IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1184: ARNULF, BISHOP OF LISIEUX

[Col. 0009]

## NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. XI, p. 774)

[Col. 0009A] Arnulf, a Norman by birth, nephew of John I, his predecessor, and younger brother of John, bishop of Sées, was educated from childhood in the best disciplines at the school of Sées through his brother’s diligence, and was likewise trained in integrity of character. He gave such proofs of his approved disposition that he became regular archdeacon of that church. At that time he went to Rome to study canon law, and from there sent to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, his treatise on the schism which arose after the death of Pope Honorius II. In it he attacks most fiercely Girard, bishop of Angoulême, a partisan of Peter Leonis, to the point of criticizing his whole previous life and even his most distinguished achievements more vehemently, it seems, than truthfully. He wrote this [Col. 0009B] about the year 1134: that is, after Lothair had been crowned emperor by Innocent II and before William, bishop of Poitiers, had been restored to his see. The former happened in 1133, the latter in 1135.

When John died in 1141, Arnulf succeeded him: a highly shrewd, eloquent, and learned man, elected by clergy and people. When Geoffrey, count of Anjou, opposed his election, Peter the Venerable wrote to Pope Innocent in support of the elect, with a remarkable eulogy, asking him to approve the election and not admit the intervention of the count of Anjou, who under the pretext of an appeal wished to gain delays for his wickedness, so that, in the pastor’s absence, no one might resist the wolf. St Bernard likewise wrote [Col. 0009C] Letter 348 to the supreme pontiff for this same elect against Geoffrey. The pope granted their prayers and confirmed the election of the most worthy bishop Arnulf. But because Arnulf had been consecrated by Archbishop Hugh without the count’s authorization, Geoffrey seized all the episcopal property for two years and three months. To redeem it, after the bishop had already spent nine hundred pounds of his own funds, he was compelled, with Pope Innocent’s permission, to take seventeen marks from the treasury of the church.

In the second year of his pontificate, 1142, he reconciled Henry, abbot of Fécamp, with Richard, abbot of Bernay, who refused obedience to the former. On 19 September 1143 he witnessed a charter of William, count of Ponthieu, granted in favour of Ralph, abbot of St Andrew at Gouffern, and was present, together with his brother John, bishop of Sées, at the dedication of the same church. In the same year he attended the translation of the head of St Julian at Le Mans. Since he was more seriously occupied in securing for himself the recent favour of a new ruler, repairing the ruins of his church and household, and arranging his brothers’ funerals, he could not himself go; he therefore addressed Pope Celestine II, elected supreme pontiff after Innocent, by letter. [Col. 0010B] In 1143 he also wrote to him for the regular canons of the church of Sées, established there by his brother. Arnulf tried to retain them there for twenty years despite the unpunished harassment of a successor; for this reason he went to Rome in 1145. Around this time he subscribed a charter of Hugh of Montfort giving the church of St Imerius to the abbey of Bec.

In a great necessity he lent King Louis as much gold and silver as he could. King Louis orders Abbot Suger, in Letter 52, to see that the remaining 104 marks of silver be paid to him within a month; and in Letter 55 he directs the same abbot not to refuse to give his heartfelt friend A. sixty measures of his best Orléans wine. In 1147 Arnulf divided equally between the chapter of Lisieux and the monastery of St Saviour the churches of Freville and Descaville. At Neufbourg in the same year Arnulf IV gave churches at St Philibert to the monks of Bec. On 8 May Eugenius III wrote to him that he was not to trouble the monastery of Bec in its possessions within his diocese.

On the overseas expedition, for which he took the cross at the assembly of Vézelay in 1146, he accompanied the crusaders in 1147—reluctantly, indeed, but at Pope Eugenius’s command. By Eugenius’s order he spent for this undertaking a golden chalice weighing thirty-four ounces. Eugenius entrusted to him and the bishop of Langres the governance of the Christian people while the king proceeded to Jerusalem. Arnulf appointed William, prior of St Barbara’s in his church, in his place; but when the supreme pontiff, then resident at Auxerre, excused William, Rotrou, bishop of Évreux, was substituted for him and long served as guardian of the bishopric. [Col. 0011A] In 1148 he attended the council at Acre with King Louis concerning the business of the Holy Land.

After returning, Arnulf endeavoured about 1151 to make peace between Geoffrey, count of Anjou, and Louis VII, king of France. Henry II, subsequently king of England, married Eleanor at Lisieux on 18 May 1152; shortly before, Louis the Younger had dismissed her on grounds of consanguinity.

At the beginning of 1153, after the octave of Epiphany, Arnulf hastened from Nonant near Bayeux to the funeral rites of William, prior of St Barbara’s. When they had been celebrated, he urged the brothers to choose a successor, and set the elected Daniel over the governance of the house. In the same year he subscribed the grant of the church of St Sidonius to the monks of Fontenelle. In 1154 he attended the coronation of Henry II, king of England, who shortly afterwards sent him, together with others, to Rome on certain difficult affairs. He was present in 1157 when Henry confirmed the foundation of the abbeys of Blanchelande and La Lucerne and gave judgment at Caen in favour of Mont-Saint-Michel. He subscribed a charter of the same king for the monastery of Bec; and, with Philip, bishop of Bayeux, subscribed the king’s diploma confirming gifts to the church of Trentham in Staffordshire. With the same bishop and William, bishop of Le Mans, he subscribed the king’s charter granting to the monks of Tiron, with his mother Matilda, twenty marks of silver from the Winchester treasury. [Col. 0011C] He also subscribed charters of Henry II, king of England, for St Florent at Saumur, St Stephen’s at Caen, Lyre, Blessed Mary of the Vow at Cherbourg, and Fontenay. He attended the consecration of the church of St Julian at Le Mans in 1158.

He congratulated the newly elected Alexander III by letter in 1159. Alexander replied in April 1160, informed him of the proceedings of the Council of Pavia, and praised him for having steadied King Henry, who was wavering in the unity of the Catholic Church then disturbed by schism. In 1162, at Fécamp, he attended the translation performed by the legate Henry of the relics and bodies of Dukes Richard I and II. On 13 October 1163 he attended the translation of the body of St Edward, king of England, at Westminster. By the pope’s command he delivered an address at the Council of Tours in the same year; the pope also appointed him delegated judge throughout Normandy for settling disputes, many of which he resolved between bishops and abbots. There he performed outstanding service for Alexander III against Victor, the false pope.

When Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, died in 1164, he had dedicated to Arnulf [Col. 0012A] a treatise on the Hexaemeron, of which a fragment may be found in *Anecdota*, vol. V, col. 1001. In the interest of St Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, who had engaged in bitter hostility with Henry, king of England, Arnulf went to the king in England to make peace, but in 1165 he laboured in vain to restore both parties to their former concord. Hence Arnulf is frequently mentioned in the Life of Thomas. Especially to be read is his letter to St Thomas, vol. II of the *Spicilegium*, p. 485, in which he openly declares his view about that famous conflict between the king and the primate of England, condemning the latter. Yet he did not thereby fall from the king’s favour, as certain persons attribute to his duplicitous character. On the contrary, he was admitted among the king’s chief advisers at the conference held in 1166 at the castle of Chinon in Touraine. Since the king foresaw that he would shortly be struck with a sentence of excommunication by St Thomas, whom the pope had appointed legate in England, Arnulf advised the king to notify St Thomas of an appeal to the supreme pontiff, and undertook to carry this out with the bishop of Sées.

After St Thomas’s murder he also wrote to Pope Alexander, in the name of all the bishops of England, excusing Henry and clearing him of the stain of so great a crime; see Letter 79. He occurs in documents of Val-Richer in 1170 and 1179; in the latter year he granted the monks liberty and immunity in the city and market of Lisieux. In the same year he attended the translation of the body of St Romanus, archbishop of Rouen. Two years earlier, in 1177, he had restored the chaplaincy of Bosham, formerly received from King Henry, and had given the church of St Peter at Gacé to the monastery of St Victor, Paris.

He is still mentioned in Savigny charters in 1180. In the following year, 1181, he incurred the displeasure of the king and supreme pontiff. For in that year certain canons of Lisieux brought complaints against Arnulf to Pope Lucius, and Lucius, upon receiving them, suspended him from a large part of the episcopal office. The supreme pontiff afterwards annulled the sentence rendered by the judges, but Arnulf, immediately condemned by apostolic judgment, resigned his dignity, as he had always wished to do. Before resigning, however, he consulted Peter of Blois, the most learned man among his contemporaries, as to what place he should devote himself after withdrawing from all secular intercourse with laypeople. Peter replied in Letter 44 and advised him by no means to resign the bishopric because of troubles unjustly inflicted by prince, chapter, or others; yet he teaches that it ought to be relinquished if it was obtained by canvassing. Gussanville, in notes to that letter, seems to deny that Arnulf withdrew because of King Henry II’s hatred; but the contrary is demonstrated both by Roger of Howden and Baronius, and by this letter, and by Arnulf’s own letter to Pope Lucius, found in *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 482. Nor could it have been disgraceful to withdraw for the good of peace and yield to the king.

In the letter Arnulf wrote to the abbot of Cîteaux asking leave to end his life at the monastery of the Dead Sea (Mortemer), he mentions in particular two things which drew him toward laying down the episcopal burden:

> “Worn out,” he says, “by old age and weighed down by the onset of certain illnesses, I have resolved to seek refuge in the healing remedy of medicine and to relieve limbs broken by labour with necessary rest. For weakness, illness, and old age come as though allied together to my destruction, and the pressure of so many troubles cuts off my confidence in a longer life. There is added from without the importunate harassment of affairs by which I am distracted, and which does not permit me, while I pant miserably, even to breathe for a moment. For I am frequently drawn with others into royal forced services, and am beset by the frequent injuries of those whom I cannot fail.”

But since that withdrawal did not attain its intended effect, he retired to the monastery of St Victor near Paris, as the Norman chronicles report:

> “Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, broken by old age, resigned the bishopric of Lisieux in June and went to St Victor at Paris, where he died in the following year.”

And Robert of Torigni, in his continuation of Sigebert, under the year 1182, writes:

> “Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, after governing the same church for forty years and labouring to build the church and most beautiful residences, renounced the bishopric and went to Paris to spend the remainder of his days at St Victor, in the most beautiful houses which he had built there for his own use.”

He did not remain there long, however, since he died in 1184, on the day before the Kalends of September [31 August]. On that day the Victorine necrology annually recites:

> “The solemn anniversary of our father of pious memory, Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, who, because of the great devotion which he had cherished toward our church for many years, came to us from his bishopric, became our canon, and chose this place above all other churches as a place of peace and burial for himself. He left to posterity many and great benefits as a worthy and enduring memorial of his name and love. This father gave us, for the furnishing of the altar, two Gospel-books, a cross and a chalice, three chasubles, a tunic [Col. 0014A] and a dalmatic, a casket, and two cloths. He also gave us three hundred Angevin pounds to discharge the church’s debts; and, in certain silver vessels and certain law-books, one hundred Parisian pounds for purchasing revenues. Moreover, he gave us six volumes of certain medium-sized law-books, and other books of various kinds to be kept in the library; and at different times during his life he bestowed many benefits upon us. It was therefore decreed that, when the anniversary of so great a father returns, it shall be solemnly celebrated each year, and a commendation shall be made before Mass.”

He lies near the choir, at the altar of St Denis, with this inscription:

> Epitaph of Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, who, after presiding over his people for forty years, powerful in deed and word, became our brother; after dying and being buried in the old basilica, he now rests here, having been translated.
>
> You who were rich and a great bishop, why  
> Did you exchange your lot for a poorer state?
>
> Rather, I exchanged poverty at great profit:  
> I was rich in the world; it was greater to be rich in God.

His chapel was subsequently renewed, and these verses were inscribed on the lintel for perpetual remembrance:

> This temple and the adjoining buildings were once  
> The ancient work of Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux.
>
> If you count three hundred years, thirty also, and one,  
> You have the time when I was restored for Christ.

Arnulf’s letters and epigrams survive in manuscripts in the [Col. 0014C] Vatican Library, nos. 189 and 537. Odo Turnebus, son of Adrian, first published the letters together with the sermons and poems; from there they passed into vol. XXII of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. D’Achery published Arnulf’s treatise on the schism between Innocent II and Peter Leonis, called Anacletus, in vol. II of the *Spicilegium*. There he also gives many of Arnulf’s previously unpublished letters: namely, to Pope Lucius, whom Arnulf addresses by the title “Majesty”; an apology refuting the calumnies of his opponents; letters to Pope Alexander and to Henry, king of England.

THE COMPLETE SURVIVING WORKS OF ARNULF, BISHOP OF LISIEUX, edited by J. A. Giles, LL.D., priest of the Church of England and formerly fellow of Corpus Christi College, Oxford.

(Oxford: J. H. Parker, 1844.)

[Col. 0015]

## J. A. GILES’S DEDICATORY LETTER

To the Reverend and distinguished brother Philip Wynter, Vice-Chancellor of the venerable University of Oxford and President of St John Baptist’s College, and to the other excellent men and his good brethren residing in the same college, John A. Giles, their humble fellow-priest, greetings and service in all things!

With how much joy, with what exultation of mind I was affected when I again looked through this excellent book, the use of which your fraternity had afforded me, no one could readily imagine except that one member of your fellowship who placed the book in my hands. For, having spent little time examining this codex, I found the letters which are now published in this book, written in no inelegant style and addressed to many very celebrated men, among whom are Henry II, king of England, St Thomas, and Gilbert of London; and, so far as I know, never before published.

Therefore, reverend and dearest gentlemen, as is fitting, I return to you the gift which your fraternity offered me. I most earnestly ask that Bishop Arnulf, under your protection, may deservedly obtain those praises for which he can owe me none. May your fraternity prosper.

Given at Oxford, in the year of the Lord 1844, indiction II.

[Col. 0015]

## J. A. GILES’S PREFACE

In view of the connection which once joined England and Normandy, it is easy to understand why we admit a Norman bishop among the writers of the early English Church. Moreover, Arnulf’s letters—he was related by birth to Henry II, king of England—relate many matters illuminating the ecclesiastical affairs and history of provinces outside the English dominion, which are not to be found elsewhere. We also possess from Arnulf most valuable documents concerning the conflict then arising between spiritual and temporal power; he attempted to reconcile the opposing parties.

We have thought it superfluous to give much here about Arnulf’s life. The few points which follow will suffice. Despite many opponents, but with the favour of the supreme pontiff, he was made bishop of the diocese of Lisieux in 1141 and governed it for forty years. While still a young man, he seems to have visited the Holy Land with the army of crusaders. He formed a friendship with St Thomas of Canterbury, then chancellor of the realm, and in a letter now published for the first time warns him to beware of the dangers and snares open to those dwelling at court. Nothing was more important to him than the affairs of his diocese, so much so that he incurred a heavy debt from which he was never freed. This is taught us by the letters first published in this volume. He spent the last years of his life in the community of the canons of St Victor at Paris, to which he withdrew after resigning the bishopric, repeatedly and urgently pressed by Henry II.

Seventy-one of Arnulf’s letters were published at Paris from the library of Odo Turnebus Hadrianus, octavo, 1585, and reprinted in the *Bibliothecae Patrum*. In addition, three may be found in Dom Bouquet’s *Writers of French Affairs*, in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, and in the Life and Letters of St Thomas. They now appear enlarged to nearly twice the number, through the aid of a very ancient manuscript codex which Mr Wynter, President of St John’s College and Vice-Chancellor of the University of Oxford, shared with the editor.

To Arnulf’s letters supplied by this outstanding codex are added his poems and sermons from the first edition, as well as the *Treatise on the Schism*, written at Rome by our author in 1131 on the occasion of the schism concerning the election of the supreme pontiff which arose after the death of Honorius II.

J. A. G.

[Col. 0017]

# LETTERS OF ARNULF, BISHOP OF LISIEUX, TO HENRY II, KING OF ENGLAND, ST THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, AND OTHERS

From the manuscript codex preserved in St John Baptist’s College, Oxford.

## I. PREFACE, TO GILES, ARCHDEACON OF ROUEN

[Col. 0017A] You ask that the letters which I once sent to different persons be gathered into a little book and presented to satisfy your wish. I should have consented more willingly if I knew that you would keep them as something almost secret, because awareness of their own imperfection does not presume to let them come into public view. For I fear that, if they are exposed to public sight, the meagre thinness of the style may offend the reader and their publication may be attributed to vanity—though it was not the pride of display that brought it about, but the insistence of your affection that compelled it. I had decided not to preserve them for future times, but immediately to banish them from all remembrance, because I had insufficient confidence either in the polish of my style or in my command of thoughts.

[Col. 0017B] Indeed, I would rather have condemned them to perpetual darkness than supplied envy with material for laughter. Envy mocks another’s work all the more securely because it does not expose its own to a similar risk. Others do not look upon us or ours with your eyes: whatever good is in us is more attentively magnified by you, and ready pardon is easily granted to imperfection. For the minds of those whom a passion of hatred or envy has claimed neither know the generosity of forgiveness nor attain the judgment of reason; rather, they measure everything by their feelings, assessing nothing by a consideration of merits.

Therefore I do not dare fail your wish, lest perhaps you take modesty for negligence. As friendship gains strength through mutual services, so it weakens when the neglect of either party advances. With the greatest effort I gathered whatever letters I could, for no copies of them remained with me; rather, I received them, as though begged from door to door, from those by whom they had been preserved by some chance. The older ones, namely the pursuits of my better age, have escaped me—those more recently scented with scholastic exercises—because there thoughts were handled with readier intellect, and practiced style supplied an abundance of careful expression. [Col. 0017C] Then language ran joyfully in a certain festive form, when learning joined with natural ability and shaped discoveries of matter through the fitting eloquence of fertile speech.

But what has been written most recently bears a certain defect from my present old age, because advancing age now grows dull with a more sluggish memory, and necessary occupations grant no leisure for study. The pressure of the episcopal office looks not so much to rhetorical figures as to the salvation of souls. Yet, whenever either reverence for a person or the importance of a matter draws me into writing, everything comes to me with difficulty, since old age has made me duller and unfamiliarity slower. I therefore send what I dare not refuse to one who asks; know that it is not submitted to a judge, but to a friend, before whom favour should plead for pardon rather than stricter expertise restore it to form.

## II. TO LORD POPE CELESTINE

The necessity of human nature has taken from our midst Pope Innocent, a man of glorious memory. The Church of God had been freed by his triumphs, adorned by [Col. 0018B] his virtues, and exalted by his magnificence. By making her gracious toward the lowly but formidable toward tyrants, the more terror he brought upon wickedness, the more charity he showed toward religion. This is indeed demonstrated by the advance both of regular discipline and monastic religion: throughout the cities and castles regular clerics are now found in place of secular clergy, and every desert today has more monks than it once had wild beasts.

Thus, at his death, desperate wickedness placed in itself a revived hope, so that it might then freely burst forth into criminal attempts and trample the condition of the Church, triumphant in all things. But at your elevation that malignant hope at once withered, as though under some languor; security arose for the good out of fear, and the praises of God sounded in every mouth. For no one doubts that, through the zeal of your holiness, what his pious labour planted will be propagated. Who could dare to hope for unlike or lesser things from you, whom both the beginnings of your former life so commend and the auspices of your present elevation show to have been set over us by divine will? For Wisdom, whose office it is to order all things strongly and sweetly from end to end (Wisdom 8), has accomplished this in you strongly, because effectively; sweetly, because harmoniously.

[Col. 0018C] Nor should the Roman Church alone claim for itself the praise of so great a work, nor boast enviously against us of so great concord, since for a long time the prayers of the lesser Churches had already agreed upon this very outcome, and Rome could offer us no successor more suitable to the greatness of so great a predecessor. The outstanding prerogative of your virtue indeed produced so great a unanimity, against which either no adversary existed or none dared to appear. It is also true that your electors had long before received from us, as it were, a mandate whose limits they were not to exceed, because what had long before been presumed from the foretelling of strangers was fulfilled by the voice of the inhabitants, and our desires produced their consent.

Therefore I shall speak to my lord, though I am dust and ashes. I shall speak as a devoted son to my only father. The more desires sought you, lord; the easier was the unanimity by which you were chosen; the greater the exultation with which all received you: [Col. 0019B] the more you understand yourself to be obligated to God and humankind. You owe gratitude to divine condescension and to human goodwill. You must strive that the result may be worthy of expectation: namely, that you show reverence to God and mercy to humankind.

Above all, I beg that the majesty of so great a dignity may not veil your serenity from me. Rather, may the affection of your former kindness always live for me in you, and may I perceive that you have succeeded your predecessor in favour and goodwill toward me. I would have come to you, had I not been more seriously occupied in securing for myself the recent favour of a new ruler, repairing the ruins of our church and household, and arranging my brothers’ funerals. On account of these matters I have as yet had neither time, eagerness, nor funds. But, God willing, I shall come as soon as possible, that the serenity of your face may shine upon my eyes and that the richer abundance of a new blessing close at hand may water my dryness; for such little as I am, I am wholly the most devoted servant of your holiness and of the holy Roman Church.

## III. TO THE SAME

For the church of Sées I cast myself with all my heart at the feet of your holiness, trusting in you in the Lord that the good which, by God’s authorship, was founded there under your predecessors will not be undone in your time. Yet it must be undone if the rule to be preserved is entrusted to one inexperienced in the rule; if a new planting is entrusted to an unskilled farmer; if, finally, mastery of anything is entrusted to someone who has not acquired its discipline. For a vineyard meant to be propagated is ruinously committed to one whose concern is rather to uproot it.

Thus, even if some form of election defended the Girard in question, because liberty of elections was introduced for the Churches, it is clear that what was acquired by their favour must not be turned to their injury. Yet it will be so turned if favour for an election proceeds to the detriment of the principal cause; if attention is paid not to who was elected or for what purpose, but to how he was elected; and if one investigates not the end or usefulness of the undertaking, but only the procedure of the affair.

But it is both true, and attested by the whole Church, that no election preceded this one—except for a few persons whom affection for and desire of a secular person [Col. 0020A] drew into wishing for him. The first was a youth and brother; the second, a novice from his household; the third, joined to him by I know not what blood relationship; the fourth, bound from childhood to cloistered discipline, still beardless and knowing absolutely nothing but the world. By secret letters, through the efforts of his brother, he enticed them with persuasion and promises and drew them into this schism, thinking that anything might safely be attempted against the poverty of the church. He hoped that, against all the rest, everything could be proved by the deposition of three or four witnesses of this sort, since by the nature of things there can be no proof of a denied act, while the burden of proof rests upon the claimant. Thus that undertaking was first conceived from ambition, then advanced by rash frivolity, so that it might finally be completed through perjuries.

There was also afterwards, because of the injury which he suffered, confidence arising from disadvantage. Yet if unconsidered ambition drew him into it, this must not be imputed to the innocent nor turned to the church’s detriment. Rather, let the avenging judgment of apostolic severity proceed against the authors of the crime; but let provision be made for the injured person, while preserving the church’s unimpaired rights, so that punishment may belong to the guilty, remedy to the injured, and its justice to religion. Moreover, concerning what occurred, the count excuses his own innocence in many ways, so much so that he permitted the authors themselves—although they believed they had earned his favour—to be punished at the church’s discretion. And lest he be thought to labour against the liberty of the Church, he remitted the whole settlement of the Church to the counsel of the archbishop and, naturally, of our bishops.

[Col. 0020C] Behold, lord, all things have been placed in your power, and none can resist your will. Be a diligent executor of your office, lest the merits of persons and causes be confused: so that worthy correction may restrain the guilty, pious compassion comfort the injured, and the regular community receive as father one formed in regular observance. Otherwise, may it never be said that by your workmanship a bronze head has been fixed upon a golden statue, or that where, by the privilege of your predecessors, secular archdeacons may not exist, your decree has created a secular bishop. May your holiness prosper in Christ!

## IV. TO ROBERT, BISHOP OF LINCOLN
[Col. 0020D] I received the letters of your affection, and embraced them with as much love as the favor of so great a man deserved to be embraced with rejoicing. I had indeed feared that length of time, distance of countries, or most recently your own promotion might have erased my memory from your mind, since new dignities commonly alter old friendships. For consciousness of a new dignity creates a new heart and new affections; and those made rich despise the friends of their poverty along with poverty itself, lest anything of their former need seem to remain with them. They honor and love only those whom fortune brings along, and rejoice only in attaching themselves to the exalted, lest the majesty of their dignity be burdened by the company of inferiors or the humble approach of persons of middling rank. [Note: [Col. 0019D] C., “assent.”] But [Col. 0021A] your constancy, retaining an old friend in fresh remembrance, embraces one absent with present affection; and, looking upon him more frequently with spiritual eyes, now offers him the riches, favor, and service of episcopal rank no less generously than it once offered the modest first-fruits of noble youth. [Note: [Col. 0021D] B. omits “noble.”] You believe that those should be retained whom generous affection invited to love, whom the truth of fidelity—not the deceit of self-interest—enticed, and who, as companions of the faithful person rather than of fortune, will share with you every event.

And I, for my part—whom the favor of the same order and of a similar, though not equal, dignity has raised up—admire in you this virtue of constancy: all the more admirable because you show the same affection toward those of lesser rank. Nevertheless, with you [Col. 0021B] there lived in me an old love, but not one grown stale; though it had proceeded from earliest youth, it had yet incurred no old age, but kept me with complete devotion ready for all that might please you. Since love ought not to be idle, but is nourished and renewed through reciprocal services, I have thought it right meanwhile to request this from your affection: that you love our lord, to whom hereditary right of succession owes the helm of your kingdom, as far as your honor permits; and that, whenever occasion offers, you lay upon me whatever charge you please, so that the affection of mutual love may always grow through the reciprocal performance of service. Farewell.

## V. TO SUGER, ABBOT OF SAINT-DENIS

[Col. 0021C]

To the venerable and beloved father and lord SUGER, by the grace of God abbot of Saint-Denis, ARNULF, humble minister of the Church of Lisieux, greetings.

With the lady empress and her son, duke of Normandy, I have, God willing, conceived good hope concerning the matter of which I spoke with you, so far as Normandy is concerned. They immediately sent messengers in haste to the count of Anjou concerning the other point that pertains to that quarter, begging him to direct that matter toward peace, and likewise to grant favorable counsel and assent in the matter concerning Normandy. Having resolved to follow your counsel very fully, they gladly promise that they will not prove ungrateful to your good will. Therefore let your holiness do what it so kindly and saintly promised us; and do not hesitate to inform us by familiar letters, through this courier, of the day to which, through your efforts, the royal replies to the requests of the English have been deferred.

## VI. TO LORD POPE EUGENIUS

[Note: [Col. 0021D] This letter and the following one are addressed in the printed editions and in C. to Pope Adrian. Bouquet first restored them to Eugenius by conjecture in the *Collection of the Writers of France*.]

We support with due devotion the request of the Church of Bayeux for the recall of its bishop, humbly joining our prayers to theirs before your mercy. [Col. 0022A] Everyone who has known the Church’s former losses joins in supplication with them: that Church which he raised from the dust of poverty and abasement; which he made rich from poor, venerable from despised, glorious from obscure. Whoever has observed his labor and industry in accomplishing these things will approve both his prudence in execution and his magnificence in achievement. The restoration of buildings, the recovery of possessions, and the renewal of ancient dignity—dignity which the malice and power [Note: [Col. 0022D] B., “impotence.”] of wicked men had given over to trampling—bear witness to this.

Those men, therefore, will rejoice if he departs, he by whose resistance they were cast down; and those who had been accustomed more freely to injure the rights of the Church are already readying greedy hands for plunder. Since the children and faithful members of the Church foresee the losses now threatening them, they have recourse to the singular aid of your discernment and mercy, that you may send back to them their bishop to preserve what he has gathered. For he is a man of counsel and strength, mighty in deed and word, esteemed and effective in royal counsels and ecclesiastical affairs, and greatly needed both by the archbishop himself and by all the bishops of the province to restrain and repel from God’s Church the insolence of the malicious. His return is desired by those who are wiser in the land; and if anyone murmurs secretly against him with malice, he is moved not so much by love as by envy, and not so much by the bishop’s faults as by suspicion of his magnificence. May the Lord preserve your person unharmed for many ages for His Church.

## VII. TO THE SAME

With fear I offer to your majesty letters long desired, [Note: [Col. 0022D] B. omits “desired.”] because it has been a long time since I appeared before your holiness. In truth, I was already about to come for the third time, had not the deceitful importunity of hostile chance prevented me, which [Note: [Col. 0022D] B., *quo* (“by which”) for *quae* (“which”).] for three years has violently carried this purpose of mine into contrary outcomes. First through the wars of the French, then through the unexpected death of the count of Anjou, and lastly through the royal anger that flared up again against his son—at which not only the thresholds of our city, but even those of the church itself, [Col. 0022D] trembled.

But now confidence of breathing freely is afforded both by the justice of our party and by the more illustrious valor of our duke, which at times has terrified the swords of enemies and inclined them toward peace. [Note: [Col. 0022D] B., *parant* (“prepare”) for *praestant* (“afford”).] Therefore, when, God willing, the disturbance has been removed or postponed, nothing will be able to keep me safe from hastening as soon as possible to the feet of your holiness, most gratefully accepting all the rebukes with which your fatherhood may reproach my delay, however excusable it may appear. For I do not dare despair of pardon from one whose kindness does not exclude inability arising from manifest excuse.

Again, from old boldness comes my presumption in commending to you by my prayers our venerable and beloved brother Bishop Constantine, who is coming to you. Much seems, however, to commend him to your favor: at the beginning of his new episcopate he judged that nothing should be done sooner than to seek the favor of the Roman pontiff and to devote himself wholly to the intimacy of the Roman Church, all the more devoutly because he does so more promptly.

## VIII. TO DANIEL, PRIOR OF SAINT BARBARA

Brother, we called you to undertake the care of your house not because of confidence in [Col. 0023B] your own strength, but because of trust in the goodness of God, who is accustomed to grant more abundant grace to those who are purely called to the governance of souls and humbly consent to obey. But just as you ought not to have thrust yourself forward without being called, so, once called, you ought not to refuse; for the pride of disobedience involves no less fault than the zeal of ambition.

But if, as you think, you withdraw not from pride but rather from humility and fear, this humility seems to me faint-heartedness—a fault to be avoided all the more diligently because it comes nearer to the danger of despair. [Note: [Col. 0023D] B., *quanto* (“in proportion as”) for *tanto* (“all the more”).] Even if there had ever been any reason by which you might be excused from this calling, you ought not to have excused yourself among your brothers or before our authority by letters, nor to have obeyed your own will, which you know that you have renounced. Rather, you should have offered your person—now in some sense [Note: [Col. 0024D] B. omits “in some sense.”] more ours than your own—humbly and devoutly at our feet, allowed yourself to be drawn by the desires of your brothers, and bowed to episcopal commands.

Moreover, your delay involves temporal losses and, what is more serious, danger to souls; for unguarded sheep are plainly exposed to the attacks of wolves, and every loss must be required from him who refuses, under any pretexts, to provide the watch owed. Come, therefore: with the burden itself divine grace will grow in you, and we shall cherish both your person and the house itself with our accustomed, or even greater, affection. And if some difficulty should perhaps arise within, I shall at once level everything before you with a strong hand. Come, I say; within eight days after receiving this letter, begin your journey. Admit no grounds for delay in coming except those which invincible necessity or the avoidance of enormous loss may suggest as admissible. If you do not do so, from that time we exclude you, as disobedient, by episcopal authority from entrance into all churches.

## IX. TO ARNALD, ABBOT OF BONNEVAL

Our venerable brother and friend, Abbot Philip, announced your illness to us with great bitterness, pursuing his feeling of mind with tears as testimony. [Col. 0024A] At the first hearing, this news was the more bitter to me because we had so recently rejoiced in your presence. Thus there began to occur to me the agreeable things that had come from your affection, and whatever similar things might be hoped for in the future; and reflection continually running between the two increased the force of my grief.

There came to mind that holy and sweet conversation of your charity, by which you prevail through skill to instruct the minds of listeners in matters, and soothe their ears with the sweetness of pleasant speech. I recalled how great a grace for writing divine goodness had bestowed upon you—a gift in which I do not know whether one ought more to admire the fruitfulness of your thoughts or the mastery of expression. These correspond in you with such equality [Col. 0024B] that neither the majesty of things seems cramped by the narrowness of words, nor the dignity of discourse overburdened by any excellence of thought—at least in matters which understanding can conceive or human eloquence can adequately expound. Clearly this proceeds from the teaching of Him whose Spirit enlightens the minds and tongues of His intimates both with knowledge of truth and abundance of speech.

Finally, grief turned into pity as I considered your troubles and labors, by which domestic anxiety and the savagery of a persecutor continually afflict your innocence. The tranquility hoped for in the near future also seemed as though snatched from your hands, so that fortune was thought to have begrudged you every present rest. Yet, as may be supposed, release would have granted you a better rest, because your eyes would see the King in His beauty, and He would fill you with joy by His countenance—He who has suffered you, for His sake, to be assailed by so many tribulations at present. [Col. 0024C]

Yet it is pleasant for us to enjoy your presence, even for a short time; to be refreshed by your conversation and relieved by your counsel. For if your reward has been postponed, it is not taken from you: the crown of righteousness is safely laid up for you, and the One who entrusted the faithful deposit will acknowledge as His own what belongs to Him in His own time. While my mind was thus carried away in due compassion by these reflections on your condition, a sudden and unexpected illness crept upon me, so that one might easily believe that the affection of compassion had transferred to me a portion of your infirmity. This compassion, however, is removed when the private suffering is removed; yet a mind concerned for each of us immediately began to suffer under a double affliction.

Therefore the merciful and compassionate Lord visited us both, and granted the benefit of health to each for this reason: neither could have been wholly healed without the other. Thus I have been preserved for you, and your wisdom has likewise been preserved for me, so that according to Christ’s law we may bear one another’s burdens (Galatians 6), and according to overflowing charity each may rejoice to have spent himself wholly for the other’s benefit.

## X. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER, WHEN HE WAS CHANCELLOR

[Col. 0025A]

I conducted your Bandinus as far as the king. The king, giving thanks to your graciousness, entrusted him to the chief steward of his household for instruction, so that he might provide him with necessities and admit him, more familiarly among the other nobles, to royal service. The steward indeed diligently carried out what had been commanded; but Bandinus also sometimes surpassed the command through his elegant talent, ready for everything by which the industry of a well-born youth ought to be praised.

Whether the king applied himself to hawking, hunting—pursuits in which he is greatly [Note: [Col. 0025D] B., *multus* (“much,” nominative) for *multum* (“greatly,” adverb).] engaged—or military affairs, Bandinus followed the royal movements with tireless speed. [Col. 0025B] When the others were idle, he attended alertly not only upon the king but upon everyone with him, as though he had been assigned in particular to the service of each. Accordingly, by his assiduous service he gained much praise and favor with the king and with all.

If you wish to inquire concerning his character: hating Gallic lack of restraint, he preserved the moderation of Italian severity, mindful in every respect of your instruction. Neither wanton or loose speech made him offensive; nor did royal luxuries [Note: [Col. 0025D] B., “riches.”] soften the strength of his vigorous youth; nor did any disgrace stain his reputation. Rather, the modesty of a conscience that bears witness to itself suffused his face, at every sight and every conversation, with the chaste blush of praiseworthy shame.

I learned these things upon my eventual return to court from many persons; but I was more gratified because I received these and other reports from the king’s own mouth. For he added that among so many noble youths he had none of such industry and such good disposition, and that Bandinus had advanced [Note: [Col. 0025D] B., *processisse* (“to have proceeded”) for *profecisse* (“to have advanced”).] more in a short time in learning the discipline of the royal household [Col. 0025C] than others had advanced in three years. The king had established that the boy was of noble descent, and that prudence and innate kindness of their own accord formed his noble character. He would be pleased if Bandinus remained with him for a while, yet would leave him to your decision as soon as the heat of summer had passed.

Perhaps you will think what I write flattering falsehoods; yet it is neither safe to deceive a wise man, nor fitting for a priest’s lips to be stained by a lie. [Col. 0025D] Farewell.

## XI. TO G., A NUN

Whenever I receive letters from your devotion, they bring me cause for grief and kindle in me the flame of sincere charity to love you ever more. They bring cause for grief because they recall to my mind that brother of mine whom, while alive, I loved with a special love above all others; and the more pleasant his life was to me, the more sorrow his tearful memory in death brings. My spirit rested in him, because I could truly regard him as another self. It was not identity of flesh, although he sprang from the same stock, that joined him and me to myself, but the inseparable unity of hearts in agreement. What pleased one always pleased the other; neither attended so much to his own feeling as to the other’s, so that each was always more affected by the other’s misfortune than his own, or rejoiced in the other’s advantage.

When he departed, the other part of my soul was taken from me; and within the hidden chamber of my breast my heart feels an emptiness, because the wholeness of my spirit, diminished in its better part, grows faint. But, as I have said, the recognition that you share this grief and stand in place of fraternal affection kindles in me a flame to love you more. For when you were still seven years old, a betrothal was arranged between you and him [Col. 0026B] through the intervention of your parents. They were pledging new bonds of friendship through a human marriage and contemplating the welcome pledges of future offspring. Human thoughts indeed freely dispose themselves toward human affections; but every affection is vain to which divine goodness does not grant its desired result.

While a nuptial chamber was being prepared for him and marital embraces assigned to a maiden whom nobility of birth, beauty of form, and finally virginal integrity commended, divine disposition was preparing a grave for him, that he might dissolve from the flower of youth into dust, from the glory of beauty and virtue into decay. Yet he is happy—if first, indeed because first—he entered the heavenly bridal chamber, so that he may someday share with his beloved the dwelling he has attained, and that, brought together to the marriage feast of the Lamb, you may be united in His sight [Note: [Col. 0026D] C., “feast.”] and rejoice in happiness.

Happy are you, who have at last overcome [Note: [Col. 0026D] C., “hoped for.”] the enticements of bodily wanton desire; whom zeal for divine goodness preserved untouched from contact of the same sort, so that, having been granted the gift of perpetual virginity, you may follow the Lamb wherever He goes and sing with the numbered thousands that spiritual song (Revelation 14). Your betrothal, then, has not been taken away but transformed, so that you may now be joined not to a man but to God in a spiritual union. May His desirable embrace cherish and bind you, so that His left hand is beneath your head and His right hand embraces you (Song of Songs 8:3).

[Col. 0026D] It will therefore be your task, before Him to whom you have turned with the whole service of your body and the whole devotion of your soul, to commend that man to Him with devout prayers; for prayer offered for him, prompted by this love, will not offend His jealousy. He knows that no carnal intercourse occurred between you and him; He knows that at that age your mind could not be defiled by any stain of desire. Therefore He has no cause for jealousy, none for making you less acceptable; rather, in you He will approve the chaste affection of so devout a love. I know indeed how earnestly you do this. For his memory cannot have passed away from you: in death you contemplate him no less with spiritual vision than in life you admired him with bodily sight.

Moreover, the more sincere this affection was, the more enduring will be the affection of holy love. Love generated by the passions of corruptible flesh is always subject to corruption: the more difficult it is to restrain in the beginning, the more readily it later vanishes, so that it often turns into hatred and pleasure is repaid with bitterness. It is also imperfect; many signs show that it is not born of true charity, since you must necessarily love each individual less to the degree that you allow that affection to be spread among many. Moreover, one who is loved without complaint admits no partner, because he judges that whatever he perceives has been given to another has been withheld from himself.

But incorruptible love, proceeding from the very truth of a sincere spirit, grows the more through its outpouring the more widely it is extended among many. Sharing it does not produce jealousy, but strengthens the indissoluble embrace of holy concord among all. Embrace, therefore, your present bridegroom with this charity. Seek him not with bodily eyes but with the eyes of the heart, so that you may behold his beauty, because he is beautiful, and taste his sweetness, because he is sweet. Give thanks also without ceasing, because he has kept your body untouched for the spirit, so that purity may answer purity and you may be able to offer him perpetual integrity.

## XII. TO LORD POPE ADRIAN

The bearer of this letter, Master Simon, brings pitiable wrongs to [Col. 0027C] the Apostolic See—wrongs whose redress, if that place had had a bishop, ought to have been heard by you before the offense. Hear him; and with due severity avenge his wrongs—indeed, your own—lest audacity of this kind grow insolent against the Apostolic See, especially since in those regions many shoots are already beginning to spring up in contempt of it. It must therefore be met, lest unpunished malice grow strong with the passage of time and your forbearance or over-indulgent favor furnish strength to wickedness.

For the apostolic name, which until now had been held in that land in reverence and fear, has become a cause of scandal and contempt. Nor does an appeal free the appellant from prosecution; rather, it provokes against him the judge’s severity. This man experienced it: because of an appeal, he was shut in prison and miserably tortured by hunger, and could obtain release neither from the tyrant without money nor from the bishop without injury to his case. I had resolved to plead for his cause as one bound to him; but his declared affliction will easily plead its case before your mercy, and our intercession will, as usual, rejoice in the result of your favor.

But the common cause outweighs the private one, because the liberty of God’s Church is at issue; and no hope of refuge remains if the authority of apostolic protection is rendered void. Avenge it, therefore, lest, God forbid, rashness proceed into an example; rather, let correction, loudly heard, instruct ignorance and restrain audacity.

## XIII. TO LORD POPE ADRIAN

[Col. 0028A]

In order to settle, by your command, the dispute between the abbot of Jumièges and the monks, we went down to the monastery itself, so that the condition of the Church and the truth of the facts might be more readily known to us at close hand and the controversy more conveniently concluded without expense and labor to the parties. In whatever direction blame should be assigned, it is nevertheless certain that this ancient and noble monastery has pitiably declined in spiritual and temporal matters. Such hostility has flared up between the abbot and all the monks, except three or four, that any restoration of concord between them must be despaired of for all time.

They publicly brought forth so many disgraceful accusations against him [Col. 0028B] that each party must always doubt the other’s genuine good will, because even if litigation perhaps ceased, the hateful memory of reproaches would not cease. They advanced three charges against him: first, shameful and unnatural incontinence; second, simony; third, dissipation of property, through which they said they had been reduced not merely to poverty but to extreme hunger.

To prevent the multitude of issues from causing confusion if the three charges were discussed indiscriminately, they chose first the charge of incontinence. On that charge they produced seven accusing monks who were priests, and afterward nine witnesses, likewise monks but of different orders. Having investigated their testimony more carefully, we found that five gave individual testimony concerning individual acts, and that none of them had learned anything together with another, but each separately had discovered what he stated. Of the two produced to attest one act, we found one to be a layman, of no order, formerly a knight, and therefore less suitable for offering proof of a crime against a priest. The other, left alone when the former was removed, was judged by us insufficient.

Of the last two, similarly produced to testify to one act, though a different act, one was found to be a subdeacon and a youth. When he himself began to be regarded with suspicion by the brethren because of a further familiarity with the abbot, he most firmly declared before everyone [Col. 0028D] that he had learned nothing dishonorable concerning the abbot. Therefore, excluded because of his lesser age, rank, and inconsistency of statement, he likewise left his companion alone, although the opposing party alleged, and concurring public report proclaimed, that this companion too had behaved rather wantonly.

Having carefully heard and examined all this, we judged according to the legal rule that all the evidence produced could serve not as proof but as presumption, because isolated testimonies do not merit the privilege of proof. Since a presumption must stand until proved otherwise, we adjudged to the abbot a purgation by the seventh hand: namely, three abbots and three priest-monks of known reputation and standing, by whose oaths a necessary remedy might be supplied for his wounded reputation. The monks therefore appealed to the octave of Pentecost. Apostolic letters were requested and issued, and the parties were commanded that in the meantime the reverence due to the apostolic name invoked in the appeal should not be violated by them.

## XIV. TO MASTER PETER HELVE

If the praiseworthy disposition and industry hoped for from our young man have failed, I am certain that neither instruction nor diligence has failed on the master’s part. If he had shown himself teachable, I should have owed you thanks; but his unstable and resistant insolence has made me your debtor in a greater measure. For the less obedience your instruction found in him, the more labor had to be expended and the more troubles endured. It is therefore our will that he return, so that, corrected both by us and by his father and brothers, [Col. 0029B] he may someday return to you with his will changed for the better.

## XV. TO ARNALD, ABBOT OF BONNEVAL

I had heard nothing of your arrival before your messenger reached me. For I had not seen the lord of Évreux; but on that same day, at Tours, whither we had come to the king, I received your letters from him, and the pleasant speech of our common friend made up for the brevity of the letter. I rejoiced at your safety, rejoiced at the outcome of your pilgrimage, and rejoiced that the Roman Church had recognized your prudence and integrity with due honor.

Yet the decision of your affection to visit us soon added to the fullness of my joy, so that we may be cheered by mutual sight [Col. 0029C] and delighted by the pleasant words of reciprocal conversation. For we shall share the favorable and adverse things that have occurred to us meanwhile, because such sharing among friends moves affections: it makes prosperity sweeter through mutual congratulations and adversity lighter through shared compassion. I carry more lightly what another bears with me in equal compassion; and conscious participation in joys makes gladness itself abound among friends.

Therefore I hasten with all the speed I can, and, God willing, shall reach Lisieux on the very day of the Kalends of March, where I shall remain for some days, either there or nearby. I have detained your messenger for a little while with difficulty [Note: [Col. 0029D] B., “moderately.”] because the serious affairs being conducted between the kings kept me uncertain [Col. 0029D] about my return.

## XVI. TO RALPH DE DICETO, ARCHDEACON OF LONDON

I heard that you had come to Paris for the sake of study; I heard it and rejoiced. I rejoiced, certainly, that the present sight of one whom I loved might gladden me and the pleasant exchange of conversation delight me. I also wished that some opportunity might arise to render you a service, since your merits have long anticipated any claim of mine. For although truth alone requires the affection of friendship, it does not exclude generous service; rather, friendship is thereby made more illustrious, because, as that holy man says, “the proof of love is the performance of a deed.”

It troubles me that, though you have now come a second time, you were unwilling even for a moment to turn aside to a friend, or at least to send by courier a greeting of due courtesy, committed to a few written characters. [Col. 0030A] I waited a long time; whenever anyone appeared from those parts, I imagined that he would announce to me the welcome arrival of my Ralph. So often disappointed, I now dare imagine nothing from this; but by this letter I have judged that your affection should be awakened, if perhaps it has fallen asleep, or, if it has conceived some illness through false suspicion, that it may recover through news of my constancy.

For know that nothing of my former affection for you has perished; rather, my love is, as it were, doubled, since my mind is compelled to give you the affection which it once bestowed on two. For our common friend Ralph de Flury has been taken from our midst, and in dying seems to have taken away half my soul. His memory must always be honored by me; his love must always be renewed in every way possible. I judge that friendship’s duty should be rendered to the dead in two ways: first, that he may be helped through devout intercessions with God; second, that those whom he loved may be loved with a substitute affection.

Hence our love has passed from him to you as by a certain right of hereditary succession, so that I embrace you now not with a single but a doubled affection. For this succession is due above others to you, whom he loved above others; and he assigns it to you as though by a testament, through the prerogative of special friendship. [Col. 0030C] Therefore show the manner of his friendship, and let clear signs reveal that it has drawn new strength from this new doubling.

Write something in the meantime, so that I may seem to have received the speech of each in the other. Command whatever you wish, so that in serving one I may seem to have rendered service to both. Visit us, so that in one I may be able to behold the person of each. Write, I say, because if you write, this very act can provide your studies with increased material and will neither impede the progress nor the result of your intended work. Command something, so that some proofs of enduring friendship may appear, because the confidence to ask proves it more effectively than generosity in offering. Visit us, because both our desire, the nearness of the place, and the feast itself invite you. Lord William de Vere is likewise bound by his promise to come; you will be able to comfort one another, and to double for us the joys of the holy feast. Farewell.

## XVII. TO POPE ADRIAN

The young man whom your graciousness commended to me for girding with the belt of knighthood, having made a slight detour because he had no safe passage through the city, returned ill. He was seized with such a burning fever that many believed his life was in danger. Nevertheless, strengthened by eagerness for the promised training, he was brought as far as your Milo and Father Radicosius. The father found great consolation, in the favor of your benefit, concerning his son’s sickness.

When I had advised rest for the young man, and meanwhile fulfilled through the appointed person my pledged obligation toward him, he continually obtained from his father’s indulgent affection leave to come as far as the agreed place, feigning health. [Col. 0031A] But since the illness did not abate on the journey [Note: [Col. 0031D] B., “did not set out.”], and disease was constantly added to disease by an oppressive increase, I feared that what I had thought I had guarded against by avoiding delay would happen to me through the very shortness of time.

I experienced how greatly the affections of the mind contribute to or detract from bodily strength, and how danger or health often proceeds from their quality. For he was carried more by spirit than by body: the gladness of his mind renewed his bodily strength, and desire drew him forward more strongly than illness delayed him. Thus we reached Lucca, where, as appeared, the arms could not be fitted in fewer than ten days or more; nor could the person for whom they were being prepared have received them, since he had taken to his bed.

A knight whom the father had assigned to me then began to give more useful counsel concerning the necessity, and, having considered everything, requested that forty pounds of Provins currency [Note: [Col. 0031D] B., “Prunen.”] be counted out to him for this purpose. He wished to test better horses over a longer period and to purchase all else more conveniently with greater time, because the shrewd cunning of sellers often deceives hasty buyers. I readily agreed. I could neither await the uncertainty of the boy’s health nor safely remain longer, lest, because my arrival had been announced, ambushes be prepared for me on the roads. I also added what was necessary in the name of expenses for the delay and return, lest some necessity compel him to take anything from what had been assigned for another purpose.

They seemed to me to have rendered you many thanks for your favor, and they offered thanks to me as well, as though from the surplus and fullness of your favors.

## XVIII. TO JOHN OF NAPLES AND WILLIAM OF PAVIA, CARDINALS
Having heard of the disturbance of the holy Roman Church, I grieved, because, as a spiritual son, I could not hear of my mother’s sorrow without compassion. [Note: [Col. 0031D] B., *specialis* (“special”).] For that grief lay upon me with particular force, since until now she has always loved me with such charity, honored me with such familiarity, and distinguished me with so many benefits and honors. But afterwards, when I heard upon whose person the votes of almost all had converged, I changed sorrow into joy, weeping into the lyre, and the voice of lamentation into the organ. For I rejoiced that a few had withdrawn from the general agreement, whose number can detract nothing, or little, from Catholic unity. I rejoiced, I say, because the supreme direction of affairs has been entrusted to one through whom the liberty and dignity of the Church are believed easily capable of restoration.

Meanwhile my devotion was not idle. Among those in whose eyes God has granted me some authority and favor, [Col. 0032A] I pleaded the Church’s cause; and I was the first and only one to confirm our prince, the king of the English, in favor of this father, employing the urgency that was necessary. Indeed, I would already have come to embrace the feet of your Apostolic Blessedness and to mingle a desired conversation with your charity, had not the prince’s warfare in our regions detained me through many troublesome necessities. It will therefore belong to your kindness and grace, in the meantime, to make up for my absence before him by your presence, and, if it seems expedient in any respect, to offer my service; for whatever may be indicated to me in a few written lines, I am ready to devote my entire resources, with complete devotion, to him and to you.

## XIX. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT-ÉVROUL

[Col. 0032B]

You ought to know that all the obligations of your predecessor have, by due course, passed to your person, by which your monastery stood bound at the time of his death. Further, if those same obligations had been confirmed by the intervention of any religious bond, you must believe yourselves liable under the same bond, since it is clear that you succeeded to his position and assumed all the monastery’s advantages as well as its burdens. Hence Hugh and Drogo of Cambrai [Note: [Col. 0032D] B., *Cambium*.] press us severely concerning the money which they lent to your aforesaid predecessor and to the whole chapter [Note: [Col. 0032D] B., *crediderit* (“he lent”).], and it is certain that he and the entire community confirmed its repayment by a pledge, with bodily presence furnished through representatives. For greater security, ten [Col. 0032C] trustworthy members of the monastery likewise bound themselves by an equal obligation; the creditors’ prudence judged them especially suitable persons to make payment.

Moreover, your own presence has recognized with what good faith and diligence I conducted your affair before them: I obtained remission of the interest for you and deferred the necessity of payment for a period of two years. Since no agreement could arise between you except through my intervention, I bound myself on your behalf, promising, that is, to render the promised assurance at the proper time and to fulfill the agreed terms. Yet your holiness has returned gratitude less than my services deserved, has paid less reverence to episcopal dignity, and has provided too little for its own reputation, for the fidelity of the brethren, [Col. 0032D] and for their welfare.

For if the community once consented to be bound, could the abbot’s liability or deposition release them from the debt they had incurred and the pledge they had given concerning it? Yet the blame should be laid upon you rather than upon them, since, being more earnestly occupied with spiritual matters, they entrusted to your faithfulness and diligence both their authority and their welfare. If you have undertaken the care of souls, to be discharged in good faith, you ought principally to have attended to preserving their pledged faith, especially since such a breach is commonly judged criminal even in secular affairs. And if the straightforwardness of the faithful excuses their ignorance, [Col. 0033A] then both your own fault and that which would have been theirs had they known are rightly transferred to you; and a double negligence makes you a transgressor under a double charge.

Furthermore, I warned your prudence once and again that you should be willing to entreat the creditors, even employing my intercession. This could easily have been done, so that by prayers alone both your advantage and your honor might still have been preserved. Therefore return to yourselves, abandon this contempt by adopting better counsel, and free our pledged faith—yours and that of your brethren—from this reproach, if reproach it is. For this affair has already inflicted very great harm upon your reputation, even if perhaps it has not taken away the purity of your conscience. But if you have resolved to persist in your former purpose, it is not fitting that I should [Col. 0033B] prove false to my promise; where the gentleness of counsel does not prevail, the hand of strength must be applied. Let it therefore be your concern to make satisfaction before the coming Pentecost, as was determined in our presence. Otherwise, from that day know that, by the authority through which we hold precedence over you, your fraternity is suspended from the service of the altar. I leave it to the consciences of your brethren to determine how they may offer the sacrament at the altar if satisfaction has not been made to the creditors, to whom they bound themselves, though not with their own hands, yet through representative hands.

## XX. TO THE SAME

We remember that once and again we wrote to your fraternity concerning William, formerly a monk, directing you to receive him into [Col. 0033C] your monastery, in which he made profession, and to sustain with due kindness one prepared for every humility and obedience. But if your fraternity had anything against him that would cause you to judge that he ought not to be received, you should have set this very matter before us at an appointed suitable place and time, lest either he should be deprived without fault of the fellowship of the community, or the peace of the brethren be disturbed by the intrusive arrival of a person deserving rejection. For a sheep ought rather to be carried back to the fold upon the shepherd’s shoulders than exposed to wolves’ bites—a sheep for whose salvation that priceless blood of Christ was shed and the teaching of evangelical institution concurs.

But when you neither received the monk in accordance with the commands nor, even after a second summons, presented yourself before us, we compelled you by a sterner command to come, lest episcopal reverence be turned into [Col. 0033D] contempt: you were to answer us concerning your disobedience and the aforesaid brother concerning his exclusion. Yet afterward, lest we should seem to act from any agitation, you know how readily we remitted the injury done to us, so that by our example you too might be invited to mercy.

You, however, remember how hard and inexorable you showed yourself, asserting that the often-mentioned brother had departed condemned by the public sentence of the whole chapter for a certain offense which, as you said, under your private regulations does not merit pardon. But he denied in every way both the offense and the chapter’s sentence, and entrusted his innocence to the testimony of the entire chapter with every [Col. 0034A] safeguard that seemed appropriate. Therefore, on the advice of the distinguished men who were present, we resolved to send him and religious persons to the chapter as our representatives, through whom it might send us a public attestation of the truth after diligent inquiry. You, however, urgently demanded that testimony be given against an absent man, declaring that you would not permit him or the chapter to enter on our behalf or hear anything said there; although, in an inquiry concerning a crime, the accused ought to be present and granted every opportunity to hear and answer.

Since you were unwilling to make us more fully informed concerning the crime of the often-mentioned brother, we must for the present regard as innocent one whom neither his own confession nor any testimony of another convicts. For canonical order does not permit him to be condemned merely upon your accusation, particularly since it is known that you have at some time hated him and have not yet buried the resentment of your old anger. Therefore, by these present writings, we command you to receive him without delay into the cloister with the other brethren, preserving intact every aspect of his former status; do not harass him with any troubles, but cherish him with charity all the more kindly because you have persecuted him with more severe violence. For filial devotion grows strong in the embrace of a kindly Father; and just as hatred is provoked by injuries, so favor is won by kindness.

But if your fraternity refuses to obey these present commands, know that, by the authority through which we hold precedence over you, you are suspended from the service of the altar until due judicial satisfaction has been made [Col. 0034C] both to the brother for the injury and to us for the contempt. You should know that disobedience is a crime in one who has professed the religious life; and he is bound to the most exact diligence who has pledged obedience to his superior orally and in writing, even with a bodily oath, confirmed by the sign of the life-giving cross.

## XXI. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER ON HIS ELEVATION

Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who always loves and preserves his Church, that is, the immaculate bride of his beloved Son, with wondrous kindness. For although he sometimes permits her to be troubled by injuries, yet with the temptation he provides an outcome so that she may endure it (1 Cor. 10); nor does he ever permit the gates of hell to prevail against her [Col. 0034D] (Matt. 16). For it is not expedient that a condition of uninterrupted prosperity should make her insolent, or idleness negligent; rather, affliction preserves humility and vexation grants understanding. All things indeed work together for her good (Rom. 8), while she is tested like gold in a furnace (Wis. 3); and all things contribute to the increase of her crown, while the force of adversity makes her stronger and the assault of malice more cautious.

The compassionate and merciful Lord, moreover, provides and prepares in advance, for times of tribulation, men of courage and counsel, able to repel the audacity of rashness and skilled in avoiding the craft of malice. This appeared quite clearly in Pope Innocent of holy and glorious memory, [Col. 0035A] who cast down the heretic who exalted himself against everything called or worshiped as God (2 Thess. 2), a man elevated by nobility of birth, heaps of wealth, sinful eloquence, worldly prudence, and finally public favor among secular men. Yet [Note: [Col. 0035D] B. omits *tamen* (“yet”).] in God’s champion truth prevailed over falsehood; proud ambition yielded to vigorous humility; and justice triumphed over iniquity. For we saw him exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; we passed by, and behold, he was not; we sought him, and his place was not found (Ps. 36), because he deserved neither a tomb among the dead nor a memorial inscription for his burial.

But the Lord exalted the horn of his Christ, so that through him the unity of the Church might be restored and his kingdom rule over all [Col. 0035B] things. I remember—and I do not think that this has escaped your memory—how much reverence the princes showed at his commands, how exalted he was, with what majesty the Church shone, and how greatly pure and undefiled religion advanced in his days: so much so that more religious men now inhabit deserts than formerly contained wild beasts. He considered that, for governing men, the discipline of sober severity should be employed rather than the gentleness of lax mercy. He desired to please God rather than men, lest, through seeking human favor, he might appear contemptible before God. Thus his strength shone ever more brightly amid adversities, and the later emblems of his prosperity did not shine as greatly as the mighty deeds of his preceding adversity are still celebrated.

For he did not trust in man, nor make flesh his arm (Jer. 17); rather, he trusted in the Lord, and the Lord was his confidence. Furthermore, the paintings in the Lateran palace show that such schisms have occurred more than once in the Roman Church: there schismatic usurpers are inscribed as footstools beneath the feet of the Catholic Fathers; there Wisdom by her own strength crushes and tramples the necks of the proud and lofty. This was fittingly done so that the inscription recording their victory might redound to the glory of the holy Fathers, while those usurpers either suffer the punishment of their subjection or beg forgiveness for their presumption. Therefore the chair of your holy apostolate ought not to have been without a footstool, but ought to have been adorned with a nobler [Col. 0035D] footstool.

For your victory is neither uncertain nor remote; rather, the humility of your modesty is punished for a time, because you delayed obeying the Fathers assembled in the Holy Spirit. For he is liable to equal guilt who either anticipates the Lord’s call or refuses it when offered. Yet serenity will soon return, God willing; this small cloud will be dissolved by the rays of the true Sun; and, once Catholic unity has been restored, the whole body of the faithful will hasten from every side to your feet.

Meanwhile, whatever pursuits delay the others, by whatever desires profane ambition may be drawn away, however great the rashness with which detestable envy bursts forth, I, though least of all, yet embrace with no less joy [Col. 0036A] than the others the glory of your elevation. I acknowledge you as Christ’s apostle, Peter’s vicar, shepherd and bishop of all who bear the Christian name; and with you I profess Catholic unity. Therefore I rejoice because the longed-for day—the day, that is, of exultation—has dawned, a day in which we truly believe that grace has been restored to the virtues, the rod to vices, terror to princes, and liberty to the Church. I rejoice, I say, because henceforth the word of God will not be bound; rather, his word—which is true in your mouth—will achieve with easy effect what had been thought impossible. [Note: [Col. 0036D] B., *consummabit* (“will accomplish”).]

I would therefore already have hastened to embrace the feet of your Blessedness, so that the abundance [Col. 0036B] of your blessing, being nearer and more plentiful, might water my dryness; but zeal for your advantage especially detained me. For from the time when the truth of your elevation and the error of the opposing usurpation came to our ears, I hastened to bring this matter to the knowledge of our prince, in order to occupy his uncommitted mind in your favor with such persuasions as I owed, lest the craft of malice should forestall us on any pretext. For it is easier to occupy minds that are uncommitted than to recall them from dispositions already formed.

He hesitated for a while, but immediately, strengthened by the working grace of the Holy Spirit, he promised with cheerful firmness and steadfast cheerfulness that he would recognize no one but you. When he had recently received the emperor’s letters urging that recognition of you be deferred—the emperor with whom, through letters and envoys passing back and forth, [Col. 0036C] he seems joined in very great friendship—he suppressed the general edict, lest he appear to have spurned the emperor’s requests and acted hastily to his prejudice. Yet he did not at all restrain his hand or tongue from reverencing your letters and name, nor did he wish to restrain any of us. He judged that the boastful force of an edict would carry less weight for you than the reality of action.

The authority of your apostolate is firm and unquestioned with him; and whichever way the heart of the aforesaid prince may be inclined, he will undoubtedly not follow it into error.
