It shall be my concern to keep watch, as it were, over all those around him, lest the mouths that speak iniquity gain strength, but that he himself may persevere in your obedience, as he has begun. [Col. 0036D] For I shall count myself happy if ever, in this or in another matter, I may be found grateful for your beneficence, so that your dignity may at least sometimes deign to remember my devotion among the others. It is also for you, whenever an opportunity shines forth, to visit all the provinces through frequent commands, so that from every side they may become accustomed alike to your name and to obedience, because there will be no one who will dare either not to receive your letters or to resist your commands.

## XXII. REPLY OF LORD POPE ALEXANDER

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ARNULF, bishop of Lisieux: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0037A] “The letters sent to us by your prudence,” etc. See under Pope Alexander III, for the year 1181, among the volumes of the *Patrologia* shortly to be published.

## XXIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS AND BISHOPS OF ENGLAND

Your prudence, touched by this sorrow, does not fail to know by what great storm the Church is distressed and in what danger she seems placed. The sons of Babylon, indeed, foresee it and exult, as though the magnitude of the storms promised certain shipwreck; they rush to plunder the cargo and the very planks of the vessel. But divine promise gives us security: it does not allow the gates of hell to prevail against her, but the certainty of victory compensates for the injuries of vexation. For there is no place for despair where rectitude commends the cause and consciousness of the truth sustains, for the time being, the virtue of patience.

The truth of our cause is neither unknown nor its justice uncertain. It is a matter clearer than light, which clears the affair of the cloud of perversity and frees every judgment from error. If person is compared with person, the perfection of learning and integrity of every virtue characterize ours; and this is confirmed no less by the testimony of our opponents than by our own. But if nobility of birth and the favor of powerful men sought for that very reason are taken away from the other, there will be nothing by which he may dare aspire to the height of Apostolic majesty. And if the acts of the elections are compared with each other, it is evident that our election rests upon every form of order, solemnity, and reason, while the other is full of shamelessness [Col. 0037C] and deprived of every support of reason.

Will the authority of one bishop—indeed, the one you know—and two cardinals prejudice the whole Church, so that, with the Catholic body rejected, it will be believed confined within the narrow limits of this group of four? Will an act performed afterward through a few hands, and those hands hired for the purpose, prevail against a consecration duly and solemnly celebrated by the multitude concerned? Will the violence of threatening bands of hired soldiers consecrate the shameless act of a garment thrown upon him by his own hands? For it is certain that Otto filled the church of Saint Peter, when the election was to be held there, with a multitude of armed men, so that what he did not hope to gain from his own merits and the favor of the holy Fathers, he might usurp by swords drawn against the necks of those who resisted. [Col. 0037D]

Finally, after the agreement of all had been confirmed in the person of the most holy Father Alexander, while he himself honorably refused and excused himself and repelled the cope placed upon him by the hands of almost everyone, ambition could neither conceal itself nor delay any longer. With unrestrained rashness, and while, as is said, none of the cardinals had yet accompanied him, he ran to the chair, trusting, of course, that armed men unwilling to move him could not be removed by unarmed men. With equal haste he mounted the palace, so that he might appear the first to have occupied both chairs, and might obtain through haste the elevation that he could not obtain by right. The aforesaid three followed him out of the entire body.

The others, frightened by swords rushing about, withdrew with their elect to the nearest fortress. There that adversary held them besieged and enclosed by swords for nine days, while throughout that time they begged, as best they could, for scant food. Thus iniquity even contrives for itself a pretext for lying, asserting that Otto sat alone in the chair of the apostolate for nine days before the other was elected—as though the latter had not been elected from the beginning, even though he refused; and as though the violent possession of one man could sanctify injustice and atone for the audacity of ambition.

But when they had been brought out of confinement by the favor of the senate, they were, by the Lord’s mercy, led to the place where the Apostolic insignia were kept, so that the election might be brought into effect and the elect might receive the grace of consecration from the hand of the bishop of Ostia, [Col. 0038B] to whom this belonged by special right. Finally, the cardinals and bishops exercising the office of legate in various provinces turned toward him with equal devotion. The serene calm of unquestioned peace would then have smiled upon the whole Church of God, had not that man fled to the emperor’s prepared assistance.

But the emperor, a zealous rival of his own glory rather than God’s, gladly seized an opportunity to fulfill the desire conceived from the example of his forefathers. For you know that his predecessors had for a long time aspired to subject the Roman Church to their own dominion, and had always either raised up or supported schismatics against her, in order that they might more freely exercise the authority they sought over her rights—although they owed her service [Note: [Col. 0037D] B., *jure . . . debent*: “they owe [it] by right . . .”]—and, reversing the proper order, might not direct her according to their will but overthrow her.

Yet it was well that whoever burst forth into this audacity through confidence in that power was brought to ruin, as an example to others, so that confused arrogance might thereafter cease and the dignity and reverence due to God’s Church be preserved. This emperor, however, was seduced by the flattering submission of the despairing schismatic, who placed his person and cause at the emperor’s discretion and declared that he would be nothing except by the emperor’s sole will. Thus he is said to have surrendered the insignia of the apostolate itself at the emperor’s feet, and afterwards to have received investiture from his hand through a ring; so that, with the old dispute evidently settled, royalty might seem to have triumphed over priesthood, temporal things over spiritual things, and secular affairs over ecclesiastical ones. [Col. 0038D] An unworthy crime and a wickedness detestable in every age: to overturn divine order by such rashness and destroy the liberty redeemed by Christ’s blood!

The aforesaid prince therefore pursued his undertaking as though under the shadow of piety. He convened an ecclesiastical assembly by secular power, in order to strengthen the usurpation of that schismatic by his own approval and bend as many as he could to obedience through the terrors of tyrannical power. His intention was that, by joining the force of the two swords, he might restore the former [Note: [Col. 0038D] B., *comminuta p. reformet*: *comminuta* (“shattered”) in place of *reformet* (“may restore”).] majesty of the empire; that, by the reciprocal cooperation of both powers, he might subject all kingdoms [Col. 0039A] to his own dominion.

Those whom necessity or inclination had attached to the schismatic composed a creed of falsehood and blasphemy, so that, if they could not prevail by truth, they might at least be thought to prevail by the support of a collected multitude. Should that document happen to come before your wise consideration, believe it full of falsehood. Even if it contained complete truth in every respect, nothing decreed in it could acquire any legal effect. For a proceeding cannot be called arbitration unless a voluntary submission of the parties binds it; nor can it be called a judicial sentence if it proceeds neither from ordinary nor delegated jurisdiction. Moreover, with what arrogance have they presumed to decide a common cause by private authority and impose magistracy upon us as though we were inferiors, when divine goodness has made us equals in rank and equally distinguished in dignity?

Nor should there be called a cause where no dispute could exist between consenting parties; nor can a question either be formed or resolved without contradiction. Furthermore, if what was done concerning Otto at the outset perhaps had no validity, it could by no right be confirmed by this subsequent action, since he had already received from the one able to do so the sentence of condemnation and the punishment of the anathema due to him.

I know that your wisdom abounds in stronger arguments and weightier reasons, so that you regard that conventicle of Pavia as having no force whatever, and may instruct through yourselves the simplicity even of the less intelligent. Blessed, however, be the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who in his kindness grants the Gallican Church its customary mercy: he always illuminates her with knowledge of the truth and never permits her feet to stray from the path of justice. For just as the manifest power of the Most High cast down all whom the envy of furious Teutonic rage advanced to oppress the Roman Church, so he has always granted victory and triumph to all whom Gallican devotion embraced.

Although many regions are known to have abounded in prodigies, Gaul alone had no monsters; rather, she shone brightly in purity of faith, truth of doctrine, titles of virtues, and abundant performance of good works. Therefore, after the quality of the persons has now been thoroughly examined and the acts of the elections more fully investigated, they have agreed upon the person of the most holy Father Alexander, with the approval of their truly Catholic and most serene king; and everywhere they receive and honor his letters and envoys. But because harmony has recently been restored between him and our prince, by God’s will, it was decided, out of regard for the former, to defer for a short time the edict publicly proclaiming his recognition, until our king could consult the Church of his realm and confirm by your acquiescence the consent he had formed in his mind. [Col. 0039D]

For it was not fitting for the prudence of royal excellence to decide anything in so great a matter without consulting your wisdom, lest he seem to have given his glory to another and to have valued your reverence less than he ought. Nevertheless, he showed and expressed by many indications what his will had been from the beginning in this matter: he always received Father Alexander’s envoys and letters with reverence and favor, and repeatedly declared before all that he would acknowledge no other. But Otto’s letters, when offered, he refused to touch with his royal hand as though they were something unclean and foul. Rather, in contempt of them, once the bearer had placed them upon a small wooden tablet which he himself had picked up from the ground, he immediately hurled them behind his back as high as he could in the envoy’s presence, amid the laughter of the crowd present. [Col. 0040A]

From these facts, therefore, it is clear that his will in favor of Lord Alexander is firmly fixed without any ambiguity, and that he sought your counsel more out of reverence than in order to settle any question concerning this affair. Princes and lords of the earth commonly defer greater affairs for some time, so that delay may increase authority and a more prolonged desire may reach fulfillment with greater joy. Since in this matter the prince’s favor and truth coincide, the grace of divine goodness plainly points out to you the way of answer.

Yet because of certain persons among you who say that they are joined to that schismatic by kinship, you must take careful precautions lest malice somehow prevail and the affection of the flesh supplant the charity which is from God. But when your whole body has assembled, do not wait for the opinions of anyone, nor fear their displeasure. Rather, immediately assert the resolution formed in the power of the Spirit, [Col. 0040C] lest your concealment lend boldness to perversity and the first fruits of blasphemies gain strength through your silence. Let zeal for justice therefore break forth more promptly through your mouth, from liberty of conscience and confidence in the truth, so that iniquity may be terrified as by a kind of spiritual thunder and deceit prepared for the overthrow of faith may be choked. May the Lord in his mercy direct and strengthen your minds toward good, so that through your zeal the integrity of his Church may be restored, and that Church which has freely anticipated you with such great benefits and honor may find you grateful and faithful in the time of need.

## XXIV. TO THE CARDINALS OF THE ROMAN CHURCH CONCERNING THE ELECTION OF LORD POPE ALEXANDER

How useful the diligence of our devotion has been among our princes for the recognition of the holy apostolate of our most reverend lord and father Pope Alexander will, or has, reached your knowledge through the report of trustworthy persons. Nor is boastfulness necessary on my part for the truth of the matter to become known to you, since, even if I were silent, that which all Normandy has admired and England itself has likewise recognized from afar cannot remain hidden. It is well with me, moreover, because I now receive the fruit of this diligence and the reward of my labor: my glory remains safe—namely, the testimony of my conscience—through which I perceive the fullness of Apostolic favor and the unquestioned truth of divine blessing.

Therefore I rejoice, knowing that I am truly held in my mother’s bosom, cherished in her sacred embraces, and nourished at her sincere breasts. I rejoice, I say, recognizing by what obstinate error the schismatics are enclosed in their pitiable blindness. The rays of surrounding light do not illumine their eyes; instead, the excessive brightness of manifest splendor itself overwhelms them. They have been judged and received the sentence due to their committed guilt: the Church, treating them as degenerate, has handed them over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh and expelled them from Catholic unity. Nor does the sentence lack execution; it is put into effect without delay, since meanwhile both conscience tortures them and the daily approaching triumph of the prevailing Church afflicts them.

Divine Wisdom has, moreover, more graciously provided for her Church by making the truth manifest to all, so that neither simplicity can plead ignorance nor malice dare [Note: [Col. 0041D] C., *audeat* (“dare”).] to allege anything plausible. [Col. 0041B] For if number, reputation, or any form of election defended those whom profane ambition separated from Catholic unity, perhaps some matter for error might have been gathered. But only three men from the entire body were led astray; and they were precisely those whom the Church seemed more to support than to take pride in for any achievement of theirs, since neither distinction of virtue nor learning commended them.

For was not he who preceded the others in age and rank—I mean the Tusculan—another Epicurus, accustomed to observe the hour of rest and dinner, negligent of all things and everyone unless perhaps the anticipated promise of some profit from an offer came first? This is so true that, while the others were at work, he alone, as is said, left the election prematurely because the dinner hour seemed near; he did not wish, as a greedy exactor, to be cheated of his desire or his empty hands to begin to make his entrails grumble against the negligent.

Another, confounded by the disgrace of his sought-after chancellorship and cast down from the honor of another’s preeminence, rashly presumed in malice to turn upon the Church a personal hatred conceived from envy. The third, rejoicing alone among the others in the privilege of perishable flesh, judged that nothing should be denied to blood, nothing yielded to the sacred canons; for he cannot pay due reverence to rules that he does not know. Therefore Brutus chose a Brutus like himself, so that each might match the other in equal ignorance of letters. Moreover, the discipline of Apostolic severity terrified them, lest it restrain their headlong audacity and curb the wandering excursions of reckless cupidity.

This number, this great expertise, this college so venerable and holy, sought, against the resistance of all, to draw the Church of God—the immaculate bride of His beloved Son—into its own will [Note: [Col. 0041D] B.: “pleasure.”], and to transfer her from the right hand of the King to the detestable embraces of Satan. Yet, when they saw the agreement of nearly the whole world, they would at once have returned to unity even against their will; but while they were astonished and therefore inactive, the unbridled ambition of the greater schismatic could endure delay no longer. With a cope secretly prepared, as it is said, [Col. 0042A] he snatched it from the hands of the officiant and threw it over his own shoulders with such haste that, the fringes catching at his neck, the upper part of the garment swept the pavement. Thus dressed, he ran to the chair, with none of those mentioned above yet accompanying him, himself proclaiming his own name as victor and shamelessly exhorting those prepared to vote for him and sing his praises [Note: [Col. 0042D] B.: “having prepared.”]. A remarkable spectacle, and not without a manifest omen of the truth to come: namely, that this ascent would someday turn to his ruin, as the inverted arrangement of the presumptuously assumed cloak itself foreshadowed.

Meanwhile, when the doors of the church had been opened, that infamous breed of the accursed burst in; for this is the old designation of that family, from which a pontiff was said to be chosen in order to pour out blessing upon all nations [Col. 0042B]. How blessing can be propagated from a stock of curse is not easy to see, especially through this man, in whom the disgrace of the ancient curse is heightened by deservedly incurred new execration. As armed men ran about, a kind of theatrical scene began to be staged throughout the church, as the gleam of weapons illuminated the walls and the wanton shouting of men seemingly triumphant echoed back. Finally, when the cope had been arranged by their hands, he was escorted as far as the palace, attended by them and by a few priests, whose shameful trade is to cheat the simplicity of pilgrims and continually harass the altar of blessed Peter with sacrileges.

Moreover, these beginnings of his did not enjoy a better sequel, whether one investigates the procedure of the procured execration [Col. 0042C] or the favour purchased from secular power. Did he not heap a greater crime upon the iniquity of sacrilege, since simoniacal depravity plainly intervened throughout, as is proved by money lavished upon the senate and people of Rome and openly spent on public buildings? Yet more monstrous is this: he prostituted the liberty purchased by Christ’s blood, so that the Church—which by her own right has always held dominion over all princes—might be enslaved to the service of her own official; thus she would lose the privilege of her incomparable majesty and at last be reduced to the wretched condition of servitude. We ourselves could not behold these things with our own eyes, but the truth reached us through the faithful report of those who saw them [Col. 0042D]. What was done publicly could also be confirmed for us by the testimony of many, especially since the witnesses shine with the honour of the dignity that was snatched away, and their unanimous simplicity establishes the unqualified truth.

Having therefore considered in this respect the nature of the affair and the merits of the persons involved, I gladly turn my eyes and mind to the other party, to contemplate with all the joy of my heart, point by point, the work of those who elected; and to give thanks to Him who bestowed upon your holy college the prudence and strength by which you were able both to avoid the serpent’s malice and to repel the wickedness of rampant pride. But neither does their tiny exception deserve the name of a party [Col. 0043A], nor is it fitting that our whole body be designated by the name of a party; for the separation of the lost does not diminish the number of the elect, nor does the Lord’s threshing-floor suffer loss when the grain remains and the chaff departs under the cleansing winnowing-fan.

Thus, to one reviewing all these matters, it is clear that zeal for holiness consecrated the beginnings; courage joined with prudence guided their course; patience will bring it to its due completion; and, God willing, steadfast faith will provide peace through perseverance. Nothing carnal, nothing earthly, nothing directed toward your private advantage engaged your eyes; rather, it is evident that with all your desires you have breathed after the common good and the honour of the Church, and have laboured with all your strength. Therefore your name shall be proclaimed, and from sea to sea [Col. 0043B] the glory of your excellence shall resound; it shall furnish later generations with a pattern and an example, lest they depart from justice and truth through the error of any persecution.

Moreover, the Spirit bears witness to our spirit (Romans 8) that, together with us, the public conscience of all rejects and condemns that schismatic, while it embraces with the arms of sincere charity and reverence the bishop elected for us. For his works are manifest—works, that is, of curse and scandal—whereas this man’s work is in blessing, and his favour among the nations grows daily stronger. The hearts of all are with us, even of those whose tongues protest against us under some secular necessity, so that, if the Church has not yet triumphed over all in their bodies, she has nevertheless triumphed in their hearts [Col. 0043C].

For does not divine vengeance plainly proceed against those who dissent from this unity of faith, and is not His will made known by clear signs? Has not that prince—the like of whom Rome has not had for a long time, whose right hand the Lord was said to have grasped (Isaiah 45), whose terror had spread almost to the remotest East from the day of his accession—Otto, begun to be rejected by divine judgment? Those whom even walls had formerly not rendered secure have dared to engage him at close quarters and to mock the prosperity of his successes. Truly, this is the finger of God (Exodus 8), a sudden change of the right hand of the Most High (Psalm 76), who still spares and delays correction in His wrath. “Would that he were wise, understood, and foresaw the things to come” (Deuteronomy [Col. 0043D] 32), for so many present losses are signs, as it were, of future ones.

Therefore, having duly considered everything from the beginning, my lords and fathers, it is fitting that you rejoice with great exultation because, uniquely out of all flesh, you have been chosen for this time: through you the truth of faith, through you the pattern of justice, through you the unshaken liberty of the Church, is preserved. That we stand with you in this unity, that we detest heretical depravity together with its author, is a grace owing to you who began it, from whom we received both authority and example. You yourselves, therefore, are our leaders; indeed, you are among the strongest of Israel, to whom Solomon’s bed was entrusted, to be surrounded with faithful watches because of the terrors of the night [Col. 0044A] (Song of Songs 3).

To you, as to a lamp set upon a lampstand (Matthew 5), the Eastern and Western Church alike flock. Yet the sound of truth has gone out even to the distant islands; from them, as from the ends of the earth (Psalm 18), many have already come through many dangers to hear Solomon’s wisdom (Matthew 12). Though great distances of place separate us, charity always joins without division those whom one Spirit, one faith, and one confession direct toward salvation. In this constancy we have resolved to remain with you; in it we must live with you; in it, when the divine will decrees, we must die; for neither death nor life nor anything whatever shall ever separate us from professing this judgment.

Meanwhile [Col. 0044B], although we cannot offer our personal presence to our lord and to you, the devotion of charity nevertheless in some measure supplies for absence, since we stand beside our venerable fathers, the legates of the apostolic see, labouring with them in every way for the interests of the holy Roman Church. In them the perfection of apostolic holiness and learning shines so brightly that their merits gain them more affection than the discipline of their severity commands reverence. They are men whose holiness the people admire, whose wisdom the clergy everywhere praises, and before whose stern virtue princes tremble. In short, they temper all their work with such gentleness that the severity of discipline is not lost, while the favour of the holy Roman Church grows strong in every respect.

As for that affair in which you heard that the king of the Franks had been offended against them, believe them wholly excusable and beyond all doubt; for they could never have been brought to consent to that dispensation unless irresistible necessity and the immeasurable good of a recompense immediately to come [Note: [Col. 0043D] B.: “to come.”] had drawn them to it. For venerable persons from the realm of each king had assembled at the kings’ command to deliberate concerning acceptance of the Roman pontiff, concerning which nothing had yet been publicly determined.

Those brethren, then, were pursuing the Church’s cause, not without great danger; for with very many the favour of iniquity had grown so strong that those who did not dare recommend an open rejection of the truth instead urged delay by a kind of secular cunning [Col. 0044D]. They said that the outcome of so doubtful a matter should be awaited rather than that the majesty of such great princes be exposed to uncertain hazards; that men whom waiting alone could more safely preserve unharmed ought not to be entangled by the rashness of excessive haste; that the Roman Church had always been burdensome to princes; that, when opportunity was given, her yoke should at some time be cast off, until detestable ambition had paid the penalties of its desire; that the uncertainty of the question should be dissolved by the death of one or the other claimant; and that meanwhile the religion of bishops throughout the several kingdoms could suffice until the divine will should appear through clearer signs.

There was also the pressing influence of the emperor’s legates and cardinals—the accursed John [Col. 0045A] and Guido—who thought that a brief delay would give them victory if any occasion should suspend your brethren even for a short time. Furthermore, since all believed the minds of the kings inclined in favour of our lord, the granting of delay would have been thought a surrender to the emperor’s side; and suspicion would perhaps bring scarcely less harm than knowledge of the truth. The king of the Franks had also committed the decision of the matter to the will of the king of England, publicly declaring that he would do nothing except what the latter’s judgment should prescribe for him.

Thus the counsel of delay had prevailed, on the ground that the more time was allowed, the more usefully provision might be made for either king; and that meanwhile they might draw some omen from the events themselves. Since, therefore, the whole cause depended upon the decision of the king of England [Col. 0045B], he ought rather to be heard than frightened by the harshness of any severity; for by his single favourable disposition, in a moment you gained the kingdoms of the Franks, the English, the Spaniards, the Irish, and finally even the Norwegians. Besides, from what source could anyone have presumed that offence would arise over a matter which, from the beginning, the holiness of the kings, the piety of the bishops, the fidelity of the princes, and the devout rejoicing of the people had confirmed for the sake of peace, with a written instrument also intervening? They assigned its completion not to the common rules, but to ecclesiastical indulgence, which could bring it about more quickly. If anything done by indulgence contrary to those same rules is admittedly an offence, nevertheless no crime intervened, and the preservation of the whole work’s soundness compensates for a slight wound.

This, certainly, was their zeal [Col. 0045C]; this was the purpose of the dispensation. It was not voluntarily chosen, but extorted by the urgency of necessity; for if the discussion had not been brought to a good conclusion that day, your brethren would undoubtedly have received a long, or even perpetual, rejection under the appearance of postponement.

## XXV. To Henry of Pisa, Legate of the Roman Church

After your departure, when I had suffered four attacks of an importunate tertian fever, I finally resorted to the salutary remedy of medicine; yet this proved scarcely less troublesome to me than the excessive heat which preceded it. Medical remedies, indeed, have mixed into them I know not what abominable malignity; and, lest they should confer every benefit freely, they always repay it with an accompanying injury, so that even when they have helped, they take a more dishonourable revenge. Yet I recovered, and, through God’s grace and your merits, the pleasant hope of desired health smiles upon me; our anchor is thought to be holding fast in the harbour of safety.

Some remnants of the past illness nevertheless still cling to me: emaciation, weakness akin to sickness, and a delicate appetite, whose fastidiousness no abundance and no ingenuity of attendants can satisfy. The physician says that material for a relapse is at hand, and therefore anxiously imposes a regime of more exact observance. With my lips cracked and my tongue throbbing, he allows me drink with such scarcity that he seems to wish rather to provoke thirst than to allay it [Col. 0046A]. For that race of men, distinguished always by a certain austerity, wins reverence for its art by the display of severity alone; and, as though generosity would make it cheap, condemns everything that the wretched patient’s desire demands.

Would that, as regards food, the same practice and abstinence were afforded to us both, so that sharing might remove suspicion and the compassion of kindness increase confidence! Moreover, they always attribute the defect of their ignorance to the patient’s fault, so that the sick man both perishes from hunger and is tortured by the insult of slander. Finally, advancing with sententious pronouncements to increase their fee, they rob themselves of the grace of divine mercy, so that what divine compassion has bestowed [Note: [Col. 0045D] B.: “bestowed.”] may appear to have proceeded from their diligence.

For the present, let these inconveniences excuse us before your highness [Col. 0046B], because, if bodily incapacity holds back my person, the devotion of charity nevertheless hastens to meet your majesty. I also particularly commend to you the causes of our people which are meanwhile to be argued before your tribunal, so that in them they may find in you both a friend’s diligence and a judge’s equity. Offer humble thanks for us also to my lord the king, because he compassionately regarded my illness with such generosity that, should anything happen otherwise, he undertook in royal munificence to pay the debt I had incurred, whether on his account or for any other reason. He praised the fidelity of our devotion and the zeal of our service, and recognized that they had often been beneficial to him.

Among all remedies, I received most sweetly and effectively the favour of my lord, flowing more abundantly in time of need [Col. 0046C]; its cheerfulness at once banished every injury of my illness. Happy am I, I say, if I shall ever be found not to have received ungratefully what has been bestowed upon me with such great and easy kindness; happy, if I am granted to serve his interests and glory with all my resources, all my zeal, and all my strength always! Though the greatness of the benefit exceeds the measure of my littleness, whoever devotes all that he can to giving thanks must surely be called most worthy.

## XXVI. To the Same

Your wisdom does not fail to know the terms on which our kings agreed concerning the acceptance of the lord pope. Our king sent envoys to the ecclesiastical persons of his kingdom in England, with the letters he had received from the lord pope and with that document fabricated by the schismatics concerning the assembly at Pavia, so that, with both documents laid before them as though they were the pleadings of the two parties, they might more rightly form a judgment, as it were, from a legal hearing, and more clearly recognize the truth by considering the falsehood set against it [Col. 0046D].

Since I could not be bodily present at that conference, I took care to be present at least by letter, so that the page might supply the place of my person and a faithful letter restore the force of a living voice. I judged that a copy of this letter, too, should be sent to your holiness, so that your affection might recognize my devotion—though of little use, still dutiful [Col. 0047A]. Besides, I am sending you the book of Ennodius: it is borrowed, indeed, but, if your experience approves it, I shall return it after having it copied, with all the speed possible.

I had not seen that book before it was assigned to me by your judgment; and, having seen it, I wondered with what confidence its author first published it, or with what favour others afterwards copied it. It does not seem to me worthy that so much time or money should be expended upon its study or transcription, since the work is prolix and each of its statements requires many tedious repetitions before it can be understood. At first sight it proceeds with difficulty and obscurity; and whereas a clearer style ought to disclose the difficulty of the subject matter, its dark language rather blunts understanding [Col. 0047B]. Though examining it entails much labour, attaining its meaning brings no pleasure: neither its thought pleases by resolution nor its language by elegance.

For its whole purpose [Note: [Col. 0047D] B. omits “for.”] is to say everything differently from everyone else. Accordingly, it entangles and knots up all that it says in a certain elaborate convolution, so that it ought more correctly to be called *Innodius* (“Knotty”) than Ennodius. Moreover, in verse it shortens long syllables and, by its own authority, lengthens syllables which ought to be shortened. No excellence compensates for the defect of false quantity, because neither the polish of the language nor the dignity of the subject makes up for it.

Still, everyone is bound to observe the constraints of the law he has undertaken; and whoever voluntarily binds himself to observances of this kind suppresses freedom of expression through necessity [Col. 0047C]. But a double fault does not deserve easy pardon when obscurity blunts the understanding and metrical corruption offends the ear’s pleasure. I think this book enjoyed neither notice nor favour among the ancients, and for that reason never came into many hands; rather, it lay buried for a long time in some old bookcase, until it recently emerged into the light because of the very merit of its obscurity and the novelty of its foreign name.

There are, indeed, some who esteem difficult things more highly because they marvel at what they understand less; things illuminated by the pleasant serenity of lucid speech they value less and regard as childish. Yet Seneca, our own author, Cicero, and the others whose writings are approved show that obscurity should be avoided as darkness [Col. 0047D]. Julius Caesar too, a man of distinguished eloquence [Note: [Col. 0048D] B. omits “a man of distinguished eloquence.”], declares culpable those who wish to speak or write things that people may marvel at rather than understand, and says that he himself avoids an unusual and infrequent word as one avoids a rock.

Read it, nevertheless, and judge it not by my estimation but rather by your own experience, lest my ignorance be said to have done injustice to its merits and to have deprived it of your favourable judgment. But if you seek an incontrovertible judgment about its prose, judge it according to the merits of its verses; for it is true that it displays equal skill in regard to syllabic quantities and to the nature and force of words. Farewell.

## XXVII. To William, Bishop of Le Mans

[Col. 0048A]

Lord Ralph, treasurer of Rouen, is our friend; and he knows that I have long since obtained very great favour with your holiness. Accordingly, through our intercession with you, he asks for your assistance, since he complains that he is burdened in two respects concerning the designation of the place which you assigned to him and to the lord of Poitiers for conducting the case pending between them. Although your city lies almost midway between them, it is nevertheless somewhat farther from Rouen; yet you have appointed that he be drawn farther on, as though to meet his adversary.

In this he thinks that your favour has begun to incline more readily toward the opposing party [Col. 0048B], because you were at once so generous to that adversary in your distribution of distances that you prescribed only forty miles for him to travel, but one hundred—and more burdensome miles at that—for the other. If you thought this deference was owed to him because of episcopal reverence, it should be extended only so far that lavish generosity does not become a burden or prejudice to the other party. For the judge’s impartiality ought to stand between the parties in such a manner that it provides each with equal and free equity, lest affection seem to have dictated the judgment, rather than justice, measured by the instruments of reason, to have formed it.

He therefore asks, and we earnestly entreat on his behalf, that Le Mans be assigned to them as the place for conducting the matter, after a fairer division of the distance; or somewhere nearer, so that we too may be able to attend [Col. 0048C], since, because of our familiarity and favour with both parties, we have great confidence of reconciling them. Nor can that party complain of you concerning the designation of another place and time, because a person summoned here cannot be condemned at the first summons for a single absence, until perhaps he has been summoned a second or third time, so that he may be condemned for manifest contumacy because of repeated absence. Farewell.

## XXVIII. To Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen

We received your highness’s letter concerning the injury which the lord of Fécamp inflicts upon us. It states that he consents, through your hand, to offer us a priest for the church in question. We certainly give thanks for your holy and kindly diligence toward us [Col. 0048D], but we fear the tricks of a crafty man, lest by this action he intends both to circumvent your prudence and to procure prejudice against our right.

For judgment has been rendered between us, and the judges delegated by the apostolic see have ordered him to restore what was taken from us, compel the excommunicated persons to come to satisfaction, and offer a priest through whom he may cause both church and people to obey us as pastor and bishop of their souls. If we receive a priest from another’s hand rather than his own, the possession will appear not restored to us but sequestered, and this may greatly impede our side when the question of lordship is considered [Col. 0049A]. Nor is the mere offering of a priest sufficient for obedience to the judges, unless he has also caused all that has been prescribed to be fully rendered to us.

If, however, a settlement were presently being negotiated between us which would remove every future dispute, we might be brought by the counsel of your fatherhood to every accommodation. But to add strength to an adversary who is arming himself with all his powers for combat belongs not merely to an imprudent man but to a madman.

## XXIX. To Saint Thomas, While He Was Chancellor of the King of England

To his venerable and beloved friend THOMAS, illustrious chancellor of the king of England, ARNULF, humble minister of the Church of Lisieux: greeting and abundant affection.

[Col. 0049B] I received the letter of your graciousness, and every word of it seemed to me to drip sweetness and flow with the honeyed flavour of sincere charity. I rejoiced that with you I retain the privilege of our former intimacy and favour; that it has neither migrated away through separation of place nor expired amid frequent business. I rejoiced, I say, because after your letter no doubt could remain: your dignity ought neither to incur the fault of falsehood nor descend to the baseness of flattery.

Yet the affection of true love lives equally in me toward you; and although frequent practical demonstration does not adorn it, the devotion of a ready will, conscious to itself, supplies the deficiency. For in friendship the will of minds alone is sought [Col. 0049C], and it admits no question of increase, lest it be considered prostituted or mercenary.

For it stands in its own purity through itself, so that even the performance of deeds has in it only the role of an accessory and consequence. It is not subject to the accidents of fortune, but gives and retains its dignity in itself and through itself. This is so true that friendship is usually found more rarely among the rich, and indeed, as if it hated the multiplicity of riches, seems to cling more securely to the simplicity of poverty. It is rare and therefore more precious, but nowhere rarer than among those called to deliberate upon the counsels of princes and arrange their affairs.

For, to say nothing of other things, restless ambition rules their minds; and while each fears that another will anticipate him in zeal, envy arises, which must at once turn into hatred [Col. 0049D]. This is indeed the ancient habit of envy: it judges another’s successes its own loss and regards as taken from itself whatever has turned to another’s advantage. Thus it is tormented; it conceals the torment of its mind beneath a constrained cheerfulness of face, and clothes its hidden hostility in deceitful flatteries.

Moreover, if a prince’s favour is altered toward someone and he begins to look upon him more sternly, the man formerly thronged by his companions’ favour, applause, and everyone’s diligent services goes forth at once bereft of all consolation. Those from whom he expected every kind of compassion mock him; old enemies, having gained an opportunity, seek out past injuries [Col. 0050A]; and they perversely construe even his benefits. You sail upon this sea; you must live in this tempest, in which you too must fear Sirens: the sudden laughter of applauders and the tuneful songs of flatterers.

Amid all this, let your sole confidence of escape be both sincerity of faith and integrity of honourable action. Seek glory rather in the testimony of your conscience with the Apostle (Romans 2) than purchase, at a price, the slippery uncertainty of another’s tongue or popular opinion. These pass away with greater swiftness than they come; the former, though sometimes meeting an unwelcome reception, always glories in a happy outcome. I write these things not, as they say, to teach letters to Minerva, but because, speaking with a friend, I could not restrain the course of my discourse [Col. 0050B], especially since a certain exuberance of congratulating feeling urged me on.

I commend to your charity our faithful lord Serlo, together with the few and minor matters that he carries, adding this request: during my absence, let your diligence preserve for me the favour of the prince which I have earned by most dutiful service; for in a young man it cannot long live without the nourishment of reminder, lest it expire. Fare well, always.

## XXX. To Lord Pope Alexander

A welcome opportunity shines upon me, long awaited and sought by many contrivances: namely, to see my lord’s face and visit my mother, the holy Roman Church [Col. 0050C]. It is delightful for me to expose myself to any dangers and undergo any labours, that I may at last deserve to enjoy the desired sight of your serenity and be refreshed by the pleasant address of sacred conversation. On another occasion I was to have been sent by the prince, but the troublesome hostility of wars then arising held me back; both the necessity of the Church and the advantage of the commonwealth required the efforts of my diligence for bringing them to an end. Indeed, I undertook that journey more at my own desire than by command of him who sent me, so that the embassy might appear requested rather than imposed.

But now, all things having been settled, I come not as one sent but led by devotion alone, to offer, for the good pleasure of my lord, body and spirit, and to devote to your interests all the resources of my means, as a matter of obligation [Col. 0050D]. Nevertheless, in order to come, I had to seek out something like grounds of necessity, because I could by no means have been permitted to depart unless I were thought driven by some urgent reason. For since my presence is always serviceable to the prince, he would have wished to keep me not so much for compliance with my devotion as for public interests and his own service.

When I have come, it will readily appear what should be ascribed to devotion and what charged to necessity. I come [Note: [Col. 0049D] B.: “no one.”], therefore, with permission obtained not indeed in spirit, but at least in words, since I did not wish to make an issue of his silence. For though his face did not answer my eyes, his speech nevertheless answered my wishes; nor did an opportunity sought with so great desire seem one to be rejected. I come, I say [Col. 0051A], paying no heed to enemies’ ambushes, the hardships of the road, the unhealthiness of the air, or injuries of the sea, in the assured confidence that your merits will go before me and, God willing, remove every obstacle from all places.

Meanwhile, I thought it proper to tell you the artifice of this contrived necessity which released me from royal occupations. Silvester, treasurer of my church, and John, nephew of the bishop of Séez, brought letters from your see to the bishops of Le Mans and Avranches concerning certain cases to be determined against me without any remedy of appeal. Lord William of Paris, cardinal of the holy Roman Church, happened to be present at their hearing; and in his presence the aforesaid treasurer withdrew, before the judges, all the complaints he had against me, and confirmed under a bodily pledge of faith that he would not thereafter raise them against me [Col. 0051B]. Through their intervention, I granted him favour; and though in every respect he appeared ungrateful and plainly a slanderer, I forgave every offence with that indulgence which is especially fitting between persons bound by close connection.

But John, having received an adverse judgment after the arguments on both sides had been carefully heard, appealed to the apostolic see for the Kalends of February, more to console his humiliation than to remedy his case, although he had removed every licence of appeal by the very apostolic ruling which he himself had brought back from you. Since judgments must be observed, especially where they cannot be suspended by an appeal [Col. 0051C], it is certain that no urgency of necessity draws me to reopen a matter judged; but I welcomed the occasion supplied by the appeal, lest I seem to have neglected reverence for you if, having been summoned to your presence, I had not come.

Furthermore, because I cannot evade so many dangers through rash haste, I may perhaps need to spend a considerable time smoothing the routes and preparing for safety. Therefore, if that John arrives first, it will be good and useful for you to keep him until our arrival; for the manifest truth will establish to you that both he and his uncle have committed very grave offences against your person and the condition of the whole Church.

## XXXI. To Lord Pope Alexander

[Col. 0051D]

If the letters by which I endeavoured to forewarn Your Majesty concerning the zeal which Bishop Sag. is directing toward removing religious life from his church have reached your notice, I am greatly astonished—and many have been astonished—how such an act, and a public document concerning that act, could have been surreptitiously obtained from Your Holiness. For what is this? A religious bishop had endowed an episcopal church, condemned to pitiable poverty, with revenues, buildings, ornaments, and, above all, with the religious life to which he chiefly devoted himself; and he had made it rich from poor, renowned from obscure, glorious from ignoble, if one may say so. This deed the whole Church of our regions indeed revered [Col. 0052A], and all religious persons everywhere commended, if anyone wished to consider either the charity poured out upon all or the discipline of the order.

Nor was this accomplished by him alone, but through the efforts of many venerable persons and by the authority of many; for auspices of success, ever desired, attended the endeavours of his labours, so that virtue and fortune seemed to contend toward the establishment of that church. The Apostolic See rejoiced that it had laid the first foundations of so great a religious institution; that it had never ceased to foster its advancement with continual support; and that it had secured its completion with privileges and with an anathema that would remain effective for ever. For in all its privileges this is found written in perpetuity in place of a salutation, whereby the author’s will [Col. 0052B] is plainly declared: he intended it to be stable, and did not leave it to be changed at others’ discretion. A transitory matter does not deserve to be inscribed under a title of perpetuity, since things so inscribed either retain a state of permanence or reveal the falsity of their title.

But the assertion that a predecessor cannot give law to his successor is either simply false, or else all the institutions of the holy Fathers may be overturned with impunity—those Fathers whose wisdom the peoples recount, whose praise the Church proclaims, and whose tombs the glory of heavenly magnificence adorns with frequent miracles. The privileges of Roman pontiffs must indeed be regarded as a kind of their testament: they do not expire at the death of the testator, but rather derive firmness from that very death; nor, when the person is gone [Col. 0052C], does the authority of things known to have been once religiously established perish.

Yet we do not deny that the errors of predecessors can be corrected by successors, and that even their good enactments can be changed for the better, where a greater benefit recommends the alteration and religious life suffers no harm. For nothing is to be done to the prejudice of religious life, since whatever opposes it is plainly contrary to the divine will. For this reason we have seen the secular canons, as they are called, removed in order to introduce regular canons, although their churches had obtained certain privileges of the Apostolic See while in that condition. In such cases it is clear that nothing has been done against the privileges: one ought rather to consider the author’s intention than [Col. 0052D] cling to the written letters, because his will is offended in no respect where the purpose of his will is more faithfully observed.

But if something more human has been instituted, even though documents of the Apostolic See confirm it, this neither excludes progress toward perfection nor assigns a limit to devotion. Endeavours after holiness ought always freely to extend toward what lies ahead; and what has been written must be interpreted so as not to seem jealous of our advancement. For favour is rightly granted to a lesser good when the growth of a greater good is in no way suppressed. The Church does not allow those who aspire to higher things from a desire for perfection to be impeded by obstacles, but permits them freely to break through to greater things; and thus it removes the privileges of an initial imperfection, so that, embracing the grace of a new perfection, it seems not so much to abolish the old by the new as to fulfil it. But it is not fitting to debase the sacred institutions of the ancients, or to furnish authority for defect, so that encouragements to boldness may be obtained from that from which the severity of discipline ought to have inspired fear.

Certainly there are some acts to which consent may not be given in advance; yet, if they have been done, they must be tolerated, because they cannot be remedied—or, if some compensation is possible, they must be regulated with discerning gentleness. Indulgence, however, must not precede fault, lest security nourish boldness and confidence in remission invite wrongdoing.

Therefore severity must restrain forbidden designs, lest they be carried into effect with rashness; and likewise [Col. 0053B] it must punish unlawful excesses with suitable correction, unless either the force of power rescues the guilty person or repentance moderates discipline. For then it lies within a judge’s power to mitigate the sentence and judge more gently than the laws prescribe, when the merits of circumstances or persons require it, or when the pressure of necessity compels it. Yet in judging necessity we ought not to be found faint-hearted, lest we seem to have withdrawn the material for virtue or despaired of divine grace.

I know certain prodigals of dispensations who are so lavishly kind that they reserve nothing for the laws but grant everything to personal inclinations; nor do they heed an offence against reason while seeming to themselves to have guarded against human displeasure. They measure [Note: [Col. 0053D] B.: “they measure” (*metuntur*).] desired outcomes by the prerogative [Col. 0053C] of their power rather than by the merit of reason; and, excusing every indulgence under the name of necessity, they do not endure to test the goodness of divine grace. Instead, seeking human favour before all things, they embrace fleeting breezes and empty winds through deceptive efforts. They proclaim, of course, that they are providing for the peace of the Church, while prostituting its liberty and reducing its majesty to contempt—though the Church ought, through the strength of the saints, to appear “terrible as an army set in array” (Song of Songs 6).

For formerly she used to stand fearsome over the highest powers and patiently wear down their might, while steadfastly exposed to tribulations and expecting deliverance only from the Deliverer of the poor. “For the Lord delivers the poor from the mighty, and the needy, for whom there is no helper” (Psalm 71); for he is faithful and does not allow our strength to be exceeded by the strength of temptation, but with temptation provides the outcome, that we may be able to endure it (1 Corinthians 10). Nevertheless, whenever, despairing of virtue’s effectiveness, we bend toward human favours, we exclude this grace through the faint-heartedness of despair; and, by hastening the shipwreck of truth and justice, we hinder the result of salutary experience.

Rather, according to the Psalmist’s teaching, we ought to “hope in the Lord and do good” (Psalm 36), since he does not abandon those who hope in him in time of tribulation or leave them without help on the day of the proud. We ought to exercise ourselves in his commandments and ordinances [Col. 0054A], not immediately offer our feeble hands for captivity. Victory cannot follow without struggle, nor can a crown be gained without lawful contest. The law of the contest is to employ one’s strength, embrace the virtue of patience and long-suffering, not be drawn away by favours at the outset, and not yield in despair of divine goodness; for “those who hope in him shall not be put to shame” (Psalm 21). But those who please men are put to shame, “because God has despised them” (Psalm 52). Would it not have been more useful to hope for human favour itself from divine goodness, and not provide it with a cause for offending God, since even the hearts of kings are in God’s hand and he will incline them wherever he wills (Proverbs 21)?

Furthermore, we have learned by experience that, by a kind of divine judgment, it often happens that those who, through an eager pursuit [Col. 0054B] of human favour, offend the reverence due to divine majesty, suffer loss in divine matters but do not obtain the human favour they sought. For as discipline produces caution, so ready indulgence makes the insolent more prone to boldness. They regard the gratuitous benefit of another’s generosity as the reward of their own merits, and sometimes even consider the benefit itself an injury because they have been valued less highly than their own estimation of themselves.

I fear that this has happened in your case; as will later become clear to Your Holiness by manifest indications, when a truthful report reaches your ears of how maliciously and boldly the aforesaid bishop publicly proclaimed the weakness of your position and, on his return, declared the victory of the Church’s enemies to be imminent. There are persons who heard him, through whom these and other, more malicious things will in due time become fully known to you, so that no suspicion affecting the credibility of the truth should stand in the way.

Meanwhile I shall speak to my lord. “May my words please him!” I shall speak, I say, because I have speech before him, before whom neither religious life needs an intercessor nor justice a defender. Lord, all who profess or love the observance of that order, throughout all the churches of the French and English, were scandalized upon hearing of this matter. They ask what anathema of your predecessors—indeed, what anathema of yours—has so recently been dissolved, when no necessity appears and no remedy seems to be offered for so great a wound by any compensation. All the revenues and [Col. 0054D] all the proceeds of that archdeaconry, which had been allotted to the common uses of the regular brethren, have been taken away without examination of the case and assigned to the expenses of one person, who is himself secular.

Thus they ask, having been despoiled without judgment of what was theirs by right; and, with that which religious life used to distribute to the poor having been withdrawn, they lament that they have nothing to show but empty hands. Meanwhile, amid the haircloth and filth of the poor brethren, the son of a record-keeper comes forth decked in silks and varied finery. As they behold him—the creature of a hateful unlikeness—they silently execrate and condemn, as much as they dare, this seedbed, as it were, of secularization being brought back. Their fear is increased [Col. 0055A] because another archdeaconry in the same church is still vacant, to be conferred upon the younger nephew as soon as he seems to have grown into the lawful age.

Moreover, after the former prior of the cloister had been removed, because he was believed to possess a keener mind and did not remain silent from conscience about injuries to the Church, the bishop appointed an ignorant man as prior—so that he himself might, of course, fill the ignorant man’s place and convert their goods to his own uses without opposition. Act therefore, and recall the Apostolic wisdom of domestic severity, so that Your Holiness itself may restore to proper form what has been concealed from Your Holiness. Thus may the integrity of the holy institution be reformed, and may both your privileges and those of your predecessors recover their former strength. In this way “the mouth of those who speak iniquity shall be stopped” (Psalm 62) [Col. 0055B]; your faithful people, in their accustomed liberty, will acclaim you in praise and glory of your name; and, once the terror of this example has been removed, the Church’s condition will rest in its former tranquillity.

I fear that I may perhaps have spoken more boldly than I ought to Your Majesty; but zeal for your holy reputation impelled me to speak, as did the unworthy crushing of that church, to which for many reasons I have long been bound by the deepest affection. I know that, in your ears, the devoted boldness of one who loves you will be more welcome than the deceitful assent of a flatterer.

### XXXII. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER

Whenever anyone seeks to be aided by the prayers of our humility before Your Majesty, I consider especially whether honourableness commends the person or justice commends the cause. These are indeed the two virtues which, we know, need no patronage before Your Excellency. You voluntarily show favour to them, since the one has set you forth for praise and the other as an example to the world.

Under this pretext, then, I approach to make petition for P., Archdeacon of Poitiers. His diligence in office, generosity toward those subject to him, kindness toward his associates, and finally his enlargement of new resources for his church are all said to make him useful to it. Therefore, if the nature of his cause is examined, he maintains that he possesses, in a certain archpresbyterate belonging to him, the right which the ancient custom of that church confirms both for him [Col. 0055D] and for all other archdeacons in all their archpresbyterates.

Moreover, it seems superfluous to trouble the matter with litigation, since the dispute concerns only the election of the archpriest. By custom, an election made by the archdeacon is referred to the bishop’s judgment, and the bishop may reject it by his authority if the candidate is unsuitable. But if an archpriest is appointed in his archdeaconry against his will, it will plainly be a serious subtraction from his interests and honour, since in his own archdeaconry another archdeacon will, in a way, be born alongside him.

### XXXIII. TO THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

To his dearest lord THOMAS, by the grace of God Archbishop of Canterbury and Primate of all England, ARNULF, humble minister of the Church of Lisieux: greetings and the reverence due with the fullest devotion.

We received the letters of Your Blessedness with all the greater joy because we recognized that they had proceeded from the richer abundance of your charity. For beyond that most pure affection which you bear toward us, they breathed a certain newness of life and zeal for justice, so that every letter seemed to distil the sweetness of former magnificence and of renewed life. We therefore pray that the condition of the dignity you have assumed may be so moderated by him who chose you that holiness may not take magnificence away from you, nor magnificence diminish holiness; but that they may advance with equal steps and, after the pattern of divine sanctification, sanctify and glorify the priest of Christ [Col. 0056B].

“For holiness and magnificence are in his sanctuary” (Psalm 95): neither is one greater than the other, nor is one anything without the other; but, as they are always, so together they illuminate and glorify the majesty of the everlasting Godhead. Therefore my soul has been filled with the richness of inward delight and outward abundance (Psalm 62), seeing one worthy summoned to dignity—one whom we have experienced through very many indications to possess zeal and skill in governing those subject to him. For indeed “a great prophet has arisen among us, and God has visited his people” (Luke 7).

You shall command me as one of your own, since in person and resources we are ready to obey all your wishes and serve your interests.

Farewell.

I have written this to you so briefly, not in order to reply to Your Majesty, but that you may know that we have seen both your messenger and the letters of your graciousness.

### XXXIV. TO SAINT THOMAS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

To the venerable and beloved lord and father THOMAS, by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury: may you attain prosperity and salvation through the spirit of counsel and fortitude.

The letter of your graciousness gave me great joy. Having indeed examined it carefully by reading it three times over [Col. 0056D], I found nothing that did not either express humility or breathe zeal for justice. Your zeal pleased me because robust humility commended it, and zeal and humility advanced together in mutual support. For humility ought to moderate the fires of fervour, and zeal ought to stir and kindle the moderation of humility, lest humility descend into faint-heartedness or aroused zeal exceed its bounds into fury.

Since these two embraced one another in mutual charity, I understood that constancy, a third, had joined the two; and this promises happy outcomes to holy beginnings and fortunate results to strong patience. For in you it considers neither losses nor labours, but, seeking with every effort the testimony of a sincere conscience, regards the shipwreck alike of fortune and person as less important [Col. 0057A] than justice or virtue.

Some persons, whose malice is accustomed to divine from another’s conscience what it does not know, imagined that your action proceeded from pride rather than the truth of virtue. They alleged that you wished, even in this dignity, to preserve the former practices of the chancellorship, so that no one might dare resist your power or will; that you would deem it glorious if you could claim for your own name a power formerly issuing from the slippery will of another, although reverence is more rightly due to ecclesiastical dignity than to a secular office. They said that you had been raised and advanced by divine goodness to higher things; that you no longer preserved even a seat at the foot or side, but stood over the crown of the very head—namely, that the chief assignment of it to us, and the confirmation of that assignment, depended so much upon your authority that it ought to belong to you.

Accordingly, they said, you had opposed royal commands at the beginning, so that the entire body might be believed conquered in that one instance, since no confidence of resistance would remain to others where royal orders could not prevail. They added that you had at some time said among friends that the unconsidered impulses of proud youth should not be encouraged in a prince, but that intemperance should at once be resisted manfully, lest toleration create boldness or ready indulgence confirm insolence. You knew all the movements of the royal mind: what frivolity it possesses, what it dares attempt in strength; and, moreover, the prince himself had recognized the magnificence of your prudence, which he had so often experienced as useful in opportunities and effective in difficulties [Col. 0057C]. He should not reject, because of the flattering deceits of sycophants, the salutary counsel by which he had been accustomed to support wavering matters, level rough places, and remove obstacles.

When envy in its malice had conveyed these words to the king’s notice, they asserted that he said in irrevocable anger that every resource and every device must be used to oppose you, because a contest over his dignity was being prepared against him; that concord would be impossible, because neither would you abandon your purposes nor would he be willing to permit anything to derogate from royal dignity. Thus, from the uncertain judgment proceeding from rumour and the malice of envy, varied and conflicting opinions were expressed.

But now, with the passage of time, all doubt has been removed, and the holiness of your purpose has become known through clear proofs [Col. 0057D], so that the good surely sympathize and rejoice, while deserved confusion has begun to cover the malicious. This is certain and clearer than light to all: you have esteemed any riches and the height of dignity attained as less than the justice that comes from God (Philippians 3) and the glory of ecclesiastical liberty.

For if you had preferred human favour to divine favour, and if your authority had consented to introduce the abuses of profane novelty, you could have lived not only in the utmost tranquillity but even reigned jointly with the prince more than formerly. Whatever concerned you more closely would have been regulated at your discretion; and, while the blood of the rest was exposed, your own household position would have been kept wholly unharmed. But Your Holiness, recognizing the obligation of episcopal office [Col. 0058A], preferred for the present to set power aside, expose resources, and offer your very person to every injury.

For you faithfully retain in memory that evangelical teaching, delivered by the doctrine and confirmed by the example of the supreme Shepherd: that we ought to lay down our lives for our sheep and brethren (1 John 3), not derive a detestable means of gain from their losses. Yet the burden could be lightened by sharing it, if the common cause, handled by common counsel, rested upon common support. Unity, strengthened by harmony of spirit, may indeed be shaken by troubles, but can be broken by no wickedness. Therefore, as malice gained strength, those who had believed for a time fell away in time of temptation (Luke 8), and they became not merely deserters of their leader but defected into the enemy camp.

If, however, they had persevered in their undertaking and patiently endured any outcomes whatsoever, violence would have recoiled upon itself when it struck, and disappointed cruelty would have restrained its intended designs. But when, after each person’s mind had been sounded out, private interest prevailed over the common cause, despair recovered boldness, and reviving hope raised fresh disputes from the grave. Yet while all equivocated—indeed, betrayed the cause—Your Magnificence of virtue alone remained to stand against them and “set itself as a wall for the house of Israel” (Ezekiel 13), so that it might redeem with its own blood the liberty once redeemed by Christ’s blood [Col. 0058B]. Although the cause has not yet reached the shedding of blood, devotion supplies the merit of martyrdom: it has not merely exposed but delivered your person to threats and terrors.

And although it is altogether incredible that he could devise anything more cruel against your person, still, amid so many motions of anger, one could not sufficiently conjecture what kindness lay hidden—especially when signs in every respect seemed to converge upon your destruction. For he hoped to bend you to obey through terror, and judged that you should be frightened more severely in proportion as he considered it necessary to abstain from greater injury. Finally, if he had wished to prevent your departure, neither clear weather, favouring winds, calm seas, nor the sailors’ skill could have conveyed you away [Col. 0058D]. Everywhere the hand of royal power would have met you: its vigilance could not be deceived, nor its power evaded.

And so long as the arms of the island that embraces you as a household held you, neither would such an opportunity to harm you have been open to him, nor would there have been so great material for envy’s chatter. Now, however, your silence outweighs every complaint, and your flight is more objectionable than any confrontation; for your modesty wins public favour for you and, by a kind of pattern of one excusing himself, more effectively accuses him before public opinion. Therefore, if a harsher passion had hardened his mind, he would rather harass you while present with frequent troubles than be compelled to show indulgence through any impunity. Or, if he at some time entertained a gentler intention, he would prefer that it should redound to his own generosity as a benefit [Col. 0059A] rather than to your patience as a triumph.

In short, you must frequently consider what your cause is, who your adversary is, and what efforts support your side. The justice of your cause is manifest: you contend for the liberty of God’s Church, which the Deliverer once won upon the cross and, having redeemed it at an inestimable price, restored entire to all who are enrolled under his name. For just as faith is one (Ephesians 4), so liberty too is one, consecrated and confirmed by the identity of the sacraments and the simplicity of the Spirit who works all things. The wonderful mystery of ecclesiastical unity consists precisely in this: just as there is one faith, one Spirit, and one baptism (ibid.), so there is one testament of perpetual manumission, by which the adoption of divine goodness makes us not only free but also fellow heirs.

Whenever liberty is diminished, therefore, faith too is clearly impaired; for, joined to each other by reciprocal reason, they always share alike both losses and gains.

But you must act against one whose craftiness those at a distance fear, whose power neighbours fear, and whose severity subjects fear. Such frequent success and favour of fortune have made him so delicate that he regards whatever does not obey him as an injury. The more readily he is moved, the more difficult he is to appease. In his case impunity does not encourage rashness; rather, he inflicts immediate punishment on offences. Yet he sometimes shows himself yielding toward humility and patience. He cannot endure to be overcome by force, but wishes it plainly to appear that whatever he has done proceeds from will, not incapacity [Col. 0059C]; for he seeks glory rather than success.

This might be considered highly praiseworthy in a prince if virtue and truth, rather than vanity and sweet, even harlot-like flattery, furnished the material of glory. He is great, indeed greatest among many, because he has no superior to frighten him and no subject to resist him. Nor is he assailed from without by injuries from others, through which he might be softened from the ingrained disposition of domestic ferocity. Rather, all who have grounds for contention against him resort to the ruinous compacts of a false peace rather than put their strength to the test, because he surpasses them in abundance of wealth, multitude of strong men, and extent of power.

Those, then, upon whose aid you ought to have relied, whose counsel ought to have protected you, and whose support ought to have sustained you, considering this, withdrew from you as though in a formed body. Yet they especially ought to have recognized the obligation of their own title and shown themselves your suffragans. Would that they had remembered their original profession, which, once made, extends through the entire sequence of future succession; and, when a new holder succeeds, the old obligation is always renewed in the same form. These were bound to pursue your cause—indeed Christ’s cause—through every danger, if they considered the duty of their order and the injury to ecclesiastical liberty. But you have seen with what faith and charity they began to walk with you—indeed, with God. In your necessity they judged that neither concealment should be employed [Col. 0060A], nor speech moderated, nor insults spared; rather, they strove with all effort to outdo one another, so that each might be thought either to hate you more or to have spared you in no respect.

The Roman pontiff and those with whom, together with him, rests the supreme care of governing the Church wondered that sheep should hurl swords against their shepherd, sons against their father, and finally men against themselves with such violence. For if they could have achieved what they sought, neither the very name of liberty nor any hope of liberty would have remained; but such confusion in ecclesiastical government would by now have followed that nothing would be handled in an orderly way, but everything would be mixed up in foolish error. Once the former institutions had been removed, nothing would be directed by its proper right to its due [Col. 0060B] result.

In these men, therefore, as it seems to me, you can place only empty confidence, because those who supplied the cause of discord do not devote faithful effort to reconciliation. Almost all the rest, however, who occupy the lower ranks embrace your person with the arms of sincere charity, imploring in deep but silent sighs that the Bridegroom of the Church may, for the glory of his name, bring your wishes to a happy fulfilment. Yet no one dares confess himself your friend; rather, in order to be thought more hateful toward you, they allege old causes of hostility, lest they be condemned by an unannounced proscription, as the others are. For sentence is passed upon suspicion; proofs of truth are not sought for imposing punishment; and those whom fault had not made equal in the character of their offence are entangled in the equal severity of punishment [Col. 0060C].

Indeed, their compassion ought to be most welcome to you. Though the prayers of the lowly do not move the minds of the exalted, they nevertheless overcome even the indignation of divine majesty, so that it becomes the more ready for mercy the more humbly it is reverently entreated. “For he regards the prayer of the humble” (Psalm 101). He considers the cause rather than the person, so that his justice always answers the justice of the cause, however delayed, while a reward proportioned to merits likewise comes to the person. Their devotion, therefore, can aid you before God; but before the king, just as they have no confidence of obtaining anything, so they have no boldness to petition.

[Col. 0060D] Moreover, if you consider the designs of the magnates, it is certain that they have formed a kind of pact with one another against the Church of God, so that they may continually obstruct its interests and incessantly oppose its dignities, because they consider all that is added to its honour or resources to be lost to themselves. They press on more eagerly because a favourable opportunity shines upon them in the circumstances of the time: royal power supports them, and they proclaim that in these matters they are exercising loyal care to preserve the kingdom’s condition.

They say that his predecessors possessed neither such strength nor such extent of power, and that he ought not to reign more disgracefully or act more weakly. One should attend to dignity rather than gain, since profit often smells of greed, while dignity always increases reverence and illuminates the glory of majesty. Thus they ascribe to dignity whatever has formerly been presumed under the name of power, although it accords neither with faith nor reason nor equity. He, however, embraces more eagerly than is expedient the pleasing words of flatterers, considering as loyalty what in the final result he will discover to be nothing but malicious deceit. For whoever examines their desires more deeply will understand that they cunningly prepare his favour for themselves, and for him material of labour and loss in the future.
