With all their desires and all their devices they strive for this, provided their purpose does not become known: namely, that his power may someday be restrained and that their old impunity for offences and a new licence for wrongdoing may be restored. The readier their malice [Col. 0061B], the more effective it is in doing harm, because intimacy furnishes them opportunity and high station supplies authority.

Besides this, if your discernment considers help from outsiders, they initially come forward with the favour of lavish liberality; but afterwards their affection cools through weariness of duration, and generosity grows tired under the quantity of expense. A small burden certainly becomes heavy through the length of a journey, and the burden of one’s own household often outweighs that of a stranger. The affection that has grown from preceding services clings more deeply and is more difficult to uproot; and shame always considers itself bound until at least what has been received is repaid with more abundant compensation.

It is therefore evident that those whom the favour of spontaneous charity invites to beneficence must be treated delicately [Col. 0061C]. Let no one swallow another’s freely offered cup! Rather, even without the giver’s wish, hands must be restrained, lest necessity or our own shamelessness consume another’s virtue. These are matters which it is good for your prudence frequently to consider, to weigh repeatedly with the instruments of reason, and to gather all, as it were, under one view, so that repeated comparison may more fully determine what weight each has.

Yet a middle way will be safer for you: so that the harshness of adversity may neither overturn your purpose nor the consciousness of truth harden you, lest fear make you despairing or confidence obstinate. What can be moderated without sin or danger to faith ought to be endured; and many things that cannot immediately be corrected must for a time be overlooked, until a calmer wind of gentler air breathes upon you. Different times do not always present the same outcomes; present circumstances sometimes restore to us losses of the past. Human weakness can set before itself nothing fixed concerning contingencies, nor can it rely even on the dispositions of its own minds; these too must depend upon chance events, and men must fashion distinct wills according to each of their movements.

For this is what they are compelled to seek with all their effort, though at present no prayers could obtain it from them: the sudden change of the right hand of the Most High at once teaches all fierceness to grow gentle. So it is: in the Lord’s hand are both the hearts [Col. 0062A] and the persons of men; with equal ease he can remove persons from the midst and change minds. Let purity of conscience and the turns of fortune therefore give you the firmest hope concerning this. For neither are the things that oppose you eternal, nor will divine justice permit one who hopes in it to be put to shame.

For God will incline the prince’s mind and in his goodness turn it back from its hostility, so that kingdom and priesthood may cooperate with equal assistance and show one another mutual reverence and mutual charity. Whoever considers the provident institutions of ancient wisdom, from which the rights both of ecclesiastical religion and royal excellence have flowed, will recognize that they are connected to one another by so great a necessity of reason that each derives very great strength from the other [Col. 0062B]. Hence, if either should inflict trouble or injury upon the other, it is clear that this will turn back upon the one inflicting it: for neither can the peace of the Church exist without the kingdom, nor can salvation come to the kingdom except through the Church. Therefore the injury will return upon its author’s head, and the final outcome will show that he has laid hands upon himself.

Meanwhile, if any prospect of calm should begin to appear for you, let not your wisdom reject the opportunity; rather, embrace it eagerly when it is offered. If anything has to be negotiated on this subject, do not examine every individual point with excessive subtlety, for subtlety breeds contention, and contention, as though by certain gusts of wind, stirs and kindles the smouldering fires of hatred. You will not need to resort to particulars, but should adhere more earnestly, as it were, to generalities, since the matter is safe unless expressly formulated agreements destroy freedom. For if we profess faith in return for faith, and that we are bound to reverence and obedience; if we offer our goods and persons to be employed for his honour and advantage; if we promise to observe royal dignities and ancient customs, insofar as they do not conflict with the law of God—this causes no harm, because in all these things we are in no way bound contrary to what is due. Therefore, if divine goodness should provide peace for you and yours under this or a similar wording, reserve interpretations of the words for future times; for he himself will not henceforth raise so many questions with you, and present experience will be able to make you more cautious in all things.

[Col. 0062D] But neither should you seem to seek glory or triumph among men; let all honour and all victory be attributed to the king, as to one pre-eminent—provided that you may be permitted to glory before God in the testimony of your conscience. For my part, I shall render faithful service to your peace, as devotedly as readily, because, God being witness, I sympathize with your adversity and embrace both your person and your cause with the arms of sincere charity. For it is certain that you offer your fortune and your person for your brethren like a holocaust, an offering of sweet savour: that your labour may bring us rest, your poverty may ransom our resources, and your patience may confirm for us whatever liberty remains. Accordingly, I must act in such a way as to profess myself at first sight your enemy, because one professing himself your friend would not be believed, nor would he be granted any access. Thus dissimulation may serve in winning favour, so that the effectiveness of action and the skill of speech may be directed more cautiously to your advantage. Therefore take comfort: from his coming into these regions very great benefit is beginning to appear to us, because, being present, he may more effectively be entreated by those who love you; nor will he be able to regard it as dishonourable to yield to the authority of the men of the Church, to acquiesce in their counsel, or to be moved by their prayers.

They say that he comes in a disposition gentler than usual, because certain forebodings of future bitterness disturb his mind, though he conceals it; for he understands that in many places certain sparks are being fostered against him to kindle conflagrations. He is troubled by [Col. 0063B] the envy of the French, the slanders of the Flemings, the wickedness of the Welsh, the plots of the Scots, the recklessness of the Bretons, the alliances of the Poitevins, the expenses of inland Aquitaine, the fickleness of the Gascons, and—what is more serious—the hostility of almost all whom he knows to be subject to his dominion. He also regards with suspicion the offence of the Roman pontiff, which he himself incurred by a sudden impulse. The state of the kingdom, too, is so confused because of your absence that neither ecclesiastical nor secular affairs proceed in their proper order, and no one knows what ought to be assigned to ecclesiastical law and what to secular law. For all these reasons he has resolved first to come to terms with the king of France on whatever conditions, so that, with his own terror and that king’s joined together, he may more easily subdue the rest. He has also decided, as they say, to act more mildly in many matters, so that, all injuries being overlooked, everything may be restored to peace; and then, by a swift return, to repress the audacity of the Welsh before the Scots and Bretons join with them and Albania, as has been prophesied, begins to rage. He therefore comes ready to do what is commanded, if there is anyone who knows or dares to command, judging it more advantageous to set aside for a time something of the haughtiness of his old arrogance than to wait until all or most of the things predicted converge upon his ruin. Farewell.

May the Lord preserve your person unharmed and swiftly turn your adversity toward favourable outcomes. But if you judge that these things should be shown to anyone, suppress the author’s name; for your experience does not fail to know how much it matters to me that these matters do not come to the king’s knowledge. Write to me more frequently, but secretly, so that your prudence may teach me how I ought to proceed, and so that watchful malice may not discover our mutual endeavours.

My greeting by the hand of Milo.

XXXV. TO THE SAME PERSON.

ERNULFUS to THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury.

I had scarcely spent three days with the lord of Meaux when, behold, William Duret arrived on the Kalends of April with your letters. Rejoicing at their reception no less than I was devoted to obeying them, on the following day—if indeed a pre-dawn tomorrow ought to be called “tomorrow”—after paying reverence to that most sacred day and receiving the blessing of the bishop with whom I was staying, I came to Senlis, intending to apply the utmost diligence to your command. There I approached the lord king of France, with all the humility I could, concerning the procuring of lodging for you. He replied with his customary kindness that he and the lord pope had agreed concerning your business that you should come as far as the Valley of Saint Mary, a monastery of the Cistercian Order near Pontoise, and remain there until you were summoned nearer by common counsel; nor, meanwhile, need much effort be made concerning your lodging, since it was uncertain whether you would come so far.

When I added [Col. 0064B] that provision for your lodging would nevertheless be necessary because of so great a concourse from every quarter, lest, if you should arrive, you and yours wander about unworthily, he replied that, when the time came, he would take care that provision should be made for you, both concerning lodging and in other matters, as befitted your eminence. I could extract nothing further from him, although I pressed him with great importunity. I therefore report to you what I have hitherto done in this matter, desiring, if it please you, again to hear your will. My brother’s house is yours, but it is three leagues distant from the place of the conference. Yet in the meantime I shall do what I can and shall seek lodging for you in every way nearer at hand. But I complain that news of your command came late. I beg that a messenger be hastened, so that the business may be hastened. For time is short and the confusion so great that scarcely any place remains open which is not already occupied. May my dearest lord fare well.

XXXVI. TO THE SAME PERSON.

ERNULFUS to THOMAS, Archbishop of Canterbury.

I waited for a long time to see whether perhaps something might reach my ears which I would judge worthy of communicating to your holiness. But because I see that you and yours have been consigned to oblivion, “as dead from the heart” (Ps. 30), and that there is none among all your beloved ones to comfort you (Lam. 1), I marvel in astonishment at so great a failure of charity: among those whom either the eminence of rank or manifold service seemed to have gained for you, not even one faithful friend remains who has stood firm in faith, who has not “bowed his knees before Baal” (3 Kings 19), all of them jointly, as it were, pronouncing that one must obey man rather than God. “Strange children have lied to you; strange children have grown old” (Ps. 17). And unless a people whom you did not know had served you, ready to obey at the hearing of the ear (ibid.), surely we should have been like Sodom and made like Gomorrah (Rom. 9).

I too—if it is permitted to compare small things with great—am weighed down by an indignation like that of your fortune, so great that none of those who had hitherto flattered me even in word is willing, in response to the messengers by whom I have solicited them more than once, either to “say Hail” (2 John 10) or to give any answer whatsoever. Our new archbishop, whose promotion I had hoped would greatly profit me, has never, as I hear, strained with such exertions after the favour of his king; and I have not yet experienced even a small fulfilment of his promise. It remains, therefore, that we entrust everything to God alone, saying to him: “Lord, our eyes are upon you, whence help shall come to us” (Ps. 120). “Judge our cause, you who alone are Father of orphans and judge of widows, and who render judgment for those suffering injury” (Ps. 145).

Indeed, if I dare to speak to my lord, though I am uncircumcised in lips and heart, I beseech you, by him whose cause you are pursuing, that no storm may ever cast you down from the throne of a good conscience. [Col. 0065B] Do not take it ill that you live as though a private man, once surrounded by a throng of retainers. Whatever the world inflicts, endure it as one higher than it—or rather despise it. In all things give thanks to God, whose mercy has for the present separated you from worldly tumult so that you may spend at least a little time in contemplation and quiet, and, with Mary who chose the better part, sit at his feet and hear his word (Luke 10). I beg you, Father and lord, to assure your servant concerning your welfare—without which nothing in life is pleasant to me—and concerning your condition, whose safety suffices for mine; and deign to comfort me by a letter from your blessedness, so that by your consolation I may reckon my poverty riches. Dearest Father and lord, fare well.

XXXVII. TO THE SAME PERSON.

[Col. 0065C]

To his dearest lord and father THOMAS, by God’s grace Archbishop of Canterbury, ERNULFUS, least of his faithful servants, greeting in the spirit of fortitude, knowledge, and counsel.

Placed in laborious leisure, I thought no remedy more fitting for me than to speak with you, Father, as though present, by writing something to you. Yet by continual meditation and singular affection you are present, and have deservedly claimed the whole little lodging of my heart. May it please your serenity, therefore, to turn aside for an hour from serious matters to my trifles, and to grant a little time to these things written for me—though I have written countless things for others to read on your behalf, would that as effectively as diligently. Let no one suppose, however, that these things proceed vainly from the excess of curiosity: both filial concern, desiring to be informed of the Father’s condition, dictates them, and the need arising from my own situation suggests them, hoping to bring back no small consolation merely by having laid itself open to its patron.

My leisure, I say, is laborious: it both assails my mind with heavier distresses as there is less material for action, and rarer opportunity for business provokes me, so that I may rightly say with the prophet: “Behold, in this peace my bitterness is most bitter” (Isa. 38). For in the very silence, so to speak, of action, a certain familiar unrest gives rise to a tumult of thoughts, occupying me far more variously, distracting me more hostilely, overthrowing me more deeply—especially since I am set against myself and divided, as it were, into parties, and experience in myself the wise man’s saying that no contest is more grievous than that in which the very man who conquers is conquered.

Hence the memory of past happiness burns me. For the greatest kind of unhappiness is to have been happy. Hence the narrowness of present adversity does not so much oppress me as shame confounds me; because of it my brethren have withdrawn far from me and my acquaintances, like strangers, have departed from me. And, what is more serious, we have become a reproach to our neighbours—who judge by sight—a mockery and derision to those about us (Ps. 78). He knew this who said:

> Unhappy poverty has nothing harsher in it  
> than that it makes men ridiculous.  
> —Juvenal, *Satires* 3.152

[Col. 0066B] Finally, to aggravate the disgrace of so great a humiliation, there is set against it not merely the impunity but even the glory of those who have either been the authors of this disturbance or the instigators of those who insult us, as though saying: “These are they who, wishing to establish their own righteousness, would not be subject to the king’s righteousness” (Rom. 10). “Therefore they have been given into captivity, and their possessions into the hand of the enemy.” Although the authority of the ancients has laboured, by most carefully reasoned arguments and in many ways, to reduce the movements of worldly insolence to the rule of equity, a man would deserve to be charged with madness if he dared to oppose their reasoning—or even refused to approve it. Yet when one returns to the pain of suffering itself, feeling outweighs hearing, sensuality prejudges reason, and so either weariness of life is incurred, so that that mighty standard-bearing prophet cries: “I beseech you, Lord, take away my soul” (Num. 11); or perhaps the way of good purpose is abandoned, so that David too, a man after the Lord’s heart, says: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps were nearly poured out, because I envied the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. 72).

If in these and other green trees, planted beside streams of water (Ps. 1), namely those made drunk with the abundant grace of the Holy Spirit, we see the vicissitudes of this humiliation have produced some cause of disturbance—good Jesus!—what will happen in us who are dry, or rather, to speak more truly, rotten, in whom the vein of that eternal fountain is obstructed by as many barriers of stones as we are weighed down by the burden of sins? For although the reading of sacred Scripture works great consolation of Christ within us, like David playing upon the harp, nevertheless, when we are either necessarily compelled to abstain from it or negligently grow torpid, the harp is as though silent, and the wicked spirit—which we not inappropriately call carnal sense—again agitates its Saul, that is, our concupiscence, devoted to pride and other vices. Nor is what springs up again to life under such frequent assaults easily rooted out completely.

In this threshing-floor of the most just Creator I indeed marvel and complain that many things happen in confusion: liberty seems to serve, strength to succumb, slavery to rule; and finally Fortune—most worthless of handmaids and worthy of no regard among virtues—powerfully commands Justice herself as queen, does violence to her, inflicts injuries, multiplies torments, abolishes, so far as lies in it, her proper function of rendering to each his own, and confidently dares and arrogates against her whatever it pleases as lawful, while it binds those who ought to be released, releases those who ought to be bound, exalts the guilty, and oppresses the innocent. Who indeed would deny that the reward of a triumphant crown belongs to innocence? What, good God, is more prodigious than this confusion? What is more wonderful than this prodigy? What is more effective than this wonder to move the mind, or more destructive of innocence? Hence the wise man’s tearful complaint, not without reason: “Alas for the grievous lot, whenever a cruel sword is added to unjust poison.” And Solomon: “When the wicked assume rule, the people groan” (Prov. 28).

[Col. 0067B] But lest the discourse wander too diffusely through material abundant and well-worn, we must return to the heart. And lest speech exceed sobriety, or the mind roll down from the precarious edge of questions into the precipice of error, caution is needed on both sides, lest we seem perhaps to wish to cast back upon the Creator what comes short in us through our own weakness. Before his eyes there is no rash motion and no chance event, because in wisdom he orders all things foreseen from eternity (Wis. 1). This disposition of things is certainly not less ordered because its cause is unknown to us; rather, it should be pursued with the greater piety of faith the further it is removed from human reason’s understanding. “The judgments of God are a great deep” (Ps. 35), known to him alone who beholds the depths and sits above the cherubim.

At length I must descend from the general to what touches me especially, and complain of the lot that alike enfolds me and all our people. But in vain: for our fall finds no one to lift it, nor our complaint any comforter among all our beloved ones. A stronger storm of tribulations rises against me from day to day; today has added something to my calamity which yesterday did not have, and I fear that tomorrow too may become worse than today. The lord of Rouen has made his hand heavier upon me because you have made yours heavy upon our persecutors in just reproof. That small benefit which he freely promised me last year he now refuses. I say “freely” in respect of time, though by reason it was owed to me. He pleads the offence of a temporal prince, whom he fears, when he ought rather to have heeded the judgment of the eternal Judge, who sees all things: “One must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5); and: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord” (Rom. 12).

And perhaps in all this my sorrow could be softened by no reasoning—for God has not given me a heart of stone, that I should not feel when struck or grieve when crushed—unless I recognized both that I am receiving what my deeds deserve and that my many sins deserve things more grievous; and unless I looked to you, most holy Father, who voluntarily endure what I am compelled to endure as deserved, what I have merited. From your abundance had flowed to me all that I seemed now to possess. To the glory of your power neither the powerful themselves could aspire nor the wise themselves knew how to aspire.

Truly, Father, you have possessed all these things in Christ as one possessing nothing; since you set no affection of your heart upon their abundance, you have stoutly cast them aside for Christ when necessity pressed. Again, Joseph left his cloak in the hand of the unchaste woman (Gen. 39); the young man, casting off his linen cloth, fled naked from Christ’s persecutors (Mark 14). So you have chosen, after casting aside—as has been said—the burdens of temporal things as obstacles to your journey, to take up your cross naked and unencumbered, to follow Christ, to be cast down in the house of God rather than glory with the world and dwell in the tents of sinners. Thus you seem to proclaim to my ears, not so much in words as in deeds, both the prophetic and evangelical saying: “But it is good for me to cling to God, to put my hope in the Lord” (Ps. 72); and: “What does it profit a man if he gain the whole world but suffer loss of his soul?” (Matt. 16).

This is the bronze serpent to which I look, wounded by temptations as though by serpents. This is the rock to which I hope to flee as a thorny hedgehog, beset by the stings of cares. “For the rock is a refuge for hedgehogs.” Otherwise I should have dwelt, swallowed up alive among the dead—that is, the despairing, who do not praise God. I should have been numbered with those who are in hell. I looked toward human help, and there was none. Truly, “cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm” (Jer. 17). It remains, therefore, that we look to him alone, to whom alone the poor man is left, who alone considers labour and sorrow (Ps. 9).

[Col. 0068C] Henceforth, Father—if I may speak without offence to you—there is one thing I bear more heavily than every tribulation, endure more impatiently, and lament more vehemently: although I very often see your messengers travelling about, I receive through them neither letters of visitation nor even words of greeting from you. Your condition is as hidden from me as though I had never seen you, or—as God avert—as though I were hateful to you; and I am given no knowledge concerning you except what rumour has made public, so that news only reaches me when it has already become old among others. Remember, Father, that I am one who bore the burden and heat of the day with you (Matt. 20). God knows that I stood by you with all my strength in a pure conscience—would that as wisely as devoutly, as successfully as faithfully! Others—almost all who are with you—have entered into my labours; they rejoice in your presence, are refreshed by your word, and are raised by your example; nor do I envy them.

I do not ask for temporal assistance, because my poverty suffices for me. I seek only that your name may be invoked over me and that I may live secure in your favour, which in this tempest is far more desirable to me than gold and precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. Let me at least hear through an intermediary what is granted to others to see, so that I may either grieve with my afflicted lord or share in consolation and hope, if there is any: “as in affliction, so also in labour” (2 Cor. 11). God knows, what calls me back when I often wish to go to you is not so much the difficulty of the journey as the fear that I may burden those by whom you are supported in whatever way, when it is more expedient for you to be content with a few than to be disturbed by the tumult of those clamouring around you.

Act then, Father; act steadfastly, for the crown is owed not to the beginner but to the finisher. As the saying goes: “It is the end, not the struggle, that crowns.” Drive the birds away from your sacrifice with Abraham until evening, lest fleeting glory carry off your labour, lest your enemy say: “I have prevailed against him” (Ps. 12). Refer all your works to God, that you may deserve blessing; for blessed is he “who shall seize and dash his little ones against the rock” (Ps. 136), that is, who refers his works to Christ and tests them in him, who is “a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling” (1 Pet. 2). Do not believe every spirit, but first test whether they are from God. Let boastful speech and rash action be far from you. Do everything with utmost seriousness and with counsel, so that your moderation may be known to all men. And thus you will conquer in him who said: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16). May he grant this to you—he who can do all things, whose cause you pursue—Jesus Christ our Lord, dearest Father and lord. Fare well.

XXXVIII. TO LOUIS, KING OF FRANCE.

[Col. 0069C]

To his dearest lord LOUIS, king of the Franks, ARNULFUS, humble servant of the Church of Lisieux, greeting and devoted service with every devotion.

The bearer of this letter has gladdened my soul with long-desired joy: joy for which both we and the other faithful people of the kingdom of France have sighed with long desires, and which we now receive as fulfilled with repeated exultation. God has visited his people and opened the bowels of his mercy to the whole kingdom of France, since he has appointed for you a certain heir and ordained for all the great men of the kingdom of France a just lord. For none will be so proud or obstinate as to refuse to render due service to him whom he knows to have been begotten from your flesh for the governance of the kingdom. May almighty God preserve your person, establish your kingdom, and multiply your offspring for you and for us through longer ages. Moreover, we beseech you for Bernard, the bearer of this letter, that in obtaining what his lord had entrusted to him he may find our prayers of benefit.

XXXIX. TO ARNALD, ARCHDEACON OF POITIERS.

That I judge something ought to be requested of you arises both from the honourableness of the petition and from regard for your kindness, not from confidence in the merits of earlier services. But if the performance of service has not preceded, devotion nevertheless considers itself to have deserved scarcely less, since it knows that, had opportunity arisen, it would always have shown itself ready for everything. For in all things it is not so much works that must be sought as intention; and one must inquire not so much what you have done as with what intention you did it. It is so: intention gives the work its name, and the deed itself derives its character more from the quality of the mind than from the magnitude of the benefit.

Accordingly, I offer prayers to your holiness for Master Meschinus, our friend and old companion: if there is any old resentment of mind, may it be laid aside, and may I deserve to find you favourably disposed toward that petition concerning which, furnished also with apostolic letters, he will petition the Church of Poitiers. He has promised me that from this time he will devote himself wholly to your service as to that of a master and father, so that the services of time to come may make recompense if anything has been done in the past too negligently or imprudently.

XL. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER.

The lord Remiba of Orléans is our friend, and through reciprocal services we are bound together in abundant mutual charity. Accordingly, he has asked for assistance from our prayers before your majesty, in the confidence that he knows our wishes more frequently obtain their desired effect with your kindness. Your sentence deprived him of the precentorship which he held, because of a certain offence that, as he himself maintains, he committed not through any malice but from simplicity alone. He thought that the deed did not fall under the terms of a public oath, nor did he believe that he transgressed the binding force of the oath if he did not share with others something which depended solely and individually upon his own will. When summoned by his brethren, he did not resist improperly or answer proudly, but immediately wished to correct his error publicly—if indeed it was an error.

If it is certain in this matter that neither malice preceded nor pride followed, the gravity of the offence does not exceed the bounds of clemency; and henceforth the mercy of the Roman pontiff can come to his aid, in which divine goodness has established for us both a saving remedy and a singular refuge. For, so far as guilt is concerned, it has been sufficiently punished: to a man of modest disposition shame is a greater punishment than even great losses. Moreover, while simplicity pleads for his pardon, devotion likewise pleads for favour, since it is true that he has always served the Roman Church, according to his means, with humble services. For all the reasons stated, therefore, we confidently come to make this request, because it will be glorious for us to have obtained so great a favour from your graciousness, and pleasant to have sought some consolation for a friend in such bitterness.

XLI. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER.

Those who saw my preparations for travelling through lands and exploring seas alike know to what dangers I had resolved to expose myself and what labours to undertake, that I might deserve to come before the presence of your sublimity. I was about to go, but public rumour preceded my journey with its report, so that ambushes could easily be prepared for me. For I am a man whom many causes have rendered conspicuous, and against whom zeal for justice has aroused very great envy among the enemies of the Church. They would have thought themselves successful if in my person they could both satisfy their malice and offend your majesty. Therefore our king detained me, though he had been sending me at my own desire; and he partly postponed his business and partly entrusted it to lesser messengers for conveyance.

Within my breast, therefore, the greater fervour of longing desire surges, grieving over this delay with the feeling of a wounded heart, because I am not permitted to embrace your feet or to behold your serenity with my present eyes. Meanwhile I do what I can, and whenever opportunity shines forth I devote my whole self to the honour and benefit of the Church, with such willingness that I seem to many liable to a charge of excess. For to a diligent mind nothing is enough, nor is great devotion satisfied by the performance of any work; it always stretches its endeavours onward. This zeal in your cause, this pressing constancy of unbroken labour, this unrevoked affection of perseverance lives in me toward you.

XLII. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER.

There is something in which I shall be found guilty of offence against your majesty unless I forewarn your holiness with reliable information. The Church of Sées had a bishop to whom the bond of brotherly blood joined me, but whom the favour of generous beneficence bound still more closely to me. When this holy man had taken charge of the aforesaid Church, he bestowed great care upon temporal matters and greater care upon spiritual matters. He left it adorned with treasures, supplied with buildings, and enlarged in possessions; so much so that, where there had been thirteen canons whom they call secular, and these themselves poor, at his death he left thirty-six regular canons there, together with every sufficiency of buildings and abundance of revenues. Having rendered it distinguished in temporal things, he strove always to make it more distinguished in spiritual things: a magnificent man, praiseworthy in every holiness, whose holiness did not take away magnificence, nor magnificence holiness.

What was begun and confirmed by your predecessors, apostolic men—first Honorius, afterward Innocent, and finally Eugenius and Adrian—was assisted by the devotion of Henry, most glorious king of the English, who for the same cause bestowed great goods upon the church and strengthened them by the enduring safeguard of a royal command.

> [Note: [Col. 0071D] B. omits “great.”]

Since this undertaking had drawn its beginning from the most religious man Honorius, it deserved increase from the incomparable man Innocent. By his authority, the aforesaid bishop-elect received persons from the Church of Saint Victor at Paris, whose holiness and prudence might, by their merits, consecrate the beginnings of so great a work. Through their efforts, amid various tribulations, the holy work grew so greatly that among all the churches of Gaul that church began to be reckoned among the more distinguished of that Order, whether one considered its grace of hospitality or the discipline of its Order.

Moreover, lest any suspicion should arise in the future of restoring secularity, and because a richer fruit could be hoped for from the administration of regulars, it was decreed—and likewise confirmed by the authority of the Roman Church—that archdeaconries, no less than prebends, and both the authority and administration of all things should be conferred upon regular persons; namely, so that all revenues should be brought into the common fund, lest occasion be given to greed if they were permitted to be applied to private uses. This is so certainly true that, when the often-mentioned bishop died, the Roman Church on no account permitted his successor to be consecrated bishop until he had professed that same Order in his own person and, by an oath solemnly taken in person, confirmed that he would faithfully preserve this arrangement in the Church. Such was the Church’s favour toward the religious life, lest, God forbid, a brazen head be said to have been attached to the workmanship of a golden statue.

But this bishop who has now succeeded, by the Lord’s permission, is reported to have conceived a detestable purpose: namely, to uproot this plantation completely and destroy the good which the devotion of the faithful, the authority of princes, the religious devotion of saints, and the privileges of the Roman Church have confirmed with an anathema intended to endure forever. If he cannot obtain all this from your discretion, he will at least endeavour to restore the archdeaconries to secular persons, so that carnal affection may have something to bestow upon nephews and relatives. Yet he will cloak this purpose with the appearance of piety, saying that that church does not possess persons fit to prove sufficient for offices of this kind—as though secular cunning ought to prevail over holy simplicity, or as though persons could not, by your authority, be transferred from the Church of Saint Victor, Saint Rufus, or others like them to administer these offices.

I myself was archdeacon of that Church; I was reared by its benefits and instructed by its institutions. It is just that I should always resist its losses and provide for its interests with due diligence. The memory of brotherly charity also lays upon my shoulders the duty of sustaining the good amassed by the great labour of my lord and brother. For this reason, although the bishop of that place had been one of my household and had been anticipated by me with many benefits, discord has newly arisen between him and me, because I could not endure the injuries inflicted upon those brethren and did not lend him help and counsel for the subversion of the Order. Therefore receive him and those with him prudently as our opponents and manifest enemies, since tongues that seek revenge deserve neither confidence nor ready hearing.

If perhaps any petitions concerning this affair have been presented to you, safely regard them as surreptitious; and it is unnecessary that the Church suffer any loss on their account, since, in order to preserve for you the favour and confidence of him from whom they were sent, it will be enough, without any offence at all, if his own petitions are granted. Let me speak briefly to my lord, though I am dust and ashes (Gen. 18). May my speech be pleasing to him, so that the petition of a devout will may attain the favour of its desired result.

Lord, public opinion commends your person, and the eager expectation of all holds their minds and ears in suspense concerning your deeds: iniquity hunts for material for slander, while the devotion of the faithful seeks glory for your name. Far be it from you that the holy plantation of your predecessors should be torn up by your hands or uprooted through your power! Far be it that through you the anathemas of so many Roman pontiffs should be brought to nothing! Far be it that, through you, secularity once removed should be restored by the sentence of your authority!

XLIII. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER.

I should have hastened back from England to embrace the feet of Your Blessedness; but I had to await an occasion in which necessity might seem rather to have drawn me than devotion to have brought me. For the mind [Col. 0073C] of our prince has somewhat fallen away from the affection with which he formerly embraced Your Holiness, so that he has sometimes complained among his intimates that he had found in you less favour than he had hoped. He says that you are difficult when his needs arise, scrupulous in regard to his requests, and that certain persons acceptable to you remain continually at the Curia, obscuring by their falsehoods the glory of royal serenity.

For many come to the Apostolic See from many regions, whose perverse tongues infect his ears with the poison of malice, so as to blacken his reputation, as it were, by a denunciation transmitted among all nations. This is indeed done furtively: by the working mystery of iniquity, the more a matter is said to be suppressed in silence, [Col. 0073D] the more widely it is spread; and the more secretly it is done, the more effective it is in causing harm. Yet he does not think that this proceeds from your knowledge or will; rather, their long residence with you supplies them with opportunity, and their unpunished persistence in deceit gives them boldness. He adds that whatever his enemies ask is easily obtained, whereas his own desires are examined with excessive subtlety or suspended by wearisome delay. If, therefore, any men of authority from among his people happen to come into your presence, those who attend him more intimately immediately confirm the uncertain evil of suspicion by deceitful flattery. [Note: [Col. 0073D] B.: “into evil.”] For that class of men is accustomed to make the greatest matters out of the smallest; and, just as there is no faith among them, so there is no feeling of true charity. [Col. 0074A] Each person strives to exclude another by every means he can, so that he may rejoice in having acquired for himself the privilege of exclusive familiarity. They think that whatever is taken from another will accrue to them, and they reckon their own gains always to conflict with the advantages of others. Therefore I, who have learned by frequent losses how ruinous the suspicion of princes is, even when one is innocent, judged that an opportunity should be sought by which I might either be sent by him, as formerly, or seem to be drawn by some pressing necessity. Since this was delayed—for the favour of your kindness imposes nothing burdensome upon me—I thought it proper to send a letter, so that the embassy of one devoted to you might supply for his absence, representing to your well-deserving Majesty my devotion both by [Col. 0074B] spoken word and by letter. I am yours, both a household servant and a son of the holy Roman Church; I continually remember that I have been gladdened by her favour, anticipated by her benefits, and enlarged by her honours. I shall never render anything equal to so great condescension, nor offer anything worthy of so many benefits; but although the rendering of works cannot discharge the debt, perfect charity nevertheless fulfills devoted service completely.

## XLIV. TO GILBERT, BISHOP OF LONDON

The bearer of this letter is our friend, and asks that he may be aided by our prayers before you; and this the more earnestly because he is confident that our prayers will obtain a useful result without difficulty from your charity. [Col. 0074C] He rejoices that the investigation has been entrusted to a lover of justice and truth, and that, fortified by the support of our prayers, he approaches you, so that sincere devotion to fraternal charity may cooperate with him before you for his advancement. Although a plurality of instruments may open a way for judicial examination, nevertheless the number of witnesses and the notoriety of the truth will settle the entire question; and an abandoned appeal will move the judge to act—an appeal which his adversary judged should be lodged, indeed with this cunning purpose: that he might be freer to carry out his intended plunder upon the poor man’s goods.

But your expertise does not fail to know what ought to be decided against a possessor in bad faith who has no title, concerning the principal cause; and against one who has abandoned an appeal, concerning costs and expenses: namely, that violence or fraud may not pass unpunished, nor innocence suffer undeserved loss. Moreover, the authority of the Roman pontiff has placed the business before you in a straightforward condition, by removing the obstacle of appeal, in which calumniators commonly establish for themselves an occasion of vexing others and an escape-route. Now malice, though unwilling, will obey you, as though bounded by certain limits, since it can neither go beyond our present court nor evade the sentence of your severity. Farewell.

## XLV. TO THE ABBOT OF GRISTAN

The fourteenth month is now in progress, or perhaps has already elapsed, since you departed from your monastery for another kingdom and regions beyond the sea [Col. 0075A] without your bishop’s blessing and knowledge. How great meanwhile have been the losses which that monastery has suffered in spiritual and temporal matters, both the brethren feel and the whole region attests. We are informed, moreover, that in England you engage in nothing but lawsuits and calumnies, and at great expense to your monastery range over the whole country without useful cause. Therefore we have judged that you should be recalled and enjoined, by virtue of obedience, to return to the monastery before the Kalends of August, having usefully arranged those matters, unless illness or a storm at sea prevents you. For you ought to know that more diligent care must be bestowed upon souls than upon property. Accordingly, unless you come by the appointed day, we shall have to send you a more severe command. [Col. 0075B]

## XLVI. TO WALTER, BISHOP OF ALBANO

I received the complaint which I learned from the letter most recently sent to me by you with especial pleasure, because it seemed more to awaken favour than to charge me with a fault. For you complained that, after several letters from you, you had received no reply from us, and that we had greeted your devotion, along with the rest, only in conventional words. From this I understood that your kindness comes with great desire to embrace us in mutual charity—something which I ought to have sought with much diligence and secured by many services. And I would have done so, had absence not provided me with an occasion which has until now always deprived me of the desired sight of your serenity. [Col. 0075C] It would have been a great thing for me had I found favour before your eyes in person. Greater still is the fact that of your own accord you send it to me even to the farthest West. It is indeed a noble office of praiseworthy generosity: bestowed for no merits, purchased by no prayers, obtained by no benefits.

There is nothing in this to lessen the greatness of the kindness. For among others the act of pure generosity disappears, but everywhere a transaction is conducted between contracting minds, while hope, both creditor and debtor of favour, compensates things. Yet today it is a great thing if someone answers the merits of a friend by an equal recompense of rewards; greater still is to anticipate every merit by greatness of spirit [Col. 0075D]. You have anticipated me, and by your estimation of such great condescension have made me yours; through it you show me the judgment of your esteem and the affection of your love. Therefore from the judgment of your esteem much exultation grows in me, and from confidence in your favour much assurance is prepared for every eventuality. It is indeed a great thing to have deserved at once the judgment and favour of a prudent person, since one gives lustre for glory and the other contributes to advancement. What then? What shall I render to my Lord for the things he has bestowed upon me? (Psalm 115.) Surely the whole affection of devotion, than which nothing greater can be offered, nothing more gratefully bestowed, nothing more precious esteemed. When this is bestowed, all is bestowed [Col. 0076A] which mind can contribute by thought, body by action, or resources by expenditure. May this judgment and favour therefore endure for me with you. Likewise, the affection of promised devotion toward you shall not grow cold with me, so that neither of us may need a monitor in the other’s necessities, but the result of shared service may prove the zeal of mutual charity.

## XLVII. TO THE BISHOP OF ANGOULÊME

The bearer of this letter entrusted his younger son, when the boy’s maternal uncle was going to the schools, to the uncle’s care, thinking that the bond of kindred blood would incline him to more diligent care of the child.

But the uncle spent too lavishly what had been provided for the child’s maintenance, and bound the child himself to a certain cleric under the title of a pledge; although such a contract neither held good in law nor accorded even with good morals. [Col. 0076B] For a free person cannot be bound without his own consent, and your expertise knows that a boy of that age cannot consent. Moreover, he is detained not only on account of the principal but also under the name of interest; and this enormous act is reported to have been done not by a layman but by a cleric—indeed, by one of your own household, or the son of a member of your household. Those who hear this are astonished that such things should be tolerated by you at the very beginning of your holy episcopate—things which neither the rigour of justice ought to leave uncorrected nor ecclesiastical severity pass over unpunished.

[Col. 0076C] For your cleric openly admits kidnapping; and he nevertheless shamelessly demands interest, though the Church detests it. If, because interest is odious, crafty malice converts it into expenditure allegedly made for the child’s support, we reply that, since the principal obligation has been removed, the child is not liable for the accessories; rather, he has an action for injuries because the offender removed from his father a free-born boy, who was to be devoted to liberal studies, and did not permit him to apply himself to his intended pursuits. Finally, I urgently demand my sheep from you as judge, against one who confesses the crimes; and you must take care that, in this matter, the integrity of your reputation—not fraternal affection—preserve the due feeling of compassion toward the boy. For if the accused should, God forbid, escape through your fault, [Col. 0076D] we may perhaps turn a subsidiary action from the accused against the judge. But if your gentleness should decree that this offense ought not to be punished but rather settled between them, unquestioned credit may be given to the sworn father, since he is a man of good reputation.

## XLVIII. TO ARNALD, ABBOT OF BONNEVAL

The letter which your charity most recently sent me remained for some time with the man who had received it for delivery. Thus it happened that I received it not while he was about to depart, nor while he was departing, but after he had departed; I could neither return his greeting nor send back whatever I might have conceived in my mind. I therefore did what I could: I offered for you a rich holocaust-sacrifice (Psalm 65), one pleasing through its own fatness, and one which the devout affection of the offerer made the very offering rich. [Col. 0077A] I offered, I say, a rich holocaust, in which bodily appearance veiled the marrow of divinity, and prayer proceeding from the marrow of the inmost heart contained its own melody in the sacrifice. For here is that fatted calf (Proverbs 15); here is that curdled and fat mountain (Psalm 67); here is Christ, anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows, from whose fullness, though all have received, the outpouring itself does not diminish him who pours it forth. Nothing more precious, more effective, or more useful can be offered—either to the person who offers or to the person for whom it is offered—provided that the unworthiness of the persons does not obstruct the dignity of the sacrifice.

[Col. 0077B] For the offerer must bring pure hands, lest that which is beyond price and most worthy of all veneration should either fall into the cheapness of a price or be expended upon unworthy causes. The person for whom it is offered must acknowledge it by faith, embrace it in charity, pursue it in desire, and place in it all his confidence of divine propitiation. When these things concur, the benefit of both parties is at work: those who offer for others are found to offer for themselves. This is indeed a great and praiseworthy benefit: bestowed upon another, it benefits him and nevertheless aids the giver himself. For whomever the priest embraces in the outpoured breadth of charity, all of Christ is at once the possession of all and, separately, of each; nor does participation by many divide his wholeness, nor does participation by different persons diminish his entirety. [Col. 0077C] Thus it is: whole Christ is bestowed upon you, whole upon me, and he admits you as co-heir to the entire inheritance which he nevertheless promises whole to me. For what is spiritual is neither bounded by limits nor confined by any narrowness; it is not diminished by being bestowed, nor can it suffer any loss of its integrity. Therefore I offered all for you, and yet reserved all for my own benefit, since it so turned to the salvation of both that it might direct your journey with prosperity and increase for me the favour of divine propitiation.

## XLIX. TO AEGIDIUS, ELECT OF ÉVREUX

[Col. 0077D]

Blessed be God, who calls you to episcopal office and brings you forward to bear our burdens with us. We plainly rejoice that your merits are advanced to the honour due to them; but we are moved with still greater joy because we now know that all your wisdom is being devoted to the interests of the Church. It is right that I should celebrate the common joy with particular gladness, because your goodness has always embraced my person with special affection, and I have always longed with my whole desire for the advancement of your honour. For reciprocal offices of mutual charity met from both sides, since neither desired to serve his own opportunities more than those of the other. [Col. 0078A]

Divine providence has well provided for us in this respect: though the desires of many drew your wisdom toward other regions, it has reserved you especially for our province. It is certainly just that you should be bound above all by the gifts of the land which fed you from its breasts, cherished you in its embrace, and enlarged you with its honours; that you should serve its necessities. But divine propitiation has smiled more kindly upon me, since it has neither separated me from my friend by difference of profession nor divided us by distance of place; rather, it has joined us as though by adjoining position and arranged frequent meetings for us, so that the very opportunity of place may serve the sharing of abundant offices of charity, and closeness [Col. 0078B] of minds may correspond also to closeness of bodies. Meanwhile I judge that we must persist in abundant desires and devout prayers, that divine kindness may attend the beginning of your consecration with happy omen and strengthen you, by the power of overflowing grace, for the execution of episcopal office.

## L. TO RICHARD DE ALMAR., PRECENTOR OF LINCOLN

Although I have personally entreated your charity on behalf of A., the bearer of this letter, I nevertheless judged that my prayers should be followed by a letter, so that both the speech of my living voice and the insistence of writing might declare the extent of my desire. He hopes, having obtained a letter from me, that he has obtained from you what he asks, because he is almost certain [Col. 0078C] that my prayers will by no means be frustrated of their desired result with your affection. Although the feeling of charity alone could have established every confidence between us, there is also the fact that I do not seek any loss to your interests—although, in your judgment, any losses are compensated by my favour with very great advantage.

You will therefore do gladly what is asked, so that the very ease of the favour may increase the magnitude of its merit; for the rendering of generous service often creates or strengthens the reality of friendship. For though friendship exists simply in its own purity, it is often weakened by external additions, so that, provoked by injuries, it fails, and, as though soothed by benefits, it recovers strength. Moreover, benefits themselves often make hatreds cease, and by a wonderful change affections are turned into their opposites. [Note: [Col. 0077D] B. omits “often.”] [Note: [Col. 0077D] B. omits “often.”] For you must love the person whom you hate if you learn that he has passed from former malice to a better disposition; and another’s disposition will fear your own disposition for itself, so that you always love one who loves you and hate one who hates you. Therefore the conscience of each must answer well to the other, and so proofs of hidden will must proceed back and forth, because evangelical doctrine itself has taught us that deeds must be believed. The mind of one who always loves is readier to fulfill another’s wishes than its own; and, considering it slothful to be anticipated, it always hastens with all diligence to anticipate.

## LI. TO POPE ALEXANDER CONCERNING THE DISSOLUTION OF THE MONASTERY OF GRISTAN

[Col. 0079A]

In the diocese which, by God’s permission, I serve, there is a monastery called Gristan, which once spread abroad the fragrance of sweetness; but in the days of this abbot it has long laboured under ill repute for its deeds, as those present have seen and those far away have heard. For scandals could not be kept within its domestic walls; as audacity in wrongdoing advanced, they were displayed openly to public view and resounded in public report, since neither fear of God nor reverence for men restrained the brethren of that place from such actions. The greater their enormity, the more widely and swiftly they were made known by spreading fame [Col. 0079B]; and it gave greater offense to all because such great wickedness seemed to proceed openly from a sanctuary.

For there was within no, or only slight, observance of regular discipline, and outwardly still less display of charity: they were not accustomed to receive guests or distribute anything to the poor; indeed, the impudence of their disorder reserved even the remnants of the common table for the satisfaction of private desires. These are small matters; but their madness broke out into bloodshed, so that their hands were kept free from no kind of crime. It is established that they rushed upon one another in the cloister with drawn knives, as barely closed scars and fresh wounds also attest. Had provident antiquity not removed the dagger from their knives, intemperance would often have raged even to mutual deaths. [Col. 0079C]

Within the monastery itself, a woman immersed in excessively cold water was killed by the force of the cold. For, in order that they might be believed to work miracles and might draw frequent visits from lay persons by every sort of contrivance, they promised remedies for health to anyone who allowed herself, allegedly bewitched by some charms or other, to be immersed seven times in water by them. Thus the sick woman, frequently immersed in icy water, died frozen amid the hands of the monks pressing her down, while illness could not endure the force of the cold, and profane religion provoked nature to destruction rather than God’s mercy to salvation.

A certain monk killed the kitchen servant while he was bent over performing his appointed task, because the servant was said once to have complained about the monk’s excessive visits to his wife. The monk broke the man’s neck by driving a large pestle into it with all his strength and spattered with innocent blood the dishes being prepared both for himself and for the other brethren. [Col. 0079D] Although I repeatedly admonished the abbot about these things with the charity due to him—for I was not permitted to compel him more severely—he judged that they should be overlooked rather than dealt with by monastic discipline. Thus lax connivance gave confidence to men who believed that nothing was forbidden them, since neither their own reason nor correction by another restrained them.

Furthermore, no authority of discipline remained to the abbot, because even [Col. 0080A] the discipline of those is despised by the reprobate in whom the works of a well-ordered mind are not seen. Their boldness was increased because necessities were not supplied to them in the cloister, but, in compensation for necessities withheld, freer permission to wander was granted them. Such persons are accustomed to bear poverty more patiently than a rule, and purchase from their prelates freedom to sin at the price of any degree of want. [Note: [Col. 0079D] B.: “however great.”]

Moreover, lest any opportunity for wandering abroad should be lacking to them, the abbot often sailed to England, ostensibly to manage the monastery’s goods. There, living without companion or judge and, as was said, indulging his appetite and his loins, he occupied himself little with anything besides wandering excursions and futile lawsuits. On his last stay there, he remained for almost a continuous two years, and was brought back by necessity under an episcopal edict. [Col. 0080B] On his return he found the condition of the monastery considerably worse than he had left it. When he immediately began to be beset by the monks’ quarrels, I prevented his hasty return [to England], unless he first put the monastery in order and assigned to me suitable persons to carry the burden of vicarious care.

But he disregarded the episcopal authority by which I am set over him, and the obedience which he is bound to render by the bond of his sworn profession; he returned without my knowledge, leaving no one at home who knew either how to maintain the order or administer temporal affairs. The event itself immediately showed this most miserably: the man whom he had left as steward, drunk in the refectory during supper, stabbed two of the brethren with a knife, and they at once killed him with a pole which chance provided. When this was done, the memory of former crimes was renewed; all things were as it were brought under one view before everyone, and all were condemned by the judgment of public opinion and reputation, for there was no one whom either his own conduct or consent had not made guilty. [Col. 0080C]

Accordingly, many said that all should be expelled and persons of a new order introduced altogether, so that expulsion might punish these men and the establishment of new persons restore the observance of the order. But I expelled the killers, since both reason and fear of secular power so required, and for the moment arranged what seemed necessary to me. For nothing permanent could be established, since neither their reputation nor their conscience gave sufficient assurance concerning any of them. [Col. 0080D] Yet I did what I could until, by stronger counsel, every plant which the heavenly Father has not planted might be uprooted.

This is reserved for your hands; it must be accomplished by your power, because weak hands cannot prevail against that which has sent its roots deeper. If, in this matter, you regard the common wishes of almost the whole region, those whom shared guilt and a mutual pact of consent have bound to perpetual disorder must be separated and scattered individually among regular monasteries, so that among strangers they may lose, through division and diversity of manner of life, the occasion for sin which they sought in the companionship of corrupt familiarity. It is the common wish, and would also please the prince himself, that the monastery be transformed into one of regular canons, so that the very form of the order being renewed may more fully remove all its old corruption and other monasteries may be frightened by the severity of the example. [Col. 0081A]

For there are some monasteries whose disorder has burst into such boldness that their wickedness, even when discovered, does not acknowledge its shame; rather, obstinacy is always strengthened by hardened faces. Thus that place would rise into the condition of a worthier order, and apostolic severity would everywhere be believed to be ever, as it were, present. Furthermore, our province is certainly rich in many and noble monasteries, but has few houses of regular canons, and these very poor, so that our countrymen often have to migrate into foreign regions in search of that order. Therefore it would seem good to many if the small number of monks, having been dissolved, grew into a multitude of regular clerics; and if those known to have departed from their mother’s instruction were usefully placed elsewhere, the rest might remain contained in their mother’s bosom, lest, like weaned children, they be driven to the harsher embraces of unknown mothers. For by this action a useful punishment will proceed against the guilty: removing bodily opportunity to sin, it will wholly contribute to the salvation of souls; and public wishes, more ready in their favour, will converge to consecrate the beginnings of the new planting. [Col. 0081B]

## LII. TO THE ABBOT OF GRISTAN

Your fraternity does not fail to know how many scandals and losses have come upon your house [Col. 0081C] because of your absences. Since it is certain that this matter belongs to our care, we commanded you to restrain your wandering journeys and keep the watch due over the flock entrusted to you; not to depart for distant regions unless you had first put the house in order and assigned to us suitable persons who could meanwhile take care of the house and provide beneficially for it in spiritual and temporal affairs.

But you disregarded the authority of the episcopal command—indeed, setting aside your own salvation and that of the souls entrusted to you—and departed without our knowledge, leaving no one at home by whose prudence affairs could be directed or by whose diligence they could be governed. Hence, as we believe has come to your knowledge, so many outrages were subsequently committed in that place that our region has plainly been scandalized and the monastery disgracefully defamed. Therefore by this present writing we command you to return, all excuse removed, within twenty days after receiving this letter, unless you are held back either by the severity of the sea or, God forbid, by bodily illness. Otherwise, from that day you are to know yourself suspended, by the authority through which we are set over you, from the service of the altar and entry into all churches. [Col. 0081D]

## LIII. TO LAURENCE, ABBOT OF WESTMINSTER

I give thanks to your charity on behalf of our Simon, because you have looked upon him with the eye of the goodness natural to you and, by provident generosity, granted him a benefit not temporary but enduring for a longer time. It is a great thing to help a person in need for the moment; greater to provide something renewed through days and years, something renewed again by frequent recurrence so as to be conferred again and again. [Col. 0082A] Certainly this benefit is not diminished by time but increased, and the continuing yield preserves the persistence of renewed generosity. Many advantages will follow a simple gift, and it will seem that a gift is made as often as sheaves of new recurring harvest-fruits are gathered.

It is also greater to have given some right than a physical object, since rights are sustained by repeated receipt, whereas the gift of any physical object is completed by a single delivery. You gave a right, so that the favour of your generosity might not pass away too quickly, and so that, just as the affection of virtue does not grow cold in you, the benefits of your generosity, extended into perpetuity, might gain strength. [Col. 0082B] Moreover, the prudence of discrimination accompanied your generosity, because you gave to one whose integrity, industry, and diligent service pleased you. You bestowed it neither upon an unknown person nor upon a useless one, but upon one whose merits preceded and will follow, who may repay your actions with thanks in mind and body to the full measure of gratitude, so that you may rightly glory in the outward fruit and in the testimony of conscience.

Yet I count what you have bestowed as bestowed rather upon me, because what had previously been delayed was granted immediately at the first word of my intercession, so that you seemed in this particularly to have sought my favour. Indeed, the donor’s gladness in granting was greater than the petitioner’s desire in receiving. It is a noble and praiseworthy benefit: delayed by no postponement, purchased by no prayers, obtained by no merits. [Col. 0082C] There was nothing in it to lessen the greatness of the kindness. You anticipated me, though I had resolved to seek out every occasion in order to anticipate you by some generously bestowed service. Thus your magnificence has made me your debtor, so that henceforth I must repay, not give; for what is rendered to one who deserves well does not deserve to be adorned with the name of a gift.

## LIV. TO LORD HENRY, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

Your Philip of Chaumont, while he was staying with us in the church of Rouen, became known and dear to us through his honorable conduct. His favour was enhanced by the fact that the excellence of royal blood shone in his actions, and liberal prudence shaped his activity in a way worthy of such nobility, so that he seemed to surpass others in character as in birth. Your greatness drew him away and took him from our desires, so that he might become nearer in companionship to those near him by birth, and, being wholly devoted to your service, might make progress before your magnificence both in learning and in fortune. [Col. 0082D]

He therefore rejoiced and was glad that he had experienced your beneficence in many ways, all the more cheerful because a greater confidence for the future could arise from the first fruits of your favour. Meanwhile, however, as he complains tearfully, your serenity has been stirred against his innocence, and a friend and kinsman has been somewhat removed from his conceived hope—unless it be that despair is excluded by the sincerity of his conscience [Col. 0083A] and by humble, devout submission to your discipline if any fault has been committed. For he preferred to use the means of entreaty before your mercy rather than renew his defense in contentious disputes, because, as your magnanimity does not know how to yield to pride, so it cannot endure to oppose humility.

Indeed, while he was with us, he often understood that divine goodness had granted us very great favour in your eyes—a favour all the more praiseworthy because it proceeds from the gratuitous goodness of your generous spirit. He therefore judged that our prayers should be sought from afar, so that he might offer them to us as some acceptable gift, in order that our intercession might redeem his fault, if there is one, and incline the movement of severity toward pardon. [Col. 0083B] For it will be glorious for you that so great favour should find fullness of grace before your Majesty, so that the abundance of your love may overflow from us even upon others.

## LV. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER  
*(After the death of blessed Thomas)*

To his dearest lord and Father Alexander, by the grace of God supreme pontiff of the Catholic Church, Arnulf, humble minister of the Church of Lisieux, greeting and due obedience with every affection of love.

When we had assembled together before our king, believing that we were to deliberate concerning the great affairs of the Church and kingdom, a sudden report concerning the lord of Canterbury overwhelmed us with lamentable grief, so that in a moment confidence was turned into astonishment and deliberations into sighs. For through certain men returning from England we learned by reliable report that some enemies of his, provoked, as they said, to anger and madness by repeated exasperations, rashly made an assault upon him and—what we cannot and ought not say without grief—persisted in attacking and cruelly murdering him. [Col. 0083C]

At last the disastrous report came to the king’s knowledge through certain bearers, since he could not be ignorant that vengeance for him seemed to belong especially to his office by right of power and of the sword. At the first beginning of that dreadful report he at once turned to every form of lamentation and compassion, utterly changing royal majesty, as it were, into sackcloth and ashes. He showed himself much more a friend than a prince, [Col. 0083D] sometimes stunned and, after the stunned silence, relapsing into sharper groans and more bitter grief. For nearly three days he kept himself shut in his chamber and would endure neither food nor the admission of comforters, but by grief too destructive he seemed obstinately to be inflicting voluntary ruin upon himself.

The spectacle of evils was pitiable and the alternation of griefs distressing: we who first mourned the priest then began also to despair for the king’s safety, and in the death of one man we miserably thought that both had perished. But when friends, especially bishops, asked why he did not permit himself to recover, he answered that he feared the authors and accomplices of the crime, in confidence of their old rancour, had promised themselves impunity for the offense. He acknowledged that he had incurred new enmities through recent injuries and frequent wrongs, and thought that the fame and glory of his name might be besprinkled with the slanders of his enemies and that a story might be invented that the deed had proceeded from his knowledge. [Col. 0084A] But he invoked almighty God as witness upon his soul that the abominable act had neither been committed by his will or knowledge nor contrived by his design—unless perhaps his fault consisted in his being thought still to love too little.

He also submitted himself altogether on this matter to the judgment of the Church and would humbly accept whatever might be beneficially determined concerning him. After consultation, the deliberation of all came to rest upon this: that he should seek the wisdom and authority of the Apostolic See, which Christian faith declares to overflow most abundantly with the spirit of wisdom and fullness of power, and should endeavor by lawful and canonical means to prove his innocence before it. We therefore beseech you that, according to the spirit of counsel and fortitude given you by God, your severity may repay the authors of so great a crime according to the enormity of the deed, and that apostolic compassion may be pleased zealously to preserve the king’s innocence in its proper state. May almighty God preserve your person safe for many years for his Church. [Col. 0084B]

## LVI. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER, ON BEHALF OF GILBERT, BISHOP OF LONDON

To his venerable lord and Father Alexander, supreme pontiff of the Catholic Church, Arnulf, humble minister of the Church of Lisieux, [Col. 0084C] greeting with every affection of due obedience and devotion.

The person of the lord Bishop of London I considered superfluous to commend more particularly to Your Excellency, because what is publicly known plainly needs neither formal accusation nor urgent and repeated recommendation. For the fullness of his virtue and learning has shone among us by so many proofs, has been supported by so many testimonies, and approved by so many benefits, that divine favour seems to have gathered upon him, in a richer abundance, what it distributes among many. In him, among us, both the diligent practice of frugality, the prerogative of learning, and integrity of religion surpass all occasion for envious comparison; so that no presumption would dare prefer anyone to him, or set anyone’s merits on an equality with his more outstanding merits. [Col. 0084D]

Yet for a long time this holy man has been drawn into a case; surrounded by hostile words, he has been attacked without cause and harassed by inquisitions born of envy. He has been drawn into a case, I say—if indeed it should be called a case where no contradiction could raise any question, where no litigation and no form of judicial procedure took place; where, without defendant or witness, the same man, acting as both plaintiff and judge, fashioned a solitary sentence out of his individual will. This man would have counted himself happy and endowed with every blessing if his judge had granted him the ground of a common hearing: if, being summoned, he could have come; if, being charged, he could have answered; if finally, while the outcome remained uncertain, he could have experienced the result of the fatal sentence. [Col. 0085A]

But against him an arrow was sent from another realm, from parts beyond the sea, from afar—indeed, as though from concealment—and the enemy, fearing to be foreseen, immediately struck the sword upon the head of one unaware. Fathers are accustomed to apply the rod before the staff to their children’s faults; and if moderate correction does not avail, they afterward employ harsher scourges.

> [Note: [Col. 0085D] C. reads “does not suffice” (*non sufficit*) for “does not avail” (*non proficit*).]

It would have been more useful to spare a person by whose punishment he knew he would scandalize an entire province, since, for the good of peace, mercy to many rather than punishment of one would have been beneficial. What was done appears to have proceeded more from an emotional impulse than from charity, because the presiding authority immediately expended all its power in inflicting punishment, reserving nothing for the future in which either prudence might dispense [Col. 0085B] or mercy come to aid.

Perhaps he ought first to have been suspended from episcopal office, forbidden the ministry of the altar, and excluded from the thresholds of the church, so that only at last, if obstinate, he might be struck by the sword; and thus he would appear not eagerly to have run to his brother’s destruction, but reluctantly compelled to do so. For one who hastens to blood is not to be believed to desire the man’s salvation. Rather, ecclesiastical censure also forewarns offenders, so that those beloved ones whom the outpouring of precious blood redeemed may be delivered, and may flee from the face of the bow, so that arrows provocatively aimed may descend only upon the obstinate.

And even if it be certain that passage to him by letters and envoys was not open, but every route had been blocked by lawful edicts through fear of secular power, another’s wrongdoing ought not to prejudice this man’s innocence, [Col. 0085C] nor could a punishment which he did not deserve lawfully be inflicted upon him. Yet the craftiness of power was outwitted by the ingenuity of persons who carried some letters to him; commands reached him, and he obeyed them with complete diligence, either by publicly announcing everything or by duly putting it into effect. Moreover, if in so critical a situation the authority of the presiding power seemed to need consultation, all access to him was denied to this man’s envoys; and there was no sign of paternal charity where both the opportunity for counsel and the means of remedy were removed from him.

Furthermore, we, who have learned the truth of the matter in great part both by experience and by reliable report from nearby, are permitted before Your Majesty to bear witness from a clear [Col. 0085D] conscience: the man, placed amid the threats of one power and the snares of another, always obeyed ecclesiastical commands insofar as they could reach him; and from the beginning of the discord he supplied neither its cause nor subsequently any encouragement to boldness. But the other man, as has been said, without observing either the case or procedure, publicly confounded before the Church a man whose praise is in the Church, to the scandal of all good people, and filled a holy soul alike with bitterness and grief.

Blessed, however, be God, who has established for us the holy Roman Church as a solemn refuge and a saving remedy against such things, so that through its governance [Col. 0086A] that which another’s insolence or ignorance has blackened into guilt may be restored to proper form. Indeed, what had been done was corrected by the authority of Your discretion: this man gave an oath that, at a time pleasing to you, he would obey apostolic commands concerning the matters under consideration. The innocent man therefore stood secure while awaiting Your command; but a second sentence, more severe than the first, was issued, and without any command or prior address summoning or citing him, he was again thrust into the same bond—indeed, into a stronger one—by letters of Your Majesty.
