The remedy of Your gentleness, in which he had begun to breathe again, was taken from him.

Those who heard were astonished that so much could be obtained by stealth against the innocence of the man and [Col. 0086B] against the order of your jurisprudence, since it was clear that he had in no way departed from the religious obligation of his oath, nor had later judicial inquiry condemned him in anything. It is certain and manifest to all inhabitants of that kingdom that the holy man, in those acts which were wrongly done, sinned neither by will, counsel, nor assistance. Universal testimony is borne to him from the clear conscience of all: he always faithfully obeyed ecclesiastical commands.

It is indeed true that both he and others feared the violence of the threatening power; compelled by the necessity of greater danger, they often dissembled, displayed mildness more often than rigor, and, like deceivers, sometimes placated the movement of power by carefully chosen blandishments, [Col. 0086C] in order to preserve, as far as might be possible, the truth of justice in the purity of their consciences. Certainly, at the critical point of that day, we saw the condition of the Church in our regions placed in such danger that no power, riches, or diligence could fully repair the extent of the breach. Nor would even the Roman Church itself have escaped a share in so great an evil, had not pontifical moderation extinguished the growing fire.

For this we render, from the depths of our hearts, as great thanks as we can to Your holy providence: because in paternal clemency you spared us, and by long-suffering patience sought to avert from us the evil that was believed beyond doubt to threaten our necks. Hence, after [Col. 0086D] many fears, prolonged labours, and imminent shipwreck, a harbour of safety and tranquillity begins to appear to us; and in certain hope, through your merits, we await happy outcomes and joyful events.

Moreover, though the person for whom we write can readily be excused in every respect, he nevertheless believed that the testimonies and prayers of venerable persons should be offered to Your kindness—persons who would never, by any boldness, attempt to deceive Your Holiness in anything. If Your discretion judges that it is necessary to proceed further toward complete certainty of faith, he is ready, before your legates or persons to whom you may choose to delegate the matter, to repel every charge against himself by manifest truth. [Col. 0087A] And if the matters are examined more deeply, he will be found in many respects to have earned very great praise by prudent skill.

With all desire he longed to come into Your presence, and he has now tried twice to see whether he could do so; but advanced age, the gravity of his position, the difficulty of the journey, and the weakness always allied to old age have drawn him back somewhat from proceeding. Moreover, not only our wishes for him but those of the entire kingdom—indeed, of kingdoms—throw themselves at the knees of Your mercy: that according to the spirit given you by God, you preserve his justice unharmed; or, if there is any imperfection, that your eyes may see equity, since he will obtain no benefit of indulgence which the person’s surpassing merits do not recompense.

We judged that these things should be written not to disparage anyone, [Col. 0087B] but to advance this man’s cause, because apostolic favour may provide for him and likewise, from the abundance of that same discretion and gentleness, bring aid to others.

> [Note: [Col. 0087D] The Bodleian manuscript supplies the end of the letter, which is in some manner incomplete in the printed editions, in these words:
>
> “Therefore, for the person concerning whom we write, not only our wishes but the public wishes of the entire kingdom—indeed, of kingdoms—throw themselves at the knees of Your mercy: that according to the spirit given you by God, you preserve his justice unharmed; or, if there is any imperfection, that your eyes may see equity, since he will obtain no benefit of indulgence which [Col. 0088D] the person’s surpassing merits do not recompense. We judged that these things should be written not to disparage anyone, but to advance his cause, because apostolic favour may provide for him and likewise, from the abundance of that same discretion and gentleness, bring aid to others. May the Lord preserve Your person unharmed for many ages for His Church.”]

## LVII. TO JOHN AND WILLIAM, CARDINALS, ON BEHALF OF ROGER, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK

With what faith, zeal, and affection the lord Archbishop of York exerted himself, at the beginning of this storm, for the unity of the Church and the honour of the Roman pontiff, your prudence—who in large part saw and heard these things—does not fail to know. The surpassing boldness of a valiant champion earned surpassing favour; and through frequent reciprocal services, both magnificence in support and munificence in resources combined on his behalf. [Col. 0087C]

He presumed that the favour due to persevering merits would not be lacking; but now, although his merits endure, the former favour does not shine.

> [Note: [Col. 0088D] B. omits *non* (“not”).]

Rather, their expectation of rewards has itself been turned into punishment. Yet he perseveres always; and while others grow lukewarm, his devotion does not grow cold, because he sees that wickedness has not yet wholly subsided, and that impious plans are being pursued, even after treaties have been struck, by men whose loyalty was thought utterly invincible.

Would that a truthful report might reach the knowledge of the Roman pontiff and yourselves concerning how greatly, recently, the holy exertion of a Catholic priest has succeeded with our prince—I mean the king of the English—when even the greatest [Col. 0087D] of princes were inviting him into schism and he was terrified by fear of apostolic severity. For, chiefly through this man’s strength, with our own and others’ efforts beside it, the king was confirmed in the faith and obedience of the Church. Before many ecclesiastical and secular persons, by giving bodily pledge in the hand of the Archbishop of Rouen, he publicly affirmed that he would obey the Roman pontiff in the matter you have heard of, as far as reason should dictate or [Col. 0088A] mercy should relax.

Moreover, he has long been drawn by the strongest desire to visit the Roman Church, so that by your help and counsel he might restore to favour the mind of the apostolic majesty, if it has conceived any feeling against him through false suggestion; and that he might demonstrate to him and to you by the surest proofs the sincerity of his conscience in all things. He was already preparing himself when he received a terrible warning from the king himself and from his envoys, who have recently returned from you: namely, that the emperor had made an exception of him alone, while granting security of passage to others through the king’s intervention, because he had presumed to direct against the emperor’s person a sentence of anathema [Col. 0088B] and to denounce his name in all the ecclesiastical assemblies he had frequently held.

Therefore provide for your friend. Do not allow him to be drawn to those regions by any pressure of necessity, nor permit his head to be exposed to so many and such great dangers. Moreover, it is good for the Church of God that faithful men sometimes dwell beside unfaithful men, so that through their strength and prudence wickedness may be restrained and inconstancy contained. Indeed, among us iniquity was believed to have prevailed had not the exertions of priests resisted it; through them unruliness, forcefully repressed, subsided, and those whom terror of ecclesiastical authority had, as it were, driven into flight returned to unity.

Yet we do not believe that our ship has attained the harbour [Col. 0088C] of perfect security, since even now the anchor may be torn from its obtained anchorage and the ship itself recalled to its former storms by the wind of wickedness. We therefore believe it more useful that those able to provide foresight should not be removed, but should be set as watchmen on diligent guard, so that they may prudently and earnestly observe every eventuality and confirm the momentary loyalty of men with necessary stability. We know, through many trials, that the man about whom we write is effective for this; and his devotion gives him a greater understanding for rendering thanks to you than his vexation does.

## LVIII. TO THE LORD POPE ALEXANDER, ON BEHALF OF JOSCELIN, BISHOP OF SALISBURY

[Col. 0088D] For our venerable father and dearest friend Joscelin, Bishop of Salisbury, we offer affectionate prayers to Your Majesty and render devoted thanks to Your kindness. Your mercy spared him, and reason required that his infirmity be spared, because, beset by bodily heaviness, advanced age, [Col. 0089A] and considerable weakness, he could not, as far as we can judge, come into Your presence.

Regarding the matter for which it pleased you to impose a more severe sentence upon him: judging from the depth of his conscience, from public opinion and testimony, and from our own estimate, we wholly believe him innocent of that lamentable act. Neither his honourable character, nor the gentleness for which his generous spirit is known, nor the prudence of an elderly man formed by so many years and more deeply taught by so many experiences could have deserted him. Moreover, the intention of those by whom that deed was so maliciously committed was concealed with every care, lest anyone’s foreknowledge of the conceived crime should prevent its accomplishment. For who, having conceived an intention of such [Col. 0089B] wickedness, would reveal it to any person, especially to an ecclesiastic, when the sword appeared to be drawn not against one head alone but against the neck of the whole Church?

We saw the man for whom we write, at the beginning of the storm, adhering more zealously among his fellow bishops to that aim, and enduring many injuries for the liberty of the Church and for that man’s favour. That favour toward him indeed continued until Reginald the archdeacon—who is bound to this bishop, as you know, also by an affection of blood—having entered royal service, began to carry royal commands to you which were believed in some respects to conflict with the interests of the archbishop. It was therefore decided to punish the father for the son, so that compassionate pain for his father might turn him from [Col. 0089C] those services, or a harsher punishment might be inflicted upon both.

Would that he had moderated his zeal for a time, since in the cause of the Church which he had undertaken he could have made more useful progress by prudent gentleness: if his entrance had been peaceful, if he had delayed avenging his own injuries, and had not darkened the pleasant joys of a new crown by sudden attacks. Indeed, concerning what was done about the crown, the bishops neither then nor now believe that they sinned in any respect, because, as they say, the authority of Your letters preceded it, and antiquity instructed them to do precisely this by many examples. Yet if it were established that they sinned to some degree in this, the gravity of the fault does not exceed the mercy of apostolic goodness; and, as to the rest, according to the manner appointed by Your Holiness, this man’s innocence will become clear to your diligence with all doubt wholly removed. [Col. 0089D]

Therefore we beseech you, and now venture to offer our prayers with confidence, because this is the time for mercy and, after prolonged scourges, for the bowels of paternal compassion to abound. Far be it from Your kindness to cause a venerable man, cherished for so many virtues and distinguished by so much praise, to spend the last stage of his old age in grief and bitterness! Certainly, no boldness would have compelled us to offer these prayers unless, according to the truth of the facts and the man’s merit, we believed him worthy of apostolic mercy.

## LIX. TO BALDWIN, BISHOP OF NOYON

[Col. 0090A]

Some priests from your bishopric came to us. Since they were said to be experienced and instructed in such work, we retained them to establish confraternities and make collections for rebuilding our church. But after travelling through the bishopric, and having stayed among us for some time, nearly all departed in secret flight, as though in a formed company. They left me personally bound to creditors, under their surety, for a total sum greater than thirty pounds.

> [Note: [Col. 0089D] B.: “some” (*quidam*).]

I, of course, paid the whole amount, keeping faithfully to my promise. They also took seventy shillings from R., the priest who bears this letter, by the same fraud, although they had given us a corporal oath, touching the holy Gospels, that they would keep good faith with us in carrying out the entire undertaking. Therefore we most earnestly beg Your brotherhood, dear to us, pursuing not so much recovery of the money as punishment for so great a fraud and injury, that your justice may give us satisfaction and correct so serious a crime by due punishment. [Col. 0090B]

## LX. TO AEGIDIUS, BISHOP OF ÉVREUX

Regarding the case that is being contested between us and that abbot, Your belovedness need not at present be troubled, because we neither wish nor ought to make you hostile to the prince or unwelcome to the abbot. [Col. 0090C] We have decided to seek a remedy through another man whom neither fear can so readily deter nor deceptive flatteries soften.

But, as is plain to see from the letters, a greater authority in no way holds you back from action; nor does the petitioner’s supplication impose necessity except upon one willing to accept it. If you have the same intention concerning the abbess, we shall regard it as a kindness if she wishes to forewarn us and if Your favour does not permit us to be wearied in vain at the appointed place and day. For a man who explores the slippery winding paths of the twisting serpent cannot walk simply: when he believes he has made the greatest advance, he finds himself cunningly returned to the very beginning.

## LXI. TO THE LORD POPE ALEXANDER

[Col. 0090D] Apostolic authority delegated to the lord Henry, Bishop of Senlis, and to us, to decide by judicial procedure within two months, without appeal, the case disputed between the venerable brother Hugh, Abbot of Saint-Vincent at Senlis, and the priest Garner

> [Note: [Col. 0090D] C.: Garinus.]

concerning the church of Marins. We appointed a suitable place and time for both parties within the period assigned to us; and, having associated with us religious and prudent persons—namely, the abbots of Saint-Victor of Paris, Sainte-Geneviève, Augy, and Mortemer; Geoffrey of Auxerre; Richard of Courcy; and [Col. 0091A] Richard, then Archdeacon of Coutances and now Bishop of Avranches, together with many others—we strove with complete faithfulness and diligence to obey the apostolic commands.

The abbot, acting as plaintiff in this matter, brought a possessory action against the priest. On the question of fact he employed the testimony of many people, and at last put forward seven selected witnesses: five regular priests, canons, and two other priests known to us by experience. We subjected them to careful examination and found them wholly consistent in the testimony of all. We also heard the priest’s allegations and gave him liberty to say what he wished against the persons of the witnesses; but although many things were proposed and carefully examined, nothing was found by which he could exclude any of them [Col. 0091B] or detract in any respect from any person’s reputation.

Having therefore received the oaths of the seven aforesaid witnesses, we restored possession of the church to the abbot, because it seemed to us that the truth ought to be established by the assertion of so many and such worthy witnesses. The priest nevertheless appealed to the hearing of the Roman pontiff; but because recourse to appeal had been removed from the case by apostolic authority, as Your prudence knows, he could not lawfully appeal, nor ought we to have heard him. By the authority which we exercised, we commanded the lord Archbishop of Rouen, in whose diocese the aforesaid church lies, to ensure that our judgment was inviolably observed; and he prudently acquiesced, as was fitting, [Col. 0091C] as is readily apparent from his letter.

But because we have heard that the priest is attempting to reopen what was done, at the abbot’s request we bear testimony to the truth before Your Highness: namely, that we received the mandate from apostolic majesty in the form we have stated and settled the matter according to the reasoning and procedure we have described.

## LXII. TO THE LORD POPE ALEXANDER

The lord King of the English received your envoys and letters with all the greater joy and eagerness because they seemed to promise him a greater measure of Your kindness. Therefore, having graciously heard Your request for peace with the Archbishop of Canterbury and restoration of his people, he granted that the archbishop might return to his archbishopric, receive it in the complete condition in which he held it when he departed, and henceforth possess it in good peace and security—for the honour of God and the Church, while preserving, of course, the former dignity of his kingdom. [Col. 0091D]

It seemed to us that this proposal pleased your envoys, who were certainly prudent men, so much that they immediately absolved those who were present. To absolve those in England, one of them—Master Vivian—consented to cross over at once; the other agreed to remain on this side of the sea for carrying out the agreed peace. Later they withdrew their agreement: they refused to accept the provision for preserving royal dignity in the future, and declined to execute what had been arranged, although the archbishops, bishops, abbots, religious persons, and magnates of the kingdom who were present had earnestly urged them with many prayers for the good of so great a peace. For, in preserving royal dignity, liberty or dignity of the Church did not seem to us in any way to be burdened. [Col. 0092A]

Indeed, ecclesiastical dignity advances rather than supports royal dignity, and royal dignity has customarily preserved rather than removed ecclesiastical liberty. For ecclesiastical and royal dignity meet as though in mutual embrace: kings do not obtain salvation without the Church, nor does the Church obtain peace without royal protection. Therefore, cast down at the knees of Your mercy with all the devotion we can muster, we humbly and earnestly beg that Your wisdom should not embrace, as it were, the letter-shapes and verbal formulations [Col. 0092B] rather than the matter itself. Instead, according to the spirit of discernment given you by God, act so that the cause of one man may not turn to the ruin of many—indeed, of nearly countless persons—for the good of peace is sometimes advanced more by the gentleness of favour than by the severity of discipline.

## LXIII. TO THE MONKS OF BERNAY

As we took care to anticipate your election with more indulgent favour, so, insofar as lies in us, we approve it now that it has taken place and embrace the elected person in the arms of abundant affection. But concerning your sending an envoy to appoint for you a day of blessing, I am greatly astonished that, whereas this should have been requested through the prior [Col. 0092C] and an appropriate number of senior persons, you sent a man alone and without letters, neither serious in character nor advanced in age. He did not fear to provoke me, though I was responding to everything quite kindly and beneficially, with arrogant words, nor to arouse great indignation by his insolent audacity.

Having therefore given the fool the answer fitting for his folly, we have thought it proper to reply to you, as brothers beloved in Christ, through our own messenger and letters, lest anyone—God forbid—compel you by deceitful malice to despair of our kindness and favour. Know, then, that within ten or twelve days, God willing, I shall return to your church; and then we wish the prior to come to us with an appropriate number of brethren and with the elected [Col. 0092D] person, so that through them the election may be presented to us, as canonical order requires, and confirmed by the protection of our authority.

Then, after consultation between you and us, a suitable day may be assigned for the blessing. If any obstacle appears, we shall take every care to remove it, and, with divine grace always preceding, to bring the business to its completion.

## LXIV. TO THE LORD POPE ALEXANDER

Your Majesty delegated to our lowliness, for judicial decision, the case disputed between Hermerius the priest and the Abbot of La Couture concerning diminution of the parish-priesthood of the church of Bruslum. [Col. 0093A] The priest Hermerius alleged that the priesthood of the said church, which he held from the abbot, was being curtailed by violence. He urgently demanded that its full integrity be restored to him, as his predecessors had possessed it, offering a multitude of witnesses as proof, wherever need or reason should require.

The abbot replied that a controversy concerning the same matter had existed between his predecessor and Gervase, Hermerius’s predecessor; that by appeal the case had been transferred from the presence of the lord Bishop of Le Mans to the hearing of the Archbishop of Tours; and that there all litigation had been concluded by amicable settlement. On this matter he produced the lord archbishop’s letters, fully containing the terms of the agreement, under the designation of a grant. [The following words, *non mereat*, are materially uncertain.] Many things appear to be missing.

## LXV. TO THE LORD POPE ALEXANDER

[Col. 0093B]

I would count myself happy and endowed with every blessing if divine goodness would bring me even once more to see Your face, so that the serenity of Your countenance might shine upon my longing eyes and the fuller abundance of Your blessing, close at hand, might water my dryness. But advanced age, the affliction of accidental weakness, and the very distance of places make me despairing, because perhaps neither time would permit sufficient space nor weakness sufficient strength for travelling through so many regions.

Meanwhile I do what I can. Though absent in body, I am always present to you through the earnestness of anxious devotion; and I stand ready and faithful, whenever opportunity shines, in every place to seek the prosperity of your condition [Col. 0093C] and the peace of the holy Roman Church. For in all things the favour and beneficence of you and your predecessors have made me your debtor; and nothing troubles me more than that all I can do is insufficient for the thanks I owe.

But the less my merits are, the more inclined is my heart to service, the more earnest to act, so that devotion may supply the deficiency of weakness—a devotion which, wherever it is sincere, ought by a sounder judgment to be considered more acceptable than any work. All your legates whom Your authority sent to our regions from the beginning saw this and tested my loyalty and diligence by clear proofs of events; as Your Majesty was also able to learn from the letters of those who came most recently. [Col. 0093D]

For when the business for which they had come had declined into a miserable rupture, and all who had intervened departed in despair of agreement, at last, out of the fervour of charity, I approached alone of my own accord. Having thoroughly and prudently discussed everything of benefit with your legates, I recalled our prince, already returning to England, from the journey itself; and through my agency divine kindness inclined him toward the good of peace. In this all saw divine mercy work an unexpected miracle: so great a prince was turned from such a movement of indignation and wrath to works of peace and humility, made himself amenable and obedient to your legates for reverence toward God and favour toward you, as your knowledge learned from his letters and theirs. [Col. 0094A]

Certainly, if it please you to judge that in what was done there lay honour for the Church of God and advancement for yourselves, what you accomplished is great—indeed, very great—provided that someone shall take care to commit it to execution and bring it into effect. This, indeed, should no longer be considered difficult, because, through the Holy Spirit working for His Church, such sincerity of devotion then bound the prince that no repentance and no shamelessness can recall him. I recount these things not for boasting, nor in order to seem to proclaim my merits, but because I desire that my zeal, approved by so many proofs, should not fall from [Col. 0094B] your memory. Let my former favour always continue with Your Majesty, so that in my final days—to which the unwelcome necessity of old age brings me—the hand of your protection may always stand more strongly by me in times of need. Do not allow my repose to be shaken by vexations, nor my church to be deprived of its right by any malignity, so that I may preserve it in the condition to which, through your merits and with God’s help, I brought it.

> [Note: [Col. 0093D] B.: “brought [it]” (*perduxit*) in place of “I brought [it]” (*perduxi*).]

Thus, when dying, I may leave it rich though once poor, glorious though once obscure. Since, because of the evil of the times that obstructs me, I cannot by myself attain this completion, I always turn at every opportunity to the customary help of Your kindness and to the singular protection of the holy Roman Church. For I have experienced you as gracious in every petition and wholly effective in overcoming my difficulties. [Col. 0094C]

I therefore send to the feet of Your Holiness the bearer of this letter, Master Gilbert, whom I commend to you alike by his honourable character, his learning, and the especial favour in which blessed Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, held him. Through him the truth and justice of our affairs may become more fully known to you, and a single man’s spoken account may more conveniently supply what the letter’s brevity omits. I therefore ask that Your goodness receive him with the kindness which you have always customarily shown to me and mine, and that you take care to put an end to the long duration of our affairs, concerning which I have already received from you first, second, and third judges. But both my hope and their investigation have been frustrated by many devices, so that I could not even reach a hearing. [Col. 0094D] You may place unquestioned trust in what this man tells you on my behalf, because it is worse than sacrilege even to attempt in any respect to deceive Your Holiness.

## LXVI. TO RICHARD, ARCHDEACON OF POITIERS

That Your affection bears a kindly concern for my old age is evident by many indications, especially because with such great and generous zeal you provide helpful assistance for my weakness. For frequent occasion draws me into various labours; and the malice of the time gives no credence to excuse, but regards what belongs to infirmity as laziness or pretence. So great is this pressure that necessity is often compelled to assail power itself, and, by wretched efforts, to restore the failing strength buried by age. [Col. 0095A]

It is harmful, however, to burden health with labours, lest distress perhaps increase the force of pain and illness acquire some new growth from the injury of strain. Your generosity therefore found assistance for old age and a remedy for labour, by which so weak a body may be invigorated and the pressure of vexations moderated. For I received from you two horses chosen with especially exact care. Their very beauty commended them at first sight; afterward, closer inspection approved them as free from every fault.

They travel smoothly: they do not shake their rider with any unevenness; their even gait does not diminish their speed; nor does a hoof, ever checked by any turf, stumble. There is no need to restrain them with a bridle or urge them with spurs, [Col. 0095B] for they submit to every rider’s service with such ease that they seem to have explored the rider’s every wish. Finally, their movement advances with such sweetness that the man who rides them believes himself not to be walking forward but gliding, and judges more truly that he is being conveyed not so much on a horse as in a little boat.

The very variety also adds to the increase of pleasure, because novelty breaks up the tedium of sameness. Nor need I always remain on the same saddle, but may ride now this horse, now the other, as I please. They seem to have restored my former strength and former endurance; I follow the rides of younger men with such ease that I feel my limbs not merely held together, but even invigorated by pleasant motion. [Col. 0095C] You have restored me to myself—or rather, to those who once enjoyed my services but now employed me in service—and, graciously led out from the enclosures of domestic confinement, I have been brought back to the customary joys of public fellowship.

## LXVII. TO HENRY, KING OF ENGLAND

HENRY, by the grace of God illustrious King of the English, etc.: R., Archbishop of Rouen, and ARNULF, Bishop of Lisieux, greeting in Him through whom kings reign.

So much the more promptly and diligently did we judge the embassy entrusted to us [Col. 0095D] ought to be carried out, as delay seemed the more dangerous in so critical a situation. Accordingly, having girded ourselves for the labour of the journey undertaken, we heard the king of the Franks; and, first offering a most courteous greeting and thereby forestalling his displeasure, we could by no entreaty obtain an answer to your greeting. We set forth in order each article of our embassy, repeatedly pressing the advantages of peace and the disadvantages of discord. He, however, received our words patiently in every respect, the greeting alone excepted. When the course of our embassy had thus been carefully completed, and a short interval had passed, he began contemptuously to reproach us with deceits and evasions by which, he complained, he had very often been outwitted. He said that you had frequently broken the pledged faith mutually agreed between you, [Col. 0096A] upon the slightest pretext; and that in all matters you had shown yourself so unstable that henceforth he would place no trust in you.

Let it not burden you, most illustrious king, that we report what we heard. For this is the duty of messengers: to conceal nothing of the commission laid upon them, and to suppress or diminish nothing of the answer. He added that he had held a most fixed intention of attacking you before your son had come to Chartres; and he alleged the following grounds of dissension and hatred: that you do not allow his daughter to return to her husband; that you do not restore her dowry to her; that you have stirred up against him, out of hatred for him, peoples subject to his jurisdiction from the mountains of Auvergne as far as the Rhône; and that, to the detriment of his crown, you have received the count of Saint-Gilles as your liege-man. Finally, [Col. 0096B] he even confirmed by oath that he would never thereafter have either treaty or peace with you, unless with the consent of your wife and your sons.

Therefore you must now use sounder counsel in guarding your fortresses, and especially in protecting your person. For, with one purpose, all France has conspired for your destruction. Nor is it enough for him to lay waste the face of the land with fire and sword; rather, against your person—may this never be!—he is plotting an abominable crime. We strongly advise that, if you have taken anything away or injured anyone, you restore what was taken and turn enmities back into favour. For what especially summons your enemies to battle is their sense that you have enemies within; and those who eat sweet food with you will, when opportunity is given, greatly increase their treachery against you.

“Cursed [Col. 0096C] is the man who trusts in man, and makes flesh the strength of his arm” (Jeremiah 17). What is more lovable than sons? What more intimate than a wife? Yet your wife has departed from your side, and your sons rise up against their father. Therefore that man, most prudent among men, did not speak without cause when he said: “Do not trust a friend. From her who sleeps in your bosom guard the doors of your mouth. For the son dishonours the father, and a man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Micah 7).

Certainly, we judge that the aid of him should be sought in whose hand are the hearts of kings. In his name David’s smallness overcame Goliath’s greatness. In his name Samaria, when Ben-hadad besieged it and it was so consumed by famine that an ass’s head was sold for thirty pieces of silver, was delivered in the twinkling of an eye [Col. 0096D] and overflowed with an abundant supply of provisions. For one who hopes in him shall not be weakened. If battle rises against you, hope in this. If camps rise against you, let not your heart fear (Psalm 26); for he will teach your hands for battle (2 Samuel 22).

Take to yourselves as help the prayers of the Church. If you have offended her in any respect, make due satisfaction, and henceforth show her every reverence. For she is Christ’s bride, and Christ considers injuries done to his bride as his own; nor is there anything that more incites your enemies to conflict than their belief that you have been less devoted to the Church of God. May our dearest lord prosper, and through the power of the Most High may he bear away glory and triumph over those who rise against him in pride and wrongdoing.

## LXVIII. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER

[Col. 0097A]

We are now compelled for the fourth time to repeat petitions which we have made three times and which your majesty has always heard with great kindness, because the number of judges most recently delegated has impeded the conclusion of the case. For the prolonged and frequent absence of the deans of Bayeux and Évreux prevented the third colleague, namely the lord bishop of Avranches, from proceeding with the business, since nothing had been entrusted to him without the present cooperation of one or both of the others.

For my own part, I wondered that your majesty should command a priest—indeed, a bishop—to be obliged to stand before deacons, an old man before young men, when rather the lesser are customarily judged by the greater, inferiors by superiors, and younger men [Col. 0097B] by elders. Yet I was ready, with every reverence, to accept the commands of whatever judges you appointed. But the cunning of the opposing party, established in possession of the things at issue, now, as always from old times, buys off days and times through delays; and though I have always appeared before the judges on every day and at every place, it has not yet once deigned to appear in court.

For at times, as hitherto always, the violence of secular power is set against us; at other times, the cautiously purchased favour of the judges admits every sort of delay against us, even delays plainly futile. Although our Church continually protests, monks have presumed, with sacrilegious audacity, to seize parish churches and tithes from lay hands by purchases or other unlawful means; and they have always been defended by secular power, so that possession ill acquired might nevertheless be preserved by an evil protection. They now endeavour to oppose the duration of this violence as a prescription of long possession, although possession that is violent or interrupted cannot avail for prescription—where, namely, neither opportunity for bringing suit nor a legally useful day is granted to the plaintiff.

We therefore ask that your goodness take care to set an end to our labour, which we have pursued ineffectually for thirty years; and that you join with the lord of Avranches, whom your choice assigned to us as judge, whom your choice assigned to us as judge, whomever you please, provided that he is known to possess zeal for God and judicial expertise, and is of such [Col. 0097D] age and rank that neither our rank appears to suffer insult nor old age humiliation. Hugo, archdeacon and our nephew, bearer of this letter, will explain our petitions more fully to your majesty, since we did not think fit to insert them in this letter, lest its length become wearisome.

## LXIX. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER

Your compassion does not fail to know what losses, labours, and injuries the Church of Canterbury has suffered in this time. But the compassionate and merciful Lord has now looked with an eye of mercy upon her, long afflicted and worn out by pitiable grief. Through the glorious mighty works of blessed Thomas, the new martyr, [Col. 0098A] by which divine majesty repeatedly illumines her, he has begun to recall her to the state of her former dignity and eminence.

It is certain that among other things a miracle has recently occurred there, such as no hope or confidence had previously presumed: namely, that a person was elected to govern the Church without designation by secular power, whereas previously no one could be promoted there unless secular power had first named him. Although many devices had been attempted to bring that act back under the old abuse, through the merits of the aforesaid martyr every contrivance was always frustrated; because he could not endure that the freedom of the person should be entrusted to another whom he had redeemed for himself by his own blood, unless that person’s election were free and his entry canonical.

For if the old practice of violence had so recently regained strength, perhaps many would have judged the shedding of that precious blood vain, and that the victory won through such great labours had collapsed into failure. But now the whole province breathes hope for the liberty desired for so long, and rejoices that the testament confirmed by Christ’s blood is again sealed with new blood. Accordingly, while all rejoice together at the triumph of liberty newly won, the Spirit having been invoked and gently guiding them into one agreement, a man was elected whose religious devotion, prudence, and magnificence were judged suited to so great a work—not from outward indications, but because over a long time this had been established by the evidence of events within the household itself. No envy, ambition, or force dared oppose it, because [Col. 0098C] that holy man seemed to be consecrating the beginnings of his successor and to be placing at the altar, of which he himself had been priest, a priest pleasing to him.

This joy was reserved for the felicity of your times, that it might add this title to the glory of your achievements: that everywhere your strength should restore liberty to the Church.

Blessed be God, moreover, who inclined the mind of our devout son, the elder king, to this agreement. He supports with due favour this act which he had formerly been accustomed to forestall by a necessary designation. But the son whom the premature affection of his father caused to be consecrated to succeed him in the kingdom began to oppose so great a good, at the prompting of those who were able to draw him away from his father’s bosom [Col. 0098D] and to turn the simplicity of his youth to his own harm rather than to his father’s. Their purpose, therefore, is always to set him against his father, so that the hatreds which they have sown between them may grow stronger from every cause, lest he should ever return to himself, acknowledge the debt of natural affection, and begin to return to his father’s embrace.

Your prudence must therefore carefully provide against this: lest the violence of necessary designation—which in the father has wholly expired through God’s grace and your glory—rise again in the son because of your forbearance or dissimulation; lest it seem not so much removed as transferred to another, and prepare to press forward with all the greater violence because it sees the father’s renunciation standing in the way of its design. Therefore receive kindly the person in whom the beginnings of liberty, long desired, have begun to be consecrated; [Col. 0099A] and grant him, from the magnificence of apostolic power, the confidence necessary for accomplishing so great a work, so that our first fruits may grow strong under your auspices and be completed with a joyful result.

The eyes of all the faithful and the prayers of all the Churches look longingly to you, so that those who possess liberty may have confidence in retaining it, and those who do not may conceive hope of gaining it. Moreover, this work, this endeavour, was the continual aim of that martyr: to redeem the liberty of the Church over which he presided. This is the fruit of his labour, the reward of his blood, the prize of his passion. Since he chose this man as, so to speak, heir and successor in preserving liberty, it is glorious for you to cooperate with the martyr and to add your completion to his beginnings, so that your action, as though quickened by the same Spirit, may join his action.

Therefore send him back with all speed to the work to which he has been so holily and so solemnly called, lest malice derive an opportunity from his absence and the shoots of revived secular power begin to spring up. Rather, through him may your Holiness seize the newborn children and dash them against the rock; and, the badge of former servitude removed, may the Church of God go forth rejoicing and, triumphing always over ancient wickedness through his merits and yours, begin to appear terrible to her enemies like an army drawn up in battle array. Let your wisdom further understand that not only the desires of that province and kingdom, but also those of other kingdoms, [Col. 0099C] make supplication—wherever the mighty works of that saint have reached, whether by report or by present sight.

## LXX. TO WILLIAM, BISHOP OF LE MANS

It is true that, in an archbishop’s election, the presence of the suffragan bishops is desired, so that the matter may be usefully arranged by the counsel and confirmed by the assent of those over whom he is to preside. The canons of Tours, however, maintain that they intended nothing offensive toward you through presumption or pride, but, compelled by great necessity, hastened what was done. For if they delayed, many hindrances and obstacles detrimental to the Church would arise for them. They also greatly doubted whether the bishops could arrive at a suitable time, since the storm spread everywhere kept each one occupied with his own prayers and many necessities.

We have heard, moreover, that what has been done displeases many of them not; rather, they confirm it with their consent, because if anything in the procedure of the act was observed less fully, the merits of a person of acknowledged worth make amends. Certainly, diligence in observing due order is required in elections so that provision for a suitable person may be made for the Church’s welfare more cautiously and faithfully. Yet the merit of the person must always be embraced more particularly than one should oppose the principal good by any observances. For what was introduced for a person’s benefit ought not to be turned against that person’s injury; and favour for the person ought to be greater than concern for the procedure, which was instituted, it is clear, rather to discover a suitable person than to exclude one.

[Col. 0100A] On this matter, we have judged it right to join our desire with the desires of many, and our prayers with their prayers, before your excellency: may your kindness incline toward consenting to and bringing about this act. Since the matter principally concerns you, your favour may be recognized more readily in the execution and completion of the work. For by doing this you will obtain praise and gratitude from many. Nor is it good that your Holiness, amid so many disturbances and scandals which, because our sins demand it, arise ceaselessly on every side, should inflict so much disturbance and labour upon your Church, of which you are, as it were, the greater and first-born son, in avenging an injury that can be borne. Perhaps, too, if the matter is brought before a higher judgment, it will have a favourable outcome. It ought to be more satisfactory to your prudence that the entire completion of the affair should proceed, as from your own benefaction, with the thanks of many, than that it should issue against your will from superior authority.

## LXXI. TO LORD POPE LUCIUS III

Last year certain canons of our Church of Lisieux, acting with the knowledge of a few rather than of the whole body, brought letters to your majesty, freely writing down against me whatever falsehoods they wished. Since they could not rely upon any truth falsely alleged against me, and knew me to be known and acceptable to the holy Roman Church from the beginning of my youth, with the integrity of my reputation brightly distinguished before her by much renown, they proceeded more boldly to lie by an astonishing device: they invented many things, indeed countless things, so that falsehood might seem to lend authority to falsehood, so that even the liars themselves might not be judged liars because of so many lies, and so that their deceptive assertion might appear to bear witness to falsehood.

[Col. 0100C] For it could scarcely be believed that anyone would presume to darken your sincerity with so many and such great lies; and there was no one able to answer in my name. It was enough for them if they could, even for a moment, blacken my reputation in any respect and draw your Holiness somewhat into uncertainty. You heard them, and heard them more favourably than was expedient for me. For though absent and innocent, and never summoned by any citation, I was punished and suspended from a great part of my episcopal office; and you sent them back further encouraged to say and do whatever they wished, so that any others also might be invited and encouraged more freely.

I was astonished, and those who heard were likewise astonished, on what grounds so harsh a sentence could at once have been pronounced against a son, indeed a special son. Yet I held back my hands, nor in my trembling did I even raise them to defend my head; and your indignation confirmed me in resigning the bishopric, which I had always desired. For this I give thanks to your Holiness: you have so mercifully freed me from an unbearable burden and allowed me to proceed more freely to care for my soul.

My adversaries, having obtained letters and judges at their own discretion, strove by many devices [Col. 0101A] to obstruct my course. By virtue of your letters they immediately summoned me to the tribunal of the bishop of Avranches and the abbots of Bec and Savigny, although, for many reasons, the whole province was known to be hostile to me. From them, on charges so numerous and so grave, no postponement or opportunity for deliberating upon a response could be obtained. At the outset, while we were conducting the case, the judges admitted that they had no knowledge of law and would receive neither procedural exceptions nor any other legal pleas, but would attend only to what the letter appeared on its face to require.

Adding to my burden were the king’s displeasure and the untiring activity of Walter of Coutances, whom they had made leader of the faction that they had sworn against me, with the bishopric promised to him. In every matter he preserved for them royal help and favour; and, using the king’s seal which he himself held, he confidently presumed to authenticate whatever he wished against me, even without the king’s knowledge, so that it might be thought to proceed from the king’s will. Thus equipped with these deceits, even the judges departed from the truth of judgment through fear, prepared indeed to do whatever their adversaries might command them.

They charged, therefore, that I had squandered the Church’s goods extravagantly, although it was established that I had acquired twelve hundred pounds and more in perpetual revenues, had added five hundred pounds to the treasury, and had spent twelve thousand pounds upon buildings which remain standing; and that the episcopal church itself had been renewed in part by my expenses and acquisitions. For the common fund [Col. 0101C] of the canons I also acquired six hundred pounds yearly and in perpetuity, and I increased the episcopal table by five hundred pounds and more yearly and in perpetuity.

From the treasury itself, however, that I may omit nothing, I took seventeen marks at the beginning of my promotion, because I was compelled to redeem from the hand of the count of Anjou all the episcopal goods which he had withheld from me for two years and three months, because I had been consecrated canonically elected without his designation. This I did by the permission of my lord Pope Innocent of glorious memory, after I had first spent nine hundred pounds of my own money and more on that cause. On the Jerusalem expedition, moreover, to which Pope Eugenius, the holy Father, sent me against my will, I expended by his command a gold chalice [Col. 0101D] weighing thirty-four ounces, although he had granted me leave to take more for my own need if necessary.

Besides, lest it perhaps seem boastful, there was meanwhile such an outpouring of hospitality, repeatedly enhanced by generous gifts, that such liberality could scarcely have been expected from a man of my modest means. This is everywhere confirmed by the public testimony of those who saw it and of those who experienced it.

I begged the judges, after considering the amount of what had been added and what had been taken away, to allow an account of compensation—if indeed it seemed proper to appraise what had been spent upon such pious and necessary causes and afterward restored more than seventy-sevenfold. I was heard in nothing, because new fear and the obstinacy of old hostility had closed their mouths [Col. 0102A] and hearts; and their hatred no longer seemed concealed, but their audacity had burst forth in everything.

They therefore condemned me to give one hundred pounds to the canons, though they had expended these on the Church’s needs and lawful expenses; and from the wholly new chapel which I had prepared for myself they took away my chasuble, dalmatic, and tunic. Thus they sent me away deprived of money and stripped of sacred vestments. When this came to your hearing, you shattered their sentence with apostolic severity and, as may be understood from your letters, wished to free me from their obstinacy.

I therefore ask that your judgment remain firm in its decree, that your letters obtain their effect, and that you cause to be restored to me what was taken away [Col. 0102B] through an unjust cause, so that what had been intended for them from the beginning may reach the brethren to whom I have withdrawn. For they insult me, distribute at their own discretion what had been assigned to pious purposes, and rejoice with shameless exultation that I have departed, as it were, naked and destitute. Therefore may your mercy do what you have begun, and command with strict severity that what has been, as it were, decreed by you be brought to completion, lest simple or ignorant malice rejoice in our losses.

## LXXII. TO THE ABBOT OF CÎTEAUX AND HIS BRETHREN

Worn out by age and weighed down by the onset of certain illnesses, I have decided to have recourse to the saving remedy of medicine and to relieve limbs broken by labours with the necessary rest [Col. 0102C]. For weakness, sickness, and old age come against me as though leagued for my destruction, and the pressure of so many troubles cuts off my confidence in a longer life. Added from without is the oppressive vexation of affairs by which I am distracted; it does not permit me, panting miserably, even for a moment to draw breath.

For I am often dragged with others into royal compulsory services, and am harassed by the repeated wrongs of those whom I cannot fail to assist. Meanwhile all intermediate resources are consumed by such great labours and expenses that neither my body suffices for endurance nor my means for expenditure. Moreover, if these things did not also obstruct the salvation of souls, a good man might judge the losses [Col. 0102D] of the present more tolerable if they furthered the gain of eternal things. But as human wickedness always advances and daily grows worse, goods, bodies, and souls alike are involved together in a similar ruin and are often brought to a fearful end.

Since it is the part of a wise man to avert such misfortunes by prudent foresight, I had to seek a suitable place where neither the tumult of lawsuits might disturb my rest nor the incursions of a crowd interrupt me; but where, by a better example, the pursuits of uprightness might always flourish and every opportunity might serve the works of true virtue. Although I was invited to many places by the prayers and wishes of many, one house of your order, called Mortemer, pleased me above all, because it appeared well suited to me in many respects.

[Col. 0103A] For we are joined to one another by great affection from long-standing friendship, and old acquaintance has strengthened mutual goodwill by reciprocal services. Therefore I decided to build for myself, outside the boundaries within which the stricter decrees of abstinence are observed according to your order, a house at moderate cost. Its restrained size will suffice for necessary uses, yet will not exceed the measure of a regular building. Certainly, we shall be excluded; yet household provisions will be granted so prudently and mercifully that strictness may prevent any violation of regular observance, while mercy does not exclude us from the Church and the holy conversations of the brethren.

Moreover, no separate entrance has been reserved from outside, so that the occasion of useless visitors may be removed and nothing may enter except through the common gate, under the eyes and careful oversight of the holy gatekeeper. [Col. 0103B] I know that they have conceived great joy at my residence among them; and may the benefits they expect indeed come to them from it, so that the result may prove worthy of their expectation and something may be added to their good opinion of my choice. But because we know that place belongs particularly to your care, we thought it right to make our intention known to you, asking that it please your charity also; that we may be protected by the holy aid of your prayers; and that your authority may gladden the desires of the holy brethren and confirm the matter by some reply or command.

## LXXIII. TO RICHARD, ARCHDEACON OF POITIERS

[Col. 0103C] I have judged it all the more gladly proper to send you the book on ecclesiastical offices because I should wish you, freed from secular concerns, to devote your whole effort to the divine offices. But if at some time necessity, income, or the favour of a superior draws you to those secular concerns, always remember your order. Do not involve yourself in matters whose execution does not suit your profession; leave them to those through whom they are more properly carried out. There are also certain matters in which you ought wholly to deny your presence: namely, where corporal punishment or a judgment of blood is to be inflicted, because the severity of secular laws in many respects does not accord with the gentleness of ecclesiastical compassion.

## LXXIV. TO THE LEGATES ALBERT AND THEODWIN

[Col. 0103D]

Roal., bearer of this letter, brought me letters of your highness. Having examined them carefully, I suspected them to be false, because in part they seemed to contain a solecism and in part to command something contrary to your custom. I therefore judged that he himself should be sent back to you with the same letters, lest I be accused of negligence or rashness in carrying out your command; instead, instruct me more clearly and fully what you wish to be done.

It would be useful for this man to be sent to another judge, before whom he could more conveniently seek redress nearby, since for certain necessary reasons I have decided to remain for some time during these days in more distant places. It would be both difficult and excessively costly to provide there the means for the necessary instruction.

## LXXV. TO NICHOLAS, A MONK OF THE MONASTERY OF ARRAMATO

I read the letters of your discretion with no small astonishment, and I grieved that the wisdom of a prince and your religious devotion had been deceived by the fraud of an impudent young man. As to what you wrote—that, at my intercession, you had restored him to further favour, and that I had extorted this from you by frequent letters—know that I have never sent you or anyone else a letter on his behalf, nor have I ever at any time made any request to anyone for him.

For he is connected to me by no kinship, commended by no merits, and bound by no familiarity. Indeed, he very rarely dares present himself before my eyes, because, stained with notorious infamy, he fears even to appear in public, his guilty conscience accusing him. Yet I have already received from him a second letter of the count, which seemed to have been dictated by the tenderest affection, since nothing was lacking from its content that either love could have commanded or inquisitive diligence discovered.

Moreover, that letter bore the style of your learning; and its handwriting, compared with letters recently received from your Holiness, showed me by certain indications that it was entirely the same hand. As to your assertion that he forged the count’s seal and, by forged letters in the count’s name, received borrowed money, if you do not judge that his merits warrant indulgence, it will be necessary to charge him in due judicial order while he denies the accusation. [Note: [Col. 0103D] B., “while he distrusts” (*diffidentem*).] Perhaps the evidence required to convict him will be lacking; and, if the case reaches the testimony of witnesses, they may perhaps meet with a disappointing failure in the very examination.

But even if the action succeeds, the debtor’s poverty will doubtless defeat it, unless your kindness in this case chooses to assist him with its accustomed generosity and your compassion, at a suitable time, renders to his merits the gratitude due for favours. Many might also judge it inhumane if your generosity brought a freeborn young man into danger, if your good will did not pardon, at least for a single offence, a person of that age after so many benefits conferred.

Yet if you resolve to pursue this injury with harsher insistence, I ought not to judge another’s servant: let him stand or fall before his own master. Nor would I have him shut in a prison-workhouse or bound tightly in iron fetters; nor ought your goodness to wish him bound with harsher chains for so small a sum. He is yours, because you have made him yours by your benefits and instruction. He is also, as you have written, a canon of the lord count; therefore proceedings must be brought against him before that count, and he is bound to recognize the forum to which he is subject and to obey the judgments of his own judge.

But the person whom, as you write, your magnificence sent to me through him, altered for the fourth time, has been received; as though he had wings, perhaps he flew away, or perhaps he judged that he should still be reserved for more distant times, [Col. 0105A] so that a more advanced change might make him more welcome.

## LXXVI. TO BARTHOLOMEW, BISHOP OF EXETER

Jor., your bearer of this letter, lived with us through many days of his youth, so that he might be trained in the divine offices in our Church and instructed among the scholars in the liberal disciplines. His modest diligence pleased both our brethren and ourselves; and the first rudiments of virtue promised good hope for what remained. In addition, his sweet and pleasant voice among those chanting in church could move even hardened hearts to devotion.

When he returned to [Col. 0105B] his native land, he rejoiced that he had found acceptance with you, so much so that your favour raised him through benefices and promoted him to the order of subdeacon. Later, drawn back to regions beyond the sea by some opportunity unknown to me, he received the remaining orders without your permission and authorization. I thought that your kindness would not be greatly stirred by an act committed not from presumption but from simplicity.

Your severity, however, suspended him from exercising the orders received with insufficient caution and, as he asserts, added this formidable threat: that he should not be restored by you unless this were granted him by higher authority. He therefore came to the cardinals through many labours and great dangers; but they would grant him nothing until they had first been informed of the truth of the matter by the testimony of your letters. They also say that they will write nothing into England until they have spoken with the lord king; for what reason they have decreed this, we do not know.

Meanwhile, we make supplication and, having been anticipated by an older favour, continue that favour, asking that our prayer may benefit him with you, so far as either justice ought to allow or mercy to assist.

## LXXVII. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT-ÉVROUL

Regarding those matters for which you incurred sentence, we do not believe that you have forgotten how you promised to abide by our command and obey our instructions. For certain reasons we have still delayed prescribing the form of the command [Col. 0105D] and imposing the manner of satisfaction, because in this matter we wish to employ such moderation that whatever we do may appear to proceed from sincere charity, and that, by our example, you may be summoned to the humility and obedience due—provided that the discipline of ecclesiastical institution is maintained insofar as we judge expedient for your salvation and ours.

Therefore, lest the matter remain longer in suspense, and since the approaching Lenten season is especially dedicated to penitence, we command you, bound by the obligation under which you lie, to present yourself before us at Lisieux on the Wednesday not of the present but of the following week. Thus, with the counsel of religious and prudent persons [Col. 0106A] employed, what is commanded to you may be arranged with the Lord’s help. For we must prepare our consciences for the Paschal feast, so that through worthy fruits of repentance we may deserve to share in the Lord’s resurrection.

## LXXVIII. TO THE ABBOT OF THE COURT OF GOD

For your son F., we offer your fatherhood thanks with all devotion, because you abound toward him in such plentiful bowels of charity that your religious devotion directs him with all care toward salvation and, in his needs, your indulgence bestows a fatherly affection. He has chosen to be lowly in the house of his God rather than dwell among his own in the tents [Col. 0106B] of sinners; but the favour of your kindness relieves the austerity of the order he has sought, and your condescension recompenses the humility of his lowliness.

It is certain whose favour you seek to merit in this and in other things. But although your rewards are secure to you, our devotion nonetheless adds its affection in thanksgiving. Happy, then, shall I be, if I am ever found not to have received ungratefully, if I am granted at some time to repay in some measure the excellence of your merits.

## LXXIX. TO THE ABBOT OF CÎTEAUX
Two priests of our diocese, namely Arn. and Ric., intending to renounce the world, at the frequent exhortation and through the efforts of our brother Will., now abbot of Pinu, first surrendered into our hands the churches which they had held and then, with the utmost readiness of devotion, entrusted themselves and their possessions to the venerable and religious man Ric., abbot of Valascia. [Note: [Col. 0105D] B.: “of our diocese.”] We, duly favouring their devotion, and out of regard for the abbot of Valascia—who is bound to us by the closest affection because of the merit of his sincere religious life and diligence—remitted without any difficulty the obligations of accounts and all other matters in which they were liable to us, since they had been our officials; and we delivered them, free and absolved, into the abbot’s hand, together with their means, to serve God perpetually in the aforesaid monastery.

Afterwards, when they were expected to enter upon the probation of that devout monastery, the abbot of Pinu, having turned his purpose in another direction, most vehemently dissuaded them from the work of which he had formerly been the most ardent promoter. He objected that one of them, before he had even reached the years of puberty, had at his persuasion solemnly pronounced in the monastery of Chaelix a public vow of religion, adding the promise that he would neither alter nor revoke that intention thereafter. On this pretext, to the great amazement of prudent and religious men, he led away alike the devout and the undevout, doubtless for the reason that the other—the one whom he strove to withdraw—had been allowed to remain perpetually in the monastery of his own religious profession.

But the abbot of Valascia, being a man of long patience and great gentleness, delayed pursuing the wrongs done to himself and his monastery until the holy assembly of your whole body. [Note: [Col. 0106D] B.: “according to.”] He hoped, indeed, that whatever had been done wrongly would there be reformed without evasion, where neither excuse obstructs truth nor greed equity.

For my own part, as concerns my Church, I cannot pass the matter over on any ground. For one of those whose recall is under discussion, namely Arn., on the advice and through the agency of the abbot of Pinu, pledged for four Angevin pounds a certain book which a devout contribution of the parishioners had bestowed upon his church, although under anathema I had forbidden him to do this or to presume to remove anything belonging to the Church without my knowledge. [Note: [Col. 0107D] B.: “formerly.”] [Note: [Col. 0107D] B.: “or.”] Therefore, since, though often warned and required, he has not restored the book to his church, know that he has departed excommunicated and suspended from every ministry of the priestly office until he makes satisfaction for the sacrilege.

LXXX. TO HENRY, ABBOT OF FÉCAMP.

We believe that your prudence faithfully remembers the case formerly committed to us by apostolic authority, which was in dispute between you and the poor bearer of this letter. In this matter, as in others, showing more ready service to the favour dear to us of your goodwill, we induced him to settle with you a large claim for a small sum, and to submit himself entirely to your will, so that he might receive even that small amount more advantageously in the future.

But for a long time now he has harassed us with pitiable lamentations, maintaining that your magnificence withholds from him the agreed settlement, and that neither the misery of a poor man nor the truth of the agreement moves your holiness in any respect. If anything has at some time perhaps been paid, it has always been after many exertions and delays, and either of less value in appearance or inferior in quality. We therefore ask and earnestly beseech you that your favour may provide in this matter for its own honour, for the poor man’s justice, and for relief of our trouble; and that you cause to be given to him, not merely faithfully but generously, what was promised before so great an assembly of venerable persons. Otherwise, this wandering and obstinate man may perhaps be compelled to seek the assistance of the apostolic majesty, bringing against both us and you a common complaint: namely, that its mandate was fulfilled by us with insufficient fidelity and that the faith of the settlement was observed by you with insufficient truth.

LXXXI. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER.

Your majesty delegated to our lowliness, for canonical decision without impediment of appeal, the case contested between William, priest, and Matthew, clerk, concerning the church of Godarville. Both parties having therefore appeared before us, Will. alleged that he had lawfully possessed the aforesaid church and had later been despoiled of it by violence without any judgment whatever. He therefore urgently sought from us restoration of possession.

To prove the possession which he claimed, he produced four priests as witnesses; one of them proved incompetent, while the other three were found sufficiently concordant under examination. He most firmly denied that Matthew had ever possessed it; and he said that Matthew, before judges delegated by your sublimity—namely the lord of Rouen, who was then governing the church of Évreux, and Lord Giles, now bishop of Évreux, who was then exercising the office of archdeacon in the Church of Rouen—had brought suit concerning the same church and at last had publicly renounced that suit before them, abjured the same church, and received forty shillings in compensation for expenses he had incurred. [Note: [Col. 0108D] C.: “Rotrou.”]

To prove this he put forward a priest, an acolyte, and a certain layman, who were likewise found concordant under examination. The matter, moreover, was very well known to the aforesaid judges and to the whole Church of Rouen, because it had been carried out before almost the entire community. Since the objection of abjuration seemed prejudicial, however, and the testimony of those produced did not give us sufficiently certain assurance, we judged that the case should be deferred until the full truth could become known to us through the judges to whom the case was said to have been delegated and the venerable persons likewise said to have been present.

When they had come with me into the presence of the lord archbishop and I had diligently required from him testimony of the truth, William, without awaiting his testimony, appealed to your hearing on the first Sunday of Advent. Since he could not be compelled to proceed against his will, and since at his own request and in his own favour the impediment of appeal appeared to have been removed, I ought not to turn that removal to his injury. Having accordingly put the other party back into the possession in which he had been, I gave both parties the letters they requested, through which the truth of what was done before us may become known to your majesty.

LXXXII. TO HENRY, ABBOT OF FÉCAMP.

Our friends who recently set out for Jerusalem have turned me from a horseman into a pedestrian. Since it is unworthy that a man of my standing should be restored to horseback through the hands of humble persons, I judged that this matter should be referred to your glory—you whom not only the dignity of knightly rank but also the eminence of royal blood has exalted.

I considered it all the more fitting to reserve this for your merits because your industry renders those to whom it gives more prudent: in the very liberality of your giving you preserve, among prudent men, a friendly economy, so that a friend may always find with you something pleasing, while you yourselves do not lack an appropriate occasion for generosity. Thus, with you, both learning and revenue are profitably sought: abundance makes men wealthier, and prudence wiser. Your discernment operates between the two in such a way as to preserve what belongs to virtue on either side while separating and repelling what belongs to vice, lest extravagance abolish sobriety or parsimony ever draw tight hands that ought to be open.

Yet if one must err in either direction, I would rather be found easy than difficult, sometimes readier than slower. Among all gifts, however, a horse is what makes the giver liable to the greatest number of complaints. For if it lacks anything of excellence, those to whom it is given immediately attribute the fault to the giver; and they ascribe the imperfection of the thing—even when it perhaps arises from poverty—to imperfection of will. If it walks too roughly, they accuse the giver of jolting them and declare themselves doomed to a fall if its hoof, checked by chance, strikes against a turf-clod. If it is stubborn, they say that it has inherited stubbornness from its former master, who was accustomed to listen more slowly to friends than a horse obeys spurs. If its form is less elegant or it has less beauty, they maintain that the ill-formed thing [Note: [Col. 0109D] B.: “well-formed.”] is not sufficiently suited to the dignity either of giver or recipient.

Meanwhile, if there is any cursing to be done, they curse not the horse but rather its author, who seems to have inflicted an injury through so many causes of offense rather than conferred a benefit. They openly declare that they do not wish anything further to be requested from one who gave what it would have been better to refuse than to bestow with an added harm. It is also certain that some are found not only fault-finders but ungrateful as well, inventing false defects in the thing given so as to appear released from every obligation of gratitude.

Yet whoever receives is immediately bound by the very act of receiving; and if the gift remains in his possession, a legal defence, as it were, of prescription confronts the person alleging defects. For in gifts there is no action for reduction of price nor an action for rescission; the exception of voluntary liberality defeats every claim. But if the favour of those who receive does not answer benefactors, virtue will nevertheless not lack its own reward. Considering rather the gains of inward fruit, it finds sufficient glory simply in the testimony within itself of a happy conscience concerning good done.

Virtue is not subject to the judgment of external arrangement; standing in the majesty of its own purity, it does not seek rewards from those less worthy. Yet it neither rejects what honourably comes from them nor, through desire for them or use of them, abandons anything it knows to be better. But if anyone is drawn by external gain, he cannot, as that wise man says, expect any outcome except one like its material; for one intent on things of chance will experience only chance events.

LXXXIII. TO LORD WILLIAM OF PAVIA, CARDINAL.

The frequent benefits bestowed have proved how great a favour divine goodness has long granted me in your eyes. I have indeed been grateful with my whole heart, but no performance of the service owed could compensate for the majesty of your condescension. Still, I count myself happy if I am ever found not to have received ungratefully what you have always bestowed freely and with such cheerfulness, and if my devotion may recognize itself as redeemed by any token of mine.

Meanwhile, on every occasion I turn to that same proven goodwill, certain that in your excellency the truth of friendship can neither suffer diminution nor incur any old age. Therefore I earnestly ask that Master G., whom I send to the lord pope on certain business, may be commended to your benevolence, so that, instructed by your counsel and supported by your aid, he may attain the desired result in the affairs he carries.

LXXXIV. TO THE LEGATES ALBERT AND THEODWIN.

I received the command of your sublimity that, near the day of the Lord’s Circumcision, I should cause Ric. Urselli to appear before your presence, to answer a certain Rob. concerning the church of Cormorlem, which the latter claims lawfully belongs to him. I have done as you commanded, for it is my purpose to obey all your commands in every respect with complete humility and diligence.

The man who has been summoned complains that the time assigned is excessively short, since in so little time he cannot, with much labour and great expense, procure the necessary preparation. He is a man of importance, and must seek assistance from remote and scattered places and afterwards travel into another province to come before you, though not even fifteen days have been allowed him for complete preparation. This, clearly, has been craftily sought by his adversary, who has conceived no confidence in justice and truth, but hopes, because of the man’s inability, to extort something through harassment and some settlement.

The church in question is situated in the diocese of Bayeux, and the case never at any time came for examination before its own bishop. But the other party, having procured letters from the apostolic see, transferred the case—because the truth of the matter was publicly known in the Church of Bayeux—to a foreign bishop, namely the bishop of Avranches, in order that he might there assert whatever he pleased more boldly. Yet the lord of Avranches, a truly religious and prudent man, having inquired more diligently into the truth, learned that Ric. had possessed it continuously for more than thirty years, had always served it through vicars, and had received its benefices by his own right.

It was also established that Robert was the son of a priest who was known to have been vicar of that very church, and that he had prepared material for this fraudulent claim of possession from the fact that he had at times received there what fell to his father for performing parochial duties and had spent it on his own needs, those of his mother, and those of the rest of his father’s household. He was therefore repelled, and peace in the lawsuit was granted to Richard; but he appealed to the hearing of the Roman pontiff for the Kalends of February.

Richard has sent representatives and awaits the apostolic majesty’s answer, hoping that what was so rightly done by a religious bishop under its command will be confirmed by that authority. It is not expedient for our province, in which unchastity daily grows so shamelessly strong, that priests’ sons should be attached to their fathers’ altars, lest the crime of incestuous concubinage appear to have been permitted by indulgence lavishly extended either by the pope himself or by you, and lest the offspring of filth defile the sanctuary of the Lord by the example of paternal depravity.

Let your eyes therefore see what is equitable: whether, for recognition of truth already known, the bishop to whom the case belonged in the first instance according to due order should be awaited in respect of the legation he received at your will; whether deference should be shown to the appeal to the apostolic see; whether a religious bishop who investigated the matter under delegation should be believed; and finally, whether a longer period should be allowed, so that, once everything has been examined, our intervention may appear to have benefited our son in maintaining his right.

LXXXV. TO ALBERT AND THEODWIN, CARDINALS.

For the venerable man Reginald, bishop-elect of Bath, we remember having petitioned your excellency: namely, that he was elected in concord by that church and received by the unanimous will of all. This is so certain that nothing in the whole kingdom is better known; nor is there anyone who proposes to oppose the person or wishes in any respect to impugn the act of election.

He peacefully administers the affairs and property of the Church with full authority, arranging and dispensing everything that an elected bishop can perform apart from the grace of consecration.
