But because he cannot attain the completion of that grace without consent of your authority, that church has sent to you venerable persons chosen from its whole body, who, on behalf of all, may seek from your goodness with eager wishes and implore with earnest prayers the completion of his promotion.

We saw them: Thomas, archdeacon, and A., a monk of that church—for that church has a community of monks, not a college of clerks—and Master Lanulf, men certainly learned and prudent and of integrity approved by many. They were pursuing this affair with every effort by delegation of all; but they could by no means find a way to reach you. We laboured with them, as did many others, yet no safe means of gaining access to you could be found—especially since the younger king, who resides in those regions, is said to oppose the matter.

To support their wishes, they carefully obtained letters both from our humility and from others, and sent on the business a messenger who could conceal himself by the garb of a stricter religious life and by poverty, since it could not otherwise be done. Since the accomplishment of so important a matter has been prevented only by the urgency of present wars and chance events, we believe it accords with your holiness and office—and we have judged that devout prayers should be added to the same end—that you complete and confirm what remains. Do not permit the wishes of the church to be mocked or its interests to be further obstructed.

LXXXVI. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER.

There is a matter which grievously troubles both my own and other churches: the rapacious and intemperate audacity of certain monks. In order to indulge themselves more freely, they purchase the protection of secular power; first they withdraw all obedience from bishops, and then, with sacrilegious rashness, presume by every kind of compact to receive parish churches, together with altars, tithes, and other benefices, from lay hands.

In these transactions neither canonical order nor episcopal consent is required of them. Having diverted all things to private ownership, they appoint hired priests there in such extreme poverty that they have nothing which would suffice even for a shepherd or a runner, either for their own maintenance or for bearing the burdens of the Church. This is widespread; but in my diocese this evil has raged more fiercely. They now oppose us not under any pretext of reason, but through deceits, gifts, and the protection of secular violence.

To reform this according to the order of ecclesiastical institution, I have obtained from your sublimity first, second, and third judges against a certain abbot and the monks of a monastery in our diocese, namely Saint-Evroul; but although the abbot has always resisted by many devices, nothing has yet been brought to completion. Meanwhile our priests, in prosecuting the case before the judges appointed, have been exhausted by great expenses and afflicted by much labour.

We have other cases as well against the same abbot, concerning his manifold and obstinate disobedience, although he is bound by the bond of sworn profession to render us obedience and reverence. We also have a case of another perjury which he openly incurred before many venerable persons after physically swearing that he would make satisfaction at our command. After sentence of suspension and anathema, he presumed for five years and more to celebrate masses and the other divine offices, until, after the truth we allege had become known before your legates, he submitted to be absolved by us more from necessity than from penitence. He swore, namely, that at our command he would answer explicitly for three transgressions and fulfil the prescribed manner of satisfaction.

The same abbot is also answerable to you and to our church concerning a privilege obtained from you by fraud. Having discovered the falsity, you have now for the third time ordered him to be sent to you with the privilege. There is also a certain hermitage granted by us and its founder to certain regular and religious brethren, newly occupied by the aforesaid abbot and monks after an appeal to you had been made; and certain other matters which the fidelity and diligence of our messenger will fully explain to your reverence in all truth.

LXXXVII. TO HENRY, BISHOP OF BAYEUX.

I remember that I formerly petitioned your excellency for the bearer of this letter, because the urgent requests of certain persons whom I could not fail induced me to petition on his behalf. You granted the request in part, in that you moderated for a time the imposition of a more severe sentence; nevertheless, the desired benefit of complete release has not yet smiled upon him.

Those who pressed from the beginning with lavish prayers continue to press, and all the more earnestly because they know that your affection is accustomed to grant my requests. Repeated petition compels me therefore to repeat my prayers and casts me at the knees of your charity, that this man may rejoice to have found, through multiplied petitions, a remedy of fuller grace.

I have also heard that the lord archbishop and the lord of Avranches have written for him and have mercifully forgiven the fault which he incurred, because, when summoned before you, he preferred humbly to confess what he had done rather than, by a doubled fault, darken his conscience with lies or despair of your mercy. I therefore judged that my prayers should be joined more confidently to their prayers and counsel, so that, if your majesty deems their admonition worthy of obedience, my intercession too may support so great an authority.

LXXXVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS OF CANTERBURY AND TARENTAISE.

We have heard that the case of our venerable brother Reginald, bishop-elect of Bath, has been entrusted by the apostolic majesty to your experience. We rejoiced that the examination of truth has been committed to lovers of truth, before whom neither justice can incur danger nor innocence loss.

If you consider the man, he is one whose prudence, integrity, virtue, and industry have become publicly known by many and highly convincing proofs. If the act of election is examined, the unanimous wishes of all those to whom it belongs have converged upon his person, and they confidently trust that the condition of the Church, shaken for many years, will be restored by his magnificence.

As for what has been objected against him, by persons to whom it does not belong to object, as falsely as it has been imprudently: definite proofs will show you that it is nothing but a charge born of hatred and envy. We, to whom truth could more certainly and easily appear at close hand, have learned through the testimony, believed worthy of credit, of many persons and through public assertion that the birth now complained of preceded his father’s sacred orders, and that his father at that time could lawfully, had he chosen, have served as a knight or contracted marriage.

Proceed, therefore, and examine with impartial judgment this calumny, which you will find to have arisen from no source other than the zeal of malice, according to the spirit and authority given you by God. Do not permit the wishes of the church to be mocked any longer through delay; but, once the favour of the blessing duly owed has been granted, send him as soon as possible to the church destined for him, so that the hopes of that long-afflicted church may at last grow strong for a better future and that people may rejoice to have obtained the help of the consolation they desire.

LXXXIX. TO ROTROU, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN.

That monk L., formerly of Cormel, for whom, as you write, your holiness has received an apostolic rescript, left that monastery and was mercifully received back three times. When he left a fourth time, the abbot and brethren refused to receive him because of sacrileges committed in the Church—such as shame itself forbids one to recount—and because he had fathered two offspring by prostitutes outside the monastery gates. Convicted and confessing publicly before us, Abbot P. of Celles, and our brethren, he obtained letters of dismissal from the abbot. Having forsworn for life the abbey and the whole banlieue, or jurisdictional district, of the monastery—because he had publicly threatened to set fire to it—he departed.

Later, when he brought the matter to the notice of William of Pavia, cardinal, in the presence of myself and the abbot, the cardinal, after the truth had been set forth, repelled and condemned him by authority of the apostolic see. Thereafter, having wandered through various lands, utterly casting off the monastic habit and becoming an apostate, he publicly gave himself over, to speak more sparingly, to every sort of dissoluteness.

Finally, if he has attempted to deceive the apostolic majesty—before which these facts could not have been known—by lies, that ought not to prejudice truth and justice before you, to whom we shall make known in every respect the manifest truth of what we say. You know, moreover, that apostolic prudence determines nothing in doubtful matters, but that all its mandates contain an implicit condition: namely, that the petitions rest upon truth, and that for those to whom such mandates are sent, full examination and judgment of the case remain reserved to the judge.

Let your holiness therefore provide for the peace of the monastery and for cloistral discipline, lest, if the author of wickedness is restored, the audacity of the rest—corrected through his punishment—revive, and their malice again grow strong through the example of an overly lenient pardon.

XC. FORM OF A SETTLEMENT CONCERNING A CERTAIN COMMISSION.

Cases brought before our hearing, whether by our ordinary jurisdiction or by superior delegation, must, just as they are decided with impartial judgment, be confirmed once decided by the testimony of truth, lest a renewed dispute arise with any audacity to revive an old lawsuit.

We therefore received by apostolic delegation, for final settlement without impediment of appeal, the case disputed between our venerable brother Simon, abbot of Saint Andrew’s, and the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem concerning the testament of the illustrious man Hugh of Pinu. Having heard the allegations of both parties, when the grave necessity of judgment seemed imminent, each party entrusted itself to our discretion, and the entire litigation was settled by us through amicable composition.

We decided that the money said to have been deposited with the aforesaid abbot by the aforementioned illustrious man should be distributed for necessary and pious purposes according to the tenor of the testament, as was made manifest to us by the testimony of those produced by the brethren of the Hospital. Accordingly, after assigning an appropriate share to creditors, needy persons, the abbot himself, and various other poor people, we assigned the largest share to the brethren of the Hospital, in consideration of their religious life and poverty. Having secured the consent of all concerned and provided for their interests, we judged that the abbot himself should be completely absolved from this dispute.

XCI. TO HENRY, ELDER KING OF ENGLAND.

I was intending to come to you, but old age, infirmity, and weakness restrain me, as though I were bound with certain fetters of disabling incapacity. I am also harassed in many directions by many wrongs, for which I expect no remedy except from the favour of your goodness.

I therefore send to you John of the abbey, a man faithful and devoted alike to you, whom I ask you to hear in my place and to whom I ask you for a moment to incline your royal ears at my request. I beseech your excellency to remember the faith, devotion, and service which from the beginning of your youth I have always rendered to your honour and advantage; and may my merits at times obtain their due response from you in my need. Let not your magnificence deem it fitting to crush the weakness of my old age; rather, cherish by royal generosity one who has always submitted himself, with all humility and patience, to your will, and allow—indeed, cause—my last days, during which I shall still be with you for a short time, to be completed in joy.

The purity of my conscience does not permit me to despair of your wisdom, before which I have often deserved favour in many and very great matters. If anything was ever done less wisely through ignorance or simplicity, faithfulness, truth, and the constant diligence of devoted service always made amends. In sum, the harsh counsel of one who truly loves is better than the deceptive flattery of one who flatters, as your majesty experienced quite recently by weighty evidence, when, although your friends had almost despaired, the terror of your magnificence prevailed and all the efforts of your enemies were, by God’s favour, crushed alike through your prudence and valour.

I still remember—and nothing will ever be able to tear this from my memory—that in the early days of your rule your sublimity received me into greater favour and that you always acted upon my counsel, which you used more frequently, in complete tranquillity. It brought you no loss, no labour, no embarrassment of any kind; rather, the great deeds of all your undertakings seemed to proceed almost miraculously. There was no one who presumed to oppose your power, because at that time reason ordered all your actions, justice directed them, and mercy moderated them.

But after the lying crowd of flatterers grew strong and was able freely to pour in the deadly blandishments of poisoned honey, justice began to yield to favour and reason to will; and by treacherous diligence it sometimes transformed into contrary inclinations minds formerly formed by better counsel. Hence, certainly, arose what has happened: for a root which derives no freshness from justice and truth cannot ultimately yield pleasant and useful fruit.

It is indeed true that good things are sometimes shaken by afflictions and evil things prosper for a time in a kind of deceptive happiness; but by divine judgment the outcome at last always answers to the merits of things. Thus it is: the unhappy outcomes of unconsidered actions are followed by late repentance, which provides material for grief but restores none of the losses that have occurred. Hence that celebrated saying of the Wise Man: “Do everything with counsel, and after the deed you will not repent” (Ecclesiasticus 32).

Counsel, moreover, is a rational deliberation truly thought out concerning whether something should or should not be done, as the eloquence of Tully defines it for us. Let my lord understand that three things constitute the definition of counsel: unity, diligence, and reason—so that what is done or said may rest upon unity, be directed by care, and be shaped by reason. For whatever does not receive from truth a stable substance is necessarily liable to collapse and failure: that which arose from nothing is reduced to nothing and does not endure in the solidity of any foundation; it has shone out as if from some empty illusion of falsehood.

Even in matters that are true, judgment must always be applied with the pressing diligence of reason, lest anyone presume, in confidence of power, to disturb another’s peace or invade another’s right. Rather, continually embracing the measure of justice and cautiously casting the keen sight of the mind in every direction, he should show reverence to superiors, favour to inferiors, and charity to neighbours. Thus let everyone measure all disposition by his own conscience, taking care to render himself to others in benefits and injuries such as he would wish to find them in his own needs.

Those who rule, however, are bound to recognize more strictly the obligation of their office: they should know that they have received dominion for guardianship rather than violence, and should think that God, who has care of them, has conferred upon them eminence of rank, abundance of wealth, and glory of power for no other reason than to place them in the work of ministry. In due time they must render account for every particular beneath the severe examination of the strict Judge.

Whoever, then, has accepted the danger of administration must prepare to render account, since he who entrusted it threatens to exact it even to the last farthing. If glory does not descend with such powerful persons—and no ascent is promised to them, but descent—what will one offer to the claimant who has kept back nothing with which he may pay? Surely flesh and spirit: for nothing of what has been seized will remain, nor can there be another manner of satisfaction except that he pay eternal punishment who has nothing else by which he can be released from an everlasting debt.

They ought to remember that they have been entrusted by him who redeemed them at the price of his own blood and freed them even through the bitterness of death. From him they have the same nature of substance; the same price of redemption, the same consummation, and the same reward belong to all. There is no ground on which some may glory in privilege against others, except that those who preside are exposed to a heavier fall and greater danger.

I have written at greater length because devotion supplied an abundance of words, and every point seemed necessary to me, so that faithful admonition might make you mindful of your glory. Would that the royal majesty valued and recognized men of virtue and the counsels of the strong, lest the spirit of wickedness and falsehood, by deceitful flatteries, weaken the strength of royal power and draw and incline it toward works of malice or failure.

XCII. TO HENRY, ELDER KING OF ENGLAND.

As I told you in Normandy, I came into England to fulfil vows of prayer to the Lord. When thereafter I was drawn with great desire toward the presence of my lord, I heard that you were making for York and the remote regions beyond it; no hope or confidence of reaching you remained to me.

Yet I set out, though at a slow pace, because old age and weakness do not permit me speed, but hold me bound as though with certain knots of disabling incapacity. Let it therefore please my lord to direct me where and when I may meet your majesty, lest what strength remains to me be consumed in an uncertain and therefore wandering journey.

For I desire as soon as possible to see my lord’s face, so that the welcome serenity of the royal countenance may shine upon my eyes, and, through the accustomed kindness shown me, I may recover breath after wrongs and prolonged labours. Farewell.

XCIII. TO HENRY, ELDER KING OF ENGLAND.

I set out for England to plead my cause, and immediately hastened to see my lord’s face, since both devotion and necessity summoned me to do so. You heard me and granted some of my requests; yet you deferred greater matters for the future, adding nevertheless a promise, in the reassuring hope bestowed on me by which I take comfort. For you promised that thereafter you would examine my conduct carefully and, according to the quality of my merits, justice would in due time be rendered me before you. Rejoicing, I trusted in the sincere truth of my good conscience: no fault would allow your Excellency to be angered or your goodwill darkened; nor would the crafty malice of envious men now outwit your prudence. Rather, according to the Gospel’s teaching, you would believe the deeds themselves, and your judgment would proceed from the evident proofs of the facts. Would that, in considering the present circumstances, your graciousness might sometime remember the devoted loyalty and service I have shown continually, and what has at times accrued, beyond that of others, to your honour and advantage through my particular counsel and industry; and finally what labours and expenditures I have always borne with you in complete cheerfulness—by which the strength of body and material resources has been worn down and exhausted over thirty uninterrupted years. I would say that I had succeeded—indeed, I would glory with joy of heart—if I had felt that even a little of these things had remained in your memory: matters in which you could in no way have been deceived, but which you have always recognized by direct knowledge and manifold result.  

From the second year of your reign, indeed, I perceived that your favour—which had always embraced me abundantly—had been diminished through the accusations of certain persons. In good faith I had admitted them to intimacy and counsel, believing that their prudence and industry would be useful to you and that through them I would be maintained in the goodwill before you which I had deserved. But what has happened to me is what unhappy experience has proved to happen to many: I have been somewhat thrust aside by those advanced through my own diligent efforts. Thus it is: among those most acceptable and intimate to exalted men, loyalty and affection are often rare; and by many arts they strive to get ahead, since each believes whatever has been taken from another is to be assigned to himself.  

Understanding this, I judged that I must press more strongly for your honour and advantage, so that my effort and perseverance might bring confusion on deceivers and restore to me the fullness of your favour, of which it was evident that some remnants still remained. I made some progress, but I could not attain the former fullness; and in these latter days I feel him more violently embittered whom, in these latter days, God is witness, I had hoped wholly to win back by sincere loyalty and most ready services. Let my lord indeed return to his heart, for the time for mercy has come. I do not propose henceforth to allege anything before you concerning my merits, but humbly to implore mercy alone. The more desirable mercy is, the more highly it ought to be valued in princes; and if it is glorious to bestow it upon penitent offenders, surely it ought not to be denied to innocence.  

My long life and extensive travels have made me known and esteemed throughout the world; and many may perhaps judge it inhuman if your graciousness pursues my innocence and the time of my extreme old age with severity; if you render a harsher judgment upon ambiguous suspicion than upon the truth of facts; if you cause me to enter the enclosure of the grave, now imminent, with tears and mourning; if you allow the condition of the Church to be shaken, which, in my days, your serenity’s benefits have made rich from poor, exalted from humble, renowned from obscure.  

## XCIV. TO WILLIAM, DEAN OF BAYEUX

As your prudence knows, the authority of the Roman pontiff delegated to us and to you the cause pending between the bishop of Le Mans and Clement, on the condition that, if either of us should be unwilling or unable to attend, the other should nevertheless decide it without impediment from an appeal. By this it is plainly understood that, in the absence of one, the whole authority of inquiry and judgment is entrusted to the other. The absentee has no right to commit his functions to someone else, because the whole authority to decide the case is granted to the other, as the superior authority of the one who delegated it has prescribed. Since the pressing urgency of many matters presently draws me into England, you must take the place of both parties and determine the cause by your sole judgment.  

## XCV. TO . . . . .

You saw how much I achieved with our Lord in England—you who endured with me the weary persistence of importunate petition, and at last carried away the humiliation of a harsher rebuff. I fear that he has become hardened against me and will never readily return to himself, because anger or hatred once conceived is not ordinarily easily appeased or restored to favour. From the second year of his reign, indeed, by frequent and utterly certain indications, I understood that ever since then he has oppressed my innocence, openly or as though covertly, under a certain guise of dissimulated severity, and has cut off every accrual of honour or advantage deriving either from me or from my own people.  

Neither purity of loyalty, nor assiduity of service, nor unremitting labour, nor excessive expenditure, nor skill in counsel zealously and effectively directed toward great and greatest matters and the glory of his majesty, could avert the bitterness of resentment conceived without cause. Rather, by a remarkable perversity, merits which ought entirely to have recovered favour sincerely provoked hatred. I therefore pressed on more vigorously, and, as though determined to overcome it, strove to heap merit upon merit, so that, when the radiance of praiseworthy deeds was seen, the baffled malice of flatterers might blush, and frequent, devoted truth might wring favour even from an unwilling lord.  

I made no progress; yet meanwhile he continually made use of my service, and, excluding me from matters which he could freely order according to his own will, he diligently and deliberately called me to consider greater affairs—matters in which the scale of the business, the danger of its outcome, and the pressure of its difficulty compelled him to seek counsel. Twenty years have passed since I have sweat miserably in this struggle, because a sincere conscience sustained untiring perseverance, and because of the continual display of outstanding merits. I have not sinned; but if perhaps there is any sin, its guilt does not exceed the freedom of royal clemency. At least he ought, without pain to me, to have been moved by the losses of a Church that had done no wrong, lest he derive glory from another’s affliction or draw sweet pleasure for himself from another’s bitterness.  

Yet it is astonishing that, amid the injuries I suffer and my abundant tears, zeal for a love deeply rooted in my heart has not yet been torn away. Nothing is more bitter to me than that he charges his most loyal servant with the crime of treachery, repays one who loves him with hatred, and permits me to breathe no confidence for the future in his esteem and favour. I am sending him a letter full of all humility and supplication, as you will be able to see from its copy. I would like it to be offered to him, once a suitable opportunity has been found, in the presence of your charity, so that, through your intervention, he may consent to hear it once in its entirety. And I ask you to inform me by letter whether you receive any answer or anticipate any result.  

## XCVI. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER

The complaint of a certain distinguished man is brought before the hearing of Your Majesty. For several reasons I am bound to him in many ways, so that I am rightly obliged, with justice leading the way, to furnish timely counsel and assistance in his necessities. He has a wife to whom the succession of her entire paternal inheritance was believed to belong. Unexpectedly, a girl is produced and brought forward from the secrecy of a clandestine upbringing—a girl whom the whole land knows to have been born of adultery during her husband’s prolonged absence. The man identified as her father, publicly questioned before the bishop of the place, before the archbishop of the province, and even before the king himself, most steadfastly denied that she was his. Almost all those connected with her by close kinship have not dared to give testimony to her legitimate birth.  

Under this hope of fraudulently obtaining the inheritance, she married a certain man who, with his supporters, solicits the false father by threats as well as promises, in order to turn him away from his public avowal of the truth. An appeal has been made to you, before whom deceit or violence cannot prevail against truth and justice. We have therefore judged it all the safer to write to Your Majesty, since we bear witness not as petitioners concerning an uncertain matter, but concerning a truth that is known.  

## XCVII. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER

[Col. 0120C]

If a certain priest named John of Grimouville comes before Your Majesty, receive him with discernment, for he has been excommunicated and remained under excommunication for about ten years. He laid violent hands on a monk, himself a priest, and would, it is said, have killed him outright, wounded and covered in much blood, had not those standing with the monk vigorously driven him off. Since by this act he had clearly incurred sentence of anathema, he neither wished to seek absolution from the Roman pontiff nor to make satisfaction to the monk, nor would he obey us in any respect. Instead, withdrawing to remote parts of another diocese, he secretly received priestly orders while under the aforesaid bond; and in those parts, without my knowledge, publicly ministered in the order thus received.  

Blind ambition had led him from the first years of his youth to commit this perversity: namely, ambition to acquire a certain parish church in our bishopric, which he believed he could secure through the violence of the common multitude to whom he was related. Though he spent twelve years and more on this, neither any merit nor any justice required me to grant his request, because on this account he repeatedly offended me and did not cease to harass the Church with many injuries. When the priest who had served in that church for about forty years died, I appointed a suitable person at the presentation of the monks of Préaux, to whom it belonged; and I did so all the more swiftly so that there would be someone able to resist his obstinacy, lest he imagine he could more easily seize the vacant church.  

Frustrated and deprived of every comfort of his long-standing hope, he obtained letters from your legates to the archbishop, and they sent him to the latter, taking away from me—without my knowledge and against my will—ordinary jurisdiction over him. Before the archbishop, because the matter was conducted among relatives and persons aware of the facts, evidence was so strongly brought against him that his crimes could easily be established and his false accusation detected. Caught by the signs of manifest truth, and having no other opening available, he appealed from the archbishop, whom he had chosen as judge, to Your hearing, hoping that, if the examination of the case were delegated, he could outwit the judge with deceitful oaths or extort something by vexations.  

Since, when one person succeeds by falsehood, the boldness of many gains strength from the example, it is publicly important that Your kindness not be too credulous toward the perversity of people of this kind, and that judges receive their appointment not from the parties’ choice but rather from your own tested judgment. They press upon you with obstinate requests for judges whom they think may be bought off, or with whom they are connected by familiar favour for every contingency. Therefore, if the man about whom we write is found in your presence, please have inquiry made: by which bishop he was first ordained and by which he was last ordained; who absolved him from the shedding of a priest’s blood; by whom and at what time the church he seeks was given to him. For the priest died within these three years, although he is known to have ministered there continuously for more than forty years; nor could the church by any right have been conferred upon this man while the priest survived. If, after my ordination—of which he first made use—he transferred to another bishop without my knowledge and dismissal, let him acknowledge the hand of his ordainer and the title he received; for by law I am not bound to receive a cleric ordained by another, especially one secretly ordained, and particularly one whom I know to be entangled in such grave crimes.  

## XCVIII. TO HUGH, ARCHDEACON OF LISIEUX, HIS NEPHEW

I joyfully received your letter concerning repentance and conversion. Would that it proceeded from holy purpose and rested in the stable truth of faith. But since the teaching of truth instructs us to believe deeds, I shall consider your deeds; may they be such that they ought to erase the memory of former things and bear fitting fruits by which prior losses may be repaired. If, however—to say less—your negligence has tarnished the disposition which from the beginning you had experienced in many ways as freely helpful and kind, merits progressing from their assumed colour to their former brightness may restore it. The benefits conferred upon you, moreover, ought to restrain your noble character from giving offence until you have made some return of thanksgiving, however slight.  

Certainly, one condemned as ungrateful proves himself unworthy of every benefit, so much so that for this reason a freedman may be reduced again to slavery; and one who does not impart to another the mercy he has received is condemned by divine judgment, in respect of that which was remitted him, to payment of the very last farthing.  

## XCIX. TO HENRY, ELDER KING OF ENGLAND

Hearing of your imminent crossing, I took care to come to you with all speed, as to my lord, so that the serenity of the royal countenance might shine upon my eyes and the weakness of my old age and infirmity might be restored by the favour of your gracious speech. I came indeed, but everything turned out very differently from what I had hoped, since I was thought worthy to be heard only in a few matters and was not granted even a partial hearing in any matter. I came, I say, intending, as I supposed, to say to you a final farewell, and to receive the same from you with joy, so that, after all my merits and your exceeding benefits, at my final departure harmony might answer one another in the good of perpetual charity and peace of heart.  

Whatever may happen, however, or whatever turn the outcome of future events may take, my glory toward you is the testimony of my conscience. I am entirely free of every fault; and among all those whose loyalty and devotion have benefited your honour and advantage, my merits—if I may say so modestly—may be equalled with greater ones. For thirty years have passed in which I have always sweated in the struggle of your service. If at any time the envy of accusers stirred any movement of your mind against me, I stood all the more securely and pressed on all the more manfully and effectively, so that the lies of flatterers might rightly be rejected through my loyalty and magnificence.  

I began as a boy, and have accompanied you almost through adolescence, youth, manhood, and into the years of old age. I have spent my entire body and soul, effort and labour, money and time; and nothing has ever been more delightful to me than serving your honour and interests. I did so in the assured expectation that in my last days royal Excellency would respond generously to me. If I have not offended, why do I suffer? Why does my lord not rather trust the truth of my deeds than the uncertain suspicions and lies of accusers? But if I have offended in a way that should be judged worthy not of pardon but of punishment, the power of punishment remains with you—provided, however, that judgment proceeds not from uncertainty but lawfully from the truth of the facts.  

In short, this single thing, and that the chief thing, I would seek from my lord by every prayer: that some hope of his goodwill may be left to me, which I may keep in my bosom like a hidden treasure, and in which I may be allowed at all times to breathe freely. When I withdrew from you, I was going to say certain things, but no suitable opportunity appeared. I therefore send them to you in writing on a slip through the bearer of this letter. Whatever of them you may please to do, I shall receive with every expression of thanks; whatever you choose to defer, I shall bear silently with all humility and patience.  

## C. TO WALTER OF COUTANCES

[Col. 0123A]

Your favour felt compassion for me because I was dismissed by the lord king as you heard and saw, and it grieved for my humiliation and losses. In that moment of exceedingly grievous sorrow, I was so overcome in spirit by bitterness that I could not see what I should do; I chiefly considered swift flight the remedy, and therefore I left the face of his anger as quickly as possible, like a fugitive. But on my return, while my mind was carried away by many thoughts of escape, I considered that he might judge my quick departure to be not fear but rather contempt and pride, because I had not pursued his displeasure with prolonged supplication and long prayers.  

I therefore resolved to return to him with all speed, so that wiser repentance might seem to repair what had been less well done and the pride he had suspected might be removed by the substance of humility. From my house near Bayeux I reached Cerisy; and there the weakness brought on by my debility grew so severe that I could not proceed without danger to my bodily health, because the effort and eagerness of returning had consumed almost all my bodily strength. When I had therefore taken to bed, I could do nothing except send a letter and messenger in my stead, so that the truth of the letter and the diligence of the messenger might explain my affairs to my lord. I judged that he should especially be sent to your affection, so that through your effort he might be introduced to the king at an opportune moment and, if it can be arranged, you might hear the letter, thereby receiving a fuller occasion to know what you should do or say. The letter contains nothing but humility and supplication, so that, if he wishes to remember royal generosity, he ought rightly to be inclined to grant its request.  

## CI. TO HENRY, ELDER KING OF ENGLAND

You promised me generous assistance from royal munificence, so that I might withdraw from this position, in which I cannot remain long without danger to my salvation, and, with the Lord’s favour, move to a safer life. Thus my case was presented before your countenance; necessity and poverty pleaded my cause, when you considered in me both the advance of advanced old age and that my resources were insufficient to meet my debts. Your graciousness exceeded all my merit, and the fullness of your favour fittingly answered my importunity.  

Would that my lord remembered that Lord Peter, your legate, a man of great honour and prudence, not only suggested and approved this action to you, but also praised it highly as a benefit worthy of royal majesty: namely, that in such need you should extend the gracious hand of generous bounty to your faithful and true lover, whom you have so often found prompt, loyal, and useful in your necessities, by many proofs. Would that my lord, according to the Gospel’s teaching, believed deeds and was not deceived by the flattering blandishments of flatterers, who regard as wholly lost whatever they see bestowed on another’s advantage. Let your goodness, therefore, review in impartial truth my whole life, in which I have stood continually beside you from my youth, so that favour due to merits may be repaid.  

You know, lord, that I am a man of many days, known in many regions and welcome to many persons. Many, too, would be pleased at your Majesty’s magnificence if they saw or heard that I left you with tears not of bitterness but of devotion. I am ready to depart, and no circumstance delays my withdrawal, if only your benefit has satisfied my needs. Have mercy, then, have mercy on me, because the time for mercy has come; so that, having laid aside every burden of temporal affairs, I may pass into the repose of divine contemplation, where devoted diligence may continually offer efficacious prayers for both my salvation and the honour and welfare of your Majesty.  

The archbishop of Rouen, the bishop of Bayeux, and certain other faithful men of yours, to whom this had been entrusted by you, discussed the matter with me. I readily accepted their persuasion, so that your discretion need not have any doubt about my departure, provided your generosity bestows the desired fulfillment upon my hope as promised. Do, then, what befits your magnificence and truth, and what the unconquerable urgency of my necessity demands: that, wholly separated from the episcopal office, I may be freed from the importunate summons of the approaching council.  

## CII. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER

Called with others to the council, I could not come with the others, because many causes rendered me incapable of that labour. First is old age: I have passed my seventieth year. Second is the Jerusalem expedition imposed upon me by the Roman pontiff. Third are the grievous falls by which once and again I fell from the height of my seat and was injured, so that during some ten years my former strength has not been restored by any remedies. Though one cause might miserably have sufficed, three meet together with equal urgency, so that incapacity seems to have bound me with a threefold cord.  

I greatly desired to come, that I might celebrate with others the glory of your victory and that the abundance of your blessing, as though from close by, might water my dryness. I prayed to see the venerable assembly of so many and such great fathers, to be instructed by their words, trained by their examples, and, if I could, to cooperate in restoring the liberty of God’s Church, which I grieve to see lost in many regions. Let my lord and father, therefore, hold my incapacity excused and, in merciful kindness, release me from a command I cannot fulfill. For although I do not come in bodily presence, I nevertheless stand present in complete desire and reverence.  

I would most willingly have come, because necessity presented me with many reasons to come, which perhaps it would be harmful to pass over and tedious to press upon your many and great occupations. Later, God willing, they may be dealt with more fully and conveniently through your favour.  

## CIII. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER

So long as the Church in which, by God’s permission, I serve keeps me bound, I must sometimes attend to the needs of those entrusted to me and, so far as I can, provide the help owed with due diligence. I ask, therefore, that, if any causes from our bishopric come before you, you entrust them to persons who possess zeal for God and skill in judgment. For in these days a new malice harasses the Church of God, arising from the rapacity of monks and the audacity of clerics. Having deceitfully or violently seized whatever they desire, they then claim after an appeal that they have been despoiled, so that by the oaths of three suborned witnesses they may somehow prevail.  

Indeed, the person to whom the appeal has been made sometimes embraces the appellant with a certain favour and, in avenging his own injury, sometimes wounds an innocent person’s cause. On this matter we ask Your kindness to provide, in delegating judges, that you do not entrust your judgments, or those of your representatives, to men hostile and envious toward us, whose names the bearer of this letter will indicate to you more fully. Although they publicly offer us nothing but reverence, they are more inclined to injure us whenever any covering, however thin or slight, is drawn over their purpose. Entrust matters to all others in the whole world as you please, without distinction of rank or age.  

## CIV. TO LORD CARDINAL PETER

The matter for which your favour pleaded with the lord king on my behalf has come entirely to nothing, because he has chosen rather to await certain unfortunate outcomes against me than to help me by any unqualified favour. Since I have not received the benefit I hoped for, I must do what is necessary with my own resources. I have therefore resolved, after entrusting episcopal care for the present to faithful men, to withdraw somewhere beyond the province—where there is no rest and no joy—to a place where rest may benefit both mind and body and frugality may assist repayment. Thus, once I have soon been freed from the importunate pressure of creditors, I shall immediately return to the one aid of the Roman pontiff, that he may both release me from the vexations of my present distress and dismiss me, with the necessary absolution and blessing, to follow the course of my devotion.  

I have therefore come into France, intending to come to the council if by any means I could. But having found more certainly that this is impossible for me, I send, with the letter of my excuse, a messenger whom I ask you to hold commended to your favour and to assist generously through your favour in what he tells you on my behalf. Know, moreover, that I take great pride in the favour of your familiarity and friendship, which, though I have not earned by a corresponding display of deeds, you will believe to be supplied by sincere devotion.  

## CV. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER

My lord, I have long wished to ask you for release from the episcopal office, because my mind and body fail for many reasons and I am adequate neither to this diligence nor to its labour. It is therefore clear that my prelateship is now not merely useless but harmful to the Church; and nothing remains except prudently to prepare for my imminent burial, lest the hour of death overtake me negligent and repentance come too late to aid one already overtaken. But because I could not freely withdraw while hindered by many things, the lord king of England, at the counsel and urging of Lord Peter, your cardinal legate, promised me the means of royal assistance by which I might be freed from the debt that most restrains me, and might be permanently provided, wherever I went, for my support from the episcopal goods—goods which through my own effort have recently been abundantly acquired.  

But now he has withdrawn his mind and held back the hand believed to be generously extended. To put it mildly, he permits me to be miserably harassed by his officers and tax-gatherers, to such an extent that he compels me to leave the entire province because I could not with any patience look upon what the Church suffers most unworthily. Besides other things which he has recently added to the accumulation of misery and servitude, he has, by his own authority, established a prefect in the city which has always hitherto enjoyed a special liberty among all others and answered in all things only to its bishop. Before my very eyes this prefect violently usurps my revenues for himself every day, subjects the citizens to the most unworthy injuries, and does not allow me to exercise the authority I have always possessed.  

I am less than a guest in the city of which I had always been lord; indeed, I am freer in other cities than in my own, in which blessed Peter—whose honour founded the Church—has always claimed every right, secular as well as ecclesiastical, for himself. Let Your wisdom remember that I was freely elected to this bishopric without any violence or nomination by secular power. I was consequently deprived of its revenues until Pope Innocent, of glorious memory, by his special authority, with strong hand and outstretched arm, placed and confirmed me in my see with the full integrity of its possessions and the liberty due to it. Surely it will seem a grave derogation from your glory if so illustrious a work of your predecessor is nullified before your eyes and the Church which among others was accustomed to rejoice in great privilege descends, first maimed into servitude and then into poverty.  

I ask, indeed, and, prostrate upon the knees of your mercy with humility and longing, I beg that Your Majesty grant me release from an unbearable burden and lead me freely out from the vexations by which I am miserably tormented. Meanwhile, however, the day of my departure and resignation must be left to my own decision, lest malicious cunning deceive me and rejoice to insult my simplicity when it sees it deceived. For if the bishopric should now become vacant in any manner, secular power will surely lay greedy hands upon all the Church’s goods, to confiscate them according to the old abuse. Nor will creditors receive any satisfaction—creditors who have long lent, without any interest, for construction and other needs of the Church. I shall be found guilty before God of violated faith, and deservedly condemned before men by public reproach and infamy.  

I have therefore resolved, after entrusting care of the Church to prudent men, to withdraw somewhere beyond the province, where there is no joy and no rest for me, to a place where rest may benefit both mind and body and frugality may assist repayment. Once I have been freed from the importunate pressure of creditors, I must meanwhile be furnished with letters from Your Holiness so that I may be allowed immediately to withdraw; otherwise I would need to spend much time and labour returning to you, which my advanced age and failing health do not permit me many days to undertake.  

## CVI. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER

Long ago divine graciousness advanced me to the episcopal office and, beyond my merits—indeed, contrary to them—raised me by favour. At first I acquiesced more readily because I had experienced neither the labour nor the danger of that office. Considering the holiness of the order and the power of the dignity, I hoped that holiness would come to me from the one and magnificence from the other. I wished these to converge in one and cooperate toward the same result of perfected virtue: that holiness might not remove magnificence, nor magnificence holiness, but that each might draw dignity from the glory of the other.  

Experience, however, taught me sorrowfully that what I believed had turned out otherwise, when the weakness of the flesh attacks the efforts of reason and manifold occupation resists the will once formed. As I seek a remedy, therefore, and devotedly long to attain salvation, I have understood that nothing is more effective or more certain for this purpose than, according to Christ’s teaching, to embrace the example of his humility, patience, and poverty together. Rejecting all things that could impede the way of truth, I must enter some community of religious brethren and a house of religious discipline, so that, once the things offering the vanity of the world are excluded, regular restraint alone within may curb wandering affections, and, with the little ones dashed against the rock, the pursuits of sincerity may always grow strong.  

But bound to the episcopal office, to which my lord and father Pope Innocent of glorious memory advanced me by special affection, I could neither rightly nor lawfully depart by my own authority until I had first been released by the Roman pontiff, whose right hand had bound me. I therefore petitioned Pope Eugenius, of holy memory, first; I also petitioned Adrian while you were aware of the matter, indeed while you were chancellor. But in that respect I found your favour less ready and your assistance less effective. Both refused me, because I was still considered of robust age and strong body, and no knowledge or recollection had yet apprehended any failing arising from bodily decline.  

Compelled by necessity, I therefore obeyed and exercised my faint-heartedness in repeated labours, while zeal for ecclesiastical liberty consumed me—a liberty which I see continually afflicted from then onward with ever greater losses. I could not keep silent, yet I accomplished little except by solitary murmuring, because no one stood with me and everyone’s votes cried out against me. Thus all the ruler’s anger was turned against me and my Church; neither patience could soften his displeasure toward me nor supplication calm it.  

Yet I endured as long as I received even a little comfort in anything and the restoration of ecclesiastical liberty seemed possible by any means. Whatever divine goodness may have provided in this matter, I have become almost wholly useless in mind and body to myself and God’s Church. My spirit has failed scarcely less than my body, since old age dulls the powers both of mind and body, and memory does not preserve faithfulness to thoughts. I am therefore distressed on every side: the force of daily persecution bears upon bodily weakness, while among varied thoughts reason suffers the torpor and stupor of indolence. Devotion once drew me, but now the invincible force of necessity drives me on, as the incompleteness of whatever works I have undertaken, together with the slowness of my tongue and confusion of my speech, bears witness.  

## CVII. TO RICHARD, BISHOP OF WINCHESTER
For a long time I have sent neither letter nor messenger to the lord king, although very many troubles pressed me hard. I feared that his indignation would be exacerbated rather than appeased by my name, and that supplication itself would provoke him to harm rather than to help. But now I can delay no longer, because his ministers openly proclaim that they have a command from him to harass me and my church in every way, if they wish either to retain or to obtain his favour. They therefore strive more fiercely and compete with one another to outdo each other in every wrongdoing. William, son of Ralph, the chief [Col. 0128D] and master of them all, induced by the entreaties of Walter of Coutances, through whom he thinks he will secure the king's favour more firmly, makes Walter many assurances which I can never believe proceeded with the king's knowledge. For he now aspires so shamelessly to my bishopric that there is scarcely any longer concealment of the promises; Hubert—would that you knew him!—having been set aside for this purpose, he has won over several of the canons and even bound them by oaths to consent, when I die, to the royal will that Walter be elected. Therefore William, Ralph's son, ceaselessly urges that I be harassed by frequent injuries, so that, worn out by distress, I may be compelled to resign. In this he has proceeded with such violence that he has driven me from my city and stripped me of all revenues, [Col. 0129A] even forbidding me to leave the land, so that he might leave me nothing in the land and not allow me, even hungry, to seek elsewhere. He further ordered by a general edict that none of my clerics should give me anything; and if anyone was found to have offered anything, all his goods were confiscated and seized. It is hard for me that royal power harasses me so severely through Walter; but harder still is that he has divided the church into parties by the oaths begun and separated the greater part from my obedience. If by chance I wish to exercise any episcopal justice upon anyone, William, Ralph's son, does not permit it, but violently usurps all ecclesiastical power, claiming churches, offerings, altars, tithes and prebends, and every kind of alms, all my authority having been wholly set aside, [Col. 0129B] for his own jurisdiction. Moreover Walter's shamelessness and blind ambition are now so great that through the bishop of Bayeux, the chancellor, William son of Ralph, and the archbishop, he has caused me to be admonished; and he himself has negotiated with me that I should receive from him the money which the king had promised me for payment, provided that I made the canons swear an oath concerning his election. I plainly answered that he was a simoniac, and that I would receive nothing from him, but from the king under precisely the form established for both him and me by Lord P., the legate.

It is sweet and pleasant to communicate to your conscience what I suffer; and it is some remedy to me that I do not doubt that you sympathize and grieve with me. I send the king letters full of every humility, [Col. 0129C] the reply to which I have certainly thought should be sent to you, so that, if an opportunity should perhaps present itself to you, you may know how you ought to speak and act. For you alone are the one in whose faith and charity I trust. I have indeed no confidence in the king; but I ought not to leave the land until I have first approached him, lest my departure seem to arise from his severity rather than from my pride. Whatever may happen, however, communicate to me your advice in familiar letters; for I shall remain here under no persuasion unless he restores to my church its liberty.

CVIII. TO HENRY, KING OF ENGLAND.

[Col. 0129D] No circumstance can erase from my memory how many and how great benefits, how much honour, intimacy, and favour royal excellence once bestowed on me over a long period; rather, the former love with which I have always loved you, and the affection owed you, endure. I have often been troubled and afflicted with many injuries and losses; but none of these has ever been such as could diminish either my zeal or the truth of my loyalty. Now, however, the testimony of my conscience is my glory: for as long as royal goodness admitted me to its counsels and affairs, the unstained integrity of my loyalty shone forth in all things, and the effectiveness of affairs commended my diligence. I therefore rejoiced that favour answered the wish of my lord, [Col. 0130A] and counted myself happy and endowed with every blessedness if anything seemed to occur through my exertion that increased his advantage or honour. Yet, although what I suffer is very bitter, nothing is more bitter to me than that I find my lord's will gravely changed toward me; for, if his favour endured, I would regard any injuries and losses of fortune as trifling. I would indeed rejoice, breathe again in contemplating him and remembering his favour, and the joys of that sweetness, surpassing all else for me, would compensate every bitterness. I had hoped that his favour for me would endure until my death, so that at last, in this sweetness, I might seem to have fallen asleep in everlasting sleep as if in his arms. But affairs have now [Col. 0130B] turned to the contrary—not, certainly, through any fault of mine, but through the envious prompting of informers—and in place of my lord's former love I experience hatred, and in place of generous beneficence oppression; nor does any counsel meet me in need or relief in oppression. I should assuredly have failed, had not the consciousness of my enduring innocence sustained me, and had I not still believed that some memory of my many services remained with your generosity of spirit: for what cost him so much to bestow and was received by you with such liberality of mind could not be erased by a light wind of falsehoods, since from the whole time during which I stood by you there arises absolutely no evidence of my idleness or fraud. I therefore believe that in the secret chamber of your breast there still lives a certain spark which [Col. 0130C] will in its time grow strong against the deceits of flatterers, and that your old faithful bishop of Lisieux, always ready and effective for every need of yours, may appear joyfully among the rest. Meanwhile, because there is no limit to the evils frequently inflicted upon me and the church which I serve, and because they cannot be borne with tolerable patience, I flee to the feet of your mercy. Even if my merits seem an obstacle, at least have pity on the church, for it is time to have pity on her, for the time has come, before her liberty, possessions, and rights descend to irrevocable ruin. I offer you my extreme old age, whose better years have long been consumed in your service; [Col. 0130D] and it is now utterly unworthy that it should be trampled upon by the excellence of your majesty. You show your power against a leaf carried by the wind and crush dry straw, unless it please you to lift away the hand that oppresses and mercifully raise up its liberty. Nothing, however, distresses me more than that, although I may not have deserved otherwise, I see the church burdened on my account. Hence I have no desire or wish to retain this prelacy longer, especially in this weakness of mine and under the disadvantage of your indignation, under which no bishop can prosper nor any church flourish. But if it please your majesty to restore it to its former liberty and establish its rights for ever, I am ready [Col. 0131A] to resign, provided that, out of regard for mercy, a small provision is reserved for my support. If, however, your highness cannot be inclined to this, I shall endure until the end of my life whatever divine wisdom dictates that I must endure. For I could not abandon it destitute without danger to my salvation; but, according to my strength, with God's grace I shall wait more manfully, in all humility and patience, until your wisdom returns to your heart. Certainly no quarrel, even if I could raise one, shall break forth from me against reverence for you; rather humility will overcome your excessive power, because as it cannot be repelled by force, so of itself it will rest in its own kindness. Yet I ask for nothing which the kingdoms of all Christians do not possess, and which my predecessors in the time of your predecessors, and I for thirty years and more under you and your father, possessed undisturbed. May my lord prosper, and may the succession of the everlasting kingdom confirm his present kingdom. I have thought it right to note my complaints to you separately and briefly, lest a longer discourse perhaps produce weariness.

CIX. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER.

There is one thing which wounds me more disgracefully than all else: namely, the failure of my archbishop in every necessity. It is clear that, almost buried, he has grown old more in mind than in body; wholly enslaved to the king's exactions, he entirely annuls whatever I have episcopally ordained in my bishopric and permits no reverence [Col. 0131C] to be shown me, because in every evil deed they think themselves justly released by any sentence of the archbishop. Thus he absolves both clerics and laymen whom we have condemned by ecclesiastical anathema, restores them to their altars from which they had canonically been deprived for ever, and orders them to have pastoral care of the people and to celebrate the sacraments while under that excommunication, although he has neither learned nor sought any ground whatever for my action. It is certain that he does this in order to gain the king's favour for himself through harassing me, because he is the king's minister in all his perversity and pays no attention whatever to ecclesiastical dignity. When all these matters have become known to your majesty, [Col. 0131D] it will be necessary for your favour to provide for me, lest I be exposed to his and his followers' injuries; for from of old they pursue me solely through envy, and now confront me more boldly through confidence in royal power. I have entrusted this matter and certain others to my messengers to bring before your mercy; I beg that they be heard more kindly by you and sent back instructed, because I always have my burial before my eyes as if present, and I would already have hastened it by the conversion I have resolved upon, had these and the other obstacles to be reported to you not arisen.

CX. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER.

I give thanks to your majesty because you have mercifully relieved me of the episcopal burden, under [Col. 0132A] the condition I requested; yet I still cannot depart, lest I seem to have fled when the wolf came and to have left the church established, as it were, in its supreme tribulation. For, as you have heard, from of old a violent anger of our prince has blazed against it, and neither its affliction yet ceases nor his indignation rests. It increases day by day, and more devices of fearful severity are brought forth; so much so that, as the bishops openly attest, he has commanded his ministers to trouble me by every means and afflict me and mine with wretched losses. This has now gone so far that his chief agent, William son of Ralph, has lately deprived me of all my revenues, even of the city itself and the episcopal see, on the sole [Col. 0132B] pretext that I could not produce a poor knight whom he alleged that he had summoned to court for an ecclesiastical matter and for whom he falsely asserted that I had stood surety. Since he was also my nephew, William threatened to bind him in fetters and shut him in prison if by any chance he fell into his hands, imputing to him without any truth that he had taken from the hands of those dragging him to prison a certain deacon who was being dragged from my table and the bishop's residence by William's officers. After doing this, though he had left me nothing in the land, he nevertheless forbade me to leave it, so that he might leave me nothing within and not allow me to seek anything outside. He also prohibited, and publicly proclaimed by royal edict through markets and fairs, that anything be [Col. 0132C] given to me by my priests or clerics; and, if anyone was found guilty under the edict, he had his immovable goods sold by auction and his movable goods confiscated. Walter of Coutances, to whom the lord king of England has openly granted the bishopric should I resign through death or weariness, kindles and multiplies this evil against me. Indeed, because Walter is great with the king, his opposition harms me scarcely less than the king's; for while the king is occupied with greater matters, Walter of Coutances, whose business is being pursued, presses constantly and cannot bear to wait for the failure of my old age, but rather strives to forestall it by steadily imposed weariness. To carry this out more faithfully at close hand and act as his deputy, he has placed a certain Hubert, one of my canons, in the church and city itself, [Col. 0132D] who daily reconciles to him whichever canons he can, and has bound some by oaths in a sacrilegious faction, so that when I die or resign they may consent to the royal will that he be elected. He therefore, as he began, watches every vigil and eventuality closely, and with the cooperation of the aforesaid William has already bent many by promises, threats, and entreaties, so that they obey me with greater difficulty; raised up in pride, they now openly seem to glory in the favour of the new bishop. It is therefore certain that some of them have entered into a mutual compact: William is to manage the absent Walter's business in Normandy, and Walter, in return, is to preserve William's favour with the king in England. Since Walter perceives me inclined to resign the bishopric, [Col. 0133A] he offered to pay the debt by which he thought I was chiefly held fast, if the canons would agree to his election through my exertion. Certainly the lord king, through the intervention of Lord Peter, your legate, had promised to assist me generously in this matter; but when, with a closed hand, he did not fulfil what he had promised, Walter came forward ready to pay, and I openly answered him that he was a simoniac and that I would receive nothing from him for a matter of this kind. Let your kindness therefore provide for me according to its custom, for I am constantly beset on many sides; indeed most people regard me as removed from the bishopric because of the king's promise, which no one is ignorant was made to Walter. On this and my other troubles I have thought it necessary to send messengers to your majesty, [Col. 0133B] so that, having heard everything through them, your mercy may assist me, since the brevity of a letter does not allow everything to be written.

CXI. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER.

Your predecessor Pope Innocent, of glorious memory, committed to my governance, without any lay nomination, the church which, God permitting, I serve; he removed every obstacle of secular power and, in God's strength, triumphed splendidly for my peace. He also diligently pursued all my work with unwearied favour, always supported it with needed help, and fortified it with protection. When, at the beginning of my office, I at once undertook to cleanse the church of its customary lacuna and remove the old concubinages of the canons, [Col. 0133C] he applied the hand of necessary severity; so that in one day, relying on his power, I made eighteen concubinages be publicly renounced by canons. Once the church was cleansed, and those who had sinned purified by fitting satisfaction, the whole province proclaimed the splendour of my church; and its renowned discipline advanced so far that many round about were drawn to due continence by our example. I rejoiced that my church had offered others a model of continence, and that holy shame prevented them from returning, as it were, to their vomit. While those whom apostolic majesty had, as it were, snatched from Satan's jaws remained, no disgrace of fornication or incest stained our community; [Col. 0133D] instead they competed with one another in efforts toward honourable conduct. But when, as time passed, the common fate required that I install new men, and the newcomers were not bound by the oath of the old, as the age continually declined for the worse, the youth of some began to indulge in secret excesses and draw some of the older men with them into similar pleasure; public shame scarcely allowed anyone to suspect anything discreditable about them. As their number increased, so did their boldness; they trusted that even a slight covering kept them safe, and nothing could easily be made manifest. Nor could I pronounce sentence on suspicion alone, while their multitude protected them through the transgressing mass. Yet what many committed could not remain hidden, since the swaddling-clothes [Col. 0134A] of new births provided most certain proof, and the entire neighbourhood celebrated the recent cradles. I learned this and first used admonitory prayers, threats, and some punishment; but an evil already rooted for a long time could not easily be torn out. When I resolved to act more severely, they, terrified by consciousness of guilt and fear of a notorious crime, presumed to conspire and even swear an oath, chiefly at the advice of my deaf nephew, the treasurer of the church—namely, that man whom you know, who, though I have anticipated him with many benefits from childhood, nevertheless never ceases, for certain reasons, to harass me with implacable hatred and does not fear to incur double perjury. By your command, before Lord William the cardinal and the bishops of Le Mans and Avranches, [Col. 0134B] he swore bodily that he would no further bring the accusations he then advanced against me; and afterwards, taking confidence from the king's anger, he forswore himself. When I lodged a complaint with you at Bourges through the archpriest of Aosta and our archdeacons, after an inquiry you sent him back to me, excommunicated and bound with that same bond; you also added entreaties of your kindness that I spare him and, after receiving again whatever security I wished, preserve for him the benefices he had held. I therefore did what you commanded, and after again receiving his ill-omened oaths I absolved him, because you granted him this mercy also out of regard for me. He swore again and for some time remained quiet through necessity; but, having newly learned that the king's anger against me had grown fiercer, [Col. 0134C] he forswore himself a third time and devoted himself with all zeal to the king's service, having received hope that the king's violence would not fail to give effect to his wickedness. He also summoned to himself those whom notorious infamy of life compelled to despair. Eleven of these were gathered in the number of transgression; thirty others, but of the better number, resisted, prepared by prudent counsel for every canonical action. Before anything had been said or done by me, however, those men, shouting with equal madness, strove to interpose the obstacle of an appeal, trusting in its name alone; and by that name alone they withdrew from me all obedience in everything, permitting right and wrong with shameless audacity. When I most urgently asked [Col. 0134D] on what heads or articles they were appealing, so that reverence might be more faithfully observed toward the appeal if there was one, I could not wring it from them; they would neither tell nor write to me, saying that they were afraid and therefore appealed against all that could be said or done. Nor did they all say the same thing: each confusedly advanced different things, wholly divided and dissenting in every respect. I bore it patiently, pronouncing no sentence on any except two against whom we proceeded under the authority of your letters; we therefore ask your excellence to confirm your own act. As for the others, though they are condemned by the public testimony of all for adulteries, incests, and other crimes, we have deferred to the appeal—though there was none—more timidly observing reverence for your name alone. [Col. 0135A] When your messengers have more fully reported their offences to your holiness, appoint judges who have zeal for honour, skill in judging, the necessary confidence in your authority, and a suitable place where cases can be decided and sentences pronounced; for we scarcely believe that they can be restrained except by flight and secular power. But those whom I presume to bring before you may safely be judged canonically by you. No judge in Normandy is good for us, nor is there safety in litigating in Normandy, because what they have not done against us to escape condemnation they will cry that they have done for the king's favour. If in this matter they have perhaps stirred up any schism against us—indeed against you—it will be yours, as your wisdom knows, [Col. 0135B] to vindicate the injury done to the Church of God.

CXII. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER.

It has come to your knowledge that Hamon the priest publicly keeps a concubine, and that he has kept her in the same house, at the same table, and in the same bed for thirty years and more, and has begotten a very large offspring by her. This act has always been so manifest and notorious that he kept it hidden under no covering whatever, but delighted to make it still more evident by the solemn marriages of his daughters. When I had received your majesty's letters directing me to admonish him both to make satisfaction and to desist, I repeatedly admonished him in chapter before all the brethren, [Col. 0135C] employing even the terror of your holy pronouncement; yet I was not heard in any way, because he would not remove her from sharing his side even for one day or night. I repeatedly sent persons to discover whether he ever showed reverence to God or you; but the mother and daughters stripped two priests whom I once sent and violently laid impious hands on them. Yet, by God's mercy, they were at last rescued by men who came upon them, and rejoiced to have escaped their hands as though from she-wolves' teeth. The priest presumes to defend this inveterate crime as though by a certain prescription, and would not separate her from himself even for a moment. We therefore, having assembled venerable men—four abbots, three archdeacons, [Col. 0135D] the precentor and head of our church, and several canons and religious monks—had your letters read publicly and, observing in all things the judicial procedure as instructed, took care to carry it into effect. We have accordingly thought it right to send you the judges' testimonies with the witnesses' subscriptions, lest what is known to be supported by your authority and by so great reason can be blackened in any respect by anyone's false allegation. It is good that one man's punishment should advance the discipline of many, lest, with so manifest a guilt, concubinaries be said to have triumphed over ecclesiastical honour under your cognizance. Let your zeal therefore impose silence on the condemned man, and cause his churches, which in the diocese of Sées he procured to be transferred to the son of his priesthood, [Col. 0136A] to be assigned to suitable persons by another bishop than the one through whom they were wrongly bestowed. They are several; and what is known to have been amassed in one man's greed may benefit several honourable persons.

CXIII. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER.

There is a matter which, though long concealed, I must now reveal to your mercy, so that I may find some remedy for it with your kindness. I have reared sons and exalted them, but they have not only despised me but have also hated me (Isa. 1). They are my nephews, whom I have reared almost from their cradles with indulgence, educated with great care, enriched, and made illustrious with honours, so that among [Col. 0136B] others they shone with a certain special glory. Yet they return no gratitude for my services, nor do they care in any way to provide for my advantage or honour. They are moved solely because I did not confer upon their little nephews whatever fell vacant in the church, but, summoning learned and honourable men from every quarter, adorned my church with persons so venerable that there is none in the whole province which can equal it in their merits. If any among them should perhaps be found blameworthy, they are redeemed by the virtues and prudence of the others; nor does the unworthiness of some make the church deserve to be slandered. They say that I do this in contempt of my blood and to abase them, whereas by natural affection they ought to have been promoted more warmly by me. Among them, to pass over the rest, one is harmful to me: first I conferred on him two prebends worth one hundred pounds in the churches of Lisieux and Bayeux, [Col. 0136C] an archdeaconry worth two hundred pounds, three parish churches worth fifty pounds, and a deanery worth fifty or sixty pounds in the church of Lisieux; for nothing I did seemed enough unless I made him sit beside me as my equal or superior. Having gained what he wanted, he immediately began to contend with me for power, to count as empty everything I said, and contentiousnessly twist everything to his own will. I endured this for a long time; the boldness of kinship and an almost equal power armed him still more. Others stood by him, and I had scarcely any conflict except with my own blood, until at last some others, frightened by fear of their own licentiousness, joined his side to seek aid. But at last I began to prevail over the others through the authority and protection of your letters. There is indeed one matter to which it is fitting that you apply the hand of your prompt severity, [Col. 0136D] because an enormous offence and the ruin of many souls are involved in it. In the deanery is a parish church whose revenues are known to be shared by the dean and priest. Its priest has been publicly condemned for three very grave crimes—concubinage, incest with his brother's concubine, and perjury in a general synod—because he could not clear himself; and he has accordingly been stripped of every ecclesiastical benefice. When afterwards he presumed to retain the church by force and to celebrate divine offices while the dean was present and consenting, he was again bound by a sentence of anathema. Yet afterwards the dean installed him in that same church and, though I always forbid it, has him serve at the parish altar to the people's curse; nor does he fear to receive from his hand the revenues which that man receives under the curse. [Col. 0137A] Though suspended by me, he nevertheless has him administer spiritual things, because he promises him protection in every necessity. It is a schism and an iniquity greater than any heresy, where the sacraments are known to be profaned and a people of five hundred souls to be involved in the danger of a perpetual curse.
