You formerly also disapproved that I had conferred the deanery and the greater archdeaconry upon one dean with lavish generosity, since this is known to be contrary to ecclesiastical institution; and you charged the bishops of Bayeux and Évreux to divide the dignities among different persons, so that not even your rescript, which is known to have been obtained from you by fraud on this matter, should stand in the way. But one of the judges died, and the double mandate could not be completed by the delegation of one. It is therefore necessary that your holiness complete what it began and delegate the execution of the matter to other judges, [Col. 0137B] through whom equality may be restored to the Church in its dignities, lest one consume the other in so great a confusion, and the ambition of an ungrateful and degenerate man be checked.

CXIV. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER.

Your highness delegated to my venerable brothers, the bishops of Bayeux and Avranches and the treasurer of Lisieux, the dispute between me and Nicholas de Cust., clerk, concerning a certain prebend which the same Nicholas had resigned into our hand to be granted to Gilbert the archdeacon, on the condition that the first which should fall vacant be assigned to Nicholas by way of compensation. In the meantime, however, canonical rank was retained for him, so that he should hold, with the others as a canon, a stall in choir, a place in chapter, and the dignity of serving at the high altar. Subsequently, when a prebend became vacant, I conferred it upon another, namely John of Alençon, without Nicholas's knowledge or consent, thinking that, because he was my familiar and household servant, he would bear patiently what I did and await without offence another benefice [Col. 0137D] from my favour. When Nicholas was by no means pleased upon learning this, he brought a complaint against me to the ears of your mercy; and by apostolic authority you ordered that same prebend to be restored to him. You also commanded that this be carried into effect without any appeal or contradiction, and that I ensure Nicholas's peaceful possession of it against all violence. When Nicholas had delayed presenting these letters for some time because of various obstacles, another mandate from you issued to the aforementioned judges: if I had not fulfilled all that you had ordered concerning Nicholas's restoration, we were, relying on your authority, to confer on the said Nicholas the prebend of the Chapel, which was said to be vacant in the church, so that both the truth of the promise might be fulfilled and Nicholas should not lack his restoration. But the prebend was by no means vacant, [Col. 0138A] because it had already been given by me, under your letters and through your intervention, to Hugh de Nunaut, archdeacon of Lisieux; nor could your mandate be fulfilled except by conferring the first prebend. I therefore, having carefully considered the content of your mandate and been induced by the admonition of the lord bishop of Bayeux, your delegated judge, conferred upon Nicholas the prebend first promised, just as is expressly contained in your mandate, which still exists, lest by omitting this I be convicted of having been insufficiently obedient and of having shown too little respect to you. Since the colleagues of the aforesaid bishop of Bayeux had excused themselves from attending for various reasons but had committed their functions to him by letters, he nevertheless pursued our act under the authority entrusted to him by you. He wrote to the chapter what had been commanded by you and carried out by us; he ordered Nicholas to be received as a canon [Col. 0138B] and all things belonging to the prebend to be conferred upon him. He also informed them that this mandate of yours could be suspended by no appeal or contradiction, as they were also permitted to see from your rescript. Since the canons proved insufficiently obedient in this, it will be yours to decree what you must. John, however, presumed to hold the prebend by force; having sought the support of secular power, he did not fear to remove the aforesaid Nicholas from the goods of his prebend through royal officials. He interposed an appeal while Vespers were being sung outside the church, with neither his adversary nor your judges present, although you had removed every right of appeal. Lest blame for failure to fulfil your mandate could be laid upon me, I thought it right to write to you what prevents its fulfilment, so that, by this precedent, support from secular power may not be sought against your majesty; but because you have decreed it so justly and holily, cause it to be carried into effect with power. [Col. 0138C] Because of the violence of secular power, which he did not fear to exercise against a sentence proceeding from your authority, he has been solemnly bound by me with the due bond of anathema; nevertheless, bound by it, he presumes to present himself before your sight. Even our archbishop could not deny his own authority in the case, although the man enjoys his favour and the archbishop opposes us in almost everything. Therefore take vengeance on the opponent; let the severer discipline of apostolic majesty proceed against the rash man, the contemner, and his accomplices, lest he make others contemners by like audacity. For they preserve no reverence for pontifical authority, but cloak the injuries they inflict under the covering of a frivolous appeal and, adding the secular power which they purchase, weaken all the force of ecclesiastical institution and enervate what seemed to possess the vigour of true authority. Your wisdom knows that this is practised very extensively in our regions; but beneath your gentleness and forbearance [Col. 0139A] wickedness daily grows strong, and there is nothing, however slight, that the Church of God dares to vindicate. Instead, by sacrilegious presumption, all things are ordered through secular power. Would that my Lord might at least stretch out to me the tip of his finger for a moment, so that under the protection of ecclesiastical liberty, for which I have always been zealous, I may be permitted to finish the few days that remain to me!

CXV. TO RICHARD, BISHOP OF WINCHESTER.

I believe you faithfully remember that William of Ferendona held the vicarage of that place from the time of Thurstan, throughout the whole time of Thurstan and Richard his son, down to my own time. When the king’s generosity had conferred the chaplaincy upon me, after Richard’s death—through whom William had held it during Richard’s life—I granted that same vicarage to the aforesaid William in perpetuity, adding certain things which his service and devotion to me appeared to have deserved. Thus I presented him to you as bishop, and you graciously confirmed by episcopal authority what I had done. Later, through your intercession, I gave the church to our nephew, while naturally preserving for William the vicarage which I had previously granted him; and this too was conceded by your kindness, and William remained in the same possession for several years. At last it pleased your goodness to remove him from that church and, although he was entirely without fault, to retain certain of his movable goods [Col. 0139C]. I am therefore bound to this poor man, because for some time he has been faithful and devoted to me; nor can I refrain from interceding for him before your holiness with whatever prayers I can. Consider what you are doing: it is not good that, for so slight a matter, the conscience of a priest and bishop should be stained. Nor can his poverty fail to move me, since he once offered himself and his possessions to my will with particular generosity.

## CXVI. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER

In the bishopric which, by God’s permission, I serve, a certain parish church became vacant. At the presentation of a distinguished man, William Marmion—who was said to possess the patronage of the church—I granted it to a suitable person, with absolutely no objection from anyone. After the man to whom I had given the aforesaid church had held it peacefully for some time, he died by the common lot of mortality; and, at the presentation of the same William as before, I assigned it as was proper to another person. When the person to whom it had last been granted had held it for four years by ecclesiastical authority, the man who had presented him raised a suit concerning the patronage in a secular court, although from ancient times such cases had always belonged to episcopal jurisdiction. That litigious man accordingly won the patronage of the church in the secular court, with nothing reserved for episcopal justice. Afterwards he brought a suit against the clerk whom I had received [Col. 0140A], demanding that he be removed completely from the church, although the clerk had been presented and had also been ordained to certain orders while that man held the patronage.

He made this demand not indeed in his own name, but in that of a four-year-old girl whose future marriage he hoped for, although, because of her age, he could contract with her neither betrothal nor marriage. Among us, however, an unforeseen change of patrons is not accustomed to cause a change of clerks; rather, the person found in office at the time is bound to recognize the patronage of the new successor. When we were preparing to proceed to judgment, this man appealed to your tribunal, fixing the feast of the Nativity of the Lord as the date of appeal; and, preserving the due reverence owed to an appeal made to you, we reserved the remainder for your majesty [Col. 0140B].

## CXVII. TO CARDINAL PETER

I do not think that the holy, useful, and wholeheartedly embraceable counsel which your wisdom gave me when you exercised the office of legate in our regions has fallen from your memory; nor was anything more deeply rooted in the desire of my whole heart. I hoped that what I desired could soon be accomplished, because the lord king, through your counsel and admonition, promised to assist me by royal generosity in discharging the debt by which I was especially burdened. But he wholly withheld his hand from payment; and, when he publicly granted the bishopric to Walter of Coutances, he released to Walter the payment of the money if I should die [Col. 0140C] or depart.

Walter himself, both through Ralph, the king’s chancellor, and in person, immediately offered ready money to be counted out, provided that I caused the leading persons and the greater part of the chapter to assemble for his election. I plainly replied that this was simoniacal, and that I would accept nothing from him in such a matter. He was angered; nor has his rash ambition yet ceased. Made more secure by the king’s permission after my removal, he seeks to drive out by harassment the man whom he cannot remove by bargains. I am therefore dragged by a threefold cord: the king’s anger crushes me, his officials steadily afflict me at his command, and Walter—having bound some of the canons to himself—acts as though he were lord, and in many matters as possessor [Col. 0140D].

This has now gone so far that the king’s chief agent, William son of Ralph, recently deprived me of all my revenues, my city, and even my episcopal see itself, and compelled me for approximately ten days to wander through other people’s houses, living on other people’s bread. Yet I have not dared wholly to resign the bishopric, lest I be said to have fled when the wolf came; but meanwhile I have judged that I should withdraw to the church of Saint-Victor until I receive my envoys, whom I have sent to the lord pope and to you, with the aid and counsel which your grace wished me to seek. For, although I am sound in health, old age nevertheless brings me such weakness that I cannot walk even seven steps [Col. 0141A], mount a horse, or dismount, unless I am lifted by others’ hands.

## CXVIII. TO CARDINAL THEODWIN

When you exercised the office of legate in our regions, you received me with great familiarity and favor, and in every need of mine you always supported me with generous counsel and assistance. This indeed was great; but much greater still was that, when great distances of place had separated us from one another, your affection endured, and at the Apostolic See you always labored to act as a special advocate in our affairs, so that your petition might never be deprived of its desired result. Therefore I ought not to be forgetful or ungrateful toward your beneficence [Col. 0141B]; rather, whenever a favorable opportunity graciously shines forth, I devote every effort and all my ability to rendering you due thanks. Meanwhile, I stand ready, with all my affection, for every service to you, should divine goodness at any time grant me the fulfillment of my desired purpose.

For the present, I commend to you with my customary confidence the bearers of this letter, my envoys, so that the business they carry may be successfully completed through your efforts. They carry many matters, all supported by complete truth and most worthy of every acceptance—especially before holy judges of conduct and defenders of ecclesiastical integrity. From copies of the letters which they carry to the lord pope, moreover, you will be able to learn everything and judge with complete certainty in what spirit these things are said.

## CXIX. TO LORD POPE ALEXANDER

[Col. 0141C]

The bearer of this letter, Fulk, will be strongly commended to you by his poverty and innocence, if his fortunes and case should come to the knowledge of your holiness. In the bishopric which, by God’s permission, I serve, there is a parish church with modest revenues; nevertheless, the priest serving there at any given time had customarily held all of them in full, by the name and right of the priesthood. I, however, granted the personship of that church with lavish generosity to our canon, named Gervase, while reserving to my own judgment the distribution of the goods between the person and the vicar who should serve the church.

Later Gervase presented to me a vicar to undertake the care of the church. After remaining in the church for some time, this man publicly took as his concubine the mother of the lord of Fundi, a noble boy; and, having begotten offspring by her, he openly displayed his shameless offense before the whole people, rejoicing that he had, as it were, taken her in lawful marriage, and taunting the other concubinary priests because he had been distinguished above them by a more noble cohabitation [Col. 0141D]. When that boy, namely the lord of Fundi, had grown up and reached lawful age, although no complaint had been raised against the priest by him, the priest secretly fled from the church, furtively carrying off such of the church’s goods as he wished.

The church accordingly stood for some time without a priest, while the people wandered without a shepherd. Although sought by public edict and by a sentence of anathema [Col. 0142A], he was nowhere found; and, entangled in the crimes of incest, theft, and sacrilege, he hid wherever he could. Gervase was therefore compelled by necessity to seek a vicar and offer him to me. He presented to me the bearer of this letter, a deacon, to be ordained priest, so that he might hold the church’s vicarage in perpetuity, with a suitable portion of the benefices assigned to him—at my discretion, certainly, because Gervase had formerly been accustomed to give others what was necessary with excessive stinginess.

After we assigned what we thought fitting in moderation, Gervase, giving corporal faith into my hand, confirmed that he would maintain it peacefully and without any diminution. I therefore ordained him and entrusted the care of the people to him. He occupied the office for several years and months, administering the church and its appurtenances with due diligence [Col. 0142B]. But when the son of the concubine—the noble boy of whom I spoke—happened to die, the former man, now more secure, boldly returned to the bed of his former filth and wickedness, and attempted to obtain the church which he had held before. Gervase openly aided him, because he promised to pay Gervase a larger yearly pension.

The bearer of this letter was accordingly drawn into litigation before our archdeacons, since I was absent. When he felt himself being severely pressed by the efforts of Gervase and his fellow canons, he appealed to your tribunal; and from Lent until the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul he peacefully ministered in the church. On that very day, however, the aforesaid invader violently burst into the church, seized the priestly vestments and put them on, celebrated the entire parish office, and desecrated the holy altar by sacrilegious usurpation [Col. 0142C]. Since, when summoned to appear before us concerning this, he contemptuously refused to come and did not cease to celebrate divine services, he was publicly excommunicated by us and excluded from all communion of Holy Church.

Yet he has not therefore stopped, nor does he stop. With Gervase supporting him and secular power sought for assistance, he persists, involving with himself in the guilt of deserved cursing the people of a large parish. It has at times been said that he falsely claims to do this by the archbishop’s authority, although he himself has never presumed to appear; the archbishop has said no word to me on the matter; nor does it belong to him to intrude upon our bishopric or, without hearing the case, to bind or absolve our priests [Col. 0142D].

## CXX. TO BARTHOLOMEW, BISHOP OF EXETER

I do not think that what I have done for you, or what your holiness promised me, has fallen from your memory. For I gave you letters to the king, by which he was moved against me; and, taking occasion from them, he granted you the chaplaincy, since it seemed to him that I had wholly resigned it to you. He even had the letters copied and brought the copy into Normandy. When I asked him why the chaplaincy had been taken from me, he replied that he had not taken it from me, but that I had granted it to you by the testimony of the letters which he produced [Col. 0143A]. He said that he intended to uphold what I had done, because in this matter he did not wish in any way to oppose my will.

Your prudence ought to remember that, long ago, you asked me not to hinder your advancement if by any means you could obtain it from the king—provided, that is, that through your hand the whole income of the chaplaincy should remain mine for as long as I lived. Under this explicit condition I did for you whatever you wished, as the king himself publicly declares. Nor did I wish to demand any securities from you, because the word of a priest and bishop seemed sufficient assurance to me—a word repeatedly given with strong affirmation. I commit the whole matter to your conscience, so that it may judge between you and me with righteous judgment, and so that you yourself may both make the case and render the judgment.

## CXXI. TO GILBERT, ARCHDEACON OF LISIEUX

[Col. 0143B]

I have received the letters of the lord king, the lord bishop of Winchester, and yourselves; from them I have nothing certain which I can at present answer. You have enjoyed my generosity for some time, and it certainly has not been fruitless to you. You had no need ever to present petitions to me or attempt any violence. Out of sheer generosity I did for you what I did, despite the envy of many; nor could any dissuasion impede my favor. May I receive from it the fruit I deserved, and may those who envied me from the beginning not laugh and mock!

Would that you had been pleased to proceed by the former path. For wherever greater power exerts its influence, what is obtained is said to have been extorted through fear of power. Meanwhile I am in Burgundy, waiting in suspense for the envoys whom I sent to the council in defense of my case—namely my nephew Hugh and others. When they arrive, I intend to return to Normandy, where I shall be able to reply to you and the others with fuller counsel, as may appear expedient for the honor and advantage of my church [Col. 0143C].

Meanwhile, know that I am not free to do what you request, because this matter has been otherwise settled and confirmed, both by the consent of your chapter and archbishop and by the authority of the Roman pontiff, with an anathema likewise imposed. An apostolic rescript on the matter was publicly read in our general synod and strengthened by the public assent of all the priests. Times and various developments will therefore come in which divine grace may give us counsel; for, as it seems to me, you are preparing to depart from us unless you are recalled by my diligence [Col. 0143D].

## CXXII. TO RICHARD, BISHOP OF WINCHESTER

Your generosity sent me through Gilbert the archdeacon what you know. I accepted it gladly, but would have accepted it more gladly if it had seemed offered not so much to relieve poverty as rather to honor me by the agreeable quality of the gift. I had hoped from your charity for a gift of another kind, one pleasing more by its character than by its weight. For I had asked for a palfrey, so that, in accordance with your customary practice, your kindness might provide for my infirmity [Col. 0144A]. But, for a private reason, as I suppose, you wished to send a hidden gift, although its elegance might reveal it.

Whatever it may be, I retain it with thanks. However great it may have been, I nevertheless judge the magnitude of the generous benefit by your affection and greatness of spirit. I know that your prosperity is often beset by many troubles, and that you sympathize with my sufferings; your own sufferings sometimes teach you this. Yet the Lord sometimes frees the poor from the powerful, and one for whom no helper appears is mercifully raised up by divine help.

## CXXIII. TO NICHOLAS, BISHOP OF MEAUX

There is with you a certain Henry, born in my territory and bishopric, who was irregularly advanced by a foreign bishop to the orders which he held. As time passed, he became implicated in many crimes and was publicly convicted and confessed of counterfeiting coin, which throughout the whole city of Bayeux he was not afraid publicly to pass and, by detestable malice, to use in defrauding the unwary. He was arrested by royal officers, shut in prison, and bound with iron fetters. At last, through great effort and labor, he was released by the bishop of the city, after formally abjuring the entire province of Normandy forever, and was brought before the archbishop. The archbishop broke the circle of his tonsure, stripped the priestly garments from his head, degraded him, and immediately expelled him from the whole land [Col. 0144C].

He has a brother named Amfred, entangled in crimes no fewer or less sparingly committed. Having lost whatever he obtained from me or from his other lords, and being unable to dare appear after remaining long in hiding, he was finally said, after fifteen years, to have obtained letters of pardon from our prince. These granted him the public peace and permitted him to recover his former inheritances from his former lords, if he could obtain them by any means. Received back by others, he could at last scarcely be received by me even through many intercessors. I restored to him the inheritance which he had formerly held from our church, on the agreement that, in recompense for the inheritance forever lost, he would pay a sum of money which he swore he would pay at a fixed time. His brother H. [Henry], who pursued his business with all zeal and entire fidelity, stood surety and, by a bodily oath, confirmed that he would pay at the appointed time if his brother did not [Col. 0144D]. The entire time has elapsed, and what was promised by them has not been fulfilled.

I have therefore thought it right, dear friend, to write and truthfully report all this to your charity, so that you may compel Henry, who is with you, to satisfy me according to justice, and so that his character may be more certainly made known to you through my declaration and letter.

## CXXIV. TO THE ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX

Richard of Blosseville, formerly abbot of Mortemer, was born in our bishopric. From the lower orders to the rank of priesthood he was promoted through the laying on of our hands [Col. 0145A], and was instituted to a definite benefice. While he had commendably served as a soldier among us in lay dress, once placed under the yoke of a stricter life he deserved commendation, in your habit, for the excellence of his conduct. At length, promoted to the place of abbot on account of the merits of his outstanding life, he shone like a lamp in your order. He benefited his subjects by the example of good conduct and inclined the hearts of princes to love your entire order.

But the devil, the plotter who is accustomed to envy the deeds of the just and to devise a blemish for the elect, sharpened against him the tongues of certain malicious men. By false inventions they injured his reputation among good and serious men, seeking only to remove him so that they might more freely deviate from the path of the order [Col. 0145B]. Therefore we believe that your holiness was misled in removing him, and that, as we believe, the full truth of the matter was not made known to you. It is also said that the Uscan abbot is driven against him by the flames of concealed envy and lent his ear to Richard’s detractors more readily than was proper.

We also wonder why, after removing him, you committed him to the custody of the aforesaid abbot, who is said to treat him poorly and to impose a stricter custody upon him than he should. We therefore beseech your holiness to provide another place for him, where he may be treated more honorably and serve the Lord with a more peaceful mind. Know that this would greatly please our prince, and that he would be deeply obliged to you if you provided a useful and honorable condition for the man whom he has so long embraced in the arms of sincere charity [Col. 0145C].

## CXXV. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

As you know, our lord king has for a very long time been moved against me and does not cease to harass me in many ways, both personally and through his justiciars. Thus he caused one of my nephews to live in exile from the country for two years. At your intercession, he was reconciled through your favor and that of our lord Count T., your brother—if only the reconciliation had proved as genuine as hoped. Having recently been driven out once more, he obtained, through your and the count’s efforts, access to a second reconciliation. He therefore clings on as best he can and finds no settled severity; but, trembling, he awaits the outcome of fortune between exile and prison [Col. 0145D].

The king also holds another man joined to me by a similar bond of blood. Without the king’s order, his chief official has confined this man in a prison cell for many months, knowing that by doing so he would win the king’s favor. But when the king learned the wickedness of these men and considered that he had been afflicted wholly without cause, he promised that he would release him entirely; and, I think, he would have done so had someone been present through whom the release could be carried out. Concerning this matter I appeal to your kindness and favor, tested for me in many great affairs: if a suitable opportunity should perhaps arise, let this man too be freed and released by a petition which you make for him to the king. I believe it can easily be accomplished, because if his own justice is insufficient for the liberation of an innocent man, whatever is lacking will be fulfilled by the favor due to your reverence [Col. 0146A].

## CXXVI. TO RICHARD, BISHOP OF AVRANCHES, AND HIS COLLEAGUES

A dispute over the election of an abbot arose long ago in the monastery of Grestain in our bishopric. Through earlier appeals it was carried as far as the Roman pontiff, who delegated it to the lord bishop of Poitiers for determination, together with certain other judges. As he, with those whom the lord pope had added as colleagues, diligently applied himself as was proper to deciding the case, it was necessary to obtain evidence from afar [Col. 0146B], and it could not easily reach his presence. He therefore ordered us, in his place, to hear the parties’ pleadings and receive the depositions of witnesses, seal them as customary, and send them to him, so that he might proceed to judgment according to judicial order.

I am concerned about the case because the monastery is in our bishopric, and I would most gladly labor for the peace of that house, since the lord king is greatly angered against its brothers; for they do not consent to the expression of his will as others do. Since, therefore, divine grace has brought the case in part before your experience, we rejoice in the Lord, most confidently trusting in your prudence and religious devotion, because you will endeavor to preserve both the justice of God and the liberty of the Church. We offer you our earnest prayers that you may apply yourselves more diligently to preserving the monastery’s peace and the prince’s favor, since without his favor the matter cannot proceed except with great harm [Col. 0146C].

## CXXVII. TO HENRY, KING OF THE ENGLISH

To his most reverend lord Henry, by God’s grace illustrious and glorious king of the English, Brother Arnulf, canon of Saint-Victor at Paris—would that he were regular—greetings: prosperity, glory, and salvation.

In the bishopric of Lisieux there is a parish church at Wacevum, which I had long held in my own hand and gave to the regular canons of Saint-Victor, before I joined them, so that it might contribute in some measure to my expenses when I had transferred to that church [Col. 0146D]. It is a small matter, but I had nothing by which I could give greater help to the poor brothers. In that same parish, however, there is a prebend of the church of Lisieux, which I gave to my nephew Hugh of Nonant, as I had been accustomed, out of lavish generosity, to give him almost whatever I could; nor could anything of the kind have come to him more agreeably in that region. He rejoiced, and I likewise exulted, hoping that in time I should receive from my generosity some return, especially from my nephew.

But past experience should have taught me otherwise, had not affectionate indulgence and compassion for so close a kinsman deceived me. I had tenderly reared him from infancy, born of my sister; I had carefully had him educated, enlarged his revenues, and resources voluntarily stood ready for me in every grant I might make to him. In the bishopric of Lisieux I gave him five churches worth approximately one hundred pounds, likewise a prebend in the church of Lisieux worth fifty pounds, and an archdeaconry worth one hundred pounds and more—so much as the extortion and injuries inflicted on those subject to him could yield [Col. 0147A]. Yet his frequent ingratitude could not restrain me from such gifts; rather, I continually heaped useless coals upon his head with all zeal.

I pass over the fact that, by right of the archdeaconry, he was bound to me by homage and fealty—would that he had kept this in more faithful remembrance. I have learned that affection does not create loyalty in him; rather, greed or reverence for superior power does. Use him without fear: he will not dare deceive your majesty. But, prompted by fear rather than devotion or ready loyalty, he will always proceed with prompt action to carry out every one of your wishes [Col. 0147B].

I had hoped that he would at least look kindly upon my final days, and be moved by my old age, weakness, and voluntary poverty, so that in every need he might generously place his own resources at my disposal and in time mercifully relieve my want from what I had given him. Yet he violently usurps a portion of the small benefice which I bestowed upon the poor canons—or rather, which I had as it were reserved for myself—although the aforesaid brothers had peacefully held it for several years, and their predecessors from ancient times. I urgently asked him to consider the justice of God, that of the poor church, and my own poverty; but I could make no progress in preventing him from continually presuming to extend audacious hands and more shamelessly usurping the right of the poor [Col. 0147C].

There is also in that parish a small chapel, having no parishioners and absolutely no revenues, belonging from ancient times to the right of the parish church. It was almost wholly destitute of service and buildings; the priest of the same parish alone visited it when he wished, for devotion’s sake, and divine services could not honorably be celebrated there. Fulk the dean, to whom the parish then belonged, diligently rebuilt it under parish right and constructed his own houses in the old little cemetery adjoining it, altering at his pleasure the use of burial there.

From this chapel Hugh of Nonant removed the priest, after taking the keys and priestly vestments, although the priest had earlier appealed to the Roman Church and in the very act continued to appeal. Thereafter Hugh continually caused his own priest to celebrate divine services there while under anathema, and he violently removes and has removed the parishioners from the authority of the priest whom they had always acknowledged. He does so in order that, if the matter comes to trial, he may seem to enjoy the advantage of a possessor by this device [Col. 0147D].

The correction of so great an outrage belongs to you. I hope for no remedy from elsewhere, because Roman aid is distant and costly for the poor of the Church, though we ought not despair of its assistance. Apply, therefore, your royal hand, in which we place greater confidence. Restrain the unbridled greed of this man; cause those brothers peacefully to possess that church, with its chapel and appurtenances, in their former undiminished condition—as their predecessors are known to have possessed them for a long time, and as they themselves possessed them for the last two or three years—and make him restore likewise the fruits he has received [Col. 0148A].

I beg my lord to remember how, at my last departure from him at Gisors, he gladdened my soul and sent me away enriched by the abundance of his generosity, adding the word of a royal promise that henceforth he would help me in every need, as freely as he had ever done, and would drive away every trouble from me. For nothing is more grievous to me than that the man who ought in all things to stand with me disturbs with implacable malice what I had hoped would gladden the brothers, and does not cease, with tireless greed, to persecute me even to the grave. Nor does he fear to disturb the order of law, although those who possessed the property ought not to have been dispossessed without judgment [Col. 0148B].

They must therefore first be restored, with the fruits and expenses; then a penalty for his offense must be imposed at the judge’s discretion. Let my lord therefore restore me to myself and, in his merciful goodness, restore the repose I hoped for, so that I may be permitted to think without disturbance of the things that concern God [Col. 0148C]. Nothing is more fitting to royal majesty than to restrain the audacity of the proud and, by royal power, preserve its justice for the just and simple.

## CXXVIII. TO HENRY, KING OF THE ENGLISH

At my departure from you at Gisors, you ordered William son of Ralph to have two hundred English pounds paid to me for my chattels. He accepted your command with due willingness and promised me, with such strong assurance, that he would do it that I thought there could be no doubt. He accordingly appointed a date for me in mid-August; I then sent to him in complete confidence, but received nothing. He appointed another day, namely the feast of Saint Michael [Col. 0148D]; yet at that time too nothing was paid to me, nor was any further date assigned for payment.

Thus deceived so often, I thought I could do nothing but send a messenger to your kindness, so that you might cause what you so generously granted to be truly carried into effect. Moreover, your magnificence established for me two hundred pounds annually, for as long as I should live, from the provostship of Lisieux, with your assent and seal, and the approval of the canons and archbishop. This was to be paid in four installments, that is, every three months, so that at this feast of Saint Michael a fourth part should be paid to me, with the remaining portions paid at their proper times. For delay concerning the bishopric, as you know, ought not to turn to my disadvantage [Col. 0149A]; rather, you must cause payment to be made without delay or reduction.

Let your magnificence therefore command both things to be done, for Hugh of Nonant would have greatly frightened me if I thought his words deserved belief. He came to Paris and, when I expected words of joy, told me before the abbot and brothers that your promises would by no means be fulfilled to me and that I must seek support elsewhere.

## CXXIX. TO RICHARD, BISHOP OF WINCHESTER

To his venerable and beloved lord and father Richard, by God’s grace bishop of Winchester, Brother Arnulf, canon of Saint-Victor at Paris—would that he were regular—wishes prosperity, glory, and salvation [Col. 0149B].

For a long time the favor of sincere charity has joined me to you, and the love that arose has never ceased to grow through agreeable increases. When royal counsels often brought us favorable counsel, and royal favor bound us in close embrace, no envy ever arose between us in either direction; rather, each rejoiced in the other’s advantage as in his own. This was praiseworthy and was even called wonderful by many, because envy does not admit a partner in the intimacy of princes: each thinks another’s rejection his own gain, considers favor doubled for himself when the other is removed, and believes whatever is diminished in the other to have increased for himself [Col. 0149C].

Between us, on the other hand, mutual loyalty rejoiced in the advantage of either, and nothing could deter either from showing truer favor. Unshaken truth preserved its freedom in all things and rejoiced to demonstrate its own sincerity by manifest proofs. I have seen our prince, at times inflamed against me by false accusations and directing against me, as it were, certain darts of his indignation, so softened by you that anger was sometimes turned to favor and some were enabled, in security, to share conversation with me and enjoy public intimacy and favor. In this your love’s strength and truth often shone: it did not timidly yield, but rather rejoiced to meet the matter with gentleness and courage and to restore me to my lord’s favor [Col. 0149D].

We rejoiced in one another, and equal love met equal love, striving to serve our common favor by common advantages and services. Since this has plainly been maintained between us by faithful efforts down to the present, I must now take more careful thought that faithful perseverance may be brought to its pleasing fulfillment. You have long known that I had proposed, with the Lord’s favor, to withdraw into religious life, but secular business held me back, hindered by many obstacles. At last, however, by God’s grace I overcame everything and went to the church of Saint-Victor at Paris, leaving all that seemed to impede my progress and advancement. Poor and naked, I followed Christ poor and naked, as he himself taught and drew me [Col. 0150A], desiring with all longing to conform to his humility and poverty, insofar as his mercy going before should grant this to me.

Until now I have lived for my flesh, too little concerned for the salvation of my soul, though I had proposed and desired at least to consecrate my final days to the Lord. Divine mercy preserved that purpose until the suitable time and brought me to it—indeed weakened by old age, yet sound in all my body and limbs, and in the whole strength of my mind—because in this hope I always confessed the Lord and found relief in his mercy. Blessed be God, who appointed this way for you through my example, and may he lead whatever way he has prepared for you and me to the same fulfillment of divine blessedness.

## CXXX. TO HENRY, KING OF ENGLAND

[Col. 0150B]

To Henry, by God’s grace illustrious and glorious king of England, his dearest lord, Brother Arnulf, canon of Saint-Victor at Paris—would that he were regular—wishes prosperity, glory, and salvation.

While I was still living among you in Normandy, the malice of wicked men who falsely suggested to you that I was thinking or wishing something against your glory often stirred up your indignation against me. Yet they could never establish their falsehood by any deeds. For God—whom it is criminal to invoke as a witness to falsehood—is witness that, whatever occasion arose, I never did anything to the detriment of your honor; rather, the memory of your former generosity always prevailed. Although many disadvantages came upon me for that reason, nothing was ever more distressing to me than knowing that your mind had been stirred against me, and that I was not permitted to rejoice, as I had always done, in the assurance of your affection.

Whatever they may have said, their lies could not prevail against me with your goodness so far as to cause any grave scandal. You always preserved me and kept me unharmed from everyone, while my adversaries wasted away because their envy did not rejoice in obtaining its desired result against me. In your mind there lived an unfailing spark of royal goodness, which recalled to you the sincerity of my enduring loyalty and the diligence of my former service; it did not allow malice wholly to prevail, but against all their lies the living memory of my previous merits shone forth. For if the affection of former charity had entirely died out, it could not have revived so easily in feeling. Yet at my last departure, at Gisors, your royal kindness smiled fully upon me.

Although the abundance of royal munificence did not delay in accompanying my departure, among all things—and indeed above all things—I counted it greater that henceforth it promised me the truth of an enduring favor. This is what sustains me in its frequent remembrance: that I now feel myself embraced not so much by the bodily arms of my lord as by the arms of sincere charity. For it will be sweet to me if, dying, I seem to have fallen asleep in my lord’s arms, if your favor attends me in death into the presence of the higher Lord. This is why, now freed from all worldly business, I do not cease to implore his mercy with frequent sighs: that, after the governance of this present kingdom which you hold, he may grant you the joys of the eternal kingdom and mercifully command that I, as one born in your household, be joined to you.

May my lord live and always gloriously surpass every envy. I know that you remember that a gracious word proceeded from the sheer truthfulness of your sincere heart: that henceforth you would always hear me kindly, and that a moderate petition would not return rejected from you. I counted this great—indeed, greatest of all. Yet your generous promise will not make me an importunate claimant; rather, I shall always petition with cheerful modesty. [Col. 0152A] But lest the length of this letter cause weariness, I have entrusted to the bearer what I request, to be communicated to you orally. They are indeed few and small matters when referred to my lord’s excellence; but whatever comes from my lord’s favorable generosity will be very great to me.

## CXXXI. EXCUSE OF A CERTAIN BISHOP

The shortness of time, an unforeseen summons, dangerous journeys, the intolerable harassment of robbers, and the necessary attention to medical treatment render us excusable to your fatherhood. Yet to the election already made and the consecration to be performed, we offer our gracious assent from the heart. For since he is strong in character and morals, vigorous in ability, and flourishing in learning, we believe that, planted in the house of God, he will flourish with divine assistance and bear fruit. [Col. 0152B]

[Col. 0151]

# SERMONS OF ARNULF, BISHOP OF LISIEUX

## I. SERMON DELIVERED AT THE COUNCIL OF TOURS

[Col. 0151C]

### Preface to Giles, Archdeacon of Rouen

At the request of certain persons I have been compelled to commit to writing the sermon delivered at the Council of Tours. Although they stood nearby, the tumult of the crowd prevented them from hearing or understanding sufficiently what was said. I have done what was asked, but unwillingly, because some things gain more favor from simple delivery than careful examination earns them praise. For in matters intended to be spoken publicly, one must serve a common understanding, so that the minds of all may immediately grasp everything said. Therefore the discourse proceeds in nearly ordinary words, lest a more subtle artifice, like some cloud of difficulty, obscure the light of things and words.

And because a discourse of this sort is ordinarily intended to move the emotions, it is fitting to urge it onward, as it were, by frequent pauses and shorter clauses, lest the speech grow sluggish in longer periods, while the mind, stirred as by interruption, rises to attention. If, therefore, the mind is to be moved toward something by the ordering of understanding, the clarity of speech must in every respect be observed; for darkness always attracts more hatred than favor, and the foot of one walking more often stumbles unless it is guided by a preceding gaze.

But in writings, the judgments of readers seem to be invited with a certain confidence. Words are arranged not so much to shape emotions as to be exposed to public examination. In what is set before the eyes, inspection is repeatedly made: now the value of the thought, now the ornament of the speech, is sought, so that the merits of one’s studies may be weighed at leisure by the assessment of reason. In other cases, however, the rapidity of utterance excludes delay for examination, where we scarcely follow the slipperiness of a running tongue even with swift understanding; and often what is said more rapidly rouses sluggish people more forcefully and shapes their feelings.

[Note: [Col. 0151D] C reads “diligence” (*dligentiae*).]

For this reason it did not seem to me that what was spoken should be reduced to writing. Rather, just as it was spoken almost extemporaneously, so it should immediately have passed away with the occasion; for the opportunity supplied it, while it was being spoken, with favor more than any skill of ability could have done. For the matter at hand was the schism which in these days has emboldened secular power, especially against the freedom of God’s Church. Therefore we treated unity and freedom with greater care, so that consolation might make firmer the spirits of those present for persistence, and exhortation make them stronger for resistance.

Read, therefore, but with the same indulgence of affection with which you began: that your eyes may see what is imperfect in me, and that what you read may not be subjected to an exacting examination, but that you may always judge more kindly with a mediating fairness.

[Note: [Col. 0151D] B reads “custom” (*morem*) for “delay” (*moram*).]

[Note: [Col. 0152D] B reads “they follow” (*consequuntur*) for “we follow” (*consequimur*).]

[Col. 0153A]

### Sermon

My lords and fathers, the authority of our lord who presides—namely, the Roman pontiff—has imposed today’s sermon upon me. I accept this assigned duty more from the necessity of obedience than from willingness of mind. I would prefer that this honor had fallen to another, whose life was more commendable and whose abundance both of learning and eloquence was greater. For who am I, that I should presume to offer any speech of my own into the ears of so many, so prudent, so venerable persons? Yet who am I that I should dare to oppose the command of the Roman pontiff? I am constrained on every side. I stand between modesty and necessity. The one advises me to be silent; the other draws me, as by a certain violence, into speech.

For one must obey without delay; yet modesty restrains my tongue, obstructs my understanding, and before your reverence makes me fearful and confused with a kind of stupefaction. For I know that three things are usually required in a preacher: holiness of life, fullness of knowledge, and a more fruitful vein of eloquence. Holiness of life is sought because, unless the preacher’s life is commendable, his preaching will not be welcome. For when a person’s life is despised, it follows that his preaching too is despised. He must fear lest, as soon as he begins to speak, the divine voice immediately rebuke and condemn him: “Why do you recount my statutes, you who have cast my words behind you?” (Psalm 49).

[Col. 0153C]

Perfection of knowledge is sought so that the preacher may have from the treasure of his heart the means to bring forth things new and old; so that he may know how to explain learned speech to those who await it, and temper what he says according to the qualities of persons—knowing to whom he should give milk to drink rather than solid food, and for whom he should provide stronger nourishment. Eloquence is desired. For what purpose? Because just as, if he has no learning, he will have nothing to say, so, unless he has eloquence, he will have no way to say it. Both are necessary: to have something to say and to know how to say it.

The excellence of thoughts calls for elegance of speech, so that the dignity of the words may correspond to the majesty of the subjects, and things and words may meet each other as in a certain harmony. Thus, for the preacher’s speech to be worthy of every acceptance, religion is required in the preacher for the reverence of his speech, knowledge for instruction, and eloquence that it may commend itself pleasantly. That is, the speech should be holy, prudent, and distinguished.

But I, who am brought forth before you, have nothing in myself except a sinful conscience, scant learning, and imperfect eloquence. Therefore it would have been more fitting for me to be silent than to speak, to be fed rather than feed, and to offer you my ears rather than my tongue. I have no confidence in myself; rather, I turn to the holiness of him who commands me and to your merits. Through your intercession, perhaps the grace of him who said, “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ezekiel 2), will grant me something. The necessity of obedience opens my mouth; may his grace, through your merits, fill it with fitting speech!

[Col. 0154A]

In every discourse, therefore, my dearest lords and fathers, it seems to me that two things must be most carefully observed regarding its principal purpose: the cause and the time. Reason supplies the cause; opportunity makes the time fitting. Opportunity, as the eloquent man said, is fitness drawn from time. So it is. Unless what is said draws an evident basis from reason, it is judged idle in itself. If it is said inappropriately, it is judged troublesome. Things that are idle or troublesome rarely obtain the desired result. Therefore, although many matters from holy writings might usefully and credibly be brought forward for everyone, speech should chiefly turn to those matters to which urgent necessity impels us and evident usefulness invites us.

To what? To consider with you the unity and freedom of God’s Church. Without these two, the Church cannot stand safe—indeed, cannot stand at all. For unless the Church has unity, it will not be one; if it is not one, it will not exist. For everything that exists exists because it is one; and what is not one loses substance together with unity. Likewise, unless it has freedom, it will be wretched; and for it, being wretched amounts to not existing—indeed, it is worse to be wretched than not to exist. “It would have been better for that man if he had not been born” (Matthew 26), was said of Judas, because it was better for him not to have been born than to have been born for such misery.

[Col. 0154C]

Therefore, my dearest lords and fathers, if the Church’s condition is to be preserved unharmed, its unity and freedom must be carefully provided for. In these days and this tempest, as we experience miserably, each is oppressed by many troubles and assailed by many injuries: the ambition of schismatics endeavors to divide the one, while the violence of tyrants seeks to take away the other. Yet both will be impossible to them through God’s grace. For it is impossible to divide the spiritual sacrament of ecclesiastical unity, which has been joined and established between Christ and the Church by an indissoluble covenant, with the Father himself as its author. It is impossible to take away God’s Church’s own freedom, which the shedding of the Lord’s blood consecrated.

Although chaff may sometimes fly off and depart from the Lord’s threshing floor through the winnowing fan of frivolity or vanity, the fruit of the threshing floor is not diminished by their departure but purified. Likewise, although the princes of darkness rise violently against God’s Church, the gates of hell cannot prevail against it. Thus, my lords, the Church’s unity is always safe for us, and its freedom always safe; for neither can the seamless tunic be torn, nor Christ’s blood be rendered ineffectual. And though some who were with us have gone out from us, they were not of us; yet the truth of unity has not been divided because of those whom the perversity of their own wickedness separated from us.

Although the tyrants of the earth of whom we spoke rage against temporal goods and even our bodies, so as to devour our flesh, they are weakened and fall. And though they busy themselves with plundering useless burdens, God’s Church nevertheless freely disposes, by its own authority, what must be administered. Indeed, it thrusts them back by spiritual power into prison as wicked servants, binding them there, as it were, with certain fetters: the bond of anathema and the reproach of perpetual curse. In this too divine power appears praiseworthily to work a miracle: while we remain in our unity and freedom, they separate themselves alone from catholic unity and subject themselves to detestable slavery.

But we, dearest brothers and lords, must not return evil for evil, nor be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good. Therefore we must direct the fullest charity toward recalling those who are outside, that through the Lord’s mercy they may be joined to our unity; and that those who attack the peace of ecclesiastical freedom, led by better counsel, may come to their senses. Thus, both through their restoration and through the repentance of these others, the fruitfulness of unity may increase and the unshaken tranquility of desired freedom be preserved.

[Note: [Col. 0155D] B reads “will be served” (*servietur*) for “will be preserved” (*servetur*).]

[Col. 0155C]

To this end we ought to apply every diligence, endure every harassment, and undergo every danger. For this is the special obligation of our profession: we are bishops. For this we wish to be sanctified by ecclesiastical sacraments, enriched with benefices, and distinguished by honors. For this reason too we hold the first seats in the council, the first places at banquets, and greetings in the marketplace. For the same reason multitudes of people bow before us, that they may receive from our hand some portion of the blessing entrusted to us. For they seek to receive from our fullness what we have received from Christ’s fullness.

This is the order: the oil goes before upon the head; from the head it descends upon the beard—upon Aaron’s beard—and flows down from the beard to the hem of the garment. From the head, namely Christ, to the beard, namely the prelates of the Church; from the prelates to the people, to those subject to them. In the head is the fullness of all perfection, and every perfection of fullness. “For in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Colossians 2), namely, solid and perfect fullness. In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (ibid.). In him is the whole Spirit of the Father. Nothing has been taken from perfection there; nothing diminished from fullness there. And from this fullness we all have received, greater and lesser alike: from the fullness indeed, but not fullness itself, for he reserved fullness for himself.

Among us, however, there have been divisions of graces: “There is one Spirit, who works all things in all persons,” not all things in each person; “for he distributes to each as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12). For he breathes where he wills (John 3), and inspires as much as he wills. But we, placed between Christ and the people, have received the privilege of grace and attained the prerogative of dignity. The privilege of grace, because what is to be poured out from us into others is first and more abundantly poured into us. The prerogative of dignity, because we are higher and nearer.

[Col. 0156A]

We are higher, because we have been appointed princes over all the earth. “You shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Psalm 44). This was said of the apostles—and surely also of us, who occupy the apostles’ places with merits truly smaller, but with consolations greater. What kind of principality is ours? Certainly one exalted and strong. “Your friends, O God, are greatly honored; their dominion is greatly strengthened,” says the Prophet (Psalm 138). We are nearer, for he calls us friends; and, as proof of a more gracious friendship, he shows us that not a part but an abundance of the whole intimacy has been granted to us. “I shall no longer call you servants,” he says, “but my friends, because I have made known to you everything that I heard from my Father” (John 15).

It is true. To us it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to the rest, in parables, “so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand” (Mark 4). We have eyes to see and ears to hear. Many and great are your gracious acts toward us, good Jesus; many and beyond estimation are your benefits. Your grace freely goes before and follows us. There is nothing, or little, that we can claim for our own merits, since you continually bestow grace upon grace in lavish generosity. What, then, shall we repay you? “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid to me?” (Psalm 115).

Does he seek repayment? He truly does, for he is also a strict creditor. He does not call in his debtor merely for the principal, but also for interest. “Why,” he says, “did you not put my money into the bank, so that when I returned I might have demanded it from you with interest?” (Luke 19). Since he seeks repayment, let us consult the Prophet as to what may worthily be offered to such majesty as repayment. It is fitting that he who taught us about the quality of our principality should also teach us about the measure of repayment. For what is offered under the name of repayment must redound to honor and add to favor; otherwise it does not produce favor but offense.

Let us therefore hear what he says: “You shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Psalm 44). Behold his merit toward us; but what repayment he seeks from us, he immediately adds: “They shall remember your name, O Lord” (ibid.). As repayment he seeks only that the memory of his name be offered to him. Of what name? He has, of course, many names. Some are names from the Old Testament, with hidden significance; some belong more especially to the New Testament, breathing sweetness and displaying grace. Though they unquestionably drew their origin from the Old Testament, they have gained greater celebration and frequency from the present newness. What are they? Jesus Christ: *Jesus* means “Savior”; *Christ*, “Anointed.” Where there is anointing, there is sweetness; plainly, this name Christ breathes the sweetness of anointing, while Jesus promises the grace of salvation.

[Col. 0157A]

Yet I believe that in this place the Prophet intends another name, because those names provide devotion and confidence by their sweetness and grace; but here he seeks remembrance of another name, whose severity may give us the caution of diligence and the fear of reverence. What is it? God. “God” means fear. In this place he requires us to be fearful and prudent. For he has entrusted to us his inheritance, which he entrusts only to those who fear him. “You have given an inheritance to those who fear your name, O Lord” (Psalm 60).

His inheritance is that which he himself received from the Father by the merit and petition of his Passion. “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations for your inheritance” (Psalm 2). This inheritance is the whole body of believers, known by the name of Church, which contains catholic unity. He entrusted this to our faith and commended it to our care. Therefore, for its care and protection, we must employ every diligence with all fear. No threat should frighten us; no persecution delay us.

[Note: [Col. 0157D] B omits everything following “delay us” through Homily II, p. 10, line 12, “may grow strong,” and makes the two homilies one. In place of what it omits after “delay us,” B has the following: “We have become sharers in consolations. It is right that we should also be companions in tribulations. We must stand against them and set ourselves up as a wall for the house of Israel. This, certainly, will not be easy for us, but it will nevertheless be possible if we steadfastly agree to remain in catholic unity. Furthermore, we are brothers from the same Father,” etc.]

Rather, at every fitting occasion we should faithfully meet them, and embrace the divine help in hope, a hope that does not disappoint. For victory does not lie on earth for us, since Christ, her bridegroom—the conqueror of every aerial power—is her defender for salvation. He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through the ages. Amen.

## II. SERMON ON THE SAME SUBJECT

[Col. 0157C]

In yesterday’s sermon, my dearest lords and fathers, we discussed with you the unity and freedom of God’s Church. Our chief purpose, with every effort, was that your good and holy will might be made more eager amid adversities by the exhortation of God’s word; and that your confidence in the recognition of divine protection and grace, and in the continual growth for the better of our mutual and unbreakable brotherhood, might grow strong.

For we are brothers from the same Father, Christ, and from the same mother, the Church; through regeneration by water and Spirit we have been transferred from children of wrath to adoption as the glorious children of God (Ephesians 1). It is therefore good, because useful; pleasant, because delightful, for us who are joined by this spiritual brotherhood to stand in unity, so that among us, as in the primitive Church, the multitude of believers may be of one heart and one soul. May there be in us one Spirit and one faith. For unity of faith produces concord; concord is the mother of unity; and unity of faith grants freedom.

For from faith we have life and victory. “My righteous one lives by faith” (Romans 1). “This is the victory that conquers the world: our faith.” And the saints conquered kingdoms through faith: the kingdom of Satan, the kingdom of the world, and the kingdom of heaven. This is more apparent regarding the kingdom of the world and Satan’s kingdom; yet “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11). Thus unity of faith, and the faith of unity, conquers every kingdom.

[Col. 0158A]

Therefore we must apply ourselves with all our efforts and urge one another to stand together. If we stand together, each will gain more confidence and strength from the other. If we stand together, we shall be able not only to resist our adversaries, but to challenge them with confidence. If we stand together, God’s Church will appear terrible as an army arrayed in battle order. “Let us stand,” says that prophet, “let us stand together. Who is my adversary? Who disputes with me? Let him approach me” (Isaiah 1). Because he felt someone faithfully standing by him, he spoke with confidence.

We too, my lords and fathers, have some who faithfully stand by us. We have the grace of the citizens above standing by us; we have your merits and prayers standing by us; we have the faith and devotion of catholic kings standing by us, who profess catholic unity with us in word and carry it out in deeds—almost all, indeed, who are known by the Christian name. Compared with so great a multitude, the exception of one is small. One is excepted, and he alone. “Woe to him who is alone, for if he falls, he has no one to lift him up” (Ecclesiastes 4).

Yet even he will, through God’s mercy, be converted and live, for among the rulers of the earth he is much to be praised for prudence and strength—unless he has resolved to place his own glory before divine glory. May he be humbled beneath the mighty hand of God and recognize that the primacy of the Church takes precedence over his own rule. May he understand that, if he confesses Christ, the bridegroom and lord of the Church, he must likewise confess the Church, which is the bride, as his lady. Moreover, he has a particular reason why he ought to recognize the holy Roman Church as his lady; otherwise he may plainly appear guilty of ingratitude. For if we turn to ancient histories, it will be certain that his predecessors received the empire by no right other than the grace of the holy Roman Church alone. Therefore rulers can claim no more right than the generosity of the giver bestowed upon them.

[Col. 0158D]

Moreover, Christ himself stands by us. For he did not entrust the Church to us on the condition that he would abandon it; he is always present. “I will not leave you orphans,” he says; “I go and come to you” (John 14), intending to remain with you until the consummation of the age. Therefore he is our helper and protector for salvation (Psalm 32). With the help of so many who stand by us, no threat should frighten us, no persecution call us back. Rather, we must stand against them and set ourselves up as a wall for the house of Israel.

And God is faithful: “he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but will provide with the temptation the outcome, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians 10). Indeed, he invites us to confidence in attaining victory by his own example: “Take courage,” he says, “I have conquered the world” (John 16). If the world has once been conquered, it was not unconquerable. It will be easier for us to conquer one already conquered than one unconquered. Christ undertook to conquer it and conquered it. Once it was said: “Look, Lord, and consider, for the enemy has risen up” (Lamentations 1); now, however, it is said that the enemy has been cast down. We may confidently attack one who lies fallen and conquered. For if he has been cast down, he will not rise again; if conquered, he will not presume. No resurrection or presumption of his will prevail from this time forward.

[Col. 0159B]

Yet I fear that perhaps someone may murmur, saying that it is presumptuous to emulate an example of such perfection. “It was easy,” he says, “for Christ to conquer the world, since he created the world.” For his name is Almighty, to whom willing and being able are the same thing. But it is not so with me, since I am weak and all my bones are troubled (Psalm 6). That is, every strength of my nature has been shaken by the corruption of sin, and therefore my substance is as nothing before him.

But by no means, my lords and fathers, ought we to lose confidence or despair. For just as Christ’s words are set before us for instruction, so his deeds are set before us as a pattern. And just as by instruction it is impossible for us to attain the fullness of his knowledge, so by examples we cannot attain equality with his virtues. Yet, though we cannot reach the height of his majesty, we may nevertheless advance to some likeness, at least, of his holiness. It is beneficial to imitate him, even though no one can equal him. Our perfection lies beneath his perfection. We must follow, even if we cannot overtake; we must press on, not with the same strides, but along the same path and in the same footsteps.

If examples among human beings are also sought, we can find many people who conquered the world. Let us consider the Apostle: a sinful human being like us, though not sinful to the degree we are; one who calls himself the least of the apostles and unworthy to be called an apostle because he persecuted God’s Church. “I have fought the good fight,” he says, “I have completed the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness” (2 Timothy 4). The Apostle fought; from the contest he obtained victory, and from victory he obtained a crown. He ran and completed the course, and therefore attained the prize—the same prize that is the crown.

But who are you, who seek a crown without victory, victory without contest? In fact, it is impossible to have conquered without contest; in law, it is unreasonable to demand a crown without victory. “For no one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Timothy 2). The law of contest is perseverance: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24). Salvation, certainly, is the same as the prize and the crown.

[Col. 0160A]

If a greater multitude of human examples pleases you, nearly innumerable thousands of martyrs will present themselves to us, who ran with all desire toward this contest and at last received a victory indeed bloody, but nevertheless with joy and glory. Did not the apostles go from the council rejoicing because they had been deemed worthy to suffer disgrace for Jesus’ name? (Acts 5). Did not Stephen, among the stones themselves, petition and pray for those stoning him? (Acts 7). Did not Peter and Andrew preach the truth from the cross? Did not Lawrence joyfully mock the tyrant from the gridiron? Did not the invincible courage of Vincent hasten to anticipate even the executioners themselves at the rack?

[Note: [Col. 0159D] B omits *non* (“not”).]

But if an example is sought from the weaker sex, Agatha went most joyfully and gladly to prison, and as though invited to a banquet, commended her contest to the Lord in prayer. The day would fail me first—indeed, the whole span of a longer year would expire—before the victories of the saints could be fully recounted. These were truly strong men, most skilled for war, who conquered pride by humility and tyranny by patience.

But the merciful and compassionate Lord deals more kindly with our weakness. For he himself is aware of our weakness, since he knows our frame. He therefore makes our endurance bearable. Truly, as has been said, he provides an outcome with the labor. No contrivances of ancient cruelty are now brought against us. Rather, we are permitted to ride in horses and chariots, sometimes to feast magnificently every day upon great and marvelous things far beyond our station, to be clothed in costly honors, and to abound in riches.

[Note: [Col. 0159D] B reads “are permitted” (*sustinentur*) for “we are permitted” (*sustinemur*).]

[Note: [Col. 0160D] B omits “daily” (*quotidie*).]

We preach Christ’s poverty in words, but display it less in example—unless perhaps contempt for riches and holy humility spiritually restore his poverty in us. For poverty itself is not required of us, but contempt for wealth. “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Psalm 61): he did not say that they should not increase, but that the heart should not be set upon them. He forbade the heart to be attached, not the hand. Certainly the Prophet proclaims himself poor and needy amid every abundance of riches.

We may therefore lawfully possess riches, provided that we do not consider ourselves their masters but their stewards; provided that we understand the property of the poor to be Christ’s property, if revenues are distributed for the Church and for the needs of the poor. Otherwise clear reason will prove us thieves and robbers if we presume to handle, according to our own will, things belonging to others against the will of their owners.

Since riches must be distributed rather than retained, they can nowhere be distributed more justly or more generously than to those who follow the Church in exile, who have suffered loss of their goods for Christ’s cause. The cause is common, but every loss and all harassment have been directed against them. For we sit in dignity within the walls of our own households and courts, while they, shamefully and violently driven from their seats, wander through regions. Divine mercy provides us every consolation in abundance, while they patiently and silently await from other people’s hands the provisions of life. A long company of our attendants and dependents stands by us; they are compelled to live an almost solitary life among strangers.

[Col. 0161A]

Yet if support obtained by begging has given them some consolation, it is unworthy to demand benefits from those to whom you ought habitually to give them. Let us therefore open to them the depths of compassion, pour out upon them every feeling of sympathy and reverence, and embrace them with every kindness and favor. For then we shall fulfill Christ’s law, if we bear one another’s burdens. They are prudent men, commendable for much integrity, whom the Lord has chosen to be tested like gold in the furnace (Wisdom 3), so that through their expenditure of persons and possessions the Church’s victory may be brought to completion.

Blessed are those to whom it has been given to exchange transient things for eternal things. More blessed are those who have suffered death or bodily injuries and have compensated the priceless blood of Christ with their own unworthy and corruptible blood. For what? Have we not expended Christ’s blood for the cause of our redemption, so that we might repay it to him at the time of repayment, namely when he himself demands it? “The sinner borrows and does not repay” (Psalm 36); but we, by the Lord’s mercy, shall repay, since we confess ourselves bound not merely by a civil legal device but naturally, through the reality of the matter itself.

[Col. 0161C]

Would that it might be granted me also, good Jesus, to exchange my temporal things with you for your spiritual things. Would that you might be pleased to receive my blood for yours, though unpaid. Or, because a mutual valuation cannot be made between the blood lent and owed—namely, yours and mine—may I at least be released and absolved by your most gracious acceptance, by which you customarily reckon righteousness as received without works, and rewards without merits: that is, by the grace of a good act you confer the grace of recompense.

## III. SERMON AT A SYNOD
Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent servant whom the lord has set over his household [Col. 0161D], to give them food at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom, when the lord comes, he finds watchful (Matt. 24). The Church, as you know, dearest brothers, is called the congregation of the faithful. The faithful are those enrolled under the Christian name, who derive the dignity of the Christian name from the acknowledgement of the Catholic faith. For this faith is concerning Christ and from Christ, and therefore is called Christian from the name of its proper author; but Catholic—that is, universal—both because of the precepts of its general rules and because of the uniform outcome of eternal recompense for all.

For this faith is no longer [Col. 0162A] assigned to particular persons or confined within any narrow limits of place; rather, the doctrine of truth has been poured forth from the lost sheep of the house of Israel to all nations, after the sound of apostolic preaching went out into all the earth (Rom. 10). Therefore, after the darkness of ignorance has been cleansed away through this faith and the obscurity of ancient figures wiped away, the merciful and compassionate Lord so illumines his Church with knowledge of the truth that he also forms it by works of charity, so that, as grace goes before, he may grant her to embrace him and present himself for her to see. For this he called her from darkness into his marvellous light; for this he assumed her with himself into the unity of the same body. For this he freed her from the slavery of corruption at the cost also of his own blood [Col. 0162B].

For she herself is the price of his blood, the recompense of his passion, the glory of his majesty. That the acquisition of this inheritance redounds manifestly to his glory we learn from his own rejoicing, because in receiving her from the Father he commends her with greater zeal and even exults joyfully: “The measuring-lines have fallen for me in pleasant places; indeed, my inheritance is splendid to me” (Ps. 15). She is splendid because she is beautiful and comely; beautiful because she is altogether beautiful, having neither spot nor wrinkle (Eph. 5). How great a zealot he is for this brightness and beauty is clearly shown even by the multitude of names by which he frequently calls her. For a multitude of names expresses a multitude [Col. 0162C] of love. He could not be content with one name: by them he distinguishes the diversity of virtues in her and reveals in himself the full affection of love toward her.

Now he calls her chosen, now beloved, now bride, or queen, and by many other names full of spiritual mysteries and illumined by sacred significations. Yet for the present I have resolved to be content with a few, because I speak to the wise, to whom the names and the sacraments of the names are more fully known than to me.

She is called chosen: “Come,” he says, “my chosen one, and I will set my throne in you.” She is called chosen on account of the eminence of virtues by which she excels. But this throne, which is said to be established in her, is the throne of the Most High; and it can be placed only in what is exalted [Col. 0162D], because he is the one who dwells on high—indeed, in the highest places: “I dwell in the highest places,” he says, “and my throne is in a pillar of cloud” (Ecclus. 24). He dwells in the highest places because the heaven of heavens is the seat of his habitation. Paul also finds him above the third heaven (2 Cor. 12).

This throne is in a pillar because, just as a pillar is lofty and slender, so the way that leads to life is lofty and narrow (Matt. 7); and life is Christ. But that this throne is said to be established in a cloud requires closer consideration. For does he not dwell in inaccessible light? [Note: [Col. 0162D] B omits “not.”] (1 Tim. 6). Is he not the true light that enlightens every person [Col. 0163A] coming into this world? (John 1). That is, the everlasting light that will shine upon the saints of God, for they shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt. 13). And his throne is as the sun in the sight of the Father. Truly, he is light and dwells in light. Yet for the present a cloud has been interposed between us and that light, preventing us from perfectly beholding it with the eyes we now possess; indeed, clouds and darkness are round about him (Ps. 96).

Yet we see something of it: through a mirror, in an enigma (1 Cor. 13), and by means of intervening bodily instruments. For the visible things created by him are like a mirror and instruments for us, through which we may in some fashion contemplate his invisible things.
