For his invisible things are perceived from him through the things that have been made [Col. 0163B]. But, God willing, we shall see more perfectly in the future, when we shall see him as he is (1 John 3), when we shall know even as we are known, when our eyes shall see the king in his beauty, when we shall be transformed from glory into glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3).

This, it seems to me, was what the Prophet desired when he said: “When shall I come and appear before the face of the Lord?” (Ps. 41). It is as though he said: I see a little, but a cloud is set before me, a veil interposed; I do not see except through bodily instruments. I would have all these things removed, that I might see face to face; that Christ, my life, might appear to me, and that I might appear with him in glory.

[Col. 0163C] Again, she is called beloved because she herself loves. She would not be loved unless she loved, for he does not love those who do not love him: “I love those who love me” (Prov. 8). Yet he goes before in loving, because he first loved us; but he loves for this purpose, that he may make people loving. For unless the one who is loved answers him with reciprocal love, the affection of divine love is withdrawn. But how great is the mutual affection of alternating charity between him and the one who loves him is difficult for us—indeed impossible—to explain. Not even Solomon’s wisdom could fully relate it to us, although he pursued with the greatest care now their embraces and kisses, now spices and ointments, now the languor of the spirit, now the failing of the soul, now the burning zeal of inquisitive emulation [Col. 0163D], now the tender affection of delicate compassion. It is enough for me to have touched upon these things briefly, because your religious devotion has more fully known them within yourselves through spiritual experience itself.

The third name we proposed is that she is called bride. By no other name could the mystery of unity and the perfection of sincere charity between them be expressed more clearly. For what unity and charity are truer than that two should become one flesh and be animated by one and the same spirit? For he was assumed from her into the unity of the same flesh, and she from him into the unity of the same spirit. “Therefore the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2): certainly Christ and the Church. For the Word was made flesh [Col. 0164A] (John 1); and the whole body of the Church is animated and governed by the Spirit of Christ.

The Church negotiated wisely: she gave flesh in order to receive the Spirit; and he, assuming an animate body, bestowed his divinity upon us. This covenant was celebrated in the person of Christ, when divinity was joined with humanity and humanity with divinity. These betrothals were there confirmed by the authority of the Father and the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit. For as yet they are only betrothals: the wedding has not yet been celebrated, the marriage not yet consummated. But all will be fulfilled in the future, when the bridegroom comes. Those found ready will enter with him to the wedding; the unready will be shut out by the doors.

Those brought in to the wedding of the Lamb [Col. 0164B] will feast there in his sight; there they will delight in joy (Ps. 67); there they will be made drunk with the abundance of his house, and he will give them drink from the torrent of his delight (Ps. 35). There those now empty will be filled with the good things of his house (Ps. 64), and the hungry will be satisfied (Ps. 106), because his glory will appear (Ps. 16). There the bride will receive the crown that the Lord has prepared for her for ever. Therefore she is also worthy to be called queen.

And rightly so, because she is the bride of the king. Christ is the king whose bride she is, both king and son of a king. He does not possess an accidental kingdom, but an inherited one, because it is from the Father: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your justice to the king’s son.” He speaks to the Father: “God the Father, give to the king”—that is, Christ, your Son—the judgment and justice of the king, namely yourself, who are king: the power and knowledge of judging. For justice and judgment are the preparation of his throne (Ps. 88). In these two things the whole authority of royal majesty consists: judgment vindicates through the severity of power and restrains evils committed so that they may not be committed again. It punishes transgressions and checks audacity. Justice, however, guides and forms through the discernment of knowledge. It forms for virtue and guides toward salvation.

Therefore the Father is king, and the Son is king. The Father is king from eternity; the Son likewise, according to divinity, is king from eternity. They are not two kings of one and the same kingdom, but one king. Yet Christ, according to humanity, was made king in time [Col. 0164D], and the Church was constituted queen of the same kingdom with him.

“The queen stood at your right hand” (Ps. 44). Christ is said to sit at the right hand of God the Father, that is, amid the more excellent goods of his glory, because of the rest of consummated glory which he received. The Church is said to stand at Christ’s right hand, not sit, because she is always stationed in readiness. “The queen stood at his right hand.” In this phrase it seems to me that the prophet foresaw a threefold state of the Church.

First, it seems to me that he considers her standing at the right hand of the Crucified, where she receives and observes, for her salvation, the sacraments flowing from his side. [Note: [Col. 0163D] B reads ejus (“his”) for sibi (“to/for herself”).] “There stood,” he says, “by the cross of Jesus his mother and his mother’s sister, [Col. 0165A] Mary of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene” (John 19). And the disciple whom Jesus loved stood there. Peter stood, and perhaps other faithful persons following from afar to see the end. The centurion also stood, openly declaring that this truly was the Son of God (Matt. 27). At that time nearly the whole universality of the Church consisted in that small number. Moreover, one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out (John 19): the blood of redemption and the water of regeneration. In these two, the power and efficacy of all the sacraments are believed to have flowed forth. For we are saved in faith in the Passion and in the washing of baptism: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16). For the blood of Christ cleanses our consciences from dead works to serve [Col. 0165B] the living God. And the water seen to come out from the temple of Christ’s body, from the right side, saved all whom it reached.

Therefore three bear witness on earth: the Spirit, the water, and the blood (1 John 5). For the Spirit bears witness concerning Christ, because the Spirit is the one who testifies, since Christ is truth (ibid.). But the water and blood bear witness to us for salvation.

The second state of the Church is from the time of Christ’s resurrection until the consummation of the world. During this time she is a pilgrim upon earth, and meanwhile soberly appropriates these temporal goods for the uses of honourable necessity. Yet she wholly abides spiritually in the knowledge of the sacraments [Col. 0165C], the exercise of virtues, and the contemplation of heavenly things. Thus she is in a sense seen to stand also in the present, since these things are spiritual and granted to her by the gift of divine goodness, so that from her reception of present gifts she may have firm expectation of future ones.

But the third state of the Church will be fulfilled in the future, when all things are consummated: then his right hand will embrace her, and the fullness of eternal blessedness will cherish her.

[Col. 0165D] “The queen stood at your right hand” (Ps. 44). In this expression we do not wish to assign a plurality of kingdoms to Christ and the Church, because there is one simple kingdom, which the eternity of the Godhead establishes for Father and Son according to divinity, and which grace communicated in time to the Son of the Virgin and to the Church. Therefore there is no impropriety in calling the Church queen, even queen of heaven, when the Psalmist confidently calls her children gods and sons of God: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81).

Thus, my lords and fathers, as we have said, a multitude of names expresses a multitude of love, and their diversity also designates a diversity of mysteries. Therefore Christ—the Chosen One—has entrusted this so splendid and acceptable Church, the chosen one to the chosen one, the beloved to the beloved, the bride to the bridegroom, the queen to the king, to your faith; he has commended her to your prudence, so that you may devote every diligence and every care to her care and keeping, with fear of his name [Col. 0166A], in order that every work of hers may be directed by your zeal toward the good, insofar as it is possible for you, and that she herself may remain whole and unharmed under your defence and Christ’s protection.

For faith and prudence are required in a steward so that through his faithfulness his lord’s advantage may be preserved, and through his prudence troubles threatening the household may be driven away.

[Note: [Col. 0165D] “May be driven away.” In place of what follows this word, B has: “It has been established; in your time it shall not be dissolved,” etc., through “May your holiness prosper in Christ”; these are from Letter 3, to Pope Celestine.]

Thus the increase of the Lord and the advancement of the household may always grow. They are Christ’s sheep. Although he is their Lord, he nevertheless professes himself their shepherd, so that he may declare both his authority over them and his affection toward them: that they may obey him as Lord by hearing his voice, and that he, as the good shepherd, may place and preserve them beside the water of refreshment in the place of pasture [Col. 0166B]. “My sheep hear my voice” (John 10). Behold what he seeks from those who are his: to be heard as Lord. “And I, the Lord, know them” (ibid.). Behold how he returns to them the kindly affection of mutual knowledge and recognition.

How great a grace of charity he extends to them is readily shown by the price of redemption which the beneficence of the Redeemer expended for their liberation. For they were bought at a great price: namely, the inestimable blood of the Crucified. Though Judas set a price upon it, it cannot fall beneath the cheapness of any price, for nothing in created things is comparable to it: it is exalted above every creature and placed at the Father’s right hand.

Humanity did not know how highly his humanity could be valued, because, though it had derived [Col. 0166C] likeness from the image of its Creator, it could by no hope or reasoning presume or foresee either the humility of the incarnation or the bitterness of the Passion. Indeed, the creation of things in some measure displays the glory of divine majesty, because the wonderful work declares the wisdom of its maker; and through the visible things made by him his everlasting power and divinity become known. It seemed that he had made what he had made in order that he, unknown through the ages, might come into the knowledge of rational nature, and that there might arise, as it were, a commerce of mutual knowledge: while he knew our frame, we in some measure understood the unity of the divine substance.

But that he was made lower than the angels (Heb. 2), that for a short time he was enclosed in the bridal chamber of a virgin’s womb and took the form of our servitude [Col. 0166D], that he endured human insults and finally the pain of the Passion—manifest truth declares that this was singularly expended for our salvation, so that his temporal death might free us from the sentence of ancient condemnation and the ratification of the New Testament might call us back to eternal life.

For he himself is the singular price of redemption, offered with equal kindness for individuals and for all, so that no one may claim for himself the magnitude of greater grace, nor anyone the pre-eminence of any privilege. Equality of redemption followed uniformity of creation, so that it might equally benefit all toward the future outcome of predestined recompense [Col. 0167A]. For it could have furnished material for pride or envy if a more abundant pardon had preferred some over others, as though the rest had been condemned through some defect of inferior essence or lesser mercy.

Therefore, if we carefully consider humankind’s origin and course, there appears in regard to humanity the incomparable goodness of the Creator, the wonderful charity of the Redeemer, and the swift grace of the Saviour. Concerning this, we have been entrusted with what was formed by such goodness, preserved by such charity, and finally believed destined to be raised to such glory—a matter of great condescension. But the greater the condescension, the greater the danger; and the greater the rewards that recompense diligent effort, the greater is the punishment for negligence. For just as God is the rewarder of good things, so he is the Lord, the God of vengeance (Ps. 93): with him, as nothing is left unrewarded, so nothing is left unpunished.

Blessed, therefore, are those servants whose faith and prudence will please the Lord when he comes. He will set them over all his goods: that is, over the things which the Lord has prepared for those who love him. He will reserve nothing hidden, but, as though his generosity were poured out upon all, will lavish the riches of his glory—the fullness, namely, of heavenly joys—and will admit them as co-heirs of the heavenly kingdom. Thus they may receive from his hand the diadem of beauty; made beautiful by it, they may contemplate, with unveiled face, him who is beautiful beyond the children of men in form (Ps. 44), and delight in [Col. 0167C] the abundance of peace, through the same our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honour and dominion (1 Tim. 6) for ever and ever.

IV. SERMON ON THE ANNUNCIATION OF THE GLORIOUS VIRGIN MARY

[Note: [Col. 0167D] Absent from the printed editions.]

“The angel Gabriel was sent to Mary, a virgin betrothed to Joseph” (Luke 1). What had been predestined from eternity, what had long ago been promised through many prophetic oracles, at last, dearest brothers, began on this day to be fulfilled through the working of divine grace. For God the Father had decreed from eternity that his Only-Begotten Son should be incarnate for the redemption of humankind, so that by the mystery of his incarnation [Col. 0167D] the ancient cunning of Satan might be undone and by the condescension of humility his power and pride might be broken.

Perhaps this had not been disclosed to the angels even from the beginning. But the greatness of the counsel lay hidden within the secret of divine goodness until a messenger privy to the secret should be sent, to announce the benefits of freedom to be granted to the human race. Thus the angel Gabriel was sent, made privy to the divine secrets, as a faithful interpreter of the divine will and, as it were, fulfilling the interpretation of his own name, to foretell that the strength of God would assume the weakness of flesh.

If, therefore, we consider the speech of the promised greeting itself, the messenger of salvation rightly set forth words of salvation, being sent to announce the salvation of all and remove destruction. The Virgin was the first to receive both the word and affection of salvation, because in her humble condition she gave faith and assent to all that the angel revealed. Therefore she was utterly cleansed from original sin and from any actual sins that there might have been, so that no corruption of sin nor desire of corruption might remain in her [Col. 0168A]. For divine magnificence prepared for itself such humanity in the Virgin as it intended to assume from her, so that, having recovered the dignity of the first creation, incorrupt divinity might be united incorruptly to nature.

Therefore she could rightly be called full of grace, since she first received the fullness of her own sanctification; and she could immediately exult in a singular privilege: that she should be both mother and virgin, and that opposites should find a harmonious outcome in her [Col. 0168B]. For nowhere else had fruitfulness known virginity, nor had the simple purity of virginity known fruitfulness; nor had they ever been joined by mutual communion or any covenant. Both, indeed, are good and praiseworthy; but in others the privilege of virginal chastity is greater. In Mary, fruitfulness is more excellent than virginity, if the fruit of fruitfulness and the merits of virginity are rightly compared.

For this fruit, proceeding from the truth sworn by the Lord to David, has been placed upon his seat—established upon his throne and kingdom by perpetual right—so that from the efficacy of the sacraments firmness may grow, and strength from the sanctification of virtues [Col. 0168C]. This fruit and shoot, growing into the magnificence and glory of divinity joined to it, was made higher than every earthly creature, so that nothing is either stronger in power or more excellent in dignity. Thus in Mary the honour of fruitfulness derives its substance from the quality of its own fruit, where no losses but increases of any virtues concur. In others, however, the loss of virginity is restored by the benefit of offspring, and the joys of received children compensate for the glory of virginity lost.

For in others, prior losses receive consolation from the quality of the outcome, when the fruitful woman receives both relief from pressure and the increase of hoped-for offspring. But the virgin who turns away carnal allurements in both mind and body, and diligently restrains the force of desire through modesty, advances toward reward in proportion as she more fully renounces herself through the grace of continence [Col. 0168D]. Thus the fruitful have what they should render thanks for; the virgin has what she should hope for. In them, the merits of virginity pass into thanksgivings; in her, those same merits of virginity continually grow strong toward reward.

But in our Virgin childbirth or conception brought no loss; rather, she attained a height of honour so much greater as she was consecrated by a more wonderful conception. Virginity and fruitfulness therefore meet in her as though in mutual embraces: the glory of virginity redeems her fruitfulness, and the fruit of fruitfulness raises her virginity [Col. 0169A]. Her fruitfulness, therefore, is to be venerated for many miracles, embraced for many benefits, and celebrated with many praises. In it the sublimity of divinity so meets humility that weakness is not overwhelmed by glory, nor majesty in any respect deprived of its own dignity.

Certainly in others virginity is greater than fruitfulness to the extent that corruption is less than integrity, because fruitfulness is preceded by a certain disapproved pleasure, since carnal intercourse and the passions of corrupted flesh do not permit it to be without fault. Hence the Psalmist remembers that he was conceived in sins, because in him sin was transmitted in both respects from a corrupted origin, and desire, proceeding from ancient corruption, supplied the tinder of sin.

But in [Col. 0169B] Mary’s fruitfulness divinity alone was operative. When the power of the Most High overshadowed the Virgin and the coming Spirit consecrated the unity of flesh and Word (Luke 1), no vice could arise from what was not vicious, nor ought the author of virtues to take away virtues but rather to bring them. Therefore he did not remove the singular privilege of her chosen chastity but added the honour of fruitfulness.

Thus virginal modesty recognizes new offspring, and nature marvels that flesh is made fruitful by the Spirit and that the law of human propagation is wholly changed: there is neither conception from pleasure nor the bringing forth of offspring with pain. For from eternity God from God and flesh from the mingling of flesh were born in time; now, by the operation of the Spirit alone, God is formed into man and man into God [Col. 0169C]. This is wonderful and possible to divine majesty alone: that humanity and divinity—this flesh and that Spirit—should constitute a unity, however great;  that the impassible should show himself to us as passible, the eternal as temporal; that we should be permitted to behold with bodily eyes him whose excellence the spiritual eyes of the citizens of heaven do not attain.

Our faith must indeed conceive this with a sounder understanding: it must proclaim a unity not of substances but of person, and must not believe that one passed into the other by any confusion or mixture. For the Word, always abiding in the eternal simplicity of his own divinity, is neither composed through admixture with another nor transferred into something else by the abolition of himself; rather, the substances [Col. 0169D] and natures alike remain in themselves. Christ, like a giant surpassing all in incomparable strength, eagerly ran the freely undertaken course of our mortality.

Therefore, to bring the purpose of divine predestination to effect, the angel was sent to the Virgin and today disclosed the mystery of the divine will hitherto delayed: as it was eternally provided by the whole Trinity, so it is also announced by the whole Trinity as to be fulfilled. For he says: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (ibid.). Therefore let us weigh with earnest consideration the force and order of the words. First, the Holy Spirit is announced as about to come upon the Virgin; afterwards she is proposed to be overshadowed by the power of the Most High, that is, the Father [Col. 0170A]; so that, when the Virgin’s conception had been prepared, an ineffable final generation of the Son might arise, separated from her womb yet flesh in the womb.

Here you see the Angel plainly expressing the presence of the whole Trinity: the Spirit comes upon her, the Most High overshadows her, and the Son is said to be incarnate. It is clear, therefore, that what was done is the work of the whole Trinity, although only one was incarnate. That is, one alone from the whole Trinity displayed the substance of the entire Godhead in this act, while one alone personally carried out the ministry of human redemption.

Thus temporal generation was added to eternal generation, and temporal birth likewise added to eternal birth, so that what is eternal might remain perfect in its eternity, while what is temporal might receive the state of its perfection not so much from nature as from miracle. For the person of a human being must come from the union of two human beings; but here new offspring proceeds and is formed from the simple antecedent substance of one human being alone. When this humanity was assumed, the excellence of divine majesty was so infused into our lowliness that, through the wondrous intercourse of flesh and Word preceding it, the whole is called man and the whole is called God; and one is predicated of the other by a new form of expression. For this predication declares unity, not essence or nature [Col. 0170B]; neither reason nor nature allows either to subsist in the other, or substance in substance. [Col. 0170C] Rather, a certain ineffable personal, as it were, consolidation produces unity.

For the essence of flesh did not pass into the essence of the Word, nor did the Word assume the passions of the flesh; but the distinction of unmixed natures always preserves their own properties.

Therefore, if evangelical authority tells you that the Word was made flesh, understand “made” as nothing other than “united.” Do not let confusion or mixture establish this unity for you. Rather, revere the individual substances, each abiding in itself, with due estimation, and set before yourself one and the same singular person from the plurality of such diverse things. Thus if, concerning Christ—that is, God and man—you hear something now human, now divine, understand it to be predicated [Col. 0170D] not from the same cause but with each predicate referring to different grounds.

That he is at one time called Almighty, at another Creator of all, at another the only-begotten Son of the Father from eternity, is known to belong to him from the substance of divinity. But that he was born of a woman, made under the law, bore the shame of the cross and the bitterness of the Passion, no one doubts to have proceeded from the nature of humanity. But if you see something that belongs particularly to one substance attributed to the whole person which embraces both substances, know that by reason of assumption it belongs to the whole person. Yet do not assign bodily passions to divinity or divine majesty to humanity.

For the Angel says that what was to be born of the Virgin would be called the Son of God [Col. 0171A], although this title cannot belong to it on account of what comes from the Virgin. But divine goodness did not wish to remove the dignity of the name from that to which it had destined the truth of the same substance to be communicated.

For the accomplishment of this, after many ages, one untouched by every desire was appointed. By this announcement, her vow of perpetual virginity was confirmed rather than removed, since the Angel had formed her husband to a like assent. No inclination to carnal intercourse remained on either side; rather, the devotion of the faithful man gladly chose to devote itself to guarding and serving virginity and the Virgin.

Therefore the holy Virgin, secure in her vow, proceeds wisely to the marriage prepared for her by the Holy Spirit, and embraces of souls, rather than bodies, are joined in a sacred covenant [Col. 0171B]. Certainly, in contracting the betrothal at first the man may perhaps have had another intention; but instructed by the Angel, he immediately turned wholly to the desire of perfect continence, so that their souls might correspond to each other in equal mutual likeness and no disagreement of divergent wills might seem to create division.

Therefore, let no one say that the betrothal was removed, but rather that it was consummated by the ensuing marriage. Nothing was taken from the holiness of the sacrament of their resolve; instead, the shared manner of life joined them in marital union. Moreover, although neither the act nor the will of carnal intercourse intervened, it is nevertheless evident that there was a marriage, because that contract derives its substance not from the mingling of flesh but from the will alone of persons lawfully consenting.

[Col. 0171C] Therefore, if neither desire nor carnal embraces are required for this, and if all that is necessary to produce a marriage is known to have intervened, it is clear that they were true spouses, so that he should rightly be called husband and she wife. If, however, it is said that marriage cannot be contracted unless consent to carnal union is shared, so that neither spouse may be able to deny the other the access required: that is indeed true if they agree in this intention and contemplate the desired pledges of future offspring. But if they resolve to renounce this condition, whether through love of chastity or through some hindering incapacity, while establishing that they will observe the law of marriage in all other respects, then the shared manner of life and the agreed service due under reciprocal authority form the substance of the intended contract [Col. 0171D]; and the faith and grace of sacred fellowship establish its perpetual reality.

For what reason compelled her to grant this consent unwillingly, when the perpetual integrity of the Virgin pleased him and it was his own vow to venerate, in the Virgin’s natural condition [Col. 0172A], the holiness of perpetual continence? And if an example may be drawn from lesser things to greater, perhaps some expressed likeness may be found in the virgin Cecilia. Having consecrated to the Lord the gift of perpetual virginity by a familiar vow, as a kind of holocaust, she nevertheless did not refuse to contract marriage with Tiburtius through the intervention of friends. She trusted in the Lord that divine wisdom would preserve in her the chastity devoted to him, and that Cecilia might seem humbly to have yielded to her parents’ wishes.

Therefore, while the instruments played, the young man predestined to life hastened to nuptial embraces and eagerly sought the desired entrance to the virginal bed. But she, with sighs and prayers arising from awareness of her vow [Col. 0172B], begged the Lord that no stain of carnal desire might steal upon her, to the shame of her spirit and body, but that he might preserve her body wholly untouched for her sincere spirit.

Thus the prudent virgin came to an amicable agreement with him, as by a kind of compact: she persuaded him to the same resolve to preserve chastity, and, after he had been purified by the water of baptism, led him on to the triumphal crown of glorious martyrdom. Who, then, would say that no marriage took place because they chose to abstain from carnal contact, when we frequently see many unite in marriage from whom extreme old age or some infirmity has taken every hope and possibility of such intercourse?

But it is certain that what can equally be present or absent as something accidental is not of the substance of the thing; and marriage is observed more holily and purely without that which cannot be without fault unless excused through the good of marriage. Surely, then, why should there not at least be a like privilege of circumstance and will, allowing them to enjoy the same effect, when some are unwillingly constrained by the necessity of incapacity while others are formed by the affection of devotion and zeal for holiness [Col. 0172C]?

From all this it is clear that the Angel could rightly call her a virgin and Joseph her husband: no violence or injury at all was done to the vow of virginity by a willing husband. Rather, he always devoted diligent effort, with every care, that he might faithfully and devoutly fulfil the office of ministry which he had undertaken—being instructed by the frequent admonition of angels, and with the Holy Spirit always directing every work of holy diligence to the good—to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0173]

**TREATISE OF ARNULF, BISHOP OF LISIEUX, ON THE SCHISM ARISING AFTER THE DEATH OF POPE HONORIUS II**

**PREFACE**

[Col. 0173A]

To the venerable Geoffrey, by the grace of God bishop of Chartres and legate of the Roman Church, Arnulf, archdeacon of Sées, his humble and devoted cleric, greeting.

Were I present, I would not refuse, to the best of my powers, to render faithful service in conducting the business of your legation. For both the common cause of the suffering Church would summon me, and devotion bound by your benefits, and the favor of the Roman pontiff, by which I confess myself to be more closely obligated. But since my long-desired studies of Roman law have led me into Italy, distance of place has indeed withdrawn my bodily service, but it has not suppressed my spiritual affection. For the inward witness of my secret conscience knows how faithfully I sympathize with the suffering Church, how affectionately I grieve amid adversities for the Roman prelate, and how wholly I judge myself indebted to you in mind. Therefore, since the opportunity of rendering bodily service has been taken away, I could not at least restrain my pen; but I have attacked Girard of Angoulême, setting forth, as briefly as I could, the origin of his birth, the character of his conduct, the cause of his elevation, and what he is doing or has done from the beginning of this storm—the sole offering which the affection of one absent could make. To refute him, when his pen had ranged too freely concerning Peter Leonis, I have added what concerns the person of the lord pope, the order of his election, the support of princes, the consent of peoples, and what the irrefutable authority of all religious persons approves concerning this matter. [Col. 0173B–C]

I venture, perhaps presumptuously, to offer this work itself to your greatness, although the meagerness of so spare a discourse by no means deserves to come before the gaze of your wisdom. Yet I know that with you kindness more often produces pardon than the strictest severity produces punishment. For he who refuses forgiveness for a lighter fault sometimes provides the occasion of a graver one. Yet if you should wish to call anything to judgment, recognize not the quality of the work but the intention of its maker. I confidently expose myself to the peril of this examination, fearing neither the inquiry nor the sentence pronounced from it. For although learning, rather than affection, supplies rhetorical color, if we do not obtain this praise of skill, we shall at least obtain the favor due to good will. [Col. 0173C–D]

Reason also required that this be directed especially to you, since everything alleged in this particular cause belongs to the task entrusted to you. For while the Roman prelate stands tirelessly in Italy to resist Peter Leonis, he has left you in Gaul to resist Girard, so that head may be set against head and right hand matched with right hand. For just as Peter is the leader and author of this schism, so Girard is, among all others, its chief instrument. In this matter what ought to be thought of your faith and prudence has been manifestly proved, since he preferred no one to you—he who would neither approve one unknown to him nor exalt one known to him above the merits of his own virtue. He judged you to be a man animated by charity, stirred by obedience, compelled by knowledge, and prepared for victory by courage. In you he found steadfastness in faith, humility in service, prudence in execution, and perseverance amid difficulty. [Col. 0174A]

Who could deny that you are fortunate in this estimate of his? Who would not call you blessed in so great a mark of his esteem? Certainly, however, the messenger is worthy of the sender, the commission worthy of its recipient, and fairest of all is the hope of both, which awaits so renowned a victory with assured outcome. For he himself will conquer in you, and you will conquer in him, while he supplies you with authority and you render obedience to authority. You will conquer, I say, and will bring back Aquitaine, once the enemy has been captured and subdued; so that, presented through you to him who sent you, he may be punished for a new crime by a new kind of penalty. For the impenitence of a hardened heart does not deserve pardon. This reward at least for my good will I ask of you: that then, among those who now serve, as it were, under your command, I may be allowed to follow the chariot of the triumphant one and to sing the praises—indeed, the triumphal proclamations—of the Church conquering in you. Farewell. [Col. 0174B–C]

## Chapter I

For some time now, Girard, I have endured you anxiously, while every day the stench of your crimes rises to us and the ever graver sound of your raging wickedness assaults our ears. Yet until now I have kept silence, waiting in credulous expectation for your repentance, or believing that the vengeance of the divine hand ought not to be deferred longer. But whereas we ought to set before ourselves examples of divine long-suffering and patience in dealing with you, you rise ever more violently, an untiring persecutor of the Church of God every day. How long, then, will you abuse God’s patience? How long will that immeasurable ambition blind your mind, and this unquenchable thirst for money turn you aside from truth? Do you not see your wretched old age, the approaching failure of your decrepit body by natural necessity, and the enclosure of the gaping grave? [Col. 0174C–D]

Do you not perceive that the growing measure of divine long-suffering toward you is heaping up the punishments of eternal condemnation, so that no excuse can now lessen divine vengeance? The entire labor and leisure of your accursed body, all the cunning of your reprobate mind, all the time of your detestable life, has been spent so that you might appear to serve the Church while you fought against the Church. But now God has revealed the counsels of your heart and uncovered your hidden darkness, lest human judgments about you be deceived any longer by doubtful opinion. It is plain that you were a traitor to the Church whose patron you pretended to be. It is plain that you were merely a hunter after money, though you had been appointed a hunter of souls. But because you are an animal man, fleshly and carnal alike, you could not perceive what belonged to God and scorned to behold His invisible things. Yet lest I seem to have undertaken this speech against you from rashness of spirit rather than reason, I choose to set forth the sequence of your deeds, by which you may be found contemptible to human beings, detestable to angels, and condemnable by God. [Col. 0175A–B]

What you have been from the first time of your episcopate; what you did at the beginning of the storm’s rising in the Church; and by what deeds you have not ceased afterward to harass her—all this will be treated in order. Your base origin and the familiar poverty of your father’s house must therefore be passed over: these drove you beyond all the bounds of your native Normandy, so that you stood as a stranger and beggar at the thresholds of an unknown people. I pass over the ignoble earnings of your childhood, the shameful reputation of your adolescence, and the avaricious dealings of your youth, lest the ears of those to whom these writings will come be polluted by the filth of your incontinence and greed alike. I come to the years of your manhood, in which not a commendable life nor prior deliberation, but chance and the impelling agitation of minds blinded by preceding discord, brought you to the episcopate. [Col. 0175B–C]

For when the divided multitude of electors rose against one another, and alternating support demanded different persons, fortune turned the voices of all toward you—not because the Church was believed to have been suitably provided for in you, but so that the uproar might somehow find an end. Each side preferred knowingly to accept you, though unworthy, rather than appear to have been overcome by the other. I recall that miserable and utterly wicked spectacle: while the remaining crowd followed you as you ran ahead, you hurried before the clergy to the chair, lest their foolish impulse should change when reason returned—although others are usually dragged there and often compelled against their will. On that day truth and mercy departed from the Church of Angoulême; deceit and impiety succeeded them; the state of affairs changed for the worse; every institution lost its splendor. [Col. 0175C–D]

The adornment and worship of the Church were diminished; that venerable religious dignity of ecclesiastical order perished; the reverend gravity of princes and the commendable propriety of the people disappeared. You built the episcopal church from dead stones, not to adorn the house of the Lord, but so that it might furnish an occasion for collecting money and so that no lying excuse might be lacking against a suspicious people while what was collected was concealed. Whatever you exacted for your greedy avarice was said to be sought for the work of the Church; and, after spending one smallest portion out of many and of the greatest sums, you wished to be believed to have distributed everything alike. [Col. 0175D–0176A]

When, therefore, you had been raised to the episcopate by such a lot, you began to exalt yourself in the insolence which poverty had formerly restrained; in the wantonness which, as a private person, you could not exercise; to persecute whomsoever among the good you pleased; to drain the province through plundering and exactions; to frame judicial decisions solely according to the purchase of gifts; to alter the condition of all things; to undermine the fortunes of nobles; and to hand over the whole administration to your nephews, whom the same cause that had driven you had expelled beyond the borders of their native soil, and to exalt them to the dignities of the Church as though they surpassed Plato in learning, Cato in morals, and Scipio in birth. [Col. 0176A–B]

Nature brought them forth from an obscure station, illiterate and shamelessly given over to illicit pursuits. Of them—lest a new digression be undertaken out of order—it is enough to say that the nephews were worthy of their uncle: nature’s bond of consanguinity, upbringing, and the example drawn from you had formed them in the likeness of your life, so that they derived from nature their beginning, from education their advancement, and from example the authority of ambition, avarice, and lust. As for the other dignities and benefices of the Church, which you could not gather into one heap and bestow upon these same persons, the richer man was considered the worthier. Integrity was not regarded; rather, you waited for hands laden with gifts. [Col. 0176B–C]

You handled the dedication of basilicas, the blessing of altars, and the appointment of priests in the same manner as everything else, so that you thought plainly that nothing ought to be done unless the expectation of some profit had preceded it. You gave no favor to virtues, inflicted no punishment upon vices, and trained no one in innocence of life.

If any report of incest of any kind emerged, or if someone burned with love of chastity against uncleanness, he was reduced to silence by your restraint. One of your archdeacons made the abbess of Angoulême pregnant through a depraved sexual approach. The swelling of her growing womb and the natural outcome revealed the crime. Since the citizens found this incredible because of the enormity of the offense and the contempt of God involved, the groans of the abbess in labor and the infant’s new-born cries established its truth. [Col. 0176C–D]

The whole city was therefore struck with amazement: by what impatience it could have been conceived, by what recklessness undertaken, and finally by what shamelessness completed—that a man who was guardian of souls, the episcopal eye, a pillar of the Church, should not merely have compelled by word but defiled by deed the bride of the Lord, the mother and guardian of His virgins; should have entered the father’s bed with an adulterous mind; and should have inflicted upon one devoted to God an injury as insulting as it was disgraceful even toward a human being. The count, to whom the abbess was joined by the same brotherly blood, was stirred to vengeance; and, having first resolved to punish the adulterer with the sword, he came to you that a canonical sentence might be pronounced. [Col. 0176D–0177A]

The illustrious man, about to disclose the matter, checked his voice three times amid the account, judging that his mind was made foul by contemplating the crime and his tongue by recounting it. At last, by a certain indirect expression, he explained what he had begun, like one who cannot bear for a serpent or hidden coals to lie concealed longer, yet refuses to touch either with a bare hand, lest he be burned by the one or defiled by the other. Who could adequately praise the prince’s severity at his first awareness of the crime, his discretion in carrying out vengeance, and the modesty shown in his report? Who, then, would not expect at least from this example a great rigor of justice in a prelate? The answer of the pontiff, worthy of remembrance, survives in the account. [Col. 0177A–B]

The count repeated that the event had occurred not without contempt for God, contrary to nature and astonishing to the age—an offense which even paganism, ignorant of divine religion, had decreed must be punished by the supreme penalty. But you, disregarding the duty imposed by your age and the dignity of your order and episcopal office, followed every word with a more lascivious laugh. You said that you could not sufficiently admire the prince’s simplicity in calling it contrary to nature and astonishing to the age that a woman had conceived by a man; rather, the miracle would lie in the opposite case, if it happened that a man should be impregnated by a woman. O astonishing obstinacy of mind! O detestable shamelessness of tongue! O answer worthy of deposition! [Col. 0177B–C]

Episcopal indignation was expected to blaze against the crime; but senile wantonness smiled upon it as though in congratulation, and what a censorial judgment ought to have punished with gravity, this new Proteus confirmed by his authority. You cannot excuse yourself from having granted the people certain permission to do similar things, since, while all hung upon your words, you condemned neither in word nor deed a new and unheard-of crime, but marked it as though lawful by your smiling expression.

Who, then, being of sound mind, would not from this plainly understand the remaining parts of your mind and life? If a man is found unrestrained and most wanton in greater offenses, will he refrain from a lesser crime? Why should he? Because one who does not abstain from incest and sacrilege, wherever the flame of lust or a sufficiently kindled greed exists, does not hesitate to defile his body by simple fornication or fill his hands by robbery. [Col. 0177C–D]

What follows from this? Because one who is not offended by the filth of another’s crime but delights in it will not condemn the same thing when he has experienced it in his own desire. What then? If you scorned to show zeal for the bride of the Lord and to avenge the injury done to God Himself, are you shown to have acted negligently in guarding human marriages and not to have cared for injuries done to persons themselves? Truth itself bears witness concerning the analogous case: what is hastened to be done in green wood will not be delayed in dry wood.

## Chapter II

Moreover, lest abundant material, free opportunity, and unshaken confidence should be lacking for the exercise of these deeds also, the legation of the Roman Church was sought and obtained. The overflowing guilt of a wounded conscience distressed you on one side; on another, the well-known severity of the bishops of your province; and on another, the suspect preeminence of the archbishop of Bordeaux, whose neighboring position your works had not always escaped. Your ambition too seemed confined, as it were, by certain narrow limits, since the spoils of one bishopric did not fill your jaws. Thus, as though complete order had secured everything in your bishopric and no occurrence offered occasion for a new enterprise, you brought it about that you should preside by singular authority over five archbishoprics and exercise in them the functions of the Roman pontiff. [Col. 0178A]

I do not think it surprising that this was obtained by stealth from the Roman Church, since amid so great a multitude of affairs and so heavy a burden of business the human mind sometimes grows weary; nor is there always a sure discernment of spirits by which the unworthiness of deceitful desires may be constrained and due assent supplied to rightful claims. Yet the legation you sought was not entrusted to you without consideration, insofar as human reason could judge. For it was believed that you had been elevated to the episcopate not by the outcome of chance but by reason. It did not seem credible that in your election clergy, prince, and people, and in your examination fellow bishops and the archbishop, had all been entangled in the blindness of the same error. [Col. 0178A–B]

Nor had any Roman yet heard anything of your deeds, which crafty concealment did not permit to be known to nearby persons, nor distance of places to those far away. In short, lest truth be denied in any respect, you possessed a recognized discretion in managing affairs, confirmed indeed by extensive learning and adorned by eloquence in both modes of speech. Whenever divine grace bestows such gifts upon an ungrateful person not from zeal of charity, they are believed to have been added as testimony to a just condemnation. Therefore, when the Roman pontiff considered the weight of his responsibility, he gladly received you as a participant in his burden, believing that you would be a faithful and prudent minister. [Col. 0178B–C]

Thereafter, armed with the prerogative of unshaken authority, you ravaged the Church of God with unrestricted power, now despoiling and now increasing the possessions of individuals, changing the lowest into the highest and the highest into the lowest, so that you seemed plainly to be the author of men’s fortunes, and all might either praise or complain of you concerning the condition of their estate. Thereafter your greed, spread over wider expanses, rejoiced that abundant matter for its rapacity was not lacking. Why should I mention your manifest exactions? Why the losses incurred by households through fear of justice? Why describe general synods and venerable persons wearied by travel from far-off regions, so that, presiding over a general council, you might boastfully survey the extent of your authority and satisfy ambition by the sight of those subject to you? [Col. 0178C–D]

How perverse everything was in this undertaking is easy to see. The authority of the holy Fathers decreed that councils should be held so that instruction in virtues and correction of evils might proceed from them, and so that the mother Church, beholding the resources of her own army, might know herself more fully; thus, rising more sternly against vices, she might begin with greater confidence the triumphs of impending wars. But who doubts that you convened them in order to indulge your greedy mind and lust of dominion, and, when the profits of individual cases, separately considered, did not supply a measured satiety, to create it from the assembled multitude of many? [Col. 0178D–0179A]

Alas, the pitiable loss of the falling Church! I seem to see you seated like a fat bull upon the high synodal chair, while the Catholic Fathers arranged below languish in equal despair, tossed by the uncertain wave of a sentence about to fall, whatever truth-conscious argument they might advance in their cases. But evil men rise, the more boldly as they press forward more shamelessly, encouraged and led on by confidence in a promised or bestowed gift. I recall this with a certain movement of indignation in my mind, when I remember that what is known to have been instituted for the adornment of the Church was expended upon your intemperance. The honor of councils has been made common and their dignity abolished by those over which you are known to have presided and in which you framed new decrees for peoples in Roman fashion. [Col. 0179A–B]

Deeply angered by this, an old Venetian mocked him wittily and honorably. When summoned among his fellow bishops to attend one of your councils, he carried before him a rough and unshaped pastoral staff and wore an old garment already torn by many rents. Asked why he had appeared in attire so cheap and ridiculous, he replied, fortified by the freedom of conscience: “Such an assembly befits such an adornment.” [Col. 0179B–C]

What you were from the beginning of your episcopate has been set forth in a less than full, but truthful, account. Now it must be added in turn what you did when the storm of disturbance rose against the Church.

## Chapter III

When Pope Honorius, of blessed memory, was removed from the midst of men, rendering his body to earth and his spirit to heaven—the due owed to each—and when canonical election had substituted one worthy of succeeding him, that Peter, Peter Leonis, invaded the Church of God. Here I wish to describe the character of each man, so that you may be proved to have chosen one like yourself from among two, and, greedy yourself, to have worshipped the greedy one. Yet obscenity of language must be spared when Peter’s life is narrated, and the truth of events must be covered with graceful speech, so that consideration for the readers’ decency may seem to have been observed. [Col. 0179C–D]

I therefore prefer to pass over the ancient origin of his birth and his equally ignoble lineage. Nor do I think his Jewish ancestry should be alleged, ancestry from which he derived not only the material of flesh but also certain first beginnings of inborn error. For he himself is material sufficient and abundant; no one can suppose that there is or has been anything more shameful in his house than he. His grandfather, having amassed incalculable money by manifold usury, condemned the circumcision he had received by the water of baptism. He was ashamed rather of his weakness than of his error, lest his family, confounded by the reproach of unbelief, should be condemned to perpetual obscurity. [Col. 0179D–0180A]

Having therefore received the sacraments of faith, when he was grafted in as a new citizen, he became Roman in rank. As the succession brought him a numerous progeny, and since “queen Money bestows lineage and beauty,” through successive marriages he brought all the nobles of the city into alliance with himself—while the enemy of humankind was already contriving that, as by some old leaven, the entire mixture of Roman purity might be corrupted. From this mixture of diverse families, Girard, your Peter arose: one who displays a Jewish likeness in face and reflects unbelief in desire and affection.

From the cradle itself, from his nurse’s breasts, the prophetic ambition of his parents destined him for the apostolic office; and after the first rudiments of letters, it sent him to Gaul for education, so that conformity in manners and language might secure for him the goodwill of that kingdom. Thus throughout the years of his childhood, to speak dishonorable things more honorably, he gave himself up to whatever another might desire; and, an importunate exactor through fear of the Roman name, he did not shrink from growing up at others’ expense. Yet these matters were carried on somewhat more modestly while the discipline of the school restrained him, the daily insistence of his lessons hindered him, and a certain natural incapacity removed some crimes from his age. [Col. 0180A–B]

But after adolescence gave him both the power to sin and freer license to wander, whatever pride or wantonness there may be, then truly, proud and wanton, he shamefully devoted himself to every excess. Certainly, since in these deeds he deigned to revere neither God nor man, he aroused against himself such infamy that, once his birth, ambition, and life had become known, people throughout all nations commonly believed and publicly declared him to be Antichrist. This belief was strengthened by the fact that he was descended from Jews; that he began to seek dominion over the whole world under the pretext of the Roman see; that, given over to vices, he redeemed his infamy by no virtue; and that he was thereafter to possess the infinite wealth of his father and grandfather. [Col. 0180B–C]

He himself gloried so greatly in the reproach of this name that he did not blush even to be called the ruin of the world. The Church of Vézelay is witness: while old workshops were being pulled down for rebuilding, with him listening, he earnestly requested to be brought there to contemplate the ruins of the walls. When asked why he so eagerly wished to see this, he said: “The ruin of great things delights me, because I am foretold to be the ruin of the world.” After this he also took on the monastic habit, so that he might cover the vices of his mind with a sheep’s garment, hide the disgrace of his former life beneath the name of Cluny, and obtain through association with good persons a reputation for virtue. [Col. 0180C–D]

In this too he sought the aid of the Church of Cluny for the things which his foreknowing mind promised itself for the future, since among the churches of Gaul none is more illustrious in the name of religion, none more prudent in discernment of counsel, none more ready for the services of charity; and none can render assistance in affairs either more promptly or more effectively. Finally returning to Rome, he was admitted, through the efforts of his father and brothers, to that most holy assembly of venerable elders; and, made a cardinal, he was honored with the name and enriched with the title. [Col. 0180D–0181A]

Perhaps no breath of Peter’s infamy had reached the ears of the supreme pontiff; and so, each person reverencing the high rank of so great a man, feared to disturb holy ears with shameful reports. Under this ignorance, therefore, while his monastic habit, the sacrament of priesthood, and his parents’ power were considered, he was received through the silence, not the consent, of the Fathers. Some were silent through fear or affection for paternal power; others hoped for better things in the future. For association with the good corrects and improves some; others, fearing punishment for transgression, turn abstinence compelled by necessity into the sincere inclination of the will.

[Col. 0181B]

Then, when he performed the office of legate in various regions, he studied to satisfy his greed rather than justice, so much so that he thought only those affairs had had a good outcome for him which were proved by added profits and a purse subsequently filled. Where no intervening causes afforded an opportunity for plunder, exaction, full of blandishments or threats, was never absent. Twice daily, at enormous expense, banquets were prepared; and such was the luxury and superfluity of foods that potters often had to be sought out for exquisite varieties of dishes and instructed to fashion new vessels of an unfamiliar construction. [Col. 0181B–C]

The potter was taught to mold jars of marvelous design: in the middle, across their width, they contained a partition like that of a throne. The upper compartment, holding food, breathed out smoke through narrow openings of a small mouth; the lower part, perforated on every side with latticed arches, enclosed coals. An attentive servant poured in an abundance of incense until, once the foods were cooked, the ingenious cook transferred the fragrance itself into flavor. This gluttony plainly exceeded human nature. Natural reason has assigned the perceptions of human senses by a fixed law, allotting to each one its own qualities of things and leaving nothing confusedly shared by one with another. But here, when the smell of incense is transferred into food, what belongs to smell is appropriated by taste, and an unknown confusion occurs among the qualities of things and a sharing among sensory perceptions that is not natural. [Col. 0181C–D]

Nor could this lack contempt for God, since, amid the fiery desires of gluttony, an exotic flavor is sought in that which is burned upon sacred altars; which the prophetic devotion of the three Magi offered as a sign of the Godhead in Christ; and which alone, among earthly things, is believed to be and to have been an offering pleasing to God in the time of both laws. I pass over the fact that this extravagance occurred not only in wealthy but also in poor churches, which afterward had to pay for it with many fasts and sufferings from cold. And when he had harassed poor bishops or abbots with expenses more lavish than they had learned at home, he proceeded with sufficiently shameless sacrilege even against the ornaments of churches, so that he seemed plainly, with reckless audacity, to despoil the bride of the Lord and strip her of her jewels. [Col. 0181D]

[Col. 0182A]

Such lavish feasts were followed by such filth of lusts that whatever came in his way was commonly approached by him. It is said—though it is scarcely lawful even to say it—that he defiled his sister from Tropea by bestial incest and by that abominable monstrosity fathered sons from her who were at once his nephews; made father of his nephews and uncle of his sons, he so confused the laws of nature that he made the same persons brothers and relatives to one another. He was now not merely a Jew, but worse even than a Jew. No distinction of sexes, places, times, or professions was observed. Yet it would be more fitting to pass these things over in silence, lest, if I state that he admitted such matters indiscriminately, silence might have passed them over more honorably. Such was his conduct at home, and he did not refrain from the same things during his legations. [Col. 0182A–B]

For, to pass over worse things, a girl was led about with him whose clothing and tonsure gave her the appearance of a young man in order to deceive observers; she endured all his passions and soothed all his desires. She was the more pleasing, and as it were an affectation of a miracle of novelty, because while she presented a man in face and a woman in all other parts, both sexes seemed displayed in her single body. The people of Montpellier and the surrounding province bear witness that they saw this. And lest sameness should provide satiety, other women were sought with whom he might engage in nightly embraces; amid that very shameful intercourse he boasted to them that he himself would become pope. Many cities in Gaul and Aquitaine testify with certain faith that this was said in their presence: “Rejoice that you have come into the embrace of so great a man, whom the whole world awaits as its future pope.” [Col. 0182B]

Did such conduct promise you the rank of the apostolic office, Peter? Did Christ, the bridegroom and defender of the Church, teach or show by His example the stewards of His household to act in this way? “Be holy,” He says, “for I am holy” (Gal. IV). Therefore whoever is to succeed Christ must walk as He walked. And if anyone is to follow after Him, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow Him (Matt. XVI). But he does not take up the cross unless, chastising his body and reducing it to servitude (I Cor. IX), he is not given over to “reveling and drunkenness, beds and shameless acts” (Rom. XIII), and does not transgress the law of God. [Col. 0182B–C]

Nor does he follow Christ unless, intent upon divine works, he orders ascents in his heart until God is seen from strength to strength. But you, Peter, while you plunge from vice to vice in an unbroken fall and darken the light of the divine countenance marked upon you—while the image of God is already disfigured and His likeness obscured by crimes—by what recklessness do you presume to be Christ’s successor when you have not first assumed His likeness? For there is no agreement between Christ and Belial, no communion between light and darkness. [Col. 0182C–D]

## Chapter IV

This is he, Girard—this is your pope: the man whom you receive, whom you assign as the sole fitting head to the whole body of the faithful; who, as bridegroom of the Church, vicar of Christ, successor of Peter, and pattern of life for the faithful, should instruct the flock by the word of preaching and, of course, by the example of such conduct. But now consider in turn who is the man whom you reject. [Col. 0182D–0183A]

If his lineage is investigated from the account of his birth, he will be seen to have been born faithful from faithful parents. If the plan of his parents in his education and instruction is considered: it was that he might dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of his life and behold the delight of the Lord. If the quality of his person is considered—so that his bodily appearance may first be described—he is a man of moderate stature, neither made insignificant by shortness nor monstrous by an excessive size. In his eyes and countenance appears a vigorous simplicity and a modesty of face that proves the chastity of his soul. [Col. 0183A]

Indeed, his face shines with such dignity that it inspires a certain reverence even in one who looks upon it. Among the other gifts of His generosity, divine power has granted him this special grace: he reconciles to himself with gentle kindness all who see him and gains their affection by sight alone. For heavenly goodness has breathed into his eyes something divine, which is generally judged full of grace, worthy of reverence, and fitting for honor. His voice is gentle, yet not softened into excessive effeminacy, so that favor is not lacking to its sweetness nor authority to its greatness. His countenance is continually cheerful; laughter occurs very frequently in the course of speech, yet with such propriety of manner that it can increase rather than diminish the dignity of both his words and face. [Col. 0183A–B]

This draws observers all the more because it seems in him to be a certain beginning of that eternal joy, of which I judge that he has received certain first fruits even in the body.

But if the integrity of his life is considered and everything is brought under examination from his earliest years, there is nothing disfigured by crime, nothing condemned by infamy. For in him childhood produced nothing unfree, adolescence nothing unrestrained, youth nothing shameful, and mature age nothing unbecoming. Unshaken faith laid the foundations for good works. He is prudent in counsel, kind in conversation, and renowned in eloquence, which neither pride in words makes haughty nor abundance makes diffuse. [Col. 0183B–C]

He enjoyed so great a reputation and favor for goodness among all that, what is otherwise very rare, before the time of his election he had no enemy. His sobriety in food and drink was such that not distaste, but the measure of abstinence, set their limit. His dress, moreover, was entirely appropriate to the time of the apostolic office: clerical profession did not exclude it, nor did the dignity of the cardinalate disdain it. For what garments he now wears does not depend upon his own choice, but has been decreed by the ancient ordinance of the holy Fathers. [Col. 0183C–D]

The aforementioned dignity of the cardinalate was not sought by him, but was freely conferred because of the merit of his purer life and fuller learning. He so performed the duties of that office as to enlarge it by his own praises. His title became more illustrious through the goodness of its holder, and he shone not so much through his own dignity as through the glory of his administration. He had surpassed the others by so great a prerogative of outstanding goodness that there seemed to be no room left for envy; each plainly perceived that his own efforts could not aspire to equality with him, and that his preeminence detracted nothing from the praises of any other. [Col. 0183D–0184A]

Lastly, had not that faithless adversary of the human race laid snares for God’s Church in Peter Leo, no question of succession would now have remained after Pope Honorius; for a singular man seemed already fashioned by divine providence for a singular dignity. It is plain that, by the counsel of divinity itself, he was formed such as he was, so that, when the violence of this persecution rose against the Church, there might be one who would securely set himself against the storm and bring aid to the little vessel in danger amid the waves. And although the conscience of almost everyone destined him for this burden, he himself did not seem capable of filling the place of dignity already attained. For it is the judgment of a wise man to believe concerning himself below his own capacity. [Col. 0184B] He taught this quite clearly about himself when the circle of his electors enclosed him and he was called to the height of the apostolate: they pressed him with prayers, entreated him with tears as he protested, and even restrained with their hands his resistance to the cope they had thrown upon him. When, resisting with all his strength, he tore the garment placed upon him a second time—as they say—and they nevertheless thought they must persist, they feared, if any trust may be placed in holy elections, that exhausted by such struggling and constriction in their hands, he might die, and immediately breathe out a soul choked by sobs.

Therefore, withholding their hands until he could breathe a little, while a third cope was being fetched from a distance, amid tears still streaming and sobs bursting forth everywhere, he addressed those standing by thus:

“It would be expedient for this pressing [Col. 0184C] business to be handled with the emotions excluded, lest mutual zeal impede charity and the common good be turned aside by private hatred or favour. For emotion often deceives minds already preoccupied, so that hatreds reject the worthy and the unworthy are preferred through favour’s prompting. I see that this favour has here claimed the chief force for itself, where reason alone ought to have prevailed after merits had been weighed in an equal balance. For when with one accord you strive to set me over so great a dignity, an examination of merits plainly does not prevail; rather, an over-indulgent favour openly prevails, rendering me acceptable to you now and hitherto in imperfect works. By that favour you once wished me to belong to this holy fellowship, though the quality of my character had cast me down far below it. Yet even if a man of no virtue and slight learning occupied that place, your wisdom supported my weakness, since the same Lord made us ministers in the same rank and of the same charge. But now it is necessary to judge by merits, not favour, and to appoint a priest who is not merely favoured but worthy. Here no comfort can be derived from equality, where a singular prerogative excludes a partner in office. Let goodwill therefore be set aside, and let the person be compared with the office to which he is called. So great an honour requires a life of proved worth, learning, and distinguished reputation: a worthy life to obtain for him divine favour; learning to confer capacity for the tasks to be undertaken; and celebrated renown to furnish conspicuous authority. [Col. 0185A] Such men are readily found among this very number. Who am I, under whose judgment the supreme direction of affairs should rest? Who, I say, am I, whom Rome should hail as pope, who should be numbered not merely among the foremost, but as the first of the foremost? He who sets an unworthy man over others wrongs the dignity itself.”

As he said such things—and would have said much more had he been allowed—the despairing assembly of those present answered him in this manner: “The losses entailed by excuses are excluded by the imminent danger and the crisis of necessity. For the lion stands in ambush, ready for prey, awaiting an opportunity—as you yourself know—from his youth; unless his assault is forestalled and his attack blunted, no hope of liberty, no discipline of honour at all, will remain. The ancient dignity of the Roman Church [Col. 0185B] will perish; its glory will be changed into reproach; and a power feared by the ends of humankind will turn into contempt. For if he is—as indeed he is—contemptible in life and stained with disgrace, the power itself must acquire contempt from the man. Who good would not refuse to be subject to one infamous? Who would not reject being constrained to honour by the will of one less honourable? If, moreover, this honour ought rightly to be bestowed upon the worthier man, Peter’s precedence, burdened with countless crimes, surely condemns us before all. We shall plainly be charged with having confessed worse things about ourselves than report has spread concerning him, if he is preferred before us as though worthier. It will also be judged that what we do not condemn in another does not displease us; and, by tolerating it, we shall incur the guilt of consent, convicted both by the truth of the matter and by public opinion.

“This Roman Church was—yes, until now it was—the head of the world: in it flourished the most steadfast faith, supreme authority, incomparable honour, unshaken severity, the highest discernment in affairs, and piety known throughout the world. It was, I say, once a terror to the wicked, a protection for the good in peace, and a singular refuge in necessity; from its integrity the lesser Churches drew strength, and, as though from an uninjured head, its wounded members derived the beginnings of their healing. But now departure from the faith, desolation of ancient power, and the ruin of every good thing are imminent. Its manifest fall appears when the man of sin, the son of perdition, is revealed, so that he may oppose and exalt himself above everything called God or worshipped, [Col. 0185D] sitting in the temple of God and showing himself as though he himself were God (2 Thess. 2). Therefore, as the Apostle plainly says, we know that either he himself is Antichrist, or that in him the times of Antichrist are being prepared for us, and that the latter’s forerunner and minister is emerging.

“Behold, he is already preparing helpers for his intrusion, and a faction conspiring in the Church of God is being assembled—a faction bound to him by lineage, power, lavish gifts, promises, and a long-standing criminal conspiracy. The wolf attacks sheep deprived of their shepherd, and hastens first to usurp the vacant see—something which perhaps he would not dare presume if a shepherd had been installed. For only when Moses is absent does the people cast the calf. Yet if thereafter ambitious rashness compelled him to attempt this, the faithful [Col. 0186A] people would at least find someone to follow. Concerning this, the holy Church has established her supreme counsel in you: that she may be governed by your foresight and set free through your earnest effort. She nourished you and, when she had no need of any service from you, received you, that in perfect tranquillity she might rear you at her breasts and cherish you in her own embrace. Now she asks a return and claims the recompense of her benefits: namely, that you assist her in necessity and not refuse aid to her oppression. Will you not hear your mother crying aloud? Will you not console her desolation? Will you not heed her entreaty? When she stretches out before you the requested hand to support her as she falls, will you not sustain her?”

“But you allege your unworthiness as a pretext for evasion, as though we did not know your prudence and the merits of the outstanding [Col. 0186B] parts of your life. Indeed, if you believed yourself worthy, you would seem unworthy by that very estimate. You also say that no consolation can here be hoped for from equality, as though counsel could not be supplied by inferiors and help by those who obey. Does not that burden chiefly rest upon us: that, as in the human body, he who presides bears the form of the head, while the rest bear the likeness of the members, so that he who rules may make the decision and the labour of those who obey may resolve the difficulties? You hesitate, too, with praiseworthy modesty to undertake the summit of so great a dignity, in which the supreme prerogatives of kingdom and priesthood meet, joined in a wondrous covenant. But we invite you not to honour, but rather to danger. We are not ignorant of what that adversary plots [Col. 0186C] against us. Already he draws swords; already he sharpens arrows. He trusts that no road to the apostolate lies open to him except through the shedding of our blood. Yet however much danger of death threatens us, we prefer to seek the reward for our blood from the divine hand rather than have the blood of the Church demanded from our own hand—although we seek you as a companion in death, indeed wish you even as our forerunner. Let your throat, like ours, be exposed for sacrifice; for it is not lawful for one who gave the spirit to deny it when it is demanded back. Therefore, if the calamity of your desolate mother moves you at all; if the overflowing tears of those standing by move you at all; if any love of honour, if the virtue of obedience moves you at all, consent. If you consent, we offer obedience; if you refuse, we exact the penalty for disobedience. For the authority to command and also to punish which belongs to the pope while he lives remains with us after his death [Col. 0186D] until another is brought in.”

After these words they prepared to pronounce sentence of excommunication, meanwhile holding before him the cope that had been brought from afar. What was he to do? Seek safety in flight? But an unbroken ring of elders shut off that route. Ask for a delay? But Peter’s machinations and the urgency of the matter denied that it could be obtained. Refuse forever? But they threatened him with the sword of the Spirit, immediately menacing the punishment of anathema. Therefore, judging himself shut within the straits of a double death and liable to one or the other by necessity’s law, he accepted the danger of bodily peril; for, refusing to undergo the sentence of anathema, [Col. 0187A] he exposed himself to the snares—indeed, to the power—of Peter Leo.

I shall not linger over the manner in which Peter’s intrusion proceeded on the following day, except to say that a shameful man, defiled by infamy and condemned by public opinion, was afterward promoted by [lacuna] and his relatives. I return especially to you, Gerard, so that you may know what you did when the storm arose, and that your ears may be battered by hearing of the evils you committed.

## CHAPTER V

When the schism was reported in Gaul, and many people, with varying favour for the parties, said many things while the faithful people were carried away by a twofold uncertainty, Louis, king of the Franks, the foremost Catholic prince among kings, was the first to respond. He summoned bishops, all who in Gaul were held to be of proven religious life, the clergy, and the great men of the realm, and established a general council. Although he acknowledged that he was under obligation to Peter Leo for services rendered to himself and his father, he nevertheless wished to arrogate no decision in the matter to royal eminence. He entrusted all authority to the bishops and fathers who had assembled from the monastic order, so that every determination might be committed to and made by them, because the whole administration of the Church rests with holy bishops; and it is not believed that divine counsels are hidden from abbots whom contemplation of divinity refreshes.

Since you, Gerard, could not attend this council, you sent a messenger bearing letters sealed with the image of your disfigurement. You stated that, having known both persons and more fully investigated the manner of the election, you had found beyond doubt that justice stood with Pope Innocent, because he was plainly a man of outstanding honour; his election had occurred first in time and had been celebrated by the leading persons of the Roman Church. You stated further that Peter had afterward usurped the chair through the power of wealth, a man so discredited in life and reputation that, even if any form of election defended him, his character and infamy would nevertheless not permit his promotion. You declared that this judgment would be accepted by you and those subject to your legation, and that the Churches of Lyons and Vienne, together with almost all Italy outside the walls of Rome itself, had accepted it.

There were also present there venerable persons who had been at Rome during that same crisis and knew the course of events clearly, especially those who had perceived each matter by eyewitness testimony.
