There were likewise voluntarily delegated testimonies on this same subject from others who were absent; along with the persuasions of persons whom firm faith held to possess the Spirit of God, since the minds of so many people perhaps converged upon the same decision. For as the faith of the good is one, so also is the Spirit one; but the spirit of the wicked is manifold and their will ambiguous.

At last, therefore, after divine favour had been implored with many tears, while the merits of both persons and the partisan commitments supporting them were compared, Peter was found so much less worthy that, by comparison with him, a grave injury seemed to be done to the other person. The disparity in the parties’ support was so great that Peter had no support yet beyond the walls of Rome, whereas the greater party within the city had elected the other, and nearly the whole Church, beyond the city and to the ends of the earth, now acknowledged him as Father. Accordingly, taking their judgment from the decree of Pope Leo the Great—where the votes of parties had divided—they considered that canon law required preference for the man supported by greater approval and merits. Since by this reasoning, under the Lord’s inspiration, they agreed upon Innocent as pope, you immediately wrote to him concerning your obedience and due submission. Yet you asked to be honoured by his rescript and to have the office of legation which you had held confirmed.

It seemed simoniacal to purchase your favour with the office of legate. Moreover, since he had decided to visit those regions at the same time, no place could remain for a legate in his presence. For a legate performs the service of an absent person, not of one present. Already such a clamour of your bad administration had reached Roman ears that the regret over what you had once obtained was greater than any desire to restore it to you. You took the refusal badly and grieved that the horns of your power had been cut short. Made now lower than those who had formerly been beneath you, and considered useless as in old age, you judged the cessation of an accustomed benefit an injury of plunder and were inflamed with a rash desire for revenge. For rejection supplies causes for anger, and innate pride produces indignation; ambition added blindness. Since these things know no rest and cannot be idle from their effects, indignation produced contempt for the party you had already adopted, blindness produced lack of judgment, and anger shaped reckless ventures.

Having therefore despised what you had rightly undertaken and turned indiscreetly to another side, you rashly conceived plans contrary to your earlier course. What often happens in human affairs occurred: around an object more eagerly sought, the desires conceived made a precipitous hope firm. You sent a legate to Rome to offer for sale to that same Peter, whom you had already vowed to support, your favour in exchange for the office of legation, and to bind to himself a servant like himself as minister to his lord. The bargain was completed without difficulty; and as indiscriminate blindness led you on, you bound yourself as a minister of schism in order to be granted a useless privilege. A new legation was created for you, but an empty one; and all that lies between the Alps and the limits of the West was subjected to your jurisdiction by a grant that was ineffective. And lest the prescribed bounds of the aforesaid territories perhaps seem too narrow to your excessive ambition, it was added that wherever your foot should tread, there your legation should be. You found, Gerard, a man lavish with what belonged to another; but if you consider the substance of the matter carefully, though very great things were written back to you, you received very little. For Peter bestowed upon you nothing that could be possessed either from himself or in his name. Yet the bounded vastness of those lands filled your ears, and the estimated magnitude of the thing immediately satisfied your desire with empty delight. But a most fitting outcome awaited your ambition: at the first trial of events you discovered the gift to be useless. Therefore, sending out messengers in every direction, you began to solicit the neighbouring princes, namely those who, not yet knowing the truth of the matter, were as yet committed to neither party.

## CHAPTER VI

You laboured especially to ensnare Henry, king of the English. Since, with a cauterized conscience, you did not dare openly to urge a Catholic and wise prince to accept Peter Leo, you urged him with remarkable subtlety to accept neither—though your speech appeared somewhat more inclined toward Peter. You said the matter remained doubtful; many supported each side; some had acted hastily and were already led by much repentance. Peter Leo’s power in the city, you said, was impregnable, especially since he was supported by the strongest fortifications, great wealth, and a very large body of relatives. You asserted that many held him condemned not by justice but rather by envy, because the others feared his penetrating intelligence, greatness of spirit, and irresistible power. Yet, you said, no one could deprive him of dominion over the city, in which the head of the Church had always been located and to which it would, no one doubted, finally return.

You said that he and those with him were sufficiently supplied from their own resources and possessed all the civil revenues belonging to the apostolate; that he need not look to other people’s means or be compelled by lack of household resources to overturn anything. If Henry received the other claimant, it would be burdensome to him and his kingdom; and, worse even than loss to a king, dishonour would follow if the other party prevailed. Nothing, you said, was more intolerable than a needy Roman under whose authority one was placed. He should therefore dissemble and await the outcome of events rather than be followed by belated repentance for a premature decision. It was more useful, you said, to avoid dangers without loss than voluntarily to confront dangers themselves at great cost.

The wise king recognized the hidden cunning of the serpent in your speech and poison concealed beneath honey. You had uttered those things, evidently, not in the spirit of one offering good-faith counsel but of one deceiving, so that, after the lord pope had first been fraudulently excluded by any artifice, a more convenient access might appear to you for speaking on Peter’s behalf. For it is easier to win over affections uncommitted to favour our party than those already occupied by favour for the other side. The king, however, believed that he should not dissemble but should voluntarily meet the needs of the afflicted Church as its helper, lest by your persuasion he be proved headless and become alienated from his mother’s breasts.

A most great king, whose example summons almost all princes to justice; whose munificence toward the poor and liberality toward all are things which all kings can more readily admire than wish or be able to imitate; whose wisdom neither his spacious kingdom nor his duchies can contain, but which pours forth in every direction upon the surrounding powers.

But when, Gerard, you had sent the same recommendations to the kings of Spain and the princes of Brittany, and the fabricated lies you had arranged brought you no hoped-for fruits, you began, with more frenzied madness, to rage within your domestic walls. You found in the count of Poitou a companion in error and an assistant of schism. His anger at the refusal to depose the aged Catholic bishop of Poitiers, and at his petition being unheard contrary to the most sacred canons, had likewise driven him away from Catholic unity.

These, Gerard, are the things you did for the Church and against the Church at the beginning of the storm. Although I may perhaps have related them in rude and unpolished speech, at least I was able to follow truth alone. For I have written nothing that I did not either know myself, receive from a credible authority, or that at least public report does not affirm; and thus it should appear no less credible to others, since so many testimonies support its truth for me. If now I gather up the parts of the division I set forth, there remains only the final part of my purpose, in which something must be said concerning the troubles by which you do not cease to harass and persecute God’s Church. For if anyone wished to recount everything, neither tongue would suffice for speaking nor pen for writing.

## CHAPTER VII

Having received Peter Leo’s letter, you began to travel throughout Aquitaine preaching doctrines contrary to your former preaching: namely, that Peter Leo, under the name Anacletus—but more truly Antichrist—was pope, whose apostolate the principal see received and whose claim the obedience of the whole city confirmed. You described the other as driven from the city, wandering without a fixed see with a few supporters, leading peoples astray and separating them from the Church; as one whom the Lateran chair did not recognize and to whom the Roman populace gave no obedience. To believe such a man pope, you declared, seemed an insanity like calling a man without a kingdom king or naming one deprived of principality a prince.

As though now, Gerard, places determined justice, the departure from that city destroyed the right of his dignity, and the favour of the Roman people alone ought to be preferred to almost all peoples. For did he, sitting at the Lateran, consecrate in the principal church of blessed John the most Christian prince Lothair as king? Did he adorn Lothair, despite his resistance, with the proper solemnity, both with the title of empire and with the imperial diadem? Does a great part of the nobles and the consent of the whole people accompany him? Is residence in the city, and entrance and departure at will, open to him? Even if he lacked all these things altogether, none of them could detract from his justice. But since hidden hatred spurred you to revenge, you did not deny your tongue to falsehood, so that words poisoned with the venom of lies might wound the simple-hearted with the wound of unbelief.

Since this was your one purpose, your one pressing labour, and the one perseverance of your labour, divine power for a short time forestalled your raging assaults; and the first proof of the futility of the power you hoped for came when your legation was turned into imprisonment. You were captured and shut up in prison for some months, until full recognition of the truth confirmed those whom favour had predestined, and those who had first hoped because of the legation granted you afterward despaired because of your confinement. But when the prison was opened, you came forth like a leopard from a cage. If its rage has long been held back in a prison and by chains and it happens to escape free, it rises more boldly, and no shedding of blood can satisfy it. You still thought that by your authority you could overturn all that the holy Church had decreed, and that the weight and decisive moment of affairs rested with you. In this I do not know whether to marvel more at your blindness or your arrogance. What arrogance is greater than for a man almost alone to rise against that which divine providence has confirmed, which all religious devotion has confirmed, which the favour of all kingdoms has confirmed, and which you yourself, insofar as it concerns you, have confirmed? What blindness is greater than to hope for victory against the whole world when no help from God precedes and only the feeble aid of a human being follows?

You cannot deny that you have incurred both the guilt of falsehood and of inconstancy: a most fickle deserter, an unfaithful advocate now of this party, now of that. In each of your actions a double path and a double aim are marked, and your ambiguous expression reveals the divided affections of your mind. For just as some unnatural deformity has distorted your bodily eyes so that, by a marvellous discord, they cannot converge to behold the same object, so too the eyes of your mind—that is, reason and feeling—are at variance.

Abusing the forces of the count, you expelled the Catholic bishops of the Churches of Poitiers and Limoges and irregularly imposed others upon them. One of these, a man of less than reputable life, with no learning and almost wholly tongue-tied even in common speech, had formerly been rejected by the Roman Church from governing the same Church of Poitiers and removed by canonical decision. Yet now he did not refuse, by his own authority, to usurp the rights of his still-living father, although as a son he was bound to him by the bond of obedience and had dedicated himself wholly into his hands, even after giving bodily homage. The other, endowed neither with secular learning nor literary knowledge, an adulterer notorious to all, is carried off by a demon almost every night; first falling from his bed to the ground, he is said to cry out horribly throughout the day and even to wander about the house while asleep. To avoid lingering too long over their qualities: they are proved unworthy of the first orders, let alone the priesthood, let alone episcopal office. Yet you could judge none worthy but men like yourself, nor form members unlike yourself and your head, Peter. For every work always reveals its maker, and in it there is found, as it were, an expressed image of the maker’s will or knowledge.

Why should I mention the most celebrated monasteries laid waste after holy abbots had been expelled, and younger men installed over the burdens of the same charge through money or favour? Under their administration the monasteries have now begun to suffer so great a decline that in those which recently flourished in singular religious discipline almost no traces of virtue or rule remain. For those whose burning desires the monastic order had formerly restrained find in the opportunity of entrusted administration licence to pour themselves out. Nothing is more effective in endangering religious life than enduring an irreligious shepherd.

Here, Gerard, I call you to account. Setting aside for a little while the old question about the apostolate—as though, by Peter’s grant, a right of legation could have come to you—I demand a canonical order in these acts. You condemned men despoiled of their goods, violently expelled from their sees, unsummoned, unadmonished, and absent, with no bishop sitting alongside you. But even if we grant that these matters proceeded in canonical order, I demand regular discipline and a rational form in the installation of others. For in whatever promotions of those men you are shown to have observed neither justice nor even the shadow of justice.

Perhaps the recollection of so great a power flatters your arrogant ears: you who were able to forestall these things according to your will. But lest you take excessive pleasure in this, consider next how much you have benefited yourself and your party. A third part of the bishopric of Poitiers does not acknowledge the bishop you installed, and almost the entire body of nobles refuses obedience to him. Indeed, he is rejected with such unanimous conviction that even his natural brother judges him excommunicated on this very ground and holds no communion with him. Meanwhile the Catholic bishop rules in full authority as far as the gates of the city, and the leading persons of the pontifical Church accompany him, following him into exile after abandoning everything, in the pattern of blessed Peter. Others dwell in the vaults of the city, reclining over pots of meat, fearing destruction rather of nation and place than of soul. But the bishop of Limoges, removed from his city by scarcely the distance of one stadium, dwells in the castle of Saint Martial outside the city gates; from there the man who usurps for himself the seat of the episcopal chair may hear every day the bells ringing for his excommunication. Nor does the land of Angoulême anywhere acknowledge you as its shepherd; there too many glory in the name of the Catholic party.

I postponed until the end of this discourse mention of your usurpation of the archbishopric of Bordeaux, so that your unbridled ambition might become clear from an irrefutable proof. You were bound to the Church of Angoulême by a spiritual marriage; yet an impudent lust of dominion was inflamed by contemplation of the aforesaid dignity. Unable to endure the losses of your now declining affairs, you rushed, in compensation for the frustrated legation, into the embrace of a wealthier adulteress, as it were. As the husband of the daughter, you did not shrink from foully defiling the mother by incest, nor from appearing as a two-headed monster, an ill-omened prodigy for the age. No request of the people and no election of the clergy preceded this; rather, the whole body—or at least by far the greater part—still opposes you, considering you excommunicated and longing intensely for the Catholic party.

## CHAPTER VIII

Come then, so that, as it were, the sum of everything may be concluded in a brief recapitulation from the beginning: because you withdrew from what you had accepted, you condemn yourself either of rashness or of inconstancy. For either your assent to this party was rashly added, or it was certainly withdrawn with excessive inconstancy. That the first refusal of this party removed your favour is no firmer proof of blind ambition. Perhaps that very thing might have been disguised with some veil of invented falsehood; but the transfer of your favour to the other party only after you had obtained the same legation deprived you of every means of defence. In short, the confusion of archbishop and bishop in one person proves that you now act not only unlawfully but shamelessly.

Since these facts concerning you are open to the whole world, by what semblance of justice do you still claim that name for yourself, publicly trying to persuade us that you act thus, if not from knowledge, at least from zeal? Do not these acts show that you sin not imprudently through simplicity, but contemptuously through arrogance? “When the wicked man comes into the depths, he despises” (Prov. 18). At least consider the failing limbs according to nature’s law: it is time to put an end to wickedness and offer to God, who awaits it, the acceptable gift of remnants useless to the world. Turn your face, bent down to the depths, upward; direct your monstrous eyes toward the opposite side, so that you may see how good and pleasant it is to dwell together in unity.

But because, as a night-owl, you cannot endure to look upon daylight, blind man, prick up your ears—unless obstinacy of heart has made them deaf as well. Hear, therefore, with whom you dwell and whose fellowship you reject. That unbelieving body which you follow is Peter Leo’s household, not yet wholly purged from the leaven of Jewish corruption. And that tyrant whom Sicily, the nurse of tyrants, supports: successor of Dionysius, heir of his court and omen, one who bought the empty title of king; formerly duke indeed, but now neither duke nor anything else, because the alien title which the tyrant usurps against justice is, by certain right, held to have no validity in him. To this number the count of Poitou alone is added: a man of pleasures, a merely animal man, not attaining the secrets of spiritual things, enslaved to error because his unlawful petition was rejected. If anyone should say that the holy Church is contained within so small a number, Christ’s inheritance would seem not merely diminished but wholly abolished.

Where then is your holy David, and where is that ancient promise of yours? Where is Paul? Where are the testimonies of the holy Scriptures? For that holy king says, speaking in the person of the Father to the Son: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. 2). And elsewhere: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 71). And Paul says: “God exalted him and gave him the name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend” (Phil. 2). Perhaps you will say that what they declare has already been fulfilled and that these passages do not prevent the present power from facing ruin. But “there shall be no end of his kingdom”; for he rules with a rod of iron.

As for our party—if so slight an exception compels us to call the almost entire whole by the name of a party—every emperor, every king, every prince, indeed every person honoured with the Christian name, acknowledges it. Yet, if there is any faith in me, I give little heed in so divine a matter to the favour of princes and people who are still held captive by worldly affection. Their agreement chiefly matters to me in this: their authority moves me, draws me when moved, and holds me when drawn—those to whom it is given to know the mystery of God’s kingdom, and whose citizenship is already said to be in heaven in part (Phil. 3). Such truly are those who inhabit the perpetual snows of Chartreuse, and those who, issuing from the Cistercian or Cluniac monastery, have spread the rays of their light in every direction. Removing earthly things from their hands and minds by sounder counsel, they mortify the body with rough clothing, food both scanty and dry, vigils, and many labours, striving with all the strength of their souls for that reward which grace has promised to those who love God. Their life is holy, their speech wise, their discernment in divine things keen, and no cloud of earthly density darkens it.

God indeed permits them to be afflicted by troubles, that they may be tested like gold in a furnace; but temptation does not grow beyond their capacity. Although he still delays them in part on earth, so that prolonged desires may increase their promised crowns, they are nevertheless not thought excluded from divine counsels: “their angels always see the face of the Father” (Matt. 18), and by the familiar visitation of the Holy Spirit their angels cause them to be enlightened. Nor, even in the present life, does his reward desert those who endure. As it is written: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have made my soul glad” (Ps. 93). “I go,” he says, “and I come to you, and your heart shall rejoice” (John 16). What then? Shall the chosen party of which I speak be deprived of the fruit of its work, and shall divinity change its promise? Far be it! “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent” (Ps. 109). Therefore the promised Holy Spirit dwells in the minds of these people, which he has prepared as fitting temples for himself, and necessarily enlightens them with full knowledge of the truth. For if the Spirit is God, and God is truth, then surely where the Spirit is present, ignorance of truth does not remain. What more need be said? Lest our discourse exceed the proper bounds of brevity, let it suffice to have spoken a few things out of many, lesser things out of the greatest.

[Col. 0195]

# POEMS OF ARNULF, BISHOP OF LISIEUX

## I. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

[Col. 0195A]

God, eternally being born, endures to be born in time  
under the condition of humanity.

The sacred power of the Father overshadows the virgin womb,  
bringing it about that the Word should become flesh.

The offspring, bearing a form like that of both father and mother,
The form gives expression and restores to each its own appearance.

Thus His form imitates the Father’s paternal form,  
so that, when He is seen, the Father Himself is seen in Him.

And, fashioning for Himself a body from the virginal body,  
He takes on from a human being a human likeness.

One person displays two forms; and God,  
made man, preserves what is proper to each nature:

For here God in the flesh preserves the simplicity proper to His nature,  
and the flesh preserves its own nature in the Godhead.

They are not mingled; for neither does the Godhead, confused with it, dissolve the flesh,  
nor does the flesh, when mingled, dissolve God.

The glory of the Godhead reigns in the assumed flesh,  
nor do fleshly veils burden majesty.

And, as virginal faith cleansed the ancient guilt,  
the flesh was sanctified by the coming of the Godhead.

Faith believed and produced a pure mother,  
and, magnified by God, she magnifies God.

The virgin’s integrity, fruitful while modesty remains unharmed,  
conceives and bears a man without a man.

Nor does the birth, begotten without a man and brought forth without an opening,  
unseal the enclosure of her guarded modesty.

Therefore reciprocal exchanges mingle in a new covenant,

[Col. 0195C] and the old wrath is transformed into a new peace.

For divine things, reconciled by a kindly favour,  
meet human things in steadfast faith.

The slave is adopted; the exile returns; the prisoner  
comes forth; and, once the obstacle has been removed, the formerly barred gate stands open.

## II. To Henry, Bishop of Winchester

What grace distributes through manifold forms,  
that she bestowed upon you wholly and all at once.

All at once she bestowed whatever virtue  
the human body and the cultivated mind can possess.

No other body was worthy of such a mind, nor was this  
mind worthy to be clothed in any other body.

Thus soul and limbs, limbs and soul, are fitted to one another,

[Col. 0195D] so that no disparity burdens them.

For a royal mind reigns in a royal body,  
and strong limbs befit a great-hearted man.

Ordered manners adorn bearing and countenance,

[Col. 0196A] and a comely form accords with your character.

An exalted understanding and vigour of intellect kindle  
your lofty eyes with keen light.

Reason forms the mind, eloquence the tongue,  
and a full stream proves the water fruitful.

A celebrated thought shines with rhetorical refinement:  
this wins minds, that pleases ears.

Things give worth to words; words give distinction to things.  
I do not know whether you please more or profit more.

## III. On the Renewal of Spring

Whatever winter, like unsightly old age,  
had long made devoid of its own beauty,

spring renews; and, with a new flower of puberty,

[Col. 0196B] commands all things to return to tender days.  
[Note: [Col. 0195D] B: “threefold,” *ternos*.]

The bonds of the ancient union seemed broken,  
and holy love, convulsed by hatreds, seemed to yield.

The sacred fellowship of the elements seemed torn apart,  
and each seemed to wish to devour its own offspring.

And, turned with equal fury into an ancient tumult,  
they seemed to hasten death, hateful to things.

Aged autumn, looking upon seeds entrusted to the cold,  
had believed that its investment had perished.

But now a hidden fire and the secret power  
of nature, conscious of a holy purpose, stir them;

applying causes to seeds and seeds to causes,  
nature, instructed, shapes them according to her heavenly work.

The rising sun, bright with a cheerful face, having regained  
its fires, loosens the earth gripped by frost.

[Col. 0196C] And, making the airy face serene with new splendour,  
the gentler breeze gladdens the cleansed day.

From every side exuberance stirs the youthful world,  
and prodigal earth opens her fruitful womb.

The ground is clothed with grass, the tree with leaves;  
the vine offers its bud, the field lilies, the thorn a rose.

In turn the elements exchange both their work and their wealth,  
and aid one another with equal favour and material.

Therefore nature, refashioning the world’s old age,  
is borne under her own auspices toward her own desires:

for power, ever attending will,

[Col. 0196D] does not allow a goddess to have willed anything in vain.  
[Note: [Col. 0196D] B: “now,” *num*.]

The world rises joyfully and boldly in hope;  
the old man thinks of advancing into the face of a boy.

Nor does he fear a return of the old and mournful form,

[Col. 0196D] believing winter utterly dead, not merely gone away.

And, elated by the success of new prosperity,  
he ordains future ages according to his wish.

[Col. 0197A] Therefore he appoints his fourth years to be shortened,  
so that all things may rejoice in three seasons.

Thus the year may not be dissolved by waters or lie numb with cold,  
and the seasons may flow in perpetual mildness.

## IV. On the Alternating Succession of the Seasons

The seasons, revolving again in their ancient circuit,  
change and restore their effects in turn.

Mother winter preserves the seeds of father autumn,  
to be restored in steadfast trust by new spring.

Spring, preceded by the icy old age of the barren world,  
is released into offspring and luxuriates in new growth.

Nature, cherishing what has been produced with kindly favour,  
advances it, under summer’s auspices, into maturity.

At last all things yield to autumn’s harvests,

[Col. 0197B] and the remaining year heaps up for it all its wealth.

What winter conceived, spring bore, and summer nourished,  
autumn reaps and completes at its own pleasure.

Only seeds suited to future conceptions are preserved,  
born to renew the powers disposed for them.

Thus the year departs in order to return, returns in order to pass away,  
recalling and hurrying on its headlong wheel.

Thus established alternation carries on the everlasting months,  
renewing the old and making the new grow old.

Divine wisdom often plays this game,  
and, moving what is to be changed, remains itself unchanged.

## V. To a Beggar-Poet

I hate begging verses, the venture of a poor Muse,

[Col. 0197C] and prayers composed in verse, Caecilianus.

An importunate demand stirs up grievous anger  
and bears the goads of a double shamelessness.

Whoever asks immediately begins, by that very act, to be troublesome;  
if he asks with any added artifice, he is more so.

For a prayer shaped by the pursuits of art  
acquires a certain blemish from the suspicion of deceit.

And a demand mingled with tricks wounds in both ways:  
insidious greed deceives and squeezes one dry.

Accordingly, doubled annoyance makes verses hateful,  
and metre retains none of its own charm.

If, then, you wish to preserve the Muse’s favour,  
let her charm ears with unpurchased speech.

For anyone who asks that his ear be filled with praises  
and his hand with gifts is importunate.

## VI. To Scaeva, on Not Refashioning an Old Woman

[Col. 0197D]

Scaeva complains that the beauty of his ageing mistress withers  
and that her tender days have grown old.

Therefore he diligently explores foreign arts  
and purchases new appearances at great cost;

and, tormenting her face with every cosmetic that might restore it,  
he laments that medical hands have been able to do nothing.

Scaeva cannot deceive nature by such care;  
no art refashions a deformed old woman.

If you wish to call back into the light a face buried away,  
and restore your mistress’s appearance, take away her days.

[Col. 0198A] Take away her days: accumulated years create the injuries of age  
and, multiplied, multiply the skin’s wrinkles.

## VII. To a Young Man and Girl Looking at One Another More Affectionately

Your eyes meet one another with gentle favour,  
and your inmost hearts smile with a shared desire.

Your faces answer one another with reciprocal blushes;  
and tender modesty reveals the affection on either side.  
[Note: [Col. 0197D] B: “both,” *utrumque*.]

A mutual will, running freely back and forth,  
makes your minds enter into a playful covenant.

The flame of your eyes gleams in alternating rays,  
and an entangled gaze binds your eyes in alliance.

The souls themselves seem almost to have exchanged  
their proper seats and to dwell in new bodies.

[Col. 0198B] Grace joins the silent embraces of your souls  
and prepares an omen in bodily bonds.

A happy union will proceed with its bond doubled,  
and bodies will join their own spirits.

Fruitful expectation will grant the desired fruits,  
and anxious wishes will bear joyful days.

## VIII. To Wanton Companions

From my earliest time my mind, trained in the pursuit of virtues,  
undertook to avoid disgraceful paths;

but, so that my life might be safer among you,  
I was a cautious dissembler of uprightness.

I wished my favour to be thought no different;  
it was not true Venus that granted it to me, but feigned Venus.

[Col. 0198C] My ingenuity served you at a mere nod,  
deceiving you indeed, but by a better deceit.

My earnest mind had shut itself within its own integrity,  
lest virtue and disparity make me burdensome.

But when perfection could not be concealed  
and virtue disclosed itself by its own signs,

the malicious tongue began, pricked by envy’s goads,  
to languish and drip poison among its people.

I confess that I wished to please; I am ashamed, because to please  
the shameful, or to please for shameful reasons, is shameful for a good man.

I ought openly to have broken silence, not buried myself  
with guilty persons through silent fear.

For silent virtue serves wickedness, and acquits  
the guilty if it does not point out that they are guilty.

To flatter a fault with any favour is itself a share in the fault,

[Col. 0198D] for by flattering you foster it, and by fostering you commit it.

He supplies hidden assistance and furnishes power to act  
who is silent, though he could have opposed evil.

For virtue neither loves nor endures even the shadow of vice,  
nor does it draw darkness into its own light.

## IX. Upon the Tomb of King Henry, in Which His Brain and Heart Are Buried

Of Henry, whose name the public voice celebrates,  
here in this place lie, in part, his buried members.

Neither earth could contain him while he lived,  
nor could one place bury him when dead.

[Col. 0199A] Divided into three, he gives up his rights to their respective  
parts, and thus makes three kingdoms illustrious through three parts.

Heaven is assigned to his spirit; Neustria to his heart and brain;  
England, which gave him his body, possesses the body.  
[Note: [Col. 0199D] B omits the two verses from *Neustria* to *cuique*.]

A good part, a better part, a best part—his portion is given respectively  
to the English, Normans, and inhabitants of heaven.

From here he drew his fathers and his spirit; but by chance, among the English,  
he was born; here he wielded the sword, there he bore the sceptres.  
[Note: [Col. 0200D] B: “those men,” *illos*.]

When the final night of November released him as he departed,  
the first day of December divided him.

## X. How One Should Give to a Poor or a Rich Person

[Col. 0199B] A small old broken object, condemned by a threefold defect of beauty,  
expressed a simple thought.

If someone takes care to give something to a needy man,  
let him consider the burden of poverty.

One must not give him an elephant, nor a Parthian tiger,  
nor anything that compels him to be still more needy.

I do not want a gift that makes a poor man poorer;  
I want what I may rather approve for its usefulness.

What does it avail me if empty honour has made a gift illustrious,  
when my hearth grows cold because its fire has gone out?

The destitute man needs feeding with bread, not being mocked with honour;  
cold gratitude comes from an empty stomach.

By contrast, whatever gift one gives to the rich  
should be fashioned more for honour, less for usefulness.

Let it distinguish rather than relieve, lest it be approved

[Col. 0199C] merely because it was a gift, rather than because it was such a gift.

And since the image of the giver’s mind is present in what is given,  
nor can the giver disguise his feeling,

give in such a way that you may always seem to have given gladly,  
lest curtailed gifts reveal a miserly hand.

## XI. Epitaph of the Empress Matilda, Daughter of King Henry and Mother of Another King Henry

Of royal offspring, royal stock, and wife of Caesar,  
great Matilda lies enclosed here in a small place.

By the titles of her virtues she surpassed the summit  
of human honour—a woman possessing nothing womanish.

On the tenth of September, after receiving kingdom following kingdoms,  
she is believed to have continued into the eternal day.

## XII. On the Same Woman

[Col. 0199D]

Matilda was mother of a king and born from kings,  
and had exalted her lineage by a nobler marriage-bed;

but, shining more brightly with the outstanding praise of virtues,  
she had surpassed the fortune of birth and marriage.

On the tenth of September, in the first hour, she passed  
from our night, restored to the true day.

## XIII. Beneath the Cross, in the Person of the Crucified One

[Col. 0200A]

Thus, by the cross I lift up the cross; dying, I triumph over death;  
though slain as man, I give life to man.

Grace prescribes commandments; form, the figure; reality, the sign; life, death; the crown, the yoke.

## XIV. To His Nephew, When He Was a Young Man

Once all Normandy considered me a celebrated poet,  
and scarcely did all France grant me an equal.

The one considered me among the foremost; the other called me first  
among her own—Normandy said “ours,” France “hers.”

Yet everywhere I was celebrated with varied honour:  
illustrious abroad and especially honoured at home.

[Col. 0200B] Now perhaps a new age has brought forth you, a new poet,  
as a model for the unpolished and an object of envy for the good.

Learning, making an old poet out of a boy,  
has bestowed upon your age words not belonging to it.

Your words savour of old age, and the page that proclaims Virgil himself  
blooms with the grey hair of one still beardless.

My Muse herself, marvelling at your days and at words beyond your years,  
grew pale before your verses and mine.

And when, as usual, I had taken up my tablets,  
she deprived my tongue of voice and my hand of the stylus.

Therefore I yield to you the Muses and sacred Helicon,  
and leave you the sweet waters of the holy spring.

Cultivate those Muses whose favour belongs to us;  
you can retain it only by diligent devotion.

## XV. Epitaph of Algar, Bishop of Coutances

[Col. 0200C]

When the ashes of Bishop Algar were buried, nature  
could not bury the merit of the man.

For, filling earth with his honours and heaven with his virtues,  
he died to us in order to live for himself.

Since earth and heaven alike speak of this man,  
it is enough to have commemorated him in a brief inscription.

One day, conscious of his merits, took him from earthly things  
and restored him to heaven, together with Martin.

## XVI. Epitaph of Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen

Among bishops, worthy of special honour,  
Hugh here lays down the burden of our flesh.

His entrusted limbs are enclosed in a brief tomb,

[Col. 0200D] yet neither hemisphere encloses the man’s deeds.

Whatever grace distributes and apportions among all persons,  
she had bestowed and granted upon this man.

Accordingly, abundance made him fruitful in the fruits of virtues,  
and the man was magnified beyond man.

At last, after the happy times of his celebrated life,  
a mournful hour took away the veteran old man.

Your equal, Martin, and destined to share your lot,  
he obtained by dying the same day with you.

# A.D. 1184–1190: William, Archbishop of Tyre

[Col. 0201]

## Historical-Literary Notice

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latinitatis*, III, 170)

William, formerly archdeacon (History, book XXI, chapter 1), Archbishop of Tyre, or Tyrian, from the year 1174 (book XX, chapter 9) in Phoenicia, apparently a Jerusalemite by nationality, but excellently educated in letters in overseas schools in Italy (book XIX, chapter 4)—concerning whom, besides the editors and especially Bongars, Aubertus Miraeus should be consulted in the *Auctarium*, pp. 61 ff. of the edition prepared by me—was a judicious man. He wrote the distinguished work *History of Deeds Done in the Lands Beyond the Sea*, from the time of the successors of Muhammad and from the year 1048, and especially from 1100 to A.D. 1184, in twenty-three books, the last of which he left scarcely begun. He is praised by Antoninus of Florence, James of Vitry, Paul Emilius, and others.

It first appeared at Basle in 1549, folio, with Nicolaus Brillinger and Johann Oporinus, through the efforts of Philip Poissenot. Then it appeared there again in 1564, folio, with Heinrich Petri, with a Life of William prefixed, edited by Heinrich Pantaleon, and with Basil Johann Herold’s continuation to the year 1521 appended in six books; these had appeared separately at Basle in 1560, folio. Finally, it was published from the careful recension of Jacques Bongars, in *Gesta Dei per Francos*, Hanover, 1611, folio, p. 625, but with Herold’s continuation omitted. Bongars himself testified that he possessed several unpublished French translations of this work, likewise continued by those translators. There also appeared Gabriel du Préau’s, or Prateolus’s, translation, *La Franciade Orientale*, Paris, 1573, folio; and an Italian translation by Giuseppe Horologgi, *Guerra sacra*, Venice, 1562, quarto, and at Venice, edited by Tommaso Baglioni, 1610, quarto. Pagi observed, at A.D. 1182, no. 11, that William, in dating events, followed Eutychius as guide and sometimes went astray; Pagi also remarks, at A.D. 1155, no. 9, that William seems insufficiently fair toward the knights of Jerusalem.

In the preface to the *History*, William testifies that, at the request of King Amalric, who himself supplied Arabic copies, he also composed another history, extending from the time of the deceiver Muhammad to the present year, which is, from the incarnation of the Lord, 1184, a course of five hundred and seventy years. He professes that the author whom he chiefly followed was the venerable Sa‘īd, son of Batrīq, patriarch of Alexandria—namely, the very man whose *Annals* we possess under the name of Eutychius. This is the work *On the Deeds of the Eastern Princes*, which William mentions (book I, chapter 3), or *On the Eastern Princes and Their Actions* (book XIX, chapters 15 and 21). Bongars already observed that students of history must most grievously regret its loss; for there is no doubt that William added much to the Eutychian narratives.

He also recorded the acts of the Lateran synod held in A.D. 1179, which he says he attended in book XXI, chapter 26. “If anyone,” he says, “desires to know its decrees and the names, number, and titles of the bishops, let him reread the work which we carefully composed, at the request of the holy Fathers who attended that synod; and which we ordered to be placed in the archive of the Church of Tyre among the other books which we bestowed upon that Church.” This work too is now lost.

[Col. 0201]

## Another Notice

(Bongars, *Gesta Dei per Francos, or a History of the Eastern Expeditions and of the Frankish Kingdom of Jerusalem*, etc.; Hanover, Wechel Press, 1611, folio; Preface, no. XI.)

… There follows the foremost of all historians: William, Archbishop of Tyre—a man of no ordinary learning, delightful beyond that age, of varied experience, keen judgment, and, so far as one may judge, of upright life and disposition; elegant and weighty also in expression. I have nothing to say about his parents or his original descent. But Baldwin the jurist, who makes him a Frenchman, and the author of his Life, prefixed to the second Basle edition—that of Heinrich Pantaleon—who makes him born of German parents, rest, so far as I know, on no evidence. Unless it be that some people so foolishly love their homeland that they think themselves permitted to claim for it every excellence found anywhere.

In the preface to the work and to book XXIII, when he speaks of love of country, the sweetness of his native soil, and the calamity and miseries of his homeland, he certainly means Syria and the kingdom of Jerusalem which he treats. For, even if we grant the author of that Life what is true, namely that one may have two homelands, one cannot have two native soils (book XIX, chapter 4): “We had not yet returned from the schools, but were still detained beyond the sea in the study of the liberal arts.” Therefore he was Syrian.

Moreover, the old French histories which expound and continue this very history of William expressly say that he was born at Jerusalem. Brother Stephen Lusignan, himself a Cypriot and author of a *History of Cyprus*, reports—on what authority I do not know—that William was related to the princes of the kingdom of Jerusalem. In his childhood he saw Ralph, patriarch of Antioch (book XV, chapter 17), that is, unless I am mistaken, about A.D. 1140. When the divorce between King Amalric and Agnes of Edessa was being concluded, he was studying in the schools, etc. (in the passage [Col. 0203] cited above). This occurred in 1162. Our French writers state, at book XXI, chapter 1, that he devoted himself to learning in France, which is probable. For at that time the city of Paris, “like a fountain of gardens and a well of living waters,” irrigated the whole surface of the earth, offering delicate bread and delights to kings, and, to the whole Church of God, breasts sweeter than honey and honeycomb, as James of Vitry says, *History of the West*, chapter 7. Hence he became dear and familiar to the king because of his learning, as appears from book XIX, chapter 3.

In 1167, unless my calculation deceives me, Archbishop Frederick conferred upon him the archdeaconry of the Church of Tyre at the request of King Amalric and many other honourable men (book XX, chapter 1). Nor did the man thereafter receive much leisure, since the very abilities and learning which commended him to princes exposed him to others’ envy. For he immediately went as envoy on a matter of the greatest importance to the emperor at Constantinople, and returned after successfully completing his embassy (book XX, chapter 4). A little later, perhaps in 1169—for we intend to trace these matters more precisely in the chronology—drawn away by domestic business and avoiding the undeserved indignation of his archbishop, he went to the Roman Church (the same book XX, chapter 18).

Upon his return, King Amalric, much concerned for the education of his nine-year-old son Baldwin, entrusted the royal boy to him, with many entreaties and under the pledge of royal favour, to be trained and instructed in the liberal arts (book XXI, chapter 1). Later the same king, on the advice of the princes, honoured him with the office of chancellor in the sacred palace, “that,” he says, “there might be someone to have charge of the royal letters” (book XXI, chapter 5; book XIX, chapter 24; book XXII, chapter 5; and the preface to the work).

In May 1174, by the unanimous wish of clergy and people, and with the king’s assent, as was customary, he was called to govern the Church of Tyre. Ten days later, on the sixth day before the Ides of June, he received consecration at the hands of Amalric, patriarch of Jerusalem, in the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre (book XXI, chapter 9). In the following year he himself, by virtue of his office, bestowed the same rite of consecration upon the bishops-elect of Sidon and Beirut. In 1176 he arranged the funeral of William, marquis of Montferrat, the king’s brother-in-law (book XXI, chapter 13). In 1177 he departed for Rome, summoned to the Lateran synod, and at the request of the Fathers present set down in writing its decrees and the names and titles of its bishops (book XXI, chapter 26).

Returning from the synod, he left at Brindisi Henry of Troyes—that is, the count of Champagne—departing for the East with a great company of nobles (book XXI, chapter 30). At Constantinople he remained continuously for seven months with Emperor Manuel, to the great benefit, as he says, of himself and his Church. He received from Manuel instructions for the prince and patriarch of Antioch. To carry these out, he reached the harbour of St. Symeon on the fourth day before the Ides of May and went aside to Antioch. Having completed them, on the day before the Nones of July, after a year and ten months since he had departed for the synod, he returned to Tyre (book XXII, chapter 4). There, a little afterward, when Master Odo, archdeacon of his Church, was called to the bishopric of Beirut, William conferred upon him the rank of priesthood and episcopal dignity (same book, chapter 7).

After Jerusalem was lost in 1188, when the affairs of the kingdom were despaired of, he was sent as an ambassador to the West. Roger of Howden writes that he attended the conference between the kings of France and England between Gisors and Trie: “There was present,” he says, “the Archbishop of Tyre, who, filled with the spirit of wisdom and understanding, preached the word of the Lord in a wonderful way before the kings and princes, and turned their hearts to taking up the cross. Those who had formerly been enemies, while he preached and God cooperated, became friends on that day; and they received the cross from his hand. In that same hour the sign of the cross appeared above them in heaven,” etc. Matthew Paris adds that William of Tyre received from the lord pope the office of legate in the matter of the cross. His name survives in John of Salisbury, letter 275, where “Archbishop of Tyre” is badly printed as “Archbishop of Terenza.” Gerald of Wales also mentions this embassy, *Expugnatio Hibernica*, book II, chapter 23, as does William of Newburgh, *English Affairs*, book III, chapter 23. Unless perhaps this was another man, a third person of that name, rather than our William; we shall consider that elsewhere.

But the man who wrote the Life of our William prefixed to the second Basle edition—whether he was Heinrich Pantaleon, as I readily persuade myself, or someone else—adds the following assertions without, so far as we have observed, attending to these facts. He says that William, already an archdeacon, was invited by the cardinals and by Pope Victor IV himself; that during almost two years in the Roman school, by disputing, lecturing, and laborious study, he acquired the name of a most learned and acute philosopher and other distinctions of learning and erudition; that it was even proposed that he should be enrolled among the purple-clad senators after being enriched with wealthy benefices; that he placed everything after his love of homeland; and that, when the kingdom was declining, such was his reputation that, by everyone’s acclamation, money from a collection was entrusted to him alone. He also says that William delivered a most splendid funeral oration for Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. We have no leisure at present to examine these claims; yet we did not wish to pass them by, though stated without authority, as if they were so certain.

The miserable yet memorable end of our William would be unknown to us without the French writers. Since their words, faithfully set forth as far as we can, both shed light on these matters and furnish grave instruction for life by their example, while containing several rare details not found elsewhere, we thought it appropriate to add them.

“There were at that time in the land beyond the sea two clerics who were archbishops: one of Tyre, the other of Caesarea—not Caesarea called Philip’s, but maritime Caesarea. The former was named William, and no better cleric was then considered to exist in the whole Christian world. The latter was named Heraclius, an Auvergnat by nation. He had departed, a poor cleric, for the land beyond the sea; through the elegance of his appearance he gained the favour of the queen mother, and through her influence became Archbishop of Caesarea.

“It happened during the time of these two clerics that the patriarch of Jerusalem died. The archbishops were therefore summoned to the city for the election of a patriarch. When all had assembled, the Archbishop of Tyre approached the canons of the Holy Sepulchre, to whom the election of the patriarch belonged, and spoke to them these words, having first asked leave:

‘Lords, in the Scriptures I find that Heraclius in Persia acquired the Holy Cross and carried it to Jerusalem; but that another Heraclius, in his own time, would demand it from Jerusalem and lose it. Therefore, by God, I beg you: do not call Heraclius patriarch. For if you nominate him, I know that he will be accepted by the king; and I know further that, with him as patriarch, the city of Jerusalem and the entire land will be lost. Do not suppose that I say this inflamed by desire for the patriarchate. Instead, by God, choose two men other than ourselves; and, if you cannot find them in this region, we promise you our assistance in obtaining a patriarch from France through the counsel of good men.’

“The canons of the Holy Sepulchre did none of this. For the queen mother had asked them to nominate the Archbishop of Caesarea. They did in fact nominate him together with William of Tyre. For such is the method of electing a patriarch in the land beyond the sea, as also of archbishops, bishops, and abbots: the canons elect two and offer them to the king, who chooses one of the two. If they are presented in the morning, the king must choose one before the signal for Vespers; if in the evening, after the office has been sung, on the following day. The apostles followed this procedure after Judas’s death when they elected two, Joseph Justus and Matthias; and it is still observed in the Holy Land. Thus the king is elector and chooses whom he wishes.

“When those two archbishops had been presented to the king, he chose Heraclius of Caesarea, having pledged his word on behalf of the latter to his mother. Having thus become patriarch of Jerusalem, Heraclius immediately summoned all the archbishops and bishops to render obedience. They all came, except the Archbishop of Tyre. For he appealed Heraclius himself to Rome, affirming that he would certainly demonstrate that Heraclius was such a man as ought not to be patriarch.

“Having lodged the appeal and arranged his affairs, he crossed the sea and came to Rome. The pope rejoiced at his arrival and received him with great honour, as did the cardinals; nor did they remember any cleric ever having been treated at Rome with so much honour by pope and all the cardinals. The pope wished him to sing Mass and ordered the cardinals to vest themselves in order to serve him at the altar. He had now gained so much influence with the pope that, had he survived, Heraclius’s deposition would have been certain if he came to Rome.

“Now I shall tell you how that man died before Heraclius appealed to Rome. When Heraclius learned that he had gone to Rome against him, and was certain that he would be deposed if William lived until Heraclius’s arrival, he approached one of his own physicians, induced him to follow William to Rome, and to remove him by poison. This succeeded. Therefore, after the Archbishop of Tyre died, the patriarch came to Rome, obtained whatever he wished from the pope, and returned to Jerusalem.

“But hear what manner of life he lived after his return from Rome to Jerusalem … [lacuna] When our Lord Jesus Christ saw these sins and these defilements in the city in which he had been crucified and had poured out his blood for the redemption of the people, he could no more endure them than he had formerly endured those of Sodom and Gomorrah. Therefore he so cleansed the city of its foul and stinking luxury that, of all those—men, women, and children, I say all—who possessed it in the time of Patriarch Heraclius, only two altogether escaped slavery. One was named Robert of Corbie, who had been present with Godfrey of Bouillon at the taking of the city; the other was named Fulco Folie, otherwise Fiole, who was the first of all persons born in the city after Godfrey had taken it. Since they did not wish to depart, Saladin granted them freedom to remain and ordered all necessities of life to be supplied to them.”

The truth of this remarkable narrative, though its chronology is not sufficiently explained—of which we shall consider the proper time—is supported both by the event and by reputable writers. By the event: for just as the Cross was recovered under Emperor Heraclius, so under Patriarch Heraclius—as the Archbishop of Tyre had foretold—both the Cross and the city were lost. By writers: Marino Sanudo, book III, part VI, chapter 24, says: “In the year 1180 Patriarch Amalric died, whose simplicity was of little benefit to the Church; Heraclius succeeded him. At his election it was publicly said that under Heraclius the Cross would be lost, just as it had been recovered under Emperor Heraclius; and this indeed occurred.” Paul Emilius, near the end of book V of *The Deeds of the Kings of France*, under King Philip Augustus, says: “The most holy Cross, as though the fateful pledge of the sacred kingdom, was now handled by hands less holy.” Authors contemporary with that time survive who state that the priests were sunk in crimes and wickedness, and that the patriarch himself lived neither chastely nor uprightly.

But let us return to our subject. William had formed the plan of writing history long before he began, and had gathered what was necessary for so great a work. At last he began at the request of King Amalric (Preface and end of book XX), equipped with traditions and eyewitness evidence, with no written text as guide.

It is not probable that a scholarly and learned man, who had crossed the sea and, as people then spoke, had also crossed the Alps, had not read so many books published about this route by persons who had travelled it. The aforesaid Orderic Vitalis records that many others, both Latins and Greeks, had written on so memorable a matter. We have seen one Greek account in the Royal Library, written in the vernacular language through the assistance of Isaac Casaubon and frequently cited by Johannes Meursius in his *Lexicon Graecobarbarum*; but this account, as I recall, touches upon this holy war in only a page or two. Yet our author seems to have neglected and counted as nothing what others had formerly proclaimed and what we collect at such expense and with such zeal.

Up to the reign of King Baldwin III, which begins in book XVI, he wove his narrative from the reports of others, to whom, as he says, fuller memory of former times still ministered. The events following he either saw himself or drew from those who had personally taken part in them, as he himself testifies in the preface to book XVI. In book XII, chapter 24, he also says that he reports what he heard from certain elders who steadfastly affirmed that they had been present at all the aforesaid events.

Nor did he complete this span in one sustained effort. Twice he openly pauses and, as it were, recovers breath and spirit—once in that same book XVI, as though about thereafter to publish matters more certain, and again after completing book XXII, when he approaches, reluctantly, the description of the extremities of his homeland.

It is evident that he did not put the finishing hand to this most useful work. For he both repeats and emphasizes certain things which it would have sufficed to say once; he touches lightly upon certain things not previously mentioned, as though they had already been explained; nor do the dates correspond everywhere. In the Preface he identifies the present year as 1184, which in Book I, chapter 2, he makes 1182—the reading required at the end of chapter 21 of Book XIX, where 1172 is commonly printed. And in Book XXI, chapter 26, he says that he had then presided over the Church of Tyre for six years, which falls in the year 1180. From these facts it is established, as I have already said, that he worked on this book repeatedly at different times, and that the section now read first was written last.

In Book XXII, chapters 7 and 13, he speaks of an event occurring while he wrote: “he is said,” he says, “to be besieging and attacking [them] with frequent hostile engagements,” etc. He divided the work, or volume, into books, which he also calls treatises, and the books into chapters. He wrote twenty-three books, as he himself states in the Preface; but that he did not finish the twenty-third is apparent from the fact that old manuscripts copied shortly after his lifetime do not differ from one another by a single letter, more or less, nor do the chapter-headings prefixed to the books promise anything beyond what we possess. And although the French translators have carried the history further, even beyond William’s death, one Palatine manuscript at Heidelberg does not exceed the Latin by so much as a word.

For I do not understand what John Herold means when, in the preface to his continuation of the *Sacred War*, he asserts—on the sworn testimony of great men—that this same William completed his history down to the death of Emperor Frederick II Augustus. On that reckoning he would have surpassed one hundred and twenty years of age, unless we suppose that Herold wrote “Frederick” the First in place of the Second. Thus perhaps he would have Paul Aemilius as a supporter, as we shall say presently. There, therefore, he stopped, diverted by business and forestalled by death; yet he intended to continue, and proposed to increase the number of books “according to the amount,” he says, “of material which should arise,” although he had previously resolved not to reach the decline of his country and the final disasters of his people (Preface to the work and Book XXIII).

Indeed, in the English Cambridge manuscript, Book XXIII is read joined to Book XXII, the copyist judging that this one or two pages was not to be entitled as a separate book. He embraced nearly a hundred years, or rather, as he himself more exactly calculates later, eighty-four years (Preface). His diligence in seeking the truth is clear from Book IX, chapters 16, 17, 7, 20, and 18. His hesitation and conscientiousness in doubtful matters are clear from Book XXII, chapter 5, end; chapters 8, 25, and 27, end; and Book XX, chapter 20, elsewhere. Thus he reports even recent events doubtfully when there has been insufficient time to investigate their truth (Book XXII, chapter 19, etc.). Pursuing general matters, he does not devote much attention to particulars (Book XVII, chapter 24). He excuses his public and private occupations if anything should perhaps occur in which the reader may rightly take offense (Preface). Finally, throughout the whole work, he displays the modesty, prudence, and piety which he promises in the Preface and makes evident there. He mentions Patriarch Heraclius without hatred, at the end of Book XXII, chapter 4.

Perhaps he may seem too harsh toward Guy of Lusignan, Count of Jaffa. After saying that he was unequal in strength and prudence, he calls him an unknown man, indiscreet and utterly useless (Book XXII, chapters 25 and 27). Even if the other statements are true—as they are not far from truth—he should not have called unknown one whom, in chapter 1 of the same book, he had called sufficiently noble, the son of Hugh le Brun. For he had mentioned both Hugh of Lusignan and Hugh de Lusignan, surnamed le Brun, in Book X, chapter 19, and Book XIX, chapter 8; and had given the same family Raymond of Poitiers, brought from the farthest reaches of England, as prince of Antioch (Book XIV, chapters 10, 20, and 21). But, God granting life, we shall discuss that most illustrious family in the genealogical work.

Certainly Guy was unequal in virtues to so great a burden: the unhappy men of his time experienced it, and we learn it from the history itself. Yet he had to contend both with the strength of his enemies and the envy of his countrymen. The princes of the kingdom took it ill that a foreigner, the king’s brother-in-law, afterwards guardian of the kingdom and finally successor, should rule, when men more noble, prudent, and even wealthier could have been found in the kingdom, as our author himself says in Book XX, chapter 1. James of Vitry, long resident in the kingdom, observes in his *History of Jerusalem*, chapter 72, that those new natives of Syria, whom he says were called Pullani, were not merely ungrateful but troublesome in many ways toward those who came from distant regions out of devotion or to aid them.

Emperor Conrad and King Louis, at Damascus, experienced the stings of their envy and the grievous blows of their treachery, to the great detriment both of the commonwealth and of the kingdom itself (our author, Book XVII, chapters 5 and 7). Count Thierry of Flanders experienced them too (Book XVIII, chapter 18). Nor is this disposition of natives toward foreigners entirely without reason. For it seems unjust that men who have borne countless labors in the kingdom’s service throughout their lives should be neglected by newcomers reaping the fruits of such great labors, and should lose the hope of reward. Tyrius himself, Book XVII, chapter 7: “Thus you, but not for yourselves.” But this is a question for another place.

Here, however, let us admire the providence and just judgments of God. When He had determined, most deservedly, to destroy our people, He gave them as king Guy, fetched from the heart of France, from the highest nobility of Poitou; while at the same time, when He was raising the fortunes of the Saracens, He produced Saladin from the dust, a son of the land, but a prince most perfectly endowed with every virtue. Let any hatred our author bore toward Guy, if there was any, therefore be excused by his love and pity for his native land. Nor was it unknown to Brother Stephen of Lusignan, of the Order of Preachers, who published a history of the kingdom of Cyprus, first in Italian and then in French. He, himself descended from Guy, attributes the cause of this hatred to the relationship by which our William was connected with the magnates of the kingdom, from whom Guy, being a foreigner, seemed to have wrested the kingdom’s succession.

The same Stephen recounts other things as though written by William which we read nowhere—he himself being otherwise little educated in letters or learned by reading. Our author, however, repeatedly extols the Count of Tripoli, Guy’s rival: Book XXII, chapters 9, 16, and 29; and Book XXIII, chapter 1. He also mentions Emperor Manuel of Constantinople with affection, in Book XV, chapter 23, and Book XXI, chapter 12; and he reveals the reason when he praises Manuel’s beneficence toward himself, Book XX, chapter 4, and Book XXII, chapter 4. For he himself truly says of Saladin’s virtues:

> By no other lure today are the hearts, even of the subjects of any other men, more commonly won over to princes; and nothing binds the minds of strangers more than generosity.

This both covers even conspicuous faults and reveals even hidden virtues.

This history is praised by Antoninus, Archbishop of Florence, who lived in 1450, title 17, chapter 9, §§3 and 12: “Lord William, Archbishop of Tyre, says in his Chronicle”; and elsewhere he employs William’s very words. So too, very often, though without naming him, does James of Vitry, who was close to his time. But in title 16, chapter 13, at the beginning, the William whom Antoninus cites as author is William of Malmesbury; to William’s words he then adds the very words of our author, which are found in Book I, chapter 17.

Paul Aemilius, a weighty authority, in Books IV and V of *On French Affairs*, repeatedly refers to our author by the title of Bishop of Tyre and quotes his words. But in Book VI, what he says was transmitted by Tyrius, an author of that period, concerning the death of Emperor Frederick I raises in me a scruple and some doubt. For Emperor Frederick died in 1190, indeed close to Tyrius’s lifetime; but we have previously established that Tyrius did not continue writing beyond 1180. Tyrius lay hidden in libraries in Aemilius’s time and had not yet been printed. It is therefore probable that Aemilius came upon a continuation of this history made by another—such as several French continuations which we possess—and read and possessed it all as Tyrius’s work; and

> [lacuna] In a long work, it is permissible that sleep should creep in.

Blondus cites William in explaining these matters, calling him “a French writer,” Book IV, Decade II; but in that book and the preceding one he repeatedly names another William, distinct from our author. Therefore I doubt it. In other respects Blondus, though a good and necessary historian, treated this subject rather negligently. This commonly happens to those who undertake to embrace everything and to write what are called general histories, cheating readers with a magnificent title. I advise young men to avoid them; let others read them with attention and judgment, lest, while the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit.

Moreover, our William composed a work whose loss students of history cannot but deplore most bitterly, especially because its subject is obscure and has been illuminated by the diligence of no writer, and of which

> To us scarcely the faint breath of fame makes its way:

*On the Deeds of the Western Princes*, Book I, chapter 3; or *On the Eastern Princes and Their Acts*, Book XIX, chapters 15 and 21: from the time of the deceiver Muhammad down to the year of the Lord 1184 (Preface). It embraced a sequence of 570 years (Preface and Book I, chapter 3), or 577 years, as Book XIX, chapter 21 has it. This variation confirms what I said above: this work of ours was not revised by the author. He completed it at the urging and request of the same King Amalric, who supplied Arabic copies (the same Preface and Book XIX, chapter 21)—an undertaking altogether praiseworthy, royal, and, through the concern thereby shown for God, to whom kings are nearest, tantamount to raising the dead and restoring them to life.

It is also admirable in a king that amid utter and profound barbarism, amid the shrill sound of trumpets, the thunder of arms, and daily dangers most immediately present, he cultivated letters and procured an abundance of books for scholars’ use—things neglected by others even in the deepest peace.

We have related above that he published a writing on the Lateran Council. Antonius Possevinus, in the *Apparatus*, writes, following Simler’s copyist, that several of his letters to Bernard of Antioch survive. Both are mistaken: those letters to Bernard of Antioch—which we have not seen—belong not to this William but to another William, likewise Archbishop of Tyre, William the Englishman. Bernard died when our William was scarcely born, namely about the year 1127; and shortly afterwards that other William also died, as is clear from our author, Book XIV, chapters 10 and 11.

But Philibert Poissenot, provost of Saint-Morand in Maxima Sequanorum, first enriched us with this history, as John Herold indicates in his *Continuation of the Sacred War*: printed by Johann Oporinus in 1549.

> **[Note: Col. 0207]** *History of the Sacred War*, comprising twenty-three books, concerning Jerusalem and the Land of Promise, and thus almost the whole of Syria, recovered by Western Christian princes; continued in a connected narrative down to the reign of Baldwin IV, over eighty-four years; a work filled with an astonishing variety of matters most worthy of knowledge, and destined to be as pleasant as it is useful to students of history. Written about four hundred years ago, it is now published for the first time through the efforts of the most learned Philibert Poissenot. The author is William, formerly Metropolitan Archbishop of Tyre and Chancellor of that same kingdom. Basel: Nicolaus Brylinger and Johann Oporinus, folio. **[Col. 0208]**

Later, Nicolaus Brylinger published it in 1564, corrupted despite promising a corrected text, through Heinrich Pantaleon.

> **[Note: Col. 0209]** *A Most Truthful History of the Sacred War, Pleasant and Most Useful to Read*, arranged in twenty-three books, in which Jerusalem and the land formerly promised and granted to God’s people, together with almost the whole of Syria, were recovered by Western Christian princes in the year 1099 of restored salvation, with great piety and courage. It is continued and described in a certain sequence of narrative for eighty-four years, down to the reign of Baldwin IV. Its former author was William, Metropolitan Archbishop of Tyre and most faithful Chancellor of the kingdom of Jerusalem. **[Col. 0210]** Now published much more corrected than before, together with a continuation of the entire history of the Sacred War, extending in six books down to our own times and setting forth in order the disasters and changing fortunes of the kingdom and city of Jerusalem; with a preface by Heinrich Pantaleon, a life of the author himself, and descriptions of many most noble cities.

Pantaleon himself does not deny that he faithfully corrected a very ancient copy; that in certain places he also substituted more familiar words for obsolete ones, and complete sentences for incomplete ones; and that he thus issued it again much improved—indeed! We, following the oldest copies as exactly as we could, have filled lacunae from them in many places; in Book III we restored the whole missing fifth chapter, and in other places entire periods; and we corrected words beyond counting. We have permitted ourselves nothing.

We used the Pithoean, Cambridge, and Paris Navarre manuscripts. Admitted through the kindness of the master and fellows, we saw and consulted the Cambridge manuscript in the library of the College of Saint Benedict; and before we approached it, Merlin Higden had supplied us with an account of it, Stephen Le Sieur having secured access for us. Albertus Miraeus pointed us to the Paris manuscript kept in the College of Navarre; subsequently Timothy Hoyus, son of Andrew, sent its readings differing from the received text, carefully and judiciously collected. All three are of entirely sound authority, written close to the author’s own time.

The subscription indicates that the Navarre manuscript was given by Anselm, Bishop of Meaux, whom Demochari calls incorrectly Aurellus and Ausellus. He lived about the year of the Lord 1200, that is, shortly after our archbishop. French translations helped establish the true reading and elucidate the history: the Palatine Heidelberg translation, which a rubricated inscription indicates belonged to Isabella, Queen of Norway—George Michael Lingelsheim obtained it for us long ago, and Janus Gruterus assisted in consulting it recently; and the Fauchet translation, supplied to us by Denis Godefroy, jurist.

We have appended to Tyrius a list of the Patriarchates of Antioch and Jerusalem, following the manuscripts; for in printed editions it is placed at Book XIV, chapter 12. We have given the names as they stood in the manuscripts, differing from the common forms and certainly very corrupt; Albertus Miraeus’s diligence will, we hope, provide them in corrected form.

[Col. 0209]

# HERE BEGINS THE HISTORY OF DEEDS DONE IN THE OVERSEAS PARTS, FROM THE TIME OF MUHAMMAD’S SUCCESSORS TO THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1184, PUBLISHED BY THE VENERABLE WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF TYRE.

## HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE.

[Col. 0209A] **WILLIAM**, by God’s forbearance unworthy minister of the holy Church of Tyre, to the venerable brethren in Christ into whose hands this present work may come: eternal salvation in the Lord.

No prudent person can doubt that it is dangerous and full of great hazard to describe the deeds of kings. For, leaving entirely aside the labor, unceasing study, and continual wakefulness which undertakings of this kind ordinarily demand, a double precipice is certainly threatening to historians, and they can scarcely avoid one or the other. In escaping Charybdis, they run upon Scylla, who, girded with dogs, knows no less well how to cause shipwrecks. For either, in pursuing the truth of events, they kindle against themselves the envy of many; or, to soften their indignation, they conceal the course of events—wherein there is certainly no lack of fault.

For deliberately passing over and intentionally concealing the truth of events is recognized as contrary to their duty. And falling away from duty is, beyond all doubt, a fault—if duty is truly defined as the appropriate action of each person according to the customs and institutions of his country. Yet to pursue the unstained course of events and not abandon the rule of truth is something that often provokes indignation, in accordance with the old proverb: “Compliance breeds friends; truth breeds hatred.” Thus they will either fall away from the duty of their profession by rendering improper compliance, or, in pursuing the truth of the matter, they must endure the hatred of which truth itself is the mother.

These things indeed commonly oppose one another and make themselves troublesome by mutual importunity. For, according to the judgment of our Cicero: “Truth is troublesome, since hatred arises from it, and hatred is the poison of friendship; but compliance is more troublesome, because, indulging faults, it permits a friend to rush headlong.” He seems to fulfill this in himself who, for the sake of compliance, suppresses truth contrary to the obligation of duty. The deed of those who, from a zeal for flattery, shamelessly wrap lies around the details of events is held so detestable that they ought not even to be counted among writers. For if it is wrong to conceal the truth of events and thereby fail in a writer’s duty, it will be judged a much graver sin to mingle the stain of falsehood with truths and to pass down to credulous posterity, as truth, that which departs from truth.

Moreover, another danger, no less—and perhaps more—formidable commonly confronts writers of histories and must be avoided with all one’s powers: namely, that the dignity of the deeds performed should suffer loss through dryness of expression and meagerness of style. For words ought to be suited to the things under discussion, and the writer’s language must not fall below the elegance of a nobler subject. Therefore great care must be taken lest the magnitude of the material collapse under the weakness of the treatment, and lest by fault of the narrative that which is by nature rich and solid emerge thin or feeble. For, as the outstanding orator says in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*:

> To commit one’s thoughts to writing when one can neither arrange nor illuminate them, nor draw the reader by some delight, belongs to a man who makes an intemperate misuse both of letters and of leisure.

We seem to have fallen into this dilemma and multiplicity of perils in the present case. For in the work we have in hand we have inserted many things concerning the character, life, and bodily condition of kings, whether commendable or subject to blame, as the sequence of events seemed to demand. Their descendants, reading these matters, may perhaps bear them impatiently and become inflamed beyond measure against the chronicler; they will deem him either malicious or deceitful—both of which, as the Lord lives, we flee as pestilential things to do.

For concerning the rest there can now be no doubt: we are presumptuously exerting ourselves upon a task unequal to our powers, and our language does not sufficiently rise to the dignity of the matter. Yet what we have done is not altogether without value. For beginners in painting, not yet admitted to the mysteries of the art, are accustomed first to lay down clay-colored pigments and sketch the first outlines, to which a more skillful hand is accustomed to add finished beauty with nobler colors. So we first laid foundations with the greatest labor, upon which a wiser architect, observing the rule of truth—which we have abandoned nowhere—may more artfully build splendid halls in a more excellent treatise.
