Amid so many snares of dangers and such doubtful risk, it would have been safer to remain quiet, to keep silence, and to dismiss the pens to leisure. But the most urgent love of country presses us—for a well-disposed man is bound to spend even his life for his country, if necessity requires it. It presses us, I say, and by the authority in which it excels commands us imperiously not to allow the deeds done there during the course of almost a hundred years, buried in silence, to suffer the harm of oblivion; rather, let them be diligently set down through the service of the pen and preserved in the memory of posterity.

We therefore obeyed and yielded our hands to him whose assistance we could not honorably refuse, paying little attention to what judgment posterity would make of us, or what our bloodless speech might deserve in so excellent a subject. We obeyed—would that it had been as effectively as willingly, as commendably as devoutly—drawn more by the sweetness of our native soil than by strength equal to the labor undertaken; relying not on the aid of talent but on the fervor of pious affection and the sincerity of charity.

There was added besides the command—by no means easily to be disregarded—and repeated urging of Lord King Amalric, of illustrious memory and renowned remembrance in the Lord, whose holy soul may enjoy rest. At his request, and with Arabic copies supplied by him, we composed another history extending from the time of the deceiver Muhammad to this year, 1184 from the Incarnation of the Lord, covering 570 years; in it we chiefly followed the venerable Seith, son of Patricius, Patriarch of Alexandria.

In this work, having no Greek or Arabic written guide, but equipped only with traditions, except for the few things which we ourselves beheld by eyewitness testimony, we arranged the sequence of the narrative. We took our beginning from the departure of the valiant and God-beloved princes who, called by the Lord, left the Western kingdoms and claimed by strong hand for themselves the Land of Promise and almost all Syria. From there down to the reign of Lord Baldwin IV—who, in the order of kings, counting Lord Duke Godfrey, who first obtained the kingdom, held the seventh place—we carried the history forward with great diligence for eighty-four years.

And so that the zealous reader might lack nothing for a fuller understanding of the condition of the eastern region, we briefly and concisely set forth beforehand how long and how great a yoke of servitude it had endured; what was, in the intervening period, the condition of the faithful living there among unbelievers; and what occasion caused the princes of the Western kingdoms, after so long a period of continual servitude, to be stirred up for their liberation and to assume so great a burden of pilgrimage.

If anyone considers the multiplicity of occupations by which we are greatly wearied—both those concerning the distinguished and God-protected metropolitan see of Tyre, over which we preside not through any election by merit but solely by the Lord’s forbearance; those concerning the affairs of the lord king, in whose sacred palace we hold the office of chancellor; and other necessities which arise in greater number than usual—he will be more inclined to indulgence should something occur in this present work that gives more just offense. For the mind, inwardly occupied with many things, ordinarily rises more weakly to examine each thing carefully; and, divided, it cannot spend on individual matters so much diligence as it customarily applies, when wholly present to itself and undivided, to its single and particular studies. Hence it more readily deserves pardon.

We have divided the entire volume into twenty-three books and have marked each with definite chapters, so that whatever the reader sees to be necessary among the elements of the history may more easily be found. Provided life accompanies us, we intend to add to what we have set forth whatever changing course of future events shall bring forth in our times, and to increase the number of books according to the quantity of material that arises.

We certainly hold—and this opinion does not deceive us—that the present work brings forward a witness to our incompetence. Though we might remain hidden by silence, we disclose our deficiency by writing, while we embrace the duty of charity. Yet we would rather be found without that knowledge which puffs up than lack that charity which builds up. For many who entered the wedding feast without the former were found worthy of the king’s table; but he who was found among the guests without the latter deserved to hear: “How did you come in here without a wedding garment?” (Matthew 22:12). May He who alone can do so, the compassionate and merciful Lord, avert this from us.

Yet, knowing that in much speaking sin is not usually absent (Proverbs 10:20), and that the tongue of wretched man, placed on a slippery surface, easily deserves punishment, we fraternally invite and exhort our reader in the Lord: whenever he finds a just ground for criticism, let him freely make use of it, with charity intervening, and through our correction acquire for himself the reward of eternal life. Mindful of us in his prayers, let him obtain from the Lord that whatever faults we have committed in this present work may not be imputed to us unto death, but that the Savior of the world, of His gratuitous goodness and innate mercy, may mercifully pardon them. We, wretched and useless servants in His house, quite rightly fear His tribunal, excessively dreading our accusing conscience.

# BOOK I BEGINS.

[Col. 0213]

## CHAPTER I. How, in the time of Emperor Heraclius, Omar son of Khattab, third after Muhammad and leader of the Arabs, occupied all Syria.

Ancient histories relate, and the traditions of the East likewise preserve, that when Emperor Heraclius governed the Roman Empire, the pestilential doctrine of Muhammad, Satan’s firstborn—who, falsely claiming to be a prophet sent by the Lord, had deceived the eastern regions and especially Arabia—had grown so strong, and the contagion so spread that it had seized all the provinces, that his successors were now compelling unwilling peoples to submit to their error not by exhortations or preaching but by swords and violence.

For while the aforesaid emperor, victorious on his return from Persia, whence he had brought back the Lord’s Cross in glory, was still remaining in Syria, he ordered, through the venerable Modestus, whom he had ordained bishop at Jerusalem, that the ruins of the churches which Chosroes, the most wicked Persian satrap, had thrown down in hostility should be restored to their former state, the necessary funds having been supplied. Omar, son of Khattab, third after the aforesaid deceiver, successor in error and in rule, had already violently occupied Gaza, the distinguished city of Palestine, with innumerable forces of Arabs.

Afterwards he entered the territory of Damascus with his legions and the immeasurable multitude which he led with him, and captured Damascus, while the aforesaid emperor was still in Cilicia awaiting the outcome. When word was brought to him that the Arabs, raised to such arrogance and trusting in their numbers, did not fear to invade Roman territory and seize its cities for themselves, he saw that he lacked the strength to meet so great a multitude and suppress its insolence. He therefore preferred to return safely to his own lands rather than commit himself, with forces unequal to the task, to the uncertain hazards of war.

Thus, when he departed—the man bound to furnish protection to afflicted citizens—the Arabs’ violence prevailed, so that suddenly and within a short period they occupied every region from Laodicea in Syria to Egypt. Who this Muhammad was; whence he came; how he broke forth into such madness as to dare falsely to call himself a prophet and sent by God; what his life and conduct were; how long and where he reigned; whom he finally had as successors; and how those who followed him in the same error filled almost the entire world with his pestilential doctrines—all this we have discussed carefully elsewhere, as is plainly understood from what follows.

## CHAPTER II. What occasion caused him so suddenly to occupy the East; and how, coming to Jerusalem, he ordered the Temple of the Lord to be rebuilt.

[Col. 0214D] It certainly assisted their design that a few years earlier the aforesaid Chosroes had violently entered that same Syria, destroyed cities, burned the suburbs, overthrown churches, and carried the people into captivity. Having broken into the Holy City, he slew thirty-six thousand citizens there by the sword in hostility and carried away with him to Persia the Lord’s Cross and Zacharias, bishop of that place, along with the remaining people both of the city and of the whole region.

For this most powerful king of the Persians took as wife a daughter of Emperor Maurice, named Maria—Maurice being so intimate a friend of blessed Pope Gregory that Gregory received one of his children from the sacred font. By virtue of that marriage Chosroes received the washing of regeneration and remained a most friendly ally of the Romans as long as the aforesaid emperor lived. But when Maurice was afterwards treacherously murdered by the Emperor Phocas, who succeeded him in the empire, Chosroes abhorred the treachery of those who had allowed so wicked a man, still stained with the blood of his lord’s murder, to reign over them. Treating them as guilty of a hidden complicity and conscious of that crime, he violently entered the borders of the empire and fiercely ravaged their lands, wishing, at his wife’s instigation, to avenge the death of his father-in-law. Having subdued the other regions subject to Roman authority, he finally seized Syria, as we have said, killing its people by the sword or leading them away with him to Persia.

The Arabs therefore entered and found the land empty of inhabitants, and thus found a greater opportunity to subject it to themselves. Having taken Jerusalem, the city beloved by God, which was involved in equal calamities, they spared the small number of people praying there, on condition that they serve them as tributaries under the strictest terms. They allowed them to retain their bishop, repair the church which, as stated above, had been destroyed, and freely preserve the Christian religion.

While the above-named ruler remained in the same city, he began diligently to ask the citizens—and especially the venerable Sophronius, bishop of that place, who had succeeded the late Modestus of pious memory—where the site was on which the Temple of the Lord had stood, which is recorded to have been destroyed, along with the city itself, by Titus the Roman commander. They pointed out and marked the place for him, displaying some remaining traces of the ancient structure. Having allotted funds sufficient for the expense, assembled craftsmen, and supplied materials as desired, both various kinds of marble and many different kinds of timber, he ordered a temple to be built.

When this had been happily completed a little later in accordance with his design, such as it is known to be at Jerusalem today, he enriched it with many and innumerable possessions, so that resources might always be available for maintaining its structure, renewing its old parts, and keeping its lamps supplied, through the agency of those serving in that temple. What its form is and what elegance there is in its construction, since this is known to almost everyone, is not the business of the present work to discuss.

Moreover, both inside and outside the building of this temple there survive very ancient memorial inscriptions in mosaic, in letters of the Arabic language, believed to date from that period. They clearly state the builder, the amount of expenditure, and when the work was begun and completed.

## CHAPTER III. How long Syria endured the yoke of servitude under alternating rulers; and how beneficial to the faithful living under the rule of unbelievers was the friendship concluded between the mighty Emperor Charles and Aaron, king of the Persians.

Thus the city beloved of God and most holy, being subjected—our sins demanding it—to the rule of unbelieving enemies, bore the yoke of unmerited servitude amid continual sufferings for four hundred and ninety years, though under alternating conditions. For amid frequent changes of affairs it changed masters still more frequently; and according to their disposition it received intervals now bright, now clouded, and, like a sick person, was burdened or drew breath according to the character of the present times. Yet it could not recover fully, since it was oppressed by the violent domination of unbelieving princes and a people without God.

Nevertheless, in the days of that admirable and praiseworthy man, namely Aaron, surnamed Ressith, who ruled over the whole East—whose exceptional generosity and courtesy, and whose singularly commendable character, the whole East even to this day admires and extols with imperishable praises—through the intervention of the most pious man of immortal memory, the lord Emperor Charles, peace was granted to the people of God and the prince’s favour mercifully bestowed, to their great consolation. For these two had established mutual goodwill between themselves, through frequent exchanges of envoys, supported by a wonderful bond of alliance; so that the Christians seemed to live rather under the Emperor Charles than under the said prince.

Of him the Life of the aforesaid glorious man reads as follows:

> When Aaron, king of the Persians, who held almost the whole East except India, had formed such harmonious friendship with him that he preferred Charles’s favour to the friendship of all kings and princes throughout the whole world, and judged that he alone ought to be honoured and magnificently treated by himself. Therefore, when Charles’s envoys, whom he had sent with gifts to the most sacred sepulchre of our Lord and Saviour and to the place of the Resurrection, came to Aaron and made known to him their lord’s wishes, he not only allowed what was requested to be done, but even granted that sacred and saving place should be assigned to Charles’s authority. Joining his own envoys to those returning, he sent Charles immense gifts among garments, spices, and the other riches of Eastern lands—having, a few years earlier, sent him, at his request, the elephant which he then possessed as his only one.

Nor did he frequently send the consolations of his benefactions and extend works of mercy merely to those faithful Christians living at Jerusalem under the power of unbelievers, but also to those dwelling in Egypt and Africa under the impiety of the Saracens. As is read in his Life:

> He was most devoted to the support of the poor and to gratuitous generosity, which the Greeks call *eleemosyna* [almsgiving]; so that he took care to do this not only in his own country and kingdom, but also beyond the seas, in Syria, Egypt, and Africa—at Jerusalem, Alexandria, and Carthage. Wherever he learned that Christians were living in poverty, he used to send money, sympathizing with their need. For this reason especially he sought the friendship of kings beyond the sea: that some relief and alleviation might come to Christians living under their dominion.

But if anyone wishes to know by what and how great changing vicissitudes of affairs, times, and dominions, during this intervening period, both the aforesaid city devoted to God and the entire adjoining region were scourged, let him reread that history which we have composed with much labour, entitled *On the Deeds of the Eastern Princes*, embracing in chronological sequence the events from the time of the aforesaid deceiver Muhammad down to this present day, the year 1182 from the Incarnation of the Lord, a period of five hundred and seventy years. [Col. 0217A]

## CHAPTER IV

How it came into the power of the Egyptian caliph; how, when the most wicked Heque reigned, the yoke of servitude became more intolerable for the faithful; and concerning the destruction of the church at Jerusalem.

At that same time there was a very bitter and persistent rivalry between the Egyptians and the Persians for supremacy. A greater fuel and incentive for their hatreds was supplied by their observance of conflicting traditions. Even to this day, in their reciprocal disputes, each people calls the other sacrilegious, refusing mutual communion, so that they even wish to differ in names. Those who follow the Eastern superstition are called in their language *Sunni*; but those who prefer the traditions of the Egyptians are called *Siha* [Shīʿa], and seem more nearly to agree with our faith. What difference of error exists between them is not a matter to explain at present.

At last the Egyptian kingdom grew powerful and occupied provinces and regions as far as Antioch. Along with the rest, the Holy City fell under its authority, under the common laws of conquest. Under this rule—as captives are sometimes granted more lenient times—its afflictions began to be somewhat relaxed, until, human wickedness having reached its full measure, Hequen was appointed caliph over that kingdom.

Surpassing by far alike the malice of his predecessors and that of his successors, he became a proverbial tale to posterity and to those reading of his madness. For he was so singular in every impiety and wickedness that his life, hateful to God and men, requires a special treatment. Among the many destructive acts he ordered, he commanded the church of the Lord’s Resurrection to be utterly demolished. It had been built, at the command of the lord Emperor Constantine Augustus, through the venerable Maximus, bishop of that place, and afterwards restored by the most reverend Modestus in the time of the lord Heraclius.

A certain official of his, namely the governor of Ramla, named Hyaroe, received the written order sent to him and, after razing the aforesaid church to the ground, carried the royal command into effect. At that time the venerable Orestes, the uncle of that most wicked king—the brother of his mother—presided over the same church.

He is said to have done this in order to furnish the unbelieving peoples with proof of his own perfidy. For the charge of Christianity was brought against him, because he had been born of a Christian mother. Wishing to cast this off as though it were a crime, he dared to perpetrate the aforesaid outrage, thinking that no reproach could remain which might be laid against his person or afford his rivals an occasion for attack once he had destroyed the fountainhead of the Christian religion and the cradle of the Catholic faith. [Col. 0218A]

## CHAPTER V

What was the condition of the faithful among unbelievers at that time.

From that day the condition of the faithful in that city began to be far worse: first because of the most just grief which they conceived at the fall of the church of the Holy Resurrection; then because their burden was doubled through multiplied compulsory exactions. For beyond the excessive taxes and imposts demanded from them contrary to custom and to the privileges granted by his predecessors, he also forbade the festivals which, until that day, under other rulers they had celebrated rather freely, both secretly and openly.

The more celebrated the day, the more strictly they were confined within the enclosure of their dwellings and did not dare to appear in public. Nor were they allowed even the safety of refuge at home; rather, by stones and filth thrown in upon them, and by violent breakings-in, they were harassed all the more as the feast-day was more solemn.

Moreover, for any trifling word, at any allegation made by an accuser, without investigation of the case, they were dragged away to crosses and punishments. Their goods were confiscated, their possessions taken away, and their sons and daughters seized from their parents’ houses; sometimes by whippings, sometimes by blandishments and promises, they were compelled either to apostatize or to be fastened to gibbets.

The patriarch who was then over them received the first insults and reproaches. Then, both publicly and more privately, he urged them to patience, promising everlasting crowns in exchange for the temporal evils they endured. Admonished by his words and example, despising transient injuries for Christ, they consoled one another in mutual charity.

It would take too long to recount in detail how many torments these servants of God suffered in their own bodies, that they might become heirs in the house of the Lord and emulate the laws of their fathers. Yet let us bring forward one example out of so many thousands, so that your love may perceive how, for frivolous causes, they were carried off to the final punishments.

A certain citizen among the unbelievers, pursuing our people with insatiable hatred, a treacherous and wicked man, devised something by which he might bring them to death. Secretly he threw the carcass of a dog into the court of the temple, whose cleanliness its guardians and the whole city took every care to preserve. At dawn, those who came to the temple for prayer found the foul and stinking corpse and, almost driven mad, filled the whole city with cries. Immediately the entire populace assembled, and everyone asserted as certain that the Christians had done it.

What more need be said? The destruction of them all was decreed, and it was judged that so accursed a crime must be expiated by death. But the faithful, trusting in their innocence, were prepared to undergo death for Christ. And while executioners stood ready with drawn swords to kill the people, a young man full of spirit came forward and said:

> It is dangerous, brothers, if this whole church thus perishes. It is more expedient that one should die for the people and that the whole nation should not perish. Grant me this: that you may keep an annual memory of me in blessing, and that the honour due to my family may be preserved forever. I, by the Lord’s aid, will avert this slaughter from you.

They gratefully accepted his words and readily granted what he had requested. They confirmed that, on Palm Sunday, his fellow tribesmen should bring into the city in solemn procession an olive branch, symbolic of our Lord Jesus Christ, in lasting remembrance of him.

When this had been done, the aforesaid young man presented himself to the leading men of the city, confessed himself guilty, and declared all the others innocent. On hearing this, the judges acquitted the others and delivered him to the sword. Thus, laying down his life for his brothers, he received his rest in piety, having the best reward laid up in the Lord. [Col. 0219B]

## CHAPTER VI

How, after the wicked father, his excellent son Daber succeeded to the government of the kingdom; and how, at the request of the lord Romanus, emperor of Constantinople, the church was rebuilt, John Carianites cooperating and the monk Constantine supplying what was necessary.

At last divine mercy came, took pity on the afflicted, and brought no small consolation to desperate circumstances. For when the aforesaid wicked prince was removed from human affairs, the shaking ceased in part, his son Daher obtaining the kingdom.

At the request of the lord Romanus, emperor of Constantinople, surnamed Heliopolitanus—whose friendship he had obtained by renewing the alliance which his father had violated—he granted the faithful permission to rebuild the aforesaid church. When this had been granted, the body of faithful Christians living at Jerusalem recognized that their own resources could not suffice for the restoration of so great a work. They therefore sent envoys to the aforesaid Romanus’s successor, the lord Constantine Monomachus, who then held the sceptre. Humble petitions were offered, setting forth how great was the sorrow and desolation in which the people had remained after the church’s destruction; and they earnestly begged that he would extend the generous hand of imperial munificence toward rebuilding the church.

Their embassy was managed by a certain John surnamed Carianites, a Constantinopolitan by birth, noble indeed according to the flesh but far nobler in character. Renouncing worldly rank and following Christ, he had assumed the religious habit and lived at Jerusalem as a poor man for Christ. Sent therefore to the same lord emperor, he laboured faithfully with due persistence and unflagging care, and obtained an order from the God-beloved Augustus that necessary and sufficient expenses for the work of the aforesaid building should be supplied from his own treasury.

Having obtained the petition sought by the faithful people, he returned joyfully to Jerusalem. There, reporting the success of his journey and the granting of their requests, he revived the whole clergy and people, as though recovering from a serious illness. The venerable patriarch Nicephorus then presided over that church.

Thus, permission having been secured and funds supplied from the imperial treasury, they built the church of the Holy Resurrection which now stands at Jerusalem, in the year 1048 from the Incarnation of the Lord, fifty-one years before the liberation of the city and thirty-seven years after its destruction. When it was built, they received consolation against imminent dangers and a thousand perils of death.

Yet frequent injuries and new kinds of compulsory exactions did not cease against the same faithful people: spitting, blows, chains, prisons, and finally every kind of punishment, by which the people of God were incessantly afflicted. Nor was this branding inflicted only on those in the same city, but also on those at Bethlehem and Tekoa, where faithful Christians alone dwelt.

For whenever a new governor arrived and a newly appointed official was sent by the caliph, fresh accusations were contrived against God’s people and varied pretexts invented for extortion. Whenever they wished violently to exact anything from the lord patriarch and the people jointly, if by any chance their demand was delayed, they immediately threatened to demolish the church. They suffered this almost every year, the governors pretending that they had before them a written order sent from the royal majesty: if the Christians dared to attach any difficulty or delay to payment of the taxes or imposts, their churches would immediately be razed to the ground.

So long as the kingdom of the Egyptians or Persians prevailed, the faithful enjoyed better conditions under their rule. But after the kingdom of the Turks again began to grow strong, and their advance extended beyond the Egyptian and Persian frontiers, the Holy City too fell into their power. During the thirty-eight years in which they held it occupied, the people of God began to be wearied by greater hardships, so that what they had endured under the Egyptian or Persian yoke seemed light to them. [Col. 0220C]

## CHAPTER VII

Concerning the rise and first origin of the Turkish people.

Since in the present work we must frequently say a great deal about the Turkish people—what they themselves have repeatedly done bravely and magnificently against our people, and what our people have done against them; and since they still persist with great insolence in attacking our people—it does not seem foreign to our purpose to insert into the present narrative something concerning the rise and first origin of this people and its progress to this height of greatness, which it is recorded to have maintained for many years.

The Turkish people, or Turcomans—for they had the same origin—were at first northern, wholly uncultivated, and without any fixed abode. They wandered and roamed everywhere, following the convenience of pastureland, having neither cities nor towns nor any settled habitation. When they wished to travel, those belonging to the same tribe moved together, having as a kind of prince one of their elder fellow-tribesmen. All disputes arising among those of the same tribe were referred to him; both sides of the disagreement obeyed his decision; and none might evade his judgment with impunity.

When migrating, they transported all their possessions with them: horses, flocks and herds, male and female slaves. For in these their entire wealth consisted. They nowhere practised agriculture and knew nothing of the contracts of buying and selling, but procured life’s necessities for themselves solely through exchange.

When, attracted by the pleasantness of grassy places, they wished to pitch tents somewhere and remain for a time without disturbance, they were accustomed to approach through certain of their number who seemed more prudent the rulers of the regions. Having made agreements on terms acceptable to the parties and promised a fixed tribute, they stayed according to the agreement, under the prince who ruled the region, in its pastures and woods.

It happened that a very great multitude of that people, travelling separately from the others, entered Persian territory and found a region very suitable to them. Having paid the king then reigning the tribute originally agreed between them, they remained there for several years. But their population increased beyond measure and there was no end to their multiplication, so that their presence became very suspect to the king and inhabitants, who had, as it were, a prescient apprehension.

Accordingly, after taking counsel, they decided to drive them violently from the bounds of the kingdom. But, changing their plan, they judged it more expedient to weary them with multiplied compulsory exactions and the customary burdens, irregularly adding new ones, until they should depart of their own accord without coercion.

After they had for many years endured the weight of injuries and the excessive demands of tax collectors, they resolved in common counsel that they would endure them no longer. When this became known to the king, a public proclamation was issued ordering them all to leave the kingdom within a fixed time.

Crossing the river Cobar, which bounded the kingdom on that side, they beheld more freely and carefully the innumerable multitude of their own people. Previously, because they had lived apart, they had known neither their number nor their power. They wondered how so great and countless a people could ever have endured the arrogance of any rulers and borne the harshness of compulsory services and taxes. They came without doubt to believe that they were inferior neither in numbers nor in strength to the Persian people or to any nation, and that they lacked nothing for forcibly gaining the neighbouring regions except that, unlike other peoples, they had no king of their own.

Desiring unanimously to make a king for themselves, they counted their entire multitude and found among them one hundred families more distinguished than the rest. They ordered each family to bring one arrow; and, corresponding to the number of families, they bound together a bundle of one hundred arrows. Covering it, they called a certain innocent little boy and directed him to put his hand beneath the covering under which the bundle of arrows lay concealed and draw out a single arrow, on the condition that a king should be chosen from the family whose arrow emerged by lot.

It happened by chance that the boy drew the arrow of the family of the Seljuks. Thus it was established among them all, as had been previously ordained, that a prince should be created from that tribe.

They then ordered that one hundred men be selected from the same tribe, surpassing their fellow-tribesmen in age, character, and valour, and that each bring a single arrow inscribed with the name of its owner. Again making a bundle from these and carefully covering it, they summoned again the same boy as before, or perhaps another of the same innocence. He too was induced to draw out one arrow, and he drew one inscribed with the name Selduc.

This man was exceedingly handsome, noble and illustrious in his tribe, advanced in age but sound in strength, and highly experienced in military affairs; his whole bodily bearing displayed the distinction of a great prince. Setting him over themselves by common decree, they raised him to the royal throne, paid him the reverence due to kings, and bound themselves, by an agreed covenant and oaths physically sworn, to carry out his commands.

He immediately made ample use of the authority conferred upon him. A public proclamation was issued ordering them, after recrossing the river and moving all their forces over it, forcibly to occupy the Persian territories from which they had previously departed and to claim the neighbouring kingdoms, so that thereafter they should not be compelled to wander through foreign countries and endure the intolerable arrogance of other nations.

And it came about that within a few years they subdued to themselves not only the Persian kingdom but all the kingdoms of the East, having overcome the power of the Arabs and other nations that possessed dominion. Thus a contemptible and lowly people suddenly rose to such a summit that it occupied the whole East. This happened scarcely thirty or forty years before our Western princes undertook the journey of pilgrimage with which this work is concerned.

And so that there might be at least a difference of name between those who had made a king for themselves and thereby acquired such immense glory, and those who still persisted in their primitive roughness without abandoning their former way of life: the former today are called Turks, while the latter retain their ancient name, Turcomans.

Having subdued the Eastern kingdoms, they also proceeded to invade the most powerful kingdom of the Egyptians. Descending into Syria, they forcibly subjected Jerusalem and certain other neighbouring cities to themselves, burdening the faithful inhabitants whom they found there with harsher than usual sufferings and wearing them down, as we have said, by a multiplicity of compulsory exactions. [Col. 0222D]

## CHAPTER VIII

How many and how great were the vices to which the world was subject at that time.

[Col. 0223A]

Not only in the East, then, were the faithful oppressed by the impious; in the West and almost throughout the whole world, especially among those called faithful, faith had failed and the fear of the Lord had been removed from their midst. Justice had vanished from human affairs; equity was overcome, and violence ruled among the peoples. Fraud, deceit, and circumvention broadly enveloped everything. Every virtue had yielded and given place as useless, as malice entered in.

Indeed, the world seemed to have declined toward evening, and the second coming of the Son of Man appeared nearer at hand. For the love of many had grown cold, and faith was not found upon the earth. With all ranks confused, everything was thrown into disorder, and the world seemed to wish to return to its former chaos.

The greater princes, who were bound to guide their subjects in peace, disregarded the bond of peace. Contending with one another over trivial causes, they gave regions over to fire, carried out plundering everywhere, and exposed the goods of the poor to be seized by their impious retainers. Amid so many snares, no one’s resources were safe. It was deemed sufficient cause for a person to be dragged off to prisons or chains and to endure undeserved tortures in his own body that he was believed to possess something.

No mercy was shown to the estates of churches and monasteries; privileges granted by pious princes brought no advantage to the possessions of the saints, nor did they retain their customary immunity and ancient dignity. Sanctuaries were broken open, and utensils dedicated to heavenly uses were violently seized. The sacrilegious hand made no distinction between sacred and profane; with the distinction removed, the garments of the altars, the vestments of priests, and the vessels of the Lord lay open to plunder.

Those who had fled to churches were dragged from the bosom of God’s house, from its innermost sanctuaries, from the courts of basilicas, to death and punishment. Wicked highwaymen, girded with swords, occupied the public roads and laid snares for travellers; they spared neither pilgrims nor religious men. Nor were cities or towns free from these outrages, in which assassins made every street and public square dangerous to the innocent. The more innocent a person was, the more snares he faced.

Every kind of fornication too was practised everywhere without shame and with impunity, as though lawful. Not even among relatives and kinsfolk were the bonds of marriage secure. Chastity, friendly to heaven and pleasing to God, was commanded to depart as though it were a worthless thing. Nor was there any place for frugality or sobriety where luxury, drunkenness, and all-night gambling had preoccupied the entrances and taken possession of the halls.

The clergy did not differ from the people by a nobler life, but, as it is written in the prophet: “Like people, like priest” (Hosea 4:9; Isaiah 24:2). For bishops had become negligent, “mute dogs, unable to bark” (Isaiah 56:10), respecters of persons, anointing their own heads with the oil of the sinner; after committing the flocks entrusted to them to the wolves that came, they deserted them in the fashion of hirelings.

Forgetful of that saying of the Lord, “You received freely; give freely” (Matthew 10:8), they did not avoid the Simoniac heresy, defiled by the filth and stain of Gehazi. What more? To state it briefly: “Every vice stood on the brink,” and “all flesh had corrupted its way” (Genesis 6:12). Nor could the Lord’s portents above in heaven and signs below on earth call back those inclined to evil: for there were plagues and famines, terrors from heaven, and great earthquakes in various places (Matthew 24:7), and the other things which the Lord carefully enumerates in the Gospel.

But, obstinate in dead works, like a sow in the mire (2 Peter 2:22), and like beasts rotting in their own dung, they abused the Lord’s merciful patience, as though the Lord said of them: “I struck them, and they did not grieve; I healed them, and they have not been healed” (Jeremiah 5:3). [Col. 0224B]

## CHAPTER IX

How, sins demanding it, the Persians occupied all the regions as far as the Hellespont.

The Lord, provoked to wrath by these and similar things, not only permitted the faithful in the land of promise to bear the yoke of the aforesaid servitude and to be wearied beyond their strength by multiplied hardships. He also raised up an adversary, a scourge of peoples and hammer of the whole earth, against others who still seemed to enjoy their liberty and were certain that all things would succeed according to their desires.

For while Romanus, surnamed Diogenes, ruled among the Greeks and administered the empire of Constantinople in every prosperity, there came forth from the remotest borders of the East Belpheth, a most powerful satrap of the Persians and Assyrians. He drew after him an infinite multitude of unbelieving nations, said to exceed counting and to cover the whole surface of the earth.

Advancing with chariots and horses, flocks and herds, and a most splendid display, he entered the bounds of the empire and subjected everything to himself, from the open country around the cities to walled cities and most strongly fortified towns. There was no one to resist; no one who, striving for safety, for children and wives, and, what was more serious, for liberty, placed himself in opposition.

Meanwhile word was brought to the emperor of the sword hanging over them, the greater force, and the hostile army devastating the Christian empire. Anxious for the commonwealth, he summoned campaigns of cavalry and gathered as many infantry forces as the impending necessity required and as the whole empire could furnish. In short, with his legions gathered and abundant cavalry, he advanced to meet the enemy. He encountered, with a strong hand but deprived of divine favour, one who already held the heart of the empire and had advanced into its interior.

The struggle on both sides was most fierce, with forces almost equal but with greater hatreds, such as grief at sacrilege and zeal for the faith commonly inspire. In short, the Christian army perished; the battle line of the faithful was laid low; the blood redeemed by Christ was shed by unbelievers. And, more wretched still, the emperor was captured.

Those portions of the army which escaped returned, announcing the disaster that had occurred. Those who heard were struck with consternation, gave themselves to bitter lamentation, and despaired of life and safety. Meanwhile the unbelieving man, though magnificent, exalted by so great a success and made more haughty by the victory granted him, ordered the emperor to be brought before him. To insult the Christian name and faith, seated upon the royal throne, he commanded that the emperor be placed beneath his feet; and, in the presence of the assembled princes, mounting and descending as though upon a footstool, he used the imperial body.

At length, in return for this great service, he restored him to liberty and allowed him to depart with a few of his nobles who had been captured with him. But when the princes of the empire heard this, they set another over themselves, judging him unworthy to exercise the sceptre and hold the Augustan dignity after enduring such indignities in his own body. Moreover, deprived of his eyes and shamefully treated, he was scarcely permitted to live a private life.

The aforesaid prince, freely fulfilling his purpose, occupied all the regions from Laodicea in Syria to the Hellespont, which flows past Constantinople: thirty days’ journey in length and ten or fifteen in breadth, with their cities and municipalities, all the people having been taken captive. “The Lord delivered them into the hand of the enemy, and those who hated them ruled over them” (Psalm 105:39).

Among these was captured—the last to be taken—the noble and outstanding chief city, ruler of many provinces, the first see of the Prince of the Apostles; and it became a tributary servant to unbelievers (2 Kings 8:2).

Thus he brought under his jurisdiction, within a short time, Coele-Syria, both Cilicias, Isauria, Pamphylia, Lycia, Pisidia, Lycaonia, Cappadocia, Galatia, both Pontuses, Bithynia, and part of Asia Minor: noble provinces, distinguished by every advantage and filled with populations of faithful Christians. He took peoples captive, demolished churches, and in fury persecuted Christian worship until it was extirpated.

Had he possessed a fleet of ships, he would beyond all doubt have subjected even the imperial city itself. For he had instilled such fear in the Greeks that they scarcely believed the walls of the royal city and the intervening sea to be sufficiently secure protection.

These things and the like added to the sum of the miseries of the faithful people living at Jerusalem and in its territory, and plunged them into the abyss of despair. For while the empire had formerly stood in prosperity, as stated above, frequent assistance from the imperial house had not been lacking in their necessities; the unimpaired and secure state of the empire, the fortunate success of neighbouring cities, and especially that of Antioch, had fostered in them some hope that freedom would one day come. But now, bearing anxiety for themselves and for others, and exhausted to utter collapse by adverse reports, they melted away and wasted within themselves, desiring death rather than life and certain of perpetual servitude. [Col. 0225D]

## CHAPTER X

How, at the same time, crowds of the faithful came to the Holy City, and under what condition they were treated both within and outside it; and how the city was again surrendered into the hands of the Turks.

[Col. 0226A]

Amid the snares of so perilous a time, a considerable multitude of both Greeks and Latins, prompted by devotion, came to the venerable places. But to those approaching the city through a thousand kinds of death and through enemy territory, entrance was denied unless they paid the gatekeepers at the Golden Gate the sum fixed as tribute. Yet those who had lost everything on the journey and had scarcely reached the desired places with their limbs intact had no means from which to pay the tribute. Thus it happened that a thousand or more such persons, gathered before the city [Col. 0226B] and awaiting permission to enter, wasted away and died of hunger and nakedness. Both the living and the dead among them were an intolerable burden upon the distressed citizens. For they strove both to feed the living and somehow sustain them with food, and to commit the dead to burial, although these tasks exceeded their resources. Those who were permitted to enter the city at the customary price caused the citizens still greater anxiety, since they feared that, while carelessly wandering about as though wishing to visit the holy places, they might be assaulted with spittle and blows, or finally be secretly suffocated and perish. Therefore, wishing to avert these evils, the citizens, moved by brotherly charity and concerned for the lives and safety of pilgrims hurrying to the holy places, followed in their tracks, fearing that some evil mischance might befall them.

[Col. 0226C] There was nevertheless in the city a monastery of the Amalfitans, which to this day is called Saint Mary of the Latins; and beside it a hospice, where there was a small oratory in honour of Saint John Eleemosynarius, Patriarch of Alexandria. It was under the care of the abbot of the aforesaid monastery, and to such wretched newcomers food was there supplied, insofar as possible, both from the monastery and from the gifts of the faithful. For scarcely one in a thousand arrived who could provide for himself. Having lost their travelling provisions and been worn out by the immensity of their hardships, they could scarcely escape alive.

Thus the citizens had no rest either abroad or at home; death threatened them every day [Col. 0226D], and a harsh and intolerable servitude, worse than any manner of death, lay upon them. Their miseries were further increased because the churches which they had restored and preserved with so many and such great labours were violently entered after their restoration. While the divine offices were being celebrated, the invaders, producing terror among the faithful with fury and uproar, sat upon the altars, making no distinction between places; they overturned chalices and vessels devoted to divine service, trampling them underfoot; they broke marblework and subjected the clergy to insults and beatings. Even the lord patriarch himself for the time being, as though he were a base and contemptible person, they threw headlong from his own seat to the ground by his beard and hair. Often too they seized him and, dragging him about like a worthless slave, thrust him into prison without cause, in order thereby to afflict the people who sympathized with their father.

[Col. 0227A] This, then, was the kind of most dreadful servitude which the people devoted to God endured with pious long-suffering for those four hundred and ninety years, as we have said. With groans, tearful sighs, and unceasing insistence in prayer, they cried to the Lord that, sparing them when corrected, he might mercifully turn away from them the scourges of his wrath. For they had descended into the depths of evils; and thus “deep calls to deep” (Ps. 41:8): the abyss of miseries deserved to be heard by the abyss of mercies, from him who is the God of all consolation. At last the Lord, mercifully looking upon them from the throne of his glory and wishing to set an end to such great labours, resolved by fatherly providence to procure for them consolation according to their desires. [Col. 0227B] The manner of this and the ordering of the divine dispensation, by which he willed to relieve the prolonged affliction of his people, we have undertaken to write in this present work for the perpetual remembrance of Christ’s faithful.

## CHAPTER XI. On the arrival of the man of God, Peter the Hermit, and his conference with Simeon, the venerable Patriarch of Jerusalem

At the same time, while the aforesaid city, pleasing to God, was subjected to such hardships as we have described, a certain priest named Peter, from the kingdom of the Franks, from the [Col. 0227C] bishopric of Amiens, who was called Hermit both in fact and in name, came to Jerusalem, drawn by the same ardour, among those who approached the venerable places for prayer and devotion.

This man was small in stature and, as regards his outward appearance, contemptible in person. Yet:

> In a small body a greater strength held sway.

For he was of lively intelligence; he had a keen and pleasing eye, and eloquence flowed from him naturally and without lack. Having entered the city, in accordance with the common law established for Christians wishing to enter, by paying the tribute, he was received as a guest by a certain faithful man, who himself belonged to the number of Christ’s confessors. From him, diligently inquiring—as he was a capable man—he was fully instructed not only about the present danger of the time, but also about the [Col. 0227D] persecution suffered by their forebears over many preceding years. Whatever was lacking to the full instruction supplied in words was later completed by the testimony of his own eyes. For, remaining in the city and visiting the churches, he himself learned more fully what he had previously grasped from the reports of others.

Hearing that the patriarch of that city was a religious man who feared God, Peter wished to confer with him about the present state of affairs and to learn more perfectly from him about certain other matters. He approached him, and, being admitted to his presence, they refreshed themselves with mutual conversation through a faithful interpreter. The patriarch’s name was Simeon. From Peter’s speech he gathered that Peter was a prudent man, experienced in many matters, and powerful [Col. 0228A] alike in action and speech; he therefore began more confidentially to set forth everything that was most grievously afflicting the people of God dwelling in the city.

As Peter, sympathizing with fraternal grief, could not restrain his tears and diligently asked whether any way of deliverance might be found against these impending evils, the righteous man replied:

“Peter, the just and merciful Lord deigns not to hear our tears, groans, and sighs, because our sins obstruct them. For our iniquity has not yet been fully cleansed, and therefore the scourges have not yet ceased. But if your people, true worshippers of God—whose strength, through the surpassing mercy of the Lord, remains still unimpaired, and whose empire flourishes far and wide in a manner terrible to our enemies—were willing [Col. 0228B], in brotherly compassion, to sympathize with our present sufferings and to procure a remedy for the calamities that oppress us, or at least to intercede for us with Christ, there would be hope for us that our affliction would soon end. For from the empire of the Greeks, though they are nearer to us both by kinship and by place, and though they possess greater abundance of riches, we have henceforth no hope of any consolation. They scarcely suffice for themselves; and all their power, as your brotherhood may have heard, has withered, so that in a few years they have lost more than half their empire.”

Peter replied: “Know, holy Father, that if the Roman Church and the princes of the West have a diligent and trustworthy informer concerning this calamity which you suffer, without any doubt [Col. 0228C] they will endeavour, both promptly in word and in deed, to procure remedies for your evils. Write therefore carefully both to the lord pope and to the Roman Church, and to the kings and princes of the West; and strengthen the letter with the authority of your seal. For my part, for the remedy of my soul, I do not refuse to take this labour upon myself. With the Lord as my helper, I am ready to meet all men, stir all men, earnestly declare the immensity of your sufferings, and diligently invite each one to hasten a remedy.”

The speech pleased both the lord patriarch and the faithful men who stood by; and, after abundant thanksgivings had been offered to the man of God for his compassion, they gave him the letter he had requested.

## CHAPTER XII. The revelation made to Peter himself in the church of the Holy Resurrection

[Col. 0228D] Truly great are you, O Lord our God, and there is no end to your mercies. Truly, good Jesus, there will be no confusion for those who hope in you. For whence came such confidence to this needy and poor pilgrim, deprived of the means necessary for life and far removed from his native land, that he should dare to undertake a task beyond his strength and trust in the fulfilment of his vow? Was it not because he had cast his care upon you, his protector? Was it not because, inflamed with the ardour of charity, sympathizing with his brethren and loving his neighbour as himself, he strove to fulfil the law? His strength was insufficient, yet charity urged him on. And although what his brethren imposed upon him appeared difficult and impossible [Col. 0229A], love of God and neighbour makes it light, because “love is strong as death” (Song 8:6). Faith therefore works through love (Gal. 5:6), and such faith merits before you; nor are merits idle before you. Hence you do not permit your servant to waver long, but reveal yourself to him and strengthen him by your revelation, lest he falter, giving him a revelation by which he may rise stronger to fulfil the work of charity.

For one day, when the aforesaid servant of God was more than usually anxious about his return home and the fulfilment of the embassy he had undertaken, he fled in full devotion to the fountain of mercies and entered the church of the Lord’s Resurrection. Having spent the night there and become exceedingly wearied by prayers and vigils, overcome by fatigue, he lay down on the pavement [Col. 0229B] to yield to the sleep that overtook him. When slumber, as usual, had fallen more deeply upon him, our Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him, as though standing present before him, and imposed upon him the same embassy, saying:

“Arise, Peter; hasten, and fearlessly carry out what has been enjoined upon you. For I shall be with you. It is time for the holy places to be cleansed and for my servants to be aided.”

Peter awoke, strengthened in the Lord by the vision he had seen. More ready to obey and following the divine admonition, he promptly broke off delay and prepared for his return. Having performed the customary prayers and received leave and a blessing from the lord patriarch, he went down to the sea. There he found a ship of merchants intending to cross to Apulia. Embarking upon it [Col. 0229C] and enjoying a favourable voyage, he arrived at Bari. From there he went to Rome and found Pope Urban in those parts. He presented to him the letters of the lord patriarch and of the faithful dwelling at Jerusalem; he explained their miseries and the abominations committed in the holy places by unclean nations; and he faithfully and prudently executed the embassy entrusted to him.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the dispute between Emperor Henry and Pope Gregory VII, and how Urban, Gregory’s successor, kindly received Peter on his return from Jerusalem

Some years earlier, Henry, king of the Germans and likewise emperor of the Romans, had been involved [Col. 0229D] in no small dispute and controversy with Pope Gregory VII, Urban’s predecessor, concerning the ring and staff of deceased bishops. For a custom had grown up, especially in the empire, that when the prelates of churches died, their ring and pastoral staff were sent to the lord emperor. He would then invest one of his household officers or chaplains and send him to the vacant church to discharge the pastoral office there, without awaiting the election of the clergy.

The lord pope, judging that this was done contrary to every principle of propriety and perceiving that ecclesiastical rights were trampled underfoot by this practice, admonished the emperor once, twice, and three times [Col. 0230A] to desist from such detestable presumption. When he could not recall him by these salutary warnings, he bound him with the bond of anathema. The emperor took this action most indignantly and began to persecute the Roman Church; against the lord pope he raised up Guibert, Archbishop of Ravenna, a highly learned and very wealthy man, as an adversary. Relying on the emperor’s forces and trusting in his abundance of wealth, Guibert violently expelled the aforesaid venerable man and seized the apostolic see. He was so delirious and so lacking in sound understanding that he believed himself to be what he was falsely called.

The unhappy world, already set in evil and pursuing the dangerous and unprofitable paths mentioned above, was made by the occasion of this schism to decline still further into worse things. It cast behind its back all reverence for God and humankind, following what was harmful and turning away from what was salutary. [Col. 0230B] Bishops were seized; and any prelates of churches who did not agree with the emperor in this perversity were imprisoned as though guilty of murder, their goods confiscated. Nor were injuries inflicted upon them only for a time: they were excluded permanently, and successors were intruded in their place.

Thus Pope Gregory, fleeing the emperor’s anger, withdrew to Apulia, where he was honourably received and kindly treated by Duke Robert Guiscard of Apulia, through whose aid he had escaped the hands of the aforesaid emperor. At last he came to Salerno, where he ended his earthly life and was buried. [Col. 0230C] After Pope Victor, who held the see after him for only two months, the aforesaid Urban succeeded him. Urban, avoiding the fury of Henry, successor of the aforesaid Henry and nonetheless obstinate in the same wickedness, hid himself in more fortified places among his faithful adherents, nowhere wholly safe.

While he was situated in this adversity, he kindly received the aforesaid venerable man Peter, returned from Jerusalem and carrying out the office of the embassy already mentioned. He promised in due time to be his faithful fellow-worker in the cause of which Peter was the bearer. Peter, meanwhile, traversed all Italy, inflamed with divine zeal; crossing the Alps, he visited every Western prince individually. He urged them anxiously, rebuked them, exhorted them; and, grace cooperating, persuaded some [Col. 0230D] by his admonitions not to delay in assisting their brethren set amid so great an affliction, nor to permit longer the profanation by the filth of unbelievers of the holy places which the Lord had deigned to honour with his own presence.

Nor did he think it sufficient to spread this message among princes unless he also encouraged the common people and those of lower rank to the same end with pious exhortations. Therefore, travelling through nations and kingdoms with pious concern, he faithfully fulfilled his embassy even among the poorest and most despised persons, preaching this same message. The Lord, regarding the merit of his faith, had bestowed upon him such grace that a people rarely gathered without fruit from his preaching. He was extremely necessary to the lord pope, who had resolved to follow him beyond the mountains without delay, in this same cause. [Col. 0231A] For Peter, fulfilling the office of a forerunner, had prepared his hearers’ minds for obedience, so that the pope, desiring to persuade them of the same thing, might more easily obtain his purpose and more swiftly incline the hearts of all to himself.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Pope Urban’s entry into the regions beyond the mountains, and the synod held at Clermont

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1095, in the fourth indiction, while Henry IV reigned as king of the Germans and likewise emperor of the Romans, in the forty-third year of his reign and the twelfth of his empire; and while the illustrious lord Philip, son of Henry, reigned as king of the Franks in France, the aforesaid Pope Urban, seeing that human wickedness [Col. 0231B] had exceeded all bounds and that all things were being carried downward as though naturally inclined toward evil, held a council at Piacenza, attended by persons from all Italy and very necessary for correcting human offences. Then, fleeing the anger of the aforesaid emperor, he departed Italy, crossed the Alps, and entered the kingdom of the Franks.

There he saw, as he had previously heard, that divine commands were everywhere trampled down, the teaching of the Gospel was despised, faith had perished, and charity and every virtue were in peril; while, conversely, the dominion of the adverse power and prince of darkness stretched exceedingly far and wide. Greatly distressed, as the duty of his office required, he considered how he might meet so many monstrous vices and prodigies of sins, which were sprouting so miserably and had enveloped the whole world. [Col. 0231C] He resolved to summon a general council, first at Vézelay, then at Le Puy. But finally, at Clermont, a city of Auvergne, by the accompanying grace of God, a sacred assembly of bishops and abbots gathered in the month of November from all the provinces beyond the Alps, with certain princes of those regions also present.

There, after ordinances had been established on the advice of prelates of the Church and men who feared God—ordinances which seemed directed to restoring the fallen condition of the Church—and after canons had been promulgated which might advance moral reformation and the correction of enormous offences, and which might restore the peace [Col. 0231D] that had perished from the earth, as Peter the Hermit urged, who bore the due concern imposed upon him in the matter entrusted to him, the pope at last turned to this exhortation, saying:

## CHAPTER XV. The lord pope’s exhortation to the people concerning the journey to Jerusalem

You know, most beloved brethren—and it is fitting that your charity should know—how the Restorer of the human race, taking flesh for the salvation of us all and dwelling as a man among men, honoured with his own presence the land of promise which he had long ago promised to the fathers; and by the works of his assumed dispensation, together with the frequent display of miracles, made it specially illustrious [the supplied text reads *in ignem*, literally “into fire,” evidently an uncertain or corrupt reading]. This the sequence of both the Old and the New Testament teaches in almost every syllable. [Col. 0232A]

It is certain that he loved it with a certain prerogative of affection, so that he deigned to call that part—indeed, that small portion—of the world his inheritance, though “the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Isa. 34:1). Hence through Isaiah he says: “Israel is my inheritance” (Isa. 19:25); and likewise: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5:7). Although from the beginning he dedicated the whole land to himself as a pre-eminent portion, he nevertheless adopted the Holy City still more particularly as his own, as the Prophet testifies: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the tents of Jacob” (Ps. 86:1). Glorious things are said of it: namely, that in it the Saviour, teaching, suffering, and rising again, wrought salvation in the midst of the earth. It was chosen from ages past to be conscious of such great events and the familiar chamber of mysteries. [Col. 0232B]

It was indeed chosen, as he who chose it testifies when he says: “From Jerusalem, the city which I have chosen, a Saviour shall come to you.” Although God, because the sins of its inhabitants demanded it, may often have permitted it in his just judgment to be handed over to the ungodly and to bear for a time the yoke of harsh servitude, one must not suppose that he rejected it as though repudiated by himself. For it is written: “God chastens every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6); whereas he stores up wrath for the one to whom he says: “My jealousy has departed from you; I will no longer be angry with you” (Ezek. 16:42). Therefore he loves it, and the ardour of his affection toward it has not cooled; for he says to it: “You shall be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord, and a royal diadem in the hand of your God; you shall no longer be called Desolate, but you shall be called My delight is in her, because the Lord has taken pleasure in you” (Isa. 62:3). [Col. 0232C]

Yet this cradle of our salvation, the homeland of the Lord, the mother of religion, is violently possessed by a people without God, the son of the Egyptian slave-woman; and, having enslaved the children of the free woman, he imposes upon them the harshest conditions—he who, in a reversal rightly deserved, ought to be serving them. But what is written? “Cast out the slave-woman and her son” (Gen. 21:10). For the impious race of Saracens, followers of worldly traditions, has for many years oppressed with violent tyranny the holy places where the Lord’s feet stood, having subdued the faithful and condemned them to servitude. Dogs have entered the holy places; the sanctuary has been profaned; the people who worship God has been humbled. The chosen race suffers unworthy forced services; the royal priesthood serves in mud and brick; the city of God, once the ruler of provinces, has been made tributary. [Col. 0232D]

Whose soul would not melt away? Whose heart would not waste away as these things return to mind? Who, dearest brethren, could hear them with dry eyes? The temple of the Lord—from which the zealous Lord drove out sellers and buyers lest his Father’s house become a den of thieves (Matt. 21)—has become a dwelling-place of demons. This same spectacle stirred the great priest Mattathias, forefather of the holy Maccabees, to a commendable zeal, as he himself testifies: “The temple of the Lord is as an insignificant man; its vessels of glory have been carried off captive” (1 Macc. 2:8). The city of the King of all kings, which delivered to others the rules of undefiled faith, is forced against its will to serve the superstitions of the nations. [Col. 0233A]

The church of the Holy Resurrection, the resting-place of the sleeping Lord, endures their rule and is defiled by the filth of those who will have no share in the resurrection, but will be assigned, as fuel for eternal fire, to everlasting flames. Venerable places devoted to divine mysteries—which received the Lord in the flesh as a guest, saw signs, and experienced benefits, and which in themselves exhibit full proofs of all these things to faith—have become sheepfolds and stables for beasts of burden. The praiseworthy people whom the Lord of hosts blessed groan in exhaustion beneath the burden of forced labour and shameful exactions. Their children, dear pledges of Mother Church, are seized in order to serve the uncleanness of the nations and are compelled either to deny the name of the living God or to blaspheme it with sacrilegious mouths. Or, detesting impious rule, they are cut down by swords like sheep, to be joined with the holy martyrs. [Col. 0233B]

For the sacrilegious there is no distinction of places, no regard for persons. Priests and Levites are killed in sanctuaries; virgins are compelled to fornicate or to perish under tortures; nor does maturer age avail married women. Woe to us, who have descended into this misery of so perilous a time—a misery which David, the faithful king chosen by the Lord, foresaw in spirit and mourned, saying: “O God, the nations have entered into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple” (Ps. 78:1). And again: “They have humbled your people and afflicted your inheritance” (Ps. 93:5). “Why, O Lord, are you angry to the end? Will your wrath burn like fire?” (Ps. 78:5; 88:47). “Where are your former mercies, O Lord?” (Ps. 88:50). Is it true what is said: “God will not forget to show mercy; he will not restrain his mercies in his anger”? (Ps. 76:10). “Remember what has befallen us; behold and see our reproach” (Lam. 5:1). “Woe to us! Why were we born to see the ruin of our people and the destruction of the holy city, and to sit there while the holy things are given into the hands of enemies?” (1 Macc. 2:7). [Col. 0233C]

Therefore, most beloved brethren, arm yourselves with zeal for God. “Gird each one his sword upon his thigh, O mighty one” (Ps. 44). Gird yourselves and be sons of the Mighty One. For it is better to die in battle than to see the evils of our nation and of the holy places. If anyone has zeal for the law of God, let him join himself to us. Let us assist our brethren. “Let us burst their bonds [Col. 0233D] and cast their yoke from us” (Ps. 2:3). Go forth, and the Lord will be with you. Turn against the enemies of the faith and of the Christian name the arms which you have unlawfully stained with mutual slaughter. Redeem by this service pleasing to God the thefts, arsons, robberies, murders, and all other deeds whose perpetrators will not possess the kingdom of God, so that these works of mercy and the united intercession of the saints may obtain for you a swift pardon for the offences by which you provoked the Lord to wrath.

Therefore we admonish and exhort you in the Lord, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of sins: sympathize with the affliction and labours of our brethren and co-heirs of the heavenly kingdom—for “we are all members of one another,” “heirs indeed of God and co-heirs with Christ” (Rom. 8:17)—who dwell at Jerusalem and in its surrounding territories. Check by due punishment the insolence of the unbelievers, who strive to subject kingdoms, principalities, and powers to themselves; and oppose them with all your strength, for they have resolved to erase the Christian name. Otherwise, it will soon come to pass that the Church of God, bearing the yoke of undeserved servitude, will suffer loss of faith, as the superstition of the heathen prevails. [Col. 0234A]

Some of you know the depth of their affliction, having seen with your own eyes the things of which we speak; and the letter brought to us directly through the hand of Peter, the venerable man now present, instructs us concerning their present circumstances. Trusting in the mercy of the Lord and in the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, we remit the penances imposed for their sins to those faithful Christians who take up arms against them and undertake the burden of this pilgrimage. [Col. 0234B] Those who die there in true penitence need not doubt that they will receive forgiveness of sins and the reward of eternal recompense.

Meanwhile we receive under the defence of the Church and the protection of the blessed Peter and Paul, as sons of true obedience, those who, with the ardour of faith, undertake this labour in order to conquer them. We decree that they shall remain secure from all disturbances, in property as well as in person. But if anyone rashly presumes in the meantime to molest them, let him be struck with excommunication by the bishop of the place; and let the sentence be observed by all until what has been taken away is restored and suitable satisfaction has been made for the damages inflicted. Bishops and priests who do not vigorously resist such persons shall be punished with suspension from office until they obtain the mercy of the apostolic see.” [Col. 0234C]

Having said these things, he ended his speech, directing the prelates of the churches who were present, when they returned home, to exhort and diligently invite their people to the same undertaking with all urgency and due concern. Having said this, he ended his speech; the synod was dissolved, and, bidding one another farewell, they returned home. Before all else, in accordance with the decrees of the synod, they worked faithfully to ensure that peace—which in the common tongue is called a truce—should be observed inviolate by all, so that no hindrance might be given to those wishing to go or to travel about for necessary provisions.

## CHAPTER XVI. Which princes offered themselves for the expedition, and concerning the sign of the cross which those about to depart marked upon their clothing as a sign of their vow and future pilgrimage

[Col. 0234D] Thus the Lord gave to his faithful servant, who preached with great power and with exalted glory in the word, an efficacious message and speech worthy of all acceptance in the eyes of all, according to the merits of his faith. And the matter seemed to have proceeded from the Lord, so that both great and small embraced his command with complete eagerness, although it appeared exceedingly arduous and difficult. Nor had the ardour of this desire, kindled by his speech, armed only those present for the expedition: the same report, spreading far and wide, kindled even absent persons, burning with an equal vow, toward the same purpose.

The bishops, as they had been commanded, showed themselves faithful fellow-workers, inviting their people to the same end and travelling through their dioceses [Col. 0235A], spreading the word of life among the people. Not one jot fell upon the ground without fruit, so that it could truly be said that the Lord’s word was being literally fulfilled: “I came not to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10:34). Husband was divided from wife, wife from husband; fathers from sons, sons from parents. No bond of affection could hinder this ardour. Thus many monks went forth from cloisters, and recluses from the cells in which they had voluntarily shut themselves up for the Lord.

Yet the Lord was not the motive in every case, nor did discretion, the mother of virtues, awaken every vow. Some joined others lest they abandon friends; some lest they be considered idle; some from mere frivolity; or in order to evade and deceive their creditors, to whom they were bound under the burden of many debts. [Col. 0235B] Thus all hastened for diverse causes. In the Western kingdoms there was no one who wished to remember age, sex, rank, or condition, or who, deterred by any persuasion, would abandon what had been begun. Rather, all alike gave their hands; all with one heart and voice professed the vow.

What is written in Tobit seemed fulfilled: “Jerusalem, city of God, nations shall come to you from afar, bringing gifts; they shall worship the Lord in you, and shall hold your land as holy, calling upon the great name in you” (Tob. 13:13). Among those present at the council, many joyfully received the word planted within them. Foremost among them was Lord Adhemar, Bishop of Le Puy [Col. 0235C], of blessed memory, a man of venerable life, who afterward exercised the office of legate of the apostolic see and in that expedition presided over the people of God with equal fidelity and prudence. So too did Lord William, Bishop of Orange, a man truly religious and fearing God.

Among the absent princes of both kingdoms, those inflamed by the same ardour likewise prepared themselves for the expedition, frequently exhorting one another and fixing a definite day upon which, after collecting necessities and summoning companions for the journey, they would set out. The undertaking of which we speak truly appears to have been arranged by divine providence, and the word truly to have gone forth from the Lord. [Col. 0235D] For the people ran together in companies wherever they heard that one of the princes had vowed the journey, so that they might join his company, invoke his name over themselves throughout the whole journey, and promise him service and loyalty. And because this saying was publicly repeated:

> “May scabies seize the hindmost; it would be shameful for me to be left behind,”

they laboured competitively to equip themselves with necessities, each eager to outstrip the others.

It was indeed divinely ordained; for this purifying fire was necessary, by which the excessive offences of the past might be washed away, and this useful occupation, by which future offences might be avoided. For among mortals there was no regard for God or reverence toward humankind. Moreover, it had been agreed by all, and enjoined by command of the lord pope, that all who bound themselves by vow to the aforesaid journey should imprint upon their garments [Col. 0236A] the saving sign of the life-giving cross, and should bear upon their shoulders the memorial of him whose place of suffering they intended to visit. In this they imitated him of whom it is said, as he hastened toward our redemption: “His dominion was made upon his shoulder” (Isa. 9:6). Of him also the saying of Isaiah may rightly be understood: “The Lord will raise a sign among the nations and gather the dispersed of Israel” (Isa. 11:12). And the Lord’s command seemed to be literally fulfilled: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16:24).

## CHAPTER XVII. The names of the princes from the kingdoms of the Franks and Germans who undertook the journey.

[Col. 0236B] From both kingdoms, as a pledge of the pilgrimage to come, the following had armed themselves with the sign of the cross: the illustrious lord Hugh the Great, brother of King Philip of the Franks; Lord Robert, count of Flanders; likewise Lord Robert, count of the Normans, son of King William, king of the English; Lord Stephen, count of Chartres and Blois, father of Count Theobald the Younger; Lord Adhemar, bishop of Le Puy; Lord William, bishop of Orange; Lord Raymond, count of Toulouse and Saint-Gilles; together with many other illustrious and noble men. There was also the vigorous and distinguished Lord Godfrey, duke of Lorraine, and with him his brothers, namely Lord Baldwin and Lord Eustace; likewise Baldwin, [Col. 0236C] surnamed of Bourcq, kinsman of those mentioned above, son of Lord Hugh, count of Rethel; also Count Warner of Grez; Baldwin, count of Hainaut; Isuard, count of Die; Rainbald, count of Orange; William, count of Forez; Count Stephen of Albemarle; Rotrou, count of Perche; and Count Hugh of Saint-Pol.

Among the greater men who nevertheless were not counts, illustrious and noble men also freely offered themselves for this service pleasing to God: Henry of Esch, Ralph of Baugency, Hebrard of Pusato, Gento of Bearn, William Amanen, Guast of Bederz, William of Montpellier, Gerard of Roussillon, Gerard of [Col. 0236D] Ceresy, Roger of Barneville, Guy of Possesse, and Guy of Garland, seneschal of the king of the Franks; Thomas of Fère, Galo of Chaumont; and likewise the aforesaid Peter the Hermit, with the immense multitude which he had gathered with much labour from both the kingdom and the empire. About the Alps there were Lord Bohemond, prince of Taranto, son of Lord Robert Guiscard, duke of Apulia; Lord Tancred also, his nephew through his sister; and many others whose number or names we do not possess.

All these, awaiting a suitable time, were ready, with immense forces of fighting men, to enter upon Christian warfare and devoutly dedicate themselves, for Christ’s name, to the hardships of so great a pilgrimage. When winter had passed and the first beginnings of the following spring appeared, [Col. 0237A] when the cold had been driven away and a welcome mildness restored to the earth, they prepared horses, brought out their weapons, arranged their baggage, and invited one another by mutual embassies, those who were to set out together.
