They carefully determined in advance when they ought to undertake the journey, where they should assemble, and by what route they might travel more safely and conveniently.

For so many and such countless multitudes could not find the necessities of life in any one region. It was therefore carefully arranged that each of the greater princes should lead his own forces separately and should not proceed by the same route. Nor did their armies assemble before reaching the city of Nicaea. For, as will be said below, the duke with his forces came through Hungary; the count of Toulouse and the bishop of Le Puy through Dalmatia; [Col. 0237B] while the remaining princes reached Constantinople by way of Apulia, though at different times.

Meanwhile they made ready what was thought likely to suffice for so great a journey, striving to measure their provisions by the length of the road, though ignorant that a man’s way is not in his own hand. For human frailty does not know what the morrow may bring. Nowhere in all the provinces of the West was there a single idle household. Each had domestic concerns suited to his station to occupy his attention: here a father of a household, there a son, elsewhere an entire household prepared itself for migration. Frequent letters were sent, by which those intending to depart together encouraged one another, sharply reproving delay and urging greater haste.

[Col. 0237C] As those appointed leaders of the companies summoned the others, the embraces of loved ones were parted with sobs and sighs; bidding one another a final farewell, they separated with kisses. A mother accompanied her son, a daughter her parent, a sister her brother, a wife her husband—bearing little children in their arms and nursing at their breasts—with tears and wailing as they departed; and, after saying farewell, they followed with fixed eyes those whom they could not follow on foot.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Walter Sans-Avoir, the first to set out, reaches Constantinople.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1096, on the eighth day of March, a certain Walter, surnamed Sans-Avoir, [Col. 0237D] a noble man and valiant in arms, was the first to undertake the journey with a vast multitude of foot soldiers—for he had very few knights with him. Passing through the kingdom of the Germans, he descended into Hungary.

The kingdom of Hungary is enclosed by intervening marshes and great rivers, and is inaccessible, so that entrance or exit is open to those wishing to enter or depart only at certain places, and those exceedingly narrow. At that time a most Christian man, King Coloman, ruled this kingdom. Learning of Walter’s arrival and being informed of his purpose, he commended the man’s pious intention, graciously received him, granted his expedition passage through Hungary, and did not withhold the privilege of public trade.

[Col. 0238A] Walter passed through the kingdom in complete peace and arrived safely at the river Maros, recognized as the eastern boundary of that kingdom. Having crossed it, he and his forces entered Bulgarian territory and came to the place called Belgrade. Unknown to him, however, some of his company had remained across that same river at a place named Maleville in order to buy provisions and gather necessities for the journey. The Hungarians seized them, stripped and beat them, took all their possessions, and sent them back to their companions.

Although the whole army compassionately shared their distress and deeply grieved with their companions over the misfortune that had occurred, they saw that it was exceedingly difficult and almost impossible to cross the river again and delay their intended journey because of new complications. They judged it better to overlook the injury for the time being than rashly to aim at what they could not attain. They placed hope in him in whose service they had undertaken to fight: the injury gratuitously inflicted upon Christ’s servants would not pass unpunished, but they would receive fitting recompense from him who promised his faithful ones, saying: “Not a hair of your head shall perish; by your endurance you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21:18).

Continuing their journey, they came, as stated above, to Belgrade. There Walter requested from the Bulgarian duke who governed the place permission to buy supplies; unable to obtain it, he encamped before the city. There, unable to restrain his army suffering from want of food, [Col. 0238C] he endured a very grievous loss among his people. For, since they could obtain absolutely no goods for sale from the Bulgarians at any price, his army went out to procure food for themselves by whatever means they could, lest they be forced to perish for lack of necessary sustenance. Finding Bulgarian flocks and herds, they began violently to drive them away and bring them into their camp.

When the Bulgarians heard this, they took up arms and marched out against those who were carrying off their animals, wishing to recover their plunder; they made war upon the raiders. Gaining the upper hand, they burned alive, after setting fire to a certain chapel in which they had taken refuge in hopes of salvation, one hundred and forty men who had incautiously become separated from the main body of the preceding company. The rest were put to flight.

Walter, knowing that he led a stiff-necked and undisciplined people, left behind those who, guided by their own spirit, had become incorrigible. With the remaining companies he prudently and cautiously passed through the forests of the Bulgarians, spreading far and wide, and arrived at Stralicia, the distinguished metropolitan city of inland Dacia. There he complained to the governor of that city of the loss and injury unjustly inflicted by the Bulgarians upon God’s people, and obtained full justice concerning everything that had been done. Moreover, the same duke, an eminent man who feared God, treated him most humanely and granted a general right of trade, so that necessities might be sold to him and his people in fair measure and at a just price. [Col. 0239A] Lest anything required by humane laws should seem lacking in his service, he also supplied guides for the road to conduct them as far as the imperial city.

Upon reaching it and being brought before the lord emperor, Walter obtained from his magnificence permission to keep his army in places near the city, with leave to buy and sell, until the arrival of Peter, at whose command he had undertaken the journey. The emperor granted this.

## CHAPTER XIX. Peter the Hermit follows; passing through Hungary, he experiences Hungarian treachery.

Not long afterward Peter, having passed through Lorraine, Franconia, Bavaria, and that [Col. 0239B] region called Austria with an innumerable army—nearly forty thousand men, gathered from every people, tribe, tongue, and nation—reached the borders of Hungary. He therefore sent an embassy to the lord king and obtained permission to enter, provided that he wished to have a peaceful entry and pass through the kingdom without disturbance or scandal. Having received this permission and accepted the stipulated condition, he entered the kingdom with all the forces following him.

Passing through it in complete peace, with an abundant supply of food provided by the inhabitants at a fair price and on good terms, he reached the above-mentioned Maleville. There he learned that the inhabitants of that place had inflicted great injury upon the companions who had preceded them in following Walter, and had exercised no small cruelty toward them. Seeing also their spoils and weapons hanging on the city wall as trophies, they were stirred by righteous anger, immediately seized their arms, and forcibly broke into the town. Nearly all the inhabitants were either killed by the sword or drowned in the nearby river.

In that tumult, it is said that, as their deserts demanded, about four thousand Hungarians fell that day; while one hundred men of Peter’s expedition are said to have perished. Having thus seized the town by force, they remained there for five continuous days because of the abundance of provisions which they found in it.

[Col. 0239D] But the Bulgarian duke named Nicetas, who had earlier forbidden Walter and his forces a market in goods for sale, learned that the followers would retaliate against him for the wrong which he too had committed against those who had gone before. Distrusting the fortifications of the place which he governed, he abandoned Belgrade and fled. The inhabitants likewise each deserted the town with his household and withdrew far into the shaded recesses of forests and groves with their flocks and herds.

While Peter was still staying in the captured stronghold, he learned from certain reports that the king of Hungary, bitterly grieving over the slaughter of his people which he had heard of, was summoning military forces from throughout his kingdom and was vigorously arming himself to avenge his own. Peter gathered every boat he could find on either bank of the river and commanded that his forces be transported across with all speed. He took with him flocks and herds and very rich spoils, which he had brought from the forcibly stormed place in overflowing abundance.

[Col. 0240A] When these had been conveyed to the farther bank, they encamped before Belgrade, which they nevertheless found deserted. From there, passing with wagons and carts, flocks and herds, and their entire company through the dense woods spread widely about for a journey of eight days, he appeared with his forces before the city of Niš, most strongly fortified with towers and a solid wall and full of brave men. Having crossed, by a stone bridge, the river which flows past that city, he pitched camp there.

As his army was already suffering from want of provisions, he sent an embassy to the governor of the city and amicably requested that goods for sale—especially those necessary for life—be made available to the pilgrim people devoted to divine service on good terms and at a just price. [Col. 0240B] The governor replied that this could not be done unless the army first bound itself by giving hostages that no injury or violence whatsoever should be inflicted upon the inhabitants as they supplied the market. When this condition pleased both parties, hostages were given and the citizens came out carrying goods for sale.

## CHAPTER XX. At the Bulgarian city of Niš, a dangerous disturbance arises between the pilgrims and the Bulgarians.

Thus a more abundant supply of food was made available to the whole expedition, and buying and selling were conducted between the two peoples in mutual goodwill. That night passed in complete peace and mutual goodwill. In the early morning, after the hostages had been restored, they prepared for the journey. While they were setting out and the greater part—indeed, nearly the entire army—had gone ahead, certain men of disturbed mind, worthy of divine punishment, remembered a quite trifling quarrel which they had had the preceding night with a Bulgarian over buying and selling. Somewhat separated from the companies ahead, they set fire to seven mills which turned in the river beside the aforementioned bridge and suddenly reduced them to ashes.

[Col. 0240D] These sons of Belial were Germans, about one hundred in number. Nor was their fury satisfied with the deed they had committed: with equal wickedness they also set fire to certain dwellings outside the circuit of the wall. When their crime was complete, they made haste to join the unsuspecting crowds, as though they had no consciousness of the wrongdoing.

But the duke, who had treated them very graciously the previous night, saw that he was being repaid in a manner far from worthy of their deserts—namely, compelled to receive punishment for a benefit conferred. With judgment not sufficiently fair, he visited the deed of a few upon all, regarding everyone as robbers and incendiaries. He summoned the citizens, urged them to take up arms, and himself went ahead with a great multitude, encouraging his men by word and example to pursue the aforesaid expedition and persuading them to exact vengeance as from sacrilegious persons.

[Col. 0241A] They therefore marched out unitedly, pursued those ahead, and violently attacked the rear of the advancing army, pressing them fiercely with swords. Finding apart from the crowded masses those wrongdoers who had not yet joined the camp, they put them to death in most just indignation. But, whether by chance or deliberately mixing the just with the wicked, they stabbed many innocent people under the same penalty. They seized the carts and wagons carrying both food and all their household goods; they also seized old men and sick persons, married women with boys and girls, who could not keep up with the others at an equal pace, and led them away bound in chains. Having completed the slaughter, sated with the blood of the slain and laden with spoils, they returned home.

## CHAPTER XXI. Peter recalls his fleeing army and again seeks a peaceful settlement with the Bulgarians; but the latter error was worse than the former, and his forces are scattered.

Meanwhile the venerable man Peter, all the companies marching ahead, and all the principal men of the expedition were wholly unaware of this disaster that had befallen their people and continued the journey they had begun. Then a man riding at full speed on a very swift horse came in hasty flight and announced the calamity, setting forth in order the slaughter and captivity of their men.

[Col. 0241C] Once this was known, by the common counsel of the prudent men they retraced the road by which they had come all that day. Recalling the forces, they looked upon the signs of the slaughter and the bodies of their slain brethren, not without tears and groaning, and halted before the city in which they had pitched camp on the previous night.

Peter and the more discerning men with him had in this action a single eye and pure intention. They had returned so that, once the cause of the evil was known and the source of scandal cut off, a fuller peace might be restored between the two peoples and they might return more safely to their purpose with consciences cleansed. They therefore sent prudent and honourable men to the governor and leading men of the city, and carefully investigated [Col. 0241D] what cause had intervened to bring about so great an uproar and such a shedding of innocent blood so suddenly.

Once the cause was known, those sent understood that the Bulgarians had run to arms in reasonably just indignation, but that the time was not at all suitable for demanding vengeance for the injuries inflicted. They therefore exerted every suitable means and all diligence to ensure that peace should be restored and that they should recover intact their booty, baggage, companions, and everything they had lost.

While they persisted in this, with the agreements almost reduced to a settlement satisfactory to both sides, a disturbance arose in the camp through the rash passion and reckless audacity of certain men, acting without counsel. Some undisciplined men wished violently to avenge the injury they had suffered. Peter, desiring to restrain their madness and avert a slaughter, sent certain prudent men of great authority to try to call them back from the attack and fury with which they were pressing the citizens as enemies.

[Col. 0242A] When he achieved nothing and they would not obey his admonitions, however salutary, he issued a public proclamation to the army, strictly commanding, under the obligation of promised obedience, that no one should give assistance or aid to those who in their rashness had dared violate the peace that had been restored. The army obeyed this command and sat as though acting as an arbiter, awaiting the end of the disturbance that had begun and the outcome of the affair.

Those who had been sent to the governor for the sake of peace saw that the turmoil stirred among the people could not be calmed but was increasing more and more, and that they could not accomplish their purpose. They returned to camp with the business unfinished and laboured with Peter, the man of God, to restrain the crowd. But this too could not be brought about. There were about a thousand men who had rushed into this rashness.

[Col. 0242B] An equal number of townsmen came out to meet them, and a great battle was joined by both sides before the city. Those in the city saw that something like a schism had arisen among the outside people. Hoping that, because these men had provoked the quarrel against Peter’s will and opposition, the remaining part of the army would in no way provide them support, they opened the gates and all came out together. They killed nearly five hundred of our men on the bridge; almost all the rest, ignorant of the ford as strangers to the place, were drowned in the river.

When the army saw this and could not endure such injury to its own men, all rushed to arms. As the forces clashed, there was an immeasurable slaughter, so that the latter error was worse than the former. The common people and undisciplined mob, unable to withstand the Bulgarian assault, began to flee; by their example and flight they compelled others, who were fighting manfully, to turn their backs.

[Col. 0242C] Thus the entire army fled; with the ranks thrown into confusion, there was no one to resist. In this tumult the oft-mentioned Peter lost all the money which he had collected from the donations of faithful princes in order to supply necessities on the road to the poor and needy. The wagon in which his entire wealth was carried was captured. The Bulgarians pressed on more vigorously, killed about ten thousand of them by the sword, seized all the wagons and baggage, and captured a great multitude of women and children.

Those who escaped followed woodland hiding places and byways; only on the third day, summoned back by sounding trumpets and blaring horns, did they gather around Peter and those who had escaped with him and withdrawn to a somewhat elevated hill.

## CHAPTER XXII. Peter, having gathered the remnant of his routed forces, reaches Constantinople; after crossing the Bosporus, he encamps in Bithynia.

At last, on the fourth day, those who had been scattered gathered together again; coming out from the hiding places in which they had lain concealed for three days, they formed a body of nearly thirty thousand and again prepared for the journey. Although they had imprudently lost nearly two thousand wagons and carts, they considered it disgraceful to abandon their undertaking and continued on their way, though with much difficulty.

[Col. 0243A] As they travelled, suffering greatly from lack of food, a messenger of the lord emperor came to their camp. Producing an imperial command, he publicly addressed Peter and the other leaders of that army:

“Grave reports and a most discordant account, noble and illustrious men, have reached the imperial hearing concerning you: it is reported that in his empire you inflict outrageous violence upon the inhabitants of the land and his subjects, stirring up quarrels and disturbances. Therefore, by his authority, if you ever seek to find favour in the sight of his majesty, we command you not to presume to remain in any of his cities for more than three days, but to direct your expedition toward Constantinople as swiftly as possible, continuing your journey at a suitable though restrained pace. We shall go before your army and arrange for necessities of life to be supplied to you at a just price.”

On hearing this, the spirit of men already wasting away through lack of food revived. Understanding the lord emperor’s clemency toward them, they were raised to greater hope. After they had sufficiently pleaded before the bearer of the imperial letters, for the occasion, their innocence and the injury gratuitously inflicted upon them without desert by the Bulgarians, which they had borne patiently, [Col. 0243C] they followed the aforesaid guide, abstained from every outrage, hastened their journey, and reached Constantinople.

There they found the aforesaid Walter, who awaited their arrival with his forces. Their armies joined, and they pitched camp in the place assigned them. Peter, summoned by the lord emperor, entered the city. Standing before him, he was questioned concerning his purpose and the reason for so great a labour. Being a high-minded and eloquent man, he explained it fully and informed him that the great, God-worthy princes of the western lands would shortly follow. He did so with such firmness of mind and elegance of speech that the princes of the palace admired his spirit and wisdom, while the emperor himself commended him more warmly.

[Col. 0243D] The emperor therefore treated him graciously, heaped richer gifts upon him, and ordered him to return to his people. After the army had refreshed itself for several days with provisions and rest, ships were prepared by imperial command. Crossing the Hellespont, they landed in Bithynia, the first province of the Asian diocese bounded by that sea, and finally reached and encamped at a place on the same sea named Civitot.

## CHAPTER XXIII. In his absence, his army drives off booty from the Nicaean district and storms a town near Nicaea.

This place lay on the frontier of the enemy. There the army remained for almost two continuous months in great abundance of provisions; scarcely a day passed without a supply of goods for sale and the refreshment required at the time. Dissolved alike by abundance and idleness, that wretched stiff-necked people, as the provocations of insolence issued from their fatness (Psalm 72:7), began to form companies separately against the orders of their leaders and to scour the country for ten miles or more, driving off flocks and herds.

[Col. 0244A] They had nevertheless repeatedly received admonitory letters from the lord emperor, directing them not, before the arrival of the greater princes said to be following, to wander too far abroad or provoke the enemy against themselves. Rather, they were to remain cautiously in the place assigned. Peter, deeply concerned for the people committed to him, had gone to the imperial city in order, if possible, to reduce the price of goods for sale and obtain more favourable terms of trade.

The stubborn and refractory people, taking the opportunity of his absence, began to behave still more madly. Their confederates, forming a separate party of about seven thousand foot soldiers and three hundred knights, disregarded the prohibitions of others with deaf ears and marched in ordered formations toward Nicaea. From places adjoining that city they gathered flocks and herds in very great numbers and returned safely to camp.

[Col. 0244B] The Germans and men of that language saw that the Latins had prospered in the venture for which they had gone out. Moved by love of plunder, they too decided to attempt something similar, so that they might gain a name and increase their domestic resources. At length about three thousand men of the same nation, joined with two hundred knights, set out for Nicaea. In that district there was a town at the foot of a mountain, scarcely four miles from Nicaea. Arriving there, they attacked it fiercely and with all their strength from every side. Although the townspeople resisted most vigorously, they stormed and seized it by force.

Having killed its inhabitants and taken all their possessions, they were drawn alike by the pleasantness and abundance of the place. They fortified the castle and proposed to remain there until the arrival of the princes.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Süleyman, prince of the Turks, retakes the aforesaid town and kills by the sword everyone whom he finds there.

[Col. 0244D]

Süleyman, ruler and governor of that region, had heard long beforehand of the coming of the Christian princes. In the meantime, gathering innumerable forces of brave men from throughout the East by entreaty, payment, and every means at his disposal, he had returned to those parts in order to provide the citizens and country with the desired protection against hostile attacks.

When he heard that the aforesaid band of Germans had stormed his town and presumed to hold it after storming it, he hastened there with all speed. Besieging the castle, he took it by force [Col. 0245A] and put to the sword everyone whom he found within.

Meanwhile a report resounded in the camp, and the widely circulating rumour announced that the German companies which had recently gone out from camp had entirely fallen into Süleyman’s hands. Greatly distressed in mind, they expressed their grief with groans and tears which they could not restrain because of their anguish of spirit. At last, when the truth had been more fully learned, a disturbance arose among the common people in camp. The crowd cried out and earnestly demanded that they should not overlook the monstrous injury inflicted upon their brethren, but that all alike, horsemen and foot soldiers, should take up arms and march out to avenge the blood of their slain brothers.

The leaders of the army and those with fuller experience in such matters wished to follow the lord emperor’s counsel and to restrain this proposal and moderate the indiscriminate zeal of the raging people. But the untamed populace rose against them and, relying on the support of a certain Godfrey surnamed Burel, the leader of the faction, began to heap insults upon its superiors. It ascribed to cowardice, not prudence, their failure to pursue with an avenging sword the killers of their brethren.

## CHAPTER XXV. The entire army is stirred against Süleyman over the slaughter of its brethren, and, fighting him, is destroyed.

[Col. 0245C] At last the opinion of those worse disposed prevailed. All took up arms, leaving behind the weak, women and little children, and those without weapons. They assembled twenty-five thousand armed foot soldiers and five hundred knights very well armoured. Having arranged their companies and formed battle lines, they marched toward the mountainous country on the Nicaean side through the aforesaid forest.

They had barely advanced three miles when Süleyman, entering the same forest with an innumerable multitude of his own men, was hurrying to make a sudden attack upon our camp in the place named above. Hearing unusual cries in that forest, he immediately learned that our forces, having left camp, were coming to meet him. Leaving the mountains and forest, he moved into the open plain.

[Col. 0245D] Our men likewise arrived there, wholly unaware of the enemy’s approach. When they discovered the hostile army stationed nearby, they encouraged one another with shouts and rushed against the enemy, pressing them at close quarters with swords and demanding from the hands of their foes the blood of their slaughtered brethren. The enemy, with every desire and ardent purpose, received with swords our men rushing upon them. Knowing that the matter concerned their lives, they resisted bravely, inflamed by righteous indignation and confident in their numbers.

At length, as the forces fought vigorously and quite manfully on both sides, our men were overwhelmed by their multitude. Unable to bear the weight of battle longer, their formations broke up and they turned to flight. The Turks nevertheless pressed after them with swords, pursuing them all the way to their camp and inflicting an immeasurable slaughter.

[Col. 0246A] In that engagement there fell among the noble men following Peter’s camp Walter Sans-Avoir, Rainald of Breis, Fulcher of Orléans, and countless others. For of the twenty-five thousand foot soldiers who had left camp and the five hundred knights, scarcely one survived who escaped either death or captivity.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Victorious, Süleyman plunders our camp; he carries off or kills the remnant of the people, besieges the fortress of Civitot, but withdraws upon hearing the emperor’s embassy.

Having gained this victory and been made more arrogant by his present success, Süleyman violently burst into the camp. Finding no one now able to resist, he destroyed with the sword the remnant that remained. He killed with the blade the old, the sick, monks and the entire clergy, and elderly married women, sparing only boys and girls still under age, whose age and appearance caused him to spare them for enslavement.

[Col. 0246B] Near our camp, on the seashore, stood an old, half-ruined fortress, uninhabited, so that it had neither bars nor doors. Compelled by necessity and believing that they might find safety there, about three thousand pilgrims withdrew into it. They blocked the approaches by placing shields in the way and rolling up great millstones, and armed themselves for defence as the urgency of necessity required.

While those under siege, fighting with all their strength for life and liberty, drove back the Turks pressing them fiercely, in hope of attaining safety, a messenger hastened to Peter and reported the slaughter of his people. He informed him that the survivors of the now destroyed population were closely hemmed in within a certain half-ruined fort, suffering from want of arms and food.

[Col. 0246C] Peter went to the lord emperor and, humbly pouring forth prayers, obtained an order that troops be sent there with all speed to deliver the remnants of the people from the imminent dangers. This was done. For when the Turks heard the lord emperor’s command, they immediately ceased attacking the fort. Taking with them those whom they had put in chains, and carrying off splendid spoil—tents and pavilions, horses, mules, and every kind of property belonging to our people—they returned to Nicaea.

Thus that stiff-necked and ungovernable people, because they did not know how to obey better counsel, fell headlong by its own force into utter ruin; and, because it did not know how to bear the yoke of wholesome discipline, it reaped the fruitless fruits of its own ways and was delivered over to the swords of its enemies.

## CHAPTER XXVII. A certain German priest, Gottschalk, again leads an army and reaches Hungary; he does not shrink from committing shameful deeds against the Hungarians.

After Peter’s passage into Bithynia, not long afterward, a certain priest named Godescalc, a German by nation, following in Peter’s footsteps and fired with the desire for the same pilgrimage, endowed with the gift of exhortation, had encouraged many men from throughout the kingdom of the Germans to undertake the same work. Having gathered companions for the journey, numbering about fifteen thousand, he entered the borders of Hungary, being admitted without difficulty. There, although provisions were offered to his army by the Hungarians, at the king’s command, on good terms, they abused the abundance of food and gave themselves up to drunkenness, turning to inflict monstrous injuries upon the inhabitants. Thus they practised plunder, violently seized goods publicly brought for sale in the markets, and slaughtered the people, disregarding the laws of hospitality.

When this became known to the lord king, he was inflamed with anger and ordered the whole kingdom to be summoned; he commanded the people, and also the leading men of the land, to arm themselves in vengeance for such injuries. For in very many places they had committed grave, exceedingly shameful, and unreportable acts, which the king could not overlook except at the cost of the hatred of his subjects and the reputation of cowardice. Therefore, when the army of the whole kingdom had been assembled, they rushed unanimously and headlong upon them as upon enemies deserving the utmost punishment, intending to inflict death for such offences.

At last, at a place called Bellegrava, situated at the very centre of their kingdom, they found the confused multitude of those senseless men. Having learned beforehand of the king’s approach, and knowing of his indignation, they feared in accordance with their guilty consciences; they had seized their weapons, prepared, as it were, to repel force by force and ward injuries away from themselves. When the Hungarians saw them taking up arms and resolved upon resistance, they realized that they could not attack them without great slaughter among their own men—for they were strong men, accustomed to the use of arms, and not likely readily to yield up their lives for nothing. Therefore, according to their custom, they attempted by stratagem what they could not accomplish by force. They sent an embassy to the aforesaid Godescalc and the chief officers of the army, and deceitfully addressed them in peaceful words, saying:

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Letter of the King of the Hungarians to the aforesaid Godescalc and his army; and their miserable destruction.

[Col. 0247D] A grave complaint concerning your army has reached the lord king: namely, that you have inflicted exceedingly grievous and outrageous injuries upon the people subject to him, thus repaying, by an unjust rule, your hosts, who treated you kindly. Nevertheless, the wisdom of the lord king knows fully that not all of you are guilty of these deeds; rather, he is certain that among you are prudent men who fear God, to whom the outrageous conduct of others is displeasing, and against whose will and resistance those acts were committed which justly provoked the lord king to anger.

Therefore, fearing to cast the crime of some upon all, lest he involve the righteous with the wicked, he has resolved to set bounds to his anger and, for the present, to spare those who share the Christian profession. We therefore advise that, in order that his indignation may wholly cease, you hand over without any condition both your persons and all the property which you have here, together with your arms, into the hands of the lord king. Otherwise not even a single one of you will be able to escape death, since you stand in the midst of his kingdom, are not his equals in strength, and have no power of flight.

Godescalc, therefore, and the commanders of the legions, to whom from the beginning the madness of the unruly people had been displeasing, trusting in the king’s kindness, in simplicity of spirit brought the people—though resisting with all their strength and ready to fight for their lives—almost forcibly to the decision that they should surrender themselves, with their arms and all their property, into the lord king’s power, thereby making satisfaction for all the offences by which they had injured him.

At last the whole people consented. Once their arms had been handed over and all their property surrendered to the king’s officers and agents, they found death while awaiting pardon. For the Hungarians fell upon a people fearing no such thing, deprived of the protection of arms and not unreasonably relying upon the king’s clemency. Making no distinction between righteous and wicked, they carried out a most savage slaughter, so that the entire place was polluted with the corpses of the slain and the blood of those killed, and scarcely any trace of so great a multitude remained.

Yet some escaped the common danger. Guided by the Lord’s mercy, they avoided the Hungarian swords and returned home; by reporting the slaughter of their companions and the disastrous event that had occurred, they made better informed those who were about to set out and were bound by vows to undertake the same journey. They warned them always to suspect the malice of that wicked people, to proceed more prudently, and to learn to conduct their affairs more cautiously.

## CHAPTER XXIX. How an innumerable multitude of senseless men followed the preceding armies, slaughtered the Jewish people, and proceeded without discipline.

At the same time, after a short interval, countless crowds from the western regions had assembled with the same purpose, an innumerable body of foot-soldiers advancing everywhere rashly and without a leader or governor. Yet among them were certain noble men: Thomas of Feria, Clarenbald of Vendoliolo, William the Carpenter, Count Herman, and several others. But the people, impatient of discipline, submitted to none of them in any respect; disregarding the instruction of prudent and better-disposed men, they ranged everywhere freely and indiscriminately in unlawful conduct.

Thus it came about that, whereas they ought to have carried out their undertaken journey in the fear of the Lord and, mindful of the divine commandments, made pilgrimage for Christ while keeping evangelical discipline, they turned instead to madness. In the cities and towns through which they passed, they cruelly butchered the Jewish people, who feared no such thing from them and were living without precaution. This occurred especially in the cities of Cologne and Mainz, where Count Emico, a powerful and noble man, eminent in that region, joined their bands with a large retinue—not as befitted his noble birth, neither a censor of conduct nor a reprover of outrages, but a participant in their crimes and an instigator of their wicked deeds.

After passing through Franconia and Bavaria, they reached the borders of Hungary and came to a place called Meeszeburg. Thinking that they would be allowed to enter freely and without difficulty, they found the approach closed and halted on this side of the bridge. This place was a stronghold, heavily fortified by the great rivers Danube and Lintace, and surrounded by deep marshes, so that even a very great multitude could not easily force its way in against the will of those guarding the entrance. The number of those who had arrived was said to be two hundred thousand foot-soldiers, and about three thousand horsemen.

The king of Hungary had ordered that passage be refused to those wishing to cross, fearing that, remembering the injuries which he had inflicted upon Godescalc’s legions, once admitted they might wish to arm themselves in revenge. For the recent event and the enormity of the bloody slaughter, widely reported everywhere, compelled the king to fear for himself. Nevertheless, they obtained from those assigned to guard the aforesaid town, and from the commanders of the legions guarding that part of the country, permission to send envoys to the king, who might humbly approach him to seek peace and obtain freedom of passage. Meanwhile they encamped in grazing places on this side of the marshes, awaiting the outcome.

## CHAPTER XXX. How they besieged the castle of Meeszeburg, killed seven hundred Hungarians, and at last, turned to flight by divine intervention, were nearly all killed by the Hungarians.

[Col. 0249C]

Meanwhile, those who had been sent to the king returned after a few days, their business having wholly failed. When the leading men in the army learned from their report that they could obtain no favour from the king, they resolved to lay waste the lands which the king possessed on this side of the rivers and marsh, to burn the suburbs, and to act with hostility against his possessions.

While they were earnestly engaged in this, it happened one day that seven hundred men from the army of the aforesaid king crossed secretly by boat and unexpectedly encountered the pilgrims, as they happened to come forward to defend the country against the injuries inflicted upon it. Since the royal men could neither avoid them nor return to their own side, being obstructed by the waters, nearly all were killed, except for a few who, having lost their horses, sought safety in the reed-beds and marshes.

Elated by this victory, they further resolved to construct bridges, storm the stronghold, open the way by the sword, and enter the kingdom by force. In accordance with this plan they roused their companies; advancing by the bridges they had newly built toward the walls, shielded by their shields, they prepared more boldly to undermine the wall and force an entrance. Their persistent efforts had now brought matters to the point that, with the wall pierced in many places, entrance seemed on the very point of being open to the pilgrims. Those inside the town had fallen wholly into despair, utterly losing hope for their lives.

But suddenly, divine fear having been sent upon them, those who had seemed victorious abandoned the assault, left behind the greater part of their baggage, and turned to flight, wholly ignorant of the reason for their flight. Nor is any other cause said to have existed except that, by their many sins, they had provoked the Lord to anger, following impiety, which is accustomed to strike terror into its own worshippers. “The wicked flees when no one pursues,” according to the saying of the Wise Man (Prov. 28:1).

The Hungarians, whose situation had thus improved, saw the enemy’s columns turn their backs and pursued them as victors, though previously they had feared them. Those whom, hemmed in by marshes beneath the walls, they could scarcely withstand, they now pursued of their own accord, inflicting in return not merely terror but death. Count Emico fled with the greater part of the disorderly bands and returned to his homeland. The other nobles named above withdrew through Carinthia and reached Italy; after crossing it, they entered Apulia. From there, following those leaders who were making the same journey and had planned to sail to Durazzo, they crossed into Greece.

Thus nearly the whole West was shaken by these and similar disturbances. Almost every nation moved in separate bands: some undertook the journey under leaders, while others advanced almost headless. Yet the short route which those who had descended through Hungary were certainly known to have found was wholly denied to later travellers because of their insolence and the excessive outrages which they repeatedly and undeservedly inflicted upon the inhabitants of the country. This made those who followed more anxious to win the favour of the king of the Hungarians.

# BOOK II BEGINS.

[Col. 0249]

## CHAPTER I. At what time Duke Godfrey began his journey, which nobles accompanied him, and how he reached Hungary.

In the same year, 1096 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in August, on the fifteenth day of the month, the magnificent and illustrious Godfrey, Duke of Lorraine, set out after the departure of Peter the Hermit and the lamentable disaster of his army, as we have related; after the previously mentioned slaughter of Godescalc’s legions; and after that further kind of misfortune which, as we have said, is reported to have befallen the following multitude before it reached Hungary. Having summoned his companions for the journey and arranged the baggage in the customary manner, he began his march.

The noble, illustrious men who joined his camp, worthy of everlasting remembrance, were: Lord Baldwin, his brother by the same mother; Lord Baldwin of Mons, Count of Hainaut; Lord Hugh, Count of Saint-Pol, and his son Engelram, a young man of outstanding character; Lord Count Garner, surnamed of Gres; Lord Renard, Count of Toul, and his brother Peter; Lord Baldwin of Bourcq, kinsman of the same duke; Lord Henry of Ascha and his brother Godfrey; Dodo of Cons; Cono of Montaigu; and many others whose names or number we do not possess.

All these, travelling together in one undivided company, reached peacefully, safely, and unharmed, on the twentieth day of September, the province called Austria, at a place called Tollenburch. This is the place where the river Lintax marks the boundary between the empire and the kingdom of Hungary. On arriving there, greatly concerned about what was said to have happened to Godescalc and his legions, they deliberated how they might safely continue the undertaking they had begun.

At last, by common counsel, it was decided to send an embassy to the king of Hungary, in order to learn more fully what cause had brought about the destruction among them of the army of their preceding brethren; and, when an opportunity was found, to approach the lord king concerning peace and, laying aside old complaints, to endeavour to obtain free passage through Hungary. For to take other routes seemed a loss to the journey they had begun.

Accordingly, the noble Godfrey of Ascha, brother of Henry, was sent with certain honourable and noble men to perform this embassy, since he had long enjoyed the friendship of that king. Reaching the king and offering the appropriate words of greeting, he faithfully carried out his instructions and spoke to the king as follows:

## CHAPTER II. Embassy of the same duke to King Coloman of Hungary through Godfrey of Ascha, and the answer of the same king to the duke.

[Col. 0251D]

The illustrious and magnificent Lord Godfrey, Duke of Lorraine, and the other princes who are worshippers of God and are with him, devoted to divine service, have sent us to Your Highness, wishing to learn through us why the people of the faithful—whose remnants we found on the road coming to meet us—met such inhumanity among you, who are said to belong to the number of the faithful, that it would have been safer for them to turn aside to any enemies whatsoever.

If the fault of the aforesaid people was so great that it deserved to be punished with the utmost penalties, those who sent me are prepared to bear their destruction with equanimity. For whatever punishment is inflicted according to desert provokes less anger and must be endured with greater patience. But if the contrary is true, and innocent people were maliciously accused without any cause in order that you might hand them over to death, they cannot overlook the injury inflicted upon the servants of God; rather, they are prepared to avenge their brothers’ blood. They therefore await your answer through our ministry, and will shape their dispositions in accordance with it.

Having said this, he ceased speaking. The king, surrounded by a company of his attendants, replied in these words:

Godfrey, man of friendship, whom on account of your merits we long ago granted our favour, I am pleased that you have come to us—both so that we may renew an old friendship and so that before so discerning a judge we may establish our innocence. We indeed belong, as you say, to the number of the faithful; and would that we might fulfil in action the virtue of this name! But those who preceded you—both those following Peter the Hermit, those adhering to Godescalc, and those who attempted, on the borders of our kingdom, to storm our castle and force their way in to us—were followers of Christ neither in deed nor in name.

For when we first received Peter and his armies as guests, sharing with them the goods in our country both freely and at a just price, like a serpent in one’s bosom and mice in one’s bag they poorly repaid their hosts. At the farthest borders of our kingdom, when they ought already to have rendered thanks for the benefits bestowed upon them, they broke into one of our cities, utterly destroyed the people within it, and departed like violent robbers with their spoils, flocks, and herds.

The expeditions of Godescalc, admitted without trouble or difficulty as though we had suffered no injury whatever from their predecessors, did not fear to engage in plunder in the midst of this kingdom, inflict violence, cause fires, and commit slaughter on trivial pretexts. By the enormity of their crimes they provoked the Lord to anger. Since we could not endure the sufferings of our subjects, we also took action, providing a remedy for an endangered situation.

Therefore, deterred by the example of the former groups, lest for a third time we should experience the injuries of detestable bands, it seemed more prudent to exclude from the borders of our kingdom such troops of impious men—plainly hateful to God—than to suffer monstrous injuries and losses from them or engage in hostile conflict with them. Let this statement suffice as our defence before you, a prudent and energetic man. For—as the Lord lives—we have declared the pure truth exactly as it is.

Having said this, he ordered that the same envoys be treated hospitably and with every honour, until, after taking counsel with his own men, he should send messengers to the aforesaid princes bearing an appropriate reply. At last he sent several of his own household together with the envoys who had come to him, and wrote to the duke and princes in these words:

We have indeed heard, and have long known by report, that among your people you are held to be a great prince, illustrious and outstanding in merit; and that even wise men far away admire the sincerity of your faith and the praiseworthy constancy of your spirit. Drawn also by the good fragrance of your name and the radiance of your deeds, we have resolved to esteem and more readily honour you even in your absence. We also believe that the noble men with you, inflamed by zeal for the Christian faith, have a pious purpose.

Therefore we do not wish those merits by which friendships are usually won to lie idle and dormant in us. We are prepared to extend due charity to all and to abound in deeds of brotherly love toward them. Since such an occasion presents itself, we ask that you come in person to our castle called Ciperon, so that we may enjoy with you the conversation long desired and grant a fitting assent to your wishes.

## CHAPTER III. The king and our princes meet; Baldwin, the duke’s brother, is given to the king as a hostage; after Hungary has been crossed and his brother restored, the duke is honoured by the king with many gifts.

When the duke had heard the king’s embassy and taken counsel with his men, he arrived on the appointed day at the designated place with three hundred horsemen selected from the entire company. There, after crossing the bridge, he found the king and was received by him most graciously and with great honour. At last, after they had shown one another much mutual goodwill, it was agreed that, once hostages selected from among the nobles had been given, all resentment laid aside, and peace fully restored, the entrance to the kingdom should be opened to the duke and his legions.

So that he might have fuller assurance concerning the legions of so great men when they had been admitted—lest, perhaps trusting in their strength and numbers on some occasion, they should presume to disturb his kingdom—the king requested as hostage Lord Baldwin, the duke’s brother, together with his wife and household. The duke readily assented and gave his brother as hostage on the agreed terms; his legions having been admitted, he entered the kingdom.

The king faithfully fulfilled his promise. Throughout all the regions through which the army was to pass, he issued an edict commanding that necessities for food be supplied to the legions at a fair price and just weight, and that a continuous market of goods for sale should accompany the travelling crowds. The duke, meanwhile, had proclamations announced throughout all the camps, privately and publicly, under penalty of death and confiscation of all goods: no one was to dare inflict plunder, violence, or injury upon those approaching the army; rather, in the bond of peace, they were to conduct buying and selling transactions in brotherly charity.

And so it happened, under the Lord’s mercy, that while crossing the whole of Hungary, they did not offend one another even by a slight word. The king accompanied the advancing army with enormous forces of his own, almost keeping pace with it on its left side and taking the hostages with him, prepared to quell immediately by his presence any disturbance that might arise.

At last they reached Malevilla, frequently mentioned above, and halted on the bank of the river Sava until a crossing could be prepared for the army. Since they found only a few ships, insufficient for transporting so great a people, they constructed rafts. After a thousand armoured horsemen had been ferried across to secure the farther bank against any enemy ambushes and provide the transported people with a safe resting-place, the people eagerly crossed over to the opposite side.

Scarcely had the common people crossed by water, together with some of the princes, when the king suddenly appeared with a great retinue of his men. He restored Lord Baldwin, his wife, and the other hostages into the duke’s hand, as had been agreed at the beginning; and, honouring both the duke and the remaining princes with abundant gifts, he returned home. The duke followed the forces that had crossed over, and then passed to the farther bank with the remaining princes and people. Coming to the Bulgarian town of Bellegrava, which we mentioned above, he encamped there. From there, after arranging the baggage and preparing the legions for the journey, he crossed the forests of Bulgaria and its widely extending woods, reaching first Niz and then Stralicia.

## CHAPTER IV. Our legions enter the emperor’s land: the entrance is described, and the misery of the Greeks is shown.

[Col. 0254B]

From places which were once provinces richer and filled with every kind of resource, one may infer how great are the misery of the Greeks and the weakness of their empire. For after the Latin princes at Constantinople had failed, the empire passed into Greek hands under the first Nicephorus, through the exigency of sins. Immediately the barbarian nations, trusting in Greek weakness, invaded their provinces and began to treat the inhabitants of the country at their own pleasure.

Among these, the uncultivated nation of the Bulgars, coming from the northern region, had occupied all the lands from the Danube to the imperial city and, again, from the same river to the Adriatic Sea. Thus the names and boundaries of the provinces were thrown into confusion, and the whole tract—said to be thirty days’ journey in length and ten or more in breadth—is called Bulgaria, while the wretched Greeks do not know that this very name proclaims their disgrace.

On the Adriatic Sea lay the two Epirus provinces; the metropolis of one of them is Durazzo, once the kingdom of Pyrrhus, the vigorous and remarkable king of the Epirotes. In the region through which the duke and his company were to pass lay two Dacias: Riparian Dacia, which they left on their left after crossing along the banks of the Danube; and Mediterranean Dacia, through which they travelled, passing through and traversing the once eminent cities of Niz and Stralicia. There were also other provinces in the same region—Arcadia, Thessaly, Macedonia, and the three Thraces—which were involved in the same calamity as the rest.

Nor had the Greeks lost only these aforesaid provinces through their softness. Later, after the Bulgarian people had been subdued by their emperor Basil, they even now do not permit inhabitants to enter or cultivate the more remote provinces, especially those bordering foreign kingdoms and providing access to them—namely, the two Dacias. Thus forests and thickets spread widely over the land, affording no convenience to those who wish to enter; they place greater confidence in the difficulty of the roads and the armour of brambles than in their own power of resistance.

In the same manner, they leave deserted and uninhabited First Epirus, which begins at Durazzo and extends for four days’ journey to the mountain called Bagularius, through which all the other princes had passage. Thus, for those wishing to approach, deserted and trackless woods, lacking provisions, serve as an obstacle in place of barriers.

The lord duke therefore crossed the aforesaid Mediterranean Dacia, which is also called Moesia. Having overcome the defiles commonly called those of Saint Basil, he descended to flatter places that furnished an abundance of food and reached Philippopolis, a noble and exceedingly wealthy city. There he learned that Lord Hugh the Great, brother of Lord Philip, king of the Franks, together with certain other nobles, was being held in chains by the emperor. He therefore sent messengers with all speed, by letters and spoken word, earnestly warning and requesting the emperor to allow those men—bound by the vow of the same pilgrimage and imprisoned without guilt—to depart free.

For that illustrious man, having set out almost before everyone else, had crossed the Alps and descended into Italy. From there he reached Apulia; crossing the sea with a small company, he stopped at Durazzo to await those who followed. He did not fear that any misfortune would befall himself or his companions in the kingdom of the Greeks, who were said to be marked by Christian profession. There, however, he was bound and chained by the governor of the region, handed over to the emperor to be treated as he pleased, and taken away.

Thus the emperor kept him in prison as though he were a robber or guilty of homicide, awaiting the arrival of the princes who were said to be following, so that, if they arrived prosperously, he might appear to have released him because of their favour; but if not, he might consign him to perpetual fetters.

## CHAPTER V. The duke sends envoys to the emperor to release Hugh the Great and the other nobles whom he held in chains; the entire region is given over to plunder, and at last our men reach Constantinople.

At that time a wicked and deceitful man, Alexius by name, surnamed Comnenus, presided over the empire of the Greeks. He had been greatly honoured in the imperial palace by Lord Nicephorus, surnamed Botoniates, who then ruled under the sceptre. Holding the office of megadomestic—that is, what we are accustomed to call chief seneschal—and second in rank after the emperor, he had treacherously rebelled against his lord and benefactor. Five or six years before our people arrived, he had deposed his lord, seized the empire, and presumed to retain by force what he had violently occupied.

The duke’s envoys therefore came to the emperor and most urgently demanded the release of the aforesaid nobleman with his companions, as they had been instructed. When the emperor flatly refused them, they returned to our forces, which had already passed Adrianople and were encamped there in pasture-lands. When the duke and the other princes learned from the report of these messengers that the emperor was entirely unwilling to release the aforesaid nobles, they decided by common counsel to give the whole region over to plunder by their legions.

They remained there continuously for eight days and ravaged everything. Hearing this, the emperor sent envoys to the duke, asking him to make his army cease from plunder and to receive the nobles whose release he had demanded, now freed. The duke willingly agreed to this request. Having forbidden plunder to his men and restored order among his legions, he reached Constantinople and encamped outside the city, pitching his tents with strong forces and a plentiful army.

The aforesaid noblemen—namely Lord Hugh the Great, Drogo of Neelle, William the Carpenter, and Clarenbald of Vendoliolo—came out to meet him and entered the duke’s camp outside the city to give thanks for their release. He received them graciously, with great affection and due honour, kept them with him kindly for some time, and fraternally sympathized with the hardships which they had endured without deserving them.

## CHAPTER VI. The emperor invites the duke to him; the duke refuses to enter; grave hostilities arise between them; by the emperor’s deceit, the duke’s army is moved to a narrower place.

Meanwhile, scarcely had they ended their mutual embraces and refreshed themselves with reciprocal conversation when the emperor’s envoys arrived, urging the duke to hasten to enter and visit the lord emperor with a few companions. After taking counsel, however, the duke delayed going there. The emperor, greatly angered by this, prohibited the market in goods for sale to the legions that had arrived with the duke.

The leaders of the people, seeing their want and the lack of provisions, again resolved together to range far and wide through the suburbs with great armed forces. They collected flocks and herds from every side and brought every abundance of food into their camp, so that even the lower ranks had more than enough. Seeing the whole region exposed to plunder and fire, and fearing that something still worse might happen, the emperor ordered commerce restored.

As the solemn day of the Lord’s Nativity approached, our princes resolved among themselves, out of religious regard, to refrain for those four days from every kind of plunder and injury. When these days had passed in complete quiet and tranquillity, an envoy of the emperor came, using peaceful words but with deceit. He advised them to cross the bridge near the palace called Blachernae and transfer their legions to the many palaces situated on the shores of the Bosporus, where they would lodge.

He could readily persuade them, for the severity of the approaching winter and the unprecedented harshness of the rains were extreme. Their tents could scarcely keep out the dripping water; their food and all their goods were damaged and rotted by the continual wetness. Neither human beings, pack animals, nor any other living creatures could endure much longer the penetrating force of the cold and the frequent—indeed almost unceasing—onslaught of snow. All were continually afflicted beyond their strength.

Although the emperor seemed to sympathize verbally with these conditions, his mind was far otherwise. His whole purpose hastened toward placing the legions in narrower quarters, where they would have less freedom to range abroad and he himself would acquire greater power to restrain them as he wished. To make this more fully understood, something must be inserted concerning the location of the aforesaid city.

## CHAPTER VII. Description of the location of the city of Constantinople. The duke sends envoys to the emperor; our army unexpectedly suffers a Greek ambush.

[Col. 0257B]

The Black Sea (which takes its name from the adjoining region) lies to the north of the aforesaid city, at a distance of thirty miles from it. A portion of it descends southward like a river through certain narrows; running straight for a distance of two hundred and thirty miles between the most ancient cities of Sestos and Abydos—one in Europe, the other in Asia—it flows into our Mediterranean Sea. This current, issuing from the aforesaid sea, after descending continuously for thirty miles from the first mouth by which it enters, [Col. 0257C] forms a bay westward, five or six miles long and about one mile broad. This narrow sea, extending from the Black Sea to the Mediterranean for two hundred and thirty miles, is called the Bosporus of the Propontis, or the Hellespont.

That this is so is attested by Solinus in the seventeenth book of *On Memorable Things*, where he says:

> The great gulf of Europe begins at the Hellespont and ends at the mouth of Lake Maeotis; and all this breadth, which separates Europe from Asia, is narrowed to a strait of seven stadia. This is the Hellespont, which Xerxes crossed by means of a bridge made of ships. From there the Euripus extends to the Asian city of Priapus, where Alexander the Great crossed in his desire to possess the world; and the sea, [Col. 0257D] having spread out from there, is again confined in the very broad expanse into the Propontis, then is compressed to five hundred paces and becomes the Thracian Bosporus, by which Darius transported his forces.

The causes of these names seem to have been drawn from the ancient fables of the poets. For the Bosporus is so called because Jupiter, having assumed the form of a bull, is said to have carried Europa, daughter of Agenor, across that sea. The Hellespont, however, is named from Helle, sister of Phrixus, who is likewise said to have crossed the sea upon a ram together with that same brother.

In the common tongue it is called the Arm of Saint George, the boundary of Europe and Asia, and it has the length already stated. Its breadth, however, is not everywhere the same: according to the situation and arrangement of the neighboring regions, it is at one point narrowed to a space of one mile, [Col. 0258A] while elsewhere it spreads out to thirty miles or more.

The aforesaid bay, stretching westward as we have said, is a harbor most famous among those possessed by the world for its convenient anchorage. Below it and the Bosporus, in a certain angle, lies the aforesaid city, formerly called Byzantium: once an obscure place, and almost the least among the cities of Thrace; now, distinguished by the happier name of its enlarger Augustus, it has become the chief city of the provinces and the customary seat of empire, envying Old Rome both its name and the prerogative of its dignity. First founded by Pausanias, king of the Spartans, according to what is contained in the third book of Paulus Orosius, it has the form of a triangle with three unequal sides. Its first side extends directly along the harbor from the angle contained between the harbor and the Hellespont, [Col. 0258B] where stands the church of Saint George called Mangana, as far as the new palace called Blachernae. The second runs from the same monastery of Saint George to the Golden Gate along the Hellespont. The third extends from that same gate to the aforesaid palace of Blachernae across open country, notable for its walls, towers, and outer fortifications.

A certain river enters the harbor. It is small in summer, but in winter, swollen by rainwater, it is usually more torrential; a bridge has been laid over it. Having crossed this bridge, our army had established itself for lodging between the Black Sea, the Bosporus, and the harbor, in the many buildings situated on the very shore of the Bosporus. [Col. 0258C] While they remained there awaiting the arrival of the other princes, the duke was repeatedly pressed by the emperor’s embassies to enter and visit him. Suspecting his friendliness and dreading an interview, he feared to comply with the summons. Yet, seeing that it would be wholly improper and contrary to the rules of honorable conduct neither to come in person nor at least to send suitable representatives on his behalf, he sent to the emperor the noble lord Conon of Montaigu, the lord Baldwin of Bourcq, and Henry of Ascha, to make his excuse.

When the emperor saw the duke’s firmness and that he could by no means summon him into his presence, he again prohibited the sale of provisions. Yet not even thus could he soften the resolve of the steadfast man. Therefore, increasing his pressure, he secretly sent archers, who came by ship to the place where the duke had pitched camp; at earliest morning, in the very dawn of day, they pierced with arrows many of our men who had gone down to the sea and who were watching from the windows, killing very many.

## CHAPTER VIII. The army returns to the city, and a great battle is joined. A very great slaughter of Greeks takes place.

When this was reported to the duke, he summoned the leaders of the people and, by common counsel, ordered his brother to take a portion of the troops and hurry to seize the bridge by which they had crossed, lest they should be cut off in those narrow places and suffer losses among their people. He, [Col. 0259A] energetic as he was, took five hundred armored men and hurried to the aforesaid bridge, which he seized by force. For by now not only those who had landed from the ships showed themselves as enemies: the whole city was arming against them in hostility.

When our men perceived that adversaries had deliberately and carefully been prepared against them, and that even all the citizens were rushing to arms for their destruction, they set fire to all the palaces in which they had been lodged, burning them continuously for six or seven miles—both private buildings and imperial ones. Then, with trumpets sounding and the signal of the horn-blowers, they gathered from the various quarters to which they had dispersed for lodging; seizing their arms, they hurried after the duke, who was already hastening toward the bridge with his battle-lines drawn up. [Col. 0259B]

Those with greater experience of warfare feared greatly that, if the bridge were occupied by the enemy, they would be found in a narrower place and more easily overwhelmed. Therefore, with such urgency that they scarcely waited for the infantry units, the entire body of cavalry assembled there. But the lord Baldwin, the duke’s brother, as we have said, had hurried ahead and seized the bridge by force against the enemy’s will; having driven them off and put them to flight, he secured for our men the far bank of the river. The duke and the whole army, crossing without difficulty with their baggage and every kind of equipment, again took their stand before the city in open and spacious ground.

There, after a battle had been fought between the church of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian—today called in the common speech Bohemond’s Castle—and the new palace called Blachernae, which lies in an angle of the city near the harbor, about the evening hour, countless persons having been killed, our men forced the Greeks, unable to bear any longer the weight of battle, to withdraw within the city. [Col. 0259C] Our men, having gallantly held the field as victors, pitched camp in a place suitable for that purpose. And perhaps, had the citizens attacked again, a more dangerous engagement and a greater slaughter would have followed, hatred supplying their fury, had not the onset of night put an end to the conflict on both sides.

Here for the first time it became clear, and was manifest beyond doubt, with what intention that wicked emperor had ordered the camp to be moved: namely, that he might confine a people he suspected in that narrow place as though within barriers. [Col. 0259D]

## CHAPTER IX. The people rush to arms and devastate the whole region; great abundance of provisions arises in the camp.

At length, when daylight had returned, a public proclamation was issued that the people should rise to arms. One part, assigned to specified commanders, was to scour the whole countryside and bring in supplies of food—which the emperor had forbidden them to buy—either by force or by purchase, sparing neither flocks nor herds, grain nor any kind of provision. Another part was to remain in the army with the duke and certain other magnates for the defense of the camp.

[Col. 0260A] Having discovered the emperor’s deceit and that of his men, they armed themselves with every precaution they could against his snares. Thus those who went out to forage spent six continuous days, with a great multitude both of horsemen and foot soldiers, ravaging the suburbs for a circuit of up to sixty miles. On the eighth day they brought such an abundance of provisions into the camp as exceeded all expectation; they could scarcely draw before them the crowds of flocks and herds, wagons, and beasts of burden.

## CHAPTER X. A messenger of Bohemond comes to the duke and urges him not to meet the emperor; the duke’s reply.

While these events were taking place in the camp, behold, a messenger of Lord Bohemond stood before the duke, bearing letters from that prince in these words:

> Know, most excellent of men, that you have to deal with a most savage beast and a wicked man, whose purpose is always to deceive and by every means to persecute the whole Latin nation to the death. My judgment of him will one day be confirmed by your own judgment as well. For I know the malice of the Greeks and their stubborn, obstinate hatred of the Latin name. Therefore, if you please, leave the city and withdraw toward Adrianople or the region around Philippopolis; command the forces committed to you by the Lord to recover in fertile places, with food and rest. By God’s aid, I shall come quickly at the beginning of spring, to furnish you, as my lord, with counsel and aid in brotherly charity against the impious ruler of the Greeks. [Col. 0260C]

After the letter had been read and its meaning fully understood, the duke, by the common counsel of the princes, replied in writing and orally as follows:

> Dearest brother, I know—and have long been taught by report—that the cunning Greeks have always ardently sought, with inexorable hatred, to persecute our people. Whatever knowledge of this I previously lacked, I learn more fully every day by experience. Nor do I doubt that you are moved against them by righteous zeal and judge their wickedness rightly. Yet, keeping the fear of God before my eyes and considering my purpose, I fear to turn arms owed to unbelievers against a Christian people. Nevertheless, the army that is dear to God, who is with us, most eagerly awaits your welcome arrival and the presence of the other princes devoted to God. [Col. 0260D]

## CHAPTER XI. The emperor sends his son John Porphyrogenitus as a hostage and invites the duke to him. The duke enters; the emperor adopts him; peace between them is restored.

The emperor, greatly troubled with his intimates and household—both because he saw the whole region exposed to plunder and could not bear the groans and lamentations of his people, and because he had learned that an embassy from Lord Bohemond had arrived and that Bohemond himself would soon come—again urged the lord duke through his messengers to enter his presence. He feared that, if the princes who were coming should meet together before he had [Col. 0261A] made the duke well disposed toward himself, they would unanimously agree upon his destruction. He therefore pressed more eagerly to reconcile the duke’s mind to him first, earnestly urging and exhorting him to receive his son John Porphyrogenitus, whom he was sending as a hostage, and then to enter his presence without any misgiving.

This proposal pleased the princes. The emperor’s son was received through Conon of Montaigu and Baldwin of Bourcq, most noble men who had been sent for this purpose, and was entrusted to careful custody in the duke’s brother’s keeping. The duke himself, taking the remaining princes with him and leaving his brother in command of the army to care for it, entered the city and offered the emperor his long-desired presence.

The emperor received him with great honor, in the presence of illustrious men who wished to see the man of whom they had heard much and whom they had partly come to know. He honored the princes who had come with him with greetings befitting their rank and likewise admitted them to the kiss of peace. He inquired carefully after their welfare; running through the names of each one, he showed himself gracious and kind to all, so as to gain their favor. [Col. 0261B]

At length he addressed the duke in these words:

> Our empire, dearest duke, has heard that you are most powerful among your princes. It is not unaware of the pious purpose which you diligently pursue, armed with the commendable fervor of devotion. What is more, widespread fame proclaims you to be a man of steadfast spirit and sincere faith. Hence, as the refinement of your character demands it, you have earned the favor even of many who have not seen you in person. Therefore, wishing also to embrace you with the whole affection of our heart and to honor you more fully, we have determined today, in the presence of the magnates of our sacred palace, to adopt you as our son, placing our empire in your power so that through you it may remain unharmed and safe before the people now present and those yet to come. [Col. 0261C]

Having said this, he clothed him in imperial garments and, with a certain ceremony customary in the court for such adoptions, adopted him as his son according to the custom of the country. Peace and favor were thus fully restored between them.

## CHAPTER XII. The duke, laden with gifts, departs with temporary leave; a market in provisions is supplied; the duke’s forces cross the Bosporus and encamp in the district of Chalcedon.

[Col. 0261D]

After this, he opened his treasuries and, in accordance with his generosity, bestowed upon both the lord duke and his companions enormous gifts of gold, gems, silk fabrics, and precious vessels, altogether surpassing human estimation both in elegance of workmanship and in the value of their material. Thus they were loaded with gifts to the utmost and marveled at the incomparable abundance of riches and the prince’s munificence. Nor did he exercise such generosity toward the duke only once: from the feast of the Epiphany until the Ascension of the Lord, every week there was supplied to him from the imperial palace as much gold coin as two strong men could carry on their shoulders, and ten bushels of bronze coins. [Col. 0262A] Yet he kept nothing of all this for himself, but generously distributed it among the nobles and the people according to what seemed necessary for each.

Having taken leave of the lord emperor for a time, they departed and returned to the camp. They then sent back to his father with an honorable escort the emperor’s son John, whom they had held as a hostage in the camp until the lord duke’s return. The emperor, by a publicly proclaimed edict, imposing the penalty of death upon its violators, ordered that every necessity be sold to the duke’s army at a just price and fair weight. Likewise, the duke publicly proclaimed in the camp, under penalty of death, that no violence or injury was to be inflicted upon the emperor’s men. [Col. 0262B] Thus, behaving with sufficient propriety toward one another, they carried on their mutual trade in complete peace.

At last, in the middle of March, the duke heard, at the emperor’s suggestion, that the other princes were stationed nearby and were arriving with their armies. Since both his common soldiers and his lords wished it, he made ready ships, crossed the Hellespont, and stationed his army in Bithynia, the first of the Asian provinces encountered. There he encamped in the district of Chalcedon.

Chalcedon is a city of Bithynia where, in the time of the elder Lord Pope Leo and the Lord Emperor Marcian, the fourth general synod of six hundred and thirty-six fathers assembled against the impieties of the monk Eutyches and Dioscorus, patriarch of Alexandria. [Col. 0262C] It is a place near Constantinople, separated only by the Bosporus; hence everyone could see the neighboring city, and those compelled by pressing business could go to the imperial city and return to the camp three or four times a day without difficulty.

The emperor had induced the duke by his persuasions to cross earlier, not from sincerity of faith, but by his customary deceit: he wished to prevent the duke’s forces from joining those of the others when they arrived. Indeed, by the same device he compelled each of those who followed later to cross separately, so that never were two armies together before the city.

## CHAPTER XIII. Bohemond hastens on; the nobles who follow him are listed; the emperor secretly prepares ambushes for him.

[Col. 0262D]

Meanwhile, while these things were being done around Constantinople by the emperor and the duke’s men, Lord Bohemond, son of Robert Guiscard and prince of Taranto, had crossed the Adriatic Sea with his army before the onset of winter and reached Dyrrachium. Waiting in the wildernesses of Bulgaria for those who followed him, he advanced gradually.

Very many noble and powerful men from Italy and other provinces had attached themselves to him and joined his camp.
