For perpetual remembrance, we include in part their number and names: Tancred, son of Marquis William; Richard of the Principate, son of William Ferrebrachia, [Col. 0263A] brother of Robert Guiscard; Ranulf, his brother; Robert of Anxa; Herman of Carni; Robert of Surdavalle; Robert, son of Tristan; Humphrey, son of Ralph; Richard, son of Count Ranulf; the count of Rosinolo with his brothers; Boel of Chartres; Albered of Cagnano; and Humphrey of Monte Scabioso.

All these followed Lord Bohemond’s banners and reached the city of Castoria, where they celebrated the feast of the Lord’s Nativity. Since the citizens did not offer provisions for sale to the passing people, they were compelled to seize by force flocks, herds, and the other necessities of life, inflicting losses upon the inhabitants, who detested them as enemies. From there they advanced and encamped in a most fertile region called Pelagonia. [Col. 0263B]

When they heard that there was nearby a town wholly inhabited by heretics, they hastened there with all speed. They violently seized the fortress, set the buildings on fire, and destroyed the townspeople partly by the sword and partly in the conflagration; they carried off all the booty and rich spoils from it.

When the emperor heard that the forces of the aforesaid Lord Bohemond were approaching, he secretly ordered the commanders of his armies, whom he had stationed in those regions for winter quarters, to pursue them continually from the flank as far as the river Vardar, with all the forces of those districts, so that, should a suitable opportunity arise by night or day, secretly or otherwise, they might attempt to harass the advancing army. For he regarded Lord Bohemond’s arrival with the deepest suspicion, since he had suffered many injuries from Bohemond and from his father, and often. Yet, being a crafty man, able alike to pretend and to conceal his purpose, he sent certain nobles of his household to this distinguished man and addressed him with peaceful words in deceit, testing whether he might somehow deceive him. The tenor of the words which he had sent by the aforesaid messengers, both orally and in letters, was as follows:

## CHAPTER XIV. Letter of Emperor Alexius to Bohemond. The emperor’s army secretly attacks Bohemond’s camp. Some are captured and reveal the emperor’s malice.

[Col. 0263D]

Our God-protected empire knows and does not in the least doubt that you are a great, powerful, and distinguished prince, the son also of a magnificent, mighty, and capable prince. On account of your merits, we have hitherto always held you dear and acceptable, although we have not seen you in person. And now, because we have heard that you have girded yourself for the service of God and the offices of piety, and have entered into fellowship in this pilgrimage with the other princes devoted to God, we desire more strongly to love you and more readily to honor you; this purpose is fixed in our ready will.

Therefore, our dearest one, command the people who follow you to spare our subjects. Make violence, plundering, and arson cease; come as quickly as possible into our presence, confident of our abundant honor and favor, with which we have proposed to anticipate you in many ways. We have also ordered the bearers of this letter to procure necessities for your armies at a just price, so that an abundance of things for sale may attend them without interruption. [Col. 0264A]

Although these words of the emperor seemed outwardly to contain much kindness, they concealed poison mixed within. But Bohemond, a shrewd and astute man who knew the emperor’s malice, concealed his own purpose and acted more cautiously, thanking the emperor for deigning to concern himself with his condition.

Thus, guided by these men, he came to the river Vardar. Part of the army had already crossed the river and stood on the farther bank, while another part was still preparing to cross. Then the emperor’s soldiers, who had been following the traces of our army with an innumerable host, thinking they had found an opportunity, rushed hostilely upon that part of the army still making ready to cross, pressing their attack with all possible violence. [Col. 0264B]

When Tancred understood this, he flew to the scene like lightning, being a man of the greatest dispatch. Swimming across the intervening river, he reached the far bank. Nearly two thousand horsemen followed him. At the very first onset of their arrival, they broke up the enemy’s companies with their swords; having put them to flight, they pursued them for some distance, killing them. After killing very many, they captured some as well and brought them before Lord Bohemond. [Col. 0264C]

When these captives were questioned more carefully as to why they were pursuing a Christian army, they answered that they were men of the emperor and were obliged, in return for pay, to serve in arms at his command. Then it became fully known to all that whatever the emperor said to them was deceit and trickery. Yet, because they had to pass through his territories, Bohemond preferred, despite the wishes of others, to conceal the injuries rather than provoke him uselessly to anger.

## CHAPTER XV. The duke meets Lord Bohemond and brings him, almost against his will, to the emperor; there Bohemond is greatly honored. Meanwhile Tancred transfers the forces to Bithynia, where they join the duke’s companies.

[Col. 0264D]

Having passed through Macedonia and all Illyricum, he hastened his journey at a fitting pace and began to approach the city. When he was stationed nearby, on the Thursday before the Paschal solemnity, he again received an embassy from the emperor, urging him to leave his army and enter the emperor’s presence with only a few of his household. He paused for a while and delayed carrying out what was commanded, suspecting the emperor’s malice.

While he wavered in uncertainty, behold, the illustrious Duke Godfrey, overcome by the emperor’s urgent and repeated entreaties to go out and meet Lord Bohemond and bring him confidently into his presence, magnificently met that noble man with an honorable escort of princes. [Col. 0265A] They received one another with mutual embraces and the kiss of sincere affection. After pleasant conversation and reciprocal inquiries concerning each other’s condition, Lord Bohemond was urged by the duke to enter the emperor’s presence, as he had been summoned. Although at first he showed himself reluctant and did not sufficiently heed the duke’s advice, suspecting the emperor’s conference as stated above, he was afterward overcome by honorable persuasion and, with the duke leading the way, entered the emperor’s presence confidently.

There he was received by the emperor with the kiss of peace, manifold favor, and many honors. After many private deliberations between them, Lord Bohemond, as it is said, became the emperor’s man, having rendered manual fidelity and taken a bodily oath in the manner in which vassals usually render them to their lords. [Col. 0265B] When this was done, gifts from the imperial wardrobes were offered to the aforesaid man—gold, garments, vessels, and precious stones, incomparable both in price and in worth.

Once these matters had thus been settled peacefully, while Lord Bohemond was still staying in the palace, Tancred, a man commendable in every respect and Bohemond’s nephew through his sister, deliberately avoided the emperor’s presence and conference. In the meantime he transferred the entire army to Bithynia beyond the Bosporus and encamped in the district of Chalcedon, where the army of the lord duke, transferred there some time before, was waiting for the arrival of those who followed. When the emperor learned fully [Col. 0265C] that Lord Tancred had thus avoided his presence, he took it very badly. Yet, in the manner of a prudent man, concealing the injury, he repeatedly heaped immense gifts upon the princes then present and sent them with great honor back to their own camp beyond the Bosporus.

There, with their forces joined and united in complete affection, both armies remained within sight of the city, awaiting the arrival of the princes who were following, so that, once their forces had been joined, they might unanimously pursue the journey they had undertaken. Necessary food was supplied in sufficient quantity to the people stationed there, both from the imperial city and from the neighboring suburbs, so that they enjoyed an abundance beyond their wishes.

## CHAPTER XVI. Count Robert of Flanders arrives with his men, is summoned and received by the emperor, receives immense gifts, crosses the sea, and joins the aforesaid princes.

[Col. 0265D]

Meanwhile the illustrious Robert, count of Flanders, had crossed the sea with his company at the beginning of winter, descending from the coastal Apulian city of Bari to Dyrrachium. He had avoided the severity of the approaching winter in fertile places full of woods, pastures, and every convenience. At length, near the beginning of spring, he set out and pursued with great urgency the other princes who had already crossed the sea, in order to join them.

Before he reached Constantinople, as had happened to the others, he received imperial envoys who commanded him to leave the army and come with only a few companions into the emperor’s presence. But having been fully informed how those who preceded him had conducted themselves with the lord emperor, he reached Constantinople and entered the palace with a few companions. [Col. 0266A] There he was received by the emperor with great honor and treated kindly. Following the example of the others, he rendered the stipulated oath of fidelity in person. He consequently obtained greater favor and received enormous gifts; his companions too were honored with like generosity according to their respective rank.

After some days, during which his army rested near the city with food and leisure, and after he had repeatedly entered the emperor’s presence and sufficiently discussed with him such matters as seemed necessary, he took leave, transferred his troops, and sailed to his fellow travelers. They received him kindly and with full affection, and he joined his following to their armies. [Col. 0266B]

There, as day by day they refreshed one another with mutual conversation about the various events that had befallen each of them on the journey, and recalled their hardships in a pleasant shared remembrance, their discussion finally returned to the pressing issue: that they might inquire more carefully among themselves when and how they should set about bringing their undertaking to completion. While they were concerned about this and criticized the delay of their companions who were following, charging them with allowing time to pass fruitlessly, behold, a messenger informed them that the Count of Toulouse and the Bishop of Le Puy were both present and would soon enter the city. [Col. 0266C]

## CHAPTER XVII. The Count of Toulouse and the Bishop of Le Puy hurry through Dalmatia with their forces, enduring great hardships on the journey through that region.

These two great and illustrious men had remained constantly and inseparably united with their forces from the beginning of the journey they had undertaken. With them were noble men, most distinguished among their own people alike for nobility and refinement of character: namely, Lord William, bishop of Orange; Rambald, count of the same city; Gaustus of Bederz; Girard of Roussillon; William of Montpellier; William, count of Forez; Raymond Pelet; Centonius [Col. 0266D] of Béarn; William Amaneu; and many others, whose names, though we do not possess them, are nevertheless certainly written in the book of life. For they left country, kindred, friends, and widely spread estates, followed Christ, and embraced voluntary poverty.

All these, following the aforesaid venerable men with every reverence, descended into Italy. Having passed through Lombardy, they went through the region called Friuli, crossed into Istria near Aquileia, and finally descended thence into Dalmatia. Dalmatia is a far-extending region situated between Hungary and the Adriatic Sea. It has four metropolitan cities: Zara, Salona—also called Spalato—Antivari, and Ragusa. It is inhabited by a most fierce people accustomed to robbery and slaughter. [Col. 0267A] It is entirely occupied by mountains and forests, great rivers, and pastures extending far and wide, so that it has little cultivation of fields; its inhabitants place their whole hope of livelihood in flocks and herds. The few who inhabit the seacoasts differ from the others both in customs and language and use the Latin tongue; the rest use the Slavic language and wear barbarian dress.

Having entered this province, they found the journey very difficult, especially because of the pressure of winter and the extreme unevenness of the terrain. They also endured a severe shortage of food and provisions, suffering dangerously from hunger for several days. The inhabitants of the region abandoned their towns and fortified places and fled with wives, children, and all their possessions to the mountains [Col. 0267B] and dense forests, like wild beasts; they feared the sight of our people. Yet, following from a distance and secretly in the army’s wake, they would find elderly and sick persons and very old women, who traveled slowly, separated from the rest, and kill them.

The count, bearing the due responsibility for the entire multitude, sent ahead some of the princes to lead the columns; he himself always marched last with a very large body of armored men and was the last to take lodging. Moreover, the air was cloudy and the darkness continuous, almost tangible, so that those who followed could scarcely keep track of the footsteps of those ahead, while those who went in front could scarcely distinguish the ground before them at the distance of a stone’s throw. [Col. 0267C] For the land, as we have said, abounded in streams and rivers and was almost entirely marshy. Every day it gave off such dampness and such thickness of fog that the air became almost suffocating.

Furthermore, the Dalmatian Slavs, as natives familiar with the country, followed the army from the flank through steep mountain paths and dense forests. Emerging from the woods, they overwhelmed the unarmed people in frequent attacks. The count and the other magnates, however, often charged such men, killing many by piercing them with lances and cutting them down with swords. They would often have killed more, had the forests not been near at hand and provided the fugitives with an immediate refuge.

Yet it happened one day that, after some of the aforesaid evildoers had been captured, [Col. 0267D] the count ordered their hands and feet to be cut off, so that their companions, at least frightened by this punishment, might fear to pursue the army. After three continuous weeks spent in so arduous a journey across part of the region, they came to the place called Scodra and found the king of the Slavs there. The lord count, being a kind, gracious, and merciful man, sought to establish friendship through lavish gifts, hoping to obtain the favor of the natives for his people and thereby at least secure trade and an abundance of goods for sale. Yet even by this means he could not soften the ferocity of that people, whom afterward he found far more savage.

After they had crossed all Dalmatia in great hardship for about forty days, they finally reached Dyrrachium. [Col. 0268A]

## CHAPTER XVIII. At Dyrrachium an imperial envoy meets this count; the Bishop of Le Puy is captured by Bulgarians but, through the Lord’s mercy, is released. Again, at Rodosto, an embassy of both the emperor and our princes meets him.

The emperor, suspecting the count’s arrival because he was a prudent and magnificent man and was drawing larger forces after him, sent well beforehand an embassy of honourable men to meet him at Dyrrhachium, commanding them to greet him most courteously on his behalf and to treat him honourably upon his arrival. Obeying this command, they appeared before him and addressed him gently in speech and by letter, presenting the emperor’s letter, whose tenor was as follows:

[Col. 0268B] “Long ago, most beloved count, the celebrated report of your wisdom and the widely diffused fragrance of your integrity reached the ears of our empire; and, as your merits required, it invited us to affection for you, our intention being to love and honour your person most devotedly. Therefore we have awaited your arrival with great desire, wishing to discuss many matters of public business with your nobility, so dear to our empire. We therefore earnestly advise that, passing through our lands without disturbance or scandal, you hasten to us, secure in our favour and in the manifold honour with which we have resolved to anticipate you. We have moreover instructed the bearers of this letter [Col. 0268C] to arrange that your people may be supplied, on good terms, with an abundance of goods for sale and with continual commerce.”

Both the count and his army were greatly encouraged by this letter. Taking the road again, they passed through forests and mountains and the whole country of the Epirotes; after the toil of many days, they finally descended into a district named Pelagonia, abounding in every kind of provision, and there pitched camp. There the lord bishop of Le Puy, a man of venerable life, having pitched his tents apart at some little distance from the camp in search of more convenient lodging, was captured by Bulgars who attacked him. But because so great a bishop was still necessary to the people of God, by chance, through God’s mercy, he was preserved alive. For while one of the robbers was demanding gold from him, he defended him [Col. 0268D] against the others; and when a tumult arose among them at the sound of their quarrelling, the whole army was stirred. Seizing their arms, they attacked the aforesaid criminal assailants and rescued the lord bishop with his companions.

At last, resuming their journey, they passed through Thessalonica and all Macedonia, and, after unbroken exertions for many days, reached the maritime city of Rodosto, situated on the Hellespont, four days’ journey from Constantinople. There once more an embassy from the emperor met the count, as did messengers from the princes who had gone ahead. They urged and earnestly exhorted him to leave the army behind to follow gradually, while he himself came quickly with a few men, so that, after concluding business with the emperor, he might, when his army arrived, [Col. 0269A] catch up with the others more promptly and cause no hindrance to people wishing to proceed quickly. He too had sent envoys ahead, and on their return they encouraged him to do the same.

## CHAPTER XIX. The count, leaving his army, hastens to the emperor, but reaches no agreement with him. The emperor deceitfully orders an attack upon his army.

Accordingly, overcome both by the urging of the imperial envoys and by the word of the princes who encouraged him to make haste, the count left his army in the care and charge of the bishops and other nobles in the camp. He himself entered Constantinople with a few men, and, having repeatedly been summoned and preceded by imperial apocrisiaries, presented himself to the emperor. [Col. 0269B] There he was honourably received by the emperor and by the distinguished and illustrious men attending him, and was treated with the greatest kindness and every mark of humanity.

Afterwards, assailed with flattering persuasions and much insistence that he should offer the emperor fealty and an oath according to the form followed by the other princes who had preceded him, he most steadfastly refused. Meanwhile, while these matters were taking place at Constantinople, the emperor, angered because the count refused to perform homage to him in the manner of the others, secretly commanded the primicerii of his legions stationed in those regions to fall suddenly upon the count’s army and harass it by every means they could, not even shrinking from carrying out slaughter among them. [Col. 0269C]

He dared attempt this because he trusted that he had bound all the princes to himself by the fealty they had given and because all their armies had crossed that sea, from which it was not easy to cross back. For every ship arriving there, whether for commerce or for conveying people across, was immediately required to leave the farther shore, so that the crusaders should lack ships and think of returning in vain. By flatteries and crafty persuasions, as we have said, he had compelled them to cross one by one, lest, with their forces joined, they might assemble before the city. For he regarded the arrival and union of our people with suspicion and feared it all the more as formidable. What he had bestowed upon the princes as though generously [Col. 0269D] was neither generosity nor favour, but the product of desperate fear and fraudulent cunning. Yet as our people proceeded in simplicity of spirit and sincere faith, they could scarcely be persuaded of Greek malice and of the wicked prince’s persistent deceit and treachery—especially since he abounded toward them in such generosity and feigned favour.

## CHAPTER XX. During the count’s absence his army is secretly attacked by the Greeks. The count is enraged; the emperor, repenting of the deed and fearing for himself, seeks the intervention of the princes, asserting his innocence.

Thus the centurions, captains of fifty, and commanders of military units who had received the emperor’s command executed the imperial order. Having forewarned their troops, they secretly attacked the expeditions of the lord count by night; finding them unprepared and fearing nothing of the kind, they killed many of them, so that before they awoke and seized their arms, shameful flight and miserable slaughter had taken place. [Col. 0270A] At length, however, warned by the more honourable men, our people recovered themselves; regaining courage and strength, they inflicted many losses upon the predatory band of the emperor and its men.

Although for the time and place our men had resisted bravely enough, yet, considering the difficulty of the road and the repeated perils that arose unexpectedly almost every day, they melted inwardly, as men repentant of having undertaken the journey. They grew less and less ardent in what they had begun, being worn out ever more severely by the weariness of their labours, [Col. 0270B] so that not only many common people but even many of the greater men repented of the enterprise. Distrusting the completion of their purpose and forgetting their vows, they planned to return. Had they not been recalled by the warnings and exhortations of the bishops and clergy, and rekindled to pursue their vow, they were ready to abandon the ranks and attempt a return home at whatever risk.

When this was reported to the lord count, he was pierced inwardly with grief of heart and cried out that he had been betrayed. Sending several noble men from among his faithful followers, he charged the emperor with the shameful accusation of treachery, declaring that, while he was in the emperor’s service through his invitation and repeated embassies, the emperor had, contrary to all good custom, ordered arms to be taken up against his army. [Col. 0270C] He also made known to the princes—at whose request and insistence he had hastened on after leaving his army—the lamentable disaster that had befallen his people and the emperor’s utterly manifest fraud, demanding from them, as from brothers, vengeance for these things.

If the count’s power to avenge his men’s wrong had equalled his feeling and will, then beyond all doubt neither threats, terrors, nor the intervention of any princes could have shaken him from the resolve he had conceived. For he was said to be a spirited man, ever mindful of injuries, and one who possessed great firmness of purpose. Seeing, therefore, that the affair had gone too far and repenting of what he had done, the emperor summoned to himself the princes—namely, the lord duke, the lord Bohemond, and the lord count of Flanders—who still remained with their legions on the farther shore of the sea, [Col. 0270D] so that through their intervention he might reconcile to himself the lord count’s anger.

They came at his summons; and although what had happened displeased them greatly, yet seeing that there was no opportunity for demanding vengeance, they privately admonished the lord count and urged him with honourable persuasions to overlook the injury, which they regarded as common to them all, lest, while pursuing vengeance, he undertake a labour of many days and hinder those wishing to proceed on the way of the Lord. At length, through the pious intervention of the princes, the count, as a prudent man, softened his anger and yielded to their counsel, entrusting himself to their decision.

[Col. 0271A] They then met the emperor privately and unanimously declared how grievously they regarded what had happened. Understanding their indignation and the steadfastness of their unanimity, the emperor made his defence before the count and the entire court, both foreigners and his own household, swearing and solemnly affirming that the event said to have occurred had happened neither with his knowledge nor by his command. Nevertheless, notwithstanding this claimed innocence, he said that he was prepared to make satisfaction to the count.

Thus day by day Greek deceit and the emperor’s fraud were more and more exposed, so that there was now no prince to whom it was not manifest, clearer than the noonday light, how great was the hatred with which he pursued our people and how odious to him was the whole Latin race. [Col. 0271B] Yet because their purpose hastened toward other things and they strove after an undertaking more pleasing to God, they judged it safer to overlook the injuries inflicted than to turn aside from so pious a task which they had conceived and undertaken, or to furnish an obstacle to it.

## CHAPTER XXI. Through the princes’ intervention, the count is reconciled to the emperor. He invites the emperor to proceed with the other princes. Those who had crossed the sea advance toward Nicaea. The count follows them immediately.

Accordingly, in obedience to the princes’ exhortation, the count was reconciled to the emperor. Giving, as the others had done, an oath of fealty in the prescribed form, he returned to full favour and was honoured with immense gifts and lavish generosity [Col. 0271C] beyond both number and weight. The other princes too received renewed gifts; taking leave, and especially urging the count not to delay after them, they crossed the Hellespont and rejoined their forces in Bithynia.

Meanwhile the lord count’s army also reached Constantinople and immediately, by his command, crossed over to those who had preceded it and was joined to the other armies. The count himself remained in the city for several days on account of household affairs, at once managing domestic business and, as a prudent man, continuing to be concerned for public matters. For, as the other princes had requested, he frequently and respectfully urged the emperor, [Col. 0271D] as each of them before him had done separately, to accompany those departing and to consent to be the leader and guide of the Lord’s army.

Repeatedly urged by each of our princes, especially by the lord count of Toulouse, to deign to be leader and companion of the Lord’s army and to accept precedence over the peoples who had dedicated themselves to divine service, the emperor excused himself. He said that he had very fierce enemies around him—the Bulgars, Cumans, and Pechenegs—who continually ranged around the borders of the empire, seeking an opportunity suddenly to attack and disturb his peace. Therefore, although participation in so great a pilgrimage and the expectation of a share in its future reward greatly accorded with his desires, [Col. 0272A] he could not abandon the care of his kingdom or provide the surrounding enemies with an occasion for mischief.

But everything he said was deceit and fraud. He alleged these matters for no other reason than that, envying our people’s progress, he wished under some pretext of his devising to withhold his assistance from them and to hinder their advance by every means permitted him. Those who had already crossed the sea—namely the lord Godfrey, the lord Bohemond, the lord Robert, count of the Flemings, and the lord bishop of Le Puy—made up their baggage and prepared again for the march, intending to proceed slowly toward Nicaea and thus wait for those who followed. After travelling for a day toward Nicomedia, the great metropolis of that province, namely Bithynia, the venerable priest Peter the Hermit came out to meet the advancing armies from neighbouring places where he had avoided the rigours of winter. With the few survivors of his own company, he greeted the princes and joined their assembly.

[Col. 0272B] Received kindly by all and carefully questioned regarding the fate of his people, he laid out the matter in order: the people who had gone ahead with him had been stiff-necked, unbelieving, and utterly ungovernable; and the misfortune that had befallen them had occurred more through their own fault than through any act of another. The princes, therefore, sympathizing with him and the distress of his followers, generously bestowed many things upon him and those who followed him. Thus the army was increased, and by God’s grace, as forces from different places joined into one, it became more numerous. Proceeding with suitable discipline, they reached Nicaea. There, arranging their camps in a circuit but reserving places for the princes yet to come, they besieged the city on the fifteenth day of May.

[Col. 0272C] The count of Toulouse, having concluded his business in the imperial city, received leave from the emperor and was again honoured with lavish gifts. With those whom he had kept with him, he pursued the camp with all speed and quickly arrived at the aforesaid city.

## CHAPTER XXII. Robert, count of the Normans, and the lord Eustace, brother of the duke, arrive at Constantinople with their legions and are received by the emperor with immense gifts and great honour. Then, crossing the Hellespont, they join the other princes.

[Col. 0272D]

Meanwhile the illustrious lord Robert, count of the Normans, and other most distinguished men in the same company—namely, the lord Stephen, count of Chartres and Blois, and the lord Eustace, brother of the lord duke Godfrey—sent another embassy to announce to both the lord emperor and their brethren that their arrival would be soon. With them were Stephen, count of Aumale; Alan Fergant and Conan, both men of distinction from Brittany; as well as Rotholdus, count of Perche, and Roger of Barneville.

All these, with many other eminent and noble men, had gone down into Apulia with the count of Flanders and the lord Hugh the Great in the preceding year, [Col. 0273A] about the beginning of the approaching winter. While the others crossed to Dyrrhachium, they, avoiding the severity of the season, spent the winter in convenient places in Apulia and in the regions of Calabria. At last, near the beginning of spring, having summoned their travelling companions and prepared their baggage, they went down to the sea and, following the footsteps of the others, reached Dyrrhachium. From there they continued their journey with all urgency, wishing to make up for the delay they had made in Apulia.

Finally, with the Lord’s help and enjoying the desired calm, they passed through the intervening provinces—Illyricum, Macedonia, and both Thraces—and reached Constantinople. There, called by the lord emperor and entering the palace according to the custom observed by the others, they were received with great honour by him and by the distinguished men attending him. [Col. 0273B] At last, after many discussions, held both jointly with the three and separately with each of them, the emperor urgently sought from them by flattering persuasion and many promises the same thing that he had obtained from the others.

But they kept the example of the others before their eyes, for they had been sufficiently informed of everything before coming to the emperor, saying among themselves, “For we are not greater than our fathers.” Rendering the fealty demanded and taking the oaths according to the form of those offered by their predecessors, they bound themselves to the emperor. Consequently they were received into greater favour and judged worthy to carry away greater gifts. The treasuries having been opened, they received gifts in gold, costly garments, vessels remarkable both for their material and workmanship, and silken fabrics of marvellous and unheard-of value, such as they had never previously seen. [Col. 0273C] These exceeded the measure and worth of our possessions and filled even those upon whom such generosity was bestowed with astonishment.

Burdened with such gifts, they took leave from the emperor, lest they should seem to devise reasons for delaying their travelling companions. Crossing the Hellespont, they hastened toward Nicaea with their legions, where the whole Christian army was encamped. They were received by the princes who had gone before with great embraces of affection and with the eager welcome of all; having obtained their assigned place, they pitched camp.

[Col. 0274A]

## CHAPTER XXIII. A certain Tatinus, intimate of the emperor, joins our princes: a man exceedingly deceitful and notorious for wickedness.

A Greek named Tatinus, very intimate with the emperor, had also joined our camp. He was a wicked and faithless man, his nose mutilated as a sign of his perverse mind. By imperial command he had been designated to be their guide and companion on the road, when our people asked for a guide as a further precaution. He was chosen because he was said to possess complete knowledge of the places [Col. 0274B] and because the emperor placed great confidence in his malice and intricate deceitfulness. He had also joined our princes with a small band of his own men, so that there might not be lacking a goose to squawk among swans, and a perverse serpent among eels.

For he reported to the emperor, with a maliciously distorted interpretation, everything done on the expedition and everything said by each person; and in return, through frequent messengers, he received from the emperor instructions for contrivance and fraud. Here for the first time, out of the different armies which had followed different princes by different routes, through different places, and at different times, there was made one army of the living God, recovering its wholeness from the multitude of parts coming together.

[Col. 0274C] For since those God-beloved commanders and captains of the armies had set out upon their journey, leaving their homes, they had nowhere been granted the opportunity to see one another and confer and deliberate together upon public affairs, until they met and pitched camp before the aforesaid city. There, when the number of the legions was counted, they were found to have six hundred thousand foot soldiers of both sexes and one hundred thousand armoured horsemen. All stood before the aforesaid city, giving every effort to its conquest and consecrating to the Lord, with all devotion, the first fruits of their labours.

# HERE BEGINS THE THIRD BOOK.

[Col. 0273]

## CHAPTER I. Description of the city of Nicaea and its privileges; how Soliman, who ruled there, had gathered immense Turkish forces against our people from the whole East, lying in ambush to attack them.

[Col. 0273D]

Nicaea is one of the cities of Bithynia. It formerly stood in the relation of a suffragan city to Nicomedia, the metropolis of the same region; but later the lord Emperor Constantine the Elder freed it from Nicomedia’s jurisdiction, out of reverence for [Col. 0274D] the first holy synod which assembled there. For in this city, in the time of the lord Pope Sylvester, the venerable Alexander, patriarch of Constantinople, and the aforesaid Emperor Constantine Augustus, the holy synod of three hundred and eighteen Fathers assembled against the impieties of Arius and his followers. Having condemned their destructive sickness and demonstrated the truth to the whole Church of God by the testimonies of the saints, it set forth an uncorrupted rule of faith.

Later, in the same city, in the time of the most pious Emperor Constantine Augustus, son of Irene, the seventh general synod again assembled against the Iconoclasts—that is, the assailants of holy images—under the lord Adrian, bishop of Rome, and the venerable Tarasius, patriarch of Constantinople. In it the aforesaid heretics received, from the orthodox Church, the sentence of condemnation which their treachery deserved. [Col. 0275A]

The city has a most advantageous situation, standing in a plain, though not far from mountains which surround it almost on every side. It has excellent fields, rich soil, and likewise many advantages of woods and groves. A lake of great breadth and immense length lies beside the aforesaid city and stretches westward; along it one may travel by boat from various directions. Swelling in the wind, it beats against the very walls, providing the city with a very great defence. [Col. 0275B] On its other sides, moreover, a ditch encircled the wall, flooded by the flow of springs and streams; this could create a great obstacle for those wishing to approach the city in order to attack it.

Furthermore, it was filled with a warlike population and was exceedingly notable and fortified with lofty, very closely spaced walls and towers, solidly constructed, so that our men, upon approaching, marvelled at the city’s defences and the strength of its construction. The lord of this city, as also of the whole region and the adjacent provinces together, was a very powerful Turkish satrap named Soliman, surnamed Shah—a Persian word meaning “king” [Col. 0275C]—a shrewd and vigorous man.

When he heard of our people’s arrival and was greatly concerned about it, he had gone down into the East long before to seek aid from the rulers of those regions against the approaching forces of the faithful. By persuasion, repeated entreaty, and the provision of pay, he had brought with him innumerable Turkish forces both from Persia and from neighbouring provinces. He hoped, relying on their help, to rescue the aforesaid city and the whole region from their impending danger.

A short time before, Soliman’s uncle, named Belfetofh, the greatest sultan of the Persians, had violently seized all these provinces—which extend for thirty days’ journey from the aforesaid Hellespont to Syria and for an equal journey from our Mediterranean Sea northward—in the time of Romanus, surnamed Diogenes, emperor of Constantinople and third predecessor of Alexius; and he had handed over most of them to the aforesaid Soliman. [Col. 0275D] Soliman therefore possessed, and claimed as his own by right of ownership, all the provinces from Tarsus in Cilicia to the Hellespont, so that he had officials within sight of Constantinople itself who exacted dues from passersby, collecting the taxes and revenues of the entire region for their lord’s benefit.

He himself, with the multitude that he had gathered at such labour, was in the neighbouring mountains, scarcely ten miles from our army, [Col. 0276A] seeking an opportunity to attack our people while preserving the safety of his own men and to free the city from their pressure.

## CHAPTER II. Our people attack the city fiercely, but the citizens retain free passage across the lake. Soliman sends the citizens a letter of encouragement.

When our armies reached the aforesaid city, they began to attack it fiercely, though their troops were still confused and their camps had not yet been arranged in settled order. Nevertheless, those present assigned fixed places to themselves and suitable places to those still to arrive, devoting all their efforts especially to denying the citizens entrance and exit. But the lake joined to the city, as stated above, greatly impeded their purpose. [Col. 0276B] Embarking and disembarking in prepared vessels, the citizens travelled unharmed at will to different places. Since our people had absolutely no supply of ships, they could in no way hinder these movements. Yet they took every possible measure to prevent approach to the citizens by land, watching all roads and entrances with utmost vigilance.

Now Soliman, learning that his city was troubled by siege, sent two of his household to travel by boat down the lake to the city. To console the citizens and more fully encourage their resistance, he sent them the following encouraging message:

“The arrival of this fortunate barbarian people, which has presumed to set a siege around our city, need not make you greatly afraid. For we are stationed nearby with a great company of brave and noble men, awaiting still greater forces which are following us. Soon, when our strength has been gathered together, we shall suddenly attack their camp. Therefore you too be ready, so that, while we attack from without, you may also come out with the entrances opened and press them unanimously, bringing us aid. [Col. 0276C]

“Nor should you be alarmed at their numbers. Coming from distant regions and from the setting of the sun, they have been wearied by the long duration of their journey and the expense of their exertions. They have neither horses able to bear the weight of war nor strength and determination equal to ours, who have come fresh. You yourselves remember how easily we triumphed over their immense multitude, putting more than fifty thousand of them to destruction in one day. Take courage, therefore, and do not fear: tomorrow, before the seventh hour of the day, you will receive full consolation, delivered from the enemy.”

[Col. 0276D]

## CHAPTER III. The bearer of the letter is captured and reveals all the enemy’s secrets to the princes. The count of Toulouse, who alone was absent, quickly arrives after being summoned by the other princes.

Accordingly, the men who had been sent, seeking where they could most conveniently put out by boat, put in along the shore. While looking about for a more suitable landing-place, one was suddenly captured when our men rushed upon them; [Col. 0277A] the other perished in the tumult, pierced by a sword. The captured man was brought unharmed before the princes and, through threats and terror, was compelled to confess everything plainly: for what purpose and by whom he had been sent. His report established that Soliman had sent them to announce his arrival to the citizens; that he was stationed nearby with immense forces assembled; and that on the following day he would secretly attack our camp.

When the commanders of our legions learned that Soliman was hastening to arrive, they ordered the man in question to be committed to custody. They sent swift messengers to warn the lord count of Toulouse and the bishop of Le Puy, who had not yet reached them, to hurry as quickly as possible. Having received their brethren’s message, these men did not delay through anxiety. Rejecting every delay and travelling throughout the whole night, very early before sunrise they entered the camp with a great multitude, banners raised, in the gleam of arms and with great noise. [Col. 0277B]

They had scarcely put down their baggage in order to establish themselves with the others in their assigned place when, about the third hour, as the man held in chains had foretold, Soliman descended from the mountains with immense cavalry forces—estimated at fifty thousand—and advanced into the plain, intending to approach the city. Seeing this, our people immediately rushed to arms. Trumpets gave warning; the blare of horns roused the cohorts; they drew up their forces and re-formed their battle lines. Observing in full the discipline of warfare, of which they had complete experience and familiar practice, omitting nothing that circumstances required, they prepared to meet the enemy. [Col. 0277C]

## CHAPTER IV. Soliman descends from the mountains and violently attacks the camp; his army is overthrown; tokens of victory are sent to the emperor, who rewards the princes.

Soliman, having sent forward a certain battle line of ten thousand cavalrymen, hastened toward the southern gate, which had been assigned to the lord count of Toulouse for its guard. He did not know of the count’s arrival, and, as he had supposed yesterday and the day before, [Col. 0277D] he believed he would find the gate undefended; but his expectation was frustrated, for he found there forces almost greater than elsewhere.

Still ignorant of all this, he hastened to the aforesaid place and attacked the legions of the lord count with great force, though they had scarcely yet put down their baggage. They received him remarkably; his efforts were shattered and his first battle line was completely broken, and its men had already turned to flight. Then Soliman followed with greater forces, restoring courage to those who had already dispersed and compelling them to return with him once more against our people.

But the duke, the lord Bohemond, and the count of Flanders, with their contingents armed to the last detail, saw that greater enemy columns and denser squadrons had arrived and that the count’s army was being strained beyond its strength by their oppressive numbers and fierce pressure. They attacked unanimously and hurled themselves upon the enemy legions, pressing them at close quarters with swords and lances. [Col. 0278A] Although the enemy seemed to retain strength and courage to resist for about one hour, after roughly four thousand of them had been killed and some captured, they turned to flight.

Having gained this first victory through the Lord’s help, our people continued the siege, their camps set around the city without interruption. From that day onward, neither Soliman nor any ruler of the unbelievers dared attempt anything similar so long as the siege lasted. The aforesaid princes performed excellently in that battle; likewise the lord Tancred, Walter of Garlande, seneschal of the king of the Franks, Guy of Porsessa, and Roger of Barneville won renowned fame in that action.

To strike fear into the enemy, our people ordered many heads of the slain to be hurled into the city by missile engines; and, sending a thousand of these heads and several captives to the emperor, they thereby gained much favour with him. [Col. 0278B] He accordingly sent a substantial sum of money and various kinds of silks with great generosity to reward the leaders of the armies, ordering that provisions and goods for sale should be brought to them in every abundance and without delay.

## CHAPTER V. The princes occupy their assigned positions, and the city is besieged and attacked on every side; certain nobles fall in battle.

[Col. 0278C]

Our princes judged it expedient for their purpose to surround the city with siege works on every side, as stated above, and to place the princes in suitable positions, so that pressure assailing the citizens from all directions might more easily compel them to surrender. By common counsel, they divided the circuit into equal portions, assigning one portion to each prince. They stationed the lord duke with his two brothers and their legions on the eastern side.

The lord Bohemond, with the lord Tancred and the other princes who had followed him, whose names we set down above, again occupied the northern part of the city with his army. [Col. 0278D] The count of Flanders and the Norman prince, with their own cohorts, were stationed next to them in order. The southern quarter assigned to Raymond, count of Toulouse, and the bishop of Le Puy was occupied by them with their companions. Next to them the lord Stephen, count of Blois and Chartres, had placed his camp with the lord Hugh the Great and certain other illustrious and noble men.

Thus, with the city enclosed on every side, the princes decided to procure from the neighbouring forest suitable timber for their needs, and to construct with all speed machines fit and necessary for undermining the wall, commonly called *scrofae* (“sows”); likewise missile engines, called in the common tongue *mangana* (“mangonels”), and stone-throwers. [Col. 0279A] Calling in craftsmen, they diligently exerted every effort, so that when the work had been completed, they might strive to attack the city.

While they laboured intensely at this, and had attacked the city in hostile engagements for a period of seven weeks, one day, in a battle appointed according to custom, they lost by a wretched misfortune two noble, distinguished, and valiant men in arms: the lord Baldwin, surnamed Calderon, struck by a stone, and the lord Baldwin of Ghent, struck by an arrow, as they fought most courageously in the assault on the city. Afterwards, when by counsel and decree of the princes the army again renewed the attack, William, count of Forez, and Galo of the Isle, ardently assailing the enemy in that battle, were pierced by arrows and died. Guy of Porsessa also, a nobleman from the kingdom of the Franks, was seized there by a grave illness and gave up the flesh. [Col. 0279B]

The people of God, deeply distressed at their fate, honourably committed them to burial, rendering them, out of piety and charity, such funeral rites as are customarily offered to noble and distinguished men.

## CHAPTER VI. A certain engine set against the wall is crushed by the citizens, and many of our people perish beneath it. The lake obstructs our efforts.

Again, on a certain day, while all the princes round about were vying with one another in applying their engines to the wall, and striving by every means in their power to weaken the walls and make for themselves an entrance—eschewing, after the manner of valiant men, idleness and slothful leisure—Count Herman and Henry of Ascha, noble and renowned men from the kingdom of the Germans, by the strenuous exertion and great courage of their retainers and household, applied to the fortifications a certain very skilfully constructed engine. The machine was framed of oak beams, and stout walls had been woven about its perimeter, so that twenty exceptionally strong knights admitted within it seemed able to stand secure from every discharge and cast of missiles, even the largest millstones sent in to undermine the wall. But at last, when this machine, as has been said, had been brought up to the walls, the townspeople above, pressing hard in defense of the wall, shattered it so completely with the impact of great stones that, its joints having come apart, it crushed all who were beneath it. The whole army therefore grieved for the aforesaid nobles, because the labor of many days had been spent uselessly, and not without expense; it grieved also for the brave men who had perished by so miserable an accident. Yet they comforted one another with the hope of obtaining victory, and especially because they did not doubt that a better life would befall those who laid down their lives for Christ in such a cause. For they considered it, not without reason, the equivalent of martyrdom to lose one’s life in such a struggle. Therefore, despising death and counting this present life as nothing, they exposed themselves more confidently to every danger, made more courageous by that hope.

[Col. 0280A] The princes accordingly pressed on unanimously with the assault upon the city on every side; and each considered it glorious to show himself diligent in the quarter assigned to him and to harass the besieged still more. The work raged exceedingly, and through continual engagements and almost unbroken fighting, the citizens were denied repose. Yet the lake adjoining the city greatly impeded our efforts and held their exertions short of the desired result, furnishing the citizens with every kind of comfort. For by sailing over it they brought in supplies of food and provisions more freely, and sometimes introduced a multitude of cattle, in sight of our men, who were unwilling to oppose them.

## CHAPTER VII. Our men bring ships from the sea on wagons; they take possession of the lake; the citizens marvel at our men’s device and despair.

[Col. 0280B]

The God-beloved princes therefore assembled and deliberated particularly on this point: by what means they might more advantageously meet this difficulty. At length it was agreed by common counsel that a very large part of the people, together with several divisions of knights, should be sent to the sea, in order to drag thence to the lake ships—either intact or taken apart in sections—upon carts and wagons, or by whatever other contrivance might be devised; otherwise, their efforts being rendered fruitless and their labors and expenditures consumed, the undertaking would come to nothing.

Those to whom this task had been assigned reached the sea; and, the Lord mercifully directing their routes and purpose, they found ships of a moderate size. Having obtained them readily from the lord emperor, they drew them out of the sea and placed them on the dry shore. Then, joining three or four wagons together according as the length of the ships required, and placing the ships upon them, within the space of one night they hauled them for seven miles or more as far as the aforesaid lake, using ropes laid upon the shoulders and necks of men and horses. Among them were some not at all small vessels, but such as could carry one hundred or fifty fighting men. When the ships had been received and launched upon the lake, the Christian army rejoiced beyond measure. The leading men hastened to the lake, brought in rowers skilled in navigation, and placed aboard with them men brave in arms and commendable for courage, having the utterly certain hope that, with the Lord as author, they would shortly possess the city.

But when the citizens saw upon the lake more vessels than usual, they were astonished and uncertain whether this were an equipment of their own people, intended to bring them aid, or of the enemy. At last, when they learned that our men had brought the ships from the sea with much labor, transported them by land, and put them into the lake, they marveled both at our men’s strength and at their contrivance, by which they had brought to completion a desperate and almost impossible undertaking.

## CHAPTER VIII. The city is again attacked on every side. The Count of Toulouse strives to weaken, by engines and every art, a tower facing him; but, the citizens resisting, the work is consumed.

[Col. 0281A]

Thus, after the citizens’ movement over the lake had been forestalled by the introduction of the fleet, it was publicly decreed and proclaimed that each division, as it had been placed under particular princes, should once more arm manfully for the attack upon the city and inflict on the citizens, with greater urgency than usual, as much injury as it could. Accordingly, the several princes encouraged their forces and sent them, armed, into battle; and an assault far fiercer than customary took place. Pressing the engines more vigorously, some strove to undermine the wall, while others hurled great millstones in an effort to weaken the fortifications.

[Col. 0281B] In the southern quarter, assigned to the lord Count of Toulouse for attack, there stood a tower distinguished above the others alike by height and thickness, beside which the wife of the aforesaid Soliman was said to have her dwelling. For several days the count had devoted all his efforts to overthrowing it, but without result. Though he had assailed it continuously with the shots of two missile-engines, the solidity of its construction prevented him from dislodging even one stone. Therefore, lest he should seem defeated and abandon what he had begun, he redoubled his efforts and multiplied the engines also; hurling greater masses of stone and rocks of astonishing hardness, he began to make fissures in it, until, worn by blows, it was reduced to dust.

[Col. 0281C] Seeing this, the army joined forces, encouraged one another, crossed the rampart, and, drawing near to the wall, strove to throw down—or at least pierce—the aforesaid tower. But the citizens, having learned that the tower threatened to collapse, filled it inside with stones and mortar, so that, if the wall undermined or weakened by engines should happen to fall, a new work might take the place of the old and impede those who wished to penetrate within. Our men, meanwhile, sheltered beneath an exceedingly solid covered engine which they had forcibly brought alongside the wall, endeavored to undermine the wall. At length, with iron tools and much labor, they made an opening through which two armed men could readily enter.

[Col. 0281D] The citizens, on the other hand, were fully prepared to resist the attackers’ importunate pressure, opposing contrivance to contrivance and strength to strength with no lesser spirit. With bows and crossbows, every kind of weapon, and the throwing of hand-stones, they strove to drive the enemy away and repel the attacks made upon them.

## CHAPTER IX. A memorable deed of Duke Godfrey. The citizens set fire to our engines; the lamentable fate of a certain nobleman.

Among those defending the wall against the attackers was a man more audacious than the rest, remarkable also in bodily stature and strength, who wrought great slaughter among our men with his bow. Moreover, puffed up by the success he had enjoyed for too long, [Col. 0282A] he assailed our men with insults and reproaches, calling them indolent and charging them with cowardice. He raged thus importunately in the sector assigned to the lord duke and his divisions for attack. The illustrious man, Lord Godfrey, could not endure this. Taking up a crossbow and seeking a suitable position, he aimed at the aforesaid taunter and, sending a bolt through his vital parts, struck him down dead upon the ground, repaying him with a just return for all that he had inflicted upon our men.

This deed greatly terrified the man’s companions in that work, who, encouraged by his example, had been resisting more boldly in that quarter; so that they hurled missiles and shouted insults less and less. Yet others, who in the remaining sectors labored more diligently in defense of the city, knowing nothing of this deed, nevertheless defended themselves from towers and walls with all diligence, striving with all their strength to inflict slaughter and wounds upon our men. They also directed pitch, oil, fat, and other substances that commonly supply fuel for fires, together with burning torches, against our machines; and in the many places where these were not more carefully guarded, they consumed them.

[Col. 0282B] Those, however, whose diligent labor had been directed in the southern sector toward the overthrow of the aforesaid tower continued their care and effort. But when they saw that all they had undermined in the wall on the preceding day had been repaired during the following night, they began to grow less determined, seeing that they were making no progress. And when they were nearly abandoning the undertaking, behold: a very brave and noble knight of the army of the Count of the Normans, wishing by his own example to encourage the rest, armed with mail and helmet and covered by a shield, crossed the rampart and fearlessly approached the wall. He intended to tear down the new masonry of stones which the citizens had set in place that same night and reopen the breach made on the previous day.

[Col. 0282C] But while the citizens above pressed upon him with every violence, none of the others dared come forward to bring him aid, nor could he accomplish his intention. For he was crushed beside the wall by great masses of stones and perished, our men looking on and unwilling to assist. Raising his lifeless body to themselves with iron hooks, they cast it down within the walls to be exposed to the mockery of their people; at last, having stripped it of mail and helmet, they threw it back outside the walls to our men.

[Col. 0282D] When he had been committed to burial with the due funeral rites, the people mourned for him, greatly praising his courage and regarding his death as precious in the sight of the Lord. They did not doubt that through it his soul would be joined to the chosen spirits; for, as we have said, all shared one mind and the same conviction: that those who fell thus in battle deserved eternal life and would be placed in the predestined light among the portion of the saints.

## CHAPTER X. A craftsman offers himself to the princes; he constructs an engine, undermines a tower, and brings down what he has undermined.

Meanwhile, according to the custom they had established among themselves, [Col. 0283A] the God-devoted princes of our divisions assembled. Having discovered that they were making no progress but were instead consuming their labor and effort to no purpose, they carefully considered among themselves, after putting the matter to deliberation, what counsel was needed in so great a necessity. While they persisted in this, suffering much anxiety, a certain Lombard by nation came to the princes. Seeing that the devices of all craftsmen were frustrated and that labor was being wasted without fruit, he professed skill in this art. He declared that, if sufficient public funds and necessities were supplied to him for completing the work, he himself, with the Lord as author, would within a few days throw the aforesaid tower to the ground without loss to our men and provide a broad open entrance for all who wished to enter.

Public funds were therefore supplied in every sufficient measure, and a suitable wage was also assigned as recompense for his labor. With the material furnished as he desired, he constructed a machine of marvelous ingenuity, so that those within it could bring it beside the wall without danger to themselves, despite the enemy’s opposition, and, concealed inside, need not fear to undermine the wall. This he demonstrated all the more fully by the actual result.

[Col. 0283B] Having constructed and equipped the engine on every side according to his wish, he assembled beneath the same machine brave mail-clad men furnished with arms and iron tools necessary for undermining the wall. With his workmen he placed it very skilfully and ingeniously beyond the rampart and brought it up against the fortifications. The citizens, however, persisting in their accustomed boldness, hurled great millstones and cast fire upon it. But because of the steep height of its roof and its sloping sides, these could not adhere so as to damage those underneath; consequently they began to despair of their customary means of assistance, marveling at the strength of the engine, which they could in no way harm, and at the craftsman’s contrivance.

[Col. 0283C] Those sheltered beneath that covered engine, entirely secure from the enemy’s attacks, applied all their strength to breaking through the wall and overthrowing the tower. In place of the stones they had dislodged, they set posts and timber supports, lest, once the lower part of the wall had been undermined, the upper part should suddenly collapse and crush the machine, which could by no means bear the weight and immense fall of so great a mass.

[Col. 0283D] When therefore so great an undermining had been made as seemed sufficient for bringing down the tower, they set fire to the supports holding up the wall that was to fall, and placed beneath them material fit to feed the flames. Then they abandoned the machine and hurried back to their own people with all speed. About midnight, when all the material of the supports had been consumed and reduced to ashes by the devouring flames, the tower fell with such a crash that it shook even those at a distance with a certain horror; like an earthquake, it troubled hearts and inspired fear. At the sound, the divisions awoke, ran to arms, and took courage, as though they were about to force their way into the city.

## CHAPTER XI. Soliman’s wife flees with her two sons and is captured. The citizens despair; they negotiate surrender with the Greek Tatinus; the princes send messengers to the emperor concerning it.

[Col. 0284A]

Soliman’s wife, who until then had endured with much hardship the troubles of the besieged city, was terrified, in womanly fashion, by the fall of the tower. Having prepared ships, she secretly left the city and intended to remove herself with her maidservants and household to safer places. But our men, who were in vessels on the lake and had been assigned to block the citizens’ entrances and exits, carefully surveying everything in prudent fashion, found her as she departed, captured her when found, and presented her, together with her two very young sons, to the princes. They ordered her to be guarded carefully under close custody with the other prisoners.

[Col. 0284B] The citizens, greatly dismayed both by the opening made accessible to the enemy and by the capture of so eminent a woman, utterly despaired of their strength. They sent an embassy to request a truce from the princes, intending to negotiate with them concerning their surrender. But Tatinus, whom we mentioned above, perceiving—as he was a most astute man—the inclination of a people ceasing to defend itself, assembled the leading men of the city and advised them, in their surrender, to honor the lord emperor. He maintained that this army of pilgrims, now present, was hastening to other business; they had entered upon this siege not as their principal purpose but incidentally and, as it were, in passing. The lord emperor, however, would remain constantly near them; from his very commendable clemency they could confidently expect much and always look for better things.

[Col. 0284C] It was therefore best, he said, that in this matter they should prefer the emperor to men unknown to them and to a barbarian people; thus the surrender, which they could not avoid, should be made into his hand, and the emperor should recover through them the city whose rule he had unjustly lost to Turkish violence not many years before. Persuaded by these and similar arguments, the assembly of citizens chose to surrender the city into the emperor’s hand, together with their own persons and all their property, with their safety preserved.

Yet this was not unwelcome to our princes, since their whole purpose was hastening toward other objectives and it was not their intention to remain attached to these matters. They nevertheless hoped that, according to the terms of the agreements, the spoils of the city would be preserved for the army as compensation for its labor and the losses it had endured. Before they would discuss the terms of surrender or satisfy the citizens’ wishes in this respect, however, our whole army received back into freedom the captive brethren whom the often-mentioned Soliman had taken both from the army of Peter the Hermit at the castle of Civitot and whom the citizens had captured during the siege.

[Col. 0284D] It therefore came about, with the connivance of the princes and the consent of the people, that messengers were sent to the emperor, saying:

> The princes and Christian army who, at the city of Nicaea, faithfully labored in its siege for love of Christ’s name, have, with the Lord as author, compelled it to surrender through great care and urgent exertion. Therefore, addressing ourselves to your serenity, we earnestly advise and exhort you not to delay sending some of your princes with sufficient forces to those regions, so that they may preserve for the honor of your name the city that has been surrendered and may be able to remove hence the multitude of prisoners. For we, having resigned the city to your highness, shall not delay, with the Lord as author, to continue the journey we have once undertaken.

## CHAPTER XII. The emperor, having sent messengers, receives the city; thanking the princes, he sends gifts. The people are indignant and complain that the agreements have been broken; the emperor restores to liberty, with gifts, those taken to Constantinople.

[Col. 0285B]

On hearing this, the emperor, joyful and rejoicing, sent to those regions certain of his household, in whose loyalty and ability he trusted, with large forces, to receive the city and fortify it once received. They claimed for him all the property of the prisoners, whether gold and silver or any kind of household goods. He sent magnificent gifts to each of the princes and sought their goodwill by letters and by spoken words, offering them great thanks for so honorable a service and for so great an increase of his empire, gained through them.

But the common people and men of lesser rank, who had labored most zealously in the siege of the aforesaid city in order that they might repair the losses they had suffered from the plunder of the captive citizens and the abundant property found within the city, saw that he did not reward their labors with sufficiently fair recompense. Seeing also that he intended to carry into his own treasury and fisc what by agreement ought to have been made public, they bore it with great resentment, so that they regretted both the labor they had expended and the costs which, as it seemed to them, they had wasted uselessly.

[Col. 0285C] The princes too steadfastly declared that the same emperor had acted deceitfully in regard to the terms of the agreements. For the following clause was said to have been inserted in the series of agreements made between them: if, throughout the whole course of their expedition as far as Syria, by the guiding mercy of the Lord, it should happen that any city formerly belonging to his empire were captured, then, once the city with its adjoining dependencies had been restored to the emperor, the booty, spoils, and all remaining property should pass entirely, without objection, to the armies as recompense for their labor and reimbursement of their expenses.

[Col. 0285D] Although it would have been quite easy and practicable for our men to drive the emperor’s household far from the city and send them back empty to their lord—and although they would have seemed to do so by right, for it is unjust to keep faith with one who strives to act contrary to agreements—nevertheless, keeping the fear of the Lord before their eyes and hastening toward greater things, they passed over the matter by common prudence. With honorable persuasions they restrained the people, who were bearing it with resentment, so that, unencumbered, they might fulfill their purpose.

The Greeks sent for this purpose entered the city, received the citizens’ weapons, and completed the surrender. Then they came out to the camp, stood before the princes, and pleaded for the lives and safety of the citizens, declaring that the citizens had restored the city to the lord emperor and had subjected their necks to the yoke of his authority.

[Col. 0286A] Thus, the city having been taken and forces deemed sufficient for its defense having been assigned, Soliman’s wife and her two sons, of whom we have spoken, together with a great multitude of prisoners, were transported to Constantinople. There the emperor treated them not only mercifully but also very generously, and within a few days restored them to their former liberty. He is said to have done this with the intention both of reconciling to himself the favor of the Turks and of provoking them, by his benefits, to be more inclined toward injury against us; and also of not deterring others, should any city at some time happen to be besieged, from making a similar surrender. The city of Nicaea was taken in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1097, in the month of June, on the twentieth day of the month.

## CHAPTER XIII. The siege ended, the army resumes its journey. The princes separate from one another. Soliman again comes upon them with innumerable forces.

The siege having ended, the army was again summoned by the princes’ command to set out; and, its baggage having been made ready, it began the march on the third day before the Kalends of July [29 June]. After advancing for two days with the divisions together, they happened on that night to encamp beside a certain bridge, following the convenience of water. At earliest dawn, before sunrise, while darkness still remained, they again prepared to march; and after crossing [Col. 0286C] the bridge, whether by chance or intentionally, the princes separated from one another with their forces.

For Lord Bohemond and the Count of the Normans, Count Stephen of Blois, Tancred, and Count Hugh of Saint-Pol took the left-hand route and traveled separately that day. They reached a valley called Gorgoni, and there, beside the bank of a running stream, having the convenience of pasture and grass, they pitched camp about the ninth hour. They spent that night quietly there, though cautiously, having posted guards in a circle. All the rest took the right-hand route, completed that day’s march, and pitched camp in similarly grassy places with convenient water, scarcely two miles distant from the camp of the men aforesaid.

[Col. 0286D] Soliman, mindful of the injury done him and continually recalling how he had lost through them his splendid city, his wife, and his sons, strained with all his strength to repay them in kind and, if possible, lay some ambushes for them. Again gathering immense forces of soldiers, he followed our army on the left, keeping almost equal pace. Having scouts among them to keep him constantly informed of the condition of those advancing, he continually waited for an opportunity to fall upon them. But, learning from those same scouts that the army had been divided and that the other part, which appeared weaker in strength and numbers, was nearer to him, he judged that he had found a suitable moment and came down from the mountains with that innumerable company of his men.

[Col. 0287A] Scarcely had the dawn of the following sun announced its coming and the denser shadow of night begun to disperse before the approaching light, when those stationed on watch, so that they might discern from afar whatever enemy ambushes there might be and warn the army, saw the enemy. They sounded their trumpets and, running with the greatest speed, announced that the enemy were at hand. Thus all the divisions, awakened by the trumpeters’ blast and the heralds’ cry, ran to arms and made ready their horses, as if they were about to fight at close quarters. It was morning, on the very day of the Kalends of July [1 July].

The whole multitude was accordingly arranged in battle lines; commanders of fifty and centurions were placed over the individual companies, and chief officers were appointed over the wings of infantry troops. Their baggage and impedimenta, together with the whole helpless multitude of old men, women, and the infirm, were stationed, as though in safety, beside a neighboring reed-bed, screened by carts and wagons, so that the fighters might advance more freely to battle.

[Col. 0287B] Messengers were sent to the remaining part of the army, from which they had rashly separated, earnestly warning and exhorting them to hasten, and informing them of the great straits in which they stood. When, according to military discipline, everything in Lord Bohemond’s camp appeared to have been arranged in order, behold: about the second hour of the day Soliman arrived, bringing with him innumerable Turkish battalions. What seemed more astonishing to our men was that, in this multitude—said to exceed two hundred thousand men—not one person except a horseman could be found. Our men, as has been said, had with them divisions of both kinds indiscriminately.

## CHAPTER XIV. Battle is joined. William, Tancred’s brother, falls; Bohemond’s entire army is brought into the utmost peril; Tancred is nearly captured.

As the Turkish army approached, such tumult arose in the camp that scarcely anyone’s speech could be heard. The clash of weapons, the noise of horses, the dread sounds of trumpets and drums, and the cries and howls of the men themselves competing with one another seemed to rise to the stars; and these things struck great terror into divisions unaccustomed to and less practiced in such warfare.

[Col. 0287D] The Turkish battle lines then rushed upon our army and discharged such a multitude of arrows that they filled the air like hail; scarcely anyone in our divisions could be found unwounded. Hardly had one cloud of arrows descended from the bows before another, no less thick, was released; whatever the first had left untouched, the second did not leave unharmed. Our men, to whom this kind of warfare was unfamiliar—and therefore harder to endure because less tested by experience—saw their horses failing beyond remedy and themselves dying from sudden wounds, from which they could take little precaution. Charging the enemy with swords and spear-points, they strove to drive them away.

But the enemy, unable to sustain the force of the charge, deliberately scattered in different directions, in order to elude its impact; finding no one opposed to them, they returned to their own men, frustrating the hope conceived by our forces. When our men returned to their own side with their effort unsuccessful, the Turks again formed up together; sending forth anew a multitude of arrows like rain, they left scarcely anyone untouched by a deadly wound.

[Col. 0288A] Nevertheless our men resisted as best they could, protected by mail, helmets, and shields; but their horses and the unarmed populace were struck down everywhere, without distinction. In that battle almost two thousand notable men of both orders fell. Among them was William, a young man of distinguished promise, son of the marquis and brother of Lord Tancred; fighting bravely for his own men, he died pierced by an arrow. Robert of Paris also, a man valiant in arms, ended his life by the same kind of death. Lord Tancred likewise, striking among the enemy, prodigal of his life and forgetful of his station, was scarcely and forcibly rescued from the hazards of death by Lord Bohemond, against his will and unwillingly.

The enemy battalions therefore gained strength; and, as our men were nearly failing, their bows hanging from their shoulders and their use neglected, they pressed forward at close quarters with swords. Thus, the companies having been broken, our men took flight and returned to their baggage and impedimenta. There, gathered round the carts and wagons amid the thickness of the reed-bed, they supposed they might find some refuge.

## CHAPTER XV. The remaining princes arrive; they aid their oppressed brethren; Soliman is put to flight; his army perishes; our men carry off exceedingly rich spoils. The army is reunited.

[Col. 0288C]

While the army of the faithful was thus afflicted and Lord Bohemond’s force was utterly collapsing in failure, behold: the illustrious and magnificent men Duke Godfrey, Count Raymond, Hugh the Great, Baldwin and Eustace, the duke’s brothers, and other God-devoted princes, leaving the infantry multitudes of their own camps with every kind of baggage behind them, came swiftly to aid their men, bringing with them forty thousand excellently armed knights.

When they reached Lord Bohemond’s camp, those who had almost already been overcome took heart again and, their strength restored, returned once more to the contest.
