Seeking to avenge the injury done them and to redeem their earlier reverses, [Col. 0288D] they rushed more boldly upon the enemy and pressed them manfully with swords. Those whom they had previously feared as if superior, they struck down with a strong right hand, now unable to resist.

The bishop of Le Puy, with the other ministers of the same office, admonished the people and exhorted the princes not to relax their hands, but, certain that victory would be divinely granted, to avenge the blood of the slain and not allow the enemies of the faith and of the Christian name to glory longer in the slaughter of the faithful. With these and similar words the men of God incited the people to battle and infused into their minds whatever strength they could.

[Col. 0289A] Our men therefore charged with greater violence than usual and pressed more fiercely with swords; breaking up the enemy formations, they put them to flight, not without innumerable slaughter. They pursued the fugitives with such relentless pressure that, for three or four miles beyond the enemy camp, which had been pitched in a fertile valley, they continued to kill them. Thus, after the enemy had been scattered in great confusion and very many killed, and after some captives whom they had been forcibly carrying away from among our men had been recovered, they returned to the enemy camp. There they found boundless stores of gold and silver, most ample quantities of provisions, flocks, herds, droves of asses and pack animals, troops of camels such as our men had never previously seen, some horses, and pavilions and tents of varied colors and unheard-of forms. Carrying all these things away with them, laden with most abundant spoils, they returned to their own camp, driving off booty and taking trophies.

[Col. 0289B] It is said that on that day about three thousand powerful and renowned men, holding the highest rank among the enemy, fell; while among our people, of the common and lowest classes of both sexes, four thousand perished. For the memory of the ancients records that only two of the leading men fell there. The battle was fought from the second hour of the day until the eighth, with varying fortune, on the day of the Kalends of July [1 July], though the forces and numbers were vastly unequal. For those who followed Soliman were said to exceed one hundred and fifty thousand men, counting only horsemen; whereas the number of our knights present and fighting in that great battle scarcely reached fifty thousand.

[Col. 0289C] After so great a victory had been divinely obtained, the armies were summoned back together. In order that they might restore the wounded by granting them some rest, for three consecutive days they tended their bodies in pleasant places with green pastures and cared for the horses, amid every abundance of food and the boundless supplies which the enemy had brought and left behind in flight. In that most perilous crisis our greater princes acquitted themselves excellently; and certain men of lesser rank also won enduring glory in the same action: namely Baldwin of Bourg, Thomas of Fère, Reinald of Beauvais, Galo of Calvomont, Guastus of Beders, and Chirardus of Cheresi. From that day it was decreed by common counsel that thereafter, with their formations united, they should march together in an indissoluble bond, so that they might share adversity and enjoy prosperity together.

## CHAPTER XVI. Having entered Pisidia, the divisions suffer exceedingly from lack of water. The army is miserably endangered.

After they had made the necessary halt there for three days, as we said above, for themselves and their horses, the trumpets sounded again; they prepared to resume their march and continue the road upon which they had begun. Having crossed the whole of Bithynia and entered Pisidia, while seeking a shorter route they happened to descend into a dry and waterless region. There, worn down by the twofold distress of excessive heat—such as blazing July commonly brings—and grievous thirst, [Col. 0290A] the people began almost to perish. It is said that on that day more than five hundred persons of both sexes gave up their breath from the anguish of thirst and the violence of the heat.

It is related that on that day something occurred which no other history records: pregnant women, constrained by the extremity of thirst and the violence of the heat, were forced to bring forth their offspring before the time appointed by nature. Overwhelmed by distress, they cast their children into the camp—some alive, some dead, others half-dead. Others, possessing a greater measure of maternal feeling, clasped their children and rolled along the roads; forgetful of their womanly sex, they uncovered their private parts, being more concerned by the imminent danger of death than to preserve the modesty due to their sex.

Nor did the stronger sex avail the men greatly, [Col. 0290B] as, fainting from sweat and heat, with mouths open and nostrils gasping for air, they sought against the urgency of thirst a remedy of moisture which they could not find. Nor were human beings alone exposed to such great dangers. The beasts assigned to carry burdens, and every other kind of animal, their inward parts dried up and the vital passages blocked, refused their service. Nor did their masters’ care benefit the delicate birds by whose prey and flight the nobility are accustomed to be entertained—nisus-birds, namely hawks and herons—for they breathed out their life in their owners’ hands.

Even the little dogs, keen of scent and suited for hunting, their masters’ darlings, abandoning the masters to whom they had been accustomed faithfully to cling, panted and thirsted and perished everywhere [Col. 0290C] along the roads. And what was far more perilous than all this: the trusty horses, companions in battle, in whom their lords placed much confidence for their own safety, and which had formerly displayed their spirit with hoof and teeth, collapsed under the pressure of thirst and the danger of excessive heat as though they were worthless pack animals.

At last, when all were suffering so severely from lack of water, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation mercifully came to their aid. For the river so long desired and so diligently sought was found at last. Reaching it, they hurried competitively toward the water in their excessive longing; and there, finding an abundance of water such as they had wished for, they exceeded all measure in drinking and fell into a graver danger. For many who had escaped the peril of thirst, as commonly happens in such circumstances, setting no limit to the avidity [Col. 0290D] of their drinking, found in the abundance of water the death which they had seemed to escape. Nor did many animals alone perish through this mishap, but many human beings as well.

At last, with the Lord’s help, delivered from these dangers, they descended into a region sufficiently rich and fertile, most delightful with streams, groves, and pastures. They pitched camp in grazing places near Lesser Antioch, which is known to be the metropolis of the aforesaid Pisidia.

## CHAPTER XVII. Certain princes separate from one another and range through the surrounding regions. The duke, fighting a bear, is nearly killed.

Here for the first time certain princes deliberately separated themselves from the army, leading off separate forces. [Col. 0291A] The first of these was Lord Baldwin, the duke’s brother; with him were Count Peter of Staden, Count Rainard of Toul, his brother Baldwin of Bourg, and Guillebert of Montclair, with seven hundred horsemen and several companies of foot soldiers. The second was Lord Tancred; with him were Richard of the Principate, Robert of Ansa, and certain other noble men, with five hundred horsemen and some infantry as well.

Yet all had one and the same purpose: to test the roads, reconnoitre the surrounding regions, try their fortune, and report to the princes who had sent them whatever outcome circumstances of place and time might bring about, so that the army might advance more prudently and with less danger. Leaving the camp, they first continued along [Col. 0291B] the royal road, passing the neighboring cities of Iconium and Heraclea. At length turning to the right, they began hastening toward the seacoast.

The duke and the other princes who had remained in camp, drawn by the pleasantness of the place in which they had encamped and by the nearness of the woods, entered the forests eagerly for hunting, in order to grant themselves some recreation amid so many hardships and to withdraw, if only briefly, from the consuming cares by which they were continually troubled. There, carried by diverse paths toward different desires, they encountered various turns of fortune.

Among them the duke too, entering the woods for recreation and exercise, happened upon a bear of enormous and dreadful size. The beast was fiercely pursuing a poor pilgrim carrying dry wood, who scarcely found refuge from the face of his pursuer and proclaimed with loud cries the danger threatening him. By chance the duke was present; being exceedingly compassionate toward his brethren, he rushed swiftly to bring aid to the sufferer. Seeing the duke approach with his sword, the beast disregarded the man whom it had been pursuing and turned, armed with teeth and claws, upon a stronger enemy. At length, when the duke’s horse had been dangerously wounded, the duke was left on foot, yet continued to press the attack with his sword.

The bear, however, confronting him with open jaws and a terrifying roar, held the duke’s advance in contempt and, scorning the sword, tried to close with its adversary in hand-to-hand combat. The duke, thrusting back its charge with his sword, strained with all his strength to pierce it with the blade. [Col. 0291D] But the bear avoided the sword, bound him in an embrace with its forelegs, and tried to throw him to the ground, so that, once he lay beneath it, it might more easily tear him with teeth and claws.

Truly an outstanding knight, not abandoning his sword, and being a man of very great strength, he seized the beast with his left hand and with his right drove home the point. Plunging the sword in up to the hilt, he brought death upon his struggling opponent. Yet, himself wounded and most dangerously injured in the leg, he gained a victory bought at great cost in blood. Weighed down by his wound and weakened by excessive loss of blood, he lay upon the ground and could not raise himself.

At length the aforesaid poor man, who had escaped death through the duke’s aid, cried out and reported to the army what had happened. The whole people ran thither, where it was said that the brave champion, the defender of the armies, lay wounded. [Col. 0292A] Placing him upon a litter, the other princes carried him back to the camp amid the groans and tears of all, applying the attentive care of surgeons, by whose skill and effort, with suitable remedies, he might recover fully.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The Count of Toulouse falls mortally ill. The army passes through Lycaonia and reaches Marash. Baldwin’s wife dies.

At the same time the distinguished and illustrious Lord Raymond, Count of Toulouse, was also seized by a grave illness and likewise carried upon a litter. He became so severely afflicted that, when set down upon the ground, he almost breathed his last, as though about to die. Therefore the venerable Lord William, bishop of Orange, [Col. 0292B] rendered to him, as though already dead, the offices due to the souls of the faithful.

Thus the armies of such great men, seemingly deprived of the counsel of their leaders, almost fell into despair of completing their journey and fulfilling their vows. Deeply concerned for their condition, all with one spirit and with tears poured out prayed to the Lord that they might be restored to health. Prayers for them were offered in the celebration of the divine offices by that whole pilgrim Church. The merciful Lord graciously heard their supplications and desires; favorably granting the wishes of the people who prayed, He restored them to health and complete recovery.

Having thus crossed Pisidia, they entered Lycaonia and reached Iconium, the metropolis of that region. Finding it deserted, they suffered the greatest [Col. 0292C] scarcity of provisions. For when the Turks learned of our people’s arrival, they had no confidence of resisting in any of their cities. Rather, after stripping their cities and laying waste the whole countryside, they fled with wives and children, flocks and herds, and every sort of possession to inaccessible mountains. Their sole hope was that our people, worn out by scarcity of food, would hasten through their territories.

Nor were they deceived in this expectation, since our people, fleeing the barrenness of the region and the lack of provisions, hastened their march as much as possible. Passing thence through Heraclea, they arrived at the city of Marash and pitched camp, remaining there for three continuous days. There the wife of Lord Baldwin, the duke’s brother, who had been worn down by a long and severe illness, and whom he had entrusted to his brethren when he departed, was called from this present light and rested in the Lord with a blessed end. [Col. 0292D] She was a noble lady of English descent, named Gutuera, commendable in life and character; they buried her there with honorable funeral rites.

## CHAPTER XIX. Tancred descends into Cilicia and besieges Tarsus. He honorably receives Baldwin, the duke’s brother, when he comes into the same region.

Meanwhile the wholly commendable Lord Tancred, following shortcuts by chance and the first to arrive in Cilicia, besieged Tarsus, the metropolis of that province, with those who had followed him. Cilicia is one of the provinces [Col. 0293A] included in the East. According to ancient authorities, we call the diocese of Antioch the East. Cilicia has Coele-Syria on the east and Isauria on the west; on the north, the ridges of Mount Taurus; and on the south, the Cyprian, or Myrtoan, Sea.

It contains two metropolitan sees: Tarsus, the homeland and birthplace of the Doctor of the Gentiles, of which we are now speaking; and Anazarbus, each with its suffragan cities. Thus there are rather said to be two Cilicias, First and Second. According to ancient traditions, Tarsus is said to have been founded by Tarshish, the second of the sons of Javan, son of Japheth, the third son of Noah; evidence for this is the city’s name, derived from that of its founder.

Solinus, however, thinks otherwise concerning the city’s founder, saying in the forty-third chapter of *On Marvels*:

> Cilicia has Tarsus as its mother-city, founded by Perseus, the most noble offspring of Danaë. The river Cydnus cuts through this city; some have related that it rushes down from Mount Taurus, others that it is diverted from the channel of the Hydaspes.

Yet both accounts may be true: Tarshish may have first founded it, and Perseus may afterward have rebuilt or enlarged it.

After Lord Tancred and his men had persisted in this undertaking for several days, he compelled the citizens, both by threats and by persuasive promises, [Col. 0293B] to admit his banner and set it upon the highest tower, thereby seeming to give a sign of their impending surrender. This was upon the condition, however, that he would keep them unharmed until the arrival of Lord Bohemond and the larger army; that he would not meanwhile compel them against their will to leave their homes or abandon their property; and that they, upon that lord’s arrival, would surrender the city to him without difficulty. This proposal seemed good and acceptable to Lord Tancred.

The aforesaid city, like the entire rest of the region, had Christian inhabitants, namely Armenians and Greeks, except for a few men who exercised military authority and governed the fortifications, oppressing the people by violent lordship. The faithful were not permitted to bear arms, but devoted themselves to trade and agriculture.

Meanwhile Lord Baldwin, the duke’s brother, with those who had come with him, having followed byways, suffered the most severe [Col. 0293D] scarcity of provisions. At length, after many wandering circuits, he happened to reach a mountaintop from which he could freely survey the land of Cilicia below, with its cities as far as the sea. Having learned that there was a camp near Tarsus, he supposed it to be the enemy’s encampment and began to fear for his journey. Nevertheless, wishing to discover whose region it was and whose camp he had seen from afar, he descended with his whole company into the plain in his customary boldness.

But Lord Tancred, forewarned by those whom he had stationed on higher lookout points and guarding against enemy ambushes, summoned his companions and took up arms. Thinking that these were enemy troops bringing aid to the city, he met them without fear, trusting in the Lord; and, raising his banners and encouraging his men by exhortation, he advanced to meet the newcomers. [Col. 0294A] When, however, they drew near one another from both sides and looked each other over, they recognized that the arms were not hostile. Approaching more confidently, they rushed into each other’s embraces; and after welcome conversation together, they returned with their joined forces to the city to continue the siege. There Lord Tancred received them with great hospitality and full charity, and that night they enjoyed a generous feast of the flocks and herds he had gathered from the neighboring country.

## CHAPTER XX. Baldwin orders Tancred’s banner cast down from the citadel of the city and sets up his own there. Tancred departs in anger. Guelfo occupies Adana.

[Col. 0294B]

When morning came, Lord Baldwin and those with him saw Lord Tancred’s banner set upon the upper citadel of the city. Spurred by envy and forgetful of their profession—by which, as though brothers of one womb, for as long as they had travelled together, they had maintained unity of spirit in the bond of peace and had resolved to maintain it perpetually—they were angered that Tancred, in their presence, should have presumed to introduce his banners into the city, though they possessed forces much stronger and more numerous.

Lord Tancred, being a modest man, wished to soothe their indignation and maintained that what had been done regarding his banner did not in the least bring dishonor upon them. For before their arrival, and before there was any expectation of their arrival, he had secured those terms with the citizens by his own strength. But Lord Baldwin, prompted and urged as far as possible by his companions, did not distinguish the merits of the case. Instead, led beyond what was proper by his own temper, he provoked Lord Tancred with insolent words and arrogantly carried the matter so far that they nearly turned their arms against each other and inflicted mutual slaughter.

Calling the citizens to him, he publicly threatened that unless they removed Tancred’s banner and raised his own in its place, he would deliver the city and all its suburbs round about to destruction, against the will of the man who had pledged them security. [Col. 0294D] Seeing that Baldwin’s forces were far more numerous and vastly stronger, the citizens, on the same terms and under the same agreement which they had previously made with Lord Tancred, cast down the former banner and placed Lord Baldwin’s upon the same citadel.

When Lord Tancred saw this, deeply affronted by so great an injury, he rightly conceived indignation. Yet, with sounder judgment and godly patience, he restrained his feelings, fearing that an excessively dangerous discord might arise among the ranks of the faithful. Breaking camp, he withdrew to the neighboring city named Adana. On arriving there, he was not permitted to enter, for a certain Guelfo, a Burgundian by nation, had gained possession of that city. Separated from the larger army with others, he had led a party apart; happening upon that city, he had driven out the Turkish forces and occupied it by force.

When Lord Tancred learned that the aforesaid city had, by God’s aid, come into the power of our people, he sent messengers to ask the lord of the city to open entry for himself and his companions, for the purpose of lodging and purchasing necessities of life. [Col. 0295A] They were admitted, and all that was necessary for life, both for themselves and for their horses, was supplied in sufficient quantity, partly without charge and partly for payment. For the aforesaid Guelfo had found that city overflowing with gold and silver, flocks and herds, grain, wine and oil, and every convenience.

## CHAPTER XXI. Tancred forcibly takes Mamistra in the same region.

At dawn Lord Tancred entered the city, followed the royal road, and hastened on his journey. [Col. 0295B] With all his company he arrived at Mamistra. Mamistra was one of the noble cities of that province, distinguished by towers and walls, a numerous population, rich fields, fertile soil, and exceptional pleasantness.

Pitching camp beside it, within a few days he attacked the city with continual assaults and unceasing combat. With God’s aid, having slain the unbelievers found in it, he captured it by force. There he found inexhaustible stores of riches and every abundance of provisions. Distributing appropriate shares among his men according to the quality of their services, he enriched them all. Redeeming the scarcity of food they had suffered through welcome abundance, they freely supplied food for themselves, their horses, and all their draught animals, restoring their bodies with rest [Col. 0295C] and provisions alike.

## CHAPTER XXII. Baldwin occupies Tarsus. Three hundred of our men perish miserably before the city gate.

But after Lord Tancred’s departure, Lord Baldwin repeatedly urged the people of Tarsus, mingling forceful threats with his admonitions, and ordered that the city be opened to him and his company admitted. For he did not think it honorable to remain idle and sit uselessly occupied until the army’s arrival.

When the citizens saw that Tancred had been unable to resist him, and that, if they refused, he would attack the city at close quarters, they made a virtue of necessity. Distrusting their own strength, they opened the gates and admitted Lord Baldwin [Col. 0295D] with his entire company. They assigned to him two towers for his temporary occupation, while the rest of his companions were received as guests throughout the city in the houses of the faithful. The Turks who governed the city still held other towers under their own control. Although they were more numerous and still quietly possessed the stronger defenses of the city, they distrusted the company of our people whom they had admitted and had no hope of relief. They therefore sought an opportunity to escape secretly with their wives, children, and every kind of possession.

That same night three hundred men from Lord Bohemond’s expedition, following Tancred, arrived at the aforesaid city. [Col. 0296A] By Baldwin’s order they were forbidden entrance into the city. Wearied by their long journey and lacking necessities, they urgently begged for the hospitality of the city and the opportunity to buy provisions. Those within, men of lower rank, sympathized with their brethren and added their prayers; but the newcomers were not admitted because they were said to belong to Bohemond’s household and were hastening to Tancred’s assistance.

Nevertheless, the people inside did not fail in fraternal compassion. Since they could not go out, they lowered bread in baskets and wine in skins over the wall by ropes, providing sufficient means for the men to pass that night. Thus, settling themselves as best they could before the city gate, because they were not allowed to enter, they rested.

That same night, when both those within and those outside had given themselves to sleep and were enjoying welcome rest in the deep silence of the night, the Turks and other unbelievers in the city departed secretly and silently through the opened gates with their wives, children, male and female servants, and all their household goods, abandoning the city. They could not live comfortably with the guests whom their people had received, since they suspected their cohabitation; yet departure was open to them, for they retained one or two city gates in their power. But in order to leave behind them a bloody victory over their enemies, after sending ahead all their baggage and impedimenta, they slaughtered nearly all those whom they found outside the gate, burdened with sleep. [Col. 0296C]

## CHAPTER XXIII. The people take up arms against Baldwin, but are eventually pacified. A fleet of Western men arrives at Tarsus.

When morning came and the full light of day had spread abroad, those who had rested in the city arose and found it empty. Astonished at the enemy’s secret flight, they inspected the walls and entrances, diligently seeking by what way they had left. While examining every detail carefully, they discovered the slaughter that the departing Turks had wrought upon the servants of Christ. Struck with deep pain and rightly overwhelmed by grief, they gave themselves to lamentation. Dividing from one another, [Col. 0296D] the lower class took up arms against Lord Baldwin and the leaders, laying upon them the death and destruction of their brethren because they had denied to their companions on the road the favor of hospitality, which rightly extends itself to all who are in need.

Thus the people, stirred by just indignation, made an attack and rushed upon their chiefs. Unless the latter had withdrawn into the higher towers, the people, nearly equal in number, would have repaid the slaughter outside by slaughter among their own leaders. At length, when the disturbance and the schism which had arisen among the people for a just cause were becoming more serious, Baldwin anxiously began to labor to calm the tumult, defending himself before the people.

After peace had therefore been obtained for the moment and silence ordered, the armed foot-soldiers’ crowd rested somewhat; then he began to plead his cause, declaring himself innocent and swearing and protesting that he had excluded them from the city for no other reason than because he had pledged his faith that he would admit no one until the duke’s arrival. [Col. 0297A] Consequently, through the intervention of certain nobles and by gentle persuasions—necessary, however, for the time and place—the people were calmed and rested for a while, Baldwin having been reconciled to the common people.

After they had remained there for several days in complete tranquillity, the scandals having been quieted, behold: a fleet was seen on the sea, scarcely three miles distant from the city. Horsemen and foot soldiers alike hurried competitively down to the shore. Speaking with the sailors from the coast, they learned from their account that they were men of the Christian profession.

Asked concerning their homeland, they answered that they came from Flanders, Holland, and Frisia. In those regions they had practiced piracy for eight years, but at last, pierced in heart and repentant of their sins, they had put out upon this sea for the sake of prayer, intending to journey to Jerusalem. [Col. 0297B] Learning that they were faithful men, the others invited them into harbor; welcoming them with the giving of hands and the kiss of peace, they brought them, after securing the fleet, as far as Tarsus.

One of them was a leader named Guinemer, from the district of Boulogne, in the land of Count Eustace, father of Lord Godfrey. When he recognized Lord Baldwin and knew that he was the son of his lord, he resolved to leave the fleet and go with him to Jerusalem. He was exceedingly rich, having become wealthier through the wicked craft he had long practiced, and had many men in his service. Bringing the greater part of them with him, he resolved to follow Baldwin. Accordingly, after arranging from both companies a sufficient guard of five hundred men for the city, they determined again to advance and try their fortune.

## CHAPTER XXIV. After taking Tarsus, Baldwin comes to Mamistra. He and Tancred fight one another, but are soon reconciled.

As they proceeded and did not abandon the royal road, it happened that they came to Mamistra, which, as we said above, Lord Tancred had shortly before forcibly occupied and held [Col. 0297D] with a strong hand. Arriving there and thinking that they would not be admitted into the city, they lodged outside in the suburbs.

Tancred, hearing that Baldwin had pitched his camp near his city, was exceedingly angry. Remembering the injuries which he had undeservedly suffered from Baldwin, he raged in spirit; inflamed with anger, he summoned his men to arms, ready to make fitting repayment for all that Baldwin had inflicted. First sending a number of archers to wound or seize and carry off their horses scattered through the pastures, he himself suddenly rushed into their camp with five hundred armored horsemen. Before they could take up arms, he had almost crushed them all.

At last they took up arms and made ready to resist, and a bitterer battle occurred, each side fighting more fiercely. [Col. 0298A] As the forces fought one another with excessive hostility, many fell, and some were captured on either side. At last Lord Tancred’s force, inferior in strength and numbers and unable longer to bear the weight of battle, turned and fled to take refuge in the city.

Between the aforesaid city and Lord Baldwin’s camp was a river crossed by a very narrow bridge. When Lord Tancred’s household hastened to return to the city, the bridge’s narrowness created an obstruction, and many of both ranks perished, while others took refuge within the city. And perhaps, as hatreds burned on both sides, they would have suffered greater losses, had not night fallen and ended the conflict.

There were captured from Lord Tancred’s company Richard of the Principate, his kinsman, and Robert of Ansa, noble and distinguished men, by whose counsel and urgings Lord Tancred had hastened to the aforesaid vengeance. From Lord Baldwin’s household, the distinguished and noble man Gillebert of Montclair was captured. [Col. 0298B] Because these men were missing, the forces on both sides were greatly troubled, thinking that they had died in the previous day’s engagements.

At last, when the rising sun restored daylight on the following morning, their hatreds subsiding and their indignation somewhat softened, they remembered their profession and returned to their senses, divine mercy looking upon them. Sending an embassy and seeking terms of peace, they restored the captives on both sides, made mutual satisfaction to one another, and returned to full friendship, joined by the kiss of peace. [Col. 0298C]

## CHAPTER XXV. Baldwin returns to the larger army. Tancred attacks and takes all Cilicia. Neighboring princes hasten to win his favor with gifts.

Thereupon Lord Baldwin, with all his company, returned at his companions’ urging to the larger army, which had already reached Marash, as we said above. For he had heard how greatly and through what dangerous chance the duke had suffered before Antioch of Pisidia; therefore, deeply concerned for his safety, he wished by being present to learn more fully of his condition.

Tancred, however, taking with him the remaining people who had arrived [Col. 0298D] in the fleet, and strengthened by these additional forces, ranged throughout all Cilicia. Every enemy stronghold he found there he stormed and burned, putting to the sword the enemies found within them. Coming to the place named Lesser Alexandria, he likewise took it by force after storming it and subjected the whole region to his authority.

When the satraps dwelling in the mountains, both Armenian and Turkish, heard that Tancred, with strong power and a numerous army, was subjecting the whole province to himself, they feared that he might ascend against them also, capture their peoples, and overthrow their towns. They hastened to win his favor and form an alliance of friendship by sending embassies in competition with one another. In order more easily to bring their purpose [Col. 0299A] to fulfillment, they sent immense gifts of gold, silver, horses, mules, and silk stuffs, making treaties and turning aside the anger and indignation of so great a prince by abundant generosity. [Col. 0300A]

Thus he was a man successful in all things; the Lord was with him and directed all his works as those of a faithful servant.

# BOOK FOUR BEGINS.

[Col. 0299]

## CHAPTER I. Baldwin, the duke’s brother, having returned to the larger army, at Pancratius’s urging again takes up arms, descends into the northern region, and occupies the whole country as far as the Euphrates.

[Col. 0299A]

[Col. 0299B] While Tancred was thus manfully subjecting all things in Cilicia to himself, and while the larger army had already arrived at Marash, the aforesaid Baldwin, having seen the brother for whose sake he had returned to the army and learned of his recovery, grew restless again. Stirred by rivalry with Tancred and envious of the courage publicly celebrated in him, he gathered companions and again proposed to set out and try new adventures.

But those whom he approached on this matter had heard how, relying upon a larger company, he had swollen with malice against Lord Tancred at Tarsus in Cilicia; they feared to go with him. For that fault had made him almost detestable to everyone. Had respect for the duke not restrained them, Bohemond and his men would not have left unpunished [Col. 0299C] the injury he had inflicted upon Tancred. It therefore happened that he found few companions for that journey.

His brother, the servant of God, severely rebuked him. Baldwin acknowledged his guilt with every humility, promised fitting satisfaction to the noble man for what he had done, and received pardon because he had offended contrary to custom and more through another’s prompting than from an impulse of his own. Thus he was reconciled to the favor of all. In other respects he was a man wholly commendable, and no report of such conduct concerning him was heard again.

Now a certain noble Armenian named Pancratius was intimate with him. Baldwin had made him his companion at Nicaea after Pancratius escaped from the emperor’s prison, and had always retained him as a companion of his journey. [Col. 0299D] This man was brave in arms, but of perverse faith and exceedingly deceitful. At almost every hour he pressed Lord Baldwin insistently to take up arms and go with him into a country which he could easily occupy with few men.

At last, having joined to himself two hundred horsemen and a considerable body of people, and with the aforesaid Pancratius as guide, he set out toward the north and entered a most wealthy region. The inhabitants of that region professed Christianity and worshipped the true God, except for a few men dwelling in the garrisons, who treated the faithful people at their pleasure; these people were forbidden to bear arms.

Entering the region, Baldwin found the Christian inhabitants abhorring the rule of the unbelievers and surrendering their fortresses to him. [Col. 0300A] Within a few days he gained possession of the entire country as far as the great river Euphrates. His name became so formidable to the surrounding enemies that they abandoned even fortified strongholds of their own accord and fled, though no one pursued them.

[Col. 0300B] The faithful who received him gained such courage from his presence, and from courage such confidence, that, as is written in the prophet: “One would put ten to flight, and two ten thousand” (Deut. 32:30). Nor did the common people alone thus cleave to him in spirit; the Christian princes of those regions also allied themselves with him. Cooperating in his purpose, they devotedly offered him their service with combined forces and resources.

## CHAPTER II. His fame spreads far and wide; he is summoned by the citizens of Edessa. Having crossed the Euphrates, he hastens there, suffers ambushes on the road, and the people of Edessa meet him and bring him into the city with great rejoicing.

After these things, when several days had passed, [Col. 0300C] report went abroad and spread far and wide through the neighbouring provinces the name and deeds of the illustrious man, proclaiming his commendable valour, faith, and steadfastness of spirit. This report reached the citizens of Edessa and, as the rumour grew, filled their whole city: that such a great prince had arrived from the Christian army as might utterly break the yoke of their servitude and restore them to liberty. Therefore both those who governed the city and the elders, in whom resided all the authority of that city, sent an embassy and endeavoured by letters and word of mouth to summon him to themselves.

Edessa is a noble metropolis of Mesopotamia, called by another name Rhages. This is the city to which the elder Tobias [Col. 0300D] sent his younger son Tobias, to demand from his kinsman Gabael ten talents of silver, which he had lent him while the latter was still a child. Immediately after the Lord’s Passion, its citizens received through the apostle Thaddaeus the saving teaching of Christ, being in all respects found worthy both of the preaching of so great an apostle and of the Saviour’s letter, which He sent in reply to their king Abgar, as is found in the first book of the Ecclesiastical History written by Eusebius of Caesarea. Persevering in the purity of faith which they had received from the beginning and from the times of the apostles, they endured the yoke of unbelievers only to this extent: that they were compelled annually to pay them tributes and taxes; and they were compelled to ransom by almost unceasing exactions their vineyards, fields, and all estates situated outside [Col. 0301A] the city. Yet within the city no one except a believer dared reside.

For this city alone, among all the cities of that region, remained in its unimpaired freedom, neither subdued by the unbelievers, who had long since occupied the surrounding provinces, nor tolerating any inhabitant of a different profession. But living outside, in neighbouring cities and frontier strongholds, they inflicted such troubles upon the aforesaid citizens that they were unable to leave the city or transact their affairs outside it.

A certain Greek by nation governed this city, a man much worn down by old age and without children of either sex. From the time when the entire province was subject to the empire of Constantinople, he had been sent to that city [Col. 0301B] as governor; and, when the Turks came before the term of his governorship had elapsed, he was compelled by necessity to remain and continued his jurisdiction, since he himself could not return home and the people could not compel him to withdraw from administration. Yet he was a useless ruler, unable either to repel injuries from his subjects or to secure any peace for them.

The citizens therefore conferred among themselves, though with his knowledge and good will, and sent envoys, as stated above, to Lord Baldwin, so that he might provide some remedy for their troubles. When Baldwin understood the request of the people and elders, he took counsel with his own men and agreed. Preparing for the journey, he crossed the Euphrates with only eighty knights, leaving the rest of his household on this side of the Euphrates, throughout the castles and towns which the lord had bestowed upon him, [Col. 0301C] for their protection.

Now the Turks who dwelt beyond the Euphrates, having learned beforehand of his arrival, prepared an ambush for him. There was on the road a town ruled by an Armenian; Baldwin withdrew into it in order to avoid the ambush laid for him, and was kindly and hospitably received by the lord of the place. When he had rested there for two days and did not dare proceed, the Turks, who had lain there in ambush for the two days and had grown weary of a longer delay, suddenly appeared before the said town with their banners raised and in stronger squadrons, violently carrying away the booty they found in the neighbouring pastures. Since our men were inferior both in number [Col. 0301D] and strength, they did not dare go out against them, but kept themselves within the town. At last, on the third day, when the Turks had departed and returned home, Baldwin continued the journey he had begun and arrived at Edessa. There he was met by the aforementioned governor of the city, with all the clergy and people; amid trumpets and drums, hymns and spiritual songs, he was received with great honour and the favour of all.

## CHAPTER III. The governor of the city, repenting of what he had done, envies Baldwin’s successes; he tries to break the agreements, but finally, overcome by the people, fraudulently adopts him as his son.

But the governor who had caused him to be summoned began secretly to reflect upon the honour and favour which the people had shown to the newcomer, and to envy him; and he recoiled from the terms of the agreements [Col. 0302A] which he had first proposed. For he had summoned Baldwin on the understanding that, during his lifetime, he should be an equal participant in all the city’s goods, revenues, and taxes, and that after his death Baldwin should possess everything in its entirety. But changing his purpose, he began to offer this: if Baldwin would furnish aid to the city and its citizens against Turkish aggressions and ward off violence, he himself would assign, at the discretion of a good man, an honourable annual recompense for his labour.

Baldwin utterly rejected this proposal, unwilling to earn wages from him as though he were some common soldier, and prepared to depart. But when the citizens learned of it, they hastened to the same governor, warning and urgently pressing him not on any account to let so great a prince, so necessary to their liberty, leave; rather, in accordance with the earlier terms of the agreement, he should bind him to themselves, so that henceforth both he and the whole city might enjoy the peace they desired. [Col. 0302B]

Seeing the unanimous urgency of common people and elders, and the ardour of affection which they had conceived for Baldwin, the governor judged it dangerous to resist and oppose their requests. Therefore, though unwilling and viewing Baldwin’s entry with suspicion, he nevertheless gave his assent. Under the pretext of an increased recompense, he adopted Baldwin as his son and, in the presence of the citizens, solemnly bestowed upon him an equal share in all his goods for as long as he lived, and the entire succession after his death. The people rejoiced, placing in Baldwin all their hope of complete liberty.

From that day, trusting in Lord Baldwin’s protection, they recalled more freely than before the injuries they had suffered from the governor and resolved in their hearts to avenge them whenever place and opportunity should arise—a resolution whose subsequent outcome made most evident.

## CHAPTER IV. At the citizens’ request he besieges Samosata. The citizens conspire against their useless governor, remembering the injuries he had inflicted upon them.

Near them stood a most ancient city, exceedingly well fortified, called Samosata. It was ruled by an unbeliever, a Turk by nation named Balduc, a valiant man in arms but deceitful and wicked. He inflicted many troubles upon the said citizens, repeatedly imposing tributes, taxes on their fields, and manifold forced services; [Col. 0302D] and, to secure all this, he held their children as hostages. Showing these children no humanity, he compelled them to serve him in mud and brick-making.

Because of these troubles, all the citizens fell at Lord Baldwin’s knees and unanimously prayed, striving with tears to implore him to deign to protect them from Balduc’s oppression and to bring it about that they might recover their children, whom he held against their will. Baldwin wished kindly to grant this their first request, and thereby to win greater favour among the people. Having summoned the people and armed them, he came in strong force to the place mentioned. There, after attacking the city for several days in frequent engagements and with great persistence, [Col. 0303A] while the Turks within resisted stoutly and relied upon the fortifications of the place, he saw that he made no progress. He therefore left seventy knights in a nearby position, somewhat fortified, to give the people of Samosata no rest and continually lay ambushes, while he himself returned to Edessa.

The citizens saw that Lord Baldwin was a valiant man and successful in all things. They judged it unworthy that one who deserved, as liberator of the city and founder of its peace, to possess all things and order everything at his discretion should have as his equal in the city a useless man. They therefore summoned Constantine, a noble and powerful man who held very strong fortresses in the neighbouring mountains, and jointly resolved that, once their governor had been killed, they would establish Lord [Col. 0303B] Baldwin as their governor and sole prince.

For the citizens hated the governor, as his deserts required. He was said to oppress them with many vexations, violently extorting gold, silver, and every valuable thing from them. If anyone tried to resist, he immediately stirred up against that person the hostility and hatred of the Turks by giving them money, so that they feared not only that their vineyards, gardens, and crops would be burned, and their flocks and herds carried away, but also that they would frequently be in danger of their lives.

## CHAPTER V. The Edessans kill the aforesaid governor and set Baldwin over themselves as lord; Baldwin in turn purchases Samosata at a great price from Balduc, who ruled it.

[Col. 0303C] Therefore, assembling together, mindful of these evils and seeing that through the guest whom they had received a greater path lay open toward gaining the liberty long desired, they rushed to arms by agreement. They attacked with great force the tower in which the governor resided, fiercely seeking to pull it down. Seeing the people’s ardour and the indignation justly conceived against himself, the governor summoned Lord Baldwin and, anxious for his life, begged him to intercede with the people for his safety, pouring out his treasures for that purpose.

Baldwin wished in good faith to avert from him the citizens’ violence and restrain them from that purpose. But when he saw that he achieved nothing and that the people were becoming ever more enraged, he returned to the governor and earnestly warned and urged [Col. 0303D] him to provide in whatever manner he could for his life and safety. The governor, however, like one in despair, sought a remedy where none existed. Lowering himself by a rope from a window, he was pierced by a thousand arrows and died before he reached the ground. They dragged his dead and lifeless body through the streets and cut off its head; even so, they scarcely satisfied the indignation conceived against him.

On the following day, though Lord Baldwin was unwilling and resisted, they set him over themselves as lord, swearing bodily oaths to preserve their fidelity. They solemnly introduced him, with every mark of glory, into the city’s citadel, and delivered to him all the treasures and the immeasurable riches which the governor had amassed over many past years; the whole city was then settled in peace. [Col. 0304A]

Balduc, whom we have said governed the city of Samosata, saw that Baldwin was advancing from day to day and subjecting the whole region to himself. He offered the said city for sale at the price of ten thousand gold pieces. After much deliberation, Lord Baldwin saw both the strength of the place and that it could not easily be overcome by force. He accordingly paid an immense sum and received the city and the hostages of its citizens with great glory. By this action he first won such favour among the citizens of Edessa that they now regarded him not only as lord but as father, ready to fight to the death for his safety and glory.

## CHAPTER VI. He besieges the city of Sororgia. He forcibly captures the besieged city, thereby winning boundless favour among his people.

[Col. 0304B]

In the same province was a city called Sororgia, likewise filled with unbelieving inhabitants and situated near Edessa. It was ruled by a Turkish satrap named Balac. He too inflicted many injuries upon the said citizens and harassed them with continual troubles. The Edessans therefore petitioned Lord Baldwin and readily obtained his agreement to assemble an army and besiege the said city. Accordingly, on the appointed day he set out thither and fulfilled the people’s desire by laying siege to it.

Having encamped around it and set siege-engines in suitable positions with adequate provisions, he began to attack the city more vigorously. But when the citizens saw the man’s determination and lost confidence in their own strength, shaken by excessive fear, they sent an embassy to him and obtained peace on the condition that, when they surrendered the city, their lives and safety should be preserved. [Col. 0304C]

Having received the city, Baldwin left a sufficient number of his own household as its garrison and appointed one of them to manage his affairs there. He imposed an annual tribute upon the citizens and returned to Edessa with great glory. As a result of this city’s capture, the route was opened for those wishing to travel freely from Antioch to Edessa. For, being located in the middle of the road between the said city and the Euphrates, it had formerly obstructed travellers. Having said these things about Lord Baldwin, let us return to what remains to be related concerning the main army. [Col. 0304D]

## CHAPTER VII. Men sent by the main army forcibly capture the city of Artasia. Stirred by this report, the Antiochenes hasten there with a large force; they set an ambush for our men, attack the city, and return without accomplishing anything, though they first fortify the bridge.

Meanwhile, while Lord Baldwin thus laboured in the regions of Edessa beyond the Euphrates, the main army, as has been said, had come through steep mountain passes and valley slopes as far as Maresia. The said city had Christian inhabitants, except for a few who lived in its garrison and treated the rest according to their arbitrary will. Hearing of our army’s arrival, these men were terrified [Col. 0305A] and secretly fled, leaving the city to believers alone. When the army, devoted to God, reached it, they encamped in green pastures before the city walls, strictly forbidding any violence to be inflicted upon the citizens. Thus an abundance of goods for sale was supplied there in complete peace.

Having learned reliably from the natives that another city lay nearby, abounding in every good thing and much more fertile than the rest, held by the Turks and called Artasia, Robert, Count of Flanders, set out thither with all speed by common counsel. He took with him certain nobles—namely Robert of Roseto and Goscelo, son of Conon, Count of Monteacuto—and a thousand armoured men. Upon arrival, he immediately [Col. 0305B] surrounded it with a siege.

The Turks, trusting in the place’s defences, abandoned the city and withdrew into the citadel. But the Armenians and other faithful inhabitants of that city, learning that those who had arrived in such a blaze of arms belonged to the army which they had long awaited with intense desire, were raised to hope of liberty. They seized arms and turned their swords against the Turks who had oppressed them with violent domination for many years. Thus they suddenly killed them all, threw their heads outside, opened the gates, and most devoutly invited the faithful who were outside into the city as guests, supplying them and their horses with necessities in the fullest observance of hospitality.

This city is also called Calquis and, like the aforementioned Maresia, is one of the suffragan cities subject to the see of Antioch. It lies fifteen miles from Antioch. [Col. 0305C] When this news spread far and wide through the region, it stirred up the citizens of Antioch to take arms and prepare themselves to destroy those who had assembled at Artasia, killed its citizens, and captured the city. Chosen from those who had gathered at Antioch for the city’s protection, nearly ten thousand men hurried there with all haste.

As they approached the place, they sent ahead thirty light-armed horsemen with very swift horses, while the rest remained behind in a concealed position to lay an ambush. [Col. 0305D] Those sent ahead ranged freely and excessively before the city of Artasia, as though they were raiders driving off booty, in order to entice our men incautiously into pursuit. Our men inside the city, unable to bear their insolence and excessively unrestrained forays, rushed eagerly to arms. Pursuing them with some lack of caution, they descended upon the ambush deliberately prepared for them. The men emerged from hiding and tried to cut our men off from the city, so that, if they fled there, they could not find refuge from the larger force attacking them.

Yet by the Lord’s aid, our men bravely repelled them and withdrew safe and unharmed, with all their company, into the said city. Seeing that it was no easy task to claim the city for themselves so suddenly, the enemy surrounded it with a siege. But after attacking the city for a whole day and making no progress because those inside resisted stoutly, and hearing also that the main army was approaching, whose arrival it was exceedingly dangerous to await, they adopted the sounder counsel and returned to Antioch, having first fortified the bridge in the middle. [Col. 0306A]

The count and those with him diligently held the city which the Lord had bestowed upon him until the main army arrived. But meanwhile Goscelo, son of Lord Conon, Count of Monteacuto, a youth endowed with excellent character, was seized by a severe illness and died. He was there buried with honourable funeral rites.

## CHAPTER VIII. The main army reaches Artasia; from there, after sending forward men to reconnoitre the roads, they come to the bridge and cross the river despite the enemy.

[Col. 0306B]

Hardly had the Turks who had come from Antioch departed from Artasia at dawn, when news arrived that the main army had entered the territory of that city and encamped not far from it. Concerned for their brothers said to be suffering siege at Artasia, they sent fifteen hundred armoured men to assist them by common counsel, commanding that, if they could gain free access to the city after the siege was raised, Lord Count of Flanders and the other nobles there should leave guards sufficient for the city’s defence and return to the army. [Col. 0306C]

Lord Tancred had also returned from Cilicia, having received the same form of command, after bringing the whole region under his authority. Others likewise returned who had been scattered in every direction and drawn away by diverse undertakings, except Lord Baldwin, brother of the duke, who was prospering more and more each day in the regions of Edessa through the Lord’s mercy leading the way.

Thus, with the army restored and its dispersed parts gathered again, they decreed almost by an edict that henceforth no one should dare separate from the army unless commanded. They broke camp and marched their ranks toward Antioch by the shortest routes. Since a river lay across their road and they had heard that the bridge over it was very strongly fortified, they feared the army might suffer some obstruction there. They therefore ordered Lord Robert, Duke of the Normans, to go ahead with his company and reconnoitre the roads, so that, if any difficulty occurred, he might make it known to the legions following and render the princes better informed on the matter. [Col. 0306D]

The leaders of his army, bearing standards, went before it: noble and distinguished men, commendable in the practice of arms, Lord Evrard of Puyset and Roger of Barneville. The count, separated from the army with his companies and preceding the larger forces, reached the said bridge. It was a stone bridge, solidly constructed throughout, with very strongly fortified towers at both ends. One hundred brave men, valiant in arms, accustomed to the use of the bow and skilled in archery, were assigned to guard these towers and forcibly prevent those wishing to cross from approaching the fords and river.

Moreover, seven hundred horsemen had come from Antioch and occupied the farther bank of the same river, intending to bar our men’s crossing to the utmost of their power. The river over which the said bridge was built is called the Orontes, and in the vernacular is called Fer. Flowing from that place past Antioch, it descends thence to the sea. Some are wont to imagine that it is the river Pharpar of Damascus, but we know that those who assert this are led astray by error. [Col. 0307A] For Pharpar and Abana, rising in Lebanon and flowing through the plain of Damascus past the city itself, hasten eastward, where they are said to disappear in a sandy desert. The Orontes, however, first rises near Heliopolis, otherwise called Malbec, flows through Caesarea and the aforementioned Antioch, and descends into the Mediterranean Sea.

When the Norman count arrived at the bridge, he and his forces were prevented from crossing both by those in the towers on the bridge and by those who occupied the farther bank of the river. A most fierce conflict therefore arose there: our men strove forcibly to cross the river, while the enemy endeavoured to oppose their crossing altogether and keep them away from the fords by sending down a hail of arrows. [Col. 0307B]

While both sides laboured fiercely in this manner, behold, the main army arrived. Learning that the count and those who had preceded him were occupied in battle around the bridge, they quickened their march in order to bring help to their struggling companions, drive out the enemy, and prepare an easy crossing for themselves. When all the legions had arrived, summoned by heralds’ cries and trumpets, they seized their arms and pressed forward with all their strength. The enemy was put to flight, and they forcibly occupied the bridge.

Others, unable to fight beside the bridge because of the narrowness of the ground, so that they might not grow sluggish in idleness, found a ford, crossed the river, and occupied the far bank after expelling the enemy. [Col. 0307C] When the whole army, with wagons, vehicles, and every kind of baggage, had crossed the river, they encamped on this side of the river, five or six miles from the city, on broad, green pastureland. On the next day they moved forward again and, following the royal road between the mountains and the river, pitched camp less than one mile before the city.

## CHAPTER IX. Description of the city of Antioch and its rank.

Antioch is a glorious and noble city, holding the third—or rather the second, for this is much disputed—rank in dignity after the city of Rome. It is chief and governor of all the provinces contained in the eastern region. In ancient times it was called Riblah, the place to which Zedekiah [Col. 0308A] king of Judah was brought with his sons before Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians; there he ordered Zedekiah’s sons to be killed in their father’s presence, and then had Zedekiah himself deprived of his eyes.

After the death of Alexander of Macedon, Antiochus, who obtained a portion of Alexander’s kingdom, surrounded this city with towers and a very strong wall, restored it to a better condition, and ordered it to be named Antioch after himself. He made it the capital of his kingdom and appointed it as the permanent familiar residence for himself and his successors.

Here the prince of the apostles held his episcopal chair and was the first to exercise pontifical dignity, when the venerable Theophilus, a most powerful man in that city, dedicated a basilica in his own house. Luke, who derived his origin from the same city, wrote for him both his Gospel [Col. 0308B] and the Acts of the Apostles; Luke also succeeded Saint Peter as the seventh in the line of bishops in the same Church.

Here too the first assembly of the faithful was held, in which the name “Christians” was established. For previously those who followed Christ’s teaching were called Nazarenes; afterwards, deriving their name from Christ, all the faithful were called Christians by the authority of that synod. Therefore, because Antioch freely and without difficulty received the preaching apostle and was unanimously converted to Christ’s faith, it first discovered and taught the name which, like poured-out ointment, gives off fragrance far and wide. It was given a new name and called Theopolis, “City of God,” so that the city which had previously borne the name of a wicked and impious man might thereafter be called the dwelling and city of Him who had called it to the faith. [Col. 0308C]

It received from the Lord a fitting reward for this: having ruled as teacher of former error over many regions subject to it, it should afterwards have the same regions as suffragans in the way of the Lord and in honourable discipline of conduct. The patriarch of this God-beloved city is said to have twenty provinces under his jurisdiction. Fourteen of these have individual metropolitans with their suffragans; the remaining six are administered, with their suffragans, under two primates, called in common speech *Catholici* (“Catholics”), one of whom is Aniensis and the other Hirinopolitanus, who is of Baghdad.

All these are called by one name, namely “the East,” as may be gathered from the Synod of Constantinople, which states:

> “Let the bishops of the East administer the affairs of the East alone, while preserving the honour of the primacy of the Church of Antioch, which is contained in the canons of the Nicene Synod.”

## CHAPTER X. The province in which it is situated, and a description of its site.

It lies in a province called Syriaceles, recognized as a part of Greater Syria, and has a most advantageous and pleasant position. It extends through valleys, possessing excellent soil and fertile land, nearly everywhere irrigated with streams and fountains, and of singular charm. It slopes westward amid mountains from the east [Col. 0309A] and is about forty miles long; its breadth varies with the terrain from four to six miles.

At its upper end it has a lake formed from adjacent springs, exceedingly rich in fish. It is one mile from the river which runs through the valley and flows into the sea beside the city; from this lake a stream issues and is afterwards led into that same river lower down near the city. The mountains which enclose it on either side, although very high, pour forth sweet, clear waters and, on their slopes and sides up to their highest summits, offer remarkable suitability for agriculture.

The mountain on the south, like the river which passes the same city, is called Orontes, according to Jerome, who says that Antioch lies between the river Orontes and the promontory Orontes. Its lower part, stretching near the sea to an immense height, claims a special name and is called in the vernacular Mount Parlier. Some consider it Parnassus, dedicated to Bacchus and Apollo. Their opinion seems supported by the spring of Daphne, which some deem the Castalian spring, sacred to the Muses and famous for philosophers’ schools according to the tenor of ancient fables. It is said to rise at the foot of the same mountain, in the place called Bohemond’s Ladder, near the said city. [Col. 0309B]

But this opinion is far from the truth. Parnassus is known to be a promontory of the region of Aonia, which is part of Thessaly, as Ovid describes it in the first book of the *Metamorphoses*:

> Fertile Phocis separates the Aonians from the Actaean fields,  
> while it was still land; but at that time it was part of the sea,  
> a plain of waters suddenly arisen.  
> There a mountain, Parnassus by name,  
> with two peaks strives for the lofty stars  
> and rises with its summit above the clouds.

This mountain, however, is called Cassius according to Solinus. In chapter forty-one of his *Polyhistor*, he says:

> Near Seleucia is Mount Cassius, close to Antioch. From its summit, while it is still the fourth watch of the night, the orb of the sun is seen; and after a brief turning of the body, as its rays scatter the darkness, night is seen on one side and day on the other.

But lest the equivocal name Seleucia deceive you, know that there are two cities, each called Seleucia. The first is the metropolis of Isauria, more than five days’ journey from Antioch; the other is near Antioch, scarcely ten miles from it, at the mouth of the river Orontes. That place is today called the Port of Saint Simeon. [Col. 0309D]

The aforesaid spring is called Daphne and Castalian, where a shrine dedicated to Apollo is said to have stood. Pagan superstition used to frequent it in order to obtain oracles and answers concerning doubtful questions. After Julian the Apostate had deserted Christ and the teaching of piety, while he was staying in the region of Antioch on his way against the Persians, he frequently visited the place in order to consult Apollo concerning that undertaking. Theodoret affirms this in chapter thirty-one of the *Tripartite History*:

> “When Julian sought responses from the Daphnean Python concerning victory in the Parthian war, and the god blamed him for the proximity of the body of the martyr Babylas, Julian ordered the body to be removed.”

The same matter is stated somewhat more fully in the tenth book of the *Ecclesiastical History*, as follows:

> “Julian gave another proof of his madness and frivolity. For when at Daphne, in the suburb of Antioch beside the Castalian spring, he sacrificed to Apollo and received none of the answers he sought, he asked the priests of the demon the reason for its silence. They said that the tomb of the martyr Babylas stood nearby, and that for this reason answers were not given.”

Although the said spring is called Castalian, it must not be understood as the Castalian spring also called Pegasaean, Caballine, and Aganippe. [Col. 0310B] That spring is recorded to be in the aforesaid Aonia, according to Solinus, whose words are:

> “At Thebes are Mount Helicon, the grove of Cithaeron, the river Ismenus, and the springs Arethusa, Hypodia, Salmace, and Dirce; but before all others, Aganippe and Hippocrene. Since the first inventor of letters discovered these by the hoof-print of a horse while seeking the places where it had settled, poets took licence to spread abroad both tales together: that the hoof of a winged horse had opened the spring, and that its drink bestowed learning by inspiration.”

The mountain to the north, commonly and customarily called the Black Mountain, appears rich and fertile, irrigated by springs and streams, and offers its inhabitants many advantages in woods and pastures. In ancient times, many monasteries of religious men are said to have existed there; even at present it shelters and sustains many venerable places of those who fear God. [Col. 0310C]

Through the middle of this valley the river already mentioned carries its waters to the sea. The city is situated nearer to, and more directly beneath, the southern mountain, between the mountain and the river. Its walls begin in the higher parts of the mountain and run down the mountain slope to the river, enclosing a vast space containing both the descending side of the mountain and the plain which stretches from the mountain’s base to the river.

Within the circuit of the walls are enclosed two mountains of remarkable height. On the summit of one, which appears the higher, stands an exceedingly strong and impregnable fortress. The two are separated from one another by a very deep but narrow valley, through which a torrent descending from the mountains enters and flows through the middle of the city, providing many conveniences for the citizens. [Col. 0310D]

There are also several springs in the city, chief among them the one at the eastern gate called Saint Paul’s Gate. The spring of Daphne too, three or four miles from the city, is brought in by conduits and an artificial aqueduct, supplying water at appointed hours in many places by an elaborate system. The walls, whether on the mountains, the slope, or the plain, are of very solid construction, extremely thick and of proportionate height, surrounded at equal intervals by numerous towers excellently suited to defence. [Col. 0311A]

In the lower western part, near the far end of the city, the river lies so close to both walls and mountain that the bridge by which it is crossed joins the city gate and wall. Some reckon the city’s length at two miles, others at three. It lies ten or twelve miles from the sea.

## CHAPTER XI. Who was lord there, and how, on hearing of our men’s arrival, they had previously fortified the city by assembling forces from neighbouring cities.

Acxianus, a Turk by nationality, was lord of this most distinguished city. He had belonged to the household of the great and most powerful prince, the Persian sultan—Belfetoh, namely, of whom we have spoken above—who had violently subjected all those provinces to his rule. At length, after subduing peoples and nations, wishing to return to his own country, he distributed among his nephews and household dependants all the provinces which he had claimed for himself, so that, mindful of such great benefits, they might remain bound to him for ever by the tie of fidelity.

In this distribution Nicaea, with its adjacent provinces, was assigned, as stated above, to his nephew Soliman. To another nephew, named Ducac, he granted the city of Damascus, together with its dependent cities and neighbouring territories; and he conferred upon both the title and dignity of sultan—upon Soliman because, bordering on the Greeks, he endured perpetual and uninterrupted conflicts with the empire of Constantinople; upon Ducac because he maintained continual and almost unbroken warfare and a stubborn struggle with the Egyptians, whose growing power and formidable strength were feared by the aforesaid sultan. To one of his servants, named Assungur, father of Sanguin and grandfather of Noradin, he granted the famous city of Aleppo. By the same liberality he granted Antioch, with limited territory, to this Acxianus, of whom we are now speaking. For the Egyptian caliph possessed all the country as far as Syrian Laodicea.

Accordingly, when he heard that so great an army of Christian princes was approaching, Acxianus repeatedly sent messengers and urgently appealed, both orally [Col. 0311D] and by letters, to all the princes of the whole East—especially to the caliph of Baghdad and to the eminent Persian sultan, more powerful than all the rest. It was quite easy and straightforward for him to persuade them to grant what he sought; for they had been warned long beforehand of our arrival. Soliman, who had observed our numbers and unconquerable courage by actual experience and with eyewitness certainty, had made them better informed through a trustworthy report.

Both therefore pressed their requests with great urgency and begged for assistance with abundant tears: the one, that he might avenge the injury inflicted upon him; the other, that he might render his country secure from attack and repel their violence from himself. They promised him aid and the assistance he had invoked [Col. 0312A]—a promise which, as the event later showed, they fulfilled in a faithful sense.

Meanwhile Acxianus, anxious concerning our arrival, gathered and brought in forces from the neighbouring provinces and adjacent cities with all possible diligence. Expecting the siege day by day, he collected stores of food and provisions and assembled weapons. With eager effort he urged the citizens to bring in material for constructing engines of various kinds, iron, steel, and all the other things customarily necessary for such use. Competing with one another in concern for the public welfare and the city’s defence, they applied all possible diligence, so that they might lack none of the things which are accustomed to bring relief to besieged citizens.

They therefore ranged through the district and stripped the suburbs, carrying with them grain, wine, oil, and the other necessities of life, as well as flocks and herds. Thus they filled the city with supplies and, with much foresight and no small labour, fortified themselves against the impending assault of their enemies. Many noble and important men had also assembled there from all the regions through which that same army had passed, fleeing before our forces. Because of the site’s fortification and strength—which seemed impregnable without anyone’s summons—they had resorted to the city in the sole hope of securing safety. Thus, with their numbers enlarged, the city was said to contain, among both citizens and gathered auxiliaries, six or seven thousand cavalry; while the forces of infantry ready for battle [Col. 0312C] were said to exceed fifteen or twenty thousand.

## CHAPTER XII. The deliberation of our princes, and the approach of the expeditionary forces to the city

Seeing that the city lay nearby, our people assembled before approaching it, in order to deliberate concerning the action before them. Some of the princes, because winter was imminent, tried to persuade the others to postpone the siege until the beginning of spring. They maintained that the army was dispersed among cities and castles and could not easily be recalled before spring.

Moreover, it was said that the emperor of Constantinople would send them immense forces [Col. 0312D] as reinforcements, and that a newly arrived army would also come from beyond the Alps. They argued that both should be awaited, so that, with their forces multiplied, they might attain their purpose more easily. Meanwhile the army, divided into detachments, should be sent to more prosperous places for winter quarters, so that, when spring returned, their strength restored and their horses refreshed by fodder, they might again rise stronger for the duties required of them.

Others, however, judged it far more expedient to invest the city immediately and suddenly with a siege, lest, if a delay were granted, the citizens might fortify it more carefully and might have greater leisure to gather larger forces summoned to their aid. In this great debate the party prevailed which argued that the work must be undertaken at once, that delay was dangerous, and that the forces of the expedition must not be separated from one another [Col. 0313A].

It was therefore resolved by common counsel that they should advance unanimously against the city and surround it with a siege. Accordingly, breaking camp and approaching the city, they halted before it and encamped on the eighteenth day of October. Although the number of our people able to draw the sword was said to be three hundred thousand, women and children not included, they nevertheless could not surround the city on every side with their encampments. For, apart from the mountains which, as stated above, enclosed the walls—where no attempt was made to establish camps—the uninterrupted siege could not contain the whole part of the city which extended across the more level ground from the foot of the mountain to the river.

At this arrival of our people and placing of the camps, although our army approached with much uproar—the blare of trumpets, the neighing of horses, the clash of arms, and confused shouting that seemed to rise to the stars—the city remained so quiet throughout that entire day and for several following days that no sound or disturbance was heard from it. One might reasonably have thought it empty of defenders, though it was in fact abundantly supplied both with provisions and with numerous troops excellently armed.

## CHAPTER XIII. The princes are stationed at suitable positions around the city and encircle it with a siege; the citizens are struck with fear

[Col. 0313C] In the part of the city situated on the plain there were five entrances through gates. On the upper side, facing east, was one gate, today called the Gate of Saint Paul because it lay beneath a monastery of that apostle situated on the mountain slope. Opposite it was a second gate, at a distance equal to the city’s entire length: the western gate, today called Saint George’s Gate because it was near that martyr’s basilica.

On the northern side there were three gates opening toward the river. The uppermost was called the Dog Gate and had before it a bridge across which one crossed a marsh adjoining the walls. The second, today called the Duke’s Gate, lay, together with the former, at a distance from the river of about one mile. The third was called the Bridge Gate because there was there a bridge by which the river was crossed. From the aforementioned Duke’s Gate, which was the middle one, as far as this last gate on that side, the river lay so close against the walls that thereafter, continually adjoining the walls, it did not recede from the city.

They left this gate and Saint George’s Gate unbesieged, since the army could reach either only after crossing the river; they invested the other three upper gates with the siege. Lord Bohemond therefore besieged the uppermost gate with those who had followed his camp from the beginning. Below him, Robert, count of the Normans; Robert, count of Flanders; Stephen, count of Blois; and Lord Hugh the Great extended their camps with their Normans, Franks, and Bretons from Lord Bohemond’s camp as far as the Dog Gate [Col. 0314A].

Around that same gate Lord Raymond, count of Toulouse, and the bishop of Le Puy, with the other nobles who had followed their camps and with the countless multitude of Gascons, Provençals, and Burgundians, had placed their camps, occupying all the ground as far as the next gate. Around this next gate Duke Godfrey, with his brother Eustace, Baldwin of Hainaut, Rainard of Toul, Conon of Montaigu—illustrious counts and distinguished men—and the other nobles who had followed his camp from the beginning, together with Lorrainers, Frisians, Swabians, Saxons, Franconians, and Bavarians, placed his camp. He occupied the remaining ground almost to the Bridge Gate, positioned, as it were, in a triangle between the city, the river already adjoining it, and the camps of the other princes.

In that district were orchards, all of which our people cut down, making from them enclosures for themselves and barriers for their horses. The citizens who watched the camps from the towers and walls through the battlements marvelled at the gleam of weapons, the diligent energy of the works, the manner of lodging, the disposition of the camps, and the multitude alarming both in strength and number. Comparing the present time with what had gone before, and the present affliction with their former tranquillity, they feared for wives and children [Col. 0314C], for their ancestral homes, and, what is most precious to mortals, for liberty. They judged fortunate those whom kindly death had removed from such great dangers, and to whom death had been granted lest they be engulfed in so many calamities.
