Thus, day by day, they waited in suspense for the destruction of their own people and the assault upon the city, as though certain that such a siege, which strained with all its strength toward that end, could not be lifted without the city’s ruin and the shipwreck of its freedom.

## CHAPTER XIV. Our people construct a wooden bridge over the river in order to go out more freely for forage. The citizens make sudden sorties against the camp of the count of Toulouse

Those in the camps were accustomed to cross the river out of necessity in order to obtain fodder for their horses and food necessary for themselves, and to go a little farther afield. Since they often hastened there and returned unharmed in complete safety, while the citizens still kept themselves within the city and did not yet venture to range outside, they had made it their habitual practice to cross the river several times a day. This was done with great difficulty, for the river was impassable on foot and had to be crossed by swimming.

The inhabitants of the city, aware of this, often—openly, but more frequently in secret—crossed the river by the bridge and inflicted slaughter and wounds upon our people as they wandered about carelessly and were separated from one another in seeking necessities. They relied chiefly upon the confidence that our people could not easily return to camp, being impeded by the river [Col. 0315A]. Likewise, those in the camps, although they saw their men ill-treated before their eyes, could not readily bring them the desired aid.

The princes therefore judged it altogether expedient to build a bridge there out of whatever material could be found, so that they might more easily counter the enemy’s ambushes and more swiftly receive their men who wished to return to camp. It would also provide their infantry, summoned for their own needs and especially for those wishing to descend to the sea, with a shorter and unobstructed route.

Having found several boats, both in the river and in the upper lake, they bound them together with suitable fastenings. They then laid beams upon them and appropriate wooden material, and covered these above with woven wicker hurdles, so that it provided firm passage even for several persons wishing to cross abreast [Col. 0315B]. From this undertaking the people gained greater convenience.

This wooden bridge stood about a mile from the stone bridge adjoining the city. It was placed near the duke’s camp, opposite the gate assigned to the duke’s custody, which is still called the Duke’s Gate after the man to whom it had been entrusted. Thus his camp lay immediately between the aforesaid gate and the newly constructed bridge.

Nor did dangers threaten our people merely through the bridge just mentioned and the gate adjoining it. Many perils also came upon them through the upper gate, third from that one, which is still called the Dog Gate. As stated above, there was there a stone bridge over a marsh adjoining the city, formed by the continual outflow of the spring at the eastern Gate of Saint Paul, together with the constant course of other channels and rivulets.

Through this bridge night sorties were made into the camp of Lord Count of Toulouse, to whose custody that gate had happened to be assigned; and there were sometimes sudden assaults by day as well. Opening the gate, the citizens launched a sudden hail of arrows; and, after wounding or killing many of his company, they trusted that they could be pursued only by way of the bridge. Having attacked and inflicted slaughter, they at once returned across the bridge to the gate and withdrew unharmed within the city [Col. 0315D]. As a result, the aforesaid count, the bishop of Le Puy, and the other nobles whose camps stood in that quarter suffered a greater loss of horses and much greater damage in horses and mules than did the forces of the other princes.

## CHAPTER XV. The count tries various measures against them; at last the gate is blocked by masses thrown before it

The count and the reverend bishop, unable patiently to endure such losses among their men, summoned their forces and ordered all unanimously to prepare for demolishing the aforesaid bridge, having found hammers and iron tools. Thus, on a certain day, armoured men, protected with helmets and shields, assembled at the bridge and attempted with great exertion to destroy it. But the solid strength of the construction resisted harder than any iron, while the citizens hindered their work by shooting arrows and hurling stones. Seeing that they were making no progress, they abandoned the undertaking.

Changing their plan, they decided to erect an engine opposite the bridge, so that, through the diligence and persistent efforts of armed men stationed in it, the citizens’ sorties might be restrained. Suitable material having been brought together as desired and craftsmen summoned, the engine was quickly completed in all its parts within a few days. With much labour and danger to those drawing it, it was set up before the bridge in the form of a lofty tower and entrusted to Lord Count for guarding [Col. 0316B].

Seeing the engine close to the wall, the citizens hurried there with all speed. Again directing projectile engines against it, they hastened to weaken it by frequent hurling of millstones. Those stationed in the towers and on the wall likewise strove vigorously, with arrows and every kind of missile, to keep from the bridge the men in and around the engine. While those on the wall pressed and shot from every direction so frequently that the discharge and multitude of arrows drove our men somewhat back, others opened the gate and sallied out with great violence. They forcibly occupied the bridge, fought hand-to-hand with swords, approached the engine, expelled those assigned to guard it, set it ablaze, and quickly reduced it to ashes.

When our princes saw that not even thus could they fully check the attacks made through that gate, on the following day they erected three projectile engines, in order at least by their continual shooting and the hurling of stones to weaken the walls and gate and prevent the citizens from going out through it [Col. 0316C]. So long as the engines continued shooting, no one dared to leave by that gate; but when their operation slackened, the citizens again returned to their usual sorties, inflicting many injuries upon the neighbouring camp.

Seeing that they were making no progress even thus, our people, at the advice of certain men, carried beyond the bridge immense rocks, scarcely movable by a hundred hands, and very large tree trunks, by the strength of a thousand armoured men, while the whole army protected them. They piled these before the gate in such a great heap that thereafter the gate was useless for the citizens to open, their attempts being obstructed by the mound of millstones [Col. 0316D]. Thus by this expedient the citizens’ attack through that same gate was broken, and their sudden sorties ceased.

## CHAPTER XVI. As our people go out for forage, the enemy attacks; a most fierce battle occurs: many fall from both armies, some pierced by weapons and others drowned in the river

[Col. 0317A]

On a certain day three hundred men of our army, both cavalry and infantry, crossed our bridge in search of forage and began, as usual, to scatter across the countryside in search of necessities. This practice had arisen from pressing need, but also from the fact that they had often returned unharmed from those regions, even though they carried back many supplies. They therefore promised themselves a security far too careless, imagining that such success would continue for ever and that no adverse chance, as commonly happens in warfare, would intervene.

Watching them from the city, the citizens emerged in greater numbers, crossed the stone bridge, and hastened with all speed toward those whom they had seen wandering carelessly. Suddenly attacking them, they killed many and put the rest to flight. As these men hurried toward the bridge of boats, intending thereby to reach the camp, the first arrivals occupied the bridge; many of the others, wishing to cross the ford, found death in the waters where they had expected salvation. Others too were forced unwillingly from the bridge into the riverbed by the crowd pressing upon them [Col. 0317C]. For the most part, the violence of the waters overwhelmed them and dragged them, entangled together, into the depths, greedily swallowing what it afterward refused to restore.

When this became known to our people, several thousand armoured men rushed to arms, crossed the river, and met the enemy returning from the slaughter of our men and rejoicing in the spoils. They pursued them eagerly as far as the city bridge, inflicting very heavy slaughter upon them. But when the citizens saw the slaughter and wounds of their people and pitied those who were failing, they opened the gate and crossed the stone bridge in a great multitude and with more than usual boldness. To bring their men the aid they needed, they charged our forces courageously. Our men at first resisted stoutly; then, overwhelmed by the force of the multitude, they were put to flight and pursued without ceasing as far as the bridge of boats.

In this action very many of our infantry fell by the sword, and many more were drowned in the river. Of the cavalry, as they crowded too closely upon the bridge while fleeing before enemies in pursuit, some were hurled headlong from the bridge into the river. With horses, armour, helmets, and shields, they afterward disappeared, suffocated in the swallowing depth of the waters [Col. 0317D].

Thus our army endured a siege no lighter than that suffered by those within the city. Restrained both by the citizens, who could not fail to know whenever our men went out, and by foreign enemies concealed in forests and mountains, laying ambushes for our people and frequently triumphing over them, they did not dare to go beyond the camps or roam farther in search of provisions. Even within the camps, moreover, they could not stay in sufficient security; all feared lest the immense host of enemies, said to be gathering from many places, should suddenly fall upon them. Thus a prudent man might reasonably have been uncertain whom one ought more to fear, or whose condition was better: that of the besiegers or of those who appeared to be undergoing siege.

## CHAPTER XVII. Necessary supplies having been consumed, famine begins to prevail; the people suffer want; tents rot in the excessive rains; the army dwindles away

To recount individual occurrences which happened almost daily in various places during so great and continuous a siege would be long, and very contrary to the brevity in history that we deliberately seek. Let us therefore omit particulars and pursue the general matters.

Amid these varied and continual events of war, when the siege had already been prolonged almost into its third month, provisions began to fail in the camps and the army suffered from scarcity of food [Col. 0318B]. At the beginning they had possessed a very great abundance of necessities, and their horses had not lacked fodder. But, like imprudent men, they thought that this condition would continue; they made no reserve for themselves. Abusing the abundance granted them, they squandered within a few days provisions which might have sufficed for many days if they had been distributed with suitable moderation.

There was no restraint in the camps, nor frugality dear to prudent persons; everywhere was extravagance, everywhere excess. All moderation failed, not only in food for people but also in fodder for beasts of burden and horses. Hence the army was reduced to such want that, as famine increased, almost the entire population perished.

They therefore formed associations, swearing to one another that they would divide in equal shares and in good faith everything they acquired as gain. Companies of three or four hundred set out together and searched the entire district in order to procure food by whatever means they could. At first, before the citizens had become accustomed to sally against them and lay ambushes, while the suburbs still abounded far and wide in flocks, herds, grain, wine, and other foods [Col. 0318D], they returned with much booty, rich plunder, and abundant provisions. This had been the source of the abundance previously found in the camps.

But now the neighbouring districts had been exhausted. The Turks, who had earlier wasted away in fear, had recovered their strength and courage and defended their own territory. Thus the foraging parties either returned entirely empty-handed, or—what happened more often—all were killed, and no one remained to inform the camp even of their destruction.

Famine and hunger increased daily. Bread could scarcely be found for two solidi—enough for a single person to eat once a day. An ox or heifer, which at first had been sold for five solidi, was sold for two marks. A lamb or kid, formerly obtainable for three or four denarii [Col. 0319A], could scarcely be found for sale at five or six solidi. Eight solidi scarcely sufficed to provide a horse with necessary food for one night.

Consequently, those who had brought with them more than seventy thousand horses when they arrived had scarcely two thousand in the camps, the rest having perished from hunger and cold. Those that appeared to survive wasted away daily from starvation and gradually failed under the violence of the cold. Moreover, the pavilions and tents of the camps had rotted, so that many who still had food were compelled to die, worn down by the harshness of the cold. Such was the flooding of the waters and the excess of rain that food and clothing rotted, and there was no place where they could keep either their heads or their necessary belongings dry [Col. 0319B].

So great a pestilence overwhelmed the legions in the camps that there was now no place for burial, and funeral rites were denied to the dead. If any still seemed to have some vigour remaining, lest they too should perish in the same danger, they secretly made their way either to the territory of Edessa, to Lord Baldwin; or to Cilicia, to those who governed cities there; or to any other places already under our people’s power. Thus, with some departing, others consumed by sickness and hunger, and still others killed by the sword, the army had been so diminished that scarcely half of it seemed to remain.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Bohemond and the count of Flanders go out with a great force to forage. Meanwhile the citizens secretly attack the camps, inflicting loss and injury upon our people

[Col. 0319C]

The princes devoted to God, seeing the people’s distress and the hardships by which they were constantly oppressed, were melted by compassion and worn away by grief for the perishing army. As they were accustomed often to do, they assembled to deliberate how and what remedy they might apply to such great evils. At last, after many opinions of different kinds, it seemed more expedient that certain magnates, taking with them part of the army, should enter enemy territory in order to bring back booty and the necessities of life; while the others should remain in the camps meantime and guard the army with every care.

Accordingly, this task was assigned to Lord Bohemond and the count of Flanders, while the count of Toulouse and the bishop of Le Puy were left to guard the camps [Col. 0319D]. For the count of Normandy was absent, and Lord Godfrey, duke of Lorraine, lay sick in bed under a severe illness. Taking therefore suitable forces from both cavalry and infantry—such as the exhausted army could furnish—they departed into enemy territory.

When the citizens heard that Bohemond and the count of Flanders had gone away, that the count of Normandy was absent, and that the duke was ill, they seized the opportunity afforded by the moment and, with boldness greater than usual on both accounts, resolved by common counsel to attack our camps and not neglect the opportunity which the princes’ absence appeared to offer. Having called together a multitude of every kind from the whole city, they assembled at the Bridge Gate. Opening the entrance, some crossed by the bridge and others by the ford below it, competing to rush into the camps.

But the count met them with a small body of cavalry. Having killed two of them, he compelled the rest to withdraw into the city. It happened in that engagement that our cavalry pursued an unmounted horse whose rider they had thrown to the ground, in order to capture it. When the miserable and undiscerning crowd saw this, supposing that our cavalry were fleeing out of fear, they too took to flight. In their terror, crowding one another into narrow space [Col. 0320B], they themselves caused their own deaths.

Seeing that our people were fleeing, though no one pursued them, the citizens again came out over the bridge and pressed after the fugitives. Pursuing our people from the stone bridge to the bridge of boats, they inflicted great slaughter on them. For as our men crowded and obstructed one another’s way, fifteen cavalrymen and twenty infantrymen perished, some by the sword and some in the river. Greatly encouraged by this success, the enemy returned to the city in triumph.

## CHAPTER XIX. Those who had gone out to forage find and defeat enemies, and return with booty and abundant spoils

But the aforesaid princes, Lord Bohemond [Col. 0320C] and the count of Flanders, who had gone out by common counsel to forage and relieve the scarcity in the camps by ample provisions, compensated in some measure for this misfortune of our people by more fortunate achievements. After capturing a certain enemy village full of every good thing, Bohemond sent scouts in different directions, so that on their return they might inform him of the condition of the region and, if possible, gather greater booty.

Some of them returned and reported that a body of Turks was nearby. Against them Bohemond sent the lord of Flanders with a respectable escort, himself following with larger forces as though to bring aid should he fail. The count, being a vigorous and noble man, charged the enemy courageously and did not return to Bohemond until he had put the rest to flight and killed one hundred of them with the sword.

As he returned victorious to the larger forces, other scouts suddenly reported that much stronger battle-lines were approaching from another direction. Bohemond sent the same count of Flanders against them, with multiplied forces and an enlarged escort; he himself followed behind with the remaining troops, ready to descend to their aid if necessary [Col. 0320D].

Through the mercy of the Lord going before them, the enemy were caught in certain narrower places. When they saw that the affair must be decided with swords rather than arrows or bows—being unfamiliar with this manner of fighting—they turned to flight. Our men pursued them for nearly two miles and inflicted great slaughter upon them. They then returned in triumph to the camps, safe and unharmed, with horses, mules, rich spoils, and varied booty gathered from the whole region [Col. 0321A].

The army rejoiced in the success of their brethren and began to recover a little from its hardships. Yet because the booty was small and could scarcely suffice so great a multitude for a few days, the army’s need was not greatly relieved.

## CHAPTER XX. Sueno, son of the king of the Danes, following the army, is slain with his forces by the Turks near the city of Finiminis

[Col. 0321B]

Meanwhile a report, full of grief and anxiety, came from the regions of Romania, striking all hearts and adding a sadder burden to their present miseries. It was said—and was indeed true—that a certain noble and powerful man, son of the king of the Danes, named Sueno, a man distinguished and illustrious in birth, character, and appearance, had been inflamed by desire for this same pilgrimage. Bringing with him fifteen hundred excellently armed young men of the same nation, he was hastening to aid our people and to the present siege.

Having departed rather late from his father’s kingdom, he had hastened greatly to join the legions that had gone before him with all his company. But, impeded by private affairs, he could not attain what he desired. He therefore led his troops separately, alone and without the company of any other princes, took the road, followed the route of the others, and reached Constantinople. There he was treated quite honourably by the emperor. Reaching Nicaea safely and hastening onward to the army in the regions of Romania, he descended with all his company.

While encamped between the cities of Finiminis and Terma, and being somewhat insufficiently cautious, he was secretly attacked at night by immense Turkish forces. They were slain by the sword in their very camp. Yet, having perceived the noise of the approaching enemy, though only when they were too near, they ran to arms; before they could more fully prepare to receive the enemy, they were overwhelmed by the unexpected multitude, and nearly all fell [Col. 0321D]. Nevertheless, resisting long and bravely, lest they should seem to have surrendered their lives without cost, they left the enemy a bloody victory.

## CHAPTER XXI. Tatinus, a deceitful man, leaves the army, supposedly to arrange trade in provisions and to ask the emperor for assistance, never to return
Tatinus also, of whom we have made mention above—the emperor’s *apocrisiarius* [envoy], who had been attached by that emperor to our army, ostensibly as a guide for the journey, and who had followed our legions up to the present day—seeing the hardships under which the army was pressed, and fearing, as indeed he was cowardly, that the princes might not persist in their purpose and that in a single day the entire people might be cut down beneath the swords of the enemy, came to the assembly of the princes. With great urgency he began to persuade them to raise the siege and move the whole army to the cities and neighbouring strongholds, where they might find the necessities of life more abundantly and inflict frequent hardships upon the Antiochenes, until the army of the lord emperor—whom he had assembled from various nations in countless thousands to bring them aid—should arrive about the beginning of spring.

He further added that, since he had resolved from the outset to share in their labours and desired to have fellowship with them alike in prosperity and adversity, he was willing, for the common favour and public advantage, to take upon himself the greater labour: namely, to hasten directly to the emperor, compel him to expedite the army, and cause provisions necessary for sustenance to be conveyed from every district on this side of the city. Although our princes had recognized his mind as deceitful and treacherous both then and from the beginning, nevertheless no one opposed his proposal or set himself against his designs.

Then, in order to cloak his fraud and contrivance under whatever pretext he could, he left behind his tents and most of his household—either disregarding their safety or secretly instructing them to follow him to the appointed place on the stated day. Thus he departed as though he would soon return. But afterward that faithless and wicked man, destined for everlasting death, did not appear. He left behind a ruinous example; for from that day onward, whoever could secretly withdraw from the camp undertook concealed flight, forgetful of their oaths and of the public profession which they had embraced from the beginning in fervent vows.

Meanwhile the famine grew stronger, nor could the princes apply any immediate remedy to so great an evil. For although, two by two, selected princes with great bodies of troops entered the enemy’s territories in turn, and often returned victorious to their own side, they brought back neither plunder nor provisions necessary for sustenance. The enemy, having learned of the expeditions of those accustomed to go out for plunder, transferred their flocks and herds, and whatever other animals they possessed, to inaccessible mountains and more remote places, where our men had no access and where, even if they arrived, it was not easy to drive off the prey.

## CHAPTER XXII. As famine grows and a pestilential plague overtakes the people, the bishops proclaim a three-day fast. Duke Godfrey recovers fully, and the army receives consolation from his restoration.

At the same time, as famine, plague arising from famine, and other dangers increased around the army day by day, the elders of the people and those whose judgment was more practiced, seeing that men’s sins demanded this and that the Lord, provoked to anger, was justly inflicting these scourges upon a stiff-necked people, gathered together. Keeping the fear of the Lord before their eyes, they began anxiously to deliberate how, by quickly repenting of their offences, making worthy satisfaction for past sins, and guarding against like faults in the future, they might render the Lord’s indignation merciful toward them.

Therefore, by the command and authority of the lord bishop of Le Puy, who discharged the office of envoy of the Apostolic See, and of the other bishops beloved of God—with the consent and earnest request that this be done of the lay princes and the whole army—a three-day fast was proclaimed, so that, with their bodies afflicted, their souls might rise more strongly to prayer. When this had been completed with all devotion, they jointly decreed that foolish and frivolous women should be separated from the army. They prohibited adultery and every sort of fornication under penalty of death; likewise feasting and drunkenness, the dangerous game of dice, reckless oaths, fraud in weight and measure, every deception, theft, and robbery.

These decrees having been confirmed by the agreement of all, they also appointed definite judges to hear such matters, granting them full authority both to investigate and to impose punishment. Some violators of these ordinances were nevertheless later found. Having been formally accused and convicted before the aforesaid judges, they suffered penalties proportionate to their offences according to the severity of the laws, thereby deterring others from similar acts. And by the Lord’s superabundant grace, when the people had been recalled to the fruits of a better life, the fiercer anger of the Lord abated in part.

For immediately Lord Godfrey, who was as it were the singular pillar of the entire army, began fully to recover from the severe illness by which he had long been afflicted as a consequence of the wound inflicted upon him by a bear near Antioch in Pisidia. The entire army therefore received very great consolation amid its affliction from his recovery.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The troublesome activity of scouts sent by the enemy is checked through a memorable deed of Lord Bohemond.

Meanwhile rumour and widely circulated report had already filled the whole East, nor had they left untouched even the kingdoms of the south and foreign nations: so great a force of Christians had arrived and was besieging Antioch with a mighty hand. Therefore each king, concerned for his own position, sent scouts to our army, in order that through them they might be better informed concerning the character, courage, and purpose of so great a multitude. Their number in the camps was so great that almost daily, as some departed to report the army’s condition to those who had sent them, fresh persons of the same sort arrived.

Nor was it difficult for such men to conceal themselves among our people. Sharing their languages, some pretended to be Greeks, some Syrians, others Armenians, and by their speech, manners, and dress assumed the persons of such peoples. The princes assembled to deliberate what should be done in order to provide for the commonwealth. Seeing that such scouts could not easily be expelled from the camps, since in language, manners, and dress they differed in no way from the aforesaid nations, they judged, until they had deliberated more fully what should be established against them, that it was best to share their counsels with fewer persons, lest, disseminated among many, they should reach those who would reveal them to the enemy for the injury of the Christian people.

When they could devise no further measure against the wickedness of such men, Lord Bohemond, being, as he was, of penetrating intellect and sharp understanding, is said to have told the princes: “Brothers and lords, cast this entire concern upon us. For, with God as author, we shall find a remedy suitable to this disease.” Thus, when the council of princes was dissolved, each returned to his own camp.

Bohemond, mindful of his promise, at the first twilight of night, while others in the camp were as usual busied with preparing supper, ordered several Turks whom he held in chains to be brought out. Handing them over to executioners, he commanded that they be slaughtered; and, with a large fire kindled beneath, he ordered them to be carefully roasted as though for the evening meal and prepared most diligently. He instructed his men that, if anyone asked what such a supper meant, they should answer: “It had been agreed among the princes that all enemies or enemy scouts captured henceforth should themselves be compelled, in a similar manner, to furnish food for the meals of both princes and people.”

Those who were on campaign, hearing that such things were being done in Lord Bohemond’s camp, were astonished at this novelty and all ran there. The scouts in the army, terrified by the event and supposing that the decree they heard proclaimed was entirely serious and without pretence, took what had happened as clear evidence. Fearing that something similar might befall them, they left the camps and returned home, saying to those who had sent them: “This people surpasses the savagery of every nation, even of wild beasts. It does not suffice them to plunder cities, castles, and every kind of property of their enemies; to put them in chains; to torture them more cruelly in the manner of enemies; or at least to kill them—unless they also fill their bellies with their flesh and fatten themselves on their enemies’ fat.”

This report spread to the remotest regions of the East, terrifying not only neighbouring nations but peoples far away. The entire city also trembled, terrified by the novelty of the report and the harshness of the deed. Thus, through Lord Bohemond’s diligence and contrivance, this plague of scouts was in part restrained, and our counsels were less frequently revealed to the enemy.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The Egyptian caliph sends envoys to the princes, seeking an alliance and attempting to win their favour.

Furthermore, the Egyptian caliph, the most powerful among the princes of the unbelievers in wealth and military strength, had sent his envoys to our princes. The reason for this embassy was as follows. From long before, an ancient hatred and grievous enmities had arisen between the eastern peoples and the Egyptians from the difference in their religious error and their opposing doctrines. These had continued unrelentingly to the present through an unbroken succession of time, so that the aforesaid realms, often clashing in mutual encounters, competed to extend their frontiers against one another and to push their boundaries forward in turn, as has been explained more carefully in the first book of this work.

As now one side, now the other gained the advantage according to changing times and varying fortunes, their kingdoms likewise grew, so that whatever happened to one seemed to have been lost by the other. At that time the Egyptian ruler possessed all the regions from the borders of Egypt to Laodicea in Syria, a journey of thirty days. But the sultan of Persia had, shortly before our arrival, seized Antioch, which bordered the lands of the Egyptian kingdom; and he had occupied all the regions as far as the Hellespont, as we have said above.

The Egyptian, therefore, suspecting the expansion of the Persians or Turks, greatly rejoiced at the report that, after Nicaea had been lost, Soliman and his followers had been badly treated, and that our people had laid siege to Antioch. He regarded the Turks’ loss as his own profit and their troubles as the highest tranquillity for himself and his people. Fearing, therefore, that our men might abandon their undertaking and grow weary from the long duration of their labour, he sent trusted envoys selected from his household, to urge our princes to continue the siege; to promise them his help and support; to win the princes’ hearts and favour; and to conclude treaties and friendship with them.

Faithfully carrying out their master’s command, these men travelled by ship and arrived in our camps, very solicitous concerning all that had been entrusted to them. Although our princes received them very hospitably and honourably, and frequently admitted them to conferences so that they might communicate their instructions, they marvelled at our men’s endurance, strength, types of weapons, and patience in toil. They viewed the forces of so great a multitude with apprehension, foreseeing in their minds what would come to pass. For what their lord deceitfully planned to bring about the overthrow of others, he was afterward compelled to experience himself. For when Antioch had been conquered and restored to the Christian faith and its former liberty, all the territory which the faithful people now hold from that city to the River of Egypt, bordering Gaza, a journey of fifteen days, the faithful people have powerfully wrested it for themselves from his violent dominion through the grace of almighty God.

# THE FIFTH BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0325]

## CHAPTER I. The citizens of Antioch call for and obtain aid from their neighbours; their auxiliaries pitch camp near the castle of Harenc.

[Col. 0325C]

Meanwhile the citizens of Antioch, together with their lord, greatly anxious about their position, saw the endurance of our men and their perseverance in hardships. Neither famine nor the severity of the cold could turn them back from their undertaking; rather, amid so many troubles, they strove to continue their purpose. Sending letters and frequent embassies, they tried to summon neighbouring rulers to assist them, earnestly imploring and seeking to persuade them that, moved by compassion for brothers, they should not delay to bring speedy help.

They also suggested the following advantageous method by which aid might be brought to them. The allies should approach the city and conceal themselves secretly in ambush, awaiting the time when the citizens, as usual, should engage the enemy near the bridge and be detained there. Once those both within and without were deeply engaged in this business, the allies should fall suddenly upon them and overwhelm them while unprepared. Thus, attacking them before and behind, they would leave not even one able to escape death.

By their persistent entreaty, a huge army was therefore assembled from Aleppo, Caesarea, Hama, Emesa, Hierapolis, and other neighbouring cities. Approaching secretly and without noise, as they had been commanded, they silently pitched camp near the castle called Harenc, scarcely fourteen miles from Antioch. Their purpose was, following the plan received from the Antiochenes, to fall unexpectedly upon our men while they were occupied in attacks on the city.

But trustworthy inhabitants of the region, who are known often to have been very useful to our people, reported their situation and arrival. Warned beforehand, the princes assembled to deliberate upon the matter. Finally they decided that all the knights in the army who possessed horses fit for use should, armed at the first twilight of night, secretly and quietly leave camp, following the banners of their respective princes in silence. The infantry, however, were to remain in camp, diligently guarding it until, with God’s aid, their departing leaders returned.

## CHAPTER II. Our princes, leaving infantry for the defence of the camp, go out with cavalry to meet the enemy and return victorious to camp.

Accordingly, at the first twilight of night, as had been arranged, they left camp by the bridge of boats and led out scarcely seven hundred knights. They made for a place midway between the lake mentioned above when we described the situation of the city, and the River Orontes, which lie about one mile apart. There they rested that night.

[Col. 0327A]

That same night the enemy likewise crossed the river by the upper bridge, entirely unaware of our men’s approach. At dawn, when the first light came upon the earth, our men seized their weapons with all speed and formed their army into six divisions, assigning designated commanders. The Turks, already stationed nearby and informed by scouts that our men were coming to meet them, likewise sent forward two divisions from their forces, followed by the larger mass of the remaining troops.

By divine action, our men—scarcely seven hundred, as stated—formed into squadrons according to military discipline and seemed, as though strengthened from heaven, to be countless thousands. As the opposing legions gradually advanced against each other, the enemy’s first divisions rushed upon our men with great force; after discharging a shower of arrows, they withdrew to their own troops.

Our men, disregarding their attack, pressed forward against them with lances vigorously brandished and swords. They compelled them to be packed together in a single mass. The narrowness of the terrain, the lake on one side and the river on the other, prevented their dispersal. Seeing that they could not resort to their customary tactics of ranging freely and shooting arrows, and unable to withstand our men’s onset, they crowded together in fear of the swords and placed their sole hope of safety in flight. Turning their backs, therefore, they fled.

Our men pursued them eagerly as far as their aforementioned camp called Harenc, ten miles from the battlefield, killing them and inflicting boundless slaughter. The townspeople, seeing their own troops turned to flight and nearly all fallen beneath enemy swords, feared to remain in the fortress after their defeat. They set fire to the town and fled as well. But Armenians and other faithful inhabitants of the region, of whom there was a large number there, occupied the said stronghold and immediately surrendered it to our princes before they returned to camp.

About two thousand of the enemy fell that day. Bringing back five hundred heads, encouraged to good hope and rejoicing in the double triumph granted them, they returned to camp with a thousand strong horses—of which they had great need—and abundant spoil, offering the Lord most ample thanksgiving.

## CHAPTER III. The citizens, learning of the defeat of their auxiliaries, are grievously dismayed.

Meanwhile the citizens spent the entire night awaiting the promised aid and passionately longing for daylight, so that, while the enemy attacked from without, they themselves might likewise emerge from within and overwhelm our men, unaware of these events and caught unprepared. But when, with the dawn now breaking near the end of the night, they saw no sign at all of the others’ arrival, and learned from scouts that our princes had gone out to meet them, they gathered together and hurried out through the gates of the city. For almost the whole day they inflicted very severe attacks upon our men, until the watchmen stationed on the higher parts of the city signalled our men’s arrival, whereupon they withdrew into the city.

Stationed upon the towers, walls, and higher places, they saw the legions approaching, though they did not know whether the camp approaching belonged to ours or theirs. At last, when our men came closer, they began to recognize their weapons and saw them dragging booty and trophies. Learning that they were returning victorious and that their own forces had been destroyed, they gave themselves over to grievous lamentation, their great hope having been disappointed.

Our men approached the city and entered camp. As a sign of victory and to increase the enemy’s grief, they caused two hundred Turkish heads to be hurled into the city by missile engines. The rest they ordered suspended on stakes before the city, so that these and those might increase and multiply their afflictions like a thorn in their eye. The number of those who had intended to come to the aid of Antioch is said to have been twenty-eight thousand, as was more fully learned from the testimony of captives. This happened in February, on the seventh day of the month, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1097.

## CHAPTER IV. Our men build a fortress. Genoese ships arrive in the harbour. The people go down to the sea and, encountering an ambush, are partly destroyed.

At the same time, our princes decided that a fortress should be built upon a hill above Lord Bohemond’s tents, so that, should the Turks at any time attempt to break into our expeditions, the new fortification might obstruct them and serve as a bulwark for our camp. When this had been done and assigned to careful guard, the whole army was so securely placed as though it had been enclosed all round by the city’s walls. This new fortification lay to their east; to the south were the city wall and the marsh adjoining it; while to the west and north lay the river, bending toward the city.

When the siege had now extended into its fifth month, certain Genoese ships, carrying pilgrims and provisions, came from the sea into the mouth of the river. They waited there, frequently sending messengers and requesting that some of the princes be sent to escort them safely to camp. The enemy knew that those on the expedition often went down to the sea, and that those aboard the ships were no less desirous of returning to camp. They therefore blocked the roads and routes, repeatedly laid ambushes for travellers, and slaughtered them there. Hence men did not dare approach camp except in a very large company.

In those same days our princes had decided to build a fortification at the bridgehead, where there stood an oratory of the enemy’s superstition, so that the enemy might have less freedom of exit across the bridge. But because countless persons from the army had gone down to the sea and intended, after completing their business, to return to camp, Lord Bohemond and the Count of Toulouse were selected from among the princes, together with Lord Evrard of Pusato and Count Garner of Gres. They were to escort to the sea the Egyptian envoys who wished to return, and to bring back to camp those in the harbour, both the newcomers and those who had descended from the camp to meet them.

When the Antiochenes heard that these princes had gone down to the sea, they sent four thousand light-armed soldiers to meet them and commanded them to lay an ambush. If the others returned unwarily, they were not to fear to attack them courageously. On the fourth day, as our men were returning, drawing with them a multitude of unarmed people and pack animals laden with provisions and every kind of equipment, the enemy suddenly came out of ambush against them in certain narrow places.

The Count of Toulouse led the way, while Lord Bohemond guarded the rear ranks. Although they were vigorous men and worthy of praise in every respect, they could not govern the undisciplined populace as they wished, give them strength, or supply strength to those whom nature had denied it. After resisting for a long time, both for their own honour and to ward off danger from the others, they saw that delay was bringing danger upon themselves and that they ought not to labour longer to no purpose. Taking thought for their own safety, they abandoned a conflict far too unequal and withdrew to camp with those of their men who could follow them.

But the common people, leaving baggage and impedimenta behind, fled partly into the woods and partly to the mountains. Those unable to flee fell and were killed by the enemy’s swords. There was a very great slaughter of our people there. Some gave us differing accounts of the number killed; nevertheless, the opinion of most is that up to three hundred persons of both sexes and all ages fell.

## CHAPTER V. The duke’s plan and remarkable deed in response to the disaster that had occurred.

Meanwhile a report reached the camp that all those ascending from the sea had utterly perished on the road through enemy ambush and a sudden attack; concerning the life or death of the princes, however, there was no one able to report anything certain.

Lord Godfrey, a vigorous man and most ready for arms, bearing as great a concern for God’s people as for his own children, summoned all the princes and legions and ordered them to take up arms without delay. A proclamation was issued forbidding anyone, under penalty of death, to withdraw himself at such a critical necessity; all were to hasten to arms in order to avenge their brothers’ blood.

Without delay, all the legions assembled as though one man. Having brought them together, he crossed the bridge of boats. Dividing the army into divisions, he placed commanders over them: Lord Robert, Count of Normandy; the Count of Flanders; Lord Hugh the Great; and his own brother Lord Eustace. Assigning a division to each, he stationed them in suitable positions, gave them courage by his words, invited them to valour, and explained his plan to them as prudent men, saying:

> “If, as has been reported to us, through our sins and with the Lord’s permission, the enemies of the Christian name and faith have triumphed over our lords and brothers, I see, illustrious men, that nothing remains except that we should die with them or avenge so great an injury done to the Lord Jesus Christ. Believe me: neither life nor safety is dearer to me than death or any kind of suffering, if the blood of so many princes has been shed upon the earth without punishment, or if the destruction of so great a people devoted to God does not find swift vengeance.
>
> “It seems to me that the enemy, somewhat elated by their present victory, will behave more carelessly. Presuming upon their strength, they will not hesitate to return through us toward the city, carrying spoil and trophies. Prosperity commonly makes those to whom it presently smiles more heedless; conversely, greater resourcefulness commonly comes to affairs that are miserable and distressed. Therefore, if it seems good to you, let us stand ready here; cherishing a just cause, let us place sure hope of victory in him whom we believe ourselves to serve in arms. And if the enemy wishes to return by way of us, let us receive them at the sword’s edge, in the manner of enemies—mindful of the injury inflicted upon us and not degenerate from the virtues of our fathers.”

This speech pleased them and seemed good in the eyes of all. While they still stood upon this matter, behold: Lord Bohemond, returning from the sea, entered the camp, and after a short interval the count followed. The people received them with tears and overflowing affection, having been almost deprived of the consolation of such great princes. When they learned the duke’s plan, they approved it and declared that it ought to be done.

Axcianus, knowing that his men had won and fearing for their return—especially because legions had left the camp in greater numbers than usual—ordered by public proclamation all in the city capable of bearing arms to assemble at the Gate of the Bridge, so that they might not delay to aid their men upon their return, should need arise. Our men, having sent scouts, carefully inquired by which route they were coming, placing their hope of victory in the Lord.

## CHAPTER VI. The enemy return victorious and are cut down by our swords before the city gate; two thousand of them fall. The duke cleaves an armoured man in two.

Without delay, while the divisions were arranged and standards raised, they awaited the enemy’s arrival. Then men rushed in announcing that the enemy were nearby, and with loud cries urged our men to arm and go forth to meet them. As the enemy drew near, close enough that our men thought they should advance, they invoked heavenly aid, encouraged one another, brandished their spears, remembered their former valour, and charged them together, pressing closely with swords.

As our men attacked them with their accustomed vigour and remembered the injury they had suffered, allowing them no respite, the enemy’s strength failed. Their knees gave way in the anguish of fear, and they turned to flight, striving eagerly toward the city bridge. But the illustrious Duke of Lorraine, experienced in such affairs, had forestalled their design. He occupied with his men a spot somewhat higher before their bridge, and those whom the venerable princes pursued with swords, seeking to escape over the bridge, he either cut down or violently compelled to return to the battle from which they had fled, there to perish.

The Count of Flanders pressed them, a vigorous man well acquainted with the use of arms; with his followers he struck down the enemy ranks, courageously and repeatedly throwing in their faces the evils they had committed against our men. The Count of Normandy likewise, not degenerate from his father’s valour, laboured most bravely in the same work. The Count of Toulouse, inflamed by zeal for God; Hugh the Great, mindful of royal blood and not falling away from the height of such dignity; Count Eustace, the duke’s brother; Baldwin, Count of Hainaut; Hugh of Saint-Pol; and other nobles pursued the enemy with such determination and raged against them with such courage that, their strength broken, they were slaughtered with impunity like cattle.

Axcianus ordered the city gates shut behind his men whom he had sent out to fight, intending to inspire them with greater courage and to make them fight more fiercely through despair of return. But while he believed that he was serving their interest, he thoughtlessly led his own men to ruin. For when they could no longer withstand the onslaught and pressure of our arms, flight was their only remedy of safety; wholly frustrated in this hope, they were cut down everywhere by swords and perished, though by that route they might have escaped death.

There was such a crash of weapons in the camp, such ringing and flashing of swords, such neighing of horses, and such shouting of the people, that, had the kind of weapons not made a clear distinction between them, indiscriminate confusion could have exposed many to imminent dangers or delivered them from adverse chances.

The matrons of the city, together with their daughters and little children, and likewise the old men and the unarmed populace, watched from towers and walls the slaughter of their people. With groans and tears they mourned their destruction, judging the times now past fortunate, and likewise those happy to whom friendly death had long ago been granted, so that they need not be involved in these calamities. Those women whom they had formerly regarded as fruitful and blessed mothers, they now, changing their song, called fortunate to be barren and proclaimed far happier than mothers.

Meanwhile Axcianus saw that his people had utterly failed and that what remained was exposed to the sword and near to destruction. He ordered the gates opened with all speed, so that the remnants of the people might be placed in safety. But when the entrance was opened, such was the crowd and tumult of fugitives across the bridge that, as the enemy pursued and they pressed one another in fear, countless men were hurled into the river.

Although the Duke of Lorraine had conducted himself excellently throughout the battle, at the bridge, as evening was already falling, he gave so great and remarkable a proof of the courage in which he uniquely excelled that his famous deed deserves perpetual remembrance and made him distinguished throughout the army. For after, with his accustomed strength, cutting off the heads of many armoured men without repeating a stroke, he split through the middle an enemy who pressed him too boldly, though he wore armour. The portion above the navel fell to the ground, while the remaining portion was carried into the city upon the horse on which it sat. The people were astonished at the novelty of the deed and did not permit so marvellous an act, which they proclaimed everywhere, to remain unknown.

About two thousand of the enemy are said to have fallen that day. Had not unwelcome night, envious of our men’s glory and victory, come on prematurely, the affair of Antioch would undoubtedly have been concluded that day. So evident were the traces of slaughter committed around the bridge and in the river that, its colour changed, the entire river flowed blood-red to the sea. It is also reported—and this became more fully known through certain faithful persons who left the city and joined our men—that twelve of their greater satraps were cut down by swords in that engagement, inflicting irreparable loss upon the city.

## CHAPTER VII. Our men build a fortification at the bridgehead and send a sign of victory to the ships.

[Col. 0332C]

With daylight at last restored to the world in its customary course, the princes again assembled and gave thanks to the Almighty for the victory bestowed, in order to deliberate upon the business at hand. All agreed that it was expedient to return to their earlier plan and build a fortification at the bridgehead, both to prevent the citizens from leaving and to afford their own men safer freedom of movement. There stood there, as we remember having said, an oratory of their superstition, where they had also assigned a place for the burial of their dead. During the preceding night and the portion of the following day already elapsed, they had carried their dead bodies thither and buried them.

When this became fully and certainly known to our people, they violently rushed in, on the pretext of plunder; they violated the tombs, dug up the buried, and extracted from the monuments gold, silver, and precious garments which had been committed to burial with the dead. Those who had previously been uncertain of the number slain, because the battle had been concluded by night, were by this disclosure better informed and took fuller joy in the previous day’s affair. For, apart from those drowned in the river by various mishaps, those buried in the city, and those mortally wounded who still awaited imminent death, fifteen hundred were found in the aforesaid place. Of these, they sent three hundred or more heads toward the port, greatly delighting our men who had returned thither from the conflict of the preceding day, and greatly frightening by this deed the Egyptian envoys, who had not yet departed from the port. Consequently, those who had escaped the danger of the previous day and were hiding in mountains, caves, woods, and thickets, on hearing of our victory made their way to the camp; and many soldiers whom they had believed to have fallen in battle returned safe and sound, by the Lord’s aid.

The people who had scattered to various places having thus been gathered back, they unanimously and zealously raised a solid-walled fort at the approach to the bridge, using the very stones which they had dug out of the tombs; and, once erected, they secured it with a deep ditch. When the princes deliberated concerning its guard, and none of them wished to subject himself to so great a burden, each alleging various reasons in excuse, the man beloved by God, Count Raymond of Toulouse, offered himself voluntarily and undertook the care of the new garrison for the public good. Thus he fully recovered the favour of the whole expedition, which throughout the year he had seemed greatly to have forfeited. For from the previous summer through the whole succeeding winter, owing to a certain illness, he had lain so inactive and nearly useless that he alone seemed to neglect the care of the army, which each of the other princes bore according to his strength and zeal with untiring effort. He showed generosity to no one and granted no one the favour of affability; and this was the more remarkable in him because he was said to be able to do more and to possess more than all the others.

Therefore, in order to excuse at once both idleness and avarice, he gladly undertook the aforesaid burden. Moreover, he is said to have given five hundred marks of tested silver, entrusted to the bishop of Le Puy and certain nobles, for replacing the horses which had been lost in the conflict. Encouraged by this action, his retainers, having confidence that the loss of their horses would be made good, pressed the enemy more vigorously than usual. The ill will which the lord count had incurred was softened, so that he was called by all the father and protector of the army.

## CHAPTER VIII. The city is suddenly more closely hemmed in: a new fortification is established above the Western Gate.

[Col. 0333D] Thus the Bridge Gate, through the aforesaid new garrison—in which the lord count had stationed five hundred strong men—was so blockaded that the citizens could leave by it only at the greatest peril, while our men moved about more freely to procure necessities. The enemy, however, could now leave only through the Western Gate, situated between the foot of the mountain and the river. Although their departure by that gate could not be very dangerous to our men, whose camps were all placed beyond the river, nevertheless the enemy seemed to possess too free a licence for roaming abroad, and through that gate alone the necessities of life were still brought into the besieged.

The princes, men of virtue and immortal memory, therefore met again to consider this necessity and decided that the present undertaking urgently required a fortification to be established beyond the river, at a suitable place, with one of the princes stationed there, so that this licence of roaming might be cut off. Although all agreed that a fortification should be built, no one offered himself to undertake its defence. As they hesitated and the work made no progress, Lord Tancred, a distinguished and energetic man, was chosen for this task. But when he sought to plead the slenderness of his resources, the aforesaid Count of Toulouse contributed a hundred marks of silver for the building work; and, lest the partners in the labour should lack suitable pay, forty marks each month were assigned to them from the common funds.

Thus, on a hill adjoining the same gate, where a monastery had formerly stood, a garrison was placed and prudent, robust men appointed for its defence. Lord Tancred guarded it, as resolutely as successfully, with due vigilance, unharmed until the enterprise was completed.

Further downstream there was a recess between the mountains and the same river, grassy and notable alike for the pleasantness and abundance of its pastureland, scarcely three or four miles from the city. Because of the lack of fodder in the city, the Antiochenes had transferred most of their horses there. When our men learned this, they secretly summoned companies of cavalry and, taking certain indirect routes in order to conceal their purpose, converged upon the place. Having killed some of the horsemen in charge of the herds, they led back to camp two thousand fine horses, excluding mules and she-mules. At that time there was no kind of plunder or booty more necessary to the army, for they had lost nearly all their own horses—some in battle, some through hunger, cold, and countless other misfortunes.

## CHAPTER IX. Those who had scattered return to the army. Baldwin sends gifts from Edessa to each of the princes.

Thus, with the city enclosed by siege on every side, so that the citizens now had neither free exit for attending to affairs outside nor entry without difficulty, they began to suffer severe hardship and many troubles. A failing food supply and sudden scarcity greatly afflicted the citizens; the reduced supply of fodder for the horses caused them to waste away from hunger and compelled them to refuse all service.

Our men, however, were granted freer opportunity to proceed both to the sea and to other places to which necessity drew them. Thus the scarcity of food in the camps was largely relieved—a scarcity under which the army had suffered very dangerously throughout the winter. For the harshness of winter having passed and the mature mildness of spring having returned, the sea was calm, and the fleet in the harbour could sail and return more safely. The difficulties of the roads also having been removed by the benefit of warmer weather, those drawn by domestic and household concerns to procure supplies could go out.

Those who had hidden in the camps and neighbouring towns, fleeing the harshness of camp life, now likewise returned to the camp with the return of milder weather. They repaired their arms and, their strength renewed, again prepared themselves for battle. Lord Baldwin, brother of the duke, of whom we have spoken above, heard that the army was suffering such want. Out of the abundance of riches which, as we have said, the Lord had bestowed on him with great generosity, he resolved in compassionate charity to relieve their poverty from his own plenty. Sending magnificent gifts—gold, silver, silks, noble and valuable horses—he enriched the household resources of each prince.

Nor did he show himself generous and liberal only toward the great men, but also toward many among the common people; he more earnestly won back the favour of all and stirred everyone to affection for himself. Moreover, lest he should seem to have done too little for his lord and elder brother, he assigned for payment to his brother all the revenues which he possessed in the land on this side of the Euphrates, around Turbessel and in its adjacent suburbs, in wheat, barley, wine, and oil, as well as fifty thousand gold pieces.

In addition, a powerful Armenian satrap, an intimate of Lord Baldwin named Nichossus, sent through his messengers to the duke, as a gift from Lord Baldwin, a tent of remarkable workmanship and enormous capacity. But Pancratius laid an ambush on the road, and the aforesaid tent was seized from the servants carrying it; it was then sent as a gift from Pancratius to Lord Bohemond. When this became known to the duke, and he learned from the servants of the aforesaid Nichossus that matters had proceeded thus, he joined to himself the count of Flanders, whose friendship he had especially enjoyed throughout the expedition, and approached Lord Bohemond to demand the restoration of the gift intended for him and violently taken away.

Although Bohemond invoked the claim of the noble Pancratius’s gift and maintained that he justly possessed what the duke demanded, nevertheless, lest there be disturbance among the people or scandal among the princes, overcome by the urgent entreaties of the other princes, he restored the gift which had been presented to him. Harmony between them was thus more fully restored.

We greatly wonder, therefore, that a man distinguished by such moderation and conspicuous for such dignity of character demanded back so insistently a thing trivial and easily despised. No explanation occurs to us except what is written:

> Nothing is wholly blessed in every respect;

and this:

> At times even good Homer nods.  
> —Horace, *Ars Poetica*, v. 359.

And also this third saying:

> In a long work it is permissible for sleep to steal in.  
> —Horace.

For the laws of the human condition ordain that we should more often experience in ourselves a falling away from the good.

## CHAPTER X. The arrival of hostile forces is reported in the camp. Stephen, count of Blois, feigning illness, goes down to the sea, never to return.

[Col. 0336A]

Meanwhile a widespread report declared that the most powerful ruler of the Persians, at the urging of the Antiochenes and their continual petitions, was sending innumerable forces from all his empire to aid them; and that he had commanded, by edict, an infinite multitude of Turks to advance into Syria under appointed commanders. This rumour did not have its origin and growth solely from outside sources; those who left the city and sought refuge in our camp also unanimously affirmed the same thing.

As the report increased more and more every day and the enemy were said already to be threatening at the gates, fear shook our army. So great was this fear that Lord Stephen, count of Chartres, a most powerful man and illustrious prince—whom the princes, on account of his exceptional prudence, had set over their counsels as a father—feigned illness. Having taken leave of his brethren, he descended to the sea with all his household and retainers and with the entire wealth in which he greatly abounded. He said that he intended to stay at Lesser Alexandria, situated on the coast not far from the harbour, where Cilicia began, until he had fully recovered and regained his strength and could return.

When he departed, almost four thousand men who had arrived in his company followed him. Reaching the sea, he withdrew to the aforesaid Alexandria and awaited the event. He had resolved that, if our men succeeded favourably in the battle expected to take place, he would return to the army as though recovered from illness; but if not, he would try to return to his homeland in the ships he had prepared, with perpetual disgrace and loss of reputation.

The princes who remained in the camp were dismayed by this notorious deed, which incurred lasting infamy. Sympathizing with the noble man, who had marred both the honour of his family and his own reputation by so great a fault, they began anxiously to deliberate how they might guard against so serious an evil, lest those who remained, provoked by his ruinous example, dare to attempt something similar. At last they resolved by common counsel that a public proclamation should forbid everyone without exception to leave the army. A penalty was attached: if any person, whatever office he held or whatever rank he possessed, secretly withdrew from the camp without the princes’ permission, he was to lie under perpetual infamy as a sacrilegious person or murderer and, moreover, be compelled to undergo the ultimate punishment.

Thus it came about that, from love of valour as well as fear of punishment, no one thereafter dared withdraw even a short distance from camp without permission obtained from the princes. All unanimously showed themselves obedient to their leaders without difficulty or complaint, like men living under monastic enclosure.

## CHAPTER XI. The condition of the city is described. Bohemond’s friendship with a certain faithful man in the city is recounted.

[Col. 0337A]

This city, beloved by God, had, as we have said, received from the time of the apostles the teaching of Christ and the easy yoke, preached to it by the prince of the apostles; and it had borne them faithfully and devoutly down to the present day. While the whole East was being shaken, and the successors of Muhammad violently subjected all provinces to the impiety of superstition and perverse doctrines, this city rejected their corruption and refused, as long as it could, to bear the rule of an unbelieving people.

For when the heresies of that seducer had occupied all regions from the Persian Gulf to the Hellespont and from India to Spain, this city, alone and singular as it were amid perverse nations, preserved the integrity of faith and stood courageously for its freedom. Barely fourteen years had passed since, assailed by an intolerable storm of enemies, its famous citizens, exhausted by long sieges and no longer able to resist, had been compelled to surrender the city to the enemies of the Christian name and faith.

Accordingly, even when our army arrived, almost all the inhabitants of the city were believers, but they possessed no authority in the city. While they were occupied with trade and other mechanical crafts, only Turks and unbelievers were permitted to serve as soldiers or administer the chief civic offices. Consequently, Christians were not permitted to handle arms or admitted to the care of military affairs. Especially after news of the arrival of the western Christians had reached the ruler of the city, they were held in such suspicion—and particularly after the city had been encircled by siege—that they were permitted to leave their homes and appear in public only at specified hours.

Among them were very noble families, tracing the distinction of their blood from ancient and high-born ancestors. One family, eminent for nobility, was called Beni Zerra, which in Latin means “sons of the armourer.” They were called “sons of the armourer,” either after their first ancestor, who practiced that craft, or because they themselves pursued the occupation of weaving coats of mail. It is, however, more probable and seems likely that some of them still worked at that art, so that, just as they possessed the name by inheritance, they did not abandon the craft handed down by succession.

Accordingly, in the western part of the city, near the gate today called that of St George, there was assigned to them a tower popularly called that of the Two Sisters, where they might peacefully devote themselves to their craft, which seemed highly useful to the lord and to the city. In this family there were two brothers. The elder, who was the head of his kinsmen and family, was called Emirfeirus, a very powerful man and joined to the lord of the city by close familiarity. He served as notary in the ruler’s palace and was distinguished by considerable rank.

This man, being very resourceful and shrewd, heard that Lord Bohemond was a magnificent and illustrious prince and took the leading part in all undertakings outside the city. Immediately after the city was surrounded by siege, he won Bohemond’s friendship through faithful intermediaries. Throughout the siege he remained faithful and devoted to this purpose, so that almost every day he informed him more fully about the state of the city and Acxian’s intentions. Being a discreet and prudent man, he concealed as far as he could this friendship which he had entered into with Lord Bohemond, lest its discovery by others bring danger upon himself and his people.

Lord Bohemond in turn concealed the friendship of this good man and kept the secret as though buried within himself. Thus not even their own household members and servants, despite the messengers continually passing between them, could perceive any indication, however slight, of their association.

## CHAPTER XII. A plan communicated through messengers between Bohemond and the aforesaid faithful man.

Since this friendship had continued between them for nearly seven months, so secretly as we have said, they frequently held familiar conversation concerning how the city might be restored to Christian freedom. When Bohemond had repeatedly reminded him of this matter, the man is said once to have replied through his son, the bearer of secrets:

> You know, best of men and dearer to me than my own light, how sincerely I have loved you since, by the Lord’s help, we entered into this mutual friendship. I remember also that I have found in your word steadfastness altogether firm and worthy of a good man. Therefore, day by day you have made yourself more deeply known to me and have become far dearer.
>
> Yet concerning the matter of which you have often reminded me, I have sometimes considered anxiously, weighing its alternatives in a fair balance. If I could restore my native city to its former liberty and, having expelled the unclean dogs beneath whose violent rule we are oppressed, bring in a people who worship God, I am certain that eternal rewards would not fail me, nor fellowship in eternal blessedness with holy souls.
>
> But if, having once undertaken a difficult and arduous enterprise, I should be unable to bring it to completion, it is certain and beyond anyone’s doubt that my house and the name of my illustrious family would be utterly destroyed, so that its name would never again be remembered.
>
> Nevertheless, since the hope of gain commonly invites mortal minds to such deeds, if you could obtain from your companions that the city delivered to you through our effort should be claimed as your own, then, for your sake—to whom I wish every good thing as to my own children—I will, by the Lord’s aid, to whose bond you are joined with me, undertake the aforesaid work, difficult though it may appear. I will without difficulty hand over to you this most strongly fortified tower, as you see, over which I have full authority; through it all your men will be able freely to enter the city.
>
> But if, as you are equals, you have resolved to divide the captured city among yourselves in equal shares, I will not enter into this danger for the sake of men with whom I have no relation. Therefore work diligently and strive, for the public good and salvation, to obtain this from your fellow princes. You may know beyond all doubt that on whatever day I learn you have obtained it, I shall not delay opening for you the entrance to the city, as you seek to persuade me.
>
> Know also that unless this is done shortly, it may perhaps be delayed forever. For almost every day messengers and letters come to the ruler of the city reporting that those who have assembled from the whole East to support him are encamped near the Euphrates, bringing with them two hundred thousand cavalry. If they find you outside the city, it will be difficult for you to withstand both the citizens and the multitude of enemy newcomers.

## CHAPTER XIII. Bohemond works to have the city entrusted to him; only the count of Toulouse opposes.

From that day Lord Bohemond began anxiously to sound out and carefully examine the minds of the individual princes: what they intended, and what they would decide concerning the besieged city if it were captured. He nevertheless concealed his purpose, except from those whose favourable assent to his wishes he knew he could securely expect. When he understood that he could make little progress with some of them, he deferred the matter to a more suitable time.

Duke Godfrey, however, the count of the Normans, the count of Flanders, and Lord Hugh the Great had agreed to his request and gave their willing assent. They approved the noble man’s secret, admired his prudence, and kept the matter hidden within themselves, never to be disclosed to anyone. The count of Toulouse alone differed from the others in this matter.

Accordingly, the affair nearly fell into a dangerous delay. For neither would Bohemond’s friend undertake so much labour and expose himself to such great dangers for the sake of the others; nor did Lord Bohemond press the matter with so much insistence for the common good as for his own domestic and family advantage. Nevertheless, he continued his friendship with the aforesaid man through gifts and services, fulfilling the obligations of sincere friendship; and by frequent messengers sent and received, they mutually nourished and strengthened the affection once conceived.

## CHAPTER XIV. Those hastening to aid the Antiochenes besiege Edessa; but Baldwin resists bravely, and they withdraw empty-handed and cross the Euphrates.

Meanwhile those sent by Acxian and the citizens into Persia to request aid, having completed their business as they wished and obtained the petition they had submitted, were returning home. That magnificent ruler, sympathizing with the troubles of the Antiochenes of which he had heard, and wishing to counter our efforts and cut short our strength lest we violently oppress any part of his realms, sent into Syria innumerable forces of Persians, Turks, and Kurds. He placed over them a familiar retainer in whose courage, loyalty, and ability he had great confidence, and under him appointed centurions, captains of fifty, and subordinate commanders, all of whom were both to obey and to govern under his authority.

He also issued to the governors of all regions subject to him letters having the force of law, commanding peoples and nations, tribes and languages that all, without excuse, should follow his beloved son Corbagath, whom he had placed over his armies by reason of his merit; and that all should submit to his authority, obeying in everything whatsoever he might determine to command according to his own free will.

Having gathered the aforesaid legions by his lord’s order, along with those encountered throughout the march, he entered Mesopotamia with two hundred thousand men and encamped near Edessa. There he learned from many reports that one of the Frankish princes, against whom he had been sent, possessed both that city and the whole surrounding province. Before crossing the Euphrates, he therefore decided to attack and forcibly occupy the aforesaid city.

Lord Baldwin, having learned beforehand of his arrival, had carefully fortified his city with provisions, arms, and brave men gathered from all sides; thus he was little troubled by the enemy’s threats and terrors. When a public proclamation ordered the troops to surround the city with siege and attack the besieged place with all their force, the more experienced among them saw that, because the citizens resisted vigorously, they could make little progress. They approached their leader and after much persuasion finally induced him to leave aside incidental concerns and carry out his principal design: he should cross the Euphrates and hasten to Antioch, his chief destination, in order to raise the siege there. For on his return, once victory had been obtained, scarcely one day’s work would be required both to occupy the aforesaid city and to put Baldwin in chains.

Having spent three continuous weeks there in labour and expense, he ordered the legions to cross the river. He too crossed, and pursued his purpose more diligently. This delay in the Edessan region was the reason Lord Baldwin could not be present at the aforesaid siege; it was also the cause of our men’s safety. For if he had come directly against them, as Bohemond’s aforesaid friend had reported, their situation would have stood in grave danger before they obtained the city. Indeed, even after the city had first been obtained by God’s grace, they could scarcely endure his arrival.

## CHAPTER XV. Our men send scouts, anxious about the enemy’s arrival.

Meanwhile the rumour of the coming of so great an army had spread in advance and filled the camp. With many people reporting the same, it was held almost certain that the enemy were stationed nearby. Greatly concerned, the princes sent experienced men, whose fidelity and ability they could rightly trust, in different directions, so that with the utmost care they might inquire through persons whom they could not lawfully distrust and learn more clearly whether matters were as commonly reported.

The following were chosen for this duty: noble and valiant men-at-arms—Drogo of Neelle, Clarenbald of Vendoil, Gerard of Cerisy, Rainard, count of Toul, and several others whose names we do not possess. Scattered in different directions with their companies, they investigated diligently with all possible care. Sending their own scouts farther onward, they learned with certainty that armies were converging and assembling from every quarter, as rivers run into the sea. At length they returned quickly and fully informed the princes who had sent them, who no longer doubted.
