Thus, seven days before the aforesaid prince arrived with his legions, our leaders had been forewarned. They instructed the scouts not to make the matter known to the people, lest the common soldiers, exhausted by hunger and the long duration of their labours, be too greatly shaken by fear and think of flight—as had recently happened even to some of the leading men.

## CHAPTER XVI. Meeting together, they deliberate. Bohemond reveals the secret entrusted to him by his friend.

[Col. 0341C] Meeting together concerning the matter in which the success of the whole enterprise seemed to rest, they began, in humility of spirit and contrition of heart, to deliberate among themselves what ought to be done in so great a necessity. At last some thought that all those engaged in the siege should leave the city and advance two or three miles to meet the approaching multitude. There, invoking heavenly aid, they should test the fortune of war against the proud prince who had excessive confidence in his own power.

Others thought it more expedient to leave part of the army in the camp, to restrain within the walls citizens seeking to depart and join the enemy, while the stronger and better-armed part, according to the first proposal, should meet the approaching enemy three miles away in the power of the Almighty and there engage them, if this were so ordained by the Lord.

As they debated this more earnestly among themselves and each offered his opinion as he thought fit, Lord Bohemond called aside from the crowd, more privately, the leading princes: Duke Godfrey, Lord Robert count of Flanders, Lord Robert count of the Normans, and Lord Raymond count of Toulouse. Having brought them together in a private place, he addressed them:

> I see, dearest brothers and partners in God’s service, that you are worn down by much anxiety concerning the coming of this prince who is said to be on his way. In the deliberation already proposed, swayed by different desires, you have reached different conclusions; yet neither party is directing itself to the point upon which the whole issue depends.
>
> For whether we all leave, as some among you wish, or whether a part remains in the camp, we seem to have expended labour, effort, and resources uselessly for so long a time. If all depart, the siege will be dissolved and our purpose frustrated: the citizens will recover their freedom, either by going out freely and joining the enemy or by admitting supporting troops into the city.
>
> But if a portion of the legions remains in the camp, I see the same result must necessarily follow. How can one part, with the enemy’s reinforcements present, restrain the citizens inside the city, when all of us together, with our strength united and undivided, and the citizens cast down without any hope of support, could scarcely restrain them?
>
> One of two things, I believe, will certainly occur: either, united to their reinforcements, they will attack us with combined strength and greater power; or at least, having admitted auxiliary forces, they will carefully furnish the city with food and arms. Thus, even if by the Lord’s aid we should defeat the enemy outside, no confidence would remain to us of obtaining the city.
>
> Therefore, most reverend fathers, I think all our effort ought to hasten to this end, and all our concern should turn upon this: before the arrival of this great prince, the city should first pass into our control.
>
> If you seek the means by which this plan of ours may be carried into effect, so that we may not appear to propose impossibilities, we have at hand a short path by which the desired end may easily be attained. I have in the city a friend, faithful so far as the human eye can judge, and very prudent. As I remember having already told some of you, he has in his power a most strongly fortified tower. Under certain conditions, pledged by good faith, he is bound to surrender it to me whenever I demand it.
>
> For this act I have promised to give him much money; and, if the enterprise should obtain the desired result, I have pledged in good faith to grant to him and his heirs in perpetuity substantial estates and complete freedom, as wages for his labour.
>
> If, therefore, it seems good to your eminence that the city captured by our care and effort should pass under our jurisdiction to be possessed by hereditary right, I am ready to fulfil my agreement with this friend of mine. But if not, let any one of you labour and obtain the city by whatever effort he can; let him possess it peacefully and undisturbed. Here and now I yield to him my claims and renounce my right.

## CHAPTER XVII. The rejoicing princes grant the city to Bohemond; he secretly negotiates with his friend concerning the city’s surrender.

The princes, having heard these words, rejoiced with great joy; and, concurring in a welcome assent to the proposal offered—except Count Raymond of Toulouse, who most obstinately declared that he would yield his own claims to no one—they granted the city with its appurtenances to be possessed in perpetuity by hereditary right. They mutually pledged themselves and, giving their right hands, bound themselves not to reveal to anyone the secret entrusted to them. They also warned and earnestly exhorted Lord Bohemond [Col. 0343A] to devote all diligence to completing the matter, lest he allow a dangerous delay to intervene.

When the meeting had been dissolved, he, being a man impatient of delay and ardently pressing forward his purpose, summoned his friend by the customary messengers. Informing him that he had obtained everything from the princes according to his wishes, he made his friend’s mind happier than usual. He therefore admonished and invited him, under the pledge of their mutual faith, that on the following night, with God as author, the matter should be brought to completion.

Meanwhile, as is said, something had occurred which nevertheless encouraged him toward the undertaking already conceived. For while he was occupied with the extensive service and care which he had in his lord’s household and throughout the whole city, he is said by chance [Col. 0343B] to have sent home, for some urgent but unknown reason, his son, who was already of age. On arriving there, the boy discovered a detestable thing. He found one of the chief Turkish princes engaged in illicit sexual intercourse with his mother. Horrified and inwardly pierced with grief of heart, he hastened back to his father and disclosed the abominable deed in detail.

The father, moved by the bitterness of the act and inflamed with marital zeal, is reported to have said: “Is it not enough for these unclean dogs that they unjustly oppress us beneath the yoke of slavery and daily impoverish our estates by exactions? Must they also violate the laws of the marriage-bed and dissolve the rights of marriage? If I live, by God’s aid I shall put an end to this insolence of theirs, repaying them a compensation worthy of their deserts.”

Having said this, he concealed the injury; and he sent his son—who knew the secret and was ashamed of the outrage done to his mother—by the customary route to Lord Bohemond, earnestly warning him to prepare every necessity for the aforesaid undertaking. As for himself, there would be no delay in him to prevent the promise being fulfilled on the following night. He further instructed him that about the ninth hour all the princes, each with his own retinue, should leave the camp as though setting out to meet the enemy; but that, about the first watch of the night, they should return secretly and silently, and about midnight hold themselves ready according to his instructions.

Bohemond therefore secretly brought the young man to the princes who knew the secret, and laid before them in order the plan which he had received from the father through him [Col. 0343D]. Astonished at the man’s resourcefulness and the sincerity of his loyalty, they approved the plan and agreed that it ought to be carried out.

## Chapter XVIII. The citizens regard the aforesaid man with suspicion; he declares his innocence before the prince.

In those same days there occurred something which often happens in great affairs. The citizens, especially those more closely charged with the care of the city, began to foresee—not from any evident signs, but rather from suspicion—that a secret negotiation for the surrender of the city was underway; and this report began to be on nearly everyone’s lips. Therefore the leading men of the city assembled and approached the prince [Col. 0344A] to deliberate upon the matter; for it seemed plausible, and many presumptions supported it.

There were in that city, as we have said, many Christians who, although wholly innocent of this charge, were nevertheless held suspect. Among them was the aforesaid nobleman; and although Acxianus had no small confidence in the sincerity of his loyalty, the other magnates entertained the same suspicion of him. When they were before Acxianus and anxiously deliberating about the affair, they mentioned this man among the others who seemed suspect. Indeed, they seemed to have the greater reason for suspecting him because he was an enterprising man and more powerful in the city than the other Christians.

The aforesaid prince, being in some measure persuaded by them, ordered him summoned. When he stood before him, discussion of the matter was deliberately continued in his presence, so that his counsel might be heard and it might plainly be discovered from his speech whether he was rightly suspect or not. But, being an astute man of very quick discernment, he immediately perceived that the meeting had been convened on his account and that he was suspect among them. Accordingly, in order skillfully to conceal his purpose and establish his innocence before them, he is reported to have said to those assembled to test him:

“You, venerable men and chief princes of this city, entertain a concern that is highly commendable and can have place only in a prudent man. For one prudently fears what can happen [Col. 0344C], and abundant caution in a capital matter does no harm. Thus you appear not to have been stirred lightly in showing this concern for liberty, life, wives, and children.

“Yet, if you are willing to accept our counsel, there is a fairly short way by which a fitting remedy and suitable care may be applied to this danger which you fear may come. This most detestable affair, which you so prudently fear may occur, can in no way be brought about except through the agency of those set over the towers and walls and assigned to guard the gates. If you distrust their loyalty, let them be changed frequently, lest, remaining long in any fixed place, they be able to contract a ruinous familiarity with the enemy.

“For an affair of this kind is not easily accomplished, but requires a long time; nor can the weight of so great a matter rest with a private person unless also some of the leading men of the city, corrupted by bribes into an equal partnership in the crime, become involved. But a sudden and frequent change of guards will cut off every opportunity for such dangerous dealings.”

Having said this, he seemed to establish his innocence and somewhat to mitigate the suspicion conceived against him. His speech pleased them and appeared good in everyone’s eyes. His counsel would at once have been put into effect, had not the day already declined as night came on, so that so great a change in the city’s arrangements could by no means be made at that time. They nevertheless ordered that the city be guarded with watchful care and exact diligence [Col. 0345A], wholly unaware of what the aforesaid man was secretly arranging. But he, knowing that the matter was soon to undergo the greatest change, busied himself carefully to see that in the meantime his purpose might be fulfilled before any obstacle arose.

## Chapter XIX. The severe distress endured by the Christian people in the city; and how the slaughter prepared for them was delayed.

From the very first entry of our people, when the siege was established around the city, the citizens had regarded Greeks, Syrians, Armenians, and all others professing the Christian faith, of whatever race, with suspicion. Therefore they immediately expelled from the city those of lesser means who could not support themselves and [Col. 0345B] their little households with necessary food, lest they burden the city; retaining only the wealthy, those with large estates and food sufficient in their homes.

Even these they afflicted with such compulsory services and requisitions (*angariae* and *parangariae*) that those expelled from the city seemed better off than those to whom they had granted residence in the city as a supreme favor. They frequently imposed money-fines upon them, violently extorting whatever they seemed to possess; and they dragged them unwillingly to every filthy task and civic burden. If engines had to be erected or beams of immense weight transported, that work was immediately imposed upon them. They were compelled to carry stones, mortar [Col. 0345C], and every material necessary for building works; they were also obliged to supply millstones for missile engines to cast outward, and to work the ropes by which these were hurled, compelled without interruption and without any rest, according to the will of their overseers.

Finally, after faithfully and devotedly performing the services imposed upon them, they received blows with the fist and lashes as their reward, suffering undeserved insults. Nor did this suffice those unclean dogs beneath whose violent domination they were oppressed. In order to complete their unheard-of wickedness, eight days before they summoned, as stated above, the aforesaid man as a suspect, they had secretly taken counsel and decreed that all Christians dwelling in the city should be killed suddenly by night. Had not a great and prudent prince of the city, who had always shown himself a friend to the Christians, against the wishes of the others secured an eight-day reprieve for carrying this out, the whole body of Christians would beyond all doubt have fallen by the sword that very night, when the armed agents charged with executing that most destructive plan were sent out.

The aforesaid postponement of eight days had been granted for this purpose: that in the meantime they might see whether the siege would be lifted. If our people persisted in the siege, what had been decreed would then be executed; but if they withdrew, the citizens condemned to death would be spared. The respite had elapsed, and that was the final night. A secret edict had already been issued that the sentence should be carried into execution [Col. 0346A], when Bohemond and the aforesaid Emirfeir had agreed that our people would carry out their purpose on that same night. It had been firmly determined that what had long before been planned between them should be fulfilled—and, by God’s aid, it was fulfilled.

Thus it happened that, when our people occupied the city that same night, the leading men of the city were less alarmed by the sudden tumult, thinking that the noise in the city signified nothing other than the violence which they had ordered to be inflicted upon their Christian fellow citizens. And when the city had been violently broken open, very many enemies were found in the homes of the Christians, assembled there in order suddenly to kill the unsuspecting people, as had been commanded them.

## Chapter XX. In accordance with the counsel of the aforesaid man, the army leaves the camp, intending to return at night.

[Col. 0346B]

Accordingly, about the ninth hour, a herald’s proclamation was sent throughout the camp, publicly ordering all men of the knightly order to arm themselves and follow the chief princes, ready without delay to execute whatever should be commanded them. Not only the common people were ignorant of this secret; it had been revealed even to only a few of the leading men.

Thus, in accordance with the prudent man’s counsel, all the troops of cavalry left the camp, followed the standards of the princes, and pretended to go far away until the coming of night brought its customary darkness over the earth. Concealed by it, they returned secretly and silently to the camp [Col. 0346C].

This man of God, who had shown such favor to our people, had a half-brother of a very different mind and purpose. Since he had little confidence in his brother’s loyalty, he had communicated none of his secret to him; rather, suspecting him, he concealed his purpose as far as he could. On the same day, while our legions were leaving about the ninth hour, the two brothers stood together at the battlements of the wall, looking out over the camp and watching the forces depart.

The elder brother was anxious to know the younger’s intention and carefully probe his will. Therefore he began and said to his brother: “My brother, I pity this people who have embraced the grace and faith of our profession, for whom so sudden a destruction is being prepared. Ignorant of what the morrow will bring, they go out confidently and, as though their affairs were secure, seem to fear nothing. Yet if they knew how great the snares being prepared for them were, and how great a ruin was near at hand, perhaps they would provide otherwise for themselves.”

His brother replied: “You wear yourself out with foolish anxiety and are exhausted by undiscerning compassion. Would that they had all already fallen beneath Turkish swords! Since the first day of their entry, our condition has become much worse; and it can scarcely be that so much advantage will come to us through them as the troubles we have suffered on their account.”

Thus he who had previously doubted whether to communicate his purpose to his brother now shrank from him as from a pest, abhorred him in his heart, cursed him in his conscience, and, lest Christ’s service should be hindered through him, began to plan his death [Col. 0347A], preferring the public safety of the Christians to brotherly affection.

## Chapter XXI. Bohemond urges his friend to complete the undertaking; he kills his dissenting brother and admits the Christians into the city by a lowered ladder.

Meanwhile Lord Bohemond, wholly intent upon fulfilling his wishes and preventing the desired result from being delayed through his own negligence, went among the princes and urgently urged them to be watchful. He had ready at hand a ladder skillfully woven from hempen ropes, which was to be fastened below with iron hooks and above to the battlements of the wall.

Now at midnight, when the whole city had given itself to rest and, after continuous watches and immense labor [Col. 0347B], strength had yielded to sleep, he sent a household interpreter, very close to him, to the aforesaid friend to inquire carefully whether he still wished his lord’s household to be at hand in support. On arriving, the interpreter found the man awake at the battlements. When in a low voice he had conveyed his lord’s words, the man replied: “Sit quietly and be silent until the captain of the watch, who approaches with a great retinue and the blaze of lamps, has passed this place.”

For it was the custom in the city that, besides the guards assigned to individual towers, their chief magistrate should make the rounds of the walls three or four times in the night with a large retinue, carrying lighted torches before him, so that if he found anyone overcome by sleep or behaving negligently, he might subject him to due punishment. Passing by, this man of such great authority found the aforesaid man awake, praised his diligence, and hurried on confidently to the further posts.

When the man saw that an opportune hour for action had presented itself, he addressed the interpreter aside: “Go quickly and tell your lord to come in haste with chosen men.” The interpreter returned more swiftly than speech to his lord, found him ready, and he secretly summoned the other princes. In the twinkling of an eye, as they had been forewarned, each followed with his household retinue, and they suddenly stood like one man before the tower long beforehand designated, so that no cry or noise could be heard from them.

Meanwhile the aforesaid man entered that tower and found his brother heavy with sleep. Knowing his brother’s mind to be hostile to his own plan, and fearing that through him an obstacle might arise to a matter now almost accomplished, he pierced him through with a sword—at once pious and criminal in the deed [Col. 0347D].

After this, returning to the battlements and seeing present those whom he had ordered to be summoned, he exchanged mutual greetings with them and lowered a rope, by which he drew up the raised ladder. The ladder having been set upright and firmly fastened both above and below, no one was found who, at the command of the man above or at Lord Bohemond’s order, dared climb up and make such an experiment upon himself. When Lord Bohemond saw this, he himself climbed first, fearlessly.

Having crossed the ladder and already laid his hand upon the battlement of the wall, the man inside grasped it; recognizing Bohemond’s hand, he is reported to have said: “May this hand live!” Then, in order to win greater favor from him and from all the Christians—because he had pierced through his half-brother, who had not consented to so holy an undertaking—he led him into the tower and showed him his brother lifeless and bloody with his own blood.

Lord Bohemond therefore kissed the man’s steadfastness and the sincerity of his loyalty. Returning to the wall, he put his head out briefly through the battlement and, in a subdued voice, began to invite his men to climb. But they still hesitated; none dared climb, judging everything said from the wall to be a trick. When he realized this [Col. 0348B], he returned to his men by the same ladder and gave manifest proof of his safety. Consequently they climbed eagerly, and in a moment filled the wall; they occupied not only that tower but also several adjoining ones. We have heard that among the others the Count of Flanders and Lord Tancred climbed up, and that the rest were directed by their instruction.

## Chapter XXII. Those admitted open a gate; the army, now made aware of the secret, rushes into the city. The city is stormed.

The princes, seeing that the number and prudence of those who had already climbed up sufficed to open one or more gates, returned with all speed [Col. 0348C] to the camp, in order to prepare their forces and, when the signal was given by those inside, not delay entering the city.

Those who had climbed onto the wall, strengthened from on high, under the leadership of the aforesaid man who had admitted them, had already occupied ten towers in one uninterrupted stretch, killing their guards. Yet the whole city still slept, so that no sound whatever was heard. On that side of the wall by which our people had climbed there was a postern gate. Descending to it, they broke its bars and bolts and forced it open. Admitting those waiting outside, they increased the number of those within enormously. Then, rushing in force to the gate called the Bridge Gate, they killed its guards with the sword [Col. 0348D] and forced it open.

Meanwhile some of Lord Bohemond’s household had carried his banner up onto the mountain overlooking the city and set it beside the upper stronghold in a fortress at a most elevated place. When they perceived that the glowing dawn announced sunrise, they gave a signal with horns and trumpets and began to make a great noise to encourage those in the camp to enter the city.

The princes, recognizing the meaning of the signal they had agreed upon, seized their arms, suddenly gathered their troops, and rushed into the city, taking possession of the approaches and gates. Meanwhile the common people, awakened, who until then had been unaware of the secret, saw that the camp was almost deserted; following the others, they eagerly poured into the city.

The citizens, awakened by so great a tumult [Col. 0349A], at first wondered what this unusual cry could mean. Then, seeing the unfamiliar movement of armored men through the city and the slaughter occurring everywhere in streets and squares, they understood the situation. Leaving their houses, they tried to escape with their wives and children. While avoiding the ranks of armed men, seeking hiding places and a way of safety, bewildered as to what to do, they rashly threw themselves among the armed men.

But those inhabitants of the city who were Syrians, Armenians, and Christians of other nations greatly rejoiced at what had happened. Seizing arms, they joined the companies of our people; and because they had greater knowledge of the places, they led others after them and showed them the byways of the city. They opened whatever gates were still shut by killing their guards and breaking the bolts [Col. 0349B], thus admitting the rest of the army.

This reversal seemed to them to have come from the Lord: those who had been subjected to unclean dogs beneath the yoke of unjust slavery, mercilessly worn down by compulsory service, requisitions, and torments, now in turn repaid equivalent injuries and brought destruction upon them. The entire army of our people had now entered; they had freely taken possession of the gates, towers, and walls; and the standards of the princes and the well-known emblems, set in the highest and most conspicuous places, gave proof of victory.

There was slaughter everywhere, mourning everywhere, everywhere the wailing of women. When fathers of households had been killed, their households were slaughtered indiscriminately; houses were broken open, vessels plundered, and all their property was surrendered as spoil to the first arrivals. The victors ran through places formerly inaccessible and, drawn by the lust for killing and desire for gain, spared neither sex nor rank; nor did age make any difference in their eyes.

Meeting one another through the streets and squares of the city, they carefully asked where the houses of the powerful were and where the wealthier inhabitants had lived. They rushed there in joined bands; after killing the household servants and breaking open the inner rooms, they pierced with swords the children of nobles and mothers of households, dividing among themselves by equal lot the household goods, gold, silver, and precious garments. More than ten thousand citizens, it is said, were killed that day [Col. 0349D]; their bodies lay unburied everywhere in the streets without distinction.

## Chapter XXIII. The citizens withdraw into the stronghold; Acxianus, fleeing outside the city, is killed; many are hurled headlong from the mountain.

Acxianus, seeing that the city had been delivered to the enemy, that they had seized the towers, walls, and the whole city, and that the people [Col. 0350A] who had escaped slaughter were rushing into the stronghold, feared that the Christian army, pursuing them thither, would surround the stronghold with a siege. Therefore, alone and without a companion, he went out by a postern, distraught yet seeking some swift means of preserving life and safety, and took flight.

As he wandered alone, aimless in the anguish of grief, he happened to meet some Armenians. Recognizing him at once, they approached as though intending to show their customary respect. But when he, as if beside himself, allowed them to come near, they understood from his solitary flight that the city had been conquered. They violently threw him to the ground and, drawing his own sword, cut off his head. They carried it into the city and offered it before the whole people to the princes.

There were in the city certain nobles who had come from distant regions to aid the people of Antioch in the exercise of arms. Ignorant of the terrain, once they learned that the city had fallen under our people’s control, they were uncertain what to do and anxious for their lives, and resolved to withdraw into the upper stronghold. As they hurried there with all intent, they happened to encounter our people from above; trapped in the narrowness of the ground so that, because of the mountain’s steepness, they could neither climb nor descend, they were pressed from above by our men. Trying to flee in any manner whatever, about three hundred were hurled down with the horses and arms in which they were equipped. With necks broken and limbs crushed [Col. 0350C], they scarcely left any trace of themselves.

But those who were more agile, having knowledge of the terrain either from the city or the neighboring province, at first light, after learning that the city had been breached, went out in joined bands through the gates which were already beginning to open, in order to flee to the mountains. Our people pursued them closely: some were brought back and forcibly fettered; others, having escaped on horseback, fled to the mountains and preserved their lives and safety.

About the fifth hour of the day, when our men who had gone out returned, and those who had been scattered throughout the city were gathered together, it was carefully sought out and certainly learned that no provisions at all had been found in the city. This was not surprising [Col. 0350D], since it had been enclosed by continuous siege for almost nine months. Yet such and so great an abundance of gold, silver, gems, precious vessels, tapestries, and silk fabrics was found that one who had formerly begged in hunger was now made wealthy and possessed everything in abundance.

In the whole city scarcely five hundred horses fit for arms were found, and even these were wasted by emaciation and perishing from hunger. Antioch was therefore taken in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1098, in the month of June, on the third day of the month.

# Here Begins the Sixth Book

[Col. 0351]

## Chapter I. The mountain is described, and part of it is occupied by the enemy, guards being stationed there. Men are sent to the sea to summon the people; and, provisions having been brought in, the city is fortified.

[Col. 0351A]

When the tumult had been quieted, the swords drunk with blood, and the victors wearied by continuous killing, and when the city had at last become quiet, the princes assembled. Understanding that much labor remained and that the undertaking was not yet completed, they assigned guards to the gates and walls and decided to climb the mountain and attack the stronghold.

A herald’s proclamation was issued, and they compelled all the companies to ascend the aforesaid mountain in haste. Having arrived there, they perceived from the fortification of the stronghold that it was altogether impregnable and could be reduced only by hunger. Seeing that they would uselessly expend labor and effort, and that the matter required the delay of many days, they turned to other measures.

This mountain, which overlooks the city, is divided by a very deep valley and an exceedingly steep precipice, so that the part facing east is lower and has a broad level summit suitable for vineyards and cultivation. Yet the separation by that deep ravine is so great that it seems rather like two mountains than one mountain divided into two. The part stretching westward is far higher and more peaked; on its higher section the stronghold is situated, with a solid wall and very strong towers. On the east and north [Col. 0351C] it has the aforesaid immense, abyss-like precipice, so that one cannot even conceive how the stronghold could be harmed from those two sides.

To the west, however, there was a lower hill. Between it and the stronghold lay a valley, but a small one, neither broad in width nor steep in depth. Through it ran the sole and only route for those wishing to descend from the stronghold into the city, dangerous enough in itself even without anyone attacking. The princes of our people therefore decided to occupy this hill, lest, perhaps, enemies admitted through the gate of the stronghold might have an open descent into the city to the injury of our people.

Accordingly they stationed there prudent and valiant men, leaving them what was necessary both in arms and food. They built a solid wall with battlements, placed engines on it in suitable order so that they could repel attacks by the enemy, and then the princes descended into the city to deliberate upon more important matters, intending to return to the same place when these affairs had been completed. For they had resolved that all should remain there until the stronghold was taken, except the lord duke, who, by common counsel of the princes, had assumed custody of the Eastern Gate, together with the fortification outside the city which our people had strengthened and committed to Lord Bohemond [Col. 0352A].

Hearing that the great prince mentioned above—namely Corbagath—would soon arrive and had already entered the territory of Antioch with innumerable forces, they decided to send one of the princes to the sea, in order to summon back those of their brethren who had gone there to gather provisions and food, and to order that everything necessary found there be carried to the city as quickly as possible.

It happened that during the two days which seemed to remain before the arrival of the larger forces, they labored with every care, moving about everywhere and bringing into the city whatever food and fodder they could collect from any source, striving with all their effort to transport it there. The inhabitants of the suburbs and cultivators of the fields also, knowing that the city had been restored to the Christians, diligently brought in whatever they could carry. But what was brought in from every side was little, almost nothing; for the long siege, which had exhausted the entire region during nine continuous months, had left nothing by which even a few days’ relief could be given to our people.

## Chapter II. Three hundred men sent ahead by the main enemy army range before the city. Roger of Barnavilla, imprudently confronting them, is killed.

On the day after the city was taken, while our people [Col. 0352C] were very anxious about guarding the city and bringing in provisions, behold: three hundred horsemen from Corbagath’s army, sent ahead in order to discover whether they might find any of our people outside the city behaving incautiously, fully armed and mounted on swift horses, laid an ambush near the city.

Thirty of them, who appeared to have the swifter horses, began to range as far as the city, deliberately pretending ignorance and riding about carelessly. When our people in the city saw them moving about in this way, they took it badly, deeming it utterly shameful if no one went out to meet them.

Therefore a valiant man-at-arms, whose exploits in that army were many and distinguished—Roger of Barnavilla, of the retinue of Lord Robert, Count of the Normans—took fifteen companions and hurried out from the city to meet them, intending, as was his custom, to perform some notable deed. As he charged more boldly against those raiders with reins loosened, they suddenly, but deceitfully, turned to flight and kept up their flight until they reached the ambush of their own men. Then those who had lain concealed rose up; their number being restored, they rushed back by a circuitous path upon those pursuing their companions and put them to flight.

Roger and his men, unequal in strength and number, tried to withdraw into the city. But Roger, overtaken by the speed of the enemy’s horses, was mortally pierced through the chest by an arrow, fell from his horse, and died [Col. 0353A]: a man to be mourned forever by his own people, and, so far as lay in him, a most faithful champion of the Christian expedition.

While the others withdrew into the city, the enemies, before the eyes of all who were on the wall and in the towers, no one offering assistance, cut off the memorable man’s head and returned unharmed. After they departed, our people brought his body into the city with honorable funeral rites, not without tears and the groaning of all, and, in the portico of the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles, gave it a magnificent burial as the last duty of humanity, in the presence of the princes and the entire people [Col. 0353B].

## Chapter III. The great prince approaches and pitches camp in the mountains above the stronghold. The duke is driven back at the Eastern Gate; two hundred of our men perish.

But on the following day, the third dawn after the city’s liberation, at first light around sunrise, the oft-mentioned most powerful prince, with forces infinite and even greater than had been reported, covered the entire region visible from the higher part of the city with the multitude of his men. Having crossed the upper bridge, he pitched camp between the lake and the river, which seem to be separated by a distance of about one mile [Col. 0353C].

The multitude of his expeditionary forces and the number of his soldiers were so great that even that notable plain, in which, as we have said, Antioch lay, scarcely sufficed for their camps; some also occupied the neighboring hills by pitching their tents there.

Finally, on the third day after he had encamped before the city, seeing that he was too far from it, he took counsel with his men in order to bring nearer aid to those defending the stronghold and to be able to introduce his own men into the city through the gate below the fortress. Breaking camp, he climbed into the mountains and enclosed the entire southern side in an unbroken siege, from the Eastern Gate to the Western Gate.

Near that same Eastern Gate there was a certain fortification on a somewhat elevated hill. From the beginning it had been built to protect the camp and had first been entrusted to Lord Bohemond for safekeeping. But after the city was taken, when he began to exercise general command, they assigned this fortification, together with the neighboring gate, to the custody of the lord duke [Col. 0353D].

When the enemy pitched their camp around this fortification and made very frequent attacks upon those within it with great persistence, their duke, unable to endure their violence, went out with his retinue to bring aid to those in the fortification, who were nearly failing, and to break up the camps placed before the gate. But as the duke went out to assist his men, a huge multitude of Turks met him. Unable to withstand a force far superior both in strength and number [Col. 0354A], he barely escaped their swords and fled back into the city.

There, while the enemy pressed on with extreme violence, the undisciplined crowd was crushed more fiercely and, because of the throng, prevented one another from entering. Nearly two hundred men, some trampled down, some wounded, and some captured, perished miserably.

## Chapter IV. Our people dig a trench within the city at the foot of the mountain; battle is fought there, and the enemy are defeated. The enemy commander descends from the mountain and besieges the city from below.

Thus, when the duke had been thrown into confusion, though he seemed as it were the foremost of all, the Turks were raised to such boldness that, by the gate of the upper fortification, descending into the city by certain well-known shortcuts, they suddenly fell upon our men; and finding them unprepared, they killed many, for the most part with arrows and swords. But when our men pursued them, they quickly made for the mountain and withdrew into the upper citadel, having other routes thither than by the hill which our men had occupied and carefully fortified. Since this happened frequently, and many of the people in the city perished through this stratagem, the princes assembled to devise a remedy for so great an evil.

Accordingly, by common counsel, Lord Bohemond and the lord Count of Toulouse drew a very deep trench, of suitable width, between the lower part of the city and the slope of the mountain, so that the attack of those accustomed to descend from the mountain might be checked and the people within the city might rest in peace. And, to make the trench more serviceable for their defence, they built a fortification there, all the companies applying themselves faithfully and zealously to the work as though for their own safety. But the Turks, who still held the upper fortification and those who were outside in the siege, having been admitted by the upper gate and descending by hidden paths, repeatedly attacked this new fortification and laboured with all the force they could command to overthrow it.

It happened one day that a body of Turks, issuing from the upper parts by their usual shortcuts, more numerous than usual, began to assault with such force those within the aforesaid newly built stronghold that, unless the princes assigned to guard other parts of the city, together with all the people scattered through the city, had come to their aid promptly, they would almost have overcome Lord Bohemond, Evrard of Puyset, Ralph of Fontaines, Reibald Creton, Peter son of Gilo, Alberic, and Ivo—brave and noble men who had gathered within it for its defence. But the duke, the Count of Flanders, and the prince of the Normans arrived with great force and so repressed the enemy’s insolence that, after killing many and taking some captive, they compelled them, driven into flight and roughly handled, to flee with all speed not merely from the fortification but from the entire city. Returning to their lord, these men proclaimed the strength of our people and the marvellous steadfastness of their courage, so that the following prophecy seemed fulfilled in them: “The tongue of your dogs [shall have its portion] from the enemies” (Psalm 67:25). For those who had persecuted the faithful people extolled its renown.

Meanwhile Corbagath, having remained continuously for four days in the mountains, as we have said, saw that he was making no progress and that forage for the horses was failing. He broke camp and again descended with all his forces to the plain. Having crossed the river at the lower ford, he divided his troops into detachments spaced at equal intervals, stationed his commanders in a circle, and enclosed the city in siege. On the following day, when certain men detached from the army challenged our men to battle, it happened that they dismounted from their horses and, rashly pressing those upon the wall, suffered losses among their own. For Lord Tancred, having gone out through the Eastern Gate, suddenly fell upon them; before they could return to their horses, he killed six of them and put the rest to flight. Cutting off their heads, he brought them into the city to console the people, who were shaken by deep grief at the loss of Roger of Barneville, who had been killed there.

## CHAPTER V. The people within the city suffer greatly from hunger. Certain nobles secretly flee from it; Bohemond is placed in command of all.

Meanwhile the people who, a few days before, had besieged this same city and violently taken it when it was under siege, now, with fortune reversed—as the vicissitudes of events commonly are—endured a siege themselves and were troubled beyond measure by severe hunger and exhausted by labours exceeding their strength. Outside was the sword, and within, terror. For, apart from the well-founded fear they had conceived from the numerous armies besieging the city from outside, they had no peace while the enemy still held the fortification from which, as has been said, incursions were very frequently made.

Thus it came about, as their sins required, that many, falling into despair, forgetful of their profession and prodigal of the oaths they had taken, were secretly lowered by ropes and in baskets over the wall and, abandoning their companions, fled to the sea. Some of them fell into the hands of the enemy and were enslaved in perpetual servitude. Others reached the sea and compelled those on the ships to flee, after cutting their anchors, saying: “A great prince has come here with innumerable forces and violently retaken the city which we had captured. The whole number of our people has been destroyed and the princes slain; we ourselves, with the Lord’s help, escaped their swords. Therefore cut your ropes and make haste to flee, lest, coming down to the sea, they involve you in equal danger.” They themselves boarded the ships with them and took flight.

Those who fled in this way included not only common and low-born persons but also noble men distinguished by great lineage: William of Grandmesnil, a renowned man of Apulia, who had as his wife the sister of Lord Bohemond, and his brother Alberic; William the Carpenter, Guy Trousseau, Lambert the Poor, and many others whose names we do not retain, because, being erased from the book of life, they are not to be inserted in the present work. Some also, which was far more abominable, through fear of future danger and impatience with hunger and hardship, went over to the enemy, wickedly renouncing Christ’s teaching and faith. By informing the adversaries of our condition, they brought almost the final danger upon our people.

Others who remained in the city nevertheless conceived, for the most part, hopes of escape. But the venerable bishop of Le Puy and the illustrious prince Lord Bohemond forestalled their plans. For, placing prudent men at each gate—men in whose experience and fidelity they could rightly place confidence—and assigning noblemen to the towers, they maintained watch by night and day with unwearied diligence, so that no avenue of escape at all was open to anyone, however swift or cunning. And that they might exercise more freely the general authority granted to them, all, from the greatest to the least, swore that until the Antiochene undertaking had been completed and the war expected to follow had been brought to an end, they would devoutly and faithfully obey the commands of Lord Bohemond.

Accordingly, he continually, night and day, accompanied by his household and intimate retainers and by those in whom he had greater trust, went about the lanes and streets, walls and towers of the city with great concern, carefully investigating lest anyone behave incautiously or any entrance be left open to the enemy’s snares.

There were four strongholds requiring especially vigilant guard: first, the upper one, situated opposite the upper citadel; second, the one below, established within the city above the trench, against the incursions of those accustomed to descend into the city from the gate of the upper fortress; third, the one outside the Eastern Gate, built before the capture of the city to guard the camp; and fourth, the one constructed at the bridgehead, by which the Bridge Gate had most recently been besieged. The Count of Toulouse had abandoned care of this last position when, after the capture of the city, he entered the city with the others.

After the city had been taken, the Count of Flanders entered this fort and carefully strengthened it with five hundred brave and valiant men, fearing that if it should by chance fall into the enemy’s hands, our people would be denied passage in and out across the bridge, and the condition of those under siege would thereby become much worse.

## CHAPTER VI. The Count of Flanders, unable to preserve the stronghold before the Bridge Gate, voluntarily abandons and burns it. The enemy prince sends certain captives of our people to Persia.

It happened one day that Corbagath, seeing that our people had excessive freedom to go out and come in, and that the aforesaid stronghold near the bridge greatly obstructed his efforts, ordered some two thousand armoured men of his own to arm themselves and attack the stronghold with all their strength. They immediately obeyed his command. Having placed suitable posts around the trench of the said fortification, they assailed the place from the first hour of the day until the eleventh with uninterrupted attacks and engagements, showering it with arrows as fiercely as they could. The count and his men resisted bravely and defended with all their strength the place whose protection he had undertaken.

When, near sunset and with evening approaching, the attackers saw that they were making little progress, they ended the assault and returned to camp. But the count, fearing that their forces would be increased and that on the following day they would undertake a similar operation, and knowing that he could in no way defend the aforesaid fortification against so great an army, set fire to everything in the silence of the deep night, committed it to the flames, and withdrew with his companions in this undertaking into the city. At daybreak, those who had attacked the fort the previous day returned for the same purpose, having taken with them another two thousand men. But when they hastened to the place and found it deserted and for the most part destroyed, they returned home without accomplishing anything.

During the same days, some men from the enemy army secretly went out and happened upon certain of our people, poor and needy men travelling incautiously, whom they captured. They brought them before their prince and set them before him, that they might dedicate to him as their lord the first fruits of their success and booty. But he, scorning the wretchedness of the captives in both arms and appearance—for their bows were wooden, their swords foul with rust, and their clothing torn by continual toil and showing age through constant use; the pilgrim people had no spare changes of clothing to use in turn—is reported to have said:

“Behold the people that ought to trouble foreign kingdoms; for whom, instead of great riches, it ought to suffice if bread were given them as to base hired servants in whatever corner of the earth. Behold the weapons by which the prowess of the East ought to be scourged—by which a struck sparrow would scarcely perish. Bind them and put them in fetters, and present them, together with their weapons and this clothing of theirs, to my lord who sent me, that from these he may understand how insignificant it is to triumph over such men, and what sort of people those are whom this miserable nation boasts that it has subdued. Let him therefore cast aside his concern and lay all this anxiety upon me; for it will soon come to pass that these unclean dogs shall cease to appear, and, utterly consumed, shall no longer be counted among peoples.”

Having said this, he ordered them handed over to certain persons appointed for the purpose, who were to lead them in chains, in accordance with his order, to the Great Sultan in Persia. He thought it a very easy matter to subject to himself men whose courage he had not yet tested. Since he had thought this would add to his glory by enabling him to disparage them before his lord, it was afterwards turned to his own disgrace. The more contemptible, in his judgment, were those by whom he went away conquered and confounded, the greater was the insult inflicted upon him and the greater the shame incurred. For it is usually a kind of consolation to the defeated, making their misfortune lighter, if they are said to have been overcome by brave and valiant men; whereas, conversely, victory won by the unworthy and insignificant doubles their shame and increases their dishonour.

## CHAPTER VII. As the famine intensifies, the people unwillingly resort to unclean foods.

Thus, with the city enclosed on every side by siege, and with the people no longer permitted to go out or come in and procure their needs outside, the condition of our people became much worse. Since no food supplies were brought in, a famine more severe than usual arose in the city, so that, through lack of provisions and the harshness of pressing hunger, the starving people, in order to obtain nourishment, resorted to exceedingly shameful expedients.

There was no distinction in food even among the refined; there was none of that legal distinction between clean and unclean. Whatever chance offered, whether freely or for payment, was turned into food; thus the roaring and hungry belly was filled, if what had been taken was at least sufficient for that purpose. Nobles felt no shame, nor free-born persons embarrassment, at forcing themselves as unwelcome guests upon others’ tables, greedily coveting what was in others’ hands, and importunately asking for what was often refused.

Modesty had fled from matrons to whom it had once been familiar, and reverence from virgins. Forgetful of their birth, gaunt of face, and with piteous cries that could have moved hearts of stone, they sought food everywhere without fearing refusal. But those whom the severity of hunger could not overcome so that, laying aside shame and hardening their brow, they would descend to begging, hid in secluded places and wasted away within themselves, choosing rather to die than expose themselves publicly to ask for something.

One might see men formerly robust, whom outstanding courage and illustrious nobility had made conspicuous and distinguished above all others, supporting themselves upon staffs because of extreme weakness and carrying their half-dead limbs through lanes and streets, their countenances cast down, begging alms from passers-by if not with their voices. One might likewise see crying children, still needing the nourishment of milk, abandoned everywhere at the crossroads, their mothers withholding maternal care because they were not even sufficient for themselves, so far as to obtain anything necessary for themselves.

Scarcely anyone in so great a population was self-sufficient. Resources had failed almost everyone, and begging had become, as it were, customary for all. Or if any person still possessed household means, he nevertheless remained in need when what was necessary was not available for sale. Those who had formerly been judged generous and lavish among their own people in providing sumptuous meals sought the most hidden retreats and places inaccessible to others; taking whatever refreshment they could, they greedily consumed what they had gathered from anywhere, sharing none of their food with anyone.

Why say more? Camels, horses, asses, mules, and every unclean thing and things unworthy to mention—animals strangled or dead of themselves—whenever they could obtain anything of them, they considered the greatest delicacies. With these they drove off their pressing hunger and somehow sustained their wretched lives. Nor had the calamity of this most miserable famine enveloped only common people and those of middling rank; it had also thrust itself most grievously upon the greater princes. It was all the more burdensome to them because, providing for more people, they required greater resources and could not deny their generosity to those who asked.

To recount what happened to each of the great men—although ancient traditions still preserve this—and the want in which the pious princes suffered for Christ would be far from the brevity proper to history and would require separate treatises. But, to state it briefly, scarcely does any history record such great princes and such a great army enduring elsewhere, without collapse and with such patience, so many hardships.

## CHAPTER VIII. The enemy secretly almost take one of the towers; Henry of Esch resists bravely and, after killing many, forcibly retains the citadel.

Meanwhile, while the city was thus surrounded on every side by siege through the effort and activity of Corbagath and his men, and the enclosed people could go nowhere out while no one could enter to them, and while they were exhausted beyond their strength by almost unceasing fighting both in the city and outside it, it happened that, failing in themselves through the duration of their toil and the pressure of hunger, they guarded the city less watchfully and less diligently. Since nearly all their concern was occupied with obtaining food for their bodies, they necessarily became more negligent in attending to other matters.

Thus it happened one day that a tower near that through which our people had been given entrance into the city, being guarded too carelessly, almost gave the enemy an opportunity to attack the city again. Some of the enemy, hoping that they could occupy it in the silence of the night and thereby have a descent into the city open to them, as it had formerly been open to our people, secretly set ladders against the wall in order to take it. By the twilight of night, about thirty had climbed onto the wall and were about to enter the empty tower.

As they laboured more eagerly at this task, it happened by chance that the commander of the watch, inspecting the walls, came to the place where these things were being done. Recognizing their plot, he loudly called out and roused those in the neighbouring towers, announcing that the tower had been deceitfully occupied by the enemy. Those keeping watch in that district were aroused by the alarm. Among them was the brave and distinguished Henry of Esch, who, with two kinsmen, namely Franco and Sigemar, from the village called Machela on the river Meuse, hurried vigorously to that place, fearing that perhaps the city had been treacherously surrendered to the enemy by persons corrupted with money.

When he arrived, he and those gathering to him from the neighbouring towers bravely attacked the enemy. With his accustomed valour he drove them from the said tower in a moment, despite their very great resistance, killing four of them with the sword. The other twenty-six—for thirty had already climbed up and were intending afterward to admit others—were hurled from the wall, their legs, arms, and necks broken. Yet the brave man lost his companion Sigemar, pierced through by a sword; Franco, mortally wounded and almost half-dead, he had carried home.

## CHAPTER IX. The enemy descend to the sea, burn the ships, and kill many of our people on the road.

As hunger pressed the besieged more heavily every day and famine grew more dangerously severe, the people suffered more grievously. Therefore, overwhelmed by the multitude of their straits and the unremitting burden of daily affliction, some who disregarded life and safety secretly left the city and descended through the midst of the enemy ranks, through a thousand dangers, to the sea, where there were still some Greek as well as Latin ships, in order to buy food and bring it back to the city for sale. Others, however, went away never to return, to free themselves from so many dangerous misfortunes; they had no hope that the affairs of those left in the city could improve, or even that they could avoid the enemy’s swords.

When the Turks learned that our people were descending secretly to the sea by hidden routes and at night to seek food, and were wandering about near the city, they sent out persons familiar with the region to lay ambushes for them and inflicted very frequent massacres upon them. Since they often succeeded in this, they dispatched two thousand chosen horsemen to the coast, to kill the sailors and merchants, burn the fleet, and henceforth cut off every kind of trade. Thus, with that means of commerce cut off, all sustenance might fail the Christians altogether and every hope of survival be blocked. And this was done.

For, carrying out the command, they burned some of the ships, killed for the most part such sailors as they found unprepared, and put the rest to flight. Terrified greatly by this report, those who customarily came from Cyprus, Rhodes, and other islands, and from Cilicia, Isauria, Pamphylia, and other coastal regions for trade, thereafter feared to return there or bring merchandise and did not dare approach. Hence the condition of our people, though previously exceedingly dangerous, became yet more dangerous, since trade in goods for sale wholly ceased.

For while merchants had free access by sea, although what they brought in was small and unable to supply so great a population, it nonetheless provided some consolation to our people and somewhat relieved their need. But the enemy, returning from the coast, also found certain of our people on the road and killed them all with the sword, except a few who were able to hide in thickets, brushwood, and the recesses of caves. This evil report afflicted our people no less than the enormity of the famine itself; for whenever they heard of the death of their own people, their grief was renewed. Thus, exhausted beyond their strength by so many hardships, immense toil, the daily destruction of their companions, and the severity of misfortunes, they began to despair of life, to take less care for their own defence, and to obey the princes less readily.

## CHAPTER X. Stephen, Count of Chartres, goes to the Emperor at Constantinople.

Meanwhile William of Grandmesnil and the others who had fled with him arrived at Little Alexandria, where Lord Stephen, Count of Chartres and Blois—whose return both the princes and all the people awaited day after day with burning desire—was still pretending illness. They reported what was happening at Antioch; and, lest they themselves should seem to have abandoned their companions for a slight and frivolous cause and out of cowardice, they exaggerated the extent of the hardships and affliction. Although it was great and incomparable, they made it greater by their deliberate account and spoke of great things as greater still.

Nor was it difficult to persuade him of anything that could increase his fear, since he himself had earlier abandoned his companions for the same reason and fled from their fellowship, feigning illness. Thus, after taking counsel together and having ships ready, they put to sea. After sailing for some time, they came to one of the coastal cities. Anxiously seeking to discover exactly where the emperor was, they learned through the differing yet truthful report of certain persons that the emperor had pitched camp near the city of Finiminis with countless forces of Greeks and Latins, on his way to Antioch, as though to bring assistance to our people, as he was bound to do by agreement.

Besides the forces which he himself had gathered from every nation, nearly forty thousand Latins had joined him. These had been left behind in the emperor’s lands by the forces which had gone before, whether because of poverty, the illness of themselves or their people, or other pressing reasons. Now, having recovered their strength and heartened by the emperor’s presence and his innumerable forces, they eagerly strove with all their spirit and mind to hasten to join their fellow travellers, confident of making the journey.

When the aforesaid Count Stephen heard that the emperor was staying there, awaiting greater forces and preparing to depart, he took a shortcut with those accompanying him and hurried with all speed toward the emperor’s army. Arriving there, he was received honourably enough, though with amazement, by the emperor; for the emperor knew him, and when Stephen had originally crossed with the others, he had gained the emperor’s friendship. The emperor carefully questioned him concerning the life, safety, and condition of the princes, and concerning the reason why he had returned separately from the others. He replied:

## CHAPTER XI. His speech to the same emperor, full of falsehood and destructive to the faithful.

“Your faithful men, most invincible emperor, who not long ago crossed over through your exalted power and, by your generosity from your abundance, became wealthier, reached Antioch by a highly prosperous course after the capture of Nicaea. Having besieged the city itself in unbroken siege for nearly nine continuous months, they violently made it their own, through the Lord’s mercy preceding them, except for the city’s fortification, which is situated on a higher mountain, overlooks the city, and cannot be overcome by any force.

“When they believed the undertaking finished and thought that, now the city had been taken, they had escaped every danger, the last error became worse than the former and they fell into dangers much greater than those they had suffered. For scarcely had three days elapsed after the capture of the city when, behold, Corbagath, the most powerful prince of the Persians, with infinite forces of Easterners and a multitude exceeding all number, enclosed the same city in siege. Denying entrance and exit to the besieged from every side, he afflicts the princes and all the people with such numerous and great hardships that one cannot even hope for their lives.

“It is not easy to comprehend the number of those besieging them. To state it briefly, their forces have covered the entire region adjoining the city like locusts, so that even the ground seems to lack room for tents. Our people have been so worn down by hunger, cold and heat alike, slaughter and destruction that they have all gathered inside the city and scarcely seem able to suffice for its defence.

“Moreover, you should know that even the consolation customarily brought by ship from your empire, both from the islands and other coastal cities, has been utterly cut off. For the enemy, having sent out part of their forces, have occupied the entire region between Antioch and the sea, so that, after the fleet was completely destroyed and sailors and merchants killed by the sword, they have cut off from our people every hope of trade and confidence in obtaining food. Nor, they say, is there enough food left even in the city to meet the need of a single day.

“To increase the accumulation of their miseries, they do not even possess a safe refuge within the city. For men are secretly and repeatedly admitted into the city through the upper fortress and make incursions; dangerous conflicts occur in the very middle of the city, through its lanes and streets. Thus our people have no less concern about internal conflicts than about those brought upon them from outside.

“Therefore we, together with the captains and noblemen here present with us, seeing that our brethren’s affairs could not prosper, met with them and repeatedly and fraternally warned them to take thought for themselves and cease wishing to undertake an impossible matter against the will of God. When we could not turn them from their purpose, we took care for our own safety, lest we should imprudently be involved in equal calamities.

“And now, if it please you and your illustrious advisers judge it so, cease advancing, lest the fortunate expeditions which you are leading with you be involved in equal dangers. For it is more prudent to withdraw with the enterprise unattempted and affairs still intact than rashly to encounter, by some chance event, so many and such great dangers in the face of a multitude supplied by the entire East. The illustrious men here present, partners in the same lot, are witnesses to what we say; as is also Tatinus, a prudent and shrewd man whom your highness sent with us. Recognizing the failure of our people, he very wisely withdrew himself from their company in order to make these matters known to your majesty.”

There was in the emperor’s aforesaid army a brother of Lord Bohemond, named Guy. When he heard this, he was almost driven mad, lamenting the fate of his brother and friends. At first he opposed the count’s account, reproaching him with cowardice because he had imprudently withdrawn himself from so great a body of princes. But the aforesaid man, William of Grandmesnil—illustrious by birth, though not so in character—restrained him. William had as his wife the sister of Guy and Lord Bohemond.

## CHAPTER XII. The emperor returns home; believing the words of the aforesaid count, he disbands the forces gathered to aid our people.

Having heard these things, the emperor summoned a council of his princes and deliberated whether he should proceed or whether the army ought to be recalled home. After a reasoned deliberation suited to the time and the matter, it was finally judged expedient by common counsel that it was safer to bring the army home unharmed than to provoke against himself all the kingdoms of the East and recklessly entrust himself to the uncertain hazards of fortune and battle.

The emperor placed such faith in the words of the aforesaid count that he not only believed matters to be as Stephen had asserted, but even feared that the aforesaid prince, having, as was said, killed our people, might enter his empire with all the multitude which he was said to be leading. He feared that he might again be forced to lose Nicaea and all Bithynia, which he had recovered through the labour and zeal of the pilgrim princes.

Taking precautions against this possibility, he ordered all the provinces, on his return from Iconium to Nicaea, to be given over to fire and plunder on both sides, so that, should the enemy by any chance wish to direct their expeditions against his empire, the devastated region, deprived of food and emptied of inhabitants, might at least provide some obstacle. Thus, through the action of the aforesaid count, the Christian army, which had the greatest need of it, did not receive the assistance which the emperor was prepared to give according to his agreement.

Yet, to those who consider the matter inwardly and investigate it carefully, it may seem that, although the aforesaid count’s deed can in no way be excused, since its source and first cause were vicious and at variance with honour, nevertheless what followed from it, through the providence of him who alone can and knows how to bring even things begun with an evil purpose to better ends, certainly redounded to the glory of those princes and of the people of God who seemed to have been so overthrown. For those who had borne the burden of the day and the heat, and who, leaving wives and children, had resolved to serve the Lord as pilgrims, deserved to carry away glory for their labours—a glory which, had the emperor been present, he would have begrudged all the others. For it would have appeared that he had completed the undertaking, owing to his pre-eminent authority and the greater number of his forces, if he had been present with his expeditions; and so the palm of victory would rightly have belonged to him. It is therefore believed that the Lord arranged matters so that those who had laboured faithfully and devoutly amid countless dangers might carry away the fruit of their labour and the title of victory.

## CHAPTER XIII. On learning of the emperor’s withdrawal, the enemy press their attack more fiercely. Our people despair and refuse service. Bohemond sets the city on fire to draw them from their hiding places; the princes contemplate flight, but the duke resists.

The report of the emperor’s withdrawal meanwhile filled the city through the accounts of many; it added a further burden to the troubles under which they were incessantly oppressed and hurled almost all headlong into the abyss of despair. They abhorred the memory of the aforesaid count and condemned it forever; they cursed William of Grandmesnil and all participants in that impiety, praying that they might have their portion with Judas the traitor in everlasting fires. For they had not only withdrawn themselves from the common labours, but had also deprived God’s people of so great a support as, in their view, the Lord had prepared for them. [Col. 0364C]

But Corbagath, and the chief princes who were in his camp, just as, when the emperor’s arrival had been learned through scouts, had rightly been held in suspense, suspecting his strength and not without reason fearing the power of the empire, so now, having learned through the same men of his departure, raised themselves to still greater insolence. As though they had conceived certain hope of victory, they pressed and hemmed in our people more boldly and more closely. Thus the faithful in the city were reduced to such calamity, and placed at the uttermost extremity of manifold misery, that no hope of safety and no avenue of consolation seemed any longer to remain. Despair had so prevailed and seized all men that, when Lord Boamund, to whom the general care of the whole army had been entrusted above all others, went about the city, he could achieve nothing either by words or by blows: he could not draw even one man from the houses in which they hid, nor assign them to keep watch or to meet the enemy, whether within or outside the city, whose many ambushes they endured. [Col. 0364D]

Therefore, on one day, after the heralds and officials had exhausted themselves with shouting and returned without accomplishing their business, when he saw that they were wasting their effort in vain and that he could bring no one out of hiding, he ordered fires to be set in many places by his servants and the city to be burned, so that at least through fear of the fire those might come forth publicly who, with hearts frozen, withheld zeal and service from God’s cause. Thus it happened that those whom previously he could not obtain at all he afterward found rushing competitively to perform their duties. It is also said that the princes, despairing of life and safety, after holding a private consultation among themselves, had secretly resolved that they themselves would flee by night, abandoning the people and the whole multitude, and hasten to the sea. When this became known to the duke and to the venerable bishop of Le Puy, they summoned them and assailed them with just reproaches, setting before their eyes what an everlasting mark of infamy those noble men had deserved for themselves and their posterity: they had withdrawn themselves from so great a fellowship of Christ’s faithful, contrary to moral honour, blackening the titles of their noble birth. [Col. 0365A]

There was therefore among God’s people such a lack of food, such distress of hunger, and so many and such great hostile pressures, both from without and from within, that nowhere could consolation or remedy be found against them. Great and small, involved alike in calamities, bestowed upon one another no comfort. Remembering the wives and children whom they had left at home, and the ample estates which they had relinquished for love of Christ, they recalled these in their minds and complained, as it were, of the Lord’s ingratitude: that he did not regard their labours and the sincerity of their devotion, but allowed them to be handed over to their enemies as though they were a people alien to God. [Col. 0365B]

## CHAPTER XIV. A revelation is made to a certain Peter; the Lord’s lance is found. The people are strengthened again.

[Col. 0365C]

While God’s people were thus afflicted, the Lord looked upon them and heard their groans, sending them consolation from the throne of his majesty. A certain cleric named Peter, as is said, from the region called Provence, approached the bishop of Le Puy and the lord count of Toulouse, maintaining that Saint Andrew the apostle had appeared to him in a dream and had very urgently admonished him three or four times to speak with the princes and tell them that they should seek with all diligence the lance with which the side of our Lord Jesus Christ had been pierced. It had been secretly deposited in the church of the Prince of the Apostles, and he had indicated its place by sure signs.

Approaching the aforesaid men beloved of God, he set forth in order the message which, he testified, had been laid upon him, asserting that he had been compelled to this by many terrors from that same apostle. For when he had often declined to undertake this mission because he was poor and without any wisdom, he declared that he could not evade the apostle’s most urgent command except at peril of death. They privately communicated the matter to the other princes and placed the same cleric before them, that they might learn from him the manner and form of the command. Giving credence to his words, they assembled at the place which he had designated to them within the enclosure of the aforesaid church. There, after the earth had been dug out to some depth, they found the lance, as he had foretold. [Col. 0365D]

When the people heard this, they ran unanimously to the church, as though consolation had been sent down from heaven. Honouring the precious discovery with gifts and offerings, they began in some measure to breathe again after their anxieties and to be restored with greater strength for divine service. There were also some others who said that they had seen visions of angels and holy apostles. Since these visions seemed mutually consonant, greater faith was placed in them, and the people rose immensely from their dejection. Therefore, at the urging of venerable men who feared God, all the princes again made a vow and, having given bodily oaths, mutually bound themselves: if the Lord mercifully delivered them from their present danger and granted them the victory they desired over their enemies, they would not separate from one another until, with the Lord’s aid, they restored the Holy City and its glorious sepulchre to the Christian faith and to their former freedom. [Col. 0366A–B]

## CHAPTER XV. By the common counsel of the princes Peter the Hermit is sent as envoy to the enemy; he fearlessly carries out his embassy.

After they had suffered this intolerable affliction continuously for twenty-six days, the people, recovering their courage, again girded their loins with strength and abounded in endurance beyond their usual measure, strengthened by a hope divinely implanted. All, from the greatest to the least, unanimously agreed that an end must be imposed upon these troubles and that battle must promptly be joined with the enemy, so that, by the aid of divine power, they might drive away those who relied upon their own strength and reclaim in freedom the city which the Lord had given them. [Col. 0366C]

For they judged it better to test the fortune of war once than to waste away in perpetual hunger and be tormented by the unceasing burden of pressing troubles. This was the subject everywhere discussed: they should go out from the city and fight the enemy. Nor was this merely the intention of the nobles; common people too, inflamed with the same desire, accused the princes of idleness and reproached their delays.

The princes therefore assembled together and, recognizing the divinely inspired fervour of the people, resolved by common counsel to send an embassy to the enemy’s leader and offer him one of two alternatives: either he should withdraw, leaving the city to be possessed forever by our people, since from the beginning it had been theirs by right and now, by the Lord’s act, had returned to that condition; or he should prepare himself for battle and undergo the judgment of the sword. Peter the Hermit, a man of venerable life, of whom we have said much above, was chosen to carry out this task. A certain Herluin was joined with him as companion and associate, a man possessing some knowledge of the Persian idiom and Parthian language, likewise prudent and discreet. They were instructed to deliver the message just described, with this further division: if the enemy should be found to prefer battle, it should be his choice whether he wished to fight alone against one of the princes; or to set a fixed number of his men against an equal number of ours; or to bring the whole armies and legions on both sides together in battle. [Col. 0366D–0367A]

Having obtained a temporary truce and requested peaceful leave to send the embassy, the two aforesaid men set out with their appointed companions for the prince’s tent. There, finding him with his commanders and satraps, Peter the Hermit—though small in stature, a man of great spirit—boldly and faithfully discharged the duty of his embassy.
