Approaching the aforesaid Persian satrap and showing him no reverence whatsoever, he spoke firmly and fearlessly:

“The sacred assembly of the princes beloved of God who are in Antioch has sent us to your nobility, warning you to cease from harassing them and from assaulting the city which divine mercy has restored to them. For Peter, prince of the apostles, a faithful and wise steward of our faith, converted this city from idolatry to the faith of Christ by the power of his word, the grace in which his exhortation excelled, and also the greatness of his signs, making it our own possession. Now the Lord, strong and mighty, has restored it to us after you had occupied it by force, but without right. Therefore, because they bear due concern for their ancestral inheritance and Christ’s familiar dwelling-place, they offer you one choice out of many: either desist from besieging the city and troubling its people, or on the third day from this you shall test the issue with them in a contest of swords. [Col. 0367B]

“And lest you perhaps excuse yourself from the offered contest and find a plausible pretext for evasion, they give you the choice of one among several courses: either fight alone against one of the princes, and, if victorious, possess all, or, if defeated, cease; or let several fight against an equal number on the same terms; or let the entire legions on both sides test the events of war.”

He, scorning the embassy, is said to have replied:

“It does not seem to me, Peter, that the affairs of the princes who sent you here stand in such a condition that they ought to propose alternatives to me, or that I am bound to choose anything according to their will. By our sword they have been brought to such a pass that they no longer have freedom even to choose; rather, they must take up and lay down their will according to ours. Go therefore and tell the foolish men who still do not understand their condition, who sent you here to us, that all whom I can find of full age, of either sex, I shall preserve alive, assigned to the service of my lord; but all the rest I shall cut down with the sword like useless trees, so that no memory of them remains. Had I not considered it preferable that they be consumed by the bitterness of hunger rather than perish by the sword, long ago, after breaking down the walls and violently occupying the city, they would have reaped the fruits of their ways, subjected to avenging swords.” [Col. 0367C–D]

## CHAPTER XVI. Peter returns to the nobles; he reports the enemy’s arrogance to our people; war is proclaimed.

But Peter, having understood the disposition and learned the arrogance of the prince to whom he had been sent—an arrogance gathered from the multitude of his men and his incomparable riches—took leave and returned to his own side. When he had been received within the city and wished to give the replies he brought with him and make them known to the princes who had sent him, the whole multitude, both of the leading men and of the common people, was present, eagerly desiring to hear the form of the reply and the outcome of the embassy. [Col. 0368A]

As Peter had resolved, in the presence of all the people, to set forth in sequence the pride, threats, and excessive haughtiness of the prince to whom he had been sent, the illustrious Duke Godfrey feared that, if everything were disclosed in order to a people worn down by continual suffering and already failing under the immensity of their hardships, the multitude would be too greatly terrified and lose heart. He therefore restrained Peter when he wished to proceed with his account, led him apart from the larger crowd, and urged that, omitting the rest, he should briefly state only this in sum: the enemy demanded battle and was wholly preparing for it.

The people, then, understanding from Peter’s words that the enemy sought battle, all alike from the greatest to the least, inflamed by equal desires, eagerly sought this very thing. They received the news with such joy that they seemed entirely forgetful of the sufferings they had endured and certain of victory. As all shouted approval and signified, both by voice and gesture, their unanimity and common agreement, battle was proclaimed for the next day. The people returned joyfully to their quarters and spent that whole night sleepless in their desire for battle: they brought out weapons, prepared horses, cleaned mail-coats and helmets, fitted shields, and sharpened swords. No place was granted to sleep, no indulgence to slumber. [Col. 0368B–C]

Furthermore, a public order was issued and proclaimed by heralds that, at first dawn before sunrise, each man, having taken up arms and equipped himself for battle, should join his own division and follow the banner of his own prince. When morning came, about the first light of day, the priests and ministers of the Lord celebrated the divine offices in the churches and completed the sacrifice. They exhorted the people, after making the customary confessions in a spirit of humility and a contrite heart, to receive the body and blood of the Lord as communion against the perils of the world. Having forgiven offences and laid aside resentment, if any remained, and having more fully restored charity, they were to go forth to battle with greater confidence and truly be hearers and members of him who said: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). [Col. 0368C–D]

When the divine offices had been celebrated and all the divisions had been fed by the heavenly gift, such grace was divinely infused into them that those who yesterday and the day before, sluggish and dejected, emaciated and bloodless, could scarcely lift their eyes or raise their heads because of weakness, and, wasted by fasting and overcome by toil, had sought hiding-places forgetful of their former honour, now came voluntarily into public. Throwing off cowardice and as though their strength had returned, they carried arms manfully and presumed to plan war with their accustomed courage, promising themselves victory. [Col. 0369A]

In so great a people scarcely anyone of any condition or age could be found who did not meditate bold deeds, rise to arms, and foretell victory for himself. Priests, clothed in sacred vestments, went about the troops and assemblies, carrying crosses in their hands and invoking the aid of the saints. They promised indulgence for sins and full remission of offences to those who laboured bravely in the battle-line and wished to be defenders of their fathers’ traditions and the Christian faith. Likewise bishops exhorted princes and commanders of the army, both privately and publicly, insisting with all the grace of exhortation divinely given to them; they blessed the people and commended them to the Lord. Among them, the chief worshipper of Christ was the lord bishop of Le Puy, who continually devoted himself as a whole burnt offering to the Lord through exhortations, fasts, prayers, and generous liberality in almsgiving. [Col. 0369A–B]

## CHAPTER XVII. The battle-lines having been arranged, they leave the city, leaving the count of Toulouse for the city’s defence.

They assembled therefore at earliest dawn, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July [28 June], before the gate adjoining the bridge. Invoking aid from heaven, all unanimously, as one man, drew up their battle-lines before leaving the city and assigned to the drawn-up ranks their order and manner of advance.

In the first battle-line they placed Hugh the Great, brother of the king of France, as commander and standard-bearer. They associated with him Anselm of Ribemont, a man commendable in every respect, and other nobles whose number and names we do not have. Over the second they set Lord Robert, surnamed the Frisian, count of Flanders, with those who had followed his camp from the beginning. Lord Robert, duke of the Normans, was commanded to lead the third, together with his illustrious nephew Count Stephen of Albemarle and other nobles who had come in his company. The bishop of Le Puy, Lord Adhemar of good memory, commanded the fourth battle-line with his own household and that of the lord count of Toulouse, carrying with him the Lord’s lance. [Col. 0369B–C]

The fifth was ordered to be led under the command of Count Rainard of Toul, his brother Peter of Stenay, Count Garner of Grez, Henry of Esch, Rainard of Ammerbach, and Walter of Dommart. The sixth battle-line was commanded by order of the princes by Count Rainbold of Oringis, Louis of Moncons, and Lambert, son of Conon of Montaigu. The illustrious and magnificent Lord Godfrey, duke of Lorraine, arranged the seventh according to military discipline, together with his venerable brother Eustace. Tancred, a man vigorous in arms and distinguished by nobility of character, commanded the eighth. Count Hugh of Saint-Pol and his son Enguerrand, Thomas of Fère, Baldwin of Bourcq, Robert son of Gerard, Rainold of Beauvais, and Galo of Calvignymont were commanded to arrange the ninth. The tenth was commanded by Count Rotold of Perche, Everard of Puiset, Drogo of Moncy, Ralph son of Godfrey, and Conan the Breton. Iscard, count of Die, Raymond Pilet, Gaston of Béziers, Gerard of Roussillon, William of Montpellier, and William Aiman held the eleventh. [Col. 0369D–0370A]

In the twelfth, which was the last and more densely filled than the rest, Lord Boamund was appointed commander and leader. He was ordered to march last, so that he might provide timely support to those preceding him and take provident care for those most heavily pressed by the enemy. They left in the city the lord count of Toulouse, who was dangerously ill with a severe sickness, for its defence against those who still remained hostile in the garrison, lest, in the princes’ absence, believing the city empty, they might attempt attacks upon the weak and sick, old men, women, and the unarmed populace. On the hill opposite the garrison they also made a very strong wall of lime and stones with battlements; upon it they placed several missile-throwing engines, leaving there two hundred men, strong in body and equipped with weapons, to defend the place. [Col. 0370A–B]

## CHAPTER XVIII. The enemy’s leader prepares to prevent the sortie, but our men break out courageously.

Their ranks thus arranged and drawn up for battle, they resolved by common counsel that Lord Hugh the Great, the lord count of Flanders, and the duke of the Normans should lead the remaining forces. They commanded all to observe this order of advance: infantry should go first, with cavalry following and carefully protecting them. It was also established by public edict and promulgated as a common law that no one should dare to covet the enemy’s spoils; rather, all should unanimously devote themselves to killing the enemy until, victory gained and the enemy overthrown, they could lawfully return to gather spoils. [Col. 0370C]

Corbagath, from the beginning—and especially after Peter had been sent to him—suspected that our men would suddenly emerge against his camp. He had therefore agreed with those in the garrison that, whenever our people contemplated a sortie and prepared to go out, the townsmen should promptly signal this to the camp. Thus, about the first hour of the day, while our men were arranging their battle-lines, those in the garrison, having discovered it, gave the agreed signal and conveyed the news at close range to the camp. Wishing to thwart our purpose, the enemy sent forward about two thousand of their men to meet our people near the bridge and prevent them from going out. In order to press more boldly and shoot more readily, they dismounted and formed themselves as infantry, occupying the farther part of the bridge. [Col. 0370D]

But our men, their battle-lines arranged and set in fitting order according to military discipline, opened the gate and emerged in succession, keeping their stations and divisions distinct. While the aforesaid enemy who had assembled to restrain our sortie laboured more vigorously at their purpose, Lord Hugh the Great, who, as we said, commanded the first division, sent forward bodies of infantry and archers and charged upon them more boldly. At first they tried to resist, but at last, unable to bear our attack, they were violently broken and put to flight. He pressed them with such vigour that they could scarcely regain the horses from which they had dismounted. When they had begun to flee, Anselm of Ribemont, a man worthy of remembrance, who was stationed in the first battle-line, immediately charged. He gave an example of valour memorable for all ages: heedless of safety, he boldly threw himself into the midst of their wedges; casting down some, piercing others, and striving fiercely amid their slaughter, he drew to himself the eyes and admiration of every rank. [Col. 0371A–B]

Seeing this, Hugh the Great, Robert count of Flanders, Robert count of the Normans, Baldwin count of Hainaut, and Eustace, the duke’s brother, hastened more swiftly to assist the aforesaid noble man, admiring his courage. Joining their strength, they charged and powerfully shattered whatever force yet remained. Inflicting countless slaughter upon them, they pursued the fugitives almost to their camp.

## CHAPTER XIX. As our men leave the city, dew is poured down from heaven, in which all received consolation.

Something worthy of remembrance occurred as our men went out from the city. While they were ready for departure and were already directing their battle-lines outside the gate, with the enemy who had intended to block the exit partly killed and partly turned to flight, a most pleasant dew, slight but very refreshing, was sent down from heaven upon our army. It descended so gently that the Lord seemed, as it were, to have poured into it his blessing and grace. [Col. 0371C]

Everyone sprinkled by that heaven-sent shower received such complete cheerfulness and soundness of mind and body, as though he had suffered no labour or hardship in the whole expedition. Not only men but horses also had their former vigour completely restored by God. Though for many previous days they had had only leaves and bark of trees for fodder, throughout that day they surpassed the enemy’s horses, which had been fed on barley and straw, both in speed and endurance. Thus, from the dew of that blessing, so great a hope of victory and grace of strength appeared to come to our divisions that this seemed to have been said of them: “God will set apart a voluntary rain for his inheritance” (Psalm 67:10). They did not doubt that they had manifestly received the grace of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0371C–D]

When the divisions had been led outside the city, they decided it was more useful to direct the lines toward the mountains, which lay about two miles from the city, and so occupy the whole plain, lest the enemy, possessing countless forces, might pass secretly or violently between them and the city, as they were accustomed to do in battle, surround our men on every side, and cut off access to the city for fugitives. They advanced at a slow pace, yet so that the battle-lines did not intermingle or the ranks become confused. [Col. 0371D–0372A]

By an operation of divine power, those who within the city were thought fewer than the enemy—indeed, almost nothing in comparison with them—appeared outside the city to be as numerous and as formidable as the enemy, or more numerous, or at least no fewer. He who had formerly known how to multiply five loaves, after the hunger of five thousand had been satisfied, into so great a quantity of fragments (Matthew 14:17), wished by no lesser miracle to increase, for the glory of his name, a people acceptable to himself and zealous for good works. Among those advancing to battle were devoted priests and Levites, clothed in white vestments and carrying in their hands the wondrous sign of the cross. Those who remained in the city climbed upon the walls, clothed in priestly garments; persevering in tears and prayer, with hands outstretched they prayed without ceasing to the Lord for the faithful people, that he would spare his people and not give his inheritance to the nations for reproach. [Col. 0372A–B]

## CHAPTER XX. Curbagath arranges his battle-lines; battle is joined hand-to-hand. Soliman, charging from the rear, heavily oppresses Boamund’s division; the princes come to its aid. As they falter, the Turks set fires to raise smoke.

Meanwhile the enemy’s leader, having learned of our sortie, both from the signal he had seen in the city’s garrison and from the reports of those who, defeated by our men as they emerged, had fled, summoned the elders and commanders of the expedition. He now began to regard as serious what he had previously treated as a game, and he began to regard with suspicion the arms and scanty numbers he had formerly seemed to despise. Therefore, by common counsel, though relying especially on the experience of the Antiochenes, he drew up battle-lines and arranged troops, carefully distinguishing who should lead and who should follow, and disposing everything with due concern. [Col. 0372C]

Among other measures, before our people had occupied all the open ground between the city and the mountains, he sent one battle-line, distinguished by prudent and powerful men and said to be commanded by the illustrious Soliman, prince of the Nicaeans, of whom we have very often spoken above, toward the sea. His purpose was that, if our people were defeated and turned to flight, those wishing to descend to the sea or re-enter the city might be met by this force, so that God’s people might be crushed between two millstones: those pursuing behind and those meeting them in front. He placed the rest on the right and left, under their individual commanders, and, under promise of his favour, sternly ordered them, mindful of their former courage, to strive to fight vigorously and manfully, counting as worthless whatever an army so unwarlike, a hungry mob, an unarmed and ill-considered populace might attempt. [Col. 0372C–D]

When the whole plain had been occupied and provision carefully made that they could not be surrounded by the enemy, our men, with trumpets sounding and the standard-bearers of the divisions going ahead, advanced step by step toward the enemy’s battle-lines. When they had approached so closely that the enemy could now shoot arrows at them, the first three battle-lines made an assault and unanimously charged, pressing forward hand-to-hand with lances and swords. Our infantry, armed with bows and crossbows, advanced before the bodies of cavalry, eagerly and competitively throwing themselves forward; the following squadrons of cavalry gave them all the protection they could. [Col. 0373A]

While the first battle-lines fought bravely in the contest, behold, those following them, joined to them and brought forward with no less impetus, made those who had preceded them still more outstanding in audacity and strength. When all the battle-lines except the last, commanded by Lord Boamund, had reached the enemy and were fighting them courageously, so that many had been killed and the enemy’s troops were almost broken and turning to flight, and when the duke with his contingent had already completely put to flight a stronger and denser enemy corps, behold, Soliman returned with the division which, as we said above, he had led toward the seacoast. He boldly and violently charged Lord Boamund’s division from the rear, sending such a multitude of arrows that it covered the whole line like hail. Then, laying aside their bows and neglecting their use, they pressed on with clubs and swords, so that Lord Boamund could scarcely withstand their troublesome attack. [Col. 0373B–C]

As he was more severely pressed and the division he commanded was nearly broken, although he himself, in the manner of a valiant and strong man, fought in the midst of the enemy with a few companions, the duke was suddenly summoned with his forces, and with him the distinguished Lord Tancred; they swiftly came to provide aid to Lord Boamund. At their timely arrival the enemy’s strength was immediately weakened and all their force withered away, while our men pressed more courageously and dealt wounds and death.

When the enemy saw themselves unequal in strength and unable longer to withstand the weight of the attack, they resorted to other devices. By their customary artifice they struck fire and set it beneath stubble. There was much hay there, very dry, and stubble altogether fit for burning; catching the fire placed beneath it, these supplied welcome fuel and, though producing only a small flame, gave off a black and dense darkness of smoke. Enveloped by it, our battle-lines pressed the enemy less vigorously, because the smoke greatly hindered their sight, as did the dust raised by the throng of horses and foot-soldiers. [Col. 0373C–D]

In this great darkness of smoke deliberately raised, the enemy pursued our men and killed some of the infantry. But the cavalry, carried away by the advantage of their horses, avoided that dangerous cloud; returning to the same struggle and trusting in divine aid, they continued the contest. Their strength renewed by God’s gift, they turned the enemy to flight with pursuing swords and did not cease their pursuit until they had forcibly compelled them to return to their own already broken formations.

## CHAPTER XXI. The enemy’s leader flees; their legions are destroyed; those who escaped are put to flight.

[Col. 0374A]

In that region there was a small valley through which, in winter, a torrent flowing down from the mountain customarily descended, and by its rushing course had worn out a channel in the valley. Beyond this, after our army had compelled the enemy to flee, they tried to resist for a while upon a somewhat higher hill and, with the sound of trumpets and the noise of drums, attempted to recall their broken legions once more. Our princes pursued them without pause and hastened up: both those who had laboured in the rear, where the greater struggle had been waged against Soliman—Lord Duke Godfrey, Lord Boamund, Tancred, and certain other nobles, victorious by the Lord’s help—and those who had crushed the battle-lines opposed to them at the front, namely Hugh the Great, both Roberts, count of Flanders and count of the Normans, and many others worthy of everlasting remembrance. [Col. 0374A–B]

Having crossed the barrier, they violently drove the enemy from the aforesaid hill and, once more dispersing them from one another, compelled them to take flight because they could not withstand our people’s steadfastness. Corbagath, avoiding the crowd from the beginning, had taken his stand on a hill and continually sent out messengers, who frequently returned to inform him about the outcome of the battle. While he waited anxiously to learn with what end so great a matter would conclude, he suddenly saw his legions utterly scattered, falling apart and cohering in no way with one another. Terrified by this sight, and advised by those accompanying him to look to his safety, he abandoned the camp, forgot his men, and fled as quickly as possible. Such fear seized him that, waiting for no one and changing horses in succession so that they might suffice for flight, he scarcely considered himself safe even after crossing the Euphrates. [Col. 0374B–C]

The remaining battle-lines, deprived of their leader’s support and lacking both the will and strength to resist, escaped by flight along the same route, so far as their horses could carry them, and evaded the swords of their pursuers. Our men, fearing exhaustion of their horses, did not dare to pursue far, except Lord Tancred and a few others, who pursued them while cutting them down for three or four miles until sunset. So great a fear had divine power cast upon them that they did not even attempt either to resist or to repel the attacks of their pursuers. Ten of our men seemed to them like many thousands, and there was no one who could offer consolation to the fugitives fleeing before our people. [Col. 0374C–D]

Here it was clearly made known that “there is no counsel against the Lord” (Proverbs 21:30), and the truth of the saying that “the Lord does not forsake those who hope in him” (Judith 13:17) was made evident and manifest by the event itself: a poor and starving people, trusting in God’s aid, was able to overcome so great a multitude of strong men and, beyond its own expectation, to confound in a single battle the whole East abandoned by God.

## CHAPTER XXII. Returning from the slaughter of the enemy, our men carry off infinite spoils from their camp.

[Col. 0375A]

The battle having thus been completed, and our princes having obtained by divine grant the victory, they returned to the enemy’s camp. There they found such an abundance of necessities, such stores of Oriental wealth, that there was neither number nor measure of the gold, silver, gems, silks, and precious garments, nor of vessels commendable alike for workmanship and material. There was likewise such an abundance of horses, flocks, and herds, as also of grain and provisions, that even those who had previously suffered the utmost want no longer knew what to choose.

Gathering the enemy’s pavilions and tents, of which they stood greatly in need—for age and the violence of the rains they had often endured had so damaged their own that they were now useless—they found in them manifold treasures. They also carried into the city the maidservants and little children whom the fugitives had left behind.

Among other things, they found the marvellous tent of their greatest prince, constructed like a city, with towers, battlements, and walls, woven of the finest silk in varied colours. From its centre, as from a principal banqueting-hall, attached quarters extended away in many directions, distinguished as though by streets; it was said that two thousand persons could sit within them spaciously.

Thus laden with spoils and enriched with booty, they carried everything into the city, keeping a solemn day in joy and exultation, giving thanks to Him by whose gift it had come about that, after overcoming so many dangers and passing through so many toils, they had obtained the victory for which they had hoped.

Those who were in the citadel, seeing that their own people had failed and that no necessary hope of relief remained, offered terms: they were to be allowed to depart safely, taking freely with them their wives, children, and all their property. The citadel was then surrendered to our princes, whose banners were placed upon the highest towers. Thus, through the overflowing grace of the Lord, once the city’s garrison had been recovered and victory secured, those who yesterday and the day before had been poor and almost starving began to abound in every kind of good.

Indeed, even the mightiest and most distinguished among them had been reduced to begging. To say nothing of the common soldiers, Count Harmannus, a nobleman from the German kingdom, had been brought to such poverty that bread from the duke’s table was assigned to him, as though it were a great gift, for his daily allowance. Henry of Ascha also, a man of singular worth, would have been utterly consumed by hunger unless the same lord duke had received him at his table as a guest. Even the duke himself, while the city was under siege and before they went out to battle, suffered such want that, having no horse, he could scarcely obtain by many entreaties from the Count of Toulouse the horse on which he rode in battle.

For both he and the other princes had already spent whatever money they had brought with them in generous almsgiving and works of piety, especially those directed to the common good, with ready devotion. Hence many noblemen, distinguished among their own people both by birth and courage, had exhausted their resources and become destitute by the day appointed for battle. Lacking horses, they went out to fight partly on foot, partly upon asses and cheap pack-animals. But the Lord, the kindly Comforter, seeing their poverty, bestowed overflowing riches upon them before the sun inclined toward its setting, once the enemy had been defeated.

There was renewed there, more manifestly, that ancient affair at Samaria concerning the measure of fine flour and barley bought for one stater. For he who in the morning could scarcely provide for himself had, by evening, enough to feed many.

This occurred in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1098, in the month of June, on the twenty-eighth day of the month.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The city having been put in order, they cleanse and restore its churches; they diligently establish clergy in them.

When the princes had returned from battle and the city had been settled in complete tranquillity, all took care—and especially the patron of the army, the venerable lord Bishop of Le Puy, with the cooperation of the other bishops in that army and the support of the people—to restore to their former splendour both the principal church of the city, which had been dedicated in honour of the Prince of the Apostles, and the other basilicas established throughout the city; and to restore in them a clergy devoted continually to divine service.

For the impious Turkish people had profaned the venerable places. Having driven out the ministers of divine worship, they had assigned the buildings to profane uses: in some they housed horses and pack-animals as in stables; in others they carried on activities unworthy of the places. They had even scraped from the walls the venerable images of saints—images which the simple people and the worshipping people of God, commendable in their devout simplicity, use as books, since in place of reading they stir the less learned to devotion. As though raging against living persons, they had gouged out their eyes, mutilated their noses, smeared them with mud taken from filthy places, thrown down the altars, and defiled the Lord’s sanctuary with unspeakable deeds.

It was therefore resolved by common counsel that, without delay, clergy should be restored in these churches and their former dignity re-established, with revenues assigned to sustain those who served the Lord in them. Accordingly, from the enemy’s spoils they offered gold and silver, from which were made candlesticks, crosses, chalices, Gospel-books, and the other vessels necessary for ecclesiastical use; also silks for priestly vestments and coverings for altars.

They likewise installed with great honour in his own see the lord patriarch, John by name, who, like a true confessor of Christ, had suffered innumerable torments from the unbelievers after the arrival of our people. In neighbouring cities which had customarily possessed cathedral rank, they appointed bishops. They did not, however, venture to elect or consecrate a patriarch of our Latin people while he who had formerly been ordained there was still alive, lest two should be seen to occupy one and the same throne—something clearly recognized as contrary to the sacred canons and the decrees of the holy Fathers.

Yet later, scarcely two years having elapsed, he, a Greek, saw that he did not preside usefully enough over the Latins; therefore he left the city and went to Constantinople. After his departure, the clergy and people of that city assembled and set over themselves as patriarch Bernard, bishop of Artah, a man of Valence by nationality, who had followed the Bishop of Le Puy on that expedition and had been his chaplain.

As they had promised from the beginning, they unanimously granted authority and lordship over the city to Lord Bohemond, except the Count of Toulouse, who held with his own guards the gate adjoining the bridge and its adjacent towers. These Bohemond later recovered, as shall be said below, after the count had departed from the city and the soldiers had been expelled. Since among his own people Bohemond had been called *princeps* by title of rank, the custom prevailed thereafter that the lord of Antioch should be called “prince.”

# BOOK VII BEGINS.

## CHAPTER I. Hugh the Great and Baldwin, Count of Hainaut, are sent as envoys to the emperor; Count Baldwin perishes on the road; Hugh the Great does not return. The Bishop of Le Puy dies; a plague arises.

The affairs of the city having thus been arranged, they decided by common counsel to urge the emperor of Constantinople through their envoys not to delay giving them assistance in person, according to the agreements he had made with them. He was to proceed toward Jerusalem and promptly follow them, as he was bound to do by his promise; otherwise, if he neglected the terms of the agreement, they themselves would by no means wish to regard themselves as bound by it.

Men noble and illustrious were chosen to carry out this mission: namely Lord Hugh the Great, brother of Philip, king of the French, and Lord Baldwin, Count of Hainaut. One of them disappeared when enemies attacked on the road; his fate is uncertain to this day. Some say that he fell in battle; others maintain that he was captured by the enemy, put in chains, and carried into the more distant East.

Lord Hugh the Great, avoiding the ambushes of the attacking enemy, reached the emperor unharmed. There, by his distinguished deeds, he cast a great cloud over himself and greatly diminished the honour of his lineage. For although in the expedition he had performed many noble deeds and thereby won immortal renown, in that embassy he tarnished his merit: after accomplishing the business, he neither brought back an answer to those who had sent him nor took care to return. His offence was the more conspicuous because he was more illustrious by birth. For, in the words of our Juvenal:

> Every fault of the mind bears a crime more conspicuous in itself  
> in proportion as he who sins is held to be greater.

Immediately after the city was taken and the victory completed, when affairs had already been settled in tranquillity, so great a disaster arose among the people from hidden causes that scarcely a day passed on which thirty or forty funerals were not borne out; thus what remained of the people was almost wholly destroyed.

In this pestilential plague and contagion, which indiscriminately enveloped everyone far and wide, the venerable man of holy life and immortal memory, Lord Adhemar, Bishop of Le Puy, entered upon the way of all flesh. Amid groaning, tears, and the heartfelt sighs of all, he was buried with great honour in the basilica of Saint Peter, at the place where the Lord’s lance was said to have been found, as a father and the chief ruler of the whole people.

By the bitterness of the same disaster Henry of Ascha, a man commendable both for noble birth and valour, died at the castle of Turbessel and was buried there. Rainard of Amesbach also, a knight famous alike for prowess and lineage, died of the same calamity and was buried in the vestibule of the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles. Almost the entire female sex likewise perished there from the same plague, so that within a few days nearly fifty thousand died.

Those curious about such matters, wishing to assign causes for so great an evil, disagreed among themselves. Some said that it happened from certain hidden disorders of the air; others assigned as its cause that the people, having long been afflicted by severe hunger, once they attained abundance of food, ate with excessive greed, seeking to compensate for their former lack, and thus brought upon themselves the cause of death through immoderate gluttony. They adduced as a clear argument for their view that those who were temperate and took food sparingly fared much better and returned to health.

## CHAPTER II. The people cry out that they should go to Jerusalem; the journey is deferred until the Kalends of October. Bohemond descends into Cilicia and takes possession of the whole region.

Meanwhile, both in order to escape the disaster and in view of the pilgrimage they had undertaken, the people began to cry out and insistently demand that the princes again prepare for the journey toward Jerusalem, for which they had come, and lead the Lord’s army, thereby satisfying the principal purpose that had summoned them all from their homelands.

For this reason the princes assembled and began deliberating upon this request of the people, so favourable and worthy of being heard. Some were inclined one way, some another. To certain of them it seemed more expedient to set out at once without delay and satisfy the people’s wishes. To others, because of the approaching heat of summer, the lack of water, the weakness of the people, long afflicted by severe hunger, and the lack of horses, it seemed best to defer the journey until the beginning of milder weather and the Kalends of October. In the meantime new horses could be acquired, the old ones restored, the people brought back to their former condition by food and rest, and everyone’s strength renewed, so that they might rise stronger for the labour of the journey.

At last the latter judgment pleased all, and by common agreement a respite was taken until the appointed time. But in order both to avoid the danger of the impending plague and to find elsewhere a greater abundance of necessities, the princes separated from one another on the condition that they should return without delay at the agreed time.

Bohemond descended into Cilicia and took the cities of Tarsus, Adana, Mamistra, and Anavarza; after stationing guards, he claimed the entire region for himself. Others also scattered through the neighbouring cities, living apart from the crowds and attending separately to themselves and their horses. Many of both common and noble rank eagerly crossed the Euphrates and hastened to Edessa, which was governed by Baldwin, the duke’s brother, hoping to deserve some gift from him. He received them with great honour, treated those staying with him kindly, bestowed many gifts upon them, and sent them cheerfully back to their own people.

## CHAPTER III. Lord Hasarth seeks the duke’s aid against his lord Rodohan. The duke summons his brother Baldwin and hastens there.

It happened in those same days that Rodohan, prince of the people of Aleppo, had fallen out with one of his satraps who governed the castle of Hasarth. Their hatred had reached such a point that Rodohan summoned troops from all the regions subject to him and besieged the aforesaid castle.

Seeing that he could not easily resist his powerful and angry lord except through the aid of the Franks, the lord of the garrison sent an embassy to Duke Godfrey through one of his faithful Christians. He sent gifts, that he might more easily win the duke’s favour; sought his friendship; and devotedly promised his service, desiring to bind himself to him by an indissoluble bond of alliance. So that the duke might place fuller faith in his words and have no doubt in any respect concerning his promise, he sent his son as a hostage, praying and asking that the duke free him from the present danger, in return for a reward proportionate to his deserts at an appropriate time.

Persuaded by these and similar arguments, the venerable man formed an alliance of friendship with the said nobleman and received him into his favour. He then sent a messenger commanding that his brother, the Count of Edessa, be summoned to him with military forces, so that he might free his friend by raising the siege.

Rodohan had scarcely remained with his forces before the castle of Hasarth for five days when Duke Godfrey, leaving Antioch in great numbers, both of his own followers and of friends whom he had invited to pursue this undertaking, was hastening energetically in strength to that region to assist his friend.

Those who had been sent by the nobleman to the duke, seeing that everything had been accomplished successfully and according to their wishes, and having won greater favour for their lord in the duke’s sight, could not personally make their lord more fully informed about it. For the hostile army had surrounded the castle so completely on every side that no entrance or exit was open to anyone. They therefore released two pigeons, expertly trained for this service, and tied to their tails little letters containing the substance of their embassy, so that they might more carefully inform their lord of all that they had obtained. Restored to their freedom, the pigeons returned in a moment to the place from which they had been sent. Their keeper and fosterer caught them together, untied the little sheets, and presented them to his lord. Once he had read them, he was raised to such hope that he who had formerly feared the besieging multitude and had long despaired of resistance was no longer afraid to provoke them of his own accord.

## CHAPTER IV. Baldwin meets his brother with enormous forces. The remaining princes provide aid. Rodohan flees. Some of our men perish on the road; up to ten thousand enemies are killed.

Meanwhile, after the duke had advanced with his company for the distance of one day’s journey, his brother met him with three thousand strong men, excellently armed. The duke received him kindly with complete charity and brotherly affection, disclosed the course of his undertaking, and carefully explained the alliance which he had made with the aforesaid nobleman. His brother approved all this, but first advised that, because his forces did not appear sufficient to raise so great a siege by force, before proceeding he should summon to his aid the princes who had remained at Antioch, so that he might undertake the affair with greater confidence.

Accordingly the duke accepted his brother’s advice. He sent an embassy and urgently entreated Lord Bohemond and the Count of Toulouse, inviting them humbly, under the claim of fraternity, not to delay bringing assistance to him for the sake of his distressed friend; at a favourable time they would receive a fitting return. He had indeed invited them earlier, before leaving the city, and had very amicably sought their help. But prompted by envy because the nobleman had sought the duke’s aid before theirs, they had refused to follow him. Now, reminded by the renewed summons and seeing that they could not honourably reject the duke’s entreaties, they gathered their forces, followed him, and joined his expedition.

When they had assembled, they numbered about thirty thousand fighting men. Rodohan, however, though said to have forty thousand Turks, distrusted his own strength and feared the arrival of our men, whom his scouts had learned would soon be present. He therefore broke up his expedition and returned to Aleppo.

While our army, unaware of Rodohan’s flight, continued its journey, many men of both ranks followed from a distance behind them from Antioch, intending to join the marching forces. Not a few, separated far from the preceding column, as we have said, accidentally fell into enemy ambushes deliberately laid for them. The Turks, greatly superior in both skill and strength, overcame them, captured some, and killed many.

When this became known to the duke and the other princes, they abandoned their intended journey and unanimously pursued the malefactors. Before the latter could withdraw to their own retreats and find their accustomed hiding places, our men encountered them by chance. Receiving them with the sword and attacking them boldly, they scattered them in a moment. They rescued their own men whom the enemy was carrying away in fetters; killed very many of the enemy; captured countless others; and put them to flight, having almost destroyed them to the last man.

These were about ten thousand of the chosen troops of the oft-mentioned Rodohan, drawn from his household and personal retainers. This accomplished, our army assembled again and arrived victoriously at the appointed place. The lord of the garrison met them with three hundred horsemen. Before all the assembled forces, he bowed his head, knelt with his knees fixed upon the ground, first gave great thanks to the duke and then, with much devotion, to the other princes. By bodily oaths given before all the people, he bound and surrendered himself faithfully to the Christian princes, declaring that no day and no event would ever separate him from their favour and service.

Thus the business having been happily completed and their friend delivered according to their desire, the army returned to Antioch, while Baldwin, the duke’s brother, returned to Edessa.

## CHAPTER V. To avoid the plague, the duke withdraws into his brother’s territory; there he destroys the towns of certain traitors. Some other princes also hasten there to obtain Baldwin’s generosity.

The duke, seeing that the aforesaid pestilence still reigned in the city and that the disaster was spreading more and more among the people, yielded to his brother’s request. His brother had earnestly begged him in person to come down into his territory and there avoid the heat of August and the harmful effects of the pestilential air. Taking with him his household retinue and a great multitude of needy people, so that he might charitably provide them with necessities, he entered his brother’s territory. He stayed within the districts of Turbessel, Hatab, and Ravendel, disposing of the whole region at his own will and often enjoying his brother’s presence.

While he was staying there, the inhabitants of the region, and especially religious men living in the many monasteries situated there, brought serious complaints against Pancratius and his brother Covasil in his presence. These two brothers were Armenians, men of distinction but exceedingly deceitful. They possessed fortified towns in that region and, trusting in their defences, harassed the inhabitants of the district, especially the monasteries, with burdensome and unlawful exactions. Their audacity had advanced so far that, while the siege of Antioch was still continuing, they had dared to rob on the road the envoys of the Count of Edessa, who were being sent with gifts to his brother; and they had sent to Lord Bohemond the gifts intended for the lord duke, in order to gain his favour against the Count of Edessa.

Having heard the complaints and moved by just indignation, the duke sent fifty of his knights with the people of the region. They violently broke into the brothers’ strongholds and, after breaking them open, razed them to the ground, in order somewhat to curb their intolerable insolence.

While the duke remained in those parts, almost all the leading men of our army, and countless common people as well, eagerly flocked to the said count, seeking some relief from the pressing hardships of poverty. This was especially so after the garrison of Hasarth, situated midway along the road, had come into the allegiance of our men. He received them all with such honour and rewarded them with such generosity that even those who had come for this purpose marvelled.

## CHAPTER VI. The citizens of Edessa, angered because their count used only Latins, conspire against him; Baldwin, warned of this, kills the conspirators.

As crowds of our people often flocked to the oft-mentioned city, there came to be so great a multitude of Latins in it that the citizens began to find it burdensome. For those frequently received as guests imposed hardships upon them, wishing to exercise excessive authority over the people. Baldwin also made less and less use of the counsel of the noble citizens through whose assistance he had acquired so great a city.

They were therefore inflamed with fierce indignation against him and his men, greatly regretting that they had made him their ruler. They feared that one day he, to whom nothing seemed sufficient, would strip them of all their goods. They consequently formed a conspiracy with the neighbouring Turkish princes and began to consider how Lord Baldwin might either be killed suddenly by some accident or at least driven from the city. To make themselves better prepared for this plan, they deposited their treasures and all their property with friends in neighbouring castles and cities.

While they frequently deliberated upon this with great concern, the report of a certain man, who possessed an abundance of sincere loyalty and affection for Baldwin, brought the matter to his ears. Finding very many credible and convincing indications of it, he sent a large force of his attendants and ordered all those murderers seized and bound in chains. Finally, when the affair had been more fully understood through their confessions, he ordered the leaders of the conspiracy blinded. Those who had been less guilty he banished from the city after confiscating their property. He added the substance of others to his treasury, but mercifully allowed them to remain in the city and punished them only by a monetary fine.

Having thereby received nearly twenty thousand pieces of gold, he distributed generous payments to those who had come to him and by whose aid he was subjecting cities and neighbouring fortified towns to himself. He inspired fear among both citizens and neighbouring peoples by his name alone. Therefore many devoted all their attention to contemplating his destruction, so much so that his father-in-law, fearing to suffer severe demands even for the remainder of the dowry which he had promised with his daughter but had not yet paid, secretly fled to the mountains where he held his strongholds.

## CHAPTER VII. Balas plots treason against the count; the count takes precautions; some of Balas’s companions are captured. Fulcher of Chartres lessens the loss. The traitor Balduc is killed.

There was in that same region a certain nobleman of Turkish origin, named Balas, allied with the count. He had formerly been lord of Sororgia and, before the frequent arrival of Latins, had been very intimate with the count. Seeing that the count’s affection toward him had cooled, whether at the citizens’ urging or through his own malice, he approached the count, praying and asking him to come in person and take possession of the one stronghold that remained to him. He declared that the count’s favour was enough for him and that he regarded it as a great inheritance. He further asserted that he wished to bring his wife, children, and all his property into the city of Edessa, for he pretended greatly to fear the indignation of his fellow tribesmen because he had become friendly with Christians.

Persuaded by these words, the count appointed a day on which he would come to the place and satisfy Balas’s request. On the appointed day he took with him two hundred horsemen and, with Balas leading the way, arrived at the designated place. But Balas had secretly fortified the town, bringing into the stronghold one hundred Turks, strong and excellently equipped with arms. They hid so completely in the garrison that none of them appeared.

When they had halted before the town, Balas asked the count to enter the castle with only a few intimates, lest, if that entire multitude were admitted, he himself should suffer some loss to his property. He had almost persuaded the count entirely, when certain noble and prudent men around him, somehow foreseeing treason, forcibly restrained him as he was about to enter. They rightly regarded the man’s malice as suspicious and thought it safer first to make the experiment by means of others.

The count accepted their prudent advice and ordered twelve of his own strongest men, excellently armed, to enter the stronghold. He himself remained outside with the rest of the cavalry in a place sufficiently near, waiting quietly until he could see the outcome with his own eyes. Those who entered experienced in themselves the deceit and malice of the wicked traitor. The hundred Turks of whom we have spoken, armed from head to foot, emerged from their hiding places and violently seized the deceived knights, who attempted resistance but in vain, and put them in chains.

Learning this, the count was exceedingly grieved and especially troubled for his loyal men whom he had lost by such treachery. Approaching nearer to the stronghold, he began earnestly to admonish Balas. Invoking the oaths by which Balas had pledged him fidelity, he urgently demanded that, upon receiving a vast sum of money, he return those whom he had treacherously captured. Balas absolutely refused unless Sororgia were restored to him.

Seeing that he was making no progress—for the stronghold was situated amid lofty rocks and was unconquerable by art or force—the count returned to Edessa, painfully enduring the captivity of his men and turning over in his mind with great anxiety the treachery he had suffered.

A certain Fulbert of Chartres, a man highly experienced in military affairs, commanded the aforesaid city of Sororgia and had under him one hundred very active horsemen. When he learned of the fraud suffered by his lord, he sympathized with all his heart and was consumed with the desire to avenge so great an injury. Therefore, one day, having placed an ambush in a suitable place before the oft-mentioned town, he approached deliberately with a few men as though to drive off plunder, intending that the enemy should pursue him.

Those in the fortified town, seeing him carry off booty from the pastures, seized their arms and eagerly pursued him in flight beyond the ambush he had laid. Then, recovering strength and joined by those who had been lying hidden, Fulbert’s party fell upon them. Having killed some and scarcely allowed others refuge in the town, he captured six alive. In exchange for these, after a short interval, he recovered an equal number of his own men. Four of those six escaped after deceiving their guards and regained their liberty; but the wicked and impious man ordered the remaining two to be beheaded.

From that day Lord Baldwin avoided the friendship of the Turks and regarded their loyalty as wholly suspect, as he immediately showed by clear evidence. There was in the same region a man of the same race, named Balduc, who had sold the ancient and very strongly fortified city of Samosata to the count for an agreed price. By agreement, he was bound to bring his wife, children, and whole household into Edessa; but, seeking frivolous pretexts, he postponed carrying out his purpose, looking for an opportunity to do mischief. When Balduc came to him as usual and offered trivial reasons for delay, Baldwin ordered him beheaded, lest he suffer something similar at his hands.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Count of Toulouse occupies Albara and appoints a bishop there. A German fleet arrives in the harbour. The disaster does not cease.

Meanwhile, while the duke was staying near Turbessel and these things were occurring in the regions of Edessa, the Count of Toulouse departed Antioch with his retinue and a large body of poor people. So as not to languish in idleness, he besieged the extremely well-fortified city of Albara, situated in the province of Apamea about two days’ journey from Antioch, and violently compelled its besieged citizens to surrender.

After taking the city and subjecting to himself the adjacent district with all its suburbs, he selected as bishop of that place a certain Peter, a native of Narbonne, from his own household—a man of honourable life and very devout. He immediately granted him half the city and the entire territory, giving thanks to God that, by his labour and effort, the East had a Latin bishop. By the count’s command, Peter went to Antioch to receive the gift of his consecration, and there received the fullness of episcopal authority.

Later, after the Church of Antioch had been organized, Bernard, the first Latin patriarch of that city, transferred the rank of his metropolitan see to that church. Having received from him the honour of the pallium, Peter became archbishop.

At that time there was with the Count of Toulouse a certain nobleman named William. When the city of Antioch had been broken into, he had by chance captured the wife of Acianus, prince of the people of Antioch, along with two young grandsons, sons of Samsadol, and held them in chains. For their ransom the aforesaid Samsadol gave the said nobleman an immense sum of money, and the mother and children were restored to their former liberty.

At the same time a great multitude of men from the German kingdom, from the region of Regensburg, numbering about fifteen hundred, arrived by a favourable voyage in the harbour of Saint Symeon. All were consumed by the same calamity within a short time. For three continuous months, until the Kalends of December, that pestilential disease afflicted the people so severely that in that period more than five hundred noblemen of the knightly order died, while among the common people the number was beyond counting.

## CHAPTER IX. They besiege the city of Maʿarrat; they take the besieged city. Lord William, Bishop of Orange, dies. Gulferus de Turribus is distinguished.

On the Kalends of November, when, as though by agreement, all the princes who had withdrawn from the city after escaping the disaster had now returned, and when the city of al-Bara had already been taken, as we have said, they resolved by common counsel to attack the very strongly fortified city of Ma'arrat, eight miles from al-Bara, lest nothing be done in the meantime. For they could not endure the outcry of the people [Col. 0386A], who were demanding the road toward Jerusalem. Having therefore made the necessary preparations, on the appointed day Count Raymond of Toulouse, the Count of Flanders, and the Count of the Normans set out to fulfill their purpose; the duke also, and his brother Lord Eustace, and Tancred, together with them, enclosed the aforesaid city in siege.

The inhabitants of that place were exceedingly proud and arrogant because of their great wealth, especially because on one occasion, in a certain engagement, they had killed many of our men. They still gloried in this, despising our army and heaping insults upon its princes. They even fastened crosses upon the towers and walls, and with spittle and certain other most disgraceful acts grossly subjected them to insult, in contempt of our people. [Col. 0386B] Therefore, stirred by greater emotion and fierce indignation—such as the pain of sacrilege could inflame—they attacked the city with continual assaults. Had they had an abundance of ladders, they would on the second day after arriving there have broken forcibly into the city.

At last, on the third day, Bohemond arrived with larger forces and continued the siege on the side of the city which had remained unbesieged. A few days after his arrival, our men, angry that they were being detained there so long to no purpose, wove hurdles, raised wooden towers, and constructed missile-engines; impatient of delay, they strove to assault the city more fiercely. After leveling the rampart with much labor, our men endeavored to undermine the wall. [Col. 0386C] Those inside, resisting with all their strength, hurled stones, fire, beehives full of bees, and quicklime with all the force they could muster, in order to drive them back from the wall. But through God’s power and mercy they could injure none, or only a few, of our men. And our men pressed the attack more vigorously from every side, in proportion as they saw the citizens losing strength and their efforts being frustrated.

When the assault had continued from the first dawn of day until sunset, the citizens, exhausted by unremitting labor and now offering less careful resistance, were confronted with ladders placed against the wall, and our men forcibly climbed the walls. Among them a nobleman from the diocese of Limoges, Guilferus, surnamed de Turribus (“of the Towers”), was the first to mount the wall. Many followed him [Col. 0386D] and occupied certain towers of the city; but the untimely onset of night prevented them from proceeding further in the enterprise and claiming the whole city for themselves. Postponing the matter until the next day, our knights and the body of leading men kept watch around the city throughout the night, so that the enemy might have no exit, intending to return to the same work early in the morning.

But the unruly common people, worn out by prolonged labor and tormented by the severity of a long famine, saw that no enemy appeared upon the walls and that the whole city lay quiet without noise. Without the knowledge of the leading men they entered the city; finding it empty, they secretly and silently seized all its spoils. For the citizens had withdrawn into underground caves, in order to secure their safety, at least for the time being. When morning came [Col. 0387A], the princes arose and took possession of the city without battle, carrying off little spoil from it. Learning, however, that the citizens had hidden in subterranean refuges, they set fires and sent in great quantities of smoke, compelling them to surrender. Dragging them out by force, they partly cut them down with swords and partly reduced them to captivity in fetters.

There died there Lord William, of blessed memory, bishop of Orange, a religious man who feared God. The duke, after remaining there with the others for fifteen days, returned to Antioch, having attended to private business with the Count of Flanders.

## CHAPTER X. The duke returns to his brother, obtains leave, and, returning to the army, suffers an ambush on the road but escapes unharmed.

[Col. 0387B]

At the same time Lord Godfrey, duke of Lower Lorraine, seeing that the people were preparing to depart and were urgently inviting the princes to do the same, resolved, before leaving that region, to see his brother and refresh himself by conversation with him. He therefore set out with a familiar retinue and went down into his brother’s territory. After seeing him, completing the business for which he had come, and taking leave, he was returning to Antioch, to the other princes who awaited him.

When he was already five or six miles from the city, it happened that he came to a pleasant grassy place beside a spring which poured forth sweet [Col. 0387C] and clear waters. The appearance of the place itself invited him to stop and take food. While his companions were busily engaged in this, and a meal appropriate to place and time was being prepared, behold, suddenly, from the reed-bed of a marsh adjoining that place, enemy horsemen, armed from head to foot, rushed upon the diners. Yet before the Turks could reach them, the duke and his men had seized their arms and mounted their horses. Thus, after an engagement between them, by the Lord’s favor the duke prevailed, so that, after killing many, he put the rest to flight and then returned gloriously to the city.

## CHAPTER XI. A dispute arises at Ma'arrat between the Count of Toulouse and Bohemond. Bohemond occupies the count’s positions at Antioch. The princes meet at Rugia, deciding nothing useful. The people suffer famine.

[Col. 0387D]

After the capture of the aforesaid city, a great dispute arose between Lord Bohemond and the Count of Toulouse. The count had proposed to give the city to the bishop of al-Bara; but Bohemond was unwilling to surrender to the bishop, at the count’s discretion, that part of the city which he had occupied, unless the count first surrendered to him the towers which he held at Antioch.

At length, disregarding the matter being conducted at Ma'arrat, Lord Bohemond returned angrily to Antioch. There, after capturing the towers held in fortification by the retainers [Col. 0388A] of the Count of Toulouse, he forcibly expelled the count’s household from them, and thus possessed the whole city without a partner. The count, seeing that his rival had departed and that he could dispose freely of the captured city as he pleased, granted it to the bishop of al-Bara, as he had previously proposed.

But while he and that bishop were arranging how, by assigning guards drawn from each order, they might preserve the city unharmed from the enemy, the people, learning this, began to take it very badly. They complained among themselves that the princes were creating delays and raising quarrels and disputes among themselves over every city captured, so that their principal purpose seemed wholly neglected. Therefore, meeting together, they resolved among themselves that, whatever the cause and in the count’s absence, they would destroy the city [Col. 0388B], lest it thereafter provide any obstacle to the fulfillment of their vows.

Meanwhile it happened that the princes met at Rugia, situated roughly midway between Antioch and the aforesaid Ma'arrat, in order to deliberate about the route in response to the people’s outcries; the count, summoned there, arrived. Since they disagreed among themselves, nothing harmonious or useful concerning their purpose was decided. While the count delayed there, the people left at Ma'arrat, seizing the opportunity afforded by his absence, utterly demolished the towers and walls, despite the strong opposition and repeated resistance of the aforesaid bishop, so that on his return the count would have no further grounds from this city for contriving delay.

When the count returned, he was deeply distressed at what had happened; nevertheless, seeing the people’s determination, he prudently pretended not to notice the deed. Yet the people pressed him more boldly, praying and demanding that he offer himself as leader to God’s people for completing the journey begun; otherwise they themselves would appoint any one of the knights over them, to command their army and lead them on the way of the Lord.

Moreover, famine in that army was so severe that, when food supplies failed, many, contrary to custom, having taken on the dispositions of wild beasts, turned to eating unclean animals. It is also said—if indeed it is lawful to believe it—that many, through lack of food, went so far as to eat human flesh. Nor was disaster absent from [Col. 0388D] the people, nor could it justly have been absent where the wretched multitude sustained itself on such unclean and pestilential foods—if indeed they ought to be called foods, being consumed contrary to nature.

Nor had that great and terrible scarcity, which afflicted the people, been momentary or brief. Rather, they had remained for about five weeks or more around the city which they were attempting to capture, exposed to this danger. There, not only through incidents of war but also through various illnesses, distinguished and noble men perished. Among them Engelrand, son of Lord Hugh, Count of Saint-Pol, a young man of the finest character, was seized by a severe illness and met his final day.

## CHAPTER XII. The count enters enemy territory and brings back plunder. Unable to bear the people’s outcry, he sets out. The Count of the Normans and Tancred join him.

[Col. 0389A]

In all this, the illustrious and distinguished Lord Count of Toulouse, troubled in mind and spirit, wavered uncertainly within himself. The distress of the people in danger afflicted him, and necessity weighed upon him; yet the desire for the journey, by which both great and small were inflamed, allowed him no rest, since with continual cries and repeated protest they importunately demanded it.

Wishing therefore to devise a fitting remedy for both maladies, but certain that the other princes [Col. 0389B] would not follow him in this matter, he appointed the people the fifteenth day for beginning the journey, in order to satisfy both the clamoring people and his own conscience. And lest, in the meantime, the people perish from the famine, which had become exceedingly severe, he took part of the cavalry and such of the foot-soldiers as seemed strongest, leaving the remainder within the city, and went down into enemy territory to procure, at whatever risk, the necessities of life for the multitude.

Entering with a very large retinue into a most fertile enemy region, after breaking into several fortified places and burning some suburbs, he brought back flocks and herds, male and female slaves, and enormous supplies of food, so that the fasting and hungry people were restored to complete satiety. Shares were also allotted, in proportion to each person’s lot, to the companions who had remained to guard the city of Ma'arrat. [Col. 0389C]

After returning, the count began anxiously to consider what he should do, as the people again cried that the appointed day for beginning the journey was now at hand and that they rejected every delay. Seeing that the people were maintaining an honorable cause and that he could no longer endure their insistence, although he was alone and no prince had resolved to follow him, he set out with his own retinue only, after setting the city on fire and reducing it to ashes.

Seeing, however, that he had few knights, he asked the bishop of al-Bara to depart with him. The bishop kindly granted the count’s request and placed a certain nobleman, William of Cumliac, in charge of his possessions [Col. 0389D] with seven knights and thirty foot-soldiers. This man guarded the property entrusted to him in good faith and with complete devotion; within a few days he had forty knights in place of seven, and eighty or more foot-soldiers in place of thirty, multiplying his lord’s resources enormously.

Thus, setting out on the appointed day, the count departed, waiting for none of the others. There were about ten thousand persons in his company, of whom scarcely three hundred and fifty were knights. As he departed, the Count of the Normans and Lord Tancred, each with forty knights and a numerous body of foot-soldiers, joined him, proving inseparable companions on the journey.

As they traveled, they found such abundance of provisions on the way that the people lacked nothing further. [Col. 0390A] Passing through Caesarea, Hama, and Emesa, commonly called Camela, they received from their rulers both guides and a market for goods for sale on the best terms; moreover, from the inhabitants of the towns and cities through whose territories they passed, they received many gifts of gold, silver, flocks, herds, and every kind of provisions, so that they might spare the region. Thus their army increased day by day and advanced into a better condition, abounding in all necessities in full sufficiency.

They also acquired a great number of horses, both as gifts and by purchase, horses of which they had suffered the greatest shortage. Before joining the remaining princes, they had more than a thousand in their army besides those they had formerly possessed. At length, after proceeding for several days by an inland route, it was decided by common counsel to return to the coast, so that they might more easily learn the condition of the other princes whom they had left behind in the territory of Antioch, and obtain trade in necessary goods from the ships which came by sea from Antioch and Laodicea.

## CHAPTER XIII. The count’s army endures attacks by brigands on the journey; the count prudently attacks them. A resisting castle is broken into. Camp is pitched before Arqa, and envoys of the neighboring peoples come to the princes.

Throughout that journey, from their departure from Ma'arrat [Col. 0390C], everything had indeed gone very prosperously for them, except that, more frequently toward the end of the expedition, certain brigands had habitually made secret attacks. They killed or captured some of the old and sick, who could not keep pace with the army. The count cleverly countered their tricks. Lord Tancred and Lord Robert, duke of the Normans, together with the bishop of al-Bara, marched ahead of the army; the count himself remained behind the army in ambush with certain distinguished and eminent men, so that he might meet at an opportune moment those aforesaid evildoers who followed the marching army from behind in order to overpower the unsuspecting.

Thus, when the evildoers attacked in their usual manner, the count came out from hiding [Col. 0390D] and confronted them. Rushing upon them suddenly, he struck down them all, bringing their horses, spoils, and several captives back to the expedition with great rejoicing. From that day the people advanced safely and without difficulty, abundantly supplied with necessities. In all the region through which they passed, there was no city or fortified town to right or left whose inhabitants did not send gifts to the army and its leaders, and seek a treaty and friendship from the passing force.

There was one exception. Its inhabitants, relying on their numbers and the natural defenses of the place, neither offered a market for provisions nor did they, after obtaining a treaty, send gifts to the leaders; rather, joining their forces, they attempted to obstruct our expedition. Seeing this, our men, inflamed by just indignation, attacked them unanimously. In a moment they scattered their bands, captured some of them, and forcibly broke into their town. [Col. 0391A] Plundering their flocks, herds, horses grazing in the surrounding pastures, and all their possessions, they carried them away with them.

Envoys of neighboring rulers were also present in that army, sent to obtain peace. Seeing our men’s strength and boldness, they returned home in order to secure full peace for their lords and to inform those who had sent them more fully of our men’s resources and courage; but they soon returned with horses and other gifts. After several days, having crossed the intervening country in complete tranquility, they came down into the plains near the ancient city of Arqa, very strongly fortified by its site and not far from the sea, and encamped quite close to the city.

## CHAPTER XIV. Description of Arqa. Captives of our people held in the city of Tripoli urge that the city be besieged.

Arqa is one of the cities of the province of Phoenicia, situated at the foot of Lebanon upon a most strongly fortified hill, four or five miles from the sea. It is widely spread out and has a plain of excellent soil and fertile ground; it also lacks neither very pleasant pastures nor the advantages of running water. According to the traditions of the ancients, it is said to have been founded by Aracheus, the seventh [Col. 0391C] son of Canaan, who named it Arachis after himself; later, after the name had been corrupted, it came to be called Archis.

Our men pitched their camp around it, as we have said, not by chance but because they had been warned by letters and exhortations from some of our people held captive by the enemy. In the city of Tripoli, a very noble city situated on the seashore, five or six miles from Arqa, there were several of our people being violently detained. From the beginning of the siege of Antioch, and especially after the city had been conquered, our men had begun, under compulsion of want, imprudently to roam the surrounding regions in order to procure food, voluntarily exposing themselves to plunder by the enemy around them. [Col. 0391D] As a result, there was scarcely a city or town that did not hold captives from our people. In the city of Tripoli mentioned above, more than two hundred of our people were held in this condition.

Learning of our men’s arrival, they informed the princes that they should by no means leave Arqa, but should enclose it in siege. In this way they could either take the city within a few days, or extort an immense sum of money from the ruler of Tripoli to induce him to abandon the siege, and obtain the release of their captive brethren. This is what happened. They came immediately to the city, pitched their camp closer about it, and enclosed it in siege: both to test what had been reported to them and to await the other princes [Col. 0392A], who were believed likely to follow shortly.

## CHAPTER XV. Some men leave the camp and courageously occupy the city of Antaradus; they return with rich spoils and continue the siege.

A hundred knights and two companies of two hundred foot-soldiers left this camp and, following Raymond Pilet, came to the city of Antaradus, commonly called Tortosa, twenty miles or more from the siege, to see whether they could find anything necessary or useful to them. Antaradus is a city situated on the seashore, having nearby a small island about two miles away, where the ancient city of Aradus, famous for many centuries, once stood. [Col. 0392B]

The prophet Ezekiel mentions it, addressing the ruler of Tyre thus: “The inhabitants of Sidon and Arad were your oarsmen” (Ezek. 27:8). And again below: “The sons of Arad, with your army, were upon your walls all around you” (ibid., 11). The aforesaid city received its name from Arad, being called Antaradus because it stood opposite the aforesaid Aradus. Both are situated in the province of Phoenicia, and both cities had one and the same founder: Aradius, the youngest of the sons of Canaan, son of Ham, son of Noah.

When the aforesaid portion of the Toulousan lord’s army approached this city, they began to attack it fiercely. But since the citizens resisted very courageously [Col. 0392C], they could make little progress in capturing it. When night came, they postponed the undertaking until the next day, so that, once their companions who intended to follow them had arrived, they might rise in the morning with greater strength for the same task.

But the citizens, fearing that larger forces would arrive that night and that they would ultimately be unable to resist them, left the city with their wives, children, and household, and fled to the neighboring mountains for safety. At first light our men encouraged one another, unaware of what had happened that night, to continue the work of the preceding day and arm themselves for attacking the city. Coming close, they found it empty and entered it fearlessly and resolutely, finding it overflowing with provisions [Col. 0392D] and plunder. Laden to the utmost abundance, they returned to camp, reporting in order everything that had occurred in the meantime and gladdening the entire army with their success.

## CHAPTER XVI. Duke Godfrey, with the Count of Flanders and the remainder of the expedition, reaches Laodicea; he releases Guynemer from captivity and restores his fleet to him. Bohemond escorts those departing as far as that city.

Meanwhile, about the Kalends of March, the people who had remained at Antioch, seeing that the appointed day for beginning the journey was at hand, began urgently to press Lord Godfrey, duke of Lower Lorraine, Lord Robert, Count of Flanders, and the other princes [Col. 0393A] to set out and, since they wished to fulfill their vow, to provide leadership. They pointed to the faithfulness and steadfastness of the Count of Toulouse, the duke of the Normans, and Lord Tancred, and to the remarkable favor they had shown God’s people by faithfully leading them for many days already upon the way of the Lord.

Persuaded by these and similar arguments, the aforesaid princes packed their baggage and prepared necessities for the journey. Taking with them the entire multitude of cavalry and infantry who desired and intended to proceed toward Jerusalem, they assembled at Laodicea in Syria on the Kalends of March, following the aforesaid princes, numbering about twenty-five thousand able-bodied armed men.

Lord Bohemond also escorted them thither with his retinue. [Col. 0393B] Yet he could neither proceed with them nor remain there longer, lest he seem rashly, even temporarily, to neglect newly captured Antioch, surrounded by enemies and left unguarded.
