Still, mindful of the fellowship and the bond he had made with the other nobles on the way of the Lord, he escorted them to the aforesaid place, readily offering with devoted zeal every service and kindness in his power, so as to impress his memory more deeply upon those departing.

He then returned, after saluting the princes and taking leave with much weeping and sighing, to give diligent care to the city entrusted to him, leaving the people at Laodicea. Laodicea is a noble and ancient city on the seashore [Col. 0393C] which, having faithful inhabitants, was alone among the cities of Syria subject to the jurisdiction of the Greek emperor.

A certain Guynemer of Boulogne came there with his fleet—the same man whom, as we recalled above, we mentioned as having arrived with a fleet at Tarsus in Cilicia when Baldwin, the duke’s brother, had taken that city. While rashly attacking Laodicea without first assembling adequate forces, intending to bring it under his rule, he had been captured by its citizens and imprisoned with nearly all his company.

Because he had come from the land of the duke’s father and had been useful and honorable to the duke’s brother at the aforesaid Tarsus, the duke requested his restoration from the governor of the city and the local leading men. Not daring to oppose the duke’s word in any respect, they restored to him [Col. 0393D] Guynemer with all his companions and the fleet which they had brought. The duke placed him in command of his own fleet and ordered him to follow at an equal pace as they traveled by land; and so it was done.

## CHAPTER XVII. The duke and the army with him besiege Gibelet. A deception by the Count of Toulouse intervenes. Hastening to Arqa, they join the other princes; the siege makes no progress.

The aforesaid army departed from Laodicea in Syria, taking up those whom they had found in that city, and those who had left Antioch, Cilicia, and neighboring cities later because they had been detained by household business and domestic concerns. Following the seacoast, they reached the city of Gabala, commonly called Gibelet, twelve miles from the aforesaid Laodicea. [Col. 0394A]

After they had besieged the city for some time, encamping around it, the official in charge of the city, an agent of the Egyptian ruler—for this was the first of the coastal cities subject to Egyptian power—offered the duke six thousand gold pieces, together with great gifts, if he would abandon the siege. When he could not bend him, as one who despised base gifts, he turned to other measures. He sent envoys, in whose loyalty and skill he trusted, to the Count of Toulouse, promising him the aforesaid money if he could free the city from the duke’s hands.

The count, it is said, secretly accepted the money offered and invented a report that an innumerable enemy host was descending from the Persian region, intending to avenge the wrongs suffered by the Persian people under the command of Kerbogha at Antioch; he claimed that a war no less serious than the former was being prepared anew, and that he had received entirely trustworthy messengers concerning all this, whose word admitted no doubt. [Col. 0394B]

He therefore sent an embassy through the venerable lord bishop of al-Bara and dispatched letters, anxiously urging the duke and the Count of Flanders not to delay, but, after lifting the siege, to hasten to meet their brothers’ shared dangers in fraternal sympathy. Hearing of their brothers’ need and of the danger said to be imminent, they proceeded in simplicity of spirit. They immediately lifted the siege and hurried their march. Passing the city of Valania, which lies below the fortress of Margat on the shore of the sea, then Maraclea, the first of the Phoenician cities encountered by those coming from the north, and Antaradus, commonly called Tortosa, likewise one of the cities of the aforesaid province on the seashore, they arrived there. [Col. 0394C]

Finding it empty of inhabitants, they admired the proximity of the island lying westward opposite that city, where they found several of our ships advantageously anchored. Taking this shortcut, within a few days they halted with all their multitude before the city of Arqa. Lord Tancred met them there [Col. 0394D] and explained to them in detail the count’s entire deception. Consequently they encamped separately, far from the tents of those who had preceded them.

The count, seeing that the minds of the other princes had become alienated from him, tried to reconcile them to himself by sending gifts. Thus, after a short interval, having been reconciled with the princes except Lord Tancred, who raised serious charges against him, the expeditions gathered into one body around the city. Since the count had already spent many days there fruitlessly before the duke’s arrival, there was hope that, when the remaining princes arrived, the city might easily be overcome and the labor of the besiegers attain its desired end. But the contrary happened. [Col. 0395A]

For neither before nor afterward did the people have the Lord favorable to them in that undertaking. Whenever they tried to attack the city and applied themselves to various methods of assault, whether to [uncertain missing word] in order to bring down the wall, or to launch assaults against it, new obstacles continually arose; every effort was frustrated, their work proved vain, and their expenditure was wasted. It was thus made manifest that divine favor had withdrawn itself from their endeavors in this enterprise. The people were killed, and noble and distinguished men fell uselessly.

There fell there, by a miserable accident, each struck by a stone, Anselm of Riburgismont, a man valiant in arms and worthy of everlasting remembrance; and Pons of Baladun, a nobleman and a retainer of the Count of Toulouse. [Col. 0395B]

For this reason the people were unwillingly detained there, though they intended to complete the journey they had begun. Hence they gave no eager effort and devoted little concern to the undertaking. Especially after the duke’s arrival, even the retainers and household men who had come with the Count of Toulouse deliberately withdrew, so that the count, wearied by tedium, might follow the course of the other princes, who were themselves held there unwillingly and against their consciences under the count’s compulsion.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The controversy concerning the Lord’s lance is renewed. Its discoverer enters a burning pyre and dies a few days later.

The controversy was renewed there concerning the lance found at Antioch: whether it was that lance from the Lord’s side, from which blood and water flowed, or a fabricated thing. The people greatly doubted it, and the leading men wavered in complete uncertainty. Some said it truly was the lance wet with the Lord’s blood, which had opened his side and had been revealed by divine inspiration for the consolation of the people. Others asserted that it was an invention of the tricks of the Count of Toulouse, a fiction devised for profit. [Col. 0395C]

The principal instigator of this dissension was a certain Arnulf, a retainer and chaplain of the Count of the Normans: a learned man indeed, but of impure conduct and a promoter of scandals, concerning whom much will have to be said below. While contradictory discussion of the matter continued for a long time among the people, the man who claimed that this revelation had been made to him ordered a very large pyre to be kindled, so that he might prove the matter to the people and remove every doubt. With the Lord as his author, he promised to establish by the certain test of fire, for the unbelieving, that nothing fabricated or shadowed forth by invention had occurred in the matter, but that everything had been brought about solely by divine revelation for human knowledge and their consolation.

Accordingly, a very large pyre was kindled, whose blazing heat could terrify even those standing around. On the Friday preceding the holy Pascha of the Lord—the day on which the Savior of the world is recorded to have suffered for our salvation—the whole people, from greatest to least, assembled in order that so great a matter might receive a full [Col. 0396A] trial. The man said to be about to undergo so dangerous an ordeal voluntarily was Peter Bartholomew, a cleric indeed but only slightly learned; and, so far as one may judge by human appearance, he seemed a simple man. After making a prayer before the surrounding crowds, he took the aforesaid lance with him and passed through the fire, apparently uninjured in the people’s view.

Yet this action not only failed to end the controversy but raised a greater one. For within a few days he died. Since he had previously appeared healthy and vigorous, some maintained that the fire he had attempted was the cause of his swift death, saying that in it, as an advocate of fraud, he had incurred the cause of death. Others said that he had escaped the fire safe and sound, but that after emerging from it he had been overwhelmed and crushed by crowds rushing upon him in devotion, to the point of causing his death. Thus the matter which had come into doubt received no resolution and brought in greater uncertainty.

## CHAPTER XIX. The envoys whom our princes had sent to Egypt return.

At the same time, our envoys, who had gone down into Egypt at the invitation of the Egyptians—envoys sent, as we have said, by the caliph of Egypt to the siege of Antioch—returned after a year to the princes who had sent them, having been detained both violently and deceitfully. Envoys of the Egyptian ruler came with them, bringing statements very [Col. 0396C] different from those which they had previously brought.

Formerly the Egyptians had earnestly sought, with many urgent requests, to obtain the favor and assistance of our princes against the arrogance of the Turks and Persians. But now they had changed their tune. They thought they were granting our people the highest favor if they permitted two or three hundred unarmed persons at a time to go to Jerusalem and, after completing their prayers, return unharmed. Our princes treated this statement as a mockery and compelled the aforesaid envoys to return, declaring that the army would not come there in small groups according to the proposed terms, but would proceed to Jerusalem united in its ranks, intending danger to his kingdom.

The cause of this change was something arising from our victory at Antioch. For the Turks suffered such danger there, and their sword was so broken throughout the East, their lofty glory so turned to shame, that wherever they had business with other nations they were defeated in every place and came away worse in every conflict. In accordance with their condition, as the Egyptian kingdom grew stronger against them, they had lost Jerusalem to an officer named Emireius, commander of the Egyptian king’s forces. The Turks themselves had violently taken Jerusalem thirty-eight years earlier. Hence the enemies who had formerly dreaded the Turks as stronger now saw them cast down [Col. 0397A] and weakened through our men’s achievement; they consequently despised the help of our people, which they had previously sought with the utmost urgency.

## CHAPTER XX. Envoys of the emperor arrive, complaining about Bohemond. They announce that the emperor will come; the princes disagree; battle is joined with the Tripolitans, and the enemy are defeated; our men return victorious to camp.

Moreover, envoys of the emperor of Constantinople had arrived, complaining greatly about Lord Bohemond, who presumed to retain Antioch contrary to the law of the agreements and the terms of the oath he had sworn. Before the princes they alleged that all who had passed through the emperor’s territory, having personally sworn oaths to their lord upon the holy Gospels, had promised that they would presume to retain, as far as Jerusalem, none of the towns or cities that had belonged to his empire, but would surrender them, once captured, to his imperial authority. Of the other provisions of the agreement, however, they retained no memory whatever.

It is certain that this had been agreed between him and the princes at Constantinople; but at the end of the agreement there had been added the condition that he himself, with all his following and very great forces, should pursue them without delay and furnish assistance in their necessities. To this, by the common counsel of the princes, the reply was made that the emperor had first violated the agreements; and therefore he rightly forfeited the claims which could have belonged to him under the law of the agreement. For it is unjust that faith should be kept with one who strives to act contrary to the compact. For, although he had been bound by agreement to our princes to follow them immediately after assembling his armies, to provide them with uninterrupted commercial supply by ships by sea, and to order an abundance of goods for sale to be furnished throughout the journey, he fraudulently neglected to perform either obligation, though he could easily have brought both to effect.

Therefore they wished what had been done concerning Antioch, since they seemed to have done it lawfully, to remain settled and unshaken: namely, that he to whom it had been granted by their common generosity should possess it in perpetuity by hereditary right. The envoys of that emperor further pressed their point, wishing to persuade the army to await the emperor’s arrival, which they promised would take place on the Kalends of July [1 July]. They promised that he would give immense gifts to each prince, and would also grant the common people, with great liberality, pay sufficient for their honorable maintenance.

While they deliberated about this, they disagreed with one another. The count of Toulouse judged it advantageous to await the arrival of so great a prince—either because he believed it would indeed occur, or because, on that pretext, he sought to keep the princes and the people in place until he could claim for himself the city which he was besieging. For he considered it shameful and dishonorable to abandon his declared purpose so openly, unable to fulfill his desire. To the others, however, the opposite course seemed far better: that they should press on with the journey they had begun and happily complete the vow for which they had endured so many labors. They judged it more expedient to avoid the emperor’s deceits and artifices, which they had experienced so often, lest they again become entangled in his labyrinths and windings, from which afterward they might not easily be freed.

Thus contention broke out among the princes, and their wishes agreed in scarcely any respect. Consequently, the ruler of the city of Tripoli, who had previously offered an infinite sum of money if our expedition would raise the siege and depart from his territory, upon learning of the schism that had arisen among the princes, not only refused to pay the money previously offered, but voluntarily resolved to meet our men and test his strength against them.

It was therefore decided by common counsel that, leaving the bishop of Albara and several other powerful men at the siege to guard the camp, the princes should proclaim battle, draw up their lines, and, with their forces properly arranged in order, march toward Tripoli. Arriving there, they found the governor of the place, together with the entire multitude of the citizens, both cavalry and infantry, outside the city; there, having likewise formed their ranks, they fearlessly awaited our men’s arrival.

For since the count of Toulouse had spent two months and more in the aforesaid siege without result and had made no progress at all, the Tripolitans had begun to despise them and to regard our army with less and less apprehension, as though, fallen away from the prowess of which they had formerly heard, they suffered in themselves a failure of their customary courage. Therefore, once our men had reached the city and had been permitted to behold the enemy legions drawn up against them, they charged them at once with greater spirit. At the first attack they scattered the enemy’s companies, put them to flight, and by fierce pressure compelled them to race one another back inside the city, having slain seven hundred of their number by the sword. Of our men, however, three or four are said to have fallen. There they celebrated Easter, on the fourth Ides of April [10 April].

## CHAPTER XXI. The governor of Tripoli obtains peace from our men with much money and gifts. By the counsel of the faithful who lived in those regions, the princes choose the coastal route.

[Col. 0398D] Having gained the victory, they returned again to camp. There all the people nevertheless began to shout and cry aloud that, abandoning that ruinous siege, they should take the road toward Jerusalem, whither their entire desire hastened. The people’s vehement insistence prevailed; and, after the camp had been burned, the duke, the count of Flanders, the count of the Normans, and Tancred, in satisfaction of the people, abandoned the siege and directed their expeditions toward Tripoli as though intending to continue their journey—despite the count of Toulouse, who was unwilling and did his utmost to hold them back.

Those who from the beginning had followed the camp of the aforesaid count were more inclined to do this, so that, deserting him, they eagerly followed the aforesaid princes. When he learned this, and saw that he could recall them neither by prayers nor promises, he made a virtue of necessity and followed the others, though unwillingly.

Having advanced scarcely five miles and encamped before the city of Tripoli, the governor of that place, who managed the affairs of the Egyptian caliph in that region, laid aside the arrogance with which he had previously believed himself able to contend on equal terms with our princes. Coming to know himself, he sent an embassy to the princes and obtained the following terms: by giving fifteen thousand pieces of gold, in addition to gifts of horses, mules, silks, and precious vessels, and by restoring every captive of our people whom he held, they should depart from the province entrusted to him and, as they passed by, spare the three cities under his authority—namely Arqa, Tripoli, and Byblos—with their dependencies.

[Col. 0399B] He also sent flocks and herds, and an abundant supply of provisions, lest scarcity of food compel them to plunder the suburbs and molest the cultivators of the fields. They also summoned certain faithful Syrians, inhabitants of Mount Lebanon, which rises above those cities on their eastern side, exceedingly lofty and stretching its ridges high into the air. As prudent men familiar with the localities, who had joyfully come down to them to show the affection due to brotherly love, they were asked for counsel as to what road they might take toward Jerusalem more safely and conveniently.

After faithfully weighing the advantages and shortcuts of all the routes leading there, these men finally recommended the coastal road, so that they might take a more direct route and not lack the assistance of their ships, which followed the advancing army. In our men’s fleet were not only the ships of Guynemer and his companions, who, as we have said, had come down from Flanders, Normandy, and England, but also ships of the Genoese, Venetians, and Greeks, which frequently arrived from Cyprus, Rhodes, and other islands laden with merchandise for sale, bringing great consolation to our legions.

Taking guides, both from among the aforesaid faithful men and from the household of the prince of Tripoli, they followed the coast, with the ridges of Lebanon on their left. Passing Byblos, they encamped on the bank of a river near a place called Maus. There, resting for a day while waiting for the weak populace and those unable to follow so quickly, they took their ease.

## CHAPTER XXII. As they proceed, they pass cities situated on the seashore and arrive at Lydda and Ramla.

At last, on the third day, they encamped before the city of Beirut, beside the river which flows near the city. There, having been given money by the governor of the place on condition that they spare the trees sufficiently, and supplied with enough provisions, they rested for one night.

On the following day, arriving at Sidon, they set up their tents beside the streams, taking advantage of the convenient water supply. There, for some reason unknown to us, the ruler of the city showed our princes no kindness; rather, presuming upon his own strength, he began to harass our army. This did not turn out very well for him. For some of our men, provoked by their raids and no longer able to overlook them, charged upon them; after killing several, they compelled the rest to retreat into the city. Thus they spent that night in camp in complete tranquility, their harassments having ceased.

When morning came, they decided to delay there for a while so that the people might recover their strength. They sent out some of the more agile men from the army to gather necessities for food from the neighboring towns. These all returned safely with flocks, herds, and an immense abundance of provisions, except for a certain nobleman, Walter of Verra. While the others were returning, he proceeded farther afield in order to gather a larger booty, and, carried off by an uncertain fate, ceased to appear—to the great grief of all, who were deeply troubled by his uncertain end.

On the following day, having crossed terrain largely rocky, they went through more level ground. Leaving on their right the ancient city of Sarepta of the Sidonians, the nourisher of the man of God Elijah, they crossed the river which runs between and reached Tyre, the distinguished metropolis of that region, the most ancient dwelling-place of Agenor and Cadmus. There they encamped near that remarkable fountain, admirable through the ages, in gardens and beside a well of living waters. They rested one night in broad suburban grounds filled with many conveniences.

When day returned, they again prepared themselves for the journey. Having surmounted the narrow passes lying most dangerously between the towering mountains and the sea, they descended again to the plains subject to the city of Acre. There, encamping beside the city on the river which flows past it, they received gifts from its governor and citizens and obtained merchandise on favorable terms. The governor also became familiar and friendly with our princes, promising that if, after Jerusalem had been captured, they could maintain themselves in the kingdom without opposition for twenty days, or overcome the power of the Egyptians, he would surrender the city of Acre to them without any difficulty.

Proceeding thence, leaving Galilee on their left, they came between Carmel and the sea to Caesarea, the metropolis of Second Palestine, formerly called by the ancient name Tower of Straton. They encamped beside the river which flows from marshes adjoining that city. There they celebrated the holy day of Pentecost, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June [29 May], scarcely two miles from the aforesaid city.

Three days later they resumed the labor of their journey. Leaving on their right the coastal places, Antipatris and Joppa, they crossed the wide plain of Eleutheria and reached Lydda, which is Diospolis. There is shown to this day the glorious tomb of the distinguished martyr George, who, according to the outward man, is believed to rest in the Lord there.

The enemies had recently demolished entirely the church which the pious and orthodox emperor of the Romans, the august Justinian of illustrious memory, had ordered to be built with great zeal and ready devotion in honor of that martyr. They feared, when they heard of our men’s arrival, that the church’s beams, which were very long, might be turned into engines and siege-machines for taking the city.

Learning that a certain noble city called Ramla lay nearby, they sent ahead the count of Flanders with five hundred knights, so that he might sound out the citizens’ intentions and discover what they proposed to do. As they approached the city, they saw that no one came out to meet them. Entering through the gates, which they found open, they discovered the city wholly deserted. For on the preceding night, learning of our men’s arrival, the inhabitants had departed with their wives, children, and entire households, leaving the city empty. The count immediately sent back a messenger to report this to the army and advised them to hasten to the city.

After completing their customary prayers, they came to the city and spent a full three days there amid an abundance of wheat, wine, and oil. They appointed as bishop of that church a certain Robert, a Norman by birth, from the bishopric of Rouen. They granted him both cities, namely Lydda and Ramla, together with their adjoining suburbs, to possess by perpetual right, dedicating with all devotion the first fruits of their labors to the distinguished martyr.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The people of Jerusalem diligently fortify their city with brave men, arms, and provisions. They drive most of the faithful inhabitants out of the city.

[Col. 0401C]

Meanwhile, the people of Jerusalem, frequently informed by messengers of our men’s approach and knowing that the entire multitude said to be coming had the special and chief purpose of taking that city, strove to fortify it with all possible diligence and anxiety. They competed with one another in gathering and bringing into the city the necessities of life, every kind of weapon, timber, iron, steel, and everything customarily providing a defense for those under siege.

The Egyptian ruler, moreover, who in that same year had recovered the aforesaid city after expelling the Turkish government with much effort, upon learning that our army had departed from Antioch, ordered the towers and walls to be repaired with the utmost zeal possible. To win for himself the faith and favor of the citizens, he ordered payments from his own treasury to be distributed with great liberality and remitted forever the payment of taxes and duties. Accordingly, both to provide for their lives and safety and to be elevated by the privilege of such great freedom, they eagerly obeyed the royal will. Summoning citizens from nearby cities and suburban places—strong, industrious, and well-armed men—they diligently fortified the city.

Moreover, all meeting unanimously in the exceedingly spacious court of the Temple, so that they might forestall and prevent our men’s arrival, resolved to kill all the faithful who lived in that city, utterly demolish the church of the Lord’s Resurrection, and uproot the Lord’s Sepulchre from its foundations, lest on its account or for the sake of prayer the people of the faithful should thereafter propose to come to or frequent the city.

But at length, learning that by this means they would stir up greater hatred among our peoples against themselves and provoke their destruction more violently, they changed their counsel. Having violently extorted all their money and everything they seemed to possess, they took fourteen thousand pieces of gold from the patriarch who then governed the city, from the city’s people, and from the neighboring monasteries. Therefore the same venerable man had to sail to the island of Cyprus, so that he might have the means of paying so large a sum of extorted money—for the estates of all together did not suffice for this—and might in some manner relieve his own poverty and the want of the people. There he begged the faithful for the aid of alms and pious generosity, to send it for the sustenance of the exhausted and starving people of God living at Jerusalem and within its borders.

Nor did even this seem sufficient to them. After extorting all the people’s goods by interrogations and severe tortures, they drove all the rest from the city, except only old men, infirm women, and little children. These, hiding in suburban villages until our men’s arrival, expected death every day, not daring to enter the city. Nor was safe rest granted to them outside among the persecuting population, since the inhabitants of those places viewed all their activity with suspicion and pressed upon them with burdensome and intolerable compulsory services.

At that same time, in that city beloved of God, there was a man of venerable life and outstanding faith named Gerald. He governed the hospice mentioned above, in which poor people who came to the city for prayer were lodged and received such refreshment as place and time permitted. Believing that he had some store of money, and suspecting that he might contrive something harmful to them at our men’s arrival, they put him in chains and beat him, torturing him so that they broke the joints of his hands and feet and rendered most of his limbs useless.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The people of Bethlehem send envoys to the princes; Tancred is sent there and occupies the church and the place.

When they had completed three days there, they assigned several guards to defend the more fortified part of the same city from enemy ambushes, and at the first light of dawn prepared to carry out their purpose. Taking as guides prudent men knowledgeable about the localities, they reached Nicopolis.

Nicopolis is a city of Palestine. While it was still a village, the sacred book of the Gospels called it Emmaus; and the blessed evangelist Luke says that it lies sixty stadia from Jerusalem. Sozomen says of it in the sixth book of the *Tripartite History*:

> After the devastation of Jerusalem and their victory in Judaea, the Romans called this place Nicopolis, “City of Victory,” from the event of the victory. Before this city, at a crossroads where Christ is known to have walked with Cleopas after the resurrection, as though going to another village, there is a healing spring. In it human ailments are washed away, and likewise other animals afflicted by various sicknesses are cleansed. The tradition that this occurs derives from an occasion when Christ appeared at the spring with his disciples and washed their feet; from this the water became a remedy for various ailments.

The aforesaid historian thus relates these matters concerning the fortress of Emmaus.

[Col. 0403B] There they spent that night peacefully, amid an abundance of water and provisions necessary for food. About midnight an embassy of the faithful dwelling in the city of Bethlehem came to Duke Godfrey, praying and urgently requesting that he send there some portion of his knights. For enemies from all the neighboring towns and suburban places were gathering and hastening toward Jerusalem, both to defend the city and to find a plan for their own safety within it. The aforesaid faithful feared that, if these enemies came into their region, they would demolish the church, which they had repeatedly redeemed from the same enemies at great cost in order to prevent its destruction.

The request of their faithful brethren having been heard and received with compassionate feeling, the duke ordered one hundred picked and swift knights from among his men to hasten to the aforesaid place to bring aid to the faithful. Lord Tancred was assigned to them as commander and companion on the journey. Guided by inhabitants of the place, they arrived at their destination at first light. The citizens received them honorably with hymns and spiritual songs; and, as people and clergy led them in, they entered the church and beheld with blessed eyes the lodging of the blessed woman in childbirth and the Saviour’s manger, in which the food of blessed animals rested.

There too the inhabitants, through the immensity of their joy and exultation, sang votive songs to the Lord and, as a sign of victory, set Lord Tancred’s banner over the church.

But those remaining in the army, longing for the journey’s end and knowing that the venerable places stood nearby—for love and reverence of which they had already endured so many labors and dangers in the third year—passed a sleepless night, earnestly imploring the dawn, so that they might behold the happy conclusion of their journey and witness the blessed completion of so long a pilgrimage. The night seemed to them to prolong its course beyond custom and improperly to seize for itself a portion of the coming light. Every delay seemed dangerous and hateful to eager minds, according to the proverbial saying: “For a desiring heart, nothing comes quickly enough”; and likewise: “By delay the vow had increased.”

## CHAPTER XXV. The advancing army arrives at Jerusalem; meanwhile a disturbance arises in which some of the enemy fall.

[Col. 0404A]

After it became known in the camp that the duke had received the messengers from Bethlehem that night and had sent some of his men ahead to assist them, the common people roused one another and reproached delay. Without waiting for leave to proceed or for the opportunity that daylight usually gives travelers, they rose in the silence of the untimely night and, against the princes’ wishes, set out on the march.

After they had proceeded a little way, a noble and valiant man, Gaston of Béziers, separated from the army with a company of thirty swift knights and began, as dawn was already breaking, to hasten toward Jerusalem. His purpose was that, if he found outside the city any herds or flocks, he might drive them back with him to the expedition. When he had already drawn near to the city, animals appeared before him as he had wished, with only a few shepherds in charge. At the sight of our soldiers the shepherds fled in terror into the city.

Gaston meanwhile was returning to the army, driving along the animals left without guards, when, behold, the people of Jerusalem, aroused by the shepherds’ cries, seized their weapons. Eager to recover by force the booty that had been driven away, they zealously pursued him as he departed. The distinguished man, fearing the multitude of his pursuers, abandoned the prey and, seeking safety by flight, halted with his company on the summit of a certain hill.

While he waited there for the outcome, behold, through the valley below that place Lord Tancred, returning from Bethlehem to the army with the aforementioned hundred knights, was hastening along. The aforesaid nobleman met him and related in order what had happened to him. Their forces being joined, they turned back and pursued those who were taking the booty away. Before these could withdraw into the city, our men suddenly charged them, killed many, put the rest to flight, and forcibly carried off the recovered booty again to the army with great joy.

When they were asked from where they had gathered that prey, they replied that they had carried it away from the territory of Jerusalem. At hearing the city’s name—the city for which they had endured so many and such great labors—they could not restrain their tears and sighs through the fervor of devotion. They cast themselves upon the ground, worshiping and glorifying God, by whose gift it comes about that he is worthily and praiseworthily served by his faithful, and who had deigned graciously to hear the vows of his people, so that according to their desire they might deserve to arrive at the places for which they longed.

Advancing a little farther, they beheld the holy city nearby. With groans and sighs poured forth in spiritual joy, marching on foot and for the most part barefoot, they pressed more ardently onward on the journey they had begun. Suddenly they halted before the city and set their camp around it in the order assigned to each by the greater princes.

What had been foretold through the prophet seemed fulfilled, and the word of the Lord was historically displayed:

> “Lift up your eyes, Jerusalem, and see” (Isa. 49:18) the power of the king. “Behold, your Savior comes” [to free you from the bond].  
>   
> “Arise, arise, stand up, Jerusalem” (Isa. 51:17); “loose the bonds from your neck, captive daughter of Zion” (Isa. 52:2).

# BOOK EIGHT BEGINS.

[Col. 0405]

## CHAPTER I. A description of the site of the holy city, showing what regions and places it has around it.

[Col. 0405A]

It is certain that the holy city Jerusalem, beloved of God, is situated upon lofty mountains; and ancient authority relates that it lies in the tribe of Benjamin. To the west it has the tribe of Simeon, the land of the Philistines, and the Mediterranean Sea. Where it approaches that sea most closely, it is twenty-four miles distant from it, near the very ancient town of Joppa. Between itself and the aforesaid sea it has the fortress of Emmaus, later called Nicopolis, as we have stated above, where after his resurrection the Lord appeared to two disciples; also Modin, the blessed stronghold of the holy Maccabees; Nob, the priestly village, where David, hungry with his young men, ate the bread of the Presence as given by the priest Abimelech; Diospolis, which is Lydda, where Peter restored to health Aeneas, a man paralyzed and lying upon a bed for eight years; and the aforesaid Joppa, where that same Peter raised Tabitha, a disciple full of good works and alms, from the dead and restored her living to the saints and widows. There also, while lodging with Simon the tanner, he received Cornelius’s messenger, as is contained in the Acts of the Apostles.

To the east it has the waters of the Jordan and the wilderness adjoining it, familiar to the sons of the prophets, at a distance of about fourteen miles; and the wooded valley where now lies the Salt Sea, also called Lake Asphaltites and the Dead Sea. Before the Lord overthrew Sodom, as is read in Genesis, this entire region was watered like the paradise of God (Gen. 13:10).

On this side of the Jordan lie the city of Jericho, subdued by Joshua, Moses’ successor, more by prayer than by fighting, where afterward the Lord, passing by, restored sight to a blind man (Matt. 20); and Gilgal, Elisha’s refuge. Beyond the Jordan are Gilead, Bashan, Ammon, and Moab, which were afterward received as a portion by Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. All that region is today called Arabia by a general designation.

To the south it has the lot of Judah, in which are Bethlehem, the Lord’s familiar resting-place and blessed site of the Lord’s birth and cradle; the city of Tekoa, dwelling-place of the prophets Habakkuk and Amos; and Hebron, also called Kiriath-arba, the venerable burial-place of the holy patriarchs.

To the north it has the city of Gibeon, renowned for the victory of Joshua son of Nun and made famous by the miracle of the sun held fixed; and the tribe of Ephraim, in which are Shiloh, at one time guardian of the Lord’s tabernacle; Sychar, homeland of the Samaritan woman with whom the Lord conversed; and Bethel, worshipper of the golden calves and witness to Jeroboam’s sin. There is also Sebaste, the tomb of John the Baptist, Elisha, and Obadiah; it was once named from Mount Somer, on which Samaria is situated, the lofty throne of the kings of Israel. Hence the whole aforesaid region is called Samaria even to the present day.

There is likewise Neapolis, formerly called Shechem, bearing the name of its founder. There, according to the account in the book of Genesis (chapter 34), Jacob’s sons Simeon and Levi, in vengeance for the rape which Shechem, son of Hamor, had inflicted upon their sister Dinah after becoming enamored of her, struck down both him and his sons with the edge of the sword and burned their city.

## CHAPTER II. By what names and how many the city is called, and how David made it the throne of his kingdom. How Aelius Hadrian transferred it from the slope to the mountain’s summit. And further matters concerning its site.

Jerusalem, the metropolis of Judaea, is situated in a place entirely lacking streams, woods, springs, and pastures. According to ancient histories and the traditions of eastern peoples, it was first called Salem, then Jebus; afterward, in the time of David, who drove out its Jebusite inhabitant, enlarged it after reigning seven years at Hebron, and made it the throne of his kingdom, it was called Jerusalem.

Thus it is read in Chronicles:

> Then David and all Israel went to Jerusalem, that is Jebus, where the Jebusites were inhabitants of the land. And those who lived in Jebus said to David: “You shall not enter here.” But David captured the stronghold of Zion, which is the City of David. And David said: “Whoever first strikes down a Jebusite shall be chief and commander.” So Joab son of Zeruiah went up first and became chief. David dwelt in the stronghold; therefore it was called the City of David. He built the city all around, from the Millo to the circuit, while Joab built up the rest of the city (1 Chron. 11:4 ff.).

Later, under the reign of his son Solomon, it was called *Hierosolyma*, as though “Jerusalem of Solomon.”

As the distinguished writers and illustrious historians Hegesippus and Josephus relate, Titus, son of Vespasian, the magnificent ruler of the Romans, besieged it in the forty-second year after the Lord’s Passion, the Jews’ merits demanding this. He took the besieged city and utterly razed it after taking it, so that, according to the word of the Lord, “not one stone remained upon another” (Matt. 24:2).

Later Aelius Hadrian, the fourth Roman emperor after Titus, restored this same city; hence it was called Aelia after him, as is read in the Council of Nicaea: “Let the bishop of Aelia be honored by all,” and so forth. Previously it had stood on a steep slope, declining in part toward the east and in part toward the south, situated on the side of both Mount Zion and Mount Moriah, so that only the Temple and the fortress called Antonia stood on its summit and upper part. This emperor transferred the entire city to the mountain’s summit, so that the place of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, formerly outside the city, was enclosed within the circuit of the walls when the city was rebuilt.

The city is smaller than the greatest cities but larger than middling ones. It is oblong in shape and longer on one side, yet four-sided, surrounded on three sides by very deep valleys. On the east it has the Valley of Jehoshaphat. The prophet Joel mentions it, saying:

> “When I restore the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem, I shall gather all nations and bring them down into the Valley of Jehoshaphat; and there I shall enter into judgment with them concerning my people and my inheritance Israel” (Joel 3:2).

At its bottom is built a noble church in honor of the Mother of God, where she is believed to have been buried; and her glorious tomb is shown to the people who come there even to this day. Beneath it also the torrent Kidron, swollen by rainwater, customarily flows during the winter months. The blessed evangelist John mentions it, saying: “Jesus went out across the torrent Kidron, where there was a garden” (John 18:1), and so forth.

To the south it has the valley adjoining the aforesaid one, called Ennon [Hinnom], which was the boundary between the portions of Benjamin and Judah in the allotted division, as is written in Joshua (15:8):

> “And it went up through the valley of the son of Ennon, along the southern side of the Jebusite, that is Jerusalem; and thence rose to the summit of the mountain opposite Gehennon toward the west.”

In this valley there is today shown the field bought with the price of the Savior, for whom Judas, that most wicked merchant, delivered the Lord to the Jews; it was assigned as a burial-place for strangers and is called Acheldemac [Akeldama].

Concerning this valley Chronicles also writes, speaking of Ahaz:

> “He it was who burned incense in the valley of Ennon and made his sons pass through the fire according to the rites of the nations whom the Lord destroyed at the coming of the children of Israel” (2 Chron. 28:3).

To the west it has that part of the valley in which the old pool, celebrated in the time of the kings of Judah, is identified; from there it extends to the upper pool, today commonly called the Patriarch’s Pool, which is near the old cemetery, in the cave called the Lion’s Cave.

From the north the city is approached by level ground. There the place is identified even today where Stephen the protomartyr, stoned by the Jews, praying on his knees for his persecutors, gave up his spirit.

## CHAPTER III. That it contains within its walls part of two mountains; that the church of the Lord’s Resurrection is situated there, while the Temple of the Lord is on high; and what is the form of each church.

[Col. 0408A]

Situated upon two mountains, as David recalls when he says, “Her foundations are upon the holy mountains” (Ps. 86:1), it contains within the circuit of its walls, for the greater part, their summits, separated by a small valley which also divides the city through its middle. One of these mountains, on the west, is called Sion; and from it the whole city is often named, as in: “The Lord loves the gates of Sion above all the tabernacles of Jacob” (Ps. 86:1). The other, on the east, is called Mount Moriah, mentioned in the Second Book of Chronicles [Col. 0408B] in these words: “Solomon began to build the house of the Lord at Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, which had been shown to David his father, in the place which David had prepared on the threshing-floor of Ornan the Jebusite” (II Chron. 3:1).

On the western mountain, as it were on its highest summit, stands the church called Sion from the name of the mountain; and not far from it is David’s Tower, built with the utmost solidity. Rising above the whole city spread beneath it, it forms, together with the towers, walls, and outer works attached to it, something like the city’s fortress. On the same mountain also, but on the slope facing east, stands the church of the Holy Resurrection, circular in shape. Since it lies upon the slope of the aforesaid mountain, the overhanging and adjoining incline rises almost above the height of the church and makes it dark. [Col. 0408C] Its roof, made of beams raised high and ingeniously interwoven in the form of a crown, is open and permanently uncovered, so that the necessary light may enter the church; beneath this wide opening lies the Saviour’s tomb.

Before the entry of our Latins, the place of the Lord’s Passion called Calvary or Golgotha; the place where the wood of the life-giving Cross is said to have been found; and the place where the Saviour’s body, taken down from the Cross, is said to have been anointed with ointments and spices and wrapped in a linen cloth, as was the Jewish burial custom, lay outside the circuit of the aforesaid church, in very small chapels. But after our people, aided by divine mercy, had taken the city by force, [Col. 0408D] the earlier building seemed to them far too narrow. Therefore, the former church having been enlarged by a structure of the greatest strength and considerable height, the old building being continuously incorporated within the new, they wonderfully enclosed the aforesaid places.

On the other mountain, which lies to the east, upon its south-facing slope, is the Temple of the Lord, on the spot where, according to the account in the Book of Kings (II Kings 24) and Chronicles, King David bought the threshing-floor from Aureuma, or Ornan, a Jebusite. There he was commanded to build an altar to the Lord, upon which he later offered burnt offerings and peace offerings; and he called upon the Lord, who answered him by fire from heaven upon the altar of burnt offering. There too, by the Lord’s command, his son Solomon, after his father’s death, built the Temple. What its form [Col. 0409A] was, how it fell under Nebuchadnezzar king of the Babylonians, how it was rebuilt under Cyrus king of the Persians by Zerubbabel and Jesus the high priest, and how this same Temple, together with the entire city, was later destroyed under Titus, prince of the Romans, is handed down by ancient histories. It is sufficient here to explain who was the builder of the present structure and what is its design.

At the beginning of this volume we said that the builder of this edifice was Omar, son of Catab, who was the third successor, after the deceiver Muhammad, to his error and kingdom. That this is so is clearly declared by ancient written records inscribed both inside and outside the building itself. Its form is as follows. A square court, its length and breadth each scarcely the distance to which a bow may shoot, bounded by sides equidistant from one another, [Col. 0409B] is enclosed by a strong wall of moderate height. It is entered from the west by two gates, one of which is called Beautiful, where, according to the Acts of the Apostles, Peter set upon his feet the man lame from his mother’s womb, who was asking alms of passers-by. We do not know the certain name of the other. There is one gate on the north; another on the east, which to this day is called the Golden Gate. On the south it has a royal building, commonly called Solomon’s Temple.

Above each of the gates adjoining the city, and at the corners of the aforesaid enclosure, were exceedingly lofty towers, in which, [Col. 0409C] at fixed hours, the priests of the Saracens’ superstition used to ascend in order to invite the people to prayer. Some of these still remain, but others have been thrown down through various accidents. Within these precincts no one was permitted either to live or even to enter except barefoot and with washed feet, gatekeepers having been stationed at each entrance to supervise this matter carefully.

In the middle of this enclosed court is another, higher level space, likewise quadrilateral and with sides equidistant in every direction from the lower court. It is approached by steps at two places on the west, at as many on the south, and at one only on the east. At each of its corners [Col. 0409D] stood a small chapel; some still exist, while others were pulled down in order that other buildings might be constructed there.

In the middle of this upper court the Temple is built, octagonal in shape and with the same number of sides, adorned within and without with marble slabs and mosaic work, and having a spherical roof artfully covered with lead. Both courts, the enclosing lower one and the enclosed upper one, are paved with white stone, so that in winter the rainwater which runs down in great quantity from the Temple building, and which they receive in no smaller quantity from elsewhere, flows very clear and free from mud into the numerous cisterns contained within the aforesaid precincts.

Within, in the middle of the Temple and beneath the inner circle of columns, [Col. 0410A] is a somewhat elevated rock, with a cave beneath it cut from the same rock. Upon this rock the angel is said to have sat who, because of David’s rash numbering of the people, struck the people until the Lord commanded him to spare them and return his sword to its sheath. There David later built the altar, as we have said, after buying the threshing-floor for six hundred shekels of gold of the most exact weight. Before the coming of our people and afterward for fifteen years, this rock lay bare and exposed; later those in charge of the place covered it with white marble and built an altar over it and a choir, where the clergy celebrate the divine offices.

## CHAPTER IV. That the city is situated in a dry and waterless place. Of the fountain of Siloam. And how the citizens, having heard of our arrival, destroyed the reservoirs and blocked the springs.

[Col. 0410B]

The region in which the aforesaid city devoted to God is situated is called Judaea; it is also called First Palestine. Judaea, indeed, received its name after the ten tribes followed Jeroboam son of Nebat and withdrew from Rehoboam son of Solomon, while only two tribes—Benjamin and Judah—remained attached to him. Thus the territory of both tribes was called Judaea from the name of Judah. Hence too the saying in the Gospel: “Return into the land of Judah.” For this reason Rehoboam himself and his successors were called kings of Judah, while the kings of the remaining ten tribes were called kings of Israel [Col. 0410C] or of Samaria.

Palestine is so called, as it were, from Philistia, deriving its name from the Philistines. There are said to be three Palestines. The first is that properly called Judaea, whose metropolis is Jerusalem; the second has Caesarea Maritima as its metropolis; the third has Bethsan, or Scythopolis, as its metropolis, the rank of which is today held by the Church of Nazareth. Whether it is called in this way or that, it is certain that it forms part of the land of promise and of Syria. This may be understood from the homily which says: “It is customary among the Syrians, and especially in the region of Palestine, which is a part of Syria and in which the Lord deigned to appear bodily, to join parables to almost all their speech.”

The same region lies, as it were, at the navel of the land of promise, according to [Col. 0410D] the description of that land’s boundaries in Joshua, where it is written: “From the wilderness and Lebanon, and from the great river Euphrates, unto the western sea, shall be your boundaries” (Josh. 1:4).

The place where the city stands is dry and waterless, utterly without streams, springs, or rivers; its inhabitants use rainwater alone. During the winter months they collect rain in the many cisterns which they possess in the city, and preserve it for necessary uses throughout the year. We are therefore greatly surprised that Solinus calls Judaea renowned for waters. For he says in his *Polyhistor*: “Judaea is renowned for waters, though the nature of its waters is not uniform.” We can find no explanation except to say either that he did not [Col. 0411A] ascertain the truth of the matter, or that the former appearance of the land was later changed.

It is nevertheless certain that Hezekiah, king of Judah and friend of the Lord, when he learned of the approach of Sennacherib, son of Salmanassar king of Assyria, blocked up the springs outside the city. Of him it is written thus in the Second Book of Chronicles: “When Hezekiah heard that Sennacherib had come, and that the whole force of the war was directed against Jerusalem, he took counsel with the princes and mighty men to block the heads of the springs which were outside the city. With this being the unanimous decision, he assembled a very great multitude, and they blocked all the springs and the brook that flowed through the middle of the land, saying: ‘Let not the kings of Assyria come and find an abundance of water’” (II Chron. 32:2).

Foremost among these was the spring called [Col. 0411B] Gihon, concerning which it is written in the same book: “This is Hezekiah, who stopped up the upper outlet of the waters of Gihon and diverted them beneath the west side of the city of David” (ibid., 30). Gihon is a place to the south, situated in the valley of Ennon in the middle of Jerusalem, where today stands a church in honour of the Blessed martyr Procopius. There Solomon is said to have been anointed king, as is written in the Third Book of Kings: “Take with you the servants of your lord, set Solomon my son upon my mule, and bring him down to Gihon. Let Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anoint him there king over Israel and Judah; sound the trumpet and say: ‘Long live King Solomon’” (III Kings 1:33).

Yet it is certain that this was before the time of the aforementioned Solinus. For that Solinus lived after Titus, prince of the Romans, who destroyed the city, [Col. 0411C] and before Aelius Hadrian, who rebuilt it, is clearly inferred from reading his *Polyhistor*, in whose fortieth chapter it is written: “The capital of Judaea was Jerusalem, but it was razed. Jericho succeeded it, and this too ceased to be the capital, having been subdued in the war of Artaxerxes.”

Outside the city, at a distance of two or three miles, are a few springs; but they are few in number and provide a very slight supply of water. Near the city, however, on the southern side, where the two aforementioned valleys join, about a mile distant from the city, is a very famous spring, Siloam. The Lord sent to it the man blind from birth, that he might wash there and see (John 9). It is a small spring, rising from the bottom of the valley, [Col. 0411D] and its waters are neither pleasant nor continuous; its flow is intermittent, and it is said to give water only every third day.

Moreover, when the citizens learned of our arrival, they blocked the mouths of the springs and cisterns around the city for five or six miles, so that the people, worn down by thirst, might abandon the siege. Consequently, during the siege our army later endured limitless hardships, as will be related below. Those within the city, besides the greatest abundance of rainwater which they possessed, also received springs brought in from external areas and conveyed by aqueducts into two pools of very great size, situated near the enclosure of the Temple, outside it indeed but within the city. One of these [Col. 0412A] is still regarded as the Sheep Pool (*Piscina Probatica*), in which sacrificial victims were formerly washed. It is said in the Gospel to have five porticoes (John 5), and into it an angel was said to descend and stir the water, with the result that whoever first entered the pool after the stirring of the water was healed. In it the Lord healed the paralytic and commanded him to take up his bed.

## CHAPTER V. At what time our army arrived before the city; what was the number of our people and of the enemy; and in what order the camps were placed.

Therefore, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1099, in the month of June, on the seventh day of the month, the legions of our people encamped before the aforesaid city. The number of those who arrived—of both sexes, every age, and every condition—is said to have been about forty thousand. Of these scarcely twenty thousand foot soldiers could be equipped for service; there were fifteen hundred cavalrymen; all the rest were either an unarmed crowd, or sick and weak persons. [Col. 0412B] In the city there were said to be forty thousand strong and very well-armed men. For a great multitude had assembled there from neighbouring towns and adjacent suburbs, partly to seek their own safety by taking refuge in the city from the approaching army, and partly to protect the royal city from imminent dangers, furnishing it with weapons and provisions.

After our leaders had approached the city, they carefully considered with those acquainted with the country how they might attack it more easily and advantageously. Seeing that they could make no progress either from the east or from the south because of the depth of the aforesaid valleys, they resolved to besiege it from the north. From the gate now called Saint Stephen’s, facing north, as far as the gate below David’s Tower, named after that king just as is the tower situated on the western side of the city, our princes encamped. [Col. 0412C] First in their order was Lord Godfrey, duke of Lorraine; after him Lord Robert, count of Flanders; in the third place Lord Robert, count of Normandy; in the fourth, near the corner tower likewise named after David, Lord Tancred and certain other nobles held their positions. From that same tower to the Western Gate, the count of Toulouse with his following besieged the city.

Later, however, since the tower overlooking his camp strongly protected the aforesaid gate lying, as it were, beneath it, and because of the valley between the city and his camp, he saw that he could not make much progress by attacking the city on that side. By the advice of certain prudent men acquainted with the region, he transferred part of his camp to the mountain on which the city was built, between the city and the church called Sion, which is distant from the city by the range of one shot of a bow, on the northern side; [Col. 0413A] leaving another part where it had been before. He is said to have done this in order that his men might approach the city’s capture more easily, and that they might protect the aforesaid church from injury by the enemy. For this was the place where the Saviour is said to have supped with his disciples and washed their feet; there also the Holy Spirit is said to have descended upon the disciples in tongues of fire on the holy day of Pentecost. Ancient tradition likewise maintains that there the pious Mother of God paid the debt of death, and there too the tomb of Stephen, the first martyr, is marked to this day.

## CHAPTER VI. On the fifth day after the siege they attack the city; under the guidance of a certain faithful man they go down into the woods, bring back timbers, and construct engines.

[Col. 0413B]

The camps having therefore been placed as we have said—from the northern gate, commonly called Saint Stephen’s, to the corner tower overlooking the Valley of Jehoshaphat—the city remained unbesieged from there as far as the opposite corner of the city, situated on the southern side above the slope of that valley, and from there as far as the southern gate, now called the Gate of Mount Sion. Thus scarcely half the city was enclosed by the siege.

On the fifth day after our army had taken its position before the city, it was publicly ordered and proclaimed that all, unanimously, from the greatest to the least, equipped with arms and protected by shields, should prepare to attack the city; and so it was done. Rising all together, [Col. 0413C] they assaulted the besieged parts of the city with such force, and continued their attack with such care and courage, that after breaking the outer walls they compelled the citizens to withdraw in fear behind the inner walls and forced them to despair of resistance. Had they possessed ladders that day, or fitted engines for taking the ramparts during that fervour of attack, they could beyond all doubt have claimed the city for themselves.

After labouring at this from early morning until about the seventh hour of the day, they saw that they could not make much progress without engines. They therefore postponed their undertaking for a time, intending, with God as author, to resume it more successfully when the engines had been completed. While the princes were anxiously deliberating where material suitable for wooden devices [Col. 0413D] might be found—for the entire surrounding country appeared to provide no such resource—a faithful native happened to be present, a Syrian by nation. He directed some of the princes to certain more secluded valleys, six or seven miles from the city, where they found many trees, not altogether suitable for the intended work, yet of some considerable height. Having craftsmen and woodcutters there, they loaded upon camels and carts as much as seemed necessary for the aforesaid work and brought it to the city.

The craftsmen and those most skilled in such work having been assembled, they applied every effort and untiring diligence, competing with one another to construct from the material at hand towers and missile engines called mangonels or petraries, together with battering-rams and digging-sows for undermining the wall, using axes, adzes, and every sort of such tool. [Col. 0414A] Wages were given from the contributions offered by the people’s devotion to craftsmen whose own means did not suffice, so that they might work without charge. For the resources of none of the princes were sufficient to pay the builders’ wages, except the count of Toulouse, who continually had greater abundance than the rest. From his own treasury, without a contribution from the people, he supplied his craftsmen with their necessary expenses; he also provided stipends for many nobles whose travelling resources had failed.

While the greater princes were thus engaged in greater concerns, other noble and distinguished men, raising their banners, led the people to places where, as they had learned from natives, there were thickets and low woodland. There they gathered branches and withies, carrying them away by horses, asses, and every kind of beast of burden, in order to weave hurdles and supply the larger works. [Col. 0414B] The work was thus in full heat, and everyone’s diligence was watchful. In so great a multitude there was no idler, nor was anyone allowed to languish in leisure; rather, each performed some service, without regard to what suited anyone’s rank. Whatever could be useful was judged honourable to handle.

Rich and poor alike laboured at the work, and inequality of condition counted for nothing where their zeal was equal and their ardour in carrying out the work no different. Whoever was greater in rank was more diligent in frequent service; whoever was lower was nevertheless admitted to some task. They counted as nothing all that they had suffered throughout the entire journey, provided they might reap the fruit of such labour and enter the city for which they had endured so many adverse chances. They considered light whatever might be commanded, so long as they believed that by cooperating in this one matter they might deserve to attain the fulfilment of their vow.

## CHAPTER VII. The people are exhausted by thirst; while seeking water far away and the other necessities of life, they are frequently killed by the enemy.

Meanwhile the army was grievously exhausted by extreme thirst. [Col. 0414D] For, as we have said, the land adjoining the city is dry and waterless, having no streams, springs, or even wells of living water except at a distance. When our arrival had been heard of, the inhabitants had blocked all of these, by throwing in dust and by other methods available to them, in order to make the place less fit for maintaining a siege. They had also destroyed the cisterns and reservoirs of rainwater, so that they could not retain water, or had maliciously concealed them, lest they offer relief to the needy and thirsty people.

Yet many faithful citizens of Bethlehem and of Tekoa, the city of the prophets, were present in the army. Under their guidance the people went out to springs four or five miles from the siege. [Col. 0415A] There, only with the greatest difficulty—crowding one another and preventing each other from drawing water—after very long delays caused by the mutual hostility which they created for one another, they carried back muddy water in skins. A draught of it, by which a thirsty person could scarcely refresh his life once, was sold at a high price.

Moreover, the spring of Siloam near the city, which we mentioned above, could not suffice for the toiling people, since it did not have continuous water and at fixed times gave forth insipid water. The harshness of thirst and the double pain of distress were further increased by the fierceness of summer and the burning heat of June. Labour too, and the dust stirred up, caused dryness in mouth and chest.

Thus, scattered and going out separately, they searched diligently for water. [Col. 0415B] When a few thought that they had found the waters they sought, a great crowd with the same purpose suddenly came upon them, so that quarrels sometimes arose among them at the springs they had found; while they obstructed one another, they often came to blows. Those who were infantrymen could somehow provide relief for themselves, using the water they found sparingly. But those who had great numbers of horses could only with the greatest difficulty lead their thirsty horses three or four miles to water.

The neglected animals, for which their masters could not provide—horses, mules, asses, as well as flocks and herds—wandered through the fields with slow step and failing strength. Consumed by thirst [Col. 0415C] and dryness, they wasted away, failed in themselves, and died as though melted within. Hence there was in the camp a very great stench and a pestilential, most dangerous corruption of the air. In this siege the grievous hardship of thirst seemed to afflict the people no less than lack of food had tormented them at Antioch.

While seeking food and fodder for horses in the adjoining suburbs, they scattered incautiously and wandered through the countryside in excessive security. Learning of their movements, the townsmen secretly emerged through the unbesieged areas and at times attacked such parties, killing many and more often leading away their horses. Some of those wounded, however, who escaped in flight, were rescued by better fortune. The number of our people diminished every day; the following day took something away from what the preceding day seemed to possess, since many almost daily perished through the various misfortunes to which mortal weakness is subject. [Col. 0415D] No one came from elsewhere to fill the places or perform the duties of those who had fallen. Conversely, the enemy’s strength increased and their reinforcements multiplied; these had free entrance into the city through the unbesieged parts and joined the citizens to the destruction of our people.

## CHAPTER VIII. The citizens construct engines, prepare to resist, and subject the faithful living among them to compulsory services.

While our entire army was labouring to construct engines, weave hurdles, and join ladders, and was greatly occupied with this task, the citizens likewise devoted every vigilance to repelling devices with devices and exerted their whole care to find a means of resistance. Having an adequate supply of timber and tall trees, which before our arrival they had brought into the city with much diligence and ample foresight for its defence, they eagerly erected within engines equal to ours but constructed of better material. [Col. 0416A] They pursued this with all zeal, lest they should be found inferior in either skill or material in this kind of equipment. Maintaining continuous watches upon the wall and in the towers, they observed with the greatest care nearly everything done in the army, especially whatever concerned the construction of such devices, and reported it to the leading men of the city, so that by rival skill, striving to imitate everything, they might answer our contrivances on equal terms. This was quite easy for them. For inside they had much greater stores than we had outside of workmanship, smiths’ tools, iron, bronze, ropes, and all else usually needed for such purposes.

Nor were the citizens alone compelled to work at this by public decree: they imposed unheard-of compulsory services and severe requisitioned transport-services (*parangariae*) upon the faithful who lived with them and endured a servile and utterly degraded condition. [Col. 0416B] They did not merely wear them down with violent exactions; they dragged them to chains and prisons, suspecting that they favoured our people and would disclose to them the condition and secrets of the city. None of the faithful dared climb the wall or appear in public unless burdened with some necessary object, as though he were a beast of burden being driven. They were compelled to carry loads; and whoever had experience in a craft was compelled to render manual labour.

At the slightest accusation from any informer, they were seized for punishment. They were compelled to receive as guests those who had come into the city from neighbouring towns and nearby cities, and to supply them with necessities. Although their resources did not suffice for even scanty and wretched sustenance for their own household and dependants, they were nonetheless forced to share their property with strangers, so that they themselves were the first to suffer want. [Col. 0416C] Furthermore, if anything was needed for public works, the houses of the faithful were broken into before all others, so that if such an item were found in them, it might be violently extorted from the owner of the dwelling.

Whenever summoned, in any place or at any time, by night or by day, and even if through some chance they delayed instead of following the first summons without an interval of time, they were disgracefully dragged away by beard and hair—so that even their enemies’ pitiable condition might draw tears. Indeed, the weight of their sufferings and labours was immeasurable and without end. Thus, exhausted beyond measure, they had now reached utter collapse, so that they preferred to die in the Lord rather than continue this temporal life. [Col. 0417A] Their life was scarcely distinguishable from death in its misery: no time was permitted even once a day for taking food, nor was any rest, however slight, granted for necessary sleep. Whatever misfortune occurred was wholly laid to their charge. They had no unhampered departure from their own homes into public, nor any unmolested return to their homes; they lay open to every accusation, and everyone was afforded opportunity to accuse them.

## CHAPTER IX. A Genoese fleet puts in at Joppa; men are sent from the army to bring them to the siege; those sent suffer enemy ambushes on the journey.

[Col. 0417B]

Meanwhile, while these things were taking place around Jerusalem during the siege, a messenger arrived to report that Genoese ships had put in at the harbour of Joppa. He asked the princes to send some military force from the army, by whose guidance and strength those who had landed might approach the city.

Joppa is a maritime city, of which Solinus says in chapter 39 of *On the Marvels of the World*: “Joppa is the most ancient town in all the world, having been founded before the inundation of the lands. The town displays a rock which still retains the marks of Andromeda’s chains, she having, according to no idle report, been exposed to a sea-monster. Indeed, M. Scaurus displayed the bones of that monster at Rome among the other marvels during his aedileship. The matter is recorded in the annals. Its measurements are also contained in trustworthy books: the length of its ribs exceeded forty feet, and its height surpassed that of an Indian elephant; moreover, the vertebrae of its spine exceeded half a foot in breadth.” [Col. 0417C]

Jerome also attests the same in his epitaph for Saint Paula, in these words: “She saw Joppa, the harbour of fleeing Jonah; and, to touch briefly upon the tales of the poets, the rock-bound Andromeda.”

It happened that, in accordance with their request and by common counsel, the lord count of Toulouse, who was richer than the others, sent there a nobleman of his following named Galdemar, surnamed Carpinnelle, with thirty knights and fifty foot soldiers. After they had departed, the princes perceived that those sent were insufficient for so great a task. They therefore again asked the same count to send more men. Yielding to their advice, he dispatched after the men who had first left the distinguished and eminent men Raymond Pelet and William of Sabran, with fifty knights, for the aforesaid service. [Col. 0417D]

When Galdemar, who had left first, had come down into the plains about Lydda and Ramla, six hundred enemies met him. They immediately attacked, killed four of his knights and many more of the foot soldiers. While our men resisted as best they could and, though few, encouraged each other to battle, it happened that the aforesaid two noblemen following them arrived with all speed and, before the engagement was broken up, joined the fight. Thus our forces united with one another; divine power was present, and, pressing hard upon the enemy, they killed two hundred of their number and put the rest to flight.

Yet in that conflict the noblemen Gilbert of Treva and Aicard of Montmerla fell. When news of their deaths became known among our expeditionary forces, it brought no small grief. Our men, however, having been granted victory by divine power, reached Joppa safely, as they had intended. [Col. 0418A] There the aforesaid sailors welcomed them with immense joy, and they refreshed one another with mutual affection and gracious conversation.

While they delayed there for some time, until those who had arrived in the ships had arranged their baggage and prepared themselves for the journey, an Egyptian fleet, which lay concealed near Ascalon waiting for an opportunity to do harm, suddenly arrived by night off the same city. When our men learned this, they went to the sea and first attempted to protect the ships from enemy attacks. But later, recognizing that they could not resist the enemy’s multitude, they took the sails, ropes, and other tackle from the ships and, leaving the ships, withdrew with all their possessions to the protection of the stronghold.

One of the ships, however, which had gone out to plunder, was returning laden with spoil to the same place. Learning that the enemy fleet had occupied the harbour of Joppa, it was driven by favourable winds to Laodicea. [Col. 0418B]

At that time Joppa had become a wilderness and was empty of inhabitants. A short time before our arrival, its citizens, despairing of their defences, had abandoned the place; our people held only the citadel. Their preparations made and ready for the road, with the military party that had come down for this purpose going before to provide guidance, the Genoese set out for Jerusalem with all their possessions. There they were joyfully received by the legions and brought great comfort to the camp. They were prudent men and, in the sailors’ manner, highly skilled in the craft of construction: cutting, shaping, and joining beams, and erecting engines. They had also brought with them many other devices of every kind useful to those on the expedition, [Col. 0418C] so that what before their arrival could scarcely and only with difficulty be hoped to be brought to completion was easily accomplished through their work.

## CHAPTER X. Those who had arrived in the fleet join the army and provide very great assistance in erecting engines. The count of Toulouse and Tancred are reconciled.

But those who had remained with the expedition, faithfully persisting in the work begun and applying themselves with all diligence to the construction of siege-engines, had already completed the greater part of the task. For the duke and the two counts, namely the Norman and the Fleming, had set over the work a certain distinguished and splendid man, Lord Gaston of Béart [Col. 0419A], and had asked him to give careful attention to ensuring that the craftsmen did not perform their assigned task negligently.

They themselves often went out, leading the people with a strong hand, to cut timber and carry the felled wood to the building work. Others cut undergrowth, shrubs, withies, and smaller branches of trees, and eagerly piled them up so that hurdles might be made from them, with which the engines could be covered on the outside. Others stripped the hides from animals, whether slaughtered or dying of thirst and drought, clean and unclean alike, so that the engines might be protected with them over the hurdles, lest fire cast by the enemy should perhaps consume the structures. Nor was the work carried on with such fervour only in the northern quarter, through the efforts of the duke and the two aforesaid counts [Col. 0419B]. From the corner tower as far as the western gate, which lies below David’s citadel, Lord Tancred and many other nobles who had pitched camp in that quarter applied themselves to the same task with no less concern, giving it the most diligent attention.

But in the southern quarter the army and entire household of the Count of Toulouse laboured tirelessly and with every diligence on the same undertaking; and the more ardently because he was wealthier and had lately received greater supplies, both of men and of necessary materials.
