For all who had come from the ships had joined his camp and had brought equipment exceedingly necessary for the building work. Having ropes [Col. 0419C], hammers, and other iron tools with them, and also excellent craftsmen highly experienced, as we have said, in constructing and erecting engines, they afforded very great assistance in bringing the work to completion. The Genoese who had arrived were commanded by a certain nobleman named William, surnamed Embriaco, whose skill in workmanship was very great.

And when the whole army had toiled at this for four weeks, the undertaking was now, after much labour, approaching completion. Therefore, after taking counsel together, the leaders set a day for assaulting the city. But because a serious quarrel had arisen between the Count of Toulouse and Lord Tancred, and enmities had also arisen among certain others for various reasons [Col. 0419D], it pleased the bishops, the leaders, and the entire people that, first, charity should be fully restored among them, so that with sincere hearts they might implore divine aid.

### Chapter XI. Litanies Are Proclaimed for the People. The Whole People Ascends the Mount of Olives.

On the appointed day, therefore, litanies were publicly proclaimed for the whole people. Taking up crosses and the patronage of the saints, the bishops and all the clergy, clothed in priestly and Levitical garments, went barefoot before the people who followed with great devotion, as far as the Mount of Olives. There the venerable man Peter the Hermit and Arnulf [Col. 0420A], a member of the household of the Count of Normandy and a learned man, addressed the people in exhortation, encouraging them, so far as they could, to steadfast endurance.

Now the Mount of Olives lies opposite the city on the east, about a mile from the city, with the valley of Jehoshaphat lying between. Hence the blessed Luke says that it is “a Sabbath day’s journey from Jerusalem” (Acts 1:12). And from this place our Saviour, as the disciples watched, was raised into heaven on the fortieth day after his resurrection, and a cloud received him from their sight.

When the faithful people had come to this place, in a spirit of humility and with contrite heart, having implored help from above with groans and tears, and having reconciled the aforesaid leaders with one another and recalled the whole people to mutual charity, they descended from the mountain [Col. 0420B] and ascended to the church of Mount Zion, which, as we have said, stands on the summit of the hill in the southern part of the same city, close to the city.

The citizens stationed in the towers and on the wall, wondering what this circuit of the people could mean, shot missiles into the companies with bows and crossbows; some of our men, behaving incautiously, were therefore wounded. They also treated crosses, which they had placed on the wall in insult and contempt of our people, shamefully with spitting and other unclean acts; and they shamelessly heaped abuse and blasphemous words upon our Lord Jesus Christ and his saving teaching. Yet the people, pursuing their vow with all devotion and inflamed with that anger which the pain of sacrilege could produce [Col. 0420C], came to the aforesaid church. There, after prayers had again been completed and the day appointed on which they would assault the city with one accord, they returned, having encircled the city, to their camp. Whatever remained unfinished for the completion of the work was ordered to be hastened with great speed, lest any defect create an obstacle for those wishing to attack the city.

### Chapter XII. The Duke and the Two Principal Counts Move Their Camps by Night; Engines Are Raised Around the City.

When, therefore, the appointed day for attacking the city arrived, on the night preceding that day [Col. 0420D], the duke and the two aforesaid principal counts saw that the part of the city which they had besieged was most strongly defended by the citizens with engines, arms, and brave men—and all the more strongly because the enemy thought that danger was greatest on that side. They also saw that on the following day they could hope to accomplish little there because of the strength of the position. With remarkable foresight and astonishing labour, before the parts had been joined together, they moved the engines and the siege-tower piece by piece, along with their camp, to the area between the gate of St Stephen and the corner tower, which stands to the north above the valley of Jehoshaphat.

For it seemed to them—and it was indeed so—that because the city had remained unbesieged on that side, it was guarded by the citizens with less diligence. Thus it came about that the transferred engines, after watch had been maintained throughout the night, were assembled with much labour and placed in suitable positions before sunrise [Col. 0421A]. The siege-tower too was brought against the walls where the wall seemed lower and the approach from outside flatter and more convenient, so that those in the towers and those in the engine seemed almost able to fight at close quarters. Nor indeed was the labour slight. They had moved these implements nearly half a mile from the place where they had first camped and had assembled their parts and raised them there before the sun rose.

At sunrise the citizens approached the wall to see what our men were doing outside. With astonishment they saw that part of the camp and all the military apparatus which had been seen there yesterday and the day before yesterday had vanished. Carefully surveying the adjacent ground and examining the circuit of the wall, they learned that the duke’s camp had been moved and observed the engines raised in the quarter we have mentioned [Col. 0421B].

That same night, in other parts of the city too, according to the various places where, as we have said, they had encamped, they had kept watch and laboured continuously and raised their engines. For at almost the same moment the Count of Toulouse brought the siege-tower he had constructed with great care against the wall, between the aforesaid church of Mount Zion and the city. The remaining leaders, beside the corner tower which today is called Tancred’s, had likewise placed against the wall a wooden tower of almost the same height and strength, with equal diligence and an equal burden of labour.

The effectiveness of these engines was alike, and their construction was not dissimilar. Since they were square structures, the side facing the city was strengthened by a double framework; and the outer layer could by a certain contrivance be lowered, so that, when laid upon the wall, it might serve those seeking to enter as a bridge. Yet the engine was not unprotected on that side; rather, when the front section was lowered, the part beneath it protected the tower no less than its other sides [Col. 0421C].

### Chapter XIII. The City Is Assaulted and a Most Violent Conflict Takes Place on Both Sides; but Nightfall Ends the Contest.

As day advanced, the entire armed multitude of our people came, as agreed, to assault the city, all holding one and the same purpose: either to lay down their lives for Christ or to restore the city to Christian freedom. In so great a multitude there was no old man, invalid, or one too young in age whom zeal did not move and the ardour of devotion did not kindle for battle. Even women, forgetting their sex and unmindful of their accustomed frailty, dared, beyond their strength, to take up the use of arms.

Approaching the battle with one mind, they strove to bring the prepared engines nearer to the wall, so that they might more boldly assail those resisting from the towers and wall. But the citizens, resolved to resist their opponents in every way [Col. 0422A], endeavoured to drive our men away from the wall by blows of missiles, the discharge of innumerable arrows, and the hurling of stones, both those thrown by hand and those cast with dreadful force from throwing-engines.

Our men, no less actively protected by shields and covered hurdles, shot frequent missiles with bows and crossbows and hurled fist-sized stones, striving fearlessly to approach the wall and denying those in the towers any respite or courage to resist. Others stationed beneath the engines strove either to advance the siege-tower with poles or, directing very large millstones against the walls with throwing-engines, to weaken and bring them down by repeated collisions and continuous blows. Others, using smaller engines called mangana, cast smaller stones in an effort to restrain those in the battlements from harassing our men.

Yet neither those labouring to advance the tower could make sufficient progress as they wished, because a great and deep ditch lying before the outer wall greatly impeded the engine’s approach; nor did the labour of those trying to breach the walls with engines avail much. For the citizens had hung down from the battlements sacks filled with straw and chaff, ropes and tapestries, beams of enormous size, and mattresses stuffed with cotton, so that by their softness and flexibility they might blunt the blows of hurled millstones and frustrate the efforts of the attackers [Col. 0422C]. Moreover, they had raised inside many more engines than ours, with which, by shooting arrows and casting stones, they discouraged our men from the work begun.

Thus, while both sides pressed on with all their courage and contended with every effort, a dreadful, violent conflict beyond human expectation continued from morning until evening, and the stubborn encounter was such that a multitude of missiles and arrows fell like hail upon both peoples, while the stones hurled met and struck one another in mid-air, inflicting diverse and manifold causes of death upon the combatants.

The labour was equal and the danger the same for those serving under the duke, under the Count of Toulouse, and under the other leaders as well. For, as stated above, the city was attacked in three places with equal zeal and comparable ardour [Col. 0422D]. Our chief concern was to fill the ditch with rubble, stones, and earth, and to make a way by which the engines could advance. The citizens’ foremost and more urgent care, conversely, was to thwart this purpose. Therefore they resisted with all possible determination those undertaking this work, and eagerly hurled onto the engines firebrands, missiles ignited with sulphur, pitch, paste, and oil, and substances that usually provide fuel for fire, in order to burn them.

Moreover, they directed against our siege-towers the blows of huge engines which they had prepared inside with such skill that they almost broke the legs of the engines, pierced their sides [Col. 0423A], and nearly hurled to the ground in astonishment those who had climbed to the upper platforms in order to attack the city from there. But our men, meeting the fires that had been cast upon them, poured water down in abundance to check the violence of the flames.

### Chapter XIV. On That Night Both Besiegers and Besieged Remain in Great Anxiety.

Night intervened and ended this most dangerous, exceedingly violent, and still uncertain conflict of both sides. Although their bodies seemed to have some sort of rest during the night, their minds, wakeful with immoderate care, laboured no less. Within, they were tormented by gnawing anxiety and, mindful of their purpose [Col. 0423B], burned with anticipation as they eagerly awaited daylight, that they might return again to the contest and test the fortune of battle, hoping in the Lord that they would carry off the palm and the more favourable verdict.

Yet they were greatly troubled, fearing that the enemy might in some manner secretly set their engines on fire. Therefore they kept continuous watch and passed that entire night without sleep. The citizens, likewise, were tortured by consuming worries, greatly afraid that those whom they had seen pressing them with such violence on the previous day might seize the opportunity afforded by the silence of the deep night and secretly enter the city by breaking through the wall or setting up ladders.

Accordingly, not sluggish in their concern but burning with diligent watchfulness, as men whose lives were at stake, they made the circuit of the wall throughout the night, placing officers of the watch in every tower [Col. 0423C]. Moreover, the older men and those more deeply concerned for the commonwealth went about the city streets, warning others to remain constantly watchful for their wives and children, their households, and the public safety; to inspect gates and streets, lest any path be open to the enemy for ambush.

Both sides were thus troubled by these cares, and wakeful anxiety permitted no place for rest. The condition was worse for them when the fighting ceased and their minds burned without finding rest than it had been the previous day while they were labouring in battle.

### Chapter XV. On the Following Day They Return to the Same Work, and the City Is Assaulted More Violently Than Usual. The Sorceresses Who Had Come to Bewitch Our Engine Perish.

[Col. 0423D]

As night was drawing toward day, when dawn, the herald of approaching light, announced the sunrise, the people arose with all eagerness for battle once more. Each man returned to the duty to which he had been assigned on the preceding day. Some, stationed beneath the throwing-engines, hurled huge millstones of exceptional size and solidity against the walls. Others, placed in the lower part of the siege-tower, devoted every effort, by skill and strength, to advancing it. Others, stationed on the highest platform, harassed those in the towers with bows, crossbows, and every kind of missile; with all the zeal and tireless persistence they could muster, they kept them below the battlements so that they would not dare extend a hand [Col. 0424A].

Others gave all their attention to levelling the ditch and breaking down the outer wall, so that the siege-tower might be brought nearer to the city walls. Still others, and these were a very large crowd, kept the citizens away from the battlements with arrows and thrown stones, lest they obstruct those sweating to bring the engine forward.

But the citizens, seeing the greater pressure exerted by our men, applied themselves all the more carefully to opposing devices, in order to repel force with force and skill by comparable contrivance. They returned missiles and stones with equal strength against the attackers, and with remarkable vigour impeded those trying to advance the siege-tower. And, in order at one stroke to frustrate all our men’s efforts [Col. 0424B], they continually hurled fire in fragile pots and by every means they could, together with sulphur and pitch, fat and grease, tow, wax, dry wood and straw, and everything that commonly feeds a fire and supplies fuel to flames.

There was therefore very great slaughter among both peoples, and on each side many were laid low by various misfortunes and unforeseen events. Some were smashed to pieces by the blows of the most powerful engines; others, pierced through hauberks and shields by arrows and a multitude of missiles, suddenly collapsed and died. Others, crushed by fist-sized stones thrown by hand or sling, either died at once or, with limbs shattered, were rendered incapable for many days or permanently. Yet none of these dangers deterred them from the work they had begun [Col. 0424C], nor could all these things diminish their ardour for battle; nor was it easy to determine which people fought with greater zeal.

Nor do we think it should pass without mention that, on that same day, an event worthy of report is said to have occurred. There was outside, among our engines, one which hurled stones of astonishing weight into the city with dreadful violence and force, causing manifold slaughter among the citizens. Since they could accomplish nothing against it by any skill, they brought two sorceresses to bewitch it and render it powerless by magical incantations. While these were practising their spells upon the wall and uttering incantations, a millstone suddenly discharged from that same engine crushed both of them together with three girls who had accompanied their steps; it knocked their lives from them and cast their lifeless bodies down from the wall below [Col. 0424D]. Thus there was applause and great rejoicing in the camp, while among the citizens, conversely, great sorrow increased.

### Chapter XVI. A Divinely Given Signal Is Made from the Mount of Olives, and the Wearied People Return to Battle More Fiercely.

Since the matter had been drawn out until the seventh hour of the day without decisive victory and remained sufficiently uncertain and doubtful, our men, despairing and exhausted beyond their strength by the immensity of the labour, began to press the attack less vigorously. They had already resolved to withdraw a little the siege-tower, almost broken by continuous blows, and the other engines which had caught fire and were now smoking, and to postpone the engagement until the following day. The people were already gradually dispersing in despondency, their spirits almost broken, while the enemy insulted and boldly challenged them to battle more fiercely than usual.

But behold: divine power was present, bringing the necessary consolation desired by the faithful in a desperate situation. For from the Mount of Olives a certain knight—who, however, was not seen afterward—gave a signal to our forces to return to the attack and renew the engagement, waving a shining and resplendent shield. Encouraged by this sign, Duke Godfrey, who with his brother Eustace was stationed on the upper platform of our siege-tower, both to attack the city and to guard the structure more carefully [Col. 0425B], began to summon the people and the leading men back with loud cries.

And, through the mercy of the Lord going before, the whole people returned to battle with rejoicing and with such fervour that they appeared to begin the battle afresh, as though their strength were whole. Those who had previously withdrawn through weariness or wounds now, their spirits restored and their strength doubled, voluntarily offered themselves and pressed on more boldly. The leaders and those who seemed to be pillars of the army went before the others and made them braver by their example. Nor, lest they seem excluded from so great a labour, did the women remain idle: they brought drink in vessels to the men toiling in the struggle, lest they fail, and encouraged them to battle with effective words [Col. 0425C].

There was such joy in the camp that, now almost certain of victory, within an hour they levelled the ditch, broke through the outer wall, and violently brought the siege-tower against the city wall. The citizens, as stated above, had hung from the wall beams of great length and great strength to blunt the blows of the engines. Two of these beams were cut loose from the ropes by which they were fastened and thrown to the ground by our men in the siege-tower. Those below received them at great risk and carried them beneath the engine. At last they placed them under the bridge which, as will immediately be said, they raised from the siege-tower onto the wall, to give it greater strength. For the bridge was woven from frail timber and could not have supported the people crossing it without this supporting reinforcement [Col. 0425D].

### Chapter XVII. In the Southern Quarter the Count of Toulouse and His Men Assault the City No Less Fiercely.

Meanwhile, while these things were being pursued with such zeal in the northern quarter, the Count of Toulouse and those with him in the southern quarter attacked the city with all possible urgency and with the same ardent zeal. Having filled the ditch, at which task they had laboured continuously for three days, they brought their siege-tower forward with a strong hand beside the wall, so that those in the towers and those in the engine could almost wound one another with lances.

The zeal of the people on both sides was equal, and their persistence not dissimilar. They applied themselves to the work all the more diligently because this was the day on which a certain servant of Christ, living on the Mount of Olives, had confidently promised that the city would be taken [Col. 0426A]. Moreover, the sign of the waving shield which they too had seen from the same Mount of Olives had greatly inflamed them and made them more confident of winning victory.

The undertaking of the two armies seemed to advance at an equal pace, as though it were carried forward with equal diligence by the same author, who had determined to reward the devotion of his servants with fitting recompense. For it was time that they should receive the fruit of so great a labour and the wages of service faithfully rendered.

### Chapter XVIII. The Duke and Those with Him Lower a Bridge onto the Wall from the Wooden Tower; They Send Their Men In. The City Is Taken, the Gate Is Opened, and Our Army Is Admitted.

[Col. 0426B]

The forces of the duke and counts, therefore, which, as we have said, were attacking the city in the northern quarter, had progressed so far with the Lord’s help that, the enemy being wearied and no longer able to resist, the outer fortifications having been broken down and the ditch entirely filled, they could approach the wall without danger; for their opponents rarely dared to inflict any injury on them through the barriers.

Those in the siege-tower, at the duke’s exhortation, had set fire to a cotton-filled mattress and to sacks full of straw. The north wind fanned the fire and drove dark smoke into the city. Under this more violent pressure, those assigned to defend the wall, unable to open their mouths or eyes, stupefied and confused by the choking gulf of smoky darkness, abandoned the guarding of the wall [Col. 0426C].

When the duke learned this, he ordered with all speed that the beams which had been captured from the enemy be carried upward. Placed at one end in the engine and at the other upon the wall, they supported the movable side of the siege-tower when he ordered it lowered. Thus, laid over the aforesaid beams, it served as a bridge, resting upon suitably strong support. What the enemy had supplied for themselves was therefore turned to their injury.

When the bridge had thus been arranged, the renowned and illustrious Duke Godfrey entered the city first of all with his brother Eustace, urging the others to follow. Ludolf and Gislebert followed at once [Col. 0426D], brothers by the same mother, noble men worthy of everlasting remembrance, born in the city of Tournai; after them came an innumerable multitude of cavalry and infantry, so that neither the engine nor the aforesaid bridge could support any more.

Seeing that our men had now occupied the wall and that the duke had introduced his army, the enemy abandoned the towers and ramparts and withdrew into the narrow streets. Our men saw that the duke and the greater part of the nobles had taken possession of the towers. Therefore, no longer waiting to ascend by the engine, they eagerly set ladders against the wall, of which they had a very great supply. For by public order, each pair of knights had prepared one ladder for themselves. Climbing up them with one accord, they awaited the duke’s command and joined the others who were on the wall.

Immediately after the duke entered the Count of Flanders and the Duke of Normandy; the valiant and in every respect commendable Lord Tancred; Hugh the Elder, Count of Saint-Pol; Baldwin of Bourg; Gaston of Béart; Gastus of Beders; Gerard of Roussillon; Thomas of Feria; Conan the Breton; Count Raimbald of the city of Orange; Louis of Monzón; Conon of Montaigu and his son Lambert; and many others whose number and names we do not have [Col. 0427A].

When the duke knew that all these had been received safely inside the city, he sent some of them with a suitable escort to the northern gate, now called the Gate of St Stephen, to open it and admit the people waiting outside. The gate having been opened with all speed, the entire army entered everywhere and without distinction [Col. 0427B].

It was Friday, at the ninth hour. It seems to have been divinely arranged that, on the day and at the hour at which the Lord had suffered in the same city for the salvation of the world, the faithful people fighting for the Saviour’s glory should likewise obtain the happy fulfilment of their desire. For it is said that on that same day the first human being was created and the second was delivered to death for the salvation of the first. Thus it was fitting that his members and imitators should triumph over his enemies in his name.

### Chapter XIX. The Duke and His Men Range Through the City and Inflict Innumerable Slaughter. The Count of Toulouse Enters by Force from the South and Brings in His Forces. Some of the Citizens Withdraw to the City’s Stronghold.

[Col. 0427C]

The duke and those with him ran through the streets and squares of the city in close formation, with drawn swords, covered by shields and helmets, and struck down indiscriminately by the sword’s edge as many enemies as they could find, sparing neither age nor condition. Everywhere the slaughtered lay in such abundance, and the heaps of severed heads were so great, that no one could find a way or passage except over the corpses of the dead.

Our leaders had already reached almost the middle of the city by different routes, inflicting innumerable slaughter; an endless multitude followed them, thirsting for the blood of the unbelievers and wholly bent upon killing [Col. 0427D]. Meanwhile the Count of Toulouse and the other leaders with him, still fighting about Mount Zion, did not know that the city had been captured or that our men had won victory. But when they were alerted by the great shouting and dreadful noise caused by our entry and the slaughter of the citizens, the citizens resisting in that quarter wondered what the unusual cry and tumultuous shouting of the people could mean. They learned that the city had been forcibly breached and that our forces had entered; therefore, abandoning the towers and wall, they fled in different directions and strove to secure their own safety.

Since the city’s citadel lay nearby, most of them withdrew into the fortress. The army, however, freely and without difficulty laid a bridge across the wall and applied ladders to the ramparts [Col. 0428A], eagerly entering the city without opposition. Once inside, they immediately opened the southern gate, which was adjacent to them, so that the rest of the people might be admitted without difficulty.

Then the distinguished and valiant Count of Toulouse entered, as did Count Isoard of Die, Raymond Pelet, William of Sabran, the bishop of Albara, and many other nobles whose number and names no history has handed down to us. All these, armed to the teeth and joined in companies, ranged through the middle of the city and inflicted dreadful slaughter. Those who had escaped the duke and his men, thinking that by fleeing to other quarters they could avoid death somehow, encountered these men and perished more dangerously; escaping Scylla, they fell into Charybdis [Col. 0428B]. So great was the slaughter of the enemy throughout the city, and so great the shedding of blood, that it could produce weariness and horror even in the victors.

### Chapter XX. The Citizens Retreat into the Temple Precinct. Tancred Pursues Them There. Innumerable Slaughter Takes Place, and Boundless Blood Is Shed There.

The greater part of the people had fled into the court of the Temple, since the place seemed more secluded within the city and was especially strongly fortified by wall, towers, and stronger gates. Yet such flight brought them no safety. For Lord Tancred immediately went there with a very large part of the entire army and forcibly entered the Temple [Col. 0428C]. After an innumerable slaughter, he is said to have carried away from it limitless quantities of gold, silver, and gems; yet afterward, when the tumult had subsided, he is believed to have restored them intact.

The remaining leaders, after killing those whom they had encountered in the other parts of the city, heard that the fleeing people had gathered within the Temple enclosure. They went down there together and, having sent in a multitude of cavalry and infantry, cut down with swords everyone they found there, sparing no one and filling all places with blood. By the just judgment of God, it is certain that this happened so that those who had defiled the Lord’s sanctuary with superstitious rites and made it alien to the faithful peoples might pay for this offence by the loss of their own blood and expiate their sacrilegious crime through death [Col. 0428D].

It was horrible, indeed, to behold the multitude of the slain, to see fragments of human limbs scattered everywhere, and the entire surface overflowing with splashes of shed blood. It was distressing to observers not only to see the bodies of the dead mutilated, torn apart in their principal limbs, and with heads cut off; but it was also terrible to behold the victors themselves, drenched in blood from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, and they struck those who met them with a certain horror.

It is said that as many as ten thousand of the enemy fell within the Temple precinct alone, apart from those slain throughout the city, who filled the streets and squares and were said to be no fewer in number. The remaining part of the army ranged through the city, dragging into public view like cattle the wretched people hiding in alleyways and side-streets [Col. 0429A] and wishing to escape the danger of death, and cutting them to pieces.

Others, divided into bands, entered houses; having seized the head of the household together with wives, children, and the entire household, they either pierced them with swords or hurled them headlong from high places to the ground, so that they died with broken necks. Whatever house each person had broken into, he claimed for himself, together with all its property, by perpetual right. For before the city was taken, they had agreed among themselves that, if the city were carried by assault, whatever each person acquired should be possessed by him forever, as property, without challenge.

Thus, more carefully searching the city and more violently pursuing the slaughter of the citizens, they broke into the city’s byways [Col. 0429B], recesses, and more hidden inner rooms. They fixed shields or any kind of weapon at an entrance as a sign to those approaching not to enter there, but to pass the place by, as though it had already been occupied by others.

### Chapter XXI. When the City Has Been Put in Order, the Tumult Is Calmed; Having Laid Aside Their Arms, They Visit the Holy Places in Prayer and Observe a Solemn Day.

Subsequently, after the city had been utterly subdued and its citizens slain, when the tumult had somewhat abated, the princes met together before laying aside their arms. They arranged that guards should be assigned to each tower for greater security, and that reputable men should be stationed as gatekeepers at every city gate, until, by common agreement and public decree of the princes, someone should be set over the city to care for it and administer all things at his own free discretion. For they reasonably suspected the plots of the surrounding enemies and prudently feared sudden attacks.

[Col. 0429C]

At length, when the city had thus been put in order, they laid down their arms and, in a spirit of humility and with hearts truly contrite, barefoot, with washed hands and cleaner garments put on, began with groaning and tears to visit with every devotion, and to kiss with heartfelt sighs, the venerable places which the Saviour had chosen to adorn and sanctify by his own presence. Especially they visited the church of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection [Col. 0429D], where clergy and the body of the faithful—who for so many years had borne the all too harsh and undeserved yoke of servitude—met the princes with crosses and the patronage of the saints, rendering thanks to the Redeemer for their restored freedom, and led them into the aforesaid church with hymns and spiritual songs.

It was most delightful to behold, and full of spiritual joy, with what devotion and what fervour of pious longing the faithful people approached the holy places; with what exultation of mind and spiritual gladness they kissed the memorial of the Lord’s saving dispensation. Everywhere were tears; everywhere sighs—not such as grief and anxiety are wont to force out, but such as fervent devotion and the perfected joy of the inward person are wont to offer up to the Lord as a burnt offering.

[Col. 0430A] In the church and throughout the entire city there was such a cry of people giving thanks to the Lord that the sound seemed almost to rise to the stars; and it might deservedly have been said of them: “The voice of joy and exultation is in the tents of the righteous” (Psalm 117 [118]:15).

Works of mercy, kindled by pious longing, indeed flourished throughout the city. Some confessed to the Lord the sins which they had committed and ought to lament, binding themselves by vow not thereafter to commit deeds requiring lamentation. Others lavishly distributed all their substance among the aged, infirm, and needy, considering it the greatest and sufficient wealth that they had been divinely granted to see this day. Others, with knees bent and bare, with sobs and heartfelt sighs, visited the venerable places [Col. 0430B], filling all things with the sprinkling of their tears; of these the saying was truly directed to the Lord: “Streams of waters have flowed from my eyes” (Psalm 118 [119]:136).

Why say more? It is difficult for our speech to comprehend how boundless was the holy devotion among the faithful people. Eager to surpass one another, they strove with one accord in works of piety, mindful of the heavenly benefit and keeping before their eyes the divine grace which had deigned to reward their immense labours. For who was so iron-hearted, who of mind so adamantine, that his inward parts would not melt when he was permitted to gather the most worthy fruit of so great a pilgrimage and count the wages of the service he had rendered?

Yet those whose minds were more exalted saw this gift as the pledge of the future recompense which the Lord promised to give his saints [Col. 0430C]: through the bestowal of present gifts, the expectation of future ones might be made firm; and through the Jerusalem that is a pilgrim here, they might arrive at that Jerusalem “whose participation is in the same” (Psalm 121 [122]:3). Meanwhile bishops and priests, performing the sacred offices in the churches, offered sacrifices and prayed for the people, giving thanks for the benefit bestowed.

## Chapter XXII. The bishop of Le Puy, and certain others who had fallen asleep on the journey, were seen in the city and appeared to many.

On that day Lord Adhemar, a man of virtues and immortal memory, bishop of Le Puy, who, as we have said, had died at Antioch [Col. 0430D], was seen in the holy city by many. Many venerable and trustworthy men steadfastly affirmed that with their bodily eyes they had seen him first of all ascending the city wall and encouraging the others to enter; and afterward, on that same day, he visibly appeared to very many as they visited the venerable places.

Moreover, many others who throughout the whole journey had devoted themselves to divine service and had received a pious falling asleep in Christ appeared to many in that city, entering the holy places with the others. From this it was plainly understood that, although they had departed this temporal life, having been called to eternal blessedness, they had not been defrauded of their desire. Rather, what they had sought with pious zeal they attained in full effect [Col. 0431A], presenting to us a great proof of the future resurrection.

And it was fitting that, just as at the Lord’s resurrection many bodies of saints who had fallen asleep arose and appeared to many in the holy city, so, while faithful peoples were cleansing the place of the holy Resurrection from heathen superstition, the ancient miracle should be renewed: that those who had devoted themselves to such pious service of the risen Lord might themselves be believed to have risen in spirit.

Since these and similar things were granted to God’s people in the holy city through an overflowing heavenly grace, miraculously rather than merely marvellously, there was such gladness of mind and inward exultation of heart among the people that, forgetting the countless hardships they had endured, they called themselves happy to whom it had been granted to behold this divine gift. [Col. 0431B] The city exulting spiritually raised its cry to the Lord, and—as though by the Lord’s command—a celebrated solemnity was observed. Thus the prophet’s oracle seemed fulfilled literally: “Rejoice with Jerusalem, and exult in her, all you who love her” (Isaiah 66:10).

## Chapter XXIII. The faithful men living in the city render immense thanks to Peter the Hermit, to whom they had entrusted their embassy, and honour him as was due.

Finally, the faithful who had seen the venerable man Peter the Hermit in that same city four or five years earlier, and to whom both the lord patriarch and other leading men, of clergy and people alike, had entrusted their letters for stirring up the princes of the western kingdoms [Col. 0431C], recognized him again. With bent knees and all humility they reverenced him, recalling his earlier arrival and the favour of acquaintance which he had deigned to establish with them. They gave thanks because, solely out of pious concern, he had pursued their embassy so diligently and faithfully; and above all they praised the Lord, who is glorious in his servants, because, beyond human expectation, he had directed this man’s paths and made his word effective in his hand, so that he turned nations and kingdoms without difficulty to endure such great labours for Christ’s name.

Truly this saying seemed to have proceeded from the Lord who says: “The word which shall go forth from my mouth shall not return to me empty, but shall prosper in all things for which I send it” (Isaiah 55:11). Therefore, individually and collectively, they strove to anticipate him with manifold honour, attributing to him alone after the Lord the fact that the condition of harsh servitude which they had endured for so many years had been dissolved and that the holy city had been restored to its former freedom.

The lord patriarch, as stated above, had sailed to Cyprus for the security of the commonwealth and the salvation of the citizens, seeking alms from the faithful of that region [Col. 0431D], from which he might pay the tributes and extraordinary taxes imposed beyond their means, lest the tax collectors, through lack of payment, destroy the churches or consign the people to the sword, as they had been accustomed to do in former times. For he knew absolutely nothing of all that was happening about the city and feared that he was about to return to his customary dangers; but meanwhile the Lord had, beyond hope, procured tranquil peace for him.

## Chapter XXIV. The city is cleansed of the corpses of the slain. Those who had withdrawn into the citadel surrender to the count of Toulouse. That day is appointed to be celebrated forever.

When the prayers had been completed and the venerable places visited with every devotion, the princes judged it expedient to cleanse the city—and above all the precinct of the Temple—lest the corpses of the slain generate a pestilential corruption of the air. Therefore this task was imposed upon citizens who had escaped death by chance, bound in fetters [Col. 0432B]. But because they did not seem able to suffice for so great a burden, a daily wage was also offered to the poor among the army, that they should attend to this work and clear the city without delay.

When this had been arranged, the princes returned to their respective quarters and used as lodgings whatever houses their households, moving about, had meanwhile prepared. Finding the city full of provisions and abounding in every good, all from greatest to least began to enjoy fuller abundance. For in the broken-open houses were found immense stores of gold and silver, gems and costly clothing, wheat, wine, oil, and also water, the scarcity of which they had suffered during the siege. Thus those who had claimed houses for themselves could have enough for every need [Col. 0432C] and charitably supply their needy brethren.

It came about that on the second and third days and thereafter the best possible trading terms for saleable goods were offered in the public market, so that even the lower populace abounded in every necessity. Accordingly, observing festive days and days of rejoicing, indulging their bodies with food and rest—which they especially needed—they were somewhat refreshed, admiring the abundance of God’s gift and keeping perpetually before their eyes the memory of the heavenly grace with which the Lord had deigned to abound toward them.

For a fuller memorial of so great an event, it was decreed by common resolution, and received and approved by the common vow of all, that this day should forever be observed by all as solemn, and more celebrated among celebrated days. On it, to the praise and glory of the Christian name, whatever had been foretold in the prophets concerning this event as though by prophecy should be rehearsed; and intercession should be made to the Lord for the souls of those through whose praiseworthy and welcome labour that city, beloved by God, had been restored to Christian faith and its former liberty.

Meanwhile, the portion of the enemy that had fled before the sword and taken refuge in the citadel of David, seeing that our people had claimed the whole city and that they could not endure the siege longer, sought and obtained from the lord count of Toulouse—who had lodged nearer that tower—that they might have free departure with their wives, children, and all the property which they had brought in with them [Col. 0433A], together with safe escort as far as Ascalon. They surrendered the citadel to him.

Those charged with cleansing the city worked diligently and ardently; some corpses they consumed by fire, others they committed to burial, as the shortage of time permitted. Suddenly, within a few days, they made the city clear, restoring it to its customary cleanliness. Hence the people could more confidently frequent the thresholds of the venerable places and could gather and converse more freely in the streets and squares of the city.

The aforesaid city was taken in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1099, in the month of July, on the fifteenth day of the month, Friday, about the ninth hour of the day; in the third year since the faithful people had taken upon themselves the burden of so great a pilgrimage. Pope Urban II presided over the Holy Roman Church; Henry IV administered the Roman Empire; Philip reigned in France; and Alexius held the sceptre among the Greeks. By the mercy of the Lord, to whom be honour and glory through ages without end. Amen.

# Here Begins the Ninth Book

[Col. 0433]

## Chapter I. On the eighth day after the capture of the city, the princes meet to elect one of their number to govern the city and region; the clergy indiscriminately strive to oppose it.

[Col. 0433B]

After the holy city had been restored to the Christian people by the Lord’s overflowing grace, and affairs had been brought to some degree of tranquillity, seven days having passed in great joy, yet in the fear of the Lord and spiritual gladness, the princes met on the eighth day. Having invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit, they were to deliberate upon choosing someone from their own body to rule the region and exercise royal care over the province.

While they were engaged in this, certain clergy assembled, swollen with the spirit of pride, seeking their own interests rather than those of Christ Jesus. They said [Col. 0433C] that they had more secret words which they wished to convey to the princes sitting within the council chamber. Admitted, they said:

“It has been reported to the clergy that you have met in order to choose one of yourselves as king. Your purpose seems to us holy, useful, and deserving to be carried out with every care—provided, however, that it be approached in the proper order. Spiritual matters are certainly worthier than temporal matters, and those things which are worthier should rightly come first. Therefore, unless a perverse order is deliberately sought, it seems to us that a person pleasing to God and religious, who knows how to preside over and benefit the Church of God, should first be chosen before proceeding to the election of secular authority. If you wish to proceed in this order, it pleases us greatly; we are with you in body and spirit. But if otherwise, we judge invalid and decree devoid of force whatever you arrange without our concurrence.”

Although this demand on the surface seemed to possess some appearance of propriety, inwardly it contained great malice, as the following will show. The leader of this faction was a certain bishop from Calabria, namely the bishop of Martirano, who was joined in excessive intimacy with one Arnulf, concerning whom enough has been said above. He was striving to install this Arnulf in the patriarchal see, although Arnulf was in minor orders, the son of a priest, and marked by excessive incontinence—so much so that during the expedition he presented himself as a singer to the people and supplied material for foolish and lewd men singing in chorus [Col. 0434B]—contrary to the sacred canons and against the will of all honourable men.

For he was a man of perverse mind, setting honesty at nothing; and therefore he could readily agree with the aforesaid Arnulf, according to the saying: “Each person delights in the company of those like himself.” For, as the old proverb has it, like readily join with like. This same man had seized the church of Bethlehem, having made an agreement with Arnulf that, if through his support Arnulf were promoted to patriarch, he himself might perpetually possess the said church without dispute or hindrance. But approaching death forestalled all these schemes of his, as will be related below.

Indeed the clergy’s vigour of religion and honesty had failed, and, without restraint or discrimination, they flowed everywhere into unlawful things after Lord Adhemar, bishop of Le Puy, of pious memory in the Lord and legate of the Apostolic See, had passed away. Yet Lord William, bishop of Orange, a religious man who feared God, took up the same care after the passing of that blessed man and administered it faithfully as long as he lived; but after a short time he rested in the Lord at Maʿarrat al-Nuʿmān. When these men had died, it came about as the prophet says: “Like people, like priest” (Hosea 4:9), excepting the lord bishop of Albara and a few others who had the fear of the Lord before their eyes.

## Chapter II. The princes disregard the clergy’s opposition, elect the lord duke, and present the elected man at the Lord’s tomb with hymns and songs.

[Col. 0434D]

The princes, however, considered the aforesaid words light and frivolous. Persisting in the work they had begun, they nevertheless continued their deliberation. Some relate that, so that they might proceed in the election more according to God and according to the merits of the persons, they separately took certain members of the households of each of the great princes and compelled them to take an oath, so that when questioned concerning the character and conduct of their lords, they would tell the truth without admixture of falsehood. This was done so that the electors might thus be more fully and faithfully informed of the merits of those to be chosen.

Afterward, questioned more carefully by the electors under the obligation of the oath they had taken, they were compelled to confess privately many faults of their lords and nevertheless enumerate their virtues, so that by plain and open judgement it might be established what each candidate was like. Among them, when the household members of the lord duke were questioned, they replied that, in all the lord duke’s conduct, what seemed most strange to his household was that, once he had entered a church, even after the divine service had been completed, he could not be separated from it. Rather, he demanded from priests and those who seemed to have some knowledge of such things an explanation of every image and painting [Col. 0435B]. Thus, while his companions had other desires, this became a source of weariness and disgust to them; and meals prepared at a fixed and suitable time were taken too late, after long and most unwelcome waiting, and therefore less seasonably and more tastelessly.

Hearing this, those holding the office of electors called blessed the man in whom these things were found, and whose supposed fault another would count as a virtue. Finally, agreeing with one another after many stages of deliberation, they unanimously elected the lord duke and most devoutly presented the elected man at the Lord’s tomb with hymns and songs.

It is said, however, that the greater part of the nobles agreed upon Lord Raymond, count of Toulouse [Col. 0435C]. But, understanding that unless he obtained the kingdom he would immediately return home, drawn by the sweetness of his native soil, they invented many charges against the lord count, even against their consciences, in order that he might be regarded as unworthy. Yet he, nevertheless despising his homeland and following Christ with the greatest devotion, did not turn back; but, stretching forward, he pursued to the end the pilgrimage which he had once undertaken and voluntary poverty, knowing that “he who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matthew 24:13), and: “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62).

## Chapter III. The duke, having been promoted, demands from the count of Toulouse the Tower of David which he had received from the enemy; the princes disagree, but at length he obtains the tower he sought.

[Col. 0435D]

When the lord duke had, by common vote and the unanimous concurrence of all, attained the summit of royal power, the count of Saint-Gilles held the city’s stronghold, namely the citadel of David, which, as we have previously related, the enemy had surrendered to him at the beginning. It was situated in the higher part of the city toward the west and built of enormous squared stones, from which one could look over the entire city below.

Seeing that this, as the city’s final refuge, was lacking to him, and judging his supremacy incomplete without it, the duke began to demand it from the lord count before the assembly of the princes. The count alleged that, because it had been surrendered to him by the enemy, he wished to retain it until Easter, when he intended to cross over and return home, so that meanwhile he and his men could remain in the kingdom more honourably.

But the duke said that unless he had the tower, he wished to abandon everything; he maintained that it was altogether dishonourable that, when he had been appointed lord, another should hold the city’s stronghold and thus appear almost his equal or superior. The count of Normandy and the count of Flanders supported the lord duke’s side. Those who supported the lord count of Saint-Gilles were also his household men, aiding the opposing side so as to furnish their lord, at least by this means, an opportunity to depart.

It came about that, until it should be decided by law to whom the tower ought to yield, the count placed it by common counsel in the hands of the lord bishop of Albara, as in sequestration [Col. 0436B]. But, without awaiting judgement, the bishop is said to have handed it over to the lord duke before the case was formally joined. When some later charged him with this, he publicly asserted that force had been used against him.

Therefore the lord count, greatly embittered and full of indignation because he had lost the tower so ignominiously, as it seemed to him, and because the other princes—insufficiently mindful of the benefits he had often conferred upon them on the journey—behaved less than amicably toward him, went down to the Jordan and washed in its waters. He then prepared to return home, satisfying the wishes of his own men.

## Chapter IV. The bishop of Martirano, a crafty and wicked man, strives to promote one Arnulf, his like, to the patriarchate, but does not succeed. The Lord’s Cross is found.

[Col. 0436C]

Meanwhile the aforesaid bishop of Martirano, a crafty and wicked man, did not cease to stir up the uneducated populace against the pious princes and to spread among the people the claim that the princes, from envy and so that they might more freely trample the Church without a shepherd, did not wish to provide for it. Taking with him accomplices of the same faction, he elected the aforesaid Arnulf, despite the opposition of others; and, relying on the support of the count of Normandy—whose intimate companion and table-fellow he was and had been throughout the expedition—he enthroned Arnulf in the patriarchal see, while the foolish populace dutifully offered its votes.

But neither long rejoiced in his devices [Col. 0436D]. Arnulf was forced to lay aside the dignity rashly assumed, and the shameless advocate of his disgrace soon gathered the fruits of his ways.

At the same time, in a separate part of the church of the Holy Resurrection, a portion of the Lord’s Cross was found. Long before, the faithful, suffering under the yoke of the gentiles and admitting only a few persons into the secret, had hidden it for greater security because of fear of the gentiles. Through the care and labour of a certain Syrian man who knew of this precious deposit, it was found and enclosed in a silver reliquary. They bore it first to the Lord’s tomb and then to the Temple of the Lord with hymns and spiritual songs, while all clergy and people followed it. All alike received it as a consolation sent from heaven, judging that they had received a reward worthy of their labours and hardships [Col. 0437A].

## Chapter V. The identity, origin, and ancestry of Duke Godfrey are set forth.

Therefore, once the aforesaid lord duke had been established by God’s grace at the summit of the kingdom, and all scandals which had arisen had been cut off, the kingdom began to grow strong and be confirmed in his days. He reigned for one year. Human sins required it, lest the new planting of the kingdom should be refreshed by the longer consolation of so great a prince and receive comfort against the troubles pressing upon it.

He was taken from the midst, lest wickedness should alter his heart, as it is written: “Men of mercy are gathered, and there is none who considers it” (Isaiah 57:1). He was born in the kingdom of the Franks, in the province of Rheims, in the city of Boulogne situated beside the English sea, drawing his origin from illustrious and religious forebears.

His father was Lord Eustace the Elder, illustrious and magnificent count of that same region, whose deeds were many and memorable. Even now, among the elders of neighbouring regions, his memory is blessed and preserved in pious recollection as that of a religious man who feared God. His mother was Ida, a distinguished woman and, among the noble matrons of the West, eminent both for excellence of character and for nobility of birth: sister of the eminent duke of Lorraine, Godfrey, surnamed “the Hunchback” (*Struma*). Since he afterward had no children [Col. 0437C], he adopted as his son his namesake nephew and made him heir to all his inheritance; when that duke died, the nephew succeeded him in the same duchy.

Godfrey had three brothers by both parents, to whom excellence of character and distinction in virtues rightly showed them to be brothers of so great a prince: namely Lord Baldwin, count of Edessa, who later succeeded him in the kingdom; Lord Eustace, count of Boulogne, named after his father, who succeeded to the paternal possessions and held the county after his father; and Lord William, an illustrious man, in no way inferior to the honour and prowess of his father and brothers.

The daughter of Eustace, Matilda by name, was married by the illustrious and magnificent king of the English, Stephen. Eustace himself, though summoned by the eastern princes to succeed in the kingdom after his brother Lord Baldwin died without children, refused to come, fearing that his accession could not be celebrated without scandal [Col. 0437D]. The first two followed their lord and brother on the expedition; the third remained at home.

As he was firstborn according to the flesh, so also in the inward person he bore the pre-eminence of character, and the birthright rightly belonged to him. Lord Godfrey was a religious man, gentle, devout, fearing God, just, turning away from every evil, serious and steadfast in speech; despising worldly vanities—which was rare in that age, especially in the military profession; constant in prayer, assiduous in works of piety, remarkable for generosity, gracious in affability, mild and merciful; praiseworthy and pleasing to God in all his conduct.

He was tall of body, so that he was considered shorter than the tallest and taller than men of medium height; of unmatched strength, with very solid limbs, a manly chest, a handsome face, and moderately fair hair and beard. In the use of arms and military exercise, by the judgement of all, he was almost without equal [Col. 0438A].

## Chapter VI. His mother’s prediction concerning the future standing of her sons.

The mother of these great princes, a holy, religious woman pleasing to God, while they were still of tender age, being filled with the divine spirit, foresaw their future conditions and uttered, as though by an oracle, the rank prepared for them in adulthood. Once, as little boys are accustomed to do, they were playing together about their mother; becoming tired, they repeatedly returned to their mother’s lap. It happened that, while they were hidden beneath her cloak, their father, the venerable count Eustace, entered.

As they jostled one another, moving their feet and hands while covered by the cloak their mother wore, the count asked what it was that moved so frequently there. She is said to have answered: “Three great princes, of whom the first will be duke, the second king, and the third count.” Divine mercy afterward fulfilled this by its gracious dispensation, and the event that followed showed that the mother had spoken truly.

For first, Lord Godfrey, as has been said, succeeded his deceased uncle and received his duchy; afterward he also attained the kingdom of Jerusalem [Col. 0438C] by the election of all the princes. The second in age, Lord Baldwin, succeeded him in that kingdom. The third, Lord Eustace, succeeded to all his father’s estate upon his father’s death and obtained their ancestral inheritance, as has been said.

We deliberately pass over the tale of the Swan, although the account of very many affirms it to be true, from which it is commonly said that they were of swan descent; for such an assertion seems to depart from the truth. Leaving these things aside, let us return to continue what we had begun concerning the lord duke. Among his other deeds, which he performed excellently in his accustomed manner, something memorable is said to have happened which we have judged worthy to insert in this account.

## Chapter VII. A memorable deed of his is recounted in a certain judicial duel.

[Col. 0438D]

In a certain single combat, which he entered most unwillingly but could not decline, according to the custom of the region, without impairing his reputation, there stands a deed of his worthy of remembrance and of this narrative. This distinguished man had a dispute in the court of the lord emperor with a certain noble and powerful man—one of the princes and said to have been his kinsman—over certain very great estates and widely spread property. A day was appointed for each party to make trial of the matter, and when it arrived, both defendant and plaintiff appeared in court.

[Col. 0439A] When the suit had been formally joined, the aforesaid nobleman advanced the claim in vindication of the property, while the duke resisted as best he could. In accordance with the laws of the land, a judicial duel and single combat were adjudged between them. The leading princes of the empire exerted their utmost efforts to prevent such distinguished men from giving the people an unworthy spectacle of themselves and submitting to so great a peril, in which the honour of either might be endangered; but they made no progress.

The imperial sentence was put into execution. With the crowd standing in a ring and the princes positioned around them according to custom, they entered the place appointed for the coming contest, to test uncertain Mars. While these illustrious and magnificent men fought there most vigorously and bravely, it happened by chance that, when the duke struck a blow against his opponent’s shield, his sword broke, so that scarcely a piece of half a foot’s length remained in his hand above the hilt [Col. 0439B].

Seeing that the duke’s situation had become much worse, the princes present declared a truce, approached the emperor, and by supplication obtained permission to negotiate a settlement between such eminent princes. While they were carefully negotiating between the two and urging what made for peace, the duke rejected them altogether; persisting irrevocably, he resumed the contest and returned to the same matter.

His adversary, seeming almost superior because his sword was intact, pressed more violently and gave the duke no rest. Then the duke, resorting to his accustomed strength, in which he was singularly pre-eminent, and inflamed with anger, rushed upon him. With the hilt which he held in his hand, he struck his opponent with such force about the left temple that he cast him down upon the ground as if half-dead, so that he seemed almost wholly deprived of life.

The duke then threw away the fragment of his own sword, took in hand the sword of his fallen enemy, summoned the princes who had earlier approached him concerning a settlement [Col. 0439C], and earnestly asked and urged them, while negotiating peace, to rescue the distinguished man who had now succumbed from so ignominious a death. Marvelling at the duke’s outstanding valour and incomparable mercy, they obtained peace and ended the controversy with so honourable a conclusion that the duke was nevertheless regarded by all as victor and worthy of immortal glory.

## Chapter VIII. The distinguished deed of the same man in Emperor Henry’s victory over Rudolph, the pseudo-king of the Saxons.

That deed also, of no lesser glory, is frequently remembered among men; and we have judged it worthy of insertion in the present account. The Saxon people, the fiercest among the German nations, refusing to bear the yoke of the Roman Empire and wishing to range more freely, having cast off the rule of discipline, had revolted from the lord emperor Henry. So obstinate were they in their insolence that, in opposition to the aforesaid Augustus, they set up for themselves as king a certain count, Ralph by name, a nobleman of their own people.

Moved by this injury, the emperor summoned to his presence all the princes of the empire. When they stood before him, he laid before them the outrage, which was known to all, and invited them to vengeance. They, emulous for the empire’s glory and deeply aggrieved by the Saxons’ monstrous crime, eagerly offered themselves; they pledged their strength, declared that so great an injury against the Roman Empire must not be ignored, but that so heinous an offence must be punished with death; and decreed that the crime of violated majesty should be struck by the avenging sword.

Accordingly, at the appointed place and on the fixed day, by agreement and at the lord emperor’s command, countless thousands gathered, drawn from every region of the empire—ecclesiastical princes as well as others—to invade the Saxon country by force and exact vengeance for such great injuries. [Col. 0440A]

When the day of battle approached and, their legions drawn up, each army stood ready for combat, the emperor summoned the princes and asked to whom he might safely entrust the imperial standard and appoint as commander-in-chief of so great armies. By common counsel they answered that the lord Godfrey, duke of Lorraine, was before all others fit and sufficient for such a burden. Therefore, as one chosen by so many thousands and, in the judgment of all, pre-eminent beyond others, he entrusted him with the eagle, though he was greatly unwilling and resistant.

It happened on that day that, while the armies clashed on either side and pressed one another most fiercely with swords, the duke, bearing the eagle before the emperor, advanced toward the battle-line commanded by the false king Ralph. The emperor directed the line under his command there. Reaching it, and breaking and scattering the king’s line, the duke, in the emperor’s presence and before certain princes, drove the standard which he carried through the king’s vital breast; piercing him through, he cast him lifeless to the ground, then raised again the imperial standard, though stained with blood. [Col. 0440B–C]

When the Saxons saw that their king had fallen, they too gave way, surrendering themselves to the lord emperor. After satisfaction proportionate to their offence had been imposed, and after fortresses and hostages had been received—by whose intervention they bound themselves never again to attempt anything similar—they were restored to favour.

We have inserted these matters in order that it may be made known how great was, among the greatest princes of the earth, this illustrious man of whom we speak. For no one can doubt that it is a very great thing to be designated, in the judgment of all, the best among so many princes, who are said to have had no equals in the world; especially since he confirmed their judgment by so distinguished a deed and, through the present proof, showed what they truly thought of him. [Col. 0440D]

There were also many other splendid and admirable deeds of this illustrious man, which even to the present are recounted by all as celebrated history. Among other things, when he had already resolved to undertake the pilgrimage, he granted to the church of Liège, by pious liberality, to possess in perpetual alms the castle from which he derived his surname—namely Bouillon—renowned and most famous for its lands, situation, fortifications, conveniences, and broad territory extending far and wide. [Col. 0441A] But we, who have undertaken to describe only what he did in our region, return to our subject.

## CHAPTER IX. How abundantly he exercised pious liberality toward the churches at Jerusalem; and how, out of humility, he refused to be adorned with the royal diadem.

After he had obtained the kingdom, and after only a few days had passed, being a religious man, he began to offer to the Lord the first fruits of his concern in those matters pertaining to the adornment of God’s house. For he immediately established canons in the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre and in the Temple of the Lord; and assigned to them ample benefices, which they call prebends, together with suitable dwellings around the aforesaid churches beloved by God. [Col. 0441B] He observed the order and institution maintained by the great and very large churches beyond the mountains, founded by pious princes; and he would have bestowed still more, had death not overtaken him.

This man, beloved by God, had also brought with him when undertaking the pilgrimage monks from well-disciplined cloisters—religious men, distinguished by holy conduct—who throughout the journey performed for him the divine offices in ecclesiastical fashion, by day and by night. Once he had obtained the kingdom, at their request he settled them in the Valley of Jehoshaphat and bestowed upon the place, for their sake, a very extensive estate.

It would take long to enumerate what and how great were the things he granted to the churches of God by his pious liberality. Yet from the text of the privileges granted to the churches it may be gathered how numerous and great were the gifts which this man, full of God, bestowed upon venerable places for the remedy of his soul. [Col. 0441C]

When he had been elevated, he refused, for humility’s sake, to be adorned in the holy city with a golden crown in the manner of kings. He was content with, and showed reverence for, that crown of thorns which the Restorer of the human race bore in that same place, even to the gibbet of the cross, for our salvation. Hence some, in their catalogue of kings, hesitate to count him among them, failing to distinguish merits and attending more to what is outwardly performed in the body than to what a faithful soul pleasing to God deserves. But to us he appears not merely a king, but the best of kings: a light and model for others. For a faithful prince is not to be thought to have despised the rite of consecration and the sacraments of the Church; rather, he humbly rejected worldly pomp, the vanity to which every creature is subject, and a crown destined to perish, so that elsewhere he might obtain one that does not fade. [Col. 0441D]

## CHAPTER X. The Egyptian prince rouses all his military forces and strength against our people and sends them into Syria.

At the same time, when the city had recently been captured and the princes who had devoted it to divine worship had not yet separated from one another, a report arose—and it was indeed true—that the prince of Egypt, the most powerful among the eastern rulers, had summoned military forces from every region subject to his rule and had assembled countless armies. He took it grievously that a barbarian people, having come forth from the uttermost ends of the earth, had entered his kingdom and violently occupied a province subject to his authority. [Col. 0442A]

Calling to him the commander of his army, al-Afdal, who was called by another name Emir, he commanded him to gather all Egypt’s might and every force of the empire, march into Syria, and wipe this presumptuous people from the face of the earth, so that its name might never again be remembered.

This Emir was an Armenian by name,* deriving his origin from Christian parents; but choked by the vastness of his riches, he had apostatized from his Creator, abandoning the faith by which the righteous live. In that same year in which the city, protected by the Lord, was besieged by the faithful people and restored to the Christian faith, he had recovered it for his lord from Turkish power. He had scarcely held it peacefully for eleven months when the Christian army, by the Lord’s favour, delivered it from the yoke of unlawful servitude. [Col. 0442B]

Thus angered that he had so briefly enjoyed his victory, and that the possession acquired for his lord through him seemed—and indeed was—momentary, he gladly undertook the task imposed upon him, hoping more easily to triumph over those who had darkened his fortune. Taking with him the whole army and all the forces which the Egyptian dominion, then at the height of its power, could furnish, he marched into Syria in fierce spirit and intolerable arrogance, resolved to destroy our people so that not even its memory might remain.

But the Lord, “terrible in his counsels over the children of men” (Psalm 65:4), willed otherwise. [Col. 0442C] Coming with splendid cavalry and enormous forces, he encamped before Ascalon. Great forces from all Arabia and the territories of Damascus had joined their expedition. Though the Turks had not previously been on sufficiently good terms with the Egyptians, but had mutually regarded one another’s strength with suspicion and alternately laboured to diminish the other’s rival dominion, nevertheless, out of fear of our people—if not through mutual goodwill—they united in order to devise something for the overthrow of our newly arrived men. They judged it preferable to endure the arrogance of their own rivals and even bear their yoke rather than experience the harsh and exceedingly fierce swords of the barbarians. Thus, the innumerable forces of Egyptians, Arabs, and Turks gathered together and moved their camp into the plain of Ascalon, as we have said, intending to march thence upon Jerusalem. They did not suppose that our army would dare to meet so vast a multitude. [Col. 0442D]

## CHAPTER XI. The duke, on the other hand, after litanies and prayers had been completed at Jerusalem, gathers the princes near Ramla and assembles an expedition.

When this was heard, our princes, bishops, clergy, and all the people gathered together, bearing spiritual arms. Before the Lord’s Sepulchre, with groaning and tears, prostrate in contrite and humbled heart, they prayed that the Lord would mercifully deliver his people from the threatening dangers—his people whom he had hitherto mercifully preserved victorious—and that he who had willed the place of his sanctification to be cleansed would not allow it to be further defiled, for the glory of his name. [Col. 0443A]

Then, barefoot and with hymns and spiritual songs, they approached the Temple of the Lord in the same fervour of devotion. Pouring out their hearts before the Lord, they prayed, saying: “Spare, O Lord, spare thy people, and do not give thine inheritance to the nations for destruction” (Joel 2:17).

When these customary rites had been completed, they received the bishops’ blessing and appointed prudent men to govern and guard the city in the meantime. The duke and the count of Flanders then left the city and descended into the plains of Ramla, leaving the other princes in the city. [Col. 0443B]

The illustrious men Lord Eustace, the duke’s brother, and Lord Tancred had gone, by the duke’s command, at the invitation of the citizens of Naples, that they might receive that city without disturbance. Delayed there both by the place’s abundance and in order to assign it a sufficient guard, they knew nothing of the matters just described. But summoned by the lord duke, they returned without delay and joined the other princes.

The duke and the count of Flanders, arriving at Ramla and learning the facts more fully, were certain that the aforesaid Emir had encamped with his forces before Ascalon. They therefore sent a messenger with all speed, commanding that the remaining princes, who had stayed in the city awaiting definite information, be summoned. [Col. 0443C]

## CHAPTER XII. Battle is joined, and victory is divinely granted to our people, who obtain innumerable riches.

The count of Toulouse and the other princes devoted to God, having learned through the duke’s messenger that the enemy had arrived in such overwhelming numbers and had encamped so near, invoked aid from on high. Gathering such forces as they could have for the time and place, they descended into the plain of Philistia, to the place now called Ibelin, where they had learned that the lord duke was located. They had twelve hundred horsemen and about nine thousand foot soldiers.

After our army had rested there during the day, about the eleventh hour a huge multitude appeared in the plain, seemingly at some distance. Thinking it an enemy army, they sent forward two hundred lightly armed horsemen to inform the rest concerning its condition and numbers, while they themselves prepared for battle. But when those sent forward came closer, they recognized herds of oxen and formations of horses and camels. There were, however, horsemen tending the animals, guarding the herds as shepherds would. [Col. 0443D]

When our army reached them, without awaiting combat both the shepherds and the horsemen placed over them fled, leaving the flocks and herds without a guard. Some were nevertheless captured, and from their report our people learned fully the enemy’s position and intention: the aforesaid prince had pitched camp near them, about seven miles away, intending to come after two days and destroy our army. [Col. 0444A]

Now certain of battle, our men formed nine battle-lines: three they placed in front, three in the centre, and ordered three to follow, so that wherever the enemy might approach them, he would find a triple rank of battle-lines opposed to him. No one could be certain of the enemy’s numbers, for their multitude was boundless and each day some increase came to their strength.

Thus, having gained without opposition a spoil which exceeded all numbering because of its vast multitude, they spent that night there rejoicing, yet after the fashion of prudent men, experienced in military discipline, maintaining unceasing watchfulness and the proper guards about them. [Col. 0444B]

At dawn the battle was proclaimed by herald’s cry. Their ranks drawn up, commending the outcome to the Lord, they hastened unanimously against the enemy, placing their hope of victory in him for whom it is easy to overcome many with few. The Egyptians and those Syrians who had joined them, seeing our men’s attack and irresistible courage, began, with a judgment far different from before, to distrust their strength. They placed less and less confidence in their own numbers, supposing the entire multitude that confronted them to be companies of men.

In truth, as has been said, our men were few; [Col. 0444C] but the spoil mentioned above had, by chance and with no one leading it, attached itself to our legions, so that when our men halted it did not go forward, and when they advanced it continually followed them without a guide. Therefore, believing our numbers boundless and our forces incomparable, the enemy fled without anyone pursuing them, scarcely hoping to find safety even in flight.

On that day, by an unknown chance, the bishop of Marturana—the foment of scandals and author of seditions—was lost; no one knew his end. Yet whatever happened, once removed from human affairs he ceased to appear. It is said, however, that he had been sent by the lord duke to summon the princes who remained in the city and, while returning, was captured and killed by the enemy, or consigned to perpetual imprisonment. [Col. 0444D]

Thus, victory having been granted from on high, our army reached the enemy camp. There it found such an abundance of varied equipment and foreign riches that, sated to the point of nausea, they disdained honey and cakes; and even the poorest and most lowly could say:

> Abundance has made me poor.  
> —Ovid

Thus, while their adversaries fled and the palm of victory was granted to us without labour, both the princes and the entire Christian army returned to Jerusalem with immense thanksgivings, laden with spoils and bringing with them unheard-of booty. They rejoiced and exulted in the Lord, like victors dividing the spoils after the capture of plunder.

## CHAPTER XIII. The princes separate: the Norman and the Fleming return to their homelands; the count of Toulouse returns to Constantinople; Tancred is appointed over the city of Tiberias.

[Col. 0445A]

When these things had thus been accomplished, the princes beloved of God and devoted to him—the lords count of the Normans and count of Flanders—having happily completed the course of the pilgrimage which they had undertaken, prepared to return home.
