Setting out, they came by ship to Constantinople and to the lord emperor Alexius. Treated kindly by him and dismissed with honourable gifts, they returned, through the Lord’s aid, safe and sound to their own country.

One of them, namely the count of the Normans, upon returning home found the state of affairs far changed, contrary to his expectation, from that which he had left when setting out abroad. For while he was serving the Lord on the expedition, his elder brother William, surnamed Rufus, king of the English, died without children. Though the right of succession and the first claim to the kingdom belonged to him by merit, his younger brother Henry persuaded the magnates of the realm that his brother, having been made king at Jerusalem, had no intention of returning; by this deception he obtained the kingdom of England. [Col. 0445B]

When the brother returned, he began urgently to demand the kingdom from Henry, as he could by right. Since Henry wholly refused it, he prepared a fleet, gathered forces, and invaded England by force. There his brother met him with all the strength of that kingdom, ready to fight him. But mediators of peace intervened, and peace was restored between them on the condition that the king should pay his elder brother a fixed sum of money every year as tribute. When this had been done, the duke returned peacefully to his own land.

Later, when the duke demanded from the king certain castles which the king held in Normandy even before he had been raised to kingship, and the king refused to restore them, the duke besieged them in order to seize them by force. Hearing this, the king crossed into Normandy with great forces, fought his brother, captured him, and consigned him to perpetual imprisonment, where he died. The brother thereafter succeeded to all his possessions. [Col. 0445C]

The lord count of Saint-Gilles, returning as far as Laodicea in Syria and leaving his wife there, intending soon to return to her, again travelled to Constantinople with an honourable retinue, to the same lord emperor. There he was magnificently received by the emperor, treated kindly, and sent away with immense gifts and abundant generosity. After two years, as will be related below, he returned safely to Syria, to his wife and household. [Col. 0445D]

The lord duke, retaining with him the illustrious and noble Lord Tancred, Count Garnier of Gres, and certain other nobles, administered wisely and vigorously the kingdom committed to him by the Lord. In his customary liberality he granted and bestowed upon the aforesaid Lord Tancred, to possess by hereditary right in perpetuity, the city of Tiberias, situated on Lake Gennesaret, with the whole principality of Galilee; likewise Caiphas, also called Porphyria, a maritime city with its appurtenances. [Col. 0446A]

In this principality Tancred conducted himself so pleasingly and praiseworthily before God that, even to the present day, his memory is blessed among the people of that province. He also established the churches of that diocese with great care and endowed them with ample estates: namely those of Nazareth, Tiberias, and Mount Tabor; moreover, he bestowed ecclesiastical ornaments. No small part of these was lost by those venerable places through the fraud and malicious litigation of later princes. Yet from what remains they still provide their necessities, praying for the soul of him who abounded in such pious liberality and such heartfelt charity toward God’s churches.

Because he was faithful in little, the Lord set him over much; and he entered into the joy of the householder, receiving a hundredfold for all that he had given. For soon, within two years, as his merits required, he was called to the principality of Antioch. There too he further ennobled that Church—glorious and noble from apostolic times—by many generous gifts. He also enlarged the principality, extending its boundaries far and wide after bringing several cities under his rule and subjecting fortresses, as will be told below. [Col. 0446B]

## CHAPTER XIV. Bohemond, prince of Antioch, and Baldwin, count of Edessa, come to Jerusalem and celebrate there the Nativity of the Lord.

While these things were occurring in the kingdom, Lord Bohemond, prince of Antioch, and Lord Baldwin, brother of the aforesaid lord duke and count of Edessa, learned from many reports that their remaining brethren and companions in so great a pilgrimage, aided by divine favour, had claimed the holy city for themselves and happily completed the purpose of the journey. They agreed upon a fixed day on which, once the necessities for travel had been made ready, they would set out thither through the Lord’s aid, in order to complete the purpose of their labours by paying their vows to the Lord and to offer brotherly support to the lord duke, Lord Tancred, and the other princes. [Col. 0446C]

For these two illustrious and magnificent men had remained behind, one at Antioch to preserve the principality, the other at Edessa to protect the county from attacking enemies. Immediately from the beginning, after Antioch had been captured, it had been arranged by common foresight that neither should abandon the cities granted them by God, devoted to God’s worship. Rather, each was to devote unceasing care to their defence, lest, should the enemies return with renewed forces, wars might revive and their former efforts thus have been in vain.

Although each was heavily occupied, they pressed on with their purpose for completing the pilgrimage and set out on the fixed day. Lord Bohemond, taking with him those drawn by desire for the same pilgrimage, and large forces both of cavalry and infantry, had already reached the maritime city of Valenia, beneath the castle of Margat, where, against the citizens’ wishes, he had pitched his tents. [Col. 0446D–0447A]

Lord Baldwin followed him immediately and found him at that city; joining their forces, they continued the journey they had begun. In those same days men from Italy had arrived at Laodicea in Syria. Among them was a learned and prudent man, very religious and a lover of honourable conduct, Lord Daimbert, archbishop of Pisa; there was also a bishop from Apulia, bishop of Ariano. These joined the camps of the aforesaid princes. Their number thus increased, so that the mixed multitude of both sexes, cavalry as well as infantry, was said to amount to twenty-five thousand.

Setting out and following the coast, they encountered only enemy cities. Thus they could with the greatest difficulty, and amid want of provisions, complete the journey undertaken. Since they had no commerce and could find nothing for sale, their travelling supplies had failed in their chests. The severity of the cold and the violence of the rains also drove many to their last extremity; for it was winter, the month of December. Only the Tripolitans and Caesareans, throughout so long a journey, offered provisions for sale to the travellers. Even so they proceeded in great lack of food and distress of hunger, having no pack animals or animals fit to carry burdens. [Col. 0447B]

At last, protected by divine mercy, they reached Jerusalem. There they were devoutly received by the lord duke and by the whole clergy and people. Visiting the holy places with contrite heart and humble spirit, they learned by the evidence of sight what they had previously understood by word and teaching. After celebrating the day of the Lord’s Nativity in holy Bethlehem, they saw the manger and the wondrous cave where the pious Mother of God, gate of salvation, wrapped the Restorer of the world in swaddling clothes and fed him, crying, with milk. [Col. 0447C]

## CHAPTER XV. Daimbert, archbishop of the Church of Pisa, is appointed patriarch of the Church of Jerusalem.

Since the Church of Jerusalem had remained without its own bishop until that day, for about five months, the princes then present assembled to provide for the Church of God in this matter. At length, after much weighing of deliberations, by the common counsel of all they placed the aforesaid venerable man, Lord Daimbert, in the patriarchal see. For what we said had previously been done concerning Arnulf, having been done imprudently, was as quickly and easily undone. [Col. 0447D]

Once this man of God had been installed in the see, both Lord Godfrey and Lord Bohemond, prince—the former receiving the kingdom, the latter the principality—humbly received investiture from him, judging that they rendered honour to one who was believed to exercise on earth, as a minister, the office of him whose representative he was. Thereupon possessions were assigned to the lord patriarch: both those which the Greek patriarch had held in the time of the pagans, from the days of the Greeks, and certain others newly granted, so that the patriarchal household might have the means of honourable support. [Col. 0448A]

When these matters had been duly completed, Lord Bohemond and Lord Baldwin, having received leave from the lord duke and preparing to return to their own territories, descended to the Jordan. Thence, following the bank of that river through the Illustrious Valley and passing Scythopolis, they reached Tiberias. Having taken there the provisions necessary for their journey, they proceeded beside the Sea of Galilee, entered Lebanese Phoenicia, passed Paneas—Caesarea Philippi—on their right, entered Ituraea, and came to the place called Heliopolis, also called Malbec. Returning thence to the coast, through divine mercy they reached Antioch safe and sound.

## CHAPTER XVI. Through the efforts of malicious persons, bitter disputes arise between the duke and the patriarch concerning the Tower of David and a fourth part of the city.

[Col. 0448B]

Meanwhile at Jerusalem, through the zeal and activity of certain malicious persons, whose constant desire is to sow scandal and envy others’ peace, a dispute was raised between the lord patriarch and the lord duke. The patriarch demanded from him the holy city dedicated to God and the citadel of that city, together with the city of Joppa and its appurtenances.

After the dispute had been pursued for some time, the duke, being a humble and gentle man who feared the words of the Lord, surrendered a fourth part of Joppa to the church of the Holy Resurrection on the Feast of the Purification of Blessed Mary, in the presence of all the clergy and people. [Col. 0448C] Later, on the holy day of the following Easter, in the presence of clergy and people assembled for the feast, he surrendered Jerusalem, with the Tower of David and all its appurtenances, into the lord patriarch’s hand, on this condition: that he himself should meanwhile enjoy and use the aforesaid cities with their territories, until, after one or two other cities had been captured, the Lord should permit the kingdom to be enlarged.

If in the meantime the duke should die without a lawful heir, all these things were to pass into the lord patriarch’s dominion without difficulty and with every objection removed. Although we learned all this from the reports of others, and although some of it was committed to writing in certain documents, we have included it in the present narrative. Yet we wonder on what grounds the lord patriarch was moved to raise this dispute against the duke, since we have nowhere read or heard from trustworthy persons that the kingdom had been given to the lord duke by the victorious princes on the condition that he knew himself bound to any person by an obligation of annual or perpetual payment. [Col. 0448D] Nor should our ignorance be judged gross or supine, since we have investigated the truth of these matters more diligently than anyone, with the particular and deliberate purpose of committing them to this present writing, as had long been our intention.

## CHAPTER XVII. For what reason a fourth part of the city passed into the right and power of the lord patriarch.

Nevertheless, it is certain that the patriarch of Jerusalem possessed a fourth part of the city as his own, from the entry of the Latins and even from many times before. How this happened, and from what source and cause this possession began, must briefly be explained. For after investigating these matters with particular diligence, we finally arrived, through frequent inquiry, at the discovery of this fact. [Col. 0449A]

Ancient traditions report that while that city was held by unbelievers, it never enjoyed continuous peace, nor even peace for a short interval; rather, it was continually wearied by frequent wars and repeated sieges, as neighbouring rulers sought to claim it for themselves. Consequently its towers and walls, collapsing into ruin both through age and through the work of besiegers, left the place broadly exposed to the enemy’s attacks.

At the time when the Egyptian kingdom surpassed all other kingdoms in the east and south in power, riches, and worldly wisdom, the Egyptian caliph, wishing to extend the boundaries of his empire and spread his dominion far and wide, sent armies and violently occupied all Syria as far as Laodicea, which borders Antioch and is the boundary of Coele-Syria. He appointed governors over cities on the coast and inland, imposed taxes, and made the entire region tributary. He commanded the citizens of every place to rebuild their city walls and erect strong towers around them. [Col. 0449B]

Under this general law, the governor at Jerusalem compelled the inhabitants of that place to obey the common regulations and restore the walls and towers to their former condition. When portions of the future work were assigned, it happened, more through malice than through comparison of resources, that a fourth part of the construction was assigned to the wretched Christians dwelling in the city. These faithful people had been so exhausted by forced labour and compulsory transport services (*angariae* and *parangariae*), tributes, taxes, and the performance of other degrading duties, that the resources of them all scarcely sufficed to repair one or two of the said towers. [Col. 0449C]

Seeing that pretexts were being sought against them, and having no other refuge, they approached the governor. With tears they begged him to impose a burden proportionate to their means, for they were wholly incapable of carrying the burden laid upon them. He ordered them to be excluded from his presence under severe threat and said: “It is sacrilege to violate the edicts of the supreme ruler. Therefore you will either complete the work imposed upon you, or you must fall beneath avenging swords as persons guilty of violated majesty.”

At last, through multiplied intercessors and the intervention of gifts, they obtained a respite from the governor, until they might send envoys to the lord emperor at Constantinople and implore his alms for carrying out the aforesaid work. [Col. 0449D]

## CHAPTER XVIII. Further concerning the same matter, and what venerable places the aforesaid part contains.

Accordingly, the envoys appointed for this purpose came before the aforesaid ruler and, not without the sighs of their hearers, set forth as carefully as they could the groans and tears of the faithful people; recounting in order the spittings upon them, blows, chains, prisons, plundering of goods, crosses, and tortures which that wretched people suffered unceasingly for Christ’s name, and the new pretexts then being sought against the same common people for their destruction. At that time the sceptre was held by the prudent and magnificent lord Constantine, surnamed Monomachus, who administered the empire of Constantinople vigorously and manfully. Moved with full charity by the troubles and continual afflictions of Christ’s faithful, he graciously assented to their tearful petitions and promised money by which the imposed work might be completed. He added, however, the condition [Col. 0450B] that he would grant them the aforesaid money on this understanding: that, if they could obtain it from the ruler of the region, no one but Christians should be permitted to live within the circuit of the aforesaid wall which they proposed to raise from imperial alms. He therefore wrote to the Cypriots that, should the faithful of Jerusalem obtain this concession, they were to supply them, from the revenues and fiscal dues owed, with such a sum of money as might suffice for the aforesaid work.

They, however, having returned home, related in sequence to the lord patriarch and to the people of God how they had proceeded. Rejoicing, they embraced the proposal and worked with every effort faithfully to fulfil the stipulated condition which the lord emperor had added. Envoys were therefore sent to their great and supreme ruler—the caliph of Egypt [Col. 0450C]—and, divine favour accompanying them, they obtained from him the aforesaid petition and, moreover, secured a charter strengthened by his subscription and seal. At last, the affair having been happily completed, they returned home and, with the Lord’s help, finished the allotted portion of the wall, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1063, while Bomensor Elmostensab reigned among the Egyptians and permitted this to be done, thirty-six years before the liberation of the city.

Until that day the Saracens had indeed lived indiscriminately with the faithful; but from that hour, on hearing the ruler’s command, they necessarily moved to other parts of the city, leaving the aforesaid quarter without opposition to the faithful. In this respect the servants of Christ seem to have greatly improved their condition. For scandals arose far more frequently from cohabitation with the sons of Belial, and many troubles were added to them. At length, living separately and without the admixture of tares, they dwelt more peacefully. If they had disputes, they referred them to the judgment of the Church and, through the arbitration of the lord patriarch then in office, settled their controversies among themselves. Thus, from that day and for the reason already stated, the aforesaid fourth part of the city had no judge or lord other than the patriarch; and the Church claimed it for itself perpetually as though it were its own property.

The aforesaid quarter is bounded as follows: from the western gate, called David’s Gate, by the corner-tower [Col. 0451A] surnamed Tancred’s, as far as the northern gate, called that of Stephen the protomartyr, runs the circuit of the outer wall. Its inner boundary is the public road which stretches directly from the same gate to the money-changers’ tables, and thence to the western gate. It contains the venerable place of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection; the house of the Hospital; both monasteries, namely that of monks and that of nuns, each called “of the Latins”; also the patriarchal residence and the cloister of the canons of the Lord’s Sepulchre, with their appurtenances.

## CHAPTER XIX. What was the state of the kingdom at that time; how the duke besieged the maritime city of Assur; and why he raised the siege.

[Col. 0451B]

At the same time, when nearly all the princes who had come on the expedition had returned home, so that only the duke—to whom the kingdom had been entrusted—and Lord Tancred remained, the latter being retained by the lord duke as a prudent, valiant, and fortunate man to share his burden of care, the resources and military forces of our people were so slight that, even when all were summoned and hastened together, scarcely three hundred horsemen and two thousand foot soldiers could be found.

Moreover, the cities that had come under our rule were very few, separated from one another by intervening hostile places, so that it was extremely dangerous to travel from one to another whenever necessity required it. All the countryside, even within our own borders, [Col. 0451C] was inhabited by unbelievers and Saracens, and no enemies were more savage toward our people than these; they were the worse because they were neighbours. For no plague is more effective in inflicting harm than a familiar enemy. Not only did they slaughter our men when they travelled incautiously on public roads and hand them over to the slavery of the enemy; they also prevented cultivation of the fields, in order to afflict our people by famine, preferring to endure hunger themselves rather than supply any assistance to those whom they regarded as enemies.

Nor, when they left the cities, were the roads free from danger; even in houses situated within city walls, because of the scarcity of inhabitants and the breaches in the walls lying open to enemies, scarcely any place could be found safe [Col. 0451D] for rest. Night-thieves broke into cities that were empty and only thinly inhabited by stealthy incursions, overwhelming many persons in their own dwellings. Consequently, some secretly and many openly abandoned the possessions they had acquired and returned home, believing that those who strove to defend the country would one day be overwhelmed by enemies and that none would be able to rescue them from the impending disasters.

These persons gave occasion for the enactment that annual prescription should take effect and favour those who, persevering amid hardship, had possessed anything peaceably and without challenge for a year and a day. This measure was introduced, as we have said, because of resentment toward those who had abandoned their possessions through fear, lest, returning after a year, [Col. 0452A] they should be admitted to reclaim them.

Although the kingdom suffered from such great want, the God-fearing and God-beloved man nevertheless undertook, with the Lord’s help, to enlarge its borders. Having summoned military assistance and the people of the region, he besieged the maritime city bordering Joppa, once called Antipatris but now commonly called Assur. Yet since it contained strong and valiant men, abundantly supplied with arms, provisions, and all other necessities for such purposes, while the duke outside endured severe want—especially because he lacked ships with which to deny the besieged either entrance or exit—he was compelled by necessity to raise the aforesaid siege. He waited for a more suitable opportunity, granted him by God in the course of time, to present itself for completing the enterprise; but prevented by an untimely death, he did not attain his desired purpose.

## CHAPTER XX. A memorable occurrence which befell him during that siege.

During the same siege there occurred something worthy of memory, which we have thought fit to insert in the present account. From the mountains of Samaria, in which the city of Neapolis is situated, certain petty rulers of the surrounding districts came down to the aforesaid siege, bringing gifts of bread and wine, figs and raisins. They did this, we believe, more in order to spy out the strength and numbers of our people and learn more fully their condition than to bring gifts to the duke. When they arrived in the army, they urgently requested to be brought before the duke. Once admitted to his presence, they offered the presents they had brought.

The duke, however, being a humble man who entirely avoided worldly pomp, was seated upon a straw-filled sack laid on the ground, waiting for those whom he had sent out to forage. Seeing this, they were stunned with amazement and asked why so great a prince and so admirable a lord—who had come from the West, shaken the whole East, and seized a mighty kingdom by the strength of his hand—sat so without display: he had neither carpets nor silken stuffs about him in royal fashion, nor was he attended by armed retainers [Col. 0452D] so as to make himself formidable to those approaching him.

While they were making these inquiries, the duke asked what they were saying. When he had learned, he replied: “The earth might rightly suffice as a temporal seat for a mortal man, since after death it will provide him with a permanent dwelling.” Those who had come with the intention of testing him, on hearing this and admiring the man’s reply, humility, and prudence, departed saying: “Truly this is the man who ought to conquer every land and to whom it is appointed, by the merit of his life, to rule peoples and nations.”

The inhabitants of the neighbouring regions alike marvelled at and feared the valour and success of this foreign people. They were carried into still greater admiration and fear because they had learned these things from the report of their own countrymen, whom they were bound to trust more fully. [Col. 0453A] This remarkable event was proclaimed even to the furthest regions of the East.

## CHAPTER XXI. Bohemond, prince of the Antiochenes, is captured near the city of Melitene.

While these things were taking place in the kingdom of Jerusalem, it happened that a certain Gabriel, an Armenian by nationality, governor of the city of Melitene beyond the Euphrates in Mesopotamia, feared Persian attacks and was unable to withstand their harassment. He sent envoys to Lord Bohemond, prince of the Antiochenes, inviting him not to delay in coming, since he would immediately receive the aforesaid city upon certain stipulated conditions.

When the magnificent Lord Bohemond heard this, he promptly accepted the man’s invitation. Taking his customary company, crossing the Euphrates, and entering Mesopotamia, he had almost reached the aforesaid city when a most powerful Turkish satrap named Danishmend, having learned of his arrival, suddenly fell upon his company. Overwhelming them while unprepared, he put some to the sword; the rest, unable to withstand the multitude of enemies, he put to flight. Lord Bohemond himself, through the exigency of his sins, was captured by the enemy and delivered over to their chains.

Elated by this success and relying upon the numerous army which he had brought with him, Danishmend surrounded the same city with a siege, hoping soon to possess it. But those who had escaped the aforesaid danger arrived at Edessa [Col. 0453C] and related in order to the count what had happened to the lord prince and themselves. On learning this, the valiant man, sympathizing with the lord prince as with a brother born of the same mother and inwardly moved by the perilous outcome of the affair, summoned his military forces with all speed. Having taken what was necessary for the journey, he hastened swiftly to those parts.

The aforesaid city is said to be three days’ journey from Edessa. Completing the journey promptly and early, he was already close to the city; but Danishmend, hearing of the count’s arrival, raised the siege and withdrew into the more distant parts of his realm, avoiding battle and taking with him Lord Bohemond, whom he held in chains. When the count heard that Danishmend, fearing his arrival, [Col. 0453D] had departed from the siege, he pursued the fugitive for three days. Seeing that he made no progress, he returned to Melitene. There he was received most splendidly by the aforesaid Gabriel, with great honour, treated excellently, and received the city upon the same conditions on which Gabriel had offered it to Lord Bohemond. These matters accomplished, he returned home.

## CHAPTER XXII. A memorable deed of the duke in the country of the Arabs.

Meanwhile, while the distinguished Lord Duke and those who, after the departure of the others, had remained with him at Jerusalem to preserve the kingdom were suffering such want and oppressed by such poverty as scarcely anyone could express in words, trustworthy scouts reported [Col. 0454A] that certain Arabs in the parts of Arabia beyond the Jordan, in the land of the Ammonites, were behaving incautiously. If they were suddenly attacked, great gains might be made.

Persuaded by this report, the illustrious man secretly summoned such forces of horse and foot as the newly established kingdom could furnish, crossed the Jordan, and entered enemy territory. The enterprise was happily accomplished; and while he was returning with an immense booty of flocks and herds and countless captives, a certain nobleman and distinguished leader among his people, an Arab of ability and an ardent lover of military discipline, obtained peace through intermediaries and came to him with an honourable company of nobles from the same nation. [Col. 0454B]

He had heard from many reports of the might and renown of this people, which had descended from the West, subjected the whole East to itself after traversing so many regions and enduring such a multitude of hardships, and especially of the duke’s singular courage and exceptional prowess. He therefore passionately desired to see him. Approaching and paying due reverence with a fitting greeting, he urgently and repeatedly begged the duke to deign, before his eyes, to strike with his sword a very large camel which he had brought for that purpose, so that he himself might bear witness to the duke’s prowess before others.

Since the duke had come from a distance to see him, he agreed. Drawing his sword, he cut off the head of the camel before him as easily [Col. 0454C] as if he had been ordered to cut through something fragile. At this sight the Arab was astonished at such immense strength, but in his own mind attributed it chiefly to the sharpness of the sword. Having obtained permission to speak more freely, he asked whether the duke could do something similar with another sword.

The duke smiled and ordered the nobleman’s own sword to be given him. Taking it, he ordered another animal of the same kind to be brought before him. Striking it, he cut off its head with a single blow and without difficulty. Then the oft-mentioned nobleman first began to marvel with intense astonishment, recognizing that the force of the blow proceeded not from the edge of the iron but from the man’s strength. He found true what he had heard concerning the man’s courage. Therefore, offering [Col. 0454D] gifts of gold, silver, and horses, he secured the favour of the lord duke; and, returning home, he became the herald to all with whom he spoke of the prowess he had seen in the duke. The duke himself returned to Jerusalem with the booty and spoils.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The duke’s death and burial.

In the same month, namely July, the same Lord Godfrey, illustrious governor of the kingdom of Jerusalem, was seized by a severe and incurable illness and began to be sick unto death. At last, as the disease gained strength and did not yield to remedies, he received the viaticum of our salvation; devoutly repentant and a true confessor of Christ, he entered upon the way of all flesh, to receive a hundredfold and to possess eternal life with the blessed spirits. He died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August [18 July], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1100. He was buried in the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, beneath the place [Col. 0456A] of Calvary where the Lord suffered; this place has also been assigned for the burial of his successors down to the present day.

# HERE BEGINS THE TENTH BOOK

[Col. 0455]

## CHAPTER I. Lord Baldwin, count of the Edessenes, succeeds his deceased brother in the kingdom.

[Col. 0455A]

When the lord duke Godfrey, of illustrious and pious memory in the Lord, the first distinguished ruler of the kingdom of Jerusalem among the Latins, departed from this light but attained a better light, [Col. 0455B] the kingdom stood vacant for three months. At last, whether by the final judgment of the lord duke or by the common counsel of the few princes who were present, Lord Baldwin, count of Edessa and brother of the aforesaid duke by both parents, was summoned to assume the kingdom, to which he was entitled by hereditary right, and succeed his brother in the same office of care.

In his youth he was suitably instructed in liberal learning and, as is said, became a cleric. By reason of the nobility in which he was singularly eminent, he obtained benefices—commonly called prebends—in the churches of Reims, Cambrai, and Liège. At length, for reasons unknown to us, he took up arms; laying aside the clerical [Col. 0455C] habit, he became a knight. In time he married an illustrious and noble Englishwoman, Lady Godehilde by name. Taking her with him, he followed his brothers, Lord Duke Godfrey and Lord Eustace—men of valour and immortal memory—on that first expedition, fortunate and successful in every respect.

Before the army of the faithful reached Antioch, however, his aforesaid wife, worn out by prolonged suffering, ended her life a good death at Marash and was buried there, as we have said above. Afterwards, called by the duke of Edessa and adopted by him as his son, Baldwin succeeded after the duke’s death to the county with its appurtenances, as has been carefully related above. He married the daughter of a certain noble and eminent Armenian prince named Tafroc, who with his brother Constantine possessed impregnable strongholds around Mount Taurus and numerous forces of valiant men; on account of their immense riches and power, they were considered kings among that people.

It is not necessary to repeat at length his family origin according to the flesh, the distinction of his ancestors, or his birthplace; for, when we recorded above the deeds of the lord duke, we sufficiently explained the noble birth which was common to both brothers.

## CHAPTER II. The bodily appearance and character of the same Lord Baldwin.

He is said to have been very tall in body [Col. 0456A] and much taller than his brother, so that, as is said of Saul, “he was taller than all the people from the shoulders upward” (1 Samuel 10:23). His hair and beard were dark, though his complexion was moderately fair. He had an aquiline nose and a slightly projecting upper lip, with the line of teeth beneath somewhat recessed; yet not so much that it could be reckoned a defect.

He was grave in gait, manner, and speech; he always wore a cloak from his shoulders, so that to strangers, by the gravity he displayed more than by speech and dress, he appeared more a bishop than a secular person. Nevertheless, as one who did not doubt himself heir to corrupted stock and the first curse, he is said to have suffered impatiently from the frailty of the flesh. Yet he took such care to manage discreetly affairs connected with that failing that he gave scandal to none, imposed violence upon none, and inflicted grievous injury upon none. What is rare in such cases, knowledge of the matter could scarcely reach even a few of his chamberlains. Yet if, in the manner of sinners who seek excuses to excuse sins, an advocate [Col. 0456C] should seek an excuse for him, he seems to have had some excuse before men, if not before the strict Judge, for this sin, as will be said below.

He was neither swollen with excessive fat nor emaciated by immoderate thinness, but of a medium bodily build. He was ready for arms, agile on horseback, tireless and attentive whenever the affairs of the kingdom called him. It seems superfluous to praise in him magnificence, courage, experience in military discipline, and the other outstanding gifts of a well-ordered mind which, as though transmitted to him by hereditary right from his ancestors, he and his brothers possessed continually—especially since he proved such an exact imitator of the lord duke that he counted it a fault to depart from his footsteps.

All the less should this be praised because he enjoyed excessive intimacy with a certain Arnulf, a wicked and thoroughly evil man, archdeacon at Jerusalem, whose intention and disposition were said to be inclined to every evil deed. We mentioned him above: he had seized the patriarchal see. Baldwin was guided by his counsel, which was counted against him as a reproach. [Col. 0456D]

## CHAPTER III. Count Garner, after the duke’s death, seizes the tower and secretly summons the aforesaid Baldwin through messengers.

After the lord duke had died and been committed to burial, as we have stated, those to whom he had entrusted the execution of his testament according to his final will abandoned the dead man’s decision and preferred their own will to his judgment. For they neither handed over the citadel of David to Lord Patriarch Daimbert nor resigned the city to his authority, as was contained in the testamentary documents and as the duke of pious memory in the Lord had stipulated in the church of the Lord’s Resurrection on the holy day of the most recently past Easter, in the presence of clergy and people, by the agreements made between himself and the lord patriarch.

The leader in this act of defiance was a certain Count Garner, surnamed of Gres, a most fierce knight and kinsman of the lord duke and the count. Immediately upon the duke’s death, he seized the aforesaid tower and carefully fortified it. Without the knowledge of the others, he secretly sent envoys to Lord Count Baldwin, urging him to come with the utmost speed and without delay. Meanwhile, when the lord patriarch repeatedly pressed him concerning the matter, asking him to satisfy the duke’s final will and surrender the Church’s right, he devised evasions, spun out delays, and sought by every means to gain time until the summoned count could arrive while his right remained unimpaired. He hoped to find great favour with the oft-mentioned count for such loyalty; but, beyond everyone’s expectation, he fell from that hope.

For it happened that within five days the same count died by chance, all considering it miraculous and attributing it to the merits of the lord patriarch that an enemy and persecutor of the Church had perished by so sudden a death. Yet the Church’s condition did not improve upon his death. Those in the garrison made little of what had happened and remained there until the arrival of the count of Edessa. The lord patriarch, however, knowing that the count had been summoned and fearing his arrival, wished by every means to prevent his advancement. He therefore sent a letter to Lord Bohemond, prince of the Antiochenes, setting out the whole sequence of events. To make the matter clearer, we have thought fit to insert his reply in the present account.

## CHAPTER IV. Letter of Lord Daimbert to the prince of Antioch.

You know, dearest son, that although I was ignorant and unwilling, you chose me, from an intention nevertheless good and holy, as ruler and patriarch of that Church which is the singular mother of all Churches [Col. 0457D] and mistress of the nations; and, elected by the common assent of clergy, people, and princes alike, you placed me, though unworthy, in the seat of this highest dignity, God’s grace going before.

How many dangers, labours, and persecutions I endure while established in this eminence—assailed by a thousand injuries—my own mind knows, and Christ, the beholder of all things, knows. For while Duke Godfrey still lived, misled not so much by his own decision as by evil counsels, he scarcely left the Church to hold those things which the patriarch who had been there in the time of the Turks had held. Thus, when the holy Church ought to have been honoured and exalted more greatly, it then endured greater reproaches of desolation and disgrace.

Yet he came to his senses through God’s mercy and, abandoning his purpose of impiety, gave to the church of the Holy Sepulchre a fourth part of Joppa on the day of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Afterwards, on the day of the Easter solemnity, refusing any longer to be proud-minded or to place his confidence in worldly pomp, touched by divine prompting, he freely restored all that belonged by right to the Church. He became a man of the Holy Sepulchre and ours, and promised that henceforth he would faithfully serve God and us.

Accordingly, he restored to our authority the Tower of David together with the whole city of Jerusalem and its appurtenances, and whatever he himself held in Joppa. Yet this was on the condition that, because of the insufficiency of temporal resources, he should retain these things by our permission until God enlarged him through the capture of Babylon or other cities. If he should die without a male heir, all these things were to be restored to the Church without any contradiction. When he had confirmed all this before the whole clergy and people on the solemn day of Easter, before the most holy Sepulchre, he also ordained the same upon the bed of the illness from which he died, in the presence of many trustworthy witnesses.

After his death, Count Garner rose up as an enemy against the Church of God. Holding the faith and covenant of justice of no account, he fortified the Tower of David against us; and by envoys sent to Baldwin he directed him to come as quickly as possible, to plunder the Church of God and violently seize its possessions. Therefore, struck by God’s judgment, he died on the fourth day after the duke’s death. But after he died, low-born men of the common people still hold the same tower with the whole city, awaiting Baldwin’s arrival for the ruin of the Church and destruction of all Christendom.

But I, who am left only to the mercy of God and to your affection, dearest son, surrounded by every misery and by the malicious calumnies of those who plot against me, turn to you alone—for in you alone, after God, I trust, and in the solidity of your affection I fix the anchor of my hope. To you alone, I say, I relate with tearful voice and anxious heart the sufferings which I endure, or rather which the Church endures.

If you possess any piety and do not wish to prove a degenerate son of your father’s glory—your father who, by tyrannical force, rescued the apostolic lord Gregory, imprisoned by an impious hand, from the city of Rome and thereby earned a name memorable through all ages—then, putting every obstacle aside, hasten to come. Having prudently arranged the care of your land and kingdom among your wiser knights, mercifully assist the holy Church in its miserable travail. You surely know that you yourself have promised your aid and counsel, and have voluntarily made yourself debtor to the holy Church and to me.

Write therefore to Baldwin, forbidding him, without our permission and embassy—since he joined you in choosing me patriarch and ruler of the Church of Jerusalem—to come in any manner to devastate the holy Church and seize its possessions. Show him that it is unreasonable to have endured so many labours and dangers for the same Church in order that it might be free, if it must now be compelled, vile and abject, to serve those over whom it ought by maternal right to rule and preside.

But if he resists justice and refuses to accept reasonable terms, I adjure you, by the obedience you owe blessed Peter, to prevent his arrival by whatever means you can, even by force if necessary. And whatever you intend to do concerning the matters I command, make it known to me, dearest one, by sending your helmet to me in haste through this same messenger whom I send to you.

## CHAPTER V. Baldwin approaches Jerusalem and discovers an enemy ambush near the Dog River.

We do not believe, however, that this letter reached Lord Bohemond. For in the very month in which the duke of good memory, released from the flesh, passed to the Lord, Bohemond had been captured by the enemy shortly before or shortly afterwards, as has been carefully set forth above.

Lord Baldwin, count of Edessa, was enjoying prosperous fortune, having restored to him the noble metropolis of the Medes, Melitene. Having thoroughly subdued the enemies round about, he had obtained through God’s grace some peace for himself and his people, when suddenly a messenger hurried from Jerusalem and announced the death of the lord duke. Learning that the friends and faithful men of his dead brother urgently summoned him to hasten to succeed to the kingdom, he gathered a company of two hundred horsemen and eight hundred foot soldiers. Entrusting the land to a kinsman, a prudent and eminent man, namely Lord Baldwin of Bourcq—who succeeded him both in that county and later in the kingdom—he set out for Jerusalem on the sixth day before the Nones of October [2 October]. Some marvelled that he had proposed to undertake so great a journey through the midst of enemy territory with such a small force.

When he reached Antioch, he ordered his wife, the maidservants attending her, the cumbersome household goods, and the greater part of the baggage to go down to the sea. There he ordered a ship to be prepared, in which she might be conveyed honourably as far as Joppa. For this alone of the maritime cities had come under our rule; all the rest were still held by unbelievers. He appears to have acted thus in order that, as he passed through enemy regions, he might be freer for whatever business occurred and altogether better prepared for sudden contingencies.

From there, reaching Laodicea in Syria, he followed the coast through Gabulum, Valenia, Maraclea, Antaradus, and Arca, until he reached Tripoli. There, in camp outside the city, he was met with gifts and honour by the king of that city. The king informed him that Duqaq, king of Damascus, had laid ambushes for him along his route. Departing thence and passing through Byblos, he reached the river called the Dog River. At this place there is a most dangerous passage between lofty mountains, inaccessible because of the roughness of their rocks and their very steep ascent, and the stormy sea. It is scarcely two cubits wide and four stadia long.

The inhabitants of the region, together with some Turks who had assembled for this purpose from distant parts, had occupied these narrow places and perilous path in order to block the passage of the lord count. When the count reached this place, he sent ahead some of his men to investigate. They discovered that certain of those who had fortified the place had crossed the river and gone down into the plain. Seeing this, our men feared that greater ambushes had been left behind them and reported the situation to the lord count through one of their number.

Without delay, he arranged his battle-lines and advanced to meet them, finding them ready to fight. Falling upon them with a spirited charge, in the first clash he broke up their formation, killing many and putting the rest to flight. He then ordered the baggage set down and the camp pitched there. Since the place was rather confined between the mountains and the sea, they passed the night wakefully in great danger. Both those who had occupied the approaches in the mountains and those who had come down in ships from Beirut and Byblos harassed them, shooting a multitude of arrows throughout the night and exposing our men to many dangers at the edge of the camp. They afflicted them with such severe distress that, although the river was near at hand, they could not water that night the horses, tired from the journey and thirsty from the excessive heat.

## CHAPTER VI. The enemies are defeated, and Baldwin, his route made clear, reaches Jerusalem.

Afterwards, when day broke, the count took counsel with his men and ordered them, having packed their baggage for travel, to begin their return. Sending ahead the weaker men and those less able to bear arms, he himself followed with the stoutest, enduring assaults not only from the rear but from either flank. This he had devised, with his usual great prudence and cunning, in order to deceive the enemy—not because he distrusted his own company, but so that, as they pursued him in what they supposed was flight, he might find the enemy in open country and engage them more freely; for he greatly feared the narrow passes.

While his army thus struggled on its return, the enemy, imagining that fear was making them hasten their withdrawal, pressed them all the more insolently, the more deeply they supposed them cast down by terror. Descending competitively from the narrow places, they began to pursue our men most urgently through more open ground; so that those who were in the ships, eager for plunder, leapt ashore, hoping without difficulty—as though the enemy had already been defeated—to carry off the trophy. But when the count saw that they had abandoned the mountains and, now holding the plain, were pressing hard upon our men, he ordered his troops to turn back. Raising the standards, he moved back against the enemy, who were pressing on more fiercely. The battle-lines followed him; inspired by the example of their advancing lord, they charged more boldly. Before the enemy could, as usual, withdraw into the mountains, our men raged against them with drawn swords, sparing none until utter destruction.

The enemy, unable to endure our men’s assault and astonished and dismayed by the strength and persistence of the slaughterers, made no effort at defence. Placing their hope in flight alone, they sought safety by that route. Thus those who had come out from the ships did not dare return to the sea; and those who fled to the mountains, running heedlessly into dangerous precipices, found a thousand avenues to unforeseen death. The enemy having thus been overthrown, our men returned in triumph and rejoicing to the place where they had left their baggage and equipment. Resting there for the night, they blessed the Lord, “who brings down the mighty and exalts the humble.”

On the following day they retreated as far as the place called Junia. Giving due attention and care to themselves and their horses, they divided among themselves, according to military custom, the booty and the captured slaves. The next morning, the lord count, wishing prudently and faithfully to provide for his company, took several of the more mobile knights and boldly approached the place where the battle had occurred the preceding day. He wished to discover whether the enemy still held the narrow defiles, or whether the place lay open for those wishing to pass through. Seeing that the passage was free of enemies and could be traversed without difficulty, he summoned his men. On hearing the welcome report, they came to the place, joined the lord count without molestation, and crossed the place they had long regarded with suspicion and justly feared. Reaching the settlement of Beirut, they encamped before the city; then, following the coast, they passed Sidon, Tyre, and Ptolemais, until they came to the place called Cayphas.

But the count, regarding Lord Tancred with suspicion because of the exceedingly grievous and undeserved injury which he himself had inflicted upon Tancred at Tarsus in Cilicia, allowed none of his men to enter the aforesaid city [Col. 0461C], fearing that the eminent man, mindful of the offence, might wish to repay him in kind. Tancred himself was absent; nevertheless his citizens came out to meet the lord count and, with great kindness and fraternal charity, offered to trade on favourable terms in merchandise for sale, especially in the things necessary for sustenance. From there, travelling by Caesarea and then Arsuf along the coastal route, they arrived at Joppa. There, received solemnly by all the clergy and people, with everyone’s favour he conducted himself as their lord. Departing thence for Jerusalem, he was met by all the clergy and people, Latins as well as people of other nations, who joyfully brought him in with hymns and spiritual songs as their king and lord [Col. 0461D].

## CHAPTER VII. Patriarch Daimbert, fearing Baldwin’s arrival, leaves the patriarchal house and withdraws to the church on Mount Sion.

At the same time Arnulf, of whom we have spoken above—the first-born of Satan, son of perdition—seeing that, as his merits required, he had fallen from the chair of James, which he had seized with rash audacity, began to trouble and disturb the peace of Lord Daimbert, whom that same church had set over itself by the common concurrence of all. Immediately after the duke’s death, he had accused him before Lord Baldwin the count on many charges. He had also stirred up part of the clergy against him, being, as he was, most malicious and a sower of scandals [Col. 0462A].

He was powerful too and overflowing with wealth, holding the archdeaconry of that city and, in place of stipends, the Temple of the Lord and the site of Calvary. Thus, since he was both rich and clever in doing evil, he had very great influence among the clergy, and still more among secular persons. Therefore the lord patriarch, seeing the malice of the said Arnulf, who had been given to him as a thorn, and the count’s credulity, and viewing his arrival with suspicion, left the patriarchal house and withdrew to the church on Mount Sion. There, avoiding occasions of scandal, he devoted himself in private to reading and prayer. For this reason he had not been present at the aforesaid lord count’s reception, nor at the honour bestowed upon him by the citizens.

## CHAPTER VIII. The count directs expeditions toward Ascalon; crosses the Jordan; enters the enemies’ lands; and finally returns to Jerusalem.

[Col. 0462B]

After the count had remained in the city for several days, allowing himself and his horses some rest, and had arranged the affairs of the kingdom as far as seemed sufficient for the moment, he—being a laborious man who shunned idleness—assembled an expedition from both those whom he had brought with him and those whom he found in the kingdom. Suddenly and unexpectedly he appeared before the city of Ascalon. Since the citizens feared to come out against him, and he saw that he was making little progress, he followed the plain lying between the mountains and the sea and found the suburbs. Their inhabitants had left their homes and withdrawn with their wives and children, flocks and herds, into underground caves [Col. 0462C].

They were robbers and brigands, breakers-up of public roads, who by frequent raids between Ramla and Jerusalem had made the route exceedingly dangerous, often savagely attacking unwary travellers with the sword. When this became known, the count ordered the attack to be pressed more vigorously. Fire was applied at the mouths of the caves, and he had smoky material added, so that the smoke might torment those shut in and force them to surrender, or the suffocating air compel them to breathe out their lives. Thus those inside, unable to endure the heat of the fires, ash, and oppressive smoke, surrendered unconditionally into the count’s hands [Col. 0462D]. Sparing them not, as their apparent deserts required, he ordered one hundred of them beheaded.

Taking the provisions found among them that were necessary for the use of men and beasts, he traversed the territory of the tribe of Simeon and then climbed into the highlands. Passing the famous burial-place of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—Hebron, namely, also called Kiriath-arba—he descended through the vineyards of Engaddi to the celebrated valley where the most salty sea lies. Then, passing through Zoar, small indeed, but the place which knew how to save Lot fleeing from Sodom, they entered the borders of the Moabites and explored all the Syria of Sobal, seeking anything by which they might injure the faithless people and improve their own circumstances [Col. 0463A]. Yet throughout that whole journey they achieved nothing except that they supplied themselves, their horses, and their beasts from the enemies’ goods. For the inhabitants of the region, forewarned of their arrival, had fled to inaccessible mountains and their customary strongholds; so that our men, travelling through the whole region, found it empty and without inhabitants. Finally, seeing that he was accomplishing nothing and that the feast of the Lord’s Nativity was approaching, the lord count retraced the road by which he had come and entered Jerusalem on 21 December, the feast-day of St Thomas the Apostle.

## CHAPTER IX. The patriarch and the count are reconciled; the count is anointed king.

[Col. 0463B]

Therefore, in the year 1101 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Lord Daimbert the patriarch and Lord Baldwin the count having been reconciled through the praiseworthy intervention of certain prudent men, on the holy day of the Lord’s Nativity, in the church at Bethlehem, in the presence of clergy and people, the prelates of the churches, and the princes of the kingdom, Lord Baldwin was consecrated and anointed king by the hand of the aforesaid Lord Daimbert the patriarch, and solemnly crowned with the royal diadem.

## CHAPTER X. Tancred, mindful of an old injury, departs from him when summoned by the Antiochenes.

Thus, once Lord Baldwin had, as stated, obtained the throne of the kingdom and been confirmed in it, Lord Tancred—of illustrious remembrance and pious memory in Christ—remembered the injury that he had suffered undeservedly at the hands of that same Lord Baldwin at Tarsus in Cilicia. Being a religious man and a lover of his own conscience, he feared to bind himself to Baldwin by any tie of fidelity, since he could not love him with pure charity. He therefore surrendered into the king’s hands the city of Tiberias and Cayphas, which Lord Godfrey of illustrious memory had generously granted him for his exceptional merits. Taking leave, while all grieved at his departure, he withdrew to the region of Antioch [Col. 0463C].

For he had been summoned repeatedly by the princes of that region, to administer and care for the principality until the return of Lord Bohemond—if the Lord should ever deem it worthy to bring him out of prison—as the man to whom the entire inheritance would by hereditary right devolve if Bohemond were not permitted to return. On his arrival at Antioch, the people and the leading men immediately conferred upon him general and unrestricted authority. The king, for his part, granted Tiberias, surrendered to him, to a certain Hugh of Saint Aldemar, a noble man and valiant in arms, to possess by hereditary right. And the kingdom was at peace for four months.

## CHAPTER XI. Having crossed the Jordan, the king carries off innumerable spoils from the enemies’ territory; and his praiseworthy deed is described.

It happened during those same days, on the advice of certain men whose office it was to investigate the state of neighbouring regions and the enemies’ weaknesses, that the king secretly assembled a great force, crossed the Jordan, and entered the lands of the Arabs. Passing into the interior of the wilderness habitually inhabited by the aforesaid people, he reached his destination. There, by night, he suddenly fell upon them while they were off their guard in their very tents. They made booty of certain men, and of all the women with their little children, as well as all their property; and they carried off infinite spoils and an unheard-of multitude of camels and asses [Col. 0464A].

Most of the men, however, having learned from a distance of our men’s approach, fled swiftly on horseback into the farther desert in search of safety, abandoning their tents, wives and children, and all their property to the enemy. As they travelled back, driving herds and captives before them, a distinguished woman, wife of some great and powerful prince, caught up in the common misfortunes of that same movement, was involved. Her time to give birth was at hand; and in the very journey, overcome by the extremity of pain customary for a woman in labour, she gave birth. On hearing this, the king ordered her taken down from the camel on which she rode and a bed prepared for her on the ground from the booty, as comfortably as circumstances allowed. He gave her food and two water-skins; at her request, he also gave her a maidservant and assigned two she-camels, on whose milk she might be nourished. Wrapping her in the cloak he himself wore, he left her there and proceeded with his army [Col. 0464C].

That same day, or the next, the great Arab satrap, accompanied by many of his followers and tracking the footsteps of our army according to his people’s custom, came upon his wife lying there. He was deeply grieved and distressed at having lost his wife, a noble lady who was close to childbirth, and regarded everything else as nothing in comparison. Seeing and marveling at the humanity which the lord king had displayed toward her, he began to extol to the stars the name of the Latins and especially the king’s mercy. From then on he was faithful to him as far as he could be, as he later demonstrated by clear proof at a time of great necessity [Col. 0464D].

## CHAPTER XII. Western princes again prepare for the expedition and arrive at Constantinople with immense forces.

While these events were occurring in the East, the western princes heard of the great marvels which the Lord had wrought through His servants who had undertaken the pilgrimage: how He had led His army across so many lands and through so many varied and manifold dangers into the Promised Land, and how He had subdued nations and humbled kingdoms before them. They rejoiced in their brothers’ success, but took it hard that they had not been worthy to share in their fortunate achievements. Those who had remained behind joined together and firmly resolved among themselves to renew the expedition [Col. 0465A].

Foremost among them was the illustrious and magnificent William, count of Poitou and duke of Aquitaine; also Lord Hugh the Great, brother of Philip king of the Franks and count of Vermandois, who had joined the first expedition but, after Antioch was taken, had been drawn home by lack of resources. There was also Lord Stephen, count of Chartres and Blois, a prudent man of great counsel, who, after Antioch had been captured, had feared the coming battle and deserted his companions in shame and dishonour, purchasing perpetual infamy through disgraceful flight. Seeking to redeem this earlier failure and erase the disgrace he had deserved, he prepared himself for the journey, gathering an honourable company.

Lord Stephen, count of Burgundy, an illustrious man distinguished by great nobility, also prepared for the same journey; and many other nobles, distinguished in their regions by life, lineage, and arms, inflamed with the same desire, made ready to depart. They waited for the appointed day, when the greater princes would set out and they might join their legions [Col. 0465B]. When the designated day and suitable season came, the necessities for the journey having been arranged and companions summoned, they set out and, following the tracks—if not the devotion—of the first expedition, reached Constantinople. There they were received quite honourably by Emperor Alexius and found Lord Raymond, count of Toulouse, who had been so great and commendable a prince in the first expedition.

As we stated above, Raymond had left his wife and most of his household at Laodicea and returned to the emperor to seek help, in order that he might return to Syria and claim one or more of its cities for himself. For he had resolved, once he had undertaken the pilgrimage, to persevere in it permanently and never return to his own lands. Glad to have found such an energetic and prudent man, and having received the emperor’s permission and more abundant gifts from him, they took the count as their leader. Crossing the Hellespont with their legions and following the route of the former army, they arrived at Nicaea in Bithynia [Col. 0465C].

## CHAPTER XIII. Emperor Alexius, in accordance with his customary Greek fashion, plots against them through the Turks; the pilgrims are for the most part destroyed; and the survivors, following the count of Toulouse, arrive at Jerusalem.

[Col. 0465D]

But that same emperor, envying our people’s successes in the ancient Greek manner, although, as stated above, he had treated them kindly enough in his own country, nevertheless secretly urged the enemy, through frequent agents, to destroy them. By repeated letters and continual messengers’ journeys he made the enemy more fully informed of their arrival, warning them not to allow so great a people to pass freely through at their own peril. He acted the part of the scorpion: since there is nothing in its face that one need fear, one does wisely if able to avoid the poison of its rearward tail.

Thus, their arrival having become known through him and his agents, the enemy summoned forces from the whole eastern region and gathered military assistance through both entreaties and payment, wishing to obstruct the journey of those whom they knew intended to cross. Our men, whether deliberately or by chance, became divided from one another and began to advance by various routes. They became, as though deliberately, like sand without lime, having no bond of charity among themselves and utterly despising the discipline observed by the former army [Col. 0466A]. Therefore, as their merits required, a powerful adversary was raised against them, and they were delivered into the hands of the enemy, so that in one day more than fifty thousand persons of both sexes fell by the sword.

Those whom God permitted to escape the enemy’s hands found safety however they could, stripped and empty, having lost their baggage and all their possessions. At last, more by chance than skill, they reached Cilicia. At Tarsus, the metropolis of that province, they lost Lord Hugh the Great, taken away by fatal necessity. He was magnificently buried in the church of the Doctor of the Nations, who had been born in that same city. Refreshed there for several days, they resumed their journey and reached Antioch [Col. 0466B].

Lord Tancred, administering the principality of that city, showed them every favour of humanity according to his custom, especially to the count of Poitou, because he was nobler and far more powerful than the others, and had suffered greater losses than all the rest in the aforesaid disastrous expedition, having lost everything completely. At last, drawn by the desire to see the holy places, those whose horses had failed hurried toward Jerusalem by ship, while those who still had horses went by land. They gathered at the coastal city of Antaradus, commonly called Tortosa [Col. 0466C].

There, on the counsel of Lord Raymond, count of Toulouse, they attacked the city, since it seemed capable of being taken. With the Lord as author, they captured it by force within a few days, killing its citizens by the sword or consigning them to perpetual slavery. Surrendering the city to the lord count and dividing its spoils among themselves according to the law of war, they continued their intended undertaking; but the said count remained behind to defend the city, against the wishes of the others, who tried to draw him along with them.

## CHAPTER XIV. The king besieges Antipatris and captures it by force.

[Col. 0466D]

Meanwhile, while the aforesaid army, as stated, was suffering misfortune in the regions of Romania, the king of Jerusalem, unwilling to grow sluggish in idleness and eager to enlarge the kingdom’s borders, devoted every effort to expanding its narrow limits. Near the beginning of spring a Genoese fleet arrived in the harbour of Joppa and was received with great honour by the king and the citizens of that city. Since the Easter feast was near, they drew their ships ashore and went up to Jerusalem for the festival. When the customary Easter celebration was completed, the king caused the consuls, leading elders, and commanders of the aforesaid fleet to assemble through prudent men skilled in exhortation [Col. 0467A]. He asked whether they intended to return, or whether they wished to devote themselves for a time to divine service and the increase of the kingdom, in return for suitable pay.

After conferring with their men, they replied that, if they could remain in the kingdom on honourable terms, it was and had been their purpose from the beginning to labour faithfully for a time in God’s service and for the kingdom’s growth. Accordingly, an agreement satisfactory to both sides having been reached and confirmed by reciprocal oaths, it was established that, as long as they wished to remain in the kingdom with the aforesaid fleet, if any city or town of the enemy should be captured by force with their assistance, they should receive, to divide among their associates without any hindrance, one-third of the booty and money taken from the enemy; the remaining two thirds being reserved for the lord king [Col. 0467B]. Moreover, in every city recovered from the enemy under the same terms, they would receive by agreement one district belonging specifically to the Genoese citizens.

Encouraged by this hope and trusting in heavenly help, the lord king assembled military forces, horsemen and foot soldiers, from the cities he possessed, and besieged by land and sea the coastal town of Arsuf. This place is also called Antipatris, so named after Antipater, Herod’s father. It is a fertile place, possessing many advantages in woods and pastures. Duke Godfrey of blessed memory had besieged it in the preceding year; but since he saw that he made no progress—for he did not have ships enough to prevent the besieged from being supplied by sea—he returned without accomplishing his purpose [Col. 0467C].

After they had surrounded the garrison by stationing troops all around, the king ordered a siege-tower constructed of great beams. When it had been assembled and, through the craftsmen’s effort, brought up to the walls, it collapsed broken to the ground, because, owing to the large number of men mounting it, it possessed less strength than was needed. In this mishap nearly one hundred of our men were seriously injured. Some were captured by the enemy, who hung them from gallows in the sight of our men. This greatly stirred our army’s indignation. They pressed the attack more boldly and confined the enemy within the town, filling them with such fear that they seemed no longer even to think of defending themselves [Col. 0467D].

Our men, applying ladders to the wall, appeared already to have taken the towers and ramparts. Then the townspeople, despairing of their lives, secured through negotiators from the lord king the following terms: if they surrendered the town, they, with their children and wives, would have free and undisturbed departure, abandoning their movable goods, and a safe escort as far as Ascalon. The stronghold having thus been taken, guards were left there to defend the place diligently, and the king immediately went to Caesarea, intending without delay to besiege it.

## CHAPTER XV. The same king besieges Caesarea, a coastal city, and assaults it while under siege.

[Col. 0468A]

Caesarea is a city situated on the coast, whose ancient name is the Tower of Straton. As ancient histories relate, Herod the Elder enlarged it and, adorning it with noble buildings, named it Caesarea in honour of Caesar Augustus, establishing it by the authority of the Roman ruler as the metropolis of Palestine Secunda. It is a place richly supplied with running waters and irrigated gardens, but lacking a harbour. Yet we read that Herod himself laboured uselessly, at great expense and with painstaking care, to provide ships there with some secure anchorage.

When the king arrived there with his army, the fleet following by sea at an equal pace, they laid siege around the city. Setting missile-engines in appropriate positions, they attacked it more vigorously. By frequent engagements at the city gates they struck fear into the citizens; with volleys of great stones they weakened towers and walls, shattered the houses within, and granted the besieged no rest [Col. 0468B]. Meanwhile an engine of remarkable height was constructed, much taller than the towers, from which our men might more freely attack the city.

For almost fifteen days both the citizens and our army continued in this enterprise: the latter striving with all their might to inflict hardships, the former with equal zeal to repel them, while both fought more boldly in constant encounters. Our men recognized that the citizens, softened by idleness and enervated by long repose, were unaccustomed to arms and unequal to such great exertions, acting more feebly each day and being exhausted by the burdens of war. They reproached one another for delay and mutually encouraged themselves. They did not wait for the construction of the engine to be completed, but made a united attack and pressed more fiercely than usual. Having forced the citizens back within the walls, they inspired such terror that, despairing of life, the citizens neither strengthened the walls for protection nor made any effort at defence [Col. 0468C].

Perceiving this, our men applied ladders to the walls, and suddenly, competing to climb, took the towers and ramparts. Through the efforts of some, the entrances were opened, and the king entered with his men after the city had been forcibly breached. The armed men now ranged about everywhere; breaking into houses, which the citizens believed to be safe refuges, killing householders, and seizing vessels, houses, and every desirable thing in them, they slaughtered the household and occupied the courtyards. It is needless to speak of those whom our men chanced to meet in the city’s lanes and streets, since even those who diligently sought side-streets and hiding places could not avoid the massacre. Many, too, who perhaps otherwise would have received mercy, brought upon themselves the causes of their death: swallowing gold and precious stones, they roused the greed of their pursuers so far that these cut them open down the middle to search their entrails for the hidden objects [Col. 0468D].

## CHAPTER XVI. An innumerable multitude of citizens is killed in the city’s oratory, and an archbishop is assigned to the captured city.

[Col. 0469A]

In an elevated part of the city stood the public oratory, where, it is said, Herod had once built a temple of marvelous workmanship in honour of Caesar Augustus. Nearly the whole population of the city had fled there, since it was a place of prayer, in hope of obtaining safety. When it was broken into, so great was the slaughter of those who had taken refuge within that the bases of the killers were stained with the blood of the slain, and it was dreadful to behold the multitude of corpses.

In this same oratory there was found a vessel of the most vivid green colour, formed in the manner of a basin. The aforesaid Genoese considered it to be emerald and accepted it as their share for a great sum of money, offering it to their church as an outstanding ornament [Col. 0469B]. Consequently, even to this day, when magnates pass through their city, they customarily display this vessel as though it were a miracle, maintaining that it truly is an emerald, as its colour suggests. After almost all the adult citizens had been killed in various places, scarcely any young girls or boys below puberty were spared. Here one could truly see fulfilled literally what is written in the Prophet: “The Lord delivered their strength into captivity, and their might into the hand of the enemy” (Psalm 77:67).

Therefore, when the sword ceased and the slaughter of the people was complete, all the booty and possessions were gathered together. In accordance with the agreement, one third was allotted to the Genoese, while the remaining two thirds fell by lot to the lord king and his men. Here for the first time our people—who had entered the expedition poor and destitute, their resources exhausted, and had remained in the same want until that day—began to grow wealthier, laden with spoils and enriched with money, and supplied with more abundant possessions [Col. 0469C].

The city’s administrator, called *emir* in their language, and the jurist who presided over the administration of justice, also called *cadius* in their language, were brought before the lord king as he sat in judgment. These two were deliberately spared, in hope of a future ransom; nevertheless they were shackled and handed over to appointed guards. Since the king had no leisure for a longer stay there, being recalled by his affairs, he elected as archbishop a certain Baldwin, who had come on the expedition with Duke Godfrey. Leaving some of the army behind to guard the city, he himself hastened with the rest to Ramla [Col. 0469D].

## CHAPTER XVII. On arriving at Ramla, the king waits for the enemy army said to be coming; fighting them, he wins victory.

Ramla is a city situated in the plains near Lydda, which is Diospolis. I have not found its ancient name; indeed, a widespread opinion holds that it did not exist in ancient times. Ancient histories report that after the time of the deceiver Muhammad, his successors, the Arab princes, founded it [Col. 0470A]. When the Christian army first arrived in Syria, it was a famous city, frequented by many peoples and surrounded by towers and a strong wall. But after our legions poured into those regions, its inhabitants all abandoned the city and fled to Ascalon because it lacked an outer defensive wall or a rampart, and because Ascalon was more strongly fortified.

Our men, finding the city empty, as stated above, fortified a castle in one part of it with walls and a rampart, judging it difficult to occupy so great a circuit of walls with few inhabitants. A report was circulating, not far from the truth, that the Egyptian caliph had sent one of the commanders of his army, with an immense multitude, toward Ascalon [Col. 0470B]. In his customary manner he ordered him to depart without delay and either utterly destroy by the sword or bring bound to Egypt that needy and beggarly people who had dared to enter his territories and did not fear to disturb his peace.

Those said to have arrived following that commander numbered eleven thousand cavalry; the number of foot soldiers was said to stand at twenty thousand. This report compelled the lord king to hasten from Caesarea, fearing that, relying on their multitude, they might plan dangerous incursions into the kingdom. On reaching Ramla, he waited for almost a month; but when he saw that they did not advance, he returned to Joppa. At length, in the third month, the Egyptian legions mentioned above, fearing to disregard their lord’s command and dreading his displeasure and anger over their delay, made a virtue of necessity, raised their spirits, restored their strength, formed their battle-lines, and strove to enter our borders and fight us [Col. 0470C].

When this was reported to the lord king, he gathered as many troops as he could around Lydda and Ramla, drawing upon the kingdom’s limited forces, since the restricted extent of his possessions could provide no more. He had two hundred and sixty cavalry and nine hundred infantry. When it was established that the enemy were approaching, the king went out to meet them and ordered six battle-lines formed. Once these were arranged, with the wood of the Lord’s Cross carried before them by a certain devout abbot with great fear of God, they beheld the enemy formations. Seeing them, they invoked help from above, raised their eyes toward heaven, and, unafraid of the enemy’s multitude, boldly hurled themselves against them, fighting manfully with swords, knowing that the matter concerned their very lives [Col. 0470D].

The enemy in turn resisted with all their strength, fearing for the wives and children, estates and possessions they had left in Egypt should they fail to return victorious, and laboured according to their ability to repel the attacks. It happened that the enemy’s first battle-lines charged one of ours and, overwhelming it with a great multitude, drove it into flight. Pursuing and pressing it with greater cruelty, they almost wiped it out completely. But our remaining battle-lines, resisting and pressing the enemy more fiercely, inflicted an astonishing and unheard-of slaughter.
