The lord king, as befitted so great a prince, encouraged now one group, now another, by word and example; and with the battle-line he commanded, he brought help to those who were oppressed and failing, supplying strength and courage [Col. 0471A].

After the battle’s outcome had long been uncertain, victory was divinely granted to our men. The enemy turned to flight, deprived of their commander, who had fought bravely in the struggle but perished pierced by swords. Seeing the enemy formations broken, with their companies partly fallen by the sword and partly in irreversible flight, the lord king commanded, on pain of death, that absolutely no one should dare seek to seize the spoils. Instead, they were to pursue the enemy without sparing their swords and kill all of them until not one could be found. He himself was first in pursuit of the enemy, taking with him troops of cavalry and swift infantry. For almost eight miles as far as Ascalon, he did not cease to kill the enemy and inflict great slaughter. When night fell, he summoned his companions by trumpet and returned to the battlefield, where he rested that night as victor, after dividing the spoils among his men according to military custom [Col. 0471B].

It is said that about five thousand of the enemy were killed there. Of our men, after a count was made, seventy cavalrymen were found missing; of the infantry, many more, although their exact number is not known.

## CHAPTER XVIII. He then proceeds to Joppa and comforts its terrified citizens.

[Col. 0471C]

But those who had put our line to flight in the conflict of the preceding day pursued the fugitives as far as Joppa. Equipping themselves with the weapons, coats of mail, shields, and helmets of the men who had fallen behind, they stood boldly before the city, shouting to the inhabitants that the lord king and the entire Christian army had fallen in battle. They represented as clear proof that the citizens could see and recognize the very well-known arms of his familiars and household servants. Hearing this, the citizens and the queen who was in the city, believing the report true, gave themselves over to lamentation. Taking counsel with the elders and those of more practiced judgment, they believed there was but one remedy: to send an embassy [Col. 0471D] to Lord Tancred, prince of Antioch, asking him to hasten to the aid of the endangered kingdom, now deprived of its ruler, since, after God, all the hope of the faithful people rested in him.

But the king, having spent that night in the open country, when daylight had returned to the earth, recalled his victorious troops and set out toward Joppa. As they were proceeding, they encountered our men who, on the preceding night, had terrified the city by their disastrous report. Seeing our forces, these men thought them to be their own companies, for they held it virtually certain that our army had been entirely destroyed the day before. Approaching all the more confidently, they had almost thrown themselves into our ranks when the lord king, exhorting his men and himself charging first against them, drew after him a headlong body of horsemen. All of these, fighting unanimously for their lives, pressed the enemy bravely; having hemmed them in closely, they dealt with them by the sword and allowed none anywhere to escape. Thus, after very many of them had been killed, and the remainder had turned to flight out of fear of death, our men, rejoicing and giving thanks to the Lord, laden with spoils and enriched with the enemy’s goods, completed the journey they had begun, hastening toward Joppa.

But the people of Joppa, shaken in spirit by what they had heard, when they saw our ranks returning, as though awakened from a heavy sleep, opened the gates with tears of joy. They went out to meet them, explaining what sorrowful reports they had heard concerning them, and into how deep an abyss of despair they had fallen. Having entered the city, they kept a joyful and festive [Col. 0472B] day, recounting to one another how great was the mercy the Lord had shown them.

When the lord king learned how the queen and those about her, in the mental anguish which they had suffered through the extremity of fear, had written to Lord Tancred, he sent a messenger with all speed and by letter informed that distinguished prince—anxious for the kingdom’s misfortune and already equipped for the journey—of his remarkable success. Receiving the messenger, Tancred, exulting and rejoicing at the lord king’s victory, rendered boundless thanks to the Creator.

## CHAPTER XIX. The princes who had newly arrived take Tortosa and, after taking it, hand it over to the count of Toulouse; then they hasten to Jerusalem; the king goes out to meet them as far as Beirut.

[Col. 0472C]

Meanwhile, those princes of whom we had previously made mention, who in the regions of Romania had lost so great an army through a disastrous misfortune, as we have said, arrived at Antioch. Proceeding thence, they handed over to Lord Raymond, count of Toulouse, the city of Tortosa, which, as was stated above, had been cleared of the enemy.

As they hastened toward Jerusalem, lest their journey perhaps be impeded at the River Canis, the king went out to meet them with troops he had taken with him and secured the difficult passes. Nor was what he undertook for their sake insignificant: before he reached the place mentioned, he had to pass by four noble and populous enemy cities—Ptolemais, Tyre, Sidon, and Beirut. While therefore the lord king with his men held the difficult passage, there arrived the illustrious men: Lord William, count of Poitiers and likewise duke of Aquitaine; Lord Stephen, count of Blois; Lord Stephen, count of Burgundy; Lord Geoffrey, count of Vendôme; Lord Hugh, brother of Lord Raymond, count of Toulouse, lord of Lusignan; and many other nobles. They were exceedingly glad and joyful, both because they found open the route which they had long regarded as exceedingly dangerous, and because they found the lord king coming to meet them.

Meeting one another, they rushed into mutual embraces; after exchanging words of greeting, they joined in kisses of peace, refreshing themselves with reciprocal conversation, [Col. 0473A] so that they seemed already forgetful alike of their labors and losses, as though they had suffered no adversity. Taking them with him and treating them kindly according to the laws of humanity and with full charity, the king brought them to Jerusalem. Since the Paschal solemnity was near, when the festival days there had passed, they reached Joppa, intending, as it were, to return to their homeland. There the lord count of Poitiers, who was under great financial pressure, likewise embarked on a ship and arrived quite safely in his own country. Both Stephens likewise embarked; but after being long and greatly tossed about at sea and driven by contrary winds, they were compelled to return to Joppa.

## CHAPTER XX. The Egyptians enter our territories with innumerable forces. The king meets them, fights them too rashly, and is defeated.

[Col. 0473B]

While all these remained there together, the men of Ascalon, joined by those Egyptians who had escaped from the aforesaid battle, assembled a great army, said to amount to twenty thousand men, and entered our territory around Lydda, Saurona, and Ramla. When this was reported to the lord king, he behaved, contrary to his usual manner, with excessive imprudence. He summoned no military forces from the neighboring cities, but relied upon his own strength; nor did he wait even for those who were with him in the city. Hurrying with excessive haste—indeed, rashly—he left the city with scarcely two hundred knights.

The noblemen, however, borrowing horses [Col. 0473C] from friends and relatives, judged it disgraceful that they should remain at leisure amid so great an emergency and not share in their brothers’ hardships. They went out together, following the lord king. But the king, who had too heedlessly gone far ahead of the others, when he beheld the enemy’s legions and marvelled at their number, began to repent of what he had done, reflecting upon the truth of the saying:

> “Impulse manages all things badly.”  
> —Statius

He wished he had not come; but he had so deeply plunged into the enemy’s ranks that neither shame nor the danger of death now urged retreat upon him. Those in the enemy army who were more prudent and had greater military experience, seeing our men advancing contrary to custom without formations of infantry and with their squadrons of horse confused, having set aside military order, began to have greater hope of victory. Becoming bolder, they formed their lines in order and rushed upon our men in a single attack, pressing them all the more spiritedly because they saw that our men had more completely neglected their customary order.

Overwhelmed by the powerful onset of so great a multitude and unable to bear the weight of battle, our men, after many had been slain, turned to flight. Yet those who fell in the conflict left the enemy a bloody victory over themselves: fighting bravely to their last strength, they cut down many of the enemy at close quarters with their swords and had almost driven the remainder, their formations broken, into [Col. 0474A] flight. But then, recovering courage, considering our small number and their own multitude, and exhorting one another, they again threw themselves in with greater violence and, as we have said, put our men to flight. Those who escaped unhurt withdrew to the town of Ramla, believing that there they had found safety.

In that battle both Counts Stephen fell, along with other nobles whose number and names we do not possess. We ought, it seems to us, to rejoice for this noble man, illustrious among his own people both by nobility of blood and magnificence of deeds: namely Lord Stephen, count of Chartres. For it is certain that the Lord, according to His great mercy, dealt with him in such a way as to allow him, by an excellent end, to erase the old stain of disgrace which he had miserably incurred by fleeing the Antiochene expedition. Henceforth that which he redeemed by so fortunate an end will deservedly not be reckoned against him as a blemish. For we believe that those who are said to fall while fighting for Christ’s name, in the battle-line of the faithful and in Christian warfare, merit not only the complete removal of disgrace but also the complete remission of sins and offenses.

## CHAPTER XXI. The king, fleeing from the battle, takes refuge in the fortress of Ramla; through the help of a certain Arab he is rescued, while others are killed there.

The king, although he placed little confidence in the town’s fortification, nevertheless withdrew inside the stronghold with others in order to avoid the imminent danger of death, seeing that, surrounded by enemy ranks, no other means of escape was open to him. While all night long he was anxious for his life and safety, consumed by heavy cares, behold, in the silence of deepest night, slipping away from the enemy army, there came to the town’s vicinity, alone and without attendants, that aforesaid noble prince of Arabia, to whose wife, as we have related, the lord king had shown such humanity a short time before. Mindful indeed of the benefit conferred and avoiding the sin of ingratitude, he spoke in a subdued voice to those on the wall, saying: “I bear more secret words for the lord king; arrange for me to be brought before him, for it is expedient.”

When this had been reported to the lord king, he admitted his message and ordered him to be brought in. Once admitted, the man disclosed to the king who he was, [Col. 0474D] recalled the benefit he had received from him in the person of his wife, and declared himself, on that account, perpetually bound to return a like service. He instructed the king to leave the garrison, revealing the enemy’s plan: at dawn they intended to surround the fortress with a siege and condemn all found inside to death. Accordingly, he urged the lord king to go out with him, promising that, with God as author and as one acquainted with the country, he would place him safely beyond danger without difficulty.

At last the king went out with him, attended by very few, lest by drawing a larger crowd he might stir up the enemy army against himself. Following him, he climbed into the mountains. There the aforesaid nobleman left him and returned to the enemy’s expeditionary force, promising his service and ready devotion at a suitable time. The enemy, however, having gained the victory, surrounded with a siege and assailed from every side the men who had withdrawn into the town. They seized them by force and, treating them as they pleased, put some to death and bound others in fetters, consigning them to perpetual slavery.

It is not recorded that, up to that day, so great a slaughter of noble and valiant men had occurred in the kingdom. The kingdom was almost thrown into confusion, and everyone’s strength was broken; the hearts of prudent men melted within them. Unless the Dayspring from on high had swiftly visited them in mercy (Luke 1), they were ready, falling into the abyss of despair, to abandon the kingdom. For our people were few, [Col. 0475B] and they could not safely reach the East from overseas, fearing the many hostile coastal cities lying on both right and left. As we have said, from Laodicea of Syria to the remotest borders of Egypt, our people held only two coastal cities: Joppa and newly captured Caesarea. Those who did arrive, after completing their prayers, immediately returned, seeing the weakness and near collapse of our people and fearing to be involved with them in their common disasters.

## CHAPTER XXII. The king, fleeing by byways, reaches Arsuf, then Joppa. Men from throughout the kingdom assemble to aid the king; battle is joined with the enemy, and our side emerges victorious.

[Col. 0475C]

The king, therefore, fleeing into the mountains as stated above, separated from his companions on the road, was saved by the swiftness of his horse and the guidance of the aforesaid nobleman. All night he hid trembling in deserted places. At daybreak, accompanied by two companions whom chance had provided, he followed out-of-the-way routes through the midst of enemy ambushes and reached Arsuf. There he was joyfully received by his men who were in that town and, having taken food, recovered strength; for as he traveled he had nearly collapsed from hunger and thirst.

Something that seems divinely arranged also happened to him. That same day, scarcely an hour before, a very great number of the enemy had withdrawn from the town; all day without interruption they had waged war before its gates against the townspeople. Had the king found them still holding that place when he arrived, he could scarcely have escaped their hands. Meanwhile varying reports concerning the king were circulating. For the few who had escaped from the battle, arriving in Jerusalem, declared that the king had fallen among the rest. The bishop of Lydda, who, after hearing of and almost seeing the slaughter of those captured in the Ramla garrison, had left his church and fled to Joppa, when asked about the king confessed that he knew absolutely nothing. Yet he firmly declared that those who had taken refuge in the stronghold had miserably ended their lives; nor did he deny that he himself had secretly escaped by flight in order to preserve his life.

Thus throughout the whole kingdom, wherever this report reached, there was mourning everywhere, groaning and tears everywhere; everyone despaired of life and wished for a swift death, lest they see the evils of their people and behold the desolation of the kingdom. When grief, mourning, and sighing had thus occupied the whole kingdom, behold, the king, shining like the morning star amid the mist, came out from Antipatris and suddenly reached Joppa by ship. There, received by the citizens with joy, he drove away the darkness of their unexpected calamity and brought serenity, his presence wiping out whatever misfortune had occurred. This report therefore went out through all the borders of the kingdom; those whom the first rumor had cast down in spirit the second raised to good hope.

Meanwhile Lord Hugh of Saint-Omer, lord of Tiberias, warned by the Jerusalemites to assist the lord king, had arrived at Arsuf with eighty knights to give the king aid. Hearing this, the king took with him those whom he could find at Joppa and went to meet him, fearing that the enemy, freely scattered through the country, might lay ambushes for them as they approached, or might gather forces and openly endeavor to block their route. Meeting them, therefore, and joining them in many joyful embraces, they united their companies and entered Joppa amid great rejoicing by the citizens. Messengers were then sent, and he urged those in the mountains to come to his aid. They assembled promptly and, because the enemy more freely held the intervening country, followed indirect routes; within a few days they reached Arsuf. From there, though with difficulty and at peril of their lives, as enemies met them on the way, they reached Joppa with God’s help.

[Col. 0476C] The knights who had newly arrived were of mixed quality, about ninety in number. Having received them, the lord king was encouraged to good hope. Seeking to repay the injuries the enemy had inflicted and to return their evils with interest, he properly equipped and, according to military discipline, arranged both squadrons of horse and companies of infantry. Relying upon the Lord’s aid, he went out to meet the enemy, making light of their multitude.

The enemy were nearby, about three miles away, weaving together hurdles, ladders, and machines of various kinds from selected timber. They intended—and regarded it as easy—to attack the hostile city and capture the king, besieged within it with all the citizens, like worthless slaves. While they were busily engaged in this work, behold, the king was already present with his army. Seeing that they were being voluntarily challenged to battle by men whom they had considered defeated, the enemy seized their weapons and prepared to meet them, fearing nothing from those whom they thought completely exhausted.

Yet when our men charged, ready to repay double for all that they had suffered, fighting with all their strength for wives and children, for liberty and fatherland, like lions whose anger is fiercer when their cubs have been taken, strength being poured upon them from above and divine grace going before them, they shattered the enemy’s ranks with the sword. Having killed very many of them, they compelled the rest disgracefully to take flight. It did not seem expedient for our men to pursue longer, [Col. 0477A] because of their small numbers. Instead, returning to the enemy camp, they gathered abundant booty—asses, camels, pavilions and tents, provisions, and various kinds of food—and returned victoriously to Joppa while all the people applauded. The kingdom then rested for about seven months.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Meanwhile Tancred brings the most noble cities of Apamea and Laodicea under his rule.

While these various and manifold events were thus taking place in the kingdom, Lord Tancred, an illustrious man, gathered troops from all his domains and summoned forces both of horse and foot; he besieged Apamea, the noble seat and metropolis of Coele-Syria. There, after he had for some time persevered with the due effort of an excellent prince, employing every means by which enemy strongholds are usually overcome and omitting none of the measures which customarily inflict more grievous distress upon besieged persons, through laborious exertion and unflagging diligence, divine mercy going before him, he gained possession of the city and extended the borders of his principality immensely.

Thence, on the same day, it is said, he reached Laodicea, which was held by Greeks, and brought it under his authority, pursuant to earlier terms agreed between himself and the Laodiceans: on whatever day he should lay claim to Apamea, they would on that same day surrender Laodicea to him without difficulty. Both these most noble cities are recorded to have been founded by Antiochus, son of Seleucus, who gave the cities the names of his daughters, one called Apamea and the other Laodicea.

But our discussion here concerns Laodicea in Syria. There is another Laodicea, numbered among the seven cities of Asia Minor, as is written in the Apocalypse of John:

> “What you see, write in a book and send it to the seven churches: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea.”  
> (Revelation 1:11)

The latter Laodicea was made a colony by the deified Severus, according to Ulpian, who says of it in the *Digest*, under the title *On Censuses*: “There is also Laodicea in Syria, to which the deified Severus granted Italian law because of its services in the civil war.” Thus, with its lord advancing his affairs, Tancred accomplished in a single expedition what was the work of many days, receiving at once two cities [Col. 0477D] whose broad, widely spread territories included many towns and suburban districts. He was indeed a man who loved God and was beloved by God, distinguished by faith, conspicuous for vigor, pleasing to the people through his merits, and successful in all things.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Baldwin of Le Bourg, count of Edessa, marries the daughter of Duke Gabriel.

Lord Baldwin, count of Edessa, likewise a magnificent and wholly praiseworthy man, who, as stated above, had succeeded the lord king in the county of Edessa, administered the land subject to him energetically and successfully, being greatly feared and dreaded by the surrounding enemies. Since he had neither wife nor children, he married Morsia, daughter of a certain Gabriel, duke of Melitene, [Col. 0478A] of whom we have made mention above, and received with her a large and very necessary sum of money as dowry. The aforesaid Gabriel was Armenian by nation, language, and dress, but Greek in faith.

It happened that, while Baldwin was in a most favorable position and enjoying complete tranquility, a cousin of his, namely Joscelin of Courtenay, a nobleman from France, from the region called Gâtinais, came to him. Since Joscelin possessed no land or property, Baldwin granted him very extensive holdings, so that he would not be compelled to turn aside to some unknown person to seek a benefice. He gave him the whole part of his territory lying about the great River Euphrates, in which were the cities of Coritium and Tulupa; and the large, strongly fortified towns of Turbessel, Hamtap, and Ravendel, with certain others. Baldwin retained for himself the territory beyond the Euphrates, nearer to the enemy, keeping only one city from its inland districts, namely Samosata.

He was a man endowed with worldly prudence and circumspect in affairs; very provident in the care and management of his household; an excellent master of a household and provider of useful things; generous where necessity required, but otherwise moderately sparing; a most diligent guardian of household goods; sober in taking food; and little concerned with the dress and adornment of his own body. Thus he managed with great industry the aforesaid portion of territory liberally granted him by the lord count, and abounded in every good thing.

## CHAPTER XXV. Bohemond, freed from the enemy’s chains, returns to Antioch and kindly receives the patriarch Daimbert, who has fled to him.

[Col. 0478C]

At the same time Lord Bohemond, prince of Antioch, a magnificent and wholly praiseworthy man, upon whom divine grace looked favorably, returned to Antioch after four years in which he had been held in the enemy’s chains, having been ransomed for a price. There he was gratefully received by the lord patriarch, the clergy, and all the people; by his long-desired arrival he gladdened the whole province and likewise the kingdom.

Learning how prudently and faithfully his kinsman Lord Tancred had administered the principality entrusted to him in Bohemond’s absence and had vigorously extended its borders by taking two outstanding cities, Bohemond gave him immense thanks and treated him kindly. He granted to him and his heirs, to possess in perpetuity, a very large part of the region, as his merits seemed to require. Not long afterwards, as will be said below, he entrusted the entire principality to him.

Meanwhile Arnulf, the Jerusalemite archdeacon of whom we have spoken above, according to his custom sowed scandals between the king and Lord Patriarch Daimbert and fostered hatred. The enmity between them, formerly seeming to have been quieted, began to spring up again. Their indignation against each other grew to such a degree that, after the clergy had been stirred against him through the labor and contrivance of that same deceiver, the religious man and lover of peace, unable to bear continual vexations, left both church and city. Destitute and poor, in need alike of counsel and assistance, he fled to Lord Bohemond. Bohemond honorably received him on his arrival and was moved to all the greater mercy toward him because he knew that Daimbert’s care and efforts had advanced him to the church of Jerusalem. So that he should not remain with him in any condition unworthy of so great a man, Bohemond generously assigned him the church of Saint Gregory, situated within the city of Antioch, with immense estates and many revenues, with the consent of Lord Bernard, patriarch of that place. Daimbert remained there continuously with him until his passage into Apulia, as will be related below.

## CHAPTER XXVI. After Daimbert’s expulsion, a certain Ebremar is irregularly appointed at Jerusalem. The king besieges Ptolemais but gains nothing; on his return he is mortally wounded.

[Col. 0479B]

But the king, led astray by the wickedness of the aforesaid Arnulf, set aside fear of God and, after expelling Lord Patriarch Daimbert, proceeded to do something still worse. He deceived a certain simple and religious priest named Ebremar and intruded him into the patriarchal see. This simple man had come on the first expedition and was acceptable to all because of the uprightness of his manner of life. Yet in this matter he was found to possess exceedingly gross and complacent ignorance: while the lord patriarch was alive, he believed that he was permitted to usurp his see.

In the same year, 1103 from the Incarnation of the Lord, about the beginning of spring, after the solemnity of the Lord’s Resurrection had been celebrated at Jerusalem, the lord king summoned military forces from throughout the kingdom and besieged Ptolemais. Ptolemais is a maritime city of the province of Phoenicia, one of the suffragan cities subject to the metropolitan see of Tyre. It has a harbor both within and outside its walls, where it can provide ships with a calm anchorage. It is also quite conveniently situated between mountains and sea, possessing rich and excellent farmland, while the River Belus flows past the city.

A widespread tradition says that the twin brothers Ptolemy and Accon founded and fortified it with strong walls, then divided it, as it were, through the middle and named the parts after themselves. Hence even today it bears two names, being called Ptolemais and Accon, just as almost all Syrian cities have two or three names. The lord king therefore arrived there with his forces. Since he had no naval army, he could not greatly pressure it toward surrender. But after cutting down the orchards around it, killing some of its inhabitants, and carrying off the flocks and herds found outside the city as booty, he lifted the siege and was returning home.

Wishing to return by way of Caesarea, he encountered, at a place called the Cut Rock, near ancient Tyre, between the coastal towns of Capharnaum and Dora—today called the District—robbers and breakers of public roads. Charging violently upon them as they lay in ambush, he killed many while others escaped by flight. By chance, however, one man hurled a javelin at the king; the weapon entered from behind through the lattice of his ribs, near his heart, and by the blow almost delivered him to death. Yet through the diligent attention of physicians, after incisions and cauterizations, he obtained some measure of recovery, though he was permanently afflicted by pain from that wound, which returned at certain intervals.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Before the city of Tripoli, the count of Toulouse builds a fortress called Mount Pilgrim.

At the same time Lord Raymond, count of Toulouse of blessed memory, having gained possession of the city commonly called Tortosa, as stated above, vigorously and most bravely extended his borders in every direction, as an outstanding, magnificent man and a true worshipper of God. Concerned with driving the enemies of the Christian name from those territories, he founded a stronghold on a hill before the city of Tripoli, scarcely two miles from it. Because it was established by pilgrims, he gave it a name derived from that fact, so that it should forever be called Mount Pilgrim (*Mons Peregrinus*); and to this day it retains the name imposed by its founder. It was well fortified both by its natural position and by the skill of craftsmen.

From there he continually inflicted hardships on the citizens of Tripoli almost every day, so that the inhabitants of the entire district and even the inhabitants of the city itself paid him annual tribute. Nor did they obey him less in everything than if he possessed the city itself without opposition. In that place there was born to him by his lawful wife, a woman devoted to God, a son called Amphossus after his ancestors, who later succeeded him in the county of Toulouse.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The king besieges Ptolemais again; relying upon Genoese assistance, he takes the besieged city by force.

In the year 1104 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in May, the same lord king, having summoned all forces and all the people, from the least to the greatest, hastened to besiege once more the Ptolemais mentioned above. The chief occasion for this was that, at the same time, a Genoese fleet had arrived in Syrian waters, numbering seventy beaked vessels, commonly called galleys. When the king learned this, he immediately sent an embassy to the consuls and invited them in friendly words to serve Christ before returning home. He also set before them the familiar example of their fellow citizens, through whose effort and work he had brought the city of Caesarea into the kingdom, not without enduring glory for the Genoese citizens and no small gain.

At length, prudent men intervening and faithfully seeking to bring the matter to completion, the Genoese gave this answer: if one third of the revenues and dues collected from maritime traffic in the harbor were granted to them in perpetuity, and if in the city they were given a church and, in a quarter, full jurisdiction, they would labor faithfully to take the aforesaid city. These terms pleased the lord king and his princes; strengthened by the bond of faith, they were recorded in writing by both sides for perpetual remembrance.

On the appointed day, therefore, the Genoese by sea and the lord king with his men by land, having pitched camps in a circuit, enclosed the aforesaid city in siege. They prevented the citizens from entering or leaving and inflicted upon them the kinds and degrees of hardship customarily imposed upon besieged persons. They also set up engines around it, such as ingenious minds devise for the destruction of enemies, battering the towers and walls with them and breaking even the inner buildings by launching great millstones. Moreover, harassed by repeated engagements both from the fleet along the seashore and from the opposite side by the royal army, and with many citizens killed in various incidents, they found it hard to withstand the besiegers’ persistence and frequent assaults.

After twenty continuous days in which our men had labored hard in attacking and the others in repelling injuries from themselves, terms were proposed: those wishing to depart would have free passage, with wives, children, and movable goods, to whatever regions they chose; while those wishing to remain in their houses and not abandon their native soil would enjoy favorable conditions on payment each year of a fixed due to the lord king. They surrendered the city to the king. Once it had been taken, he assigned the Genoese possessions and dwellings according to each man’s merit. Then for the first time those arriving by sea enjoyed secure tranquility, a more convenient harbor having been acquired and the coast being somewhat cleared of enemies.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Carrhae of Mesopotamia is besieged by Tancred, Baldwin, and others. The citizens, compelled by famine, take counsel concerning surrender of the city.

[Col. 0481C]

In the same year, Lord Bohemond, together with all the magnates of that province, and likewise Lord Tancred, as well as Lord Baldwin, count of Edessa, together with his kinsman Lord Joscelin, met one another and pledged their faith that, crossing the Euphrates, they would besiege the city of Carrhae, neighbouring Edessa and held by the unbelievers. In accordance with this plan, summoning military forces competitively from their own lands and gathering aid from every quarter, they crossed the Euphrates on the appointed day and arrived at Edessa. [Col. 0481D]

Present also on that ill-fated expedition were venerable men and eminent lights of the Church: Lord Bernard, patriarch of Antioch; Lord Daimbert, patriarch of Jerusalem, who was then staying at Antioch as a wanderer, exile, and fugitive; and Lord Benedict, archbishop of Edessa. All these, assembled at the aforesaid city and striving to carry their purpose into effect, reached the appointed place with their armies.

Carrhae, according to ancient histories, is the place to which Terah, fleeing from Ur of the Chaldeans and hastening toward the land of Canaan, brought Abraham his son and Lot his grandson through his son Haran, and dwelt there, as is contained in the Book of Genesis (ch. 11). There he himself died; and there Abraham received the Lord’s answer that, leaving his land and his kindred, he should follow the Lord’s promises. It is also the place where Crassus, dictator of the Romans, drank the gold for which he had thirsted, when the Parthians offered it to him.

When they arrived, they enclosed the city in siege, as they had originally intended. Nor was it greatly necessary to assault it otherwise than by preventing the citizens’ entrance and exit, for they had little—indeed almost no—food within. The cause of this scarcity was that Lord Baldwin had long laboured to bring the inhabitants of that place into want, so that, tormented at last by hunger, they might surrender the city to him. The method by which he sought to accomplish this purpose seemed suitable to him.

Between Edessa [Col. 0482B] and the aforesaid city, which are scarcely fourteen miles apart, a river runs between them. Drawn off through channels, its irrigation made the surrounding plain rich and fertile in crops. From ancient times the land in question had had this division: what lay on this side of the river belonged peacefully to the Edessans, whereas the people of Carrhae possessed as their own what lay beyond it. Lord Baldwin saw that no food at all reached the enemy city from outside, but that they derived their entire subsistence from those common lands. He therefore preferred to forgo this advantage himself rather than permit the enemy—who could not conveniently obtain supplies elsewhere—to be fed from the intervening territory. By frequent raids he had long before prevented cultivation on his own lands, hoping that he could provide his citizens with a sufficient food supply from the region beyond the Euphrates and from the territory lying between Edessa and that river. Meanwhile, deprived of the advantage which they had customarily obtained from the aforesaid common lands, the people of Carrhae would be driven into intolerable want—as the outcome indeed clearly showed. He had already imposed this prohibition several years earlier.

Thus, when they besieged the aforesaid city, as we have said, they found it suffering from a severe lack of provisions. Yet the citizens, having learned far in advance of our men’s arrival, had through messengers and letters appealed to the princes of the East, declaring that unless help came swiftly, [Col. 0482D] they were ready to surrender. But, seeing that no assistance was supplied to them from that quarter and that the pressure of famine troubled them more severely each day, they took counsel together and chose rather to yield up the city than waste away within from hunger and melt away through lack of food.

## CHAPTER XXX. Our men, disputing over dominion of the city, lose it; the citizens receive supplies; battle is joined there; our men are defeated, and a disaster most dangerous to our side occurs.

They therefore came out and surrendered themselves into the hands of the besiegers without any condition. But envy spurred on contention among the princes; and while Lord Prince Bohemond and [Col. 0483A] Lord Count Baldwin disputed with one another as to which of them the city should be delivered, and whose banner should first be brought into the city, they delayed occupying the surrendered city until morning, so that they might deliberate more fully concerning that frivolous question.

Thus they learned by experience how true is the saying:

> Delay brings danger with it;

and again:

> It harmed those who were ready to delay.

For before the next day had dawned, so vast a multitude of enemies arrived, and so numerous and formidable an army of Turks, that our men despaired even of their lives. Those who came brought with them an unlimited quantity of provisions. They had prudently and cunningly agreed among themselves to divide into two divisions: while one fought against our men, whatever the outcome, favourable or adverse, the other would bring provisions into the city.

And so it happened. For as soon as the day had advanced somewhat, the leaders of the opposing side marshalled their troops and drew up their battle-lines, as though about to fight immediately, setting apart those entrusted with the care of the baggage. Yet those preparing for battle entertained no hope either of winning victory or of resisting for long. It seemed sufficient for their purpose alone if, while our men were occupied with them, the besieged citizens could receive the food brought to them.

When our princes saw the enemy preparing for battle, they too arranged their lines and troops in proper order. Both patriarchs endeavoured by exhortatory speeches to add courage to the soldiers; but, deprived of the Lord’s grace, they were helped neither by words nor by admonitions. For at the very first encounter [Col. 0484A] their enemies gained the upper hand, and our men shamefully turned their backs upon the enemy. Abandoning camp and baggage, they sought safety in flight, but could not find it. The enemy, casting aside their bows and neglecting their use, pressed on with swords and almost annihilated them all by slaughter.

The count of Edessa and his kinsman Lord Joscelin were captured there, bound in chains, and carried away into more distant enemy lands. But Lord Bohemond, together with Lord Tancred and both patriarchs, escaped the tumult of battle and, carefully avoiding short routes, reached Edessa unharmed. The archbishop of that place, however, being a simple man, became entangled in the fighting crowds and, bound and chained, increased the number of captives. [Col. 0484B]

It happened that a certain Christian, assigned to guard him, was moved by the bowels of charity once he learned that he was a bishop. Setting his own life in place of the other’s life, he allowed him to depart unharmed. Protected by the Lord, the archbishop at last returned to Edessa within a few days and was received with great rejoicing by the citizens.

Meanwhile, while the prince was still staying at Edessa, he heard that, as sins required, the count had been taken prisoner. With the citizens’ consent, he entrusted the city and the whole region to Lord Tancred for safekeeping, on the condition that, when Lord Count Baldwin returned from prison, Tancred should immediately surrender it to him without difficulty. The prince himself took Lord Joscelin’s land into his own care. Neither before nor afterward, throughout the whole East during the time of Latin rule, is there recorded anywhere a battle so dangerous, a slaughter of brave men so great, or a flight of our people so disgraceful. [Col. 0484C]

# BOOK ELEVEN BEGINS.

[Col. 0483]

## CHAPTER I. Bohemond, prince of Antioch, entrusts the principality to Tancred, crosses the sea, hastens to France, and marries the daughter of the king of the Franks. The patriarch of Jerusalem goes to Rome. The king abandons his lawful wife without examination of the case.

[Col. 0483C]

After the summer had passed, Lord Bohemond, burdened by a heavy load of debt, sought to prepare himself to repay what he owed and to bring back with him from overseas greater forces of soldiers. He therefore entrusted the care and general administration of his principality, with full jurisdiction, to his beloved kinsman Lord Tancred, and sailed to Apulia; Lord Daimbert, patriarch of Jerusalem, went with him. [Col. 0483D]

After reaching Apulia and remaining a short time in his own region, Bohemond took an honourable company of his followers, crossed the Alps, and came to Lord Philip, the illustrious king of the Franks. Among other things, he obtained two of Philip’s daughters from him. One, born of legitimate marriage and named Constance, he joined to himself as wife by a marriage alliance. The other, named Cecilia, had been borne to the same king by the countess of Anjou—who, despising her husband, had gone over to the king—while his wife was still alive. Bohemond sent her from Apulia to be the wife of his nephew Lord Tancred. [Col. 0484C–D]

When his affairs with that king and in the other regions beyond the mountains had been completed, he returned again to Apulia with a vast multitude of horsemen and foot-soldiers wishing to cross the sea. Lord Daimbert, however, went to the Roman Church and set forth the extent of the wrongs he had suffered, fully revealing at the same time Arnulf’s highly effective malice and the king’s hostile purpose, by which he sought to humble the Church of God. He moved all to compassion for himself and obtained the favour of everyone.

The king had committed not only the enormous offence, contrary to ecclesiastical discipline, which we mentioned above in connection with Lord Patriarch Daimbert. He had also dismissed, without examination of the case, his lawful wife—the woman whom he had married at Edessa while he was count there—though she had neither been convicted nor confessed, disregarding the law of marriage. He forcibly compelled her to become a nun in the monastery of Saint Anne, mother of the Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary. [Col. 0485A]

This place is in Jerusalem, on the eastern side, near the gate called Jehoshaphat, beside the pool which in ancient times was called the Sheep Pool. There is shown the crypt in which, according to ancient tradition, Joachim and the aforesaid Anne had their dwelling; and there the perpetual Virgin is said to have been born. Three or four poor little women, professing the monastic life, were there; because of the wife who was brought in, their possessions were enlarged and their patrimony expanded.

Various accounts circulated among different persons concerning why he had separated from his wife. Some said that the lord king dismissed her so that, by taking a wealthier and nobler wife, he might improve his position and relieve the poverty under which he was heavily oppressed by obtaining wealth elsewhere in the form of a dowry. Others asserted that the queen, being imprudent and insufficiently discreet, had observed the obligations of the marriage-bed with too little caution. [Col. 0485B]

Although she had at first seemed gladly to assume the religious habit and, in the first period of her conversion, had appeared to live quite honourably in that monastery, she eventually seized an opportunity offered by contrived frauds. Going to the king, she obtained permission, on the ground of the needs of her monastery, to visit her kinsfolk who were at Constantinople, in order to relieve its poverty. Under that pretext she left the kingdom and began to devote herself wholly to filth and impurity. Casting off the religious habit, she prostituted herself to every passer-by, sparing neither her own reputation nor showing reverence for the royal dignity which she had possessed. [Col. 0485C]

## CHAPTER II. Lord Raymond, count of Toulouse, dies. His nephew William Jordan succeeds him. Rodwan, a great Turkish prince, enters our territories; Tancred meets him and puts him to shameful flight.

In the following year, which was 1195 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Lord Raymond of blessed memory, count of Toulouse—a religious man who feared God, altogether praiseworthy, whose admirable deeds and life distinguished by virtues deserve a special treatment—entered the way of all flesh as a true confessor of Christ, on the day before the Kalends of March [28 February]. He died in his town which he himself had founded before the city of Tripoli, called Mount Pilgrim. [Col. 0485D]

His nephew William Jordan succeeded him in the same concern of the siege. In that work he laboured energetically and manfully until the arrival of Count Bertrand, until, after suffering a dispute concerning the same matter, he withdrew somewhat from the enterprise, as will be related below.

We believe that the steadfastness of spirit of this venerable man, admirable indeed and worthy of praise to those present and future alike, was exceptional: once he had undertaken the pilgrimage for Christ, he did not disdain patiently to bear it until the final end of his life. Although in his own country, as an illustrious and very powerful man with a very extensive patrimony, he could have abounded in every good thing according to his desires, he chose rather to be lowly in the Lord’s service, leaving his land and kindred, than to abound in sinners’ tents among his own people. [Col. 0486A]

For the other princes who had professed the same pilgrimage, once the holy city had been restored to freedom, returned to their own lands as though they had attained the fulfilment of their vows. But he feared to lay down the cross which he had once taken up. Though his familiars and household urged him strongly, now that he had fulfilled his vow, to return to the homeland that desired him, he preferred to offer himself as a burnt offering to the Lord rather than give himself over to worldly allurements. He imitated his master, who, when told, “Come down from the cross” (Matthew 27:40), preferred, once his passion had been completed, to be taken down by others’ hands rather than abandon the purpose of our salvation which he had begun. [Col. 0486B]

In the same year Rodwan, a very powerful man and lord of Aleppo, summoned aid from neighbouring regions by both entreaty and payment. Entering the territory of Antioch in great numbers, he terrorized the whole region with raids and harassed it with frequent burnings. When Lord Tancred heard this, he summoned his forces and military troops of both cavalry and infantry and marched to meet him where reliable report had learned that he had assembled his troops.

Tancred therefore left Antioch and directed his army toward Artah. [Col. 0486C] On arriving there, he found the enemy’s immense multitude, as had been reported to him. Invoking aid from above and obtaining it according to his merits, he charged them bravely. They attempted at first to resist, but soon fell into disorder and were driven into flight. Countless enemies were slain and many captured; the banner of the aforesaid Rodwan was taken. Rodwan himself, to preserve his life, had been the first to flee. And, much to the consolation of our men, as compensation for those whom they had often lost in similar affairs, they claimed for themselves many excellent horses, violently taking them from the enemy after throwing down their riders.

## CHAPTER III. The Egyptians pour into the kingdom with immense forces; the king meets them, captures some, kills many, and puts the rest to flight.

[Col. 0486D]

In the same year, certain of the Egyptian caliph’s princes came to him and said:

> That people of pilgrims, who in recent times violently entered your kingdom and, prodigal of their own lives, have hitherto resisted the commanders sent by you, acquired this boldness through confidence in the multitude which the earlier army had brought in. But now, since the greater part of them have returned home and they have been deprived of the support of incoming pilgrims, they have become fewer, their resources having been wholly exhausted by frequent expeditions. Therefore it seems expedient to us, if it likewise seems good to your majesty, that you send one chosen from among your great men to those regions, to free that land, occupied by that unhappy people.

The speech pleased the caliph and seemed excellent in his sight. Ordering a huge army to be gathered and a very large fleet prepared, and appointing leaders separately for each force, he sent them into Syria. When they reached Ascalon, they brought great terror upon the entire kingdom. [Col. 0487A]

Hearing this, the king swiftly reached Joppa with all the forces of the kingdom. By public proclamation he commanded all persons from every city to assemble there without delay. Those who had been summoned therefore arrived with all speed, including Lord Ebremar, patriarch of Jerusalem, who likewise came carrying with him the saving wood of the life-giving Cross. When they had assembled and our numbers were counted, they were found to have five hundred horsemen and two thousand foot-soldiers. The enemy, however, were said to number fifteen thousand, apart from those serving in the fleet. [Col. 0487B]

Leaving Ascalon, they commanded the fleet to hasten toward Joppa. They themselves, passing through Ashdod, divided into two bodies. They ordered one to proceed toward Ramla and provoke the lord king to battle, while the other hastened to Joppa, so that, while the king was occupied against the first, it might attack that city with those who had by then arrived there in the fleet.

Accordingly, according to the plan just described, the army was divided in two. One part entered the district of Ramla and, drawing up battle-lines, gave clear evidence of its arrival by the blare of trumpets and the din of drums. This was intentionally done in order that, by drawing the lord king and his forces against themselves, the other division, following the coast, might safely reach Joppa. But their plans came to nothing. For when they saw the king and his army drawing near, their hearts melted under the pressure of fear. Recalling the other division, they scarcely believed they still had enough men to escape his hands. [Col. 0487C]

The opposing forces therefore came together. The king, charging with his men against the enemy, pressed them more vigorously. Encouraging his battle-lines both by word and example, he redoubled their strength. Lord Patriarch Ebremar displayed the life-giving wood of the Cross to those about to fight, ran through the ranks, and admonished and exhorted them to remember him who wished to accomplish salvation for us sinners upon that same wood. He also commanded them, for the remission of sins, to fight bravely against the enemies of the Christian name and faith, expecting their reward from him who is accustomed to repay his own a hundredfold. [Col. 0487D]

Thus our men became more courageous and pressed the enemy more fiercely. Calling upon heaven’s aid, they killed an innumerable multitude and put the remainder to flight. The governor of Ascalon fell in that encounter, but the commander of the entire army escaped by fleeing. About four thousand of the enemy are said to have been killed that day; sixty of our men were found among the dead. By the Lord’s merciful guidance, therefore, our men gained the enemy camp and endless droves of camels. Taking with them innumerable asses and horses, excellent spoils, and many captives, they reached Joppa with joy and exultation. [Col. 0488A]

That day a certain nobleman was also captured, who had once been administrator in the city of Acre; the king is said later to have received twenty thousand gold pieces for him. The enemy fleet nonetheless remained in Joppa’s harbour. But after learning of their men’s destruction, and with a south wind supplying the necessary breeze, they withdrew into the harbour of Tyre. Later, wishing to return to Egypt, they were suddenly caught in a storm at sea. Separated from one another by the force of the whirlwind, twenty-five of their ships, unable to withstand the strait, were driven onto our shores. Of their rowers and sailors, excepting the dead, our men put more than two thousand in chains.

## CHAPTER IV. Patriarch Daimbert, returning with the enforcement of apostolic letters, dies at Messina in Sicily. Ebremar, intruder upon that see, hastens to Rome. Ghibelin, archbishop of Arles, is sent as legate and is later installed as patriarch.

[Col. 0488B]

Meanwhile Lord Daimbert, patriarch of Jerusalem, had been detained for a long time by Lord Pope Paschal and the Roman Church, who wished to learn more fully whether the king of Jerusalem and those who had expelled Daimbert wished to allege anything against him by which they might appear to have acted lawfully. Once no one appeared to make any objection against him, and nothing else could be found blameworthy in his conduct except that he had been expelled by royal violence, [Col. 0488C] he was ordered to return to his own place and recover the see from which he had been wrongfully driven, with the fullness of favour and the enforcement of apostolic letters.

At length he came to Sicily and, while making a necessary stay at Messina and awaiting passage, was struck by a serious illness. On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July [16 June], he entered the way of all flesh. He had sat in peace for four years, and in exile for three.

Ebremar, the intruder upon that see, heard that Lord Daimbert was returning with the fullness of favour in order to recover his see. Before learning of Daimbert’s death, he decided to cross the sea to the same Roman Church, intending to plead his innocence: that he had been placed in that see unwillingly and against his resistance. When he arrived, he could obtain nothing except that a legate should be sent with him, who, being established in Jerusalem, might investigate his case more fully. [Col. 0488D]

Lord Ghibelin, an elderly and aged man, archbishop of Arles, was appointed to carry out this task. By the pope’s command he set out for Jerusalem and, summoning a council of the kingdom’s bishops, fully investigated Lord Ebremar’s case. When it had been established to him by suitable witnesses, sufficient and beyond every objection, that Lord Daimbert had been expelled without lawful cause through Arnulf’s factions and royal violence, and that Ebremar had occupied the see while the pontiff was still alive and in communion with the Roman Church, he deposed Ebremar from the patriarchate by the authority which he possessed. [Col. 0489A]

But, considering the man’s great religious devotion and remarkable simplicity, Ghibelin granted him the church of Caesarea, then vacant, to hold. Later, while clergy and people disputed concerning the appointment of a patriarch for the church of Jerusalem, a day was specifically appointed to discuss the matter according to custom. After much deliberation on both sides, they unanimously agreed upon Lord Ghibelin, legate of the Apostolic See, and placed him in the patriarchal seat. The aforesaid Arnulf is also said to have arranged this maliciously, so that an old and decrepit man could not live long in that see.

In the same year, 1107 from the Incarnation of the Lord, the Ascalonites, employing their customary malice, had laid an ambush in suitable places on the public road descending from Jerusalem to the sea: five hundred horsemen and one thousand foot-soldiers. [Col. 0489B] They had heard that a company of our men was leaving Joppa and intending to go to Jerusalem. Wishing to accomplish by deceit what they could not achieve by force, they lay hidden in the aforesaid ambush. Then our men, wholly ignorant of all this, continuing their intended journey, fell into their trap.

Though they were greatly distressed, uncertain whether to yield or fight, the enemy’s attack took away time for deliberation. Seeing that they must either perish shamefully or fight them bravely, our men made necessity a virtue and took courage. Renewing their boldness and attacking fiercely, they reduced to mental stupefaction those whom they had formerly found terrifying. Unable any longer to bear our men’s assault, the enemy turned to flight after many had been killed and some captured; our men pursued them for some time. At last, aided by divine grace and victorious, having lost only three of their number, they proceeded to Jerusalem. [Col. 0489C]

## CHAPTER V. The nobleman Hugh of Saint-Omer, lord of Tiberias, builds a castle in the mountains above Tyre, called Toron; soon afterward, fighting the Damascenes, he is mortally wounded but dies victorious. The Ascalonites also, seeking to lay an ambush for our men, fall into the snare they had prepared.

[Col. 0489D]

At the same time, while the city of Tyre was still held by the enemy and impeded our progress by every means, the noble and powerful man Lord Hugh of Saint-Omer, of renowned memory in the Lord, who after Lord Tancred governed the city of Tiberias, harassed the citizens of Tyre by frequent secret raids, insofar as the distance between the places allowed. For the two aforesaid cities are about thirty miles apart. Since his soldiery was often endangered in going and returning, because between those cities there was no stronghold or any kind of fortification into which his men could retreat and escape the pursuit of the enemy, [Col. 0490A] this illustrious man added a castle on the high mountains overlooking Tyre and about ten miles from it, at a place whose ancient name was Tibnin. Since it stood upon a very lofty, peaked mountain, he gave it the name Toron.

The place lies almost midway between the sea and Lebanon, equally distant from Tyre and Paneas, in the tribe of Asher. It is commended for healthfulness and the agreeable mildness of its climate. Its soil is rich and entirely suited to vineyards and trees, and is also exceptionally suitable for crops and cultivation. Thus it afforded its founder the desired advantage for the aforesaid undertaking in those days; and even to the present day, both by the abundance it yields and by the great fortification in which it excels, it provides incomparable benefits to the city of Tyre and to the whole kingdom. [Col. 0490B]

Without delay after the establishment of this stronghold, the same nobleman entered enemy territory with seventy knights. He fought four thousand Damascenes once, and a second time that same day was heavily repulsed by the enemy. On the third occasion, however, attacking under better auspices and with courage granted by God, and likewise with stronger forces received through the Lord’s help, he put the enemy to flight. Yet he himself died, mortally pierced by an arrow: a prudent and valiant man, highly commendable and welcome to king and kingdom alike because of his merits. Two hundred of the enemy were killed in that battle, and our men recovered the same number of horses.

After those days many signs and portents were seen in the heavens in the East. For during forty days and more, a comet was seen near the beginning of the night, trailing a long tail. Again, from sunrise until the third hour, the sun appeared to have two companions beside it, equal in size but inferior to the sun in brightness. A rainbow, distinguished by its colours, was also seen around the sun. All these things were certainly understood to portend new events for mortals. [Col. 0490C]

## CHAPTER VI. Bohemond returns from France to Apulia, enters Greek territory with immense forces to ravage it, and at last, wishing to return to Syria, dies, leaving his son Bohemond behind.

At the same time Alexius, emperor of Constantinople, a malicious and wicked man, placed many obstacles before those wishing to travel through his territories to Jerusalem. For against the first expedition—which, as was said above, had greatly benefited him—he had stirred up Soliman, the most powerful prince of the Turks, and barbarian peoples from all over the East. Against the second expedition, led by the count of Poitou, he had likewise incited the same nations and unbelieving peoples through frequent embassies; thus, through his malice, the later expedition almost entirely perished. [Col. 0490D]

Nor had he shown hostility toward our people merely once or twice. Whenever an opportunity presented itself to inflict harm upon them or prepare disasters for them, he counted it as profit. Yet to those present before him he gave gracious replies and lavish gifts, so that he might deceive them more conveniently, observing the custom of the Greeks, of whom it is said:

> “I fear the Danaans, even when they bring gifts.”  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid* II.49

Suspicious of the progress of all Latins generally, and unwilling either that their forces should increase or their power expand, wherever he could furnish an obstacle, he allowed their journey to be impeded. [Col. 0491A]

Lord Bohemond, therefore, mindful of these wrongs, returned from beyond the mountains and took up the cause of all Latins. He had five thousand horsemen and forty thousand foot-soldiers. On the seventh day before the Ides of October [9 October], he arrived by ship in the territory of the aforesaid emperor. Having almost entirely destroyed and plundered all the coastal cities, he ravaged all Epirus, both First and Second. At length he besieged Dyrrachium, metropolis of Epirus I, and gave the surrounding country to fire and plunder. He used the neighbouring regions at will, preparing, through the Lord’s help, to proceed forcefully farther into the empire in order to avenge the injuries done to the Latins. [Col. 0491B]

When the emperor learned that Lord Bohemond had entered his borders with a great Latin army, he too assembled his armies and went forth to meet him, stationing his forces nearby. There, mutual friends intervened, and the emperor concluded a treaty with Bohemond, confirming it by oaths: henceforth he would give faithful counsel and aid, without fraud or evil intent, to Christ’s faithful wishing to cross into the East; nor would he allow their journey to be impeded by those whom he himself could restrain.

When these terms had been agreed and confirmed by the bond of faith, Lord Bohemond too gave a bodily oath and promised to preserve friendship and fidelity forever. He then returned to Apulia and dismissed the crowd of pilgrims, who, bound by vows, were obliged to complete the journey to Jerusalem. He himself remained at home, still occupied by domestic concerns. [Col. 0491C]

In the following summer, after necessities for the journey had been partly prepared and ships assembled, while he was preparing to depart and had summoned forces from every quarter, he was seized by a severe illness and passed into death. He left as heir of his principality and name his only son, born to Lady Constance, daughter of Lord Philip, the illustrious king of the Franks. In the same year his father-in-law, Lord Philip, illustrious king of the Franks, also died. [Col. 0491D]

## CHAPTER VII. Again immense Turkish forces from the eastern regions attempt to occupy the territory of Edessa; but Tancred and the king resist them bravely.

During these same days, while the aforesaid nobles—Count Baldwin, namely, and his kinsman Joscelin—were still held in chains by the enemy, the Turks, taking occasion from their absence, gathered an infinite multitude and innumerable forces from the eastern gulf. Descending into Mesopotamia, they began to ravage the regions around Edessa as enemies, violently occupying certain strongholds, [Col. 0492A] giving the suburbs to the flames, taking the cultivators captive, and themselves devoting their efforts to agriculture. Thus no safe place could be found outside the circuit of walled towns, and, with agriculture failing, provisions altogether failed.

Lord Tancred, to whom the care of the region had been entrusted, was being kept occupied in the regions around Antioch; he had also undertaken the care of that city, as we have said, when Lord Bohemond departed. Nevertheless, hearing how great was the enemy’s harassment in those regions, he summoned the lord king of Jerusalem, explained the reason for the summons, and himself called together from all the towns and garrisons whatever forces he could. The king came to him within a few days as he hastened thus and concerned himself for the region; joining their armies, they crossed the Euphrates. [Col. 0492B] On arriving there they found the enemy, as had been reported to them, roaming at will throughout the whole country. Once they learned of our men’s arrival, the enemy began to draw together, and to exercise less freely the licence which they had formerly enjoyed in roaming about.

Having repeatedly learned the strength of our people, they feared to fight them. Yet they had not resolved to return home. Rather, knowing that neither prince had a free interval in which he could remain long in that region, they strove to delay them until weariness should induce them to hasten their return, while the Turks themselves returned to their customary attacks. Our men, therefore, recognizing their purpose, adopted the most useful plan which the urgency of circumstances permitted. They ordered gathered from the region around the Euphrates, which abounded most richly in grain, abundant supplies of every sort of food. Crossing the river, they loaded horses, camels, asses, and mules, and brought into the towns and garrisons provisions in abundance, sufficient for a long time; above all, they fortified the city of Edessa with supplies beyond all need. [Col. 0492C]

Thereafter they took little concern for the populations of the towns and garrisons, since these were very well provided with arms, men, and food. Recalled by weightier matters, they returned to the Euphrates. While they were crossing the river in a few small boats, carrying over their forces in small numbers, the enemy followed our men’s tracks and attacked some of the rear party who were still awaiting passage, holding the farther bank. [Col. 0492D] They killed some and carried off the rest captive, in the presence of the lord king and Lord Tancred, who were unable to bring them aid; for the river lay between them, and they could not cross it at fords, nor was it easy to carry so great an army back in a few little boats.

Our men, deeply grieved for those poor people whom they had seen killed in their presence and partly taken captive, returned home. They also ordered the magnates who governed the country on this side of the Euphrates to fortify it more carefully. Those captured and killed upon the bank of the Euphrates were poor Armenians, who, fleeing the Turks’ harassment, had intended to make their way [Col. 0493A] to safer places.

## CHAPTER VIII. Count Baldwin of Edessa returns from the enemy’s chains, and Joscelin with him; they provoke war against Tancred.

In the following year, 1109 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Lord Baldwin, Count of Edessa, having been held in chains by the enemy for five continuous years together with his kinsman Joscelin, gave hostages for a stipulated sum of money which they had agreed to pay for their ransom. They recovered their freedom and returned home; and the Lord dealt quite mercifully with them also. For their hostages, committed to a certain fortress under appointed guards, happened—whether weighed down by sleep or wine—to inflict death upon those guards. Afterwards the hostages themselves reached home, secretly, by roundabout ways, wandering by night. [Col. 0493B]

When the aforesaid count approached the city of Edessa, Lord Tancred is said to have denied him entry. Yet at last, mindful of the oaths which had been exchanged when the city had been surrendered to Lord Tancred upon that same count’s capture, he came to his senses and ordered both the city itself and the whole region to be restored to him. Moved by this wrong, the two thereafter jointly declared war against Tancred. Joscelin especially, whose strongholds lay on this side of the Euphrates and were nearer to the Antiochene territories, harassed the prince more severely.

It happened one day that Joscelin, calling a multitude of Turks to his assistance, planned incursions into the prince’s land. The prince, foreseeing this, met him. In the battle which followed, nearly five hundred men of Lord Tancred’s army fell in the first encounter. But at length, recovering their courage and reforming their battle-lines, they struck down a great multitude of Turks and put Joscelin and his men to flight. [Col. 0493C] The leading men of the region, however, and those of more practiced judgment, seeing that the enmity of such great men was exceedingly dangerous and could bring great injury upon the Christian people, intervened and reconciled them to one another.

## CHAPTER IX. Bertrand, son of the Count of Toulouse, comes down into Syria with a Genoese fleet, seeking to succeed his father; William Jordan opposes him. Byblos is taken.

[Col. 0493D]

At the same time Bertrand, son of Lord Raymond, the late Count of Toulouse, arrived with a Genoese fleet near the city of Tripoli. There his kinsman William Jordan was blockading that same city by siege, as he had continued to do from the day of the death of the aforesaid venerable man, who had died while engaged in this undertaking. Immediately upon Bertrand’s arrival a dispute arose between them. Bertrand asserted his right to his father’s succession, while William alleged the merits of his own labour, expense, and four continuous years of effort. The former wished to succeed to his paternal possessions as lawful heir; [Col. 0494A] the latter strove to claim for himself the place which his own persistence had conquered.

While this controversy continued for a long time, mutual friends intervened to negotiate peace. The mediators agreed that, for the sake of peace, the towns of Arqa and Tortosa, with their dependencies, should be granted to William Jordan; while Tripoli, Byblos, and Mount Peregrinus, likewise with their dependencies, should belong to Bertrand. This was done and ratified with the consent of both parties. William therefore became the man of the prince of Antioch for the portion assigned to him, rendering him fealty by the joining of hands; Bertrand received investiture of his assigned portion from the lord king of Jerusalem, solemnly rendering him fealty. It was also added to the terms of the settlement that, if either died [Col. 0494B] without children, the other should succeed to the whole.

When the aforesaid dispute had been settled by this agreement, a quarrel arose from a slight cause between the armed retainers of the two households. William, the often-mentioned count, rode swiftly to intervene and make peace; but he was struck accidentally by an arrow and died. Some said that Count William perished through the tricks and machinations of Count Bertrand; yet to this day no certain author of that wound has appeared. Thus, with his rival and competitor for the aforesaid city removed, Bertrand alone remained in the enterprise.

The Genoese fleet with which he had arrived consisted of seventy galleys. Its commanders were two noble Genoese men, Ansaldus and Hugh Embriaco. Seeing that they were spending their efforts for the time being around the city of Tripoli, [Col. 0494C] they judged it useful meanwhile to undertake something worthy of remembrance. Having privately urged Count Bertrand to be present with them overland, they directed the fleet toward Byblos.

Byblos is a maritime city in Phoenicia, one of the suffragan cities understood to be subject by metropolitan right to the see of Tyre. The prophet Ezekiel mentions it, saying: “The elders of Byblos and its wise men, O Tyre, provided sailors for the service of your varied merchandise” (Ezek. 27:9). Again, in the Second Book of Kings it is written concerning the same city: “Moreover, the men of Byblos prepared timber and stones to build the house of the Lord” [Col. 0494D] (3 Kings [1 Kings] 5:18). In ancient usage it was called Eve, and is believed to have been founded by Eveus, the sixth of the sons of Canaan.

Arriving there and surrounding it by sea and land, they found the citizens greatly terrified and despairing of their defense. The citizens sent an embassy to the commanders of the fleet, the aforesaid Ansaldus and Hugh Embriaco, declaring that, if they would grant free departure to those wishing to leave with wives and children, and permit those unwilling to abandon their homes to remain in the city under favourable conditions, they were ready to open the entrances and receive them as lords. These terms having been accepted as they wished, they surrendered the city to the two men. One of them, namely Hugh Embriaco, held it until a specified time on payment to the Genoese treasury of an annual fixed tribute. He was the grandfather of the Hugh who now governs that same city and bears both his name and surname. [Col. 0495A] Once the city had been taken, the fleet returned to Tripoli.

## CHAPTER X. King Baldwin hastens to Tripoli; the siege intensifies, and the city is taken.

Hearing that the aforesaid Genoese fleet, after taking Byblos, was still lingering near Tripoli, the lord king hurried there. He intended to see whether he might retain the Genoese on some terms, so that, relying on their aid, he could claim one of the maritime cities for himself. Four rebels still remained upon our coast: Beirut, Sidon, Tyre, and Ascalon. These greatly hindered the new plantation of our people from attaining growth. [Col. 0495B]

When he arrived, he cheered all who were engaged in the siege, both by sea and land, with his presence, and made them more zealous in the work begun. At once, upon his arrival, those labouring outside in the siege seemed to have found the greatest comfort; so that their courage appeared to have increased, and they did not doubt that their strength had grown. For the besieged, conversely, desolation came in greater measure than usual, and their hope of resistance utterly collapsed and was enfeebled. The stronger they saw their enemies become, the weaker they considered themselves; and they thought that whatever accrued to the enemy was entirely taken away from themselves.

Our men, therefore, as though new and fresh, renewed [Col. 0495C] their assaults and pressed the enemy more fiercely than usual wherever opportunity offered—as though they had only then begun the siege which they had prolonged with much labour for almost seven continuous years. The citizens, seeing our men’s strength grow day by day while their own diminished, worn out by prolonged exertions and having no hope of relief, took counsel together about how they might put an end to such great evils.

They accordingly sent embassies both to the lord king and to the lord count, promising to surrender the city on the condition that those wishing to depart should be allowed to do so freely and without hindrance and to convey their households, with all their possessions, to places of their choice. Those unwilling to leave were to be permitted safely and peacefully to remain in their homes and cultivate their possessions, on payment each year of a fixed rent to the lord count. [Col. 0495D] Having heard the citizens’ requests, the king, after taking counsel with the count and the other magnates, judged it advantageous to accept their wishes and receive the city without delay. This proposal pleased all; having given their agreement and summoned the citizens before them, they granted the petition.

After oaths had been sworn that the aforesaid agreements would be observed toward them in good faith, without fraud or malicious intent, they received the city, opening the entrances to those wishing to enter. The aforesaid city was taken in the year 1109 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in June, on the tenth day of the month. There Count Bertrand became the liege man of the lord king, rendering fealty by the joining of hands; and for this reason his successors, to the present day, are bound to render the same to the king of Jerusalem. [Col. 0496A]

## CHAPTER XI. Count Baldwin of Edessa goes down to his father-in-law Gabriel at Melitene, where he performs a highly memorable deed.

During these same days it happened that Lord Baldwin, Count of Edessa, released from the enemy’s chains, had many knights but lacked the means to pay them the wages due for their service and faithful performance of duty. Having conceived a shrewd and very cunning plan, he set out with these fellow-soldiers to visit his father-in-law at Melitene, a very wealthy man. He had carefully arranged and preordained what was to be done after arriving in his father-in-law’s presence. [Col. 0496B]

Having made ready the necessities for the journey, he arrived there. After the customary exchange of greetings, and after the sign of peace had been reciprocally given with embraces and full affection, he was received by his father-in-law magnificently, far beyond the demands of hospitality, as a member of the household and an affectionate son. When the count had remained there for several days, and father-in-law and son-in-law had perhaps prolonged part of a day in necessary conversation, the count’s knights approached—as had previously been agreed among them—and thrust themselves into their conference.

Then one of them, made as it were spokesman by the authority of all, addressed the count: “You know, Count—and no one knows better than you—how faithfully and how bravely this company of knights now present has for a long time served you, following your faith and promise; [Col. 0496C] how great were the hardships and troubles it has endured in watchfulness, thirst, hunger, cold, and likewise the assault of heat, in order to make you and the region divinely entrusted to you safe from injuries inflicted by enemies, and to turn aside from the citizens and the remaining people dwelling there the attacks and troubles of unbelievers and enemies of Christ’s cross. This fellowship calls you as its witness, having at times been necessary to you.

“You know how much time has now passed since we served you without wages; how often necessity compelled us to demand payment; how often you granted us the postponements we requested, while we, sympathizing with you, bore them patiently from day to day. Now our circumstances have reached the point at which we can wait no longer. Poverty is invincible; it refuses us further respite and denies that more time can again be granted to you.
