Choose one of two things: either pay the debt and relieve our want, or produce the pledge which you gave, according to the agreement.”

Gabriel wondered what this assembly could want of him and what so solemn a speech portended. At length, instructed through interpreters, he understood the matter; but he asked what sort of pledge the lord count had given as security for the promised wages. When the count, restrained as though by shame, gave no answer, their spokesman replied: “He mortgaged his beard to us: unless the stipulated wages were paid to the knights on the appointed day, [Col. 0497A] that beard was to be shaved without objection.”

Hearing this, Gabriel, stunned by the novelty of the act and clapping his hands, began to gasp and to be exceedingly distressed. For it is the custom among Eastern peoples, Greeks as well as other nations, to cultivate their beards with every care and concern, and to regard it as the utmost disgrace and the greatest shame that can ever be inflicted if even one hair of the beard is removed from them, through any mishap, with insult.

He asked the lord count whether matters stood as had been said. The count replied, “Yes.” Again marveling more strongly and almost beside himself, Gabriel asked: “Why have you thus pledged a thing which must be guarded with such care—the token of a man, the glory of his face, the chief mark of a person’s dignity—as though it were a trivial thing that could be separated from a man without disgrace?”

The count replied: “Because I possessed no worthier thing through which I could make full satisfaction to the knights, who pressed me so aggressively. Nor should my lord and father trouble himself greatly about this. For I hope, through the Lord’s mercy, that having obtained a postponement from the knights, when I return to Edessa I shall satisfy their demands and redeem the pledged security with my honour intact.”

The knights, however, as instructed, unanimously declared that they would immediately depart from him and threatened him unless he paid promptly. [Col. 0497B] Hearing this, Gabriel—a simple man and ignorant of their collusion—pondered anxiously what to do. He chose rather to pay from his own resources what his son-in-law, regarded as his son, was bound to pay the knights, than to endure such great disgrace for him.

He asked the amount of the debt. The answer was: thirty thousand Michaelites, a type of gold coin then famous in public commerce, named after a Byzantine emperor called Michael, who had distinguished that coin with his own image. Gabriel therefore promised to pay the stipulated sum for his son-in-law, on this condition: that the lord count should solemnly promise in good faith that henceforth, in no circumstance and under no necessity, he would wish to pledge himself so to any persons whatsoever. Once the money had been paid and leave taken of his father-in-law, the lord count and his men returned home wealthy, with bulging purses and poverty driven away. [Col. 0497C]

## CHAPTER XII. Through the king’s efforts, the Church of Bethlehem is raised to cathedral rank.

[Col. 0497D]

In the following year, 1110 from the Incarnation of the Lord, the king, watchful and maintaining untiring care over how he might honour the kingdom entrusted to him by God and offer something worthy of acceptance to God his protector, resolved in the devout fervour of his mind to raise the Church of Bethlehem, which until that day had been only a priory, to cathedral dignity. How this was done will be made more fully and perfectly clear from the decree of that same most pious king issued on this matter, which reads as follows:

“By divine grace inspiring it, the people of the Franks, admonished thereto, liberated the holy city of Jerusalem, long wearied by the oppression [Col. 0498A] of pagans and polluted by the aforesaid filth. There, death, which had invaded the human race through the first parent’s transgression, was destroyed by the death of the Saviour. This city, worthy of divine worship, was besieged by the aforesaid people on the seventh day before the Ides of June; and on the Ides of July, with God fighting for it, it was taken.

“After the city’s capture, in the year of the Lord 1100, divine ordinance prompting it, the clergy, Raymond of Saint-Gilles, Robert Count of Normandy, Robert Count of Flanders, Tancred, the other leading men, and the whole multitude of Franks chose that my dearest brother, the most pious and merciful Duke Godfrey, should preside over it. That man worthy of God, governor of the holy city, having completed the first year of his rule, rested in peace, God being gracious, on the third day of the following year.

“To him succeeded I, Baldwin, by divine will the first king of the Franks, chosen by the rejoicing clergy, princes, and people. Reflecting with shining devotion upon the preeminence of the Church of Bethlehem and the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, in which my head, adorned with a diadem, had first shone venerably, I judged it wholly fitting that it should be endowed with episcopal dignity. [Col. 0498B] Continually considering what I had conceived in purity of heart, I finally brought the matter to the attention of Arnulf, archdeacon, a most renowned man, and of the chapter of Jerusalem, earnestly requesting that he and that chapter advise me concerning it. In compliance with my most just request, both on behalf of the see of Jerusalem, which thereafter seemed as though bereft of its father, and on behalf of this affair, they decided to go to Rome.

“Arnulf the archdeacon and Aichard, then dean, undertook this embassy and went to Rome. With the Holy Spirit cooperating, they found honourable counsel on both matters from Lord Pope Paschal II, pontiff of the universal Church, and returned to Jerusalem. Lord Pope Paschal then sent after them to Jerusalem Gibelin, Archbishop of Arles, a man radiant with the beams of wisdom and shining with every excellence of character; in Arnulf’s and Aichard’s presence he had entrusted to him that embassy. [Col. 0498C]

“Accordingly, received with joy by me, clergy, and people, Gibelin, by command of Lord Pope Paschal, through my good will, the assent of the Jerusalem chapter, the favour of the whole council, and his own deliberation, made all arrangements. In the Church of Bethlehem he decreed that Aschetinus, an illustrious man governing that same church—whom the chapter of Jerusalem, with my consent and that of my magnates and people, had elected and appointed bishop at Ascalon as cantor of that church—should hold episcopal primacy. He subjected the Church of Ascalon to the see of Bethlehem by parochial right, in accordance with our command and judgment.

“At last I, Baldwin, by God’s grace king of Jerusalem and first among the Latins, gladly and earnestly confirmed the matters already stated. I further commanded, gave, and granted that the bishop and his successors should hold and possess firmly and freely: the town of Bethlehem, which I had granted to the church for the salvation of my soul, of my most merciful brother Duke Godfrey, and of all my relatives; one village in the territory of Acre, named Bedar; another in the territory of Neapolis, named Seylon; another adjoining Bethlehem, [Col. 0499A] called Bethbezan; and two villages in the territory of Ascalon, one named Zeophir and the other Caicapha, with their dependencies.

“I also rendered the aforesaid church entirely free from the claim by which the Church of Jerusalem harassed it, through an exchange of lands and vineyards around Jerusalem that were in my domain. We further decree that, if any cleric or layman, led by most wicked avarice, should after my death presume to violate what, at my request, has been established concerning the Church of Bethlehem—renowned for the Nativity of our Lord and Saviour—through the help of the Holy Spirit, by Lord Paschal, supreme and venerable pontiff of the Roman see, and confirmed through Gibelin, his legate and Archbishop of Arles, he shall, unless warned and brought to repentance, be liable to the crime of unlawful seizure and, deprived of our whole kingdom, be severely judged. [Col. 0499B]

“Furthermore, I grant that any of my magnates, or any knight or burgess, inspired by God’s Spirit, who wishes from his own revenues to give something to that church for his own soul and the souls of his people, shall be free to carry out his pious will, and the donation lawfully made from his goods shall remain valid forever.

“This record of our grant and confirmation, and account of the acts performed, was made in the year 1110 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the third indiction, while Lord Pope Paschal II presided over the Roman Church, and Gibelin, Archbishop of Arles and vicar of the Apostolic See, was patriarch-elect at Jerusalem.” [Col. 0499C]

The witnesses of this declaration are:

Arnulf the archdeacon; Aichard the dean; Eustace Grenier; Anselm, keeper of the Tower of David; Ralph of Foritanet; Pisellus the viscount; Simon, son of the duke; Anfred, a religious man; Gerard the chamberlain; and many others.

## CHAPTER XIII. The city of Beirut is besieged by land and sea, and is taken in the second month.

[Col. 0499D]

In the same year, the aforesaid worshipper of God and magnificent victor, the same lord king, tirelessly concerned with how he might enlarge the kingdom entrusted to him by God, took advantage of certain galleys that had wintered in the kingdom. In February, having assembled from the whole realm as large a multitude of Christian people as his resources allowed, he besieged the city of Beirut.

Beirut is a maritime city in Phoenicia between Byblos and Sidon, one of the suffragan cities understood to be subject to the metropolitan see of Tyre. It was once highly favoured by the Romans, so that, granted citizenship under the law of the Quirites, it was reckoned among the colonies. Ulpian testifies to this in the *Digest*, under the title “On Censuses,” speaking of the province of Phoenicia: “There is also the colony of Berytus in that province, favoured by Augustus’ benefactions.” And, as the deified Hadrian says in a certain address: “An Augustan colony which possesses Italian right.” [Col. 0500A] It received from the same Augustus not only Italian right but also the authority to teach—an entitlement granted to few cities—as is evident in the first book of the Code, in the constitution beginning *Cordi nobis est*, where it reads: “And Dorotheus, teacher of the Berytans.”

It is believed to have borne in ancient usage the name Gerse, and to have been founded by Gerseus, the fifth of the sons of Canaan. On reaching it, the king summoned Lord Bertrand, Count of Tripoli, and began to press the city with vigorous effort. Some ships, filled with brave and warlike men, had come from Tyre and Sidon to bring aid to the city. If these ships had enjoyed free entry and departure, those engaged in the siege would have expended their efforts in vain. But when the fleet arrived, on whose help the king had relied in undertaking the present operation, the ships, fearing to commit themselves to sea, immediately withdrew within the harbour. Thus the citizens were denied both entry and exit by sea. [Col. 0500B]

Near the city was a pine forest that supplied besiegers abundantly with much suitable timber for constructing ladders and every kind of siege-engine. From it they raised wooden towers, assembled missile-throwing engines, and made the devices customarily necessary for such operations. They attacked the city with continuous assaults, allowing the besieged no rest for even an hour, by day or night. Taking turns and relieving one another in succession, they exhausted the citizens by intolerable labour.

After they had worked manfully at the undertaking for two continuous months, reproaching one another for delay, one day they assailed the city in several places more fiercely than usual. Some men leapt from wooden towers that had been forcibly brought against the walls onto the rampart; others followed them, some in the same way and some ascending by ladders. Descending into the city, they forcibly opened its gate. [Col. 0500C] Our army thus entered without difficulty and occupied the entire city, while the citizens fled to the sea.

Those who were in the ships, hearing that the king and his men had broken into the city, also leapt from the ships and seized the harbour. Repelling with swords the citizens who had fled there for safety, they forced them back toward the enemy. Thus the wretched citizens, unhappily trapped between two hostile bodies, perished by the sword in the middle, now attacked by these, now by those, until the king, beholding the excessive slaughter, proclaimed by herald’s voice an end to the killing and ordered that life be spared to the survivors who begged mercy. The aforesaid city was taken in the year 1112 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in April, on the twenty-seventh day of the month. [Col. 0500D]

## CHAPTER XIV. A fleet of Danes and Norwegians comes down into Syria; with their help the king besieges and takes Sidon; and a remarkable incident involving the king is related.

[Col. 0501A]

In the same year a people departed from the western islands, especially from that western region called Norway. Hearing that the holy city of Jerusalem had been taken by Christ’s faithful, and wishing to hasten there out of devotion, they prepared a suitable fleet. Embarking in it, with a favourable wind, they sailed the British Sea, then passed Calpe and Atlas, entered the straits of this Mediterranean inlet, crossed our sea, and made land at Jaffa.

The commander-in-chief and highest leader of the aforesaid fleet was a certain young man, tall in stature and handsome in appearance, brother of the king of Norway. [Col. 0501B] After reaching the harbour of Jaffa, they undertook their intended journey and visited Jerusalem, for whose sake they had come. When the king learned of their arrival, he hastened there with all speed. Speaking kindly and familiarly with the aforesaid nobleman, he began carefully to inquire whether that naval army would remain in the kingdom and dedicate its services to Christ for a time, so that through its exertions one of the cities of the unbelievers might be added to the faithful people.

After consulting together, they replied that they had come for this very purpose and were animated by the intention of devoting themselves to Christ’s service. In accordance with that purpose, they were prepared to hasten by sea with all speed to whichever of the maritime cities the king, with his army, wished to besiege, demanding nothing for wages except provisions. The king most devoutly accepted their offer. Gathering all the strength of the kingdom and as much cavalry as he could, he came to Sidon. [Col. 0501C] The fleet likewise left the harbour of Acre and made directly for the same place, so that both armies arrived before the city at almost the same moment.

Sidon is a maritime city between Beirut and the metropolitan see of Tyre, no small part of the province of Phoenicia, with a most convenient position. It is frequently mentioned in both the Old and New Testaments. Thus, in the Second Book of Kings, Solomon says to Hiram king of Tyre: “Therefore command that cedars of Lebanon be cut for me; my servants shall be with yours; and I shall give you whatever wages for your servants you ask. For you know that among my people none knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 5:6). The Lord also mentions it in the Gospel: “Amen I say to you, if these things had been done in Tyre and Sidon,” and the rest (Matt. 11:1); and elsewhere: “Jesus went out and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon” (Mark 7:24). [Col. 0501D] Sidon is said to have been founded by Sidon, son of Canaan, and so retains the name of its founder to the present day. It is one of the suffragan cities of the metropolis of Tyre.

Our army therefore blockaded it on both sides, striking great fear into the citizens. Seeing that they could in no way resist by force or defend themselves from the dangers threatening them, they devised by trickery what they could not accomplish by strength. In the retinue of the lord king was a certain Baldwin, formerly a pagan, his intimate and, as it were, chamber attendant. When this man came to the font of baptism, the lord king had received him from the sacred font out of pious regard, given him his own name, and admitted him among his household. The noblemen of the city, seeking by whatever means to extricate themselves, secretly approached him through messengers and promised him boundless money and very extensive possessions in the city if, by killing the king, he would free them from such great calamities. [Col. 0502A]

This Baldwin was so intimate and dear to the lord king that he would usually accompany the king alone even to the more private places where the necessities of nature are satisfied. He gladly accepted the proposal and promised to carry out their request. He devoted himself wholly to waiting for a suitable time to accomplish the crime. Meanwhile some faithful persons in the city, to whom knowledge of this plot had come, feared that such an abominable plan might succeed through the lord king’s lack of caution. They wrote letters without naming a definite author and sent them by an arrow into our army, setting forth the whole matter in order. By chance they reached the lord king and, not without reason, greatly disturbed him.

He summoned the princes and deliberated what ought to be done. The man was called, confessed the crime, and, after the princes passed sentence upon him, ended his life by hanging. [Col. 0502B] Seeing that their scheme had not had a successful outcome, the citizens began another course. They sent an embassy asking that the nobles be allowed to depart, while the common people, as before, might be permitted to work the land under favourable conditions. When this was granted, they surrendered the city and went without opposition, with their wives and children, to places of their choice.

The king immediately and without delay granted the city, as a hereditary possession, to one of his magnates, namely Eustace Grenier. The fleet, having received gifts from the lord king and taken leave, returned home, accompanied by the blessing of all. [Col. 0502C] The aforesaid city was taken in the year 1111 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in December, on the nineteenth day of the month.

## CHAPTER XV. Gibelin, patriarch of Jerusalem, dies; the impious and wicked Arnulf succeeds him.

Per idem tempus, the lord Gibelin, patriarch of Jerusalem, of blessed memory, died. He was succeeded—against the will of God, as we believe—by Arnulf, the archdeacon of Jerusalem, of whom we have made very frequent mention above, commonly surnamed Malacorona (“Evil Crown”). “For because of the sins of the people, God suffers a hypocrite to reign” (Job 34:30). This man, persisting as before in his own course, [Col. 0503A] performed many utterly wicked deeds. Among other things, he gave his niece in marriage to Lord Eustace Grenier, one of the foremost princes of the kingdom and lord of two noble cities, namely Sidon and Caesarea; with her he bestowed the best portions of the Church’s patrimony, namely Jericho with all its appurtenances, whose annual revenue is said today to be five thousand gold pieces. During his pontificate he also lived an impure life, so that his disgrace was publicly known.

Seeking a pretext for this conduct, he altered the order which the first princes had carefully and after much deliberation established in the Church of Jerusalem by introducing regular canons. He also induced the king to take another wife while his own wife was still living, [Col. 0503B] as will be related below.

## CHAPTER XVI. An enormous host and innumerable forces of Turks pour in from the East upon the territory of Antioch; but Tancred, together with Bertrand, count of Tripoli, resists them bravely.

Without any long delay, after the capture of Sidon, an innumerable body of cavalry was assembled in Persia. In order to test their own strength and thereafter have cause to boast concerning it, they came up into our regions. For from the first entrance of the Latins until almost the fortieth year of their rule, that plague—like a fiercer Hydra, made newly richer by the loss of its heads—never failed to afflict our people. Indeed, in almost every year such a multitude of that detestable people burst forth from that Persian bosom [Col. 0503C] that they nearly covered the whole surface of the earth by their numbers.

But divine mercy, taking pity on our sufferings, raised up against Persian insolence and a kingdom excessively confident in itself the rival power of the Iberian people. As that power, through God’s grace, gained increase and strength, the pride of the Persians was crushed by continual successes. Those who had formerly been feared and formidable to the aforesaid people became, by a reversal of fortune, far inferior to them both in strength and in experience of arms. And those who had been accustomed to trouble foreign kingdoms, even more distant ones, now think themselves fortunate if they can find peace within their own borders, even for a time.

Iberia is a region situated in [Col. 0503D] the northern quarter, also called Avesguia, bordering upon Persia; its inhabitants are tall in body, robust in strength, and notable for great bravery. By frequent wars and continual encounters they have so worn down the forces of the Persians that the latter no longer consider themselves their equals; anxious for their own security, they have ceased to harass other provinces.

The aforesaid multitude therefore, departing from those regions, crossed Mesopotamia and passed over the great river Euphrates. Ravaging at will the country about the river, they laid siege to Turbessel, the strongest fortress of the region. Having spent a whole month there, and seeing that they made no progress, they withdrew toward Aleppo, trusting in their numbers and contriving to provoke Lord [Col. 0504A] Tancred rashly and violently into battle.

But Lord Tancred, being prudent and circumspect in action, summoned the lord king by letters and messengers, asking him to bring assistance quickly. The king, without delay gathering a great force and taking with him Bertrand, count of Tripoli, again proceeded with his troops to those parts. When they had reached the town of Rugia, they found Lord Tancred there with his forces. Marching thence against the enemy, they came before the city of Caesarea—commonly called Caesarea—where the enemy had encamped, with their battle-lines drawn up. When the two armies had caught sight of one another, the Turks declined battle and departed from the region; our men, having taken leave of one another, returned home.

## CHAPTER XVII. Tyre is besieged; but the citizens resist vigorously, and the purpose of the besiegers is frustrated.

[Col. 0504B]

Later in the same year, since Tyre alone among the coastal cities lying from Laodicea in Syria to Ascalon, the last city of the kingdom, still bore the yoke of unbelief, the lord king, who had on other occasions prospered with the Lord’s aid, resolved to reclaim it for the kingdom. Gathering from the entire coast as many ships as he could find, he formed such a fleet as was available and ordered it to hasten there with all speed. He himself summoned the forces of the kingdom and the whole people from every quarter, stationed his troops around the aforesaid city, and enclosed it in siege. [Col. 0504C]

Tyre is a city set in the heart of the sea, surrounded by the waters like an island, the capital and metropolitan city of the province of Phoenicia. That province extends from the stream of Valenia to the Cut Rock, bordering on Dora, and contains within its bounds fourteen suffragan cities. The site and advantages of this city will be described more fully below, where, with God as author, we shall deal with its final siege and capture granted by divine favour.

Once the city had been besieged, the prince, being very diligent, devoted every effort and all his attention to compelling its citizens to surrender by burdening them in many ways. Reviewing every means by which hardships are usually inflicted upon besieged cities, [Col. 0504D] he employed them all carefully so that the city might pass under his authority. By frequent assaults, almost continual engagements, battering of walls and towers, violent blows, and continual showers of missiles and arrows, he harassed the besieged.

Finally, to crown their troubles, he ordered two wooden towers to be erected, much higher than the stone structures, so that from them the city might be viewed as though lying below, and war might be brought upon the citizens, as it were, inevitably from above. But the citizens, prudent and valiant men and not entirely inexperienced in such stratagems, opposed devices to devices and strove to repel the injuries inflicted upon them by corresponding means. They began to build up two towers, bringing together stones and accumulating mortar in great [Col. 0505A] quantity, opposite the engines of our men. These towers were so raised that, suddenly and within a few days, they were found much higher than the wooden engines stationed outside. From them they could cast fire upon the engines below and were ready to burn everything without difficulty.

Seeing therefore that artifice was being defeated by artifice, and greatly burdened by the long labour and substantial expenditure which he had consumed there for more than four months, the king abandoned his undertaking, disappointed of his hope. The siege was lifted; he himself returned to Ptolemais, and the rest hastened back to their own homes.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Lord Tancred dies, leaving the principality to Roger, son of Richard.

[Col. 0505B]

At the same time Lord Tancred, of illustrious memory and pious remembrance in the Lord—whose almsgiving and works of mercy the whole Church of the saints will recount forever—paid the debt of death. While he lay upon the bed of his final illness, he had near him in his service the young man Pons, son of Lord Bertrand, count of Tripoli. Seeing the day of his death approaching, he is said to have advised both this young man and his wife Cecilia, who stood before him and who, as we stated above, was the daughter of Lord Philip, king of the French, to contract a lawful marriage after his death.

And so it came about that after Tancred’s departure from this life, and after the death also of Lord Bertrand, count of Tripoli, [Col. 0505C] the father of Pons, the aforesaid Pons took as wife the same lady, widow of the aforesaid Lord Tancred. He was succeeded in the same principality, by Tancred’s final judgment, by a kinsman of his, Roger son of Richard, on the condition that whenever Lord Bohemond the Younger, son of Lord Bohemond the Elder, should claim Antioch with its appurtenances as his own inheritance, Roger would restore it to him without difficulty or opposition. This illustrious man was buried in the portico of the church of the Prince of the Apostles, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1112.

## CHAPTER XIX. Menduc, a most powerful prince of the Turks, again enters the kingdom with enormous forces; the king meets him and is defeated; the whole region is strained beyond its strength.

[Col. 0505D]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1113, when summer had come, an unspeakable multitude again burst out of Persia, which has always been accustomed to produce evil offspring, from which, as from a harmful fountain, pestilential waters are wont to flow. It was under a most powerful prince, illustrious in titles of noble birth, named Menduc. He brought with him so vast a number that neither its exact count nor its limit could be known.

Having crossed the intervening regions, they reached the Euphrates, employing new plans. For those of the same people who had preceded them had usually first tested their strength in the region of Antioch; but these men, as became apparent afterward, had a far different intention and purpose. Crossing all Coele-Syria, leaving Damascus to their left, and passing Tiberias between Lebanon and the coast, they encamped around the bridge beneath which the Jordan flows. [Col. 0506A]

When the king heard this and learned that they relied upon their infinite multitude, he summoned to his aid Lord Roger, prince of Antioch, and the count of Tripoli. Yet before they could arrive, he himself had pitched camp nearby with his own forces. When the enemy learned this, they sent two thousand cavalry from their army. Understanding that craft was more necessary than strength, they ordered fifteen hundred of them to lie concealed in ambush, while the remaining five hundred were commanded to advance farther and, pretending to be more careless than they were, to provoke the king and his men by pursuing them.

This is known to have occurred almost exactly as they intended. The king observed those five hundred apparently incautious men, who had advanced farther; eagerly summoning his own troops, he went out to meet them and, pursuing them as they turned in flight, fell rashly into their ambush. The men emerged from their hiding places, making a huge enemy force; after gathering and recalling the first five hundred, they rushed upon our men with great violence. [Col. 0506B] Our troops attempted to resist and beat them back with their swords, but the enemy pressed upon them more fiercely. Overwhelmed by numbers, our men were forced to flee, nor did they find safety even in flight. For there was a very great slaughter of the fugitives, so that the king himself, abandoning the banner which he carried in his hands, Arnulf the patriarch who was with him, and the other princes of the kingdom scarcely escaped, leaving behind their camp and all their baggage. The enemy took possession of our camp, and, as our sins required, there was great confusion among the people of God.

All this was ascribed to the lord king, because he had acted too impetuously and trusted in his own strength more than was proper, refusing to wait for the aid he had summoned. For Lord Roger, prince of Antioch, and the count of Tripoli were near at hand and would beyond doubt have arrived on the next or the third day. Thirty of our knights fell that day, and twelve hundred foot-soldiers. [Col. 0506C]

After these events the aforesaid two great and powerful men arrived. Learning what had happened, they reproached the king for excessive rashness. Then, reunited, they pitched camp in the neighbouring hills, from which the army of the enemy could be seen below in the valley. The enemy, knowing that the remaining parts of the kingdom were without soldiery, sent detachments from their army in various directions. They began to range throughout the entire land, commit slaughter everywhere on the public roads, set fires, break into the suburbs, and capture peasants; they moved freely throughout the whole region as if everything had been subjected to them.

In those days our own household Saracens and the inhabitants of our suburban villages, called *casalia*, also deserted us. Joining the enemy’s bands, they instructed others [Col. 0507A] how to destroy us. They could do this all the better because they possessed fuller knowledge of our condition. For no plague is more effective in causing harm than a familiar enemy. Trusting in such guides and made stronger by their support, the enemy ranged through villages and castles, carrying off booty and captives. Such terror had seized the entire kingdom that no one at all dared appear outside the walls.

## CHAPTER XX. The men of Ascalon attack Jerusalem; but at last the enemy battle-lines disperse and return home.

Moreover, adding to the mass of fear and misery, the men of Ascalon—like restless worms—knew that the king, with all the kingdom’s forces, was occupied around Tiberias and that the enemy held almost the whole region. They therefore set out with a great multitude, ascended into the hill country, and besieged Jerusalem, which was deprived of military forces. They captured or killed some whom they found outside the city, and burned the dry harvests which the farmers had gathered on the threshing floors. [Col. 0507B]

At last, after remaining there for several days, they saw that no one came out against them and that all were keeping more cautiously within the walls. Fearing the king’s arrival, they returned home. But as summer was already declining into autumn, ships of pilgrims began to arrive according to custom. Those carried in them heard that the king and Christian people were suffering such hardships, and both horsemen and foot-soldiers hastened there with all speed, each striving to arrive first. Thus our army increased visibly day by day.

When the enemy princes learned this, fearing that once our strength had grown we would prepare to avenge their injuries, they withdrew into the territory of Damascus. Our men, separating from one another, returned home. But the commander of the hostile armies, who had so powerfully afflicted the kingdom, arrived at Damascus and was murdered by certain assassins, with the consent, it is said, of Doldequin, king of Damascus. His power was considered threatening, since he was thought likely to deprive that king of his realm. [Col. 0507C]

## CHAPTER XXI. The countess of Sicily, the king’s future wife, lands in the harbour of Acre.

[Col. 0507D]

After the army had dispersed and each man was returning home, a messenger came to the lord king, reporting that the countess of Sicily had landed at the city of Acre. The aforesaid countess had been the wife of Lord Roger, count surnamed Borsa, brother of Lord Robert Guiscard; she was a noble, powerful, and wealthy matron.

In the previous year the king had sent certain nobles of his kingdom to her, inviting her and earnestly requesting that she should enter into a lawful marriage with him. She communicated the proposal to her son, Lord Roger, later king of Sicily, and began to deliberate with him concerning it. At last both agreed that, if the lord king would confirm the proposal under certain conditions, they were ready to assent to his request. [Col. 0508A]

The terms were these: if the king and the aforesaid countess should have offspring, then after the king’s death the kingdom would be granted to that child without opposition or difficulty; but if the king should die without an heir born of that countess, Count Roger, her son, would be heir and would succeed as king in the kingdom without opposition or difficulty. When the envoys departed, however, the king had instructed them to labour by every means to bring her with them, yielding to whatever demands she might make. For he had heard—and knew truly—that she was a wealthy woman, and that, together with her son, she abounded in every kind of possession. He himself, by contrast, was poor and of scant resources, scarcely able to meet his daily needs and the wages of his knights. Therefore he thirsted for his poverty to be relieved from her abundance. [Col. 0508B]

The envoys thus gladly accepted the stated conditions, and, after oaths had been exchanged as required—that the lord king and his princes would observe these agreements in good faith, without fraud or deceit—the countess, while her son provided every necessity, prepared for the journey. She loaded ships with grain, wine, oil, salted meat, arms, and excellent riding horses, took an unlimited quantity of money with her, and, accompanied by all these resources, arrived in our region as stated above.

This, as has been said, was contrived through the malice of Arnulf the patriarch, so that this noble and honourable woman might be deceived. For we cannot deny that she was deceived: in the simplicity of her ways, she believed that the king was qualified to act in a capacity fitting for her lawfully to marry him. But the reality was very different, for the wife whom he had lawfully married at Edessa was still alive. After the said countess arrived, in the presence of the lord king, the patriarch, and the princes of the kingdom, the oaths were renewed in the same form in which they had earlier been given in Sicily. [Col. 0508C]

Because these proceedings had begun with a sinister intention and an eye not single, the Lord, looking upon their intention, did not grant the woman—even though innocent—the fertility usually granted in the kingdom; and mourning took possession of the end of this joy (Prov. 14), as will be said below. For it is difficult for things begun with an evil beginning to end well. Meanwhile, however, her arrival brought such great and numerous benefits to the kingdom that even the least among men might rightly say: “And of her fullness have we received” (John 16). [Col. 0508D]

## CHAPTER XXII. A severe famine arises in the region of Edessa. Baldwin captures his kinsman Joscelin and compels him violently to leave the whole region.

It happened in those days that a most severe famine arose in the territory of Edessa, both because of the unseasonableness of land and air, and because that region lay in the midst of enemies and was surrounded on every side by foes. The inhabitants could not freely devote themselves to agriculture for fear of hostilities; consequently the citizens of that city and the inhabitants of its suburbs alike were compelled by want to eat barley bread, even bread mixed with acorns. [Col. 0509A]

But the land of Lord Joscelin, safely situated on this side of the Euphrates, abounded more fully in crops and provisions. Yet although his province overflowed with every kind of wealth, Joscelin, unwise in this respect and like an ungrateful man, gave absolutely nothing from his extraordinary abundance and plenty to his lord and kinsman, who had bestowed all these things upon him. This was despite his having no doubt that the count and his people suffered extreme want.

Now the lord count Baldwin had occasion to send messengers to Lord Roger, son of Richard, prince of Antioch, to whom he had also given a certain sister of his in marriage. These envoys, after crossing the Euphrates and travelling through Lord Joscelin’s territory, were treated by him very hospitably and humanely both on their outward and return journeys. At length, as commonly happens among imprudent people, certain members of Lord Joscelin’s household began to provoke the count’s messengers with words. They reproached the lord count’s poverty while, conversely, exalting the immense resources of their own lord: his abundance of grain, wine, oil, and provisions; his immeasurable weights of gold and silver; and the number of his soldiers and foot-soldiers. [Col. 0509B]

Moreover, as a prating tongue often speaks rashly, they added that the count was not suitable for the region over which he ruled; he would act more wisely if he sold his county to Lord Joscelin and, having received boundless money, returned to France. These words sank deeply into the hearts of the messengers, although they appeared to conceal their feelings. Though they had been uttered by insignificant persons, they nevertheless seemed to reflect their lord’s mind. Having taken leave, they returned to the lord count. Arriving there, they set out in order everything that had happened on the road, together with the words which they had heard in Lord Joscelin’s house. [Col. 0509C]

When he heard this, the lord count grew angry. Weighing carefully within himself the words he had heard, he understood that all this had originated with Lord Joscelin. He was greatly indignant that a man upon whom he had bestowed such resources, and who was therefore bound by his own wealth to relieve the count’s need, should contrary to all good custom reproach him with poverty as though it were a vice. Yet he had fallen into that poverty not through trivial acts but by unavoidable necessity, which no wise or skilled person could avert—“for there is no counsel against the Lord”—and he had generously taken from himself the very riches of which Joscelin boasted in order to bestow them upon him. Full of indignation, he began to boil with anger. [Col. 0509D]

He therefore feigned illness and, lying in bed, sent word to Lord Joscelin to hurry to him without delay. When he learned this, Lord Joscelin made haste, fearing nothing and finding nothing suspicious in the journey. At last, arriving at Edessa, he found the count lying in the fortress of the city, in the inner chamber of that part called Rangulath. Entering, after offering the customary words of greeting, he asked the lord count how he was. The latter replied: “Much better, by God’s grace, than you would wish.” Continuing his speech, he added:

“Joscelin, do you possess anything which I did not give you?”

He answered: “Lord, nothing.”

“Why then is it that, ungrateful and forgetful of my benefits, overflowing and enlarged from what is mine, you do not have compassion on me, your needy benefactor? I did not come to want through recklessness, but for a cause which no wise man and no experienced man could avoid, for there is no counsel against the Lord. Why do you not return a portion of that which I gave you wholly? Moreover, why do you reproach and charge as a crime the poverty divinely laid upon me, as though it were a vice? Am I so worthless that I should sell you what the Lord gave me and flee, as you say? Surrender what I gave and return everything I bestowed upon you, for you have made yourself unworthy.” [Col. 0510A]

Having spoken these words, he ordered Joscelin to be seized and put in chains. He afflicted him in astonishing and pitiable fashion, not least through varied interrogations and tortures, until, after the whole region had been put under oath, Joscelin surrendered all that he had received as a gift from the same count. Leaving those territories, stripped of all his possessions, Joscelin first went to Lord Baldwin, king of Jerusalem. Having laid out in order everything that had happened to him, he disclosed his intention of returning to his homeland.

When the lord king heard this, seeing that he was greatly needed by the kingdom, he granted him the city of Tiberias with its territory, to possess in perpetuity, so that he might fortify himself by the support of so great a man. Joscelin is said to have ruled that city and all its appurtenances most vigorously and prudently for as long as he remained there, and to have extended its territory greatly. While Tyre was still held by unbelievers, he is said, following the example of his predecessor, to have inflicted many hardships upon its citizens. Although he appeared to be somewhat more distant from them because mountains lay between, he nevertheless often entered their territory to cause them harm. [Col. 0510B]

## CHAPTER XXIII. A great earthquake shakes the region of Antioch. Borsequin also, a most powerful Turkish satrap, ravages the same region.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1114, an earthquake shook all Syria so violently that it utterly destroyed many cities and innumerable towns, especially around Cilicia, Isauria, and Coele-Syria. In Cilicia it levelled Mamistra to the ground with many towns; it also destroyed Marash with its suburbs, so that scarcely even traces of some places remained. Towers and walls were shaken; the collapse of larger buildings was more perilous, and there was an endless slaughter of people. Very great cities, reduced as it were to heaps of stones, became mounds over the crushed and served in place of tombs for their broken inhabitants. [Col. 0510C]

The terrified populace fled the habitation of cities, fearing the ruin of dwellings. While they hoped to find rest in the open air, shaken by fear they broke off their sleep, experiencing in dreams the crushings which they had feared while awake. Nor was this enormous disaster confined to one region only: the plague had spread widely even to the farthest borders of the East. [Col. 0511A]

In the following year also, according to his usual custom, Borsequin, a most powerful Turk, gathered an innumerable multitude of his people and entered the region of Antioch as an enemy. Crossing the whole province, he encamped between Aleppo and Damascus, waiting for an opportunity to launch incursions thence into one or another part of our territories.

But Doldequin, king of Damascus, regarded their expedition with great suspicion. Fearing that they had gathered there more to devise harm against himself and his kingdom than to come and fight the Christians, whose strength they had often experienced, he became anxious. For the death of the aforesaid nobleman, who had been killed at Damascus, was attributed to him, as though that man’s death had proceeded from his knowledge or complicity. On hearing of the Turks’ arrival and learning their intention more fully, he sent embassies, with great magnificence of gifts, both to the lord king and to the lord prince of Antioch. He requested and entreated them for peace for a fixed period, giving oaths and hostages that throughout the agreed term he would maintain a faithful alliance with the Christians of both the kingdom and the principality. [Col. 0511B]

Meanwhile the prince of Antioch, seeing that they were nearer to his lands and being informed by certain reports that they intended an attack upon his territory, summoned the lord king to his aid. He likewise invited Doldequin, bound by the right of the treaty, to ensure that he came with his forces. The king, greatly concerned for the safety of the region, gathered his army, attended by an honourable company, and hastened there energetically. Taking with him Pons, count of Tripoli, he arrived within a few days at the place where the lord prince had gathered his forces. Doldequin, being nearer, had arrived before the lord king’s army and joined our camp as an ally. [Col. 0511C]

When all the forces had been assembled together, they took up a united position before the city of Caesarea, where they had previously heard that the enemy were present. When the enemy learned this, seeing that they could not withstand our men except at grave risk, they feigned withdrawal, as though they would not return again. Thereupon our men separated and returned home. [Col. 0511D]

## CHAPTER XXIV. The men of Ascalon besiege the city of Joppa; but fearing the king’s arrival, they withdraw home without accomplishing their purpose.

Meanwhile, while the king was occupied in the region of Antioch, the men of Ascalon, relying on the fact that he was absent and had drawn together with himself the chief forces of the kingdom, seized the opportunity and besieged the city of Joppa. A short time previously, a fleet of seventy ships had come up from Egypt to assist them. They ordered it to go ahead and occupy the shore of Joppa; they themselves followed in many thousands, banners raised, and suddenly halted before the city. [Col. 0512A]

Those who were in the fleet, learning of the arrival of their people by land, eagerly leapt from the ships in order to attack the city. Thus, with their ranks arranged in a circle, they surrounded the city on every side and, at the given signal, attacked it, pressing vigorously from all directions. The citizens, though few in number and far inferior in strength, nevertheless resisted bravely for their wives and children, for liberty and country—the cause for which every noble man considers it honourable to die. Strengthening the towers and walls as best they could, they drove the enemy farther away with bows, crossbows, and volleys of hand-thrown stones, and did not allow them to approach the wall. [Col. 0512B]

But the event turned out far differently for the men of Ascalon than they had hoped. Thinking they would find the city empty, they had constructed ladders sufficient in both height and number, by which they did not doubt that they could immediately burst within the walls without opposition. But because the besieged resisted bravely, they were not permitted to set the ladders against the walls; they could scarcely even throw anything at those who stood on the towers. For the Lord had granted the citizens such grace that, relying upon divine help, they did not fear the multitude around them.

The city gates were wooden, without any covering of bronze or iron. The attackers skilfully hurled fire against them and burned them in part, yet not so far as to inflict through them greater force or greater harm upon the citizens. [Col. 0512C] Therefore, after several days, the men of Ascalon saw that they were making no progress and feared that the people of the region would gather in aid of the besieged. They lifted the siege and went home. The fleet, using favourable winds, withdrew into the harbour of Tyre.

After ten days had passed, they wished to test whether they might sometime find the people of Joppa unprepared. Leaving Ascalon more secretly, having gathered a great multitude of their men, they again appeared suddenly and silently before Joppa. But the citizens, accustomed to such circumstances, were always on guard, maintaining continual watches by turns throughout the nights, so that they would always be found ready to resist. Seeing the enemy’s returned legions and renewed warfare being prepared against them, they hastened up to the towers and walls. They strove to resist all the more vigorously because they perceived the enemy’s strength to be smaller and saw that their number had diminished. [Col. 0512D] For they saw that the fleet, which on the former occasion had brought many dangers upon the citizens, was absent and would not easily return. Their confidence was also increased because the king was said to be about to come nearby. Thus, becoming more courageous and resisting more confidently, in various encounters they killed many of the enemy army who pressed upon them too boldly. After attacking the city for about seven continuous hours, the enemy saw that they were wasting their labour uselessly, recalled their troops, and returned to Ascalon.

## CHAPTER XXV. Borsequin again harasses the territory of Antioch; but when Prince Roger meets him with his supporting forces, he is put to flight in confusion and his legions are dispersed.

[Col. 0513A]

While these events were taking place in the kingdom, Bursequinus, of whom we have spoken above, who at the arrival of the lord king and of the other nobles who had assembled against him had feigned flight and withdrawal from the regions of Antioch, seeing that the king, the prince of Antioch, and also Doldequinus had separated from one another and, drawn away by domestic concerns, had returned to their own territories, judged that they would not easily be able to meet again. He therefore again harassed the Antiochene territories; ranging through the whole country, he set fire to villages and burned the suburbs, and gave over to plunder and booty whatever they could find outside fortified strongholds. [Col. 0513B] Dividing their forces into companies, they also sent them in various directions, so that they might work slaughter everywhere and, meeting unsuspecting persons either in the fields or upon the road, might either carry them off captive or cut them down with the sword. Nor did they merely break into unwalled villages by their raids, but they even violently seized walled towns. For they had razed Maarrat and Cafarda to the ground, after seizing the inhabitants within, killing some by the sword and putting others in fetters; and, holding the whole region, every day they gathered booty from every side and Christian captives from every side.

When this was reported to the prince, he summoned the lord count of Edessa and, on the twelfth day of September, [Col. 0513C] departed from Antioch and promptly appeared with his forces before the town of Rugia. He immediately sent out scouts to inform him of the enemy’s condition and intention; he himself drew up the battle-lines, arranged the divisions, and vigorously prepared himself for battle. While he laboured over these matters, faithfully assisted by the lord count in accordance with military discipline, behold, a messenger hastened up with all speed and reported that the enemy were encamped in the valley of Sarmata. On hearing this, the whole army was greatly encouraged, as though it had already conceived the hope of victory.

Bursequinus himself too, hearing of our men’s arrival, ordered his men to arm and, having drawn up his forces, urged his comrades-in-arms to act boldly. Yet, wishing to provide for his own safety, [Col. 0513D] before our men approached he occupied a neighboring mountain called Danim with his brother and certain retainers, so that he might observe his men fighting from there and more fully direct them as necessity required concerning the conduct of the battle. It happened, therefore, that while he was occupied with these matters, behold, our battle-lines began to appear with their banners raised. On seeing the enemy and despising their multitude, the lord Baldwin, count of Edessa, who with his troop was leading the others, charged them boldly and with a fierce assault shook their entire army. The remaining battle-lines, following this example, plunged into the midst of the enemy’s wedges, pressing them at close quarters with swords and blades, ready to repay the injuries which they had inflicted with excessive license upon villagers and the poor.

The enemy, having hope of resistance in the first engagements, [Col. 0514A] tried with great insolence to drive back our men; but at last, astonished by our men’s strength, assault, and remarkable steadfastness, their formations utterly broken up, they turned to flight. Bursequinus, however, seeing from the mountain summit the failure of his own men and the growing strength of ours, escaped in flight with his brother and the retainers whom he had gathered on the mountain, abandoning his banner, camp, and all baggage, and thereby saved his life. Our men therefore pursued the broken battle-lines as they fled more vigorously; cutting down the fugitives with the sword, they wrought an immeasurable slaughter for about two miles.

The prince, with part of his men, remained as victor for two days on the field of battle, awaiting his men who had pursued the enemy in different directions. [Col. 0514B] Once they had returned and all the spoils had been brought before him, he allotted fitting shares of the victory to his companions. For the enemy had taken flight, forgetful of everything, leaving their camp filled with every convenience and overflowing with great riches of every kind. Our men also recovered the booty and spoils which they had collected from different places, together with our captives whom they had thrown into chains; rejoicing, they sent them back to their homes with their animals, wives, and children. It is said that more than three thousand of the enemy fell in that conflict. After accomplishing these things, the prince entered Antioch as victor, [Col. 0514C] amid immense applause and the rejoicing of the people, preceded by horses, mules, a multitude of captives, and every variety of riches.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Arnulf, patriarch of Jerusalem, accused on many counts, goes to Rome. The king builds beyond the Jordan, in Sobal Syria, a castle called Mount Royal.

At the same time, the lord pope, having heard of the enormities committed by Patriarch Arnulf and having been fully informed of his impure manner of life, sent a legate to Syria: a certain venerable man, conspicuous for great religious devotion, the bishop of Orange. Upon arriving in our regions, he convened a council of all the bishops of the kingdom and ordered the aforesaid Arnulf to appear before him. At length, as his deserts required, [Col. 0514D] he deposed him from the pontifical office by authority of the Apostolic See.

Arnulf, however, still trusting in his tricks, by which he almost subverted the minds of all men, was compelled to cross the sea and went to the Roman Church. There, by flattering words and lavish expenditure of gifts, he deceived the piety of the lord pope and of the entire Church; he returned to his own country with the favor of the Apostolic See, retaining the see of Jerusalem with the same license of life which had previously deserved his deposition.

During the same period, since the Christian people still possessed no stronghold beyond the Jordan, the king, desiring to extend the boundaries of the kingdom in those regions, resolved, with God as author, to build a castle in the third Arabia, which is otherwise called Sobal Syria, [Col. 0515A] whose inhabitants might protect the land subject and tributary to the kingdom against the enemy’s raids. Wishing, therefore, to fulfill his purpose, he assembled the kingdom’s forces, crossed the Dead Sea, passed through the second Arabia, whose metropolis is Petra, and reached the third. There, on a hill highly suitable to his intention, he founded a stronghold greatly fortified both by natural position and by craftsmanship. Once the work was completed, he settled there both cavalry and infantry as inhabitants, granting them ample estates. Having carefully furnished the town with a wall, towers, a forewall and ditch, arms, provisions, and engines of war, he gave it a name derived from royal dignity and ordered it to be called Mount Royal because a king had founded it.

The aforesaid place possesses the advantages of fertile soil, yielding abundant supplies of grain, wine, and oil; it is singularly commendable alike for healthfulness and pleasantness, and brings the whole neighboring region under its dominion. [Col. 0515B]

## CHAPTER XXVII. The king, seeing the Holy City empty of inhabitants, brings faithful Syrians from Arabia; granting them dwellings, he establishes them as inhabitants of the city.

At that juncture, the king saw—and was greatly troubled by the fact—that the holy city, beloved by God, was empty of inhabitants, so that, for the kingdom’s other necessary business, there was necessarily a population [lacking; text uncertain] which might at least suffice to protect the city’s entrances, towers, and walls against sudden hostile assaults. He anxiously considered within himself and frequently asked others [Col. 0515C] how he might fill it with faithful peoples and inhabitants who worshipped God. For the Gentiles who had been its inhabitants had nearly all fallen by the sword when the city was violently stormed; and those who had escaped by chance were not permitted to dwell within the city. For it seemed like sacrilege to princes devoted to God to allow any persons not reckoned within the Christian profession to live in so venerable a place.

Our own people, moreover, were so few and poor that they could scarcely inhabit a single street. The Syrians, who from the beginning had been citizens of the city, had become so scarce through many tribulations and countless hardships during the time of hostilities that their number was almost nothing. [Col. 0515D] For from the arrival of the Latins in Syria—and especially after the army began, following the capture of Antioch, to advance toward Jerusalem—their fellow citizens had begun to afflict these servants of God so severely that, for any trifling word, they killed many of them, sparing neither age nor status. They suspected them of having summoned by letters and messengers the Western princes who were said to be coming, to bring about their destruction.

Thus, taking due concern for the city’s desolation, he inquired carefully whence he could summon citizens there. At last he learned that beyond the Jordan, in Arabia, many faithful people lived in villages and served the enemy under harsh conditions, paying tribute. The lord king summoned these persons and promised them better conditions; drawn alike by reverence for the place, love for our people, and love of liberty, within a short time many came with wives and children, flocks and herds, and their entire households. [Col. 0516A] Many also came without being summoned, declining the yoke of harsh servitude in order to inhabit a city worthy of God. The king granted them those quarters of the city which seemed most to need this relief, and filled them with dwellings.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. At the clergy’s suggestion, the king asks the lord pope that whatever cities he subdues may be subjected to the Church of Jerusalem. Replies of various letters are appended.

Meanwhile it occurred to the lord king’s mind—and perhaps he was led to this by the clergy’s suggestion—that he should send messengers [Col. 0516B] to the Roman Church and present petitions to the lord pope. Their tenor was that whatever cities and whatever province he might, with God as author, claim for himself by the toil of war and royal diligence, and violently wrest from the enemy’s power, should all be subject to the jurisdiction and rule of the Church of Jerusalem. On this matter he obtained a reply from the Apostolic See, the tenor of which we have considered worthy to insert in the present narrative:

> PASCHAL, servant of the servants of God, to BALDWIN, glorious king of Jerusalem: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> The boundaries and possessions of the churches which were, or are, in your regions have been thrown into confusion by the long possession and tyranny of unbelievers. Since, therefore, we cannot by present deliberation assign their certain boundaries, we have judged it not unreasonable to grant your requests: because you have vowed, for the exaltation of the Church of Jerusalem, to expose your person to the utmost dangers, whatever cities of the unbelievers you have taken or shall take shall be subject to the jurisdiction and dignity of that same Church. Moreover, let the bishops of those cities render obedience to its patriarch as to their own metropolitan, so that he, supported by their aid, and they in turn strengthened by the help of his unity, may advance in the exaltation of the Church of Jerusalem in such a manner that almighty God may be glorified by their advancement.
>
> Given at the Lateran, the fifth day before the Ides of July.

At the request also of the same lord king, [Col. 0516D] the same lord Paschal had granted to the lord Patriarch Gibelin and his successors in perpetuity a privilege upon the same matter. We have taken care to insert its text into this present narrative; its words are as follows:

> PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend brother GIBELIN, patriarch of Jerusalem, and to his successors canonically promoted in perpetuity.
>
> According to the changes of times, the kingdoms of the earth are also transferred; hence it is fitting that the boundaries of ecclesiastical parishes likewise be changed and transferred in many provinces. The boundaries of the Asiatic churches were formerly apportioned by ancient determinations, but the incursions of various peoples of differing faith have thrown those arrangements into confusion. [Col. 0517A] Thanks be to God, however, that in our time the cities both of Antioch and Jerusalem, with their suburbs and neighboring provinces, have been brought under the power of Christian princes. Therefore we ought to put our hand to this divine change and transfer, and, according to the time, arrange what must be arranged: namely, to grant to the Church of Jerusalem those cities and provinces which have been acquired, by God’s grace, through the blood of the glorious King Baldwin and the armies following him.
>
> Therefore, by the authority of this present decree, we ordain that all the cities and provinces which divine grace has already restored, or shall in the future deign to restore, to the lordship of the aforesaid king shall be ruled and administered by you, most dear brother and fellow bishop Gibelin, and your successors, and through you by the holy Church of Jerusalem, by patriarchal or metropolitan right. [Col. 0517B] For it is fitting that the Church of the Lord’s Sepulchre should receive appropriate honor in accordance with the desires of the faithful soldiers, and, freed from the yoke of Turks or Saracens, should be more abundantly exalted in Christian hands.

On account of this grant the lord Bernard, patriarch of Antioch, a man venerable for his life, became greatly indignant, since it appeared likely to redound to the injury of his Church. He sent messengers to the Roman Church to complain very strongly about the act, and in his letters rebuked the lord pope and the entire Church for the manifest injury done to himself and his Church. The lord pope, wishing to mitigate his indignation, replied in these words:

> [Col. 0517C] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother BERNARD, patriarch of Antioch: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> Although among the other apostolic sees that one stands preeminent which divine favor glorified in bodily form through the death of the Apostle Peter, nevertheless such great affection is recorded formerly to have existed between the bishops of Rome and Antioch that no difference appeared between them. For the same person of Peter made both Churches illustrious. Many ages thereafter passed during which the dominion of unbelievers impeded this unity in the persons presiding over them. Thanks be to God, however, that in our time He has restored Christian rule in the city of Antioch.
>
> It is fitting, therefore, dearest brother, [Col. 0517D] that the unity of this same affection should remain firm in us; nor should any opinion enter your mind that we wish to abase or dishonor the Church of Antioch. If, therefore, we have perhaps written anything concerning the boundaries of parishes otherwise than we ought, whether regarding the Church of Antioch or Jerusalem, it must not be attributed to frivolity or malice, nor should scandal therefore be raised against us. For both the great remoteness of the places and the alteration of ancient names which has occurred to cities and provinces have brought us much uncertainty or ignorance. Besides, we have desired and do desire to furnish our brethren not the fuel of scandal but of peace, and to preserve for every Church its own right and honor.
>
> Given at the Lateran, the seventh day before the Ides of August.

[Col. 0518A] The lord pope, however, wishing to explain his intention and the purpose for which he had granted to the lord king and the Church of Jerusalem the matter contained in his rescripts, wrote to the same Patriarch Bernard in this manner:

> PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his fellow bishop BERNARD, patriarch of Antioch: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> As we wrote to your brotherhood in another letter, we love both your person and the Church committed to you with complete affection. We do not in any way wish the honor of your dignity to be diminished; rather, we wish that the preeminence of the patriarchate of Antioch, as it has been preserved in past times, may likewise remain whole in the future, by the Lord’s favor. But what we granted, at the intercession of his messengers, to our son [Col. 0518B] Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, ought not at all to disturb your affection if you examine closely the inward meaning of our letters. For this is what was written in them:
>
> “The boundaries and possessions of churches which were, or are, in those regions have been thrown into confusion by the long possession and tyranny of unbelievers. Since, therefore, we cannot by present deliberation assign their certain boundaries, we have judged it not unreasonable to grant your requests: because you have vowed, for the exaltation of the Church of Jerusalem, to expose your person to the utmost dangers, whatever cities of the unbelievers you have taken or shall take shall be subject to the jurisdiction and dignity of that same Church.”
>
> The words which we wrote to Gibelin, patriarch of Jerusalem of happy memory, concerning the cities and provinces acquired by God’s grace through the prudence of the aforesaid King Baldwin [Col. 0518C] and the blood of the armies following him, must likewise be understood in the same sense. We wish those Churches to be subject to that Church to which they are known by ancient right to belong: namely, those whose certain boundaries can be assigned, whose boundaries and possessions have not been thrown into confusion by long possession and tyranny, and the cities belonging to those Churches. For we do not wish either ecclesiastical dignity to be diminished for the power of princes, or princely power to be curtailed for ecclesiastical dignity.
>
> Given at Benevento, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.

He also wrote to the lord king in the same manner, explaining the purpose for which he had granted assent to the king’s aforesaid petitions and stating that he did not wish the Church of Antioch to be improperly burdened in any respect, in these words:

> [Col. 0518D] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most dear son BALDWIN, illustrious king of Jerusalem: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> The concession which we made in response to your petition—that whatever cities of unbelievers you have taken or shall take should be subject to the jurisdiction and dignity of the Church of Jerusalem—has greatly disturbed both our brother Patriarch Bernard and the entire Church of Antioch. For although we granted that concession concerning those Churches whose boundaries and possessions have been thrown into confusion by the long possession and tyranny of unbelievers, they complain that, with your connivance, the Churches of which there is no uncertainty that the see of Antioch possessed them even in the times of the Turks or Saracens have been seized by the patriarch of Jerusalem. For their bishops, even when oppressed by the tyranny of unbelievers, rendered obedience to the patriarch of Antioch.
>
> Moreover, in letters sent to the aforesaid patriarch we decreed that the preeminence of the patriarchate of Antioch, as distributed by the ancient Fathers and preserved in past times, should likewise be kept whole in the future. [Col. 0519A] We therefore admonish—and in admonishing command—your zeal not to permit invasions of this kind to be made by you where the truth is manifest; rather, let every Church enjoy the bounds of its own right. For we cannot openly oppose the constitutions of our holy Fathers, nor do we at all wish either ecclesiastical dignity to be diminished for the power of princes, or princely power to be curtailed for ecclesiastical dignity, lest, God forbid, the Church’s peace among you be disturbed on either ground.
>
> We also command the clergy of Jerusalem by these present letters, since they have left their paternal possessions and homeland for, as is believed, the exaltation of the Church and the observance of religion, that they be content with the right of the Church of Jerusalem and not strive unjustly or insolently to usurp what is certainly known to belong by right to the Church of Antioch. May the almighty Lord protect you in all things by His right hand and grant you triumph over the enemies of the Church.
>
> Given at the Lateran, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.

## CHAPTER XXIX. The king descends to the Red Sea and surveys the region; worn down by illness, he sends back to her homeland the countess of Sicily whom he had taken as wife.

[Col. 0519C]

In the following year, in order that the king might have fuller knowledge of the adjacent regions and be more fully instructed regarding the situation of the provinces, he took with him men knowledgeable about the places and an escort which seemed sufficient for his purpose. Crossing the Jordan, passing through Sobal Syria, and descending through the wilderness of the desert to the Red Sea, he entered the very ancient city of Elim, once familiar to the people of Israel, where it is written that there were twelve springs and seventy palm trees. When he arrived there, [Col. 0519D] the inhabitants of that place, forewarned of the lord king’s arrival, boarded little boats and took themselves out upon the neighboring sea, wishing to escape death.

There the lord king, having marked and carefully considered the places, retraced the route by which he had come and returned to Mount Royal, namely the castle which he had newly founded. Returning thence to Jerusalem, he was unexpectedly seized by a severe illness. Exhausted beyond his strength and fearing that he might die, his conscience was troubled because he had unjustly cast aside his lawful wife and brought in another. Compunct in heart and repenting of the deed, he disclosed his conscience to religious and God-fearing men, confessed his guilt, and promised satisfaction. When he was advised that he should dismiss the queen whom he had brought in and restore to royal dignity the woman he had rejected, [Col. 0520A] he agreed, binding himself by vow that he would do so if a longer life were granted him.

Accordingly, the queen was summoned to him and he explained the matter in due order. Although she had some prior knowledge of it, since she had heard the same thing before from several persons, she nevertheless seemed to take it badly that she had been summoned so rashly and deceived by the treachery of the princes of the region who had been sent to call her. Thus sorrowful and grieved both by the insult inflicted upon her and by the wealth spent to no purpose, she prepared to return, intending, after the third year since she had come to the lord king, to go back to her homeland.

When she returned home, her son was exceedingly disturbed and conceived in his heart an undying hatred against the kingdom and its inhabitants. [Col. 0520B] For while other faithful princes from different parts of the world have striven, whether in person or through immense liberality, to foster and enlarge our kingdom like a newly planted tree, he and his heirs, down to the present day, have not even won us over with a friendly word, although they could more conveniently and readily than any other prince furnish counsel and aid in our necessities. They therefore seem perpetually mindful of the injury and visit upon the whole people the offense of an individual.

## CHAPTER XXX. Before the city of Tyre, the castle of Alexandria, popularly called Scandalium, is built.

[Col. 0520C] In the same year, after the king had recovered from the aforesaid illness, he anxiously considered how he might bring under his authority the city of the Tyrians, the only one of the maritime cities still held by the enemy. Between Ptolemais and the aforesaid Tyre he built a castle, on the same spot where Alexander of Macedon is said long ago to have founded that same stronghold in order to capture the city and to have called it Alexandria after his own name. The place, irrigated by springs, lies on the seashore, scarcely five miles from Tyre. He rebuilt it for the purpose of being a goad to the Tyrians and a means by which frequent injuries might be inflicted upon them. Today the common people, by a corruption of the name, call the place Scandalium. For Alexander is called *Scandar* in Arabic, and Alexandria *Scandarium*; but the common people change the *r* into *l* and say *Scandalium*. [Col. 0520D]

## CHAPTER XXXI. The king descends into Egypt; he takes Pharamia, falls ill, and, worn down by illness, dies on that expedition; he is buried at Jerusalem beside his brother.

In the following year, in order to repay the Egyptians for what they had often done in the kingdom, the king descended into Egypt with immense forces and violently captured an exceedingly ancient city named Pharamia; he gave the wealth of the captured city to his comrades-in-arms as plunder. Pharamia, as we have said, is an ancient city situated on the seashore, not far from the mouth of the Nile [Col. 0521A] called Carabeix. Above it is again Tampnis, a very ancient city, familiar with the signs which the Lord wrought before Pharaoh through Moses His servant.

After taking the city, the king went out to the aforesaid mouth of the Nile and marveled at the flow of waters which he had not seen before, especially because the Nile—one branch of which that channel carries to the sea—is said and believed to be one of the four rivers of Paradise. Having caught fish, of which there is a very great abundance there, they returned to the city they had occupied and, once the meal was prepared, refreshed themselves with them. When the king rose from supper, he felt himself greatly oppressed inwardly by pain; and as the suffering from his old wound grew acute again, he began to suffer more severely, so that, in danger of death, he despaired of life.

The return was therefore proclaimed to the legions by the herald’s voice. As the king’s illness intensified, he became so weak [Col. 0521B] [Col. 0522A] that he could not ride; they prepared a litter and placed him in it as he suffered anxiously. Thus, making uninterrupted marches and crossing part of the wilderness which stretches between Egypt and Syria, they reached Laris, an ancient maritime city of the same desert. There, overcome by illness and coming to his end, the king yielded to fate. The legions mourned and were overcome by the anguish of grief; his body was carried to Jerusalem. On the Sunday called Palm Branches, he was brought through the valley of Jehoshaphat into the city, where, according to custom, the people had assembled for the feast day. He was buried with royal magnificence beside his brother beneath Calvary, in the place called Golgotha. He died in the year 1118 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the eighteenth year of his reign.

# BOOK TWELVE BEGINS.

[Col. 0521]

## CHAPTER I. Baldwin, count of Edessa, is raised to the kingship; his identity and origin are described.

[Col. 0521B]

The second king of Jerusalem among the Latins was the lord Baldwin of Bourcq, surnamed “the Stinger” (*Aculeus*), a religious man who feared God, distinguished for faith and highly experienced in military affairs. He was a Frank by nation, from the bishopric of Rheims, son of the lord Hugh, count of Rethel, and of the renowned countess Melisende. She is said to have had so many sisters, and consequently such a multitude of sons and daughters is said to have been born, as is known to those who investigate princely genealogies with diligent care.

While his father was still alive, he set out upon the same route, with the same devotion as the others, in the company of the lord Duke Godfrey of illustrious and pious memory, his kinsman, together with other nobles who had undertaken the journey to Jerusalem. He left at home with his now aged father two brothers and an equal number of sisters, he himself being the eldest of them all. One brother was named Gervase, who was later elected to the Church of Rheims; [Col. 0521D] the other, Manasses. Of his sisters, one, named Mahalda, married the castellan of Vitry; the other, named Hodierna, married the lord Herbrand of Herges, a noble and powerful man. From her was born Manasses of Herges, whom we later saw, in the time of Queen Melisende, as royal constable.

After the death of the father of this lord King Baldwin, his son Manasses succeeded because lord Baldwin, the eldest, was occupied by the kingdom. When Manasses too died without children, their brother Gervase, having resigned the archbishopric of Rheims and taken a wife contrary to ecclesiastical ordinances, possessed the same county by hereditary right. He gave his only daughter, born to him by his wife, in marriage to a certain nobleman in Normandy.
