[Col. 0522B] When he died, their sister Mahalda’s son—she having married the castellan of Vitry—named Iterius, succeeded to the same county. But enough of these matters.

## CHAPTER II. Why he set out for Jerusalem, and when he was elected king.

[Col. 0522C]

After the lord Baldwin, brother of the lord Duke Godfrey of pious and illustrious memory, had been summoned to the kingdom of Jerusalem following his brother’s death and solemnly installed upon the royal throne, this Baldwin—of whom we are now speaking—succeeded, by appointment of the lord king, his kinsman, to the county of Edessa. He governed it vigorously and successfully for eighteen years and somewhat more.

In the eighteenth year of his county, with his region established in desired tranquillity, he resolved, out of devotion, to visit the king of Jerusalem—his lord, kinsman, and benefactor—and the holy places. Having therefore arranged what was necessary for the journey, entrusted his territory to faithful men in whose loyalty and diligence he had the fullest confidence, and placed the towns in safety, he set out upon the appointed road with an honorable escort, as a prudent and fully circumspect man. [Col. 0522D] While continuing the journey he had begun, behold, a messenger met him and announced that the lord king had, as was true, ended his last day by fate in Egypt. On hearing this, though greatly distressed by the death of his lord and kinsman, as was no wonder, he nevertheless did not abandon the journey he had undertaken, but hurried on to Jerusalem.

When he arrived there, it happened that on the feast day called Palm Branches, when the whole people had assembled as customary in the valley of Jehoshaphat for the solemn and celebrated procession of that great day, the count suddenly entered from one side with his men; and from the opposite direction came the lord king’s funeral procession, with the whole army which had descended with him into Egypt following its lord’s body according to custom.

## CHAPTER III. The manner of the election is set forth, and a memorable deed of Eustace, count of Boulogne, is described.

The royal funeral having therefore been brought into the Holy City, and the king honorably buried in the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre beside his brother, before the place called Golgotha, beneath Mount Calvary, those of the greater men of the kingdom who were present assembled: bishops, archbishops, and other prelates of churches with Lord Arnulf, the patriarch; [Col. 0523B] and certain lay princes, among whom was the energetic man of whom we have often spoken above, Joscelin, mighty in deed and word, lord of Tiberias. Deliberation having been held concerning the urgent matter, they advanced divergent opinions. Some said: “Lord Count Eustace must be awaited, and the most ancient law of hereditary succession must not be interrupted—especially since his brothers of blessed memory had governed the kingdom happily, with appropriate and universally acceptable moderation.” Others said: “The affairs of the kingdom and its continual necessities cannot endure such delays or allow so long a recess; rather, haste must be made to provide for the land more swiftly, lest, if necessity should arise, there be no one to lead armies out and bring them back [Col. 0523C] and administer the affairs of the kingdom, and the condition of the realm be endangered through lack of a duke.”

Joscelin aforesaid, who possessed very great authority in the kingdom, having sounded out the mind of the lord patriarch and inclined it toward himself, resolved this wavering of parties and conflict of opinions by supporting those who said that a king ought immediately to be established. He said: “Here is the lord Count of Edessa, a just and God-fearing man, kinsman of the lord king, valiant in arms, commendable in every respect; no country or province could furnish us with a better man. It is more expedient to raise him to the kingship than to await more dangerous contingencies.”

Many, accordingly, judged Lord Joscelin’s words to proceed from sincerity of faith, [Col. 0523D] knowing how the count had dealt with him not long before, as we have said, and recalling the proverb: “Every praise from an enemy is true.” Unaware that his intention tended elsewhere, they trusted his words and acquiesced. He himself, however, was, as was said, otherwise disposed; for, hoping to succeed in the county, he strove to introduce the lord count into the kingdom. Therefore, since Lord Arnulf the patriarch and Lord Joscelin embraced this opinion, the rest were easily brought to it; and, electing him king by equal vote and unanimous consent, on the following Day of the Holy Resurrection they solemnly anointed and consecrated him according to custom, and he received the royal insignia of the diadem.

Whatever the intention of the lord patriarch or Lord Joscelin in this act may have been, the Lord mercifully turned the outcome to good. For, through divine grace going before him, he showed himself a just, pious, and God-fearing man, and a man successful in all things. Yet he seems to have had a less regular accession; and it is certain that those who promoted him fraudulently excluded the lawful heir of the kingdom from his due succession. For after the lord king’s death—whether by his final command or by the common counsel of the princes of the kingdom, since we have certainly learned neither—certain noble and eminent men had been sent to summon, by common decree, Lord Count Eustace of Boulogne to succeed to the kingdom: brother of the distinguished Duke Godfrey and of Lord King Baldwin. [Col. 0524B] Having reached him, they drew him, reluctant and resisting, as far as Apulia, advancing highly honorable reasons why he ought to come.

There the aforesaid venerable man, devout and God-fearing, truly the imitator and brother of such great men, their successor alike in virtues and honorable merits, heard that meanwhile at Jerusalem Lord Baldwin, his kinsman the Count of Edessa, had been made king. The messengers sent for him urged him nevertheless to proceed, alleging that what had been done could in no way stand, being contrary to right and justice and to the most ancient law of hereditary succession. The man full of God is said to have replied: “Far be it from me that through me scandal should enter the kingdom [Col. 0524C] of the Lord, through whose blood it received the peace of Christ, and for whose tranquillity my brothers—men of virtue and immortal memory—offered their noble souls to heaven!” Having again packed his baggage and reassembled his retinue, he returned home, against the wishes of those who were striving to draw him to the kingdom.

## CHAPTER IV. The bodily appearance, character, and manner of life of the same king.

He is said to have been distinguished in appearance, tall of stature, handsome in face, with thin fair hair mingled with grey. His beard was sparse, yet hung down to his breast. His complexion was lively and, so far as that age permitted, ruddy. Skilled in the use of arms and highly adept in governing horses, he had much military experience; prudent in his undertakings, fortunate in campaigns, pious, gentle, and merciful in his works; devout and God-fearing; constant in prayer, so that through frequent mortification and kneeling he had calluses on his hands and knees; energetic, though elderly, whenever the affairs of the kingdom called him.

Having thus obtained the royal throne, he was concerned for the County of Edessa, which he had left without a lord. He summoned his kinsman Joscelin, in order to repair by free and full satisfaction the wrong he had formerly done him; and, since Joscelin knew that region more thoroughly, he gave him the county. Having received his oath of fealty, he invested him by the banner and put him in possession. [Col. 0525A] Calling thence his wife, daughters, and household, he soon received them all safely through the assistance and diligence of that same Lord Joscelin.

His wife was named Morphia, daughter of a certain noble Greek named Gabriel, of whom we spoke above. While still count, he had married her, with an immense sum of money bestowed as a dowry. By her he had received three daughters: namely Melisende, Haalim, and Hodierna; for his wife bore him a fourth, named Iveta, after he had acquired the kingdom. He was crowned and consecrated in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1118, in April, on the second day of the month, while Lord Pope Gelasius II presided over the Holy Roman Church; Bernard was first patriarch of the Latins in the city of Antioch; [Col. 0525B] and Lord Arnulf was fourth patriarch of the Latins in the Holy Church of Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER V. Alexius, emperor of Constantinople; Lord Pope Paschal; and the countess of Sicily, who had been queen of Jerusalem, die.

At the same time Alexius, emperor of Constantinople and the greatest persecutor of the Latins, was removed from human affairs. His son John succeeded him, far more humane than his father and, as his deserts required, far more acceptable to our people than his father. Yet he did not prove altogether sincere toward the eastern Latins, as the following events will show.

Likewise Lord Paschal, Roman pontiff, entered upon the way of all flesh [Col. 0525C] in the sixteenth year of his pontificate. He was succeeded by Lord Gelasius, also called John Gaetanus, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church. Lady Adelasia, countess of Sicily, also died; she had been the wife in fact, though not in law, of the aforesaid Lord King Baldwin.

## CHAPTER VI. The Egyptian army, both naval and land forces, enters the kingdom; the king and his men meet it, but do not engage. Arnulf, patriarch of Jerusalem, dies; Gormund succeeds him.

In the same year, in the summer immediately following, the Egyptian ruler then in office gathered from all parts of Egypt an innumerable multitude of horsemen and [Col. 0525D] foot soldiers. By land as well as by a naval force, he intended violently to enter our kingdom, believing he could easily either destroy so small a people by the sword or drive them, fleeing, out of all the lands of Syria. Having crossed the wilderness lying between us and Egypt, he encamped before Ascalon with numerous cavalry and an innumerable multitude of foot soldiers equipped with missiles.

But Doldequin, king of Damascus, on learning of the Egyptians’ arrival—whether of his own accord or at their invitation—again gathered a great army. Taking byways so that our army might not meet him, he crossed the Jordan, joined their camp, and tried to increase their strength to our injury. Some of the ships put in at Ascalon; [Col. 0526A] others sailed as far as Tyre, because it was a very strongly fortified city with a convenient harbor, awaiting instructions from their lord and from the commander of the fleet.

The king, having learned of their arrival long beforehand, summoned military aid from Antioch and Tripoli and gathered his own men together. He went down into the plains of Philistia to meet them. Passing the place formerly called Azotus, known to have been one of the five cities of the Philistines, he encamped near the Egyptians, so that each side could daily see the enemy camp. For nearly three months they feared to provoke one another: our men feared rashly to provoke such a multitude against themselves, while the Egyptians feared our forces, courage, and experience in battle. [Col. 0526B] The Egyptian ruler therefore considered it safer to return home unharmed than recklessly to expose himself and his men to the perils of war. When their forces returned to Egypt, and our people felt no further apprehension over their sudden departure, our men too, having received leave from the lord king, returned joyfully to their homes.

In those same days Arnulf, patriarch of Jerusalem, died—a most restless man, negligent of the holiness of his office. He was succeeded by a simple and God-fearing man, Lord Gormund, a Frenchman from the bishopric of Amiens, [Col. 0526C] from the town of Picquigny. In his days and, it is believed, because of his merits, the Lord deigned magnificently to work much for the consolation and increase of the kingdom, as the present history will relate in what follows.

## CHAPTER VII. The Order of the Temple is established at Jerusalem.

In the same year certain noble men of knightly rank, devoted to God, devout, and God-fearing, committed themselves to Christ’s service in the hand of the lord patriarch. In the manner of Regular Canons, they professed to live perpetually in chastity, obedience, and without a will of their own. The first and foremost among them were the venerable men Hugh of Payns and Godfrey [Col. 0526D] of Saint-Aldemar. Since they had neither a church nor a fixed dwelling, the king granted them temporary lodgings in the palace situated beside the Temple of the Lord, on its southern side. The canons of the Temple of the Lord also granted them, under certain conditions, the street around the aforesaid palace for workshops.

The lord king and his princes, and likewise the lord patriarch with the prelates of churches, bestowed upon them from their own lordships certain benefices for food and clothing—some temporary, others perpetual. Their first profession, and the charge imposed upon them by the lord patriarch and the other bishops for the remission of sins, was that they should protect roads and routes, especially for the safety of pilgrims, [Col. 0527A] to the best of their ability against the ambushes of robbers and raiders.

For nine years after their institution they wore secular clothing, using such garments as the people bestowed for the salvation of their souls. At length, in the ninth year, when a council was held in France at Troyes, attended by the archbishops of Rheims and Sens with their suffragans; the bishop of Albano, legate of the Apostolic See; and the abbots of Cîteaux, Clairvaux, and Pontigny with many others, a rule was established for them and a white habit assigned, by command of Lord Pope Honorius and Lord Stephen, patriarch of Jerusalem. Though they had already been nine years in this undertaking, they numbered only [Col. 0527B] nine men; thereafter their number began to increase and their possessions multiplied.

Later, in the time of Lord Pope Eugenius, they are said to have begun sewing crosses of red cloth onto their mantles, so that they might be more conspicuous among others—both the knights and their inferior brethren, called serjeants. Their resources grew so boundlessly that today, apart from the brethren, whose number is almost infinite, they are said to have some three hundred knights in convent, clothed in white cloaks. They are said to possess estates so immense both beyond and on this side of the sea that there is now no province in the Christian world that has not contributed a portion of its goods to these brethren; and they are said today to possess wealth equal to royal riches.

[Col. 0527C] Because, as we have said, they have their dwelling in the royal palace beside the Temple of the Lord, they are called the brethren of the Knighthood of the Temple. Although for a long time they maintained themselves in an honorable purpose, prudently fulfilling their profession, they neglected humility—the guardian of all virtues, which voluntarily sits in the low place and therefore has nowhere from which it can fall. They withdrew themselves from the patriarch of Jerusalem, from whom they had received both the institution of their order and their first benefices, refusing him the obedience their predecessors had rendered. Moreover, by withholding tithes and first-fruits from the churches of God and improperly troubling their possessions, they became exceedingly troublesome.

## CHAPTER VIII. Pope Gelasius dies; Calixtus succeeds him.

[Col. 0527D]

In the following year Lord Pope Gelasius II died, successor to Lord Paschal, also called John Gaetanus, a learned man. Fleeing the persecution of Emperor Henry and avoiding the violence of his rival antipope, surnamed Burdinus, he withdrew into the kingdom of France and died at Cluny, where he was also buried. He was succeeded by Lord Guy, noble by birth, archbishop of Vienne, who, after being elevated to the papacy, was called Calixtus.

Having afterward won the favor of Emperor Henry, his kinsman, and relying on his aid, he went down into Italy with the cardinals and the whole curia. At Sutri, a city adjoining Rome, he violently seized his rival and heresiarch Burdinus; moreover, mounted upon a camel and dressed in a bear’s hide, he sent him with great ignominy to the monastery of Cava, known to be situated near Salerno. There he was compelled, under the rule of that place, to lead a monastic life until extreme old age. Thus the schism was quelled which, from the time of Lord Gregory VII through the times of his predecessors Lord Urban, Lord Paschal, and Lord Gelasius, had incessantly troubled the Church for nearly thirty years—Emperor Henry having at last been recalled to the fold of the Church after long years during which he had been cut off from the fellowship of the faithful by sentence of excommunication. [Col. 0528B]

## CHAPTER IX. Gazzi, a most powerful Turkish satrap, pours into the region of Antioch with immense forces, devastating everything.

In the same year a most powerful prince among the unbelievers, greatly feared among his own people—lord of the unhappy and faithless people of the Turcomans, named Gazzi—entered the territory of Antioch with immense forces and a heavy multitude of his followers, and encamped on this side of Aleppo. Doldequin, king of Damascus, and Debeis, a most powerful satrap of the Arabs, had joined him.

When his arrival became known, Lord Roger, prince of Antioch and brother-in-law of the lord king, sent messages to the neighboring [Col. 0528C] princes—namely Lord Joscelin, count of Edessa; Lord Pons, count of Tripoli; and likewise the lord king—announcing the pressing danger and earnestly exhorting and begging them not to delay in coming with all speed to bring aid against the imminent peril.

The king therefore gathered such military forces as he could suddenly collect from the kingdom and hastened to Tripoli. There he joined to himself the count, who was likewise prepared for the journey, and pressed on along the road he had begun. Meanwhile, however, the lord prince, impatient of delay and, subject to the common law of mortals, ignorant of future events, left Antioch and encamped near the town of Artas. [Col. 0528D] This place was very convenient for supporting armies: it lay within our territory, access to it was free and easy for those wishing to join the army, and thus there was the greatest abundance of campaign necessities and the desirable convenience ordinarily found in cities.

After he had awaited the king’s and count’s arrival for several days, the lord patriarch, who had accompanied him thus far, forbade him to move; some of the princes also tried to restrain him. Yet he ordered the army to march, firmly declaring that he would await no one’s arrival thereafter. Certain nobles of the region were urging him to this, not in order to improve the army’s condition, but so that, with the army present, they might secure their lands which lay near the enemy camp. Following their counsel, he rashly departed, to his own destruction and that of his followers, from the place where he had been and ordered the camp pitched in the place called the Field of Blood.

When his army was counted, it contained seven hundred knights and three thousand armed foot soldiers, excluding the merchants who usually follow a camp for buying and selling. [Col. 0529A] The enemy, learning that the prince’s camp had been placed nearby, broke camp and pretended to direct their lines toward the town of Cerep, so that, by concealing their purpose, they might more conveniently bring their conceived plan to effect. Having arrived there and accomplished nothing that night, they encamped in the vicinity.

At daybreak the prince sent scouts, wishing to know whether the enemy were moving to besiege the town or were hastening to attack our men in camp. While he and his men armed themselves as though expecting imminent battle, messengers returned and declared in a single report that the enemy, arranged in three divisions, each containing twenty thousand horsemen, were approaching our army at speed. Learning this, the prince formed four battle lines. Riding around among them, he carefully inspected them and encouraged the formations with fitting words. While he was engaged in this, the enemy lines, banners raised, almost joined our army. [Col. 0529B]

Battle was therefore joined, both sides fighting spiritedly; but, as our sins deserved, the opposing side prevailed. The lines commanded by the noble and valiant men Geoffrey the Monk and Guy Fremel—the first assigned to charge the enemy—advanced excellently and according to military discipline. They violently broke up the larger enemy wedges and denser divisions, driving them almost to flight. But the line commanded by Robert of Saint-Lô, which should have charged the enemy more boldly, following the example of the preceding lines, shamefully halted as the enemy regained strength. Finally it took flight, split the prince’s line—which was to bring aid to the others—through the middle, and carried part of it with itself in flight, so that it could no longer be recalled.

Something worthy of record also happened in the same battle. While in the heat of combat men strove more fiercely on either side, [Col. 0529D] behold, a most enormous whirlwind arose from the north and settled upon the ground in the middle of the battlefield, visible to all. Crawling onward for a considerable distance, it carried with it such a mass of dust that, by its immensity, it blinded the eyes of both sides and prevented them from fighting. Then, rising in a circle, it lifted itself into the air like a barrel consumed by sulphurous flames. By this occurrence the enemy gained the advantage, and our side fell, almost all our men being killed by the sword.

## CHAPTER X. Prince Roger falls in battle, and our army is overthrown.

The prince, a valiant man in arms, fought manfully with a few men in the midst of the enemy. [Col. 0530A] While vainly striving to recall his men and throwing himself against the enemy’s greatest assaults, he was pierced by swords and died. Those who had followed the baggage and impedimenta made their way to a neighboring hill. Those who seemed to have escaped the enemy’s weapons, withdrawing from the turmoil of battle, saw our men gathered on the summit of the hill and, believing that they had strength to resist and that safety could be found with them, hastened to join them. Once all had gathered there, the enemy, having utterly put to the sword those in the plain, turned against them and, sending their divisions there, brought them all to destruction in a moment.

Rainaud Mansuer, one of the leading princes of that region, together with certain other nobles, had withdrawn for safety into the tower of a neighboring [Col. 0530B] town named Sarmatan. When the aforesaid Turkish prince learned this, he rushed there with all speed and violently compelled the noble men who had gathered inside to surrender. Thus it happened that on that day, out of so many thousands who had followed the lord prince, our sins deserving it, scarcely even one escaped to bear the news, while of the enemy either few or none were killed.

This same Prince Roger is said to have been a thoroughly depraved man, incontinent, miserly, and a public adulterer. Moreover, throughout the time he held the principality, he had kept his young lord Bohemond—the son of the elder Bohemond, living in Apulia with his mother—excluded from Antioch, his paternal inheritance. For Lord Tancred of blessed memory had entrusted the principality to Roger on his deathbed upon the condition that he should not refuse it to Lord Bohemond or his heirs when they should demand it.

It is nevertheless said that, in the campaign in which he died pierced by swords, he confessed his sins before God with a contrite and humbled heart in the presence of the venerable Lord Peter, archbishop of Apamea, who had been present at that moment of necessity. He promised, with the Lord’s help, fruits worthy of repentance; and thus, truly repentant, entered the hazard of battle. [Col. 0530C]

## CHAPTER XI. The king and count of Tripoli hasten to Antioch to resist the aforesaid Gazzi.

[Col. 0530D]

Meanwhile the king and the count of Tripoli advanced and reached the place called Mount Nigron. When Gazzi learned this, he sent ten thousand selected horsemen to meet them, to obstruct their approach if they could. These men departed and divided themselves into three divisions: one heading toward the sea and the port of Saint Symeon, the other two sent by different routes to meet the king.

It happened that the king encountered one of the two divisions. Through the Lord’s preceding mercy, after killing many and taking some captives, he violently broke it up and put it to flight. Proceeding thence by Latorum and Casambella, he arrived at Antioch, where he was received with the greatest longing by the lord patriarch, clergy, and whole people. [Col. 0531A] There, entering into deliberation both with his own men and with those surviving from the aforesaid battle, he asked what was most expedient amid the imminence of such great necessity.

Meanwhile Gazzi left the towns of Emma and Artas and besieged Cerep, the more confidently because he had heard that Alan, lord of that place, with his household, had been summoned from it to Antioch by the lord king—which was true. Approaching the fortress and finding the place unprepared, he sent in miners from different sides to undermine the hill on which the aforesaid town stood; when it had been propped with timbers, he intended to set fire beneath it, so that, as the earthwork gave way, the towers above and the walls might be thrown down to the ground. Fearing that, once the earthwork had been undermined, the entire fortress would plunge headlong [Col. 0531B] down, the townspeople surrendered the place on terms securing their lives, safety, and free return to their own people.

Gazzi then directed his forces toward the castle of Sardonas and surrounded it with a siege. Within a few days he received it likewise, its inhabitants surrendering it in the same manner. Impatient of delay, and especially because he believed that no one could resist him, he treated the entire region as he pleased, so that the inhabitants of neighboring places had no hope of escaping the yoke of so great a prince.

## CHAPTER XII. The king and the same count engage the aforesaid Gazzi; putting him to flight, they overthrow his army and kill many; the care of the principality is entrusted to the king.

[Col. 0531C] The king, with the count and all the soldiery he could have, left Antioch. Thinking that he would find the enemy at Cerep, he directed his forces toward Rugia; passing thence through Hab, he encamped on the mountain called Danim. On hearing this, Gazzi summoned his princes and, under threat of death, commanded them to spend the entire night sleeplessly, attending with the utmost diligence to their arms and horses. At the earliest dawn, before daybreak, fully prepared, they were to fall upon the king’s camp and, finding them still asleep, pierce them with swords, so that not even one man might be permitted to escape death.

But divine mercy had ordered matters far otherwise. The king, no less anxiously watchful with his men, spent that same night without sleep, considering what was necessary for the coming battle. A venerable man, marked with the sign of the Lord’s cross, who had accompanied the lord king to those regions, exhorted the people. [Col. 0531D] Thus armed and manfully girded to receive battle, they awaited the enemy’s expected assault early in the morning.

At the king’s command, nine battle lines were formed according to military discipline—for he is said to have had seven hundred soldiers in that engagement—and stationed in suitable order, awaiting the Lord’s mercy. Three lines were sent forward to precede the entire force. The lord count of Tripoli held the right wing with his men, while the princes of Antioch were placed on the left; [Col. 0532A] the infantry formations were stationed in the center. The king followed with four lines, intending to provide assistance to the others.

As they stood thus arrayed awaiting the enemy’s approach, behold, they arrived with a great shout, shrill trumpets, and the din of drums, charging our men with the utmost ferocity. The enemy’s chief confidence lay in their countless multitude; our men’s fuller and unfailing hope lay in the presence of the most victorious cross and in confession of the true faith. When the lines had closed and hostile legions mingled, the fight was waged hand-to-hand with swords; setting aside the laws of humanity, they fought on both sides with burning zeal and insatiable hatred, as though against utterly savage beasts.

When the enemy recognized the fierce and exceedingly dangerous resistance of our infantry formations, they exerted all their strength to destroy the infantry divisions. And it happened, by the Lord’s permission, that on that day they perished for the most part by the enemy’s swords. [Col. 0532B] But the king, seeing the infantry formations oppressed beyond their strength and the forward lines in need of aid, rushed with his adherents into the midst of the ranks. Pressing forward more boldly with the sword, he scattered the densest wedges of the enemy. The comrades of those same battle lines faithfully joined him; restoring strength and courage by words and example to men already losing heart, they charged the enemy together. Invoking aid from heaven, divine mercy came to them; after an immense slaughter of the enemy, they put the survivors, unable to resist, to flight.

About seven hundred of our infantry are said to have fallen there, and one hundred cavalrymen. Of the enemy, however, as many as four thousand were slain, apart from those mortally wounded and those put in fetters. Gazzi fled with Doldequin, king of Damascus, and Debeis, prince of the Arabs, abandoning his men exposed to death. While our men pursued them and advanced to various places, the king, with a few men, held the field until the early hours of night. At last, pressed by lack of provisions, he withdrew to the neighboring town called Hab to take refreshment. [Col. 0532C]

At daybreak he returned to the aforesaid field and sent messengers to his sister and the lord patriarch, with his own ring as a sure token of victory, reporting that, by divine grace assisting him, the gift of victory had been bestowed upon him by God. Yet he did not leave the field that day until the latest evening, when certain information had been received that the scattered enemy would not return. Finally, having gathered as many of his own men as he could then have, he entered Antioch as a distinguished victor, with the patriarch and all the clergy and people of the city coming to meet him.

This victory was divinely granted to our men in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1120, in the second year of the reign of Lord King Baldwin II, in August, on the vigil of the Assumption of Saint Mary, Mother of God. The king sent the life-giving wood of the cross to Jerusalem with the lord archbishop of Caesarea and an honorable retinue, so that on the Feast of its Exaltation [Col. 0533A] it might be honorably received by clergy and people with hymns and spiritual songs.

He himself was compelled to remain in that province because of the region’s pressing needs. There the lord patriarch and all the princes, together with the clergy and people, with united desire and free consent entrusted to the king the care and complete authority of the principality of Antioch. Thus he possessed in the principality, as in the kingdom, free authority to appoint and remove persons and to administer everything as he saw fit. Having bestowed the possessions of those who had fallen in battle upon their children or kindred of other degrees, as reason or the custom of the region demanded; having married widows to men of equal rank and fitting merit; and having more diligently fortified the garrisons where this appeared necessary with men, provisions, and arms, he took leave of them for a time and returned to the kingdom. There, in the church at Bethlehem, he was crowned with his wife at the solemn feast of the Lord’s Nativity. [Col. 0533B]

## CHAPTER XIII. A council is held at Neapolis, a city of Samaria.

In the same year, 1120 from the Incarnation of the Lord, while, as our sins deserved, the kingdom of Jerusalem was afflicted by many vexations, and while, besides the troubles inflicted by enemies, its crops had for almost four continuous years been so wholly destroyed by the ravages of locusts and devouring mice that every staff of bread seemed to have failed, [Col. 0533C] Lord Gormund, patriarch of Jerusalem, a devout and God-fearing man, together with Lord King Baldwin, the prelates of churches, and the princes of the kingdom, assembled at Neapolis, a city of Samaria, and convened a public assembly and general court.

After an address had been made to the people by way of exhortation, and since all seemed agreed that the people’s sins had provoked the Lord to wrath, they resolved by common counsel to correct errors and reduce transgressions to order. Thus, returning at last to the fruitfulness of a better life and making worthy satisfaction for their offences, they might render propitious to themselves him “who does not will the death of the sinner, but rather that he turn and live” (Ezekiel [Col. 0533D] 33).

Alarmed, therefore, by threatening signs from heaven, frequent earthquakes, calamity, the pressure of famine, and the exceedingly fierce and almost daily assaults of enemies, and seeking through works of piety to reconcile the Lord to themselves, they established by common decision twenty-five chapters, having almost the force of law, to restore and preserve moral discipline. Whoever wishes to see them for the sake of reading may easily find them in the archives of many churches.

Those present at this council were: Lord Gormund, patriarch of Jerusalem; Lord Baldwin, second Latin king of Jerusalem; Ebremarus, archbishop of Caesarea; Bernard, bishop of Nazareth; Asquitillus, bishop of Bethlehem; Roger, bishop of Lydda; [Col. 0534A] Gildon, elected abbot of Saint Mary in the Valley of Jehoshaphat; Peter, abbot of Mount Tabor; Achard, prior of the Temple; Arnald, prior of Mount Sion; Gerard, prior of the Lord’s Sepulchre; Pagan, the king’s chancellor; Eustace Granier; William of Bures; Barisan, constable of Jaffa; Baldwin of Ramla; and many others of both orders, whose number and names we do not possess.

## CHAPTER XIV. The aforesaid Gazzi again renews his campaign and enters the territory of Antioch; the king meets him. Gazzi, struck by apoplexy, dies.

In the following year, Gazzi, the aforesaid stubborn and untiring persecutor of the Christian faith and name, like a restless worm, ever seeking whom he might harm [Col. 0534B], taking occasion from the king’s absence, summoned military forces and also began to besiege certain of our strongholds. When this became known, they called upon the lord king with the utmost urgency. He, however, prompt in action, taking with him the wood of the life-giving Cross and an honorable company of knights, hastened to those parts. Having also summoned the lord Joscelin, count of Edessa, and joined to himself the nobles of Antioch, he directed his camp against the aforesaid powerful enemy. When he had arrived there, and they expected that battle would shortly ensue, the hand of the Lord struck Gazzi with the illness called apoplexy.

Therefore the magnates in his army, deprived of their prince’s support, prudently and with sound judgment avoided battle. Carrying their lord half alive in a litter, they hastened toward Aleppo [Col. 0534C]. Before reaching it, he is said to have breathed out his unhappy soul, destined for eternal fires. The king likewise, after making such a delay at Antioch as seemed necessary at the time, returned safely, through the Lord’s aid, to the kingdom. By both peoples—both in the kingdom and in the principality—he was exceedingly beloved and acceptable, as his merits required. For he faithfully and devoutly discharged both administrations, that is, of the kingdom and of the principality, although they differed greatly from one another. Nor was it easy to determine for which he was more anxious. The kingdom was his own possession, which he could lawfully transmit to his successors; but the principality had been entrusted to him. Indeed, he seemed to show even greater diligence for the condition of the Antiochenes [Col. 0534D], and in good faith continued in this office until the arrival of the lord Bohemond the younger, as will be related below.

## CHAPTER XV. The king grants Jerusalem’s citizens complete liberty and confirms it by his privilege.

At the same time, while the king was in Jerusalem, in pious liberality and princely generosity he granted the citizens of Jerusalem freedom from the customary dues which had been exacted from citizens importing or exporting merchandise. He ordered a charter, confirmed by the royal seal and to remain valid forever, to be drawn up for them. Henceforth, no Latin entering or departing, whether bringing in or taking out merchandise, was to be compelled to render anything at all under the pretext of any customary due [Col. 0535A], but was to have entirely free power to buy and sell.

He also gave Syrians, Greeks, Armenians, and persons of any of these nations—and Saracens likewise—the free right to bring wheat, barley, and every kind of pulse into the Holy City without any exaction. He also remitted the customary charge for measures and weights. By this he won the goodwill of the aforesaid peoples and earned public favor. In both respects, with a royal practice and an exceedingly commendable disposition, he seems to have provided for the citizens: both that the city might abound more fully in provisions brought in free from exactions, and that the city beloved by God [Col. 0535B] might be inhabited by increasing and more numerous residents—something which both he and his predecessor had pursued with every diligence.

## CHAPTER XVI. Doldequin, king of Damascus, ravages the territory of Tiberias; the king confronts him and destroys the city of Gerasa.

In the following year Doldequin, the faithless and impious king of Damascus, having allied with himself an Arab prince and the latter’s troops, and seeing that the lord king bore responsibility for both regions beyond his available strength, presumed upon the king’s preoccupations and began, by sending in his legions, to lay waste with great hostility our territory near Tiberias. On hearing this, the lord king gathered troops from every part of the whole kingdom and, as was his custom, hastened there without delay.

But Doldequin, having learned of the king’s approach [Col. 0535C], saw that he could achieve nothing while the king was present, and, judging it unsafe to engage him, withdrew into the more distant parts of his realm. The king, turning southward with his columns, came to Gerasa. Gerasa was one of the noble cities of the province of Decapolis, a few miles from the Jordan, adjoining Mount Gilead, and situated in the tribe of Manasseh. In its more fortified quarter—for the rest of the city had long lain desolate through fear of hostilities—Doldequin had, in the preceding year, caused a castle to be built of large squared stones at great expense. Having supplied it with provisions and arms, he had entrusted it to certain of his faithful men to guard.

When the king arrived there, he vigorously attacked the garrison. After taking the castle, he permitted the forty knights [Col. 0535D] left within it as guards to depart unharmed, on the condition that they should return safely to their own people. Having deliberated with his men whether it was more expedient to demolish the stronghold entirely or preserve it for Christendom, all agreed that the fortress should be utterly destroyed. For it did not seem that our people could maintain it without great expense, continual labor, and serious danger to travelers.

## CHAPTER XVII. Balac, a most powerful prince of the Turks, violently enters Antiochene territory; Count Joscelin is captured by him, and the king also falls into his chains, captured by the same man.

While, therefore, by God’s grace, the affairs of the kingdom were proceeding quite prosperously [Col. 0536A], the enemy of peace, envying its tranquility, devised the scandal which he hoped to introduce. Pontius, the second count of Tripoli, through an impulse we do not know, denied homage to his lord, the king of Jerusalem; and he shamelessly refused the service which he was bound to render by the law of fealty. Unable to endure so great an injury, the king assembled forces of both cavalry and infantry from throughout the kingdom and came into those regions to exact vengeance for such an affront. Before either side had suffered any damage, however, worthy and God-loving men intervened, and a fitting peace was restored between them.

Proceeding from there, he went down into those parts at the summons of the Antiochenes, on account of their necessities. For Balac [Col. 0536B], a magnificent and powerful prince of the Turks, was harassing the whole region by frequent incursions. He did so more confidently because, shortly before, suddenly falling upon the lord Joscelin, count of Edessa, and his kinsman the lord Galeran, he had captured them and consigned them in chains to captivity. Knowing, therefore, that the lord king had arrived, he began to restrain his incursions somewhat and to avoid encounter with him. For he had heard that the king was more fortunate in battle and that it was difficult for anyone to triumph over him. Yet he roamed about with an expeditionary force, as if at a distance, watching for an opportunity to inflict damage upon our people.

The king, therefore, with the forces he had brought with him, entered the land of the count of Edessa [Col. 0536C], to afford some relief to a people lacking their ruler. Going through the region, he carefully investigated whether the strongholds were fortified and possessed sufficient supplies of cavalry, infantry, arms, and provisions; and he showed due concern to remedy their deficiencies. It happened, while he was hastening toward Edessa with this same care, after leaving the town of Turbessel, that he undertook a journey by night, wishing through the same diligence to learn more fully the state of the country beyond the Euphrates and to improve everything as far as possible. He traveled with his household retinue; but while they went on somewhat incautiously, their ranks dispersed and almost all asleep, in security, the aforesaid Balac—who had learned the king’s route—lay in ambush [Col. 0536D] and suddenly attacked. Finding the king’s company unprepared and weighed down by sleep, he chanced upon the king himself, laid hands upon him, and carried him away captive. Those who went before and those who followed scattered in flight in different directions, unaware of what had happened to the king.

Balac accordingly consigned the captured king in chains to a fortress beyond the Euphrates called Quartapiert. Count Joscelin and Galeran, mentioned above, were there as well. When our princes in the kingdom heard of the grievous misfortune that had befallen the lord king, they were greatly concerned for the kingdom’s condition. Together with the lord patriarch and the prelates of the churches, they assembled at Acre as one man and, by common consent, appointed as their leader and governor [Col. 0537A] the lord Eustace Grenier, a prudent and discerning man, fully experienced in military affairs. By hereditary right and through the support of his merits, he possessed two cities in the kingdom, namely Sidon and Caesarea, each with its dependencies. They entrusted to him the care and general administration of the kingdom, until the East should be visited from on high by the lord king and, restored to freedom, he might again attend to royal affairs. But meanwhile, let us return the narrative to those matters which we had begun concerning the lord king.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Certain Armenians expose themselves to grave danger in order to free the king; they seize the castle in which the captives were held, and Count Joscelin is released.

[Col. 0537B] While the lord king and the lord count were held in chains in the aforementioned castle, certain Armenians from the count’s land learned that such great princes of the Christian name were held captive in that fortress. Counting danger as nothing, even should their undertaking fail to have a favorable result, they entered upon a new course of unheard-of enterprise. Some, however, assert that these same men were summoned through the diligence of the lord Joscelin and exposed themselves to this danger in hope of a most ample reward.

Fifty of them, who seemed the strongest, having pledged faith and bound themselves by mutual oaths, resolved that they would go there and endeavor to free the aforesaid distinguished men, whatever the danger. They therefore disguised themselves as monks, carrying daggers beneath loose garments, and proceeded to the said town, pretending that they had business concerning monasteries. By speech, groaning, and an altered expression of face, they feigned that certain persons had inflicted violence and injury upon them. They declared, with tears, that they wished to report this to the official whose responsibility it was to ensure that nothing outrageous or contrary to the order of the times should occur in the neighboring places [Col. 0537C]. Others say that they entered the town as merchants carrying cheap wares.

At length they were admitted; and, once inside the fortress, they drew their swords and killed every person who met them. In short, having obtained the castle, they freed the king and the count and fortified the castle as best they could. The king meanwhile resolved to send out Count Joscelin, so that he might gather aid for himself and his companions, by whose action they seemed to have been freed, and not delay in sending it speedily. But the Turks dwelling in the suburbs, learning that by this stratagem the king and those inside with him had gained possession of the castle, seized their arms and came to the place. They diligently endeavored, at least until the arrival of their lord Balac, to deny those in the town both entrance and exit.

Count Joscelin, nevertheless, taking with him three companions—two to accompany him on the journey, and the third to send immediately back to the lord king with news of his condition—exposed himself to the enemy’s ambushes and departed. Protected by the Lord’s mercy, without the knowledge of those besieging the castle, he set out with two companions along the route as had been arranged [Col. 0538A], sending the third back into the town. To him he gave his ring as proof that he had safely escaped the enemy’s bands. The king, with those by whose aid he had been freed, strove with all his strength to fortify the stronghold, trying to see whether he might somehow preserve it until the arrival of the aid he expected shortly.

## CHAPTER XIX. Balac again violently retakes the same castle, after the aforesaid Armenians have been put to the sword.

But Balac, troubled that same night by a terrifying vision, seemed in a dream to see Count Joscelin depriving him of his sight with his own hands. Terrified by the vision, at first light he sent messengers to the aforementioned town to behead the lord Joscelin without delay. When they came nearer the castle and learned that through this event it had fallen into the hands of the enemy, they retraced their route with all speed and returned to their lord, setting forth in order everything that had happened there.

He, however, summoned military forces from all sides, hastened promptly to those parts, stationed his troops in a ring, and surrounded with a siege those who had taken refuge in the town. There, through envoys, he held a discussion with the lord king and firmly pledged and promised that, if the king restored the stronghold to him without difficulty, he would grant the king and all his men free egress and safe conduct as far as the city of Edessa [Col. 0538B]. But the king, confident in the town’s fortifications and hoping, with the assistance of those who had entered it with him, to hold the castle by force until relief arrived, rejected the offered terms and persisted more earnestly in defending the fortress.

Balac, enraged because his terms had been rejected, summoned craftsmen and prepared many engines by which enemy strongholds are usually attacked. Pressing the siege more obstinately, he ingeniously applied himself to every means by which he might injure the besieged. The hill on which the town stood was chalky and easy to undermine. Seeing, therefore, that the place could more easily be brought down on that side, he sent in diggers and ordered vast excavations to be made beneath the hill, supported by beams and timber. Then, after withdrawing the workmen and setting fire to it, the material within was burned [Col. 0538C–D]; the hill subsided, and the tower built upon it collapsed with a tremendous crash. Fearing that by a similar fall the entire stronghold would plunge headlong, the king surrendered the castle to Balac without any conditions intervening.

Having gained the castle, Balac spared the lives of the lord king, a certain nephew of his, and the lord Galeran. He ordered them to be carried in fetters to Carrhae, a city neighboring Edessa, and there held under close guard. But he subjected the aforesaid Armenians, valiant and faithful men who had exposed themselves to such dangers in order to free the king and their lord from chains, to various tortures. Some he had flayed alive; others he had sawn in two; others buried alive; and others handed over to his boys as targets for shooting arrows [Col. 0539A]. Yet although they suffered torments before them, their hope is full of immortality; and, though tried in a few things, they shall be richly rewarded in many.

## CHAPTER XX. Count Joscelin, having assembled a great force to free the lord king, reaches Antioch; but moved by the unexpected news of what had happened, he dismisses the dispersed forces to their homes.

Count Joscelin, with those whom he had taken as companions on the journey, traveled on his intended route amid much anxiety and continual fear. With scant provisions and two skins which he had happened to bring with him, he reached the great river Euphrates. There, after deliberating with his companions in danger about how he might cross the river, he filled the skins with wind, fastened them around himself with a rope, and, with his companions—who were highly practiced in swimming—guiding him on the right and left, reached the farther bank safe and unharmed, by the Lord’s aid [Col. 0539B].

Then, in no smaller danger, barefoot, oppressed by unaccustomed exertion, exhausted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue, he finally reached his notable town of Turbessel, under the leading mercy of the Lord. Bearing full concern for the task entrusted to him, he hastened with such retinue as was necessary at the time to Antioch and afterward, with the counsel of the lord patriarch Bernard, to Jerusalem. There he set out the matter in order before the lord patriarch and the princes of the kingdom, explaining in sequence the disaster that had occurred and calling them to send aid without delay. He asserted that the king’s situation could admit no postponement, but required prompt and immediate counsel.

Accordingly, at his exhortation, the whole people of the kingdom assembled as one man. Taking up the Cross of the Lord, they joined to themselves auxiliary forces from every intermediate city and came to Antioch. There, having added to their number both the common people and the leading men of that city, they went on under the count’s leadership to Turbessel. Having there learned more fully what had happened to the lord king in the meantime, and discovered that proceeding further would be fruitless, they decided by common counsel that each should return home [Col. 0539C]. Yet, lest they seem to have done altogether nothing, they resolved, while passing by Aleppo, to test whether they could inflict any damage or injury upon the enemy. This was done as proposed. For when they passed before the aforesaid city, they forced its citizens, who had come out against them as if to fight, violently back into the city; and they remained there for four successive days against the citizens’ will.

Those from the kingdom, separated from the others and returning to the kingdom, crossed the Jordan near Scythopolis and suddenly entered enemy territory. Finding the enemy unprepared, they fell upon them, killed many with the sword, captured countless men and women, and returned joyfully and triumphantly to their homes with immense booty and rich spoils [Col. 0539D].

## CHAPTER XXI. The Egyptians again entered the kingdom with enormous forces; but when our men confront them with a strong hand, they are wonderfully overthrown.

[Col. 0540A]

Meanwhile, the prince of Egypt, judging that the king’s captivity had afforded him a great opportunity to oppress in some degree the kingdom of Jerusalem—which he had every reason to suspect—ordered military assistance to be summoned from every part of Egypt. He commanded the coastal cities, through officials specially appointed for the task, to prepare galleys and arm a fleet; and he ordered without delay all other things necessary for the use of a naval army to be made ready.

When seventy galleys had been prepared, he crossed the desert with an innumerable multitude of infantry and encamped near Ascalon with his legions. The fleet advanced as far as Joppa and took station before the city. Disembarking in great numbers, they began to harass the city on every side with uninterrupted attacks, so that, because of the shortage of defenders, they could safely approach the walls to undermine them and weaken them in many places [Col. 0540B]. Had they been allowed one further day free to assault the city, they would beyond doubt have broken down the walls and seized it by force, for there were few inside able to resist their attacks.

Meanwhile the lord patriarch, the lord Eustace Grenier, constable of the kingdom, and the other princes of the realm, having gathered all the troops then available to them, met in the plains of Caesarea at a place called Caco. From there, descending toward Joppa with their columns arranged, they directed their legions onward. Hearing this, those attacking the city hastened competitively back to the fleet, fearing our men’s arrival. When the fleet had been made ready, they bent to their oars, waiting to see what would happen to their own forces, whom they knew to be near the enemy.

Our men, meanwhile, with the Cross of the Lord leading them, armed in faith and raised to hope of victory by the cooperation of God’s grace, arranged their battle lines and drew them into proper order near the place called Ibelin [Col. 0540C]. There they found the enemy. The enemy too, according to their custom, had arranged their companies and had arrived determined, beyond doubt, to fight our men. But, seeing our men’s array and recognizing their courage by clear indications, those who had approached as lions wished to refuse battle, timid as hares and more timid than hares—indeed, wishing rather that they had never begun it.

Our mixed force, comprising every sort of common people, was said to number about seven thousand. The enemy’s force equipped for battle was said to number sixteen thousand, apart from those serving the fleet who were said to be aboard the ships [Col. 0540D]. Our men therefore rushed upon them with fierce spirit, contrite heart, and fear of the Lord. Invoking aid from above, they pressed on more fiercely with their swords and, bringing the danger of death close at hand, denied them even the chance to breathe.

At last the Egyptians marveled at the strength and boldness of our men; and what they had heard in report, they experienced under the blows dealt them and beheld with their own eyes [Col. 0541A]. They nevertheless prepared and strove to resist the injuries inflicted and to answer our men in equal measure. But greatly inferior both in courage and in strength, they failed in their purpose and took to flight. Leaving behind their camp, filled with every sort of wealth and convenience, they sought safety in flight. Our men pursued them more vigorously and cut down with swords as many as they could overtake, so that few of that great multitude escaped either captivity or death. Seven thousand of them are said to have fallen that day.

Our victorious men returned to the camp and found Egyptian treasures, immense quantities of gold and silver, most precious equipment of every kind, pavilions and tents, horses, coats of mail, and swords in abundance. Dividing the spoils according to the law of war, they became exceedingly rich and returned home [Col. 0541B]. When the fleet learned what had happened to its own men, it turned aside toward Ascalon, still in Egyptian power, to choose a secure anchorage; there it learned more fully of their defeat.

At the same time, the lord Eustace Grenier, governor of the kingdom, a prudent and discerning man, died. In his place was appointed the lord William of Bures, a distinguished man in every respect worthy of praise, lord of Tiberias.

## CHAPTER XXII. The doge of Venice comes down into Syria with a numerous fleet.

At the same time, when the need of the Eastern kingdom had become known, Dominicus Michaelis, doge of Venice and prince of the kingdom of Dalmatia and Croatia, together with the leading men of that province, prepared a fleet [Col. 0541C]. With forty galleys, twenty-eight *gatti*—larger, beaked ships—and four larger vessels fitted for carrying freight, they set out for Syria.

When they had reached the island of Cyprus, word was brought to them, their approach having already become known, that the Egyptian fleet had put in along the Syrian coast near Joppa, was remaining in those parts, and was a serious threat to the maritime cities. Hearing this, the aforesaid doge ordered his men to depart and, with his force arrayed, hastened his course toward the shore of Joppa. Meanwhile they were told that the aforesaid Egyptian fleet, having left Joppa, had withdrawn toward Ascalon, for it had heard unfavorable reports of its men who had fought our people on land and had taken refuge in its own city for that reason.

When the Venetians likewise learned this through messengers [Col. 0541D], they directed their fleet there, ardently desiring to find the enemy fleet and engage it. As prudent men experienced in such business, they arranged their fleet in the manner that appeared most advantageous. In that fleet were certain beaked ships called *gatti*, larger than galleys, each furnished with one hundred oars, every oar requiring two rowers. There were also, as stated above, four larger ships assigned to carry freight, engines, weapons, and provisions. They placed these vessels first together with the *gatti*, intending that, if they were perhaps seen by the enemy from a distance, they might be thought not an enemy force but merchant ships. The galleys followed behind.

With their force thus arranged [Col. 0542A], they proceeded toward the coast. They enjoyed a favorable wind, a welcome calm at sea, and the enemy fleet nearby. When it was about dawn and the rising light announced the coming day, the enemy sensed the fleet approaching; as daylight increased, they saw it nearer. Astounded and greatly afraid, they seized their oars, exhorting their men with shouts and gestures to cut the cables, raise the anchors, arrange the rowers, and confidently seize their weapons for battle.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The same doge violently breaks up the enemy fleet found near Joppa and puts it to flight, capturing many galleys.

[Col. 0542B] While these things were happening among the enemy in disordered confusion and tumult, fear producing confusion, behold: one Venetian galley, carrying the doge, outstripped the others in speed and by chance struck with such force the ship on which the commander of the opposing side was riding that it almost engulfed it, together with its rowers, in the waves. Then the other ships, following with great speed, each nearly sent a corresponding enemy vessel beneath the sea.

Thus a severe battle arose and an exceedingly hostile engagement on both sides, with such slaughter that even those who took part in it—though it may seem incredible—steadfastly asserted that the feet of the victors were fouled with the blood of the slain up to their very tops. The adjacent sea, moreover, took on a bloody color for two thousand paces around because of the bodies cast into it and the blood of the slain flowing from the ships [Col. 0542C]. The shore was so filled with corpses thrown up by the sea that the surrounding country contracted both a pestilence and corruption of the air from the stench of the rotting dead.

The close combat continued; these men attacked with burning zeal, while those attempted resistance. But at last, through the Lord’s aid, the Venetians prevailed and put the enemy to flight. They captured four galleys, as many *gatti*, and one very large ship; their commander was killed. Thus they won a victory memorable for ages.

Since this victory had been divinely granted them, they did not wish to waste time uselessly. At the doge’s command, they proceeded toward Egyptian territory as far as Laris, a very ancient coastal city in the desert, looking to see whether they might chance upon any enemy vessels [Col. 0542D]. This indeed happened and succeeded according to their desire, as though some certain messenger had informed them in order of everything that was afterward to occur. For while they were sailing on that sea, ten enemy ships were sighted not far from them. Hastening toward them with all speed, they captured them by force in the first engagements, killing some of the men found in them and putting others in fetters.

These ships were laden with Eastern merchandise, namely spices and silken cloths. Dividing all these things according to their custom, they became richer and, taking the aforesaid ships with them, put in at the city of Acre.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The princes of the kingdom meet with the same doge, and Tyre is besieged.

[Col. 0543A]

The lord Gormund, patriarch of Jerusalem; the lord William of Bures, constable and governor of the kingdom; and Pagan, the royal chancellor, together with the archbishops, bishops, and other princes of the kingdom, heard that the doge of Venice had reached our shores with a naval force and had so gloriously triumphed over the enemy. They sent to him prudent and honorable messengers to greet him, the leading men of the Venetian people, and the commanders of the army on behalf of the lord patriarch, the princes, and the people, and to express their joy at their arrival. They invited them to use and enjoy the resources of the kingdom freely, as citizens and members of the household, declaring that they were ready and intended to treat them, as was fitting, with the claims of humanity and the fullest grace of hospitality [Col. 0543B].

The doge, wishing both to see the holy places with the devotion long conceived and to speak with the princes who had invited him so graciously, left prudent men in charge of the fleet and himself came to Jerusalem with the leading men of his people. There he was honorably received and treated with much distinction, and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord. There too the princes of the kingdom earnestly urged him to devote himself for some time to Christ’s service and the increase of the kingdom. He replied that he had come especially for that purpose and that his whole intention was directed to it.

It was therefore decided by common counsel that, in the presence of the lord patriarch and the other princes of the kingdom, they should agree, subject to certain intervening terms, to besiege one of the coastal cities—either Tyre or Ascalon. For all the others, by God’s grace, from the River of Egypt as far as Antioch, had come under our dominion [Col. 0543C]. But while the wishes of our people were drawn toward different aims, the matter nearly descended into a dangerous dispute. The men of Jerusalem, Ramla, Joppa, Neapolis, and the neighboring districts strongly pressed for an expedition to besiege Ascalon, because it was nearer and seemed to require less labor and expense.

But the people of Acre, Nazareth, Sidon, Beirut, Tiberias, Byblos, and the inhabitants of the other coastal cities maintained that the armies ought to be directed against Tyre. They argued that, since the city was noble and most strongly fortified, every effort should be made to bring it under our power, lest it should at some time give the enemy an avenue by which they might enter against us in order to recover the region and the whole province [Col. 0543D].

Thus, through this disagreement of wishes, the matter nearly reached the dangerous impasse of which we have spoken. At last, through the mediation of certain persons, it was decided that this controversy should be determined by lot; and the form of the lot was not far removed from propriety. They wrote two slips upon pieces of parchment, one bearing the name of Tyre and the other that of Ascalon, and placed these papers upon the altar. They chose one innocent boy without parents and gave him the choice of taking whichever he wished. Whichever city’s name he brought away with him, both armies were to go there without dispute. The lot fell upon Tyre.

We heard this from certain elders who steadfastly affirmed that they had been present at all the aforesaid events. This resolution having therefore been confirmed, the lord patriarch and the illustrious men of that region, together with the whole people, gathered in the city of Acre, for the Venetian fleet lay securely stationed in that city’s harbor. Having personally sworn that both sides would faithfully abide by the terms of the agreement [Col. 0544A–B], and having arranged in advance what was customarily necessary for such an undertaking, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March they invested the aforesaid city with a double siege.

## CHAPTER XXV. Text of the charter of privilege containing the agreement of the terms between the Venetians and the princes of the kingdom of Jerusalem concerning the siege of Tyre.

But lest we pass over anything from antiquity that occurred in the meantime, it is fitting, for clearer evidence of the greater events undertaken, to set down the text of the charter of privilege containing the agreement of the terms between the Venetians and the princes of the kingdom of Jerusalem. It reads as follows:

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0544C] At the time when Pope Calixtus II and Henry IV, Augustus, emperor of the Romans, were ruling respectively the Roman Church and the empire—after, with God’s help, peace had in that same year been concluded between the kingdom and the priesthood concerning the controversy over ring and staff, and a council had been held at Rome—Dominicus Michaelis, doge of Venice and prince of the kingdom of Dalmatia and Croatia, came victoriously to the region of Jerusalem for the necessary protection of Christians with an innumerable multitude of ships and soldiers. Before this, however, he had inflicted a most grievous slaughter upon the pagan fleets of the king of Babylon off the stormy shores of Ascalon.

For King Baldwin II of Jerusalem was then, as our sins required, held captive in the pagan snare, under Balac, prince of the Parthians, together with many others [Col. 0544D]. Therefore we, Gormund, by the grace of God patriarch of the holy city of Jerusalem, together with the suffragan brethren of our church, the lord William of Bures, constable, and Pagan, chancellor, joined by the associated military force of the barons of the whole kingdom of Jerusalem, assembled at Acre in the church of the Holy Cross.

We confirmed and established to the most holy evangelist Mark, to the aforesaid doge and his successors, and jointly to the Venetian people, all the agreements of the terms written below, sworn upon the holy Gospels by all the barons whose names are subscribed. This was done in accordance with the promises of that same King Baldwin—conveyed to the Venetian doge by the king himself through his messengers all the way to Venice, according to the tenor of his letters and the statements of his messengers—and confirmed by his own hand, by the hands of the bishops or the chancellor, and by the kiss of peace, as our order requires. We establish that, without any contradiction, the matters stated and subscribed below shall remain valid, inviolate in the future, and perpetual for him and his people [Col. 0545A]. Amen.

In all the cities under the dominion of the aforesaid king and his successors, and of all his barons, the Venetians shall have a church, an entire street, one square or bathhouse, and also an oven, to possess by hereditary right in perpetuity, free from every exaction, as are the king’s own properties. In the square at Jerusalem, however, they shall have as their own only as much as the king has customarily possessed. And if at Acre the Venetians should wish to establish in their own quarter an oven, mill, bathhouse, balance, measures, and *buzas* for measuring wine, oil, or honey, every resident there who wishes may bake, grind, or bathe there without objection, as freely as at the king’s own establishments. But they may use the measures, balance, and *buza* in the following manner. When Venetians trade among themselves, they must measure by their own—that is, Venetian—measures; when Venetians sell their goods to other peoples, they must sell by their own—that is, Venetian—measures. But when Venetians purchase something acquired through trade from peoples other than Venetians, they may receive it at the king’s measures and the stated price.

Moreover, the Venetians shall in no way be required to pay any due, whether by custom or upon any other ground, when entering, remaining, selling, purchasing, dwelling, or departing, and for absolutely no cause; except only when they arrive or depart with their ships carrying pilgrims. Then indeed, according to the king’s custom, they must give the king one third. Accordingly, the king of Jerusalem himself and all of us must pay the doge of the Venetians, out of the fund of Tyre on the king’s behalf, three hundred Saracen Byzantine coins each year, on the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, pursuant to the terms of the debt.

We also promise you, doge of Venice, and your people, that we shall take nothing more from those peoples who trade with you than they customarily give, and than we take from those who trade with other peoples.

Furthermore, we confirm by this present charter to blessed Mark, to you Dominic Michael, doge of Venice, and to your successors, that part of the same square and street at Acre which has one end at the dwelling of Peter Zanni and the other at the monastery of Saint Demetrius; and another part of that same street, containing one timber house and two stone houses, which formerly used to be huts of reeds, and which King Baldwin of Jerusalem first gave to blessed Mark, to Lord Doge Ordelafo, and to his successors at the capture of Sidon. We grant you authority to hold and possess these portions, and to do with them in perpetuity whatever may please you.

Over the other portion of that same street, running straight from the house of Bernard of New Castle, formerly that of John Julian, as far as the house of Guibert of Joppa, of the Lauda family, we give you in full the same authority as the king has. Moreover, no Venetian throughout the dominion of the king and his barons shall by any device be obliged to render any payment on entering, dwelling there, or departing; but he shall be as free as in Venice itself.

If a Venetian has a plea or litigation in any matter against a Venetian, it shall be decided in the Venetian court. And if anyone believes that he has a complaint or suit against a Venetian, it shall be determined in that same Venetian court. But if a Venetian brings a complaint against any person other than a Venetian, it shall be remedied in the king’s court. Furthermore, wherever a Venetian, ordained or unordained—what we call “without language”—dies, his possessions shall revert to Venetian control. If any Venetian suffers shipwreck, he shall suffer no loss of his property. If he dies in the wreck, his remaining property shall be restored to his heirs or to other Venetians. Further, over the burgesses of whatever people dwelling in the Venetian quarter and houses, the Venetians shall have the same justice and customs as the king has over his own.

Finally, the Venetians shall possess in perpetuity by hereditary right, freely and royally, without impediment from anyone’s opposition, one third of the two cities of Tyre and Ascalon with their appurtenances, and one third of all the lands belonging to them which, from the day of Saint Peter, serve only the Saracens and are not in Frankish hands—of whichever one of those cities, or, if with God’s help the Holy Spirit should will to deliver both into Christian power through their aid or some device. That third part, as stated, the Venetians shall possess for ever, as freely and royally as the king possesses the other two thirds.

Therefore, if the aforesaid king, with God’s help, should ever emerge from captivity, we, Gormund, patriarch of Jerusalem, shall cause him to confirm the aforesaid agreements upon the Gospels. But if another should come to be raised to the kingship of Jerusalem, we shall cause him, before he is elevated, to confirm the promises set out above, as has been stated; otherwise we shall in no way consent to his advancement to the kingdom. Likewise, the successors of the barons and new barons to come shall make the same confirmations in the same manner.

Concerning the matter of Antioch, in which we know well that King Baldwin II, under the same contractual agreement, promised you that he would give himself to you Venetians in the principality of Antioch—namely, that in Antioch [it should be] as in the other cities of the king, provided that the Antiochenes are willing to observe the covenanted promises made to you—we, Gormund, patriarch of Jerusalem, together with our bishops, clergy, barons, and people of Jerusalem, promise to give you counsel and aid, and faithfully to fulfil in their entirety whatever our lord the pope shall write to us on this matter, and all the foregoing provisions, to the honour of the Venetians.

[Col. 0547A] I, Gormund, by God’s grace patriarch of Jerusalem, confirm the aforesaid with my own hand. I, Ebremar, archbishop of Caesarea, likewise confirm the same. I, Bernard, bishop of Nazareth, likewise confirm. I, Asquitinus, bishop of Bethlehem, likewise confirm. I, Roger, bishop of Lydda and Saint George, likewise confirm. [Col. 0548A] I, Gildoin, abbot of Saint Mary of the Valley of Jehoshaphat, likewise confirm. I, Gerard, prior of the Holy Sepulchre, likewise confirm. I, Aicard, prior of the Temple of the Lord, likewise affirm. I, Arnald, prior of Mount Zion, likewise affirm. I, William of Bures, constable of the king, likewise affirm. Given at Acre, by the hand of Pagan, chancellor of the king of Jerusalem, in the year 1123, indiction II.

## HERE BEGINS THE THIRTEENTH BOOK.

[Col. 0547]

## CHAPTER I. The antiquity and nobility of Tyre are described together.

[Col. 0547B]

Tyre is a most ancient city, as Ulpian, that most learned jurist, himself a native of this city, asserts in the *Digest*, under the title “On Censuses,” saying:

> It should be known that there are certain colonies possessing Italian law, such as the most splendid colony of the Tyrians in Phoenician Syria, whence I derive my origin: noble among regions, most ancient in the succession of ages, powerful in arms, most steadfast in the treaty which it struck with the Romans. For the deified Severus and our emperor granted it Italian law because of its outstanding and remarkable loyalty to the commonwealth and the Roman empire.

From this city, if we turn to the ancient histories, came King Agenor and his children Europa, Cadmus, and Phoenix. From one of them the whole region received its name, being called Phoenicia; another, the founder of the city of Thebes and inventor of Greek letters, left to posterity a celebrated remembrance of himself; while the third, daughter of the same king, gave her name to the third part of the world, so that it was called Europe.

The citizens of this place too, distinguished by extraordinary keenness of mind and liveliness of intelligence, were the first to attempt to mark the indivisible elements of sounds by appropriate characters; and, building storehouses for memory, they first among mortals handed down to posterity the art of writing and the method of marking speech, the interpreter of the mind, by characters. Both ancient histories report this, and Lucan, the distinguished narrator of the Civil War, records it, saying:

> The Phoenicians first, if fame is to be believed, dared  
> To mark enduring speech with rudely fashioned signs.

This city was also the first to distinguish purple by the outstanding colour of the worn shellfish and precious murex; hence the finest purple among them, even today deriving its name from the city, is called Tyrian. Sychaeus and his wife Elisa Dido are likewise recorded as having come from this city; in the African diocese they founded that admirable city, rival of the Roman empire—Carthage, that is. Calling their Punic kingdom, as it were Phoenician, after the region from which they had departed, they named it accordingly; and, mindful of their origin, the Carthaginians wished always to call themselves Tyrians. Hence that verse of Maro in the first book:

> There was an ancient city, held by Tyrian settlers.

And this:

> Trojan and Tyrian are held by me without distinction.

It had two names from the beginning: for it is also called *Sor* in Hebrew, while Tyre is the more customary name. Although the latter seems to savour of Greek speech—for it is interpreted “narrowness”—it is certain that it acquired this designation from its founder. For according to ancient tradition, Tyras, the seventh of the sons of Japheth, son of Noah, founded this city and gave it a name taken from his own.

How great this city’s glory was in ancient times may clearly be gathered from the words of the prophet Ezekiel, to whom the Lord says:

> And you, son of man, take up a lamentation over Tyre; and say to Tyre, that dwells around the sea, the merchant of peoples to many islands: You have said, “I am perfect in beauty, and set in the heart of the sea.” Your neighbours who built you filled up your beauty; with fir trees from Senir they built you, with all the planking of the sea.
