They took cedar from Lebanon to make you a mast; they fashioned your oars from oaks of Bashan; they made your benches from Indian ivory, and your cabins from the islands of Italy. Fine linen, embroidered from Egypt, was your sail, set upon the mast; hyacinth and purple from the islands of Elishah were your covering. (Ezek. 27:2)

And Isaiah:

> Cross the seas; howl, you inhabitants of the Island. Is this not your city, which gloried from ancient days in its antiquity? Her own feet shall carry her far away to sojourn. Who has devised this against Tyre, once crowned, whose merchants were princes, whose traders were renowned upon the earth? (Isa. 23:6)

Hiram also came from this city, the king who assisted Solomon in building the Temple of the Lord; and so did Apollonius, whose exploits are the subject of a celebrated and widely circulated history. From this city likewise was the youth Abdimus, son of Abdaemon, who with wonderful subtlety solved all Solomon’s sophistries and enigmatic proverbial sayings which Solomon sent to Hiram, king of the Tyrians, to be solved. Thus one reads of him in the eighth book of Josephus’s *Antiquities*:

> Menander, who translated the Tyrian antiquities from the Phoenician language into Greek, makes mention of these two kings, saying: “When Abibal died, his son Hiram succeeded to his kingdom. Having lived fifty-three years, he reigned thirty-four. In his time there was Abdimus, son of Abdaemon, in chains, who always prevailed over the problems proposed by the king of Jerusalem.”

And again below:

> He added that Solomon, king of Jerusalem, sent certain riddles to Hiram, king of Tyre, and asked him to solve them, on the condition that, if he could not discern them, he should pay money to the solver. Hiram confessed that he could not solve them and would suffer great monetary losses; but through a certain Tyrian, Abdimum, the questions proposed were solved. He in turn proposed others, and if Solomon did not solve them, he was to pay King Hiram much money.

Perhaps this is the man whom popular tales fabulously call Marcolf, of whom it is said that he solved Solomon’s riddles and answered him, proposing in return questions of equal difficulty to be solved.

[Col. 0549C] This same city conceals the body of Origen, as may still today be seen with eyewitness certainty. Jerome, writing to Pammachius and Oceanus in the letter beginning, “The little notes which you sent,” asserts the same thing, saying: “It is nearly one hundred and fifty years today since Origen died at Tyre.”

And, if we turn to Gospel history, this same city also produced that remarkable Canaanite woman, whose great faith, as she pleaded for her daughter grievously tormented by a demon, the Saviour commends, saying: “Woman, great is your faith” (Matt. 15:28). Leaving monuments of wondrous faith and praiseworthy patience to the daughters of her fellow citizens, she first taught them to pray to Christ the Saviour with gifts of faith, charity, and hope, according to the Prophet’s saying:

> The daughters of Tyre shall entreat your favour with gifts. (Ps. 44:14)

It is also the metropolis of all Phoenicia, which has always held first place among the provinces of Syria, both in the abundance of almost every good and in the number of its inhabitants.

## CHAPTER II. How far Syria extends, and what regions it comprises.

It should therefore be observed that the name Syria is sometimes taken more broadly, as the name of the whole; sometimes more narrowly, as applying only to one part; and sometimes it is used with a qualifying addition and denotes particular regions, as will be explained more clearly.

Greater Syria contains many provinces within its bounds. Beginning at the Tigris, it stretches as far as Egypt, and from Cilicia to the Red Sea. In its lower part, between the Tigris and the Euphrates, the first of its regions is Mesopotamia, which, because it is situated between two rivers, is called Mesopotamia—that is, the land lying between two rivers; for *potamos* in Greek means “river” in Latin. Since it is a part of Syria, it is therefore frequently called Mesopotamia of Syria in Scripture.

After this, Coele-Syria is a very large region of that same Syria; in it lies the noble city of Antioch with its suffragan cities. Both Cilicias border it, as it were, on the north, and are parts of the same Syria. Immediately to the south lies Phoenicia, the chief among its regions. Formerly for a long time single and undivided, it is now divided into two. The first is called Maritime Phoenicia, whose metropolis is Tyre, the subject of our discourse. It has fourteen suffragan cities, beginning at the stream of Valania below the castle of Margat and ending at the Cut Stone, now called the District, near the most ancient city called Old Tyre.

The cities included in this province are these: furthest south, Porphyrea, otherwise called Hepha, and in the vernacular Caiphas; second, Ptolemais, also called Acre; third to the east, Paneas, that is Caesarea Philippi; fourth to the north, Sarepta; fifth, Sidon; sixth, Berytus; seventh, Byblus; eighth, Botrys; ninth, Tripoli; tenth, Artusia; eleventh, Archis; twelfth, Arados; thirteenth, Antarados; fourteenth, Maraclea.

The other Phoenicia is called Lebanese Phoenicia, whose metropolis is Damascus, which is also sometimes called Syria, as in the saying, “The head of Syria is Damascus” (Isa. 7:8). This Phoenicia was afterward divided again into two portions: one called Damascene, the other Emesan. Both Arabias are also parts of Syria: the first has Bostra as its metropolis; the second, Petra of the desert. Syria Sobal is likewise a part of that greater Syria, and Sobal is its metropolis. The three Palestines, moreover, are parts of the same Syria: the first, whose metropolis is Jerusalem, is properly called Judaea; the second has Caesarea Maritime as its metropolis; and the third Scythopolis, otherwise called Bethsan, whose place is now occupied by Nazareth. Idumaea too is the furthest part of this same Greater Syria, facing Egypt.

## CHAPTER III. Description of the region adjoining the city, and of the advantages which it supplies.

The aforesaid city was not only extremely well fortified, as we have said, but was also distinguished by remarkable fertility and almost unique pleasantness. Although it is situated in the sea itself and is entirely surrounded by waves like an island, it has before its gates an estate wholly worthy of praise, and a plain adjoining it, of rich loam and fertile soil, yielding many advantages to the citizens. Though it appears small beside other regions, its abundance redeems its narrow extent, and makes up for countless acres by manifold fruitfulness.

Nor is it confined within such narrow bounds. It extends southward toward Ptolemais for four or five miles, as far as the place now commonly called the District of Scandarion; northward, toward Sarepta and Sidon, it stretches a like number of miles. In breadth it is at least two miles and at most three.

In this same district are many springs which issue clear and healthful waters and offer pleasant refreshment against excessive heat. Among them is one pre-eminent and most renowned in the records of fame, of which Solomon is said also to have sung in the Song of Songs:

> A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, flowing in force from Lebanon. (Cant. 4:15)

Although this spring rises in the lower part of the whole region and seems to gush forth not from mountains, as springs commonly do, but from the very floodgates of the deep, yet, raised into the upper air by human care and skill, it abundantly irrigates all the surrounding country and by the benefit of its visitation makes it fertile for many uses.

It has been raised and conducted upward by a remarkable work of stone, resembling the hardness of iron, to a height of ten cubits. In its low natural position it could not be very useful; but, made higher by art prevailing against nature, it renders itself welcome to the entire region and plentifully supplies water for the production of crops. To those approaching and wishing to behold the marvel, it appears externally as a lofty tower and displays no appearance of a spring. But when one reaches its summit, one sees, as it were, a reservoir of collected water, carried thence through aqueducts of equal height and marvelous strength into the surrounding country. Stairways of the same solid stonework have also been provided for those wishing to ascend to the top, by which even horsemen may ride upward without difficulty.

The adjoining region derives marvelous advantage from it. It nourishes not only gardens, orchards planted with fruit-bearing trees, and groves of exceptional beauty, but also sugar-canes, from which is made *zachara* [sugar], a substance most precious for human use and especially necessary to health; merchants carry it thence to the furthest regions of the world. A most elegant kind of glass, easily pre-eminent among things of that class, is also wonderfully made from the sand gathered in this plain. Carried from there even to remote provinces, it provides material suited to marvelous vessels and notable for transparent purity. Thus the city’s name is made famous among foreign nations, and merchants’ profit increases manifold.

The city was endowed not only with these advantages but also with incomparable fortifications, as will be related below. Therefore, because it was so strongly fortified and abounded in such resources, it was pleasing and welcome to the Egyptian prince, one of the most powerful of all, who ruled by unrestricted authority the entire country from Syrian Laodicea to barren Libya. Regarding it as the strength and seat of his kingdoms, he diligently furnished it with provisions, arms, and men powerful in war, judging that the other members of his body would remain secure if he could preserve the safety of its head inviolate.

## CHAPTER IV. That it was frequently besieged in ancient times.

[Col. 0552B] Accordingly, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, as has been said, each of our armies came to the aforesaid city and invested it with a siege as closely as it could. This city is situated, according to the Prophet’s phrase, “in the heart of the sea” (Ezek. 27:3), so that it is surrounded on every side by the deep except for a small space, no more than an arrow might be shot from a bow.

The elders relate that it was once an island, wholly separated from the mainland. Nebuchadnezzar, the mighty Assyrian prince, once besieged it and wished to join it to the mainland, but did not complete the work. The Prophet Ezekiel also recalls this siege, saying:

> Behold, I will bring against Tyre Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, from the north, a king of kings, with horses and chariots and horsemen and a great assembly and people. He shall kill with the sword your daughters that are in the field; he shall surround you with fortifications and cast up earthworks around you, and raise shield and spear against you. (Ezek. 26:7)

And so forth.

Josephus records this siege in the tenth book of the *Antiquities*, saying:

> Diocles also, in the second book of his *Colonies*, mentions this king. Philostratus, in his histories of India and Phoenicia, says that this king besieged Tyre for three years and ten months, while Joatabalus was reigning in Tyre at that time.

After him Alexander of Macedon joined it to the mainland and, having so joined it, captured it by force. Josephus, in the eleventh book of the *Antiquities*, records this siege, saying:

> Alexander, coming into Syria, took Damascus; having subdued Sidon, he besieged Tyre.

And below:

> Therefore, persevering more earnestly in the siege, he captured it; and, having taken it, he came to the city of Gaza.

And again below:

> After seven months had passed in the siege and two at Gaza, Sanaballus died.

Shalmaneser had also earlier besieged it and invaded the whole of Phoenicia. Josephus records this in the ninth book of the *Antiquities*, saying:

> He fought against Tyre while Elizaeus was reigning there.

Menander too, who recorded the events of times and translated Tyrian antiquity into Greek, bears witness concerning these matters, saying:

> A man named Elizaeus reigned thirty-six years. When the Cuthaeans withdrew, he sailed and brought them back. Then Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, rose again against them and invaded all Phoenicia with war. Having made peace with everyone, he returned home. But Sidon, Arca, Old Tyre, and many other cities revolted from Tyre and surrendered themselves to the Assyrian king. Therefore, because the Tyrians were not subject, the king again marched against them; the Phoenicians supplied him sixty ships and eighty oarsmen. The Tyrians sailed against them with twelve ships, scattered the enemy fleet, and took five hundred men captive. Hence Tyrian prestige grew exceedingly from this event. The Assyrian king returned and stationed guards over the river and the citizens’ aqueducts, so as to prevent the Tyrians from drawing water to drink; and when this had been done for five years, they drank water from excavated wells.

These things concerning Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, are written in the archives of the Tyrians.

## CHAPTER V. The city is described, and the condition and character of its citizens are set forth.

[Col. 0553B]

Thus, as we have said, the aforesaid city is like an island, having around it a stormy sea, dangerous because of hidden rocks and extreme unevenness. It is dangerous for strangers and persons ignorant of the localities to approach the city by sea; unless they have a guide acquainted with the adjoining waters, they cannot approach it except at the risk of shipwreck.

On the sea side it was enclosed all around by a double wall, with towers of suitable height set at proportionate intervals. On the eastern side, where there is access by land, it was enclosed by a triple wall, with towers of extraordinary height, exceedingly dense and almost touching one another. There was also a broad ditch through which its citizens could easily introduce the sea from one side to the other.

On the northern side, the city’s inner harbour has an entrance between two towers, though it lies within the walls. Outside, however, an island exposed to the waves breaks the first assaults of the surging sea and provides a safe anchorage between itself and the mainland, inaccessible to winds but exposed to the north wind.

Having therefore brought the fleet into that quarter and placed it in calm water, while the army occupied the suburbs near the city and camps were established around its circuit, they denied the citizens exit and entrance and compelled them to be content with their walls alone.

The aforesaid city had two lords. The Egyptian caliph, as the greater lord, held two portions of it. He granted the third to the king of Damascus, who was nearer, so that he might not molest it and, indeed, might offer the citizens the aid of his support in their necessities. Its citizens were noble and very wealthy, having through continual voyages filled their city with foreign merchandise and manifold riches from almost all the provinces adjoining the Mediterranean Sea for the sake of trade. Distinguished and affluent citizens had moreover fled there from Caesarea, Ptolemais, Sidon, Byblus, Tripoli, and other coastal cities already brought under our power; there they had purchased many dwellings at great price, considering it wholly impossible that a city so fortified could by any chance come under our dominion. For it appeared—and indeed still appears today—the sole and singular defence of the entire region, a strength beyond comparison.

## CHAPTER VI. The siege is established; leaders are assigned their positions; and the city is attacked by the enemy.

Having arranged their baggage and placed their possessions conveniently, they hauled all their ships ashore beside the harbour, except one galley which was always kept ready for suspicious contingencies that might arise. Having done this, they dug a deep ditch from the upper sea to the lower and thereby enclosed the whole army. Then, taking suitable timber from the ships—a great quantity of which the Venetians had brought with them—and summoning craftsmen, they raised engines of various kinds.

The lord patriarch, holding the place of the lord king together with the princes of the realm, summoned woodcutters and men skilled in construction; with the necessary material supplied as desired, he ordered a castle of great height to be built, so that they might fight almost hand-to-hand with those in the towers and look out over the entire city. He also ordered projectile engines to be made, by which huge millstones might batter the towers and walls and strike terror into the citizens.

The doge likewise, emulating the royal party with his men, raised engines of the same kind and set them up in suitable places. They pressed on with the work undertaken in every way, without slackening from their purpose. Rather, growing ever more ardent, they tightened their pressure on the citizens and continually harassed the city with their engines. By unceasing assaults and engagements, they allowed the besieged no rest.

The citizens, equally anxious to defend themselves, considered every means of repelling our attacks and inflicting damage on the enemy. From inside, opposite our engines, they accordingly raised engines of their own; hurling enormous stones from them, they continually battered our castles. By fear of the discharged millstones, they so made the ground about these castles their own that none of our men dared remain there. Even those whose lot obliged them to protect the engines were compelled to dare approach them only at a very rapid run, and could remain there only at the greatest peril.

Those stationed in the lofty towers inflicted such a multitude of javelins and arrows with bows and crossbows upon those attacking them in the castles and about the engines, and pressed them with such a discharge of hand-thrown stones, that they scarcely dared even put forth a hand. Yet our men in the castles, returning blow for blow with very great equality and repelling force with force, imposed upon those in the towers and upon the walls such a necessity of exertion that, though relieved several times a day, they could not bear the burden of battle.

Those in the engines, instructed by persons skilled in shooting, hurled huge stones with such strength and effort that, striking walls or towers, they shook the whole structure and nearly brought it down. From the collision of the stones and the crumbling mortar rose dust so immense that, like an intervening cloud, it prevented those on the walls and towers from seeing our men. If any of the projected stones passed beyond the towers or walls, they fell violently into the city and reduced large buildings and their inhabitants to tiny fragments.

Those fighting on the plain, both infantry and cavalry, courageously and manfully engaged almost every day with those who came out of the city to fight; usually our men provoked those within to battle, while the citizens sometimes made incursions of their own accord against the besiegers.

## CHAPTER VII. The Damascenes in the city resist more boldly, while the citizens become somewhat less resolute.

[Col. 0555B]

While our men thus daily tested their fortunes in the uncertain contest, now with engines and now near the gate, and mutually challenged one another with all possible vigour, Lord Pons, count of Tripoli, came at the summons of the princes of the kingdom, with an honourable company. At his arrival our forces seemed almost doubled and their boldness increased, while upon the enemy, conversely, fell fear and something like despair of resistance.

There were in the same city seven hundred Damascene horsemen. By their example they furnished courage to the noble citizens, who were soft and delicate and not greatly practiced in warfare; and they readily bestowed the necessary assistance through their own personal bravery. Yet even these men, seeing our forces and efforts improving each day, while the citizens’ resources gradually diminished and their strength daily came into danger, began to grow less zealous and wisely to evade a burden which they could not bear. They did so, however, in such a way that they neither urged surrender upon the citizens nor encouraged excessive confidence in their strength.

There was, moreover, in the city, as there is today, only one entrance and a single gate. For, as stated, the whole city is surrounded on every side by straits like an island, except at one narrow place through which access reaches the gate. There incessant and varied conflicts between cavalry and infantry occurred, as is commonly wont to happen in such a situation.

## CHAPTER VIII. The men of Ascalon come to Jerusalem to attack the city, but are badly handled by its citizens on their return.

Meanwhile, while these events were occurring at Tyre, the men of Ascalon saw that the kingdom was stripped of military forces and that all the strength of the region was detained at the siege of Tyre. Seizing the opportunity, they hurried with their entire army across the intervening plain toward the mountains on which Jerusalem is situated. They thought they would find that most fortunate city undefended and might carry off captive some of its inhabitants who ventured out incautiously.

Arriving with great suddenness, they killed about eight citizens who were heedlessly abroad in fields and vineyards. The citizens, however, though few in number, were fervent in faith and inflamed with most righteous zeal for their homeland, children, and wives. Taking up arms, they left the city and met the enemy in unanimous accord.

For three hours they faced one another, our men not daring to charge them because they had only infantry. The men of Ascalon, seeing that they could not remain there without danger, and that it was unsafe to engage beside the city with a stubborn people more courageously prepared to resist, made ready to retreat swiftly. Our men pursued them somewhat cautiously, captured seventeen of the enemy’s horses, killed four of their knights and forty-two others, and, having successfully completed the affair, returned home entirely safe.

## CHAPTER IX. Doldequin, king of Damascus, comes to raise the siege; our men meet him; terrified, he abandons his purpose.

[Col. 0556B]

Meanwhile, the Tyrians, worn out by frequent watchfulness, continual engagements, and unremitting toil, came more rarely to battle and performed their assigned duties more slackly. They were exceedingly astonished that a city which almost every day had been thronged with people arriving both by land and sea, and had been accustomed to be supplied abundantly with every commodity by both routes, should be reduced to such straits that neither citizens nor outsiders could enter or leave, and that provisions were failing and almost no stores of food remained.

Having held a council, they wrote letters to the Egyptian Caliph [Col. 0556C] and to the king of Damascus, urgently warning and entreating them to bring prompt aid to their now nearly hopeless situation. They described the pressure of the enemy, whose strength and courage increased daily; the weakness of their own people, the scarcity of food, and their intolerable distress. Having done this, and somewhat encouraged in hope while awaiting the assistance of the aforesaid princes, they urged themselves to resistance as was their custom. And although many of them were mortally wounded and could not themselves fight, they nevertheless exhorted others, as best they could, to resist.

Meanwhile it was reported that Doldequin, king of Damascus, moved by the letters and embassy of the besieged, had left the Damascene territories with an innumerable host of Turks and a very large force of cavalry, and had encamped in the diocese of Tyre beside a river [Col. 0556D]. This river was scarcely four miles from the city of Tyre. It was also said that an Egyptian fleet, larger than usual and more fully equipped with armed men, bringing the citizens both military reinforcements and necessities for food, would arrive within three days. It was further asserted that the king of Damascus was awaiting still greater military assistance, and prudently delayed crossing the river and engaging with our forces until the fleet arrived, so that, while he fought us, the fleet might have free and unobstructed access to the city.

When they heard this, our people, after consultation and prudent weighing of the alternatives, judged it best to divide the entire army into three parts. All the knights [Col. 0557A] and paid infantry, together with the lord count of Tripoli and Lord William of Bures, royal constable and administrator of the affairs of the kingdom, were to leave the camp and, when necessary, meet the Damascene and fight him with the Lord as their helper. The doge, with his men, was to board the galleys and meet the arriving fleet, try the fortune of war against it, and, like valiant men, make vigorous trial with their swords. The citizens who had assembled for the siege from all the cities of the kingdom, together with the greater part of the Venetians, were to guard the siege engines and towers vigilantly, so that the hands of those fighting from the towers should not be withdrawn, the engines should not cease their customary and ever more pressing assaults, and an unceasing engagement should be maintained before the gate.

This proposal pleased everyone [Col. 0557B], and it was immediately put into effect as seemed expedient. Thus the count of Tripoli and the royal constable, with all the cavalry, went out to meet the enemy. But after they had advanced about two miles, the enemy did not dare to appear at all. It was nevertheless certain that Doldequin had placed his camp beside the aforesaid river, originally intending to cross it. But when, on the report of certain persons, he learned that our men had adopted so prudent a plan, he judged it dangerous rashly to fight men so prudent and so valiant. Sounding the trumpets, therefore, he summoned his men and ordered them to return home.

The doge, with the fleet equipped and ready, went down as far as Alexandria [Col. 0557C], a place about six miles from the aforesaid city, today commonly called Scandarium. But when they learned that the king of Damascus had returned home and that no sign whatever of the expected fleet appeared, they again placed the galleys on shore, all withdrew to the camp, and pressed the assault upon the citizens more fiercely.

## CHAPTER X. The citizens set fire to our engines; our men resist bravely. A man from Antioch, skilled in directing missiles, is summoned by our forces.

One day it happened that certain young men of the city, wishing to make themselves more distinguished among their people and acquire enduring glory with posterity, bound themselves by mutual pledge and agreed [Col. 0557D] to leave the city secretly, set fire to our engines and towers, and return. Carrying out this plan, they left the city secretly and set fire beneath the engine most useful to us. When our men saw this, they rushed to arms and, bringing water in abundance, attempted to resist the flames.

There occurred there something worthy of wonder and of record. A young man of exceptional merit and admirable courage, seeing the engine ablaze, boldly climbed upon it and poured down the water handed up to him. When those in the towers saw this, armed with bows and crossbows, they all directed their weapons against him. Competing in shooting at him, who stood there as though he were a target for arrows, they wasted their efforts; for throughout that day he felt absolutely no injury in his own flesh [Col. 0558A].

Those who had set the fire were captured by our men and all perished, pierced by the avenging sword before the eyes of their own people. Moreover, our men saw that an inner engine was hurling very large stones so directly against our towers that it had severely damaged both of them; and because there was no one in the camp fully skilled in aiming engines and launching stones, they summoned a certain man from Antioch, an Armenian by nationality named Havedic, said to be most highly trained in this art. They immediately received him. He displayed such skill in aiming engines and launching millstones from them that whatever was assigned to him as a target he immediately shattered without difficulty. After he arrived with the army [Col. 0558B], an honourable public salary was assigned him, sufficient for him to maintain himself magnificently according to his station. Thereafter he devoted such diligence to the work for which he had been summoned, and employed such skill in it, that his arrival seemed to have brought upon the citizens not merely a continuing but a newly renewed war, and doubled their troubles.

## CHAPTER XI. Balac is killed near Hierapolis; when this report is heard, our army becomes more cheerful and attacks the city more vigorously.

While these events were taking place at Tyre, Balac, the most powerful Turkish satrap, in whose chains the lord king was held, besieged the city of Hierapolis. While he persisted in the siege [Col. 0558C], he summoned the lord of that city to him with deceitfully peaceful words. The latter, simple and excessively credulous, trusting Balac’s words, immediately presented himself. Balac at once ordered him beheaded when he stood before him.

When Joscelin the Elder, count of Edessa, heard that Balac was besieging a neighboring city, he feared that, if its former lord were driven out, a harsher adversary would be prepared for him. He therefore summoned a great force both from the regions of Antioch and from his own lands and hurried to meet Balac. Having found his army and arranged his own troops in battle-lines, he suddenly fell upon him. Balac’s army was put to flight, and by chance Joscelin encountered Balac himself. Piercing him with his sword, he brought him to the ground; and, once he had fallen, cut off his head, not knowing [Col. 0558D] that this was the commander of the army.

Thus he experienced a plainly manifest interpretation of Balac’s own dream. For one may truly say that he plucked out Balac’s eyes by cutting off his head, thereby imposing an end upon his seeing and living. Joscelin, being a most prudent man with complete practical experience, immediately sent the head of that prince by a young man, so that our people might rejoice in his prosperity and victory. He ordered the messenger to hurry through Antioch to our army, so that neither those people nor these should be deprived of so great a success. On arriving, the messenger filled every heart with delight and raised all to the highest joy.

The lord count of Tripoli, Pontius, who on that expedition had always, with his own men, obeyed the lord patriarch and the other princes as though he were one of their household retainers, and had humbly made himself available for public business out of reverence for the lord count who had sent him and for the dignity of so great an embassy, advanced an unnamed person to the knightly order, conferring military arms upon him [Col. 0559A]. [The object of promovit is absent from the supplied Latin.]

When our men on the expedition learned these things, they raised their hands to heaven and began to praise, bless, and glorify God, “who is terrible in his counsels over the children of men” (Psalm 65:4). Then indeed our army, inflamed with greater zeal, as though its strength had been renewed and its spirit restored, applied itself more fervently to the undertaking already begun; and by frequent attacks it allowed the besieged no rest at all.

The citizens, however, their food entirely consumed and suffering most dangerously from hunger, behaved more slackly, since they had no remaining hope of relief. On one occasion certain young men of the city, highly skilled in swimming, left the inner harbor and swam into the outer harbor as far as that galley which we said above was always kept ready at sea. Having firmly fastened it with a rope that they had carried with them, and cut the ropes by which the galley had been moored, they returned to the city and began to pull after them what they had secured. When those assigned to watch in the towers saw this, they began to shout. Our men, awakened by the cry, rushed to the shore; but before they had fully deliberated upon a remedy, the said young men had already brought the vessel inside the city. Since five men had been assigned to guard it [Col. 0559C], one was killed, while the other four threw themselves headlong into the sea and, swimming out, reached the shore unharmed.

## CHAPTER XII. The Ascalonites again ravage the region of Jerusalem while our army is still detained at the siege.

The Ascalonites, restless like gnats and persisting in their purpose of doing harm, saw that the strength of the kingdom was held at Tyre in the siege and that the whole region was left without troops and exposed to raids. Gathering their forces, they again ascended together into the hill country of Judaea. There, at a place situated north of Jerusalem, five or six miles from it, called Bilin [Col. 0559D] and today more commonly known as Mahomeria, they suddenly attacked and violently occupied it. Having put most of its inhabitants to the sword, the old men, women, and little children escaped the danger of death by withdrawing into a tower. The invaders then ranged without restraint through the whole neighboring region, no one opposing them; whoever they encountered, they either bound in chains or slaughtered with swords, raging at will against the country people.

## CHAPTER XIII. The citizens suffer the grievous pressure of famine and prepare to surrender. Doldequin hastens to their aid, but in vain; the city is handed over to our men.

Meanwhile the Tyrians, suffering more violently than usual from the pressure of hunger [Col. 0560A], adopted another course. Gathering in groups, they began to discuss how they might end the hardships they were enduring. They said it would be more advantageous to surrender the city to the enemy and pass freely to other cities of their own people than to waste away from hunger, or to see their wives and children melt away from want while they themselves looked on, unable to bring help.

At last, after such discussions among the crowds, the proposal was carried by common consent to the elders, the governors of the city, and the public assembly. The whole city having been gathered, the proposal was set forth and discussed more carefully in a public hearing. All agreed that an end must be made to such great evils and that peace must be obtained, whatever the outcome and on whatever terms.

The king of Damascus [Col. 0560B], moved by the citizens’ misery and hearing that they suffered the utmost deprivation, took compassion on their distress. Having summoned military forces from every side, he came down to the sea, where he had previously been, and encamped beside the river near the aforesaid city. Hearing this, our men, suspicious of his arrival, again armed themselves as though expecting battle at the gates; nevertheless, without abandoning their purpose toward the city, they pressed their attack incessantly.

Meanwhile the king of Damascus sent prudent and discerning envoys bearing peaceful proposals to the commanders of our army: namely, to the lord patriarch, the lord doge of Venice, the lord count of Tripoli, Lord William of Bures, and the other magnates of the kingdom [Col. 0560C], to explore a way toward peace. At length, after many negotiations, both sides agreed that the city should be surrendered to the Christians, on condition that the citizens, with their wives, children, and all their property, should be granted free departure. If any citizens preferred to remain in that city, they were to receive free permission to live there, their possessions and dwellings being preserved.

The common people and men of the second rank, understanding that the city would be surrendered on these terms, were greatly displeased that this proposal was being discussed among the princes and that, if the city were not forcibly broken open, booty and plunder would not be available to them. They determined unanimously to withdraw their labor from the military operations, prepared wholly to dissent from the princes. Nevertheless, the sounder judgment of the leading men prevailed [Col. 0560D]; and when the city was received, the citizens were granted the freedom to depart, as had been agreed by the terms.

As a sign of victory, the banner of the lord king was placed upon the tower overlooking the city gate; upon the tower called the Green Tower, the banner of the lord doge of Venice; and upon that called the Tower of Tanaria, the banner of the lord count of Tripoli. The banners were set up with great glory.

Moreover, before the city was either captured or besieged, the greater part of its diocese had already come into our power. Thus a certain noble and powerful man living in the mountains—Humphrey of Toron, father of the younger Humphrey, who later became royal constable—peaceably possessed almost all the hills adjoining the city, both in the fortified places and in the suburbs, nearly as far as Lebanon and within about four or five miles of the city. He had in those mountains a castle strongly fortified by natural position and craftsmanship, from which he inflicted frequent and sudden injuries upon the aforesaid citizens. The lord of Tiberias, Lord William of Bures, royal constable, and before him Lord Joscelin, count of Edessa, who had been lord of the aforesaid city, also held very extensive possessions in these same mountains, from which they frequently and unexpectedly devised dangerous ambushes against the city. Likewise, to the south, King Baldwin of blessed memory, predecessor of the present king, had founded a castle on the seashore beside a wholesome and clear spring, named Alexandria, six or seven miles from the city of Tyre [Col. 0561B]. The aforesaid city, having long before been continually wearied by these troubles, thereby afforded those besieging it greater opportunity to assault it.

It is said that during this expedition there died a venerable man named Odo, who had been appointed metropolitan to the title of that church while the city was still held by the enemy, and was said to have been consecrated by the patriarch of Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER XIV. The city having been captured, its citizens come out to the camp, and our men occupy the city.

The citizens, then, exhausted by the long siege, hurried out to our camp in order to alleviate their weariness [Col. 0561C]. They carefully considered what kind of people these were: so resolute, so patient in labor, so well trained in the practice of arms, that within a few months they had reduced so distinguished and strongly fortified a city to the utmost want and compelled it to submit to extreme terms. They wished to inspect the construction of the engines, the height of the towers, the kind of arms, the position of the camp, and even to learn carefully the names of the leaders, inquiring into everything with concern, so that they might later compose trustworthy histories for posterity from certain reports.

Our men, too, entering the city, marveled at its fortifications, the strength of its buildings, the height of its towers, the solidity of its walls, the beauty of its harbor, and the difficulty of its entrance. They also praised the steadfastness of the citizens, who, though placed in such extreme necessity of hunger and afflicted by such starvation, had delayed surrender for so long. For when the city was received by our men, only five modii of grain were found in it.

Although at first it had seemed harsh to the common people that the city should come into our power under the aforesaid agreement, it subsequently began to please them. The labor expended was praised, and they judged the work completed through their efforts and expenditures worthy of everlasting remembrance. The city having therefore been divided into three parts—two assigned to the lord king and one to the Venetians, as had been included in the earlier agreement—each returned home with great joy and full gladness.

This city was captured and restored to the Christian name on the third day before the Kalends of July, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1124 [Col. 0562A], the sixth year of the reign of Baldwin II, king of Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER XV. The king is released from captivity; he besieges Aleppo, but the siege is raised at the approach of relieving forces; the king returns to Jerusalem; Pope Calixtus dies, and Honorius succeeds him.

In the same year, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, Baldwin, lord king of Jerusalem, having been held in chains among the enemy for about eighteen months or somewhat more, obtained his freedom, by God’s help, upon payment of the money stipulated for him and the giving of hostages, and returned to Antioch. The sum stipulated for him is said to have been one hundred thousand Michaelites, a currency which held first place in public commerce and in the markets for saleable goods in those regions [Col. 0562B].

Having returned to Antioch and being anxious about how he might pay the stipulated money and recover his hostages, he deliberated with the more prudent men concerning what he could do to his advantage. He was therefore persuaded to besiege Aleppo, which suffered from lack of provisions and was almost empty. In this way, it was thought, he could easily secure either the restoration of the hostages by citizens pressed by the siege, or their payment of so great a sum as he had originally agreed for his release.

Accordingly, the entire military force of the whole principality having been publicly summoned to him, he besieged the aforesaid city. Stationing his troops around it in the customary manner, he denied the citizens entrance and exit and forcibly compelled them to husband their scanty food supplies [Col. 0562C]. They, however, repeatedly notified the eastern peoples, especially those beyond the Euphrates, by letters concerning their need: unless aid came promptly, the city would shortly fall.

Those princes, concerned for a friendly city, eagerly summoned their forces and, offering common assistance, gathered military troops. At length, having crossed the Euphrates, they hastened forward, making every effort to free the aforesaid city from the hardship of siege. Those who came to relieve the besieged numbered seven thousand horsemen, apart from those who attended to baggage and equipment and the retainers who rendered due service to their greater lords.

The king [Col. 0562D] and those with him, learning that so great a multitude of enemies was arriving, judged it more advantageous to retreat and put themselves and their expedition in safety than rashly to engage stronger enemy forces. Before the enemy expedition reached the city, our men had withdrawn into one of their fortified castles, called Ceperum. From there they came together at Antioch and then dispersed, the lord king returning to Jerusalem with his personal retinue. There he was received with great honor by all the clergy and people, as one long desired; after what was almost a two-year interval, he bestowed his welcome presence upon people and fathers alike.

In the same year Pope Calixtus II, of blessed memory, died. He was succeeded by a certain Lambert, a Bolognese by birth and bishop of Ostia, who was called Honorius [Col. 0563A]. He was elected amid contention with a certain Theobald, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. Because Honorius’s election had proceeded less canonically, after twelve days he voluntarily renounced and laid aside the mitre and mantle before the brethren. But the brethren—cardinal bishops, priests, and deacons alike—seeing his humility and foreseeing that they should introduce no innovation into the Roman Church, corrected what had been wrongly done. Confirming the same Honorius anew, they fell at his feet and rendered him their customary obedience as their shepherd and universal pope.

## CHAPTER XVI. Bursequin, a Turkish prince, ravages the territories of Antioch; the king meets and engages him; the enemy army is overthrown.

Meanwhile, while the lord king was at Jerusalem, repeated embassies reported that one of the most powerful eastern princes, named Bursequin, had gathered a great army from the eastern territories, crossed the Euphrates, and entered the region of Antioch [Col. 0563B]. Ranging through the country at will, with no one preventing him, he gave to the flames whatever he could seize outside the cities and fortified strongholds, and exposed everything to plunder by his men.

The nobles of Antioch had repeatedly attempted in vain to resist him and test their strength against him. Seeing that they made no progress [Col. 0563C], they informed the lord king—who long before had been entrusted with the care of the principality—of the situation, urgently begging him to come to them without delay.

But the king was burdened by a double responsibility, that of the kingdom and that of the principality, and devoted less care to the kingdom, to which he was much more bound. For repeatedly summoned by the troubles of the principality, he had spent there nearly all his labor and resources for almost a decade, so that while occupied with its affairs he had been captured in person and had endured, most undeservedly, the chains and prisons of the enemy for almost two continuous years. In the kingdom, however, under the protection of God’s hand, nothing adverse at all had happened to him; rather, the Lord, comforter of chosen kings, directed everything prosperously and happily in his hand [Col. 0563D].

Nevertheless, wishing to observe his commitment with every respect, he gathered as large a force as he could and hastened to those regions. Bursequin, however, being a powerful man and very experienced in arms, had joined to himself Doldequin, king of Damascus. Before the king’s arrival, knowing that he had been summoned by the Antiochenes, Bursequin besieged a castle named Caphardan and compelled those inside, pressed by many hardships, to surrender upon terms preserving their safety.

Then, passing through Lesser Syria and hoping for similar successes, he enclosed the town of Sardana with a siege. But after spending several days there and seeing that he could make no progress, he set about besieging a notable but less fortified town called Hasard. While he erected engines and prepared military equipment there, testing his strength to the injury of the besieged, behold: the king and the count of Tripoli with him, and also the count of Edessa, arrived with great forces, soon, with God’s help, to bring aid to the besieged [Col. 0564A].

As they began to approach the enemy, they arranged three battle-lines. In the first, on the right wing, they placed the nobles of Antioch; in the second, arrayed on the left flank, they stationed both counts with their men; and in the center, the lord king. They had 1,100 horsemen and 2,000 infantry.

Bursequin, seeing the arrival of our men and knowing certainly that they were, as prudent men, ready at once to fight, saw that he could not honorably avoid battle. He too therefore drew up twenty battle-lines; his cavalry was said to number fifteen thousand. The forces on both sides having been marshalled and set in order, and advancing against one another, they fell upon each other with great violence in the manner of enemies. In their fierce zeal, striking one another in turn with weapons, they inflicted slaughter and dealt death in many ways.

For in conflicts of this sort, the pain of sacrilege and contempt for the law commonly gives greater force to hatred and fuel to enmity. Battle is otherwise and more mildly undertaken between those sharing the same law and faith, and otherwise between those who differ and maintain opposing traditions. For here it suffices to provide matter for continual scandal and perpetual quarrels that they do not share in the articles of the same faith, even if there is no other cause of hatred [Col. 0564C].

The aforesaid battle-lines therefore pressed fiercely against one another. But through the presence of divine mercy—“with few” it is not difficult for Him “to overcome many,” and He says of His own: “One shall chase a thousand, and two shall put ten thousand to flight” (Deut. 32:30)—our side prevailed. The enemy was put to flight, and our men won a most glorious victory granted from heaven. Two thousand of the enemy are said to have fallen in that engagement, and twenty-four of our men.

Bursequin, seeing that events had turned out very differently from what he had expected, clothed in shame and awe, crossed the Euphrates and returned home, no longer “walking in things too wonderful” for him. The king, having gathered a great sum of money both from the spoils of the enemy and from the generosity of his faithful friends, paid the ransom and received back his five-year-old daughter, whom he had given as a hostage for himself. Having taken leave of the Antiochenes for a time, he returned safe and victorious to Jerusalem [Col. 0564D].

In the same year the king founded a castle in the hills above the city of Beirut, called Mount Glavianus.

## CHAPTER XVII. The king defeats the Ascalonites and also the Egyptians who had come to assist them.

At the same time, after the period of temporal peace and the treaty previously agreed between the lord king and Doldequin through payment of money had expired, the king, having joined to himself troops from the whole kingdom, entered the land of Damascus [Col. 0565A]. Ranging freely through the country, he destroyed certain suburban settlements. Carrying off their inhabitants with him and bringing back very great booty and exceedingly rich spoils from the enemy, he returned safe and unharmed to his own territory.

Before the troops had dispersed, scarcely three days having elapsed, word came that an Egyptian army with a great military array had arrived at the city of Ascalon. It was the Egyptians’ custom four times every year to send new expeditions to that city, so that, with their strength continually renewed, they might withstand the continual attacks of our men and the almost constant injuries repeatedly inflicted upon them.

These newly arrived men customarily sought encounters with our forces most eagerly, wishing to test our strength and give the citizens sure proofs of their own courage. Therefore in military engagements more of them were frequently captured or perished by the sword, as men unfamiliar with the country and not yet fully experienced in warfare; whereas the veteran citizens more prudently avoided encounters with our men and sometimes pursued fugitives less vigorously [Col. 0565B].

When this was reported to the lord king, in an expedition more continuous than renewed, he hastened there with the utmost speed. Upon arriving, he stationed himself with the stronger and more valiant men in an ambush at a suitable place, having sent forward lightly armed soldiers to provoke the citizens’ spirits by wandering raids and incite them to pursue.

But the citizens, seeing our men roaming freely through the places bordering their city and deeply offended by such great boldness, eagerly seized their weapons. They came out rashly in separate companies and put our men, who deliberately offered their backs, to flight. Pursuing the fugitives too rashly, they reached the place where the king lay hidden in ambush with his chosen troops [Col. 0565C].

The king did not reject the opportunity presented. He and those who faithfully stood by him cut off the enemy who wished to return to the city; engaging them hand to hand, they pressed them vigorously with their swords. Before the enemy could withdraw into the city, they slaughtered forty of them here and there. The rest fled into the city and scarcely believed themselves safe within its walls. That those who fell had been brave and among the more noble citizens was shown by the citizens’ lamentation and wailing in the city, greater than usual [Col. 0565D].

The king, summoning his men to him with sounding trumpets and the noise of drums, joyfully pitched camp near the city and rested there in victory throughout the night. He then returned safely to Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The king enters the territory of Damascus; Doldequin meets him; battle is joined; our army returns victorious.

In the following year, 1126 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and the eighth of the reign of the same Lord Baldwin, in January, by command of the lord king and the princes, all the people of the whole kingdom, from greatest to least, were summoned by herald’s proclamation throughout the individual cities. Within a few days the strength of the entire kingdom was gathered, as though one man, near the city of Tiberias, intending by agreement to enter the territory of Damascus. Arriving there, warned by the military signals, their baggage arranged and their columns advancing in order, they traversed the region of Decapolis and entered the enemies’ lands. Thence they crossed the narrow valley called the Hollow of Roob as far as the plains of Medan.

This is a broad, open plain, extending far and wide and affording an unobstructed view. Through it flows the river named Dan, which, between Tiberias and Scythopolis—formerly called Bethsan—enters the Jordan. Some, aided also by the argument of its name, suppose this to be the river which supplies the final part of the Jordan’s name. For all that descends into the Sea of Galilee and emerges from it, as far as the confluence of this river, they call Jor; what flows thence onward they call Jordan, as though Jor and Dan were joined together. Bede, however, and certain other doctors of ours of the highest authority, say that both springs rise near Caesarea Philippi, situated at the foot of Lebanon; one is called Jor and the other Dan. Gathering the streams of these two, the Jordan descends thence in its entirety into Lake Gennesar, which is the Sea of Galilee; then, issuing wholly from it, after almost one hundred miles it pours itself into Lake Asphaltites, otherwise called the Most Salty Sea, cutting through the famous valley.

Having crossed the aforesaid plains, our army reached the village called Salome. This place was then, as it is today, assigned to Christian inhabitants. Therefore our men spared the place and treated its inhabitants as brothers. They then pressed on to the place called Mergisafar, their companies drawn up in order and the cavalry assigned to suitable positions. This is said to be the very place in which Saul, the ravening wolf and persecutor of God’s Church, heard the voice saying, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4), and the rest. It seems to have been divinely arranged that, on the very day on which these events were said to have occurred there—when from a persecutor he became a chosen vessel—the army of the faithful should arrive at that place.

Gathered there, they waited for two days and saw the camp of the Damascenes drawn up against them at no great distance. At last, on the third day, the two sides came together. Their battle array having been carefully ordered and equipped on both sides, they joined arms with utmost hostility; advancing as though in evenly matched encounters, they long left the verdict of victory in doubt. Yet the king, according to his custom, pressed the enemy more fiercely. He called each brave man by name and, urging them alike by word and example, invited them to slaughter and promised victory. They, drawing their swords and falling upon the enemy, strove with the greatest courage to imitate the king as far as they could; filled with zeal for the faith, they sought at once to avenge the injuries done to God and to themselves.

Doldequin likewise encouraged his own men with speeches and inflamed them for battle with promises, declaring that they were waging a just war for their wives and children, for liberty—which was the greater cause—and for their native soil against plunderers. With these and similar appeals they persevered with no lesser spirit and no unequal strength. The infantry companies, instructed by the example of the lord king and the knights, thrust themselves more fiercely into the enemy lines and attacked more boldly. Whenever they found enemies fallen or wounded, they cut them down with their swords and blocked their paths of escape. They raised up our own fallen men and returned them to the fight; they sent the wounded back to the baggage, so that they might care for themselves. What was believed to have been especially harmful to the hostile ranks that day was that some devoted all their efforts to wounding the enemy horses, thereby preparing their riders as victims for the comrades who followed.

The king, accompanied by certain valiant and distinguished men, flashed like a lion amid the dense wedges of the enemy, inflicting a slaughter grievous even upon those who were winning, both to right and left. It is not recorded among us that up to that day such exhausting effort had been expended in a contest so dangerous and doubtful. For although the battle had lasted from the third hour of the day until the tenth, scarcely at the eleventh hour could one discern which side would gain the better result. At length, through the aid of divine mercy and the intercession on their behalf of the outstanding Doctor of the Gentiles, the enemy were put to flight, suffering a slaughter among their own men memorable for ages. More than two thousand of them are said to have fallen that day. Of our own men, after a count both of knights and infantry, it was found that twenty-four knights had fallen, and eighty infantrymen.

Thus, with victory divinely bestowed upon our men, the victorious king held the field of combat. Leading his army away with rejoicing and thanksgiving, he began his return home. While on the march, they encountered a tower in which ninety-six of the enemy had taken refuge for safety. They attacked it violently and forced the captured enemies to end their lives by the sword. Proceeding further, they likewise seized another tower by force, sparing the lives of twenty enemy men assigned to defend it, because they had surrendered the aforesaid tower to our men without difficulty. Having quickly undermined it, they cast it utterly down to the ground with a tremendous crash. Thus, having gained a manifold victory memorable for ages, they returned home joyfully.

## CHAPTER XIX. The Count of Tripoli takes the city of Rafanea. Henry, Emperor of the Romans, dies; Lothair succeeds him.

At the same time, Lord Pons, Count of Tripoli, seeing that the city of Rafanea, adjoining his territory, could be made subject to his purpose, resolved to besiege it. But, in order more easily to attain what he had planned, he both wrote to the lord king of Jerusalem and repeatedly urged him through messengers to come in person and provide assistance. The king, being energetic and faithfully attentive to the common affairs of the Christian people, took with him an honorable retinue and hurried there without delay. On arriving, he found the count equipped for the undertaking. Therefore, taking siege engines, whatever might be necessary for attacking the city, and provisions sufficient for several days, and sending infantry wings ahead to the positions assigned them, they directed their forces toward the place.

On their arrival, they surrounded the city with a siege according to plan, immediately denying the citizens both entrance and exit from the first moment of their arrival. The city, however, was only slightly fortified, both by its natural position and by the poverty of its inhabitants; worn down by many hardships, it could not resist long. For this same count had built a stronghold on a neighboring mountain, and its inhabitants, continually oppressing the aforesaid city with straits, had reduced them almost to utter exhaustion. Therefore, after attacking it vigorously for eighteen days, they compelled the citizens to surrender, first granting them, their wives, and their children free departure and promising them immunity from harm.

The aforesaid Rafanea is in the province of Apamea, one of its suffragan sees. It was taken on the last day of March. The king then returned to Jerusalem and celebrated the Easter days there with great devotion.

At the same time, Lord Henry, Emperor of the Romans, closed his final day by fate. He was succeeded by the Duke of Saxony, Lord Lothair, a man commendable in every respect. Later, descending into Apulia with an innumerable army, he violently occupied the whole region as far as the Faro, appointing as duke in Apulia a prudent and discerning man named Reinon. He compelled Count Roger, who had violently occupied that land, to flee into Sicily. After the emperor’s departure, Roger recovered it, fought the aforesaid Reinon, and, after Reinon’s death, obtained the duchy; afterwards he also became king of Sicily and of the entire province.

## CHAPTER XX. Bursequin again enters the territory of Antioch; at last he perishes, stabbed by his own men. An Egyptian fleet comes up to Syria, but returns after suffering losses and accomplishing nothing.

While the lord king was staying at Tyre, behold, a messenger hurried from Antioch and asserted by letter and word of mouth that Bursequin, the most savage persecutor of our faith, had descended with a great force into the regions of Coele-Syria; that he was besieging towns, burning suburbs everywhere without hindrance and without discrimination, carrying off their inhabitants captive, and reducing wives and children to slavery. When the king heard this, although he regarded the Egyptians with suspicion and did not doubt that they would soon arrive with the great fleet they had prepared, yet, like a prudent physician who, when he senses the more violent onset of a disease, hastens to apply remedies there, he neglected other concerns and, confronting the greater necessity, hurried more swiftly into those regions.

Hearing this, Bursequin immediately raised the siege which he had carefully established around the noble town of Cerepum, and retreated farther back into the enemy’s territory. Before the king arrived, however, he had violently seized a town of no great name, in which he captured some women with their children. For the men who had been besieged in it escaped their hands with much difficulty and danger, preferring to find safety for themselves in flight rather than be miserably entangled, together with their wives and children, in the same yoke of captivity.

Afterwards this same impious Bursequin, heir of malediction, was stabbed to death with swords by his own household and retainers, thereby reaping in his own deed both the seed of his wickedness and the fruit of his impiety.

While these things were happening in the region of Antioch, the Egyptian fleet, as had been foretold, sailed down with twenty-four galleys, surveying the entire seacoast as far as the city of Beirut. They carefully explored whether they might inflict damage upon any of our cities, or perhaps seize unexpectedly, as if emerging from ambush, anyone who incautiously passed by or approached Syria. At last, suffering from want of drink and compelled by thirst, they landed beside the streams to draw water. The people of the city, joined by certain others who had come from neighboring cities to assist them, met them and violently drove them from the water, wholly denying them its use. Pressing them more boldly with arms, they forced them to return to their ships, having slain one hundred and thirty of them by the sword.

## CHAPTER XXI. The younger Bohemond arrives at Antioch; the king restores his land to him and gives him his daughter, named Halis, in marriage.

In the following autumn, the younger Lord Bohemond, son of the elder Lord Bohemond and prince of Taranto, having made an agreement and concluded a treaty with his uncle, Lord William, Duke of Apulia, concerning the future succession—namely, that whichever of them died first should be succeeded in everything by the other—prepared ships: ten galleys and twelve others suitable for carrying baggage and equipment and for transporting arms and provisions. He directed his journey toward Syria, trusting in the lord king’s good faith: that the king would not deny him, upon his arrival and his claim for his paternal inheritance.

When he arrived and his fleet had already been safely received within the mouths of the River Orontes, the king, upon learning of it, went out to meet him with the magnates of the land. When Bohemond entered Antioch, the king graciously restored to him the whole city and territory, care for which had worn him down for eight years with ceaseless and most anxious concern. Once the principality had been restored, all the nobles and magnates of the region, in the presence and at the urging of the lord king, rendered him liege fealty in his palace.

Afterwards, through the intervention of certain persons friendly to both sides, it was arranged that the lord king should give him one of his daughters, named Halis, the second by birth, as wife, under terms agreed by both parties, so that greater favor and a more friendly relationship might exist between them. Lord Bohemond was a youth of about eighteen years, conspicuous for the beauty of his appearance; very tall, with blond hair and a pleasing face, such as would truly identify him as a prince even to those who did not know him. He was agreeable in speech, readily winning the minds of his hearers by his words; most generous, and, like his father, truly magnificent. In nobility of birth he was inferior to no mortal, for his father was the elder Bohemond, son of the illustrious Robert Guiscard, a man memorable through the ages; while his mother was Constance, distinguished and most noble among illustrious women, daughter of Philip, the eminent king of the Franks.

When the wedding had been celebrated according to custom and the daughter had been solemnly placed with the lord prince under the law of marriage, the king returned safe and sound to Jerusalem, having laid down the greater part of his burden. In the following spring Lord Bohemond assembled military forces from throughout the principality and had, through the labor of craftsmen, siege engines made that were necessary for attacking fortifications. He then besieged the town of Cafardan, which some years earlier the enemy had violently subjected to themselves by force of arms. In a short time he retook it by assault, sparing none of those whom he captured within, though they tried to purchase life at a great price and to obtain safety through money. These were the first fruits given by this illustrious and noble prince of his youth, the first proofs of his good disposition.

## CHAPTER XXII. Serious hostilities arise between the same Bohemond and Joscelin, Count of Edessa; but the king hastens there and settles them. Africans violently storm Syracuse, a city of Sicily.

Without delay, through causes hidden from us but hateful to God, serious hostilities arose between the same lord prince and Joscelin the Elder, Count of Edessa. So far did this go that, contrary to good morals and to the discipline of our times, leaving a ruinous example to posterity, he summoned Turks and bands of unbelievers to assist him. Relying on their aid, he gave the region of Antioch over to fires and imposed upon its inhabitants, servants of Christ, the yoke of an undeserved slavery. What is considered more notable and more deserving of divine punishment is that these acts are said to have been committed while the prince was absent and entirely unaware of them, as he labored in Christ’s service by fighting the enemy.

Consequently the aforesaid Joscelin incurred the hatred and indignation of all to whom this account came, and deserved the curses of all. The king, hearing this report, was first anxious lest, through the occasion of this division, the enemy might gain a wider entrance to our confusion, since “a kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste,” according to the word of the Lord (Luke 11:17). He was also concerned because both men were related to him by blood: one was his cousin, the son of his maternal aunt; the other was his son-in-law, to whom he had recently betrothed his daughter. He therefore flew swiftly to those parts to establish peace. With Lord Bernard, Patriarch of Antioch, proving a faithful and devoted fellow-worker, he restored the best peace between them.

The reconciliation was especially made possible because, in the meantime, the count fell gravely ill. While suffering most dangerously from this sickness and repenting of his deed, he bound himself to the Lord by vows that, if life and health were granted him, he would make satisfaction to the lord prince and, rendering him the fealty owed, would be reconciled to him. This indeed was done. For after recovering fully, in the presence of the lord king and the lord patriarch, they were reconciled to one another and full goodwill intervened; he rendered fealty to him by placing his hands in his, and thereafter maintained it in due observance. The king, once peace had been arranged, returned to Jerusalem.

At the same time Count Roger of Sicily is said to have sent toward Africa a fleet of forty galleys prepared with great effort. When their arrival became known, the people of that province, forewarned and prudently prepared, gave the enemy no opportunity to harm them. On the contrary, arming with no less effort the galleys that they had nearly at hand, they pursued at the swiftest speed these evildoers as they returned with their enterprise unsuccessful, and sailed as far as Sicily. Arriving there with eighty galleys, they suddenly attacked and immediately seized by force the noble and ancient city of Syracuse, made careless by long peace, secure and fearing no such thing. Having assaulted the city, they slaughtered the citizens with swords, sparing no one for sex or age; for those who were spared, slavery harsher than every death was prepared. The bishop of the place, fleeing to the outskirts with a few clergy of the church, barely escaped.

## CHAPTER XXIII. At Tyre, the first archbishop of the Latins is established.

At last, in the spring immediately following, in the fourth year after the city had been restored to the Christian faith, the king, the lord patriarch, and the chief princes of the kingdom met at Tyre and began to deliberate concerning the appointment of a bishop for that church. At length they placed over that city Lord William, a venerable man, prior of the Church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, an Englishman by nationality and commendable in life and character.

Here—God knows—we cannot sufficiently restrain our groans. For, as the proverb says, “Where love is, there is the eye; where grief is, there is the hand.” These things oppress us more deeply and, through the pain inflicted, do not allow our hearts to rest. We marvel at the prudence of that time, and we remain perplexed, judging it almost rashness. For those who, two years before the aforesaid city was restored to Christian liberty, had consecrated a bishop for themselves there, afterwards, through indolent and gross prudence, delayed until the fourth year to provide it with a bishop. Thus, while its churches were dispersed and its cathedral church deprived of its own members, the first man to assume its governance would receive the worse portion with a curse. For it is written: “Accursed is the man who makes his own portion worse.”

Yet that predecessor of ours, and those who followed after him down to our own time, deservedly escape the effect of that curse, since they did not themselves make their portions worse; rather, they necessarily accepted conditions made worse by others. May the Lord spare them and not impute to Gehenna those who treated the Church in this way.

The aforesaid predecessor of blessed memory, Lord William, having received consecration from the lord patriarch of Jerusalem, went to Rome to receive the pallium, against the will and despite the resistance of that same consecrator. There he was graciously received by Pope Honorius II, obtained what he sought with great honor, and was sent back home accompanied by apostolic letters, whose text was as follows:

> **HONORIUS**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, the suffragan bishops, clergy, and people of Tyre: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> We have received with due affection our most beloved brother William, your archbishop. Since we have learned that he was canonically elected and consecrated by our venerable brother Gormund, Patriarch of Jerusalem, we have adorned him with the dignity of the pallium, that is, with the fullness of the pontifical office. Since, through the aid of divine mercy, we believe that the greatest benefit will come to your mother church of Tyre from his person, we have thought fit to send him back to you with the favor of the Apostolic See and the support of our letters. Therefore, by this command, we direct your whole community to receive him graciously and humbly render to him submission, obedience, and reverence as to your own metropolitan and bishop of your souls.

> **HONORIUS**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother **GORMUND**, Patriarch of Jerusalem: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> Having received the letters of your fraternity, we graciously received our brother William, whom you consecrated archbishop in the Church of Tyre, and adorned him with the dignity of the pallium, that is, with the fullness of the pontifical office. We likewise command his suffragan churches to render him submission, obedience, and reverence as to their own metropolitan.
>
> Given in the territory of Bari, on the eighth day before the Ides of July [8 July].

He also sent with the same archbishop Lord Aegidius, Bishop of Tusculum, legate of the Apostolic See, a man exceedingly eloquent and learned, whose highly celebrated letters to the Antiochenes survive to this day. Through him he wrote to Bernard, Patriarch of Antioch, instructing him to restore to the lord of Tyre the suffragans whom he retained. Among other things he said:

> Therefore, through apostolic writings and our venerable brother Aegidius, Bishop of Tusculum and legate of the Apostolic See, we command you to restore to him the suffragans of the Church of Tyre. Unless within forty days after inspection of the letters which we have directed to them they render him the submission due, from that time we suspend them from the office of bishop.

What was the reason why he had been consecrated by and had obeyed the Patriarch of Jerusalem, when from the time of the Apostles until that day the Church of Tyre is known to have been subject to the see of Antioch, will be explained by the following discussion in its proper place.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Fulk, Count of Anjou, comes at the summons; the king’s eldest daughter Melisende is given to him in marriage.

In the following year, about the middle of spring, the illustrious and magnificent Lord Fulk, Count of Anjou, for whom the king had sent with the common counsel of all the ecclesiastical and secular princes in order to give him his eldest daughter, Lady Melisende, as wife, landed at the city of Acre with an honorable retinue of nobles and an equipment surpassing royal wealth. Lord William of Bures, the royal constable, also came with him. The king had immediately sent William, once freed from the enemy’s bonds, together with certain other nobles, to summon the aforesaid count.

William had been charged, when departing, to swear confidently on the soul of the king and of the princes of the kingdom that, once the count reached the kingdom safely, within fifty days the king’s eldest daughter would be given to him together with the expectation of the kingdom after the king’s death. Once he had arrived, the king, without delay and according to the terms of the agreement, gave him his aforesaid daughter in lawful marriage before the forthcoming celebration of Holy Pentecost. During his lifetime the king gave them the two cities, Tyre and Ptolemais, to possess; they held them until the king’s death.

The aforesaid count, as a prudent and discerning man, stood faithfully by the lord king throughout his life, taking part in the affairs of the kingdom and performing the duty of a son with devotion. The services by which friends are usually acquired were not idle in him toward the lord king.

## CHAPTER XXV. Gormund, Patriarch of Jerusalem, dies; Stephen succeeds him. Difficult disputes arise between the king and the patriarch.

In the same year Lord Gormund, Patriarch of Jerusalem, of blessed memory, while besieging in the district of Sidon a certain fortress called Belhasem, held by some robbers, contracted a severe, fatal illness and was carried to Sidon. There, as his sickness worsened, he met the condition of mortals and entered upon the way of all flesh, having presided over the Church of Jerusalem for about ten years.

He was succeeded by a man noble in birth, but much nobler in life and character, named Stephen, abbot of Saint John of the Valley, a place situated in the city of Chartres. He was a native of Chartres and a kinsman of King Baldwin. Before his conversion, he had been vice-lord of that city in the rank and dress of a knight. Afterwards, renouncing the world, he received the religious habit in the aforesaid cloister; then, through the support of his merits, he was advanced to the governance of that church, having been suitably trained in the liberal disciplines in his youth.

When he came to Jerusalem for prayer and devotion, and remained there awaiting a passage, it happened that, after the funeral rites of Lord Gormund the patriarch, while clergy and people were deliberating about appointing a shepherd, he was elected by the unanimous vote of all. Once consecrated, he began to raise difficult claims against the lord king, maintaining that the city of Jaffa belonged by right to himself and to the Church of the Lord’s Resurrection, and affirming that the Holy City itself would pass to the Church in the same way after Ascalon had been captured.

He was a distinguished man, steadfast in purpose, honorable in conduct, and a diligent advocate of his rights. Hence serious hostilities arose between him and the lord king, though premature death is said to have ended them. For before two full years had passed, he died. Some think that he died through poison administered to him, but we have not established this as certain. It is nevertheless reported that, as he lay in bed in his final illness, the king came in to visit him and asked about his condition; he replied: “It is with us now, lord king, as you wish.”

## CHAPTER XXVI. The king, the Prince of Antioch, the Count of Tripoli, and the Count of Edessa enter the territory of Damascus; but, routed and having lost part of their army, they return. Patriarch Stephen dies; William succeeds him.

In the following year Hugh of Payns, the first master of the knighthood of the Temple, and certain other religious men, whom the lord king and other princes of the kingdom had sent to the princes of the West to stir up their peoples for our support and especially to invite the powerful to the siege of Damascus, returned.
