A very great multitude of noble men, trusting the assurances of these men, had come into the kingdom.

Therefore, confident in their strength and assistance, all the Christian princes of the East assembled by agreement: Lord King Baldwin, Lord Fulk, Count of Anjou, Lord Pons, Count of Tripoli, Lord Bohemond the Younger, Prince of Antioch, and Lord Joscelin the Elder, Count of Edessa. All of them, after taking counsel together, gathering military forces from every side and summoning reinforcements, hastened with their columns equipped, competing to besiege the excellent and noble city of Damascus and either force it, once besieged, to surrender by violence or storm it at close quarters.

But divine providence, by a hidden yet just judgment, opposed such great exertions. For after they had reached the territory of Damascus, with God guiding their course and their success still favorable, they came to the place called Mergesaphar. There the men of the lower division separated themselves from the army. It is their customary duty in camp to range far and wide through the outskirts to seek provisions necessary both for the use of men and for fodder for beasts of burden. Lord William of Bures was assigned to guard them with a thousand knights.

But these men, as is customary with such people, separated from one another and began rashly to explore the whole region, deliberately moving apart and without companions, so that each might claim as his own whatever he found, without sharing it with others. While occupied with these matters, breaking into the outskirts and striving to bring plunder back to their own men, they behaved with extreme imprudence and violated military discipline.

When Doldequin, prince of the Damascenes, heard this, hoping—as indeed happened—that if he suddenly fell upon them with his men he could destroy them, being unwary and unfamiliar with the country, he took with him from every rank of his own men the swiftest and those most skilled in military affairs. In a sudden attack he fell upon our men, who, as we have said, had gone out incautiously to forage. Finding them unprepared and occupied with other concerns, he easily put them to flight; he cut down those scattered about the fields and did not cease pursuing until he had put to flight both the common men and the strength of the distinguished soldiers appointed to guard them, killing many of them.

When this became known, our men in the army, ready to repel so great an outrage and to pursue vengeance, seized their arms and prepared to go out to meet the enemy, manfully resolute in spirit and inflamed with great indignation. But suddenly the divine power—without which human affairs do not sufficiently prosper—sent such violent rains, such darkness in the air, and such difficulty in the roads because of the abundance of water, that one could scarcely hope for life, though no one was attacking except the harshness of the weather alone. The murky air, the density of the clouds, the irregular collision of the winds, and the most frequent thunder and lightning had indeed foretold this long beforehand. Yet the blind human mind, ignorant of what was to come, did not heed divine forbearance calling it back, but sought to proceed, which is impossible, against that will.

Seeing that the violence of the weather had been sent on account of their sins, they were compelled to abandon their purpose. Their condition was changed: those who had first arrived terrible and exceedingly feared by the enemy now, while the enemy was at rest and had even become superior, were a burden to themselves and regarded it as an immense victory merely to return home. Thus, on the eighth day before the Ides of December [6 December], in the year 1130 from the Incarnation of the Lord, the twelfth of the reign of Lord Baldwin, this happened almost in the same place where, four years earlier, the same king had won a distinguished and universally memorable victory over these same enemies.

It is wonderful—truly wonderful, beyond human expectation—that you, eternal Savior, humble those who presume upon their own strength; and that you pierce, as their deserts demand, with the dart of your curse those who trust in man and make flesh their arm, seeking neither a helper nor a sharer in your glory. For you have said, blessed Lord: “I will not give my glory to another” (Isaiah 48:11); “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Romans 12:19); “I will strike, and I will heal; I will make alive, and there is none who can deliver from my hand” (Deuteronomy 32:39).

And truly, Lord, this is so. For when the king, using only the strength of his own kingdom and his own troops, wholly committed himself to the overflowing grace of God, he often gained unexpected triumphs over the enemy. But when, trusting in a multitude, he presumed that he could be exalted by human agency and began, with multiplied auxiliaries, to rely upon the strength of mortals, you withdrew grace and left him to his own condition. He went away confounded amid a multitude, though in small numbers, trusting in the Lord’s aid, he had been accustomed easily to triumph over his enemies.

Thus, driven back by the divinely sent violence of the weather, with heaven warring against them, they neither took vengeance for their own men who had fallen under enemy swords nor could carry their purpose into effect. After these events, our princes separated from one another and, believing it impossible that the undertaking once begun could now easily be continued, returned home.

In the meantime, Lord Stephen, Patriarch of Jerusalem, of pious memory, died. He was succeeded by Lord William, prior of the Church of the Lord’s Sepulchre: a simple man, moderately educated, handsome in appearance, commendable in morals, a Fleming by nationality, from the place called Messines; greatly acceptable to the king, the princes of the kingdom, and all the people.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Bohemond, Prince of the Antiochenes, is killed in Cilicia near Mamistra. The king hastens to Antioch. Bohemond’s wife attempts to repel her arriving father, but through the action of the citizens the city is delivered to the king and the princess is excluded.

After the lord Bohemond, the king’s son-in-law and prince of Antioch, had returned from that expedition and withdrawn into his own province, Rodoan, son of the Accursed, prince of Aleppo and most powerful ruler of the Turks, entered the territory of Antioch. The lord prince hastened to meet him, wishing to keep him from his borders, and descended into Cilicia, being also drawn thither by other causes of a domestic and family character. There, while he was encamped in a place called the Meadow of the Pavilions, upon wide-open plains, the enemy multitude suddenly rushed upon him; deserted by his own men, he perished pierced by swords. He was a great prince and would have been dear to God had he lived, unless premature death and envious fate had withdrawn him from human affairs. By this calamity the people of Antioch were greatly dismayed: under his rule they had believed themselves secure for a long time, and had placed in his youth a confidence greater than was fitting. Falling once more into renewed lamentations, lest they again become prey to enemies without a prince to perform his office, they took counsel together and summoned the lord king of Jerusalem.

When this was reported to the lord king, he was moved by the novelty of the event. Fearing that, through the prince’s loss, some worse misfortune might befall the aforesaid region, he set aside his own concerns and began to care for those of others, reckoning nothing foreign to himself [Col. 0577A] that had happened to Christian princes. He also judged worthy of his care whatever benefit he could see might accrue to the Christian people through his labours. He therefore hastened to Antioch with rapid steps.

Meanwhile, his daughter, having learned of her husband’s death, was stirred by an evil spirit and conceived a wicked plan before she had received any intimation of her father’s coming. In order to prepare a more secure position for herself and bring her purpose to effect, she sent messengers to a very powerful Turkish commander named Sanguin, hoping through his aid, against the will of her father and of the whole people, to secure Antioch for herself forever. She had by the lord Bohemond of good memory an only daughter, who seemed to enjoy little favour with her mother. For her mother’s whole intention seemed directed to this end: that, whether she remained a widow or entered a second marriage, she herself might possess the principality forever, having disinherited her daughter.

She had also sent to the aforesaid nobleman, by one of her household servants, a very white palfrey, shod with silver, adorned with a bridle and other silver trappings, and covered with the whitest samite, so that snowy whiteness might accord in every respect. This messenger was accidentally intercepted on the road and brought into the presence of the lord king. Having confessed the course of the affair, he reaped the fruits of his journey and ended his life by the extreme penalty.

The king, therefore, hastening to Antioch because of the misfortunes already described, arrived there at the city; but, through his daughter’s prohibition, he was not admitted. Fearing her seared [Col. 0577C] conscience, she even dreaded her father’s judgment. Handing over the city to her accomplices and to those whom she had corrupted with money, she strove to resist altogether and to exercise her tyranny more freely. But the result proved far otherwise than she intended. For in that city were men who feared God and despised the insolence of the raging woman. One of these was Peter the Latinizer, a monk of Saint Paul’s, and another William of Adversa. With the consent of others, they secretly summoned the lord king through intermediaries and, by agreement, stationed the lord Fulk, count of Anjou, at the Gate of the Duke, and Count Joscelin at the Gate of Saint Paul. They then opened the entrances and admitted the king.

When she learned this, the princess fled to the citadel. Later, summoned from it by more prudent persons in whom she had full trust, she presented herself before her father, prepared to submit to his judgment. Although the father had conceived a sharper movement of indignation against her for her grave offence, nevertheless, overcome by the prayers of those intervening and not devoid of paternal affection, after recovering Antioch he granted her the coastal cities of Laodicea and Gabala, lest she should at some time attempt something similar. Yet her husband had assigned these to her, by supreme judgment, as a marriage-gift. Having arranged the affairs of that city and entrusted its care to the princes, he returned to Jerusalem, recalled by domestic concerns. First, however, he received the sworn fealties of both great and small, confirmed by bodily oaths: that, both during his lifetime and after his death, they would faithfully preserve Antioch with its dependencies for the ward Constance, daughter of the younger lord Bohemond. For he feared the malice of his own daughter, lest she should attempt—as she had done before—to disinherit the aforesaid ward.

## Chapter XXVIII. The king returns to Jerusalem; seized by a severe illness, he dies; he is buried with the other kings in the church of the Holy Sepulchre.

Having returned to Jerusalem, he fell into a most grave illness. Seeing that the day of death was near, he left his own palace and, humbly and suppliantly in the sight of the Lord, laid aside royal state and ordered himself carried into the house of the lord patriarch, because it was nearer the place of the Lord’s resurrection. He placed his hope in Him who had conquered death there, that He would make him a participant in His resurrection.

There he summoned his daughter and son-in-law, and the boy Baldwin, now two years old, and, in the presence of the lord patriarch, the prelates of the churches, and certain princes who happened to be present, entrusted to them the care of the kingdom and full authority, granting them, after the manner of a pious prince, his paternal blessing. He himself, a true confessor of Christ, assumed the religious habit and professed the regular life, if he should live; he surrendered his spirit to Him who is the Father of spirits, to receive rewards with the pious princes through the Lord’s agency.

He died in the year 1131 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the thirteenth year of his reign, on the twenty-first day of August. He was buried among his predecessors, the kings of pious memory, beneath Mount Calvary, before the place called Golgotha, amid the great care of his people and solemn rites worthy of royal magnificence. [Col. 0578D] To the present day his memory is blessed among all people because of his outstanding faith and notable deeds.

# Book Fourteen

## Chapter I. What were the character and ancestry of the lord Fulk, third king of Jerusalem.

Thus, when the lord Baldwin, the second king of Jerusalem from among the Latins, surnamed of Bourg, had been called from this world, his son-in-law, the lord [Col. 0578D] Fulk, count of Tours, Maine, and Anjou, succeeded to the kingdom. As mentioned above, the aforesaid lord king had given him his firstborn daughter, named Melisende, in marriage.

This Fulk was a red-haired man, but like David, whom the Lord found after His own heart: faithful, gentle, and—contrary to the usual traits of that colouring—affable, kindly, and merciful; exceedingly liberal in works of piety and the giving of alms. In temporal affairs he was a powerful prince and most fortunate among his own people even before he was summoned to the government of the kingdom; very experienced in military matters, and highly patient and prudent in the hardships of war. He was of medium stature, but already elderly, being more than sixty years old.

Among the defects to which he was subject by the law of mortality, he had a memory so weak and unstable that he did not retain even the names of his household servants and recognized the faces of only a few. Thus, after having shortly before bestowed the highest honour and the favour of intimacy upon a person, he would afterward carefully inquire who he was if that man unexpectedly appeared before him. Consequently he put to shame many who presumed upon their familiarity with him, when, although they had proposed to make themselves protectors of others, they themselves needed a patron with him.

His father, count of Tours and Anjou, was also named Fulk and was surnamed Rechin. He married the sister of the lord Amaury of Montfort, named Bertrada. By her he had two sons: this Fulk, of whom we speak, and Geoffrey Martel; and one daughter, named Ermengarde. She was first the wife of William, count of Poitou; spurned and put away by him contrary to the laws of marriage, she went to the count of Brittany and joined herself to him in marital affection. From them was born Conan, count of the same Brittany, surnamed the Fat.

After these three children had been born to the elder Fulk, their mother, having abandoned her husband, went to Philip, king of the Franks. He too, having rejected his lawful wife, received her as partner of his bed and companion of his cares; later, treating her with marital affection, he kept her with him against ecclesiastical law, despite the opposition and vigorous resistance of the bishops and princes of his realm. By her he had Florus, Philip, and Cecilia, of whom we have spoken above. Cecilia was first the wife of Tancred, prince of Antioch; after his death she entered a second marriage with the lord Pons, count of Tripoli.

The aforesaid Fulk, son of the elder Fulk, after his father’s death married the daughter of Elias, count of Maine, named Eremburga; by her he had two sons and two daughters. The cause of this marriage was his mother. For while this young man was serving as cupbearer in the court of the count of Poitou, his lord, he heard of the death of his elder brother. The same count seized him and cast him into chains on account of certain castles which he sought forcibly to take from him. Fulk’s father and brother had long possessed these, by hereditary right but as fiefs of the aforesaid count, within the latter’s territory.

When his mother heard this—she who had long before separated from his father and gone to the lord king of the Franks—she was moved by maternal feeling. She humbly petitioned the lord king and obtained the release of her son from chains and his restoration to his paternal inheritance. Moreover, she brought it about that the lord king gave to her son in marriage the only daughter of the above-named Count Elias, together with all her inheritance. By her, as stated, he begot two sons and an equal number of daughters.

The firstborn was named Geoffrey. He succeeded his father in the same county. To him Henry the Elder, most powerful king of the English, gave in marriage his only daughter Matilda, widow of the lord Henry, emperor of the Romans. By her Geoffrey had three sons: Henry, who now governs the kingdom of England vigorously and wisely; Geoffrey, surnamed Plantagenet; and William, called Longsword.

The second son of the lord Fulk, bearing the name of his maternal grandfather, was Elias. Rotrou, count of Perche, gave him his only daughter in marriage, promising that he would thereafter take no wife, but at death would transfer his entire inheritance to him whole and undiminished. Forgetful of the agreement, however, and prodigal of his promises, he married the sister of Count Patrick, a nobleman of England, and by her had several children. Thus the aforesaid Elias was, contrary to expectation, excluded from his inheritance.

Of the daughters, one was named Sibylla. She married the illustrious and noble lord Thierry, count of Flanders; from them was born Philip, who today administers the county of Flanders. The other was named Matilda. She had been betrothed to the son of the aforesaid King Henry of the English; but before they came together, her bridegroom, sailing for England, suffered shipwreck and was drowned in the sea. His betrothed, vowing perpetual celibacy, lived for the rest of her life as a nun in a very devout convent of women at Fontevraud.

## Chapter II. Before Baldwin the king summoned him, Fulk had come to Jerusalem on pilgrimage; and concerning his elevation to the kingship.

After his wife’s death, the aforesaid Fulk had gone to Jerusalem for prayer, before he was summoned by the lord king. There he comported himself most magnificently in God’s service and, as his merits required, won the favour of all the people, the lord king’s friendship, and the great intimacy of all the princes. For he maintained one hundred knights at his own expense in the kingdom for a whole year. At length he returned safely to his own lands, married off his daughters, found wives for his sons, and put his county in the best order.

While he was energetically and prudently attending to his affairs for several years after his return, behold: the lord king of Jerusalem, concerned about the succession—namely, to whom he should marry his firstborn daughter—after much deliberation, by the common counsel of all the princes and with the people’s approval, sent some of his nobles, namely the lord William of Bures and the lord Guy Brisebarre, to the aforesaid count. They invited him to the marriage of his daughter and to succession in the kingdom.

Having settled his affairs and organized his county, he gave his children his blessing, chose distinguished men from among his nobles, and set out in answer to the lord king’s summons. After he entered the kingdom, the king, within a few days, united his firstborn daughter to him in marriage as the agreement required, granting him as dowry the two coastal cities of Tyre and Ptolemais. He held them for about three years, yet continued to be called count as before.

When the lord king died on 22 August in the year 1131 from the Incarnation of the Lord, this count and his aforesaid wife were solemnly crowned and consecrated, according to custom, by William, patriarch of Jerusalem of good memory, in the church of the Holy Sepulchre, on 14 September, the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross.

## Chapter III. The elder Joscelin, count of Edessa, sick, confronts the enemy in a litter; having secured victory, he departs from the flesh; and concerning his son Joscelin.

At the same time, the lord Joscelin, count of Edessa, worn out by a long illness and lying in bed, awaited the approaching day of death. In the preceding year, in the region of Aleppo, a tower constructed of unbaked bricks had fallen upon him. In order to capture the enemies shut up within it more easily, he had ordered it undermined. When the undermined tower suddenly collapsed, it crushed him unawares. With great labour, his men barely pulled him out, as if buried, his limbs shattered. He had been weakened by this illness for a long time, and it still detained the soul striving to depart.

Then a messenger flew in, reporting that the sultan of Iconium was besieging one of his castles, named Cressum. When he heard this, the high-minded man—though weak and wholly powerless in body, yet strong in spirit—ordered his son to be summoned to him. He commanded him to take with him all the military forces of that region, to confront the above-named enemy manfully, and to take the place of his disabled father.

But the son began to excuse himself, alleging that the said sultan was said to be coming with a great multitude and that, in comparison with such forces, he himself had few men. The father, weighing his son’s faintheartedness and inferring from those words what he would become, ordered the military forces and the entire population of the region to be assembled. When they had been prepared, he ordered a litter fitted out for himself; mounting it, he went to meet the enemy, forgetting his pain and incapacity.

After he had proceeded some distance with the army, Geoffrey, surnamed the Monk, one of the magnates of the region, informed him that, on hearing of his approach, the sultan had lifted the siege of the aforesaid castle and hastened to depart. On learning this, the count ordered the litter in which he was carried to be set down on the ground. Raising his hands to heaven, he gave thanks to the Lord with sighs and tears and with a devout spirit: the gracious and merciful Lord had visited him with so great a favour at his end that, though half-dead and standing at death’s very threshold, he was still feared by the enemies of the Christian faith. In thanksgiving he surrendered his last breath to heaven, leaving as his heir to all his possessions without exception his namesake son, yet one greatly degenerate from his father’s glory.

This younger Joscelin was born of the sister of Leo the Armenian, a man of great power among his people. He was small in stature but thick-limbed and very robust; dark in complexion and hair, with a broad face marked by scars of the disease commonly called smallpox; his eyes were swollen and his nose prominent. He was a generous man, distinguished in military enterprises, but excessively given to drinking-bouts and to the works of Venus, serving the impurities of the flesh to the point of disgrace.

He married Beatrice, the widow of William of Saone, a woman noble in body but nobler in character. By her he had a son, the third Joscelin, and a daughter. This daughter was first the wife of Reynald of Marash, and afterward of the lord Amalric, count of Jaffa, who later became king of Jerusalem. From them were born Baldwin, the sixth king of Jerusalem, and his sister Sibylla. This Joscelin, as will be told below, through his cowardice and as his sins deserved, lost the whole region which his father had governed with fitting moderation.

## Chapter IV. The king is summoned by the Antiochenes; and the princess’s wickedness is disclosed.

In the first year of the reign of the lord Fulk, the city and the entire region of Antioch were deprived of a prince’s protection. The younger lord Bohemond had died before the lord king, leaving an only daughter as heir. Fearing that, lacking a protector, the province would lie open to enemy plots, the magnates of that region summoned the lord king to take care of those districts and make all their affairs his concern.

The wife of the deceased prince, daughter of King Baldwin and sister of Lady Melisende, was a woman exceedingly crafty and very malicious. She had some supporters of her schemes, with whose cooperation she strove to act wickedly concerning the principality. She wished to claim the entire region for herself by disinheriting the daughter she had borne to her husband; and, once she had gained the principality, then to enter a second marriage at her own pleasure.

While he lived, her father had very effectively forestalled these very schemes immediately after her husband’s death. Having expelled her from Antioch by force, he ordered her to be content with what her husband had bestowed upon her as a marriage-gift: namely, the two coastal cities of Gabala and Laodicea. But after her father’s death, thinking she had found a suitable opportunity, she again aspired to her former design.

By lavish gifts and still ampler promises she had made certain powerful men accomplices in these schemes: William of Saone, brother of Guarentin; Pons, count of Tripoli; and the younger Joscelin, count of Edessa. The magnates of that region, fearing this, strove with all their power to oppose her impious designs. For that reason, as we have said, they had summoned the lord king, so that he might aid them in these matters and the region might not lack support.

## Chapter V. As the king hastens to Antioch, the count of Tripoli opposes him, but is defeated by the king. The affairs of Antioch are placed in security.

When the embassy of the Antiochenes had been heard and the lord king was greatly moved by anxiety for that region, whose danger he feared exceedingly, he hastened at their summons and reached Beirut. But the count of Tripoli barred passage through his lands. The king therefore took with him Anselm of Brie, a nobleman and his faithful vassal, and went by ship as far as the harbour of Saint Simeon. There the noble and powerful magnates of Antioch met him and led him into the city, subjecting the whole region to his authority.

Although the count of Tripoli had the lord king’s sister as his wife, as has often been said, he nevertheless hurried after the king to Antioch in order, for the princess’s sake—whose gifts were said to have corrupted him—to oppose the king’s actions. In those regions the count possessed two castles, Arcicanum and Rugia, which he held through his wife. The lord Tancred, of pious memory in Christ, had given them to his wife when dying as a marriage-gift. The count fortified these with arms and troops, and began from them to harass the lord king and his followers.

The Antiochenes bore this very badly and persuaded the king to confront him and curb his presumptuous attacks. The king agreed to their words, remembering the injuries he had suffered on his way there when the count had barred his passage. He therefore marched thither with all the forces he could raise. Near the aforementioned Rugia, the two sides drew up their battle-lines, engaged one another in battle, and fought for a long time with an uncertain outcome. At last the king gained the advantage, put the count and his men to flight, routed their formations, and captured many of his soldiers. He brought these in chains to Antioch.

At length, through prudent men and faithful mediators of peace, the king and count were reconciled. The king restored to the count those of his soldiers whom he had taken, and the condition of the region seemed to have improved. Yet the more prudent inhabitants of that province feared that, once the lord king had returned to his own lands, internal disturbances would shake the region and so provide the enemy a greater opportunity for attack. With earnest prayers they begged the king to remain among them longer.

The king considered that, through the Lord’s mercy, his own kingdom was securely established and enjoyed full tranquillity, while the region in which he was staying greatly needed the support of a ruler. He graciously consented. By common counsel of the nobles, he administered both the city and its adjacent territory with fitting moderation, devoting to them as much care as he devoted to his own affairs—and even more exact care—in order to bring all things to the best condition. Thus he won the fuller favour of all the citizens and of the princes also, who persisted in their duty of fealty.

When their affairs had been secured and their business arranged in fitting order, and after he had stayed for a time as necessity appeared to require, he returned to the kingdom, recalled by care for his own affairs. He entrusted the care of the principality to the noble and industrious man Reynald, surnamed Mansuer.

## Chapter VI. He is again recalled by the Antiochenes. Sanguin besieges a certain castle in Tripolitan territory; through the king’s intervention at his sister’s request, he lifts the siege.

As time passed, while this king was vigorously labouring over the needs of the kingdom entrusted to him by God and, after the manner of Martha, diligently managing its affairs through assiduous provision for its many services, a messenger arrived from the Antiochenes. He reported that an innumerable host of Turks from the Persian Gulf and the whole eastern region had crossed the great river Euphrates and settled in huge numbers near Antioch.

On hearing this, the king was greatly anxious for the condition of the principality entrusted to him and for the safety of those living in it, especially because they had placed all their hope in him. He was also concerned because, as the proverb says:

> Your own affair is at stake when your neighbour’s wall is on fire.

He understood that the defeat of neighbours would rebound to his own danger. Deciding that it was an honourable duty to provide assistance to brothers in need, he summoned from throughout the kingdom reinforcements of knights and foot-soldiers, prepared for the journey, and hastened there with all speed.

As he advanced with his forces and reached Sidon, his sister, Lady Cecilia, countess and wife of Pons, count of Tripoli, brought sorrowful news. She said that Sanguin, prince of Aleppo and a most powerful Turkish satrap, had besieged her husband with the multitude of his forces in one of the count’s strongholds, named Mount Ferrand. She therefore begged the king—urgently and persistently, in womanly fashion—that he postpone for a time other matters requiring less immediate attention and quickly assist her husband in his peril.

Moved by her pressing entreaty, the king delayed his former undertaking briefly and marched there, taking with him several knights who had remained from the count’s expedition. When Sanguin heard that the lord king was hastening to raise the siege, he took counsel with his men as to what was more advantageous and voluntarily lifted the siege. He returned with his troops to his own country.

## Chapter VII. The king hastens to Antioch; he puts to flight the assembled enemies; the Antiochenes are enriched with enemy spoils.

The count having meanwhile been relieved, the king, free from this concern, returned to his undertaking and hastened to Antioch by the routes he had previously intended. On hearing of his arrival, the Antiochenes went out to meet him and received so great a guest with every joy. They hoped that through his skill they might endure without danger the violence of the enemy said to be approaching.

For even a great multitude rarely accomplishes much without a leader, and numerous companies without a commander, like sand without lime, scarcely hold together. Meanwhile, widespread and consistent reports announced that those said to have crossed the Euphrates with a strong force and an exceedingly abundant equipment had joined to themselves persons familiar with the country whom they found near the river. They had pitched camp in the territory of Aleppo and intended to ravage the whole region by sudden raids.

They had gathered from every neighbouring district into one place, named Canestrivum. There, having collected their whole multitude, they intended, guided by those who knew the terrain, to make unexpected incursions throughout the province. When the lord king learned this, he summoned military forces from the whole principality. With the men of his household whom he had with him, he left Antioch and pitched camp near the castle of Harenc. Like a prudent man, he waited for several days, because:

> “... rash impulse is a poor minister in all things.” — Statius

He waited to see whether the enemy, said to have superior forces, would provoke his men to battle or disclose their intended plan in some other way. But when he saw that they attempted nothing of the kind, instead lingering securely and quietly in their camp, perhaps still awaiting greater reinforcements, he suddenly rushed upon them. Finding them unprepared before they could seize their weapons, he pressed them with swords and pierced them with lances. Only a few were permitted, through the speed of their horses, to escape death by flight; all the rest were slain.

The enemy camp, filled with every useful thing and varied equipment, was left behind. Innumerable men—nearly three thousand—were killed. Our victors returned to Antioch with the greatest joy and the emblems of triumph, laden to satiety with enemy spoils and already desiring no more. They drove before them horses, slaves, herds of cattle, flocks, tents, every kind of booty, and every variety of captured goods.

From that time the lord king had the hearts of all the Antiochenes, both nobles and common people alike, more fully reconciled to him and possessed the favour of all. Previously, because of the princess, to whom the lord king’s presence was unwelcome and suspect, some of the greater men had opposed him, favouring the princess because of the gifts which she distributed in lavish generosity.

## Chapter VIII. The patriarch of Jerusalem and the princes of the kingdom establish a highly necessary stronghold, called Arnald’s Castle.

Meanwhile, while the lord king was detained and occupied in the Antiochene regions, making that region’s affairs his own concern as though they were his own, until a prince should be appointed there by common counsel, those who remained in the kingdom—the lord [Col. 0586A] patriarch and the citizens of Jerusalem—put their trust in the Lord and assembled their strength. Near the very ancient place Nobe, today commonly called Bettenoble, on the descending slopes of the mountains at the beginning of the plains, on the road to Lydda and the sea, they solidly founded a stronghold for the protection of travelling pilgrims.

For in the mountain passes, amid unavoidable narrow defiles, travellers had been exposed to the greatest danger, since the men of Ascalon were accustomed to make sudden attacks there. When the work had been successfully completed, they gave the place its name, calling it Arnald’s Castle. Through the Lord’s grace, this stronghold also had the benefit that passage became less dangerous and the road much safer for those wishing either to go to Jerusalem or return from it.

## Chapter IX. By the king’s counsel, messengers are sent to Raymond, son of the count of Poitou, that he may marry Constance, daughter of Bohemond.

Having gained so notable a victory and arranged the affairs of the principality of Antioch according to his free judgment, the lord king was held in very high esteem. By divine providence he had obtained the government of two kingdoms, prospered in both, and protected their people in complete tranquillity.

The leading men of that region came to him, especially those who had been eager to keep faith with their now-dead lord Bohemond, prince of Antioch, and with his daughter, still a ward. They approached the lord king privately and earnestly requested that, since he had more complete knowledge of noblemen and distinguished young men in the lands beyond the mountains, he should advise them which of so many princes they ought to summon, and with whom they might most suitably marry the daughter of their lord, heiress to her father’s possessions.

The king gladly received their request, commended both their loyalty and their concern, and joined them in considering the matter. After many candidates had been reviewed, the common counsel of all decided that a noble youth of outstanding character named Raymond, son of the lord William, count of Poitou, should be summoned. He was said to be residing at the court of the lord Henry the Elder, king of the English, where he had taken up the profession of arms, while his elder brother, the lord William, governed Aquitaine by hereditary right.

Having weighed the alternatives and considered this most expedient, they secretly sent envoys: a certain Gerard, surnamed Jeberrus, a brother of the Hospital, carrying letters from the lord patriarch and all the nobles. They feared that if Raymond were summoned openly and through persons of greater rank, the princess—being a most malicious woman—would devise obstacles.

For anyone could easily prevent his arrival. Roger, then duke of Apulia and afterward king, claimed Antioch with all its dependencies as an inheritance due to him by hereditary right. He wished to succeed as the kinsman of the lord Bohemond. For Robert Guiscard, father of the elder Bohemond, and Roger, count of Sicily, surnamed Borsa, father of this King Roger, were brothers by both parents. The younger Bohemond, son of the elder, was the father of the young girl to whose marriage the aforesaid youth Raymond was being invited. He therefore had to be summoned cautiously, lest, once his coming was known, his rivals obstruct his approach by force or deceit.

These matters having been arranged, the lord king returned to the region of Jerusalem, attended by the goodwill of all.

## Chapter X. Bernard, patriarch of Antioch, dies; Ralph, archbishop of Mamistra, succeeds him amid tumult.

[Col. 0587B]

At the same time Bernard, a very aged man of most blessed memory, simple and fearing God, the first Latin patriarch at Antioch, entered upon the way of all flesh in the thirty-sixth year of his pontificate. After his death, when all the suffragans of that most eminent see, both archbishops and bishops, had assembled according to custom in order profitably to provide consolation for the church deprived of its shepherd, and when, in the patriarchal palace, they were holding more careful mutual deliberations, as is customary in such matters, concerning this most salutary business, a certain Ralph, archbishop of Mamistra, native of the castle of Danfront, situated on the border between Normandy and the diocese of Le Mans, a military man, splendid [Col. 0587C] and exceedingly generous, highly acceptable to the populace and to the order of knights, was elected—without the knowledge of his brethren and fellow bishops—by the vote of the people alone, as they say, and was enthroned in the chair of the Prince of the Apostles. When those who had gathered in order, with God as author, to appoint a patriarch over themselves heard this, fearing the indiscriminate outbreaks of the furious, shouting populace, they separated from one another, refusing to render obedience to one whom they had not elected. Nevertheless, he occupied the church and palace and, immediately and without delay, took for himself the pallium from the altar of Saint Peter, showing no reverence whatever for the Roman Church. In the course of time he also drew some of the church’s suffragans into communion with himself.

[Col. 0587D] And, as we learned from the report of many persons, had he embraced peace with the canons of the church and not, under the prompting of a spirit of pride, presumed to disturb their possessions, he might have passed his life there in tranquillity. But since the proverbial saying is true, “It is difficult for things badly begun to end well,” compelled by his sins and rendered insolent by the abundance of his wealth, he came to regard no man as his equal, so that he presented himself as successor rather of Antiochus than of Peter or Ignatius. For he violently expelled some of the leading men of the church; others he consigned to chains and prison as though guilty of capital crimes. Among them were a certain Arnulf, a Calabrian by birth, certainly a noble and learned man; likewise Lambert, a man of remarkable simplicity [Col. 0588A] and honourable conduct, also learned, archdeacon of the same church. He thrust them into prison in a certain fortress, into a lodging full of lime, as though they were men of blood, and afflicted them for many days, saying that they had conspired against his life. By perpetrating these and similar acts upon his subjects in a savage spirit, he provoked the hatred of all against himself. Hardly even among his household and dependants, driven by the goads of an evil conscience, did any place seem safe to him. But enough of this for now; in what follows, at the proper time, we shall speak in its place of his end.

## CHAPTER XI. Pope Honorius dies; Innocent is substituted for him; a dangerous schism arises. William, archbishop of Tyre, departs from the flesh; Fulcher succeeds him; he goes to Rome, seeks and obtains the pallium.

[Col. 0588B]

While these things were taking place in the East, Pope Honorius, closing his final day, paid the debt of fate. And while the cardinals were deliberating concerning the appointment of his successor, their wishes were divided. Unable to agree upon one person, they elected two amid contention: Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo, whom, after consecrating him, they called Innocent; and Peter, surnamed Leonis, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mary in Trastevere, called “Fountain of Oil,” whom those who elected him likewise consecrated and called Anacletus. Thus a most dangerous schism arose, so that not only were the churches within the City endangered and the people perished [Col. 0588C] by mutual slaughter, but almost the whole world was shaken and kingdoms, inflamed by rival zeal, clashed with one another. At last, after many labours and immense dangers, Lord Innocent prevailed, Peter aforesaid, his rival for the papacy, having first died.

In those same days our aforesaid predecessor William, the first Latin archbishop of Tyre after the liberation of the city, laid aside the burden of the flesh and passed to the Lord. For while the city was still held by the enemy, a certain Odo had been ordained to the title of that church; but, as stated above, he had died before the liberation of the same city. He was succeeded by Lord Fulcher of blessed memory, an Aquitanian by birth, from the district of Angoulême, [Col. 0588D] a religious man and one fearing God, moderately learned, but steadfast and a lover of discipline. Among his own people he had been abbot of regular canons in the monastery called Cella. Later, however, during the aforesaid schism which arose between Pope Innocent and Peter, son of Peter Leonis, Gerard, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the Apostolic See, favoured the aforesaid Peter and, supporting the other party, harassed him with very many troubles. Unable to endure this, the man of venerable life obtained leave from his brethren and came to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer. At length, having professed the regular life and its continual observance in the cloister of the Church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, he was called to the church of Tyre. He governed that church vigorously and prosperously [Col. 0589A] for twelve years. He was the fourth before us, who now preside over that same church not through any merit of election, but solely by the Lord’s favour and forbearance.

After receiving the gift of his consecration from William, patriarch of Jerusalem, he wished, following the example of his predecessor, to hasten to the Roman Church to obtain the pallium. But he suffered plots and violence at the hands of the same patriarch and his accomplices, so that he could scarcely, and only with much difficulty, escape their hands and reach the Roman Church for the aforesaid purpose, as is plainly evident from the tenor of the letters of Pope Innocent. For he says:

> **INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WILLIAM, patriarch of Jerusalem, greeting and apostolic blessing.**
>
> The authority of the Gospel declares that the governance of the whole Church and of ecclesiastical order was conferred by heavenly privilege upon blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles.

And below:

> We are astonished that, although the Roman Church has laboured so greatly for the liberation of the Eastern Church and, by the shedding of the blood of many sons, has stirred the hearts both of churchmen and secular persons to its service, you have in no way taken care on this occasion to respond to that same mother as is fitting. For it had seemed too little to you that you had presumed to hinder our venerable brother Fulcher, archbishop of Tyre, who was coming to the Roman Church according to the custom of his predecessors to receive the pallium, [Col. 0589C] unless you also showed yourself inhuman, troublesome, and excessively harsh toward him on his return from us: so that you were unwilling either to restore to him the ancient dignity of the Church of Tyre, or, within three months after receiving our letters, to do him justice concerning the injuries inflicted there, or concerning Caiphas or Porphyreon, in accordance with our command. Yet it is surely most unworthy that the honour which would be accorded to him by the Church of Antioch, if he obeyed it, should be withheld by you or your successors.
>
> Furthermore, you are said to conduct yourself with excessive lordship over his subjects. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we command and enjoin you that, as you desire to be cherished by the pious zeal and assistance of that same your mother, and as in your necessities you desire to be aided by her protection, [Col. 0589D] you shall love and honour the said archbishop and presume in no respect to trouble him. Rather, in all matters concerning which he has lodged a complaint with you, do not delay to render him full justice within forty days after you have received these present letters; nor presume to act in any way against his subjects contrary to the statutes of the canons. Otherwise, you must fear that we shall withdraw both him and his suffragans from your obedience and retain them in our own hand.

Given at the Lateran, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January.

## CHAPTER XII. The Roman Church commands him to obey the pontiff of Jerusalem and to hold with him the place which he had previously held among the Antiochenes.

On his return from the Roman Church he received an order [Col. 0590A] that, until it should be decided to which of the two patriarchs he ought permanently to yield, he should meanwhile obey the patriarch of Jerusalem, as his predecessor had also been told to do; and that he should hold in the Church of Jerusalem the dignity which his predecessors had held in the Church of Antioch while they obeyed it. It is certain that among the thirteen archbishops subject to the see of Antioch from apostolic times, Tyre held the first place, so that in the East it is called *Protothronos*, “first in rank,” as is contained in the catalogue of suffragan pontiffs belonging to the Church of Antioch. It reads as follows:

> First see: Tyre, under which are thirteen bishoprics.  
> Second see: Tarsus, under which are five bishoprics.  
> Third see: Edessa, under which are ten bishoprics.  
> [Col. 0590B] Fourth see: Apamea, under which are seven bishoprics.  
> Fifth see: Hierapolis, under which are eight bishoprics.  
> Sixth see: Bostra, under which are nineteen bishoprics.  
> Seventh see: Anazarbus, under which are nine bishoprics.  
> Eighth see: Seleucia, under which are twenty-four bishoprics.  
> Ninth see: Damascus, under which are ten bishoprics.  
> Tenth see: Amida, under which are seven bishoprics.  
> Eleventh see: Sergiopolis, under which are four bishoprics.  
> Twelfth see: Theodosiopolis, under which are seven bishoprics.  
> Thirteenth see: Emesa, under which are four bishoprics.  
> Metropolitan sees maintaining themselves independently: eight. Archbishops: twelve.

That the Church of Tyre should therefore occupy the first place among the suffragans of the Church of Jerusalem, and that it obeys that church solely by the command of the pope, is plainly inferred [Col. 0590C] from the rescript of Pope Innocent’s letters addressed to the same William, patriarch of Jerusalem. It reads thus:

> **INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to WILLIAM, patriarch of Jerusalem, greeting and apostolic blessing.**
>
> The more highly the kindness of heavenly munificence has exalted the Church of Jerusalem in your time, the more fitting it is that you should show yourself more kindly toward your brethren and honour with mutual charity those who render obedience to you. Therefore we command your fraternity that, with a view to brotherly love, you shall love and honour our venerable brother Fulcher, archbishop of Tyre, who by command of the holy Roman Church [Col. 0590D] obeys you. Carefully ensure that you inflict no burden upon him, and that, under the pretext of such subjection—which is indeed granted to you and to the Church of Jerusalem by the beneficence of the Apostolic See—the noble and renowned Church of Tyre suffers no loss of its right or dignity. For it is unworthy that the honour which would be accorded to it by Antioch, if it obeyed that church, should be withheld by you or your successors.

Given at Albano, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August.

## CHAPTER XIII. Its suffragans are commanded to obey it; many letters are sent for this purpose.

Accordingly, upon his return, although reluctantly, the following of his suffragans, who until that day had been in the power of the patriarch of Jerusalem, were restored to him: the bishops of Acre, Sidon, and Beirut. But the patriarch of Antioch violently retained the rest—namely the bishops of Byblos, Tripoli, and Antaradus—who possessed the other bishoprics of the same church in their own hands as though they were their own. He alleged only the ground that Tyre did not obey him, not that he denied that they belonged to its jurisdiction. To prevent this and to ensure that they returned to their mother Church of Tyre, the same Pope Innocent commanded, writing both to the aforesaid bishops and to the patriarch of Antioch as follows:

> **INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren GERARD, bishop of Tripoli, R., bishop of Tortosa, and H., bishop of Byblos, greeting and apostolic blessing.**
>
> [Col. 0591B] Your brotherhood ought to know that the condition of the Church then shines forth more clearly when the ranks established in it are preserved uninjured and the reverence owed to each prelate is rendered without contention or contradiction. For each of those who is subject to another ought to consider with what reverence and honour he must honour his prelates, if he has any. If these are unjustly and undeservedly withheld, the condition of unity will certainly be shaken; ecclesiastical teaching, with careful consideration, has reduced everything to this unity by ordering all things within itself for greater firmness.
>
> Therefore, lest the honour or dignity of your churches be diminished or annulled by contention or improper rebellion, we command [Col. 0591C] and enjoin you by apostolic letters that you render to our venerable brother Fulcher, archbishop of Tyre, your metropolitan, the obedience and reverence due to him. For by apostolic authority we restore you and your churches to the Church of Tyre, which is your metropolitan see, and likewise absolve you from the oath or fealty by which you are bound to the patriarch of Antioch. But if you neglect to obey our commands and, within three months after receiving these letters, to return to obedience to our aforesaid brother, we shall, with God as author, hold valid the sentence which he shall canonically pronounce against you.

Given at the Lateran, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February.

[Col. 0591D] And lest they be hindered by the patriarch of Antioch, who had long held them and was the more powerful man, from carrying out the pope’s order, he wrote to that patriarch in these words:

> **INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother RALPH, patriarch of Antioch, greeting and apostolic blessing.**
>
> The institutions of the holy canons provide that each person should remain content with his own bounds and should not encroach upon another’s rights. Both divine and human laws forbid us to do to our neighbours what we do not wish done to ourselves. This being so, we command your fraternity that you do not hinder the suffragans of the Church of Tyre from rendering to our venerable brother Fulcher, their archbishop and metropolitan, [Col. 0592A] the obedience and reverence due to him. Otherwise the canonical sanctions are violated if obedience is withheld from metropolitans by their suffragans. For we desire that, concerning prelates and subjects, each person’s right and proper order be preserved without contradiction.

Given at the Lateran, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February.

Nor did the pope write thus only to these persons; he also enjoined those who had been held by the patriarch of Jerusalem and, out of fear of him, refused to obey the apostolic commands. He commanded them likewise, setting aside every pretext, to render obedience to the lord archbishop of Tyre, as follows:

> **INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren BALDWIN, bishop of Beirut, BERNARD, bishop of Sidon, and JOHN, bishop of Ptolemais, greeting [Col. 0592B] and apostolic blessing.**
>
> The holy Fathers wished that there should be different ranks and orders in the Church, so that, while lesser persons render subjection and reverence to greater persons, one bond might arise from diversity and the administration of each office be rightly conducted. But it grieves us, and we are greatly astonished, that although we long ago commanded you by apostolic letters to render obedience and reverence to our venerable brother Fulcher, archbishop of Tyre, your metropolitan, you have scorned to do so by alleging certain unworthy pretexts and interpretations. Yet to resist is as the sin of divination, and to refuse obedience as the crime of idolatry (1 Samuel 15). Therefore we command you and again enjoin by apostolic authority that [Col. 0592C] henceforth, putting aside every pretext, you obey the same our brother, and that, under pretext of the obedience which you render to some primate, you in no way withhold from him the subjection and reverence due to your metropolitan. If you should continue to prove contumacious, we shall, with the Lord as author, hold valid the sentence which the same archbishop has canonically pronounced, or shall pronounce, against you. But if, because you have obeyed the same our brother, the patriarch of Jerusalem should decree anything against you, we decree that such sentence is without force and judge it to be of no effect.

Given at the Lateran, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February.

## CHAPTER XIV. It is explained whence and for what reason this controversy between the two patriarchs arose, and on what grounds each defends his position.

[Col. 0592D]

Lest anyone wonder that, although we previously said that the archbishop of Tyre had fourteen suffragans by right, the pope writes to only six, it must be known that the city of Paneas, that is Caesarea Philippi, did not yet have a bishop, and that these six held the remaining bishoprics. The bishop of Sidon held, as he still holds, the bishopric of Sarepta; the bishop of Tripoli held Botrys, Arca, and Arsus; and the bishop of Antaradus, who is also called bishop of Tortosa, held Aradus and Maraclea. Of these six, the patriarch of Antioch had three obedient to himself: namely, the bishops of Antaradus, Tripoli, and Byblos. For, after the aforesaid cities had been captured, he consecrated bishops in them with the intention that, once the metropolitan see of Tyre was freed and its archbishop rendered him the obedience due under ancient constitutions, he would restore them to him without difficulty, as he was bound to do by right. These aforesaid cities lay in the county of Tripoli, and therefore the patriarch of Antioch could do this more freely, since the lord king did not hinder him.

But in the other three—Beirut, Sidon, and Ptolemais, which is Acre—the patriarch of Jerusalem consecrated bishops with the intention that, after the city of Tyre had been captured and an archbishop had there been consecrated by him, he would restore them to him. For he assumed, contrary to ancient custom, that the Church of Tyre ought someday to obey him, trusting in the letters of Pope Paschal, by which he appeared to have granted to Lord Baldwin, first king of Jerusalem, and to Lord Gibelin, third patriarch of Jerusalem, that the bishops of all cities which the lord king or his army had already acquired, or would acquire, should be subject to the patriarch of Jerusalem—as was stated above when we treated of the reign of Lord Baldwin, first king of Jerusalem.

Thus, the entire province of Tyre having been liberated before its metropolis itself was freed, the aforesaid two patriarchs divided the diocese between themselves. The Church of Antioch held and still holds what lay outside the kingdom, below the place called the Pass of the Pagan; but the patriarch of Jerusalem possessed what lay on this side and was contained within the boundaries of the kingdom. At length, however, after the city of Tyre had been liberated through the Lord’s mercy, in the fourth year after its liberation the patriarch of Jerusalem consecrated an archbishop there, as we have said, and restored to him the suffragans whom he held. Meanwhile, while the patriarch of Jerusalem had it in his own charge, it was so diminished and reduced to nothing that, among the churches within the circuit of the same city, only one was reserved for the future archbishop.

And it came about, as the common proverb says, that “from another’s hide generous leather straps were made for petitioners and the undeserving.” Even to this day the aforesaid two lords contend over our very entrails, strong to our injury and enriched from our poverty. Its limbs scattered, though in their integrity it had flourished far and wide from apostolic times, with the agreement of the holy and universal seven synods, it lies torn apart; mutilated in its more important limbs, it awaits consolation, and there is none to console it; it stretches out its hand, and there is none to help. We have become like those of whom it is said:

> “Whatever madness kings commit, the Achaeans pay the penalty.”  
> *(Horace, Epistles I.2.14)*

They feed upon our flesh—may it someday be their lot to vomit it up! Yet we do not without reason impute the cause of so great an evil to the Roman Church. For while it commands us to obey the patriarch of Jerusalem, it permits us to be unlawfully curtailed by the patriarch of Antioch. If our integrity were restored to us, we, being sons of obedience, would be ready in a willing spirit to be subject to either of them, without contradiction and without grievance. Nor should anyone think it foreign to our purpose—we who have undertaken to write history—that we have inserted these remarks on the condition of our own church. It is not fitting for us to treat others’ affairs and forget our own. For, as the proverb says, “He prays badly who forgets himself.” But now let us return to the history.

## CHAPTER XV. The count of Jaffa is accused before the king, and great tumult is stirred up in the kingdom.

[Col. 0594B]

After the lord king had returned from the region of Antioch, as we have related, behold, a most dangerous disturbance again arose. For certain persons are said, for some reasons, to have conspired against the lord king among the greater princes of the kingdom: namely Hugh, count of Jaffa, and Roman of Le Puy, lord of the region beyond the Jordan. In order that this may be more clearly evident, the narrative must be resumed somewhat further back.

In the time of Lord Baldwin of Le Bourg, who preceded this Fulk in the kingdom, a certain noble and powerful man among his own people, Hugh of Puiset, from the diocese of Orléans, set out for Jerusalem for the sake of prayer with his wife Mamilia, daughter of Lord Hugh Cholet, count of Ruci. In Apulia he had a son. For his wife had begun the journey while pregnant; and because the child was very small and could not safely be carried along, he left him there with his kinsman Lord Bohemond. Crossing the sea, he came to Lord King Baldwin, likewise his kinsman by blood. Immediately after his arrival the king granted him and his heirs the city of Jaffa with its dependencies, to hold by hereditary right. Not long afterward this noble man ended his life in death.

The king then granted his widow and the aforesaid city to another noble man, Count Albert, brother of the count of Namur, a very powerful man in the Empire, from the diocese of Liège. When, within a short time, both the aforesaid count and his wife had died, Hugh, the child who had remained in Apulia, having now reached maturity, sought and obtained from the lord king his father’s hereditary estate, which had devolved upon him by hereditary right according to the custom of his ancestors. Having obtained it, he married Lady Emelota, niece of Patriarch Arnulf and widow of the magnificent Lord Eustace Grenier. By her the aforesaid Lord Eustace had begotten twin sons: the younger Eustace, lord of the city of Sidon, and Walter, who ruled Caesarea.

After Lord Baldwin died and Lord Fulk was raised to the royal throne, serious enmities arose between the same lord king and the aforesaid count for concealed reasons. Some said that the lord king regarded the count with extreme suspicion lest he hold excessively intimate conversations with the queen. Many indications seemed to support this. Hence, inflamed with marital jealousy, he was said to have conceived an implacable hatred for him. The count was a young man, tall in body, handsome in appearance, distinguished in martial deeds, pleasing in the eyes of all; nature’s gifts seemed to have converged upon him in complete liberality. Thus he undoubtedly had no equal in the kingdom, whether in bodily elegance, nobility of birth, or experience in warfare. He was also very closely related to the queen on her father’s side: their fathers were first cousins, that is, sons of two sisters. Others, wishing to cloak such talk, said that the sole source of hostility was that the count, as though arrogant and presuming too much upon himself, would not submit to the lord king as the other princes of the kingdom did, and very stubbornly refused to obey his commands.

## CHAPTER XVI. Walter of Caesarea challenges the count to single combat; the count goes over to the enemy and is deserted by his own followers.

Meanwhile Walter of Caesarea, the count’s stepson, a man of surpassing bodily beauty, distinguished in strength and in the prime of life, allegedly prompted by the lord king, publicly accused the count before a very full court of nobles, in the king’s presence and in the manner of an accuser. He charged him with being guilty of treason against majesty and with conspiring, with certain accomplices of the same faction, against the safety of the lord king, contrary to good morals and the discipline of our time.

The count denied the crime and offered himself to undergo, as innocent in this matter, the judgment of the court concerning the accusations. These statements having been made, a single combat was decreed between them according to Frankish custom, and an appropriate day was appointed for the combat. When the court was dissolved, the count returned to Jaffa. Whether because he feared his conscience and knew himself guilty of the charge, or because he suspected the court, is uncertain; but he did not appear on the appointed day. He therefore deservedly incurred a greater suspicion of the alleged crime, even among his own supporters. The court and assembly of nobles, noting his contumacy, condemned him in his absence as guilty of the charge.

When the count learned this, he undertook an act unheard of until that day, worthy of popular hatred and every indignation. Hastening by ship to Ascalon, a city hateful to the Christian name and friendly to our enemies, he entered it to seek assistance from the enemy against the lord king. Seeing that our internal conflicts and domestic seditions advanced their own interests and caused our dangers, they readily gave their assent. Having received hostages from him and reduced their mutual agreements to accord, he returned to Jaffa. The people of Ascalon, led by persistent and obstinate hatred against us and made more secure by the count’s alliance and favour, then invaded our territories more insolently and confidently than usual. Roaming freely and unchecked, carrying off plunder, they did not fear to range as far as Arsuf, also called Antipatris.

When the king heard this, he assembled military forces from throughout the kingdom and a very great multitude of people, and besieged Jaffa. Seeing this, some of the count’s faithful followers who were with him in that same city—namely the elder Balian and certain other God-fearing men—perceived that the count had resolved to rush headlong to ruin, and that he could not be recalled from his pernicious undertaking by the wholesome advice of his faithful friends. Nor did he fear stubbornly to pursue causes of even greater danger. Leaving the benefices they held from him, they chose the better side and went over to the lord king.

## CHAPTER XVII. The city of Jaffa is besieged; the princes of the kingdom negotiate peace; meanwhile Belinas is captured by the enemy.

[Col. 0596B]

Meanwhile Lord Patriarch William, a most gentle man and lover of peace, and certain princes of the kingdom, seeing that these internal conflicts were exceedingly dangerous to the realm, reflected on the Gospel saying, “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be made desolate, and house shall fall upon house” (Matthew 12:25). Fearing—as indeed they could rightly fear—that this occasion might open a greater opportunity and advantage for the enemies of the Christian name to inflict injury, they placed themselves between the parties and tried to discover useful negotiations for peace between the lord king and the oft-mentioned count.

[Col. 0596C] At length, after many disputes, as often happens in such matters, the peacemakers decided that, for the good of peace and to confer some greater honour upon the lord king, the count should remain outside the kingdom for three years. When these had elapsed, he might, with the lord king’s favour, return to the kingdom with those whom he had taken out, without thereafter suffering any claim on account of this affair. In the meantime, all his debts and every liability that he had incurred from any source were to be discharged from the revenues of his possessions.

During the same period, while the lord king was thus occupied around Jaffa and Lord Rainerius surnamed Brus remained there with the other princes of the kingdom, the city of Paneas, besieged by Tegelmeluch, king of Damascus, was violently broken into and fell into the hands of the enemy before the king, though urgently striving to do so, could bring aid to the besieged. Its citizens and the mercenaries within it, both knights and infantry, were captured; the wife of the aforesaid noble and valiant man underwent captivity and removal with the others.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The count of Jaffa is maliciously wounded at Jerusalem; tumult again arises; but once restored to health, he crosses the sea according to the agreement.

Meanwhile, while the count of Jaffa was awaiting his departure and staying at Jerusalem as he was accustomed to do, it happened that in the street called that of the Furriers, before the shop of a merchant named Alfanus, [Col. 0597A] as he was playing dice on the man’s table, a knight of Breton birth unexpectedly drew his sword and inflicted many exceedingly hostile wounds upon the count, who feared nothing of the kind and was intent on the game, in the sight of all who stood by.

A sudden gathering of people immediately took place, and the whole city, hearing of the cruelty of this most monstrous deed, was shaken and roared fiercely. One public report was on everyone’s lips: that this could not have been done without the king’s knowledge; that the criminal would not have presumed to undertake such a deed unless he trusted in the king’s favour. The report spread throughout the populace that the count, innocent, was suffering unjust accusations, and that the king had given a most evident proof of the hatred he had gratuitously conceived against him, beyond any deserts of the count.

Thus popular favour and public goodwill came to the count, and everything alleged against him seemed to have proceeded from malice. When this became known to the lord king, he wished to clear himself of the deed and establish his innocence by manifest proofs. He ordered that the criminal be brought before judgment and, for his notorious offence—which required neither accuser nor witnesses, where due process was unnecessary—commanded that he receive the sentence his merits deserved. The court was accordingly convened and, by common consent, the aforesaid assassin was condemned to suffer the mutilation of his limbs.

When this was reported to the king, he ordered the sentence carried out, with the sole exception that the tongue should not be included among the limbs to be mutilated. He excepted it lest it be said that this was deliberately done in order that the man’s tongue might be cut out, preventing him from confessing the truth of the matter and declaring that the king had sent him. By this manifest act the king provided very prudently for his reputation and greatly restrained the indignation aroused against himself. For neither privately nor publicly, either before or after the loss of his limbs, could anything be extracted from the man to show that he had undertaken that enormous deed by the king’s command or with his knowledge; rather, he confessed that he had acted on his own initiative, hoping by this means to earn the lord king’s favour.

The count, meanwhile, delayed in order to care for his body and recover his health. When he had fully recovered, profoundly sorrowful both because of the recent injury inflicted upon him and because, exiled from his own inheritance, he was compelled to beg through unknown lands, he left the kingdom in accordance with the agreement and went to Apulia. There Lord Roger, who had by then subjected the whole region to himself, received him kindly. Thinking that rivals had expelled so valiant and noble a man from his realm out of envy, and sympathizing with him, he granted him the county of Gargano. But overtaken by untimely death, a man to be lamented by posterity, he never thereafter returned to the kingdom.

From that day, all who had been the count’s informers before the lord king and instigators of hatred incurred the indignation of Lady Queen Melisende. The disgrace of the charge apparently cast some reflection upon her as well, and the grievous sorrow caused by the expelled count tormented her heart. They had to take the utmost care for their own safety. Above all, she persecuted by every means available the elder Roard, later called “of Naples,” who had especially led the king into that cause of hatred. It was unsafe for them to approach her presence, and it was more prudent for them to avoid public assemblies. Nor was any place wholly safe for the king among the queen’s supporters and kinsmen.

At last, through the intervention of some of their intimates, her anger was appeased; with much difficulty the king reconciled the other participants in the same resentment, but only so far that they were permitted to enter her presence with the others. From that day the king became so devoted to his wife that, in order to soften the anger of her whom he had previously embittered, he would not venture to proceed even in minor matters without her knowledge.

## Chapter XIX. A truce is made with the Damascenes; the captives taken at Belinas are restored.

At the same time, when the Damascenes requested a temporary peace from the lord king, besides other things which they offered in order to obtain the treaty, they restored, according to the agreement, all the captives whom they had taken in the city of Paneas, together with the wife of the aforesaid valiant man, namely Lord Rainer Brus, whose city it was. [Col. 0598C] This wife, when she returned after two years, the distinguished and eminent man devoutly received again into the fellowship of his marital embrace. But afterwards, learning that she had not behaved with sufficient prudence among the enemy, and had not observed the honour due to the marriage bed with the caution customary among noble matrons, he cast her off. She, not denying her fault, entered a convent of holy virgins at Jerusalem and, binding herself by a vow of perpetual continence, became a nun. After her death, the aforesaid illustrious man married Agnes, niece of Lord William of Bures. After his death, Gerard of Sidon took her as his wife; from her was born Rainald, who now governs that same city of the Sidonians.

The aforesaid city of Paneas, which, as we have said, had been overcome during the absence of its lord, an official of the Assassins named Emir Ali had surrendered and delivered to our people to hold not long before this time, after accepting an agreed compensation for it, although his own people had possessed it for a long time. Without delay the king granted it to the aforesaid man to possess by hereditary right. Who the people called Assassins are, and what frivolous and God-hateful traditions they follow, we shall explain later in the appropriate place and time. For the present, it is enough to know this about them: they are a people highly suspect and deservedly fearsome to Christians, to nations of other sects, and especially to princes.

## Chapter XX. Raymond, son of the Count of Poitiers, arrives secretly and, reaching Antioch, marries Constance, daughter of Bohemond, against the will and resistance of the princess, the girl’s mother, and obtains the principality.

[Col. 0599A]

Meanwhile, those who had been sent by the Antiochenes for Lord Raymond, son of the Count of Poitiers, as we have said above, diligently seeking, as they had been ordered, where they might find him most readily, learned from reliable reports that he was staying with the lord Henry the Elder, king of the English, from whom he had also received the arms of knighthood. Therefore, taking the direct road to England, they found the aforesaid young man there. When the purpose of their journey had been disclosed to him in secret, he devoutly embraced the proposal made to him; and, on the advice of the lord king, his benefactor, he prepared the necessities for his journey and set out, unknown to anyone.

Roger, duke of Apulia, had perceived what had been devised at Antioch concerning Raymond’s summons. Therefore he had laid ambushes in every maritime city of Apulia, to capture him; for he hoped that, if he could hinder his crossing, he could more readily gain the inheritance he sought by buying off with money the magnates of that region. But Lord Raymond prudently concealed his purpose. Laying aside every display, he travelled like one of the common people, now on foot and now mounted upon cheap beasts of burden, making his way among the populace, [Col. 0599C] never showing anyone even a slight indication of noble birth or wealth. His companions and household were divided into groups: some went three or four days’ journeys ahead, while others followed, as though they had no connection with him.

Thus, clothed in a foreign and humble dress and very often performing the offices of servants, deceiving everyone by his appearance, he evaded the snares of a prudent and most powerful enemy. Arriving at Antioch, he delighted his friends by his coming, but struck no small fear into others, who, as supporters of the princess, were striving to resist his elevation.

A little before this time, though after the aforesaid envoys had been sent to summon Lord Raymond, Princess Alice, widow of Lord Bohemond and sister of Lady Queen Melisende, whom her father had expelled from the city of Antioch and ordered to be content with Laodicea and Gabala, had re-entered Antioch. Through the intervention of her sister with the king, so that he might not oppose her actions, and supported by the patronage of certain nobles, she conducted herself as lady of the city and drew everything into her own management. [Col. 0599D]

In the meantime Ralph, patriarch of Antioch, deceitful and double-dealing in all his ways, had persuaded the princess meanwhile to grant him favour and services against his clergy, who were persecuting him. He told her that Lord Raymond, who had been summoned and was said to have arrived, was intended for her and would become her husband; and he cruelly deceived her credulity with this vain hope.

But Raymond, foreseeing that without the favour and counsel of the lord patriarch he could not attain what he desired, sought, through interpreters familiar to both parties, an opportunity to secure the patriarch’s support and gain his fuller goodwill. Accordingly, Lord Raymond was required to pledge, by a bodily oath, fidelity to the lord patriarch; in return, he was to receive without difficulty the girl as his wife and the principality in complete peace. It was also inserted among the terms that, if Lord Raymond’s brother Henry should come into the regions of Antioch, the lord patriarch would faithfully endeavour to arrange for Henry to have as wife the mother of the girl, Lord Bohemond’s widow, together with the two maritime cities and their territories.

Thus, after the agreements had been made and confirmed by oath, [Col. 0600B] he was admitted into the city, while the mother was still expecting that all the preparations for the marriage would be made for her. He was immediately led to the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles, and, with the lord patriarch giving her in marriage and all the magnates requesting it, he took Lady Constance, still under marriageable age, as his wife.

When the princess heard that she had been deceived, she suddenly left Antioch and withdrew into her own territory, thereafter pursuing the prince with implacable hatred. From that day, the lord patriarch, raised from arrogance to greater arrogance, hoping that he had secured very firm foundations in the lord prince, showed himself more arrogant than usual, presumed too much upon the prince, and was utterly deceived.
