For the prince, regarding it as a great disgrace that the patriarch had extorted fidelity from him, and unmindful of the benefit received, began to persecute him as an enemy; lavish with his oath, he joined the patriarch’s adversaries.

## Chapter XXI. A description of who Raymond was, what manner of man, and from what ancestry he came.

This same Lord Raymond was distinguished by the ancient nobility of an excellent lineage; exceptionally eminent in the outstanding height of his body and in all its most pleasing proportions; a young man whose cheeks were scarcely covered by their first down; handsome in appearance beyond the kings and princes of the world; commendable in speech and affability; displaying in all his bearing the graceful elegance of an outstanding prince. [Col. 0600D] In the use of arms and experience in warfare, he was to be preferred to all who had preceded or followed him. Although himself unlettered, he was a patron of learned men; assiduous in divine worship and an eager hearer of ecclesiastical offices, especially on feast days; after taking a wife, a careful guardian and preserver of marital fidelity; sober in food and drink; exceedingly generous and liberal. Yet he was not very provident, being excessively devoted to dice and ruinous games of chance.

Moreover, among his other defects, he was rash in spirit, impetuous in action, knew no moderation in anger, lacked judgment, and was not very fortunate. In the fidelity which he had promised the lord patriarch, he forgot his oath and was prodigal of the pledged faith.

## Chapter XXII. To restrain the insolence of the Ascalonites, the king builds a castle called Gybelin, also named Beersheba.

[Col. 0601A]

The Ascalonites, more insolent than usual in those days and made bolder by their successes, ranged through the whole country with excessive freedom. That city was subject to the most powerful ruler of Egypt. Fearing that, if it were subdued, the Christian army would break into Egypt and disturb his peace, he made every effort, at infinite expense, to retain it as a wall between himself and our land. Fearing also that the strength of his people might fail under continual toil and the unceasing dangers of war, every three months he diligently sent new peoples and fresh legions to reinforce the citizens, with necessary provisions and an abundance of arms. [Col. 0601B]

Those who newly arrived, wishing to test the strength of their military service and provide sure proofs of their courage, often undertook raids and expeditions for the sake of experience, usually against the wishes of the veterans. Seeing that their presumption did not cease, that their forces were continuously renewed, and that, as though after the manner of the Hydra, citizens multiplied still more and without ceasing as others died, our people, after many deliberations, judged it best to build fortifications all around against this most monstrous Hydra—made richer by the loss of its heads and, though so often crushed, rising again grievously to our peril. From these, troops could more easily be assembled; the attacks of the roaming enemy could more conveniently be restrained from nearby; and the city could be more frequently assailed.

A suitable site having therefore been chosen, at the foot of the hills where the plain begins, in the continuous tract lying between the mountains and the aforesaid city, in that part of Judaea which fell by lot to the tribe of Simeon in the line of distribution, they prepared to rebuild an ancient ruined city named Beersheba. Summoning all the people of the kingdom, together with Lord William the patriarch and the magnates, they undertook the planned work and, under favourable auspices, completed what had been begun more successfully through the Lord’s aid: a stronghold defended by an impregnable wall, outer works, and ditch, and most strongly fortified with towers, twelve miles distant from the aforesaid Ascalon. [Col. 0601D]

In the time of the children of Israel this place was the southern boundary of the Promised Land, just as Dan—today called Paneas or Caesarea Philippi—was its northern boundary; this is often found in the Old Testament: “from Dan to Beersheba” (Judges 20:1; 2 Kings 3:10). Here Abraham, as also in many other places, is said to have dug a well, to which, because of the abundance of its waters, he gave the name Abundance.

Josephus also mentions these matters in the book of the *Antiquities*, saying: “Accordingly Abimelech both assigned him land and money, and they agreed to deal with one another without deceit, making a treaty at a certain well which they call Bersabee, a name that may mean ‘Well of the Treaty’; and so it is called to this day by the people of that province.” [Col. 0602A] It is also called “the seventh well”; in Arabic, Bethgebrim, which means “house of Gabriel.”

When the stronghold was completed in every respect, it was, by common counsel, entrusted to the brothers of the Hospital at Jerusalem. They have guarded the deposit with due diligence down to the present, and the attacks of the enemy in that quarter became weaker.

## Chapter XXIII. The Count of Tripoli is killed near Mount Pilgrim through the treachery of some of his own men; his son Raymond succeeds him and avenges his father’s death.

Not long after this, Lord Pons, Count of Tripoli, when Bezeuge, commander of the Damascene forces, had entered the territory of Tripoli, met the enemy bravely with all his forces beneath the castle called Mount Pilgrim. [Col. 0602B] His ranks having been broken and turned to flight, he was captured; and, betrayed by Syrians dwelling on the ridges of Lebanon above that city, he was killed. His son Raymond was left as heir and successor in the same county.

There also Lord Gerald, bishop of that city, was captured. But, after being detained among the enemy for some time without being recognized, he was restored to his former liberty in exchange for one captive held in chains by our people. In that battle fell a great multitude of the nobles of the aforesaid city and of men of middling rank.

After his father’s death, Raymond assembled reinforcements from the remnants of the cavalry and gathered a strong force of infantry. Suddenly ascending Lebanon with great power, [Col. 0602C] he brought to Tripoli in chains, together with their wives and children, all those bloodstained men who had induced the aforesaid powerful man to enter the territory of Tripoli by their persuasions, and whom he could discover to be guilty of his father’s death and of the public slaughter. There, before the people, in vengeance for the blood of those who had fallen in battle, he inflicted various punishments upon them and compelled them to suffer the harshest modes of death—yet modes deserved because of the enormity of their crime. Such were the first proofs of valour given by the aforesaid young count, winning for himself the affection and favour of all.

## Chapter XXIV. The emperor John of Constantinople, hurrying toward Antioch, occupies all Cilicia.

[Col. 0602D]

Meanwhile it was reported and widely spread by the accounts of many that Lord John, emperor of Constantinople, son of Lord Alexius, having summoned peoples, tribes, and languages from every part of his empire, and gathered multitudes of chariots and four-horse carriages and unheard-of forces of cavalry, was hastening to descend into Syria. Nor was this report without foundation.

For as soon as he learned with certainty that the citizens, after Raymond had been summoned, had surrendered Antioch to him and given him Lord Bohemond’s daughter as his wife, he had resolved to come to Antioch. He was greatly angered that they had presumed, without his knowledge and command, either to give his lord’s daughter in marriage [Col. 0603A] or, without consulting him, to place the city under another’s authority. Claiming the city with all the adjacent provinces as subject to his jurisdiction, he strove to assert it as his own. He maintained that those great princes—men of valour, of immortal memory, and sent by the Lord—who had come on the first expedition, too numerous to name individually, had made an agreement with his father and predecessor in the empire, Lord Alexius, through the exchange of many gifts and services: whatever cities or castles they might acquire by any chance in the whole course of that expedition, they would subject to his empire without contradiction, and would faithfully preserve them, as far as their power and ability allowed, until he himself should arrive with his forces. [Col. 0603B] He alleged that this was recorded in historical accounts and confirmed by the bodily oaths of the aforesaid princes.

It is certain that the aforesaid princes made agreements with the emperor, and that he, in return, bound himself to the princes by certain conditions; but he had certainly first failed to fulfil those conditions. Therefore those who had been parties to them firmly maintained that they were not bound to him as a violator of agreements; and they likewise excused those who had already died, saying that he had first acted contrary to his agreements, as a changeable and unreliable man who had dealt deceitfully with them. Hence they maintained that they were justly released by the law of agreements: for it is unjust to keep faith with one who strives to act contrary to agreements.

Having spent a full year, through agents sent throughout the empire, preparing for the journey with equipment worthy of imperial magnificence—chariots and horses, treasures beyond number, weight, and measure, and infinite forces—he crossed the Hellespont by ship, which in common speech is called the Arm of Saint George, and directed his march toward Antioch with a great multitude. Passing through the intervening provinces, he came to Cilicia. There he delayed, besieged Tarsus, the distinguished metropolis of First Cilicia, and seized it by force; expelling the loyal men of the lord prince of Antioch, to whose loyalty he had entrusted the aforesaid city, and installing his own men. [Col. 0603C]

He did not delay to do the same with Adana, Mamistra, Anavarza, the most celebrated metropolis of Second Cilicia, and all the cities, fortresses, and towns whatsoever of the same province. Thus he claimed for his own empire, contrary to right and justice, all Cilicia, which for forty years had been possessed without challenge by the prince of Antioch. Tarsus had been restored to Christian liberty through the hand of Lord Baldwin, brother of the lord duke; Mamistra, together with all the remaining region, through the hand of the most illustrious Lord Tancred, before Antioch had come under our power. Then, proceeding with all his armies in the might of his forces, he hurried toward Antioch. On arriving, he immediately surrounded it with a hostile siege. Having placed engines and huge siege machines at suitable stations around it, [Col. 0604A] he began to press the city more severely.

## Chapter XXV. Sanguin besieges the castle called Montferrand; the king, with the Count of Tripoli, seeks to raise the siege, but they fail and are defeated. The count is captured, and the king withdraws into the castle.

While these things were happening around Antioch, Sanguin, a most wicked man and most savage persecutor of the Christian name, seeing that the Count of Tripoli had shortly before fallen with many of his men and that the entire region was deprived of military assistance, powerfully besieged a fortress situated on a mountain in the territory of Tripoli, above the city of Rafanea, called Montferrand, of which we have also spoken above. [Col. 0604B] He fiercely attacked the townsmen enclosed within, pressed them without ceasing, and harassed them with great persistence.

Hearing this, Raymond, Count of Tripoli, a young man, son of the late Pons and nephew of the lord king through the king’s sister, dispatched messengers with all speed and anxiously begged the lord king, with earnest prayers, not to delay bringing aid in so great a necessity and in circumstances almost desperate, but to hasten to their relief.

The lord king, therefore, in fatherly fashion maintaining due concern for all the necessities of the Christian people, suddenly summoned all the princes of the kingdom and gathered military aid, both cavalry and infantry. He flew swiftly to their assistance and unexpectedly appeared in the territory of Tripoli. There also came messengers of the lord prince of Antioch, bearing grievous news. In writing and by word of mouth they declared—truthfully—that the emperor had besieged Antioch, [Col. 0604C] urging and repeatedly begging him to go there with all his forces and promptly assist his brethren placed in grave distress.

After deliberating what ought to be done in so doubtful a situation, all agreed that aid should first be supplied to the Christians shut up in the nearby castle, since that seemed a comparatively easy matter; then all would proceed together to aid the Antiochenes. The forces of the lord king and count were therefore joined, and, their strength combined, they attempted to advance against the enemy, deprived of divine favour.

When they began to approach the appointed place, Sanguin, hearing of our approach, raised the siege, drew up his ranks, and came out to meet them. Our men likewise arranged their battle lines and, deploying them according to military discipline, advanced with no less determination toward the town to bring assistance to the besieged and to fill the fortress, empty of supplies, with provisions brought in.

But the guides of the route, advancing ahead of our army, whether through error or malice is uncertain, abandoned the easier, level road on the left and, following the steep places of the mountain, led our battle lines through pathless and excessively narrow ground, where there was no suitable place for a martial engagement—neither fit for resistance nor favourable for attack. [Col. 0604D]

When Sanguin saw this, being a most shrewd man and highly experienced in warfare, and seeing that fortune favoured him, he burned with courage. Calling his men together, first among the thousands of his own men, encouraging them by speech and urging them by example, he charged into the midst of our ranks. Fighting bravely, he urged them to slaughter our men and overthrew our foremost battle lines after turning them to flight.

When the leaders of our army saw that the first lines had failed, that there was no hope of resistance, and that, hemmed in within a narrow place, they had no means of aiding the distressed, they advised the lord king to consult for his safety and withdraw into the nearby fortress. Seeing this to be the more expedient course at the time, the lord king entered the fortress with a few men, while almost all the infantry were either delivered to death [Col. 0605B] or thrown into chains.

There the young Count of Tripoli, of excellent promise, was captured, and several of the knightly order were taken with him. But those who followed the lord king entered the fortress and preserved their lives and safety in whatever way they could. On that day they lost all their baggage, horses, and beasts assigned for carrying burdens, with which they had intended to provision the aforesaid town. For those who fled and entered the castle came empty-handed, bringing no food but only the arms with which they were equipped.

Among others, that day there fell the magnificent man Geoffrey Charpalu, distinguished in nobility and skill in arms, brother of Lord Joscelin the Elder, Count of Edessa. [Col. 0605C] The death of so valiant a man caused many greater sorrow, and his grievous fall shook the entire army.

## Chapter XXVI. Sanguin besieges the castle again; the besieged summon their neighbours from every side for assistance.

Meanwhile, seeing that our people had brought absolutely no provisions into the castle, that he possessed all their supplies, had worn down all the forces of the kingdom, held the count in chains, and had the king shut up with the great men of the kingdom in a half-ruined, provisionless castle, Sanguin again undertook to shut the fortress in by siege. He hoped that none could provide aid to the besieged and did not doubt that he could overcome the stronghold within a few days. [Col. 0605D]

Accordingly, calling his divisions together, they returned laden with the spoils of our people, scorning a still greater booty because of the abundance of what they had already gathered. With his legions arrayed in a circle, he enclosed the castle in an extremely severe siege.

Within, together with the lord king, had withdrawn several of the magnates of the kingdom: William of Bures, constable; Rainer Brus, a distinguished knight; Guy of Brisebarre; Baldwin of Ramla; Humphrey of Toron, a novice and very young man; and many others. With them the king took counsel and deliberated what ought to be done in so great, confined, and pressing a necessity. They jointly resolved to summon the prince of Antioch and Joscelin the Younger, Count of Edessa, to their aid, and to invite the patriarch of Jerusalem with all the peoples of the kingdom; meanwhile they would await their coming by whatever means they could. [Col. 0606A]

At the same time, while these events were taking place around Montferrand, Rainald, surnamed the Bishop, nephew of Lord Roger, bishop of Lydda, *primicerius* of the knighthood of Saint George, a knight valiant in arms and distinguished in military deeds, while pursuing the Ascalonites as usual but incautiously, happened to fall into the ambushes laid by the enemy and was captured.

Meanwhile the messengers did not rest, but hurried with all speed. One pressed the lord prince with fitting urgency, informed him of the necessities of the king and his men, reproved delay, and urged him more insistently to hasten. Another continually stirred the lord Count of Edessa with exhortations. A third hurried swiftly to Jerusalem and roused the whole people.

But the prince of Antioch, uncertain what to do, hesitated for a while. With the emperor at his gates, he feared for the city should he attempt to depart; yet he considered it exceedingly harsh and inhuman not to assist the lord king in so great a necessity. At last, sympathizing with the troubles and distresses of the lord king and Christian people, commending his city to the Lord, he judged it better to suffer whatever adversities might come with his brethren than, while they were thus failing, to abound in prosperity and enjoy any tranquillity. He therefore summoned the magnates and leading men of the people; disclosing to all his own conviction, he invited all to assist the king, and readily persuaded them. [Col. 0606C] For all willingly concurred in the same desires most pleasing to God; and, immediately offering themselves ready, they left the city, abandoning the emperor around it, and proceeded unanimously to the lord king’s aid.

The Count of Edessa likewise armed himself with all his forces in the same resolve and hastened with remarkable speed toward the same undertaking. Lord William, patriarch of Jerusalem, also collected all the forces he could find in the kingdom, took with him the venerable wood of the Lord’s Cross, hurried there without delay, and, gathering assistance from every side, hastened to their relief.

## Chapter XXVII. Bezeuge, governor of Damascus, burns and devastates Neapolis.

[Col. 0606D] While these things were occurring around the lord king, Bezeuge, governor of the kingdom of Damascus and commander of its army, of whom we have also spoken above, heard that the kingdom was empty of its customary strength, that the king was shut in by siege at the farthest borders of the realm, and that the princes and the whole people, concerned for his deliverance, were hastening unanimously to those regions. Thinking that he had found a favourable opportunity for harm, he entered the kingdom with a large force and unexpectedly attacked the city of Neapolis, which was undefended, lacking a wall, outer works, and even a ditch.

Suddenly breaking in like a thief in the night, he raged against the unsuspecting citizens with swords and with all his fury, sparing neither age nor sex. At last, belatedly warned, those who remained fled with their wives and children, with great difficulty, into the fortress in the middle of the city, and barely escaped slaughter and fire. He, meanwhile, with no one to hinder him, roamed freely throughout the whole city, consigned everything to flames, plundered the booty, spoils, and every desirable thing in the city, and withdrew unharmed. [Col. 0607A]

## Chapter XXVIII. Aid for the king is hastened; but in the meantime still greater hardships are inflicted on the besieged.

Meanwhile Sanguin pressed the besieged with continual hardships, battered the walls with engines, and hurled millstones and huge rocks from throwing machines into the middle of the fortress, demolishing houses within. [Col. 0607B] This caused no little terror among those enclosed. The great stones hurled violently against them, together with the various kinds of missiles shot at them, overwhelmed them with such straits that no safe place could now be found inside the walls in which to shelter the wounded and weak.

Everywhere was danger, everywhere peril, and the dreadful image of death thrust itself before their eyes. Nor did their minds lack fear of sudden destruction and the presence of disastrous calamities. To this the most savage man added repeated assaults: assigning battle divisions in rotation, he renewed his forces in a certain order of succession and, when the first troops were exhausted, substituted fresh ones, so that the business of battle seemed continuous rather than renewed.

But our men, not possessing forces sufficient to introduce such alternation for their recovery, themselves bore the first and the last assaults amid unceasing toil. Moreover, their number was diminished each day, some falling through the severity of wounds, others through diverse illnesses; yet all suffered one and the same deficiency and an equal inability to endure their uninterrupted distress. For they spent the nights sleepless, assigned to watches; and by day, exhausted by continual encounters, the enemy allowed them no respite by which they might recover their spent bodies. [Col. 0607C]

To the accumulation of their evils was added that they had brought no food with them when they entered, nor had any remnant of provisions remained in the castle from the former siege. What they had determined to bring in had come wholly intact into the enemy’s hands. Thus, immediately after entering, they had eaten their horses, having nothing else; when these failed, every means of sustenance entirely failed.

The bodies even of the strong and robust wasted away through fasting, and the leanness brought on by hunger robbed even valiant men of their strength. Moreover, so great was the multitude enclosed that the food supply would not have sufficed even to give each person a small amount. Indeed, the quarters throughout the fortress were so filled with the multitude of the besieged that lanes and streets seemed strewn with rushes because of the crowds lying there. Arrows discharged carelessly also inflicted mortal wounds by chance, without any intention on the part of the shooter. [Col. 0607D]

Sanguin knew all these things fully; and he drove his men on to press the siege more boldly because he did not doubt that our people could endure them no longer. In addition, enemy companies were stationed so thickly around the town and guarded every approach with such diligence that no one could attempt to come to us, nor could anyone of our people leave, except as though undertaking a hopeless thing.

The distress of the besieged increased every day; with provisions utterly exhausted, no hope remained. By the facts themselves they were taught how violent is the dominion of hunger, and how truly it has been said: “Hunger alone captures cities” (*Lucan*, III.56).

Yet one thing still sustained the people, though perishing by every means: they awaited the assistance of the prince, the Count of Edessa, and the Jerusalemites. And, because to a desiring mind nothing comes quickly enough, every delay appeared more alarming; through postponement their desire increased, [Col. 0608B] and an hour was counted as a year.

## Chapter XXIX. Assistance arrives; but meanwhile the king inclines toward surrender and, after agreements are concluded, returns safely to his own land.

Meanwhile, while these events were thus taking place during the siege, Prince Raymond was already present with his legions, and the Count of Edessa, leading great battle lines, was not far away. The army of Jerusalem, too, following unanimously the saving wood of the Cross, was hastening onward by a forced march.

When Sanguin learned this through trustworthy messengers, he feared the arrival of such great princes. He especially dreaded that the emperor, whom he knew to be near Antioch, hearing of the sufferings of the besieged and sympathizing with them, might angrily fall upon him with his irresistible forces. Therefore, before this report could reach the besieged, he first addressed the lord king and his princes concerning peace through envoys. He said that the castle, already half-secure, could not stand against him for long; that the people, hungry and suffering famine, had lost their strength and courage to resist; and that, on the other hand, his own army abounded in necessities. Nevertheless, out of regard for the lord king, who was a great and eminent prince among the Christian people, he said that he would restore all the captives whom he had lately taken, both the count and the others, and grant the lord king and all his men free and peaceful departure and return to their own land, if they were willing to restore the castle to him wholly evacuated. [Col. 0608D]

Our people, unaware that aid was so near and besides worn down by hunger, watchfulness, toil, anguish, and mortal wounds, rendered incapable of fighting and exhausted in strength, received the proposal with the utmost eagerness. They wondered how such humanity could have proceeded from a man so cruel, but whatever its motive, they gratefully accepted the offered terms.

The agreements on both sides having been brought into a form acceptable to each, the Count of Tripoli was restored, along with a great multitude of captives. At once the lord king departed with his men. Treated quite humanely by the enemy, he surrendered the fortress to the Turks and, though ashamed, nevertheless freed from the excessive entanglement of dangers, joyfully descended from the mountains into the plain adjacent to Arqa. [Col. 0609A] There, hearing of the arrival of the lord prince and the lord count, he devoutly went to meet them. He approved their concern and brotherly affection, though he complained that their aid had come late. Offering abundant thanks because they had shown such concern for his cause and had supplied the desired aid insofar as lay in their power, and refreshed by mutual conversation, they separated and returned to their own lands.

## Chapter XXX. The prince, returning to Antioch, finds the city besieged; he resists the emperor with all his strength, but is at last reconciled with him through the intervention of certain persons.

The lord prince, whose affairs seemed to be in a strait [Col. 0609B], because he had left before his own city the most powerful ruler on earth, plotting hostile measures, returned to Antioch with all speed. Entering through the upper gate, which is adjacent to the city garrison and the citadel, he found the emperor still persisting in the same purpose. For several days engagements took place there; certain Antiochenes repeatedly made incursions, sometimes secretly and more often openly, into the emperor’s army, frequently inflicting enormous losses upon them, and dealt with them as enemies, without regard for their common profession of faith.

The emperor in turn, hurling immense rocks of enormous weight with great engines and missile-machines, battered the walls and towers from the Bridge Gate, striving to weaken and break through the city’s barriers [Col. 0609C]. Having deployed his legions in a circle, he kept the citizens at a distance from defending the wall by arrows, every kind of projectile, and a formidable body of slingers; and he tried to secure access and opportunity for undermining the walls. With matters thus situated, the wiser men of both armies feared that, unless prompt counsel remedied the situation, matters would reach a point at which, as dangers arose, suitable remedies could not easily be applied.

Accordingly, God-fearing men intervened as arbiters between the parties, bearing the sheaves of peace. Entering the emperor’s camp, they laboured to mitigate his indignation by peaceful words and every show of humility [Col. 0610A]. Then, returning to the lord prince, they carefully and prudently sought, as necessity required, to find a way to peace. At length it seemed good to the arbiters and directors of the sought alliance that the lord prince should approach the imperial magnificence and, in the presence of the illustrious and renowned men of the imperial court, together with the whole assembly of his nobles, render him liege homage with due solemnity. He was also to swear, by a corporal oath, that he would not deny the lord emperor, whether angry or reconciled, free and peaceful entry into Antioch when he wished to enter, nor deny entry to his garrison.

And if the lord emperor restored to the prince Aleppo, Caesarea, Hama, and Emesa, peaceful and undisturbed, as the agreement stipulated, then, content with these cities and others adjoining them, he should restore Antioch without difficulty to the lord emperor, to possess by right of ownership [Col. 0610B]. In recompense for the fidelity rendered, the lord emperor should grant the prince that, if by God’s aid it should happen that he acquired Aleppo, Caesarea, and the entire surrounding territory, the whole should accrue to the prince without molestation or diminution, to be possessed peacefully by him and his heirs in perpetuity, yet as a benefice—what is commonly called a fief.

Accordingly, as agreed, the lord prince went out with all his noble following to the imperial camp. There, received with due honour by the lord emperor, and after the agreements mutually made had been rehearsed to the satisfaction of both sides, he rendered his homage to the lord emperor by hand [Col. 0610C]. At once the lord emperor also granted him investiture of the aforesaid cities with all their appurtenances, firmly promising that in the summer next to come, with God’s help, he would capture them and hand them over in person. Thus, the treaty having been completed and peace more fully restored, the imperial banner was placed above the prince’s chief citadel-garrison; laden with great gifts, the prince returned with his men into the city. Because of the approaching severity of winter, the lord emperor returned with all his forces to Cilicia and took himself to the coastal region around Tarsus for winter quarters.

## Here begins the Fifteenth Book

[Col. 0609]

## Chapter I. The emperor besieges Caesarea; the prince and the count of Edessa are placed in his service.

[Col. 0609D]

When the winter months in the regions of Cilicia had passed, spring had now returned and brought a welcome mildness to the armies. A proclamation was issued, and by public imperial edict the primicerii, centurions, and commanders of fifty of the legions were ordered to equip their cohorts again, repair their military equipment, and arm the whole people [Col. 0610D]. Embassies having first been sent, the lord prince, the lord count of Edessa, and the other leading men of those regions were invited to proceed with the lord emperor to war.

When these had assembled from every quarter, about the Kalends of April, amid the shrill blast of trumpets and the sounding of drums, the emperor ordered the whole army to march toward Caesarea, in order to fulfil the agreements previously made between himself and the prince. Entering enemy territory, it encamped before the aforesaid city after a few days [Col. 0611A]. On hearing this, the prince and count summoned their forces from throughout the region and followed the emperor with all speed; suddenly they arrived with their men before the above-named city, equally inflamed with zeal.

The aforesaid city is situated, rather like Antioch, between a mountain and the river which flows past Antioch. Its greater part lies on level ground extending to the river; another part lies on the mountain slope; while its fortress, rising on the mountain summit, is established beyond the power of human forces to capture. Thus the city, together with its adjacent suburb, is enclosed by walls descending on both left and right to the river. Having crossed the river and arranged their forces in a circle, they surrounded the city with a siege from that side on which, with the suburb lying before it, it seemed more suitable for attack [Col. 0611B].

There, after engines had been suitably provided, they continually shook the towers, walls, and the citizens’ dwellings inside the walls by the heavy discharge of millstones; by repeated blows and the recurring impact of the hurled rocks, they utterly brought down, not without great slaughter among the inhabitants, the defensive structures of the buildings in which their chief hope of defence lay. The lord emperor, a man of great spirit, pressed forward his undertaking with ardent zeal. By offering prizes, he inflamed the minds of young men eager for glory toward contests and martial encounters. Clad in a cuirass, girded with a sword, and his head covered by a golden helmet, he moved among the ranks, now exhorting one group and now another with fitting words [Col. 0611C]; now, by his own example, he incited them as though he were one of the common soldiers, pressing on bravely in order to make the others more eager to press on.

Thus this man, distinguished by outstanding courage, ran about without interruption, enduring the heat of battle from the first hour of the day until the last. He allowed himself no rest even for taking food. Rather, he either urged those serving the engines to shoot more frequently and more accurately, or encouraged those labouring in the fighting, restoring their strength by successive reliefs, replacing the exhausted with fresh men and assigning vigorous men with unimpaired effort.

But the prince and the count, both, it is said, young men and excessively drawn to the frivolous pursuits of their age [Col. 0611D], were continually playing dice, to no small injury of their household resources, while the others laboured in battle and military affairs. Being themselves more slack in their concern for war, by their example they also recalled the others from the fervour of pressing action. Hearing this and troubled exceedingly by their harmful conduct, the emperor tried once and again to recall them privately by familiar and confidential admonition, setting before them his own example: although he was the most powerful of all earthly kings and princes, he spared neither bodily labour nor vast expense.

At length, after the army had persevered for several days in such encounters and continual engagements, the emperor was indignant that so small a city could resist his incomparable forces for so long. Wearied, censuring delay and accusing his men’s idleness, he encouraged them to stronger assaults and ordered them to press on more fiercely, redoubling the attacks. While they competed eagerly to break into the city, they violently occupied the aforesaid suburb, which, as we said, lay in the lower part of the city. They spared none of the citizens found there, except perhaps one who, by word, clothing, or any sign whatsoever, indicated that he would adhere to the Christian faith [Col. 0612A]. For that city had, and had had from the beginning, many faithful inhabitants, who were unjustly oppressed beneath the yoke of wretched servitude by unbelieving lords.

## Chapter II. Indignant, he raises the siege before completing the undertaking and returns to Antioch.

[Col. 0612B]

Thus, after one part of the city had been attacked, the frightened citizens, fearing the enemy’s violent incursions against their wives, children, and the inner parts of the city, requested a short truce and obtained what they asked. The lord of that city was a certain nobleman, an Arab by nation, named Machedolus. Secretly sending messengers to the emperor, he humbly begged, with profuse prayers, for the safety of the city and the security of its citizens, promising an unlimited sum of money for this purpose.

For the emperor, angered because the prince and count had behaved so dissolutely and negligently during the expedition—and especially because he seemed to be labouring for their affairs and to fulfil his promise—had conceived the greatest resentment against them. He judged their promised fidelity, like faith dead without works, to be more splendid than substantial and of no account. Firmly, with a few intimates, he had already determined that, in hatred of them and as a punishment for their unfaithfulness, whenever any opportunity offered that might at least seem to carry some appearance of propriety, he would raise the siege and return home [Col. 0612C].

Having therefore accepted money under an agreement for raising the siege, he publicly proclaimed peace to the besieged and ordered the legions to prepare for their return. Breaking camp, the emperor commanded the ranks to march toward Antioch and the entire army to hasten there. On hearing this, the prince and count, led late by repentance, tried to recall the lord emperor from his undertaking; but the emperor persisted in the purpose he had irrevocably conceived and, rejecting their persuasion, hastened his journey.

The count was said to have acted very maliciously in this matter. For secretly—though it later became clear—he was led by hatred against his lord, namely the prince; regarding all the prince’s advancement with suspicion, he, being the more cunning, misled the mind of the less prudent young man. With all his zeal he strove to make the prince incur the emperor’s indignation, so that the prince might not advance through him to greater advantages [Col. 0612D].

## Chapter III. The emperor demands from the prince the city’s citadel-garrison, as though he intended to remain in the region.

Accordingly, the lord emperor arrived at Antioch with his sons, retainers, and a considerable force. Entering the city, while the lord prince and lord count performed the office of strator—leading or attending his horse—and while the lord patriarch, with all the clergy and people, went in customary ordered procession, he was solemnly conducted first to the cathedral church and then to the prince’s palace, amid psalms, hymns, songs, the harmony of musical instruments, applause, and the rejoicing of the people [Col. 0613A].

There, for several days, he made free use, as a lord in his own house, of baths and other bodily recreations. He also exercised imperial generosity lavishly and almost prodigally toward the lord prince and count, their magnates, and citizens without distinction. Then he summoned before him the prince and count together with all the leading men of the province. When they stood in his presence, he addressed the prince:

“You know, my most beloved son Raymond, how, for your sake, and in accordance with the agreements previously concluded through the mediation of prudent men between our God-beloved empire and your fidelity, I have long remained in this region, in order to enlarge your principality and extend your possessions over the enemies of our faith [Col. 0613B]. And now that opportunity has arisen, it is time for me to fulfil my promises and subject the entire surrounding region to your authority, as the tenor of the agreements more clearly teaches.

“But you know well, and these men who stand with you in our presence know, that what we are bound to render you is not a work of short duration. Your affairs seem to require a longer stay and demand greater expenditure. Therefore, as you are bound by agreement, you must assign the citadel-garrison of this city to our custody, so that our treasures may be stored there more safely. You must also make the city accessible to our armies, so that they may have completely free permission to enter and depart without impediment [Col. 0613C]. For military engines cannot be prepared so conveniently at Tarsus, Anavarza, or other Cilician cities for bringing pressure and siege against Aleppo. This city offers another and much better opportunity for those purposes than any other could provide.

“Fulfil, therefore, what was promised; and according to the tenor of the fidelity you have rendered, carry out what is yours to do. It shall be the part of our eminence to grant generously and in overflowing measure what we are bound to render you.”

At these words the prince and his men, alarmed by the severity of the speech, long hesitated over what they should answer and anxiously considered among themselves what reply they should make. It seemed exceedingly hard and grievous that a city acquired by such danger to our people and restored to the Christian faith at the cost of so much bloodshed among fortunate princes—a city which had always been head and ruler of so many provinces—should fall into the hands of the effeminate Greek people. Without it, the remaining portions of the region did not seem capable of standing for us. Yet again, no one doubted that this was included in the prince’s agreements; moreover, he had brought in so many of the emperor’s men that it did not seem easy for him to resist one intent upon using force [Col. 0614A].

Thus matters stood in a strait, when the count of Edessa answered for them all, beginning thus:

“Lord, the speech delivered by your imperial sublimity breathes divine eloquence and is worthy of every acceptance. For we see that its entire tenor wholly concerns our advancement. Yet a new matter requires new counsel, and its execution does not rest with the lord prince alone. He must deliberate more fully on this with the counsel of his own men—namely myself and his other faithful men—so that your word and request may more easily attain their due effect, lest an outbreak of the populace should arise and impede the future execution of your requests.”

The count’s answer pleased the lord emperor. Granting a short truce so that the stated deliberation might take place, the count returned home, while the prince remained in the palace and, as was said, did not have power even over himself [Col. 0614B].

## Chapter IV. A tumult is stirred up in the city; the emperor is afraid and withdraws his demand; the disturbance is quieted when he leaves the city.

When the count had returned home, he secretly sent messengers to incite the whole people to arms by revealing the emperor’s demand. A tumult then arose throughout the city with unrestrained noise; crowds gathering from every direction raised an immense outcry. Hearing this, the count quickly mounted a horse and hastened to the palace. As though fleeing the assault of the populace, he threw himself down half-dead at the emperor’s feet [Col. 0614C].

Startled by the count’s sudden entrance, the emperor carefully asked why he had rushed so disorderly into the imperial presence, contrary to the custom and discipline of the sacred palace. He answered that necessity knows no law, and that, compelled by pursuit from the enraged people in order to avoid the danger of death, he had come contrary to the rules of decorum. When the emperor repeatedly asked him to disclose the matter more fully, he replied that he had withdrawn to his lodging to take some rest and had intended to attend to that purpose when, suddenly, the entire city population, as though one man, stood at his door with swords and such weapons as rage supplied [Col. 0614D]. They began to cry out that he was a man of blood, a traitor to his country, and a murderer of the people, who wished to sell the city to the emperor for money received from him; that they wanted the count of Edessa delivered up to them; and that he himself had scarcely escaped after his house was broken into, amid a thousand dangers.

Meanwhile a great cry arose through the city, an unrestrained disturbance, and a widely spreading rumour rang in everyone’s ears: the city had been sold to the Greeks; the garrison had already been handed over to them; the citizens would have to leave their ancestral homes and patrimonial lands and migrate. Enraged by these reports, the citizens threw from their horses any members of the emperor’s household whom they found, stripped them by force, beat them, and cut down with swords those who tried to resist. With drawn swords, they pursued them as far as the prince’s palace while they fled insults and death [Col. 0615A].

Moved by this uproar of the citizens and the loud cries of his own men, the emperor ordered the prince and magnates to be summoned. Temporarily moderating his anger, and fearing that something harsher might arise against him, he referred to the speech he had made rather freely before men that same day:

“I remember that today I held a discussion with you on one matter, from which this disturbance among the people is perhaps said to have arisen. But now let the whole body alike of fathers and common people know that, since what I said seems so hard and difficult to you, I withdraw my decision and reconsider what I proposed. Keep for yourselves both the whole city and the citadel-garrison. It is enough for my empire to maintain the existing order of affairs. I know that you are truly my faithful men and that no day can ever shake you from the fidelity you have promised and rendered [Col. 0615B]. Go out, therefore, and restrain the raging people. And if my remaining in the city is at all suspicious to them, so that they may not be disturbed on this account, tomorrow, with God’s help, we shall depart.”

At these words all praised the emperor’s purpose and extolled to the stars his provident mind, the profundity of his counsel, and the judgment of his deliberating heart. The prince and count, with the other leading nobles, went out and tried to calm the tumult by voice, hand, nods, and signs. At length silence was proclaimed; the populace was brought by friendly words to some degree of calm; and they were earnestly asked to go home, lay down their arms, and live peaceably. This was done [Col. 0615C]. On the following day the lord emperor left with his sons, kinsmen, and retainers, and ordered camp to be pitched outside the city.

## Chapter V. Envoys are sent to mitigate the emperor’s indignation and succeed; the emperor returns home.

Those of sounder judgment knew that, although the lord emperor had acted like a prudent man in concealing it, he had conceived resentment against the prince and the leading nobles, believing that the popular tumult and public disturbance had been stirred up at their instigation and by their secret activity. Therefore, to restore peace, they sent to the imperial excellence suitable envoys, men of practised judgment [Col. 0615D], to labour to have the lord prince and the magnates of the region excused before the lord emperor and to assert that they were altogether innocent of the tumult that had arisen among the people.

Admitted to the emperor’s audience chamber, the envoys spoke on the task entrusted to them, seeking to plead and establish the prince’s innocence as follows:

“Your August Majesty and imperial eminence know much better than we do that in any association, much less in cities and great gatherings of people, not all shine with equal prudence or are endowed with equal discipline. Citizens differ in their dispositions, and therefore follow different morals and different pursuits, so that, in the words of a wise man, this saying is true:

> ‘Three dinner-guests seem to me nearly to disagree.’

[Col. 0616A]

“And likewise:

> ‘As many people, so many opinions.’

“But amid this great diversity of differing characters, it belongs to a prudent man to distinguish the quality of men’s deserts and assign rewards appropriate to their merits. By this reasoning, the rash and undiscriminating heat of the common people ought not to bring harm upon those better disposed. For it commonly happens among men that the confused populace, not knowing moderation, incautiously raises quarrels and tumults; and it is certain that in all well-ordered cities, an ancient custom, approved by long use, has prevailed: the moderation of the leading men restrains popular impulses and checks audacity ignorant of bounds. Otherwise the condition of the mob would be far better than that of the nobles, and the confusion of an imprudent crowd better than the experience of discerning men, unless the sins of an ill-advised populace may be imputed to its betters.

“The undiscriminating populace committed this offence without the knowledge of the lord prince and without the knowledge of those at whose direction greater affairs are conducted [Col. 0616B]. Let it therefore suffer the penalties it has deserved, while the lord prince and the leading men are preserved unharmed. Finally, as proof of his innocence, he is ready to abide by the terms of the agreements and, if permitted, to transfer the city with its garrison into the hands of the empire.”

Persuaded by these and similar arguments, the emperor withdrew, in a more humane judgment, the excessive movement of indignation that he had conceived from suspicion alone. He summoned the lord prince, the count, and the nobles and ordered them to enter his presence familiarly. Clearing away every cloud of intervening resentment, he graciously received and offered them the greeting of mutual salutation [Col. 0616C].

At length he informed them that he had most urgent reasons compelling him to return home. Taking leave, and firmly promising that he would return again, with God’s help, in strong force to fulfil the agreements, he directed all his armies into Cilicia. When his affairs in Cilicia and Syria had been completed and the columns prepared for the journey, he returned home.

## Chapter VI. The king of Jerusalem besieges and violently captures a fortress beyond the Jordan. Our men are miserably defeated near Tekoa.

Meanwhile, while these events were occurring around Antioch, in the following summer, after no great interval, the distinguished and great lord Theoderic, count of Flanders, renowned among western princes and son-in-law of the lord king, came to Jerusalem for prayer and a devout pilgrimage, with an honourable company of noblemen [Col. 0616D]. The king and all the people received his arrival with great joy. Confident in the notable and strong force he had brought with him, they unanimously resolved, with the counsel of the lord patriarch and the other princes of the kingdom, to besiege a fortress beyond the Jordan, in the territory of the Ammonites near Mount Gilead, which was very harmful to our lands.

This stronghold was a cave situated on the side of a very steep, lofty mountain and had an approach almost inaccessible. Above it hung a most terrible precipice, continuous from the summit of the overhanging promontory down to the lowest part of the valley below [Col. 0617A]. On the other side, between the slope of the overhanging height and that precipice, the approach to the same cave was narrow and formidable. A harmful band of thieves and a troop of robbers from the districts of Moab, Ammon, and Gilead had gathered in it. Having first sent scouts skilled in the terrain and learned through them more fully about the state of our regions, they took opportunities to make frequent incursions into our territory, secretly and for the most part extremely dangerously.

Wishing to meet these evils, our people proposed, as stated, to besiege the cave. The whole population of the kingdom was summoned and military forces assembled; having crossed the Jordan, they came there and, as the unevenness and narrowness of the region permitted, occupied the approaches, pitching camp around it. With troops disposed in a circle, they invested the place with a siege [Col. 0617B]. Observing the rules of war, they turned to every means of causing harm, pressing the besieged by every means available to compel their surrender. The latter, in turn, gathering whatever ingenuity usually comes to men in desperate circumstances, vigilantly armed themselves for their defence.

While nearly the entire Christian army was labouring there in common purpose, certain Turks, seizing an opportunity, saw that the entire region beyond the Jordan had been left without soldiers and lay open to hostile ambushes. Crossing the Jordan, they left the region of Jericho, proceeded on the right along Lake Asphaltitis, also called the Dead Sea, then made for the highlands and burst into that part of the province which had formerly fallen by lot to the tribe of Judah. Reaching the city of the prophets Amos and Habakkuk, called Tekoa, they violently occupied it, finding it empty of inhabitants, and killed the few persons whom they found there [Col. 0617C]. The inhabitants of that place had fled when they learned beforehand of the enemy’s coming; with their wives and children, herds and flocks, they had withdrawn to the nearby cave of Adullam. Finding the aforesaid village empty, the Turks entered the dwellings of those who had fled and carried off what remained.

By chance there was then at Jerusalem, having come from Antioch, a man of pious memory in the Lord: Lord Robert, surnamed the Burgundian, an Aquitanian by nation, noble in birth and character, an outstanding knight and valiant in arms, master of the military order of the Temple. With some of his brothers and the few mounted men of mixed kind who had remained at Jerusalem, while a certain household knight of the lord king, Bernard Vacher, bore the royal banner and the populace followed, he hurried with all speed toward the aforesaid place [Col. 0617D].

Hearing of our approach, the Turks abandoned the place. They had begun to flee from Habehim, the home of the prophet Joel, toward Hebron, the burial-place of the patriarchs, intending from there to descend to the plains toward Ascalon. Our men, knowing that the enemy ranks had turned to flight, did not follow the same tracks as men certain of victory. Instead, with extreme carelessness, they scattered in different directions and foolishly pursued the plunder of the fugitives rather than the destruction of the enemy. When those who had fled realized this, they gathered again in their customary manner, recovered their courage, and tried as best they could to recall their scattered ranks. Falling unexpectedly upon our men, who were wandering about and overconfident, they attacked and cut them down with swords here and there. A battle was nevertheless joined by the few who resisted and gathered together [Col. 0618A].

Meanwhile those who had gone in different directions were alerted by the blast of trumpets, the sound of horns, the neighing of horses, the gleam of flashing weapons, the voices of men encouraging their comrades, and the cloud of dust stirred by horses’ hooves and carried aloft. They hurried to the place of battle. But before they could unite with the bands of those who had held out, the first men failed and were driven into flight; the enemy gained the upper hand over our defeated troops [Col. 0618B].

The enemy pursued our fleeing men in the manner of enemies, through places made exceedingly rough by rocks, wholly impassable and entirely unsuited to flight, with arrows and drawn swords. Some they killed with the sword; others they hurled headlong. Pursuing them from the aforesaid Hebron, which is Kiriath-arba, as far as the borders of Tekoa, they wrought a very great slaughter among the people. Many noble and distinguished men fell that day, among them the outstanding knight Odo of Montfaucon, brother of the military order of the Temple, whose death filled all with sorrow and lamentation. Having won the victory, the enemy rejoiced in the slaughter and spoils of our men and returned to Ascalon [Col. 0618C].

When our men on the expedition learned of the misfortune that had occurred among us, they were indeed greatly dismayed. Yet understanding that this is the law of wars—that now one side and now the other gains the advantage through varying events—they recovered courage, pressed on with their begun work more eagerly than before, and, with God’s help, captured the aforesaid fortress within a few days. They then returned home in glory and triumph.

## Chapter VII. Sanguinus troubles the kingdom of Damascus; the Damascenes request help from our men and obtain it under stipulated conditions; Sanguinus returns home.

[Col. 0618D]

Meanwhile, while these events occurred in the regions of Jerusalem, Sanguinus, restless as a worm and exceedingly elated by his successes, presumed also to claim the kingdom of the Damascenes for himself. Ainardus, governor of that kingdom, commander of its forces and father-in-law of the king of Damascus, learned that Sanguinus had violently entered his territory. He sent envoys with peaceful words to the lord king, asking and earnestly beseeching aid and counsel from him and the Christian people against this most cruel enemy of both kingdoms.

So that he might not seem presumptuously to solicit the lord king and his princes for his assistance gratuitously and without hope of much benefit, he promised to pay, each month, twenty thousand gold pieces toward the expenses necessary for this undertaking [Col. 0619A]. Moreover, once the enemy had been violently driven from his territory, he included among the agreement’s terms the restoration without contradiction to our side of the city of Paneas, which had been violently taken from us a few years earlier. To secure greater credit for all these articles of agreement, he promised to give as hostages as many sons of nobles as might be needed.

Hearing this, the lord king summoned all the princes of the kingdom and carefully set before them the character of the embassy and the sequence of its words. He sought their counsel on what answer ought to be made to such requests. At length, after consultation among themselves and a prudent weighing of the deliberation’s parts, they judged it best to bring aid to Ainardus and the Damascenes against this most savage enemy, who was a threat to both kingdoms [Col. 0619B]. They also judged that assistance should be supplied freely, lest the enemy, made stronger through our indolence by acquiring that kingdom, should receive an increase of power to our destruction. Furthermore, the added conditions made the cause more favourable; and what chiefly drew all to this course was the addition at the end of the proposal concerning the city of Paneas.

## Chapter VIII. The city of Paneas is besieged, with the Damascenes furnishing assistance.

When the general counsel had therefore been approved, the aforesaid hostages received and placed in safety, an innumerable force of cavalry and infantry was immediately ordered to assemble at Tiberias from all parts of the kingdom [Col. 0619C]. Sanguinus, however, trusting in the multitude of his strength, had entered the territory of that province with immense cavalry forces. Leaving Damascus behind him, he had reached the place called Rasaline; there he had remained with his legions for some time, uncertain whether our men would come. He seemed certain that, unless our strength prevented his design, he could easily attain his desired end.

Our men were informed that Sanguinus was remaining at the aforesaid place, and that the Damascenes, having already left their city, were awaiting the arrival of the lord king and our forces at Nuara. Upon learning this, our own troops likewise broke camp and, their standards going before them, hastened together to the aforesaid place. Hearing this, Sanguinus, an astute man, feared to engage a double army in enemy territory before our men could join the Damascenes [Col. 0619D]. He therefore abandoned the place, avoided our forces and those of the Damascenes by turning to the left, hastened into flight, and made his way by forced marches into the region commonly called the Valley of Baccar.

Our men nevertheless reached the aforesaid place, joined with the Damascenes, and were fully informed of Sanguinus’s departure. By common counsel, as the agreement stipulated, they directed all their armies against Paneas. As we said earlier, Doldequinus, king of the Damascenes, had willingly occupied this city a few years before. But afterwards the governor to whom he had entrusted it defected from the Damascenes and joined Sanguinus against them [Col. 0620A]. Therefore they worked all the more faithfully to have it handed over to the lord king, preferring that it be restored to the Christians, whose favour they enjoyed, rather than possessed by their enemy, so threatening and so formidable; from there, being nearer at hand, he could harm them more seriously and inflict greater troubles upon them.

## Chapter IX. The prince of Antioch and the count of Tripoli join the same siege, and the city is attacked with the utmost vigour.

Paneas is this city, which in the common vernacular is called Belinas, and which, before the entry of the children of Israel into the Promised Land, was formerly called Lesen. Later the children of Dan received it as their allotment and called it Lesen-Dan, [Col. 0620B] as is read in Joshua, where it is written: “And the children of Dan went up and fought against Lesen, captured it, struck it with the edge of the sword, took possession of it, and dwelt in it, calling its name Lesen-Dan, after Dan their father” (Josh. 19:47). Subsequently the same place was called Caesarea Philippi, because Philip the tetrarch, son of the elder Herod, enlarged it in honour of Tiberius Caesar and made it notable with magnificent buildings, so that it bore in one designation the name of Caesar and of its enlarger.

The forces therefore turned toward the city, reached it on the Kalends of May [1 May], and invested it with a siege on every side. Ainard with his men stationed his expeditionary forces on the east, between the city and the forest, at the place [Col. 0620C] called Cohagar; but the king and our army set their legions on the west, toward the plain. With posts thus carefully arranged in a circle, every means of access was diligently cut off from those enclosed, so that no unrestricted opportunity of escape lay open either to those wishing to enter or to those wishing to leave. Moreover, it was agreed and decreed by common counsel that trustworthy messengers should be sent to summon Lord Raymond, prince of Antioch, and the lord count of Tripoli to assist in the present undertaking; and this was done.

Meanwhile, they themselves, together with the Turks, who were equally eager and equipped for daily engagements, pressed the besieged with continual assaults. They brought up stone-throwing engines, called *petrariae*, and hurled immense millstones, shaking the walls and crushing houses within the city. With volleys of missiles and a great hail of arrows they so exhausted the townsmen that no safe place for concealment could be found within the walls. Barely protected by wall and battlements, they dared only to look upon those attacking from without while hurling stones or using bows.

There might there be seen, beyond all ordinary measure, enemies challenged by enemies in a most savage warfare; disguise had been cast aside, and they were seriously intent upon one another’s destruction. Nor was it easy to determine which hand seized arms more fiercely against the common enemies, pressed more vigorously in battle, or persevered with longer endurance under the burden of war. For our soldiers and the Damascene [Col. 0621A] cohorts had an equal spirit and a concordant desire. Their experience and practice in arms were very different; yet their willingness to inflict harm was no less.

But the besieged, though worn down by continuous assaults, by wakefulness, and by the weight of excessive labour, nevertheless resisted courageously. Striving with all their strength to protect their liberty, wives, and children, made more resourceful by the pressure of distress, they turned to every means of resistance. After these operations had continued for several days, it seemed that no progress whatsoever could be made unless a wooden tower were brought up to the walls and war made upon the besieged from above. Since no suitable timber for such a purpose could be found anywhere in that region, men were sent to Damascus by Lord Ainard’s order to bring back, with all speed, tall beams of immense size [Col. 0621B] which had long before been specially set aside for this purpose.

## CHAPTER X. With the prince and count present, an engine is erected to assault the city; the citizens stoutly defend themselves in hope of relief.

Meanwhile the prince of Antioch and the count of Tripoli, summoned by our envoys, arrived as desired with very great forces and a strong hand, and joined their camp to ours. Their arrival doubled the besieged men’s fear, and every hope of resistance seemed to have fallen. While the newly arrived men vied in testing their strength and, eager for praise and the attainment of glory, separately attacked the city with their assembled troops, [Col. 0621C] greater terror and despair were brought upon the besieged. Among our men, however, the now more certain hope of victory raised their spirits, lessened their weariness, and made them stronger each day for the assault.

Without delay, while these things were being done around the city, those who had gone to Damascus returned, bringing beams of remarkable size and the desired strength. Once these had been smoothed by craftsmen and woodcutters with all speed, and joined securely with iron nails, a tower of immense height was suddenly erected. From it the entire city could be surveyed from above, and its defenders driven back with arrows, every kind of missile, and the throwing of hand-cast stones. When it had been raised and the intervening ground between tower and wall levelled, it was brought against the fortifications, overlooking the whole city, [Col. 0621D] as though a tower had suddenly appeared built in the middle of the town.

Then the condition of the besieged first became exceedingly harsh and drove them to utter extremity. Against the stones hurled and missiles sent continually upon them by those in the wooden tower, no remedy whatever could be found. Inside there was no place that could provide safe shelter for wounded or weakened men, nor any to which those still sound and strong might withdraw after their labours, so that they could defend the others. They were now prevented even from moving along the wall; and when their companions failed, they could not bring help without danger of death. For the burdens of war and means of destruction inflicted from below, when compared with the varied dangers looming from above, [Col. 0622A] could be judged nothing or little. Thus it seemed that they were waging war not so much with men as with powers above.

From the beginning, however, the besieged had cherished—and even to this critical point continued to cherish—the hope that Sanguinus would provide them assistance, as he had pledged himself to do; but now, with danger pressing, neither help nor any means of defence seemed left.

## CHAPTER XI. A legate of the Roman Church arrives; he comes to the siege; the city is captured; a bishop having been appointed there, all the princes proceed to Jerusalem.

While these things were being done on the expedition, a legate of the Roman Church, named Alberic, bishop of Ostia, a Frenchman from the bishopric of Beauvais, [Col. 0622B] landed at Sidon. He had been sent specifically on account of the dispute that had arisen in the church of Antioch between the lord patriarch and his canons. For the same reason, a man of venerable life, Lord Peter, archbishop of Lyons, had come to Syria a few days earlier in the capacity of legate; but, overtaken by death, he could not bring the assigned affair to its conclusion. Therefore this man was substituted for that venerable person, to impose the due end upon so great a controversy, as will be stated below.

Hearing that the entire Christian army was held at the siege of Paneas, and that the lord William, patriarch of Jerusalem, Lord Fulcher, archbishop of Tyre, [Col. 0622C] and the other princes of the kingdom were staying there, he hastened there with all speed. Though those besieging the city did not slacken in their undertaking but pressed it eagerly, he, supported by the zeal of a prudent man and apostolic authority, summoned them to their purpose; adding the spur of an exhortatory address, he kindled them more fiercely to attack the city.

Meanwhile those assigned to the tower pressed the citizens with unceasing assaults. Denying them rest and raining down manifold causes of terror and peril from above, they redoubled their distress by continual exhaustion. Some were already killed by the sword, some mortally wounded, and others failing from weariness; their number diminished, and they could no longer repel, as formerly, those attacking [Col. 0622D] them.

When Ainard, governor and military leader of the Damascenes, understood this—a most prudent man and a most steadfast and faithful keeper of the treaty he had made with us—he knew that oppression opens the way to hearing, and that utter misery commonly drives men to extreme terms. He therefore secretly sent certain members of his household to invite the besieged to surrender with hope of safety, and faithfully sounded them out. At first they recoiled and pretended to go farther, as though they still seemed to possess some hope of resistance; but at last they eagerly and gratefully accepted the offered proposal.

The magistrate, however, whom they call the emir, a noble and powerful man, added this condition to the terms offered: that in return for surrendering the city, consideration should be given to ensuring that he did not fall into need, and some recompense should be made for him at the discretion of an honourable man. For it would seem shameful and improper that a noble man and lord of so famous a city, expelled from his own inheritance, should be forced to beg. Ainard, seeing that the nobleman’s request accorded sufficiently with law and equity, and hastening with all his heart that the city should come into our power, bound himself in accordance with their wish: he would assign him annual revenues, payable from baths and orchards, to a specified amount agreed between them; and he would provide free departure, with all their possessions, to the people wishing to leave. To those who wished to remain in the city and on their estates, urban and rural alike, and to depart nowhere, whether temporarily or permanently, [Col. 0623B] he promised peaceful residence on good terms, under pledge of faith.

Both the lord king and the remaining people gladly accepted this proposal and were ready to hand over the city without delay. Ainard, seeing that the agreements had reached the desired harmony and that the terms were now in no respect uncertain, privately met the lord king, the patriarch, the prince, and the count. He carefully explained the course of the matter, secretly negotiated, and urged them by every means to agree. Considering the man’s prudence and sincerity of faith, they approved the terms; freely giving their consent, they firmly pledged themselves to do everything according to his arrangement.

Thus, when the city had been surrendered, its citizens, having free departure with all their household goods, wives, and children, removed themselves to the places they desired. When our men had received the city, the lord patriarch arranging the matter and Lord Fulcher, archbishop of Tyre—under whose metropolitan jurisdiction it was certain that the church of Paneas lawfully belonged—granting his consent and approving the election, they elected Lord Adam, archdeacon of Acre, bishop of that place. They entrusted to him the spiritual care of the faithful wishing to remain there; and they restored temporal jurisdiction to Lord Rainer, surnamed Brus, from whom it had been violently taken a few years earlier.

Then, to offer thanks to God and solemn sacrifices, the lord king hastened to Jerusalem with the lord prince of Antioch, the lord patriarch, [Col. 0623D] and the lord legate. After the customary prayers had been completed and they had stayed several days at Jerusalem, the lord prince, having sounded out the legate’s mind concerning his intention against his patriarch and invited him not to hesitate to come, but to come boldly and assured of his help, returned to Antioch. For, as we have said, this same legate had been sent to investigate certain crimes imputed to that patriarch by certain canons of his church and to bring the case to its due conclusion. It is now time to fulfil what we previously promised concerning the aforesaid patriarch; and, that this may be more easily understood, the narrative must be taken up again a little from earlier events.

## CHAPTER XII. The prince of Antioch conspires with the adversaries of the patriarch of Antioch; the patriarch sets out for Rome. He is captured by Roger, duke of Apulia; but finally reconciled with him, he reaches Rome.

[Col. 0624A]

When therefore Lord Raymond first came to Antioch, as we have said, before he had received his intended wife, he gave Lord Ralph, then head of the church of Antioch, manual fealty, so that he might more easily attain his desire. Under pledge of faith, he promised that from that day forward he would not participate, by counsel or deed, in anything whereby Ralph might lose honour, life, or limb, or be captured by an evil capture; as is contained in the form for rendering fealty. Yet he did not remain faithful even for a brief time. For immediately after he had taken his wife and received the whole region through Ralph’s effort and service, he joined Ralph’s adversaries, giving them assistance and every counsel against the obligation of fealty, to Ralph’s injury.

Having so great a collaborator in their schemes, Ralph’s enemies pressed their attacks more boldly and set out for Rome. These adversaries were a certain Lambert, archdeacon of the same church, a learned man indeed and of honourable conduct, but possessing little or no experience in secular affairs; and a certain Arnulf, a Calabrian by nationality, noble by birth, learned and circumspect in worldly matters. Having formally appealed, and with the lord prince consenting and favouring them, they went to Rome. They compelled Ralph, though unwilling, [Col. 0624C] to take the same road, forced by the prince’s violence.

Arnulf went ahead and, taking a direct route to Sicily, joined to himself friends and kinsmen—for he was a native of Calabria, where he was later archbishop of Cosenza; he was, as we have said, very noble—and approached Lord Roger, duke of Apulia, whom he knew. He said: “Behold, illustrious prince: the most formidable of your enemies, the patriarch of Antioch, who took Antioch from you and your heirs forever by elevating there an unknown man against the order of law, is given into your hands as you desire, and freely. Behold, the Lord has offered him to you, and his completed sins have delivered him into your presence. [Col. 0624D] Come, rouse yourself; contrive how you may seize him. Be assured that through him an entrance may again be opened to the inheritance owed you by right of lawful succession, an entrance which was wrongfully denied you by that same man.”

Moved by these words, the duke of Apulia, being a most resourceful man, ordered ambushes placed in every coastal city, so that on arrival Ralph might immediately be captured, put in chains, and sent straightway to Sicily. Ralph, however, having a favourable voyage and fearing no such thing, landed at Brindisi. In accordance with the duke’s command, all that he had brought with him as a most powerful prince was taken away, his entire household was dispersed, and he was bound and handed over to Arnulf, to be dragged before the duke in Sicily.

There, for the first time, Arnulf was given his wish: free licence to rage against his enemy and impious persecutor and to repay in equal measure the double injuries he had received from Ralph’s hand. At length Ralph was brought into the duke’s presence. After familiar conversations and agreements had taken place between them, Ralph—being prudent, highly eloquent, and of very distinguished appearance—received back in full integrity everything he had lost, and also had his household restored. Promising that on his return he would obtain passage back through the same duke, he was dismissed and proceeded honourably to Rome.

On reaching Rome, however, he initially found access to the lord pope difficult. As a persecutor of the Roman Church, who had wished to diminish and undermine the unique primacy of the apostolic see by setting up a rival see against Rome and making the Antiochene Church its equal, he was treated as one guilty of injured majesty: he was excluded from entering the sacred palace and suspended from an audience with the lord pope. [Col. 0625B]

## CHAPTER XIII. He is accused by his adversaries; finally he returns home with the fullness of favour.

Both the lord pope and the whole Church were more inclined to burden the lord patriarch whenever they could find any respectable occasion, and they showed much favour to his adversaries. For he was highly suspect to them, because he was a wealthy and magnificent man and disdained to make the see over which he presided—namely Antioch—subject to Rome; rather, he strove to make it equal with Rome in all things, saying: “Both are Peter’s [Col. 0625C] chairs, and this one is marked by the prerogative, as it were, of the firstborn.” Accordingly, they strove in many ways to burden him.

At length, through the service of certain friends, who intervened and cleared the way with both the lord pope and Ralph’s own associates, he was admitted to the lord pope and to the solemnly assembled curia, and was received with great magnificence. When he had entered the consistory once and then a second time, his adversaries seized the opportunity and appeared publicly. Producing written bills of accusation, they were prepared to proceed with the accusation in all legal form.

But when the whole curia recognized that those who had come forward to accuse were not yet sufficiently equipped to establish fully before the lord pope and his assessors the charges made, both parties were told to remain quiet for the time being, until the lord pope should send someone from his side to Antioch, where, with witnesses and documents available, he might examine the case more fully. Meanwhile, the pallium which the patriarch had taken for himself, on his own authority, from the altar of the church of Antioch, to the injury, it was said, of the apostolic see, was surrendered and handed to the cardinals. Another pallium, taken from the body of Saint Peter, was solemnly given him by the prior of the deacons.

Thus, after staying in Rome for as long as his affair seemed to require, he received permission and returned to Duke Roger in Sicily with the fullness of favour, though the case remained undecided.
