The duke received him honourably upon his return; and after they had often and extensively exchanged private conversations and whatever seemed sufficient, the duke gave him as many galleys as he needed for his homeward journey. With favourable winds he was carried to Syria and reached the mouth of the Orontes, the river which flows past Antioch. This place is commonly called the port of Saint Symeon and lies about ten miles from Antioch. [Col. 0626A]

## CHAPTER XIV. On his return, his clergy, at the prince’s instigation, do not receive him; he withdraws into the land of the count of Edessa; finally reconciled with the prince, he enters Antioch.

After the lord patriarch, as stated, arrived in Coele-Syria and was thus near [Col. 0626B] his city, he wrote to his church that on an appointed day they should come ceremonially in procession to meet him outside the city at the place mentioned above. But relying on the prince’s favour—the prince who, as we have said, pursued him with implacable hatred in violation of the fealty by which he was bound to him—they utterly refused either to act or to obey him. By the prince’s violence they completely forbade him entrance to the city.

Understanding his clergy’s malice, the alienation of those from whom he had deserved far different treatment, and the prince’s obstinate anger, he withdrew into the mountains adjoining the city, commonly called the Black Mountains. There, staying in the monasteries with which that place abounds, he waited for the lord prince and his clergy, after laying aside their rancour, to summon him back into the city with a more humane disposition.

The prince, indeed, opposed him more than usual and more openly. Arnulf had increased the prince’s hatred and added greater fuel to it. From Sicily he had written to the prince that the patriarch had entered into secret agreements against him with Duke Roger, the prince’s rival. In support of his allegation he pointed to the fact that, while travelling home through Sicily, the patriarch had been received with gifts and much honour, and had been supplied with the galleys needed for his journey. All of this could reasonably seem to promote the persuasion.

While Ralph stayed in the places just named, the count of Edessa, the younger Joscelin, partly from hatred of the prince and partly from favour toward the patriarch, sent special [Col. 0626D] messengers diligently inviting him to come down securely and confidently into his territory with all his company. The bishops of that region favoured the patriarch and reverently venerated him as lord and father: namely, the archbishops of Edessa, Coricesium, and Hierapolis. Drawn by their invitation, he came down to them and was treated with very great honour by all the prelates of that region. The count also received his arrival, as he had promised, most courteously and with much devotion, and gladly welcomed his stay.

The prince, however, being, as was said, bought with money, restored his favour to Ralph in word but not in heart, through the mediation of certain intimates of both parties. Sending messengers, he warmly invited him with deceitful words of peace to enter the city and return to [Col. 0627A] his possessions. Hearing this, the patriarch hastened back. Taking with him those neighbouring bishops, whose essential devotion in his adversity he had experienced by certain proofs, he reached Antioch. There the entire Church and all the people met him, together with a great multitude of knights and the prince. Clothed in pontifical vestments, he was solemnly led with hymns and songs into the city and the greater church, and then into his palace.

## CHAPTER XV. The archbishop of Lyons, legate of the apostolic see, dies at Acre; Alberic, bishop of Ostia, is sent for the same matter. A synod is called at Antioch.

[Col. 0627B]

Meanwhile a legate of the Roman Church, named Peter, a Burgundian and archbishop of Lyons, was sent by Lord Pope Innocent to bring the aforesaid case to its due conclusion. He came to Syria and landed at Acre. He was a man of venerable life, simple and God-fearing, elderly and already declining into old age. As soon as he entered Syria, he went to Jerusalem to pray. Departing thence shortly afterward, he was urgently pressed by the aforesaid Lambert and Arnulf to hasten to Antioch in order to render judgment. He returned to Acre, where, seized by grave illness before proceeding further, he suddenly failed and died, poisoned, it is said, by poison administered in a drink.

The named adversaries [Col. 0627C] of the patriarch hurried to Antioch. Utterly deprived of assistance, disappointed also in the hope they had conceived from the legate’s arrival, and exhausted by weariness from the road and labours endured over so long a time, they humbly sought peace through mediators deemed suitable for this purpose. They asked for restoration of their benefices, were ready to renounce their accusation, and to render fealty. Lambert was restored to the archdeaconry. Arnulf, finding no humane treatment, again trusted in the prince’s help and, with his customary persistence, again set himself to journeys and labour. Going to Rome, he again knocked at the door, opportunely and importunately; finally, stubbornly pressing his petitions, he obtained the dispatch to Syria of the aforesaid legate, of whom we are speaking [Col. 0627D] here.

When he arrived in Jerusalem, as we have said, he completed his prayers, summoned the lord patriarch and all the bishops of the kingdom to a synod to be held at Antioch on the day before the Kalends of December [30 November], and hastened there with all speed.

## CHAPTER XVI. At the assembly of bishops an accusation is brought against the patriarch; he is summoned but delays coming. Serlo, archbishop of Apamea and his supporter, is deposed.

On the appointed day there were present from the diocese of Jerusalem Lord William the patriarch, Gaudentius, archbishop of Caesarea, and Anselm, bishop of Bethlehem. Lord Fulcher, archbishop of Tyre, was also present, greatly devoted and faithful to the holy Roman Church, [Col. 0628A] in whom the legate’s whole hope for bringing the affair to conclusion rested; he was a man of high spirit and exceptional discernment. He came with two of his suffragans, Bernard of Sidon and Baldwin of Beirut.

From the province of Antioch, because they were nearer, all were present, although their wishes were exceedingly varied and mutually discordant. For Stephen, archbishop of Tarsus, Gerard, bishop of Laodicea, and Hugh, bishop of Gibel, supported the canons’ cause against the lord patriarch. But Franco of Hierapolis, Gerard of Coricesium, and Serlo of Apamea, though Serlo had originally been his adversary, had turned toward him and openly gave their support to the lord patriarch. The others did not seem openly to incline to either side.

On the appointed day, therefore, the archbishops, bishops, and abbots sat according to custom in the church of the Prince of the Apostles, clothed in pontifical vestments, with the lord legate presiding and acting in the pope’s stead. The text of the lord pope’s mandates was read publicly. When it had been read and more carefully and fully understood, the accusers came forward: the oft-mentioned Arnulf and Lambert the archdeacon. Although Lambert had previously reached a deceitful agreement with the lord patriarch and received restoration of his benefice, he turned like a warped bow and again made himself an accuser. Several others joined them, seeing that circumstances were not responding favourably to the lord patriarch.

Here, too, one could plainly recognize the truth of the proverbial saying passed down by our Naso [Ovid]:

> “So long as you are fortunate, you will count many friends;
>
> If times become cloudy, you will be alone.”

The accusers therefore came into the public court and declared themselves ready, according to legal rules and having submitted written bills of accusation, to proceed with the prosecution and, should they fail, to undergo the penalty of retaliation. The charges on which they intended to attack him were written upon slips. Some concerned his outrageous and disorderly entry, contrary to the rules of the holy Fathers; others, his sexual incontinence and simoniacal practices.

As they urgently demanded that he appear in person, men were sent solemnly to summon him to the synod and warn him to come answer the allegations. He utterly refused to come. Thus nothing further was done in that matter on that day, except that they delivered mutually exhortatory addresses, as is customary in such cases.

On the second day they assembled again, sat in due order, and once more solemnly summoned the lord patriarch by a citation edict. As on the preceding day, he utterly refused to come. Meanwhile Serlo, archbishop of Apamea, sat in the choir of bishops without the wedding garment—that is, he was not clothed in pontifical vestments like the others. The lord legate challenged him as to why he did not agree with his fellow brothers and why he did not proceed to accuse, as he had once done.

He replied: “What I once did, I did in unconsidered passion and against the salvation of my soul: by slandering my father and, after the manner of accursed Ham, uncovering my father’s shame, I acted. But now, recalled by God’s help from my wandering error, I shall not presumptuously attempt either to accuse or judge him. Rather, I am ready to strive even to death for his standing and safety.”

He was therefore ordered to leave; and a sentence both of excommunication and degradation was passed against him. Whether justly or otherwise, he was deposed from every priestly and pontifical office. Such fear of the lord prince, who was excessively inclined to the legate’s party, had seized everyone that no one any longer possessed freedom to contradict.

A certain Peter Armoinus, keeper of the city fortress, a man exceedingly malicious, inflamed that same prince, who was insufficiently prudent and undiscerning. He hoped that if the patriarch were deposed, he could raise to that see, through the deceived prince, a certain nephew of his named Aimeric—whom the lord patriarch, to his own ruin, had made dean of that church. And this indeed was done. Serlo, therefore, whether deposed in fact or in law, left Antioch and went to his diocese. On arriving at the castle of Harenc, overtaken by illness and troubled by the weight of his cares, he took to bed; and, turning to the wall, unable to endure the enormity of the wrongs done him, he died. [Col. 0629B]

## CHAPTER XVII. The patriarch, absent as though contumacious, is deposed; ignominiously treated, he is put in chains; setting out again for Rome, he obtains partial favour, but dies of poison on his return.

[Col. 0629C]

On the third day, when they again assembled and sat in order, they sent men a third time to summon the lord patriarch by a peremptory edict and warn him to come answer the charges. Whether he feared his conscience, or knew that the synod had been assembled maliciously against him and feared the prince’s violence, we do not know with certainty; but, as before, he wholly refused to come.

He was in his palace with his household, surrounded by a large company of knights and townspeople. For all those of the city had gathered to support him, and, had they not feared the prince’s power, they were ready to drive the legate and everyone assembled for his deposition from the city in disgrace. Seeing therefore that the patriarch would not come [Col. 0629D] to him, the legate, relying upon the lord prince’s support and forces, entered the palace. There, after pronouncing sentence of deposition upon him, he compelled him violently to surrender ring and cross. Then, by the legate’s command, he was handed over to the prince and miserably bound in chains. Treated ignominiously as a man of blood, he was committed to prison at the monastery of Saint Symeon, situated beside the sea on a very high mountain.

This Lord Ralph—for we ourselves saw him in our childhood—was handsome in appearance, tall in body, with eyes somewhat oblique, though not unattractively so; moderately learned, but highly eloquent and of most agreeable conversation, possessing much charm. He was very liberal and had acquired considerable favour among men of the military class and also among those of the second rank. He was easily forgetful of promises and agreements; fickle and inconstant in his word; deceitful and excessively complex in all his ways, yet prudent and discerning. Only in this was he found less wise: he did not admit again to his favour adversaries whom he had deservedly raised against himself when they wished to return to it. For he was said—and it was true—to be arrogant and to presume too much upon himself. Hence he fell into a disaster which, had he conducted himself somewhat more circumspectly, he could easily have avoided.

Captured and chained, and held long in the monastery, he finally escaped and went to Rome. There he gained some measure of the apostolic see’s favour; but while hastening to return, he drank poison, administered by some unknown agent of crime, and died miserably. [Col. 0630B] Thus, another Marius, he experienced more fully in himself all that either fortune could do.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The legate returns to Jerusalem, holds a synod, and dedicates the Lord’s Temple.

The legate, having deposed the patriarch and completed at Antioch the business for which he had come, returned to Jerusalem. There he remained until the feast of Easter. Having first consulted the prelates of the churches, on the third day after holy Easter he solemnly dedicated the Temple of the Lord together with the lord patriarch and several bishops.

Many great and noble men from both the lands beyond the mountains and the regions on this side of the sea attended on the day of dedication. Among them was [Col. 0630C] Lord Joscelin the younger, count of Edessa, who was then staying in the city with great magnificence during the solemn days of holy Easter. When this celebration had been completed, the legate summoned the archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of the churches, and together with the lord patriarch held a council in holy Sion, the first and mother of the churches. There he discussed with them matters that seemed suited to the needs of the time.

Maximus, pontiff of the Armenians—or rather chief and eminent teacher of all the bishops of Cappadocia, Media, Persia, and both Armenias—was present at that synod; he is called the *Catholicus*. With him there was also a discussion of the articles of faith in which his people seemed to differ from us; and, on his side, correction in many matters was promised.

When these things had been duly completed, the aforesaid legate returned to the city of Acre and, embarking there on a prepared ship, returned to Rome.

But the clergy of Antioch, especially those who had conspired in the deposition of Lord Ralph, at the prince’s instigation and, it is said, through the intervention of very great bribes, elected as their leader a certain subdeacon of that church, named Aimeric, a native of Limoges, a man without learning and of not sufficiently honourable conduct. The aforesaid Lord Ralph had promoted him to dean of that church, mistakenly supposing that this would make him more obligated and faithful to himself. For from that day, Aimeric is said to have joined Ralph’s adversaries and, forgetful of loyalty to his benefactor, [Col. 0631A] conspired in his deposition. It is said that a certain Peter, surnamed Armoinus, castellan of that city, accomplished Aimeric’s promotion by his contrivances and lavish expenditure of gifts, and induced both clergy and prince to it because Aimeric was his kinsman.

## CHAPTER XIX. The emperor again comes down into Syria and summons the prince concerning the agreements previously made.

At about this time, scarcely four full years having elapsed since he had departed from Tarsus in Cilicia and from all Syria, the lord John, emperor of Constantinople, having restored his strength and recalled his legions, and stirred by the frequent messages of the lord prince and the Antiochenes, again directed expeditions—again armies—into Syria. In the abundance of his power, with chariots and horses, infinite treasures, and innumerable supplies, he set his course toward the regions of Antioch. Having crossed the Bosporus, understood to be the boundary between Europe and Asia, and passed through the intervening provinces, he reached Attalia, a very great city on the seacoast and metropolis of Pamphylia. While the lord emperor was staying there, two of his sons—Alexius, the first-born, and Andronicus, the second in age—were seized by a very grave illness and died.

The emperor summoned his third son, Isaac by name, and sent him to Constantinople with the bodies of his deceased brothers, so that, attending to them with the offices of humanity and causing the final honour of burial rites to be rendered, he might commit them to their tombs as befitted imperial magnificence. [Col. 0631C] There, after burying his brothers, Isaac remained continuously in the city, in accordance with his father’s command, until his father’s death. The father, taking with him his youngest son Manuel, continued the journey he had begun. Passing through Isauria, he arrived in Cilicia; then, having suddenly traversed Cilicia, with scarcely the report of his approach preceding him, he entered the territory of the count of Edessa with all his forces and unexpectedly encamped before Turbessel.

The aforesaid place is a very wealthy fortress, near the Euphrates, twenty-four miles or a little more distant from it. When the emperor had arrived there, he demanded hostages from the younger Count Joscelin. Joscelin, thunderstruck and astonished by his sudden arrival, seeing his incomparable forces—such as no king in that land seemed capable of withstanding—and finding himself unprepared and wholly unable to offer resistance, made a virtue of necessity and handed over one of his daughters, Isabella by name, as a hostage. He demanded this for no other reason than that, by this bond, he might hold the count more closely bound to himself and more faithful in carrying out his commands.

Thence he directed all his armies toward Antioch and hastened there with all speed. Beside a certain town named Gastun, he stationed his army in September, on the twenty-fifth day of the month. From there he sent messengers to the prince, commanding him, according to the terms of the agreement previously concluded between them, [Col. 0632A] to surrender to him the city, with its garrison and without exception all the city’s fortifications, so that he might more conveniently wage war from close at hand against the neighbouring cities of the enemy. In return, he steadfastly declared himself ready, so far as lay in his power, to fulfil with generous interpretation the agreements formerly committed to writing, and moreover to add a good and overflowing measure, according to the quality of the prince’s deserts.

### Chapter XX. The Citizens Send an Embassy to the Emperor, Reject the Agreements, and Forbid His Entry

The prince of Antioch, Lord Raymond, who had formerly summoned him by so many messages, saw himself placed in a difficult position and knew that he was bound by the terms of the agreement. He hesitated, uncertain what to do. Having summoned the leading and principal men both of the city and of the whole region, he entered into deliberation with them, seeking counsel as to what ought to be done in a matter so perilous.

After much deliberation, they unanimously judged that it was by no means advantageous for the condition of the land that so noble, powerful, and fortified a city should be handed over to the emperor on any terms. For, through Greek weakness—as had happened more than once before—they believed that the city, together with the whole region, would come into the hands of the enemy. Yet, lest the prince might deservedly be accused of breaking faith, they sought a pretext by which the prince’s less commendable action might be veiled. For, as we have stated, they had agreed at the emperor’s earlier arrival that the prince would surrender the city to him without difficulty; and afterward, while repeatedly inviting him to come into Syria, the prince had promised that he would faithfully observe this agreement.

Therefore, that they might somehow excuse the prince in this matter, they sent to the emperor envoys chosen from the nobler men of the land. On behalf of Saint Peter, of the lord patriarch, and of all the citizens, these envoys were to forbid the emperor entrance into the city and declare that they would by no means ratify the prince’s preceding actions. Nor, they said, had the prince had by right the power to make such an agreement concerning his wife’s inheritance. Neither had he possessed, nor did he possess, any power to transfer its lordship to another person without the consent of the citizens and magnates. No authority whatsoever, under any right, had been granted to either of them to transact anything to the injury of the citizens or of the princes of the land. If either or both should presumptuously persist obstinately in this, then, expelled from the city and from all its territories, they would be made exiles from that inheritance which they had proposed to put up for sale, contrary to right and to the harm of their faithful people.

Moved by these words, and already knowing the hearts of all the citizens and provincials, the emperor was greatly angered. He ordered the armies to return into Cilicia, so that, as the harshness of winter approached, he might entrust them to the milder climate of the seacoast. For in coastal regions the air is usually more pleasant in winter, and more suitable conditions are found for maintaining the legions.

### Chapter XXI. The Emperor Sends Messengers to the King of Jerusalem, Pretending That He Intends to Visit the Holy Places; He Receives the King’s Answer

[Col. 0633A]

The emperor therefore, seeing that the entry into the city so desired by himself and his followers had been wholly denied him, hoped that, after winter had passed and the welcome mildness of spring had returned, he might gain something near Antioch in accordance with his wishes, even against the will of the citizens. He concealed the purpose he had conceived and, to hide his intention, sent men of great nobility to Lord Fulk, king of Jerusalem. They announced that he would gladly come, if this seemed good to the Christians, for devotion and prayer, and in order to bring aid against the enemies in those parts.

[Col. 0633B] The king, having taken counsel, sent messengers in reply to the request: Lord Anselm, bishop of Bethlehem; Lord Geoffrey, abbot of the Temple of the Lord and skilled in the Greek language; and Roard, castellan of the citadel of Jerusalem. They said that the kingdom was very restricted and did not abound sufficiently in provisions for so great a multitude; nor could it sustain such large armies except at the risk of famine and a lack of necessities. Nevertheless, if it pleased his God-beloved imperial majesty to come with ten thousand men as far as the Holy City and the venerable places of our salvation, and to arrange something in accordance with his desires, all would go out to meet him with the greatest eagerness. They would receive his arrival with every joy and exultation of heart, and would obey him as lord and greatest prince of the world.

Hearing this, and judging it contrary to imperial glory to travel with so small a force when he was accustomed always to proceed surrounded by so many thousands, the emperor said no more. Having dismissed the messengers after honouring and favouring them with great generosity, he awaited the coming spring and spent the winter in Cilicia around Tarsus. He promised himself, and resolved, that in the following summer he would accomplish something great and worthy of lasting memory in the regions of Syria.

Meanwhile, a nobleman named Pagan, formerly the king’s butler, afterward held the land beyond the Jordan, after Roman of Le Puy and his son Ralph had, through their deserts, been disinherited and expelled from it. In the territories of Arabia Secunda he built a fortress named Crac, very strongly fortified both by the natural position of the site and by human workmanship. It stood near the most ancient city, formerly called Rabbah, the metropolis of the same Arabia, during whose siege Uriah the innocent is recorded to have been killed at David’s command and through Joab’s agency. Later it was called Petra of the Desert; hence Arabia Secunda is now called Petracene.

### Chapter XXII. While Remaining in Cilicia, the Emperor Is Mortally Wounded While Hunting

Meanwhile, near the beginning of spring, before kings usually lead out their armies to war, the emperor of Constantinople—an exceedingly eager lover of woods and groves for the sake of hunting—entered the forest with his customary retinue appointed for this purpose, seeking relief from weariness as his long habit required. While he was pursuing wild beasts with his usual diligence, carrying a bow in his hand and, as usual, a quiver heavy with arrows, behold: a boar, caught by the skill of the dogs, worn out by their importunity, and driven onward by their harsh barking, necessarily passed before the lord emperor, who had stationed himself in ambush.

Seizing an arrow with remarkable swiftness, the emperor drew the bow too far and wounded himself in the hand with which he held the bow, by the poisoned point of the arrow. Thus, from so slight a cause, he received in his own body the sentence of death. Compelled by the pain of his illness, he left the woods and went to the camp. Summoning many physicians, he disclosed the matter and did not hesitate to say that he himself was the cause of his own death.

[Col. 0634B] Greatly concerned for their lord’s safety, they applied their care. But the deadly poison, having entered within, did not heed remedies; creeping inward and advancing into the deeper parts, it blocked every avenue of recovery. They said, however, that one unique remedy, though unworthy of so great a prince, might be employed: the injured hand, in which the full force of the evil was still contained, should be cut off before it infected the other parts of his body, which were still unharmed.

When the high-minded man heard this, although he was tormented by immense pain and did not doubt that death stood at the door, he nevertheless steadfastly preserved imperial dignity, rejected the proposal, and is said to have replied: “It is unworthy that the Roman empire should be governed by one hand!”

By this disastrous event—than which none more dangerous could have occurred—the entire army was struck with amazement and dismay. Grief seized all the legions at the decline of so great a prince; sorrow and anxiety claimed every heart and filled the camp with wholly unforeseen bitterness.

### Chapter XXIII. The Younger Son Is Raised to the Empire; the Emperor Dies; the Army, Manuel Being Appointed Emperor as Its Leader, Returns Home

Meanwhile the lord emperor, a prudent and discerning man, seeing that the day of his death was certainly imminent, summoned to himself his kinsmen and relations, a great multitude of whom had always been accustomed to follow him, [Col. 0634D] together with the leading men of the sacred palace and the commanders-in-chief of the armies. He raised among them the question of the imperial succession. He was greatly uncertain what to do: whether he should entrust the reins of empire to Isaac, the elder of his sons, whom, as we have said, he had sent from Attalia to Constantinople with his brothers’ bodies, and to whom the first right in the kingdom seemed legally due; or to the younger son, who was with him, a young man of excellent and outstanding character, whom all said would become great.

He added also the reason for his doubt, saying: “If we grant the sceptres of empire to this one, we shall seem to oppose the laws of humanity, which rightly make the first-born superior. But if, observing the common judgment, we confer the government of the empire upon the other, there will be no one to lead these armies, and the strength and glory of the whole Roman empire, safely home. Since enemies lie between us, plotting ambushes and gathering support on every side, it appears certain that the legions cannot pass through except at risk, without a leader.”

Among the princes was a magnificent man named John the Megadomestic, who earnestly wished the empire to be preserved for Isaac and endeavoured to reassure the doubtful emperor concerning the safe return of the legions to their homes. But the younger son Manuel, present there with his father, was extolled by the favour and praises of the entire army, and especially of the Latins. Some of the princes likewise exerted every effort for his elevation. The father’s affection and favour also inclined more toward Manuel, because he seemed more prudent, more vigorous in arms, and altogether more gracious; above all, the emperor was troubled by his deeper concern for the army.

Thus, after much deliberation, with the Lord’s approval the younger son prevailed. In his father’s presence, and at his command, imperial reverence having been rendered to him, he was invested with purple boots, as was the custom in that empire, and was unanimously acclaimed Augustus by all the legions. Thus Lord Manuel having been raised to the imperial height, his father—of illustrious memory, an illustrious man, generous, devout, gentle, and merciful—passed to his fate.

He was of medium height, dark in complexion and hair; for this reason he is still called by the surname “the Moor.” His face was unattractive, [Col. 0635C] but he was distinguished in character and notable in military deeds. He died beneath Anavarza, a most ancient city which is the metropolis of Cilicia Secunda, at the place called the Meadow of the Pavilions, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1137, in April, in the twenty-seventh year of his reign, and in the … year of his life.

At last, when affairs in that region had been settled, the lord emperor brought his armies back safely to Constantinople. There he learned that his elder brother had already taken possession of the palace after hearing of their father’s death. By secretly sent letters, he caused him, through his Mysticus—who was in charge of the palace and all the treasures—to be unexpectedly seized, although he feared nothing of the kind, and thrown into chains. But afterward, when he had solemnly entered the imperial city, he was reconciled with his brother through the intervention and loyal efforts of their common kinsmen and the princes of the sacred palace. Thus Lord Manuel, according to his father’s final decision, acquired the monarchy in due tranquillity, never ceasing, as long as he lived, to honour his brother as the first-born with manifold marks of distinction and to favour him with fuller grace.

### Chapter XXIV. The King and the Princes of the Kingdom Found a Fortress Before Ascalon, Named Ibelin

Meanwhile Lord Fulk, king of Jerusalem, and the other princes of the kingdom, together with the lord patriarch and the other prelates of the churches, wishing to restrain the attacks of the Ascalonites, who were raging with excessive insolence, and somewhat to curb their excessive liberty of ranging through the country, resolved by common agreement to build a fortress in the plain near the city of Ramla, not far from Lydda, which is Diospolis.

In that region was a somewhat elevated hill, upon which tradition holds that one of the cities of the Philistines, named Gath, had been established, near that other city of theirs called Ashdod. It was ten miles from Ascalon and not far from the seacoast. Therefore, assembling unanimously by agreement upon the aforesaid hill, they built a strong defensive work, laying lofty foundations, with four towers. Old buildings, many traces of which still remained, supplied an abundance of stones; wells from ancient times, appearing in great number within the circuit of the ruined city, supplied abundant water both for the needs of construction and for human use.

When the fortress had been completed and finished in all its parts, it was entrusted, by common counsel, to a certain noble and prudent man, Lord Balian the elder, father of Hugh, Baldwin, and the younger Balian. All were named “of Ibelin” from the same place, for that was the place’s name even before the fortress was built there. In guarding it and in pursuing the enemies—the purpose for which the stronghold had been founded—the aforesaid man exercised diligent vigilance. After his death, his aforesaid sons, noble men and vigorous in arms, maintained it with no less diligent care until the aforesaid city was restored to the Christian name.

### Chapter XXV. Again, by the Common Counsel of the Princes, a Fortress Is Built Before the Same Ascalon, Named Blanchegarde

In the following year, the princes of the kingdom, seeing and learning more fully from the experience of events that by founding the two strongholds of Beersheba and Ibelin they had made great progress against the pride of the Ascalonites, and that their insolence had for the most part been repressed, their attacks slowed and their efforts weakened, added a third fortress. By greater difficulties and multiplied castles around it, they intended to harass the city and, as though it were besieged, to inspire it more frequently with sudden terror and danger.

There was in that part of Judaea which slopes down from the mountains and begins to border upon the plains, beside the lands of the Philistines, in the tribe of Simeon, a place eight miles from Ascalon. Compared with the highlands it could be called a hill, but compared with the flatter country it might be called a lofty mountain. Its Arabic name was *Tellesaphi*, which among us is interpreted “the bright mountain or hill.” It seemed good to the wiser men to establish a stronghold there, because it appeared both nearer to the city and more strongly protected by site and position than the other castles built for similar purposes.

Therefore, fulfilling their purpose, the lord king and his princes, together with the lord patriarch and the prelates of the churches, assembled unanimously at the place near the beginning of spring, after winter had passed. They summoned craftsmen and the whole people to supply necessities, and built a fortified town upon solid foundations and of squared stones, with four towers of suitable height. From it there was an unobstructed view all the way to the enemy city; it was greatly hateful and terrifying to enemies wishing to go out to plunder. They gave it the common name *Blancha guarda*, which in Latin means “White Watchtower.”

The fortress, completed and finished in all its parts, the lord king took into his own care. Having adequately supplied it with food and arms, he entrusted it for defence to prudent men experienced in military affairs, whose fidelity was known and whose devotion tested. They frequently went out in person, and more frequently with soldiers joined to them from the other castles built for similar purposes, to meet enemies who were coming forth and frustrate their designs. At times, provoking the Ascalonites themselves, they inflicted severe losses upon them and often triumphed over them.

Moreover, those who possessed the surrounding country, trusting in the aforesaid protection and the proximity of the fortresses, built many suburban settlements. They placed in them numerous households and cultivators of the fields. Their settlement made the entire region safer and brought an abundant supply of food to the neighbouring places. Meanwhile the Ascalonites, seeing their city encircled with impregnable fortresses, began to despair of their position more than usual. By frequent messengers they urged their lord, the most powerful prince of Egypt—to whom nothing more of the whole region remained—to take thought for the city, which was the strength of his dominion.

### Chapter XXVI. The Queen Builds a Monastery at Bethany, Endows It with a Very Great Estate, and Places Her Sister There as Superior

Meanwhile, through the Lord’s abundant grace, the kingdom having been brought to some degree of tranquillity, Lady Melisende, queen of pious memory, conceived the plan of founding a monastery of consecrated virgins, for the spiritual benefit of her own soul and of her parents’, and for the welfare of her husband and children, if she could find a place suited to her heart.

She had a younger sister among the others, named Ioveta, who had professed the monastic life in the monastery of Saint Anne, mother of the holy Mother of God. The queen was especially moved toward the aforesaid purpose on her account. It seemed unworthy to her that a king’s daughter should be subject in a cloister to some mother as though she were one of the common people.

Having considered the whole region in her mind and diligently investigated what place might be most suitable for founding a monastery, after much deliberation Bethany pleased her: the village of Mary and Martha and their brother Lazarus, whom Jesus loved; the Lord’s familiar lodging and the Saviour’s dwelling-place. This place lies fifteen stadia from Jerusalem, according to the Evangelist’s statement, beyond the Mount of Olives, eastward, on the slope of that mountain.

The place belonged to the church of the Holy Sepulchre. In exchange for it, the queen gave the canons the city of the prophets, Tekoa, and received the place as her own. Since it was almost in a wilderness and could be exposed to enemy ambushes, she ordered a very strongly fortified tower to be built at great expense from squared and polished stones, divided into the necessary rooms, so that virgins dedicated to God might not lack the support of an impregnable refuge against sudden attacks.

When the tower had been built and the place made in some measure ready for religious observance, she brought in nuns and appointed over them an elderly woman, tested in religion, a venerable matron. She bestowed much landed property upon the church, so that in temporal goods it was considered inferior to no monastery, whether of men or women; indeed, it was said to exceed any other church in abundance. Among the other possessions which she bestowed on that venerable place, she generously assigned Jericho with its dependencies, a most famous place filled with an abundance of every advantage, situated in the plains of the Jordan.

She also bestowed upon the monastery sacred vessels of gold, gems, and silver in great quantity; silken textiles for the adornment of God’s house; and priestly and Levitical vestments of every kind, as ecclesiastical discipline required. When the venerable matron whom she had placed over that house died, the queen returned to her original intention and, with the consent of the lord patriarch and the agreement of the nuns, set her own sister over the monastery. With her she added many further ornaments in chalices, books, and other things relating to ecclesiastical use. As long as she lived, she never ceased to enlarge the place for the sake of her own soul and that of her sister, whom she uniquely loved.

### Chapter XXVII. While Chasing a Hare in the Plains of Acre, the King Falls Headlong from His Horse; He Dies and Is Buried at Jerusalem among His Predecessors

It happened in those days that, when the lord king was staying with the lady queen in the city of Acre after autumn had passed, the queen wished, to relieve weariness, to go outside the city for recreation to certain suburban places watered by springs. The lord king, lest the queen should lack his companionship, decided to go as well, with his customary retinue.

While they were travelling, it happened by chance that boys going before the ranks and company startled a hare lying in the furrows. Everyone’s shouting pursued it as it fled. The king seized a lance in order to chase the hare, but, driven by ill fortune, urged his horse toward it and pressed on vigorously in pursuit. At last, hastening rashly, the horse plunged headlong; falling to the ground, it threw the king down headlong. As he lay stunned by the pain of the fall, the saddle crushed his head, so that his brain issued out both through his ears and through his nostrils.

At this mishap, the entire retinue, both those preceding and those following, terrified by the horror of what had occurred, turned back. Wishing to aid the fallen king, they found him unconscious, with neither voice nor awareness. The queen, learning of her husband’s so sudden death and wounded by this disastrous blow, tore her clothing and hair, wailed, testified to the immensity of her grief with sighs and lamentations, fell to the ground, and embraced the lifeless body. Her eyes could not contain their tears because of the continuous abundance of weeping; her voice, the interpreter of grief, was broken by repeated sobs. Nor was grief satisfied, although she was concerned with nothing but satisfying grief. The household likewise, by tears, voice, and bearing, displayed their mourning and gave sorrowful signs of excessive anguish.

Meanwhile the report of the king’s miserable death was announced and spread through the city of Acre; crowds hastened competitively to the place, wishing to see the unheard-of event that had occurred. He was then carried with tears into the aforesaid city. Though still breathing, he lingered for three days without consciousness. At last, on the fourth day—the Ides of November, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1142 and the eleventh year of his reign—he failed and ended his final day in a good old age.

He was then carried to Jerusalem with due honour. The entire clergy and people came out to meet him, and in the church of the Holy Sepulchre, on entering beneath Mount Calvary, at the right side near the doorway, he was buried with royal magnificence by the hand of Lord William, venerable patriarch of Jerusalem and of pious memory, among the other kings of blessed memory, his predecessors. He left two surviving children, still under age: Baldwin, his first-born, thirteen years old; and Amalric, seven years old. The power of the kingdom rested with Lady Melisende, the God-beloved queen, to whom it belonged by hereditary right.

## Here Begins the Sixteenth Book

[Col. 0639]

## Preface

[Col. 0639B]

What we have thus far woven together in the present history we have gathered only from the accounts of others whose memory still served more fully the events of earlier times. Therefore, with greater difficulty, as though begging for assistance from others, we have attained the truth of the matter, the sequence of events, and the number of years; although we have committed these matters to writing with as faithful an account as we could provide.

But what follows we ourselves have partly witnessed by direct observation, and it has partly become known to us through the trustworthy report of those who were present at the events. Therefore, relying on this twofold aid, we shall, with the Lord as author, commit what remains to the reading of posterity more easily and more faithfully. For the memory of recent times is usually more secure; and things presented to the mind by sight do not so readily suffer the inconvenience of oblivion as things gathered only by hearing.

For, to use the words of our Flaccus, which accord with our purpose:

> Things conveyed through the ear stir the mind more slowly  
> than things set before trustworthy eyes, which  
> the spectator himself relates, etc.

### Chapter I. A Brief Preliminary Notice; Upon Fulk’s Death, His Son Baldwin III Succeeds Him, and His Physical Appearance Is Described

[Col. 0639D]

When Lord Fulk, the third king of Jerusalem from among the Latins, had died, he was succeeded by his son, Lord Baldwin III, born of Lady Queen Melisende. As stated above, he had one younger brother, Amalric by name, seven years old. After Baldwin later died without children, Amalric succeeded to the kingdom, as will be made clear below.

Lord Baldwin was thirteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned for twenty years. He was a young man of excellent character, giving certain indications in himself of what he afterward fulfilled in full experience when he reached manhood. For when he became a man, as he excelled other men in the elegance of his appearance, face, and whole bodily bearing, so also in quickness of mind and flower of eloquence he easily surpassed all the other princes of the kingdom.

He was tall in body, taller than average, with the disposition of his limbs harmoniously and proportionately corresponding throughout to his height, so that no part of him departed even slightly from the proportion of the whole. His face was exceedingly handsome, with a lively colour indicating inborn vigour; in this respect he clearly resembled his mother and did not fall short of his maternal grandfather. His eyes were of moderate size, somewhat prominent, and of restrained brilliance. His hair was straight, though not altogether blond. His beard covered chin and cheeks with a pleasing fullness. His body was moderated by a medium degree of fleshiness, so that he could be called neither stouter, like his brother, nor thin, like his mother.

In short, his superiority of appearance was so great that even those who did not know him, seeing an exceptional dignity shining in him, received from his person a certain indication of royal majesty.

### Chapter II. His Character and Way of Life

To so great a beauty of body there corresponded in equal measure the disposition of a well-ordered mind. He possessed a mind of the greatest quickness, and a certain singular gift of freely flowing eloquence was not lacking to him. Nor did he seem inferior to any prince in the distinction of his commendable character.

For he was exceedingly affable and merciful. Although he showed himself generous to almost everyone beyond his means, he was by no means greedy for what belonged to another. He neither harassed the possessions of churches nor, like a spendthrift, plotted against the wealth of his subjects. What most rarely happens at that age, even in his youth he feared God and held complete reverence for ecclesiastical ordinances and the prelates of the churches. Endowed with quick intelligence, he had also acquired the benefit of a faithful memory. He was fairly well educated, and much more so than his brother Lord Amalric, who succeeded him. Whenever he could snatch some leisure from public occupations, he gladly devoted himself to reading. He especially attended to histories, carefully examining the deeds and characters of ancient kings and the best princes. He took great pleasure in conversation with learned men, and also with prudent laymen.

He excelled so greatly in graciousness that he would unexpectedly address even persons of low standing with personal greetings. To those wishing to approach him or casually meeting him, he would either voluntarily offer mutual conversation or would not deny it to those who asked. Thus he won for himself so great a favour among both common people and fathers that he was considered more welcome to each class than any of his predecessors.

He was also patient in hardship and, in uncertain outcomes of war, exceedingly provident after the manner of an excellent prince. In the greatest necessities, which he often endured for the enlargement of the kingdom, he displayed royal constancy and nowhere abandoned the assurance of a brave man. He had full experience of the eastern customary law by which the kingdom was governed, so that in doubtful matters even the older princes of the realm sought his experience and admired the learning of his deliberative judgment.

Moreover, he was pleasant and witty in speech. Adapting himself with a certain gracious manner to people of every sort, he made himself most agreeable to every age and condition. He was also notably urbane—though less so because he used excessive freedom of speech, publicly flinging into his friends’ faces, without distinction as to whether it pleased or wounded, whatever was noteworthy or liable to rebuke in them. Yet, because he said these things not with intent to harm but from a certain gaiety—or rather frivolity—of mind, he did not lose much favour even among those whom he provoked by freer speech. It seemed all the more pardonable because, when biting words were turned back upon himself in return, he bore them with equanimity.

Furthermore, he pursued dice and the ruinous games of gaming tables beyond what became royal majesty, and, indulging the flesh in its desires, was said to inflict injury upon other men’s marriages. But this was in his youth. When he became a man, “according to the Apostle, he put away the things of a child” (II Cor. XIII, 11). For the notable virtues that followed compensated for the faults of his earlier age. Having taken a wife, he is said to have lived with her most chastely. What he had contracted in youth, less pleasing to God and subject to reproach, under the pressure of that slippery age, he afterward wiped away by wiser counsel and reformed for the better by sounder diligence.

Moreover, he was extremely moderate in taking bodily refreshment and more abstinent than that age required, declaring and abhorring drunkenness, both in food and drink, as the fuel of the worst crime.

### Chapter III. His Advancement to the Kingdom, and How Long He Reigned under His Mother’s Guardianship
After his father’s death, on the fourth day before the Ides of November, immediately following the feast of the Lord’s Nativity, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1142, when Lord Pope Eugenius III presided over the holy Roman Church, Lord Aimery over the Church of Antioch, Lord William over that of Jerusalem, and Lord Fulcher over the Church of Tyre, [Col. 0642B] the princes assembling according to custom, together with all the prelates of the churches, he was solemnly anointed, consecrated, and crowned with his mother in the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, by the hands of Lord William, patriarch of Jerusalem of blessed memory.

His mother was a most prudent woman, possessing nearly complete experience in every secular affair and altogether surpassing the limitations of the female sex, so that she set her hand to mighty deeds. She strove to emulate the magnificence of the best princes and pursued their enterprises with no lesser step. For, while her son was still under age, she governed the kingdom with such diligence and administered it with such moderation that she might deservedly be said to equal her forebears in this respect. [Col. 0642C] So long as the son was willing to be governed by her counsel, the people rejoiced in desired tranquillity and the affairs of the realm advanced in a prosperous course.

But those of lighter mind, observing that the queen’s prudence strongly opposed their designs to entangle the lord king, induced the king by their persuasions—after the manner of others of his age, wax to be bent toward vices and harsh toward advisers—to withdraw himself from his mother’s guardianship and govern his ancestral kingdom himself. They said that it was unworthy for a king, who ought to preside over all others, always to hang upon his mother’s breast as though he were a private person’s son. As this business had its origin in ill-considered frivolity or in the malice of certain persons, [Col. 0642D] so it nearly brought ruin upon the entire kingdom, as will be shown more fully below when these matters are discussed.

## CHAPTER IV. Sanguin besieges Edessa; and the site of that city is described.

In the same year, during the interval between his father’s death and the promotion of the same Lord Baldwin to the kingdom, Sanguin, a wicked man and the most powerful of the Turks in the East, lord and ruler of that city which was formerly called Nineveh but is now, under a changed name, called Mosul—the metropolis of the region formerly called Assyria—besieged with a great host the great and distinguished metropolis of the Medes, Edessa by name, which by another and more usual appellation [Col. 0643A] is called Rages. He relied greatly both on the numbers and strength of his people and on the exceedingly dangerous hostilities that had arisen between Raymond, prince of Antioch, and Joscelin, count of that city.

This city lay beyond the Euphrates, at a distance of one day’s journey from that river. Contrary to the custom of his predecessors, the aforesaid count of that city had abandoned residence in the city itself and established a continual and permanent abode near the Euphrates, at a place called Turbessei, both because of the fertility of the place and for ease; for it was far from the tumult of enemies. Given over to pleasures, he did not show the care due to so noble a city.

The aforesaid city had as its inhabitants Chaldeans and unwarlike men among the Armenians, wholly ignorant of the use of arms and familiar only with the craft of trade. [Col. 0643B] It was rarely visited by Latins and had very few of them as citizens. Its care had been entrusted solely to mercenaries, who were not even paid wages proportionate to their service or time; rather, when seeking their stipulated money, they were commonly put off for a year or longer.

Yet both Baldwin and the elder Joscelin, after obtaining that same county, had established there a constant and permanent residence, diligently bringing in from neighbouring places an abundant supply of provisions, arms, and all other things needed at the time, sufficient in every respect. Thus it was able not only to stand secure in itself, but also deservedly inspired fear in other neighbouring cities. As we have said, the prince of Antioch and the count were divided by enmities no longer concealed but already advanced to open hatred. [Col. 0643C] Hence each had little or no concern for the other’s troubles or misfortunes; indeed, each rejoiced in the other’s losses and took pleasure in adverse events.

From all these circumstances the great prince Sanguin drew his opportunity. Bringing with him countless troops of cavalry from the whole eastern region, and summoning also the peoples of neighbouring cities, he enclosed the aforesaid city in siege and blocked every approach to the besieged, so that neither could citizens leave the city nor could any persons wishing to enter gain access to them. Those besieged were also grievously afflicted by scarcity of provisions and every kind of food.

The city was surrounded by a solid wall and protected by lofty towers; it had two strongholds, one in the upper part of the city and the other below, to which the citizens could retreat even if the city were taken. [Col. 0643D] Yet all these things, though customarily useful against enemies where there are men willing to contend for liberty and oppose the enemy bravely, lie useless where no one among the besieged is found willing to play the part of a defender. It is of little avail for cities to have towers, walls, and outer defences unless there are persons to defend them.

Finding the city empty and thereby gaining greater confidence of taking it, he stationed his legions in a circle and arranged the commanders of the legions at appropriate posts. [Col. 0644A] He then weakened the walls with engines and missile-throwing machines; and, continually harassing the citizens with frequent flights of arrows, he allowed the besieged no rest.

Meanwhile it was announced and spread abroad by rumour that this city devoted to God was suffering these straits of siege at the hands of enemies of the Christian faith and name. At this report, the hearts of the faithful who heard it far and wide melted, and zeal began to arm itself for vengeance upon the wicked. Hearing this, the count, struck by the bitterness of the event, vigorously summoned military forces. Too late mindful of the eminent city, he prepared, as though it were already dead, its funeral rites—he who had refused to care for it when sick and seeking remedies. He went about among the faithful, solicited friends, and humbly admonished and earnestly urged his lord, the prince of Antioch, through messengers, to have compassion upon his sufferings and free the aforesaid city from the yoke of future slavery.

News of this disastrous event also reached the king of Jerusalem, attesting with certainty the siege around the aforesaid city and the distress suffered by its citizens. The queen, who administered the government of the kingdom, after taking counsel with the nobles, dispatched in all haste Manasses, royal constable and her kinsman, Philip of Nablus, and Elinand of Tiberias, together with a military force, to give desired assistance to the lord count and the afflicted citizens. [Col. 0644C] But the prince of Antioch, rejoicing in the count’s adversities and giving little consideration to what he owed to the common good or to the fact that personal hatred ought not to result in public injury, sought pretexts while delaying the requested aid.

## CHAPTER V. The city is taken and its people slaughtered.

Meanwhile Sanguin pressed the besieged with continuous assaults and employed every device of harm. He left unattempted nothing that could increase the citizens’ distress and afford him an opportunity to take the place. Sending in miners through trenches and underground passages, he drove a tunnel alongside the wall and supported the undermined work with timbers set in place. [Col. 0644D] When these had been consumed by fire, a great part of the wall fell and opened to the enemy a breach more than a hundred cubits wide.

The enemy, having the access they desired, entered the city as legions poured in from every side, and put to the sword whatever citizens they encountered, sparing neither condition, age, nor sex. Thus the words seemed spoken of them: “They have slain the widow and the stranger, and murdered the fatherless; the young man together with the virgin and the nursing child, with the aged man” (Ps. 93 [94]:6).

When the city had been taken and delivered to the swords of the enemy, the wiser or more nimble citizens withdrew with their children and wives into the strongholds which, as we have said, were within the city, that they might at least provide for their lives, though only for a brief time. There such a tumult arose at the entrance from the crowds rushing together [Col. 0645A] that many perished miserably, suffocated by the crush of the throng. Among them, it is said, the most reverend man Hugh, archbishop of that city, died in the same manner with certain of his clerics.

Those who were present at the affair nevertheless lay some blame for this miserable event upon the aforesaid bishop. For although he was said to have amassed an immense sum of money, which he might have spent upon soldiers to assist the city, he preferred in his greed to devote himself to riches rather than help the people who were perishing. Thus, gathering the fruit of his avarice, he shared without distinction the death of his fellow citizens, and, unless the Lord mercifully comes to his aid, is not very secure even from an evil report. For Scripture speaks terrifyingly to such persons, saying: “May your money perish with you” (Acts 8:20).

Thus, while the prince of Antioch, overcome by undiscriminating hatred, delayed giving his brethren the aid due to them, and while the count awaited assistance from others, this most ancient city—devoted to the Christian name from apostolic times and rescued from the superstitions of unbelievers by the word and preaching of the apostle Thaddaeus—endured the yoke of undeserved servitude. [Col. 0645B] In the same city, it is said, are buried the body of the blessed apostle Thomas, together with the bodies of the aforesaid apostle and the blessed king Abgar.

This is that distinguished ruler Abgar whose letter sent to the Lord Jesus Christ Eusebius of Caesarea affirms in his history, which he calls *Ecclesiastical*, and whom he shows worthy of the Lord’s reply, setting forth both letters and adding at the end: “We found these things thus copied in the public archives of the city of Edessa, in which the aforesaid Abgar then reigned, in those documents which contained the anciently preserved acts of King Abgar.” But enough of this; let us now return to the history.

## CHAPTER VI. The king acquires the castle beyond the Jordan called the Valley of Moses.

In the first year in which this Lord Baldwin began to reign, the Turks, aided and summoned by certain inhabitants of the region, had occupied one of our castles, called the Valley of Moses, in Sobal Syria beyond the Jordan. This town lies [Col. 0645D] near the waters of contradiction, where Moses, when the people of Israel cried out and fainted from thirst, brought forth streams from a rock, and the whole people and their beasts drank.

Learning that enemies held the aforesaid fortress after killing our men who were in it, the lord king, although still very young, gathered military forces from every side and set out thither. Crossing with his expedition the renowned valley in which the Dead Sea—also called Lake Asphaltites—now lies, he ascended the mountains of Arabia Secunda, called Petracene, in the borders of Moab. From there, traversing Sobal Syria, which is Arabia Tertia and is now commonly called the land of the Royal Mountain, they reached their appointed place.

When the native inhabitants of the region learned of our arrival, [Col. 0646A] they had withdrawn with wives and children into the fortress, relying upon the fortification of the place, since it seemed impregnable. Seeing the difficulty of the site and its invincible defence, our men spent several days in vain hurling stones, shooting arrows repeatedly, and using other means of attack; then they turned to other plans.

The entire region was planted with rich olive trees, so dense like thick woods that they shaded the whole surface of the land. From them the inhabitants of the region, like their forefathers, derived every means of subsistence; if they failed, all hope of life would altogether desert them. It was therefore decided to uproot and burn them, so that, at least terrified by this loss and despairing when their olive trees had been cut down, the inhabitants might surrender or expel the Turks who had taken refuge in the fortress and restore the castle to our men. [Col. 0646B] This plan did not lack a fruitful result. For as soon as they saw their beloved trees being cut down, they changed their plan and turned to other measures. On the terms that the Turks whom they had admitted should have a free and safe departure, and that their offence should not be held against them unto death, either for themselves or for their wives and children, they restored the castle to the lord king.

Having recovered the fortress, posted guards in it, and sent in an abundance of provisions and arms, the lord king, after completing the business which had occurred at the beginning of his reign, returned victorious and unharmed with his whole army to his own lands. [Col. 0646C]

## CHAPTER VII. Sanguin dies while besieging Calagenbar; his son Noradin succeeds him.

Meanwhile Sanguin, whom we mentioned above, after subduing the city of Edessa, was raised to such boundless pride by his success that he also began to besiege a fortified city situated above the waters of the Euphrates, called Calogenbar. While he persisted in this siege, the lord of the aforesaid city arranged with certain chamberlains and eunuch attendants of Sanguin that, one night, while he was inflamed with wine and lay on his back in his tent from excessive drunkenness, he should be stabbed with swords by those same household servants. [Col. 0646D]

Concerning him, when news of his death was received, one of our men said:

> What a good event! Sanguin becomes bloody through blood—
>  
> A murderous, guilty man, Sanguineus by name.

Those who killed him, received within the walls by agreement from the lord of the besieged city, escaped the avenging hands of the slain man’s kinsmen. His whole army also fled, deprived of its lord’s support and guidance. On his death, his sons succeeded him: one at Mosul, farther within the East; the other, the younger by birth, at Aleppo, named Noradin—a provident and discerning man, fearing God according to the superstitious traditions of his people, fortunate also and an enlarger of his paternal inheritance.

## CHAPTER VIII. A nobleman of Damascus, governor of the city of Bosra, makes an agreement with the king; the army of the kingdom hastens toward Bosra; Ainard, governor of the Damascenes, attempts to impede the undertaking.

[Col. 0647A]

Not long afterward, in the second year of Lord Baldwin’s reign, a noble Turkish satrap, suffering the displeasure of Mejeredim, king of the Damascenes, for certain reasons and deprived of the favour of his governor Mehenedin, who was also called Ainard—a man whose authority throughout all the territory of Damascus was much greater than that of the king himself—came to Jerusalem with an honourable retinue, to the lord king and his mother. He declared that, if the lord king would assign him honourable compensation sufficient in the judgment of a good man, he would surrender to the Christians the city of Bosra, over which he presided, together with the town of Selcath.

Bosra is the metropolis of Arabia Prima, now commonly called Bussereth. [Col. 0647B] This nobleman was said to have been Armenian by birth, tall in body and handsome in face, displaying manly courage in his whole bearing; his name was Tantais.

Accordingly, all the princes of the kingdom were summoned for this purpose. After the elements of the deliberation had been weighed with appropriate balance and the cause of so great a man’s arrival heard, all agreed by common counsel that the aforesaid man should receive honourable and suitable recompense, and that the armies should be summoned and expeditions sent toward the territory of Bosra. For they judged it a great and God-pleasing increase to the kingdom if, through this man’s agency, the aforesaid city could be added in perpetual right to the Christian faith and to our jurisdiction.

When terms had thus been drawn up in suitable agreement on both sides, all the people of the kingdom were summoned by herald’s proclamation. After imploring aid from above and taking with them the saving wood of the life-giving cross, the lord king and all the princes came as far as Tiberias, where they encamped near the bridge at which the waters of the Jordan divide from the sea. [Col. 0647C]

Now the aforesaid Ainard had previously entered into a treaty and temporary peace with the lord king, as also with his father. He therefore had to be formally warned, so that he might have the lawful period of truce customary in that region to prepare resistance, make ready, and summon an army; otherwise, if the lord king entered his territory in a hostile manner suddenly and before formal notice, he might seem to have acted against the law of the agreements.

Accordingly, messengers were sent to the same governor. While he, as a most sagacious man, deliberately delayed giving an answer, nearly a month passed. During that interval he did not cease, both by entreaty and by payment, to summon from far and wide all the neighbouring nobles of his people to his aid. When an exceedingly vast number had gathered from every side, he sent word to the lord king and the princes:

> You are preparing, contrary to the law of the treaty made, to enter the land of my lord and to protect by an unlawful patronage his servant, who is disobedient and acts contrary to the obligations of due fidelity. We humbly ask the lord king to desist from his unjust purpose and preserve inviolate the terms of the agreements previously made. We are prepared to repay in full all expenses which the lord king has incurred for this expedition.

To this the lord king, by common counsel, gave the following answer:

> We have no intention whatever of violating the terms of the agreements and treaty concluded. But because the aforesaid nobleman came to us in order to speak familiarly with us, we cannot, consistently with our honour, wholly fail a man who has placed hope in our kingdom. It will suffice us if we may introduce him without difficulty into the city which he has abandoned for our sake. After he has returned to his fortress, let his lord deal with him according to the laws of his country and bestow upon him rewards according to his deserts. For, whether in going or returning, we shall, God being our author, entirely refrain, as we are bound to do, from inflicting injury upon our friend the king of Damascus. [Col. 0648B]

This Ainard was a most prudent man and a friend of our people. He had three daughters: one he had given to the aforesaid king of Damascus, another to Noradin, son of Sanguin, and the third to an eminent knight named Manguarth. He therefore had charge of the kingdom, both because he was the king’s father-in-law and because he was a man of very great circumspection.

The king himself, however, was idle, drunken, and given to feasting; he devoted himself solely to pleasures and was wholly abandoned to lust. As we have said, Ainard endeavoured through every service in his power to earn the goodwill of our people, and the services by which friends are ordinarily acquired were not inactive in him. Whether this proceeded from his heart and the sincerity of affection, or whether necessity compelled him against his will, was debated among prudent persons. Either could indeed have been a cause. For he regarded his son-in-law Noradin, as formerly also Noradin’s father, with no small suspicion, fearing that he might remove from the kingdom the king—again his son-in-law, a wholly useless man and sunk in gross ignorance—and remove Ainard himself from the administration. [Col. 0648C] This was chiefly why, considering our goodwill necessary to himself, he strove by every means to obtain it.

The man seemed to possess a discerning spirit of foreknowledge, for what he feared came to pass. Immediately after his death, the aforesaid Noradin, with the assent of the Damascenes, violently expelled the ruler and seized the kingdom. Ainard therefore worked faithfully to ensure that the lord king, reimbursed for the expenses incurred in assembling the expedition, might return unharmed to his own lands. And doubtless he would have acted less hostilely toward the lord king and the Christian army in this affair if he had been able to restrain, at his own discretion, the foreign nations whom he had summoned. For in many affairs we have learned, by sure experience of events, many proofs of his sincere fidelity and steadfastness. [Col. 0648D]

## CHAPTER IX. The advancing army endures countless dangers.

But while the envoys reported these things—among whom was a leading familiar of the lord king, Bernard Vacher—the people began to cry out that Bernard was a traitor, and that no one who wished by discouragement to obstruct this undertaking was faithful to the Christian people. The undiscerning crowd also began to shout loudly that they must advance, that a city so noble ought not lightly to be abandoned, that thanks must be given to the nobleman and his proposal embraced faithfully and devoutly in all respects, since he had offered Christendom so memorable a benefit for all ages, and that they must fight for it even to the death.

Thus, amid so great an uproar, the opinion of the populace prevailed, and the counsel of those more soundly disposed was scorned. Having packed their baggage and struck camp, they directed their march toward the aforesaid town. After passing the hollow of Roob, [Col. 0649B] they reached the plain called Medan, where solemn annual fairs of Arabs and other eastern peoples were customarily held. There so great a multitude of enemies began to confront our men that those who had formerly cried that they must persist in their enterprise and proceed now preferred, if possible, to turn back and judged it more expedient.

Nevertheless, seeing the enemy’s formations and astonished by their multitude, our men armed themselves as though they were about to fight at once. By the advice of those experienced in military affairs, the king immediately ordered camp to be made. Once it had been arranged, attending as best they could in their constrained circumstances to bodily needs, they passed that night sleepless.

But the enemies, multiplied beyond number and surrounding our legions on every side, did not doubt that on the following day they would have our men in fetters as booty and cheap slaves. [Col. 0649C] Our men, however, wisely maintained themselves in continual watches and with all diligence performed around themselves the duties of brave men. At daybreak, after taking counsel, they determined to proceed, for returning seemed both full of dishonour and almost impossible. Yet the enemies stationed around them seemed to prevent either course.

At last, pressing on more courageously, our men opened a way with the sword through the midst of the enemy lines and advanced together toward their intended destination. But burdened with mail shirts, helmets, and shields, they went at a slow pace and were hindered by the surrounding multitude of enemies. Although the cavalry could have moved more easily, they had to keep pace with the companies of infantry, lest the column be broken up and the enemy be given an opportunity to charge their formations. [Col. 0649D]

The divisions therefore bore with one another, and the entire people were as one man in their resolve. The cavalry had such care for the ranks of foot soldiers that they themselves dismounted from their horses, shared their labour, offered themselves to the weary as transport, and made the hardship of the journey lighter. Meanwhile the enemy, wearying the army with continual flights of arrows, attempted through multiplied attacks to break up our companies. But the more importunately our men saw them press in this way, the more they did not fear to cling to one another and persist more ardently in the course they had undertaken.

[Col. 0650A] To increase the sum of their hardships, severe thirst was added, doubled by the difficulty of the labour and the heat of summer. Their route also passed through dry and waterless places, for the whole region has no springs; in winter, however, rainwater is customarily collected in natural and artificial pools. But in those days even these had become useless. For shortly before, an extraordinary plague of locusts had occurred in that province, and their decaying bodies had polluted all such pools, rendering the water’s use abominable by the rot they produced.

This region through which our men travelled is called Trachonitis, which Luke mentions in the Gospel, saying: “Philip, tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis” (Luke 3:1). [Col. 0650B] It seems to us to be named from the *trachones*. For *trachones* are hidden underground passages, with which the region abounds; nearly all its population lives in caves and caverns and has dwellings in the *trachones*.

## CHAPTER X. On reaching their intended destination, they find the city occupied by enemies; the enterprise fails, and a return is ordered.

After traversing that part of the region with extreme danger, they arrived at the place about the last hour of the day. It was formerly called Adratum, but is now commonly called the city [Col. 0650C] of Bernard de Stampis. It is one of the suffragan cities subject to the metropolis of Bosra. There, as the inhabitants of the place joined the enemy, the hardship threatening our men became greater. Moreover, from cisterns whose mouths they saw open, and from which our men thought they could draw water easily, they lost the buckets they had lowered, not without damage. For those hidden below in underground caverns cut the ropes to which the drawing devices were attached, then let back the ropes shortened. Thus, mocked in their hope of drink, our men were compelled to suffer still greater thirst while labouring long and fruitlessly to draw water.

For four continuous days, therefore, never granted rest, our men were relentlessly afflicted, scarcely having leisure at night to satisfy bodily necessities in whatever way they could. [Col. 0650D] The enemy increased in number day after day, while our own ranks diminished: some were killed; others mortally wounded; others, despairing of life and struck by excessive fear, swelled the crowd of baggage and impedimenta by hiding beneath horses and pack animals and feigning incapacity, lest they be compelled to go out and bear the burden of enemy assaults.

Indeed, the almost unceasing density of arrows and missiles above our army was so great that they fell like hail or rain, and men and beasts alike appeared covered with darts. Observers might wonder either that the enemy could shoot so much or that our men could sustain such a labour with such invincible endurance. Our men also pressed on with darts and flights of arrows; but because the enemy army had freer mobility, it was more rarely wounded by our arrows.

At length, on the fourth day, after continued marches amid so great danger, they drew near their destination and saw the city from afar. [Col. 0651A] There, after forcibly driving out the enemy with great difficulty, they took possession of water that trickled sparingly among the rocks and pitched camp around it. There, devoting themselves briefly to refreshment, they gave their bodies such relief as circumstances allowed.

That night, having such rest as they could, our men awaited the following day with the greatest longing. But behold: in the silence of deepest night, a certain man secretly left the aforesaid city, passed through the midst of the enemy lines, and came to our army bearing a grievous message. Immediately upon arrival, he asked to be admitted to the king, saying that he had more confidential words to convey. He was admitted; and when the princes had been summoned, together with the nobleman who had governed that city and had led us into the present dangers, he reported that the city had been delivered to the enemy through the betrayal of that nobleman’s wife, and that their troops, having been admitted, held all the citadels and the fortress, excluding everyone else. [Col. 0651B]

Our men were profoundly dismayed by this unhappy report and deliberated what must be done. At length it seemed more expedient to hasten a return home, whatever the danger. Yet certain of the greater princes of the realm advised the lord king privately, in his ear, to take with him the wood of the life-giving cross, mount the horse of Lord John Goman—which was said to surpass all the other horses of that army by far in speed and endurance—and provide alone for his own safety. They said this because they entirely despaired of return and feared the imminent slaughter of all.

The king, although still under age—thereby showing what he would be in maturity—rejected this advice with royal greatness, saying that he would wholly despise his own safety if a people so devoted to God should perish in so lamentable a disaster. [Col. 0651C] Seeing that the king would not comply with their advice, though it proceeded from concern for him, they turned to other plans and began to deliberate on returning, recognizing that they could not proceed farther without the destruction of all.
