Then, for the first time, when their great hope had been cast down and they saw all their efforts frustrated, their labour rose doubly more grievous. For although they had previously suffered things exceedingly harsh, almost intolerable, and no less severe than anything that might afterward happen, the hope and confidence of taking the city had warmed the spirits of those labouring and urged them with a kind of willing spur to endurance. Seeing themselves wholly disappointed in hope, they determined firmly and irrevocably upon what they had resolved, prepared for the journey, and announced the return to all by herald’s proclamation. [Col. 0651D]

## CHAPTER XI. The returning army suffers intolerable dangers; the enemy marvel at our men’s endurance.

[Col. 0652A]

When daylight was restored to the lands, behold, Noradin, summoned to assist his father-in-law, came from the aforesaid city, bringing with him innumerable bands of Turks, and joined the enemy forces. Our men, according to their intention, set out upon the road of return. Seeing this, their adversaries came rushing to meet them with clamorous cries, seeking to prevent their retreat.

But our men, made more courageous by the very difficulty pressing upon them from every side, broke up the opposing ranks with swords and steel and violently opened a way for themselves, amid utmost danger and slaughter of their own men. It had been publicly ordered among our men that the bodies of the dead should be placed upon camels and other beasts assigned to baggage, [Col. 0652B] lest the enemy, seeing our losses, be made stronger. The weak and wounded were likewise ordered to be put upon pack animals, lest any of our men be thought dead or infirm. They were also commanded to draw their swords, that they might at least present the appearance of men in health.

The wiser enemy leaders marvelled that, after so great a discharge of arrows, frequent battles, such thirst, dust, and excessive heat, no dead or weakened man was ever found. They judged the people to be made of iron, able to bear so many and such continual hardships with such perseverance. Seeing, however, that they made no progress in this manner, the enemies turned to other devices.

The whole region was covered with thorns and low brushwood, dry thistles and a wilderness of mustard, old stalks and ripe crops. [Col. 0652C] They set fire to all of it, while a wind blowing toward our men supplied the fuel and force. By the blast of the approaching fire and the very dense cloud of smoke coming against them, our men’s misery was doubled.

Then the whole people, with cries and lamentation, turned to the venerable Lord Robert, archbishop of Nazareth, who bore the Lord’s cross, and tearfully asked, saying:

> Pray for us, father; and by this wood of the life-giving cross which you carry in your hands, on which we believe the author of our salvation hung, rescue us from these evils, for we can endure no longer.

The people, like workmen in smithies when the wind stirs soot, had been blackened and discoloured both in face and throughout their bodily appearance. [Col. 0652D] Tormented beyond their strength by thirst, made double by the heat both of summer and of the fires, they laboured on.

At the voices of the groaning people, the man beloved by God, broken in heart and deeply compassionate in spirit, raised the saving wood against the fires which the enemy had kindled against them with all their strength. Calling upon aid from above, divine power immediately came; and in a moment the winds shifted to the opposite direction, and the fires, together with the foul darkness of smoke, turned upon the enemies who preceded our army. What they had prepared for our injury they saw redirected to their own destruction.

The enemy marvelled at the novelty of the miracle and regarded as singular the Christian faith, [Col. 0653A] which could obtain so prompt a benefit from its Lord God according to its desire. Occupied, therefore, with their own necessities, they allowed our men some respite and gave them time to recover their breath.

## CHAPTER XII. An envoy is sent to the enemy to seek peace; a certain noble enemy falls; the enemy army disperses; ours advances more freely.

While our army was being oppressed by these utterly intolerable evils, the leading men—distrusting the endurance of the common people, and being those of more practiced judgment—approached the king and persuaded him to send an embassy to Ainard, requesting peace on whatever terms, provided only that the army might return home. A certain man was chosen who was regarded with suspicion, because on another occasion, in a similar embassy, he was thought to have acted maliciously against the people of Christ. Nevertheless, because he was said to have an exceptionally ready command of the language, this task was again imposed upon him.

As he was being urged faithfully to carry out the office entrusted to him, he is reported to have said: “I am suspected unjustly and beyond my deserts. Yet I shall go; but if I am guilty of the crime alleged against me, may I never be permitted to return, unless I perish, pierced by the swords of the enemy.” Thus the wretched man pronounced a sentence of death upon himself, and immediately experienced the divine judgment; for before he reached the enemy and discharged the duty of his embassy, he died, pierced by enemy weapons.

Four renowned Arab princes, brothers, sons of the distinguished and eminent Arab satrap called Merel, had assembled for the same campaign with an innumerable host of their own men. While they were harassing our men more insistently from the flank by exceedingly insolent assaults, and our men did not dare to break out against them, because, if they broke ranks contrary to military discipline, they would incur a harsher sentence as deserters from their posts, one of the household of that Turk who was with us could not bear their arrogance. Wishing to repel their insult to our men, prodigal of his life and forgetful of the regulation laid down, he courageously spurred his horse and directed the spear he held in his hand against one of the four. Piercing him with the sword amid the ranks of his own force, he cast him lifeless to the ground, and immediately returned safe and unharmed to our army. [Col. 0653B–C]

An innumerable multitude then gathered around the dead man’s body. When they learned that the unhappy man had already breathed out his soul, they burst into lamentation and testified to the immensity of their grief by an abundance of tears. Our men, rejoicing, carefully inquired who had exposed himself to so great a danger, and whose deed, so remarkable, had deserved everlasting glory. When they learned that he was a foreigner and one who might be excused for being ignorant of the regulation—especially because, having no command of the language, he had not understood the public proclamation—they treated him mercifully, though there was no doubt that he had acted contrary to military discipline. They welcomed the man’s deed as commendable less for its reasoning than for its outcome.

The enemy formation on that side was therefore broken up; and our army, having freer space, exchanged the narrow confines it had endured for more open ground. After continuing the march for several days, it again reached the Cave of Roob. Because that place was narrow and could be dangerous for travelers, the princes deliberately ordered it to be avoided. The aforesaid Ainard, governor of Damascus, seeing that the king and his forces were hastening toward the said valley, sent messengers offering, if it pleased him, to have an honorable meal prepared for him beyond the Cave. He knew that the army had been suffering for several days from lack of provisions. Whether this offer proceeded from sincere goodwill or from deceit, intending to plunge our expedition into the constricted passages of dangerous valleys, we do not know with certainty. [Col. 0653D–0654B]

Yet it is commonly held that even the gifts of enemies are rightly regarded with suspicion. By general decree, therefore, they decided to proceed by the upper road, since it was flatter and less dangerous. And because they had no guide to lead the columns and knew the country through which they were to travel, suddenly there appeared before the companies an unknown soldier, mounted on a white horse, carrying a red banner, clothed in a cuirass with sleeves short to the elbows. He went before the army. Like an angel of the Lord of Hosts, following short routes and leading them to waters previously unknown, he taught them to encamp at suitable and convenient stopping places. Thus, although the expedition had scarcely reached the aforesaid Cave in five days, under this aforementioned guide and forerunner of the journey it traveled for three further days and reached Gadara. [Col. 0654B–C]

## CHAPTER XIII. Our legions reach Gadara; the place is described; and the army returns home.

Gadara is situated in the region called the Decapolis, of which the Gospel of Mark says: “Jesus, departing from the region of Tyre, came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, through the midst of the borders of Decapolis” (Mark 7:31). In it, as its name indicates, are ten cities: Hippos, Pella, Gadara, of which we are here speaking, and seven others. When the first of our legions arrived there—for it lies on the boundary between enemy territory and our own—the enemy again began, as though their evil had revived and their madness broken out anew, to rage around the rear formations. But seeing that they made no progress, and that our men had already crossed into their own territory, exhausted by smoke, excessive heat, and weariness, they broke up their formations and began to return homeward in groups. [Col. 0654C–D]

Our men likewise, after spending that night in a tranquility greater than usual, granting their bodies worn out by labor the rest due to them, reached the city of Tiberias on the following day. Those whose memory of the event still serves them more fully unanimously affirm that no one knew this guide of whom we have spoken. For when the time came for the army to encamp, he suddenly disappeared and was nowhere to be seen in the camp; yet in the morning he again went before the army.

No memory of men now living records that, during the time of the Latins, any expedition throughout the whole East was so perilous without an evident victory over the enemy. Therefore, when the lord king had returned to his kingdom and the Lord’s Cross had also been restored to Jerusalem, the people who had remained rejoiced at the return of their people, saying: “He was dead, and has come to life; he was lost, and has been found” (Luke 15:24). Afterwards, however, the same noble man was summoned by Ainard with peaceful words deceitfully offered, as though under the appearance of reconciliation, and was treated very cruelly. His eyes were torn out, and in extreme poverty and misery he was compelled miserably to end his unhappy life. [Col. 0655A]

## CHAPTER XIV. The citizens of Edessa summon the count; the count hastens there; and, while the enemy are unaware, he recovers the city.

[Col. 0655B]

While these things were occurring among us, a miserable event, worthy of being bound into writing, took place in the regions of Edessa. To understand it more fully, the narrative must be taken up somewhat further back. After the death of Sanguin, the greatest persecutor of the Christian name, his son Noradin was detained and occupied at Mosul by a dispute concerning succession to his father’s principality. The citizens of Edessa saw that only a few members of his household remained in the city, appointed to guard the forts, while all the remaining population professed the Christian faith. They secretly sent messengers to the aforesaid Count Joscelin, informing him that the city was empty of Turks except for the few who held the garrisons, and had been left to its citizens alone.

For the citizens of that city had been, and had been from the days of the apostles, rooted and grounded in the faith of Christ; so that, as was said elsewhere, scarcely anyone—or no one at all—of another profession lived among them. They also begged and urgently exhorted him by every means to gather military forces without delay and hasten to the city, so that, when its citizens delivered it to him, he might recover it without danger and without difficulty.

He therefore moved with all speed. Taking with him Lord Baldwin of Marash, a noble and powerful man, and all the cavalry and infantry forces of that region, he crossed the river suddenly and came unexpectedly by night with all his company to the aforesaid city. There, in the silence of the dead of night, while those appointed to watches were asleep, men were let in by ropes and ladders, in order that they might open the gates for the others waiting outside. When these had been opened and everyone had been admitted without distinction, they immediately ran through the city and put to the sword every enemy they encountered. Some of them nevertheless fled and, avoiding the danger of death, withdrew into the forts. [Col. 0655C–D]

Thus the count and the Christian army with him held the city in this manner for several days. Yet he was unable to take the forts, because they were supplied with provisions, arms, and soldiers and were more carefully fortified—especially as he had brought neither siege engines nor material from which they could be made, and could find none in the whole city.

## CHAPTER XV. Noradin arrives; besieging the city, he grievously presses our men.

[Col. 0656A]

Messengers were therefore sent to make known far and wide the success which had occurred and to invite the neighboring peoples to assistance, so that by their support they might hold permanently and preserve for Christian worship the city which, by the Lord’s favor, they had thus recovered. On hearing this, the Christian people everywhere rejoiced; and in proportion to the grief they had conceived at that city’s capture, they seemed to receive consolation in equal measure.

But grief follows joy at its utmost point: suddenly the harp was turned into mourning, and a renewed pain arose, worse than the former. For Noradin, hearing that the count had recovered the aforesaid city when its citizens surrendered it, gathered military forces from every part of the East and the peoples of neighboring cities, summoned together by public proclamation. He suddenly arrived and, arranging his legions around it, enclosed the city in a siege. Thus it was with our men, as it is written: “Outside, the sword; within, terror” (Deut. 32:25). The hostile battle-lines outside denied them an exit, prepared for battle, and threatened death; within, those who occupied the forts inside the city inspired terror and harassed them with continual attacks. [Col. 0656A–B]

Our men, amid so many straits, did not know what to do. They turned plans over in their minds and frequently changed their counsels; but whichever course of deliberation they adopted, they found nothing safe and no outcome free from danger of death. At last, given the circumstances of place and time, it appeared to all expedient that they must leave the city, whatever danger or risk of death might attend it. They did not doubt that it was better to attempt an engagement with the enemy and open a route by the sword for their safety than to endure the siege; for if it continued, either all alike would perish by the sword, or, compelled by lack of food, they would be handed over to the enemy’s chains and forced to undergo a harsh slavery worse than every kind of death. This counsel pleased all; and although exceedingly dangerous, when compared with worse possibilities, it was judged the shorter course.

When the citizens, through whose work and zeal the count and his men had been admitted, heard that every hope of resistance and way of safety had failed, they feared that if they remained in the city after the count’s departure they would be punished with a most grievous death, because they would seem to be the authors of this act. Taking their wives and children, they chose to depart with the Christian army and share their brothers’ uncertain fortune rather than die a death entirely certain, or endure under unbelieving enemies the yoke of a most cruel slavery, more dreadful than every kind of death. [Col. 0656C–D]

## CHAPTER XVI. The count departs with his men, seeking to return home; Noradin pursues; he destroys the army; the count escapes by flight.

The gates having been opened, all hastened competitively to leave, as though this were their singular remedy and only path to safety. Although they did not doubt that they would have to open a road through the middle of the enemy’s formations, they considered anything that might happen after leaving the city a lesser evil.

Meanwhile, some of the enemy, admitted into the city through an entrance opened by those who held the forts, pressed them more fiercely from the rear and compelled them to hasten their departure. Those outside, hearing that some of their own men had entered the city and were already fighting our men, wished to join them. They violently seized the gate which our men had opened for their own exit; and, gathering a huge crowd from every rank, they prevented the departure and strove also to enter the city. Thereupon a battle was fought there between the two sides, exceedingly dangerous to both, as far as the narrowness of the place allowed. [Col. 0657A]

At last, driven by the force of those pressing from within at close quarters, and with our men in that sector supplying strength and courage, they opened a path with the sword against the unwilling and fiercely resisting enemy outside, after great slaughter on either side, and poured into the open fields. There one could behold a sight both pitiable to see and full of groaning in the telling: an unarmed multitude; a civilian population unfit for war; old men; the sick; matrons with tender maidens; aged mothers with little children and infants at the breast. In the narrow spaces of the gates, some were trampled under horses’ feet; some, their passages for breathing blocked by the crushing crowd, were miserably suffocated; some perished beneath the unsparing swords of the enemy.

There were killed there nearly all the citizens of both sexes who had resolved to follow our departing army. Few escaped—those who by their own bodily strength or through the aid of horses could keep company with the retreating force. [Col. 0657B–C]

Noradin, seeing that our men were equipped for return, summoned his companies to pursue the departing force, drew up battle-lines, and arranged the formations. Pressing the retreating men from the rear in continual engagements, he pursued them. The route of our men lay toward the Euphrates, which was about fourteen miles from the aforesaid city. Throughout the whole journey the lord count and his army lacked neither unceasing battle nor unremitting danger: almost at every step there were conflicts, sometimes of many men, sometimes individual combats, in which many on both sides fell.

There died there the noble man mentioned above, distinguished in military exploits, Lord Baldwin of Marash. Many other commendable men, worthy of remembrance, also fell, whose names we do not possess. May their souls enjoy holy rest; yet it is certain that their names are inscribed in heaven, because they came to rest in a glorious end for the cause of the faith and for the liberty of the Christian people. At last the count, unequal in strength, with most of his men already lost and unable to endure the enemies’ constant attacks, sought safety for his life by flight. Having crossed the Euphrates, he withdrew to Samosata. Others dispersed in different directions, as seemed most expedient to each, abandoning baggage and equipment and preserving their lives and safety. [Col. 0657C–D]

The report of this event spread throughout all the lands of the wide surrounding regions. Those whom the rumor of Edessa’s recovery had earlier made happier were now saddened by a harsher disaster: its loss again, the slaughter of the nobles, and the destruction of the Christian people. [Col. 0658A]

## CHAPTER XVII. William, patriarch of Jerusalem, dies; Fulcher, archbishop of Tyre, succeeds him; and Ralph, the royal chancellor, is forced upon the Church of Tyre by royal violence.

At the same time Lord William of blessed memory, patriarch of Jerusalem, a simple man who feared God, entered the way of all flesh. He died on the fifth day before the Kalends of October [27 September], in the fifteenth year of his pontificate. In the following January, on the eighth day before the Kalends of February [25 January], Lord Fulcher, archbishop of Tyre, was appointed in his place, the third in the number of our predecessors.

At the same time, around the day of Epiphany, lightning sent from heaven struck with a dangerous blow the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre and Mount Sion, foretelling, as we believe, every misfortune and terrifying the whole city. A comet too was seen for many days, and certain other signs appeared contrary to custom, portending future events.

In those same days, when the Church of Tyre was vacant, it happened that the lord king and his mother—who held the care and the entire administration of the kingdom—the lord patriarch, who had been taken from that church, and the suffragan bishops of the same church, met in the aforesaid city in order to provide for the church. While they were discussing, according to custom, the election of a bishop, the electors’ desires, as often happens in such cases, divided into two parties. [Col. 0658A–C]

One party demanded that Lord Ralph, the king’s chancellor, be given to them: a learned man indeed, but excessively secular; English by nation, handsome in appearance, very acceptable to the king and queen and to all courtiers. The lord king and his mother were kindly disposed toward and supported this party. The others, led by John the Pisan, archdeacon of the same church, who afterwards became cardinal of the Roman Church of Saints Sylvester and Martin, together with Bernard, bishop of Sidon, and John, bishop of Beirut, followed the lord patriarch and did not wish Ralph to be promoted. Raising an appeal, they resisted by every means those who relied upon royal violence, having the lord patriarch as their protector.

But the aforesaid chancellor prevailed by force, seized the church and its possessions, and held them for two years. At length, when the case had been decided in the presence of both parties by the Roman pontiff, under the direction of Pope Eugenius, the chancellor’s act was annulled. Afterwards the same Ralph, with the favor of Pope Adrian, who was his fellow countryman, was received into the Church of Bethlehem and ordained bishop of that place. [Col. 0658C–D]

In the aforesaid metropolitan church, by the common consent and unanimous acquiescence of all, there was appointed Lord Peter, prior of the Church of the Lord’s Sepulchre: a man of remarkable simplicity and gentleness, fearing God and departing from evil, whose memory is in blessing before God and men. He was born in nearer Spain, in the city of Barcelona; noble according to the flesh, but nobler in spirit. His life and conduct require longer and more careful treatment. But history calls us back, that, omitting particular matters, we may discuss public affairs. [Col. 0659A]

## CHAPTER XVIII. The Western people are stirred up; and, to aid the Eastern Christians, Conrad, emperor of the Romans, and Louis, king of the Franks, set out with many other princes.

After the capture of Edessa, as we have said, the report of that deadly event sounded more fully in men’s memories. Throughout the whole West there spread again and again the news that the impious race of Turks, ranging with freer license not only through the aforesaid city but through the entire East, was laying waste the cities, towns, and boroughs of our people and afflicting the Christian population more than usual with battles and very frequent invasions.

There were men who spread such reports far and wide among peoples and nations, rousing provinces made sluggish and lax by long peace to avenge such great wrongs. Pope Eugenius III also, a man full of God, bore what was called a fatherly concern for the affliction of his Eastern children and felt a fuller compassion for them. He sent to various regions of the West religious men gifted in exhortatory speech, powerful in deed and word, to announce to peoples, tribes, and languages the intolerable sufferings of their Eastern brethren and encourage them to avenge such wrongs done to fraternal blood. [Col. 0659B–C]

Chief among them, selected to carry out this God-pleasing office, was Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, a man of immortal memory, a mirror of honorable conduct, of pious remembrance in the Lord and worthy in every respect to be embraced. A diligent executor of the ministry entrusted to him, taking with him fellow ministers beloved of God for the same work, he traveled energetically and without weariness—though physically weak, both because of approaching old age and because of almost continuous fasts and an exceedingly spare diet. He went through kingdoms and traveled through regions, everywhere preaching the kingdom of God. He carefully set forth the affliction of the people in the East and the sufferings under which they were incessantly oppressed. He vividly described cities of the faithful, formerly devoted to the Christian faith, enduring the yoke of persecutors of the Christian name and the harshest slavery.

He fully taught that brethren for whom Christ had willed to die had been consigned to chains and fetters, worn down by hunger, confined in the horrible prisons of dungeons, filthy with squalor, clothed in bitterness, sitting in want and irons. He invited men to their liberation and stirred them to repel the wrongs of their oppressed brethren. He promised that help from above would not fail those willing to undertake so pious a labor, and he promised them everlasting rewards with the elect. [Col. 0659C–0660A]

As he expounded these matters with pious perseverance among peoples, principalities, and kingdoms, he received the spontaneous favor alike of clergy and laity. Giving voluntary assent to his exhortations, they pledged themselves to journey toward Jerusalem, placed the sign of the life-giving Cross upon their shoulders, and made ready for the journey. Nor was this persuasive speech effective only among plebeian and popular crowds; it reached with no less effect the highest rulers of the world and those who seemed to administer the foremost summits of kingdoms.

For the most illustrious and powerful kings of the earth—namely Lord Conrad, emperor of the Romans, and Lord Louis, king of the Franks—together with many princes of both kingdoms, embraced the message with one vow and equal desire. With every devotion they impressed the saving sign of the life-giving Cross upon their necks and garments as a pledge of their future expedition. [Col. 0660A–B]

## CHAPTER XIX. The emperor goes ahead with his expedition and reaches Constantinople. The sultan of Iconium prepares ambushes against him.

Having arranged the state of their kingdoms under fitting governance, taking with them those who, stirred by the fervor of the same desire, were bound by salutary vows, and preparing what was necessary for the journey in a manner befitting royal dignity, they unanimously set out in May on their God-pleasing pilgrimage—but under ill-omened birds and a sinister omen. For they undertook the journey as though God were unwilling and angry with them. During that entire expedition, through the demands of our sins, they accomplished nothing pleasing to God; instead, they changed for the worse the condition of us whom they believed they would aid.

They decided to march separately and lead armies distinct from one another, so that disputes might not arise among peoples differing among themselves; so that they might more conveniently provide necessities of life for their legions; and so that fodder might not fail their horses and pack-animals assigned to burdens. Having crossed Bavaria and passed over the great River Danube at Regensburg, keeping the same river on their left, they descended into Austria; thence they entered the frontiers of the Hungarians, where they were honorably received by the lord king of that land. [Col. 0660B–D]

Having traversed the kingdom and crossed both Pannonias, they passed through the provinces of the Bulgarians—namely Moesia and inland Dacia—leaving Riparian Dacia on their left. Then, reaching Thrace and passing through the famous cities of Philippopolis and Adrianople, they arrived at the imperial city. There, after more familiar conference with Lord Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, and after the holidays necessary, it seemed, for the army’s recovery and rest after so many labors, they crossed the Hellespont, which washes that city and marks the boundary of Europe and the beginning of Asia. They encamped all their legions in the district of Chalcedon in Bithynia, the first of the Asian provinces encountered, from which the city they had left could be seen nearby.

This is Chalcedon, an ancient city where the holy fourth synod of six hundred and thirty-six Fathers assembled under the Lord Augustus Marcian and Lord Leo, Roman pontiff, against Eutyches, monk and abbot, who asserted that there was only one nature in the Lord Jesus Christ. [Col. 0660D–0661A]

Meanwhile the sultan of Iconium, hearing of the arrival of such great princes and having long regarded their entry with suspicion, summoned military auxiliaries from the farthest limits of the East. He anxiously considered how he might escape the threatening dangers posed by so great an enemy. He fortified cities, restored ruined works, implored the support of neighboring peoples, and with continual anxiety awaited the arrival of those whom he had heard described as robbers, expecting day by day the destruction of his people and the desolation of his homeland.

For it was said that a multitude unheard of for ages was coming, and that their cavalry covered the whole surface of the earth; that even the greatest rivers were insufficient for their drinking, and rich regions could not furnish them enough food. Though the report preceding the truth said more than was true, the actual state of affairs could, and deservedly did, inspire great terror in princes alien to the Christian faith. For, as those present on that expedition firmly affirm, in the retinue of the lord emperor alone there were seventy thousand armored men, besides infantry, children, women, and lightly armed cavalry. In the army of the lord king of the Franks, the number of valiant men wearing cuirasses was likewise reckoned at seventy thousand, apart from the second division. [Col. 0661A–C]

Had the Lord’s grace been merciful, favorable, and accompanying them, and had the Lord deigned to visit them with His good pleasure, they might have subjected not merely the sultan but all the provinces of the East to the Christian name. But by a hidden, though just, judgment the Lord rejected their service; He did not accept the offering which they perhaps presented with unworthy hands.

## CHAPTER XX. After crossing the Hellespont, Emperor Conrad is deceived by Greek malice; his army is led into exceedingly dangerous places.

[Col. 0661D]

Meanwhile Lord Emperor Conrad, having transported all his legions across the Bosporus, crossed the same Bosporus by ship, with a few very close princes, after receiving leave from the emperor. He ordered the army to begin its march, appointing one prince over each legion. Leaving Galatia, Paphlagonia, and both Pontus regions on the left, and Phrygia, Lydia, and Asia Minor on the right, he traveled through the middle of Bithynia. Keeping Nicomedia, the metropolis of that region, and Nicaea on his right—the latter being the place where, in the time of Lord Constantine, the synod of three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers met against the impious doctrines of unhappy Arius—he traversed the whole region.

Then, following the shorter road, the whole army in ordered formations reached Lycaonia, whose metropolis is Iconium. There the aforesaid sultan, having gathered military forces and a great multitude of Turks from neighboring regions, waited in readiness, that he might meet them at a favorable place and time as they passed and prevent their further advance. For he had urged every king, duke, and prince of whatever rank in those provinces, even to the farthest bounds of the East, by both entreaties and payment, to work our harm. He declared, and repeatedly insisted through messengers, that if free passage were granted to so great and heavily armed a multitude, it would follow that they would violently subject the whole East to their dominion. [Col. 0661D–0662A]

From both Armenias, Cappadocia, Isauria, Cilicia, Media, and Parthia, an infinite number of peoples rushed at his summons, and an unheard-of multitude gathered. Relying upon the aid of all these, he conceived hope that he could resist with equal forces the immense multitude which he had heard was arriving.

The emperor of Constantinople, when Emperor Conrad departed and requested it, had supplied him with guides familiar with the roads and possessing complete knowledge of the neighboring provinces, but possessing little faithfulness. These men were believed to have been assigned to lead the army in good faith, so that unwary troops might not encounter dangerous narrow places, or that legions following impassable routes might lack provisions. Once they had brought the columns into enemy territory, they instructed the commanders of the army to take enough food for a fixed number of days, during which they would have to pass through desert places in order to shorten the route. They firmly promised that, when the stated small number of days had elapsed, the army would reach the very famous city of Iconium and enter a most excellent region abounding in resources. [Col. 0662B–C]

Obeying their word, the troops loaded wagons, pack-animals, and every kind of vehicle with provisions and, in the simplicity of their hearts, trusted and followed their leaders. But the Greeks, employing their innate malice and led by their customary hatred of our people—whether by their lord’s command or bribed by enemy money—began deliberately and intentionally to lead the legions by detours and to bring them into places where the enemy would have greater ability to crush and overcome the unsuspecting people, and a much fuller opportunity would be provided for doing so. [Col. 0662C–D]

## CHAPTER XXI. Those whom the Greek emperor had given as guides to his army maliciously depart; and the emperor’s army is endangered.

The emperor, seeing that the stated number of days had already elapsed and that the expedition had not yet reached the desired and promised place, ordered the Greek road-guides to be summoned. Before his princes he began carefully to ask them why the army had now kept to the route begun for more days than they had originally specified, and had not reached the appointed place. Falling back upon their usual fabrications, they replied and confidently asserted that, with the Lord’s help, all the legions would reach Iconium within three days. The emperor, who was a simple man, was persuaded by these words and agreed to endure even this further three-day period patiently, trusting their promises.

On the following night, after the camp had been laid out in the customary manner and the rest, worn out with labor, gave their limbs to sleep, the aforesaid pestilent men fled secretly from the army in the silence of the dead of night. They left without a guide the people committed to their trust. When daylight returned and the time came for the army to set out, those who customarily led the columns could not be found. At last the fraud of the fugitives was reported to the emperor and the army’s princes, and their malice became known to all. [Col. 0662D–0663A]

To prolong their wrongdoing and add sin to sin, those sons of Belial hastened to the army of the king of the Franks, which was said to be nearby. They lied that the emperor, who had gone ahead relying on their guidance, had prospered in everything: that he had violently captured Iconium, razed it to the ground, and won a solemn triumph over the enemy. They seem, as we believe, to have made these assertions with the intention either of precipitating the king into the same danger and persuading him to follow the same road; or perhaps of preventing aid from being sent to endangered brethren, since their affairs were believed to be proceeding as desired; or perhaps they invented this tale so that, if they said the army had perished, they themselves might not be seized for punishment as traitors through whose crime the people had fallen.

Whatever their intention in saying it, it is certain that the army, deceived by their treachery, descended into the dangers of death in which it was destroyed. [Col. 0663B–C]

Seeing that the army was deprived of road-guides, the emperor assembled a council of all the princes to deliberate what should be done. Some said they should return; others that they should proceed. Such discord of opinion arose that one could truly say: “Contention was poured out upon princes, and the Lord made them wander in a trackless waste and not on a road” (Ps. 106:40 [Vulgate; 107:40 in many modern enumerations]).

While they thus wavered, ignorant of the country and anxious because provisions had failed—for fodder for horses and pack-animals and every sort of food for men had entirely run out—it was reported, and this was not far from the truth, that enemy battle-lines were stationed nearby and that an innumerable Turkish host was present. The army stood in a barren wilderness, far from cultivated land, precisely as it had been deliberately led there by the aforesaid deceivers. For instead of turning right through Lycaonia, by which their route should have run, and where they could easily have arrived sooner and possessed every abundance by following cultivated places, they kept to the left and compelled the whole army to wander into the deserts of Cappadocia, far from Iconium. [Col. 0663C–D]

It was publicly said—and did not greatly depart from likelihood—that these exceedingly dangerous machinations had been devised with the knowledge and by the command of the Greek emperor, who envied our advances. For the Greeks are said always to have regarded, and still to regard, every increase of our power, especially that of the Germans, as suspect, since they rival the empire. They take it ill that their king of the Romans calls himself emperor; for in this they think their own emperor is greatly diminished, whom they call *monarch*, that is, one who rules alone over all, as the unique and sole emperor of the Romans. [Col. 0664A]

## CHAPTER XXII. The Turks suddenly fall upon the German legions and cut them down; nevertheless, the emperor escapes.

Thus, while the army of the lord emperor was suffering from hunger, unfamiliarity with the country, the prolonged duration of its labours, the difficulty of the roads, the shortage of horses, and the weight of baggage, the Turkish satraps and officers of various ranks, having first summoned military auxiliaries for this very purpose, suddenly made a hostile attack upon their camp and, by their unexpected assault, threw the legions—who feared nothing of the sort—into confusion.

Relying upon swift horses, which lacked none of the necessities, and upon the lightness of their arms, namely bows and quivers, they filled the area around the camp with loud cries and, with their customary agility, launched dangerous attacks against our men, slow-moving and burdened with heavy armour. Our men, however, weighed down by breastplates, greaves, and shields, and possessing horses exhausted by hunger and the length of the journey and incapable of sustaining rapid charges, although superior in strength and military skill, nevertheless did not wish to range far from the camp either to pursue the enemy or to engage with them.

The enemy, on the contrary, rushing in bands, wounded their horses and riders from a distance by an innumerable shower of arrows, like hail, and inflicted the causes of death from afar; then, fleeing with the speed of their horses, they escaped the swords of our men when these tried to pursue them. Thus the army of our people, enclosed in a ring, was grievously and relentlessly pressed by flights of missiles and arrows even unto death; nor was there any opportunity to retaliate or to engage the enemy hand to hand, since they had no power at all to seize their adversaries.

Whenever the ranks of our men attempted to charge the enemy, the latter scattered their formations, evaded our efforts, and rode off in different directions. Again, when our men withdrew to their camp, they recalled their own companies and surrounded our army; pressing harder, they denied them rest as though they were under siege.

By the hidden but just judgment of God it happened that all the strength of so many princes—which formerly seemed incomparable in arms, physical power, courage, and numbers—was suddenly shattered and, harassed by a feeble warfare, collapsed, so that scarcely any trace of its former glory remained and scarcely a remnant of such great forces survived. For of seventy thousand armoured horsemen and so great a host of infantry, whose number was innumerable, scarcely a tenth part escaped, as those who were present assert: some having been killed by hunger, others by the sword, and still others reduced to captivity in the enemy’s chains.

Yet the lord emperor escaped with a few of his princes and, with the remnant of his men, though with extreme difficulty, made his way after several days to the region of Nicaea. The enemy, having gained the victory, laden with spoils and enriched with abundant treasure—made wealthy with horses and arms to satiety—withdrew to their own strongholds, knowing the country well, eagerly awaiting the arrival of the king of the Franks, who was said to have reached nearly the same region. They hoped that, since they had routed the greater forces of the lord emperor, they could much more easily prevail over the retinue of the lord king of France; and this indeed happened.

The sultan of Iconium did not take part in this great affair; rather, a certain distinguished commander of his army, a great Turkish satrap named Paramus, by the Lord’s permission, inflicted this blow beyond expectation.

This occurred in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1146, in the month of November.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The king of the Franks, having crossed the Hellespont, arrives with his legions at Nicaea in Bithynia; they confer with one another; the emperor returns to Constantinople.

Meanwhile the king of the Franks, following almost the same route with his army, had reached Constantinople. There, after holding private discussions for a short time with the emperor, he was dismissed by him with the highest honour and with a lavish bestowal of gifts; his own princes also were greatly honoured. Between the imperial city and the Pontic Sea, which is thirty miles from it, where the Hellespont is at its narrowest and is scarcely one mile wide, he crossed the sea with all his legions and entered Bithynia.

Having gone around the inlet of the sea which, from the adjoining city—the metropolis of that part of Bithynia—is called the Gulf of Nicomedia, and which is also part of the Bosporus or Hellespont, he pitched camp in the district of Nicaea, not far from Nicaea itself. There he considered which route to take and diligently sought news of the lord emperor, who had preceded him. And behold, it was reported that the lord emperor, having lost his army, had escaped as a wanderer and fugitive with a few princes.

At first the report was uncertain and arose without any definite author; but with the passage of time it became more certain. For, after a short interval, Duke Frederick of Swabia—a young man of admirable character, nephew of the lord emperor Conrad through his elder brother, and he who, succeeding his uncle Conrad, now governs the Roman Empire vigorously and prosperously—left the lord emperor’s camp and hastened to the army of the lord king of France. He reported more fully and certainly the same things which they had first received from an uncertain source.

He had come to invite the lord king to a conference with the aforesaid lord emperor, so that, though late, the route might be discussed by common counsel. When the peril and destruction of their brethren, and the adverse misfortune which had befallen the lord emperor, were heard, the whole army of the Franks was rightly disturbed and shared the sorrow in spirit. At length the king, moved by the duke’s words and having deliberated with his men, set out with a few of his princes, Frederick acting as guide, in order to speak with him. He arrived at the emperor’s camp, which the latter had pitched nearby.

After the proper words of greeting had been exchanged and the kiss of peace given, they held friendly discussions and resolved to pursue their purpose and advance together with their forces united. Many men from both armies, however—especially from the German camp—having lost their provisions and the supplies needed for the journey, and discouraged by the immensity of their labour, forgot their vows and returned to Constantinople.

After consulting the leading men of both armies, they left on their left the route which the emperor had previously followed and directed their columns towards Asia Minor, leaving both Phrygias on their right and Bithynia behind them. Marching now inland, now by the coastal route, they passed Philadelphia on their left and reached Smyrna, and thence Ephesus, the metropolis of that Asia, illustrious for the life, preaching, and tomb of John the Evangelist.

There at last the emperor, whether ashamed because he now had only a few men whereas formerly he had led very many, or unable to bear the arrogance of the Franks, or for other hidden reasons, sent what remained of his legions by land and himself sailed from Ephesus back to Constantinople. There he was received by the emperor much more honourably than on his first arrival, and remained with him, together with his princes, until the beginning of the following spring.

There was indeed a bond of kinship between them, for their wives were sisters, daughters of Berengar the Elder, Count of Sulzbach, a great and distinguished prince and one of the most powerful men in the German kingdom. Hence the emperor’s favour towards him was more abundant, and he was bound to show still greater generosity towards him and his followers, especially through the intercession of the empress.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The king of the Franks proceeds by another route and reaches Ephesus; Count Guy of Ponthieu dies there. The Franks cross the river Maeander despite the enemy.

Meanwhile the king of the Franks, greatly concerned about the route with his princes, was remaining at Ephesus in order to restore his army when Guy, Count of Ponthieu, a man distinguished and eminent in military achievements, fell ill and died. He was honourably buried there in the vestibule of the church.

The king then set out with his army and hurried eastward as best he could. A few days after leaving there, he reached the fords of the Maeander, friendly to swans. This is the river of which our Ovid says in the *Heroic Epistles*:

> Thus, when the fates call, cast down amid the wet grass,  
> the white swan sings beside the fords of the Maeander.

He pitched camp on its banks amid pleasantly green pastures. There the Franks were first granted the sight of enemies, as they wished; for when our men sought to approach the water, enemies in great numbers came to the bank from the opposite side of the river and forbade them the use of the water.

At last, having found fords, they crossed the river despite the enemy. The ranks of our men charged; they put many of the enemy to death, took many captive, drove them into flight, seized their camp together with rich spoils and all their equipment, and courageously secured the farther bank of the river for themselves. Having won this victory and been made happier by the enemy’s booty and plunder, they passed that night in peace. At dawn they again prepared for the journey and, arriving at Laodicea, a city of that region, took provisions for several days and, as usual, set out together.

## CHAPTER XXV. The army of the Franks is overthrown by a miserable mischance; the portion which had gone ahead escapes.

[Col. 0667B] A very steep mountain, difficult to ascend, confronted the army; according to the plan of the expedition, it was necessary to cross it that day. Now it was customary on campaign each day to appoint certain distinguished men to lead the columns and others to follow behind in order to protect the unarmed people, especially the bands of infantry; and with the princes they would arrange the manner of march, the day’s distance, and the site of the next day’s camp.

On that day, chosen by lot in his turn, a nobleman of Aquitaine named Geoffrey of Rançon was leading with the royal standard. When he had ascended the mountain with the vanguard and had taken position upon its summit, although it had been arranged beforehand that those who led should camp on the top of the mountain, he proposed to proceed a little farther. For it seemed to him that the army had advanced too little that day and that much of the day still remained. Thus, with guides going before and promising a more suitable place nearby, he began to proceed farther.

Those who followed, believing that the vanguard would camp on the summit of the mountain and thinking that little of the day’s assigned journey remained, began to follow the leaders very slowly and leisurely. Thus, some crossed the mountain while others were still delayed about it, and the army was divided.

When the enemy squadrons, watching the army from afar along its flank, saw this—they who were always ready to attack if they found an opportunity and who had especially followed the army without interruption—they seized their chance. Because of the narrowness of the terrain, and because the larger and stronger part of the expedition had gone ahead and was separated, they judged that they could neither easily learn the situation of those behind nor assist them in their distress. They occupied the mountain slope, in order to make the gulf between the vanguard and rearguard still greater; then, having drawn up their lines, they attacked our men. Before our men could seize their arms, the enemy violently broke up their ranks; and now attacking at close quarters not with arrows or bows but with swords, they brought warfare and death upon them, pressing more fiercely those preparing to flee.

The narrowness of the terrain hindered our men; their horses too had been weakened by the length and difficulty of the journey, and the great quantity of baggage presented a considerable obstacle. Yet they resisted together and with equal courage fought bravely for life, liberty, and their fellow travellers. They carried on the battle with swords and lances, encouraging one another by words and examples.

The enemy, on the other hand, encouraged their own men with the hope of victory, reminding them that a few days before, at far less risk, they had defeated forces much larger than these and had easily triumphed over opponents more numerous and far stronger. Thus they fought for a long time in a contest of doubtful and uncertain outcome. But at the end, our sins demanding it, the hand of the unbelievers prevailed; and our army was reduced to a small number, very many being killed and innumerable men taken captive.

There fell that day noble and illustrious men, singularly distinguished in military affairs and worthy of pious remembrance: the Count of Warenne, a man pre-eminent among the great; Galcher of Montjay; Evrard of Breteuil; Iter of Magnac; and many others whose names we do not possess, though we should believe them written in heaven, and their memory shall be in blessing for ever and ever.

On that day, disastrous to our men and marked by most adverse misfortune, the great glory of the Franks fell; their courage, hitherto feared by nations, was crushed and collapsed, becoming a mockery to the unclean and to those who do not know God, though it had formerly been a terror to them. Why is it, blessed Lord Jesus, that this people, so devoted to you, desiring to worship the footsteps of your feet and to kiss the venerable places which you consecrated by your bodily presence, suffered ruin at the hands of those who hate you? Truly, “your judgments are a great deep” (Psalm 35:7), and there is none who can attain to them. For you alone, Lord, are able to do all things, and none can resist your will.

## CHAPTER XXVI. The king escapes the disaster and joins those who had gone ahead; the remnant of the army reaches Attalia and sails thence to Syria.

Meanwhile the king, delivered from so great and confused a danger more by chance than by skill, climbed the slope of the often-mentioned neighbouring mountain. With a few companions in flight, without a guide, amid the silence of deep night, he made his way to the camp of his men, which had been pitched somewhat farther away.

Those who had gone ahead, following the royal standard, as we said, had passed the mountain’s narrow places without difficulty and had pitched camp in a sufficiently convenient place, no one opposing them. They were wholly ignorant and unaware of everything that had happened to those who followed. Yet the minds of those who had gone ahead foreboded that something adverse had occurred, once they saw the columns broken and such delay among those behind; matters were not proceeding as they wished.

But when those who escaped and came into camp with the king made them more certain of the disastrous event that had occurred, grief immediately seized all; sorrow and anguish took possession of every heart. While each, with mournful cries and tearful sighs, sought the relative whom he had lost, and, with grief multiplied, failed to find the one sought, the columns resounded with lamentation and the companies were worn down by groaning. There was no place in the camp untouched by private grief and domestic loss: one searched everywhere for his father, another for his lord; one woman for her son, another for her husband. Since they could not find what they sought, they passed the night sleepless beneath the weight of care, suspecting every worst thing that might befall the absent.

Yet during that night some men from both divisions returned, who, escaping the danger of death by hiding among thickets, rocks, and caves in the earth, protected by the benefit of darkness, joined themselves to the others and reached the camp more by chance than by prudence.

This happened in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1146, in the month of January. From that day bread and every kind of food entirely failed in the camp; for many days thereafter they could procure no provisions of any kind. Worse still, without a guide or advance leader, wandering now here, now there, and possessing no knowledge at all of the country, they roamed about.

At length, entering Pamphylia, they travelled through rugged mountains and down the slopes of valleys, with extreme difficulty but without an encounter with the enemy, until they reached Attalia, the metropolis of that region. Attalia is a city on the seashore, subject to the emperor of Constantinople. It has fertile land, yet land useless to its citizens; for enemies hem them in on every side and do not allow them leisure to cultivate the fields. Thus the land lies unproductive, because no one can secure its fruitfulness by tilling it.

Yet it possesses many other advantages and is usually a welcome place for guests: it produces clear and healthful waters, is planted with fruitful orchards, and enjoys a most pleasant site. It generally has abundant imported grain and goods carried by sea, and supplies travellers with adequate provisions. But because it lies very near the enemy and cannot continually endure their attacks, it has become tributary to them and thus conducts trade with the enemy for necessities.

Our people, unfamiliar with the Greek language, call it *Satalia*, corrupting the name. Hence the whole gulf of the sea from the promontory of Lissidona to the island of Cyprus is called the Attalian Gulf, commonly the Gulf of Satalia.

When the king of the Franks reached it with his men, the multitude converging there caused such a shortage of provisions that nearly the remnant of the army, especially the poor, would have perished there from hunger. The king himself, however, with his princes, leaving the infantry behind, hastily embarked. Leaving Isauria and Cilicia on the left and Cyprus on the right, carried by favourable winds, he entered the mouth of the river Orontes, which flows past Antioch—a place now called the port of Saint Symeon—near the ancient city of Seleucia and ten miles from Antioch.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Raymond, prince of Antioch, honourably receives the king of the Franks at the port of Saint Symeon; he leads him to Antioch, but in the end they part badly.

[Col. 0670A] When Raymond, prince of Antioch, heard that the king of the Franks had landed in his territories—an arrival which he had long awaited with desire—he summoned the nobles of the whole region and the leading men of the people. Meeting the king with a select retinue and showing him every reverence, he led him most magnificently into the city of Antioch, the whole clergy and people coming out to meet him.

Long before, upon hearing of the king’s coming, he had conceived the hope that with his aid he might enlarge the principality of Antioch. Therefore, even before the king undertook his journey, he had sent him honourable gifts to France and bestowed presents of great value in order to win his favour. He also placed confidence in the queen’s influence with the king. She had accompanied the king as his inseparable companion on the pilgrimage and was the niece of the same prince: the daughter of his elder brother, Count William of Poitiers.

To the king upon his arrival, as we have said, Raymond showed every kindness; nor did comparable care and works of exceptional generosity fail towards the nobles and princes who accompanied him. Anticipating all in honour, according as each man’s merits required, he treated them with full liberality.

He had indeed the greatest hope that, trusting to the king’s aid and strengthened by his forces, he could subdue to himself the neighbouring cities of Aleppo and Caesarea, together with some others. Nor would he have been disappointed in this hope if he had been able to persuade the king and his nobles to it. So great a fear of the king’s arrival had come upon our enemies that they seemed no longer merely to distrust their strength, but even to despair of life.

Accordingly, in a formal meeting held in the presence of both the king’s princes and his own, the prince laid before the lord king what he had conceived in his mind and had sometimes discussed with him more privately. He showed that his requests could be carried out without difficulty and were compatible alike with honour and advantage. But when he saw that he was making no progress, since the king had irrevocably resolved with ardent vows to go to Jerusalem, he was disappointed in his hope. Changing his purpose, he began openly to detest the king’s plans, to lay snares for him, and to arm himself for his injury.

He proposed to seize the king’s wife, who consented to this purpose and was one of the foolish women, either by force or by secret contrivances. As we have said, and as she later made clear by manifest signs both before and afterwards, she was an imprudent woman, neglecting the marital law contrary to royal dignity and forgetful of the fidelity of the marriage bed.

When this became known to the king, he forestalled the prince’s designs and, providing for his life and safety, hurried his journey by the advice of his magnates. He secretly left the city of Antioch with his men. Thus the excellent complexion of affairs was changed, and the end was unlike the beginning. He who had been received with such great glory when he arrived departed ingloriously when circumstances changed.

There are those who attribute these events to the king’s excessive wickedness and say that what happened befell him deservedly, because he did not grant the requests of so great a man, who had deserved so well both of him and of his followers. They especially assert confidently that, had he chosen to devote his effort to it, he could easily have gained one or more of the cities mentioned above.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. After the winter has passed, Emperor Conrad reaches Syria by sea; Count Anfossus also lands at Acre and dies at Caesarea.

[Col. 0671B] Meanwhile the lord emperor, after the winter had passed, was at the imperial city. There the emperor of Constantinople had carefully treated him, as the laws of courtesy required and as befitted so great a prince, and at his departure had laden him with most lavish gifts. Conveyed in the fleet which imperial magnificence had assigned to him, he reached the East with certain of his princes and came to the port of Acre.

Proceeding thence to Jerusalem, he was received into the holy city by Lord King Baldwin and Lord Patriarch Fulcher of blessed memory, the whole clergy and people meeting him outside the city with hymns and songs.

In those same days there also landed at the port of Acre a magnificent and illustrious man, Count Anfossus of Toulouse, son of the elder Count Raymond, who had been so great a prince and of such great merit in the first expedition. He was eminent in his own titles, but more illustrious through the pious memory of his father. While travelling thence towards Jerusalem, in order to give thanks to the Lord for the pilgrimage happily completed, he died at Caesarea, the maritime city, a few days after landing there, having been given poison, as is said, though the author of so great a crime was unknown.

The whole people had awaited with the greatest longing the arrival of this man of illustrious memory, hoping that by his coming he would bring to the kingdom the favourable and happy omen of his father.

## CHAPTER XXIX. The king of the Franks, having departed from Antioch, hastens to Jerusalem; the patriarch of Jerusalem is sent to meet him.

[Col. 0671D] Meanwhile it was reported at Jerusalem that the king of the Franks, having departed from Antioch, was approaching the region of Tripoli. Therefore, by common counsel of all the princes, Lord Fulcher, patriarch of Jerusalem of blessed memory, was sent to meet him, that by suitable exhortations and salutary admonitions he might draw him into the kingdom. They feared that he might delay his desire for Jerusalem either because the lord prince, restoring their favour in full, recalled him, or because the lord count of Tripoli, his kinsman, detained him.

For the whole eastern region of the Latins was divided into four principalities. The first, in the south, was the kingdom of Jerusalem, beginning at the stream between Byblos and Berytus, maritime cities of the province of Phoenicia, and ending in the desert beyond Darum, facing Egypt. The second, to the north, was the county of Tripoli, beginning at the aforesaid stream and ending at the stream between Maraclea and Valenia, likewise maritime cities. The third was the principality of Antioch, beginning at the same stream and extending westward as far as Tarsus in Cilicia. The fourth was the county of Edessa, extending eastward beyond the Euphrates from the forest called Marrim.

All these great and powerful men had from the beginning hoped that, through the efforts and assistance of the aforesaid kings at their arrival, they might enlarge their territories and extend their boundaries without measure. For they had as neighbours many most savage enemies and hated enemy cities, which they desired to annex. They were therefore very anxious about the care of their own households and the increase of their domains. Thus each invited the kings to himself with messengers and gifts, wishing to forestall the others.

Among them the lord king and those in the kingdom seemed to entertain the greater hope for themselves, both because of the reverence due to the venerable places, whose love and devotion drew all men more strongly, and because they had the lord emperor among them. It was credible that the lord king of the Franks would come to him, both for the sake of completing his prayers and pilgrimage and in order that, by common counsel, they might undertake some work for the increase of Christianity.

Therefore the lord patriarch was sent, as we have said, by the princes of the kingdom. They greatly feared that the lord prince, whose relative the king was and to whom he seemed joined by a closer bond of affection, especially through the queen’s intervention, would detain him in the region of Aleppo, as indeed appeared likely. But when they learned that the two had parted on unfriendly terms, their hope increased that the king would leave there without delay and arrive at Jerusalem.

Nevertheless, against the snares of fortune, and because whatever can happen is prudently feared, they sent ahead the venerable patriarch, whose authority might influence him. Nor were they disappointed in their hope; for, following his word, the king came to Jerusalem without delay. Upon his arrival, the whole clergy and people, together with his princes, came out to meet him. With hymns and songs he was honourably received into the city with due splendour and conducted to the venerable places.

At last, when the customary prayers had been completed, a general council was proclaimed at the city of Acre, in order to deliberate upon the result of so great a pilgrimage, the end of such great labours, and the desired enlargement of the kingdom. Finally, on the appointed day, they assembled at the designated place as arranged and began more carefully to deliberate, together with the magnates of our kingdom, who had fuller knowledge of the circumstances and places, what course would be most advantageous.

# THE SEVENTEENTH BOOK BEGINS.

[Col. 0673]

## CHAPTER I. A general council is held at the maritime city of Ptolemais, and the princes who assembled there are named.

[Col. 0673A] We believe it worthy, and quite fitting for the present history, that the memory of the princes who attended the aforesaid council, having assembled from so many regions, should be handed down to posterity.

First there attended Lord Conrad, of illustrious memory, king of the Germans and emperor of the Romans. Of his ecclesiastical princes there were Lord Otto, bishop of Freising, his learned brother; Lord Stephen, bishop of Metz; Lord Henry, brother of Count Theodoric of Flanders, bishop of Toul; and Lord Theodwin, a German by nation, bishop of Porto and legate of the Apostolic See, who had followed the camp of the same lord emperor by command of Pope Eugenius.

Of the laymen there were Lord Henry, duke of Austria, brother of the same emperor; Lord Duke Welf, an illustrious and powerful man; Lord Frederick, illustrious duke of the Swabians and Vindelicians, nephew of the same lord emperor through his elder brother, a young man of exceptional character, who later succeeded him and now governs the Roman Empire vigorously and courageously; Lord Herman, margrave of the province of Verona; Lord Berthold of Andechs, who afterwards became duke of Bavaria; Lord William, margrave of Montferrat, brother-in-law of the same lord emperor; and Count Guy of Biandrate, who had as wife the sister of the aforesaid margrave. Both were from Lombardy, great and distinguished princes. There were also several other noble and notable men whose names or titles we do not possess.

There attended the most pious Lord Louis, king of the Franks, of illustrious memory in the Lord; with him Lord Geoffrey, bishop of Langres; Lord Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux; Lord Guy of Florence, priest-cardinal of the Roman Church, of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, legate of the Apostolic See; Lord Robert, count of Perche, brother of the same lord king; Lord Henry, son of the elder Count Theobald, count of Troyes, son-in-law of the same lord king, a young man of distinguished character; Lord Theodoric, magnificent count of Flanders and brother-in-law of the king of Jerusalem; and Lord Ivo of Nesle of Soissons, a faithful and prudent man. There were also many other noble, powerful, and memorable men, whose names we deliberately pass over to avoid prolixity.

From our own regions there were present Lord Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, a young man of illustrious character; with him his mother, a prudent and circumspect woman, possessing a manly heart and inferior in wisdom to no prince, however judicious; and with them Lord Fulcher, patriarch; Lord Baldwin, archbishop of Caesarea; Lord Robert, archbishop of Nazareth; Lord Rorgo, bishop of Acre; Lord Bernard, bishop of Sidon; Lord William, bishop of Berytus; Lord Adam, bishop of Paneas; Lord Gerald, bishop of Bethlehem; Robert, master of the military order of the Temple; and Raymond, master of the house of the Hospital.

Of the laymen there were Manasses, the king’s constable; Philip of Naples; Helinand of Tiberias; Gerard of Sidon; Walter of Caesarea; Pagan, lord of the region beyond the Jordan; Balian the elder; Humphrey of Toron; Guy of Berytus; and many others, whom it would be far too long to enumerate individually.

All these, as we have said, had assembled at Acre in order to determine what seemed best and most suitable to place and time, and what, with the Lord as author, they should first undertake for the enlargement of the kingdom and the glory of the Christian name.

## CHAPTER II. They propose to besiege the city of Damascus and approach it according to agreement.

Having carefully considered the matter, after the various counsels of different parties had been put forward, as usually happens in such affairs, it seemed more expedient by common counsel to besiege Damascus, a city harmful to our people. When the decision had been confirmed, a public proclamation was ordered, requiring all men to be ready on the appointed day, united in purpose, to direct their forces towards those regions.

Accordingly, in the month of May, on the twenty-fifth day of that month, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1147, military forces of cavalry and infantry from the whole kingdom, both natives and pilgrims, having been assembled, the aforesaid God-beloved kings, with their expeditions and preceded by the saving wood of the life-giving cross, arrived by agreement at the city of Tiberias.

From there, taking shorter routes, they led all the armies along the Sea of Galilee as far as Paneas, which is Caesarea Philippi. There, after deliberating with those who knew the site of Damascus and the adjoining region, and consulting the greater princes, they judged it more useful to surround the aforesaid city with a siege in such a way as first to occupy the orchards, which almost entirely encircle the city and seem to provide it with very great protection. They thought that once the orchards were occupied, it would thereafter be quite easy to take the city.

Accordingly, undertaking the route agreed upon, they crossed the most famous Mount Lebanon, which lies between Caesarea Philippi and Damascus itself, and descended into the territory of Damascus at a village named Daria, four or five miles from the city. From there the whole city and the adjoining region could be seen spread out below.

## CHAPTER III. The site of the city of Damascus is described.

Damascus is a very great city of Lesser Syria, the metropolis which is also called Phoenice Libanensis, as is written there: “Damascus is the head of Syria” (Isa. 7:8). It was named after a certain servant of Abraham, who is believed to have founded it. Its name is interpreted “bloody” or “blood-stained.” It lies on level ground, in a barren and arid territory, except insofar as it is irrigated by waters conveyed through ancient channels. For a river descending from a neighboring promontory [Col. 0675B] is, in the upper parts of that region, received into canals, so that it may more freely be led across the plain. It is directed through various parts of the surrounding country to make the barrenness of the fields fruitful; and what remains, since it has abundant waters, nourishes orchards planted with fruit-bearing trees on both banks, and flows eastward beside the city wall.

When the aforesaid kings reached the previously named place, namely Daria, with the city now close at hand, they drew up their battle lines and assigned an order of march to the legions, lest, advancing in disorder, they stir up quarrels among themselves and hinder the work to come. Thus the king of Jerusalem, with his forces, was commanded by the common decision of the princes to go first—especially because his companies were said to possess knowledge of the localities [Col. 0675C]—and to open the way for those following. The king of the Franks, with his expeditionary forces, was ordered to hold the second and middle position, so that, should necessity arise, he might bring assistance to those ahead. By the same decree the emperor was commanded to maintain the third and last position, so that he might be prepared to resist the enemy should they attack from the rear, and make the troops before him safer on the side left behind.

Accordingly, with these three armies suitably arranged in order, they moved their camp toward the city, striving to approach it. On its western side, from which our men approached, and on its northern side, the city was planted far and wide with orchards, like dense groves and shady forests, so that they extended for more than five [Col. 0675D] miles toward Lebanon. Moreover, so that ownership might not perhaps be uncertain, and so that persons might not be free to enter everywhere at will, these orchards were enclosed by a wall, though one of mud; for that region did not abound in stones. They were thus enclosed, and, according to the property assigned to each owner, surrounded with such a wall, while paths and public roads were left open, though narrow ones, by which gardeners and those responsible for the orchards could reach the city with their beasts of burden carrying fruit.

These orchards were the city’s chief defense; for because of their density and abundance of trees, and the narrowness of the roads, it seemed difficult and almost impossible for persons wishing to approach the city to pass through on that side. Nevertheless, from the beginning our princes had resolved to lead the army through these places [Col. 0676A] and open a route to the city, for two reasons: first, so that, after the stronger places and those in which the people of Damascus had greatest confidence had been occupied, what remained might seem easy and be accomplished more readily; secondly, so that the expeditionary forces should not lack the advantage of fruit and water.

Therefore the king of Jerusalem first sent his battle lines through the narrower paths of the orchards. But the army could scarcely advance, and only with great difficulty: impeded both by the narrowness of the roads; harassed by the ambushes of those hiding in the thickets; and also engaged in open conflict with enemies who held the entrances and had occupied the bends of the roads. Indeed, the whole population of the city had gone out together and descended into the aforesaid orchards, to prevent the army from passing by both concealed and [Col. 0676B] open attacks.

Moreover, within the enclosures of the orchards stood lofty and elevated houses, which their neighboring owners had fortified with men ready to fight. From these, by arrows and the discharge of other missiles, they defended the orchard enclosures, allowing no one to approach; and they made the public road, for those wishing to pass along it, extremely dangerous from afar with their arrows. Nor did these fearful ambushes threaten our men from one side alone; danger was equal on every side for the unwary, and the peril of an unforeseen death was equally to be feared.

There were also men hidden inside along the walls with lances. Through small openings, carefully arranged for that purpose in the walls [Col. 0676C], from which they could see passers-by but could not themselves be seen, they stabbed those going past in the side. In this way very many are said to have perished miserably that day. Nor were countless other kinds of danger lacking for those wishing to pass through those narrow ways.

## CHAPTER IV. Our men violently break into the city’s orchards and seize the river by force despite the enemy. A remarkable and admirable deed of the emperor is described.

Understanding this, our men pressed more fiercely. Having violently broken open the orchard enclosures, they eagerly occupied the orchards; and those whom they found within the boundaries or in houses of this kind they ran through with swords, or cast into chains as captives. When those who had gone out for the same purpose heard this, fearing to perish by the example of the others, they abandoned the orchards and withdrew in bands into the city. Thus, when they had been put to flight or slain by the sword, a free passage to the ground ahead lay open to our men.

The cavalry forces, both of the citizens and of those who had come to their aid, understood that our army would approach to besiege the city from those parts. They therefore came to the river which flows past the city, intending with bows and crossbows to keep the expeditionary forces—wearied by the march and suffering from the distress of thirst—away from the stream, and to deny the thirsty the indispensable benefit of water. But our men, to relieve the thirst which they had acquired from the hardship of their toil and from the dense cloud of dust stirred up by the feet of horses and men [Col. 0677A], hastened to the river they had heard was nearby. When they saw so great a multitude of enemies along its bank, they paused briefly. At last, gathering their strength, with necessity supplying strength and boldness, they tried once and again, though in vain, to claim the water for themselves.

While the king of Jerusalem with his men labored greatly and to no purpose over this matter, it was reported to the lord emperor, who commanded the rear columns, when he asked why the army was not advancing, that the enemy, holding the river, would not allow our men to approach. When he learned this, inflamed with anger, he quickly came with his princes through the midst of the king of the Franks’ battle lines to the conflict of those contending for the river [Col. 0677B]. There he and his men dismounted and became infantry—as is the custom of the Germans to conduct military affairs in extremities of greatest need. With shields set before them, they fought hand-to-hand with swords against the enemy. Unable to withstand their attack, though they had previously resisted stoutly, the enemy took flight, abandoned the river, and withdrew into the city with utmost speed.

In this encounter, an act of the lord emperor memorable through the ages is said to have occurred.
