With one stroke, he is said to have cut off from one of the resisting men, who fought manfully and vigorously, though armored, his head and neck together with the left shoulder and attached arm, and also part of the adjoining side. This deed cast the citizens—both those who saw it and those who learned of it from the report of others [Col. 0677C]—into such terror that they utterly despaired both of resistance and of life.

## CHAPTER V. The citizens despair and consider flight; they corrupt certain of our princes with money, and by their persuasion the army is transferred to the opposite side of the city.

Once the river had been gained and the bank granted freely to them, they encamped far and wide beside the city; and they enjoyed at will both the orchards, taken by force, and the advantage of the river. The citizens, therefore, astounded at both the number and the prowess of our army, began to lose confidence in their own strength, as though unable to resist. Fearing sudden incursions by our men, they considered nothing safe, recalling what sort of men they had found them in the previous day’s engagements.

Having taken counsel, they employed the resourcefulness which commonly attends wretched and afflicted circumstances. Resorting to their final devices, they interwove all the streets of the city on the side where our men had pitched camp with great and tall beams. Their sole hope was that, while our men labored to break such barriers, they themselves might escape by the opposite side with their wives and children. It seemed quite plain, if the Divinity were favorable to us, that the Christian people would soon possess the city. But otherwise seemed good to him who is “terrible in his counsels toward the children of men” (Ps. 65:4). For while, as we have said [Col. 0678A], the city was in dire straits and its citizens had no hope either of resistance or safety, but were preparing their baggage to depart from the place, our sins demanding it, they began to presume upon the greed of our men. By means of money they undertook to overcome the minds of men whose bodies they doubted they could conquer. Applying all their concern to various schemes, they persuaded certain princes, by money promised and bestowed in infinite quantity, to use their zeal and efforts to raise the siege, thus to perform the office of Judas the traitor.

These men, corrupted by what was given and promised, and following greed, the fuel of every vice, descended to such wickedness that by impious suggestions they persuaded the kings and foreign princes, who trusted in their loyalty and judgment [Col. 0678B], to abandon the orchards and transfer their forces to the opposite side of the city. To conceal the deceit under some pretext, they alleged that on the opposite side of the city, which faces south and east, there were no orchards that strengthened the city; nor was access to assault the wall obstructed by ditch or river. They also asserted that the wall was low and built of unbaked bricks, scarcely capable of withstanding the first attacks. There, they said, neither engines nor great exertion were needed: at the first encounters the wall could immediately be thrown down by hand, and it would not be difficult to burst into the city.

But their sole intention was to remove the army from the side [Col. 0678C] where it was stationed and where the city was most severely pressed and could not long endure, knowing that it could not remain and continue the siege on the opposite side. The kings themselves, therefore, and the leaders of the whole army believed them. Abandoning the places which they had occupied with much labor and the great slaughter of their own men, they transferred all the legions and encamped on the opposite side of the city, with the deceivers leading the way. There, seeing themselves far removed from the advantage of water, deprived also of the abundance of fruit, and with provisions now wholly failing, they complained, though too late, that deceit had intervened and that they had been maliciously transferred from fertile places.

## CHAPTER VI. Provisions fail in our camp; the treachery of the traitors is exposed; our men lift the siege and return.

[Col. 0678D]

Thus provisions failed in the camp. For, in the hope of taking the city swiftly, as they had been persuaded before setting out, they had brought food sufficient for only a few days—especially the foreigners, who could not much be blamed, since they were unfamiliar with the country. They had indeed been persuaded that they would take the city at the first attacks, immediately and without difficulty; and they maintained that, meanwhile, even if every other supply of food were entirely lacking, the nourishment provided by fruits freely available would be sufficient to feed a great army.

What, then, were they to do in their uncertainty? They deliberated both privately and publicly. To return to the places from which they had come seemed harsh and impossible. For as soon as our men left, the enemy, seeing that what they had desired had been accomplished [Col. 0679A], occupied those same places much more strongly than before and fortified the routes by which our men had formerly entered. They obstructed them with beams and great masses and stationed an innumerable body of archers to keep would-be entrants from the approaches. On the other hand, to attack the city from the side on which they had established camp seemed to require delay, but the lack of provisions allowed no prolonged respite.

Therefore the foreign princes conferred together. Seeing the manifest malice of those to whose loyalty they had entrusted their lives and affairs, and knowing that they would gain nothing, they resolved that they must return, detesting the deceits of those who had led them astray. Thus the kings and princes, greater in number than we read of having assembled in any age, clothed in shame and disgrace, compelled by our sins to return with the enterprise unfinished, went back into the kingdom by the same route through which they had come [Col. 0679B]. Thereafter, not only for as long as they remained in the East did they regard all the counsels of our princes with suspicion and, deservedly, avoid them as excessively malicious, showing themselves lukewarm in affairs of the kingdom; but, after they were permitted to return to their own regions, they remained forever mindful of the injuries they had suffered and abhorred the wickedness of those same princes. Nor did they make only themselves less ready to love the kingdom; they also made others who had not been present less willing. Consequently, thereafter neither so many nor men so fervent undertook the journey of this pilgrimage; and even those who arrived, unwilling to be ensnared by their frauds [Col. 0679C], strive even today to return home sooner.

## CHAPTER VII. Various opinions are given concerning who was responsible for so great a treachery. They again propose to besiege Ascalon, but accomplish nothing.

I remember that I often asked prudent men, especially those in whom a reliable memory of that time still survived, what had been the cause of so great an evil, who had been the authors of so great a crime, and how such a detestable design could have been brought to completion—chiefly so that I might commit what I learned to the present history. But in assigning the cause I found conflicting accounts. For some held the opinion that a certain act of the count of Flanders had given occasion to this evil. He, as we have said before, was in that army. After our legions had come to the aforesaid city, and the orchards and river had been forcibly secured and the city was now besieged, he is said to have approached each king separately and privately and, with lavish prayers, asked that the city, once taken, be given to him. This too, it is said, he obtained.

When certain nobles of our kingdom heard it, with some others agreeing with them, they were indignant that so great a prince—one for whom his own resources could suffice and who seemed to serve the Lord without payment—should demand that so great a portion of the kingdom be given to him. For they hoped that whatever increase came to the kingdom through the work and labor of these princes would accrue to themselves. Therefore, in their indignation, they descended to such a criminal offense that they preferred to preserve the city for the enemy rather than let it fall to the lot of the aforesaid count [Col. 0680A]. For it seemed wholly intolerable to them that those who had served the kingdom throughout their lives and borne countless hardships should be neglected and left without hope of reward, while others, newly arrived, gathered the fruits of such great labors—fruits which the former seemed by long service and merit to have earned.

Others say that the prince of Antioch, angered that the king of France had passed through his territory in such a manner and, forgetful of his favors, had assisted him in nothing, gave instructions to certain princes in the army and secured their cooperation, in order that by their means the king’s undertaking might not attain its desired end and that they might arrange matters so that he would be compelled to return ingloriously with the enterprise unfinished. Others say that absolutely nothing else intervened except that those who procured so great an evil were bought by the enemy with limitless money. They are accustomed to recount as a supreme miracle that afterward all that ill-gotten money was found to be counterfeit and wholly worthless [Col. 0680B]. Who the ministers of so detestable a crime were was likewise a matter of varied opinion among many people, but it has not been established to my certain knowledge. Whoever they are, let them know that one day they shall receive rewards worthy of their deeds, unless the merciful Lord graciously spares those who make fitting satisfaction.

Thus, as we have said, our men returned without glory. Damascus rejoiced at their departure, because fear of them had fallen upon its people; but for our men, on the contrary, “the harp was turned into mourning, and we became the song of our enemies all the day” (Job 30:31). The aforesaid kings, having returned to the kingdom, again summoned an assembly of nobles and attempted—though vainly—to undertake some deed by which they might make their memory praiseworthy to posterity. There were some who urged that a siege should be laid around Ascalon, which was still held by the unbelieving people. It lay, as it were, in the middle of the kingdom, and every necessary supply could be carried there without difficulty. They declared that it would be easy and readily achievable to restore it to Christian worship. But after many such words, this plan too suffered miscarriage like the aforementioned design, and while it was still being begun [Col. 0680D], it was cut short. For the Lord, in his anger, seemed to frustrate all their endeavors.

## CHAPTER VIII. Emperor Conrad returns home, while the king of France remains in Syria.

The lord emperor Conrad, seeing that the Lord had withdrawn his favor from him and that he was prevented from advancing in the affairs of the kingdom, prepared a ship, took leave, and returned to his own realm. Having arrived there, he died within a few years at Bauenberg, where he was splendidly buried in the principal church: a devout and merciful man, distinguished in person, eminent in noble birth, thoroughly experienced in military affairs, and in life and character altogether praiseworthy, whose memory “is in blessing” [Col. 0681A].

He was succeeded in the Empire by the lord Frederick, illustrious duke of Swabia, his nephew through his elder brother—of whom we have made mention above—a young man of eminent promise who had remained inseparably attached to him as companion in that pilgrimage. He now administers the Roman Empire vigorously and successfully.

The lord king of France, after spending the course of one year among us, returned to his own country with his wife and princes around the spring crossing, having celebrated Easter at Jerusalem. On arriving there, mindful of the injuries which his wife had inflicted upon him on the journey and throughout the course of the pilgrimage, he solemnly obtained a divorce from her in the presence of the bishops of his kingdom, alleging the ground of consanguinity. Without delay Henry, duke of Normandy and count of Anjou, married her before she had returned to her Aquitaine, her paternal inheritance [Col. 0681B]. Immediately after marrying her, he succeeded to the kingdom upon the death of Stephen, king of the English, who had died without children of the better sex. The lord king of France, more fortunate in his second marriage, joined to himself in matrimony the daughter of the emperor of the Spains, named Maria, a maiden pleasing to God and commendable for her character and holy life.

## CHAPTER IX. Nur al-Din enters the territory of Antioch; Prince Raymond meets him; they fight. Prince Raymond is killed.

From that day the condition of the Latins of the East began manifestly to worsen. For our enemies saw the greatest princes and kings among our people, who seemed to be the firmest foundations of the Christian people; they mocked at fruitless labors, endeavors without result, strength exhausted, and glory broken. Those whose names alone had formerly inspired fear in our enemies were now despised in person without loss. Hence the enemy rose to such presumption and boldness that thereafter they neither regarded the strength of these rulers with apprehension nor feared to press our men more fiercely than usual.

For this reason, immediately after the departure of both kings, Nur al-Din, son of Sanguin, whom we have mentioned above, summoned an innumerable host of Turks from all the East and began to rage more insolently than usual in the region of Antioch [Col. 0681D]. Seeing that the land of the Latin princes was deprived of assistance, he also laid siege to a castle named Nepa.

When this became fully known to the lord Raymond, prince of Antioch, he acted as a spirited and impetuous man, not guided by another’s counsel in such matters. Without waiting for the company of his knights, whom he had ordered to be summoned, he rashly hurried to those parts with a few men and found Nur al-Din still persisting in the siege around the aforesaid fortress. Hearing that the prince was coming, Nur al-Din feared that he might bring larger forces with him. Afraid to wait and engage him, he withdrew from the siege, moved to a safe place, and waited, wishing by frequent messengers to learn more fully what support the prince had brought with him [Col. 0682A] and whether greater aid would arrive.

But the prince, elated by his present success and, as was his habit, presuming too much upon himself, began to act less cautiously. Although he had nearby strongholds in which he could have kept himself and his men unharmed and brought them back safely, he preferred to trust himself to the open plain, judging it unworthy to appear to have yielded, even temporarily, through fear of that man; and he preferred to expose himself to the enemy’s ambushes.

That night, Nur al-Din, seeing that no larger force had joined the prince and hoping easily to overcome with his own men those whom the prince had brought, enclosed the prince’s company by deploying troops around it in a circle and besieged it in the manner of a city. When morning came, the prince saw the multitude of the enemy. Though too late, he began to doubt and lose confidence in his own strength; nevertheless, he drew up battle lines and arranged his troops as one intending to engage the enemy at close quarters. When battle began, those with him, unequal in strength and unable to bear the enemy’s multitude, took flight, leaving the prince with a few men [Col. 0682B].

The prince, however, being high-minded and singularly brave in arms, fought manfully. Amid the slaughter he had inflicted upon the enemy, exhausted by killing and spent of breath, he perished pierced through by swords. They severed his head and right arm from his body and left the remaining mutilated body among the others deprived of life. There also fell, among others, a great and powerful man, forever to be mourned by his country, the lord Rainald of Marash, to whom the count of Edessa had given his daughter in marriage. Several other nobles also fell, whose names we do not retain.

The lord Raymond was a high-minded man, highly experienced in military affairs, and exceedingly formidable to his enemies, though not very fortunate. The many deeds which he performed vigorously and magnificently during his principate require separate accounts; but since we hasten to pursue the common course of events, we cannot linger over every such episode and entrust them to our pen. He was killed in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1148, in the thirteenth year of his principate, in June, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, on the feast day of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, between the city of Apamea and the town of Rugia, at the place called Fons-muratus, “the Walled Spring.” His body was recognized by certain marks and scars, found among the bodies of the other dead [Col. 0682D], brought to Antioch, and buried with solemn funeral rites in the vestibule of the church of the Prince of the Apostles, among his predecessors.

## CHAPTER X. Nur al-Din treats the whole region as he pleases. The king hastens there to bring relief. The sultan of Iconium enters the land of the count of Edessa.

Nur al-Din, to increase his glory and as a sign of victory, and because he was believed to have killed the greatest persecutor of paganism, sent the head and right hand—which he had caused to be severed from the body of the aforesaid man for this purpose—to the greatest prince and monarch of the Saracens, namely the caliph of Baghdad, and to other Turkish satraps established throughout the East [Col. 0683A].

Deprived of the support of so great a ruler, the region of Antioch gave itself up to lamentation, not restraining its weeping and revealing its grief in frequent sighs, while with plaintive and tearful voices it recalled the outstanding deeds of the brave man. Nor did news of his death grieve only neighboring peoples; this report spread far and wide and brought bitterness to the hearts of both great and small, consuming them inwardly with bitter sorrow.

Meanwhile Nur al-Din, this same greatest persecutor of the Christian faith and name, following his father’s manner, saw that the prince of the region and the greater part of its strong men had fallen in battle, and that the whole province lay subject to his will. He at once sent out his forces and began to range through the entire region in hostile fashion. Passing close to Antioch and giving everything to the flames, he climbed to the monastery of Saint Simeon, situated in lofty mountains between Antioch and the sea, exercising his own authority there and ruling everything with unrestricted command [Col. 0683B]. From there he descended to the sea, which he had never previously seen, and washed himself in it before his men as a sign that he had come victoriously as far as the sea.

On his return, he passed by and seized the castle of Harenc, scarcely ten miles from Antioch. Having occupied it, he carefully equipped and fortified it with arms, soldiers, and provisions, so that it could withstand a siege for many days. Therefore the whole people was afraid, and the land was humbled before him, because the Lord had delivered into his hands the strength of its soldiery and the prince of the region. There was no helper, nor anyone who could bring the remedy of protection against the threatening dangers.

For in the administration of the state and principate there remained only the prince’s wife Constance, with two sons and two daughters, still under age; and there was no one to perform the prince’s office and raise up the despondency of the people. Yet at that time the lord Aimery, patriarch of the same city, a capable and very wealthy man, proved himself a vigorous patron of the afflicted region. To hire bodies of soldiers he supplied pay liberally, contrary to his usual practice, meeting the necessity of the time.

When the king of Jerusalem heard of the dangers in those regions and learned of the lord prince’s death, he was greatly dismayed. He swiftly assembled troops and hastened to the region of Antioch to bring aid to his oppressed brethren, offering by his own presence consolation to those who had lost confidence and were dispirited [Col. 0683D]. Having gathered military assistance both from his own men, whom he had brought with him, and from the whole region, he summoned them to resistance. In order that they might recover heart and learn to breathe again, he besieged the castle of Harenc, which, as we have said above, had newly been taken. But after some days, making no progress because it had been more carefully equipped, he returned to Antioch with the enterprise unfinished.

The sultan of Iconium also, hearing of the prince’s death, descended into Syria with a great multitude. Having captured many cities and several castles, he besieged Turbessel, although the count was within it with his wife and children. The king, meanwhile, sent the constable Humphrey with sixty knights to defend Hasart, lest it be occupied by the Turks. At length the count gave the sultan all the captives from his territory whom he held in chains, and twelve sets of knights’ arms. Peace having been made and the sultan departing, he was freed from the siege. On the same day he came to Hasart, and from there hurried to Antioch to thank the lord king for the kindness he had shown him. Having seen the king there and received leave from him, he returned to his own lands with the small retinue he had brought. The king, remaining at Antioch to care for the distressed region, delayed there for this purpose. Once affairs had been arranged as place and time required and tranquility had been to some extent restored [Col. 0684B], the demands of his own realm recalled him, and he returned to his kingdom.

## CHAPTER X. The count of Edessa, after the king’s departure from Antioch, is captured by the enemy and dies there disgracefully.

Meanwhile the count of Edessa, the younger Joscelin—a lax man, fallen from his country’s honor, overflowing with filth, dissolute in lust, scorning better things and pursuing destructive ones—thought that matters had gone very well for him because the prince of Antioch, whom he pursued with insatiable hatred, had fallen. He paid little attention to the truth of the saying:

> Your own concern is at stake when the neighboring wall is on fire.

As he was setting out by night for Antioch, summoned there, it is said, by the lord patriarch [Col. 0684C], he separated himself from his retinue with a young man who led his horse, allegedly in order to relieve his bowels and satisfy the more private necessities of nature. Those going before and those following alike were unaware. Robbers lying in ambush rushed upon him; he was captured and put in chains, then taken to Aleppo. There, reaping the fruits of his unclean ways, worn down by the squalor of prison and the weight of chains, consumed by anxiety of spirit and the continual affliction of his body, he ended his life miserably.

When day returned, those in his company, wholly unaware of what had happened to him, anxiously sought their lord, whom they could not find. Seeing that their search gained nothing, they returned and reported what had befallen them. Again the whole land was filled with astonishment and dismay. Though they had not known how to grieve at the misfortunes of their neighbors, now oppressed by dangers close to home, they learned by the same experience how one should sympathize with the sorrows of others. At last, after some days, they learned from the report of persons to whom it was certainly known that he was held in fetters at Aleppo.

His wife, a chaste, sober woman who feared God, such as God loves, remained with an underage son and two daughters. So far as she could, she endeavored, by the counsel of the surviving nobles, to govern the people; and, exceeding female strength, she labored to secure the strongholds of the region against the enemy with arms, men, and provisions [Col. 0685A]. Thus, our sins demanding it, both regions, deprived of better counsel and scarcely maintaining themselves, were ruled by female authority.

## CHAPTER XII. The king, with the princes of the kingdom, rebuilds Gaza near Ascalon.

While these events were taking place in the region of Antioch, not long afterward divine mercy visited the kingdom. Rising from the dust and from the extreme abasement in which, because of the frequent disasters that had befallen them, they seemed to lie, the lord king and the other princes of the Jerusalemite realm came to their senses. In order more closely to restrain the people of Ascalon, their most savage enemies, and more effectively to curb their dangerous attacks, they proposed to restore the most ancient city of Gaza, ten miles south of Ascalon, which had been destroyed and was without inhabitants. Thus, just as they had, as it were, hemmed Ascalon in from north and east by founding fortified towns around it, so it should not lack a spur from the south as well, but should be assailed from that direction by continual attacks and harassed by frequent ambushes. On the appointed day, therefore, the whole people gathered at the said place as one man; and, undertaking the work unanimously, they eagerly strove to rebuild the city.

Gaza itself had been a most ancient city, one of the five cities of the Philistines, distinguished by its buildings. Of its ancient nobility there remained many great proofs in its churches and spacious houses, though ruined, in marble and great stones, and in the multitude of cisterns and wells of living water. It stood upon a somewhat elevated hill, enclosing within its walls a very large and extensive circuit. But when our people saw that it was not sufficiently practical, and that perhaps the resources of the time were inadequate, for the whole city to be restored, they occupied part of the said hill. Having laid foundations to a suitable height, they built a notable work of wall and towers, and in a short time, with the Lord’s help, happily completed it. When completed and finished in all its parts, they entrusted it, by common counsel, to the brethren of the military Order of the Temple to guard and possess in perpetuity, together with the entire adjoining district. [Col. 0685B–D]

These men, being brave and vigorous in arms, have guarded what was entrusted to them faithfully and wisely down to the present day. They have manfully harassed the said city with frequent attacks, both secret and open, so that those who formerly ranged abroad and ravaged the whole country like enemies, and were a terror to our people, now regard it as the height of good fortune if they may live shut within their walls and enjoy quiet, having procured peace for a time by prayers or by payment. Nor was this stronghold useful merely while the said city, for whose injury it had been built, still resisted; after Gaza had been subdued, it also served the region as a great protection, like the southern boundary of the kingdom against Egypt.

At the beginning of spring, the lord king and the lord patriarch, after the inner fortification had been partly completed and the brethren of the Temple—whose diligence had been assigned to it—had been left there, returned to Jerusalem. Then an Egyptian relief force, which customarily came three or four times a year to renew the strength of the people of Ascalon, arrived in great numbers before the said town. Gathering the townspeople inside for fear of the enemy, it launched repeated and vigorous attacks. But when those commanding the force saw that they were making no progress, after spending several days at the siege they departed for Ascalon. From that day onward, as though their strength had been worn down and their freedom to harm curtailed, they began altogether to cease from harassing the neighboring region. Moreover, the Egyptian army which, as stated above, had so frequently brought aid to the already afflicted city, thereafter customarily approached only by sea, fearing the ambushes of the said fortified town in its path and suspecting its garrison. [Col. 0686A–B]

## CHAPTER XIII. Serious hostilities arise between the king and his mother; the king is crowned without her knowledge.

Meanwhile, while affairs in the eastern kingdom were proceeding with a fairly favorable course and it seemed to enjoy a certain tranquillity—though less so because the county of Edessa had been lost to us and had fallen into the power of our enemies, while the Antiochene region was wearied by frequent enemy plots—the enemy man, who is accustomed to sow tares among the wheat and who envied our prosperity, sought to disturb our peace by shaking us with internal dissensions. The cause and origin of this danger were as follows.

Lady Queen Melisende, of illustrious remembrance and pious memory in the Lord, when her husband died, as we have said, was left with two children still under age. She received the care and administration of the kingdom, as though owing to her by hereditary right, acting as the lawful guardian of her sons. By the counsel of the princes of the realm, she had administered it vigorously and faithfully, surpassing feminine strength and spirit, down to that day; and her firstborn son, Lord Baldwin, whose deeds we are now recording, even after being raised to the throne of the kingdom, greatly favored and deservedly submitted to her authority. [Col. 0686C–D]

Among the others whose service and counsel she employed, she held in especial favor a certain nobleman, her cousin Manasses. Immediately after her accession to the kingdom, she had entrusted to him the entire charge of the army and appointed him constable. Relying upon the queen’s favor, however, he became excessively arrogant, as the saying goes; insolently preferring himself to the greater men of the kingdom and showing due reverence to no one, he incurred the extreme hatred of the nobles of the realm. Had the authority of Queen Melisende not restrained them, they were ready to carry their conceived hatred into action.

He had married the widow of the elder Lord Balian, a noble matron and mother of the brothers Hugh, Baldwin, and Balian of Ramla; and thereby he had amassed riches and increased his possessions. The foremost among those who hated Manasses, both in feeling and in action, was the king himself. He maintained that Manasses deprived him of his mother’s favor and obstructed her generosity toward him. He also had many instigators in this matter, who supplied fuel to his hatred, since the power of this man was odious to them and his domination exceedingly burdensome. They urged the king to remove even his mother from power in the kingdom, saying that he had now reached adulthood; that it was unworthy for him to be governed by a woman’s will; and that he ought to entrust some care of his own kingdom to himself to govern.

Relying upon the counsel of these and similar persons, the king had resolved to be crowned solemnly at Jerusalem on Easter Day. When the lord patriarch and prudent men who loved the peace of the kingdom urgently begged him to make his mother a participant in that honor, he deferred to the counsel of the aforesaid men, so that he should not have his mother as a partner on the day he had proposed. On the following day, suddenly and without summoning his mother, he came forth before the public wearing the crown. [Col. 0687A–B]

## CHAPTER XIV. Son and mother divide the kingdom between themselves. The king forcibly enters Jerusalem and besieges his mother in David’s citadel; at last peace and tranquillity are restored.

After that ceremony had passed, he summoned an assembly of the nobles, with Count Ivo of Soissons and Walter, castellan of Saint-Aldemar, also present. He met his mother and urgently demanded that she divide the kingdom with him and assign him a portion of his ancestral inheritance. At last, after many discussions and deliberations on both sides, the inheritance was divided. The lord king was given the choice, and he took as his share Tyre and Acre, together with their dependencies, the coastal cities; Jerusalem and Nablus, with their dependencies, were left to Queen Melisende.

Thus they were separated from one another, the people hoping, for the sake of peace, that this arrangement should be endured, and that each should be content with the portion which had fallen to him. In those same days the lord king appointed as his constable a certain noble and splendid man, Lord Humphrey of Toron, who possessed great and extensive estates in Phoenicia, in the mountains adjoining the metropolis of Tyre; and he entrusted him with the care of his army. [Col. 0687C–D]

Yet even so, the goad of those pursuing Queen Melisende did not rest. From slight causes, the fire that had lain hidden beneath ashes recovered strength and began to produce a greater conflagration, far more dangerous than the former. For the king, pressed by the same men whose counsel he had previously accepted, again began to trouble his mother. He resolved to claim for himself, wholly excluding her, that portion of the kingdom which he had held with the assent of them both.

When the queen understood this, she entrusted Nablus to certain faithful followers to care for it and withdrew to Jerusalem. The king, meanwhile, gathered as large an army as he could and besieged Manasses in one of his castles, called Mirabel. Compelling him to surrender, he forced him to renounce the kingdom and the entire region on this side of the sea. Then, after occupying Nablus, he set out for Jerusalem in pursuit of his mother.

Some of those who held possessions within her share and were bound to her by fealty had deserted Queen Melisende, forgetful of their oaths and fidelity. But a few who adhered to her preserved their faithfulness intact: namely, Amalric, count of Jaffa, her very young son; Philip of Nablus; Rohard the Elder; and a few others whose names we do not retain. Hearing that her son was arriving with an army, the queen withdrew with her household and faithful followers into the citadel, trusting in the strength of its defenses. [Col. 0688A–B]

The lord patriarch Fulk, of blessed memory, seeing the times to be dangerous and days of trial impending, wished to intervene and plead for peace. Taking with him clergy who were religious and God-fearing men, he went out to meet the lord king, urging him to desist from his wrongful design and, remaining within the bounds of the agreement, to allow his mother to enjoy peace. When he saw that he made no progress with him, he condemned the king’s plan and returned to the city.

The king, however, pressing on with his design, pitched camp before the city. At length, when the citizens yielded to royal indignation and opened the gates, he entered with his forces. Thereupon he immediately surrounded with a siege the citadel into which his mother had withdrawn, fitting machines for its assault; and, with the persistence of an enemy, continually inflicted distress by crossbows, bows, and missile engines, refusing the besieged any rest. They, resisting the attack with all their might, sought to repel force by force; and, by the same methods by which the attackers strove to assail those within, the besieged did not fear to drive off their injuries and inflict equal damage upon their enemies.

At last, after several days of very dangerous fighting on both sides, when the king made little progress in storming the citadel but would nevertheless not abandon his purpose, certain mediators brought about peace and reconciliation. Queen Melisende was content with the city of Nablus and its territory, and surrendered Jerusalem, the capital of the kingdom, to the lord king. Oaths were offered on the king’s behalf and sworn bodily, that he should never thereafter trouble her over that possession. Thus, when they returned to mutual favor, tranquillity was restored to kingdom and Church, like the morning star shining amid the clouds. [Col. 0688C–D]

## CHAPTER XV. The sultan of Iconium again enters the county of Edessa; the king hastens there with all speed.

It was reported to the king of Jerusalem, and established by more reliable information, that the count of Edessa had been captured in such a miserable fate, and that the whole country, lacking a defender’s care, lay widely open to enemy attacks. That entire province, like the region of Antioch, left under a woman’s governance, demanded his attention. Taking with him Humphrey the constable and Guy of Beirut—for although he had summoned individually those in Queen Melisende’s portion, he could obtain no one from among them—he arrived in the region of Tripoli. There he took the count and his knights with him and swiftly reached Antioch.

For it was commonly said—and this was indeed true—that the sultan of Iconium, the most powerful prince of the Turks, had descended into those parts with innumerable cavalry and occupied almost the entire country bordering his own lands. Since the inhabitants were unable to resist or endure the power of his armies, they had surrendered all cities and fortified towns to him, obtaining from him safe and free departure with wives and children, and an escort without danger as far as Turbessel. This place, more fortified than the others and with more inhabitants, where the lord count had maintained his regular and permanent residence, still appeared to be secure. [Col. 0689A–B]

Having thus occupied the whole country, save a few garrisons, the sultan was compelled by more pressing concerns to return home. Yet neither the hardship of the provincials was lessened nor their anxiety made lighter. For Nur al-Din, the most troublesome persecutor of our people and a most powerful prince of the Turks, harassed the whole region with almost continual incursions, so that no one at all dared appear outside the garrisons. Thus that wretched people were incessantly ground between two millstones and oppressed beyond their strength by two very great princes, when they could scarcely have endured the power of either one alone. [Col. 0689B–C]

## CHAPTER XVI. The emperor of Constantinople sends an army into the Antiochene region; he demands the surrender of the county of Edessa; his demand is granted; the castles are surrendered to the Greeks; the king leads the Latins away.

Meanwhile, the lord emperor of Constantinople, hearing of the desolation of those regions, sent one of his princes to those parts, with immense resources and a considerable force of his own soldiers. He offered the countess and her children annual revenues of a fixed amount, sufficient to provide them honorably with sustenance forever, in exchange for the country being surrendered to him, if she would concede to his authority the garrisons which she still retained. Confident in the abundance of his wealth, he promised that, if the province were surrendered to him, he would preserve it unharmed from Turkish incursions and easily restore to his rule the other places which had been lost.

When the king arrived at Antioch and learned the reason for the imperial envoys’ arrival, the envoys themselves revealing the embassy entrusted to them, disagreement arose among the princes of that region. Some said that matters had not yet reached such a point of necessity that this ought to be done; others, on the contrary, maintained that it was necessary to do so before the land was entirely handed into the enemies’ power. [Col. 0689D–0690A]

Amid these uncertainties of deliberation, the lord king recognized that the said territory could not long endure in its present state. Care for his own kingdom did not allow him to remain there longer, nor were his resources so great and numerous that he could conveniently administer two provinces separated from each other by a journey of fifteen days. Seeing too that Antioch, the intervening province, had been deprived of a prince’s help for several years, he resolved that, on the terms already stated, the towns that remained should be delivered to the Greeks.

Although he had little confidence that the province could be preserved in that condition by Greek power, he nevertheless preferred that such a disaster should befall it while they possessed it rather than that the ruin of a people in danger and a land failing should be attributed to him. Accordingly, when agreements had been made on both sides according to the terms stated, and the consent of the lady countess and her children obtained, a day was appointed on which the lord king, descending into those regions with all his army, should put the emperor’s men in possession and surrender all the towns to them.

On the appointed day the king, as agreed, took with him the count of Tripoli and the magnates both of his own kingdom and of the Antiochene region. Leading Greeks with him into the land of the count of Edessa, he reached Turbessel. There, taking with him the lady countess and her children and all others wishing to leave—Latins and Armenians alike, men and women—he assigned the country to the Greeks. [Col. 0690A–C]

The towns still held by our people were Turbessel, Hamtab, Ravendel, Ranculat, Bile, Samosata, and perhaps some others. When all these had been surrendered to Greek authority, he prepared to depart with the entire population wishing to leave, along with their beasts and baggage, which were exceedingly abundant. For every person had resolved to leave with his whole household and family and all his belongings. With all this large multitude of noncombatants and the great quantity of baggage, he hastened to set out, intending to conduct them away safely.

## CHAPTER XVII. Nur al-Din meets the king and tries to prevent the departure. The king, though with difficulty, returns to Antioch. Nur al-Din expels the Greeks and occupies the whole country.

[Col. 0690D]

Hearing that the king had entered the region in order to lead away the population, and that, despairing entirely of preserving the country, they had surrendered the towns to effeminate and weak Greeks, Nur al-Din became bolder because of his fear of us. Gathering troops from all the neighboring regions, he hastened into those parts, wishing to meet the king and a people distrustful of their own strength and encumbered with much baggage. He reckoned that it would turn to his advantage if he could encounter such opponents.

It happened that the helpless multitude had scarcely been brought to the city of Tulupa, only five or six miles from Turbessel, when Nur al-Din had filled the whole region with his legions. Near them stood a castle named Hamtab, through which their route was to pass. Our men, wishing to hasten there and seeing the danger imminent, drew up battle lines and arranged their divisions, as though they were about to engage the enemy at once. The enemy, for their part, having formed their troops, eagerly awaited our approach, as though assured of victory. Yet contrary to their expectation, our army, preceded by the Lord’s mercy, reached the said town unharmed. [Col. 0691A]

There, after a whole night had been granted for rest to men and beasts alike, who were weary, an assembly of the nobles was called. While they deliberated concerning the next day’s march, some of the magnates requested that the said stronghold be given to them, believing that with the Lord’s help they could preserve the place by their own resources against Turkish incursions. One was Humphrey of Toron, a distinguished man and the royal constable; the other was Robert of Surdaval, a noble and powerful man of the principality of Antioch. But the lord king, seeing that neither had strength or power sufficient for the task, rejected each proposal as useless. Persisting in the agreements, he delivered the town to the Greeks and ordered the people to prepare for the journey.

There one could see noble men, and distinguished matrons with freeborn maidens and little children, leaving their native soil, ancestral homes, and kindred country with sobs and tearful sighs, and entering upon migration to another people amid weeping and lamentation. No breast was so iron that its inward parts were not moved by the tears, cries, and mournful voices of the migrating people. [Col. 0691B–C]

When daylight returned to the earth, they arranged their baggage and again took the road. And behold: enemy battle lines advanced on both sides in close formations, prepared to fall upon our column from every direction. Seeing the enemy divisions and their great multitude, our men formed battle lines out of the five hundred knights whom they had, and assigned them their order of march. They ordered the lord king to lead the way, so that he might go before the columns and direct the movement of the infantry masses. They ordered the count of Tripoli and Humphrey, the royal constable, to protect the rear, so that, with the larger and stronger forces of knights, they might endure the enemy attacks and keep their violence from the common people. They placed the Antiochene magnates on the right and left, so that the multitude in the middle should not lack, anywhere around it, the strength of brave men and armed soldiers.

Thus our people marched in the same order throughout the entire day, until sunset; and they did not lack intolerable hardship, frequent attacks, unceasing fighting, and continual engagements. So great was the number of arrows launched into the army that all the baggage seemed, like hedgehogs, to be bristling with arrows. Moreover, dust, the heat such as August usually produces, and harsh thirst exhausted the common people beyond their strength. [Col. 0691C–0692A]

At length, when the sun was already declining toward sunset, the Turks—having no provisions with them and having lost several nobles from their army—gave the signal to return and ceased to pursue our people, amazed at their incomparable endurance and perseverance. As Constable Humphrey pursued the departing enemy with his bow, having gone somewhat farther from the column, a soldier from the enemy ranks approached him. Laying aside his weapons and alternately placing his joined hands at his side, he made a gesture of reverence.

This man was a servant and intimate dependent of a most powerful Turkish prince, who was bound to the constable by a fraternal pact and was very steadfast in it. He had been sent by that prince to greet Humphrey in his master’s words and inform him concerning the state of the hostile army. He reported that Nur al-Din and his men intended to hasten home that night, since all provisions in their camp had completely failed and they could not pursue our people longer.

When the man had returned to his own side, the constable rejoined the camp. Having communicated to the lord king what he had heard, and night now being at hand, the entire people encamped in a place called Joha. In the following days, the people were brought without molestation through the forest called Marris and as far as places subject to our rule; the lord king then returned to Antioch. [Col. 0692A–B]

Nur al-Din, seeing that the count’s territory was deprived of Latin help and placing confidence in the weakness of the Greeks to whom it had been entrusted, began to burden it with frequent incursions which the Greeks did not know how adequately to withstand. At last, sending in large armies and surrounding the towns with siege works, he violently expelled the Greeks and within a year occupied the whole region.

Thus the most wealthy province, most delightful in streams, woods, and pastures, rich in fertile soil and overflowing with every advantage—a land in which five hundred knights held adequate fiefs—came, through the demands of our sins, into enemy hands and has remained outside our jurisdiction to the present day. Three archbishops were lost to the Church of Antioch in those parts: the archbishop of Edessa, of Hierapolis, and of Corica. Their churches are still held, though unwillingly, by unbelief and pagan superstition. [Col. 0692C]

## CHAPTER XVIII. The king urges the princess to take one of the princes as husband, so that he may govern the country; but he does not succeed. The king then goes to Tripoli, intending to return home.

Meanwhile, Baldwin, lord king of Jerusalem, was deeply concerned for the city of Antioch and its adjoining diocese, lest, deprived of the aid of a prince, it too should fall, like the count’s territory mentioned above, into enemy hands in a miserable fate, adding further disgrace to the Christian people together with an intolerable loss. Since care of his kingdom recalled him and did not permit him to remain there longer, he repeatedly urged the lady princess to choose from among the noblemen a husband whose counsel and service might govern the principality.

At that time there were distinguished and noble men in that region, following the king’s camp: namely, Lord Ivo of Neella, count of Soissons, a splendid, prudent, and discerning man, whose influence in the kingdom of the Franks was very great; Walter of Falcunberg, castellan of Saint-Aldemar, who later became lord of Tiberias, likewise a prudent man, of exceptional refinement, provident in counsel and vigorous in arms; and Lord Ralph of Merle, a man of the highest nobility, experienced in arms and conspicuous for great prudence. Any one of them seemed fully qualified to administer the territory. [Col. 0692D–0693A]

But the princess, fearing the bonds of marriage and preferring an unbound and free life, paid little attention to what would benefit the people, being exceedingly concerned to make provision for the flesh in its desires. Understanding her intention, the king summoned a general court at Tripoli of the princes of both the kingdom and the principality. To it he invited the lord patriarch of Antioch with his suffragan bishops, and the lady princess with her barons. His mother, Lady Queen Melisende, attended as well, accompanied by the princes of the kingdom.

After careful discussion had been held concerning public affairs, they came to the matter of the princess. Yet neither the king nor the count, her blood relatives, nor the queen and the countess of Tripoli, both her maternal aunts, could induce her to make provision in this matter for herself and the country. It was also said that she acted at the patriarch’s advice: he, being a shrewd and double-dealing man, was said to encourage her in this error so that he might meanwhile rule the whole land more freely, for he was exceedingly desirous of this. Since they made no progress in the matter, the court was dissolved and each returned home. [Col. 0693B–C]

## CHAPTER XIX. The king and his mother meet at Tripoli to reconcile the count with his wife, but do not succeed. The count is murdered by Assassins at the city gate.

In those days hostility had arisen between the lord count and his wife, the sister of Queen Melisende, from marital jealousy. Queen Melisende had come in order to settle the quarrel and to see her niece, the princess. Since she herself had again made little progress in restoring goodwill, she determined, on returning, to take her sister with her. In preparation for this, both women had already left the city of Tripoli.

The count had accompanied the departing princess for a time. Having taken leave of her, he returned after a short interval. As he entered the city gate, fearing no misfortune whatsoever, he was stabbed to death miserably by the swords of Assassins in the gateway, between the wall and the outer defensive wall. With him fell the distinguished and noble Lord Ralph of Merle, whom we mentioned above, together with one of Ralph’s knights; each of them had happened to become the count’s companion on that journey. [Col. 0693C–D]

The king, unaware of all this, was safely within the city playing dice and taking recreation. The whole city was stirred upon hearing of the count’s murder. The people rushed to arms and struck down with the sword anyone they found foreign in language or dress, thinking that they would thus discover the murderers who had perpetrated this evil; indiscriminately they inflicted death upon all.

Meanwhile, roused by the sudden cries and learning of the count’s death, the king was profoundly sad and greatly distressed in mind. Unable to restrain tears and sighs, he immediately ordered his mother and aunt to be recalled. When they had returned, after much lamentation and abundant weeping, the body was committed to burial with the proper magnificence of funeral rites. By the lord king’s command, all the nobles of those regions rendered fealty to the lady countess and her children.

The lord count had a son of the same name, Raymond, scarcely twelve years old, and a daughter named Melisende, younger than her brother. When these matters had been settled, the king returned to his kingdom with his mother and his princes. [Col. 0694A–B]

## CHAPTER XX. A vast multitude of Turks comes to Jerusalem to seize it; but our men go out and overthrow them in great strength.

Not long afterward, certain noble Turkish satraps, powerful men of great renown among their own people, surnamed the Hiaroquin—whose holy city, before it was liberated by Christians, is said to have been their inheritance—were urged by their mother, who reproached them for cowardice because they had for so long allowed themselves to be dispossessed of their ancestral inheritance. Gathering an innumerable multitude of Turks, they resolved to come to Jerusalem and claim it as owed to them, as it were, by hereditary right.

Accordingly, taking with them vast forces of fighting men and following their aged mother, who continually urged this upon them, they set out to carry out their plan, if the Lord should permit it. They reached Damascus and paused there for some time to replenish their army and recover their strength. Though the Damascenes wished to recall them from their foolish design, they did not consent; rather, having taken up provisions and packed their baggage again, they set out toward Jerusalem, as if not doubting their purpose. [Col. 0694B–D]

At length, having crossed the Jordan with all their companies and ascended the highlands in which the said city is situated, they made their way to the Mount of Olives, a neighboring mountain overlooking the city. From there they could freely behold all the venerable places, especially the Temple of the Lord, which they hold in highest and special reverence, and the whole city.

Those remaining in the city saw this. For the greater part of the army of the whole region had assembled at Nablus. Fearing that the multitude of arriving enemies would descend there, because the city was without walls, they invoked help from heaven, seized their arms, and eagerly hurried out to attack and engage the enemy with burning resolve.

The road descending from Jerusalem to Jericho and thence to the Jordan is very uneven, dangerous through rocky places and frequent precipices, so that even for those who fear nothing and have free passage, it has always made ascent and descent difficult. When the enemy fled in disorder before our battle lines pressing them more fiercely, many perished without a sword-stroke, hurled down where cliffs and narrow places allowed no means of escape. Those who took the flatter ground and tried to continue their flight met our swords and, mortally wounded, were nevertheless sent headlong to death. [Col. 0695A]

Their horses, exhausted by the length of the journey and the difficulty of the labor, could not endure the roughness of the roads and, failing completely, refused service to their riders. Thus their riders became infantry, laden with weapons and unused to hardship, and were slaughtered like cattle by the swords of our pursuers. So great was the slaughter of horses and men through the causes mentioned that the multitude of the slain impeded passage for pursuing those who went ahead.

But our men pursued all the more eagerly, scorning plunder and passing by spoils; they pressed on more fiercely with the slaughter, counting it their greatest gain to be drenched in enemy blood. Those who had assembled at Nablus, knowing that the said enemies had entered our lands, all went out together and hurried eagerly to meet the enemy at the waters of the Jordan, in order to occupy the fords and prevent those wishing to cross. There they found unsuspecting and stabbed from the side those who had escaped the pursuers. [Col. 0695B–C]

Thus the hand of the Lord was upon them that day, so that, as it is written: “What the locust left, the cankerworm consumed” (Joel 1:4). For those who seemed to have escaped the pursuers through the speed of their horses or some stratagem were cut down by the swords of men attacking from the side. If any, going ahead of the columns, had entered the Jordan, they were swept away in its swollen waters, ignorant of the fords, and drowned in the river.

Thus those who had ascended in many thousands, in high spirits and placing their hope in cavalry, were reduced to a small number and returned home clothed in confusion and reverence. It is said that as many as five thousand of them were killed that day. This occurred in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1152, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December [23 November], in the ninth year of the reign of King Baldwin IV. Our men, laden with enemy spoils and bearing away rich trophies, returned to Jerusalem to offer solemn sacrifices of praise to the Lord. [Col. 0695C–D]

## CHAPTER XXI. The king and princes of the kingdom hasten to Ascalon to ravage the orchards around the city; but, enlarging their purpose, they besiege the city.

Accordingly, after this victory had been divinely granted to our side, their hearts directed by the Lord, they were raised to good hope and, having taken counsel together, both great and small, unanimously resolved somehow to harm the enemy settled nearby, who had often inflicted grave dangers upon our people—namely, the people of Ascalon. [Col. 0696A] For the moment, they judged it more expedient to endeavour, with a strong hand, to destroy the orchards adjoining the city, from which the citizens derived much benefit, and thus at least partly to damage their insolent enemies. In accordance with this plan, all the forces of the kingdom were assembled unanimously and in strength before the aforesaid city, judging it sufficient if they could put their intention into effect.

But when our forces stood before the city, divine mercy was wonderfully present, and unexpectedly began to spur them toward greater things. For after our battle-lines had taken their position before the city, such fear seized the citizens that all hastened to withdraw within it; nor was even one person found who ventured outside the walls to meet our men. Taking occasion therefore from the fact that the citizens appeared so frightened, and guided by divine grace, they decided further to surround the city with a siege. Messengers were sent throughout all the borders of the kingdom, commanding that those who had remained at home be summoned, so that all might not delay to be present unanimously on the appointed day; and they disclosed the plan which God had inspired in them. Those who had been summoned came joyfully and without delay, joined those who had preceded them, and pitched camp with the others around the city. And, that what they undertook might be firm and that none might doubt their perseverance in the purpose, they mutually bound themselves by solemn corporal oaths not to withdraw from the siege before the city had been captured.

Thus all the forces of the kingdom having been summoned and the people assembling unanimously, the lord king and the lord [Col. 0696C] patriarch, together with the other secular and ecclesiastical princes of the kingdom, bearing with them the life-giving and venerable sign of the Lord’s Cross, pitched camp before the aforesaid city under favourable auspices, on the eighth day before the Kalends of February [25 January]. Present among the prelates of the churches were Lord Fulcher, patriarch of Jerusalem; Lord Peter, archbishop of Tyre; Lord Baldwin, archbishop of Caesarea; Lord Robert, archbishop of Nazareth; Lord Frederick, bishop of Acre; and Lord Gerald, bishop of Bethlehem; also several abbots; Bernard of Tremelay, master of the military order of the Temple; and Raymond, master of the house of the Hospital. Among the secular princes were [Col. 0696D] Hugh of Ibelin, Philip of Nablus, Humphrey of Toron, Simon of Tiberias, Gerard of Sidon, Guy of Beirut, Maurice of Montreal, Raynald of Châtillon, and Gauder of Saint-Aldemar, the latter two receiving pay in the lord king’s service. The tents having thus been arranged and set in order in a circle, and the princes assigned suitable and proper quarters, they faithfully applied themselves to the work begun, devoutly and prudently bestowing upon so great a labour the diligence it deserved.

## CHAPTER XXII. The site of the city is described, and its advantages set forth

Ascalon is one of the five cities of the Philistines, situated upon the seashore. It has the form of a semicircle, its chord or diameter lying along the [Col. 0697A] shore of the sea, while its circumference, or arc, faces eastward over the land. The whole city lies, as it were, in a hollow, entirely sloping down toward the sea. It is enclosed on every side by artificial embankments, upon which stand walls with numerous towers, bound together by solid workmanship and cement stronger than the hardness of stone; the walls are broad with suitable thickness and lofty in fitting proportion. Moreover, it is entirely encircled and more carefully fortified with outer walls constructed with the same solidity.

It has neither springs within the circuit of its walls nor any nearby; but it abounds in wells, both outside and below the city, providing sweet water fit for drinking. As a further precaution the citizens had also built within [Col. 0697B] several cisterns for collecting rainwater. There were four gates in the circuit of the walls, most carefully fortified with lofty and solid towers. The first, facing east, is called the Great Gate, surnamed the Jerusalem Gate because it looks toward the Holy City. It has beside it two very high towers, which seem to stand over the city like its strength and defence. Before it are three or four smaller gates in the outer works, through which it is reached by certain winding approaches.

The second faces west and is called the Sea Gate, because it affords the citizens an exit to the sea. The third faces south toward the city of Gaza, mentioned above, and takes its name from it. The fourth, facing north, is called the Jaffa Gate after the neighbouring city situated on the same coast. This city, however, having no suitable maritime position, neither has nor had a harbour or any safe anchorage for ships; it has only a sandy shore and a sea near it which, when winds rise, is exceedingly rough and dangerous to those approaching unless the sea is very calm.

The ground outside adjoining the city is covered with sand, incapable of agriculture, though suited to vineyards and fruit-bearing trees. Excepted are a few small valleys in the northern part which, enriched with manure and irrigated with well-water, afford the citizens some provision of herbs and fruits. There was in that city [Col. 0697D] a large population; even the least among them, as was commonly said, even a newborn child, received stipends from the treasuries of the Egyptian caliph. For the aforesaid lord and his princes took great, indeed the greatest, care for that city, judging that if it failed and came into our dominion, nothing would remain except that our princes could descend freely and without difficulty into Egypt, intending to seize the kingdom by force. They therefore used it as a wall; and with lavish generosity they supplied the citizens with aid four times a year, by sea and by land, so that while it survived and our men exhausted effort and labour around it, they themselves might meanwhile enjoy the peace they desired. For this reason they furnished the city with many necessary supplies and expenses, [Col. 0698A] sending arms, provisions, and fresh troops at appointed times, so that while our people were occupied with them, they might feel less concern about the strength of our forces.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The siege is organized; commanders are appointed over the fleet and the land forces

This city, which for fifty years and more had remained resistant and hostile to our efforts after the Lord had delivered the remaining parts of the Promised Land to the Christian people, they at last attempted to besiege—an undertaking difficult and almost impossible. For besides being equipped beyond all expectation with walls and outer walls, towers and embankment, arms and provisions, [Col. 0698B] it had a population practiced and experienced in warfare, so numerous that from the first day of the siege to the last, the number of besiegers was outnumbered twofold by the multitude of the besieged.

The lord king, the lord patriarch, Lord Peter, our predecessor and archbishop of Tyre, the other magnates of the kingdom—both princes and prelates of the churches—and the citizens of the individual towns, pitching their tents separately, besieged the city by land. They had placed Lord Gerard of Sidon, one of the great nobles of the kingdom, in command of a fleet of fifteen beaked ships, swift and ready for sailing, to prevent those wishing to approach by sea from gaining access and likewise to prevent those wishing to leave from departing. [Col. 0698C]

Nearly every day our men, now cavalry, now infantry, made frequent assaults upon the city. The defenders, meeting them with great spirit, resisted manfully, fighting for wives and children and, above all, for freedom. In these engagements now one side, now the other, as usually happens in such matters, gained the advantage; yet our side more often carried away the better result. It was said that in the camp there was such security, together with every abundance of goods for sale, that the people lived in tents and pavilions just as they were accustomed to live at home in walled cities.

The townsmen, taking special care to guard the place by night, appointed watches in rotation; their leading men likewise took turns keeping watch and inspecting the walls, spending most of the nights sleepless. Along the circuit of the walls and towers, glass lamps with glass covers had been placed in the battlements, preserving the flame maintained by poured oil; by these lamps those making the rounds of the walls were furnished with light as though it were day. Our people in the camp also assigned watches by troops as occasion required, and there was no lack of continual guard, for they feared that the townsmen might make night attacks upon the camp, or that Egyptians hastening to their aid might harm the army by sudden and unforeseen incursions. Nevertheless, at many places near Gaza there were scouts [Col. 0699A] able to announce the enemy’s arrival with the utmost speed.

## CHAPTER XXIV. In the second month of the siege, the passage of pilgrims arrives, bringing many resources for the siege

Thus, after the siege had continued in the same manner for two months, it happened, as was customary around Easter, that the passage arrived and a multitude of pilgrims came. Having taken counsel, men were sent from the army who, by royal authority, forbade sailors and pilgrims wishing to return from departing; they invited them all, with promises of pay, to the siege and to this labour so acceptable to God, and brought thither both larger and smaller ships. Thus [Col. 0699B] it happened that suddenly, within a few days, all the ships that had arrived in that passage were driven by a favourable wind and were present before the city. Vast numbers of pilgrims, both mounted and on foot, joined our forces, and the army increased each day.

There was therefore joy in the camp and hope of enjoying victory; among the enemy, however, grief and anxiety grew. Distrusting their strength, they went out less often to fight, although frequently challenged. By frequent messengers they also urged the Egyptian caliph to provide aid quickly, declaring that otherwise they would soon fail. He, however, energetically through his princes appointed over this business, equipped a fleet, assembled troops, loaded the lofty ships to the full with arms, provisions, and engines, appointed commanders, provided funds, reproved delays, and ordered speed.

Meanwhile our people, having bought ships at great cost and taken their masts from them, summoned craftsmen and raised a wooden tower of enormous height. They carefully fortified it within and without with hurdles and hides against fire and accidental hazards, so that it might offer secure protection to those ordered to attack the city from it. From the remaining timber of the ships they constructed projectile engines, which they placed in suitable positions for breaking down the walls. They also constructed *scrophae* (“sows,” covered siege-shelters) from the same material, by means of which they could safely approach in order to level the embankments. When these things had been properly prepared, [Col. 0699D] and the part of the wall considered where our tower could be applied more easily, the embankment having first been largely levelled with the aforesaid instruments, they brought the tower up to the wall with great shouts. From it the whole city could be seen at a distance, and close combat could be tried with those in the neighbouring towers.

The citizens worked hard and pressed their attack more fiercely, both from the walls and from the embankment, with bows and crossbows; but their effort was futile, for they could not injure those sheltered within, by whose labour the engine was advanced. Thus the citizens rushed toward the part of the wall opposite the tower, and those among them who were bolder were ordered to test their strength there, maintaining continual and unceasing combat with those attacking them from the tower. Yet in other parts of the same [Col. 0700A] wall as well, fighting and stubborn battle were not lacking at various places, so that scarcely a day passed without slaughter, apart from the very great number of wounded on both sides. We have heard of memorable and outstanding deeds of courage by certain men in that siege, both ours and the enemy’s. But since we are pursuing the general course of events, we give little attention to such particulars.

## CHAPTER XXV. In the fifth month, the Egyptian fleet reaches the city, bringing great consolation to the besieged citizens

After our princes had persevered in the siege for five continuous months, and the enemy’s strength seemed to have been somewhat worn down, while a hope greater than usual of obtaining the city sustained our men, [Col. 0700B] behold, suddenly the Egyptian fleet appeared, driven by favourable winds. When the people of Ascalon saw it, they raised voices and hands to heaven and shouted loudly that our men must withdraw or would soon perish.

Gerard of Sidon, commander of our fleet, seeing the enemy force approach the city, tried with the few galleys he had to meet it and prevent its arrival; but, fearing the multitude, he turned his back and fled, consulting for his life and safety. The enemy fleet, however, reached the city without fear, bringing the citizens the consolation they desired. In that fleet, it is said, were seventy galleys and other ships, wondrously and enormously large, loaded to the full with men, arms, and provisions; all these the Egyptian ruler had sent to aid the aforesaid city. [Col. 0700C]

The enemy, now as though their strength had been restored and confident in their relief force, again began to bring renewed conflicts against our men, seeking combat more fiercely and more often than before. Yet the citizens, who knew our methods, acted more cautiously; while the inexperienced men who had recently arrived, desirous of glory and wishing to display their strength and boldness, more often fell as they acted rashly, until, having themselves experienced our men’s steadfastness, they learned to attack less recklessly and to withstand more moderately the assaults of those charging them.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Princess Constance of Antioch marries Raynald of Châtillon. Nūr al-Dīn violently seizes the kingdom of Damascus. Amalric is appointed to the Church of Sidon

[Col. 0700D]

While these things were happening in the camp around Ascalon, Lady Constance, widow of Lord Raymond, prince of Antioch, had, according to feminine custom, rejected many distinguished and noble men who sought marriage with her. Secretly she chose as her husband Raynald of Châtillon, a certain soldier in paid service. She did not wish the matter to be made public until the authority and consent of the lord king intervened—for she was his cousin, and the principality seemed to stand under his protection. Raynald therefore hastened to the army and communicated the matter to the lord king. Having obtained his assent, he returned to Antioch and married the aforesaid princess [Col. 0701A]—not without the astonishment of many that so illustrious, powerful, and distinguished a woman, and the wife of so eminent a man, should deign to marry a soldier who was, as it were, a common ranker.

Meanwhile Nūr al-Dīn, a prudent and circumspect man, heard that his father-in-law Ainard, commander of the Damascus forces and administrator of the king’s affairs, who had always strongly opposed his designs, was dead. Seeing also that the king of Jerusalem and all the troops of that kingdom had long been occupied around Ascalon, and judging that they would not easily abandon the siege in order to give assistance against him to the Damascenes when they sought it, he seized the opportunity and came with a great army into the territory of Damascus, as though intending violently to seize the kingdom. There, [Col. 0701B] with the support of the Damascenes, who voluntarily submitted to him, he deprived their king, a dissolute and useless man, of his realm and compelled him, a wanderer and exile upon the earth, to flee eastward.

By this act our position nevertheless became worse. For in place of a powerless man who, because of his weakness, had been so dependent on our people as to pay annual tribute like a subject, a harsher adversary was set against us. For just as a kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, according to the Savior’s saying (Matt. 12:25), so things united commonly acquire great strength from mutual support and rise more powerfully against their enemies. Having captured Damascus and subdued the whole region, Nūr al-Dīn wished to give the people of Ascalon such assistance as he could from afar. Taking advantage of our preoccupations, he besieged the city of Paneas, situated at the furthest borders of the kingdom, [Col. 0701C] so that, summoned to help the besieged, our men might abandon the siege of Ascalon and be compelled to return without accomplishing their undertaking. But by the Lord’s mercy going before them, he fell short of so great a hope and achieved neither aim: he made no progress around the besieged city, while our men, with the Lord’s aid, secured a surrender.

At the same time, after the death of Lord Bernard, of good memory, bishop of Sidon, Amalric was appointed in his place: a man of pious memory in the Lord, abbot of the Regular Canons of the Premonstratensian Order at the place called Saint Habakkuk, or Saint Joseph, surnamed “of Arimathea”; a simple man who feared God and was of outstanding conduct. In the church of Lydda, he is said to have received consecration at the hands of Lord Peter, archbishop of Tyre of happy memory, [Col. 0701D] because from the besieged city no one was permitted to depart farther away.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Those at the siege assail the city vigorously. The citizens attempt to burn the outer engine. Part of the city wall collapses; our men, wishing to enter, are partly destroyed; our army despairs

Meanwhile those on the expedition, applying themselves with great diligence to the work begun, did not cease continually to assault the besieged city and to renew engagements very dangerous to the citizens near the gate called the Great Gate. They also weakened the towers and walls with projectile engines, [Col. 0702A] and, by hurling great millstones into the city, destroyed dwellings to their foundations, not without much slaughter.

Those assigned to guard the tower inflicted such troubles upon the citizens with bows and arrows—not only upon those resisting in the towers and on the walls, but also upon those compelled by necessity to run through the city—that by comparison with them whatever was inflicted elsewhere upon the citizens was judged slight and, however harsh, tolerable. Therefore, after taking counsel together and especially seeking the advice of those who seemed most experienced in such matters, they proposed that, at whatever peril and whatever risk to the citizens, dry wood should be placed between the wall and the tower, wood able to provide suitable material and fuel for fire; and that by secretly kindling a blaze it should be burned. Otherwise, so oppressed and afflicted to the utmost, they saw neither hope of safety nor confidence in resistance.

Accordingly certain brave men, superior in strength and courage, placing their fellow citizens’ safety before their own, exposed themselves to danger. Carrying wood to that part of the wall nearer the tower, they threw it outside into what seemed to be the space between the wall and the engine. When a very great pile of wood had been arranged—such as seemed sufficient to burn the tower—they poured pitch over it, as well as oil, *liquamen*, and other inflammable substances of this kind that usually provide fuel for fires. [Col. 0702C]

When the fire was set, divine mercy was manifestly present for us. For as the blaze immediately grew strong, a violent east wind arose, which with a mighty blast hurled the full force of the fire against the city wall. The wind, driving the flames and fire against the wall by its violence, kept watch throughout that entire night and blew without ceasing, burning the wall down to ashes. Thus, when morning came, at daybreak, the entire wall collapsed from its foundations from one tower to the next adjoining one; the crash of its fall shook the whole army. Falling with such weight, it struck the tower, and though fire had not harmed it, the fall of the wall broke certain of its principal timbers and nearly threw to the ground those keeping watch on its platforms and projections. [Col. 0702D]

Roused by the sound of this collapse, the entire army seized its arms and rushed to that place, as though a divinely opened entrance had been laid bare, intending at once to enter. But Bernard of Tremelay, master of the military order of the Temple, together with his brethren, having greatly outstripped all others, occupied the entrance and permitted no one except their own men to go in. They were said to have excluded the others for this purpose: that by entering first they might obtain greater spoils and richer booty.
