For in cities violently breached, this custom had hitherto prevailed among us as law: whatever any man entering seized for himself, he possessed by perpetual right for himself and his heirs. Yet the city could have been taken by all entering without distinction, and there would have been enough spoils for the victors.

But it is rare for a deed proceeding from a corrupt root and perverse intention to end well, because:

> Foul booty has no good outcome.

Therefore, carried away by greed, because they refused to have companions in sharing the prey, they were rightly found alone when they faced death. About forty of them having entered, while the rest could not follow, the citizens—who had first been anxious for their lives and ready to endure every extremity without resistance—saw that the entrants were few. Recovering their strength and courage, they received them with swords, cut them off, and slaughtered them. Having again joined their ranks, as though their strength were renewed, and having resumed the weapons which they had laid aside as if defeated, they rushed unanimously to the place where the wall had fallen. [Col. 0703B] Weaving together beams of immense size and huge timbers, of which they had an abundance from the ships, they filled the gap, blocked the entrance, and made the place impassable with all speed.

They also fortified the towers on either side which had been near the fire and which they had abandoned because they could not endure the violence of the flames. They renewed the fighting, again prepared for battle, and voluntarily challenged our men to combat, as if they had suffered no adversity whatsoever. Those in the tower, knowing that its foundations were less sound and that the engine had been damaged from below in its firmer supports, pressed the attack less boldly, placing little confidence in its solidity. The citizens, meanwhile, hung the bodies of the slain from ropes over the wall in the battlements, to shame our men, insulting them and expressing by words and gestures the joy they had conceived in their hearts. [Col. 0703C] But the end of this joy is seized by mourning; and what follows clearly shows how truly it is said: “Before destruction the heart is exalted” (Prov. 16:18). Our men, by contrast, were dismayed in mind and spirit, consumed by grief and bitterness of heart; having become faint-hearted, they despaired of victory.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Our men are strengthened again and encouraged to continue the siege, pressing on more courageously

Meanwhile the lord king, alarmed by the bitterness of the disaster, summoned the princes. The life-giving Cross having been placed before them—for they had assembled in his tent—in the presence of the lord [Col. 0703D] patriarch, the lord archbishop of Tyre, and the other prelates of the churches, he anxiously asked what should be done amid so great a change in affairs.

As they deliberated in the fear of God and with much anxiety, their opinions diverged and the desire of those deliberating was, as it were, divided into two parts. Some, despairing of taking the city, maintained that they had long spent their labour there uselessly; they alleged that part of the army had fallen, that princes had been wounded or killed, that funds were failing, that the city was impregnable, that its citizens abounded in every good thing, that their strength was repeatedly replenished while ours was failing; and they urged withdrawal. But others, whose judgment was sounder, encouraged them still to persevere in their intention and to hope in the Lord’s mercy, who in His loving patience does not usually forsake those hoping in Him. They urged that it was of little value for any undertaking to have a good beginning unless it is also concluded with a like end. [Col. 0704A]

They said that much time and very great expenditure had indeed been devoted, but in hope of a richer fruit which the Lord seemed, though delaying it, not to be taking away. They acknowledged that their own men had fallen, but said that there was hope that they would find a better resurrection. They asserted that it was promised to believers: “Your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (John 16:20), and “Whatever you ask, shall be done for you” (Matt. 7:8). Citing these and similar things, they opposed withdrawal and endeavoured to exhort them to persevere like brave men in their purpose.

Nearly all the secular princes supported the former opinion; the king also, wearied by adverse events, seemed more inclined toward it. On the opposing side were the lord patriarch and the lord archbishop of Tyre, with the clergy, having as their ally Lord Raymond, master of the Hospital, together with his brethren. Thus, while they disagreed and advanced various arguments on either side, divine mercy was present and caused all to approve the patriarch’s opinion, which was aided by greater merits and shone with ampler honour. They therefore unanimously resolved that they should have recourse to the Lord and, having implored aid from heaven, persevere in what they had begun until “the Dayspring from on high” should visit them (Luke 1) and look mercifully upon [Col. 0704C] their labours.

Returning therefore to their single purpose, they unanimously seized their arms, sounded the trumpets, and with clarions and heralds’ cries roused all the people to battle. Desiring to avenge the wrongs done to their slain brethren, they assembled before the city with greater ardour than usual and most eagerly challenged the enemy to battle. One could see our lines, as though they had sustained no loss or had acquired fresh strength, their fury expended, rushing upon the enemy and making assaults more violent than usual. The enemy’s squadrons marvelled; they were amazed at the invincible increase of strength among our men and at their persistence in pressing the attack. Though they tried to resist with equal effort, they strove in vain: they could neither endure our men’s pressure nor avoid their swords. [Col. 0704D]

Thus there was fighting that day with forces very unequal; but cavalry and infantry alike triumphed everywhere over the enemy and everywhere carried off the palm of victory. The enemy’s slaughter was enormous, and with overflowing measure the injury suffered by our men the day before yesterday was repaid. There was no household in the city that was not oppressed by domestic mourning and family anxiety. The city was therefore clothed with shame, and in comparison with its present danger its earlier sufferings seemed light. From the first day of the siege until then, they had never suffered equal damage, nor had a similar loss befallen them. For the strength of their soldiery had been consumed, the city’s leaders had been killed, counsel had failed, courage had languished, [Col. 0705A] and every hope of resistance had vanished.

Accordingly, by public counsel, certain leading men of the people were sent as envoys of peace to request a truce for a time from the lord king, so that, after bodies of our dead had been given and those of their own received, both sides might be permitted, according to their custom, to render the due rites and final honour to the funerals. Our men approved the requested condition; and, having received the bodies of their dead, they commended them to burial with funeral solemnities.

## CHAPTER XXIX. The people of Ascalon despair and, by common counsel, incline toward surrender

After the people of Ascalon saw the present slaughter of their own and the mighty hand [Col. 0705B] which the Lord had exercised against them, their grief was renewed, their spirit distressed, and through the enormity of their pain their souls melted within them. And that nothing might be lacking to complete their evils, it happened the same day that, when forty of their strongest men were carrying a beam of enormous size to a place where it seemed necessary, a huge stone shot from one of our projectile engines happened to fall upon the beam and crushed, together with the beam, all those who were beneath it carrying the burden.

Pressed by these heavy troubles and plunged in bitterness, the people summoned together with tears and groaning the Fathers who remained among them, so that mothers holding infants to their breasts were not absent, nor sick old men in whose breasts scarcely their last breath remained. [Col. 0705C] There, through eloquent and prudent men, the following address was delivered to the whole people by common counsel of all:

> Men of Ascalon, who dwell within these gates: you know—and none knows better than you—how dangerous and difficult a struggle we have now maintained for fifty years with this iron people, excessively stubborn in its purpose. You have learned by experience how often they have overthrown our fathers in battle; and how often sons, in their fathers’ place, have renewed wars against them, desiring to repel injuries and preserve this place from which we drew our origin, together with wives and children and, what is greater, freedom.
>
> Today marks the fifty-fourth year since this people, so grievous to us, came up against us from the farthest regions of the West and violently occupied by strong hand the entire country from Tarsus in Cilicia to Egypt. This city alone, through the merits and valour of our forefathers, has remained undiminished to the present day amid so many enemies; yet what it has hitherto suffered may be judged little or nothing in comparison with the dangers threatening now. [Col. 0705D]
>
> Even now our will to resist is no less steadfast in any respect. But the army is worn down, our resources exhausted, the burden of labour intolerable, and the ever-watchful, excessively persistent multitude of enemies, together with continual distress both of mind and body, denies us strength and prevents us from prolonging the struggle. Therefore the Fathers think—if you also think it right—that in the present emergency and miseries it is expedient to send envoys on behalf of the whole people to this powerful king who besieges us, and to try, under agreed conditions, to obtain free departure with wives and children, male and female servants, and every kind of household property; and, what we say with groaning, to surrender the city to him, so that we may put an end to such great evils. [Col. 0706A]

## CHAPTER XXX. Envoys chosen from the leading men of the city obtain from the king free departure with wives, children, and all property, and surrender the city
The proposal seemed good in the eyes of all; and, with loud and unanimous shouts, as commonly happens on such occasions, it was approved. From the whole people prudent and discerning men were chosen, bearing the marks of venerable old age, to carry the proposed terms [Col. 0706B] to the lord king and his princes. Having gone out beyond the gate after first obtaining a truce and permission to approach, they came before the lord king. When, as they had requested, access to all the princes had been granted them, they presented their proposal, setting out the agreed terms in order.

The king ordered them to withdraw for a while; and, having consulted with his princes, carefully asked what each thought. But they, bursting into tears for joy, raised their eyes and hands to the stars and rendered abundant thanks to the Creator, because He had deigned to bestow so great an abundance of His gift upon those unworthy of it. The envoys having then been recalled, the common answer was given them: the proposed terms were acceptable, provided that within the following three days they should evacuate the whole city. [Col. 0706C] Approving this, and wishing that the agreements might acquire greater force, they required oaths to be sworn to them. These were solemnly and physically sworn, by the hand of the lord king and the chosen princes, that the tenor of the aforesaid acts should be observed in good faith and without fraud. Hostages first having been given to them, whom the king had specified by name, they joyfully returned to their own people, taking with them certain of our knights, who were to set the king’s banners upon the city’s loftier towers as a sign of victory.

When our army, awaiting this with the keenest desire, saw the royal banners upon the highest towers, there arose a great shout of the rejoicing people, mingled with tears, praising with united voice up to the stars [Col. 0706D] and saying: “Blessed is the God of our fathers, who does not forsake those who hope in Him; and blessed is the name of His majesty, which is holy, because today we have seen wonders.”

Now, although by agreement they had a truce for a continuous three days, fearing our presence, they packed their baggage and, within two days, set out with wives and children, male and female servants, and every kind of household property. The lord king provided them guides for the journey and, in accordance with the terms of the agreement, dismissed them in peace as far as Laris, an ancient city situated in the wilderness. But the lord king, and likewise the lord patriarch, with the other princes of the kingdom and prelates of the churches, together with all the clergy and people, entered the city behind the wood of the Lord’s Cross, with hymns and spiritual songs [Col. 0707A]. Into their principal and most splendid oratory—which was afterwards consecrated in honour of the apostle Paul—they brought the Lord’s Cross. There, having solemnly celebrated the divine offices and given thanks, they withdrew to the lodgings assigned them and passed a joyful day, memorable for all ages.

Within a few days, the lord patriarch, arranging the Church, established there a fixed number of canons and fixed revenues for them, which they call prebends. He also ordained as bishop a certain Absalom, a regular canon of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, although Gerard, bishop of Bethlehem, strongly objected and forbade it to be done. Afterwards, when the case was brought by appeal before the Roman pontiff, [Col. 0707B] the aforesaid bishop of Bethlehem obtained, with the exclusion of the man whom the lord patriarch had consecrated there, the Church of Ascalon with its possessions, to be held in perpetual right by himself and the Church of Bethlehem.

The king, by his mother’s [Col. 0708A] counsel, distributed properties and lands measured out by the line, both in the city and its suburbs, among men who had deserved well—some also through payment—and generously granted the city to his young brother, Lord Amalric, count of Jaffa. Thus the aforesaid city was taken in the year 1154 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the tenth year of the reign of Lord Baldwin IV, king, in August, on the twelfth day of the month.

A miserable misfortune befell the unhappy Ascalonites as they departed and went down into Egypt. When the king’s men, who had been assigned as their guides and protectors against molestation, had left them, a certain Nocquinus, a Turk by race, valiant in arms but depraved in morals and faithless, who had long served among them as a fellow-soldier for pay, pretended to be their companion in their departure and descent into Egypt. [Col. 0708B] But when he saw them deprived of guides, he cast aside faith, despised humanity, and fell upon them; after taking their spoils, he departed and left them wandering in the wilderness.

# BOOK EIGHTEEN BEGINS

[Col. 0707]

## CHAPTER I. Raynald of Châtillon, prince of Antioch, shamefully mistreats the patriarch of Antioch; the latter takes refuge in the kingdom. A severe famine arises over the land.

[Col. 0707C]

Meanwhile Raynald of Châtillon, who had married the widow of Lord Raymond, prince of Antioch—an action of which we spoke above—seeing that the lord patriarch had not greatly approved of it from the beginning and still persisted in the same view, regarded all the patriarch’s conduct with suspicion. The patriarch, however, being a very rich and powerful man of supreme authority, spoke quite freely and often about Raynald’s person and deeds, both privately and publicly. There were certain persons, as frequently happens in such cases, who, seeking fuel for hatred, carried such words to Raynald. Moved thereby to indignation [Col. 0707D] and implacable anger, the prince laid violent hands upon the lord patriarch; and, in a devilish act of audacity, had him seized and shamefully brought to the castle which overlooks the city of Antioch.

And what seems sufficiently abominable: he compelled an aged priest, successor of Peter, prince of the apostles, a sickly man and one almost perpetually infirm, to sit bareheaded and smeared with honey through a summer day in the fiercest sun, with no one providing relief from the sun’s violence or, in pity, driving away the flies. When the lord king of Jerusalem heard this, he was struck with amazement, marveling at the madness of the deranged man and almost beside himself with astonishment. He sent honourable envoys—Lord Frederick, bishop of Acre, and Lord Ralph [Col. 0708B], his chancellor—by whom he addressed letters to him, rebuked the aforesaid madman by royal authority, and admonished him to desist from his perpetrated insanity.

Raynald, having seen the envoys and read the royal letters, after subjecting the patriarch to many insults, released him; he also fully restored the goods which he had violently seized from him and his people. At length the lord patriarch abandoned the diocese of Antioch and went into the kingdom of Jerusalem. There he was kindly received by the lord king and his most discerning mother, as well as by the lord patriarch and all the bishops of the kingdom, and remained for several years.

In the following year there was a severe famine throughout the whole land. The Lord, angry with us, broke every staff of bread, so that a modius of wheat was sold for four gold pieces. Had it not been for the supply of grain found in the city of Ascalon after its conquest, [Col. 0708D] the whole people would almost have perished while famine besieged the region. Yet in the following years, once the adjoining territory of Ascalon—which for fifty years had lain uncultivated through fear of the enemy—received the care of farmers, and the population of the region, the fear of enemies having been driven away, could freely cultivate the land, it filled the entire kingdom with such abundance that, in comparison with the present, one might rightly call all the preceding time barren and sterile. For, long ignorant of cultivation and never having borne the use of the ploughshare, it had retained its full strength; once it felt the husbandman’s care, it returned the seed entrusted to it with manifold interest and sixtyfold fruit.

## CHAPTER II. Upon Anastasius’s death Adrian succeeds him. Emperor Frederick is crowned at Rome. Grave hostilities arise between the pope and William, king of Sicily.

[Col. 0709A]

While these things were taking place in the East, Pope Anastasius IV died at Rome and Lord Adrian III succeeded him. An Englishman by birth, he had been abbot of the Regular Canons in the church of Saint Rufus, at the castle of Saint Alban near the city of Avignon in Provence, in the diocese of Arles. From there he was summoned to the Roman Church by Lord Eugenius, of blessed memory, and was ordained bishop of Albano, under the name Nicholas. When Lord Anastasius—who had succeeded the aforesaid Lord Eugenius—died, Nicholas had returned from Norway, the westernmost and remotest province, to which the same pope had sent him as legate. He attended the election, was unanimously chosen by clergy and people, and was called Adrian.

It happened in that same year that Lord Frederick, king of the Germans but not yet emperor, descended into Italy with an innumerable host of his men. After subduing Tortona, one of the cities of Lombardy which he had long besieged, he intended to come to Rome and be crowned there. In those days grave hostilities had arisen, for certain reasons, between Pope Adrian, of whom we have spoken, and Lord William, king of Sicily, son of Lord Roger of blessed memory. The affair had advanced to open hatred and harmful war, so that [Col. 0709C] the pope launched a sentence of excommunication against him.

Frederick, of whom we have spoken, pressing on with his purpose, hastened his march and within a few days came from Lombardy to Rome; his sudden arrival was exceedingly alarming to the pope and the whole Roman Church. At last, through mediators arranging peace and after the usual conditions had been set forth, he was solemnly crowned in the church of Saint Peter, according to custom, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July [26 June], and was called Augustus. Three days later, on the feast day of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, both proceeded beneath the city of Tivoli at a place called the Lucanian Bridge: the one adorned in imperial regalia, the other bearing the distinctive insignia of the supreme pontificate. With their troops joined, [Col. 0709D] and clergy and people rejoicing, they proceeded crowned with laurels. When the celebration of the feast day was ended, they parted from one another in good peace. The lord emperor hurried to the region of Ancona, whither the care of the empire drew him, while the lord pope remained for a time in the Roman region, in the hill towns.

Meanwhile the king of Sicily ordered his princes to besiege the city of Benevento, a familiar seat of the Roman Church, and commanded that its inhabitants be pressed by the most urgent straits. The pope took this report exceedingly ill and, wishing to repay him in equal measure, sought to arm his own princes against him; nor was he disappointed in this purpose. For he persuaded Robert of Bassavilla, the most powerful count of William’s kingdom and son of that king’s paternal aunt, [Col. 0710A] along with many other noble men—to whom he promised that the aid and counsel of the Roman Church would never fail—to rise against him.

He also urged the exiles, whom both William and his father had expelled from the kingdom and stripped of their paternal estates—illustrious and powerful men, namely Lord Robert of Sorrento, prince of Capua, Count Andrew of Rapacanina, and many others—to return to the kingdom and take possession of the properties due to them by hereditary right. On his pontifical word he most firmly pledged that the Roman Church would never fail them. He likewise incited both emperors—the emperor of the Romans and the emperor of Constantinople—to seize the Sicilian kingdom: the former, who was still in Italy, openly and face to face; the latter secretly by letters. [Col. 0710B]

## CHAPTER III. Disputes arise between the lord patriarch and the brethren of the Hospital concerning tithes and certain wrongs inflicted by them upon the churches.

Thus, while the affairs both of the Church and of the Sicilian kingdom were troubled in Italy, our eastern region also was not free from disturbance. At the same time, after the city of Ascalon had been restored to the Christians by divine favour and the affairs of the kingdom were proceeding quite prosperously amid joyful fruits, the enemy man began to sow tares over the field and to envy the tranquillity granted by the Lord.

For Raymond, master of the house of the Hospital, together with his brethren filled with the same spirit—although he was otherwise believed to be a religious man who feared God—began to cause many troubles both to the lord patriarch and to the other prelates of the churches, concerning parochial jurisdiction and the right to tithes. [Col. 0710C] Those whom their bishops had excommunicated or specifically placed under interdict, and who had been separated from the Church because of their crimes, they received everywhere and without distinction for the celebration of the divine offices; they did not deny them, while sick, either viaticum or extreme unction, nor burial when dead.

Whenever, because of enormous offences, silence was imposed upon all the churches of a city or of any town, these men were the first, by the ringing of bells and louder-than-usual shouting, to summon the interdicted people to divine worship, so that they themselves might have the offerings and other revenues due to the mother churches, and, while others mourned, they alone might rejoice. Thus they forgot the saying of that outstanding preacher: “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Rom. 12:15). [Col. 0710D]

They neither presented their priests to the bishops of the places, in accordance with the ancient ordinance of the holy decrees, so that they might celebrate the divine offices in their dioceses with the bishops’ knowledge; nor, when they dismissed them, whether justly or unjustly, did they make this known to the bishops. From their estates and all revenues accruing to them by whatever right, they utterly refused to pay tithes. This was the complaint of all bishops against them; this was the injury they inflicted upon all cathedral churches everywhere. But especially they inflicted this injury, hateful to all Christians, upon the lord patriarch and the holy Church of Jerusalem. For before the doors of the church of the Holy Resurrection, in contempt and insult to that Church, they began to erect buildings far more costly and considerably higher than the church which had been consecrated by the precious blood of the Lord and Saviour hanging upon the Cross, and which afforded Him, after the gibbet of the Cross, a most welcome burial within itself. [Col. 0711A]

Moreover, whenever the lord patriarch customarily ascended to the place where the Saviour of the world hung for our salvation, and where the redemption of the whole world was wrought and is celebrated in abundant measure, in order to speak to the people, they, to hinder his actions and the ministry entrusted to him, rang so many bells, and such great ones, so zealously and for so long, that the lord patriarch’s voice was insufficient even to shout, and the people could not hear him, however greatly he exerted himself. [Col. 0711B] Although the lord patriarch often complained to the citizens of such rashness, and their malice was proved by evidence in their presence, when summoned by many they were found incorrigible, even threatening at times to undertake more serious acts.

And this indeed came to pass. In devilish audacity and a spirit of rage, they proceeded so far that, having taken up arms, they burst into the aforesaid God-beloved church as though into the house of some commoner, and shot many arrows as though into a den of thieves. Afterwards these were gathered and made into a bundle, hung by a rope before the place of Calvary where the Lord was crucified; we ourselves saw them, and countless others saw them. [Col. 0711C]

The Roman Church, perhaps unknowingly and without duly weighing what was asked of it, seems to attentive observers to have introduced the first origin of so great an evil. For it improperly emancipated the aforesaid place from the jurisdiction of the lord patriarch of Jerusalem, to whom it had long and deservedly been subject; so that they have reverence neither for God nor for men, except those whom they fear. Yet we do not, with one judgment and without distinguishing differences, involve all in this pride hateful to God and mother of every vice; for we believe that it can scarcely happen that in so great a body all walk the same path and that there should be no difference of merits. [Col. 0711D]

But in order to record in the present history how great an increase the place in question began from so small a sowing, and how improperly it has kicked against the churches of God and has not ceased to do so even to this day, we have thought it necessary to begin somewhat further back, by the Lord’s help omitting in no way the rule of truth.

## CHAPTER IV. An account of the origin and beginning of the house of the Hospital.

When, because our sins required it, the kingdom of Jerusalem, together with all Syria and [Col. 0712A] Egypt and the adjoining provinces, had passed into the hands of enemies of the Christian name and faith—as ancient histories relate—this is known to have happened in the time of Lord Heraclius, emperor of the Romans, when the peoples of Arabia grew strong against him. Yet many Westerners did not fail from time to time to visit the holy places, though they had fallen under enemy power, either from devotion, for trade, or for both reasons.

Among those who, under the pretext of trade, attempted in those centuries to visit the aforesaid places were men from Italy, called Amalfitans from the city in which they lived. Amalfi is a city situated between the sea and very high mountains. To the east it has the most noble city of Salerno, scarcely seven miles distant from it by sea; to the west, Sorrento and Virgilian Naples; and to the south, Sicily, separated by the Tyrrhenian Sea and about two hundred miles away, more or less. [Col. 0712B]

The inhabitants of this region, as we have said, were the first to attempt to introduce into the aforesaid regions, for the sake of profit, foreign wares and goods previously unknown in the East. Thus, because of the necessary things which they brought, they obtained excellent terms from the rulers of those regions, easy access, and likewise the goodwill of the people. In those days the ruler of Egypt possessed all the coastal regions from the city of Gabala, on the seashore near Laodicea of Syria, as far as Alexandria, the last city of Egypt; and through governors appointed to individual cities he rendered his rule widely formidable. [Col. 0712C]

The aforesaid Amalfitans, enjoying the full favour both of the king and of his princes, could confidently travel everywhere, appearing as merchants and traders in useful goods and carrying merchandise about. Mindful also of the traditions of their fathers and of the Christian faith, they visited the holy places whenever opportunity was given. But since they had no familiar lodging in that city where they could stay for a while, as they had in the coastal cities, they gathered from their own people as many as they could summon for the conceived undertaking, approached the caliph of Egypt, gained the favour of his household, submitted their petition in writing, and obtained its fulfilment in accordance with their desires. [Col. 0712D]

## CHAPTER V. How the Egyptian caliph, at the Amalfitans’ request, orders a site assigned to them on which to build a church.

Accordingly, the governor of Jerusalem was instructed that a very ample place in Jerusalem should be assigned, according to their desire, to the Amalfitan men—friends and importers of useful goods—in the quarter inhabited by Christians, for building whatever sort of dwelling they wished. The city, as it is today, was almost equally divided into four parts. Only one quarter, in which the Lord’s Sepulchre is situated, was granted to the faithful for habitation; the other quarters, together with the Temple of the Lord, were occupied exclusively by the unbelievers as their homes.

By the prince’s command, therefore, a site considered sufficient for the required buildings was assigned them. The merchants contributed money, as it were by a common subscription, and, before the door of the church of the Lord’s Resurrection, scarcely a stone’s throw away, they erected a monastery in honour of the holy and glorious Mother of God and perpetual Virgin Mary, together with such workshops as could offer some convenience for the use of the monks and for receiving guests of their own people. [Col. 0713A]

When this had been done, they transferred both monks and an abbot from their own country, established the place according to a rule, and made it pleasing to the Lord by holy observance. [Col. 0713B] Because both the men who founded the place and those who maintained religious life there were Latins, from that day to the present the place has been called the Monastery of the Latins.

At the same time holy widows and continent women came to venerate the sacred places. Forgetting female fear and not terrified by the many dangers that occurred, when they arrived there was no suitable provision within the monastery’s enclosure where they could be decently gathered. The holy men who founded the place therefore took care that devout women arriving should have a separate oratory, a dwelling house, and a place of lodging. At length, by the favour of divine mercy, a small monastery was established there in honour of the pious sinner, Mary Magdalene, and a fixed number of sisters were appointed to serve women visitors. [Col. 0713C]

During those dangerous times, some also came from other peoples, both nobles and persons of lesser rank. Since access to the holy city was possible only through enemy territories, none of their travel resources remained when they reached the city. Poor and destitute, they were compelled outside the city gate to wait a long time in extreme hardship, hunger, thirst, and nakedness, until, after giving a gold coin, they were allowed to enter the city. Once inside, after visiting the holy places in order, they had no hope even of food for one day except what was fraternally supplied from the aforesaid monastery. For all the other inhabitants of the city were Saracens and unbelievers, except for the lord patriarch, the clergy, and the wretched little people of the Syrians. These were daily oppressed with so many forced labours, transport obligations, and payments of degrading dues that, placed in utter poverty and continual fear of death, they could scarcely breathe. [Col. 0713D]

For our wretched people, then, utterly afflicted and needy, since there was no one to provide shelter, the most blessed men inhabiting the monastery of the Latins arranged that, mercifully taking from their own food and clothing, they should erect within their allotted enclosure a hospice (*xenodochium*) for such persons. There they gathered the healthy and sick, lest they be found in the streets at night and slaughtered; and to those gathered there, they supplied some scant daily sustenance from the leftovers and fragments of both monasteries, of men and women alike. [Col. 0714A]

They also erected in the same place an altar in honour of blessed John Eleemon. This man, pleasing to God and in every respect worthy of praise, was Cypriot by birth; later, through the assistance of his merits, he became patriarch of Alexandria, a man pre-eminent in works of mercy, whose pious efforts and generous almsgiving the whole Church of the saints will recount forever. Hence the holy Fathers called him *Eleemon*, “the Merciful.”

This venerable institution, so generously extended toward humanity, possessed neither revenues nor estates. But every year the aforesaid Amalfitans, both those at home and those engaged in commerce, gathered money among themselves as by a common subscription and sent it through persons travelling to Jerusalem to the abbot then in office, so that food and clothing might be provided from it for the brothers and sisters, and some mercy might be shown from the remainder to Christians arriving at the hospice. Thus, for the course of many years, until it pleased the supreme Maker of all things to cleanse from heathen superstitions the city which He had purified by His own blood, that place remained under these conditions. [Col. 0714B]

When the Christian people and the princes protected by God arrived—those to whom the Saviour chose to entrust that kingdom—there was found in the women’s monastery a certain woman devoted and holy before God, named Agnes, noble according to the flesh and Roman by birth, fulfilling the office of abbess. Even after the city had been restored to the Christian faith, she lived for several years. Likewise, in the hospice there was found a certain Gerard, a man of proven conduct, who had long and devoutly served the poor in that place during the period of hostility, by command of the abbot and monks. Raymond, of whom we are now speaking, later succeeded him. [Col. 0714C]

## CHAPTER VI. The patriarch, with most of the eastern bishops, journeys to Rome to Pope Adrian.

[Col. 0714D]

Thus, after attaining such growth from so small a beginning, the brethren of the aforesaid house first withdrew themselves from the abbot’s jurisdiction. Then, when their wealth had multiplied beyond measure, they were emancipated by the Roman Church from the hand and authority of the lord patriarch. Having obtained this pernicious freedom, they thereafter showed no reverence at all to the prelates of the churches and wholly refused tithes from any estates whatsoever that came to them by any right.

Following this example, many monasteries and hospices among those places called venerable—places to which churches had first supplied their foundations from pure liberality and the duty of customary charity, and had brought them to their desired growth—eventually, grown fat, kicked back. They were separated from the breasts of their pious mother, from which they had at first, like newborn infants, been fed with milk and then nourished at the proper time with solid food. Thus the Church may rightly complain of them: “I have nourished and brought up children, but they have despised me” (Isa. 1:2). [Col. 0715A]

May the Lord spare them and grant them to return to their senses, so that they may learn to serve in fear their mother whom they have abandoned. And may He still further spare that one who, though he possessed a hundred sheep, saw and begrudged the single ewe of a poor man, to whom the Lord says: “You have killed and taken possession” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 21:19). Woe to him, whoever he may be, for according to the prophet’s judgment he is a man of blood (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 16:8).

Therefore, after the lord patriarch and the other prelates of the churches had repeatedly failed, as we have said, in seeking to recover their rights from the brethren, recourse was had on both sides to the tribunal of the Roman pontiff. [Col. 0715B] The lord patriarch, though aged and nearly a hundred years old, accordingly took with him from the prelates of the churches Lord Peter, archbishop of Tyre; and among his suffragans Lord Frederick, bishop of Acre; Lord Amalric, bishop of Sidon; Lord Baldwin, archbishop of Caesarea; Lord Constantine, bishop of Lydda; Lord Rainer, bishop of Sebaste; and Lord Herbert, bishop of Tiberias. When the mildness of spring was returning, and the sea, stirred by winter winds, began under the breath of the west wind to become more favourable, they set out and, with God’s help, reached Otranto, a maritime city of Apulia, in a prosperous voyage. [Col. 0715C]

## CHAPTER VII. With the pope’s consent, the emperor of Constantinople invades Apulia. The lord patriarch and his companions reach the curia.

Meanwhile, while the eastern bishops together with the lord patriarch had reached the borders of Apulia, as stated above, the emperor of Constantinople, acting on the pope’s word, had sent in some of his princes with immense sums of money and, with the consent of the magnates of those regions, violently invaded the country. Thus, by the time the lord patriarch and his party came from Otranto to Brindisi, the household of the emperor had already received that city into its possession, the citizens having surrendered it, while only the city’s garrison, in which there were few men, remained loyal to the lord king. [Col. 0715D]

Count Robert, of whom we spoke above, together with those who followed his party both from hatred of the king and from favour toward him, had violently seized Taranto, Bari, distinguished metropolitan cities, and the whole coastal region as far as the borders of the kingdom. The aforesaid great and illustrious men, Robert, prince of Capua, and Count Andrew, had claimed for themselves the whole of Campania, popularly called the Terra di Lavoro, as far as Salerno, Naples, and San Germano. The whole region was in such turmoil that nowhere was there peace or security for travellers.

The emperor of the Romans also, Lord Frederick, remaining with his armies in the region of Ancona, suffered such a slaughter among the legions he had led into Italy that, with the greater and nobler princes of the empire failing, scarcely a tenth remained. Therefore, unable to restrain those who remained and wished to return home, he too prepared for return, though unwillingly. Many affairs, especially those against the same king of Sicily, required his presence. [Col. 0716A]

The lord patriarch and his travelling companions anxiously considered by what route they could reach the pope amid such tumult, for battles and seditions everywhere seemed to close every approach. A certain Ansquetinus, chancellor of the king of Sicily, was also besieging Benevento. He absolutely refused passage through those regions to the patriarch’s messengers who had been sent to request an escort from the aforesaid chancellor, although that route was much shorter than all the others. At length, after taking counsel with certain prudent men, the patriarch followed the sea route and reached Ancona with all his company. From there he sent certain bishops from his retinue to greet the emperor of the Romans, who, as stated, was already returning home, and to obtain imperial letters from him to the pope concerning the patriarch’s affairs. [Col. 0716B]

This was done, although the emperor, eager to return, had already passed Senigallia and Pesaro. The lord patriarch, however, directing his journey toward Rome with his [Col. 0716C] company, pursued the lord pope, who had left the city of Narni, as though he were fleeing. At last, having come to Rome and remained there for several days, when he was told that the pope had taken up his position at the city of Ferentino, he hurried there without delay to try to pursue the matter for which he had come.

Some said that the pope was deliberately avoiding him, in order to weary him with delay and burden him with expenses; for, corrupted by countless gifts, he was said to have inclined to the Hospitallers’ side, and they had arrived before him much earlier. Others said that he had arrived with such haste because of Benevento, which, as we have said, was shut in by siege. It was, however, evident that he had granted his own favour and that of his household far too readily to the Hospitallers, while he drove the lord patriarch and his party from him with a certain haughtiness and indignation, as though they were illegitimate sons and unworthy. [Col. 0716D]

## CHAPTER VIII. Pope Adrian hastens to Benevento; the patriarch hurries there, sets forth his claims, but the curia, corrupted by gifts, suppresses justice. The patriarch returns with his business unfinished.

After he had therefore arrived at the aforesaid city, he presented himself, as customary, before the apostolic presence. There he was received badly and treated worse; and, although the cardinals were for the most part unwilling, he carried away clear evidence of the pope’s disposition and intention. Yet [Col. 0717A], relying on the counsel of certain prudent friends, he concealed all this; and, being a stern man, he continued to attend upon the pope. On feast days he was constantly present in consistory, reverently surrounded by the company of his bishops; and a throng of advocates also stood continually by him whenever needed, ready to perform their office. When, therefore, both parties had been granted a hearing, and they had for many days contended fruitlessly on either side, the lord patriarch, seeing—and learning through certain intimate friends—that he would make no progress, took leave and, reporting a worse state of affairs, set out to return home, clothed in confusion and reverence.

Of so great a multitude of cardinals, scarcely two or three were found—namely Lord Octavian and Lord [Col. 0717B] John of Saint Martin, who, while the same lord patriarch was archbishop of Tyre, had been his archdeacon—who, following Christ, were willing in piety to support His minister in his cause. All the others, going after gifts, followed the ways of Balaam, son of Bosor. The lord pope, however, pressed by domestic concerns, crossed Campania and arrived at Benevento.

Meanwhile the king of Sicily, Lord William, hearing and being repeatedly informed by embassies that in Apulia Count Robert of Bassavilla, together with the Greeks, had violently occupied the country; that in Campania the prince of Capua and Count Andrew were widely extending their dominion; and that the lord pope had withdrawn to Benevento, whence he supplied strength and encouragement to all those aforesaid—having assembled military forces from all Sicily and Calabria, advanced into Apulia with a great expedition. There, immediately near Brindisi, Count Robert fleeing, he scattered the Greek forces in the first encounter; and, having utterly crushed their army, he put their captured commanders in chains. He also conveyed to his own wardrobes, as powerfully as successfully, the very numerous *cazas* [perhaps garments] which they had brought. Then, having recovered the entire region which had revolted from him and restored the people to favour, he besieged Benevento. There he afflicted both the lord pope and his cardinals, and all the citizens, with such hardships that food failed and they became extremely anxious for their safety. Through envoys passing between them, peace was restored under certain secret terms [Col. 0717D], all those being excluded from the treaty who, at the pope’s persuasion, had plunged themselves into such labours and dangers.

Seeing, therefore, that events had turned out contrary to their hope, and that the lord pope, without securing for them the king’s favour, had made peace for himself and the Roman Church while excluding them, these noblemen anxiously began to consider how they might leave the kingdom safe and unharmed. Count Robert and Andrew, hastening with certain other noblemen into Lombardy, betook themselves to the emperor. But the prince of Capua, more unfortunate than the rest, while preparing to cross the Garigliano by boat, was captured by his own boatmen. Having already sent his men ahead and himself waiting with a few on the nearer bank, just about to cross [Col. 0718A], he was delivered to the king’s faithful men and taken to Sicily, where he was at once imprisoned and forcibly blinded, and ended his life miserably.

## CHAPTER IX. A civil disturbance arises in Egypt; the sultan flees from them and is killed by our men; his son Nosceradinus is captured.

At the same time, while the kingdom of Jerusalem was prospering tolerably through God’s mercy, it happened that the regions adjoining it on either side were, as if unexpectedly, shaken miserably. For a very powerful Egyptian, exercising the office of sultan, approached the ruler of the land—the caliph, namely, whom the Egyptians customarily worship and venerate as a supreme divinity [Col. 0718B]—as though he were the confidential manager of his affairs, and deceitfully murdered him in a more private chamber of the palace. He is said to have done this with the intention of raising his own son Noseredin to be caliph and, while his son presided over the administration of the kingdom, continuing himself free from care and anxiety.

For several days he supposed that the matter could be concealed, until, having seized the greater palace and wholly occupied the treasures, and having summoned a gathering of friends and retainers, he might be able to resist those who wished to hold against him as a capital crime what he had done. But the matter turned out very differently. For after a short interval the crime became known, and the entire people, from the greatest to the least, assembling as one man, surrounded on every side the house into which he had withdrawn after committing the murder. With one voice they demanded punishment from the man of blood who had, in wicked audacity, inflicted death on the ruler of the land.

As they pressed him more fiercely, seeing no other way of safety remained, he opened his treasures and threw gold, jewels, and whatever desirable things he possessed through the windows to the shouting people, so that, while they were more occupied in gathering them, he might somehow prepare himself for departure. Why say more? He went out with a respectable company of sons and grandsons and, despite those who had besieged him, took the road into the wilderness, intending, it was said, to go to Damascus. They nevertheless pursued him with no less vigour and tried to impede him. But his eldest son, along with other prudent men of the household, vigorous in arms [Col. 0718D], kept them at a greater distance, bore their attacks, and did not allow them to approach their own party too closely. At times they deliberately left behind gold or silver vessels, costly garments, and silks of no small value, in order to delay their pursuers and provide them grounds for quarrelling over the division of what they gathered.

At last, seeing that they could not succeed, the Egyptians returned home with the affair unfinished. But he continued his journey; and, while he thought that he had escaped the snares of fate, travelling securely and supposing that no difficulty remained, he fled Scylla only to fall into Charybdis. For our men, having heard of his passage, had laid an ambush in advance; after the manner of those intending harm, they hid silently in concealment. [Col. 0719A] He unexpectedly fell into the aforesaid ambush and, in the first encounters, was mortally pierced; there he immediately ended his life by the sword. The nobleman’s name was Habeis. His son Noseredinus, his entire household, and all the wealth which they had brought with them from Egypt were delivered into the hands of the enemy.

Thus laden with rich spoils—such as our world had never previously heard of—and heavily burdened with plunder, they divided the booty according to custom and returned home. It happened that, among the others who had taken part in this undertaking, the brethren of the Knights Templar had many soldiers and, in proportion to their numbers, carried off the larger shares of the spoils and booty. For, besides other things, there fell to their lot in the line of distribution the son of the aforesaid nobleman, [Col. 0719B] Noseradinus, a most daring man, possessing among the Egyptians exceptional experience in warfare; his very name was terrifying to the peoples of that region, and his appearance inspired unrelieved dread.

After the aforesaid brethren had held him in chains for many days, although he eagerly sought rebirth in Christ, had already learned Latin letters, and had been taught the first rudiments of the Christian faith, they sold him for sixty thousand Egyptian gold pieces to those who demanded him for death. Delivered over bound hand and foot with iron chains, they placed him in an iron cage upon camels and took him to Egypt. There, satisfying their inhuman desires, they tore him apart with their teeth and cut him into very small pieces [Col. 0719C].

## CHAPTER X. Prince Rainald occupies the island of Cyprus and violently plunders its inhabitants.

In the following year, Rainald of Châtillon, prince of Antioch, directed chiefly by the counsel of wicked men, again committed a sacrilegious crime. He violently occupied, by sending hostile forces into it, the island of Cyprus, our neighbour—full of Christian inhabitants, useful to our kingdom, and always friendly to it.

The apparent reason for this detestable invasion was as follows. In Cilicia, near Tarsus, there was a certain noble and very powerful Armenian named Toros. Owing to his own fickleness, he frequently forfeited the emperor’s favour and incurred his displeasure [Col. 0719D]. Trusting greatly in the fact that he was far removed from the empire and had his dwellings in steep mountains, he carried off booty and spoil through the plains of Cilicia. He did not fear to damage the land of his lord in every way he could, and to inflict serious and unjust hardships on the emperor’s subjects of whatever rank.

Hearing this, the emperor wrote to the aforesaid Rainald, instructing him to summon troops, drive Toros back from his borders, and make secure from his incursions the possessions of the Cilicians subject to him. If money were necessary to accomplish the undertaking, he would send enough from his own treasury at the proper time. Thus Rainald assembled military forces and, to obey the imperial commands [Col. 0720A], entered Cilicia, expelled Toros, and destroyed his army almost to total annihilation.

Expecting an honourable reward for so great a deed, Rainald thought that it was being delayed excessively. Impatient of the delay, he rushed into the aforesaid evil act. The islanders had been carefully forewarned by some of our people and had therefore gathered such forces as they could from throughout the island. But when Prince Rainald entered, he immediately routed their army and so completely crushed all their forces that thereafter not one person could be found who dared raise a hand against him. Having free passage throughout the entire island, he destroyed cities, overthrew towns, and shamelessly destroyed monasteries of men and women alike, exposing nuns and tender young virgins to outrage. Gold and silver and precious garments were without number or end; yet, compared with violated chastity, the people regarded the loss of these things as dung.

Thus for several days, raging throughout the entire country while there was no one to resist, they spared neither age nor sex and made no distinction of rank. At last, having gathered spoil from every quarter and an infinite abundance of plunder of every kind, they withdrew to the sea; and from there, with ships prepared, descended into the region of Antioch, squandering within a short time the wealth they had wickedly acquired, according to the proverbial saying:

> [Col. 0720C] “Foul plunder has no good outcome.”

## CHAPTER XI. Contrary to the agreements and treaty of peace which he had made with them, the king captures Turks and Arabs in the forest of Paneas.

At the same time, an unprecedented multitude of Arabs and Turcomans had assembled, beyond what was usual. They too dwell in tents and, like the Arabs, customarily sustain life from the produce of animals. They gathered in the forest adjoining the city of Paneas, from which it now takes its common name. For in ancient times the whole forest—both that extending north and south and that covering Lebanon itself—was called the forest tract of Lebanon. Hence it is written of Solomon that he built in it a house of costly workmanship and wonderful construction [Col. 0720D], called the House of the Forest of Lebanon. But now, as we have said, the entire forest is named after the nearby city.

Into this forest the aforesaid peoples had brought their animals, especially horses in countless number, following the advantages of pasture; but first they had obtained the lord king’s favour and had been solemnly granted peace. Yet wicked men, sons of Belial, having no fear of the Lord before their eyes, approached the king. They suggested to him—and more easily entangled him in their wickedness—persuading him to be lavish with his pledged faith and forgetful of the treaty he had made with them. They urged him suddenly to attack these men, who had brought both flocks and herds into the forest for grazing, and to give both them and their livestock to his own men as plunder. This [Col. 0721A] was done.

For the king, burdened with debt and bound by many obligations, having no means of satisfying his creditors, more readily lent an open ear to wicked instigators in order somehow to free himself, and acquiesced in their suggestions. Departing after the counsel of the ungodly, he summoned troops, suddenly fell upon them, found them unsuspecting and fearing nothing of the kind, and treated them as enemies, exposing them to plunder by his men. Those who could save themselves by flight, either by using the speed of their horses or by avoiding the enemy in the hiding places of the woods, as necessity itself taught them, were preserved alive. All the rest were either killed by the sword or reduced to harsh slavery.

The quantity of spoil and booty was so great and so unheard-of that none equal to it is said to have existed in our regions. To each of the common people and plebeians there fell by lot a very great number of horses. Yet this cannot be credited to our people as any ground for extending glory or praise, since, as violators of peace and breakers of treaty, they wickedly treated according to their will men who were unsuspecting and trusted in the king’s favour, while no one was there to resist them. But the Lord, the just requiter, the God of vengeance, did not allow us long to rejoice in such shameful gain. Signifying that even faith with unbelievers must be preserved inviolate, He brought upon us confusion and vengeance as the punishment for the crime committed. For all our sins He repaid us double and, with multiplied interest, inflicted disgrace, as [Col. 0721C] will be said in what follows.

## CHAPTER XII. Humphrey the constable grants one half of the city of Paneas to the Hospitallers; the relief being brought is captured by Nur al-Din, and the city is besieged.

During the same days, Humphrey of Toron, royal constable, since he could no longer conveniently govern and preserve alone the oft-mentioned city of Paneas—his hereditary possession—exhausted as he was by expense and continual care, divided it equally with the brethren of the Hospital, with the lord king’s consent. The aforesaid brethren, holding one half of the entire city and all its suburbs, were to provide half the useful and necessary expenses [Col. 0721D], while taking due care for the other half of the city.

The city lay on the frontier of the enemy and very near to them, so that none could approach or depart except with danger, unless coming with strong armed force or by an exceedingly secret route. After the aforesaid brethren had thus received their share of the city, they took care to fortify the place more diligently on a fixed day, having gathered supplies, weapons, and forces of men. A very large caravan of camels sufficient for the purpose, animals of every kind assigned to carry burdens, and troops to force the whole expedition into the city were assembled. They approached the place, intending to furnish the city with necessities for many times to come.

As they drew near the city with all their baggage, behold, the enemy, forewarned of their arrival, came out to meet them. Pressing them with swords and killing a great many, they scattered the column. While the rest sought safety and life in flight, the enemy seized the baggage; those unable to escape, overtaken by the enemy’s attack, either died by the sword or were put in chains. Thus the things amassed to provision the city were yielded to the enemy for its injury [Col. 0722A].

The oft-mentioned brethren, fearing the losses of similar mishaps, withdrew from their prior agreement and surrendered the city, with its burdens and revenues alike, to the lord constable. Without delay Nur al-Din, made more confident by this success, set about besieging the same city, shaken by the aforesaid misfortune. Having summoned troops and brought up engines, he suddenly stood before the city; stationing his forces around it in a circle, he enclosed it in siege.

In one part of the city was a fortress, very well supplied with arms, men, and, for the needs of the moment, provisions; if the city were taken, it could serve as a refuge for the citizens. Nevertheless, trusting in the city’s fortifications and because they had often suffered similar attacks there, they resolved to defend the city and stand bravely for it. They could have preserved it unharmed, in accordance with their wishes, had they not, confident in themselves, begun to act too rashly.

But Nur al-Din pressed them with engines and missile-throwing devices; employing the continuous and unfailing activity of archers [Col. 0722C], he gave the besieged no rest and, wearying them in many ways night and day without interruption, forced them into exhaustion. Many had been killed and some mortally wounded; few remained to carry out the duty of defence. Had not the constable himself and his son, a distinguished emulator of his father’s valour—both ready, as though for their own inheritance, to stand there personally and in rivalry—encouraged the others by their example to resist, they would certainly have failed, overcome by the immense toil and unequal to the strength of the attackers. But, as stated, the presence of their lords recalled them; and their unfailing courage, effective in animating others, restored their failing strength and made them stronger to fight.

One day, while the enemy attacked more fiercely than usual, those within the city went out through an opened gate in order to engage the enemy. Recklessly exposing themselves to battle, they provoked the enemy’s multitude against them. When the enemy rushed upon them and they could not withstand the attack, they attempted to retreat into the city. Since the gate could not be shut because of the tumult of those entering first, the enemy entered indiscriminately together with the citizens, in such numbers that, after violently capturing the city, they forced our people to withdraw into the fortress, not without danger and great slaughter [Col. 0722D].

Meanwhile the lord king was informed that the aforesaid city was suffering such distress from Nur al-Din and had almost reached the utmost point of collapse. He therefore assembled such forces of horse and foot as he could have at the time and hastened energetically with his troops to those regions, intending either to relieve the aforementioned city from siege or to test the chances of Mars and the fortune of war against Nur al-Din [Col. 0723A].

## CHAPTER XIII. The king hastens there and raises the siege; but, while returning incautiously, our army suffers dangerous enemy ambushes on the road.

When the aforesaid prince heard that the lord king was coming with this intention, unwilling to submit himself to the uncertain chances of war, he raised the siege. First, however, he set fire to and undermined the city which he had violently taken [Col. 0723B], then returned home. Yet he did not allow the force he had once assembled to disperse, but kept it with him, summoned a larger one, and lay concealed in ambush in the neighbouring woods—as though his mind foresaw what was coming—waiting for the outcome.

The king came to the city, brought the desired relief to the besieged, and remained present until what had fallen was raised up, what had been broken was strengthened, and the city, its walls restored, was returned to its former condition. Masons and all who seemed to have some experience in building were summoned from neighbouring cities and throughout the kingdom. With diligent effort they repaired towers and walls, renewed the outer defences, restored dwellings for the citizens throughout the circuit of the walls, and restored public buildings to their former state [Col. 0723C]. All these Nur al-Din had deliberately razed to the ground during the time he possessed the city, as has been stated.

When these things had been done, the king and his princes judged that their further stay in the aforesaid city was not greatly needed by its citizens, since everything had now been fully restored and the fortress had been adequately supplied for the time with weapons, provisions, and men. Dismissing the infantry companies, he resolved to return to Tiberias with the cavalry squadrons alone. He therefore departed from the city and headed south, encamping beside the lake called Meleha. There, that night, the army rested in a manner very different from what military discipline required, imprudently and without observing the rule of the camp [Col. 0723D].

For it commonly happens among men that in prosperous and favourable success they are accustomed to behave less circumspectly. In adversity, however, vigilance is generally at hand. Hence perhaps it has been said: “A thousand shall fall at your side,” namely on the left, “and ten thousand at your right hand” (Psalm 90:7). For more men, driven by prosperity and puffed up by success, are accustomed to rush headlong to destruction. Conversely, those wearied by losses and adverse events, instructed by their own dangers, learn to act more cautiously in uncertainty and always to fear fortune, which they have often found bitter in their affairs.

The king, therefore, recalling that he had driven so great a prince from the assault upon the besieged city, and supposing him to have gone far away with his forces, and judging that he could not easily again gather so many nations into one to injure either himself or his men, began, as stated, to behave somewhat imprudently and to indulge each individual more freely according to his own wishes [Col. 0724A]. The enemies lying in ambush were informed that the lord king’s army, having dismissed its infantry divisions, was behaving far too securely and imprudently around Lake Meleha; and that some of his princes, namely Philip of Nablus and certain others, had left with their retinues. Seeing events occur according to their wishes, they suddenly moved camp. Their most prudent prince hastened the business as he knew was expedient; they pressed toward those regions and reached the Jordan, which lay between them. Having crossed it, they placed themselves in ambush on this side of the Jordan, at the place commonly called Jacob’s Ford, where the royal army was to cross the next day.

But when daylight had returned to the earth, our army again set out, unaware of the night-time ambush and ignorant of what the enemy had meanwhile prepared. They headed toward the areas secretly occupied by the Turks; and while they travelled securely, fearing absolutely nothing sinister, behold, those who had assembled specifically to attack the unsuspecting suddenly emerged from ambush. With drawn swords they threw themselves upon men who were secure and feared nothing of the kind, intending, in the manner of enemies, to inflict wounds and death. Our men, though late in awakening, abandoned their various conversations [Col. 0724C] and, seeing that the matter was serious, seized horses and weapons. But before they could prepare themselves and assemble to resist, the ranks were broken in disorder, since the enemy pressed them relentlessly and fought vigorously hand-to-hand with swords; so that scarcely any of our men remained together anywhere.

## CHAPTER XIV. The king, fleeing from battle, withdraws to the castle of Safed; the army is overthrown, and very many princes are captured.

The king, with the few who remained attached to him, saw the battle lines broken and the confused army exposed on every side to the enemy for plunder. The enemy was growing stronger on all sides, while our men were not merely now failing but had failed from the beginning [Col. 0724D]. To secure his safety, he wisely climbed a nearby mountain. Avoiding enemies now on his right and now on his left, with the help of the horse he rode, he barely and with great difficulty reached the castle called Safed, situated on that mountain, amid the utmost dangers.

On that day a very great number of our princes were captured, but few were killed. For all alike—both those said to possess special knowledge and experience in warfare and ordinary soldiers—unwilling to shrink from the yoke of shameful slavery and the mark of perpetual disgrace as though they were worthless slaves of the enemy, surrendered without resistance in order to preserve their miserable lives. Among those captured there were the noble and renowned Lord Hugh of Ibelin; Odo [Col. 0725A] of Saint Amand, royal marshal; John Gotman; Rohard of Jaffa; and his brother Balian; Bertrand of Blanquefort, master of the Knights Templar, a religious man who feared God; and many others whose names we do not possess.

The Lord repaid us according to the fruit deserved by our ways. Having unjustly oppressed innocent people who trusted in our pledged faith, scorning the laws of humanity, we received disgrace weighed out in an equal balance. For our renowned men were given to the nations as an object of reproach and exposed to the enemy’s mockery; because our sins required it, they were handed over to be a shaking of the head among the peoples (Psalm 43:16). The zeal of the Lord of hosts has done these things (Isaiah 9:7). Yet He acted kindly and mercifully with us, not forgetting to have mercy and not restraining His mercies in His anger [Col. 0725B], by providing for the king’s safety. Had he fallen that day, the whole kingdom would without doubt have descended into its final peril—may God avert it. In even the most outstanding soldier the fate is that of one man; but in a king lies the danger of all. David, faithful and solicitous for the king, understood this well when he said: “Lord, save the king” (Psalm 19:10).

Meanwhile varying reports concerning the king deeply troubled the anxious region far and wide. Some said that he had perished, pierced by swords; others that he had been carried away, bound among the captives, without the enemy knowing who he was; others that, protected by divine mercy, he had escaped unharmed from the tumults of war. Therefore the entire people anxiously showed a tender concern for him, like a mother with an only son; and, not knowing what had happened to him, affectionately imagined and shared his suffering in whatever worse thing could occur. But after the region had been somewhat cleared of enemies, he himself, with very few who had withdrawn with him into the aforesaid town, joined by certain men who had by chance escaped the dangers of the previous day, hastened to the city of Acre. There he was received, as if restored from death, with the people’s applause and no little rejoicing [Col. 0725C].

This occurred in the fourteenth year of the reign of Lord Baldwin, in June, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July [19 June].

## CHAPTER XV. Nur al-Din again besieges Paneas, but makes no progress when the king again comes against him.

[Col. 0725D]

Nur al-Din, a vigorous man and tireless in continuing his successes, had traversed all the regions and gathered plunder on every side, thereby becoming wealthier. He again summoned military forces and, by an edict, called up greater numbers from Damascus and all its territories. He then set out again to besiege Paneas, suspecting nothing less than that the king or his princes, whose forces he had worn down, would bring aid to the besieged.

Having laid siege according to his purpose around the oft-mentioned city, he again acted in the enemy’s manner: with numerous engines suitably arranged, he battered towers, weakened walls, and, by the repeated work of archers and a hail-like discharge of missiles [Col. 0726A], prevented those who had withdrawn inside from performing in turn the duty of resistance. The citizens of that place, remembering how in the recent earlier siege they had failed in their purpose when they wished to defend the city, had all voluntarily retired in advance into the fortress.

The constable, departing and occupied by other concerns, had placed over that place and entrusted with supreme responsibility a kinsman of his, namely Guy of Scandelion, highly experienced in warfare but of little faith and entirely ignorant of God. Both out of regard for his commander and from concern for his own reputation, lest he obscure the honours of distinguished deeds in war, he encouraged the others by word and example to resist. He confidently promised that help would not be lacking soon and that everlasting glory awaited those who deserved well. Hence all fought as if for their own cause, making themselves astonishing and admirable to their enemies by their unceasing watches and continual labours.

The enemy, nevertheless, wholly prepared to oppose those who wholly resisted, inflicted troubles without interruption; having greater numbers appointed to relieve one another in turns, they forced into exhaustion by daily hardships those who had no means whatever of restoring their strength [Col. 0726B]. Meanwhile it was reported to the lord king, and the princes remaining in the kingdom also did not fail to learn, how greatly those besieged in the city were distressed. Therefore embassies were sent both to the prince of Antioch and to the count of Tripoli, asking them to hasten without delay to give assistance. The king, meanwhile, summoned by heralds whatever remained of the kingdom’s soldiery.

By divine favour, within a few days and sooner than expected, each of the aforesaid illustrious men arrived with a respectable company in the royal camp beneath Chastel Neuf, at the place called Nigraguarda, from which the besieged city could be seen close at hand [Col. 0726C]. When Nur al-Din heard that the aforesaid princes had joined the lord king and were prepared to approach the city, being a prudent man and most circumspect in his affairs, he raised the siege and withdrew to more distant parts of his realm. Although he had already breached the town in many places and the besieged no longer had any hope of resistance, he avoided the hazards of war and the uncertain chances of battle [Col. 0726D].

## CHAPTER XVI. Count Theoderic of Flanders arrives. Envoys are sent to Constantinople to seek a wife for the lord king.

While these varied and manifold events were taking place in the kingdom, and while the kingdom lay desolate because most of our princes had been captured, it happened, through divine mercy looking upon us, that the count of Flanders, Lord Theoderic, a renowned and magnificent man, whose entry into the kingdom had often been useful and necessary, arrived in the port of Beirut with his wife Sibylla, the lord king’s sister by the same father. The whole people received his arrival with such exultation of heart [Col. 0727A] that they seemed already to foresee that, by the arrival of him and his people, the kingdom’s unbearable troubles would in large part be relieved. Nor were those piously concerned for the kingdom’s tranquillity disappointed of their desire.

For immediately after his arrival there came an Angel of great counsel, who, directing our ways toward the kingdom’s advantage and the glory of the Christian name, mercifully went before them, as will subsequently be related. Meanwhile, however, the princes of the kingdom, ecclesiastical as well as secular, saw that the king had now attained manhood but had remained without a wife until then. Concerned, as they ought to be, for children, so that a son might succeed him in the kingdom as lawful heir, they deliberated that provision should be made through an honourable marriage for the childless king. At last, after many stages of deliberation and for several converging reasons, everyone judged it most expedient to open discussions with the lord emperor of Constantinople on this matter. His palace had no lack of noble maidens closely connected to him by kinship; and, being an exceedingly powerful prince and wealthier than other mortals, he could, from his resources, relieve our poverty and want, by which the kingdom was especially afflicted, and transform its condition into abundance.

Therefore, by common consent, Attard, bishop of Nazareth, and Lord Humphrey of Toron, the royal constable, were sent to accomplish, with God as author, what had been devised. Having arranged matters as circumstances required [Col. 0727C], they embarked and set sail for that place.

## CHAPTER XVII. The king, with all the kingdom’s forces and the count of Flanders, hastens to Antioch. Nur al-Din is struck by a hopeless illness.

Meanwhile, lest the arrival of so great a prince and of so many noble and brave men who had come with him should lie idle and fruitless, they resolved by common counsel, divine grace inspiring them, to move with all their military forces into the region of Antioch. This very matter having been communicated to both the lord prince and the lord count of Tripoli, each was privately urged to have his troops ready on a fixed day, so that on the appointed day they might make a sudden entry into the enemy’s lands. And it came about, with heaven’s favor going before, that in the region of Tripoli, at the place commonly called La Boquea, they assembled in unity, though from different directions. Thence, with their forces marshalled, they violently entered the enemy’s territory.

At first, however, they did not rejoice greatly in their success; for, though they assailed with much persistence an enemy town commonly called the castle of Rugium, they made no progress at all. But better fortune followed this weak beginning. For at the suggestion of Lord Raynald, prince of the Antiochenes, who labored to the utmost of his ability to achieve it, all the princes who had assembled directed their forces toward the Antiochene regions under happier auspices. When they had arrived there, while they were staying in the aforesaid city and deliberating what was presently most expedient, behold, the bearer of very welcome news came to the king and the princes, asserting with the utmost certainty that Noradin, the mightiest of our enemies, who had encamped with a large force near the castle of Nepa, was either dead or had fallen into an incurable and desperate illness.

In support of his assertion, he alleged that on the previous day he had seen Noradin’s camp so disturbed that his servants, especially his household retainers, and his goods were, he said, given over to plunder by all indiscriminately; and that, amid great lamentation and weeping and manifest signs of deep grief, the disbanded companies and confused army had withdrawn in different directions. [Col. 0728B] What this messenger reported was indeed probable. Noradin had fallen into a most desperate illness, so that, the ranks having broken up beyond all order, plundering went unpunished in the army and no man’s violence was restrained, as commonly happens among them when their lord has died. He himself, powerless in body, as though his limbs refused their offices, was carried in a litter by the hands of his faithful men as far as Aleppo.

Our people, therefore, having learned the state of affairs and seeing that everything was working toward their purpose, by common desire and approved counsel sent envoys to the most powerful prince of the Armenians, Lord Toros. They earnestly requested him, and strove by every means to persuade him, that, putting aside every excuse, he should see to it that he came to Antioch with military aid and deign to join so great princes in so fruitful an undertaking. He, delighted at receiving the embassy, being a vigorous and energetic man, summoned vast forces of his own, hastened his journey, and arrived at Antioch. Our people rejoiced greatly at his arrival; they led out their forces, left the city, and marched their camp toward Caesara.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Caesarea is besieged and shortly afterwards forcibly broken into.

Caesara is a city situated on the river Orontes, which flows past Antioch. Some call it Caesarea in the common vernacular and think it to be that distinguished metropolis of Cappadocia over which the blessed and eminent teacher Basil presided; but those who believe this stray from the truth. For that metropolis is more than fifteen days’ journey, or thereabouts, from Antioch. This city is in Coele Syria, a different province, separated from the Cappadocian diocese by many intervening provinces; nor is it called Caesarea, but rather Caesara, and it is one of the suffragan cities of the patriarchate of Antioch.
