The city is quite conveniently situated. Its lower part lies on a plain, but its upper part has at its summit a very strongly fortified stronghold, fairly long but exceedingly narrow. On one side the city and on the other the river give it strength beyond its natural defenses and render access impossible. [Col. 0729A] Our men, approaching it with their troops ordered according to military discipline, immediately enclosed the city in a siege, assigning in fitting order the contingents of the individual princes. When the city had thus been besieged and its inhabitants had gathered within through fear of the enemy, the king and those who had pitched camp outside set up engines and missile-throwing devices and did not cease, by continuous operations and unremitting labor, to harass the city by every means available.

The princes competed, each in the sector assigned to him by lot from the beginning, urging on his men and promising rewards, to attack the city more fiercely. While they strove with one another to be the first to break into the city, and while each sought to claim for himself the glory of the first entry, they inflicted such distress upon the citizens that on every side they believed death to be imminent. [Col. 0729B] The citizens of that place were unpractised in military affairs and occupied with trade. Moreover, ignorant of the present danger, they had never feared anything less than a siege, trusting alike in the power of their lord, whom they believed to be safe and well, and in the fortifications of the place. For these reasons they were unequal to bearing such burdens and unable to sustain continual assaults and martial engagements.

It therefore happened that, after several days, the citizens having utterly failed, our men broke through the walls under the attackers’ unceasing pressure and rushed into the middle of the city. The city having been taken by force, its townspeople withdrew into the fortress. Everything remaining in the lower city was delivered over to them, and all things without distinction were given up to plunder. For several days they used at their pleasure both the citizens’ dwellings and whatever was found in them. [Col. 0729C]

When it seemed very easy also to take the fortress, together with all those who had taken refuge there to escape, provided proper persistence were employed, a contention arose among our princes—quite frivolous, yet very harmful. The lord king, wishing to provide for the safety of the land, saw that the lord count of Flanders, being adequately supplied both with soldiers and money, could hold the place unharmed against the enemy’s power and snares. He had therefore intended the city for him from the outset; and with this purpose had decided to press the attack on the fortress more vigorously, so that, once both had been taken, he might hand them over to the lord count to preserve and assign them to him for perpetual and hereditary possession.

Although this seemed highly suitable to the other princes, and they unanimously agreed to it with willing assent, Prince Raynald raised objections. He said that the city and its appurtenances had from the beginning formed part of the inheritance of the prince of Antioch, and that whoever possessed it ought therefore to render fealty to the Antiochene prince. But the aforesaid count was ready to render fealty for that possession devoutly to the lord king; to the prince of Antioch, however—whether to Lord Raynald, then administering the principality, or to the young Bohemond, who was expected shortly to become prince—he wholly denied that he would render it, declaring: “I have never rendered fealty except to kings.” [Col. 0730A]

Thus, through the exaction of our sins, controversy having arisen among the princes over this matter, they abandoned an undertaking that was exceedingly useful and easy to accomplish. Laden to satiety with spoils and plunder, they returned to Antioch with their forces.

## CHAPTER XIX. Noradin’s brother comes over to us. Fulcher, patriarch of Jerusalem, dies. The Cave beyond the Jordan is restored to our people. The king besieges and takes the castle of Harenc in the Antiochene region.

At the same time Noradin’s brother, Mirmiram, having heard of his brother’s decline and believing that he had passed into death, came to Aleppo and obtained it without difficulty when the citizens surrendered it to him. But while he was pressing more vigorously for the fortress to be delivered to him, he learned that his brother was still alive; he therefore disbanded his forces and withdrew from the city.

At the same time Lord Fulcher, patriarch of Jerusalem, the eighth of the Latins, a religious man and one who feared God, entered upon the way of all flesh in the twelfth year of his patriarchate, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December [20 November]. At the same time, through the zeal and diligence of Queen Melisende and the efforts of those who remained in the kingdom, especially through the care and vigilance of Baldwin of Insula, to whom the lord king, when departing, had entrusted the care of the kingdom, our people recovered a fortress beyond the Jordan in the borders of Gilead: namely, a most strongly fortified cave, which the enemy had deceitfully stolen from our people a few years earlier while they were off their guard. [Col. 0730C] The messenger sent to the lord king concerning this made all the companies glad; hearing of the success, they became more cheerful.

Meanwhile our princes who were staying at Antioch, although, as we have said, they had previously been somewhat at odds at Caesara, at length received, by the Lord’s gift, unity of spirit in the bond of peace. They again resolved to undertake some notable work worthy of perpetual remembrance. It pleased all, and it was agreed by common consent, to besiege a castle near Antioch, scarcely twelve miles distant from it, very harmful to that city, and possessing broad power and jurisdiction over the suburbs, commonly called *casalia*. It came about that on the day of the Lord’s Nativity the whole army unanimously encamped around the said stronghold.

Noradin, however, was still held by the illness that had seized him, so that the most learned physicians, summoned from every region of the East, despaired entirely of his life, although they applied remedies to which his malady seemed little responsive. This appeared to our people, by the favorable ordering of divine providence, to cooperate greatly with their purpose. For it could scarcely have been possible, had that prince been safe and enjoying sound health, for our army to enjoy such free scope in regions subject to him. [Col. 0731A]

The king and those with him in the aforesaid army, turning the opportunity of the time to their own advantage, pressed their purpose and pursued the work they had begun with all the greater zeal because they knew with complete certainty that the aforesaid great man could not attend to his own affairs. The stronghold was therefore surrounded by a siege-line; they erected engines and prepared the instruments by which besieged men in fortresses are usually more severely harassed.

The castle stood on a hill not very high, so that the mound upon which it was built appeared to have been heaped up and made by human hands. Hence the wiser men in the army devoted great effort to weaving covered sheds of suitable material, under which men sent to undermine the mound might safely conceal themselves. For they thought—and this was not far from the truth—that if the mound were undermined by secret tunnels, some part of the buildings constructed upon it would necessarily collapse. They also hastened, with diligent effort, to prepare wicker hurdles, ladders of medium size, and all things customarily useful for such a purpose. [Col. 0731B]

When these had been prepared with every care, they publicly and privately commanded the leaders of the infantry companies, the commanders of the squadrons, and the officers of the cavalry, that all should zealously and watchfully devote themselves to harassing the besieged. Thus, specific sectors having been allotted to the individual princes, each pressed forward with his household and retainers as if the entire enterprise rested upon himself alone. Each was eager to show that he possessed the best followers, and they carried on the work with such persistence in continual assaults and daily engagements that they completed, by watchful diligence in less than two months, a work that would have required many days.

One day it happened that a missile engine, which by day and almost by night hurled millstones into the fortress, by chance struck the chief officer of the castle, to whom all responsibility had been entrusted, and crushed him suddenly into fragments. When he had died, the sheep were scattered as though their shepherd had been struck; and, like sand without lime, not adhering to one another, they gave up the stubborn resistance which they had previously maintained. [Col. 0731D] When our men learned this, they began to press all the harder, as the defenders seemed to them more slack in resistance. Before long, after a few intervening days, they sent an embassy to the lord king and, on condition that they should have free and safe departure and return with their goods to their own homes, surrendered the stronghold to him. Guides were given them who would conduct them safely and without molestation as far as the place they themselves requested.

Thus the castle was taken and handed over to the lord prince, within whose jurisdiction it had been. Their affairs having been brought to a fortunate conclusion, they returned to Antioch. There they took leave of one another; the lord king returned to his kingdom with the magnificent count of Flanders, while the lord count of Tripoli most dutifully accompanied them as far as Tripoli.

## CHAPTER XX. At Jerusalem Amalric, prior of the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, is elected patriarch; contention arises among the bishops over his election.

[Col. 0732A]

At the same time, after the death of Lord Fulcher of happy memory, the Church of Jerusalem was vacant. The prelates of the churches happened to assemble at Jerusalem in order to deliberate, according to the ordinances of the canons, concerning the appointment of a bishop to so great a see. But, as is said, contrary to the rules of law, through the intervention both of Lady Melisende, the king’s sister, and of Lady Sibylla, countess of Flanders, likewise the king’s sister, Lord Amalric was elected: prior of the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, a Frenchman by nation, from the diocese of Noyon, from the town of Neelle; a man moderately learned, but excessively simple and almost useless.

He was promoted despite the opposition of Lord Hernesius, archbishop of Caesarea, and Lord Ralph, bishop of Bethlehem, who lodged appeals. Having at last obtained the see, he entrusted the matter to Lord Frederick, bishop of Acre. Frederick went to the Roman Church and, in the absence of the opponents, obtained from Lord Adrian, who then presided, through great munificence, it is said, the favor of the Roman see. He returned bearing the pallium, that is, the fullness of pontifical office.

## CHAPTER XXI. Noradin besieges our cave in the region of Sueta; the king comes to its aid and raises the siege; Noradin fights our men and is defeated.

[Col. 0732C]

Meanwhile Noradin recovered through the most diligent care of physicians. After the lord king had returned to his kingdom and Noradin too had regained complete health, he went into the Damascene territories. There, lest he should waste his time in idleness and be thought to have abandoned his customary vigilance, he suddenly besieged, in the following summer, one of our fortresses situated in the region called Sueta, having assembled an army and summoned great reinforcements.

The fortress was a cave situated on the steep and extremely precipitous side of a mountain. There was no access to it either from above or below; it could be approached only from the side by a very narrow path, dangerous because of the overhanging precipice. Within, it had chambers and dwellings able to provide its inhabitants with necessary conveniences; nor did it lack a spring of living and unfailing water. Thus, so far as the narrowness of the place allowed, it was considered a sufficiently suitable site and very useful to the region. [Col. 0732D]

When this was reliably reported to the lord king, he took with him the lord count of Flanders, summoned the forces of the kingdom, and hastened there with all speed. For those inside, unable to bear the burdens of siege, had already agreed to such terms as necessity commonly extorts: namely, that unless aid were brought them within ten days, they would thereafter certainly surrender the fortress. This too was known to the lord king. Hurrying relief as much as he could, he encamped with his army near Tiberias, beside the bridge where the waters of the Jordan divide from the Lake of Gennesaret.

When Noradin heard of our men’s arrival, he was led by the counsel of Syracunus [name uncertain], commander of his army, a vigorous man with great confidence in himself. He raised the siege and advanced with his forces to meet our men. The king, hearing that Noradin intended to come against him, summoned the princes to camp at earliest dawn. After devoutly worshipping the wood of the life-giving Cross, which Lord Peter, our predecessor and archbishop of Tyre of pious memory, carried, war was declared by common consent, with the most eager approval of all. [Col. 0733B]

Their forces were set in motion and the march begun. Exultant in spirit, as though assured of victory, they hastened to the place where the enemy army was said to be. At last, finding the enemy near at hand as they wished, armed from head to foot and with their wedges, called battle-lines, arrayed in military order, they rushed unanimously upon the enemy and pressed them fiercely with their swords, fighting for their very lives. The enemy nevertheless received our men’s onset with the greatest constancy and without fear, returned stroke for stroke, and strove with courage, by manful resistance, to repel the injuries inflicted upon them.

At length, after diverse fortunes, victory was divinely granted to our men. The enemy, not without great slaughter among their own, were put to flight, and the king with his men held the field as victors. This happened on the Ides of July [15 July], in the fifteenth year of his reign, at a place named Puthaha. [Col. 0733C] Thence he advanced with the entire army, as appeared necessary, to the fortress that had been besieged. There he repaired what had fallen into disrepair and carefully provisioned the place with arms, food, and prudent men. Having happily fulfilled his purpose, he disbanded the army, dismissed it to its homes, and returned.

## CHAPTER XXII. The envoys sent to Constantinople concerning the king’s marriage return and bring the king a wife, the emperor’s niece.

Of the envoys mentioned above, who had gone to Constantinople to arrange the lord king’s marriage, Lord Attard, archbishop of Nazareth, died; through the zeal and vigilance of his faithful men, his body was brought to his own church. He was succeeded by Lord Letard, prior of the same church, a most gentle, affable, and kindly man, who still presides over that church today, now in the twenty-third year of his pontificate.

Those who survived of the aforesaid envoys—namely Lord Henfred, the constable, Joscelin Piselius, and William of Barres, distinguished and noble men, highly experienced in secular affairs—pressed the emperor with due diligence concerning the matter entrusted to them. At last, after innumerable delays and verbal riddles, such as the Greeks, cavilling at everything, are accustomed to answer with involved circumlocutions, they obtained what they sought. Terms were established both concerning the dowry and the marriage-gift; and a wife was assigned to the king, a most illustrious maiden who had been reared in the sacred inner chambers of the empire. [Col. 0734A]

She was the niece of the lord emperor: the daughter of his elder brother, Lord Isaac. Her name was Theodora; she was in her thirteenth year, singularly notable for beauty of form, elegance of countenance, and a whole bodily bearing pleasing to beholders. The dowry amounted to one hundred thousand hyperpera of full weight, apart from another ten thousand of the same currency, which the lord emperor generously granted for wedding expenses; and apart from the maiden’s trousseau, which in gold, jewels, garments, pearls, tapestries, silk fabrics, and precious vessels might fairly be estimated at forty thousand.

The king bound himself by his own written instrument before the lord emperor that he would hold ratified whatever his envoys might expressly agree with him. Through his representatives he pledged most firmly that after his death she should hold the city of Acre with all its appurtenances, for her entire lifetime, as a marriage-gift, peaceably and without contradiction. [Col. 0734B] When the agreements had thus been completed and brought into accord on both sides, leading princes of the empire were assigned to the illustrious girl as escorts to accompany her on her journey to the lord king. She set out with the royal envoys for Syria, to proceed to her husband.

It happened that in the following September she arrived safely and unharmed at Tyre with all her retinue. Within a few days, at Jerusalem, as the custom of the kingdom required, she was consecrated, adorned with the royal diadem, and, after the marriage rites had been solemnly celebrated, was given to her husband. Since at that time the elected patriarch of Jerusalem had not yet received the office of his consecration, and the advocates whom he had sent concerning his own case had not returned from the Apostolic See, Patriarch Aimeric of Antioch was summoned by royal command both to confer upon the queen the grace of royal anointing and to celebrate the customary solemnities of marriage.

After he had taken a wife, the king so wholly put aside all the frivolity with which he was said to have been afflicted beyond measure until that day that he seemed able to say with the Apostle: “When I was a child, I thought as a child, I spoke as a child; but when I became a man, I put away the things of a child” (1 Corinthians 13:11). [Col. 0734D] For he is said thereafter to have loved his wife with commendable affection and is believed to have preserved inviolate fidelity to the marriage bed until the end. Thus, putting aside his frivolous conduct as though changed from what he had been, he began to embrace serious concerns and to attend more carefully to wholesome matters.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The emperor of Constantinople comes to Antioch; Prince Raynald, making satisfaction for what he had done to the Cypriots, is reconciled to him.

In the same year the lord emperor of Constantinople, having summoned military forces from every part of the empire as imperial magnificence required and assembled a huge army from every tribe, people, tongue, and nation, resolved, after crossing the Hellespont, to descend into Syria. Having passed through the intervening provinces with all speed, he suddenly arrived with his armies in Cilicia at the beginning of December, so unexpectedly that it would scarcely have seemed credible to anyone. [Col. 0735A]

The principal reason for so hurried a march was that a most powerful Armenian prince named Toros, of whom we have spoken above, had forcibly occupied all Cilicia that lay beneath the mountains in which he held his most strongly fortified castles, from the walled city to the furthest outlying settlement. He had reduced to his own power Tarsus, metropolis of First Cilicia, Anavarza, metropolis of Second Cilicia, and other cities—Mamistra, Adana, and Sis—having expelled from them the officials of imperial administration. To surprise him unawares, the emperor had both hastened his march and concealed his purpose.

He was also moved by the grievous and sympathetic case of the Cypriots, against whom, as against enemies of the faith and detestable parricides, the prince of Antioch had exercised, as we have stated, so inhuman a tyranny. The arrival of the imperial forces was so sudden that Toros, then staying at Tarsus, scarcely had free time to flee for safety into the neighboring mountains before the legions and the first divisions of the army had already spread themselves over the open plains. [Col. 0735C]

When Prince Raynald of Antioch heard this, he was goaded by the pricks of conscience because, not long before the emperor’s arrival, he had raged with such madness against innocent and undeserving Cypriots and inflicted upon them, their wives, and their children an injury abominable before God and men. Fearing the emperor’s arrival, lest he might be stirred by the plaintive cries of those calling out against him to descend and avenge their wrongs, Raynald anxiously began to deliberate, now by himself, now in consultation with such of his more intimate associates as he possessed, what he ought to do and by what kind of satisfaction he might reconcile himself to imperial majesty for so great an offense.

Such fear of the lord emperor’s arrival had seized him, as is said, that he was unwilling even to await the presence of the lord king, though he expected him soon to arrive. Yet he could have known with absolute certainty that, through the king’s intervention and efforts—and especially because of their new family connection—he would find far better terms in the said matter. [Col. 0735D] He therefore followed the counsel of his household. Taking some of them as he chose, together with Lord Gerard, the venerable bishop of Laodicea, as his travelling companion, and having first gained the favor of certain intimates of the lord emperor who went back and forth as interpreters in this affair, he came to the city of Mamistra in Cilicia, where the lord emperor was with his forces.

There, after many negotiations, he was reconciled to imperial majesty, to the great humiliation of himself and disgrace of our people. Barefoot, it is said, clothed in woolen sleeves cut short to the elbow, with a rope tied about his neck and a naked sword in his hand, holding it by the point so as to offer its hilt to the lord emperor, he was brought before the emperor in the sight of all the legions. There he prostrated himself on the ground before the emperor’s feet, handed the sword over to him, and lay there until it became nauseating to all and turned the glory of Latin Christendom into reproach—most extreme both in wrongdoing and in making satisfaction.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The king hastens to those regions, is honorably received by the emperor, and receives countless gifts.

The lord king of Jerusalem likewise, having heard of the lord emperor’s arrival, took his brother and a select company of princes of the kingdom. Leaving behind the lord count of Flanders, who had decided to return home on the approaching crossing, he hurried toward Antioch. On arriving there, he sent envoys to the lord emperor: namely Lord Geoffrey, abbot of the Temple of the Lord, who knew the Greek language, and the noble Lord Joscelin Pessel. Through them he most dutifully offered words of due greeting and inquired concerning the emperor’s pleasure—whether he wished the king to come to him and have the king’s presence. [Col. 0736B]

They were answered that they should urge and invite the king not to delay in coming to him. Moreover, an illustrious *apocrisiarius* was sent from the imperial court to press the king, both by letter and in person, as the empire’s most beloved son, not to refuse to come to him. On the appointed day, taking a select company of excellent knights, the king arrived and was received most honorably. For the emperor immediately sent to meet him two of his nephews, brothers by the same mother: John Protosebastos and Alexius Protostrator, who held the first rank among the illustrious men of the sacred palace, accompanied by a very great company of nobles.

Then, conducted by them to the entrance of the tent where the lord emperor sat with his illustrious men, the king was brought in with great splendor. He was most graciously greeted by the emperor, raised for the kiss of peace, and placed beside him on an honorable seat, though one lower than the emperor’s. [Col. 0736D] His companions too were most graciously honored by the emperor both with words of due greeting and with the kiss of peace. He carefully asked after the well-being of the lord king and of those who had come with him; displaying a countenance more cheerful than usual, he showed by word and every gesture of his body that he had received their arrival most gladly and took pleasure in the presence offered by so great a prince and his companions.

By frequent conversations, both private and in the assembly of nobles, and by agreeable intercourse with the lord emperor during the ten days in which he constantly remained with him, the king—being a man of grace—won such favor from the lord emperor and his princes and was bound to their hearts by so strong a bond of affection that thereafter they loved him while living uniquely as a son, and, after his death, his memory among them has not ceased even to this day to be blessed.

Nor was his stay with the lord emperor fruitless. Being an ingenious man with a penetrating eye for secular affairs, he saw that the emperor had ordered the army to encamp outside the city in order to lead it against the aforesaid Toros, whom he pursued with insatiable hatred. Having first obtained permission, the king began carefully to consider how he might reconcile the said prince to the lord emperor. Toros was summoned and brought before him; he surrendered the fortresses demanded back by the emperor and was restored to fuller favor, so that, through the intervention of this same lord king, before returning home he rendered liege fealty to the emperor by his own hand. [Col. 0737B]

At last the king returned to Antioch, enriched, as befitted imperial magnificence, together with his princes by more abundant gifts and immeasurable generosity in presents, and attended by the goodwill of all. We have heard from some persons beyond every exception and worthy of trust that, apart from what the emperor bestowed with lavish generosity upon the king’s companions—which was believed to be beyond number—he was said to have given the king alone twenty-two thousand hyperpera and three thousand marks of the purest silver, besides garments, silk fabrics, and precious vessels.

On arriving at Antioch, the king found there his brother Lord Amalric, count of Jaffa and Ascalon, together with Lord Hugh of Ibelin, who had very recently been ransomed from the enemy’s bonds and had returned from captivity. They too wished to visit the lord emperor. Going there afterward, they were graciously received by that same lord emperor, honorably entertained, and, according to imperial custom, honored with more abundant gifts; they were sent back rejoicing to the lord king.

## CHAPTER XXV. The emperor enters Antioch, exercising great liberality toward its citizens; afterwards he returns home.

After celebrating the solemnity of the Lord’s Easter in Cilicia, and when the festival days had passed, he directed his army toward Antioch. When the legions had reached [Col. 0737D] the city, he stood before its gates, formidable in an innumerable multitude. There the lord patriarch, with all the clergy and people, came out to meet him, bearing Gospel books and every kind of ecclesiastical ornament. The king also, with the prince of that place and the count of Ascalon, and with all the leading men both of the kingdom and of the principality of Antioch, went out to meet him; and with the highest glory, crowned with the imperial diadem and adorned with Augustan insignia, amid the blare of trumpets and the beating of drums, with hymns and songs, they led him into the city, and escorted him as far as the cathedral church—the basilica, that is, of the prince of the apostles—and then to the palace, with the same procession of fathers and people.

There, after devoting several days to baths and other bodily [Col. 0738A] pleasures, he distributed among the people of the city, according to his custom, a most generous largesse. He then proposed to leave the city for hunting, and, to drive away weariness, drew the lord king with him as a companion in the sport to places suitable for hunting. It happened, however, that while they were engaged in this pursuit, on the solemn day of the Lord’s Ascension, as they were ranging through the woods in the manner of hunters, the king, carried away by the rush of the horse he was riding, was hurled down through ground overgrown with low brushwood and thorns, and fell headlong to the earth with his horse, breaking his arm. When this became known to the lord emperor, he sympathized with him with great kindness and, performing the office of surgeons, knelt before him and ministered to him attentively as though he were one of the common people. [Col. 0738B] His princes and kinsmen were therefore astonished and indignant that, forgetful of imperial majesty and neglecting Augustan dignity, he showed himself so devoted and familiar toward the king—something which would have seemed unbecoming even in relation to any one of them.

They therefore returned to Antioch because of the accident. Every day he visited the lord king and, renewing the poultices with the necessary ointments, carefully wrapped the bandage again, anxiously attending to him with such care as one could scarcely show to a sick son with greater devotion. When the lord king had fully recovered, the emperor ordered the commanders of the legions to be informed by public proclamation that, on a fixed day, they should march their battle-lines toward Aleppo and have the siege-machines and [Col. 0738C] military equipment carried before them. He himself, with the lord king and the princes of both realms, afterward left the city amid trumpets, drums, and the martial horns that stir men to battle; he halted, together with the whole army, at the place commonly called the Ford of the Whale. From there, having sent messengers to Nūr al-Dīn, who happened then to be at Aleppo, he obtained through envoys the surrender of a certain Bertrand, the natural son of the count of Saint-Gilles, together with several fellow-captives. Not long afterward, however, recalled by domestic concerns, he returned to his own lands. The king likewise, after the lord emperor’s departure, withdrew into the kingdom with those whom he had brought out with him.

## CHAPTER XXVI. After Adrian’s death, a dangerous schism arises in the Roman Church.

[Col. 0738D]

At the same time, Pope Adrian died of quinsy at Anagni, a city of Campania. His body was brought to Rome and honourably buried in the basilica of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles. While the cardinals discussed appointing a successor, the desires of the electors—as often happens in such matters—were divided. One party chose Lord Roland, priest-cardinal of that church, of the title of Saint Mark, who was also chancellor of the Apostolic See. They laid hands upon him, ordained him bishop, and called him Alexander. Others chose Lord Octavian, a man noble by birth, priest-cardinal of the same Church, of the title of Saint Cecilia across the [Col. 0739A] Tiber. They likewise laid hands upon him, made him bishop, and called him Victor.

On account of this schism, the whole Latin Church, our sins so requiring, came very near being divided and irreversibly separated from itself, while the greater princes of the world competed in granting favour and support to the opposing sides. At last, in the nineteenth year, when Lord Frederick, emperor of the Romans, who had supplied aid and counsel to the opposite party, returned to the unity of the Church and was reconciled to Pope Alexander in full charity, peace was restored to the Church. The darkness of error having been driven away, tranquillity shone forth like the morning star in the midst of a cloud.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Nūr al-Dīn enters the territories of the sultan of Iconium and violently occupies part of them. The king devastates the territory of Damascus.

[Col. 0739B]

Meanwhile Nūr al-Dīn, exceedingly pleased at the emperor’s departure—for his arrival had inspired him with great terror, and his presence with still greater—now felt secure from the highly suspect power of so great a prince. Seeing also that the lord king had returned to his own lands, he thought he had found an opportunity such as he had desired for many years. Having summoned troops from all his territories, he sent expeditions into the land of the sultan of Iconium, which bordered upon his own, and hastened to bring under his power the city of Marash, together with the towns of Cressum and Behetselin.

[Col. 0739C] The sultan, being far from those regions, could not easily send aid to his own people; and it was in reliance upon this that Nūr al-Dīn had presumed to attack one stronger than himself. When the lord king learned that Nūr al-Dīn was occupied in those parts with all his forces, he wished to turn his occupation to his own advantage. Knowing that the territory of Damascus, lacking the strength of fighting men, lay easily open to the ambushes of enemies, he assembled an army and entered the Damascene region. Giving everything over at will to fire and plunder, he led his army freely, without opposition, from Ofra, the famous metropolis of Arabia Prima, as far as Damascus.

There was at Damascus a certain nobleman named Najm al-Dīn, [Col. 0739D] to whom his lord had entrusted the management of his affairs on account of the extensive worldly experience he was said to possess, delivering to him the city and its dependencies to govern at his discretion. Seeing that his lord was occupied with business in a distant land, and that he himself lacked forces of fighting men capable of resisting the royal power, he acted as a prudent man, seeking to ward off imminent dangers. He offered four thousand gold pieces and requested a peace of three months; by increasing the money given to intermediaries, he obtained the peace he had sought, and also gave up six common soldiers whom he held in chains. Thus he prudently removed the king and his army from his country.

Meanwhile Queen Melisende, a prudent woman and possessed of judgement beyond [Col. 0740A] her sex, who, both during her husband’s lifetime and during her son’s reign, had governed the kingdom for thirty years and more with fitting moderation, surpassing feminine strength, fell into an incurable illness. From it she did not recover until her death, although both her sisters—the lady countess of Tripoli and the lady abbess of Saint Lazarus of Bethany—devoted every care to her. The most skilled physicians were summoned from every quarter and did not cease to administer such remedies as seemed necessary. But she, her memory for a time impaired and her body seemingly wasted away, lay bedridden for a long period, almost dissolved, with access to her permitted only to very few.

When the period which the king had set for Najm al-Dīn, the administrator of Damascus, had expired, [Col. 0740B] and the term of the truce had run out, while Nūr al-Dīn was still occupied in the regions mentioned above and had not yet completed his business there, the king again violently entered the enemy’s territory. Roaming through the country at will, he freely carried off plunder, caused fires, and collected spoils without opposition. After devastating the region, breaking into the suburbs, and taking the inhabitants captive, he again returned safely to his own lands.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Raynald, prince of Antioch, is captured by the enemy and put in chains at Aleppo.

Not long afterward it happened that Raynald, prince of Antioch, learned through scouts that in those parts which had once [Col. 0740C] belonged to the count of Edessa, between Marash and Tulupa, the land, rich in cattle and flocks and lacking fighting men, with inhabitants ignorant of the use of arms, might readily lie open to plunder. He readily gave credence to their words and, having gathered a great force, set out under evil omens.

Coming to the places mentioned, he found their reports entirely true; for he discovered beyond doubt a marvelous abundance of herds and flocks. But the people to whom these belonged were a faithful people. That whole region has Turks only in its fortresses, very few indeed, who both guard the fortresses and collect the dues of the peasants for their greater lords, whose agents they are. The surrounding settlements, however, are inhabited solely by Christians, Syrians, and Armenians, [Col. 0740D] who cultivate the land and work the fields.

Having gathered plunder from various places and brought together spoils without anyone hindering them, they were returning safe and wholly untroubled, laden with booty and enriched with goods of many kinds. But behold: Majd al-Dīn, prefect of Aleppo, a close and most faithful associate of Nūr al-Dīn, took with him the more mobile troops of the whole region. Learning in advance of Raynald’s return, he hastened to meet him, so that he might overwhelm them, burdened with baggage and booty, in some narrow or obstructed place, or at least forcibly compel them to abandon their equipment.

Thus it came about, according to the design of a prudent man, that those hurrying to meet them, guided by men who had come from the [Col. 0741A] prince’s army, reached the appointed place, quite close to the region where the prince had encamped with all the booty. When he learned of the enemy’s approach, he deliberated with his men about what ought to be done in the present emergency. They abandoned the sounder counsel—namely, to leave the booty and return more lightly equipped to their own lands without much difficulty—and chose instead not to abandon the plunder and spoils, but to fight bravely with the enemy unless the enemy themselves prevented it.

At daybreak, when the day had already advanced a little, the battle began as the forces came together. The enemy pressed them hard with bows and swords, with most stubborn determination. Our men, although at first they seemed to have the spirit to resist, at last lost heart, turned their backs, abandoned their [Col. 0741B] spoils, and chose flight. The prince, his sins so requiring, destined to pay bodily for all the impieties he had committed, was captured, bound in fetters, and led in the utmost disgrace to Aleppo with the other fellow-captives, made a spectacle to the unbelieving peoples. This took place in the eighteenth year of the reign of Lord Baldwin, in November, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December [23 November], between Cressum and Marash, at a place called Commi.

## CHAPTER XXIX. A certain John, priest-cardinal of the Roman Church, comes down into Syria as legate; disagreement arises among the bishops concerning his reception. A son, Baldwin, is born to Amalric, count of Jaffa, the king’s brother.

[Col. 0741C] In those same days, a certain John, a highly learned priest-cardinal of the Roman Church, of the title of Saints John and Paul, was sent by Pope Alexander as legate to the eastern lands. He landed at Byblos with some Genoese. Wishing, once permission had been obtained, to enter the kingdom as legate, he sounded out the views of the lord king and the other princes of the kingdom, ecclesiastical as well as secular, concerning his entry.

For, as we have said, nearly the whole world was divided because of the schism which had arisen: some favoured Pope Alexander, others the opposing party. Therefore, after much deliberation, he was instructed to remain where he was and not presume to enter the kingdom until fuller [Col. 0741D] consultation had been held with the prelates of the churches and the princes of the kingdom, and he had been informed by their common counsel what he ought to do.

Meanwhile, the lord patriarch and the other prelates of the churches were summoned to Nazareth. Some princes also attended with the lord king, and they began to deliberate what it would be most expedient to do in so great an uncertainty. All the bishops of the East, of both patriarchates, had not openly inclined to either party, though secretly some gave their support to one side and some to the other. It happened, as commonly occurs in such cases, that they disagreed with one another and their votes were divided in various directions. Some said that Lord Alexander and his legate ought to be received, [Col. 0742A] since he supported the stronger cause. Their leader was Lord Peter, of pious memory in the Lord, our predecessor, archbishop of Tyre. Others, on the contrary, preferred the cause of Lord Victor, asserting that he had always been a friend and protector of the kingdom; they held that the legate ought by no means to be received.

The king, however, taking a middle course with his princes and certain prelates of the churches, feared that the bishops might divide among themselves and that the Church might be torn apart. He advised that neither party should be received. But if the legate wished, as a pilgrim and for the sake of prayer, to visit the holy places without the insignia of a legation, permission should be granted him and freedom allowed him to remain in the kingdom until the [Col. 0742B] first crossing; thereafter he should return. The king also alleged the reason for his view, saying:

> “The schism is recent. It has not yet become known to the world which of them has the stronger cause. It is dangerous, in a doubtful matter, to choose a side for oneself by one’s own judgement and to rush into a definitive decision about an uncertain question. Moreover, there is no need for a legate in the kingdom—one who will burden churches and monasteries with expenses and weaken them by exactions.”

This was the lord king’s opinion. Although it seemed the more advantageous, the view of those who asserted that the legate ought to be received prevailed. Thus he was called into the kingdom and came; though his arrival pleased many, he later became burdensome.

At that time a son was born to Lord Amalric, count of Jaffa, by Agnes, daughter of the [Col. 0742C] count of Edessa. At his father’s request the king received the child from the sacred font and gave him his own name. When he was asked jokingly what he would give to his nephew and godson, he replied—for he was a man of agreeable and witty speech—“The kingdom of Jerusalem.” This saying penetrated deeply into the hearts of certain prudent men who heard it. They observed that, although he was still very young and his wife a girl, he seemed to foresee that he would be taken from this world without children—which indeed happened.

## CHAPTER XXX. Summoned by the Antiochenes, the king hastens there; imperial envoys arrive, requesting for their lord one of the king’s kinswomen as wife.

[Col. 0742D]

After the prince had been captured and the province of Antioch deprived of the protection of its ruler, the people of the region were again seized by fear and anxiety. Day after day, in suspense of mind, they awaited the desolation of their land, unless the Lord should protect them. At last it seemed right to have recourse to their accustomed help and to seek consolation against the impending evils from the person from whom they had often obtained what they asked without refusal. They therefore sent an embassy with tearful entreaties and humbly invited the king of Jerusalem not to delay in coming to aid a nation in despair and a people perishing, so that he might receive honour and glory from men and eternal rewards from the Lord.

When the king heard of the pitiable plight of that region, following in the footsteps of his [Col. 0743A] predecessors and sympathizing with their distress, he devoutly undertook the labour. Taking with him a suitable military force, he hurried to Antioch, where his arrival was received by clergy and people with every joy and exultation. Remaining in that city as long as the necessity of time and place required, he devoted the most exacting attention to the business of the principality as though it were his own. He entrusted the administration of the region temporarily to the lord patriarch, provided honourable expenses for the princess, and then, recalled by concern for domestic affairs, returned to his own lands.

After the lord king had returned to the kingdom, behold, there arrived envoys of the lord emperor of Constantinople, distinguished men and eminent in the sacred palace, [Col. 0743B] bringing to the lord king letters with a golden seal, together with more confidential oral messages. The first of them was the illustrious Gundostephanus, a kinsman of the emperor; the second was Triffillus, chief of the palace interpreters, a shrewd man and exceedingly diligent in imperial business. As stated above, they brought the imperial letters, whose tenor, in summary, was as follows:

> “Know, most beloved of us and most acceptable to our empire, that Irene, our happy consort of illustrious memory in the Lord, has ended the last day of her life and is to be joined to the elect spirits, leaving behind her our only daughter, heir of the common empire. Since we are concerned for the succession of the empire and [Col. 0743C] have no offspring of the better sex, we have often held diligent consultation with the illustrious men of the sacred palace concerning a second marriage. At last, with the favour and consent of all our princes, it has pleased us to join to ourselves in partnership of empire one from your blood, which our empire uniquely loves. Whichever of your female cousins you shall choose for us—either the sister of the illustrious count of Tripoli or the younger full sister of the magnificent prince of Antioch—we shall, according to your choice, placing complete confidence in your loyalty, take her, God permitting, as companion of our bed and sharer in our empire.”

When the king learned the emperor’s intention, both from the letters and from the envoys’ oral report, he promised his service, pledged his assistance, and gave [Col. 0743D] many thanks to the imperial majesty: both because the emperor proposed to associate a woman of his blood with himself in so high an eminence, and because, commending his loyalty, he left it to the king’s choice which woman he would take as companion of his bed and consort in the empire.

## CHAPTER XXXI. The king designates for him the sister of the count of Tripoli, an illustrious maiden named Melisende; but after a year the emperor rejects her and marries Maria, daughter of Prince Raymond.

The king, having deliberated with his intimates what would best suit himself and the imperial highness in the present matter, summoned the imperial envoys and persuaded and ordered them to accept as wife for their lord Melisende, a well-born young woman, sister of the lord count of Tripoli. [Col. 0744A] They received the king’s word with the greatest reverence and consented, while declaring that this must be communicated to the emperor by envoys and letters.

Meanwhile the maiden destined for so lofty a station was provided by her mother and aunt, brother, and all her friends with ornaments of immeasurable cost and beyond all measure, surpassing royal resources: necklaces, earrings, armlets and anklets, rings, collars, and crowns of the purest gold; also silver vessels of enormous weight and size. Unheard-of provisions for the kitchen, for food and drink, and for bathing were prepared, besides bridles, saddles, and, to speak briefly, every kind of equipment. All this was prepared at such infinite [Col. 0744B] expense and with such care that the works themselves proclaimed their extravagance and easily surpassed royal luxury.

Meanwhile, while the Greeks examined and searched into every particular, investigating minutely the maiden’s character and the condition of the hidden parts of her body, they sent frequent messengers to the emperor and awaited their return. A year passed. The lord king and count, together with all the maiden’s relatives and friends, took this very badly and publicly confronted the imperial envoys, proposing one of two alternatives: either they must definitively abandon the long-discussed marriage arrangement and repay the expenses, or they must stop weaving complications of delay and bring the affair to an end, as agreed, by completing it.

[Col. 0744C] The count was burdened with many expenses. He had ordered twelve galleys to be built and fully equipped, intending to escort his sister to her husband. All the leading men of both the principality and the kingdom had assembled at Tripoli, awaiting the lady’s imminent departure; and the count provided all, or at least most, of their necessities. The Greeks, however, answering ambiguously in their customary manner, endeavoured still to prolong the matter. But the lord king forestalled their sophistical manoeuvres and sent Lord Otto of Risbergis as a special envoy to the lord emperor concerning the affair, earnestly asking him to declare his will unequivocally through the same messenger.

[Col. 0744D] Otto returned to the king sooner than expected and informed him, both orally and by letters, that everything which had been arranged concerning the aforesaid marriage displeased the emperor. When the king understood this, he abandoned the matter, considering it a great disgrace that what was thought to have been arranged through his intervention and settled by his side should have come to nothing; undoubtedly, it appeared to redound to his own injury. The emperor’s envoys, fearing the indignation of the count of Tripoli, found a small vessel by chance and had themselves carried to Cyprus.

When the assembly of magnates gathered at Tripoli had dispersed, the lord king withdrew to Antioch, the care of which, as stated above, he had undertaken at the earnest request of the people of the region. On arriving there, [Col. 0745A] he found the same imperial envoys, whom he had believed had departed from Tripoli. They were engaged in daily and familiar negotiation with the princess concerning her youngest daughter, Maria. Moreover, they had with them letters of the lord emperor sealed in gold, in which he promised to ratify whatever should be confirmed through their agency concerning the present marriage with the princess or her friends.

When the king arrived and the matter was communicated to him, though he seemed to have been injured in the former affair, so that he might with good reason have withdrawn his assistance and interest from the emperor in the present one, he nevertheless intervened for the sake of his kinswoman, who was an orphan and bereft of her father’s protection. After many delays, he strove to bring the matter to completion. When the business had been completed, [Col. 0745B] galleys were made ready at the mouth of the Orontes River, in the place called the port of Saint Symeon. The girl was handed over, and certain magnates of the region, considered suitable for the task, accompanied her as companions on the journey as far as her husband; they set out.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Near Antioch the king rebuilds the castle called the Iron Bridge. His mother, Queen Melisende, dies.

While the king remained in those parts so that his presence might benefit the region, he rebuilt, [Col. 0745C] very usefully, the castle which had formerly stood over the bridge of the Orontes River—commonly called the Iron Bridge—some six or seven miles from the city of Antioch. It served to check enemy raids and the secret incursions of bandits.

While he was occupied with the affairs of those regions, his pious mother, worn down by a long illness and exhausted by continual sufferings, entered upon the way of all flesh on the third day before the Ides of September [11 September]. When word reached him, he gave proof by genuine signs of how sincerely he had loved her, gave himself over to lamentation, and for many days accepted no consolation whatsoever.

The lady Melisende, of illustrious memory and destined to be brought among the choirs of angels, was buried in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, on the right as one descends toward the tomb of the blessed and undefiled Mother of God and Virgin Mary, in a stone crypt enclosed by iron doors. It has a nearby altar, where sacrifices acceptable to the Creator are daily offered both for the remedy of her [Col. 0745D] soul and for the spirits of all the faithful departed.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Angered by the repudiation of his sister, the count of Tripoli inflicts upon the emperor whatever injuries he can.

Meanwhile the count of Tripoli was inwardly pierced by grief of heart and bitterly resented having been so deceived by the emperor. He saw that, on the emperor’s account, he had made enormous expenditures, and that his sister had been repudiated without examination of any cause, as though she were the daughter of some common man. In distress he groaned to himself and sighed from his heart, considering by what means he might repay the emperor in kind and return retaliation in the same [Col. 0746A] measure for the injury inflicted.

But against this thought there stood the fact that the emperor was among the most powerful of mortals, and that the count’s forces could not suffice to harm him even in some slight degree. Yet, lest he appear either not to feel the injury inflicted or to pass it over too negligently, driven by grief he ordered the galleys prepared for another purpose to be armed. He summoned pirates and practitioners of abominable crimes, entrusted the vessels to them, and ordered them, while ranging through the emperor’s lands, to spare neither age nor sex and to make no distinction of condition. They were everywhere and without selection to commit churches and monasteries alike to the flames, and freely to perpetrate robberies and killings everywhere, bearing arms and force for a just cause.

[Col. 0746B] Obeying his command, they took to sea and ranged through the emperor’s territories, both those on islands and those on land adjoining the sea. Interpreting the count’s command more broadly, they brought about robbery everywhere, fire everywhere, and murder everywhere. They violated churches, broke into monasteries, and made absolutely no distinction among holy places. They robbed travelers going to the holy places or returning from them of their money for the journey, leaving them naked and destitute and forcing them either to die or to drag out their lives in beggary. They likewise robbed merchants, who supported themselves, their wives, and their children by that kind of trade, of the goods they had gathered, compelling them to return home empty-handed, their principal lost together with its profit.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. At Antioch the king drinks a medicine; brought thereby into his final illness, he seeks to return to his own lands, but as the illness worsens, he dies on the journey at Beirut.

[Col. 0746C]

While the count of Tripoli, moved by zeal for his own injury, was doing these things, the king at Antioch, before the onset of winter, wished, as was his custom, to take medicine. Through Barac, physician of the count of Tripoli, he received pills: some to take immediately, and others to take later after a short interval. For our eastern princes, chiefly because women bring this about, despise the medical art and method of treatment of our Latins. Placing trust only in [Col. 0746D] Jews, Samaritans, Syrians, and Saracens, they unwisely subject themselves to their care and entrust themselves to persons wholly ignorant of medical principles.

The pills in question were said to have been infected with poison, and this was not far from the truth. The remainder, which the king had been ordered to take a second time, was later tested at Tripoli: soaked in bread and given to a little dog, it brought death upon it within a few days. From the day on which the king drank the aforesaid medicine, he suffered dysentery and a slight fever, which later turned into a hectic fever. From then until the day of his death he experienced neither relief nor recovery.

Feeling within himself the urgency of his pain and the increase of his illness, he left Antioch and reached Tripoli. There he lay ill for [Col. 0747A] several months, awaiting a remedy day by day. But when he recognized that the illness was growing worse and that no hope of recovery remained, he was carried to Beirut. He ordered the prelates of the churches and the princes of the kingdom to be summoned to him with all speed. When they stood before him, he devoutly and religiously set forth his faith article by article; in a contrite and humble spirit, confessing his sins in the presence of the bishops, freed from the prison-house of the flesh, he carried his soul to heaven, there, God granting, to receive with the elect princes an unfading crown.

He died in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1162, in the twentieth year of his reign, on the fourth day before the Ides of February [10 February], and in the thirty-third year of his age. As he had no children, his brother was appointed heir to the kingdom. His body was then brought to Jerusalem with the greatest reverence and [Col. 0747B] royal funeral rites, amid the groans and tears of all. The clergy and all the people of the city came out to meet it, and he was honourably committed to burial among his predecessors in the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, before the place of Calvary where the Lord was crucified for our salvation.

No history records, nor does the memory of living men retain, that so great a sorrow and [Col. 0748A] so many proofs of inward grief arose in our kingdom or any other at the loss of any prince. Apart from the citizens in whose cities the royal funeral procession entered, whose grief and sorrow seemed without parallel, a multitude of the faithful came down from the mountains, following the funeral procession with wailing. Thus, from Beirut to Jerusalem, for almost eight continuous days, lamentation did not cease, and grief was renewed at nearly every hour.

It is said that even his enemies grieved at his death. When some suggested to Nūr al-Dīn that he should enter our territories and devastate the land while we were occupied with the funeral rites, he is said to have replied: “We must sympathize with [Col. 0748B] and humanely yield to their just grief, because they have lost a prince such as the rest of the world does not possess today.” As we conclude this book concerning his deeds, we pray that his holy soul may enjoy rest with the pious and elect. Amen.

# HERE BEGINS THE NINETEENTH BOOK.

[Col. 0747]

## CHAPTER I. Amalric succeeds his brother Baldwin in the kingdom.

[Col. 0747C]

Therefore, after the death without children, as stated, of Lord Baldwin III, the fourth Latin king of Jerusalem, he was succeeded in that same holy city by the fifth Latin king of Jerusalem, Lord Amalric, his only brother, count of Jaffa and Ascalon, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1162; in the sixty-second year from the liberation of that God-beloved city; while Lord Alexander presided over the holy Roman Church, in the third year of his pontificate; while Lord Amalric was the ninth Latin patriarch of the Church of the Holy Resurrection, in the fourth year of his pontificate; while Lord Aimery was the third Latin patriarch in that city [Col. 0747D] of the holy Church of Antioch, in the twentieth year of his pontificate; and while Lord Peter was the third Latin archbishop of the holy Church of Tyre in that city after its capture, in the thirteenth year of his pontificate.

After his brother’s death, however, the princes of the kingdom disagreed among themselves and were differently disposed regarding the appointment of a king. A great scandal arising from schism nearly intervened, with danger. But divine mercy came to their aid as desired, for it knows how to fit suitable remedies to imperilled circumstances. Suddenly, chiefly through the favour of the clergy and people, and of a few magnates, the plans of those otherwise inclined were thwarted. In the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, by the aforesaid Lord Amalric, patriarch, with the archbishops, bishops, and all the prelates of the [Col. 0748B] churches present and cooperating, he received the grace of royal anointing [Col. 0748C] and the insignia of the diadem. On the twelfth day before the Kalends of March [18 February], the eighth day after his brother’s death, he was raised to the throne of the kingdom, which was due to him by hereditary right.

As soon as he had been made a knight and begun to bear military arms, he was made count of Jaffa. Later his brother, Lord Baldwin of illustrious memory, granted him with royal liberality Ascalon, the eminent metropolis of the Philistines, which he had conquered in his own days and restored after a long time to the Christian name—as has been more carefully set forth above in our account of the reign of that same Lord Baldwin. Lord Amalric was twenty-seven years old when he began to reign. He reigned eleven years and five months.

## CHAPTER II. A description of his character, manners, life, and conduct.

[Col. 0748D]

Amalric was therefore a man endowed with worldly experience, exceedingly prudent and circumspect in action. His speech was somewhat impeded, though not so much that it could be reckoned a serious defect; rather, he lacked the elegance of naturally flowing eloquence. He was far better in counsel than in abundance or ornament of words. In the customary law by which the kingdom was governed he was most subtle, second to none; indeed, he surpassed all the princes of the realm alike in keenness of mind and in the soundness of his judgment. In dangers and extreme necessities—which he frequently encountered while striving manfully and without cessation to enlarge the kingdom—he was courageous and provident, preserving an undaunted spirit with a kind of royal constancy. [Col. 0749A]

He was moderately educated, and much less so than his brother; yet by quickness of intelligence, the benefit of a retentive memory, frequent questioning, and a love of reading whenever the occupations of the kingdom allowed him some leisure, he was, as commonly befalls kings, sufficiently well furnished with learning. He was shrewder in raising questions and took great delight in their solutions. Above all other reading, he eagerly listened to histories, retaining them continually in memory and reciting them readily and most faithfully. He was wholly devoted to serious matters; never to mime-shows or dice. He took particular pleasure in the flight and capture of hawks and herons. He could endure hardship; since he was rather stout and excessively fat, he was not greatly troubled by the severity of cold or heat.

In this respect an evangelical man, he ordered tithes to be paid in all integrity and without burdening the Church. [Col. 0749B] Every day, unless illness or an urgent necessity prevented him, he devoutly heard Mass. Of curses and insults brought against him—frequently in public and almost continually in secret, even by low and contemptible persons—he was a most patient recipient and an excellent dissembler, so that he appeared not even to have heard what he had heard. Moderate in food and drink, he abhorred drunkenness in both. He was said also to place such confidence in his stewards that, once he had placed them over his affairs, he neither required accounts from them nor lent an ear to those alleging their dishonesty. Some, however, regarded this as a fault; others, attributing it to virtue, maintained that it was proof of sincere trust. [Col. 0749C]

These endowments and greater virtues of character were impaired by certain notable traits which seemed to cast a cloud over what has been said. He was more taciturn than was fitting, and devoid of outstanding courtesy. He wholly lacked the grace of affability which most effectively wins the hearts of subjects for princes. He very rarely addressed anyone unless necessity compelled him or another had first spoken to him. This defect appeared all the more notable in him because his brother had possessed in fuller measure the charm of pleasant speech and winning affability. He was also said to suffer impatiently from the slippery weakness of the flesh—may the Lord mercifully pardon him for it—and to make attempts upon other men’s marriages.

He was likewise a vehement assailant of the liberties of the Churches. By frequent and unlawful exactions during his days, he reduced their patrimonies to utter exhaustion, so that venerable places were compelled to burden themselves with debts beyond the capacity of their revenues. [Col. 0749D] He was covetous of money beyond what befitted royal honor. Through the intervention of gifts, he often took away, and still more often postponed, matters in a manner not permitted by the rigor of judicial censure and the moderation of law. Yet, offering an excuse for his avarice, he endeavored to give reasons even to me in more familiar conversation, saying:

“Every ruler, and especially a king, ought always to retain this provision for himself, lest he fall into need, for two reasons: first, because the wealth of subjects is safe where the sovereign is not in want; and second, because he may have at hand the means of providing for the needs of his kingdom if unexpected occasions arise. In that case a provident king ought to be abundantly generous and spare no expense at all, so that whatever he possesses may appear to be possessed not for himself, but for the uses of the kingdom.” [Col. 0750A]

No enemy of his can deny that one of these things was present in him. For in the necessities of the kingdom he spared neither expense nor the exertion of his own body. But the wealth of his subjects was by no means secure, for he frequently resorted to exhausting their estates upon the slightest pretext.

## CHAPTER III. On his bodily appearance; and on a certain question which he proposed to one of his intimates for solution.

In bodily stature he was shaped with a certain favorable proportion, being taller than men of medium height but shorter than the very tall. [Col. 0750B] His face was handsome and bore the dignity becoming a venerable prince even to those who did not know him. His eyes were bright and of medium size; his nose, like his brother’s, was suitably aquiline; his hair blond and slightly receding. His beard clothed his cheeks and chin with a pleasing fullness. His laugh, however, was uncontrolled, and in laughing his whole body shook.

He delighted greatly in conversing with prudent and discerning men, men acquainted with distant regions and experienced in foreign customs. I remember that once, when he had summoned me in familiar fashion, while he was suffering at the castle of Tyre from a lingering low fever—not very dangerously—I spoke privately with him at length during the hours of rest and a lucid interval, as commonly happens in intermittent fevers. [Col. 0750C] To certain questions of his I offered such answers as occurred to me at the time; for he was greatly refreshed by our discussion. Among them he proposed to us one question which greatly stirred me inwardly: first because it was unusual for such a question to be asked, since what the universal faith taught and had most firmly handed down as to be believed did not seem worthy even of question; and secondly because it inflicted a grave wound on my mind if an orthodox prince, and the son of orthodox parents, could entertain a scruple in so certain a matter and doubt in his conscience.

He asked whether, apart from the teaching of the Savior and of the saints who followed Christ—a teaching of which he did not doubt—reason might be found by which the future resurrection could be proved through evident and necessary arguments. Moved by the novelty of the question, I answered: “The teaching of our Lord and Redeemer is sufficient. In many places in the Gospel He most plainly teaches that there will be a resurrection of the flesh; He promises that He will come as judge, to judge the living and the dead and to judge the world by fire; that He will give the elect the kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world; and that He will assign to the wicked the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. [Col. 0750D] The devout assertion of the holy apostles and likewise of the Fathers of the Old Testament is sufficient.”

To this he replied: “I hold all these things most firmly; but I seek a reason by which the future resurrection and another life after this death may be proved to someone who denies these things and does not receive Christ’s teaching.”

I said: “Then take upon yourself the role of such a person, and let us try to find something on this matter.”

“It pleases me,” he said.

Then I asked: “Do you confess that God is just?”

He replied: “Nothing is truer; I confess it.”

I said: “And is it the part of the just to repay good with good and evil with evil?”

He replied: “It is true.”

I continued: “But this does not happen in the present life. For some good people suffer nothing but troubles and adversities in this present age, while certain evil people enjoy unbroken prosperity, as the examples of daily life teach us.”

He replied: “That is certain.”

I went on: “Therefore it will occur in another life, because God cannot fail to be a just recompense-giver. Therefore there will be another life and a resurrection of this flesh; in that flesh in which each person has deserved good or evil, he must receive his reward and recompense.” [Col. 0751A]

He replied: “It pleases me beyond measure; you have wiped every doubt from my heart.”

He was greatly refreshed by discussions of this and similar kinds. But let us return to our subject. He was exceedingly fat, so that in a womanly fashion he had breasts projecting down to his belt. But Nature, with more cheerful and kindly hand, had shaped the remaining parts of his body so that they displayed not merely ordinary comeliness but enjoyed a certain distinction of form. Even his enemies cannot deny that he was moderate in taking bodily refreshment and most abstinent from wine. [Col. 0751B]

## CHAPTER IV. That before he was crowned, he was compelled to separate from his wife, whom he had married contrary to the sacred canons.

Finally, while his brother was still alive and was prosperously administering the kingdom, he married Agnes, daughter of Joscelin the Younger, Count of Edessa. While his brother lived, he had by her twin children: namely Baldwin, whom his uncle received from the sacred font, and a daughter born first, named Sibylla, bearing the same name as the Countess of Flanders, sister of them both. Yet, after his brother’s death, when he claimed the kingdom devolved upon him by hereditary right, he was compelled to repudiate this wife.

For from the beginning, when he had married her, he joined her to himself in marriage against the will and opposition of the lord Patriarch Fulcher of blessed memory, because they were said to be related in the fourth degree of consanguinity, as was afterward solemnly proved before the face of the Church by their common kinsfolk. [Col. 0751C] For in the presence of Lord Amalric, patriarch of blessed memory, and Lord John, cardinal-priest of Saints John and Paul and legate of the Apostolic See, and in accordance with the solemnity of ecclesiastical law, the relatives of both parties personally gave oaths and affirmed that the matter was as alleged. A divorce was therefore effected and the marriage dissolved.

This provision was nevertheless added: that those born of the two should be considered legitimate and should obtain full rights of succession in their paternal property. Later, being curious about such matters, we carefully inquired into the degree of their relationship. For we had not yet returned from the schools, but were still overseas occupied with studies in the liberal arts, when these things occurred at Jerusalem. At length we learned from Lady Stephanie, abbess of the Church of Saint Mary the Greater at Jerusalem, situated before the Lord’s Sepulchre, daughter of Joscelin the Elder, Count of Edessa, by the sister of Lord Roger, son of Richard, Prince of Antioch—a woman religious and noble in birth and character, then already advanced in years but retaining these things in memory—that their genealogy was as follows. [Col. 0752A]

Lord Baldwin of Bourg, the second king of Jerusalem, a man magnificent in every respect—whose life and character, and whose favorable and adverse fortunes, we discussed more fully when treating his reign—and Lord Joscelin the Elder were sons of two sisters. From Lord Baldwin was born Queen Melisende; from Melisende were born King Baldwin III and King Amalric. Likewise, from Lord Joscelin the Elder were born Joscelin the Younger, from whom came the aforesaid Countess Agnes, in fact, though not in law, wife of Lord King Amalric; and the third Joscelin, now royal seneschal and maternal uncle of the Lord King Baldwin who reigns today. [Col. 0752B]

Thereafter, while Lord King Amalric still remained unmarried, she was immediately united in marriage to the noble and magnificent Lord Hugh of Ibelin, son of the elder Balian, brother of Baldwin of Ramla—who now possesses that aforesaid city after the death without children of his brother—and of the younger Balian, who today has as wife the widow of Lord King Amalric. After Hugh’s death, while Lord Amalric was still alive, she entered into the same relationship with Lord Reginald of Sidon, son of Lord Gerard; and with him she is said to have had a union less lawful than the one she had earlier had with Lord Amalric. [Col. 0752C] For Lord Gerard, his aforesaid father, as kinsman of both parties—as indeed he certainly was—confirmed by his own oath that, as he had heard from his elders, there was consanguinity between the persons named above. Hence the divorce followed, as has been stated.

## CHAPTER V. The king descends into Egypt; battle is joined with Dargan the sultan. Shawar introduces Shirkuh into Egypt; Dargan sends envoys to the king seeking peace.

The lord Amalric having therefore been confirmed upon the throne of the kingdom, in the first year of his reign, when the Egyptians refused to pay the annual tribute which they had stipulated with his brother, he assembled military forces and a large army and, on the Kalends of September [1 September], descended by force into Egypt. There the administrator of that kingdom, who in their language was called *soldanus* (“sultan”), named Dargan, met him with an innumerable multitude and did not fear to engage him in the desert near Egypt. But unable to withstand our men’s attack, after many of his own had been killed and some captured, he was compelled to flee and, with the remnant, to withdraw into the neighboring city which in their language is called Belbeis. [Col. 0752D]

The Egyptians, fearing that, once the lord king had defeated him, he would wish to advance farther into the kingdom with his army, judged that they had no other remedy against our attacks. They therefore broke the embankments which usually restrain the river in flood until fixed seasons, and let in the Nile, already swollen to its accustomed height, in order that at least by these barriers they might check our advance and protect themselves through the benefit of the inundating river. The lord king, having triumphed over the enemy and successfully settled matters, returned thence victorious and in glory to his kingdom.

Now this Dargan, whom we have called administrator and sultan of all Egypt, had a few days earlier driven from the same office, partly by deceit and partly by force, another very powerful man named Shawar. With friends, retainers, and such forces as he could take with him, Shawar escaped by flight and went to the Arab tribes allied with him to request their aid. [Col. 0753A] Awaiting the outcome and watching for the course of war, he lay concealed among his people, as we have said, intending at a suitable time to undertake something against his rival.

When, therefore, he heard that the lord king had returned to his own kingdom, and that his adversary persisted in his authority with his usual insolence and almost greater glory—because he had withstood so great a prince in battle and because the kingdom had suffered little harm from his departure—he hastened to Nur al-Din, the most powerful prince and king of Damascus. He implored aid from him, trusting that by it he might return to Egypt, expel his rival, and recover the realm. [Col. 0753B]

Nur al-Din, enticed by gifts and promises, hoped that if his army could once enter Egypt’s borders he might seize the kingdom by force. He therefore readily consented. He entrusted Shawar with the commander of his army, a capable man, vigorous in arms, generous beyond the means of his patrimony, eager for glory, and highly experienced in warfare. His generosity made him beloved and welcome among soldiers. This man, named Shirkuh, he sent into Egypt with a great force.

Shirkuh was already an elderly man, short of stature, very fat and corpulent; he had risen from humble circumstances to wealth and, through meritorious service, from a servile condition to be a prince. He had a white opacity in one eye. [Col. 0753C] He was most patient of hardship and endured thirst and hunger with equanimity beyond what that age is accustomed to bear.

But Sultan Dargan learned through passing messengers and public report that the enemy whom he had previously expelled was approaching with countless thousands of Turks. Distrusting his own resources, he resorted to borrowed assistance. He therefore sent envoys with peaceful words to the lord king, asking and beseeching his aid against the threatening enemies. He promised not merely the tribute agreed upon with Lord King Baldwin, but a much larger tribute, to be rendered at the lord king’s discretion; he also promised perpetual subjection and an everlasting alliance, prepared to confirm them by giving hostages. [Col. 0753D]

## CHAPTER VI. Peter, Archbishop of Tyre, dies; Lord Frederick, Bishop of Acre, succeeds him.

At the same time Lord Peter, the venerable Archbishop of Tyre, of pious memory in the Lord, entered upon the way of all flesh in the second year of the aforesaid lord king, in March, on the first day of the month. Within a few days, in the same month, he was succeeded—through the strong advocacy of the lord king—by a suffragan of the same church, namely Lord Frederick, Bishop of Acre: a man noble according to the flesh, very tall in body, a Lorrainer by nation, moderately learned, but military beyond measure. [Col. 0754A]

## CHAPTER VII. Dargan, sultan in Egypt, is killed by the treachery of his own men. Shawar becomes sultan. He invites the king; the king descends into Egypt; Shirkuh is forcibly expelled.

While the aforesaid envoys were negotiating these matters with the lord king, and their requests had almost been granted, before they could return home, the aforementioned Shawar and Shirkuh had already descended into Egypt with their auxiliaries. They engaged Sultan Dargan in battle; in the first encounter they were defeated and severely overthrown. Before they met again under the same conditions, however, the oft-mentioned Dargan was secretly struck by an arrow by one of his own men and died, lamented by his followers.
