After his death Shawar, victorious and having attained his desire, entered Cairo; he put to the sword all the friends, kinsmen, and retainers of Dargan whom he could find, and recovered his former office. [Col. 0754B] For their supreme ruler cares little which of the contenders falls or prevails, provided that there is someone to manage his own and the kingdom’s affairs and to subject himself to his service.

Shirkuh, meanwhile, seized the neighboring city of Belbeis and began resolutely to claim it as though it were his own. By deed—and perhaps by word—he made clear that, if opportunity allowed, he wished to subject the other parts of that kingdom to his own dominion, even against the will of the sultan and caliph. Shawar therefore feared that by introducing such a guest he had worsened both his own position and that of his lord, and that he had received one who, like a mouse in a bag and a serpent in the bosom, would repay his hosts badly. [Col. 0754C]

With all haste he sent envoys and a message of peace to the lord king in Syria, that, according to the agreements previously made between the lord king and Sultan Dargan, they might immediately fulfill them not merely in word but also in deed, and, if necessary, add still greater concessions. The agreements being confirmed on both sides, the king set out with all his army and descended again into Egypt in the second year of his reign. There Shawar and the Egyptians joined him; together they besieged the aforesaid Shirkuh, who had withdrawn into the city of Belbeis as into a personal stronghold. [Col. 0754D] Worn down by a lengthy siege and want of provisions, he was compelled to surrender, upon the terms that he and all his men should have free and unharmed departure and return to their own country. This was granted him; having obtained it, he abandoned the city and returned through the desert to Damascus. [Col. 0755A]

## CHAPTER VIII. Nur al-Din is defeated in the region of Tripoli and barely escapes our men’s hands by flight.

Meanwhile Nur al-Din, remaining in the region of Tripoli at the place commonly called La Bochea, was puffed up by prosperity and acted somewhat carelessly, thereby suffering a loss almost irreparable. At that time certain nobles from Aquitaine had arrived on pilgrimage: Geoffrey, surnamed Martel, brother of the Count of Angoulême, and Hugh of Lusignan the Elder, surnamed Brunus. After performing their devotions as customary, they went to the region of Antioch.

When they learned that Nur al-Din was staying with his army in the aforesaid place in the region of Tripoli, resting in leisure with excessive security and without concern, they assembled military aid and suddenly fell upon his army. They captured many, slew more with the sword, and destroyed his army almost to utter annihilation. [Col. 0755B] He himself, abandoning his sword and leaving behind all his baggage, barefoot on one foot and riding a pack-animal, greatly confounded and despairing of life, barely escaped by flight from our men’s hands. Our men, enriched by spoils and manifold wealth, returned victorious to their own country.

The commanders of this expedition were Gilbert de Lacy, a nobleman experienced in arms and master of the brethren of the Knights Templar in those regions; the two great men mentioned above; Robert Mansel, who commanded the men of Galilee in the same expedition; and a few others. [Col. 0755C]

## CHAPTER IX. Nur al-Din besieges the castle of Harim in the region of Antioch; the Prince of Antioch, the Count of Tripoli, and Calaman, governor of Cilicia, are captured.

Nur al-Din, dismayed by this adverse event, inflamed with anger, clothed in shame and disgrace, and desiring to efface the ignominy, stirred up his neighbors and allies to avenge the injury to himself and his men. By entreaty now, now by payment, he humbly invited almost all the princes of the East; he restored his strength and collected military assistance from every quarter.

Having assembled immense forces and massed innumerable thousands, he besieged one of our towns on the borders of Antioch, named Harim. Arranging his engines around it, according to custom, he began fiercely and unceasingly to press the townspeople, giving them no rest. [Col. 0755D] When this became known to our princes, Lord Bohemond III, son of Raymond, Prince of Antioch; Lord Raymond the Younger, Count of Tripoli, son of Count Raymond; Calaman, governor of Cilicia, kinsman of the emperor and administrator of imperial affairs in that province; and Thoros, most powerful prince of the Armenians, joined to themselves such infantry and cavalry reinforcements as they could gather from every quarter. They formed their columns and battle line, hurried to meet the enemy, and undertook to raise the siege against their will.

Nur al-Din and the Turkish princes with him, having taken counsel together, judged it safer to depart voluntarily after lifting the siege than rashly to engage the enemies now almost upon them. They made ready their baggage and attempted to withdraw. But our men nevertheless pressed after them; abusing success and good fortune, they were not content merely to have freed the townspeople from the siege of so many princes. Pursuing too heedlessly, with their ranks broken up, wandering here and there contrary to military discipline, they were caught in certain narrow marshy places when the Turks suddenly returned and recovered heart and strength. [Col. 0756A]

At the first onset our men were broken; and they who had formerly been an object of fear to their enemies were now, most miserably, exposed to mockery. Routed and shattered, they were shamefully cut down by the enemies’ swords like sacrificial victims. There was no one who remembered former valor, who, mindful of his fathers’ courage or his own, sought to repel the injury or gloriously fight for the liberty and honor of his country. Hurried headlong and forgetful of their rank, they laid down their arms and earned life by shameful supplication—a life which it would have been nobler to spend in manfully fighting for their country, thereby leaving a favorable example for posterity. [Col. 0756B]

Thoros the Armenian, seeing the enemy’s squadrons prevail and our battle lines collapse in turn, sought safety in flight and withdrew from the tumult of war. From the beginning he had disapproved of pursuing the enemy as they withdrew from the siege and had attempted to dissuade the others; but the more useless opinion of the rest prevailed.

Lord Bohemond, Prince of Antioch; Lord Raymond, Count of Tripoli; Calaman, governor of Cilicia; Hugh of Lusignan, whom we mentioned above; Joscelin III, son of Joscelin II, Count of Edessa; and many other nobles, seeking to preserve their lives with disgrace and dishonor, surrendered themselves to the enemy. They were miserably bound in chains like worthless slaves, carried to Aleppo, made a spectacle to unbelieving peoples, and consigned to prisons. [Col. 0756C]

At length, encouraged by success and exceedingly favorable fortune, Nur al-Din and those with him returned more confidently to the castle they had formerly besieged. Having again enclosed it in siege, they captured it within a few days and violently occupied it after storming it by force. This occurred in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1165, in the second year of the reign of Lord Amalric, on the fourth Ides of August [10 August], while he was still detained in Egypt occupied with his own affairs. [Col. 0756D]

## CHAPTER X. Thierry, Count of Flanders, arrives in Syria. Nur al-Din besieges Paneas and occupies it after besieging it.

Meanwhile our affairs, afflicted almost to complete exhaustion by so great a reversal and such adverse events, had no remnant even of hope left. All, already dismayed in spirit, feared worse things with every passing day. Behold, Thierry, Count of Flanders, the king’s brother-in-law, arrived with his devout and God-fearing wife and a small troop of soldiers. All the people received his arrival with such joy that, after excessive heat from the sun, they seemed to have received a most welcome breeze and an immediate remedy. They hoped that, supported by his assistance, they might await the arrival of the lord king and the Christian army. [Col. 0757A]

But this somewhat meager calm was miserably cut short and turned into darkness when a suddenly arisen gloomy cloud appeared. For Nur al-Din, elevated by success and favorable fortune, saw that the kingdom lacked its customary support and was bereft of its principal princes, whom he held captive. Moreover, he saw that the lord king and all the strength of the army were absent. Seizing this timely opportunity, he set about besieging the city of Paneas.

Paneas is a most ancient city situated at the foot of the famous promontory of Lebanon. In ancient times, in the days of the Israelite people, it was called Dan, the northern boundary of their possession, just as Beersheba was its southern boundary. Thus whenever the length of the Promised Land is described, it is said to extend from Dan to Beersheba (1 Kings 3:20). In the time of Philip, eldest son of Herod, tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis, as Luke relates (chapter 3), he enlarged it in honor of Tiberius Caesar and, for the perpetual memory of his own name, it was called Caesarea Philippi. [Col. 0757B]

It is also called Paneas; but our Latins, corrupting the name as they do those of almost all other cities, call it Belinas. On the east it borders the territory of Damascus, near which the Jordan has the source of its streams. This is the city of which the Gospel says that Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi and questioned His disciples (Matthew 16:13). There also Peter, chief of the apostles, received from the Lord the keys of the heavenly kingdom on account of the merit of his outstanding confession (ibid., 19). [Col. 0757C]

Nur al-Din besieged it and found it undefended, since Lord Humphrey, the royal constable, whose hereditary possession it was, was absent with the lord king in Egypt; its bishop also was absent and its population diminished. He placed engines and military siege devices around it, undermined its wall, and weakened its towers for the most part by continual hurling of stones. Within a few days he took it by storm, compelling those inside to surrender on the terms that, departing with all their possessions, they should have free and peaceful exit. He received the city in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1167, in the second year of the reign of Lord King Amalric, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November [18 October]. [Col. 0757D]

As he was departing for Egypt, the lord constable had entrusted the city to a certain faithful knight named Walter of Quesnet. Some say that he was negligent in guarding the place. They add that, at the surrender, he acted treacherously with a certain priest named Roger, a canon of that church, after taking money; hence, upon the lord king’s return from Egypt, they were greatly afraid, fearing that this would be imputed to them as a capital crime. But we have learned none of these matters for certain, except that the city was handed over to the enemy. [Col. 0758A]

## CHAPTER XI. The king, returning from Egypt, proceeds to Antioch. The prince is restored to liberty upon payment of ransom. The cave-fortress of Sidon is handed over to the enemy. Likewise, beyond the Jordan the enemy take another cave-fortress.

While these things were occurring in Syria, the lord king, having expelled Shirkuh from Egypt and confirmed Shawar the sultan in his administration, returned victoriously and gloriously to his own country. Although he had heard before of what had occurred, he now learned in full the sad events and calamities that had befallen the kingdom. Summoned by the Antiochenes to help their almost desperate situation, he compassionately answered their appeal as a brother. Taking the Count of Flanders with him and hastening his journey, he proceeded to Antioch to provide the desired relief for their affliction. [Col. 0758B]

When he arrived, he administered the affairs of the lord prince faithfully and prudently, with as much diligence and concern as he was scarcely accustomed to show even in his own affairs. He governed nobles and common people with much gentleness and provident moderation, and stationed prudent men in every city to administer in good faith and sound judgment the matters belonging to the prince’s demesne. He then returned to his own country, yet did not cease to labor with the prince’s faithful men and friends in negotiating his ransom.

Through his efforts it came about that in that same summer the prince, after being held scarcely a full year by the enemy and after payment of a great price, was restored to liberty and his former honor. Returning to Antioch, he did not rest idly, but hastened as quickly as he could to the emperor of Constantinople, who a few days earlier had married his younger sister Maria, so that he might not delay in recovering the hostages he had given, after their ransom had been paid. [Col. 0758C] The emperor received him honorably, treated him kindly, and heaped imperial gifts upon him with the utmost liberality; within a few days he returned to Antioch.

It seems remarkable that Nur al-Din, so prudent and provident a prince, who most unwillingly released our captives from his prisons and took especial pride in holding many of our men, particularly nobles, in chains, permitted the Prince of Antioch to be restored so quickly to freedom. Two explanations occur to us: either he feared the requests of the lord emperor, lest the emperor perhaps wish to have him without payment, and he would be ashamed to refuse him such a thing; or, because the prince was young and gave no promise of good hope, Nur al-Din feared that, if he held him longer, the Antiochenes would provide for themselves by appointing a stronger man and a harsher adversary would be set against him. [Col. 0758D] To a man of great discernment and foresight, it seemed safer that this man, from whom little good was expected, should rule the province of Antioch than that someone wiser and stronger should administer the region in his place, one with whom it would be more dangerous to share affairs. This, in our view, was the intention of that most vigilant man. [Col. 0759A]

At the same time Shirkuh, often mentioned above, a man ingenious in devising our ruin, suddenly and unexpectedly seized by stratagems a certain one of our strongholds situated in the territory of Sidon: an impregnable cave-fortress commonly called the Cave of Tyre (*Cavea de Tyrum*), having, it is said, bribed its guards. That it came into the enemy’s hands through the consent of those entrusted with its defence is shown by the fact that, as soon as the fortress was surrendered, all who were within went over to the enemy’s territory, except their lord, who was fortuitously captured and ended his unhappy life by hanging at Sidon. [Col. 0759B]

In the same year, Lord William, king of Sicily, of illustrious memory, son of King Roger, met his final day, overtaken by death.

At the same time, another stronghold of the same kind, again an impregnable cave-fortress, situated beyond the Jordan in the territory of Arabia and entrusted to the care of the brethren of the Knights Templar, was handed over to the same Shirkuh. The lord king hurried with a large force to recover it; but while encamped above the Jordan, he received news that the fortress had already fallen into the enemy’s hands. On hearing this, the lord king, confounded and inflamed with anger, ordered about twelve of the brethren of the Temple who had surrendered the castle to the enemy to be hanged on the gallows. [Col. 0759C]

Thus in that year, the third of Lord Amalric’s reign, our affairs suffered very great loss, as our sins deserved, so that the entire kingdom was brought into an exceedingly narrow strait.

## CHAPTER XII. The return to his homeland of the author of this history is described, and certain particulars of his advancement are set forth. Shirkuh descends into Egypt, bringing a great force with him.

While these events were taking place around us, a persistent report resounded [Col. 0759D] and was widely proclaimed: the often-mentioned Shirkuh, with a magnificent equipment, having summoned innumerable soldiers from the eastern and northern regions, was again preparing to descend into Egypt; nor was the report false. For he had approached the greatest prince of the Saracens—the caliph of Baghdad, namely—who, as though sole monarch, is understood to surpass and rule all others. Having reached him and rendered the customary reverence, he began carefully to set forth the innumerable riches of Egypt: its wonderful abundance of every good and exceptional advantage; that ruler’s inestimable treasures, revenues, taxes, and annual income of boundless amount from cities inland and on the sea; and, further, a people given over to luxury, unpractised in war, [Col. 0760A] enervated by a long peace. He added, insisted, and repeatedly recalled how both the man then ruling that kingdom and his forefathers had set up for themselves a rival seat against him and his predecessors, imprudently making themselves equal to their unique supremacy; and how they had even presumed to teach another law and contradictory traditions. By these arguments and others he stirred the caliph’s mind toward the object at which it aimed and persuaded it. The caliph therefore wrote to all the princes subject to his authority, strictly commanding them to contribute their forces, furnish assistance, and follow Shirkuh.

Hearing this, King Amalric, wishing to forestall his designs, summoned a general council at Nablus. There, in the presence of the lord patriarch, archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of the churches, princes, and people, he set forth in order the kingdom’s necessities, humbly imploring the assistance of all. It was therefore decreed and adopted by common consent that everyone without exception should give, for the kingdom’s aid, a tenth of all movable property; and this was done. Meanwhile the report was no less insistent that Shirkuh, undoubtedly having taken provisions sufficient for many days and carrying water in skins, had set out across the desert by which the people of Israel came to the Promised Land. The king, gathering such soldiers as he could have, marched out to meet him and hurried with all speed as far as Kadesh-barnea, which is in the wilderness, in order to hinder his passage. Not finding him there, he returned more quickly.

## CHAPTER XIII. The king, pursuing Shirkuh, likewise descends into Egypt to furnish aid to the Egyptians.

[Col. 0760C]

Accordingly, forces of cavalry and infantry having been summoned from every city by public proclamation, and having assembled unanimously at Ascalon, on the third day before the Kalends of February [30 January], they began their march. Taking provisions necessary for a fixed number of days, they crossed by rapid stages the desolate wilderness lying between Gaza, the last city of our kingdom, and the Egyptian territory. Having counted their men and awaited the last arrivals at Laris, an ancient town in that same desert, the whole army at last reached the city now called Belbeis, often mentioned by us, formerly called Pelusium, of which the prophets make frequent mention. [Col. 0760D]

When the arrival of the lord king became known, the sultan Shawar, startled by the sudden appearance of our men, fearing that all this preparation was directed against himself and doubting our good faith, was seized by excessive terror. Although elsewhere regarded as a prudent, energetic, and highly provident man, in this respect he was found so supine and burdened with such gross ignorance that, when informed of the reason for our journey, he could scarcely believe it. Almost too late and sluggishly, he sent scouts through the desert to bring him reliable intelligence concerning the enemy army. Those who had been sent returned and announced that the Turkish forces had reached the place called Attasi. [Col. 0761A] Then the sultan, admiring and extolling the sincerity of our faith, and carefully considering how great a concern a Christian army had shown for its friends, placed all the riches of the kingdom and of the caliph at the king’s disposal, and from that day showed himself a diligent executor of all his commands. The lord king, in turn, had at his disposal every service needed for his purposes.

## CHAPTER XIV. Cairo is described, and its first founder is identified.

Passing Pelusium and Cairo, where the royal seat and summit of all Egypt are displayed adorned with magnificent buildings, they placed their camp on the bank of the river, with on their left the noble and distinguished metropolis commonly called Babylon, but called in Arabic Macer. [Col. 0761B] We have been unable to discover a more ancient name for this city; for Babylon, or Babylonia, was a most ancient city in the East. According to ancient and indeed most ancient histories, no city of this name was ever heard of in Egypt. Hence it is probable that this city was founded after the times of the Pharaohs, who first ruled in Egypt, and of the later Ptolemies, and even after the Roman period, when they reduced the kingdom of Egypt to a province—as is known concerning Cairo. For Johar, commander of the army of Mehezedinalla, who was then ruling in Africa, is known to have founded it after acquiring for his lord the whole Egyptian province; how this happened we shall relate below. [Col. 0761C]

Some, however, confidently maintain that this is that ancient, noble, and most famous Memphis, frequently remembered in ancient histories and in the prophets, which is said to have been the capital and governing city of that whole kingdom and of many neighbouring provinces. Yet even today, beyond the Nile which flows past the city of which we speak, at about ten miles’ distance there appears an ancient and immense city displaying countless evidences of ancient nobility and exceptional magnitude; the inhabitants of the region firmly assert that it was ancient Memphis. It is therefore probable that the people of Memphis, either compelled by necessity or attracted by greater advantages, [Col. 0761D] transferred their dwellings to this side of the river and changed their former name either then or later.

But we hold it certain that Johar, as stated above, who had been sent from Africa with the armies of the great prince Mehezedinalla to conquer Egypt, built Cairo beside this same city after subduing the entire country and making its peoples tributary. He built it as a principal and familiar residence for his lord’s dominion, in the 358th year from the reign of Mehemet. In the third year thereafter Mehezedinalla, leaving Caraea, where the seat of his kingdom had been for several years, followed him and, in accordance with his lord’s disposition, established the aforesaid place as the throne of his kingdom and rendered it glorious by his own residence. This was in the 361st year from Mehemet’s reign, [Col. 0762A] and the twentieth of his own reign, as is set out more carefully elsewhere in the history that we composed concerning the princes of the East.

## CHAPTER XV. As Shirkuh approaches, the king goes out to meet him; Shirkuh forestalls the king and crosses the river.

Our men having encamped on the riverbank scarcely two stadia from the aforesaid city, they took counsel and weighed the alternatives in lengthy deliberation. They judged it best to meet Shirkuh and his men before they crossed the river and to keep him outside the kingdom’s boundaries, rather than engage them after they had crossed, when the very difficulty of returning would make them more desperate. Therefore they broke camp and hastened to the place where the enemy was said to be. [Col. 0762B] He was reported to be about ten miles from the place where our men had first encamped. But when they reached the said place, he had already crossed the river, like a most vigilant commander, with nearly his entire army, leaving behind a few men. Our men captured these and bound them in chains.

When questioned concerning his crossing, the number of his soldiers, and many other necessary matters, they informed our men. Their report disclosed something previously unknown to us: after they had crossed Syrian Sobal in the desert, a sudden and exceedingly violent storm of winds arose, dispersing so much dust from the sand through the air in the manner of clouds and thick darkness that those in the army did not dare at all to open their eyes [Col. 0762C] or mouths in order to speak with one another. Dismounting from their horses and throwing themselves to the ground, they clung to the earth, pressing their hands as deeply as they could into the sand, lest the force of the whirlwind should carry them upward, only to cast them down again.

For in that desert, as on the sea, waves of sand are raised and lowered, as in storms; so that passage through those inhospitable places is no less dangerous than navigation through waters. Having lost their camels and the greater part of their provisions, scarcely hoping to survive, with many dead and many others scattered over the broad expanse of sands, they at last, when the air had become calm again, reached Egypt after several days, following uncertain routes and wandering more than knowing their way, as has been stated. [Col. 0762D] When our army saw that Shirkuh and his men had crossed the river, it retraced the way by which it had come and again encamped beside the same city it had previously left, on the riverbank.

## CHAPTER XVI. Sultan Shawar endeavours to keep the king in Egypt by renewing the agreements.

The sultan, seeing that he had admitted into the very heart of his kingdom an enemy whom he could neither withstand nor expel from its bounds except through the lord king, anxiously considered by what agreement he might keep the king in Egypt. He feared that, exhausted by the immensity of his labour, the king might decide to return home. Nor did it seem possible by any other means that the lord king should remain in the country [Col. 0763A] unless a larger amount of tribute were fixed for him and sufficient expenses assigned to him and his princes.

It therefore pleased him—and our men too judged it expedient—to renew the former agreements, to establish with inviolable firmness the covenant of perpetual peace between the lord king and the caliph, and, with the tribute increased, to assign the lord king fixed annual payments from the caliph’s treasury. The affair seemed unlikely to end quickly, but likely to require prolonged labour and much time. After sounding out on both sides the wishes of the parties and ascertaining their intentions, the mediators of these arrangements decreed for the lord king four hundred thousand gold pieces: [Col. 0763B] two hundred thousand to be paid immediately, and the remaining two hundred thousand to be paid without difficulty at stipulated times, upon this condition and in these terms: that the lord king should personally pledge in good faith, without fraud or evil intent, that he would not leave the kingdom of Egypt until Shirkuh and his entire army had either been utterly destroyed or expelled from all Egyptian territory.

The condition pleased both parties. The lord king gave his hand, concerning the agreed terms, to those sent by the caliph. Lord Hugh of Caesarea, a young man of remarkable prudence and, beyond what that age ordinarily affords, circumspect, was sent with certain others; in Hugh’s hand the caliph was to confirm the agreements according to the agreed form; [Col. 0763C] for it did not seem sufficient for the sultan alone to bind himself in this matter.

## CHAPTER XVII. Envoys are sent to the caliph to renew the treaty; the magnificence of the royal palace is described.

Since that ruler’s palace has a custom singular and unknown in our age, it is pleasing to record carefully what we learned, from the trustworthy account of those who entered in the presence of so great a prince, about its condition and magnificence, the immensity of its wealth, and the multiplicity of its splendour. It will not be a small gain to have understood these things more carefully.

The aforesaid Hugh of Caesarea and Geoffrey, brother of Fulk, a Templar, at the beginning of their embassy, entered Cairo under the sultan’s guidance. Ascending to the palace, which in their language is called Cascere, [Col. 0763D] they were accompanied by a vast number of officials who went before them with swords and clamour. Led through narrow streets and places lacking light, they found at each entrance frequent cohorts of armed Ethiopians, eagerly competing to render the sultan the duty of salutation.

Passing the first and second guards and being admitted into certain broad and more spacious places, accessible only to the sun and exposed to the open sky, they found walks supported by marble columns, covered with gilded ceilings and projecting ornamentation, and paved with varied flooring, so that in their entire circuit they displayed royal dignity. Such elegance of material and workmanship was present that they held even unwilling passers-by’s eyes, and the extraordinary novelty of the works, inviting a desire to look, did not permit the gaze of spectators to be satisfied. [Col. 0764A] There were marble pools overflowing with exceptionally clear waters; there were diverse chirpings of many kinds of birds, unknown to our world, of unfamiliar forms and exotic colours, prodigious in appearance to us, each supplied with food according to its kind and with fare appropriate to its variety.

Admitted thence farther inward, with chief eunuchs going before, they again found buildings as much more elegant than those before as the earlier ones had seemed superior to ordinary and familiar structures. Here was an astonishing variety of four-footed animals, such as the playful hand of painters commonly depicts, such as poetic licence commonly invents, or the mind of a dreamer imagines in nocturnal visions; such as the regions of the East and South [Col. 0764B] commonly supply, but the West has never been accustomed to see and only more rarely to hear of. It seemed beyond doubt that from these places our Solinus drew the material of his *Polyhistor*.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The agreements are fulfilled; in confirmation of them the caliph gives his hand to Hugh of Caesarea.

After many winding passages and various turnings, which might detain even busy men by their spectacle, they came to the royal palace itself. There larger masses of armed men and a more numerous escort of guards, by their dress and multitude, proclaimed the incomparable glory of their lord; the appearance of the places themselves likewise displayed his opulence and surpassing riches. [Col. 0764C]

When they had entered and been admitted into the inner part of the palace, the sultan, according to custom, rendered the accustomed reverence to his lord. Prostrating himself on the ground once and then a second time, he began humbly to offer a worship as though owed to no one else, a kind of adoration. A third time he prostrated himself on the ground and laid down the sword that hung from his neck. Then, suddenly, curtains hanging in the middle, woven with varied pearls and gold and shading the throne, were drawn back with marvellous speed. His face revealed, the caliph appeared seated on a golden throne, in attire more than royal, with only a few eunuchs of his household and intimate attendants about him.

Then the sultan approached with every reverence, humbly pressing a kiss upon the seated man’s feet. In brief words he explained the reason for the envoys’ coming and the terms of the agreements, the kingdom’s most urgent need, the most savage enemies standing in its very midst, what was demanded from the caliph, and what was offered to him by the lord king. [Col. 0764D] The caliph replied with great kindness and the serene cheerfulness of a tranquil countenance that he was prepared, in accordance with the agreements entered into and accepted by both sides, to fulfil everything generously for his beloved lord king.

When our men asked him to ratify this with his own hand, as the lord king had done, those standing more familiarly near him—the private counsellors and chamberlains, in whose hands lay authority in royal counsels—at first seemed to regard the matter as utterly abhorrent and unheard of in any age. At last, however, after much deliberation and the sultan’s earnest insistence, [Col. 0765A] he extended his hand, very unwillingly, but veiled. Hugh of Caesarea then said to him, while the Egyptians greatly marvelled and were astonished that he spoke so freely to their supreme prince: “Lord, faith has no corners. In the faith by which princes customarily bind themselves, everything ought to be bare and open, and all matters inserted into any agreements under a pledge of faith ought fittingly to be bound and released with sincerity. Therefore, either you will give your hand uncovered, or we shall be compelled to suppose that on your part there is something feigned and less pure.”

At last, extremely unwilling and as though his majesty were being diminished, though smiling—which the Egyptians took very ill—the caliph offered his bare right hand into Lord Hugh’s hand. Following Hugh, who stated the form of the agreements, in almost the same syllables, he declared that he would observe the terms agreed upon in good faith, without fraud or evil intent. [Col. 0765B] As Lord Hugh related to us, the caliph was a young man with the first down of puberty, dark-complexioned, tall in body, handsome in face, very generous, and possessed of innumerable wives. His name was Elhadech, son of Elfeis. Having dismissed them, he sent the envoys gifts, a mark of royal generosity, which by their quantity and quality commended so great a prince, so that they might depart joyfully from the presence of so great a ruler and return happier to their own people.

## CHAPTER XIX. Why the Egyptian ruler is called Mulene.

Since we have spoken of his magnificence according to what we heard from those who saw and inspected it with eyewitness certainty, [Col. 0765C] let us also set forth, insofar as it has been granted us to know, the title of his dignity and its origin and development, from reading ancient histories as well as from the truthful account of many persons. It will not be without benefit to the history to make the reader better informed in this respect.

The Egyptian ruler is called by his people by two names. He is called *calipha*, which means “successor” or “heir,” because by hereditary right he holds the office and succession of their highest prophet. He is also called *Mulene*, which means “our Lord.” The reason for the latter name seems to have originated when our Joseph, in Pharaoh’s time, bought the whole land of Egypt, as the Egyptians sold their possessions because of the pressure of famine; and he subjected them to Pharaoh, together with all their peoples, from the farthest boundaries of Egypt to its uttermost limits, saying to the cultivators of the fields: “You shall give a fifth part to the king; I permit you to retain the other four for seed and for food for your households and children.” [Col. 0765D]

Thus he bought their possessions first and then their persons. For this reason the Egyptians are held to their lord by a tighter bond and are more obligated to him than inhabitants of other regions are to their rulers, since he bought both them and their possessions for a price; they are therefore bound to him in servile attachment and the lowest condition. Thus, through the remarkable diligence of their excellent administrator, in the times of the Pharaohs, then of the Ptolemies, and afterwards of the Romans, [Col. 0766A] who reduced Egypt to a province after the manner of other kingdoms, this custom prevailed: the Egyptians are servants and have been accustomed to address their ruler with that reverence.

Moreover, it is also a remnant of ancient custom that the same ruler, continually at leisure and devoted to pleasures, ignorant of disturbances and free from care, has a steward who administers all the affairs of the kingdom as another Joseph, possessing the power of the sword and exercising every right in his lord’s place. This man is called the sultan; Shawar held this office, and hence our so frequent mention of him.

## CHAPTER XX. Why he is also called caliph, and how he is an adversary of the caliph of Baghdad.

The reason for the former name is as follows. Mehemet, their prophet—or rather, destroyer—who first drew the Eastern peoples into this superstition, had immediately after him as successor one of his associates, named Bebecre. After him Homar, son of Chata, succeeded to the kingdom; after him Vhemen; after him Hali, son of Bithaleb. All these were called caliphs, as were all who succeeded them thereafter, because they succeeded their chief master and were his heirs. [Col. 0766B]

This fifth man from Mehemet, Hali, was more vigorous in arms than those before him and more practised in military affairs than the men of his age; he was also Mehemet’s cousin. He began to resent greatly that he should be called Mehemet’s successor, rather than be regarded himself as an eminent prophet and far greater than Mehemet. Nor did it suffice him merely to think this of himself, or for others to think it, unless he publicly proclaimed it. [Col. 0766C] He also added and spread among the populace the blasphemous assertion that Gabriel, the angel who gave the law, had been sent to him by God, but, deceived by error, had delivered it to Mehemet, for which he had been severely punished by the Lord.

Although these opinions seemed absurd to some of them and greatly at variance with their traditions, he nevertheless found people who believed him. Thus a schism arose among that people which has not ceased down to the present day: some say that Mehemet is greater and the most eminent of all prophets, and these in their language are called *Sumni*; others say that Hali alone is the prophet of the Lord, [Col. 0766D] and these are called *Ssia*. The aforesaid Hali was killed, and the opposing party gained power; the followers of Mehemet held the monarchy in the East and oppressed men of the contrary opinion because they possessed authority.

In the 286th year from the reign of the aforesaid seducer, a nobleman arose named Abdalla, son of Mehemet, son of Japhar, son of Mehemet, son of Hali, son of Hussen, son of the greater Hali of whom we spoke above. Leaving the eastern city of Selemia, he crossed into Africa and, having seized the kingdoms of all those regions, called himself *Mehedt*, meaning “the leveller,” as though he directed all things toward tranquillity and made the people’s ways smoother, without obstruction. He built a very great city named after himself, Mehedia, which he wished to be the capital and preeminent metropolis of his kingdoms. [Col. 0767A] Having equipped a fleet, he captured Sicily and ravaged certain parts of Italy.

He was the first of all after his ancestor Hali to dare to call and name himself caliph—not as successor, he said, of Mehemet, whom he execrated, but of the great and eminent prophet Hali, from whose line he descended, as stated above. He likewise dared publicly to hurl curses at Mehemet and his followers and to teach another rite and another manner of prayer. His great-grandson Ebuthemin, surnamed Elmehedinalla, subdued Egypt through Johar, commander of his army, and built Cairo, whose name means “conquering,” because it was to be the residence of their chief lord and supreme prince, conqueror of all things. Leaving Caroea in the African province, where four of his predecessors had lived, he descended into Egypt and established the aforesaid place as the throne of his kingdom. [Col. 0767B]

From that day until the present, the Eastern caliph, who for so many years had been monarch, has not lacked a rival ruling in Egypt, contending with him for equality and indeed setting himself above him. Whoever wishes to know these matters more fully should read the history which, at the request and urging of Lord Amalric of illustrious memory, who supplied Arabic exemplars, we wrote with much diligence concerning Eastern princes and their deeds from the times of the aforesaid deceiver Mehemet—a period of 577 years—down to the present day, the year 1182 from the Incarnation of the Lord. [Col. 0767C]

## CHAPTER XXI. The king builds a bridge across the Nile. Shirkuh descends into the Island; the king pursues him.

The agreements, as stated above, having been renewed and brought into harmony by both sides, they unanimously applied themselves to the undertaking already conceived, ready to pursue the enemy and expel him from the whole kingdom. Meanwhile night came on and provided occasion for rest; in the morning they found some change in circumstances. For Shirkuh had come during that night and pitched camp on the opposite bank of the same river, directly across from our army.

Ships and palm-tree beams, such as that land is accustomed to supply, having been gathered, the lord king ordered a bridge to be constructed. The ships were joined two by two and, with anchors fixed, were made stable. Beams were arranged above them, earth was laid upon the beams, and finally wooden towers with engines mounted upon them were erected as armament. Thus the work was extended over several days to the middle of the river; fear of the enemy prevented the completion of the remainder and advance to the farther bank. [Col. 0767D] For a month and more the entire outcome of the war remained in suspense: our men could not cross the river, and the enemy dared not range farther afield, lest our men attack from behind.

While these events occurred near Cairo, Shirkuh sent a part of his men to occupy, if possible, the nearby island, abundantly supplied with every resource, and to forestall our men, who might at some time descend there; and this was done. But when the lord king learned that the enemy had gone down into the island, he sent there Lord Milo of Plancy and Chemel, the sultan’s son, with part of the army. At last reaching the island, they found the Turks raging with extreme cruelty against its inhabitants. They met them; battle was joined, and both sides fought bravely. At length, with the Lord’s help, our men prevailed and compelled them to hurl themselves headlong into the nearby river, where those who escaped the swords were drowned in the violent waters. Thus five hundred of their horsemen perished that day by various deaths. [Col. 0768A] When this was reported to Shirkuh, deeply dismayed, he began to lose further confidence in his enterprise. [Col. 0768B]

While matters stood thus, certain princes of our kingdom—Humphrey of Toron, the royal constable, and likewise Philip of Nablus—who had not gone out with the lord king because they had remained at home for private reasons, followed the army with great speed and joined our camp. Our companies received their arrival with great joy and applause, for they were brave men, vigorous in arms, and highly practised in military affairs from their earliest years.

Having taken counsel, they deliberated what had to be done. At last, by common vote, they resolved to take the entire fleet by night, in the silence of the dead of night and unknown to the enemy, to the island lying downstream, scarcely eight miles from the place where the camp stood; and to ferry the whole army across there, about the first watch of the night. Their purpose was to cross the river without the enemy’s knowledge, fall by night upon the unsuspecting foe, and inflict whatever damage they could. The plan was therefore put into execution. Unknown to the adversaries, the fleet went down to the designated place. [Col. 0768C] The army followed in complete silence, was suddenly conveyed in the ships, and occupied the island. But while they attempted in the same manner, as arranged, to gain the other side of the river, a sudden storm of winds arose and prevented completion of the operation. They were consequently compelled to encamp on that part of the island facing the farther bank.

They nevertheless left some of our men to complete and defend the bridge that had been begun, placing over them Lord Hugh of Ibelin, a magnificent and powerful man who, as stated above, had married the widow of the lord king.

[Col. 0768D]

## CHAPTER XXII. The island is described, and the mouths by which the Nile enters the sea are enumerated. Our men, having driven out the enemy, occupy the island; Shirkuh flees into the desert.

The island of which we are speaking is called by them Maheleth. It is exceedingly rich in every good and delightsome in the fertility of its soil. It is formed by the division of the streams of the Nile; for there the river divides, not taking back together the portions that it separates until the sea. Yet, without coming together again, they enter the sea by four mouths. [Col. 0769A]

The first branch, facing our Syria, enters the sea between two most ancient maritime cities, Tafnim and Pharamiam. It flows nearer to the buildings of the latter and washes the place as it passes; from the former it is somewhat distant, about three or four miles. The second joins the straits at Damietta, an ancient and noble city; the third at Sturion; the fourth at Ressith, a place bordering Alexandria and scarcely four miles or thereabouts from it, where its waters are received by the sea’s waves.

Although we have investigated this matter diligently, no other mouths of this river have come to our notice. We therefore greatly wonder that the ancients called the Nile “seven-streamed,” as though it entered the sea by seven mouths. No solution occurs to us except that either the passage of the remotest ages altered the appearance of the places and the river changed its channel, as frequently happens with other rivers; or that men of former times did not ascertain the truth of the matter; or perhaps that when the river rises and becomes fuller in its customary flood, it finds channels other than these four through which its waters run during the time of its swelling, later returning within its bed and ceasing to enter the sea by them. If any such channels exist, we have not counted them among the mouths, because they do not carry permanent waters but flow only at fixed seasons, like torrents. [Col. 0769B]

The island having thus been occupied, only the smaller branch of the river remained. As day was just breaking, the enemy, awakened from sleep and seeing that our men had departed with the fleet, rushed to arms, fearing a sudden attack by us. Then they pursued quickly along the river, drawing out their columns, and saw that our men had occupied the island and, having sent in the fleet, were claiming as their own [Col. 0769C] the remaining portion of the river that had to be crossed. They therefore pitched camp opposite, though somewhat far from the edge of the channel, so that they had no entirely free access to the water; consequently, when leading their horses down to drink, they went farther downstream.

The following day it had been resolved at all costs to try their fortune and open a way by the sword. But during that night, without our knowledge, the enemy withdrew. When morning came and our men saw that they had gone, they quickly crossed the river and hastened to pursue them. Here, in order to hasten and enable the cavalry to advance more expeditiously, the lord king set out with cavalry alone, leaving behind the infantry supports. [Col. 0769D] He nevertheless left Lord Hugh of Ibelin and Chemel, the sultan’s son, with a large force of both our men and Egyptians, to protect Cairo and the bridge completed by our men from sudden enemy attacks.

Here the towers and all the fortifications of that noble city were handed over to our men, and the caliph’s palace, hitherto unknown to us, was made accessible to them, so that the ruler himself and all his household placed every hope of safety in our men alone. Then those “holy of holies,” hidden for ages, were disclosed to our men; secrets once astonishing and familiar to few were laid open.

The lord king also sent Gerard of Pugi and another son of the sultan, named Mahadam, again to the farther riverbank with forces from both peoples, so that, should the enemy attempt to cross the river, they might oppose their efforts. [Col. 0770A] Having therefore left behind, as stated, the greater part of the baggage, the lord king pursued the enemy upstream; for the very shape of the country provided the pursuers with a sure indication of the enemy’s route.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The region of Egypt is described, and its character is explained.

For the whole Egyptian territory, from its earliest beginnings—when it is said to be joined to the land of the Ethiopians—lies between two sandy deserts condemned to perpetual barrenness; nor does it ever experience or yield fruitful produce of any kind, except insofar as it is made fertile at fixed seasons by the bounty of the overflowing Nile. The river, however, renders the land fit for crops by its irrigation only to the extent that the nature of the adjacent places allows. For where it finds a flatter surface around it, spreading out more freely, it makes a wider extent of land more suitable for cultivation; and, becoming more widely diffused, it extends a more abundant fertility to the soil.

Below Cairo, therefore, toward the sea, finding the ground altogether flatter, it has free scope for its course; hence it produces fertility more freely and extensively, gives the kingdom its greatest increase, and enlarges its boundaries. For from the town called Facus, which faces Syria, as far as Alexandria, the furthest city of that kingdom, which touches arid Libya, the convenience of cultivated and fertile land extends for more than one hundred miles. Above Cairo, however, as far as Chus is reached—[Col. 0770C] the last city of the Egyptian diocese, said to border upon the kingdom of Ethiopia—the land is so constricted by the obstruction of sandy hills that the river, spreading out on either side, or on one side only, according to the measure of its overflow, rarely extends or contracts the lateral boundaries of the kingdom to seven or eight miles, and more commonly to four or five. For those places which the river does not irrigate are assigned to the heat of the sun and to the perpetual barrenness of which we have spoken.

The upper region is called Seith in their language. We have so far been able to find no other explanation of this name except that in ancient times there is recorded to have been in Upper Egypt a very ancient city called Sais. Plato, in our *Timaeus*, mentions it under the person of Critias, his disciple, introducing Solon, a man of the highest authority. We have judged that his words ought to be set down for greater clarity, lest anything seem lacking in authority:

“There is,” he says, “a region of Egypt called Delta, from whose summit the streams of the Nile divide. Near it was a great city named Sais, governed by an ancient custom which is called the law of Satyra. From this city Amasis was ruler,” etc.

There is, nevertheless, another district belonging to the same Egypt, one day’s journey from Cairo through uninhabitable land. Visited by the benefit of that same river through certain channels, it has a very rich and fertile soil, enjoying great abundance of fields and vineyards. The Egyptians call it Phium in their language. According to ancient tradition, Joseph—the most prudent administrator of Egypt and the best provider of useful things—made it so. Previously its soil had lain useless from the beginning of the world, wholly unacquainted with the plough, entirely without cultivation or care, like the other parts of that desert. Considering the situation of the place, because it appeared lower than the neighboring surrounding lands, and because, if certain embankments situated between the inhabited district and that part of the desert were broken through, it could easily receive the benefit of the river, he set up embankments, levelled the intervening surface, and, having prepared watercourses, introduced the stagnant Nile. Thus he made familiar to the soil a fertility unknown to it for ages.

But, not retaining its ancient name, we suppose that it was called the Thebaid in former times; whence the legion of the holy Thebans is said to have come—the legion which, under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, was crowned with martyrdom at Agaunum—and whose primicerius is recorded to have been the great martyr Maurice. Another argument is added: the finest opium found anywhere, which physicians call Thebaic, grows there.

For the land of Goshen, which is recorded to have been given to Joseph’s brothers, lies in that part of Egypt which faces Syria, as may be discovered from reading the Book of Genesis, and any attentive reader will easily find this. But this region has nearer to it the opposite part of Egypt and the farther bank of the river, which faces Libya. It is no small region; indeed, it is said to contain within its boundaries three hundred and sixty-six cities and suburbs alike.

By this condition of the place, therefore, as we have said, because the kingdom was so narrow that they could turn neither right nor left, and because the lord king and the sultan had also learned of the enemy’s route through frequent reports from scouts, they pursued them continuously for three days. At last, on the fourth day—namely, Saturday before the Sunday on which the Church of God sings “Rejoice, Jerusalem”—they were informed that the enemy were near.

## CHAPTER XXIV. A battle is joined in the desert between the king and Shirkuh, with the greatest peril to both sides.

Having therefore taken counsel as briefly as was necessary—for pressing necessity did not permit more leisurely deliberation—they declared that prudent counsel and provident courage were needed; and, in accordance with the desire of all, battle was resolved upon and a clash of swords was acclaimed.

But the distribution of those equipped for battle was very unequal. Shirkuh had twelve thousand Turks, of whom nine thousand were protected by coats of mail and helmets, while the remaining three thousand used only bows and arrows; besides these, he had ten or eleven thousand Arabs, using lances according to their custom. Our knights, on the other hand, scarcely numbered 374, apart from the base and effeminate Egyptians, who were more a hindrance and burden than a help. We also had light-armed horsemen called Turcopoles, though we do not know their number. We have heard from many reports that on that day, in so great a conflict, they were for the most part utterly useless.

[Col. 0772A] Both our men, knowing of the enemy’s proximity, and the enemy themselves, knowing of our arrival, drew up their battle lines, arranged their squadrons, and brought forth their weapons, as the situation appeared to require. Those more experienced in the former practice of warfare encouraged the others, instructed the inexperienced, inflamed their spirits with exhortatory speeches, promised victory, the reward of victory, and immortal praise.

The place where the engagement was to occur lay on the border of cultivated land and desert. It was uneven, broken by sandy hills and intervening valleys, so that neither those approaching could be seen from afar nor those departing viewed to any great distance. The place was called Beben, meaning “the Gates,” because passage is blocked between opposing hills. Lamonia, from which some customarily name the battle of this day, was ten miles distant from that place.

The enemy, however, not sluggish in their vigilance, had nevertheless drawn up their lines and occupied the hills on the right and left. Our men found it difficult to approach these with a charge, both because of the ascent and because of the softness of the sand. They placed in the center the troop commanded by Shirkuh, with the others stationed on either side. And now matters had reached the point where they had to fight at close quarters. Our men of the king’s battle line advanced and bravely overthrew as one the troop commanded by Shirkuh; they cut down with swords those who had been thrown down, and pursued Shirkuh himself as he fled.

But Hugh of Caesarea, charging the line commanded by Saladin, Shirkuh’s nephew, was abandoned by his own men, succumbed, and was captured; many were captured with him, and more were killed. There fell the noble and valiant soldier Eustace Caolet, of the region of Pontus. Emboldened by this success, the other troops joined one another, surrounded on every side the line assigned to guard the baggage and burdens, attacked it, and immediately overthrew it once it was broken. There, it is said, died the nobleman Hugh of Creona, a Sicilian by birth, a worthy and honorable young man. When that line was scattered and many had died, those able to escape the swords sought safety in flight. The enemy freely seized the baggage and burdens and carried off what they had taken.

Meanwhile, as the bodies of troops were broken up here and there and scattered through the said little valleys, battle was waged with varying fortunes, witnessed only by those who actually fought; for the others were not permitted to see it. The contest was uncertain: now one side, now the other gained the upper hand, unaware of what was happening elsewhere. Each side reckoned itself victorious in one place and defeated in another.

Our venerable brother, Lord Ralph, bishop of Bethlehem and chancellor of the lord king—whom we later succeeded in the same office—was severely wounded and lost all his baggage in the same tumult. The battle remained uncertain for a long time and postponed a definite judgment concerning the victors, until the day, now declining, urged the scattered men to return to their standards. Then at last, fearing the onset of night, those who were free began to hasten toward their own side; emerging from various quarters and eagerly seeking the king, they gathered themselves together again.

[Col. 0773A] The lord king, however, had fought victoriously and successfully at the place where he had engaged. Others had tested Mars in different places with diverse fortune, enjoying prosperity here and adversity there; therefore neither side was crowned with a certain victory. Returning with very few men, he occupied a somewhat elevated hill and, raising his banner so that the scattered might gather to him again, waited for his companions.

When some of these had been recalled, they saw before them on the twin hills the enemy who had broken the baggage-guarding line and had partly slain and partly captured it. There was no other route open to our men for returning except to pass between the middle of the aforesaid hills. Thus, intending to return and drawn up in battle formation, they proceeded at a slow pace through the enemy’s midst, whom they saw on their right and left. Against men advancing with such constancy, the enemy dared devise no hostile action. Our men joined their ranks, placed the stronger and best-armed men all around, came to a branch of the river, and crossed it safely at a ford.

That entire night our men withdrew and returned by the road by which they had first come. When they reached Lamonia, Gerard of Pugi met them. With fifty knights, one hundred Turcopoles, and Mahadan, the sultan’s son, he had held the opposite bank of the river, in order to prevent the enemy from crossing it if they should attempt to do so. He arrived most opportunely, for the lord king greatly feared that the enemy might attack them when found separated, either beyond or on this side of the river.

He was also no less anxious about the foot-soldiers whom he had left behind, as stated above, fearing that they might suddenly and incautiously encounter the enemy. Therefore he waited for them for three days at the aforesaid town. Their leader was the noble and prudent Joscelin of Samosata. On the fourth day, when our men had scarcely been received little by little and the body of infantry had again been joined to him, they continued their march and reached Cairo, where they pitched camp before Babylon beside the bridge. When the number of soldiers was counted, they found that one hundred of their own were missing; of the enemy, they asserted that fifteen hundred had fallen.

## CHAPTER XXV. Shirkuh withdraws into Alexandria. The king hastens there and besieges the city.

[Col. 0773D]

Shirkuh, however, having gathered into one body those of his men who remained, made for Alexandria through the desert without our men knowing it; and the Alexandrians immediately handed the city over to him. As soon as the king heard the report, he summoned the princes, the sultan and his sons, and the Egyptian nobles, and diligently sought their advice on what ought to be done.

After many discussions, as commonly happens in doubtful matters, it was decided—because Alexandria has no abundance of provisions or grain from its own resources, except what is brought by ship from the upper parts of Egypt—that a fleet should be stationed on the river to keep watch, so that no supplies of any kind might be brought from there to the Alexandrians. This having been done, the king himself descended with the whole army into those parts and pitched camp between the place called Toroge and Demenehut, which is eight miles from Alexandria. From there, sending out scouts, he penetrated and searched the nearby and even the distant places through the desert, lest anyone should either bring help to the besieged or, coming from there, solicit outsiders to assist them.

The fleet likewise either completely prevented anyone wishing to cross from making the passage, or allowed him to land only after he had been carefully questioned and identified. When a month had passed and that city had received no food whatever from elsewhere during that period, the people began to complain that bread had failed in their baskets and that they had no sustenance. Shirkuh, understanding this and fearing that he and his men might, along with the others, be forced to waste away from hunger, left his nephew Saladin in the city with about a thousand knights and himself escaped by night marches through the desert, though near our expedition, into Upper Egypt, from which he had descended shortly before.

When this became known to the king, he vigorously pursued him as far as Babylon. There, while the entire army was already ready to march and had resolved, with the baggage packed, to follow him, the noble and powerful Egyptian Benecarselle suddenly came to the king. He told him that Alexandria was suffering extreme want. He said that he had very powerful kinsmen in the city, governors of the community, who could easily draw the people, afflicted by hunger, in whatever direction they wished, and place the city, together with all the Turks left in it, in the lord king’s power. Moved by this statement, the king asked the princes what they thought. At length, in accordance with the unanimous wishes of all, and with the sultan also approving, they returned to Alexandria and surrounded it with a double army.

## CHAPTER XXVI. A description of the site of Alexandria.

Alexandria is the furthest of all the cities of the entire Egyptian diocese, in the part facing Libya and stretching westward. It lies on the boundary between cultivated soil and arid desert, so that immediately outside the city walls, toward sunset, there extends a vast wilderness wholly untouched by the benefit of cultivation and care.

According to ancient histories, it is said to have been founded by Alexander of Macedon, son of Philip, whose name it also bears. As Julius Solinus says, it was founded in the twelfth hundredth Olympiad, under the consulship of Lucius Papirius, son of Lucius, and Gaius Petilius, son of Gaius; Dinocrates the architect laid it out and holds second place after its founder among its memorable figures.

It is situated not far from an outlet of the Nile, which some call the Heracleotic and others the Canopic. Today, the place from which the mouth takes its name, adjoining the city, is called Ressith, the ancient names having disappeared. It lies five or six miles from the riverbed; yet, through certain channels, part of the river flows into the city at the time of its customary rise. The inhabitants carefully preserve this influx of water throughout the year in very large cisterns specifically assigned for this purpose. They also direct from it, through hidden conduits, the necessary quantity for maintaining the orchards outside the city.

[Col. 0775A] In respect of commerce, it is most advantageously situated. It has two harbors, divided by a very narrow strip of land lying between them. At the head of this intervening space stands a tower of marvelous height called the Pharos, which Julius Caesar is said to have built for necessary purposes and to which he led a colony.

From Upper Egypt, by the waters of the Nile, it receives an abundance of every kind of food and a wealth of almost all things. And from lands beyond the sea, whatever Egypt does not possess is supplied by ship in every abundance; thus it is said to surpass every maritime city in its supply of all conveniences. Moreover, from both Indies, from Saba and Arabia, likewise from both Ethiopias, and also from Persia and the surrounding provinces, everything in spices, pearls, Oriental treasures, and foreign merchandise required by our world is brought by the Red Sea—by which those peoples have access to us—into Upper Egypt, to the city called Aideb, situated on the shore of that same sea. All of it is conveyed to the river and descends from there to Alexandria.

Thus peoples of East and West converge there, and the same city is a public market for both worlds. It is indeed renowned both for ancient titles and modern ones; it was also made illustrious by the preaching and teaching of blessed Mark, the spiritual son of the Prince of the Apostles, divinely sent to that church; and adorned by the leadership and tombs of the holy Fathers Athanasius and Cyril. Holding second place among the patriarchates, it is the revered metropolis of Egypt, Libya, Pentapolis, and many provinces.

The whole fleet was brought there, and, besieging the gates and every approach, allowed no one permission to enter.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The king continues the siege and harasses the Alexandrian citizens most severely.

Meanwhile those who had remained in Syria, hearing that the lord king had besieged Alexandria and that they could reach it within a few days by continuous sailing, eagerly set out. Taking up their arms, they loaded onto ships the provisions necessary for life and set out joyfully, urging one another on.

Among them was Lord Frederick, archbishop of Tyre, our predecessor. Moved by zeal for the others and by special affection toward the lord king, he sailed down to Egypt with a quite respectable retinue. But because of the waters of the Nile, he began to suffer most dangerously from dysentery; and before Alexandria was handed over to the lord king, he was compelled, as his illness worsened, to return home.

Then, using ship masts of immense size and summoning craftsmen and woodcutters, they constructed a tower of marvelous height from which the whole city could be overlooked. Engines, commonly called stone-throwers, from which heavy, large millstones were launched against the walls, were placed in suitable positions and brought intolerable terror upon the citizens at almost every hour.

Around that same city there were orchards planted with fruit-bearing trees, delightful in their pleasantness and full of fertility, like woods and leafy groves, and filled with healing herbs. By their appearance they rightly invited passers-by to enter, and once they had entered, urged them to rest. Into these our army entered in large part, first for the sake of collecting timber for the construction of siege engines, then from mere desire to inflict harm and cause damage. They felled aromatic trees and trees suited for many uses with as much eagerness as they had scarcely been cultivated with labor from the beginning. Thus it suddenly came about that, once the ground was levelled, no trace whatever of its former condition remained. This was the injury of which the city and its damaged inhabitants complained most bitterly after they had obtained the terms of peace.

Our men therefore pressed on, striving to discover every device by which they could injure the besieged, attempting every means of inflicting harm and equipping themselves, by all possible methods, for their injury. Constant assaults also denied rest to the exhausted inhabitants. The citizens were accustomed to trade and inexperienced in military affairs; they had no practice in fighting and could therefore endure the unfamiliar labor only with greater difficulty. The Turks who had remained there, both because they were few and because they did not trust much in the citizens’ changeable and unstable temper, were infrequent in engagements and slack in encounters, and did not greatly encourage the others.

What more need be said? Daily conflicts, continual slaughter of their people, perpetual watchfulness, nighttime fears, and, above all, lack of food had worn down the populace and broken their spirit. They were now more inclined to abandon the city and, forgetful of liberty, submit themselves to any peoples whatever than to be consumed in the bitterness of hunger in their own homes with their little children and wives.

A murmur thus spread among the people; the talk was now openly circulating among more and more persons: the pestilent guests who had inflicted so great an affliction upon the citizens ought to be expelled from the city; some means or other must be sought by which the city, freed from its pressing troubles and released from siege, might be restored to its former advantages and customary liberty.

Saladin perceived this and, by secret and swift messengers, informed his uncle in detail of the city’s wretched state, the purpose of the people who were deserting him, and the extreme shortage of food. He begged him by every means to find an immediate remedy for these desperate circumstances and to provide for those who were perishing.

Meanwhile he addressed the people together with the Fathers. He urged them to fight to the death for their wives and children; he exhorted them to emulate their law and ancestral traditions; salvation, he said, stood at their gates; and his uncle Shirkuh was ranging through Egypt for their liberation and to remove the enemy, and would shortly be present with countless forces.

But the lord king, learning that there was dissension among the citizens, ordered the city to be pressed without ceasing; and the more severely he knew them to be afflicted, the more sharply he commanded the attack to continue. The sultan also, ready and indefatigable in every respect, diligently visited all the princes with full concern. With a lavish hand he provided funds for constructing engines and generous expenditures for every use of war; he gave appropriate wages to craftsmen; he gave gifts to the poor and needy, especially to the wounded, so that they might look after themselves; and he distributed something also among warriors and those whom he knew to be brave in battle.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Hearing of these things, Shirkuh speaks with Hugh of Caesarea concerning peace.

While these things were occurring at Alexandria, Shirkuh ranged through Upper Egypt. Reaching Chus, he attempted to capture the city; and, seeing that he was making no progress and that undertakings of this kind would require a longer time, while his nephew’s need pressed him to other business, he took money from those cities, hastened his return, and brought back to Lower Egypt the army which he had led.

When, on his return, he reached Babylon and saw that the king had left Hugh of Ibelin as guardian of Cairo and the bridge, and that everything had turned out very differently from what he had expected, he addressed Hugh of Caesarea, whom he held captive, in familiar conversation. Being eloquent and urbane in speech, he began to address him in carefully composed words:

“You are a great prince, noble and most illustrious among your people; and among your princes there is no one to whom, if free choice were granted me, I would more wish to communicate this secret of mine and make a participant in this conversation. Fortune has freely offered, and the event of war has granted, what otherwise would have had to be sought with many efforts: namely, that I should have the benefit of your experience for my present need.

“I confess that, desirous of glory, as commonly happens to mortals, and trusting in the wealth of this kingdom and also in the weakness of its native inhabitants, I once conceived the hope that this kingdom might someday be delivered into my hands. Therefore, with infinite expense and labor—fruitless, as I now see—and with a great cavalry force of nobles, all drawn by the same purpose, I descended into Egypt through so many dangers, expecting a different outcome from events than has occurred. For, as I see, I entered under adverse fortune; would that I might at least be permitted to return under favorable fortune!

“You are noble, as I have said, dear to the king, powerful in speech and action. Be a mediator of peace between us. Let the matter prosper in your hand. Tell the lord king: ‘We are wasting time, and the days pass without profit; much remains to be done at home, and the king’s presence is especially necessary to his own kingdom. He now expends his efforts elsewhere; for after he has driven us away, he will leave the wealth of this kingdom to its wretched citizens, scarcely worthy of life.

“‘Let him recover his men whom I hold in chains; let him also, after raising the siege, restore those whom he holds in chains and those whom he confines in the city of Alexandria. And I, once I have received from him a guarantee that we shall encounter no difficulty from his people on the journey, am prepared to depart.’”

## CHAPTER XXIX. Hugh completes the terms of the treaty with the king and the princes.

[Col. 0778A]

On hearing this proposal, Lord Hugh, being a prudent and discerning man, carefully weighed the words offered to him. Although he did not doubt that the proposed peace and treaty were advantageous to our side, nevertheless, lest he seem to be pursuing his own liberty more eagerly than the public good through this negotiation, he judged it more honorable that the initial overtures should be made through another. He later explained this intention of his to us privately.

A certain familiar servant of the king, Arnulf of Turuassel, who was likewise held captive and had been captured with the aforesaid Lord Hugh in the same battle, was sent as bearer of the message. Having received the proposal, he hastened to the king, carefully explained the cause of his embassy, and, when an assembly had been convened in the council of princes, with the sultan and his sons present, presented the formulated proposal and the terms of settlement.

The terms of peace pleased everyone. It seemed sufficient both for honor and for full fidelity to the agreements made between the king and the caliph that the city should pass by surrender into the lord king’s power; that both those enemies enclosed by the siege and those who, following Shirkuh, were scattered through the lands of Egypt should be compelled to leave all Egypt; and that the captives whom they held of our men should be released, while they themselves likewise received back their own men.

The sultan Shawar, with all the Egyptian satraps, approved the agreement and willingly accepted the harmony of the treaty, declaring that he was fully satisfied provided the most dangerous enemy and rival of the kingdom was excluded. Finally Lord Hugh appeared in person; after the terms had been discussed on both sides, he put the finishing hand and an agreed conclusion to the matter.

## CHAPTER XXX. The city is surrendered to the king, and peace is proclaimed to the Alexandrians.

A herald’s proclamation therefore announced to every troop and to all generally an end to fighting; and by public edict it was forbidden that any injury be inflicted upon the Alexandrians. Those worn down by the long siege accordingly came out rejoicing under the peace granted to them. Loathing the hardships they had endured, they loved and sought freer walks in order to relieve their weariness.

When a supply of food was found and freedom of commerce permitted, they strove to restore their bodies ruined by hunger and to revive their spirits, already failing. It was pleasant to see the peaceful groups which shortly before had feared and hated one another, and to enjoy the conversations of those whom they had recently feared as agents of their dangers and authors of death.

Our men likewise entered the long-desired city without delay. Roaming freely through its streets, harbors, and walls, they carefully observed everything, so that after returning home they might someday weave stories for their own people and delight their listeners’ minds with pleasing tales.

A tower of marvelous height called the Pharos rises over this splendid city. By its lighted torches and abundant fire, shining like a star, those unfamiliar with the place direct their nighttime sailing toward it. For Alexandria is approached by a blind sea, a most dangerous entrance, and deceptive shallows. Before sailors enter, instructed by the fires continuously maintained upon it at public expense and with an unfailing supply of fuel, they avoid the threatening shipwrecks and guide themselves into safe courses.

Upon this tower the sign of victory, the lord king’s banner, was raised. What had previously been known to few became manifest to all through the visible sign. At this sight, those who had cautiously hesitated at the first words of treaty to entrust themselves to our men, now more certain of peace, did not fear to join themselves to us and rely upon the sincerity of our pledged faith.

Above all they marveled that so small an army had easily confined within the city walls, and compelled to a shameful surrender at its pleasure, so great a multitude of citizens and so numerous a body of newcomers, all of whom had faithfully labored for the defense of the city. For our knights scarcely numbered five hundred and our infantry four or five thousand, whereas more than fifty thousand of the besieged were able to bear arms.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Having gained the victory and recovered all his own men, the king returns home.

Saladin, having gone out to the lord king, remained in the camp until the king set out on his return journey. A guardian was assigned to him to treat him honorably and keep reckless persons from injuring him.

The sultan, however, entered through the gates of the city in triumph as though a victor, surrounded by troops, with the blare of trumpets, drums, choirs, and every kind of musical instrument, an innumerable host of attendants running before him, and bands of armed men shouting. He shook the citizens with fear: he condemned some, acquitted others, investigated offenses with authority, and allotted to all the rewards of their deserts.
