At length, after imposing upon the citizens a fixed sum of money, he appointed managers of tribute and collectors of taxes and civic duties. When an immense sum of money had been exacted, he entrusted the care of the city to his faithful men and returned gloriously to the camp.

Our men who had arrived by ship, eager to return, took on the necessities for the journey, embarked, entrusted themselves to the winds, and joyfully returned home. The king also burned the engines, packed the baggage, and directed his march toward Babylon. Having joined to himself those whom he had left there, confirmed the sultan in his administration, expelled the enemy, and recovered his captured men, he entered Ascalon on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September [21 August], in the fourth year of his reign and in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1167.

# BOOK TWENTY BEGINS.

[Col. 0779]

## CHAPTER I. Lord Ernisius, archbishop of Caesarea, and Odo of Saint Amand, the king’s butler, return from Constantinople, bringing with them the king’s future wife. The king is crowned in the church of Tyre and marries.

[Col. 0779C]

Meanwhile Lord Ernisius, of good memory, archbishop of Caesarea, and Odo of Saint Amand, then the king’s butler, having carried out as prudently as faithfully the lord king’s embassy for which they had been sent to Lord Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, obtained what they had requested after two years had passed. Returning by ship and bringing the daughter of the Protosebastos of the lord emperor, who was to become the lord king’s wife, they arrived at Tyre.

When he learned this, the lord king hastened to Tyre. Having summoned the prelates of the churches and the princes of the kingdom, he married that same Maria, who had received the anointing and consecration of royalty. He himself, distinguished in royal dress and crowned with the ancestral diadem, took her in marriage by the hand of Lord Amalric, the patriarch of blessed memory, in the church of Tyre, with due magnificence, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September [29 August].

This John Protosebastos, whose daughter the king married, as we have said, was a nephew of the same lord emperor through the emperor’s elder brother. The lord emperor sent with his aforesaid niece illustrious and magnificent men, members of the imperial court—Lord Palaiologos and Manuel Sebastos, his kinsman, together with many others—to hand her over magnificently to the lord king and to ensure that none of the prescribed ceremonies was omitted.

The church of Tyre, where these things occurred, was governed by Lord Frederick, who had been transferred there from the church of Acre. Three days after the king had been crowned in that city and celebrated his marriage, in the presence and at the request of the lord king and many other honorable men, he generously conferred upon us the archdeaconry of that church, from which Lord William had been called to the church of Acre.

## CHAPTER II. A certain Andronicus, a kinsman of the emperor, carries off Theodora, widow of King Baldwin, with him through enemy lands.

[Col. 0780D]

At the same time, a certain Andronicus, a noble and powerful Greek and a relative of the lord emperor of Constantinople, came from Cilicia with a large force. While the lord king was still detained in Egypt, he remained among us until the king’s return, bringing us comfort. But, like the serpent in one’s bosom and the mouse in one’s bag, he repaid his hosts badly, proving true what Maro had said:

> “I fear the Danaans, even when bearing gifts.”

Immediately after his return, the lord king gave him the city of Beirut. When Andronicus invited Lady Theodora—the widow of King Baldwin, who held the city of Acre by way of a marriage-gift donation, the daughter of his nephew, with whom he had long stayed—to come there for the sake of seeing the city, he deceitfully carried her off, as is said. With Nur ad-Din’s support, he took her into enemy territory, first to Damascus and then into Persia.

## CHAPTER III. The churches of Petra and Hebron are established by the appointment of bishops. Stephen, chancellor of the king of Sicily and elect of the church of Palermo, comes down into Syria. Count William of Nevers dies among us.

[Col. 0781B]

In the same year almost nothing worthy of record occurred in the kingdom, except that about the season of Lent two churches in the kingdom were established with bishops appointed: one of them, the Church of Petra, which lies beyond the Jordan in the territory of Moab and is the metropolis of Arabia Secunda, had had no Latin bishop since the Latins entered the Promised Land; the other, that of Hebron, had, it is said, never had one. Yet in the time of the Greeks it had been a priory, as is known also to have been the case with the Church of Bethlehem. But the Church of Bethlehem, because of reverence for the Lord’s Nativity, deserved earlier—immediately after the liberation of the holy and God-beloved city, in the time of King Baldwin I—to enjoy the prerogative of cathedral status [Col. 0781C]. The church of Hebron likewise first deserved to be distinguished with that same dignity at that time, in consideration of the servants of God whose memory is blessed—namely Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Thus Lord Guerric, a regular canon of the Temple of the Lord, was placed over the Church of Petra and became metropolitan of Arabia Secunda; while Lord Rainald, nephew of Lord Fulcher, patriarch of pious memory, was appointed to Hebron.

In the following summer, the noble Lord Stephen, chancellor of the king of Sicily and elected of the Church of Palermo, a young man of good disposition and exceptional appearance, brother of Lord Rotold, Count of Perche [Col. 0781D], was driven from the kingdom by the intrigues and conspiracy against him of the princes of that land—while the boy king was unwilling and his mother unable to resist. With only a few companions he barely escaped their snares and arrived among us by ship. Not long afterward he was seized by a severe illness, died, and was honourably buried at Jerusalem in the chapter-house of the Temple of the Lord.

At the same time Lord William, Count of Nevers, a great prince, noble and powerful, came from the kingdom of the Franks to Jerusalem with an honourable body of troops, intending to serve Christendom against the enemies of our faith at his own expense. But untimely death, begrudging his noble and pious purposes their happy accomplishment, miserably forestalled them. For, suddenly seized by a lingering illness [Col. 0782A], after prolonged bodily suffering, he ended his life in the first bloom of his most gracious youth, amid the sighs and lamentations of all.

## CHAPTER IV. Envoys of the emperor come to the king, requesting certain agreements from the lord king. The archdeacon of Tyre is sent and concludes the proposed agreements with the emperor.

In that same summer Count Alexander of Gravina and one Michael of Otranto, intimates and envoys of the lord emperor of Constantinople, sent to the lord king, arrived at Tyre. They met the lord king privately, in the presence of those whom the king wished to share his counsels; they explained the reasons for their journey and presented imperial letters concerning all these matters [Col. 0782B].

The substance of their embassy was this. The lord emperor had perceived that the kingdom of Egypt, hitherto exceedingly powerful and very wealthy, had fallen into the hands of weak and effeminate men; and that the incapacity, weakness, and inadequacy both of its lord and of its princes had become known to neighbouring peoples. Therefore, since it did not seem that it could long remain in its present condition without its lordship and government having to pass to foreign nations, he conceived that, with the help of the lord king, he could easily bring it under his own jurisdiction. For this purpose he had sent the aforesaid envoys.

There are some who say that, concerning this same enterprise, he had first been solicited by the lord king through messengers and frequent letters [Col. 0782C]—which is more likely—that he should assist him with military forces, a fleet, and funds, receiving, under stipulated conditions, specified portions both of the kingdom and of the spoils. Accordingly, for this reason, when the aforesaid envoys came to the king and the agreements had been confirmed in terms satisfactory to both sides, I was joined to them by royal command, so that I might hasten to carry to the lord emperor, together with their letters, the counsel of the king and of the whole kingdom; and, subject to a specified form, might give binding force to the agreements arranged between them, as would be required of me.

Taking with us the aforesaid *apocrisiarii*—imperial envoys—of the lord emperor, who were awaiting our arrival at Tripoli, as the king had notified them by letter, we set out for the imperial city. At that moment the emperor was occupied in Serbia [Col. 0782D], a mountainous, forested country with difficult approaches, situated between Dalmatia, Hungary, and Illyricum. The Serbs had rebelled, relying on the narrowness of the approaches to their country and the inaccessibility of their land. Ancient traditions hold that this entire people derived its origin from deportees and persons condemned to exile, who had been sent to those regions to cut marble and mine metals; and that from this they also took their name from servitude.

It is an uncultivated people, without discipline, dwelling in mountains and forests and ignorant of agriculture; yet rich in flocks and herds, and abundantly supplied with milk, cheese, butter, meat, honey, and wax. They have magistrates whom they call *suppani*; at times they serve the lord emperor, while at other times, descending from the mountains and forests [Col. 0783A], they lay waste all the surrounding country, being bold and warlike men. On account of these intolerable injuries done to their neighbours, the lord emperor had entered their country with great strength and an innumerable host.

After subduing them and reducing their principal leader to captivity, we met the emperor as he returned, wearied by the many hardships of the journey, in the province of Pelagonia, in a city commonly called Butella, near that ancient city, the birthplace of the most fortunate, invincible, and prudent Augustus, Lord Justinian—namely Justiniana Prima, which is now commonly called Acreda. There, honourably received by the lord emperor and treated kindly with imperial clemency, we carefully explained the purpose of the embassy and journey and the terms of the agreements. He received and gladly embraced all these things, and approved what had been previously arranged [Col. 0783B]. Thus, after mutual oaths had been given in person and his authority interposed, the arrangements previously made through messengers were confirmed.

Having received imperial letters containing in full the terms of the agreements, and having successfully completed the embassy, we were dismissed with the emperor’s customary generosity, and on the Kalends of October [1 October] set out on our return journey.

## CHAPTER V. The king enters Egypt with his forces and, contrary to the terms of the treaty he had made with the Egyptians, makes war upon them.

Meanwhile, immediately after our departure, before we had returned home and before the king could have been informed through our embassy of the emperor’s aid [Col. 0783C], public report spread, as is said, that Shawar, the Egyptian sultan, was sending frequent embassies to Nur al-Din and secretly requesting his assistance, declaring that he wished to withdraw from the agreements he had made with the king and that he had unwillingly entered into some treaty of peace with an enemy people; if he could be assured of Nur al-Din’s help, he would break the agreements and wholly abandon the king.

Moved, it is said, by just indignation, the king summoned the whole kingdom, gathered forces of cavalry and infantry, and hastened down into Egypt. Some say that all the foregoing was fabricated, and that war was brought, contrary to justice and piety, against the innocent Sultan Shawar, who deserved nothing of the kind and was keeping in good faith the agreements and terms of the treaty [Col. 0783D]. They say that this pretext was sought in order that so notable a deed might have some excuse; and that the Lord, the just judge of secrets and consciences, withdrew all favour from our undertakings and denied success to these enterprises, which lacked justice.

The cause and instigator of this evil, they say, was Gilbert, surnamed Assailit, master of the Hospital at Jerusalem, a high-spirited man, lavish in a certain generosity of giving, yet unstable and fickle in mind. He expended all the treasures of that house and, moreover, borrowed money in an unlimited amount. He distributed it all among soldiers, attracting to himself everyone he could find; and thus [Col. 0784A] he burdened the aforesaid house with so great a mass of debt that there was no hope of payment. Later, despairing, he abandoned his office and resigned its administration, leaving the house encumbered with a debt of one hundred thousand gold pieces.

He is said, however, to have incurred so many and such great expenses because, if Egypt were captured and subdued, Belbeis—formerly called Pelusium—together with all its territory, would pass in perpetuity to the right of that house, according to an agreement previously made with the king. But the brothers of the military Order of the Temple withdrew themselves from this undertaking. Either it seemed to them contrary to their conscience, or the master of the rival house appeared to be the author and chief promoter of the enterprise; they refused altogether to provide their forces or to follow the king. For it seemed harsh to them to declare war, contrary to the terms of the agreements and contrary to the law of religion, against a friendly kingdom that trusted in our good faith, though it had done no wrong and was keeping faith [Col. 0784B].

## CHAPTER VI. The city of Belbeis is besieged and captured. The sultan deceives the king with promises of an immense sum of money.

Accordingly, equipped and prepared for battle, having summoned the strength of the kingdom, in the fifth year of his reign and in the month of October the king entered Egypt. Crossing the intervening desert, a journey of about ten days, he reached Pelusium. At once surrounding it with a siege, he took it by force within three days; having captured it, he put it to the sword and immediately let in his men. This occurred on the third day before the Nones of November [3 November].

When the city had been taken and most of its citizens put to the sword [Col. 0784C], neither age nor sex was spared. Those found to have escaped death by any means incurred the loss of liberty—which honourable men fear more than every kind of death—and were subjected to wretched slavery. Among others captured in the same condition were Mahazam, the son of the sultan, and one of his nephews, who governed the city and had charge of the army assembled there.

Once the city had been breached, detachments rushing in everywhere without discrimination penetrated the innermost entrances of the dwellings, opened the private chambers, and dragged out in fetters those who seemed to have escaped death by hiding, shamefully leading them away to execution. Those found in the full strength of age and capable of bearing arms they ran through with swords [Col. 0784D]. The old and children were scarcely spared, and the weaker sex received no more lenient treatment. Their precious possessions became the enemies’ plunder; all beautiful things fell to the lot of those dividing the spoils among themselves.

Terrified by these reports, Shawar did not know what to do. As the narrow exigency of the time and of affairs in so desperate a position allowed, he considered whether he should try to overcome the king with gifts and soften his anger with money, or solicit by prayers and payment the aid of the neighbouring princes of his religion. At length he decided, with prompt provision, to attempt both. He therefore sent an embassy to Nur al-Din, implored assistance, and obtained what he requested. Nur al-Din summoned Shirkuh, of whom we have often made mention, entrusted to him part of his army and no small number of his nobles, together with emirs [Col. 0785A] who would share the burden of command, and, having supplied provisions necessary for the journey and enough camels to carry the loads, sent them into Egypt.

## CHAPTER VII. The king encamps before Cairo, awaiting the money promised by the sultan.

Meanwhile, after destroying Pelusium, the king led all his divisions toward Cairo, but at a very slow pace, accomplishing scarcely a day’s journey in ten days. At last he encamped before the city, prepared siege engines, erected mantlets, and arranged the other things useful for such purposes. What was being constructed outside seemed to promise imminent assaults, to inspire fear in the besieged, and to hold before them a kind of image of death [Col. 0785B].

But those who know the secrets of the affair assert that the cause of this delay was that the sultan, shaken by fear of the approaching army, might have a longer period for deliberation and negotiate money for the withdrawal of the army. For the king’s whole purpose in hastening thither was to squeeze money from the sultan. He preferred to depart after being bought off for a price rather than expose those cities to the plundering of the common soldiers, as had happened at Pelusium, as will be made clearer below.

Meanwhile the sultan, through his own agents and the king’s intimates, tested every approach and explored every avenue of access. At length he weakened the king’s money-hungry mind by promises, offering an immense sum which scarcely the whole kingdom, after resources had been gathered from every quarter, could have paid [Col. 0785C]. He promised, so they say, two million gold pieces, if his son and nephew were restored to him and the expedition withdrew and returned home.

As afterward became clear, he did not devise this with the expectation that the promised sum could ever be paid; rather, he did so lest the king, coming suddenly upon Cairo, should find it unprepared and undefended and take it by a surprise attack. This, those who were present firmly assert, would undoubtedly have occurred if, after Pelusium had been captured, our army had proceeded there by rapid marches while the Egyptians’ spirits were still crushed and stunned by the recent disaster and the unexpected calamity of so great a city. For it seems likely that men soft and effeminate, long devoted to luxury [Col. 0785D], unskilled in warfare, still shaken by the smoke of the neighbouring city’s conflagration and the death of countless of their people, fearing for themselves what they saw had befallen others, would have had neither courage nor strength to resist.

## CHAPTER VIII. Our fleet, sent up the Nile, attempts to join our army; but, accomplishing nothing, returns home.

While these things were taking place around Cairo, our fleet, which the king had ordered to make haste when he set out from our territories, is said to have arrived by sea under favourable winds, entering through that mouth of the river commonly called Carabes. It violently captured the very ancient city named Tapnim, situated above that bank of the river [Col. 0786A], and the city was immediately given over to our men for plunder and spoil.

As our men endeavoured to hasten up the river channel to the king, the Egyptians blocked the channel with their ships and denied passage. Therefore the king sent Humphrey of Toron, his constable, to come there with a selected force and violently occupy the other bank of the river, so that from it passage might be free for them. This would have been carried out quite readily, had not the report of Shirkuh’s arrival meanwhile compelled a change of plan. They were therefore ordered to descend to the sea and hasten their return home. This was done, though they carelessly lost one galley.

## CHAPTER IX. With Cairo besieged, the king awaits the money promised by the sultan. The sultan attempts to withdraw from the agreements and implores Turkish aid.

[Col. 0786B]

Meanwhile the sultan and his men did not cease contriving how to repel the king from themselves. By tricks they accomplished what they felt lacking in strength, and by the commerce of deceit compensated for their deficiency of power. Having promised money, they asked for a truce in order to make payment. They alleged that the sum was very large and could not all be found in one place; more time should be granted for the agreements to be fulfilled. Yet, upon a payment of one hundred thousand immediately, the sultan received back his son and nephew; for the remaining sum he supplied as hostages his two grandsons, still under age.

The king then lifted the siege, withdrew about a mile, and established camp near the Garden of Balsam. There, after eight days of frequent but fruitless embassies from the sultan [Col. 0786C], he finally moved the army to a place called Syriacus. Meanwhile the sultan stirred up the whole kingdom with frequent messengers, gathered weapons from every quarter, summoned help from everywhere, brought in provisions, inspected and strengthened the weak points of the city, and pursued every means of resistance. With exhortatory speeches he urged them to fight for their lives, their liberty, their wives, and their children; he set before their eyes the lamentable fate of the neighbouring city and described the bitterness of captivity, the unbearable yoke of masters, and the most wretched condition of slavery.

## CHAPTER X. Milo of Plancy corrupts the king’s judgment by pernicious counsel. Shirkuh, summoned by the Egyptians, arrives; the king goes out to meet him in the desert, but, not finding him, returns home with his enterprise unaccomplished.

[Col. 0786D]

In the army of the lord king there was a man noble in birth but base in character, fearing neither God nor respecting any human being: namely Milo of Plancy, a shameless, noisy, slanderous, seditious man. Recognising the lord king’s excessive avarice, and wishing rather to humour him than to advise him with wholesome counsel, from the beginning he had advised and persistently, assiduously urged that the king should direct his chief effort toward coming to terms with the caliph and the sultan after fining the kingdom in the amount already mentioned, rather than forcibly breaking into Cairo and Babylon [Col. 0787A].

This was not, as is said, because he despaired that it could be done, but so that, with the soldiers and the others who had set their hands and minds upon plunder deceived, the whole profit of so great a labour might appear to be brought into the royal treasury. For when cities are stormed by force, armies generally derive much more abundant profit from the spoils than when cities are subjected to kings and princes under some bond of treaty and specified conditions advantageous only to their rulers. In the former case, amid so great a confused tumult and devastation, whatever comes to anyone’s hand by any chance is conceded by the law of war to the person who seizes it and increases the victor’s private wealth; in the latter, advantages are managed for kings alone, and whatever is so acquired is claimed by the rights of the treasury.

Although an increase accruing to kings and higher powers appears to flow over into the wealth of subjects and augment everyone’s prosperity [Col. 0787B], what enriches private households and is entered in domestic accounts is sought more eagerly. In these disputes they disagreed: the greater part demanded that everything be plundered and decided by the sword, whereas the king and his party embraced the contrary view. Nevertheless the latter opinion prevailed, and the royal will was satisfied.

When our people had been stationed in the aforementioned village, five or six miles from Cairo, there was an almost continual coming and going of interpreters and messengers, according to each person’s *. Thus the sultan sent embassies to the king, as it were in succession, declaring how diligent he was in collecting the money; he also begged that the king should not complain of the delay but wait patiently. He further warned and advised him not to come nearer, lest he alarm the caliph or the people, who had become more fully confident of the peace treaty they had concluded [Col. 0787C]. Soon, he said, once the payment had been handed over, the king would be able to return with happy auspices.

While he thus deceived our preparations by tricks that were, as it were, mocking illusions, and rendered futile both the sound counsel of those urging a direct course and the more wholesome warnings of those proposing better measures, a report suddenly arose that Shirkuh was arriving and bringing with him an innumerable multitude of Turks. On learning this, the king struck camp, packed the baggage, and returned to Pelusium. There, having taken provisions for the journey and left both cavalry and infantry to guard the city, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January [25 December] he went out into the desert to meet Shirkuh. When he had advanced some distance into the wilderness [Col. 0787D], scouts familiar with the country and worthy of belief informed the king that Shirkuh with his legions had already crossed over.

At this point a new plan was required. For, with the enemy’s forces doubled, it was not safe to delay longer. Delay entailed enormous danger; it did not seem entirely safe to engage them, the sultan no longer wished to abide by the terms of the agreements, and we could not compel him to keep the law of the peaceful settlement. Indeed, it seemed that he had intentionally and deliberately prolonged the matter by evasive delays precisely in order that, when the Turks arrived, we should be forced to withdraw.

Our men therefore returned to Pelusium and there took up the part of the army which had been left to guard the city. On the following day after the Kalends of January [2 January], with the battle lines arranged, they began their march back to Syria [Col. 0788A].

## CHAPTER XI. Shirkuh occupies Egypt, kills the sultan, and himself dies shortly afterward.

Shirkuh, seeing that the opportunity of the times accorded with his wishes and that, now the king had departed, nothing remained to obstruct his desires, brought into effect what he had previously conceived in his mind. He established his camp before Cairo and, as though his entrance had been peaceful, patiently waited for several days. Like a most prudent man, breathing nothing harsh and displaying nothing bitter, he concealed his purpose through the cunning in which he was especially skilled.

Every day Sultan Shawar went out to him in the camp [Col. 0788B] with great splendour and a very large retinue; after performing the duty of daily visitation, offering devout greetings, and giving presents, he returned. The continual regularity of these prosperous comings and goings now seemed to promise security; and what had been received respectfully yesterday and the day before began to produce a more confident familiarity.

The agent of crime therefore anticipated him while he was secure and excessively trusting in Turkish faith. Shirkuh secretly ordered his men that, when the next day, early in the morning, he went out as if to walk by the water, at the hour when the sultan had customarily made his visit, they should stab the sultan as he came. Shawar, then, at the usual part of the day, went out to the camp to render the customary visit and the due exchange of greetings [Col. 0788C]. The agents of his death met him and carried out what had been commanded. Throwing him to the ground, they cut off his head and butchered him with swords.

When his sons saw this, they spurred their horses and fled into Cairo. Terrified, they threw themselves at the caliph’s knees and begged for their lives. He is said to have answered that they might hope for life on condition that they plotted nothing secretly with the Turks. But they immediately violated the terms of the agreement and began secretly, through intermediaries, to negotiate peace with Shirkuh. Hearing this, the caliph ordered them both to be put to the sword.

Thus, with the king absent and Shawar removed, Shirkuh fulfilled his desires: he occupied the kingdom and, entering the caliph’s presence, paid him the reverence due. The caliph in turn honoured him greatly [Col. 0788D], invested him with the dignity and office of the sultanate, and, granting him authority over the sword, yielded to him all Egypt.

O blind human greed, greater than every crime! O accursed frenzy of a covetous mind and insatiable spirit! See from what a wholly peaceful and tranquil condition unrestrained desire of possession has cast us down into one so turbulent and full of anxieties. Egypt’s resources and immeasurable wealth served our needs; on that side our kingdom had secure borders; there was no one to fear from the south. The sea afforded safer routes to those wishing to travel; and our people could enter the territories of Egypt without fear, on favourable terms, for the sake of trade and commerce. The Egyptians in turn, bringing foreign riches and carrying with them articles of trade unknown among us [Col. 0789A], were advantageous and honourable to us whenever they came among us. Moreover, the immense payment of annual tribute supplied strength and increased both the royal treasury and the private wealth of individuals.

But now, conversely, everything has taken a turn for the worse; the best condition has changed, and our harp has been turned into mourning. Wherever I turn, I find danger. The sea denies peaceful access; every neighbouring region all around obeys enemies; and the kingdoms adjoining us prepare for our destruction. The greed of one man has brought in all these things, and avarice, the root of vices, has clouded the serenity granted us by God. But let us return to the history.

## CHAPTER XII. Saladin, his nephew through his brother, succeeds him after his death and gains the kingdom of Egypt.

[Col. 0789B]

After the death of the sultan and his sons—against whom, contrary to the rule of piety, we had furnished causes for undeserved death—Shirkuh, having attained his desire, obtained the principate. But he did not long rejoice in this success; for scarcely a year after gaining power he was removed from human affairs. He was succeeded by Saladin, son of his brother Najm al-Din, a man of keen intelligence, vigorous in arms, and extraordinarily liberal.

At the beginning of his rule he entered the presence of the caliph, his lord, to render him the customary reverence. It is said that with the club he carried in his hands he struck him to the ground and killed him, and put all his offspring to the sword [Col. 0789C], so that, having regard to no superior, he himself might be both caliph and sultan. For he feared that, when he came into the caliph’s presence, the caliph—since the Turks had now become hated by the people—might order him to be slaughtered. He therefore forestalled him and, like a master fearing no such thing, inflicted on him the death which, it is said, the caliph was preparing to inflict upon him.

After the caliph’s death, he plundered at his own unrestricted discretion the royal treasury, treasures, and all the precious possessions of that household, and distributed everything with extreme liberality among the soldiers. Thus within a few days, when the wardrobes had been emptied, he himself borrowed money and bound himself under the heavy burden of debt. Yet there were, it is said, persons who secretly rescued some of the caliph’s sons, intending that, if the administration of the kingdom should ever be restored to the Egyptians, there might not be lacking someone who would stand as heir to his predecessors in name, dignity, and blood [Col. 0789D].

## CHAPTER XIII. Bernard, abbot of the monastery of Mount Tabor, is appointed over the Church of Lydda. Frederick, archbishop of Tyre, is sent westward to seek aid from the princes of the West.

After the lord king had returned to the kingdom, nothing memorable was done in the first part of that year, except that, after the death of Rayner, bishop of Lydda of good memory, Bernard, abbot of the church of Mount Tabor, was enthroned in that church. But in the following spring, which was the beginning of the sixth year of Lord Amalric, the wiser men of the kingdom saw that, with Egypt subdued by the Turks, our position had greatly deteriorated [Col. 0790A]. For our most violent enemy, Nur al-Din, could now, with a numerous fleet sailing from Egypt, severely hem in our kingdom by sea and surround any maritime city with an army on both land and sea. What was more alarming, he could hinder or utterly deny passage to pilgrims coming to us.

They therefore decided that venerable, prudent, and eloquent men from among the prelates of the churches should be sent to the princes of the West, to teach and carefully impress upon them the unbearable pressures upon the kingdom, the affliction of the Christian people, and the harsh disasters threatening their brethren. By common counsel there were chosen for this ministry the lord patriarch, Lord Ernulf, archbishop of Caesarea, and Lord William, bishop of Acre [Col. 0790B]. Taking letters both from the lord king and from all the bishops, they embarked, bound for the lord Frederick, emperor of the Romans; the lord Louis, king of the Franks; the lord Henry, king of the English; the lord William, king of Sicily; and also Counts Philip of Flanders, Henry of Troyes, Theobald of Chartres, and the other princes of the western regions.

But on the following night a violent storm suddenly arose. The ship was battered, its oars broken, and its masts lowered; greatly distressed, after three days they barely escaped shipwreck and returned. In the same embassy they were succeeded by Lord Frederick, archbishop of Tyre, overcome by the persistent entreaties of the lord king and the princes. He took with him Lord John, bishop of Paneas, a suffragan of the same church. Setting sail under more favourable auspices, they successfully reached the desired harbour, though they made little progress in the business entrusted to them. For the aforesaid bishop, once he had reached France, immediately died at Paris; while the lord archbishop, after completing two years, returned entirely empty-handed [Col. 0790C].

## CHAPTER XIV. The emperor, wishing to fulfil the agreements, sends a fleet and certain of his princes into Syria.

After that summer had passed without memorable events, at the beginning of the following autumn, mindful of his faith and keeping in mind the agreements which, through our mediation and interposed effort, the lord emperor had confirmed with the lord king, he sent the fleet he had promised. In this matter he was highly praiseworthy, for, interpreting most fully in imperial magnificence the rule of amicable agreement, he fulfilled his promise with a more abundant contribution [Col. 0790D].

There were in this army one hundred and fifty long, beaked ships, equipped with two banks of oars and more suited to military purposes, commonly called galleys. There were also sixty larger vessels assigned for transporting horses, with openings in their sterns through which the animals might be led in and out, and fitted with bridges to facilitate the embarkation and disembarkation of both men and horses [Col. 0791A]. There were also ten or twelve of the largest vessels, called dromons, filled to the utmost with provisions of various kinds, numerous weapons, siege engines, and military artillery.

With the fleet he sent several of his princes: his relative Megadux, whom he placed in command of all; another man named Mauresius, very intimate with him and in whose ability, as afterward became more fully evident, he had great confidence—for later he placed him over his entire empire; and Count Alexander of Conversano, a nobleman of Apulia, whom the emperor held dear and esteemed because of his conspicuous loyalty and great devotion toward him. Entrusting them with the care of his army, he sent them eastward to us [Col. 0791B]. Having enjoyed a favourable voyage, they entered the harbour of Tyre about the end of September. From there they proceeded to Acre and took up a calm anchorage between the river and the port.

## CHAPTER XV. The king descends into Egypt with his forces, followed by the Greeks both by sea and by land.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1169, the sixty-eighth from the liberation of the city, and the sixth year of the reign of Lord Amalric, on the Ides of October [15 October], after the affairs of the kingdom had been arranged and a force had been left behind to defend the kingdom, during the king’s absence, from the ambushes and raids of Nur al-Din—whom he had left in the region of Damascus [Col. 0791C]—the entire army of both Latins and Greeks assembled at Ascalon. The fleet had already left the harbour of Acre some days earlier and was making its way toward the frontiers of Egypt *[the printed asterisk is unexplained]*.

Then, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September [16 August], they departed from the aforesaid city and, by suitable stages where water would not be lacking and with measured marches so that the infantry formations might not be burdened beyond their strength, reached the most ancient city of Pharamia on the ninth day.

A chance event had recently made the middle portion of this route, for those wishing to follow the seacoast, longer. Certain banks of sand lying between some flatter ground and the neighbouring strait had been overcome by the customary scourge and nearly continual assault of the waves [Col. 0791D]. The sea, violently breaking through the barriers, made a way for itself and claimed free access to the farther plain. Flowing in more freely, it formed a lagoon, narrow at its mouth but spreading within over broad fields. From that day onward, such a multitude of fish is usually enclosed there by marine inundations that it supplies not only neighbouring but even distant cities with abundant and unheard-of quantities of fish.

Thus, because the places nearer the sea were occupied by the standing salt water, those wishing to travel along the watery shore and descend into Egypt were compelled by necessity to make a detour around the lagoon, departing by ten miles or more before returning to the coast. We have inserted this account because of the marvel and of the newly made breach: a part of the desert formerly exposed to the heat of the sun is now subject to waves, familiar to swimming creatures and open to vessels; it fills fishermen’s nets and, becoming more productive than usual, yields fruits formerly unknown [Col. 0792A].

Pharamia, mentioned above, is a deserted city, once inhabited by a large population. It lies near the first mouth of the Nile, where it receives the sea’s waves, commonly called Carabes; joined to the desert, it stands between the river, the sea, and the wilderness, though it is three miles from the river’s mouth. When our men arrived there, they found that our fleet had come. There, after the ships had been fitted out with the necessary crews, the whole army was transported to the farther bank [Col. 0792B].

Leaving Tapnim on their left—once an eminent metropolis, now reduced to the likeness of a very small town—they took the middle road between marshy ground and the seashore. In about twenty miles, they reached Damietta in two days.

## CHAPTER XVI. The king besieges Damietta, and the armies of both Latins and Greeks toil fruitlessly in attempting to take it.

Damiata, then, is among the most ancient and most distinguished metropolises of Egypt. It lies on the nearer bank of the Nile, where that river enters the sea by its second mouth, advantageously situated between the river-channel and the sea, though about a mile distant from the latter. [Col. 0792C] Our army reached it on 27 October and encamped between the city and the sea, awaiting the fleet, which was held back by the roughness of the sea and contrary winds. After three days, when the sea had grown calm and favourable winds served it, the fleet entered the river-channel and took up a suitable station along the bank between the city and the sea.

On the farther bank of the river stood a remarkably lofty tower, sufficiently manned for its defence. From it to the city stretched an iron chain, which created the greatest obstacle for our men, so that there was absolutely no passage upstream. Yet vessels of every kind could enter freely and without hindrance from upstream, from Babylon and Cairo. When the fleet had therefore been assembled, our men too, [Col. 0792D] passing beyond the outer precincts lying between the camp and the city, pitched their tents nearer to the town, whence they had unobstructed access to the walls. But, while they delayed the assault for three days, they learned by experience how true is the saying:

> Delay harms those who are ready.

For countless multitudes of Turks arriving from the upper regions of Egypt, and ships laden with armed men, filled before the eyes of our forces—who could not prevent them—a city that had previously been almost empty. What at their first arrival they had thought scarcely able to withstand their initial attacks, they now declared could be taken only by siege-engines and military artillery.

Accordingly, craftsmen were chosen; and, with the necessary materials at hand, a tower of extraordinary height was raised at immense expense and labour, [Col. 0793A] having seven storeys, from which the whole city could be seen. Other engines of various kinds were constructed: some to batter down the walls with great millstones; others by which, as though concealed in underground chambers, miners might undermine the city walls and force those thus undermined to collapse through subterranean passages. Meanwhile, when the engines had been built and set alongside the wall by means of levelled approaches, those in the tower pressed the townsmen vigorously with arrows, hand-thrown stones, and such weapons as fury and the narrowness of the position supplied. Those beneath the missile-engines, meanwhile, hurled millstones and competed in attacking the walls and the houses adjoining them.

Seeing this, the townsmen, that they might foil art with art and counter our contrivances with equal ingenuity, raised a tower directly opposite our own [Col. 0793B] to a great height. They placed armed men upon it, to resist our men on equal terms and answer them with an effort no less powerful. They also opposed engines to engines, and devoted themselves with every care to breaking ours by whatever devices they could. They became ingenious in their own defence, and necessity gave strength to their intelligence. Those who had previously believed themselves unequal to this found, when pressed by the crisis of necessity, means formerly unknown; and, for the protection of their own safety, became keener from having been dull-witted.

There one might learn by experience how true is the proverbial saying:

> Ingenuity comes to men in wretched circumstances.  
> —Ovid

[Col. 0793C] Our men, however, when they ought to have pressed more vigorously, began to perform everything timidly and coldly. Some attributed this to treachery, others to carelessness and negligence. There, indeed, it at once became clear either that our men had too little experience, or had departed from their customary prudence, or that the commanders of the army had acted maliciously: for they ordered the tower they had erected to be brought up to the walls through steep and almost impassable ground. Although on that side of the city the walls were in many places lower and exceedingly weak, and there were many places more easily accessible for assault and capture, they raised the tower on the side held to be stronger and better fortified, where it could be brought to the walls with a difficulty [Col. 0793D] that would have arisen nowhere else. Nor did it there trouble the citizens or their buildings in any respect, but only the basilica of the holy Mother of God, situated beside the walls.

There can surely be no doubt that the delay in attacking the city when our men first arrived proceeded, as usual, from malice. They found it empty, containing only its own household population—unwarlike, effeminate men, ignorant of battle—and, had they pressed the matter more boldly as duty required, they would have seized it by force in the first engagements. The respite granted gave the besieged so much strength, and in the meantime such a multitude of brave and excellently armed men arrived, that they could withstand our attacks not only within the walls but even in the open country.

## Chapter XVII. Famine arises in the camp, and almost our entire fleet is burned; at last the siege is lifted, its works having been expended uselessly.

[Col. 0794A]

Moreover, a miserable occurrence arose: the whole multitude of Greeks who had come in the fleet began to suffer such a shortage of provisions that bread wholly failed them all, nor could any food be found among them. A grove of palms adjoining the camp was cut down for various uses; and, as the trees were eagerly felled, the starving Greeks searched with great diligence at their tops, where the branches originate, for a certain tender substance from which life-giving moisture is supplied to the branches, and which was in some manner fit for food. Thus they consoled their hunger, though miserably. [Col. 0794B] Hunger had increased their ingenuity in seeking food, and the appetite of the roaring belly had brought forth greater resourcefulness. Sustaining life miserably by this food for several days, they struggled to drive hunger away. Yet some who were not utterly deprived of nourishment found hazelnuts, raisins, and dried chestnuts to offer some relief against the violence of hunger.

Our men, however, did not lack a sufficient supply of bread and foodstuffs of various kinds; but, thinking of the morrow, they husbanded their stores, fearing that, if they heedlessly shared them with those who had no food, they too might eventually lack it. Being uncertain also of the delay, they regarded a prolonged period with apprehension. Furthermore, at that time such an abundance of rain and such unseasonable weather descended that neither the poorer men in huts nor the richer in tents could by any contrivance exclude the dripping—indeed, the overflowing downpour—[Col. 0794C] of the storms. Therefore, by surrounding their tents with a ditch so that the force of the rain might run into it, they could scarcely place themselves in safety.

During the same days an exceedingly great disaster also occurred. They had drawn the galleys and other ships of various kinds out of the sea into the channel of the river and had arranged them in what seemed a safe station near the city. Seeing that a somewhat violent wind was blowing downstream and, as it were, following the course of the Nile, the townsmen attempted to put their plan into effect. Taking a boat of medium size and filling it to the very top with dry timber, pitch, resinous liquid, and all things customarily providing fuel for fire, [Col. 0794D] they set fire beneath it and directed it, now ablaze, against our fleet, the river carrying it freely along. Nor was there lacking a southerly wind, which, taking its opportunity from the combustible material beneath, fed the flames.

The burning boat thus descended into the fleet; finding it packed closely together and unable to pass through, it lodged among the vessels. The fire it carried burned six of the beaked ships called galleys to ashes; and the growing blaze would have wholly consumed the fleet, had not the lord king, on learning of the fire, swiftly mounted a horse while still barefoot and roused the sailors, by his own actions and many shouts, to resist the flames. Separating the vessels from one another, [Col. 0795A] they escaped the fury of the widely spreading fire. Any vessels that had begun to catch fire from the neighbouring blaze, carrying fuel for it either as embers or otherwise, found a remedy through the aid of the river and the sprinkling of nearby water.

Assaults upon the city were also made, though at intervals. In these, as the issue of wars is usually uncertain, now our side and now the enemy suffered the worse outcome; yet our men more often furnished the occasion for battle. For the enemy rarely challenged them to an engagement unless provoked. Sometimes, however, the townsmen made sudden sorties against the Greek camp through a postern gate, we do not know through what confidence prompted—whether because they had heard that our Greeks were by nature weaker, [Col. 0795B] or because they considered them less able to withstand attacks while endangered by hunger. Nevertheless, their commander, the Megaduke, and others fought bravely and vigorously in battle whenever necessary. Encouraged by their example, the rank and file often pressed more fiercely and resisted more boldly even than usual.

Military forces continued to increase for the citizens by land and by water, so that henceforth those held within the walls were more an object of fear to our men than men said to be besieged suffered any inconvenience. Murmuring therefore now spread among the people, and almost everyone agreed that our men were wasting their labour uselessly: that, because the Godhead was angry, they had begun this undertaking; and that it was safer to return home than to waste away from hunger in Egypt or be delivered over to the enemy’s swords. Accordingly, through the mediation of our men and certain Turkish satraps, especially one of their princes, Jevelin, who rendered faithful assistance, and with the Greeks agreeing to the same, an alliance was concluded under certain secret terms; immediately peace was proclaimed by herald.

## Chapter XVIII. The expedition being recalled, the king returns home. On its return journey the Greek fleet almost entirely perishes, driven by adverse winds.

Thus, both citizens and those who had come to assist them went out to our camp as they pleased; and those of our men who wished to enter the city had free entrance and exit without difficulty. [Col. 0795D] At last mutual commercial dealings were permitted, and everyone was allowed to buy or exchange whatever he wished. Thus, after our men had used a common market with the enemy for goods for sale for about three days, they prepared themselves for departure.

Those who had come by land dismantled the engines and set them on fire; following the lord king, they returned by the route on which they had come toward Syria and, hastening their steps, reached Ascalon on 21 December. The lord king, hastening to Acre because of the approaching feast, reached that city on Christmas Eve. But those who had come by sea embarked under an evil omen and ill-omened birds. For at the very outset of their return journey [Col. 0796A] a sudden and extremely violent storm arose; encountering the unconquerable violence of the straits, their ships were broken and dashed upon the shores, and almost all suffered shipwreck. Thus, of so great a fleet that had come down to us, both larger and smaller vessels, only a few ships remained unharmed and capable in themselves of making the return voyage.

Although the undertaking had failed, the envoys of the lord emperor had nevertheless expended every effort required for its completion and had shown due care in administering affairs. They returned home dejected and shattered by adverse fortune, fearing that the imperial excellency would, beyond their deserts, attribute the unfavourable outcome to them, and that their lord, inflamed with anger, would unjustly ascribe to their malice or negligence what unavoidable mischance had brought about.

We remember, however, that after our own return both the lord king and certain princes of the realm diligently and earnestly inquired what cause had made so great an army, provided through the efforts of such great princes, fail thus in its purpose. For in that year we had gone to the Roman Church, drawn by private business and avoiding the undeserved displeasure of our lord archbishop. On our return, seeking an answer to the aforesaid question, we desired to learn the truth of the matter from the differing accounts of many persons; for the event was said to have fallen far short of our hopes. Drawn on by this concern, we had already conceived the plan of committing all these things to writing.

[Col. 0796C] We found that the Greeks too were not without grave fault in the matter just described. For although the lord emperor had most firmly promised to send sufficient money to sustain so great an army, his word was found defective in this respect. Once his archons had entered Egypt, where they ought also to have aided others in need from imperial munificence, they themselves were the first to be in need and to seek loans, by which they might provide their legions with food and pay; and no one gave to them.

## Chapter XIX. A very great earthquake shakes almost the entire East and overthrows most ancient cities.

[Col. 0796D] In the following summer, namely the seventh year of the lord Amalric, in June, an earthquake so great and violent occurred in the eastern regions as no such event is recorded in the memory of men of the present age. Destroying to their foundations the most ancient and strongly fortified cities of the whole eastern region, enveloping their inhabitants in ruin, and crushing them in the fall of their buildings, it reduced them to a very small remnant. There was no place to the ends of the earth where private loss and domestic grief did not cause anguish; everywhere there was mourning, everywhere funeral rites were performed.

Among these it utterly threw down the greatest cities of our provinces, Syria and Phoenicia, noble for their ancient succession of centuries. In Coele-Syria it completely levelled Antioch, the metropolis of many provinces and formerly ruler of many kingdoms, together with the people dwelling in it. [Col. 0797A] It overthrew the walls and the very strong towers around them—works of incomparable solidity—as well as churches and every kind of building, with such force that even to the present day they can scarcely be restored to a merely moderate condition through great labour, immense expenditure, constant care, and unwearied effort.

In the same province fell distinguished cities: among the coastal towns, Gabulum and Laodicea; among inland towns—though held by the enemy—Nerea, also called Halapia, Caesarea, Hamum, Emesa, and many others. The number of lesser towns was beyond counting. In Phoenicia, Tripoli, a noble and populous city, was suddenly shaken by such force of earthquake on 29 June, about the first hour of the day, that scarcely one of all those found within its circuit had any way of escape. The whole city became, as it were, a heap of stones, a mound of its crushed citizens, and a public tomb.

At Tyre also, the most famous metropolis of the same province, the earthquake violently threw down several very sturdy towers, though without danger to the citizens. Both among us and among the enemy there were towns half ruined and lying wide open to ambushes and hostile force. Yet, while each feared the wrath of the strict Judge for himself, he dreaded to trouble another. Each person’s own sorrow was sufficient, and, as domestic anxiety wore everyone down, each deferred inflicting injury upon another. [Col. 0797C] A peace was made, though brief, brought about by human effort; a treaty was concluded, framed through fear of divine judgments. And while everyone expected from above the indignation due to his sins, he withdrew his hand and restrained his attacks from the injuries usually inflicted in war.

This manifestation of God’s anger did not last merely an hour, as is generally the case. For three or four months, or even longer, that dreadful movement was felt three or four times, and often more frequently, by day or by night. Every movement was now feared, and nowhere could secure rest be found. Even the mind of a sleeper, horrified by what it had feared while awake, often compelled the body to leap up suddenly, breaking its repose. The upper parts of our province, however—Palestine, that is—were exempt from all these evils, the Lord protecting them.

## Chapter XX. Saladin enters our territory and besieges the castle called Darum.

In the same year, in December—the seventh year of the lord Amalric—a widespread report circulated and was publicized by frequent messengers: Saladin, having called together military forces from all Egypt and the territories of Damascus, and having enlarged the number of soldiers with common people and men of the second rank, was preparing to enter Palestine in order to devastate our kingdom. On hearing this, the lord king hastened with all speed into the territory of Ascalon. There he learned with certainty from trustworthy reports [Col. 0798A] that the said great and most powerful prince, with a very large army greater than usual, had been besieging for two days the castle called Darum. During those two days, allowing the besieged no rest, he had troubled them so severely and assailed those in the garrison with such numerous and repeated discharges of arrows that, with almost everyone wounded, only a few could take up arms for the defence of the place.

Having also undermined and violently breached the wall, he had already taken part of the fortified settlement, the townspeople being forced to withdraw into the citadel, which seemed more strongly fortified. His men had also violently burst into the lower part of its tower after breaking and burning the gate, while the soldiers within still defended its upper portions. Such was the report made to the lord king; and it was indeed true.

The commander and keeper assigned to that garrison was the lord Anselm of Pass, a nobleman, vigorous in arms, devout and fearing God. Had the aforesaid castle not had his presence that day, it would beyond all doubt have fallen into the hands of the enemy. When the king learned this, inwardly pierced by grief and inflamed with anger, he summoned from every quarter such aid of horsemen and foot soldiers as the shortness of time and proximity of the enemy allowed. Leaving Ascalon, he hastened to Gaza on the eighteenth day of the aforesaid month.

[Col. 0798B] The lord patriarch was present with him, bearing the venerable and precious wood of the life-giving Cross. Present also were the venerable men Lord Ralph, bishop of Bethlehem and chancellor of the kingdom, and Lord Bernard, bishop of Lydda, as well as very few of the princes of the kingdom. When their numbers were counted, they could scarcely find 250 knights and about 2,000 infantrymen. They spent that night sleepless in the place just mentioned, under the weight of anxiety and cares. Taking with them the brothers of the Temple, who had assembled there for the protection of the place, they all left the city at sunrise and directed their march toward the aforesaid castle.

The castle, we believe, lies in Idumaea—that is, Edom—beyond the torrent called the Torrent of Egypt, which is also the boundary of Palestine and the aforesaid region. The same lord Amalric had founded it a few years earlier on a somewhat elevated site [Col. 0798D], taking advantage of ancient buildings, of which certain traces still remained there. The older inhabitants of those regions relate that in ancient times there had been a Greek monastery there; hence it still bears the name Darum, interpreted as “House of the Greeks.”

As we have said, the lord king had founded there a castle of modest size, containing within itself scarcely as much space as a stone’s throw. It was square in form and had four angle-towers, one of which was larger and stronger than the others; nevertheless, it had neither ditch nor outer wall. It was about five stadia from the sea and four miles from Gaza. Some cultivators from neighbouring places and some persons engaged in trade had assembled there; they built a suburb and a church not far from the fortress and became inhabitants of that place. For the place was convenient, and poorer people could prosper there more easily than in cities. The king had established the aforesaid fortified town with the intention both of extending his frontiers and of more fully and easily obtaining the annual revenues from the adjoining rural settlements—which our people call *casalia*—and the fixed dues from travellers.

## Chapter XXI. The king, with a small body of soldiers, meets him; many of our men are slaughtered by the enemy both in Gaza and on the road.

Our army, having left Gaza and taken position on a certain elevated place along the route, [Col. 0799B] saw the enemy camp. Terrified by its immense multitude, they began to close their ranks more tightly than usual, so that because of the density of the crowd they could scarcely move. The enemy immediately charged upon our men, attempting, if possible, to separate them from one another. But our men, through divine favour, formed themselves more solidly together, endured the enemy’s attacks, and completed their march at a rapid pace.

At last they reached their intended place, pitched their tents, and the entire army halted there. The lord patriarch was stationed in the citadel, while all the rest encamped outside and near the suburb. It was about the sixth hour of the day. Thus, having had individual engagements and some clashes by squadrons that day, our men both attacked boldly and resisted bravely. As night drew on, Saladin arranged his columns and directed his army toward Gaza; that night they rested beside the torrent. At daybreak they took up position before Gaza and began to approach the city.

Gaza was a most ancient city, a distinguished metropolis of the Philistines, frequently mentioned in both ecclesiastical and secular histories; even today its noble buildings preserve many evidences of its ancient distinction. It had lain deserted for many years, so that it was inhabited by not even one resident, until Baldwin IV, king of Jerusalem of illustrious memory, before the capture of Ascalon, gathered the forces of the kingdom and at public expense built a sufficiently fortified castle in one part of the city. [Col. 0799D] Once built, he immediately gave it to the brothers of the Knights Templar to possess in perpetual right.

The castle could not occupy the entire hill on which the city had been founded, as stated above. But some persons gathered to inhabit the place and, that they might dwell there more safely, attempted to fortify the remaining part of the hill with gates and a wall—though low and weak. On hearing of the enemy’s approach, the inhabitants of the place resolved to enter the fortress with their wives and little children; they were unarmed people, cultivators of the soil, unaccustomed to such affairs, and intended to expose the rest of the city, as unfortified, to the enemy.

But Milo of Plancy, one of the magnates of the kingdom but a wicked man, wishing ostensibly to encourage the people, utterly forbade them to enter and urged them to defend the weaker part of the city. There were also sixty-five nimble young men, ready for arms, from the Jerusalem region, from the village called Macomeria. [Col. 0800A] They were hurrying to the army and happened to arrive in the same city that night. While, by command of the aforesaid Milo, they fought bravely beside the gate of the outer city for freedom and country, and vigorously resisted the enemy’s attempt to open a way by the sword, the enemy burst into the city from another side and found them between the fortress and the said gate, still denying the enemy an entrance. Charging from behind, they surrounded the unsuspecting men on every side; no longer able to resist, they slaughtered them with the sword. Yet they won a bloody victory over them, though many of the latter were killed and more were wounded.

When the inhabitants of the place wished again to enter the fortress, the enemy had already been admitted within the walls and were indiscriminately delivering them to death everywhere; entry was not permitted, and no other path of safety presented itself. Thus, after the Turks had seized the city, they spared neither age nor sex; dashing crying infants against stones, they could scarcely satisfy their rage. But those who were in the fortress kept the enemy at a distance from the towers and walls by throwing stones and repeatedly shooting missiles, and by the Lord’s favour preserved the castle unharmed.

Thus, after occupying the city and killing its inhabitants, as though holding the palm of victory, they returned toward Darum. On the march they found about fifty of our infantrymen, who were incautiously hurrying toward our army. Although these men defended themselves quite bravely and resisted stoutly, the enemy killed them all with the sword. [Col. 0800C]

## Chapter XXII. Saladin returns home. The king too, after repairing the castle, which had been partly destroyed, returns to Ascalon.

Having arranged their columns and deployed them in battle order as military discipline required, they formed forty-two companies. They ordered twenty-two of them to follow the seashore, proceeding between Darum and the sea; they commanded the remainder to take the inland route until, after passing the castle, all should reunite in a single body. Seeing the enemy return in ordered ranks, our men prepared themselves for battle. Though few in number, they trusted [Col. 0800D] in the Lord’s mercy; invoking help from above, they girded themselves for war, the Lord supplying strength and steadfastness of spirit. They regarded nothing as more certain than that the enemy had returned in order to engage our men.

But the enemy had a very different purpose. Turning neither to the right nor to the left, they were hastening back to Egypt. When trustworthy messengers had made it clear to the lord king that they had taken this road with no intention of returning, he left men behind to rebuild the half-ruined castle, strengthen it further when rebuilt, and guard it faithfully once fortified. Then, guided by the Lord, he returned with his men to Ascalon. Those who had more frequently seen campaigns in the kingdom said that they had never heard of so great a multitude of Turks assembled in any age. The enemy’s number, consisting only of cavalry, was reckoned at 40,000. [Col. 0801A]

## Chapter XXIII. In the same year Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, the glorious martyr of Christ, is slain in his own church.

At the same time, on 29 December, in England at Canterbury, the noble and eminent metropolis of that province, the passion of the most blessed and glorious martyr Thomas, archbishop of that city, was celebrated. He was a native of London and, under Theobald of blessed memory, bishop of the city of Canterbury, deserved to be promoted to archdeacon of that church. Called by Henry II, king of the same realm, to share in the royal burden of government, he became the king’s chancellor and a faithful, prudent, and most important administrator of the entire kingdom. [Col. 0801B]

At last, through the aid of his merits and after the death of the aforesaid blessed father, he was called by God’s ordinance to the church of Canterbury. While he fought manfully and with the greatest constancy against tyrannical impieties for the rights of his church, he fled that same king as persecutor and was compelled to undergo exile. In France he endured this exile for an uninterrupted seven years with wonderful and praiseworthy patience. While awaiting the peace promised by the king, he returned. Within the very church over which he presided by God’s appointment, he suffered indignities, prayed for his persecutors, was struck down by the swords of the wicked, and, crowned in his own blood, attained through a blessed exchange the crown of martyrdom. Through him the pious and merciful Lord deigns to work so many and such great miracles almost every day in the aforesaid church and throughout the entire province that the times of the apostles seem to have been renewed. [Col. 0801C]

## Chapter XXIV. The king, taking with him several of his princes, travels to Constantinople; the emperor strives to anticipate him with manifold honours.

In the following year, the seventh of the reign of the lord Amalric, the aforesaid king saw the burdens with which the kingdom was daily oppressed: the enemy’s numbers increased without cease, their power grew stronger, and their resources and riches multiplied without measure. Meanwhile the provident and judicious princes of our kingdom had now wholly passed away, and in their place a pernicious offspring was growing up, uselessly occupying the place of such great men and squandering paternal goods on detestable purposes. The kingdom had consequently reached a degree of weakness perceptible even to those with little practical judgment.

[Col. 0801D] He summoned all the princes of the kingdom and, in their presence, set forth the kingdom’s necessities and sought their counsel on how these evils might be met, lest the kingdom perish. After deliberating on the present situation, they answered unanimously, as though with one judgment: that the kingdom, through sins demanding it, had reached such a crisis that it could neither attack its adversaries nor withstand their assaults. They said that, after imploring the assistance of the western princes, he must attempt to resist these evils; they declared themselves wholly unable to find any other way of salvation.

It was therefore resolved, and this pleased the common counsel, that worthy persons of distinction should be sent to solicit and inform of the kingdom’s distress the lord pope; the illustrious emperor of the Romans; the kings of the French, English, Sicily, and the Spains; and the renowned dukes and counts, so that they might implore their help against the imminent dangers. It was also decreed that the precarious and dangerous state of the kingdom should be communicated to the lord emperor of Constantinople, because, being nearer to us and far wealthier than the others, he could more easily provide the assistance desired. [Col. 0802A] They further added that a person should be sent to him who had the prudence, eloquence, and authority to know and be able to incline the mind of so great a prince toward our wishes.

While they deliberated who might be fit to fulfil so great an embassy, the king, after taking counsel with a few intimate advisers, disclosed his purpose and revealed publicly the design conceived in his mind, saying that this could be done by no one but himself. He added that he was ready, for the relief of the kingdom’s necessities, to undertake labours and every kind of danger. When the great men of the kingdom, stunned and filled with astonishment, said, “It is exceedingly hard for the kingdom to be found, as it were, abandoned without the king’s presence,” he replied: “May the Lord rule His own kingdom, whose servant I am. It is fixed in my mind that I shall go; there is no one who can recall me from this purpose.”

Therefore, taking with him Lord William, bishop of Acre; and, from the magnates of the kingdom, Guarmund of Tiberias, John of Arsuf, Gerard of Pugi, marshal, Roard, castellan of Jerusalem, and Reinuard of Nephin—[Col. 0802C] for he had sent Philip of Naples, who had already laid down the mastership of the Knights Templar, ahead by land—he set out on 10 March in ten galleys, accompanied by a great retinue befitting royal majesty. By God’s favour he had a prosperous voyage and successfully entered the narrows of Abydos and the mouth of the Bosporus, commonly called the Arm of Saint George.

When the lord emperor—a most magnificent, provident, discerning, and in every respect praiseworthy man—heard that so great a prince and ruler of so renowned and God-beloved a kingdom was entering his empire in an unprecedented manner, he first wondered greatly what could be the cause of so arduous and unusual a journey. Then, considering the increase of his own glory, the greatness of the honour, and the incomparable gift of heavenly favour that seemed freely offered him by God—namely, that something had happened to him which is not recorded to have happened to any of his predecessors: the king of Jerusalem, defender and advocate of the venerable places of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, was coming to him—he was exceedingly delighted and arranged to anticipate the king’s arrival with manifold honours.

[Col. 0802D] Summoning his nephew John Protosebastos, most eminent among the princes of the sacred palace, whose daughter the same lord king had as wife, he sent him to meet the king. In accordance with the ancient and inviolable ceremonial and incomparable magnificence of the empire, John was to ensure that the king was received with the highest honour in the cities and places he reached; and he was to instruct him, as a son, to await the emperor’s messengers concerning his entrance into the imperial city.

This magnificent prince, meeting the lord king with an honourable retinue, accompanied him as far as Callipolis, a city situated on the shore of the Bosporus, not far from the narrows of Abydos. Since the wind was not very suitable for those wishing to hurry onward to the imperial city, the king disembarked from the galleys and rode with his household retinue as far as Heraclea, situated on the same shore of the sea. There he found in harbour his fleet, which, after receiving a more favourable breeze and sailing with prosperous winds, had preceded him on his journey. [Col. 0803B] Embarking once more, he reached Constantinople with the wind favourably attending him.

## Chapter XXV. Brought before the emperor, he is honourably received and holds frequent conferences with him concerning necessary affairs.

There is in that city, upon the shore of the sea and facing eastward, an imperial palace called the Constantinian Palace. It has an entrance from the sea, with a wondrous and magnificent landing-stage; marble steps descending into the sea itself; and lions and columns, raised in royal magnificence, of the same material. By this way entrance to the upper parts of the palace is normally open to the Emperor alone [Col. 0803C]; but, in special regard for the king’s honour, an exception to the common rules was granted, allowing him to enter by that side.

There the great princes of the Sacred Palace, meeting him with a very numerous body of courtiers, received him with the highest honour. Then, through passageways and lodgings of marvellous variety, attended by many ranks both of his own men and of the palace, he was led to the lofty imperial residence, where the Emperor sat with his distinguished companions. Before the imperial audience-chamber hung curtains of precious material and workmanship no less precious—indeed, to which that verse of Naso [Ovid] might fittingly be applied:

> The workmanship surpassed the material.

[Col. 0803D] Outside these curtains the greater princes met the king and conducted him within them. This, it is said, was done to preserve the imperial glory and to regain the king’s favour. For, in the company of his magnates, when only distinguished persons stood by, the Emperor is said to have risen familiarly to greet him; had this been done in the presence of the general court, the Emperor would have seemed to have impaired his majesty too greatly.

When the king entered, the curtains were suddenly drawn together, leaving outside those who had been beyond them. The Emperor then appeared seated upon a golden throne and clothed in imperial attire; beside him the king sat upon a fitting, though lower, throne. The Emperor bestowed upon our princes both the kiss of peace and the greetings due to them, with great graciousness; [Col. 0804A] carefully inquiring after the health of the king and his princes, he showed by word and countenance, with great cheerfulness of spirit, how gladly he had received their arrival.

The Emperor had ordered his household officers and the administrators of his Sacred Palace to prepare, within the precincts of the palace, lodgings of remarkable excellence for the king and his intimate attendants; and for each of the king’s princes he had ordered separate lodgings, very honourable ones, prepared in the city, though not far from himself. Having therefore taken leave of the Emperor, they withdrew for a time, following the king; and, having appointed the hour at which they were to return to him, the king ordered his princes to go down to their respective lodgings.

Every day, at hours specially assigned for this purpose, they held earnest discussions, both with the Emperor and among themselves, concerning the affairs [Col. 0804B] for which they had come, applying every effort to ensure that, the purpose of so great a labour and journey having been accomplished, they might return home with the desired result. Thus, in frequent private conversations with the Emperor, and also in the distinguished company of his intimates, the king explained the purpose of his journey, described the needs of the kingdom, set forth more fully the immortality of fame which the Emperor might acquire by bringing the kingdom of Egypt under his dominion, and supported with clear arguments the ease with which that aim might be achieved. Persuaded by these arguments, the Emperor gave a kindly hearing to his assertions and promised a full and desired fulfilment of his wishes.

Meanwhile, in accordance with imperial magnificence, he repeatedly honoured both [Col. 0804C] the king and his princes with an abundance of gifts, and by frequent visits showed himself concerned for their condition and safety. He also ordered opened to them, as to his own intimates, the inner parts of the palace; its inmost chambers, accessible only to his household; residences reserved for more private uses; basilicas closed to the populace; treasuries; and ancestral repositories of every desirable thing. He ordered displayed also the relics of the saints and the most precious proofs of the dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ: namely, the Cross, the nails, the lance, the sponge, the reed, the crown of thorns, the shroud, and the sandals. There was no secret thing, no mystical object kept hidden in the recesses of the sacred bedchamber since the times of the blessed emperors Constantine, [Col. 0804D] Theodosius, and Justinian, which was not familiarly revealed to them.

At times also, laying aside business, he invited the king and his companions to entertainments and novel diversions that were not inconsistent with the dignity of either. There he ordered to be displayed various kinds of musical instruments, songs of wonderful sweetness distinguished by artistic harmonies, dances of maidens, and admirable performances of actors—yet with moral propriety maintained. He also ordered public spectacles, which we are accustomed to call theatrical or Circus games, to be presented for the citizens in honour of the king, at great expense and with customary magnificence.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Their business completed and laden with gifts, both the king and his princes return home.

[Col. 0805A]
