After they had remained for several days in the Constantinian Palace, the Emperor transferred himself and the king to the New Palace, called Blachernae, in order to introduce variety, which is especially apt to relieve weariness. There, too, having assigned honourable apartments within his own palace with every obligation of hospitality fulfilled, he entertained the king kindly for several days in the very inner chambers of his forefathers. For the king’s followers likewise he caused lodgings, both honourable and convenient, to be prepared not far from the same palace.

There also, as before, the vestiarers and those to whom that duty had been assigned did not cease magnificently and superabundantly to supply expenses not merely necessary but abundantly luxurious [Col. 0805B] as well. The king toured the entire city, both its interior and exterior, together with its churches and monasteries, whose number is almost infinite, its columns bearing tokens of triumph, and its triumphal arches. Guided by great nobles and persons acquainted with the places, and inquiring from very old and prudent men into the reason and cause of each thing, he was fully instructed.

During those same days the king also sailed down the Bosporus as far as the mouth of the Pontic Sea [the Black Sea], where begins this channel called the Bosporus, flowing into the Mediterranean. Thus he visited unknown places like a man of inquisitive mind who wished to know the causes of things. When he had learned these matters fully [Col. 0805C] and returned to the city, he again sought private audience with the Emperor, desiring to bring to the wished-for conclusion the business that had occasioned his journey.

When suitable holidays had passed, the necessary matters had been discussed, and the business had happily been completed according to his wishes, the agreements on both sides reduced to terms mutually acceptable and set down in writing under the seals of both parties, he took leave; and, attended by the goodwill of all, he prepared for departure. Then imperial generosity first shone forth toward the king and his followers as if lavish, but wholly commendable. For, conferring immense quantities of gold upon the king, a multitude of silks, and exceptional gifts of foreign riches, the Emperor also loaded all the king’s followers, down to the least of the boys, with great gifts. The Protosebastos likewise, as a distinguished man, poured out his liberality upon all. The other princes too, fired by the same zeal and striving to outdo one another in generosity, offered gifts to the king, lacking neither intrinsic value nor elegance of workmanship nor favour in either respect.

The fleet having been assembled and the business happily concluded, the king entered the Bosporus—the strait recognized as the boundary between Europe and Asia—and, sailing two hundred miles from the city through that channel, passed between the famous cities of Sestus and Abydus, the homes of Leander and Hero, and entered the Mediterranean Sea. Thence, borne by favourable winds, he reached the city of Sidon on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July [15 June].

## CHAPTER XXVII. The king summons the army at Sephorim. Frederick, Archbishop of Tyre, returns from the lands beyond the mountains. Lord William, Bishop of Acre, is killed in Romania.

[Col. 0806A]

Having entered the kingdom, the king heard that Nūr al-Dīn was stationed with a large army in the district of Paneas. Fearing that he might be planning incursions into the kingdom from there, the king took such precautions as seemed expedient and went down into Galilee. Having summoned the princes of the kingdom, he encamped beside that celebrated spring which lies between Nazareth and Sephorim, so that, placed as it were in the centre of the kingdom, he might more conveniently move from there to any part of the realm should necessity call. Both he and his predecessors had customarily summoned armies there for the same reason.

In those same days, Lord Frederick, Archbishop of Tyre, our predecessor, who had been sent to seek counsel and aid for us from the Western princes, returned empty-handed after completing two years abroad. His hopes had been disappointed, and he had obtained none of the things sought in our name. He had, however, sent ahead Count Stephen, a man noble indeed by birth but not equally so in character, son of Count Theobald the Elder of Blois, Chartres, and Troyes. The king had summoned him through the same archbishop in order to give him his daughter in marriage. On reaching the kingdom and being kindly reminded by the king of that agreement, [Col. 0806C] Stephen rejected the terms formerly offered and agreed upon. After living shamefully and impurely in the kingdom for several months, he decided to return through the lands beyond it.

When he reached Antioch and thence Cilicia, intending, after first obtaining safe-conduct from the sultan of Iconium, to hasten through that sultan’s territory to Constantinople, he happened near the Cilician city of Mamistra to fall into an ambush laid for him by Milo, the very powerful Armenian prince and brother of Toros. Those concealed in ambush rushed upon him, stripped him as plunder of all the precious and highly desirable things he carried, and took them away. With many urgent entreaties he barely obtained from the robbers a worthless horse on which to be carried. With a few companions and after much hardship he eventually reached Constantinople in disgrace, hated by all the peoples of the East.

In the same year Count Stephen, his namesake but far unlike him in honour of character—a modest and wholly commendable man, son of Count William of Saône—and Henry the Younger, Duke of Burgundy, nephew through his sister of the aforesaid Stephen, entered the kingdom for prayer and devotion. After a brief stay, they returned home by way of the Emperor of Constantinople, who received them honourably and dismissed them with many gifts.

The following year, the eighth of King Amalric’s reign, Lord William of blessed memory, Bishop of Acre, was sent by the king from Constantinople into Italy. Having travelled through those regions and prudently and faithfully attempted every means of obtaining what he sought, [Col. 0807A] he was returning home by the route already traversed and was to return, by previous arrangement, to the Emperor. When he reached Adrianople, the renowned metropolis of Second Thrace, he suffered an unheard-of and undeserved death through a disastrous accident.

For at midday, weary from his long journey, after taking food he had surrendered his limbs to sleep. A certain Robert of his household, whom he himself had promoted to the priesthood and received among his familiars, was lying in the same chamber as the bishop. Recovering from a long illness by which he had been greatly afflicted, Robert was seized by madness and, taking up a sword, inflicted several wounds upon the sleeping bishop and pierced him mortally. Those outside heard him cry out and, recognizing his groans and sighs in the agony of death, wished to rush in to bring aid to their distressed lord, but could not enter because the door had been firmly fastened from within. At last they forcibly broke down the door and found their lord half-alive, with a little breath still remaining about his breast.

Wishing therefore to put the aforesaid criminal in chains and bring him to the punishments due to murderers under the law, the bishop forbade them by word and gesture. He prayed and begged that fuller pardon might be granted to Robert for the salvation of his own soul, earnestly requesting that the deed just committed should not be imputed to him unto death. He then yielded up his last breath to the Lord on the third day before the Kalends of July [29 June]. [Col. 0807B]

We have hitherto been unable to discover the certain cause of so great a crime. Some say that Robert, perpetrator of this great wickedness, had suffered from a long illness and, while recovering, was seized by the violence of frenzy and unknowingly descended to so abominable an offence. Others say that he committed so monstrous a crime out of hatred for a certain chamberlain who, relying excessively upon the bishop’s favour, was said to treat both Robert and the others badly. In the same year a certain Joscius, canon and subdeacon of the same church, was installed in that church on the ninth day before the Kalends of December [23 November].

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Milo the Armenian, brother of Lord Toros, allied with Nūr al-Dīn, ravages the territory of Antioch; the king hastens there to restrain his wickedness.

At about the same time, after the death of the magnificent and noble man frequently mentioned by us, Lord Toros, the greatest prince of the Armenians, a certain brother of his named Melier, a most wicked man, approached Nūr al-Dīn in order to claim his brother’s inheritance for himself. He asked and urgently requested military forces by which he might violently seize his brother’s inheritance. After the death of that brother, however, a certain Thomas, their common nephew through their sister, had, at the invitation of the princes of the region, peacefully possessed the whole principality of his uncle. He was a Latin, but lacked resourcefulness and was not very prudent in showing himself generous and accommodating to those who had summoned him.

Having agreed to such terms as seemed likely to please Nūr al-Dīn, Melier obtained from him a considerable part [Col. 0808A] of his army. Relying upon its aid, he became the first, contrary to the custom of his forefathers, to bring unbelievers into his paternal and ancestral inheritance. He violently entered his father’s land, expelled his nephew, and claimed the entire region for himself. Immediately after gaining power, he utterly seized, at the outset of his principality, all that the brothers of the Order of the Temple possessed in Cilicia, although he had once been their brother. Thereafter he joined himself to Nūr al-Dīn and the Turks by so close an alliance as scarcely exists even between brothers.

Thus becoming like an unbeliever and disregarding the law of the Lord, he inflicted every injury he could upon Christians, and persons captured either by chance, in battle, or in the storming of towns, he put in chains and took into enemy lands to be sold. The Prince of Antioch and the leading men of that region, seeing this wicked man rage against Christians more arrogantly than any enemy, took up arms against him. Although it is a dangerous precedent for believers to take arms against those regarded as belonging to the same profession, and although this seemed to have the character of civil war, they did not dare to overlook the wrongs inflicted upon their brethren. They therefore made war upon him and declared him a public enemy.

Meanwhile the king, hearing of the disturbance that had arisen in those parts and wishing to use his influence toward peace, went down with his household retinue to the territory of Antioch. From there he sent private messengers to the aforesaid utterly savage and God-forsaken Melier, asking and earnestly requesting [Col. 0808C] that he should come down to a conference with him at a place pleasing to Melier himself, on a suitable day. Though Melier appeared to receive this proposal gladly, his heart was far from it. Although the king attempted three or four times through messengers to bring this about, he was finally deceived by the wiles of the malicious man and made no progress in the matter.

At last, military forces having been gathered from the whole province, the entire Christian army of those regions entered Melier’s territory. In the plains of Cilicia—for it was hard and difficult to ascend into the mountains—they ranged over the country, burned crops, and tried to storm towns. Then a messenger bearing evil news came to the king [Col. 0808D] and reported, truly, that Nūr al-Dīn had besieged Petra, the metropolis of Second Arabia, which is also called Crac.

On hearing this, the king was greatly distressed. Having taken leave of the prince, he returned with all speed and with his household retinue. But before he had re-entered the kingdom, the princes of the land had prudently and vigorously assembled all the strength of the kingdom. They entrusted the command of the army to Lord Humphrey, the constable, while Lord Ralph, Bishop of Bethlehem, bore the Lord’s Cross. As they hastened energetically and without delay to their appointed destination, a messenger met them on their way and announced—again truly—that Nūr al-Dīn, having spared the city, had raised the siege and returned home. Thus when the king arrived in the kingdom, he found peace beyond his expectation, though in accordance with his wishes.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Saladin besieges the castle beyond the Jordan called Montreal; but accomplishes nothing and returns home.

In the following year Saladin, with immense forces and countless cavalry, prepared about the beginning of autumn to enter our lands, leading innumerable troops out of all Egypt. Having crossed the desert, he reached the place called the Turks’ Canna. The king, foreseeing his arrival, had gathered his armies and, taking with him the lord Patriarch and the life-giving and venerable wood of the Lord’s Cross, had pitched camp near Beersheba [Col. 0809B] so that he might more conveniently meet the approaching enemy at close quarters.

The place where Saladin was said to be with his army was scarcely sixteen miles from the royal camp; yet it was not firmly established in the king’s mind that he had reached that place. It was certain, however, that Saladin had encamped there because of the convenience of water. After deliberation with his princes, the king’s forces deliberately took different routes, as though purposefully avoiding an encounter with him. They directed the expeditionary forces and all the people toward Ascalon, verbally seeking the encounter which they had deliberately avoided while it was near. Then, coming to Darum and leading the army back from there to the place named above, they uselessly spent their resources and labour.

Saladin, following the plains of Idumaea, meanwhile went up with his troops into Syrian Sobal and besieged the castle which is the head and singular defence of the whole region. As the nature of the place permitted, he attacked it with vigorous efforts. The fortress stood on a high hill and was excellently fortified with towers, walls, and outer works. Outside the stronghold, on the slope of the hill, stood a suburb, yet in a place so lofty and steep that it feared neither assault nor the blows of arrows or engines. All the inhabitants of that place were faithful Christians, and consequently greater trust could be placed in them. Moreover, it was carefully and sufficiently furnished, according to the capacity of the place, with arms, provisions, and men. [Col. 0809D] Having spent several days there fruitlessly and seeing that he made no progress, Saladin ordered his men to return, entered the desert route, and went back into Egypt.

## CHAPTER XXX. Saladin devastates the whole land beyond the Jordan. The king keeps his army at a place called Carmel. Count Raymond of Tripoli returns from prison.

In the following year, the tenth of King Amalric’s reign, Saladin saw that in the preceding year he had not achieved much against our people. Wishing to make good his former failures, he gathered an immense army and great forces from every district of Egypt and again planned to enter the kingdom. [Col. 0810A] Entering the desert in July, so as to approach more secretly and thereby find greater opportunity for harm, he entered with his armies the same region he had invaded in the preceding year.

The king, being forewarned of his arrival, led with him the entire military strength of the kingdom and met him as far as the desert. When he was informed that Saladin had turned toward Syrian Sobal, as in the preceding year, he feared to follow him there, lest Saladin, hearing that the king was coming behind him, should enter the kingdom from the opposite side in order to ravage it. Accordingly, he went up into the mountains and, selecting a place suitable for a station, withdrew to Carmel.

This Carmel was not that mountain by the coast familiar to Elijah, but a certain village where the dwelling of foolish Nabal is recorded to have been. The king prudently chose it because of the availability of water. For there was there an ancient pool of immense size, supplying water for the use of the entire army. The place mentioned was also near the land beyond the Jordan, with only the Illustrious Valley, in which the Dead Sea lies, separating the two regions. Thus it was easier and more frequent for our people to receive news of the enemy’s deeds and learn their condition.

Meanwhile Saladin, while the king for the stated reason hesitated to approach those regions, gave everything he found outside the fortresses to the flames, cut down groves and vineyards, destroyed suburbs, and raged at will throughout the whole land. At last, having exercised his tyranny as he wished, he returned to Egypt about the end of September.

At the same time Lord Raymond the Younger, son of Raymond the Elder, Count of Tripoli, in the eighth year of his captivity—during which he had been held among the enemy in poverty and irons—restored himself to his former liberty by paying eighty thousand gold pieces for his ransom and returned to his ancestral county. The king kindly received him on his return and restored without difficulty his land, which he had preserved during the intervening period. Moreover, so that Raymond might be able to pay the cost of his ransom, the king bestowed many things upon him out of royal generosity. By his own example he also effectively persuaded his princes and the prelates of the churches to do likewise.

## CHAPTER XXXI. A description of the sect of the Assassins, and the sending of their envoy to the king.

[Col. 0810D]

In those same days an event occurred among us most dangerous and detestable, to be lamented by the kingdom and the Church to the present day and perhaps forever. That it may become more fully known, the narrative must begin somewhat earlier.

In the province of Tyre, called Phoenicia, near the bishopric of Antaradus, there is a people possessing ten castles with their dependent districts. Their number, as we have often heard, is about sixty thousand or more. They customarily appoint and elect as their master and teacher not by hereditary succession but by the pre-eminence of merit one whom, rejecting all other titles of dignity, they call the Elder. They are bound to him by such a bond of subjection and obedience that nothing is so hard, difficult, or dangerous that they do not undertake with eager minds to fulfil it at their master’s command. [Col. 0811A]

For among other things, if they have princes hateful to them or suspected by their people, one or more of their number, given a dagger, proceeds to the assigned target without considering the outcome or whether he can escape. Anxious to fulfil the command, he keeps watch and labours until, by some opportunity, he performs the imposed task and satisfies his master’s order. Both our people and the Saracens call these men Assassins—though we do not know from what origin the name is derived.

For four hundred years they cultivated the Saracens’ law and traditions with such zeal that, in comparison with them, all others were judged almost apostates, while they themselves seemed to fulfil the law. But in our days they appointed as their master a most eloquent man, subtle and of very keen intellect. Contrary to the custom of his predecessors, he began to keep with him books of the Gospels and the Apostolic book. Applying himself to their continual study, he had, after much labour, gained some understanding of the sequence of Christ’s miracles and precepts and also of the Apostle’s teaching. Comparing the sweet and honourable teaching of Christ and his followers with what the wretched deceiver Muhammad had handed down to his accomplices and dupes, everything he had imbibed with his mother’s milk began to seem vile to him; [Col. 0811C] and he came to abhor the impurities of that deceiver.

Teaching his people in the same manner, he caused them to cease observing that superstition. He threw down the prayer-houses they had formerly used, abolished their fasts, and permitted his followers wine and pork. Finally, wishing to advance toward the inner meaning of God’s law, he sent to the king a prudent man, wise in counsel, eloquent, and imbued with his master’s teaching, named Boaldelle, bearing secret words. The principal and greatest article of these was this: if the brothers of the Order of the Temple, who possessed castles bordering their country, would remit the two thousand gold pieces which they customarily took every year from those people as a kind of tribute, and would thereafter observe brotherly charity, the Assassins would hasten to the faith of Christ and baptism.

## CHAPTER XXXII. The envoy of the Assassins is killed by the brothers of the Order of the Temple, and a great commotion is stirred up in the kingdom. Ralph, Bishop of Bethlehem, dies.

The king received their embassy gladly and with gratitude. As a most discerning man, he fully assented to their request and was, it is said, prepared to repay from his own revenues to the aforesaid brothers the two thousand gold pieces whose annual payment the Assassins requested to have remitted. He had long kept the envoy with him for completion of the negotiations; then, giving him a guide for the journey and a guard for his person, [Col. 0812A] he sent him back to his own master, that the proposal made might be wholly brought to completion.

As the envoy passed through Tripoli with his travelling companion and assigned guide, and was about to enter his own territory, certain of the aforesaid brothers suddenly rushed upon him unexpectedly with drawn swords. Killing a man who relied upon royal safe-conduct and the good faith of our people, unsuspecting and fearing no such thing, they incurred the crime of violated majesty.

When the king heard this, he was violently inflamed by the atrocity of the deed with anger almost amounting to madness. Summoning the princes of the kingdom and declaring that whatever had happened redounded to his own injury, he sought instruction as to what he ought to do. Finally, by the common counsel of the princes, he was advised not to disregard what had occurred, for in it royal authority seemed to be impaired, the faith and constancy of the Christian name incurred undeserved infamy, and the Eastern Church might lose an increase pleasing to God and already prepared.

Accordingly, by common counsel, certain nobles were sent—Seiher of Mamedune and Godescalc of Turholt, specially chosen for this purpose—to demand of Odo of Saint Amand, master of the aforesaid brothers, satisfaction to the king and the whole kingdom for so grave an excess and heinous crime. A certain brother of theirs, Walter of Maisnil, an evil one-eyed man, whose spirit was in his nostrils and who possessed no discretion at all, was said to have done this with the knowledge of the brethren. [Col. 0812C] Hence, sparing him beyond what was due, the master reportedly informed the king through messengers that he had imposed penance upon the brother who committed the deed and would send him with that imposed penance to the lord Pope. He further prohibited anyone, on the authority of the lord Pope, from daring to lay violent hands upon the said brother. He added other things prompted by the spirit of pride, in which he himself greatly abounded, which it is not very necessary to insert into the present narrative.

The king, who was at Sidon on this business, found the same master with many of his brothers and the same criminal. Having consulted with those accompanying him on his journey thither, he forcibly removed the offender against majesty from their house, conveyed him in chains to Tyre, and committed him to prison. [Col. 0812D]

On this occasion the whole kingdom came close to suffering irreparable ruin. Yet the king proved his innocence before the master of the Assassins, whose envoy had perished in so disastrous an event. Toward the aforesaid brothers he used considerable moderation, and left the matter unresolved until the day of his death. It is said, nevertheless, that had he recovered from that final illness, he intended to pursue the question more carefully, through most honourable envoys, with the kings and princes of the world.

Very soon afterward, the venerable brother Lord Ralph of happy memory, Bishop of Bethlehem and royal chancellor, a man exceedingly generous and kindly, met his appointed day and was honourably buried in the chapter-house [Col. 0813A] of his church. After his death, when discussion was held in the same church concerning the appointment of a pastor, conflicting preferences led to difficult disputes. These were scarcely settled in the second year of Lord Baldwin, successor and son of Lord Amalric, and brought many losses upon the aforesaid church.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Nūr al-Dīn dies. The king besieges Paneas and withdraws after making a truce; stricken by illness, he proceeds to Jerusalem, where he dies a few days later.

At the same time, after scarcely a month had elapsed, Nūr al-Dīn, the greatest persecutor of the Christian name and faith—yet a just, shrewd, and provident prince, and religious according to the traditions of his people—died in May, in the twenty-ninth year of his reign. [Col. 0813B] On hearing of his death, the king immediately and without delay summoned all the forces of the kingdom and besieged the city of Paneas.

When the wife of the aforesaid prince heard this, she rose above feminine weakness and sent an embassy to the king, promising him a specified great sum of money if he would withdraw from the siege and grant her a temporary peace. The king, wishing to exact a greater sum, appeared at first to refuse, while nevertheless continuing the siege. Having attacked the besieged for about fifteen days with vigilant labour and diligent effort, inflicting many hardships upon them by engines and other means, he saw that they grew more resolute in resistance each day. Fully recognizing that he was making no progress, and as the envoys of the noble lady pressed him more urgently to obtain peace, he accepted the stipulated money, while twenty captive knights of our people were restored to freedom. Then, entertaining greater designs, he raised the siege and returned, complaining to his intimates that he was not quite well and was not in good bodily condition.

Having dismissed the expeditionary forces, he came with his household retinue to Tiberias, where he began to suffer most dangerously from dysentery. Fearing the illness, he then entered Jerusalem by way of Nazareth and Neapolis, riding on horseback and not yet utterly debilitated. There, as his condition worsened, he began to suffer most violently also from fever, while the dysentery ceased despite the physicians’ art. After being afflicted by that fever beyond his strength for several days, he ordered Greek and Syrian physicians and men of those nations to be summoned, urgently begging them to loosen his bowels by some decoction. [Col. 0814B] When he could not obtain this from them, he next had Latin physicians summoned. Demanding the same thing from them, he added that the outcome of everything should be imputed to himself.

They gave him a decoction, and after taking it he passed stool several times without difficulty, so that he thought himself better. Yet before his body, exhausted by the violence of the medicine, could be restored by food, the usual fever returned, and he passed into death. He died in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1173, on the fifth day before the Ides of July [11 July]; in the twelfth year and fifth month of his reign; and in the thirty-eighth year of his age. He was buried among his predecessors, beside his brother and in the same line, before the place of Calvary. He was a prudent and discerning man, wholly fit to govern the kingdom; at whose prayers and urgings we undertook to commit to writing in this present work the deeds both of his predecessors and of himself.

# HERE BEGINS THE TWENTY-FIRST BOOK.

[Col. 0813]

## CHAPTER I. On the first beginnings of Baldwin IV, sixth king of Jerusalem; on his character, age, and bodily appearance.

[Col. 0813C]

[Col. 0813D] The sixth Latin king of Jerusalem was Lord Baldwin IV, son of King Amalric, of illustrious memory, of whom we have spoken above, by Agnes the countess, daughter of Joscelin the Younger, count of Edessa, whom we have often mentioned in the preceding books. As has been said, when he was called to his ancestral kingdom, due to him by hereditary right, Lord Amalric, patriarch of Jerusalem of good memory, following in the footsteps of his predecessor Lord Fulcher, compelled him by ecclesiastical censure to put her away. For they were said—and indeed this was true—to be related within a prohibited degree of consanguinity, as we explained more carefully when we treated in sequence of the reign of Lord Amalric.

While he was still a boy of about nine years, when we held the archdeaconry of Tyre, his father, greatly concerned for his education, entrusted him to us for instruction and training in the liberal arts, with many entreaties and under the assurance of his favor. While he was with us, and we bestowed upon him vigilant care and such attention as befitted a royal child, both in moral discipline and in literary study, it happened that, as the sons of nobles who were with him played together and, as is the custom of boisterous boys, pinched one another’s hands and arms with their nails, the others expressed their sensation of pain by cries; but he, as though free from pain, endured it with extraordinary patience, although his companions did not spare him. When this happened once and repeatedly, and was reported to me, I first thought it arose from the virtue of patience rather than from a defect of sensation. Calling him, I began to inquire [Col. 0815A] what was the matter; and at last I discovered that his right arm and the corresponding hand were numb over one half, so that he felt no pinching at all, nor even bites.

I began to be troubled, recalling to myself that saying of the Wise Man: “It is certain that a numbed limb is far removed from health, and that one who is ill without feeling himself ill suffers more dangerously.” This was reported to his father; and, after physicians had been consulted, they diligently—but vainly—attempted to help him with repeated fomentations, ointments, and medicines. For, as in the passage of time we learned more fully from the event itself, this was the beginning of a more extensive and wholly incurable affliction, foreshadowed in this way. And—what we cannot say with dry eyes—when he began to reach the years of puberty, he appeared to suffer most dangerously from leprosy. As it grew excessively worse day by day, especially injuring his extremities and face, it distressed the hearts of his faithful followers with compassion whenever they looked upon him.

Yet he made progress in literary study, and every day grew more and more into a youth of good promise and admirable natural disposition. For his age he was handsome in appearance; and, unlike the custom of his forefathers, he was exceptionally well suited to mounting and governing horses. He had a retentive memory and loved conversation; he was nevertheless frugal, but also very mindful alike of favors and injuries. He resembled his father in every respect—not only in face, but in his whole body, his gait, and the modulation of his speech. He was quick of mind, but somewhat impeded in speech; [Col. 0815C] an eager listener to histories, like his father, and very obedient to wholesome advice.

## CHAPTER II. At what time he was anointed and crowned.

At his father’s death he was scarcely thirteen years old. He had a sister named Sibylla, older than himself, by the same mother, who was being brought up in the convent of Saint Lazarus at Bethany under Lady Yvette, abbess of that place and his father’s maternal aunt. Therefore, after his father’s death, all the princes of the kingdom, ecclesiastical as well as secular, gathered together. In accordance with the unanimous desire of all, in the church of the Holy Sepulchre of the Lord, he was solemnly anointed and crowned according to custom by Lord Amalric, patriarch of Jerusalem of good memory, assisted by archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of the Churches, on the Ides of July, the fourth day after his father’s death.

At that time Lord Alexander III presided over the holy Roman Church; Lord Almeric over the holy Church of Antioch; Lord Amalric over that of Jerusalem; and Lord Frederick over that of Tyre. At Constantinople ruled Lord Manuel, of glorious and pious memory; among the Romans, Lord Frederick; among the French, Lord Louis; in England, Lord Henry, son of Geoffrey, count of Anjou; and in Sicily, Lord William II, likewise son of the elder Lord William. At Antioch Lord Bohemond, son of Prince Raymond, held authority; and at Tripoli Lord [Col. 0816A] Raymond the Younger, son of Count Raymond the Elder.

## CHAPTER III. In the first year of his reign, a fleet of the king of Sicily, arriving at Alexandria, suffers an enormous loss. The count of Tripoli claims administration of the kingdom and guardianship of the king as the nearest agnate.

In the first year of this Lord Baldwin, about the beginning of August, a fleet of two hundred ships, sent by Lord William, king of Sicily, to attack Alexandria and carrying worthy forces both of infantry and cavalry, landed in Egypt. There, while its commanders and principal officers acted too carelessly, and very many of both ranks were lost, some captured and some slain by the sword, they withdrew in confusion after remaining five or six days around the city.

In our kingdom, while Milo of Plancy was administering the affairs of the realm, grave hostilities arose between him and certain princes of the kingdom. For they envied him and were deeply agitated because, without their knowledge or summons, he alone—presuming too much upon himself and scorning the others—was always at the king’s side; and because, excluding all the rest from royal intimacy, he administered the business of the kingdom without consulting them.

Meanwhile the count of Tripoli approached the lord king and, before the princes who happened then to be present, requested administration of the kingdom, maintaining that the lawful guardianship of the lord king, who was still below the years of puberty, was due to him by right of agnation. He said that this was his by several arguments: first, because he was the nearest of all [Col. 0816C] the king’s blood-relations; secondly, because he was the wealthiest and most powerful of all the king’s faithful men; and he added a third and very powerful reason. While he himself was a captive, he had commanded his faithful men from prison, under the obligation of loyalty, to surrender all his land, strongholds, and castles to Lord King Amalric, the father of the present king, and to subject all things to his commands and complete authority. He had further added, at the close of his words, that should it happen that he ended his life in prison by human fate, he had appointed the aforesaid lord king, because he was the nearest of all his relatives, heir to his entire estate.

For all these reasons he asked that this recompense be rendered to him, more as a matter of honor than in hope of any future advantage. An answer to the count’s allegations was deferred on the pretext that the lord king had too few of the greater men of the kingdom with him whose counsel he could presently use. Yet he promised that at a suitable time he would summon them more promptly and generally, and, after their counsel had been heard, would give, with the Lord’s help, a fitting answer concerning all these matters.

When this had been done, the count returned to his own lands. Almost all the people favored the count; among the barons were Humphrey of Toron, the royal constable, Baldwin of Ramla, his brother Balian, and Raynald of Sidon; and all the bishops likewise favored him.

## CHAPTER IV. Milo of Plancy is killed at Acre. Frederick, archbishop of Tyre, dies.

The aforesaid Milo of Plancy, of whom we have spoken, [Col. 0817A] was a nobleman of Champagne beyond the mountains, from the land of Count Henry of Troyes. He had been exceedingly intimate with, and a kinsman of, Lord King Amalric, so that the king appointed him seneschal of his kingdom. At last, after the death of the younger Humphrey, son of the elder Humphrey, he gave him as wife Stephanie, the widow, daughter of Philip of Nablus. By his wife’s right he was lord of Oultrejordain, that is, the region beyond the Jordan commonly called Montreal. The aforesaid widow, however, had borne twins by her former husband, namely a son and a daughter.

This man, as we have said, trusting in the excessive intimacy he had enjoyed with the lord king’s father, held the princes of the kingdom—even those greater than himself—in contempt. He was an incautious man, proud and arrogant, lavish of useless words, and presuming more than was right upon himself. In order to seem in some measure to soften the envy of others, by a contrivance too obvious to conceal its artifice, he had put forward one Roard, keeper of the citadel of Jerusalem, an ordinary man of inferior competence, as though Roard were in command and Milo merely obeyed his orders. But the reverse was the case: one bore a title more splendid than substantial, while the other, under this pretext, managed the affairs of the kingdom according to his own will.

Therefore, while he conducted himself heedlessly, spoke too imprudently, recalled all the business of the kingdom to his own direction against the will of the others, arranged everything and [Col. 0817C] disposed of everything at his pleasure, a persistent hatred was formed against him, and certain men were hired to plot against his life. When this was reported to him, he dismissed it as a trifling matter of no account. Continuing, as usual, to act incautiously, he was staying in the city of Acre when, at the first twilight of night, he was pierced with swords in the public street, shamefully and ignominiously handled, and killed.

Various opinions about his murder circulated among the people. Some said that it had happened to him because of the loyalty which he devotedly showed to the lord king; others, on the contrary, that he was secretly preparing the kingdom for himself, having sent messengers to his friends and acquaintances in France to hasten to him, with whose assistance he believed he could obtain the kingdom. But neither assertion has been established to our certainty. It was nevertheless well known that Balian of Jaffa, brother of the aforesaid Roard, had been sent to the lands beyond the mountains with royal letters and gifts, and that Milo awaited his arrival day by day.

At the same time, in the same month, Lord Frederick, our predecessor as archbishop of Tyre, a man exceedingly noble in worldly lineage, of whom we have spoken above, after being detained for some time at Naples by a very grave illness, entered upon the way of all flesh on the third day before the Kalends of November [30 October]. His body was brought to Jerusalem with fitting funeral rites and due honor, and was buried in the chapter-house of the Temple of the Lord, where he had formerly been a regular canon.

## CHAPTER V. A description of the count of Tripoli: his character and ancestry; how he assumed administration of the kingdom. The writer of this history is made the king’s chancellor.

[Col. 0818A]

At the same time, when the princes of the kingdom and the prelates of the Churches had been summoned and the king was at Jerusalem, the count of Tripoli returned again to hear the answer to his earlier petitions for the administration of the kingdom. Repeating his request and pressing the same points, while the king deliberated for two entire days, at last, with the common assent of all, administration and authority over the whole kingdom after the lord king were entrusted to him in the chapter-house of the Holy Sepulchre of the Lord, amid the acclamation of the people.

Since the course of events has introduced the count into our narrative, it is fitting that we should commit to the memory of posterity what we have learned with certainty concerning him—not because we intend to write a panegyric, but in order to explain, as briefly as the compressed style of history permits, what sort of man he was. This Count Raymond, of whom we speak, drew the seed of his bodily descent from the elder Lord Raymond, that great prince in the army of the Lord whose work, zeal, and labors restored the eastern kingdom to the service of Christ, as we carefully explained above when treating of the first princes who came in the first expedition.

The aforesaid elder Lord Raymond, of good memory, [Col. 0818C] had a son named Bertrand, who after his father’s death and the murder of William Jordan, nephew of the aforesaid count, obtained the county of Tripoli. He had a son named Pons, who possessed the same county by hereditary right after his father’s death. Pons took as wife Cecilia, daughter of King Philip of France and widow of Tancred; by her he had a son named Raymond, who succeeded him in the county. This Raymond took as wife Hodierna, daughter of Lord Baldwin II, king of Jerusalem. From them was born this Raymond of whom we now speak, who succeeded his father in the same county after his father had been killed by a sudden attack of the Assassins at the gate of the city of Tripoli.

Thus the aforesaid count was cousin to Kings Amalric and Baldwin on his mother’s side; for they were sons of two sisters. On his father’s side he was one degree more remote. For his grandmother—the mother of his father, namely Cecilia, of whom we have spoken—was the sister of King Fulk, father of Kings Baldwin and Amalric, by the same mother though not by the same father. The mother of both Fulk and Cecilia, sister of Lord Amalric of Montfort, had been given in marriage to the elder Fulk, count of Anjou. Later, after bearing the younger Fulk, she left her husband and went to King Philip of France, by whom she bore this Cecilia and certain other children. Nonetheless, King Philip, madly infatuated by love for the aforesaid countess, expelled, contrary to ecclesiastical law, his lawful wife the queen, by whom he had already had Louis and Constance. [Col. 0819A] Thus, on both sides of their parentage, the count and the two aforesaid kings were bound to one another by ties of consanguinity.

The aforesaid count was a thin man, somewhat lean, moderately tall, dark-complexioned in face, with straight hair of moderately dark brown, keen eyes, erect shoulders, and a composed mind. He was very prudent and vigorous in his actions; in food and drink, almost superhumanly sober; generous toward strangers, though not very affable toward his own people. He was moderately learned, but strove, more through the natural quickness of his mind and in the manner of King Amalric, to grasp the understanding of the Scriptures; this he had acquired with the greatest labor while in enemy captivity. He was frequent in asking questions, if he had present someone whom he judged sufficient to resolve them.

In the same year in which he assumed the administration of the kingdom, he married Lady Eschiva, widow of Lord Walter, prince of Galilee, a very wealthy woman who had borne children by her former husband. Yet after she came to him, for a hidden reason she ceased to bear children. He is said to love her together with her children as dearly as though she had borne every one of them to him. But, having briefly completed this digression, let us return to the course of our history.

At the same time, since in the preceding summer Lord Ralph, bishop of Bethlehem and chancellor of the kingdom, of good memory, had departed this life, so that there might be someone to care for the royal letters, the king, by the counsel of his princes, [Col. 0819C] called us to the aforesaid office and bestowed upon us the dignity of chancellor.

## CHAPTER VI. Saladin, summoned by the Damascenes, obtains Damascus and the remaining regions of the country. The count of Tripoli is sent against him to oppose his designs.

In the same year Saladin, son of Najm al-Din, nephew through his brother of Shirkuh, who had succeeded his uncle Shirkuh in the kingdom of Egypt, was secretly summoned by the leading men of Damascus. Their lawful lord, al-Malik al-Salih, namely the still underage son of Nur al-Din, was staying at Aleppo. Entrusting the care of Egypt to one of his brothers named Sayf al-Din, Saladin hastened through the waste of the desert into Syria in order to seize the kingdom of Damascus, and arrived at Damascus. Within not many days, when the citizens surrendered it, he received the city; then he hurried toward Coele-Syria, hoping that he would receive all its cities into his dominion without war. Nor was he disappointed in this hope. For within a short time, as the inhabitants surrendered the places and of their own accord opened the entrances, he received all the cities of that province, in violation of the loyalty owed to their lord, whose servant he had been: Heliopolis in Greek, now called Malbec, in Arabic Baalbek; Emesa, commonly called Camela; Hama; and Caesarea, commonly called Great Caesarea. He further presumed that Aleppo and the boy himself would be handed over to him through the work of certain traitors; but this was prevented by a certain turn of events.

[Col. 0820A] While these things were happening in those regions, the lord king, after taking counsel concerning what ought to be done in so sudden an event and so great a change of circumstances, deliberated long with his princes. At last all agreed that the lord count should hasten as quickly as possible to Coele-Syria with an army drawn both from the kingdom and from his own county. He was further commanded to oppose Saladin’s advances with every effort—and rightly so. For all his growth was suspect to us, and everything that accrued to him appeared to be wholly lost to us. He was a man prudent in counsel, vigorous in arms, and exceedingly liberal; and for that reason he was particularly suspect to our wiser men. For there is no other bait by which princes commonly reconcile to themselves the hearts of subjects, and indeed of all other men, nor anything that more binds the minds of strangers, than generosity—especially princely generosity.

He was therefore justly suspect to us, lest, with possessions doubled and power increased by a double dominion, he should rise against us more fiercely and harass us more violently. And this, while our efforts have come to nothing and we have tried in vain to restrain him, we now behold with tearful eyes: that he rises against us with such power by land and sea; that, unless “the Dayspring from on high” mercifully visits us (Luke 1:78), there is no hope of resistance. It seemed safer, surely, to provide assistance to the boy who was still under age, not as though some act of humanity ought to be rendered to him out of favor, but so that an adversary might be maintained against a more dangerous rival, and, while he delayed Saladin, Saladin’s attacks upon us might become weaker.

## CHAPTER VII. Reasons are assigned why enemies prevail over our people more than formerly.

I should like to depart for a little while from the thread of history, not for the useless purpose of wandering aside, but in order to introduce something not without profit. It is often asked—and rightly seems worthy of inquiry—what is the reason why our fathers, though fewer in number, often endured in battle greater enemy forces more bravely; and why, more frequently, with divine aid, they crushed larger enemy battalions and often an innumerable multitude with a small force; so that even the very Christian name was a terror to peoples ignorant of God, and the Lord was glorified in the works of our fathers.

But men of our time, by contrast, are often found defeated by fewer opponents; and though sometimes more numerous against fewer, they are found to have attempted something in vain and at times to have succumbed. When we carefully consider and examine our condition, the first cause that presents itself looks to God as its author: in place of our fathers, who were religious men and feared God, there have been born utterly ruined sons, wicked sons, violators of the Christian faith, everywhere and indiscriminately pursuing every unlawful thing—such men, or worse, as said to the Lord their God: “Depart from us; we do not desire knowledge of thy ways” (Job 21:14). Because their sins demand it, the Lord rightly withdraws grace from them, as though provoked to anger.

Such are the people of the present age, and especially of the eastern regions. If anyone attempted to pursue their manners—or rather, their monstrous vices—with a more careful pen, he would be overwhelmed by the immensity of the material and would seem to be composing a satire rather than weaving history.

A second cause presents itself: in former times, when those venerable men, led by divine zeal and inwardly enflamed by fervor of faith, first came down into the eastern lands, they were accustomed to military discipline, trained in battles, and familiar with the use of arms. The eastern people, by contrast, weakened by long peace, unacquainted with military affairs, untrained in the rules of battle, rejoiced in idleness. Therefore it was no wonder if a few more lightly withstood many, or, having defeated them in military encounters, gained the better result and carried off victory with its palm. In such matters, as those know better than I who have senses more fully exercised in them, experience hardened by long and continual practice often prevails against forces untrained and lacking skill.

A third cause, no less important or effective, again presents itself: in ancient times almost every city had different lords, to speak in the manner of our Aristotle—not subordinate one to another, who were seldom of like purpose and more often acted from contrary interests. Against men differing in counsel, or more often opposed, and mutually suspicious, battle was fought with less danger, since they could neither easily nor willingly unite to repel common injuries; nor did they readily arm for our destruction, for they feared their own neighbors no less than ours.

But now all the kingdoms adjoining us have, with the Lord thus permitting it, been reduced to the power of one man. For in recent times, the most savage man Sanguin, abhorred the Christian name as though it were a pestilence, father of the recently deceased Nur al-Din, after violently occupying other kingdoms, violently seized in our own memory the noble and distinguished Median metropolis of Rages, called by another name Edessa, after delivering the faithful who were in it to death, together with all its territory. Likewise his son Nur al-Din, having expelled the king of Damascus—more through the treachery of his people than by his own strength—claimed that kingdom for himself and added it to his paternal inheritance. Finally, the same Nur al-Din, through the service and skill of Shirkuh, made subject to himself the most ancient and immensely rich kingdom of Egypt, as we discussed more fully above when treating the reign of Lord Amalric.

Thus, as we have said, all the neighboring kingdoms obey the rule of one man and serve one man’s nod, even unwillingly; at his voice, as though one man, they arm for our injury. There is no one carried away by a divergent purpose; there is no one who disregards his lord’s commands with impunity. All these possessions are held by Saladin, of whom we have often spoken, a man indeed of humble birth and lowest station, with fortune smiling upon him too favorably: from Egypt and adjacent territories he has an immeasurable abundance of the finest and purest gold, called *obryzum*; from other provinces he has countless bands of horsemen, fighters, and men thirsting for gold, whom it is easy enough to gather for those possessing an abundance of gold.

But let us now return to the history. As we have stated, all who were present agreed that this man, so magnificent and advancing by continual successes toward the highest summit, should be resisted by every means, lest, once he had greater power, he should rise as a harsher enemy against us. Therefore the lord count, taking with him the princes of the kingdom and gathering military assistance from every side, hastened into the region of Tripoli; and there, encamping near the borders of Arqa, he settled in that part of the country called Galifa.

## CHAPTER VIII. The lord of Mosul hastens to assist his nephew. Saladin advances and occupies the whole region. The count makes an agreement with him and receives hostages.

While these things were occurring among us, the uncle of Nur al-Din’s son, a most powerful prince and, among the eastern Parthian people, a man of the greatest power, named Qutb al-Din, heard that after his brother’s death Saladin, disregarding the laws of humanity, forgetful of his own condition and ungrateful for the benefits conferred upon him by the boy’s father, had thus risen against his still underage lord. He gathered a large force of cavalry, of which he was said to possess the greatest abundance, crossed the Euphrates, and came to bring aid to his nephew against his traitors.

This was the great prince, lord of that most ancient and most famous city of Nineveh, which is said formerly to have done penance in sackcloth and ashes at the exhorting word of the prophet Jonah. But now, with its name changed and rebuilt from the remains of buildings and people at a place not very far from the older site, it is called Mosul, still retaining metropolitan dignity throughout Assyria. After arriving, he pitched camp in the plains around Aleppo.

Meanwhile Saladin, no less actively, received without war, by the voluntary surrender of their citizens, Bostra, the great metropolis of Arabia Prima, and Heliopolis, now commonly called Malbec. He then besieged the city of Emesa, called [Col. 0822D] Camela; and without any delay the citizens of the same city surrendered to him its lower part. For upon a somewhat elevated hill stood the citadel of the city, sufficiently fortified, to which the faithful men of the aforesaid boy had withdrawn; they had first strengthened it amply and carefully with both arms and provisions. He had also received the neighboring cities of the same province as their inhabitants surrendered them: Hama, Caesarea, and the entire region as far as Aleppo itself.

Those who were in the citadel of Emesa sent messengers to the count of Tripoli and to our men who, as stated, were in camp, waiting to be summoned by either side amid so great a disturbance on desirable terms. They asked them not to hesitate to come, promising that assistance against so pestilential a man would not be without gain and fitting profit. Now the lord count’s hostages were held in the same town. When he was released from prison, he had pledged them to Nur al-Din, the boy’s father, for his ransom and a specified sum amounting to sixty thousand gold pieces. There were also held there some hostages of Lord Raynald of Sidon for his brother Eustace.

Hoping that, in exchange for the assistance requested, they could recover them by some agreement from the commander of the citadel in which they were held, they hastened thither with all their forces. But finding no substance in his words—for he had hope that his aforesaid lord could lift the siege—they returned, after many shifts of deliberation, to the camp from which they had first departed.

Meanwhile Saladin, seeing that our men had withdrawn as though offended, grew more confident and, presuming greatly upon their absence, approached nearer to Aleppo. He began to challenge the army of the aforesaid prince to battle and provoke it by frequent raids. As he pressed them more and more, an engagement took place between them at close quarters and with great severity. At last, when the men of Nineveh were defeated—by the treachery, it was said, of their own men, corrupted by money—Saladin won the victory. Returning thence to Emesa, he received at last not only the city, as before, but also its citadel.

Then he sent an embassy to the count, asking the lord count not to oppose his successes, but to allow him to test his strength against the son of Nur al-Din and the others who had come to his aid. Lest the count reject even this without fitting recompense, Saladin offered to restore without payment the count’s hostages and those of Lord Raynald. This proposal pleased the lord count. Having received the hostages in accordance with the terms of the agreement, and having dismissed the other nobles who had been on the expedition with suitable generosity, they broke camp and returned home.

Humphrey of Toron, the royal constable, was said to have been mediator of all these negotiations; he was accused of being bound to the aforesaid Saladin by an excessively intimate attachment. Thus, contrary to our intention, favor was extended to the very man whom we ought wholly to have opposed, lest, made more powerful against [Col. 0823D] us, he should grow more insolent and violent than usual; and he dared to hope for support from us even while he was continually increasing to our injury. They departed from us about the Kalends of January and returned home again at the Kalends of May.

## CHAPTER IX. Mainard, bishop of Beirut, dies. The writer of this history is promoted to the metropolitan see of Tyre.

In these same days Lord Mainard, bishop of Beirut, of good memory, after being seized by illness and languishing for some time in the city of Tyre, was overtaken by death on the seventh day before the Kalends of May [25 April]. May his soul rest in peace. In the same month, when the Church of Tyre had been vacant for seven continuous months, with the clergy and people unanimously desiring it and with the king’s assent, as custom required, we were called—by God’s forbearance rather than through our merits—to govern that Church. Within ten days, in the church of the Holy Sepulchre of the Lord, through the hands of Lord Amalric, patriarch of Jerusalem, we received, by the Lord’s authorizing, the office of consecration on the sixth day before the Ides of June [8 June], though unworthy.

## CHAPTER X. The king enters the territory of Damascus and ravages it. Hernesius, archbishop of Caesarea, dies.

At the same time, while Saladin was more closely occupied in those regions, word was brought to the lord king that the territory of Damascus, without troops and without a governor, lay quite open to plunder and to the other injuries which may lawfully be inflicted upon enemies in war. On learning this, he gathered military forces, crossed the Jordan, and, passing through the forest adjoining the city of Banias and deriving its name from it, with the famous promontory of Lebanon on his left, reached the territory of Damascus. It was harvest-time.

Our men therefore ranged abroad and freely traversed the whole region, committing to the flames grain either gathered upon the threshing floors, still standing in the ground, or heaped in sheaves through the fields. The people, having learned beforehand of their approach, had withdrawn with their wives and little children to more fortified places. Thus, holding the region at their pleasure, our men reached as far as Darayya. This is a suburban place adjoining Damascus, scarcely four miles from it. From there they came also to Bedegene, a place situated at the foot of Lebanon, from which clear waters issue, and therefore called “the House of Delight.” Against the will and strenuous resistance of its inhabitants, they seized the place by force; enriched with plunder and carrying off booty and spoils, while the Damascenes looked on and could not resist, they returned home safe and unharmed after several days.

At the same time Lord Hernesius, archbishop of Caesarea, of good memory, died; and in his place Lord Heraclius, archdeacon of Jerusalem, was elected and consecrated.

## CHAPTER XI. The king again enters the territory of the enemy Damascenes and plunders the valley called Bachar. Raynald of Châtillon and Joscelin, the king’s paternal uncle, are released from enemy captivity.

[Col. 0824D]

In the second year of the reign of the lord Baldwin IV, while Saladin was still occupied with affairs in the region of Aleppo, in August, on the first day of the month, the lord king again entered the enemy’s territory, having summoned the magnates of the kingdom and assembled an army. Crossing the district of Sidon and ascending the highlands lying between our borders and those of the enemy, he reached a place endowed with almost every temporal advantage: fertile soil, watered by springs, and called Messaara. Descending thence into the valley called Bacar, he found a land which, as Scripture says, flowed with milk [Col. 0825A] and honey.

Some believe that this region was formerly called Ituraea, of which Philip, son of Herod the Elder, is called tetrarch in the Gospel of Luke (chap. III), together with the region of Trachonitis. In still earlier times, namely in the age of the kings of Israel, it was called the Forest of Lebanon, because the valley, extending to the foothills of Lebanon, is distinguished by rich soil, healthful waters, a numerous population, plentiful suburban settlements, and a pleasantly temperate climate. In its lower parts a city is shown even today, encircled by strong walls and displaying in its ancient buildings many marks of former nobility; its modern name is Amegarra. Certain investigators of antiquity suppose this to be Palmyra, once a famous [Col. 0825B] colony in Phoenicia, mentioned by Ulpian of Tyre in the Digest, New Title 10, “On Censuses.”

Having arrived there, our men began freely to range throughout the whole region, with no one resisting them, and to lay everything waste with fire. The inhabitants of the country had fled to the mountains, to which our men could not easily make their way. But they had placed their flocks and herds, for the most part, in the marshes in the middle of the valley, where the pastures were most abundant, having learned beforehand of our men’s approach.

Meanwhile the count of Tripoli, according to their agreement, entered suddenly through the district of Byblos, near the castle called Manethera, into the territory of Heliopolis; and he was reported to be burning everything in that same valley together with his men. When our men [Col. 0825C] heard this, they hurried to meet them; and they likewise, no less eager to meet us, came together as though in the middle of the valley. Hearing this, Semsedolus, Saladin’s brother, who resided at Damascus as governor, assembled troops; and, with the inhabitants of the area also gathering, he attempted resistance, drew up his battle-lines, and prepared to go out against our men.

Our men likewise, having arranged their ranks, advanced with greater eagerness. Both sides fought bravely; but, with God’s favour, many having been killed and countless others captured, the enemy was put to flight. Semsedolus escaped with a few men and withdrew to the steep heights of the mountain. Our men returned laden with hostile spoils, herds, and immense booty, though a few were lost through imprudence: they had entered the marshes to fight, did not know the paths, [Col. 0825D] and had not expected so sudden a return by our men.

The lord king and his men therefore returned in complete safety, driving herds of cattle, flocks of sheep, and every kind of household goods—the proofs of victory and emblems of success—and, by God’s aid, reached Tyre. The count of Tripoli too, returning by the route on which he had come and bringing with him innumerable spoils, happily withdrew with all his men to his own lands.

In the same year, the lord Reynald of Châtillon, who had succeeded the lord Raymond, prince of Antioch, in that principality by marrying his wife Constance, was restored to liberty after many years of captivity, which he had endured most harshly at Aleppo. His friends intervened, and a large sum of money was paid for him. At the same time Joscelin, son of Count Joscelin of Edessa and maternal uncle of the lord king, was rescued from captivity through the care and exertions of Countess Agnes, wife of Reynald of Sidon—his sister, namely the king’s mother—and returned to his former liberty. [Col. 0826A]

In the same year, on the second day of May, through our ministry in the church of Tyre, the lord Odo, bishop-elect of Sidon, formerly precentor of that same church of Tyre, and the lord Reynald, bishop-elect of Beirut, received the rite of consecration.

## CHAPTER XII. The emperor of Constantinople suffers an ignominious defeat at Iconium.

[Col. 0826B]

At the same time the lord Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, of illustrious memory and a recollection to be cherished in Christ—whose benefits and extraordinary generosity are felt by almost the entire world—was fighting, in a commendable impulse of piety, against the most savage Turkish people and their impious leader, the sultan of Iconium, for the enlargement of the Christian name. Yet, because our sins required it, he suffered near Iconium an immeasurable slaughter of his own men and disastrous losses among the imperial forces which he had brought with him beyond even human expectation. There also men of his own kin, illustrious and worthy of renowned remembrance, fell in battle. Among them was John Protosebastos, nephew of the same lord emperor through his brother, a man of exceptional generosity [Col. 0826C] and memorable magnificence. The lord Amalric had married his daughter Maria. While resisting the enemy bravely, he died, pierced by many wounds.

The emperor himself, though he recovered the greater part of his army, was utterly dismayed by this adverse event and withdrew physically unharmed into his own territory. It is said that this happened more through the imprudence of his commanders, who led the columns, than through the strength of the enemy. For although broad and open roads were available for deploying battle-lines, more conveniently drawing the baggage-trains, and transporting every kind of impediment—which was said to exceed both number and measure—they rashly threw themselves into dangerous narrow passes. There they could neither resist the enemy, who had already occupied those places, [Col. 0826D] nor were they afforded any opportunity of turning back.

From that day forward, it is said that the aforesaid emperor bore the lasting memory of this grievous disaster so deeply impressed upon his mind that thereafter he neither showed himself to his people as cheerful as he had customarily been—though they earnestly desired it, and in such cheerfulness he had been singularly pre-eminent—nor enjoyed the bodily health in which he had greatly excelled until the final day of his life. So continuously was he consumed by the renewed recollection of the event that no repose was granted to his spirit, nor the accustomed tranquillity to his mind.

## CHAPTER XIII. William the Younger, marquis of Montferrat, comes to Syria and marries the king’s sister.

In the third year of the reign of the same lord Baldwin, about [Col. 0827A] the beginning of October, the lord William, marquis surnamed Longsword, son of the elder Marquis William of Montferrat, arrived at Sidon. He had been summoned by the lord king and by all the princes of the kingdom, secular as well as ecclesiastical. Within forty days after his arrival, because in the preceding year, when he had been specially summoned for this purpose, the matter had been confirmed by sworn bodily oaths through the hand of the lord king and all the princes, the lord king gave him his elder sister in marriage. With her he bestowed upon him the coastal cities of Jaffa and Ascalon, with their dependencies and the whole county, as had previously been stipulated in the agreements. Some, by whose counsel he had been summoned, nevertheless opposed this and openly protested, not sufficiently considering that it belongs to a fickle and inconstant man to act contrary to his own deeds.

The aforesaid marquis was a young man of becomingly tall stature, handsome appearance, and fair hair; courageous in manly fashion, but so irascible that he exceeded proper measure; exceedingly generous, open-handed in disposition, and one who would never conceal any purpose. He displayed himself outwardly as the spirit he bore within. He was greatly excessive in food and especially in drink, though not to the injury of his reason. From earliest youth he was said to have possessed ample practice and experience in arms. Noble in worldly rank, he was said to have had either no equal or a very rare one. For his father was maternal uncle to the lord Philip, king of the Franks—that is, his mother’s [Col. 0827C] brother. His mother was sister to the lord Conrad, illustrious emperor of the Romans, and paternal aunt to the lord Frederick, who now, after his uncle Conrad of illustrious memory, vigorously governs the Roman Empire. Thus the aforesaid marquis was related in equal degree to each of those illustrious kings.

After taking his wife, when he had been physically well with her for scarcely three months, he fell into a most severe illness. Having suffered from it continuously for about two months, he died the following June, while the lord king was also seriously ill at that same Ascalon, leaving his wife pregnant. His body was brought to Jerusalem and, through our ministry, buried with considerable magnificence in the vestibule of the church [Col. 0827D] of the Hospital, on the left as one enters.

About that time Humphrey of Toron, royal constable, married the lady Philippa, daughter of the lord Raymond, prince of Antioch; sister of the lord Bohemond III, who now governs that same principality, and of the lady Maria, empress of Constantinople. Andronicus, kinsman of the lord emperor, had previously had her as his wife; having put her away, he secretly carried off the lady Theodora, widow of King Baldwin and his own niece, with extreme shamelessness and no less impurity. The lord Humphrey of whom we have spoken began to fall hopelessly ill as soon as he brought Philippa into his house; she likewise, seized by severe sickness, ended her life within a few days. [Col. 0828A]

## CHAPTER XIV. The long-awaited count of Flanders enters the kingdom.

In the fourth year of the reign of the same lord Baldwin IV, in the second month, about the Kalends of August, the long-awaited Philip, count of Flanders, arrived at the city of Acre. The lord king, who, still ill, had had himself carried in a litter from Ascalon to Jerusalem, was greatly heartened by his arrival and sent his princes and prelates of the churches to meet him with manifold honour.

After he reached Jerusalem, where the king was still gravely ill, the king, with the common counsel [Col. 0828B] of all—the lord patriarch, archbishops, bishops, abbots and priors, the masters of the Hospital and Temple, and all the lay princes—offered him authority and free, general administration over the whole kingdom. Thus, in peace and war, within and without, he was to possess full jurisdiction over great and small alike, and freely exercise his judgment over the kingdom’s treasures and revenues.

Having consulted his men, he replied that he had not come in order to receive any authority, but to devote himself to divine service, for the sake of which he had come; nor did he intend to bind himself to any administration, since he must remain free to return to his own lands whenever his affairs recalled him. Rather, the lord king should appoint whatever governor he wished in his kingdom; and he himself would be willing to obey him, as he would the king of the Franks his lord, for the advantage of the kingdom.

Seeing that he altogether refused what we had offered, the lord king again caused him to be most devoutly asked through his princes at least to be leader of the imminent expedition, which he had long before arranged with the lord emperor of Constantinople and of the entire Christian army, and to undertake the Lord’s battles against the Egyptians. To this proposal he gave the same answer as before.

The lord king therefore appointed as governor of the kingdom and armies, as he had already done before the count’s arrival, the lord Reynald, formerly prince of Antioch, a man of proven fidelity and remarkable constancy. If the lord king could not come in person, he was to administer the affairs of the kingdom, though in all things he was to be governed by the counsel of the lord count. When this was reported to the lord count, he replied that such a governor did not seem necessary to him. Rather, one should appoint a man to whom both the glory of war, should God so provide, and the dishonour, should the Lord permit it, would belong personally; and to whom the kingdom of Egypt would fall if the Lord delivered it into our power. To this we, who had been sent by the king, replied that the lord king could not appoint such a governor without making him king himself; and that this was neither the king’s purpose nor ours. [Col. 0829A]

When matters stood thus, he at last made the secret of his mind clearer and did not conceal the aim toward which his whole intention was hastening, saying that it was remarkable that no one approached him concerning the marriage of his kinswoman. Hearing this, we were astonished at the man’s malice and the perverse conception of his mind: although he had been received so honourably by the lord king, he was attempting, forgetful of the laws of kinship and hospitality, to plot these things for the overthrow of the lord king.

## CHAPTER XV. Those who had come with the count mislead him, warning him not to defer to the princes of the kingdom.

It is fitting to digress briefly, so that the minds of our hearers may more fully grasp the matter in which, as we learned both from the reports of many persons [Col. 0829B] and from his own confession, the aforesaid count acted maliciously. A certain powerful man had come with the lord count on that pilgrimage: namely, the advocate of Béthune, who had brought with him two already adult sons. This man, it is said, acting with the support of Count William of Mandeville, who had come by the same route with the same count, deceived the lord count and began to persuade him that he could gain the greatest advantages in the affair of the kingdom. He said that he possessed a very extensive inheritance in the count’s county, which he would grant wholly to the lord count as a hereditary possession if the aforesaid count would arrange for the two daughters of the lord King Amalric to be married to his two sons.

Now the lord Amalric certainly had two daughters: one who had been the marquis’s wife; the other, still under marriageable age, was living with her mother, the lady queen, at Nablus. By these words the count was persuaded and made himself ready to bring the proposal into effect.

But now let us return to our subject. Having understood to what end the count’s spirit aspired, we replied that the matter must first be reported to the lord king and that, after consultation, we would announce the next day what seemed proper to him. The following morning, after consultation had first been held, we returned to the count and replied that it was a custom among us, approved by long practice, that it is not honourable for a widow, especially a pregnant widow, to enter into a second marriage before the year of mourning; and scarcely [Col. 0829D] three months had passed since her husband’s death. Therefore, we could not be blamed if, contrary to the discipline of the times and our country, we had held no discussion concerning the marriage of the aforesaid lady.

Nevertheless, it would be pleasing and acceptable to all of us if, with his counsel—since he was present—the aforesaid proposal were discussed. For the lord king had certainly always intended, both in this and in every other affair, to be guided especially by his counsel and to serve his wishes insofar as could be done with honour. Let him take the lead in this matter and name a person suitable for it; and we, by common agreement, were prepared to proceed in the present affair.

Taking this badly, he said that he would do no such thing unless all the princes first swore that they would abide by his decision without objection; for it would dishonour a noble person if, after he had been named, he suffered rejection. We replied that it would be wholly contrary to the honour of the lord king and of ourselves if we gave his sister to an unknown person whose very name was unknown. At last, having learned the will of the king and all the princes, although greatly indignant and angry, he abandoned this proposal. [Col. 0830A]

## CHAPTER XVI. Envoys of the emperor of Constantinople arrive, urgently requesting fulfilment of the agreements which the king had made with their lord, and preparation for an expedition against Egypt.

At that same time there were at Jerusalem envoys of the lord emperor, eminent and distinguished men: the lord [Col. 0830B] Andronicus surnamed Angelus, the emperor’s nephew through his sister; John, a magnificent man, *megaltriarcha*; the noble Alexander, count of Cupersano in Apulia; and George Sinaites, an intimate of the imperial court.

By imperial command they had come to the lord king, judging that the time had come—as was hoped—that, upon the arrival of the lord count of Flanders, the agreements once made between the lord emperor and the lord King Amalric, and afterward renewed upon not dissimilar conditions between that same lord emperor and the lord Baldwin, who now reigns, might, by God’s aid, be brought to fulfilment. For this reason a general court had been summoned in that most holy city, with all the magnates of the kingdom assembled together.

There was one hope shared by all, and it seemed to sustain everyone: that with the help and counsel of the aforesaid count and his men, the kingdom beloved of God would receive the desired increase, and careful deliberation would be held concerning the crushing of Christ’s enemies. But suddenly, as we have said, the count changed to the sinister side; forgetful of his promises, he turned to other affairs and destroyed every foundation of our hope.

The imperial envoys nevertheless insisted that the agreements be observed, maintaining that delay is accustomed to bring danger with it. They declared that the matter was not delayed by them, and asserted themselves ready faithfully and liberally to fulfil every condition contained in the agreements. Having heard the envoys’ words, we deliberated and decided that the matter should be set forth in due order to the lord count. When he had been summoned and was present, the written text of the agreements between ourselves and the lord emperor, authenticated by his golden seal, was faithfully presented to him. [Col. 0830D]

After he had read it carefully and understood it fully, he was asked what he thought.
