He replied that he was a foreigner, ignorant of the places, and especially of Egypt, which was said to differ in character from every other region because at fixed seasons it is irrigated and wholly covered by water. We knew better, he said, both the nature of the country and the favourable time for departure. Yet he had heard from men who had frequently gone down into Egypt that the time was unsuitable for attacking it. He added that winter was near, while Egypt was covered by the backwaters of the overflowing Nile. Moreover, he had heard that an infinite multitude of Turks had assembled there. He feared besides, and especially, that provisions might fail those on the march or even after arrival, and that the army might be destroyed by the hardship of famine.

Seeing that he was seeking bare pretexts to evade the expedition under this excuse, we offered him six hundred camels to transport provisions, arms, and every other kind of baggage overland; and as many ships as he needed to carry provisions, objects required for war, and the heavy parts of siege-machines by sea. Spurning all these offers, he added that he would not under any circumstances go down into Egypt with us, lest he and his followers be forced to die of hunger. He further said that he had been accustomed to lead his armies through rich lands and that his men could not endure such privation. We should choose other regions where we might more conveniently and easily both lead an army for the advancement of the Christian name and crush Christ’s enemies; to this task he would gladly devote himself with his men. [Col. 0831B]

## CHAPTER XVII. The count obstructs the enterprise, estranged from an honourable purpose.

For our part, it was neither safe nor honourable to withdraw from the agreements. The emperor’s envoys, noble and distinguished men, were present with an immense sum of money, declaring themselves ready, as we have said, faithfully to fulfil the conventions made between us and the lord emperor. They had seventy galleys in the harbour of Acre, apart from other ships sufficient for the agreed expedition and undertaking. Moreover, it seemed extremely dishonourable and dangerous to violate our oaths.

Even if, with the agreement of the imperial envoys, the affair could have been deferred to another time, we did not consider it safe to forsake the present aid of the lord emperor, fearing his anger, which might prove very dangerous to us. Therefore, according to our agreement and as had previously been arranged, with the consent of both parties, we confirmed our expedition and prepared ourselves for the undertaking which we had long before established with the lord emperor.

When he heard this, the count of Flanders again began to rage more fiercely against us, saying that the whole affair had been contrived as an insult to him. Eventually, after much discussion, in order somehow to satisfy his will, the expedition was again postponed by common counsel of our side and the Greeks until the whole of the following April. [Col. 0831D]

After these events, the lord count, having remained at Jerusalem for about fifteen days, completed his prayers and received the palm, which among us is the sign of a completed pilgrimage; then, as though intending to depart altogether, he went to Nablus. A few days later he sent to us at Jerusalem the advocate of Béthune, together with certain others of his men. They reported to us on the lord count’s behalf that the count was ready and that the sum of his decision was this: he would follow us wherever we judged best, whether into Egypt or to other regions.

When we learned this, although it seemed ridiculous to us to change opinions so often, and though adhering to no settled purpose rightly appeared chargeable to excessive instability, we nevertheless approached the Greeks, albeit unwillingly, seeing the count’s intention. For it was not his purpose to match his words with deeds. Rather, he strove with all his power to bring us into blame and to be able to write to the princes beyond the sea that the enterprise had failed to proceed because of us. Wishing therefore to shift his own blame upon us, he had sent the aforesaid men to us, not at all hoping that the Greeks would again return to our position. [Col. 0832A]

## CHAPTER XVIII. The emperor’s envoys return home. The count makes for the region of Antioch. Balian marries the widow of King Amalric.

[Col. 0832B]

We therefore met with the Greeks, seeking to learn whether they would again abide by the former agreements and, if the count came with us, whether they would go down into Egypt. They replied that, although the time was far too short to prepare their armies, nevertheless, if the count would personally swear that he would come with us; that, should he fall ill either here or on the journey, he would send his men; that throughout the whole expedition he would labour in good faith, without deceit or malicious intent, for the advancement of Christendom; that he would neither counsel nor assist any violation, in any respect, of the agreements negotiated and written between the lord king and the lord emperor; and that he would cause his own men to swear the same—then, although it seemed to them exceedingly hard and contrary to manly constancy to change plans so often, they would come, in order that the glory of this kingdom beloved of God and of the lord emperor might be increased.

When the advocate and those sent with him offered their oath upon the stated conditions, but were unwilling either to include all the foregoing matters in their oath or to promise the count’s oath, we would no longer persist in useless words. Our conference ended; and, taking their leave, the imperial envoys deferred the often-mentioned undertaking until a suitable time and returned home.

After this the count’s envoys began to ask, since the aforesaid expedition could not now take place, what the lord count might do with the assistance of the kingdom so as not to appear wholly idle. At last it pleased those to whom this question had been put that he should proceed into the land of Tripoli or Antioch; for there it seemed that he might accomplish something for his honour and for the advancement of Christendom. Some blamed the lord prince of Antioch, who was present, and the lord count of Tripoli for the count’s opposition to the expedition into Egypt. They were said to be trying to draw him to their own regions, hoping with his aid to undertake something directed to the enlargement of their territories. But they were disappointed in their hope, because by God’s will he accomplished nothing worthy of remembrance, either among us or among them. It was fitting, indeed, that he from whom the Lord had withdrawn His grace should prosper in nothing. “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (I Peter 5:5). [Col. 0833A]

The lord king nevertheless promised that he would be his collaborator and helper, and gave him for his departure one hundred of his own knights and two thousand infantrymen. Our affairs were in this condition about the Kalends of October. Accordingly, taking with him his own men, the lord count of Tripoli, the master of the Hospital, and many brothers of the Order of the Temple, he made for the region of Tripoli.

At the same time the lord Balian of Ibelin, brother of the lord Baldwin of Ramla, married the widow of the lord King Amalric, Queen Maria, daughter of John Protosebastos, whom we mentioned above, with the lord king’s permission. With her he received the city of Nablus, which she possessed as a marriage-gift, to hold during his wife’s lifetime. [Col. 0833B]

## CHAPTER XIX. The count of Flanders, together with the prince of Antioch and the count of Tripoli, besieges the castle of Harenc and labours without result.

Having arrived in the appointed region, the count made the necessary arrangements for the journey and drew up his forces. With the count of Tripoli and his men, he entered the enemy’s lands, remaining for some time around Homs and Hama, not without damage to the enemy. [Col. 0833C]

Saladin, having completed the affairs in that region according to his wish and made peace on his own terms with the son of Nur al-Din, had gone down into Egypt, fearing that the preparations and long-promised expedition mentioned above might hasten there, as had long before been arranged. He had therefore drawn together the greatest forces of soldiers, whoever and wherever he could gather them, concentrating strength where greater dangers seemed likely to arise.

The count and his men found the region devoid of military force and could therefore range about more freely. Yet the towns and garrisons of the cities were sufficiently and amply supplied with provisions, arms, and guards. When the lord prince learned that they had entered the enemy’s territory, as they had agreed, he hastened by another route and joined them. United in person, they were also united in purpose; and, judging this more expedient in the present circumstances, they resolved to besiege the castle of Harenc.

This place lies in the territory of Chalcis, a city now commonly called Artasia, once noble but now reduced to the condition of a very small town. Each place is about twelve miles from Antioch. When they reached the site, they pitched their camp in a circle and surrounded it on every side, so that neither was there an exit for the besieged nor a free entrance for those wishing to bring them aid. They therefore constructed siege-engines and whatever is customarily necessary for such purposes. Promising, as it were, permanence in the siege and constancy in their purpose, [Col. 0834A] they made huts of wickerwork and, because winter was approaching, fortified their camp with a rampart, so that the force of torrents might not cause them any loss of goods.

Moreover, inhabitants of the countryside from Antioch and its suburban borders, and people of that occupation, zealously competed in supplying the necessary provisions. The aforementioned castle belonged to the son of Nur al-Din, and it was all that Saladin had left him in those regions. Once the fortress had been surrounded on every side, they attacked its inhabitants at appointed times and in turns, according to custom; battering the walls with siege-engines and artillery, they allowed the besieged no rest.

## CHAPTER XX. Saladin comes from Egypt with an innumerable multitude, enters the kingdom, and encamps before Ascalon. The king goes out against him with all the kingdom’s forces; a great battle with the enemy occurs before the aforesaid city.

[Col. 0834B]

Meanwhile, while these things were happening in the region of Antioch, Saladin learned that the count and the strength of the entire Christian army—which he had awaited in Egypt with no slight fear—had gone to the region of Antioch. He reasonably judged that he could invade the kingdom, now devoid of forces, without punishment and more easily achieve one of two things: either force the lifting of the siege from the besieged fortress, or, if the enemy persisted there, win a triumph over those who had remained in the kingdom.

Accordingly, having collected military forces from every side, in a great multitude and equipped more abundantly than usual with arms and almost everything customarily useful in war, he left Egypt and hastened through the desolation of the intervening wilderness to an ancient but deserted city called Laris. There, having deposited part of his baggage and lightened the burden of his loads, he selected those who appeared more mobile and more skilled in fighting. Leaving behind our towns of Darum and the very famous city of Gaza, he suddenly descended before Ascalon, after sending forward some raiders. [Col. 0834C]

The lord king, forewarned of his arrival several days earlier, had quickly summoned the military force remaining in the kingdom and entered that same city with his men a few days before. Absent, as we have said, were the count of Tripoli with one hundred of our knights, selected from a large number; the master of the Hospital with his brethren; and the greater part of the Order of the Temple. The remaining brethren had withdrawn to Gaza, fearing that Saladin might besiege it because it was the first of our cities to confront him. Humphrey, the royal constable, was also suffering, as we have said, from severe illness.

The lord king therefore had only few men with him. Yet, when he learned that the enemy were freely and hostilely roaming and raiding through the plains adjoining us, he invoked divine help, left men to guard the city, and went out from it with his troops as though to fight them. Saladin, however, had gathered his people together near the city. When the Christian army emerged and saw the enemy’s innumerable multitude, those with more experience in such matters said that it was safer to stand firm where they were than rashly to commit themselves to the uncertain hazards of war. Thus, until evening, although the two battle-lines were close to one another and there were occasional individual engagements, our men held off their assaults. [Col. 0835A]

But as evening drew on, they judged it dangerous, with so small a force, to commit themselves to camp that night, particularly when the enemy multitude was so great; and they prudently withdrew again into the city of Ascalon. This so raised Saladin and his men to presumptuous confidence that he no longer stood firmly within himself but walked in marvels beyond himself; already as though victorious, he allotted definite portions of the subjugated kingdom to his fellow-soldiers. From then on, therefore, believing that they had obtained everything according to their wishes, they began to range about more carelessly, to conduct themselves more imprudently, and to wander everywhere in troops and disordered columns. [Col. 0835B]

## CHAPTER XXI. The enemy ravage the region far and wide, burning cities and suburbs.

That night we supposed that they would pitch their camp before the city, in the district where they had been on the preceding day; or that, moving nearer to the city, they would shut it in by siege. But they, allowing neither themselves nor their horses any rest, ranged in bands throughout the whole region, and, according to the impulse of each, were carried off in different directions. Among their satraps was one named Ivelinus, a man valiant in war and ready to attempt anything; an apostate who, abandoning faith in the mediator between God and men, had turned aside to Gentile impiety. He was Armenian by birth.

With the force under his command he reached the city of Ramla, situated in the plain; finding it empty, he set it on fire. For the citizens of that place, despairing of holding it because it was not adequately fortified, had partly gone with King Baldwin on the expedition near Ascalon; another part, with the weaker force, had withdrawn with the women and children to Joppa; while some had gone up to the castle in the mountains, sufficiently strong by its position, called Mirabel. Having burned the city, the said Ivelinus hastened with all his company to Lydda, a neighboring city. Dividing his forces, he suddenly enclosed the place on every side; then, with a shower of arrows and every kind of weapon, he attacked and relentlessly harassed those shut within. [Col. 0835C]

All the people had indeed gathered around the church of the blessed martyr George. So great a terror had seized our people that no hope remained except in flight. Nor did this afflict only those who lived in the plain, where the enemy could range so freely: such dread also lay upon the inhabitants of the mountains that the citizens nearly abandoned the Holy City; despairing of defending it, they rushed in rivalry to the fortress called David, leaving the rest of the city neglected. For the raiders had advanced as far as the place called Calcalia, and in their march had covered almost the whole surface of the land; and now, leaving the plain country, they were preparing to ascend into the mountains. [Col. 0835D]

Such was the appearance of the land, desolate and oppressed with bitterness, on the day when the Lord covered it with darkness in His wrath, provoked to anger. Yet He did not restrain His mercies in His anger, nor forget to have compassion; but He turned and comforted us, and added that He might yet be more favorable (Ps. 76:7); and, according to the multitude of our sorrows in our heart, His consolations made our souls glad (Ps. 93:19). [Col. 0836A]

## CHAPTER XXII. The king leaves Ascalon and meets the enemy; the battle-lines are arranged on both sides; preparations are made for battle.

While these things were taking place in those parts, the lord king, hearing that a multitude of enemies spread far and wide had completely occupied his territories, went out from Ascalon with his men and prepared to meet the enemy. He judged it better to try the fortune of battle against them, even with an uncertain result, than to endure plunder, fires, and the slaughter of his own people.

Therefore, setting out along the seacoast and following the shore so that he might come suddenly and secretly upon the enemy, he arrived at the place where Saladin was opposite him in the plain. On arriving there, he drew up his battle-line and all his military array, both horse and foot, against him. There the brethren of the Order of the Temple joined him, those who had remained at Gaza. Then, having arranged the ranks of the soldiers, they prepared to meet the enemy. As they advanced, united in purpose to avenge their injuries, divinely kindled to manly courage by the fires which they beheld on every side and by the reported slaughter of their people, they hastened forward as though made into one man. And behold, they saw before them the enemy’s formations at no great distance. [Col. 0836B–C]

It was about the eighth hour of the day. Meanwhile Saladin, hearing that our men were approaching in hope of battle, feared the encounter which earlier he had seemed to desire. He sent men to summon his own troops, scattered in every direction; and with the blare of trumpets, the clamor of drums, and words such as are customary in such circumstances, he encouraged his companies for the conflict and strove to add strength by his speech.

There were with the lord king Odo of Saint-Amand, master of the Order of the Temple, with eighty of his men; Prince Raynald; Baldwin of Ramla and his brother Balian; Raynald of Sidon; and Count Joscelin, the king’s uncle and seneschal. Altogether, of every condition, scarcely three hundred and seventy-five men were found. Invoking help from above, and with the wondrous life-giving wood of the Cross borne before them, which Lord Albert, bishop of Bethlehem, carried in his hands, they arranged their ranks and girded themselves to fight bravely. [Col. 0836D]

Meanwhile, from different quarters, the enemy’s detachments that had gone farther off in pursuit of booty and to kindle fires came flocking back to their formations, and their numbers grew. Unless the Lord, who does not abandon those who hope in Him, had mercifully strengthened our men by some inward inspiration, they would have been compelled to despair not merely of victory, but even of safety and freedom. The enemy likewise drew up their own lines and disposed their troops according to military discipline, determining who should attack first and who should support them. [Col. 0837A]

## CHAPTER XXIII. Battle is joined; Saladin is defeated and put to flight with the utmost danger and disgrace.

Meanwhile, as the ranks of warriors gradually approached one another from both sides, battle was joined. At first the outcome was uncertain, although the forces were very unequal; afterward, as our men pressed on more boldly, grace poured down from heaven made them stronger than usual. The enemy’s legions were broken, and after great slaughter our men put the enemy to flight.

When I investigated and inquired more carefully what the enemy’s numbers had been, I learned from the truthful report of many persons that he had brought twenty-six thousand light cavalry, apart from those riding pack animals and camels, into our territories. Of these, eight thousand were distinguished troops, whom they in their own language call *Toassin*; the remaining eighteen thousand were common soldiers, whom they call *Carnagolam*. Of the distinguished troops, one thousand were all clad in yellow garments over their coats of mail, of Saladin’s own color, and stood more closely about him for the protection of his person. [Col. 0837B]

For Turkish satraps and greater princes, whom they call *emir* in the Arabic language, are accustomed carefully to rear young men—whether born of slave-women, purchased, or enslaved in war—and diligently to train them in military discipline. When they reach maturity, they give them pay according to the merit of each, and also confer generous possessions upon them. In uncertain outcomes of war, they entrust to them the care of preserving their own persons and place no small hope in them for obtaining victory. In their language these are called *Mameluc*.

These men stood faithfully by their lord, striving unanimously to ward off injuries from him and not to abandon him even unto death. They remained steadfast in the engagement until their lord fled; hence it came about that, when all the rest had escaped in flight, nearly all of these men fell. [Col. 0837C]

When the enemy had turned to flight, our men pursued them until, as day was now declining, night came on—from the place called Mount Gisard as far as that marsh commonly called Caunetum Esturnellorum. Throughout all that time and distance of flight, for twelve miles or more, the slaughter of the enemy continued without ceasing; and none of the entire number would have survived had not the untimely onset of night rescued them from the swords of their pursuers.

That they might more readily secure their safety by flight, they cast away their weapons and clothing, abandoned their baggage, and left behind the weaker men. Those who were stronger and rode swift horses, fleeing with all their might, were saved from death by the approaching night; all the rest either were captured or killed by the sword and met a more grievous end. Of our men, in the first encounter four or five knights fell; of the infantry, however, we do not know the exact number. [Col. 0837D]

Those who had escaped by flight, on reaching the aforesaid marsh, threw into the water-reeds and into the water itself whatever burden remained—namely, their coats of mail and iron leggings—so that they themselves might move more easily, and so that the weapons cast into the water might never be of use to our people or serve as a token of victory. Yet our men later recovered both fully. For, following their tracks despite the onset of night, and again on the following day, they carefully searched the said reed-bed and probed the marsh itself with poles and hooks, quickly finding whatever the enemy had concealed. We heard from certain trustworthy persons that they had seen one hundred coats of mail drawn out in a single day, apart from helmets, iron greaves, and lighter objects—useful and valuable nevertheless. [Col. 0838A]

This signal benefit, memorable for ages, was divinely granted to us in the third year of the lord Baldwin IV, in the month of November, on the seventh day before the Kalends of December [25 November], the feast-day of the holy martyrs Peter of Alexandria and Catherine the Virgin. The lord king then returned to Ascalon and waited until he had received back his men, who had pursued the fugitives by different routes; within four days he gathered them together. One could see them returning laden with spoils, leading captives, bringing herds of camels, horses, and tents, and rejoicing in accordance with the saying of the Prophet: “As victors who have taken booty, when they divide the spoils” (Isa. 9:3). [Col. 0838B]

## CHAPTER XXIV. Excessive rains and unusual cold wear out beyond endurance those who fled from the battle; countless numbers are killed and very many captured. The king returns victoriously to Jerusalem.

[Col. 0838C]

There was also another circumstance in which the divine mercy present among us was plainly made known. On the following day, and continuously for ten days, such a force of rain and such unusual severity of cold descended that one might truly believe that even the elements themselves had conspired against them. They had lost all their horses, to which, during the three days they had remained in our territories, they had allowed neither food nor drink nor any rest at all. Likewise, as we have said, they had completely cast away every kind of clothing and garment.

To crown their miseries, they had no provisions whatever and wasted away under cold, hunger, the weariness of the roads, and the burden of labor to which they were unaccustomed. Sometimes more, sometimes fewer, of them were found scattered about, men upon whom even a powerless and weak person could rage with impunity at will. For most of them, ignorant of the country and thinking that they were returning home, gave themselves up to our villagers, travelers, or those seeking them. [Col. 0838D]

Meanwhile the Arabs, a faithless race of men, seeing the disaster that had overtaken the Turks, hurried against those whom, as stated above, we had said were left with the baggage near the city of Laris. Terrified by news of the slaughter of their people, these were put to flight. The Arabs likewise pursued more harshly those who by any chance had escaped our hands; those who seemed to have escaped from us were handed over to them as booty. Thus the prophetic saying seemed fulfilled: “What the locust has left, the caterpillar has eaten” (Joel 1:4).

For this is said to be the custom of that wicked generation: under whatever leader they enter battle, they habitually avoid a contest of uncertain issue; while the outcome of wars remains doubtful, they watch from a distance; then at last they attach themselves to the victors, pursue the defeated as enemies, and enrich themselves with their spoils. Thus, for many days, captives were brought out from forests, mountains, and even the wilderness itself. At times they even voluntarily came to our people, judging it better to be consigned to prison and chains than to waste away and suffer from cold and hunger. [Col. 0839A]

Meanwhile the lord king, after the booty and spoils had been distributed according to the law of war, hastened to Jerusalem in order to render vowed thanksgivings for the benefits bestowed on him by the Lord. Saladin, who had set out with such pride and such a numerous cavalry force, struck by the divine hand, returned with scarcely one hundred horsemen; he himself, too, is said to have ridden on a camel.

It is fitting to behold and consider inwardly the abundance of this divine gift, and how, by the generosity shown toward us, the merciful Comforter wished to claim the whole glory for Himself. For if the count of Flanders, the prince of Antioch, the count of Tripoli, and that multitude of soldiers who were absent had taken part in this work divinely accomplished, then, in the manner of foolish men and because of the pride that commonly steals in amid prosperity, they would not have feared to say, if not aloud, at least in their thoughts: “Our hand is exalted, and not the Lord has done all these things” (Deut. 32:27). [Col. 0839B–C]

But now, according to His word, which is written: “I will not give my glory to another” (Isa. 42:8), reserving authority and glory wholly to Himself, He used not a multitude but the service of a few; and mercifully renewing Gideon’s miracles, He overthrew an innumerable multitude, signifying that it is He, and no other, by whose favor one pursues a thousand and two put ten thousand to flight.

Therefore let it be ascribed to Him, from whom is “every good gift and every perfect gift” (Jas. 1:17), since in this present affair there is nothing which a man can attribute to his own works. It is a gift of divine grace, bestowed not for merits: “Thine is the work, O Lord; for Thou stretched forth Thy hand, and the earth swallowed them” (Exod. 15:12); “in the multitude of Thy glory Thou hast cast down all my adversaries” (ibid., v. 7). [Col. 0839D]

## CHAPTER XXV. Those who had besieged the castle of Harenc in the region of Antioch returned home without accomplishing their purpose.

While these things were being carried out among us, the count and those with him persevered in the siege of the aforesaid castle, but uselessly. Given over to dissipation, they devoted more attention to dice and other harmful pleasures than military discipline or the law of siege required. They frequently hastened to Antioch, where, given over to baths, feasting, drunkenness, and other wanton pleasures, they abandoned the siege to idleness.

Nor did those who seemed constant and diligent there, benumbed by negligence, accomplish anything useful. They whiled away their leisure and dragged out dull, stagnant days. The count himself also declared every day that he must return, and that he was being held there against his will. This statement not only recalled those outside the siege from their honorable purpose; it also made the besieged readier to resist. Hoping that the siege would soon be raised, they resolved that it was better to endure all things for this short time, even if the hardships that could be inflicted seemed severe, than to surrender to hateful peoples the stronghold entrusted to their faith and incur the lasting disgrace of treachery. [Col. 0840A]

The aforesaid castle stood on a high site, established upon a hill that seemed, for the greater part, artificially heaped up. It offered an approach to attackers from one side only; on the other sides, although it was by no means accessible to those wishing to launch an assault, it could nevertheless be freely battered from every direction by siege engines.

After various reverses and frequent assaults, by which it appeared that the place could have been taken if the enterprise had been conducted wholeheartedly and the Divinity had been favorable, the affair, as we have said, fell into negligence. Because our sins demanded it, all the strength of our people so withered and all prudence was so emptied that, when those enclosed had already fallen into utter despair, our men began to discuss returning home. [Col. 0840B]

We cannot sufficiently wonder—for the matter seems beyond human expectation—that the Lord brought such a darkness of mind upon such great princes and in His indignation struck them with such blindness that, though no one compelled them, prompted only by envy and called back by negligence, they abandoned to the enemy a castle already almost taken.

Therefore, when the lord prince saw that the count of Flanders had so firmly resolved upon this course and was stubbornly fixed in this decision beyond recall, he accepted money from the besieged, in an amount uncertain to us, and raised the siege. The count of Flanders, returning to Jerusalem, completed there the solemn days of holy Easter and prepared for his departure. Having fitted out galleys and ships needed to carry his baggage, he began his voyage from Laodicea in Syria, intending to return home by way of the lord emperor of Constantinople, leaving behind no memory of himself worthy of blessing. [Col. 0840C–D]

At the same time, the lord Frederick, emperor of the Romans, after the twentieth year of schism, was reconciled at Venice with Pope Alexander.

Also at this time, since the walls of the holy city Jerusalem had already partly fallen down because of excessive age, a contribution was arranged among the princes, both secular and ecclesiastical. A fixed sum of money was collected, to be paid annually until, with the Lord as author, the work should be completed, so that the saying might be fulfilled: “Deal kindly in Thy good pleasure, that the walls of Jerusalem may be built” (Ps. 50:19).

## CHAPTER XXVI. A general synod is summoned at Rome. The king builds a castle by the waters of the Jordan, under ominous auguries, and hands the completed castle over to the Templars.

[Col. 0841A]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1178, which was the fifth year of the reign of the lord Baldwin IV, in the month of October, a general synod having been summoned at Rome throughout the whole Latin world in the preceding year, the following men from our East set out when called to that synod: I, William, archbishop of Tyre; Heraclius, archbishop of Caesarea; Albert, bishop of Bethlehem; Ralph, bishop of Sebaste; Joscius, bishop of Acre; Romanus, bishop of Tripoli; Peter, prior of the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre; and Raynald, abbot of the church of Mount Sion.

The aforementioned Joscius was not only making his way to the synod with us, but was also performing an embassy to Lord Henry, duke of Burgundy, in order to summon him to us. For we had unanimously agreed that we would give the king’s sister—whom the marquis had previously possessed as wife—in marriage to the same man under the same conditions. The duke had first gratefully accepted this proposal through the hand of the aforesaid lord bishop and had even, as is said, bound himself by an oath taken with his own hand to come. Yet, for certain reasons still unknown to us, he refused to come, proving forgetful of the oath he had sworn and lavish in betraying the faith by which he had bound himself. [Col. 0841B]

In the same month in which we set out for the synod, the lord king, with all the forces of the kingdom, began to build a certain castle on the banks of the Jordan, at the place commonly called Jacob’s Ford. Ancient tradition holds that this is the place where Jacob, returning from Mesopotamia, after sending messengers to his brother and dividing his household into two companies, said: “With my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I return with two companies” (Gen. 32:10).

It lies in the district of Kadesh-Naphtali, between Naphtali and Dan, which is also called Panias and likewise Caesarea Philippi. Both are known to be part of Phoenicia and suffragan cities of the metropolitan see of Tyre. It is ten miles from Paneas. There was there a moderately elevated hill. Laying foundations of suitable depth upon it, they built a wall of marvelous thickness, square in plan and of the strongest construction, and raised it to an appropriate height within six months. [Col. 0841C–D]

While they were remaining there to build it, bandits came out from the region of Damascus and so beset all the roads that travelers could neither go to the army nor return from it, nor travel any road at all, except at peril. These bandits came from a place situated in the mountains of Acre, called Bacades, commonly known as Bucael. This place lies in the territory of Zebulun and is exceedingly pleasant; although high in the mountains, it is watered by streams and planted thickly with fruit-bearing trees. Its inhabitants were insolent, strong in arms, and proud of their numbers, so much so that they made the fields and neighboring settlements of their neighbors tributary to themselves. They provided a safe refuge among themselves for evildoers and for men fleeing their deserved punishment, as well as for assailants and highway robbers, in return for a share of the booty and violently seized goods given to them. [Col. 0842A]

Thus, because of their intolerable arrogance, they had become hated and detested by all around them, both by our people and by the Saracens. Attempts had often been made to root them out completely, but the effort had not succeeded; hence they became more insolent every day.

The lord king, unable to endure their intolerable arrogance, their thefts, and the murders they had committed, suddenly and forcibly occupied the aforesaid place and put to death those whom he could seize. But most fled, having learned beforehand of the lord king’s approach, and withdrew with their wives and children into the territory of Damascus. From there they were accustomed, not forgetting their old practice, to make frequent but secret incursions into our provinces. Now, however, joined by associates of the same faction, they had entered our territories, as stated above. [Col. 0842B]

Hearing this, our people were angered that men of this sort had made the public roads so dangerous. They laid ambushes for them in suitable places and devoted careful effort to anticipating them. One night, after these men had taken booty and were descending from the mountains of Zebulun, intending to return to the region from which they had come, they fell upon our men, who had prepared an ambush for them, and reaped the fruit of their ways. Nine of them were captured, and seventy or more were killed. This occurred in the month of March, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April [21 March]. [Col. 0842C]

At the same time a synod of three hundred bishops was held at Rome in the Constantinian basilica called the Lateran, in the twentieth year of the pontificate of Lord Alexander, in March, in the twelfth indiction, on the fifth day of the month. Whoever wishes to know its decrees and the names, number, and titles of the bishops should reread the document which, at the request of the holy Fathers who attended that synod, we prepared with care. We ordered it to be placed in the archive of the holy church of Tyre among the other books which we bestowed upon that church, over which we have now presided for six years.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The king enters enemy territory and suffers enormous losses. Humphrey, the royal constable, receives there the cause of his death and dies.

[Col. 0842D]

When the castle had thus been constructed and completed in its parts, the lord king was informed that the enemy, carelessly following pasture, had driven flocks and herds into the forest adjoining the city of Paneas, without bringing with them those forces of soldiers upon which they might rely to resist an attack by our people.

Our men therefore believed that they could easily overwhelm them, unguarded and deprived of martial support as had been reported. They secretly made their way there; and, so that they might attack covertly and unexpectedly, their approach concealed from the enemy, they began their journey by night and hastened on through the night. At daybreak they came to the appointed place. There, while some hurried to one place and some to another in order to fight, and others followed much too slowly and from far behind, the battle-line in which the king was imprudently entered certain stone enclosures, where some of the enemy lay hidden. Having heard of our approach, these men had resolved to hide so that, by avoiding our attack, they might in this manner secure their own safety. [Col. 0843A]

Seeing our men rush upon them incautiously, though unwilling and despairing of life, they became stronger under the pressure of necessity itself. Suddenly leaping out and seeing our men in narrow quarters, they pressed them more boldly. Men for whom it had previously been enough to avoid the enemy by concealment now killed horses and, shooting arrows from a distance, violently hemmed in our people.

When the lord constable saw the enemy suddenly emerge, he threw himself into their midst with great force. While he fought bravely according to his custom, faithfully protected the lord king, who was in a confined position, from a more dangerous attack, and powerfully defended him from injury, he was assailed by repeated violent blows and pierced by mortal wounds. At last, when his men rescued him, he was barely restored to his horse. [Col. 0843B]

There fell in that encounter men worthy of remembrance and pious commemoration: a young man of elegant appearance and honorable conduct, noble and rich, Abraham of Nazareth; and Godescalc of Turolte, who likewise left behind a good reputation; and a few others of lesser rank.

These matters standing thus, the lord king, rescued from so dangerous a disaster by the efforts of his men, returned to the camp from which he had come, where he gathered back his men, who had been scattered disorderly in various directions. Lord Humphrey, the royal constable, as his pains increased, was carried to the New Castle which he himself was still building. This occurred on the fourth day before the Ides of April [10 April]. [Col. 0843C]

Lying there and prolonging his life in suffering for about ten days, after prudently and deliberately ordering his affairs in view of the last judgment, this man in every respect worthy of praise, to be mourned forever by his country, ended his life on the tenth day before the Kalends of May [22 April]. He was buried with due magnificence in the church of the Blessed Mother of God and Ever-Virgin, beside his noble and famous castle, namely Toron.

After his death, immediately within that same month, Saladin besieged the aforesaid newly built castle on the sixth day before the Kalends of June [27 May]. With frequent assaults and a thick storm of arrows he began violently to harass those shut inside. But behold, one of the defenders, named, as is said, Raynerius of Marum, killed with an arrow one of the wealthier emirs. At his death all were so dismayed that they withdrew, raising the siege and leaving their undertaking unfinished. [Col. 0843D]

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Saladin enters the territory of Sidon; the king summons the forces of the kingdom and meets the enemy.

In the following month, after the aforesaid Saladin had already twice, or even more often, entered the territory of Sidon by force and freely inflicted fires and slaughter upon men, no one restraining him, he again entered. Pitching his camp between the city of Paneas and the river Dan, he repeatedly sent out raiders to drive off booty and to kindle fires. He himself, as if in support, did not leave the camp but waited for their return and the outcome of their attacks.

Meanwhile the lord king was informed that Saladin was thus raging through our territories. Taking up the wood of the Lord’s Cross and summoning all whom he could gather from anywhere, he hastened to the city of Tiberias; thence he came with his men through the town of Safed and the most ancient city of Naason to the aforesaid Toron. [Col. 0844A]

There, through frequent messengers passing to and fro, he learned for certain that Saladin and his army still remained in the same place, while his more lightly armed soldiers, who had been sent forward, were laying waste the fields of the Sidonians in hostile fashion, committing killings, fires, and plundering. After deliberation, all agreed that they should meet the enemy.

Therefore, directing the army by arrangement toward Paneas, they arrived at the village called Mesaphar. Since it is situated upon very high mountains, one could look out over the whole country below as far as the foothills of Lebanon, and could see the enemy’s camp in the distance. The movements of the enemy and their fires were likewise open to everyone’s sight. Descending the mountain slope in haste, our men could not bring the companies of infantry along with them, for they were thoroughly exhausted by the length of the journey and could not keep pace with the cavalry. Thus, with the few foot soldiers found more agile, they reached the plain lying immediately beneath the mountains, at a place commonly called Mergium. There they halted for several hours, so that they might more fully determine what should be done. [Col. 0844B–C]

Meanwhile Saladin, somewhat alarmed by the king’s sudden arrival, feared for his raiders, whom he saw as though cut off from himself and his own men; he also feared that our men might rush into the camp. He therefore ordered the baggage, packs, and all equipment to be carried between the wall and outer wall of the neighboring city, so that he might be found more unencumbered for whatever event of war occurred. Thus armed for action and greatly uncertain, he awaited the outcome.

But the raiders who had gone plundering, alarmed when they heard of our arrival, set all else aside and judged it best if they could join their own formations. Having crossed the river that divides through the middle the Sidonians’ fields from the plain in which, as we said, our men were stationed, they encountered our men. Battle having been joined hand-to-hand, our men immediately, through the Lord’s favor, gained the advantage. After many had been killed or struck down and more put to flight, the enemy strove to retreat to their camp. [Col. 0844D]

## CHAPTER XXIX. Battle is joined; our men are defeated; very many of them are captured.

While these events were taking place, Odo, master of the Order of the Temple, and with him the count of Tripoli, followed by others, ascended a hill before them, having the river on their left, while on their right lay a very great plain and the enemy camp. Hearing that his men were hard pressed, exposed to danger, and given over to death, Saladin prepared to send them aid. While he remained fixed in this intention, behold, he saw his men who had escaped coming in flight. Meeting them and learning the state of affairs, he gave them courage by words and called them back into battle formation; then he suddenly threw himself upon our men, who were pursuing and were much too confident. [Col. 0845A]

Our infantry, enriched with the spoils of those who had been killed and thinking that nothing remained to complete their victory, had encamped along the riverbank and sat down at rest. But when the cavalry saw the enemy whom they thought defeated rushing upon them with renewed strength, they had neither opportunity nor leisure to arrange battle-lines and form the companies according to military discipline. Fighting in disordered ranks, they resisted for a time and steadfastly endured the enemy’s attacks. At last, unequal in strength and, because they were scattered too disorderly, unable to aid one another, they gave way and were shamefully put to flight. [Col. 0845B]

Although the pursuing enemy could readily have been avoided by other routes and safety attained, because our sins demanded it, our men chose the worse course and thrust themselves into narrow places filled with rough rocks and wholly denying escape. There they could neither advance nor return through enemy hands except at peril of death.

Those who crossed the river in order to secure life and safety mostly withdrew to the nearest stronghold, called Belfort. Others crossed the river, followed the farther bank, and proceeded toward Sidon, thereby escaping the dangerous fury of the confused battle. When Lord Raynald of Sidon, with his men, encountered them while hurrying to the army, he learned what misfortune had occurred; at their warning also, he returned to Sidon. [Col. 0845C]

This action is believed to have caused manifold loss that day. For it is likely that, if he had continued his journey and withdrawn to his castle, with the cooperation of townsmen and country people familiar with the area, he would have rescued many from the enemy—men who that night hid in caves and among rocks, but were found on the following morning by enemies roaming about and searching everywhere, captured, and consigned to chains.

The lord king, supported by the help of certain faithful men, escaped unharmed. The count of Tripoli likewise reached Tyre with a few men. Of ours who were captured there were Odo of Saint-Amand, master of the Order of the Temple—a wicked man, proud and arrogant, with a spirit of fury in his nostrils, fearing neither God nor showing reverence toward man. According to the assertion of many, he is said to have caused the aforesaid loss and lasting disgrace; in the same year in which he was captured, he is said to have died in chains and the filth of prison, mourned by no one. [Col. 0845D]

Also captured were Baldwin of Ramla, a noble and powerful man; Hugh of Tiberias, the stepson of the lord count of Tripoli, a young man of good disposition and greatly beloved; and many others, whose names and number we do not know. [Col. 0846A]

## CHAPTER XXX. Saladin besieges the newly built castle; he captures it under siege and destroys it after capture. Henry, count of Troyes, and Peter, brother of Louis, king of the Franks, come to Syria.

Accordingly, while our affairs stood thus, reduced to their lowest point, behold Lord Henry, Count of Troyes, a magnificent man, son of the elder Count Theobald—whom, when we were returning from the council, we had left at the Apulian city of Brindisi—arrived at the city of Acre with a great company of nobles. As we have said, many nobles had come in the same passage: namely, Lord Peter of Courtenay, brother of Lord Louis, King of the Franks; and Lord Philip, son of Lord Count Robert, brother of the same lord king, elected bishop of Beauvais. By their arrival our people, greatly dismayed by their earlier misfortunes, were nevertheless somewhat raised in hope, expecting that through the support of so many and such great nobles they might repel future injuries and avenge those already suffered. But, with divine providence adverse to us, they did not drive off the former evils, but fell into still greater troubles. For our most savage enemy Saladin, lifted up by successful events and favourable fortune into such pride, suddenly besieged our castle, completed only recently in the preceding April, before our men were allowed even a little time to recover breath [Col. 0846C].

The often-mentioned castle had been handed over, immediately after it was completed and entrusted to their care, to the brethren of the Knights Templar, who claimed the whole region for themselves by grants of the kings. When this was reported to the lord king, he summoned all the strength and knighthood of the kingdom, called in Lord Count Henry and the other noble men who had arrived, and hurried to Tiberias. There, having assembled all the princes of the kingdom, he proposed to bring aid to the besieged and remove the enemy from the siege. But while he waited and the preparations were postponed from day to day, word came that the aforesaid castle—as was indeed true—had been violently taken by the enemy and razed utterly to the ground, all those left in it for its defence having been killed or captured [Col. 0846D].

Thus a greater disgrace was added to the earlier losses, so that it might truly be said: “The Lord their God has departed from them.” Truly, “the judgments of God are a great deep” (Ps. 35:7); truly, “God is terrible in his counsels over the children of men” (Ps. 65:5). For he who, in the preceding year, had bestowed upon his faithful such an immense abundance of his gift, now allowed those same men to be clothed in such shame and confusion. “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?” (Rom. 11:34). What is this, Lord God? Is it because, though this multitude and number of nobles were here present, you withdrew grace, lest they should ascribe to themselves what is not given by merits but by grace? Or because, for the earlier benefit freely bestowed, they had not rendered you, their benefactor, sufficiently abundant thanksgivings [Col. 0847A]? Or because, Lord, “you scourge the son whom you receive” (Heb. 12:6), and fill our faces with disgrace, so that we may seek your holy name, which is blessed for ever? We know, Lord, and confess that you do not change. For you said: “I am God, and I do not change” (Mal. 3:6). Whatever it may be, we know that you are just, Lord, and that your judgment is right.

[Col. 0848A] At the same time the proposal that had been raised in the preceding year concerning the Duke of Burgundy and Lord Count Henry, his uncle, was renewed. It was hoped that he would come in the next approaching passage; but, as afterward became clearly evident, he refused to come for reasons still unknown.

# BOOK TWENTY-SECOND BEGINS

[Col. 0847]

## CHAPTER I. The king gives his sister, formerly the marquis’s wife, in marriage to a certain young man, namely Guy of Lusignan. A truce is concluded with Saladin, on equal terms, contrary to custom.

[Col. 0847B]

At the same time Lord Bohemond, Prince of Antioch, and Lord Raymond entered the kingdom with armed forces and alarmed the lord king, who feared that they might attempt some innovation: namely, that they might wish to claim the kingdom for themselves after depriving the king of it. For the king was more severely afflicted than usual by his illness, and every day the sign of leprosy appeared more and more plainly. The lord king’s sister, who had been the marquis’s wife, still remained in widowhood, awaiting the duke, as we have said [Col. 0847C].

Therefore the king, aware of the arrival of those nobles and suspicious of it—although each was his kinsman—hastened his sister’s marriage. Although nobler, wiser, and richer men, both among the newcomers and among the natives of the kingdom, could have been found, with whom she might much more advantageously, in respect to the kingdom’s welfare, have been placed, yet, not sufficiently considering that

> Rash impulse manages all things badly,

he nevertheless, owing to certain intervening causes, unexpectedly gave her, before Easter and without the customary ceremonies, to a rather noble young man, namely Guy of Lusignan, son of Hugh le Brun, from the diocese of Poitiers.

The aforesaid noblemen, seeing that their arrival was regarded with suspicion by the lord king and his followers, completed their prayers as customary and returned home [Col. 0847D]. Yet while both stayed for several days at Tiberias, Saladin, unaware of their presence, made an attack upon that city. He inflicted no damage on its citizens, however, and again withdrew into the territory of Paneas. While he remained there with his armies, awaiting, as later appeared, the naval force which he had caused to be prepared throughout the preceding winter—fifty galleys—the lord king, suspicious of his delay, sent envoys to negotiate a truce with him. Saladin, it is said, gladly accepted the proposal [Col. 0848B], not because he distrusted his own strength or had any fear of our men, whom he had so often defeated that year, but because, owing to extreme dryness and lack of rain, every kind of food for horses as well as men had failed throughout the region of Damascus for a continuous five years.

Accordingly, a truce was made by sea and by land, for newcomers and natives alike, and confirmed by oaths exchanged on both sides, on terms very humble so far as we were concerned. What is said never before to have happened now occurred: the pact was concluded on equal terms, our side reserving no special advantage for itself in that agreement.

## CHAPTER II. Saladin makes a hostile invasion of the region of Tripoli and devastates its crops and resources.

[Col. 0848C]

In the same year, in the summer immediately following, Saladin, having secured the provinces of Damascus and Bosra, directed all his cavalry forces toward the region of Tripoli. There he pitched camp and scattered military bands throughout the whole country. The count had withdrawn with his men to the city of Arqa, waiting to see whether an opportunity might be given him to engage the enemy without grave danger.

The brethren of the Knights Templar, being in the same region, were shut up in their fortified places, expecting almost every hour to be surrounded by siege; nor did they dare rashly to commit themselves to battle. Likewise the brethren of the Hospital, in fear, had withdrawn to their castle called Crac [Col. 0848D], judging that amid so great a disturbance it was enough if they could defend that stronghold against the enemy’s assaults. The enemy’s forces lay between the expeditions of these brethren and those of the lord count, so that they could neither give each other aid nor even send messengers capable of informing either party of the other’s condition.

But Saladin, ranging everywhere over the plains and especially through cultivated places, freely surveyed all things, since no one opposed him. He burned with fire crops already gathered into threshing-floors, crops collected in sheaves through the fields, and crops still standing in the ground; he carried off plunder and devastated everything.

## CHAPTER III. The Egyptian fleet comes to the island of Arados. The Count of Tripoli makes a treaty with Saladin.

[Col. 0849A]

While these things were happening in those regions, behold, about the Kalends of June, his naval force suddenly appeared off Beirut. When the commanders of that fleet learned for certain that Saladin had concluded a treaty with the lord king, they respected the laws of peace which he had ordained and feared to violate the terms of the treaty within the territory of Beirut or anywhere inside the borders of the whole kingdom. Hearing also that their lord was staying with his forces in the region of Tripoli, they hurried there and occupied the island of Arados—which lies opposite the city of Antarados, scarcely three miles from it—having conveniently stationed their galleys in the harbour [Col. 0849B].

Arados, it is said, was first inhabited by Aradius, son of Canaan and grandson of Noah, who built there a strongly fortified city bearing his own name; hence it was called Arados. To its east lies another city, once very noble, which, because it stands opposite the aforesaid city, as we have said above, was called Antarados; today, by a corrupted name, it is called Tortosa. There the apostle Peter, while travelling through Phoenicia, is said to have founded a small basilica in honour of the Mother of God, which to this day is much frequented by worshippers; and there, through the intercession of that ever-virgin, many benefits are said to be divinely granted to needy believers. Both cities are suffragans of the metropolitan see of Tyre, together with another adjacent place called Maraclea, which is understood to be a portion of the province of Phoenicia [Col. 0849C].

Having landed at the aforesaid island, they shook the entire region with terror. While awaiting their lord’s orders, they burned a house above the harbour of Antarados, attempting unsuccessfully to inflict greater damage upon the citizens. Meanwhile Saladin, having devastated the region as he pleased, ordered the fleet to return; he too recalled his forces and withdrew into his own territory. A few days later, however, after making a treaty with the lord count, he withdrew farther into the region of Damascus.

## CHAPTER IV. The archbishop of Tyre returns from Constantinople; Lord Louis, King of the Franks, dies.

[Col. 0849D]

At the same time, after we had spent seven continuous months with the most magnificent Lord Manuel, Emperor of Constantinople of illustrious memory—a stay very advantageous to us and our Church—on the Wednesday after Easter we obtained, after much urging, permission to return home. He entrusted to our devotion his envoys, noble and distinguished men, and generously granted us four galleys in the imperial manner. Having passed Tenedos, Mytilene, Chios, Samos, Delos, Claros, Rhodes, and Cyprus, leaving on our left the provinces of Phrygia, Lesser Asia, Lycia, Lycaonia, Pamphylia, Isauria, and Cilicia, we reached the mouth of the river Orontes and the harbour of Seleucia, now called Saint Symeon’s, on 12 May, by divine favour safe and sound in body and possessions [Col. 0850A].

It should not, however, be passed over, but constitutes no small part of the present history, that while we remained in the imperial city, as stated above, both through the necessity imposed by the approaching winter and at the command of the most fortunate lord emperor, it happened that he, with paternal foresight and a mind somehow prescient of his imminent departure from this life, joined his two children, a son and a daughter, in the bonds of marriage: the former to a wife, the latter to a husband.

To his son Alexius, still under age and scarcely thirteen years old, who bore the name of his paternal grandfather, he solemnly gave Agnes, scarcely eight years old, daughter of the illustrious Lord Louis, King of the Franks, granting imperial insignia to each in the palace of the elder Lord Constantine, in the part of the palace called the Trullus [Col. 0850B]. There, in the time of Constantine, son of Constantine, son of Heraclius, the holy and universal Sixth Synod is said to have been assembled.

He gave his daughter in marriage to a young man named Renier, son of William the elder, Marquis of Montferrat, and brother of Lord William, to whom we had given our king’s sister. The emperor had summoned him through his apocrisiaries; he was about seventeen years old and had arrived in the imperial city about fifteen days before our own arrival. After he had remained both in the city and on campaign with the lord emperor, and after the emperor returned to the city about Epiphany, in February, in the New Palace called Blachernae, the emperor assembled his court and, with imperial magnificence, gave him his daughter Maria as wife through the hand of Theodosius, patriarch of the same city. He named him John after his own father and made him Caesar [Col. 0850C].

His former wife Irene, the pious empress of blessed memory, who had been given to him in marriage from the kingdom of Germany, bore him this daughter. By Maria, whom he married second, he had only Alexius, who now rules.

But if we attempted to set down in writing the circus games, called Hippodromes by the citizens of that city, and the splendour of the various spectacles solemnly displayed to the people on those days; the imperial magnificence in garments and personal clothing, surpassing all else in precious stones and in the weight and number of pearls; the golden and silver furnishings of the palace, countless in number and weight; the value of the hangings suspended as ornament; the multitude of servants and courtiers [Col. 0850D]; the magnificence of the arrangements and marriage festivities; and the lavish munificence of immeasurable generosity poured out upon all alike, citizens and foreigners—we should be overwhelmed by the immensity of the material, even if a special treatise were devoted to it. But let us now return to our history.

Having therefore completed at Antioch the matters entrusted to us by the imperial majesty for the lord prince and the lord patriarch, and having found the lord king at Beirut as he hastened by land to Tyre, we, by divine favour, returned by uninterrupted voyage to the Church of Tyre on 6 July, after one year and ten months since we had set out for the council [Col. 0851A].

In the seventh year of the reign of Lord Baldwin IV, on 19 September, the most pious and most Christian King of the Franks, Lord Louis, a man of virtues and immortal memory, laid aside the burden of flesh and carried his soul to heaven, there to possess eternal rewards with the chosen princes. He left one son and heir, Philip, by Queen Adela, daughter of the elder Theobald and sister of Lord Henry, Count of Troyes; Theobald, Count of Chartres; Stephen, Count of Sancerre; and Lord William, Archbishop of Reims. He died in the fiftieth year of his reign and the sixtieth year of his life [Col. 0851B].

In the following month, on 6 October, in the twenty-second year of his pontificate, Lord Amalric, Patriarch of Jerusalem of good memory—a man exceedingly simple and almost useless—entered upon the way of all flesh. Within ten days Lord Heraclius, Archbishop of Caesarea, was appointed in his place.

## CHAPTER V. The king gives his younger sister in marriage to Humphrey III. The Emperor of Constantinople dies.

In the same month the lord king betrothed his sister, scarcely eight years old, to a young man named Humphrey. This was Humphrey III, son of the younger Humphrey by Stephanie, daughter of Philip of Nablus [Col. 0851C]. This second Humphrey was the son of the elder Humphrey of Toron, constable of the kingdom, whom we have frequently mentioned above. His maternal grandfather, namely Philip, was lord of the second Arabia—that is, the territory of Petra, whose principal place is today commonly called Crac—and of Sobal in Syria, now called Montreal; both lie beyond the Jordan. He later became a convert and was made master of the Knights Templar.

Accordingly, through the efforts and great exertions of Prince Raynald, third husband of the mother of this already pubescent boy, the betrothal of the aforesaid young man and the lord king’s sister was celebrated at Jerusalem. Moreover, he exchanged with the lord king, on specified conditions, his inheritance in the territory of Tyre—namely Toron, Chastel Neuf, and Paneas, with their appurtenances—which had devolved upon him by hereditary right through the death of his paternal grandfather [Col. 0851D]. The terms of these conditions are recorded, through our office and at our dictation, in the royal archives.

In the same month, on its third day, the most eminent man and of immortal memory, Lord Manuel, Emperor of Constantinople, the most generous of all earthly princes, laid aside the burden of flesh and rendered his soul to heaven. May his memory be blessed; all the Church of the saints will recount his alms and most generous benefactions. He is said to have died in the fortieth year of his reign and the forty-first of his life, so far as can yet be known.

## CHAPTER VI. The Prince of Antioch is subjected to anathema because of a concubine whom he took while his wife still lived. A conspiracy is formed against Emperor Alexius.

[Col. 0852A]

At the same time Lord Bohemond, Prince of Antioch, abandoned his wife Lady Theodora, niece of the lord emperor, and, disregarding ecclesiastical discipline, presumed to take as wife a certain *sibyl*, who, it is said, practised sorcery.

At the same time, Lord Joscelin, the king’s uncle and seneschal, had been sent by the lord king on certain affairs of the kingdom and was staying in Constantinople; Lord Baldwin of Ramla was likewise staying in that city in order to seek help from the lord emperor for his ransom. After the death of Lord Manuel, emperor of pious memory, on the Kalends of March certain noble, great, and illustrious men were discovered to have conspired against Lord Emperor Alexius, son of Lord Manuel, while plotting political change [Col. 0852B]. The emperor ordered them, once seized, to be put in chains and committed to prison as guilty of treason, though some of them were his kinsmen. He was still under his mother’s guardianship, in accordance with his father’s arrangement.

Among them were, as it were, the architects of the entire faction: Manuel, son of the elder Andronicus, of whom we have spoken above; Alexius the Protostrator, son of Theodora Calusina, niece of the lord emperor; the brother of the Logothete, who held the office of Canaclivus; and about twelve other distinguished magnates [Col. 0852C]. The emperor’s sister Lady Maria, also aware of the same plot, fled by night with her husband, the marquis’s son—of whom we have likewise spoken above—to the church of Saint Sophia. There, enclosed within the church in precarious and uncertain circumstances, she and her husband, having fortified the same church with arms and soldiers, attempted with their supporters and accomplices in the same undertaking to contrive something against her brother the emperor, aided by the patriarch of that city. But at last, when the emperor’s party grew stronger, relying especially upon Latin support, she lost hope for her life after her forces had been broken. Through intermediaries she humbly sought pardon and was reconciled to her brother after forgiveness had been granted.

## CHAPTER VII. The Patriarch of Jerusalem is sent to Antioch, to attempt a remedy for the endangered situation. Pope Alexander dies.

[Col. 0852D]

At the same time, because of the concubine whom Bohemond, Prince of Antioch, had taken after casting aside his lawful wife, the condition of the Latins of the East was disturbed, especially in the principality of the Antiochenes. For when the prince had been admonished once and twice to withdraw from so manifest an act of adultery and restore his lawful wife, he behaved like the sinner who, having reached the depth of vices, is accustomed to despise correction. With his ears stopped, he refused to hear the voice of those wisely offering their incantation; but persevering obstinately in sin, he incurred the deserved sentence of excommunication [Col. 0853A].

Giving this little heed and doubling his offence, he began to persecute in hostile fashion both the lord patriarch and the bishops and other prelates of churches in that region, laying violent hands upon them. Violating the enclosures of holy places, churches and monasteries alike, he plundered sacred property and, with impious spirit and rash audacity, disturbed their possessions. He is even said to have besieged the lord patriarch himself with the clergy who had fled to him in a certain fortified ecclesiastical stronghold, sufficiently supplied with arms, soldiers, and provisions, and to have attacked them repeatedly in hostile encounters.

Some magnates of that region, unable to endure his madness and recognizing that they owed more to God than to men, withdrew from him in heart and body, detesting his evil deeds [Col. 0853B]. Among them was Raynald, surnamed Mansel, a noble and powerful man. With those who had the more honourable cause at heart and the fear of God before their eyes, he withdrew to his own impregnable and strongly fortified refuge. There he provided safe shelter, without distinction, to prelates driven from their own sees and to others exiled for the same cause.

Because of this, the entire region was brought into such a dangerous crisis that prudent and experienced men considered it beyond all doubt that, unless divine mercy promptly came to our aid, the enemy must be allowed an entrance for our ruin and the enduring disgrace of the Christian name; the entire province would return into their power, though, with the Lord’s help, it had been taken from their hands through the diligence of faithful princes and the many labours and expenditures of the Christian people [Col. 0853C]. For the saying of Truth is true and worthy of all acceptance: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste, and house shall fall upon house” (Matt. 12:25).

The Lord King of Jerusalem, the lord patriarch, the other prelates of the churches, and the lay princes, exercising due concern, assembled and deliberated with the greatest care on what ought to be done in so dangerous a state of affairs. Although the deserts of the aforesaid imprudent and dissolute prince seemed to demand force, they hesitated to employ it, lest, perhaps, when he wished to resist with the enemy’s strength and with aid requested from them, he might expose the region to the Turks, from whom they could afterward not remove them even with the utmost effort [Col. 0853D].

They also understood that with a madman, rushing headlong into evil and already occupied by wrongdoing, prayers and salutary warnings have no place; for that would be to tell a story to a deaf ass and to cast words to the winds. Thus they did not presume to send prudent men gifted in exhortation. They endured this evil lest they should encounter a worse, awaiting help from him who is accustomed to turn about those set in the depths of the sea, “to give snow like wool, and to scatter frost like morsels of bread” (Ps. 147:5–6), so that Bohemond, warned by divine visitation and returning to himself [Col. 0854A], might rise to the fruit of a better life and be clothed from on high with the virtue of the best ruler.

At last our people, seeing that the evil was becoming worse and hoping for no immediate remedy—for not merely the person of the prince was bound by the chain of anathema, but the entire region had been placed under interdict because of the robberies and burnings committed upon the property of holy places, so that, apart from the baptism of infants, none of the ecclesiastical sacraments was administered to the people—began to fear still more, seeing that matters had reached a point at which they could not long remain without danger to all.

By common counsel they therefore arranged that the lord patriarch, Lord Raynald of Châtillon, who had once been Prince of Antioch and was stepfather of this younger Lord Bohemond, Brother Arnald of Torroja, master of the Knights Templar, and Brother Roger of Moulins, master of the Hospital, should hasten to those regions [Col. 0854B], in an attempt, if God’s grace went before them, to find and apply some remedy to so great evils, whether temporary or permanent. For we feared that the lord pope and the princes overseas might charge us with negligence—or rather malice—if we gave no sign of compassion and made no effort to provide relief while our neighbours suffered so miserable a fate.

The lord patriarch therefore set out for those regions, taking with him among the prelates of the churches Lord Monachus, bishop-elect of Caesarea; Lord Albert, bishop of Bethlehem; Lord Raynald, abbot of Mount Sion; and Lord Peter, prior of the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, prudent and discerning men, together with other companions of the same journey [Col. 0854C]. Taking with him the Count of Tripoli, who was very familiar and acceptable to the prince, so that their proposal might more readily be carried into effect, he met at Laodicea. At last, after meeting separately both the lord prince and the lord patriarch, they appointed a day for each at Antioch. There, after proposals had been put forward on both sides, they established a temporary peace: namely, that after restoration to the lord patriarch, the bishops, and the holy places of whatever they had lost, the interdict should cease and the people should again receive the benefits of ecclesiastical sacraments [Col. 0854D].

The prince himself was to endure patiently, in his own person, the sentence pronounced by the bishops; or, if he sought complete absolution, he was to dismiss the concubine and restore his lawful wife. These matters having been accomplished, they thought that they had somewhat moderated the conflagration of the region and returned home. The prince, however, remained obstinately and irrevocably in the same filth. Furthermore—and this was more dangerous for the region—because they were said to disapprove of his action, he expelled from the city and all his territory the best, most renowned, and noble of his faithful men: namely, his constable, his chamberlain, Guiscard of the Island, Bertrand son of Count Gilbert, and Garin Gainart. These fled of necessity to Lord Rupen, the magnificent prince of the Armenians [Col. 0855A], and were most honourably received by him: he immediately gave each great gifts and assigned each sufficient maintenance.

In the same year, on 27 August, in the twenty-third year of his pontificate, Lord Pope Alexander III entered upon the way of all flesh and was buried in the Lateran Church. Lord Pope Lucius III succeeded him, also called Ubaldo, bishop of Ostia, a Tuscan by nation and a native of Lucca, a man very advanced in age and moderately learned.

At the same time our venerable brother in Christ, Lord Raymond, bishop of the Church of Beirut, of pious memory in the Lord, was removed from this life on the Ides of September [13 September], and, by the Lord’s preceding grace, would enjoy eternally the rewards of everlasting light [Col. 0855B]. He was later succeeded in that church by Master Odo, an honourable and learned man, archdeacon of our church; during the December fasts we conferred upon him, by God’s authority, both priestly rank and episcopal dignity.

## CHAPTER VIII. The son of Nūr al-Dīn dies, leaving his inheritance to a kinsman, the lord of Mosul.

At the same time, Malik al-Salih, son of Nūr al-Dīn, died while still a youth. Of all his paternal inheritance, only Aleppo remained to him, with very few fortified places. At his death, by his last testament, he is said to have conveyed Aleppo and his entire inheritance, in full, to a certain son of his paternal uncle, named ‘Izz al-Dīn [Col. 0855C], son of Thebeth, lord of Mosul.

After his death the princes of Aleppo sent envoys to the aforesaid lord of Mosul, an illustrious and magnificent Turkish ruler, urging him not to delay but to come to them with all speed. Receiving the embassy, he arrived quickly and took possession of the ancestral goods due to him by hereditary right. He feared that Saladin, who had deprived the aforesaid cousin of the greater part of his inheritance, might, on returning from Egypt, violently seize this city also against the will of its citizens, especially since certain leading men were secretly giving him support.

Saladin, however, having concluded a temporary peace with us for a full two years, had gone down to Egypt to attend more carefully to his affairs there [Col. 0855D]. He was greatly troubled because he had heard that the fleet of the king of Sicily, with immense equipment and innumerable forces, had put to sea and intended to hasten toward Egypt. Yet he had conceived a needless fear on that score. The aforesaid fleet took its course westward, aiming for the Balearic Islands, adjacent to nearer Spain, one of which is commonly called Majorca and the other Minorca. There, driven by an unfortunate voyage and adverse winds, almost the whole fleet perished near Sacua Albenguenam, and twenty thousand men were dashed against the shores near maritime towns by the swelling strait.

Meanwhile, while the kingdom enjoyed, as stated, a temporary peace [Col. 0856A], a certain people of Syria dwelling in the province of Phoenicia, around the ridges of Lebanon near the city of Byblos, underwent a great change in their condition. For, having followed for nearly five hundred years the error of a certain heresiarch Maron—so that they were called Maronites after him—and having been separated from the Church of the faithful, celebrating their sacraments apart, they returned to their senses through divine inspiration. Casting aside their sickness, they approached Aimeric, Patriarch of Antioch, the third Latin now presiding over that church, and, after abjuring the error by which they had so long been held in exceedingly dangerous fashion, returned to the unity of the Catholic Church. They received the orthodox faith, ready to embrace and observe with all reverence the traditions of the Roman Church.

The multitude of this people was not small, but was said to exceed about forty thousand. They inhabited, as we have said, the ridges and mountain slopes of Lebanon throughout the bishoprics of Byblos, Botrys, and Tripoli [Col. 0856B]. They were strong and valiant men in arms, very useful to our people in the greater undertakings they frequently had against the enemy. Thus their conversion to the sincerity of faith brought great joy to our side.

The error of Maron and his followers was and is this, as is read in the Sixth Synod, which is known to have been assembled against them and in which they received sentence of condemnation: that in our Lord Jesus Christ there is, and has been from the beginning, only one will and one operation. After this doctrine had been rejected by the Church of the orthodox, they added many exceedingly destructive errors once they had separated themselves from the fellowship of the faithful. Led by repentance concerning all these things, they returned, as stated, to the Catholic Church [Col. 0856C], together with their patriarch and several bishops who, just as they had formerly led them in impiety, now provided them with godly leadership as they returned to truth.
