## CHAPTER IX. A dangerous quarrel arises between the king and the Count of Tripoli and proceeds to open hatred.

While the kingdom, as we have said, enjoyed for a time a certain tranquillity under the peace concluded between the lord king and Saladin, there were not lacking sons of Belial and pupils of impiety, who, having a restless spirit, stirred up disturbances in the kingdom and plotted internal evils. Since also the count of Tripoli, detained for almost two continuous years in the region of Tripoli by a multiplicity of affairs, had been unable to come up into the kingdom, it happened that, prompted by the concern which he bore for the city of Tiberias, his wife’s inheritance, he decided to return. Having made every preparation for the journey, and already having reached Byblos, the aforesaid wicked men deceived the all too guileless king by malicious insinuation, persuading him that the said count wished to enter the kingdom with sinister intent, in order secretly to plot his overthrow. Thus it came about that the king, lending far too credulous an ear to their deceitful words, sent an embassy and most imprudently forbade him entry into the kingdom. [Col. 0857A]

The count, upon whom so great an injury had been inflicted without deserving it, was confounded and inflamed with just indignation. Abandoning his purpose, though unwillingly, after innumerable expenses had been uselessly incurred, he returned to Tripoli. The intention of these deceivers was that, with the count absent—a capable man and prudent in every matter—they themselves might manage royal affairs at their own discretion and turn the king’s weakness to their own advantage. Among them were the king’s mother, a woman plainly hateful to God and importunate in extortion; and her brother, the royal seneschal. With a few of their adherents, impious men, they urged the king toward this course with ever greater insolence.

When this became known to the princes of the kingdom, it greatly troubled the hearts especially of those whose judgment was more practiced. They feared that the kingdom, deprived of the protection of so great a prince, might plunge headlong into ruin and, according to the Lord’s saying, being divided against itself, be laid waste (Matt. 12:25). This was especially so because the king, whose illness grew stronger day by day, became more incapacitated and less and less fit to administer the affairs of the kingdom; indeed, scarcely able to stand by his own strength, he was wholly wasting away. Seeing therefore the danger which was certainly threatened by the aforesaid act, the greater men of the kingdom made every effort to recall the count and to soften his anger. At last, after many negotiations and various counsels, although the king was unwilling yet nevertheless permitted it, they brought the distinguished man back into the kingdom. He prudently concealed the injuries done him, and peace between him and the lord king was more fully restored. [Col. 0857C]

## CHAPTER X. A disturbance arises at Constantinople; and when the wicked man Andronicus prevails, the Latin people are driven out.

While these things were taking place in our East, a great change occurred in the empire at Constantinople, and there befell the whole Latin people a grievous disaster, inflicting an unheard-of outrage with enormous loss. For the pain long conceived by deceitful and perfidious Greece brought forth and gave birth to iniquity.

After the death of the lord Manuel, most fortunate emperor of illustrious memory, there succeeded him—both by his father’s testament and by hereditary right—his underage son, named Alexius, scarcely thirteen years old. [Col. 0857D] While he was placed under his mother’s guardianship, and imperial affairs were administered through Alexius the Protosebastos, nephew on his elder brother’s side of the late emperor, both the leading men and the people of that city thought that they had found an opportunity to bring to effect what they had maliciously conceived against our people.

For while the aforementioned emperor, beloved of God, reigned, the Latin people had found such favour with him, on account of their faithfulness and prowess, that, neglecting his own little Greeks as soft and effeminate men, he, being high-minded and of incomparable valour, entrusted great affairs to the Latins alone, deservedly relying upon their loyalty and strength. Because they stood very well with him and he abounded in lavish generosity toward them, both nobles and commoners flocked to him in rivalry from every part of the world, as to their chief benefactor. Their service kindled him more and more in love for our people, and he advanced all of them to a better condition. [Col. 0858A]

Hence the Greek nobles, especially his kinsmen, and also the rest of the people, conceived an insatiable hatred against our people. Added to the fullness of their indignation, and furnishing fuel and incentive to their hatreds, was the difference in sacraments between us and them. For, excessively arrogant and separated from the Roman Church through insolence, they regard as heretical everyone who does not follow their frivolous traditions; whereas they more properly take upon themselves the name of heretics, since against the Roman Church and the faith of the apostles Peter and Paul—against which the gates of hell cannot prevail (Matt. 16)—they either devise or follow novel and pestilential opinions. [Col. 0858B]

In short, from long before they had conceived this enmity among themselves for these and similar reasons, seeking an opportunity to annihilate completely, at least after the emperor’s death, the hated Latin people dwelling both in the city and within the borders of the empire, thereby satiating their inexorable hatred.

## CHAPTER XI. The causes of the disturbance and dissension are set forth.

After the aforesaid emperor had departed this life, while, as has been said, Alexius the Protosebastos administered the empire, they considered that they had not yet found an opportunity sufficiently favourable to accomplish their wickedness. For he too, following the emperor’s example, used the counsel and assistance of our people and made them as close to himself as he could; yet in one respect he made himself utterly hateful both to ours and generally to all men. Although, in the Greek manner, he was excessively soft and strove with all zeal to indulge the flesh in unclean desires, he was nevertheless avaricious and spared the imperial treasures as though he had amassed them by his own sweat. [Col. 0858C]

It was also said that he had an adulterous relationship with the empress, although her husband was still alive but lying at the point of death, and although she had professed the religious life of a nun. Moreover, arrogant and treating no man as his equal, he arranged everything according to his own will without consulting the other princes, so that he appeared to care nothing for the rest, though equally noble and distinguished men.

Hence, through the design and efforts of the palace princes, who greatly envied him for the reasons stated above, Andronicus the Elder—cousin of the late lord emperor and governor of Pontus—was summoned from Pontus to come as their accomplice in completing their wickedness and to drive Alexius the Protosebastos from the administration which he held. [Col. 0858D]

This Andronicus, cousin of the deceased lord emperor, was a treacherous and wicked man, a sower of conspiracies and always disloyal to the empire. On account of his many crimes, in the time of the lord emperor he had endured chains and prisons; and, as his merits required, having been disgracefully treated, he wandered as an exile and fugitive over the earth, traversing all the East. In that exile he committed many shameful deeds deserving punishment. Yet at last, scarcely three months before the emperor’s death, he had been reconciled and restored to favour. To prevent him, as was his custom, from stirring up disturbances around the city and plotting conspiracies to rule the empire, he was sent to Pontus under the honourable title of governor.

His kinsmen—the emperor’s and also the Protosebastos’s—and especially those in whom he appeared to have the greatest confidence, summoned him by secret embassies, urging him to arm against the man who had disgracefully thrown his sons and certain other distinguished persons into chains. [Col. 0859A] For this man, as stated above, had consigned certain notable persons detected in conspiracy to prison, and had thereby stirred up greater envy against himself.

When the said Andronicus had been summoned, he drew with him innumerable forces of barbarian nations, approached the city, encamped along the Hellespont within sight of it, and occupied all Bithynia. Certain powerful men were sent against him to resist his schemes, but in the manner of traitors went over to him. Foremost and most important among them were Andronicus Angelus, commander of the army sent against him, and Alexius the Megaduke, commander of the fleet, both kinsmen of the emperor. [Col. 0859B]

Nor did only those who had thus openly defected to him render our party weaker; all the rest also, both nobles and the multitude of citizens, now gave their support to Andronicus not secretly but openly. They desired his arrival in the city and did all they could to procure his speedy crossing.

## CHAPTER XII. Andronicus occupies the city and palaces after killing the nobles, and oppresses the people by violent rule.

Thus it happened that, as their conspiracy gained strength, the Protosebastos was captured, deprived of his eyes, and mutilated in his sexual organs. Our people were greatly alarmed by this, fearing a sudden attack upon them by the citizens. Warned by certain persons aware of the conspiracy, those who were stronger escaped the Greeks’ designs in forty-four galleys which they found in the harbour. Others escaped the danger of death in ships, of which there was a great abundance in the harbour, loading aboard all their household goods. [Col. 0859D]

But those who were elderly or infirm and less able to flee were left in their homes and suffered the fury of impiety from which the others had escaped. For Andronicus, having secretly prepared shipping, brought into the city all the forces he had led with him. Hardly had they entered when, together with the citizens, they rushed into the part of the city inhabited by our people and slaughtered with raging swords the remaining population—those who, when the others departed, either had not wished or had been unable to leave. Although few were capable of bearing arms, they nevertheless resisted for a long time and left their enemies a bloody victory over them. [Col. 0860A]

Forgetting both the treaty and the many services which our people had rendered to the empire, after killing those who seemed capable of resistance, they set fire to their dwellings and suddenly turned their whole quarter into ashes, consuming women and little children, old people and the sick in the blaze. Nor did their impiety suffice to rage against secular places: setting churches and every venerable place on fire, they burned together with the sacred buildings those who had fled there for safety. Nor was there any distinction between laymen and clergy, except that they raged more cruelly against those who wore the habit of religion and decency.

They inflicted their first outrages upon monks and priests and put them to death with refined tortures. Among them, they seized a venerable man named John, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, whom the lord pope had sent there on Church business; in contempt of the Church they beheaded him and tied his head to the tail of an unclean dog. [Col. 0860B] Nor was rest secure even for the dead, whom every form of impiety had customarily spared, among these detestable sacrilegious persons, worse than parricides. They dragged corpses from their tombs through lanes and streets as though they themselves had suffered injuries.

Moreover, going to the hospice called Saint John’s, they put to the sword every sick person whom they found there. Those whose office of piety properly obliged them to relieve the affliction of the oppressed—namely, their priests and monks—accepted payment and invited robbers and assassins to slaughter. Searching hiding places and the inner rooms of houses, lest anyone might be concealed there in order to escape the danger of death, they handed over those discovered and violently dragged out to the executioners. And lest the killers should exert themselves for nothing, they offered them blood money for murdering the wretched. [Col. 0860C]

Those who seemed to act more mercifully sold to Turks and other unbelieving peoples, into perpetual slavery, those who had fled to them and to whom they had given hope of safety. It is said that more than four thousand persons of both sexes, every age, and every condition were thus sold to barbarian nations for a price. Thus the impious Greek people, a brood of vipers (Matt. 23), like a serpent in one’s bosom and mice in one’s bag, repaid their guests wickedly—though those guests had done nothing of the kind and feared nothing of the kind. Yet they had given them their daughters, granddaughters, and sisters as wives, and long association had made them intimate with one another. [Col. 0860D]

## CHAPTER XIII. The Latin people who had taken refuge in galleys ravage islands and coastal places in war.

Yet they are not said to have committed such a great and unprecedented crime without punishment. Those who, as stated above, had departed in galleys, and those who later followed them in other ships, having with them a very great multitude and a sizeable fleet, assembled not far from the city and awaited the outcome. When they learned fully that those who had stirred up the disturbance in the city had burned their quarters and had destroyed their wives, children, and whole household, partly by sword and partly by fire, they were moved by just indignation and burned with anger. [Col. 0861A]

Desiring with vehement zeal to avenge their people’s blood, they traversed both shores of the Hellespont, from the mouth of the Black Sea, thirty miles from Constantinople, to the mouth of the Mediterranean Sea, two hundred miles from that city. They violently seized all cities and towns situated on either shore and killed all their inhabitants with the sword. They also overran the monasteries situated both on the two shores of that sea and on the small islands scattered through it. In vengeance for their brethren’s blood, they put to the sword the pseudo-monks and sacrilegious priests there and burned the monasteries themselves together with those who had fled to them. [Col. 0861B]

From these places they are said to have carried away limitless quantities of gold, silver, gems, and silk brocades, and so were able to compensate themselves many times over for their lost property and their material losses. Besides the innumerable wealth and limitless treasures of the monasteries, accumulated over many past ages, the citizens of Constantinople had deposited there immense quantities of gold and other treasure. Carrying all these things with them and leaving the narrows of that sea, they entered the Mediterranean between Sestos and Abydos, very ancient maritime cities. Carefully ranging over the coasts of Thessaly and the cities and towns of provinces adjoining the sea, they delivered everything to fire and plunder and wrought an innumerable slaughter. [Col. 0861C]

They are also said to have found ten other galleys besides the first ones near Chrysopolis, a city of Macedonia, and many others elsewhere. Thus they are said to have assembled a very great fleet, wholly formidable to the Greeks, for their destruction. But others, who abhorred committing slaughter and plunder, boarded ships, of which great numbers were available to them, with their wives, children, and the remainder of their small possessions. Avoiding the aforesaid army, they came down to us in Syria.

Meanwhile Andronicus, having gained possession of the city as he wished and having no opponent, caused the emperor to be solemnly crowned on the feast day of Pentecost with his future wife, daughter of the king of the French, showing him every reverence. He also treated the emperor’s sister and her husband, together with the emperor’s mother, somewhat more humanely within the palace enclosure. Yet he himself freely disposed all affairs of the empire according to his own will, both inside and outside the city. It is feared, however, that he displayed this humanity, cloaked in deceit, toward those persons only until he should gradually seize the empire and subdue all men, and then more freely show what disposition he bore toward them. [Col. 0862A]

This occurred in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1182, in April.

## CHAPTER XIV. Saladin breaks the treaty which he had made with the lord king; the king meets him beyond the Jordan. The Turks storm the village of Buria and carry its inhabitants into captivity.

Meanwhile, while these things were taking place in Greece, a ship carrying fifteen hundred pilgrims was driven by adverse winds and wrecked near Damietta, within the borders of Egypt. Those who had suffered shipwreck nevertheless had hope of safety because Saladin was said to have a truce and temporary peace with us both by land and by sea. But things befell them far otherwise than either the tenor of the peace or the terms of the agreements required. [Col. 0862B]

Overcome by desire for plunder, and unwilling, on the pretext of the treaty, to let so great a multitude of Christians leave his realm freely, Saladin threw them all into chains and ordered their goods confiscated. Sending an embassy to the lord king, he began to demand from him, contrary to the terms of the agreement, conditions that were almost impossible to meet. He added that, unless complete satisfaction were made to him concerning all these matters according to his wish, he would retain the aforesaid ship as compensation and, moreover, renounce the peace agreed between them.

When his envoy failed to obtain this—because he was fabricating specious pretexts so that he might keep the ship under some contrived colour rather than alleging just causes—Saladin broke the treaty and began to consider how, practicing his old hatred in his customary manner, he might afflict the kingdom. [Col. 0862C] Having summoned his expeditions and all his foot and horse forces, together with the multitude of those who in past years, fleeing the severity of famine, had come down to Egypt from Damascus and its neighbouring territories, he proposed to return to Damascus, that from there, as from close at hand, he might harass us more effectively.

He further intended, while on the way, to damage as much as possible our territory beyond the Jordan: either by burning the crops, which were already white for harvest, or by forcibly capturing one or more of our fortresses in that province. It was said that he had especially proposed this in order to obtain satisfaction from Prince Raynald, who ruled that region, because certain Arabs were said to have been captured during the truce contrary to the terms of the agreement, and Raynald had refused to surrender them when demanded. [Col. 0862D]

Having learned through his scouts of Saladin’s arrival and purpose, the king held a general court at Jerusalem and carefully deliberated concerning Saladin’s demands. By the counsel of certain persons, he proceeded with all the forces of the kingdom into the aforesaid region, crossing the wooded valley in which lies the Dead Sea, in order to meet Saladin as he came and oppose him in his intention to ravage the province.

Saladin, however, having crossed the desert with his expeditions by a route which he had accomplished only with great difficulty in scarcely twenty days, had already pitched camp in habitable territory within our borders, near the fortress called Mount Royal, at a distance of about ten miles. There he awaited certain news concerning the state of the region and the whereabouts of the king with his forces. [Col. 0863A] The king had encamped near the ancient city named Petra of the Desert, situated in Arabia Secunda, scarcely thirty-six miles from Saladin’s army. With him was the entire strength of the kingdom; but the count of Tripoli was also detained there against his will. The king had gone there contrary to the count’s counsel, leaving the other parts of the kingdom unguarded and without troops.

For, through favour toward the aforesaid Prince Raynald rather than from consideration of the greater advantage, certain persons had urged the king to this course, paying little attention to what meanwhile might happen to the kingdom, deprived of its forces. How imprudently this was done, the immediately following outcome showed. For the princes around Damascus, Bosra, Baalbek, and Homs, seeing that the strength of the kingdom was absent and that the entire region lacked troops, secretly and quietly assembled their forces. Crossing the Jordan beside the Sea of Galilee, that is, the Sea of Tiberias, they stealthily entered our territories. [Col. 0863B]

After passing through part of Galilee, they reached a place below Mount Tabor called Buria, near the very ancient city of Nain. The people of those parts, relying on the truce, which they did not yet know had ended, were excessively secure and took too little precaution. Therefore the enemy rushed upon them secretly by night and surrounded the place on every side, so that those besieged had no avenue of flight even to the mountain which overlooked the site.

At daybreak, seeing an innumerable multitude of enemies around them, the inhabitants rushed together into the tower which commanded the suburb. Surrounding it on every side and undermining it with the utmost determination, they brought it down to the ground within four hours. Before its collapse, however, when it had already begun to crack and threatened to fall, they accepted the surrender of those who had fled into it. [Col. 0863C]

Then, freely and without opposition gathering the entire booty of both that place and the neighbouring places, they carried away in chains nearly five hundred persons, apart from those who had fallen in the fighting. For since the place was fertile and harvest-time had come, many people from neighbouring places had gone there to reap. Taking all of them away, as has been said, without opposition, they crossed the Jordan again and returned safe and unharmed to their own lands. [Col. 0863D]

## CHAPTER XV. The same man forcibly seizes our fortress in the region of Sueth, namely a most strongly fortified cave.

It happened moreover in those same days, while the king and the Christian army were still detained in the Syrian Sobal, that a highly dangerous and perpetually lamentable disaster befell our people. In the region of Sueth beyond the Jordan, sixteen miles from Tiberias, we had a very strongly fortified stronghold, said to be impregnable, from which much benefit was said to accrue to our people. For although that region bordered the enemy’s territories more closely than ours, and they could more easily have governed it at their own discretion and more confidently commanded its inhabitants, nevertheless, by the advantage of this fortress, it had been maintained for many years—and was still maintained—that authority there was divided equally between our people and them, and that revenues and tribute were shared equally. [Col. 0864A]

It was a cave situated in the side of a mountain, beneath which lay an immense precipice. From above there was absolutely no approach; from the other side there was only an exceedingly narrow path, which scarcely afforded passage without danger even to a man unburdened and free of every load. It had been entrusted to the fidelity and diligence of the noble and very wealthy Fulk of Tiberias.

The aforesaid enemy princes, who, as stated above, had stormed Buria and captured our people, approached this place and suddenly appeared before the stronghold. Within five days they captured it by assault. There was not one opinion concerning this event. Some asserted that those in the fortress, bribed with money, surrendered the place to the enemy. Others said that the enemy broke into the cave from the side, because the stone was chalky and easily dislodged, and that, entering violently, they occupied the first, lower station. Thus afterward they compelled to surrender those who were in the middle and upper chamber—for there were said to be three levels there. [Col. 0864B]

It was later discovered that the fortress had fallen to the enemy through the fault of the officers who commanded the rest. Although others wished to resist, they used their superior authority to forbid the defence; afterward, having surrendered the fortress, they went over to the enemy. Those who commanded the place were said to be Syrians, who among us are regarded as effeminate and soft. Therefore greater blame falls upon the aforesaid Fulk, who had set such men over a place of such necessity.

This report spread widely throughout the kingdom and reached our people beyond the Jordan, who wished to hinder Saladin’s crossing as he came up from Egypt into Syria and hastened toward Damascus. On learning it, all were dismayed, especially the count of Tripoli, to whose care the aforesaid fortress belonged. [Col. 0864C] Thus those who had negligently abandoned the kingdom now behaved there still more negligently and could accomplish nothing pleasing to God or useful to the kingdom. For although they ought to have met Saladin as he came, as far as the borders of our territory, and prevented him from entering the kingdom, they most imprudently allowed him to come as far as the place called Gerba, where he found an abundant supply of water, which his thirsty army particularly needed. From there he sent part of his expeditions around our fortress called Mount Royal; they cut down vineyards and inflicted other damage upon the inhabitants.

Had our people reached that place, he would without doubt have had to return to Egypt. For he dragged with him an immense multitude of unarmed people, whose water had already failed in their skins and whose bread had failed in their baskets; all these would have had to perish from hunger in the desert, since he could not advance and it was dangerous to engage our people. [Col. 0864D] Learning that he had already reached the aforesaid place, our people again resolved to meet him at the waters of Rasel Rasit. Had this been done, he would have had to continue his intended journey through a further stretch of desert, which he could not have completed without great loss of both men and beasts.

But when that purpose was not carried into effect, he reached the aforesaid waters without difficulty; and from there, without opposition, he entered his own borders in complete safety and arrived at Damascus. When our people learned this, they returned home by the same road by which they had previously come. Yet fearing that from Damascus, where he had withdrawn with all his company, he might devise some treachery and injury against the kingdom, the whole people of the kingdom assembled at the Fountain of Sephoria, between Sephoria and Nazareth. There, having with them the wood of the Lord’s Cross, and with the king, patriarch, and other ecclesiastical and secular princes of the kingdom present, they awaited the enemy’s attack day by day. [Col. 0865B]

## CHAPTER XVI. The same man forcibly enters our borders; a battle is fought near the castle of Forbelet, with an indecisive victory.

[Col. 0865C]

Meanwhile Saladin, having gathered from all his territories troops in addition to those which he had brought with him while departing from Egypt, and intending to enter our borders, came to the place which in their language is called Raseline, meaning “head of the water.” This place is said to lie a short distance from our borders and from the city of Tiberias. After remaining there for several days, he suddenly entered our territory and pitched camp at the place called Cavam, between two rivers, scarcely four miles from Tiberias.

When our people learned this through scouts, they sent the army in all haste to the aforesaid city, in order to take with them the military forces assigned to the defence of that place and the neighbouring fortresses, namely Safed and Belvoir, and immediately pursue the enemy. [Col. 0865D] But the count of Tripoli, a prudent and valiant man, highly experienced in warfare, was there suffering most dangerously from a double tertian fever. Great sorrow consequently came upon our people, who placed much reliance upon his counsel and foresight, because they were deprived, at so critical a moment, of the assistance of so great a prince.

Nevertheless, summoning auxiliary forces from neighbouring places and raising their standards, they pursued the enemy. Saladin, however, hearing of our people’s arrival, crossed the Jordan and led his expeditions into the region of Scythopolis. Scythopolis is the metropolis of Palestina Tertia, situated between Mount Gilboa and the Jordan, in plains and irrigated land. It was also called Bersan; the church of Nazareth, today located in the same diocese, enjoys its prerogative. For the aforesaid city is now seldom inhabited and has been reduced to the likeness of a small town. [Col. 0866A]

When the enemy squadrons reached that place, they began vigorously to attack a small fortress situated in the marshes there. But as the inhabitants resisted bravely and the enemy saw that they were making no progress, they directed their battle lines toward the new castle, now called Belvoir, situated in the hills between the aforesaid city and Tiberias, in order to meet our people.

Our men followed the waters of the Jordan; when they reached the aforesaid place, they left the valley and ascended into the hills, though much wearied by the discomfort of the immense heat, which had oppressed them beyond measure on the march. There they passed that night, dangerous because of the nearby enemy, maintaining unbroken watches. At dawn they descended into the plain between the aforesaid town and the village called Forbelet, and saw the enemy drawn up around them in a multitude such as they had not been accustomed to see. [Col. 0866B] The elder princes of the kingdom said that, since the first entrance of the Latins into Syria, they had never seen such forces of the enemy.

The number ready for battle was said to be about twenty thousand, whereas our cavalry were counted at scarcely seven hundred. Saladin and his princes had one common intention: to surround our people on every side so that not one might escape. Confident in the aforesaid multitude and despising our small numbers, they did not in the least suppose that our men could resist them. But He for whom it is not difficult to overcome a greater multitude with few men ordained otherwise.

Through the preceding mercy of the compassionate God, although in comparison with them our men seemed as nothing, they arranged their ranks according to military discipline and attacked the enemy squadrons with their customary courage. Enduring the enemy’s assaults with great steadfastness, they proved superior in that engagement. Yet many of our men, whom we refrain from naming individually, most shamefully withdrew themselves from the labours of war, to their perpetual disgrace. [Col. 0866C]

Baldwin of Ramla and his brother Balian conducted themselves excellently that day, fighting bravely and manfully. Hugh the Younger, stepson of the lord count of Tripoli, likewise earned a memory to be celebrated in blessing that day with the battle line of the men of Tiberias. Although he was rather young, nevertheless, beyond the strength of his age, with the aforesaid line which he commanded, he violently broke three enemy squadrons and put them to flight, returning unharmed to his own men through God’s grace. [Col. 0866D]

Of our side, few of the knightly order fell in that battle, but they attained the fellowship of the saints; of the common soldiers, more fell. The enemy’s slaughter was greater, and several of their princes also fell; their deaths dismayed the opposing side, which abandoned the field of battle. Nor should it be passed over in silence that in those days the heat was so exceptionally severe that no fewer in either army fell from the oppressive burning than by the sword. [Col. 0867A]

We could ascertain nothing certain about the number of enemy dead. To conceal their losses from our people, they carried away those who had fallen in battle and secretly buried them in their camp on the following night, lest knowledge of their destruction make our men stronger. Nevertheless, we say that in both the aforesaid incidents about one thousand of them fell.

When this had happened, Saladin, seeing that matters had turned out contrary to his expectation and that he had found opponents tougher than he had supposed, withdrew in confusion. Crossing the Jordan again, he returned to his own territory and pitched camp once more at the same place from which he had departed. Our people, recalling their battle lines, returned to the Fountain of Sephoria, whence they had earlier set out. [Col. 0867B]

On that journey a certain canon of the Holy Sepulchre, named Baldwin, treasurer of that church and bearer of the life-giving Cross, unable to endure the extreme heat, died while being carried in a litter beneath Mount Tabor, beside the torrent Kishon. Another brother and canon of the same church, Geoffrey of Neufville, who had been assigned to assist the aforesaid Baldwin on that journey, was, while carried away by concerns not his own, pierced by an arrow and perished in the aforesaid battle. For it is fitting that he who takes the sword should, according to the Lord’s saying, perish by the sword (Matt. 26:52).

## CHAPTER XVII. The same man, having summoned a fleet from Egypt, besieges the city of Beirut.

[Col. 0867C]

When the lord king, with his forces, had returned to the place mentioned above, Saladin, deeply distressed that the efforts of himself and his men had thus been frustrated, again summoned troops; again he ran through every kind of stratagem, anxiously deliberating with his followers how he might once more inflict renewed hardships upon our people. Seeing, however, that there was no more effective way to crush our men than by trying to harass them from several quarters, he sent orders and strict commands to the brother whom he had left in Egypt as administrator of his affairs, that he should speedily dispatch a fleet from Alexandria [Col. 0867D] and from all Egypt to Syria. He informed him of the plan he had in view: once the fleet had arrived, to blockade the city of Beirut both by sea and land. And lest the people of the kingdom should be able to hasten with the king to its relief, he further commanded him, gathering the remaining cavalry forces in Egypt, to enter also from the south and ravage the whole region around Gaza, Ascalon, and Darum—the outermost towns of our kingdom, facing the Egyptian district.

His purpose in this was that, while one part of the kingdom tried to confront those invading from Egypt, the remainder, weakened and reduced in numbers, would leave him freer to assail the besieged city more fiercely. And it happened according to his design [Col. 0868A] and the terms of his command. For within a few days a fleet of thirty beaked warships arrived as agreed; and his brother brought forces, gathered from throughout Egypt as far as he could, into the vicinity of Darum. Saladin himself, in order to be better prepared when the fleet arrived, sent his forces into the region popularly called the Valley of Bacar, stationing scouts on the mountains lying between that region and the territory of Beirut, which project into the sea, so that they might inform him of the galleys’ arrival. Meanwhile, he summoned infantry reinforcements from neighboring places and carefully procured whatever he judged necessary for the coming siege.

Without delay, around the Kalends of August, the aforesaid fleet landed [Col. 0868B] on the coast of Beirut. When this was reported to Saladin by scouts specially assigned for that purpose, he immediately, without delay, crossed the intervening mountains already mentioned and brought all his forces down into the plain; and he enclosed the often-named city on every side with a siege, as he had long before intended.

Among our men, who were encamped at Sephoria, conflicting reports circulated concerning Saladin’s purpose. Some said that he had decided, as was later certainly clear, to besiege Beirut; others asserted that all his attention was fixed upon acquiring Aleppo; while some maintained that he was trying to meet the lord of Mosul, the great and powerful Turkish ruler, who was said to be besieging certain of his towns near the Euphrates. But while this uncertain report was being discussed in the camp, a messenger arrived to resolve the ambiguity, declaring beyond all doubt that Beirut was under siege. There also came a messenger from the south reporting with certainty that Saladin’s brother had invaded our borders near Darum with enormous forces, had killed thirty-six light-armed soldiers called Turcopoles, and had burned certain suburbs. When this became known, the king, after deliberation with the princes, chose to meet the more dangerous threat and to free the besieged city from its impending distress; for his forces did not seem sufficient to repel both enemies from his territories at the same [Col. 0868D] time.

## Chapter XVIII. The king hastens to its relief and reaches Tyre. Saladin raises the siege.

The forces having therefore been summoned and the entire army moved, the king reached Tyre. He also ordered the fleet found being prepared both in the harbor of Acre and in that of Tyre to be made ready. Suddenly, and beyond everyone’s expectation, within seven days he assembled thirty-three galleys, excellently armed and manned by brave men.

Meanwhile, while these things were being prepared among us with great diligence and ardent hope, Saladin, besieging the city as stated above, inflicted upon the citizens every hardship he could, with both armies exerting themselves in the matter. For, arranging divisions [Col. 0869A] around the city and relieving them with successive contingents, he imposed such pressure upon the besieged for three continuous days that he allowed them no rest and granted them no interval even for the bodily refreshment they required. Yet he had brought with him no engines, missile-throwers, or other devices by which strongholds are usually captured by enemies—either because he thought that without their aid he could suddenly and easily break into the city and seize it by force, or because, expecting our swift arrival, he refused to expend so much labor uselessly. What he could accomplish without engines, however, he pursued with diligent effort and every care.

For, as has been said, he had stationed around the city in ordered sequence an innumerable multitude, relieving one another in alternating turns, who discharged such a mass of arrows upon those on the walls and towers laboring for the city’s defense that they filled both city and ramparts as though with hail. Nor did they endeavor only in this way to drive the besieged from defending the city. They also tried forcefully to introduce miners, specially summoned to undermine the wall, so that by breaking down the outer works and walls they might open entrances through which bodies of armed men could enter despite the citizens. And in order that these men might devote themselves more freely to this work, others, as stated, pressed the attack with bows and crossbows and an endless discharge of missiles; they attacked with such violence that those within scarcely dared put out a finger without danger of death.

Yet the citizens, although very few, obeyed the admonitions and exhortations especially of the city’s governor and bishop, whose courage and steadfastness in this affair deserve much praise. They countered all these devices with contrary measures and left no method of resistance untried. Against the outside archers they returned darts and arrows with no lesser skill or zeal, thereby inflicting far greater losses upon the enemy and more frequently bringing death upon those who seemed to press the attack with the greatest violence. Against those attempting to undermine the wall they employed the same art, so that they often either killed the laborers at their work or took away their digging tools.

Nor were these great hardships inflicted upon the besieged citizens only by those who had arrived overland: those who had approached by ship pressed them no less violently and no less hostilely. Saladin himself, stationed on a hill not far from the city, encouraged his men to attack by his own presence and by exhortation. He succeeded so far that one of his princes, named Choelinus, resolved that ladders should be set against the walls and proclaimed that an assault must be made by force. For it seemed shameful and disgraceful to him that so small a people could or dared resist so great a multitude of such men. While he persisted most intently in this plan and encouraged others to the same course both by word and example, he was suddenly struck in the face by an arrow near the eye, [Col. 0870A] and withdrew both himself and the others from the undertaking begun.

Having thus attacked the city for almost three continuous days, and seeing that they made no progress, those who had arrived by sea, by Saladin’s command, withdrew into their galleys and secretly departed by night around the beginning of the third night. Saladin likewise recalled his contingents and withdrew some distance from the city. Across the plains adjoining it, he began dividing his troops, ordering the towers in the adjacent suburbs to be entirely demolished. Nor did they spare the orchards and vineyards, which were very numerous around the city, but cut everything down with axe and hatchet.

In order that he might continue the siege more freely and safely, he had certain difficult and narrow passages between the city and Sidon—through which our army, coming to relieve the city, would necessarily have to pass—occupied not only by his infantry. Where the narrows were greatest, he had a dry-stone wall, without mortar, carried down to the very sea, [Col. 0870B] so that our divisions, hindered by both obstacles, might approach him less freely, while he meanwhile continued to harass the city. Although he was previously said to have held the firm and fixed intention of not departing from the siege unless the city were broken by force, he changed his mind and, as stated above, hastened back to his own lands.

The reason for this is said to have been that guards watching the routes happened to capture a bearer of letters sent into the city by certain faithful men to strengthen the morale of the besieged. They brought him before Saladin and subjected him to severe interrogation. From his confession, forcibly extracted, and from the contents of the letters, they learned that both divisions of our army were ready and would without doubt arrive within three days. Accordingly, changing their plan, they raised the siege, as has been said.

Our fleet nevertheless reached its appointed destination; but finding the city free, it returned, after no long interval, to the harbors from which it had departed. The king and his entire army, learning that the enemies had withdrawn from the besieged city, remained at Tyre for several days and then, recalling the forces, returned to Sephoria.

## Chapter XIX. Saladin crosses the Euphrates and enters Mesopotamia.

[Col. 0870D]

Meanwhile Saladin, being a most watchful man and striving with all the ardor of his mind to enlarge the glory of his name and the extent of his kingdom, treated our strength as though it were nothing and aspired to greater things. He resolved to cross into the eastern regions. It is not yet certainly clear whether he undertook this through his own initiative and his customary impetuous high spirit, or whether, summoned by the princes of that region, he attempted an enterprise so difficult and apparently beyond his strength.

Whatever confidence inspired him, he gathered great forces of cavalry and, arranging baggage and provisions according to the requirements of place and time—whatever seemed sufficient for completing so great a journey—hastened toward the Euphrates. Among us, however, the common report was that he was making for Aleppo in an effort to claim it for himself. For that city alone, with a few adjacent towns, remained from the whole inheritance of Nur al-Din and had not yet come under his power. After the death of Nur al-Din’s son, it was held, with Qutb al-Din’s permission, by the brother of Qutb al-Din, lord of Mosul; the inheritance had devolved by hereditary right upon Qutb al-Din at the death of the said young man. It was therefore believed, and plausibly so, that he had hastened into those regions in order to obtain that city. But, as the outcome revealed, he had conceived far loftier designs.

For, leaving that city behind and crossing the Euphrates, he claimed within a few days for himself the most splendid cities of Mesopotamia—Edessa, Carrhae, and many others with their dependent towns—and almost the whole region formerly subject to the authority of the aforesaid prince, the lord of Mosul, through both force and the intervention of gifts. [Col. 0871B] By lavishly bribing the leading men of the regions, who were bound in fidelity to the often-mentioned lord, and receiving their towns, he brought them all into his obedience. Thus that great and noble prince, entirely deprived of his followers’ support, was said to be unable to confront or resist him. It was even publicly reported that, having corrupted his household and retainers, Saladin had administered him a deadly drink, from which he afterwards barely escaped; and consequently, according to report, Saladin was believed already to have reached Mosul freely with his forces.

Yet conflicting reports about this affair circulated among us. Some said that he was proceeding successfully and that everything was coming to him as he wished; others, on the contrary, asserted that the great princes of those regions had united against his arrogance and that his army had been badly handled.

## Chapter XX. The king ravages the territory of Damascus as an enemy.

The king and princes of our kingdom, seeing the enemy region deprived of military forces, judged—as indeed it might rightly seem—that the desired opportunity to injure the enemy lay open. They were all the more indignant at the great arrogance of the man who had departed: scorning the kingdom’s forces, he had set out to claim foreign realms for himself without making either truce or treaty with the king. After taking counsel and gathering the kingdom’s forces, they took with them the precious wood of the life-giving Cross; and the lord patriarch accompanying them, they entered the enemy’s territory to ravage the region according to their strength.

Crossing the region of Trachonitis, which forms no small part of the diocese of Bostra, they entered Lesser Syria, whose capital is Damascus. Advancing toward its eastern side, they violently broke into a celebrated and well-known, densely inhabited place called Zora, not far from Damascus; then, ranging through much of the region, they destroyed by fire and other means of damage the outlying settlements commonly called *casalia*. [Col. 0872A] The inhabitants, having learned beforehand of our men’s approach, had removed themselves with their flocks and herds, children and wives, to more fortified places. Thus our men carried back either no booty and spoils or very little; but the grain and other necessities of life which the inhabitants could not take away, our men consumed by fire or by whatever other means could be used.

Returning while devastating everything they encountered, they passed near that region’s noble metropolis, Bostra, popularly called Bosseret. When our men discussed breaking into that city’s suburb, they saw that this could not be done suddenly but would require a longer delay than their lack of water allowed. They therefore prepared to return, fearing the severity of thirst for themselves, their horses, and all their beasts of burden. The said region is wholly arid and waterless, having neither springs, streams, nor rivers. During the winter months its inhabitants usually collect rainwater in pools and preserve it with every care for essential use throughout the whole year; but the sun’s heat and the continual mud lying over it make it tasteless. Learning of our men’s approach, they had either drained these reservoirs by breaking them open or polluted them with filth, so that the passing army could not remain there. Nor did that season allow them to carry out as much devastation as they wished. The grain and other things usually consumed by fire had already been stored in granaries which that region customarily has in underground caves; many of these, covered with earth and artfully concealed, were difficult to find. And whatever was found on threshing floors, stripped of straw and cleared of chaff, did not easily catch fire, since the great bareness did not allow fire to take hold. They could scarcely do other damage to the threshing floors than scatter the grain and carry it away for their horses’ use. Many, however, seeking means of destruction, mixed straw from one place and chaff from another with the already cleaned grain, so that it might more easily catch fire. [Col. 0872D]

The remainder of the troops which Saladin had left in that region, because they did not have sufficient confidence in their strength to dare engage our men or directly impede them, followed at a distance in groups, in order to devise something secretly against the rear of the departing army. Yet not even thus were they able to impede our men or harm the whole army or any part of it.

## Chapter XXI. He besieges, captures, and restores to Christendom the stronghold which Saladin had recently occupied.

After crossing the region and damaging it as far as they were able, our men returned and halted in that part of the same province called Suite. This is the region in which lies the stronghold that, a little before, as we have said, the enemy had deceitfully taken from us while they were staying in Syrian Sobal. It is a region distinguished by the abundance of wine, grain, and oil, and likewise by healthfulness and exceptional beauty. It is said that Job’s friend Baldad came from it, and was therefore surnamed the Suites.

On arriving there, they judged it honorable and decided that it ought to be done: they would besiege the aforesaid fortress and, by recovering the place if God granted it to them, repair the injury the enemy had inflicted upon us by its deceitful capture. Accordingly, they pitched camp before the aforesaid place and applied every labor [Col. 0873B] and effort to compel those within to surrender.

Because the place was extremely strong and so situated that it could be harmed only from above—and there only by cutting through the rock as far as the dwelling itself—they decided to station stonecutters on the upper side, together with as many necessary assistants and guards for the works as they had, so that they might labor safely and without danger from attackers. For there was a cave high on a mountainside, accessible only with great difficulty: even a foot-soldier could scarcely make his way there, since below it, down to the depth of the valley beneath, lay an immense and terrible precipice; while from the side it was approached by a path scarcely one foot wide.

Within the same cave were three chambers, placed one above another. There was access and descent between them by certain wooden ladders and narrow openings. They therefore began to cut into the cave from above—the only direction from which it could be harmed, as stated—in the attempt to penetrate by cutting into the first and uppermost chamber. All our men’s attention was directed to this, and all their labor expended upon it. Having assigned the necessary craftsmen to execute the work, and assisting laborers to roll the cut stones and fragments of rock down the steep slope into the valley below, so that the work might proceed without interruption, they established alternating shifts by day and night. When the first workers were exhausted, fresh men took their place, able and trained to bear the burden of the work.

The labor advanced greatly, both because of the number and enthusiasm of those engaged in it and because of a certain quality of the rock itself. It was chalky stone, easy to break, except that veins of very hard flint were interspersed within it. These often damaged the iron tools and repeatedly hindered those busily engaged in the work. Whatever fragments were rolled down into the valley below in order to clear the place, as stated, were observed at close hand by those besieged in the cave. [Col. 0874A] This filled them with greater fear, as they expected every hour that, once the cutting was completed, their enemies would burst in upon them by force.

Our army was divided into two parts. One part, as has been said, had pitched camp on the summit of the mountain where the cave stood, in order to protect those occupied with the work from enemy ambushes. The other remained below on the plain, with the specific purpose of denying the besieged entrance and exit. These men also sometimes approached the lower chamber of the cave by the narrow path mentioned above, and, though they made no progress, attempted to harass those within by assaults.

Inside were about seventy strong and warlike men, well supplied both with provisions and weapons. Saladin, trusting greatly in their proven courage, loyalty, and steadfastness, had left them there when he departed, entrusting the fortress to their care. Matters had now reached the point that those in the cave could not rest inside because of the frequent and almost continuous blows of the hammers. At each repeated stroke, the cave seemed to tremble and the whole structure to be shaken. They no longer feared that our men would force their way in against them, but rather that the entire cave, exhausted by the repeated hammering, would suddenly collapse and crush them all. Finally, they could have no hope whatever of relief. They already knew that Saladin had gone away to very distant regions, from which he could not easily return, and had taken the military forces with him.

Therefore, after they had endured the siege for three weeks or a little more, they sent an embassy to the lord king and, through the intervention of the lord count of Tripoli, obtained permission, upon surrendering the stronghold, to proceed freely as far as Bostra with the weapons they themselves had brought into it and with their own belongings. Thus, when they had departed and the stronghold had been recovered, we wiped away, with the Lord’s help and through His superabundant grace, the disgrace which we had seemed earlier to incur through its loss. The lord king and the other princes then took considerable care promptly, as seemed expedient, to fortify the surrendered place with arms [Col. 0874D] and provisions and to entrust it to faithful men whose loyalty and competence could not be doubted. When all this had been completed with every diligence, our army returned home.

This happened in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1182, in the month of October.

## Chapter XXII. The king again enters the territory of Damascus with his forces.

A short time after this—namely, in the following December—our people saw that Saladin had not returned and was still detained, occupied with greater enterprises in the regions around Mosul. Not wishing to lose the opportunity afforded by his absence, they again assembled, took counsel concerning the kingdom, and unanimously agreed at the maritime city of Caesarea that, having gathered the kingdom’s forces and provided for fifteen days the necessities both of men and beasts, they would again enter enemy territory, not neglecting the opportunity offered.

Accordingly, they conducted a secret expedition, taking only cavalry with them. From the enemy territories adjoining Bostra they carried off, as had been agreed from the beginning, booty in flocks and herds and also very many captives, returning safely to their own lands. Because this enterprise both set out from and returned to the region of Tiberias, the lord count of Tripoli commanded it.

On the fifteenth day, however, the king, with all the princes of the kingdom and such forces of cavalry and infantry as the kingdom could then supply, taking with him the Lord’s Cross, arrived near Tiberias, beside the Sea of Galilee, at a place called Castelletum. From there, crossing the river at a place called Jacob’s Ford, he entered enemy territory. The army then advanced, leaving Lebanon on its left and following the flatter ground. First they utterly destroyed by fire and demolition a place called Bettegene, together with its adjacent villages, delivering all its goods to destruction by various means. They then continued their march to a place called Daria, scarcely four or five miles from Damascus, which they likewise ravaged in the same manner with its neighboring villages.

The inhabitants of the region had partly gone to the ridges of Lebanon and partly fled to Damascus. Thus in the whole region our men could scarcely capture a single enemy. We did, however, lose certain of our own men who had gone out to forage and behaved incautiously. Some horsemen had come out from Damascus; trusting in their horses’ speed, they sometimes rode far ahead of the army and sometimes followed behind it, watching for a time or place to inflict harm. Falling upon the men just mentioned, they treated them in the manner of enemies and slaughtered them all.

The citizens of Damascus, coming out of the city and gathering in bands around the numerous orchards adjoining it, watched our columns from afar and did not dare advance. Thus neither our men attempted to attack them nor they our forces; but when our men departed, they withdrew into the city. Our men, having traversed and damaged the region as stated, returned home without difficulty or impediment. The lord king hastened to Tyre in order to celebrate there with us the feast of the Lord’s Nativity.

## Chapter XXIII. A tax is collected in the kingdom, by which the kingdom may protect itself against future dangers.

Meanwhile uncertain reports concerning Saladin were circulating. Some said that in Mesopotamia, around Mosul, he was making great progress and subjecting the whole region to himself. Others said that all the princes of the eastern lands had assembled to drive him forcibly out of those regions and recover from him the territories which he had claimed through deceit and the use of money. His success greatly alarmed us; and we were exceedingly concerned that he might not gain greater power, fearing that, with increased forces, he would return against us stronger.

Consequently, in the following February all the princes of the kingdom assembled at Jerusalem to deliberate upon the present condition of affairs. As stated, Saladin’s return was greatly feared, and they therefore strove more anxiously to provide every means of resistance. After many discussions, it was decided by general agreement that a tax should be collected throughout the kingdom, from which we might have cavalry and infantry forces in time of necessity, so that the returning enemy might find us ready to resist. For the king and the other princes had fallen into such poverty that they were wholly unable to fulfill their necessary obligations.

Public money was therefore collected. The manner of its assessment will be more fully evident from the text of the ordinance made concerning this business, which reads as follows:

This is the method of collecting the tax which, by the common decision of all the princes, ecclesiastical as well as secular, and by consent of the whole people of the kingdom of Jerusalem, is to be collected for the common benefit of that kingdom against impending necessities.

It has been publicly decreed that in every city of the kingdom four prudent and trustworthy men shall be chosen. Having themselves first taken a bodily oath that they will act in good faith in the present business, they shall first give for themselves and then compel others to do the same: from every one hundred Byzantines which they possess, or their equivalent, whether in property held by them or debts owed to them, one Byzantine; and from revenues, two Byzantines for every one hundred Byzantines. In compelling others, they must act in this manner: each citizen or inhabitant of the cities or places over which they preside shall privately be assessed, according to their good-faith judgment of the value of his resources, what he ought to pay toward the aforesaid contribution, each according to his means. If the person assessed declares that he has been burdened and charged beyond his means, he shall state according to his own conscience what he considers his movable property to be worth, and, after swearing that he ought to give no more, he shall be released according to the stated provision.

The four men shall be bound by the obligation of their oath to keep secret whatever has been offered them by citizens, whether great or small; and they shall likewise be bound by oath not to disclose their wealth or poverty. They must observe this rule for all whose property is worth one hundred Byzantines, of whatever language, nation, or faith, without distinction of sex: whether men or women, all shall be subject to this law. But if the said four persons appointed for this purpose know certainly that someone’s property is not worth one hundred Byzantines, they shall take from him a *foagium*, that is, one Byzantine per hearth; if he cannot pay the whole, they shall take half; and if he cannot pay half, they shall take a *rabuinum* [quarter-payment], according as they judge in good faith ought to be done. All persons, whatever their nation, language, faith, or sex, whose movable goods are not worth one hundred Byzantines shall be subject to this provision.

It is also decreed that every church, every monastery, all barons without exception, and also vavassors, must give two Byzantines out of every hundred Byzantines of revenue which they possess, just as all others in the kingdom who have revenues must do; while holders of a knight’s fee (*solidarii*) shall give one Byzantine out of every hundred Byzantines. Whoever possesses villages (*casalia*) is bound to swear that, in addition to the provisions above, he will in good faith give one Byzantine from every hearth in his villages and *casalia*: thus, if a village has one hundred hearths, he shall cause one hundred Byzantines to be paid from it by compelling the peasants. The lord of the village shall afterwards apportion the aforesaid Byzantines among the peasants of that place in suitable shares, so that each person is compelled to make the aforesaid payment according to his means and the richer do not escape more lightly, nor the poorer bear a heavier burden. The same shall apply whether a village has more or fewer hearths.

The money thus collected from each city situated from Caipha inland toward Jerusalem shall be carried to Jerusalem by those who, as stated, preside over the respective cities and castles. They shall deliver it in specified number and weight to those appointed at Jerusalem for this business. These officials shall place it separately, as they receive it from each city or other place, in individual sealed sacks in the chest kept in the treasury of the Holy Cross, in the presence of the lord patriarch or his messenger, the prior of the Holy Sepulchre, and the castellan of the same city. The chest shall have three locks and as many keys: the first key shall be held by the lord patriarch, the second by the prior of the Sepulchre, and the third by the castellan and the four aforesaid citizens appointed to collect the money.

From Caipha as far as Beirut, those presiding over the cities shall likewise carry the collected money to the city of Acre. There it shall be delivered, as from the individual cities and castles, in specified number and weight to the four men appointed to collect the money in that city. It shall be placed in separate marked and sealed sacks in a chest having three locks and as many keys. The first key shall be held by the lord archbishop of Tyre; the second by Joscelin, the royal seneschal; and the third by the aforesaid four citizens appointed to this duty in the city of Acre. These persons shall receive the aforesaid money in the presence of the said lords who hold the keys.

The money thus collected must not be spent on the lesser affairs of the kingdom, but only upon the descent into the land [that is, a major military emergency]; and so long as this money remains, the exactions commonly called *taliae* shall cease, both from churches and from cities. This levy shall be made once only and shall not hereafter be regarded as a custom.

## Chapter XXIV. Saladin besieges Aleppo and obtains it upon certain stipulated conditions. The prince of Antioch exchanges Tarsus with Rupen, leader of the Armenians.

Meanwhile Saladin, an energetic man who behaved in every respect as a vigorous prince, occupied the regions of Mesopotamia in Syria and violently claimed for himself cities of the highest importance. Among them he besieged the distinguished metropolis of Amida, which, both because of the size of its population and the exceedingly strong circuit of its walls, as well as the nature of its site, seemed impregnable [Col. 0878B]. He took it by assault; and, having taken it, handed it over by agreement to a certain Turkish prince named Nur al-Din, son of Karaslan, relying on whose service and assistance he had spent a secure period in those parts and subdued the country.

In the spring which followed soon afterward, having recalled his expeditionary forces and placed the whole region safely in the hands of his faithful followers, he crossed back over the Euphrates and returned to Coele-Syria. He stationed his army around Aleppo and laboured by every means to harass the city. The man governing that city, seeing that his brother—much stronger and more powerful than himself, namely the lord of Mosul—had been unable to keep Saladin from his territories, but that Saladin, despite his opposition, had subdued all the provinces beyond the Euphrates, feared that something similar might happen to him [Col. 0878C]. He therefore sent a secret embassy, without the knowledge of the people of Aleppo, and made an agreement with Saladin: if Saladin restored to him Semar and certain other towns, whose names we do not possess, he himself would surrender Aleppo to him.

Saladin received this embassy with the greatest delight, since from the beginning of his rule he had desired nothing more eagerly than somehow to bring Aleppo—virtually the strength of the entire kingdom—under his own authority. He readily agreed to the terms; and, when the aforementioned city with its adjacent dependencies had been handed over, he received Aleppo on the Nones of June [5 June].

Then a doubled fear first seized our people, for what they most feared had occurred. From the beginning it had seemed to them that, if he could add that often-mentioned city to his dominion, all our territory would appear hemmed in on every side, as though enclosed in a siege by his power and forces [Col. 0878D]. Accordingly, when the news became known, our people turned themselves to various measures, working to fortify the cities and towns, especially those situated on the enemy frontier; above all, the city of Beirut, which seemed to stand in greatest need of such works.

The prince of Antioch too, anxious because so great an enemy was now near, and seeing a more formidable adversary set against him, came to the king, who was then staying in Acre. He brought a small retinue, lest he leave his own land destitute of military forces, and took with him the count of Tripoli. There, in the presence of the princes of the realm, he sought aid against the aforesaid Saladin and was heard as he wished [Col. 0879A]. About three hundred knights of mixed status were assigned from the kingdom’s soldiery for the desired relief. They followed him to the region of Antioch; but, while they were ready to serve in his warfare, within a short time, having obtained his leave, they returned.

The prince himself made a temporary peace with Saladin and appeared to have obtained some tranquillity. To diminish his anxieties and enable himself to watch more closely over the Antiochene frontier and devote more attentive care to it, he transferred Tarsus, the chief metropolis of Cilicia, which he had received from the Greeks, to Rupen, the most powerful Armenian lord, who possessed the other cities of that region, for a large sum of money [Col. 0879B]. This was a prudent act. For Tarsus lay too far from him, and Rupen’s land intervened; the prince could not care for it except with difficulty and boundless expense, whereas this was easy for that nobleman.

Saladin, having arranged matters in that region as he wished, moved with his legions to Damascus. This seized our people with a fear far more violent than before, and all the more dangerous because they could gain no certain knowledge from spies of his intentions. Some thought that, after summoning a naval force, he intended to besiege Beirut as he had done in the previous year. Others maintained that he meant to capture the two fortresses in the uplands overlooking Tyre, Toron and Chastel Neuf [Col. 0879C]. Others thought he had set his heart on ravaging the territory beyond the Jordan—namely the land of Suab—and destroying the towns in that region. Some further tried to persuade others that, wearied by long and continuous expeditions, he intended, after obtaining peace for a time, to go down into Egypt, in order to restore his exhausted armies and collect again the expenditure needed for future campaigns.

Amid such uncertainties, the king and all the princes of the kingdom waited in great anxiety. They assembled the kingdom’s forces at the spring of Sephoria, where armies in the field customarily gathered from ancient practice, and awaited the outcome [Col. 0879D]. The prince of Antioch and the count of Tripoli were summoned, and forces and aid were solicited from them. Day by day they expected that Saladin would suddenly break into some part of the kingdom and bring in legions more numerous than usual.

## CHAPTER XXV. The king is seized by a severe illness at Nazareth and appoints Guy of Lusignan, count of Jaffa, administrator of the kingdom.

While our army was thus held in suspense at the spring of Sephoria, the king at Nazareth was struck with a sudden fever and became gravely ill. His leprosy, which had troubled him from the beginning of his reign and from the first years of his youth, increased beyond its usual severity. He lost his sight [Col. 0880A]; and as the extremities of his body were afflicted and decaying entirely, his feet and hands refused their service. Yet he had until then refused to lay aside his royal dignity and government, although some advised him to abdicate and, choosing a quiet life apart for himself from the royal resources, to make honourable provision for his needs.

For although weak and powerless in body, he was strong in spirit and strove beyond his strength to conceal his illness and bear the burden of royal care. Seized by the fever, as we have said, and despairing of life, he summoned his princes to him. With his mother and the lord patriarch present, he appointed Guy of Lusignan, husband of his sister and count of Jaffa and Ascalon, of whom we have made very frequent mention above, administrator of the kingdom [Col. 0880B]. He retained for himself the royal dignity and Jerusalem alone, with an annual revenue of ten thousand gold pieces; but he granted Guy the general and free administration of all the other parts of the kingdom. He ordered his faithful men and all the princes generally to become Guy’s vassals and render him fealty by hand; and this was done.

Before this, however, Guy is said to have sworn at the king’s command that, while the king lived, he would not aspire to the crown, and that he would transfer to no one, or alienate from the fisc, any city or castle then possessed by the king. It is believed that this obligation was deliberately and carefully imposed upon him and that, in the presence of all the princes, he was bound by the sacred obligation of an oath firmly to observe it [Col. 0880C]. For he had promised considerable portions to each of them—nearly all the chief members of the kingdom—in order that their votes and support might help him obtain what he sought; and, it was said, he was bound by a similar bond to fulfil these promises. We ought not, however, to affirm this as fact, since we have not established it as certain; nevertheless, the report was widely circulated among the people.

There were some to whom this change was not very pleasing. Some, through personal attachments and hidden motives, were inclined to dislike it. Others, acting from public concerns and anxiously troubled about the state of the kingdom, openly declared that the aforesaid count was unequal to the burden of so great an administration and could not suffice to manage the affairs of the realm [Col. 0880D]. Others, who hoped to improve their own circumstances through his advancement, asserted that it had been done wisely. Thus there was much murmuring and discordant talk among the people, according to the proverbial saying:

> As many people, so many opinions.

Yet he did not long rejoice in this administration, long desired and granted to him as he wished, in which at first he seemed to glory quite thoughtlessly, as will be said below. We say that the count assumed this burden thoughtlessly because he had not carefully enough weighed his powers against the office imposed on him. Unequal both in strength and judgment, he placed an unbearable weight upon his shoulders [Col. 0881A], insufficiently instructed by the Gospel parable which advises one wishing to build a tower first to sit down, calculate the cost, and carefully determine whether his resources equal the undertaking, lest, failing, he should hear: “This man began to build and was unable to finish.”

## CHAPTER XXVI. Saladin enters our borders with enormous forces and encamps near Scythopolis; our forces meet him.

With matters thus standing among us, and with the greater part of our army assembled at Sephoria, the often-mentioned Saladin, after much deliberation, summoned forces from the region beyond the Euphrates and gathered whatever mounted troops he could enlist from every quarter. With a great and fully armed host, he finally entered our borders [Col. 0881B]. Passing swiftly through Auranitis, he appeared with his legions beside the Sea of Tiberias, in the plains of the Jordan, at a place called Cavan, his army divided into various detachments. From there he hastened along the waters of the Jordan toward Scythopolis.

Scythopolis, as has often been said, is the place now called Bethsan, once the metropolis of all Galilee. Proofs of its former splendour may be gathered from the ruins of its ancient buildings and the great quantity of marble found in its shattered structures [Col. 0881C]. But it has now been reduced to nothing and is rarely inhabited, save for a small town situated amid marshes, reserved as the dwelling-place of a few people. Although these inhabitants had arms and provisions sufficient for their number and the capacity of the place, they distrusted the strength of their defence. Before the hostile army had fully approached, they abandoned the fortress, leaving all their baggage, and withdrew to Tiberias.

Thus the enemy, reaching the said place and finding it empty, treated it as they pleased, carrying away all the arms, provisions, and every useful thing inside. Then, advancing with their army divided, one part encamped near a spring named Tubania [Col. 0881D], which rises at the foot of Mount Gilboa, beside the anciently famous city called Jezreel, now commonly called Little Gerinum, following the advantage of the water supply.

Our forces were still encamped at the spring of Sephoria—of which we have made very frequent mention in these writings—waiting anxiously to see from which direction the enemy legions would break into our territory. When they learned that the enemy held the plains around Bethsan and had already occupied those regions with legions divided in many directions, they seized their arms with one accord. Following the wood of the life-giving Cross and the royal banners, they crossed the hills on which Nazareth, the city of the Lord, is situated, and descended into the great plain [Col. 0882A] whose ancient name is Esdraelon.

Having drawn up their battle lines and arranged them appropriately according to military discipline, they directed their columns toward the spring of Tubania, where Saladin, with a vast body of distinguished and chosen soldiers, had posted himself beside the waters. Their apparent purpose was to drive away the enemy and claim the advantage of the water for themselves. On arriving, they judged that they could not obtain the water without difficulty and dangerous encounters. Saladin suddenly broke camp, unexpectedly abandoned the spring, and encamped lower down toward Bethsan, following the stream from the same spring, scarcely one mile distant from our forces.

Before our men reached him, however, the enemy had begun to divide themselves in squadrons from their main force, range through the neighbouring country, and treat it in the manner of enemies [Col. 0882B]. Some destroyed the aforesaid village of Little Gerinum and gave everything found in it over to destruction; but they found few or no inhabitants, for these had withdrawn to more fortified places when they learned beforehand of the enemy’s approach. Others came to the place commonly called Forbelet, broke into the village, and treated as enemies everything that came before them. Others followed the public roads by which both horsemen and foot soldiers hurried from different directions toward our army, and inflicted many dangers on travellers, so that no one could reach our army from any direction without peril and risk of death [Col. 0882C].

Some of them even climbed Mount Tabor—something previously unheard of—and, treating at will the Greek monastery called Saint Elijah’s, attempted to break into the larger monastery itself. But the monks, all their household, and some people from neighbouring villages had taken refuge within the enclosure of the monastery, protected by wall and towers; and they manfully drove away from the entire circuit of the monastery the enemy who had climbed the mountain.

Others from the same company likewise climbed the mountain on which Nazareth stands, so that from the projecting hills they looked down upon the whole city below [Col. 0882D].
