They caused such terror among the women, children, old people, and infirm left in the city that, as they struggled competitively to take refuge in the greater church for safety, many were said to have perished, suffocated by the crowd. For a great part of the city’s men capable of bearing arms had either followed the army on the public expedition or moved with their households to the coastal cities, especially Ptolemais.

## CHAPTER XXVII. A severe famine arises in the army; at last both our forces and the enemy withdraw from each other without battle.

Thus those who had separated from the larger enemy army, scattered far and wide over the whole region [Col. 0883A], inflicted harsh and very grave perils upon those wishing to reach our legions. Such fear arose that no one dared approach our camp, either for trade or in the capacity of auxiliary; consequently famine suddenly broke out in the army.

To meet the enemy more swiftly, our battle lines had moved there without burdens or baggage, hoping that the affair would end within two or at least three days. The foot soldiers suffered especially, and above all the Pisans, Genoese, Venetians, and Lombards who had been summoned with the greatest urgency from the coast. Leaving their ships and equipment for crossing the sea—for the sailing season was pressing, with October already almost half gone—they had joined our camp along with the pilgrims whom they had undertaken to transport [Col. 0883B]. All these men, scarcely sufficient even to bear arms, had brought no provisions at all, because the camp was about twenty miles from the sea.

Envoys were therefore sent to the neighbouring cities to urge their governors to send food with all speed. Obeying the royal command with due diligence, they eagerly and without delay directed as much provision as they could to that place. The greater part reached the camp and supplied abundance sufficient for place and time; but a portion, conveyed less carefully, fell into the hands of the enemy and brought them much benefit, since they too were suffering from want.

Some of our horsemen had been sent ahead and were especially charged to secure a safe approach for those coming to the army with food [Col. 0883C]. Those whom they met were brought safely into camp; but those who lacked this protection fell into the enemy’s hands and were either killed by the sword or compelled to serve the enemy permanently.

Here indeed, had our sins allowed God to be favourable to us, the enemy’s strength seemed capable of being easily overthrown and their intolerable arrogance cast down. Never, it is recorded, had so great a multitude of both cavalry and infantry gathered from the whole eastern region; nor do any elders report that so heavily armed a force had assembled from the resources of a single kingdom. They had about thirteen hundred cavalrymen, and the number of excellently armed foot soldiers was said to exceed fifteen thousand [Col. 0883D].

Moreover, great and admirable commanders led the army, illustrious by birth and famous for military experience: Lord Raymond, count of Tripoli; Lord Henry, duke of Louvain, a noble prince of the German Empire; Ralph of Maleine, a renowned man of Aquitaine; besides the princes of the kingdom: Guy, count of Jaffa; Raynald of Châtillon, lord of the land beyond the Jordan and formerly prince of Antioch; Baldwin of Ramla; his brother Balian of Nablus; Raynald of Sidon; Walter of Caesarea; and Joscelin, the royal seneschal.

From all this it seemed very likely that our enemies had crossed the Jordan far too rashly and settled in our territory. But because our sins deserved it, “contempt was poured upon princes” (Psalm 106:40) [Col. 0884A], so that in public affairs requiring such great diligence they were said to have acted not merely negligently but maliciously. For those who seemed most able to advance the present business, it was said, hated the count of Jaffa, to whom the king had entrusted the care of the kingdom only three days before. They resented that he had committed the conduct of affairs so weighty, amid such dangers and at such a crisis of necessity, to a man unknown, undiscerning, and utterly useless.

As a result, for eight continuous days they allowed the enemy camp, situated near them and scarcely one mile from their own, to remain patiently—indeed disgracefully, in a way never elsewhere recorded in the kingdom—and to ravage the whole region as it pleased [Col. 0884B]. Straightforward men who were present, unacquainted with the malice of our princes, asked why, when such an opportunity was offered, no engagement with the enemy occurred and no arrangement for battle was made.

When the matter was publicly discussed, they gave as their reason that Saladin, commander of the enemy legions, was positioned in a place strewn with rocks, so that our lines could not reach him except at great risk. Further, he had strong troops arrayed as if in a circle, intending to attack our forces from all sides if they attempted to engage Saladin [Col. 0884C]. Some said this was indeed true and that the princes advanced the reason justly. Others claimed that it was a pretext sought out and that avoidance of battle was fraudulently contrived, lest any successful outcome be credited to the count and they appear to have achieved it well under his command.

We have recorded these differing reports as they were variously told by many persons, affirming nothing, since we have not fully ascertained the truth. It is certain, however, that for seven or eight consecutive days the enemy remained freely about the Jordan within our borders, daily inflicting many injuries upon us with impunity. On the eighth day—or rather the ninth—he recalled his expeditions and returned unharmed to his own country [Col. 0884D]. Our men returned to the spring of Sephoria, not entirely secure that he would not come back.

During the same days in which our army was held at the spring of Tubania, an event worthy of memory occurred. Although both the spring named above and the stream flowing from it had previously been believed to have no fish, or only very rare fish, they are said in those days to have supplied such an abundance as could suffice for the whole army.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Saladin besieges the city of Petra beyond the Jordan and attacks the besieged city as an enemy.

What happened was not far from their expectation. When scarcely a month had passed, Saladin renewed his strength, prepared for renewed war, recalled his troops, gathered legions, brought up engines, and carefully provided everything usually necessary for besiegers of cities [Col. 0885A]. When these matters had been duly arranged, he passed through the regions of Bashan and Gilead, and of Ammon and Moab beyond the Jordan, and set out to besiege the city whose ancient name was Petra of the Desert and whose modern name was Crac.

When this became known through spies, Raynald of Châtillon, who administered the care of that region as his wife’s inheritance, swiftly crossed to those parts, taking with him such military force as appeared sufficient for the defence of the castle. He had another matter there as well. Humphrey III, son of the younger Humphrey and grandson through a son of the elder Humphrey, called of Toron, the royal constable, was Raynald’s stepson. In those days he was to marry the king’s younger sister, whom he had betrothed nearly four years before [Col. 0885B].

Hardly had he arrived at the place named above, and hardly had they completed the wedding ceremonies, when, on that very day, as is said, Saladin appeared with an innumerable multitude. He brought siege engines and projectile weapons, with which besieged strongholds are usually battered; and, pitching his camps around it, he enclosed the place with a siege.

The aforesaid city lay on a very high mountain, encircled by deep valleys, and for many ages had lain ruined and wholly reduced to desolation. At length, under the reign of Lord Fulk, third king of the Eastern Latins, a certain Pagan, surnamed the Butler, lord of the territory beyond the Jordan, founded a fortress on the mountain where the city had stood [Col. 0885C]. It was placed on the side of the mountain where the slope was gentler and where it adjoined more closely the level ground outside. His successors—namely his nephew Maurice and Philip of Nablus—made the place more notable with a rampart and towers.

Outside this fortress, where the city had once been built, there was now a suburb in which the inhabitants had made what they considered sufficiently safe homes. To the east the town itself stood as their chief defence; on every other side the whole mountain, as stated above, was surrounded by deep valleys [Col. 0885D]. Thus, if it had been enclosed even by a slight wall, it need have feared no hostile approach. Only at two points was ascent to the summit open, and these could easily be defended by a few men against enormous enemy forces; all the remaining parts are said to be wholly impassable.

When Prince Raynald saw that the enemy had arrived, he decided—very imprudently, as it seems to those experienced in such matters—to defend the outer position and the suburb adjoining the fortress. He forbade the inhabitants, who wished to move their possessions into the fortress and provide for their safety, to abandon their homes or presume to carry away any of their movable goods. But while squadrons of both cavalry and infantry were occupied with this and laboured to prevent the enemy’s ascent, the enemy’s numbers prevailed [Col. 0886A]. They put to flight those trying to block their way, seized the mountain, and opened a path everywhere by the sword. The enemy almost gained violent entry into the fortress alongside our men struggling to take refuge there. Indeed, unless the remarkable courage of one knight named Ivenus had held them back, the enemies who had already approached would have secured for their own side an open and easy entrance through the bridge and the gate adjacent to it.

Thus the unhappy citizens, through the unwise counsel of their ruler, lost their possessions when the enemy occupied their homes with every kind of implement and all their household goods. Those who had taken refuge in the fortress, however, fearing the enemy attack, most unwisely and entirely without thought demolished the only bridge over the rampart, through which the besieged had access and exit [Col. 0886B].

Inside was a very great and useless crowd of mixed condition and sex, more a burden than a help to the besieged: actors, flute-players, and female harpists, who had come from every region for the wedding day. What happened to them was beyond expectation: while they sought entertainments and wedding revelry, they found warlike encounters and the utterly different occupations of battle. Syrians too, with their wives and children, had gathered there from the suburban places and filled the stronghold. Thus those wishing to move about found no free passage because of the crowds, and they burdened and hindered the more active men who were working at the defence [Col. 0886C]. The place was said, however, to abound in provisions, though it did not possess such a supply of arms as its defence seemed to require.

## CHAPTER XXIX. The king removes the administration from the count of Jaffa and crowns his nephew Baldwin with the royal diadem.

Meanwhile the king saw that, in the affair mentioned above at the spring of Tubania, the count of Jaffa, to whom, as we have said, he had entrusted the administration of the kingdom, had behaved neither vigorously nor prudently enough; and that through his imprudence and utter incompetence the state of the kingdom had almost collapsed. Adopting a sounder course [Col. 0886D], he took back the administration which he had entrusted to him.

Other causes too are said to have been involved. As we have stated, when he entrusted the care of the kingdom to Guy, he had retained Jerusalem for himself, together with ten thousand gold pieces payable annually for household expenses. Later, repenting of this arrangement, he wanted to exchange Tyre for Jerusalem on the same conditions, because Tyre was the strongest city in the whole kingdom and seemed more suited to his needs. Since the count appeared to receive this request unwillingly, the king is said to have altered his previous decision. It happened deservedly that one who was unwilling to show generosity in a small matter toward the man who had given him everything should lose the whole sum of affairs [Col. 0887A].

Not only was the care of the kingdom and the honour of administration taken from him; even his hope of succession was wholly cut off. By common counsel of the princes—especially Lord Bohemond, prince of Antioch; Lord Raymond, count of Tripoli; Raynald of Sidon; Baldwin of Ramla; and Balian his brother—Baldwin, still a little boy scarcely five years old, was solemnly anointed and crowned in the Church of the Lord’s Resurrection. This was done with Guy himself present and not daring to object, at the prompting and urgent urging of the boy’s mother, with the support of all the people and the assent of the clergy present.

Immediately, without delay, all the barons rendered the boy their fealty by hand in the customary form of oaths [Col. 0887B]; and every honour and glory due to royal majesty was bestowed upon him in full. The count of Jaffa alone was invited by no one to render his homage. To the wiser observers this plainly seemed, as undoubtedly it was, evidence of an animosity already conceived—indeed, of manifest hatred—as the subsequent event will make clearer.

At this moment of such a great change, the opinions of prudent men were varied and numerous. Some said that the advancement of the boy brought no advantage to the kingdom and no benefit to public affairs, since both kings were entirely incapable, the one hindered by illness and the other by age. They thought it would be more expedient, by common counsel of the magnates, to entrust the care of royal affairs and administration of the commonwealth to a man vigorous in strength and sound in judgment [Col. 0887C]. Others thought that, although what was done concerning the child could not be judged wholly beneficial, the public interest was nevertheless served because the hope of succession had been cut off from the aforesaid count, who aspired to the kingdom and was, as they said, inadequate. In this they hoped that the source of future scandals and dangerous sedition feared after the king’s death had been brought to an end.

Yet all shared one purpose and desire: that a procurator should be placed over public affairs, especially over mustering and leading armies against the enemy’s more violent than usual pressure. Nearly all agreed that this office belonged solely to the count of Tripoli and that he alone could suffice for the task [Col. 0887D].

This took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1183, in the first indiction, on the twentieth day of November.

## CHAPTER XXX. The king hastens beyond the Jordan with gathered forces to assist the besieged; Saladin raises the siege.

While these events were taking place at Jerusalem, Saladin nevertheless pressed the besieged city with still greater zeal and all his strength, allowing those shut inside no rest through his relentless assaults. He set up eight engines—six on the inner side, where the ancient city had stood, and two on the outer side [Col. 0888A], at the place commonly called Obelet. With enormous millstones launched from them, he battered the castle so relentlessly by night no less than by day that none inside dared either raise a hand, look through the battlements, or attempt any kind of defence.

The terror grew so extreme that, while the besieged were confused and did not dare show themselves, the enemy went down by ropes* to the booty which the unhappy citizens had brought into the ditch adjoining the fortress. They killed it with impunity, cut the animals into pieces, and drew them out for food, suffering no harm whatever from the townspeople. Those in the enemy army who performed the functions of cooks or bakers, and those who managed the market in goods for sale, set up their workshops in the citizens’ houses, which were full of every convenience [Col. 0888B], and freely practised their trades. They found there an abundance, as they could wish, of wheat, barley, wine, and oil, which they used forcibly against the will of the owners.

Those in the fortress did at one time attempt to erect an engine of their own. But the men in charge of the outer engines aimed their hurled stones with such skill that, because of the constant blows and fear of death which each launched stone seemed to threaten, our men abandoned their plan. They judged it better to endure patiently whatever was inflicted than to undertake that kind of defence at risk of death.

Not only were those who emerged from hiding and approached the battlements—to shoot arrows or stones at the enemy, or merely to inspect the besieging legions—exposed to such danger and shaken by fear driving them to despair [Col. 0888C]. Even those in the innermost chambers and those who had withdrawn to more secluded places, terrified by the crash and sound of the incoming millstones, seemed to hear thunder and awaited what were, as it were, thunderbolt strikes, continually apprehensive lest the shattered buildings collapse upon them.

Meanwhile the king was anxious and took every care to assist the besieged and hasten to them the help they desired. Taking with him the saving wood of the life-giving Cross and gathering the kingdom’s forces from every side, he hastened to those parts to bring aid to the besieged. He reached the Salt Sea, otherwise called Lake Asphaltites, beside the place named Segor, now commonly called Palmer [Col. 0888D]. After much deliberation, he appointed the count of Tripoli commander and leader of the entire army.

But Saladin learned through spies that the Christian army was near and that the count of Tripoli had been placed over its legions. He therefore put aside his engines, ordered his men to return, and raised the siege with which he had afflicted the aforesaid place continuously for a month, returning home. Nevertheless, the king arrived with his whole army at the appointed place and brought the citizens their desired consolation. He then ordered the return, recalled the columns, and came safely back to Jerusalem.

# HERE BEGINS BOOK TWENTY-THREE.

[Col. 0889]

## PREFACE.

[Col. 0889A]

We had resolved, wearied by the disastrous reverses that befall the kingdom more frequently than usual—indeed, almost without interruption—to grant our pens repose henceforth, and to consign to burial and silence what we had undertaken to publish for posterity. For there is no one who does not reluctantly bring into the light his country’s weakness and the failures of his own people, since it is, as it were, agreed among men and regarded as natural that everyone should strive with all his powers to exalt his country with praises and should not begrudge distinctions to his own countrymen. But all material for encomium is withdrawn from us; there presents itself only the calamity of a mourning homeland, fitted for tears and compelling tears from us, together with manifold misery.

We who, in the preceding books, have described in such style as we could the notable deeds of the brave men who held authority in our East, and especially at Jerusalem, for more than eighty years, are overcome within ourselves by abhorrence at present events, stunned by the subject matter thrust upon our eyes and ears—a subject worthy neither of Codrus’ poetry nor of the recital of any Maevius. For nothing occurs in the actions of our rulers which a prudent man would judge worthy to be committed to the treasuries of memory; nothing that may either afford refreshment to the reader or bring honor to the writer. For among us, as the prophet laments, “Counsel has perished from the wise man, speech from the priest, vision from the prophet” (Jeremiah 18:18); and among us it has become “as with the people, so with the priest” (Hosea 4:9), so that the prophetic saying may be applied to us: “Every head is sick, and every heart sorrowful; from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health in us” (Isaiah 1:6).

For we have now reached times in which we can endure neither our vices nor their remedies. Hence, because our sins deserve it, our enemies have become our head; and we, who formerly, triumphant over our foes, were accustomed often to bear away the palm with glory, now, deprived of divine grace, bring back the worse verdict in almost every conflict. Therefore we ought to have been silent; and it seemed more prudent to cast night over our defects than to expose shameful things to the sun.

But those who desire us to persevere in the purpose once undertaken, and who earnestly ask that the entire condition of the kingdom of Jerusalem, prosperous as well as adverse, be made known to posterity through our work, add their spurs. They set before us the most eloquent historians: Titus Livy, namely, who committed to writing not only Roman successes but also Roman misfortunes; and Josephus, who published in lengthy treatises not only the noble deeds of the Jews, but also the disgraceful injuries inflicted upon them. They abound also in other examples intended to urge us on; and they persuade us the more readily because it is perfectly clear that historians of events are equally bound to set forth both fortunes: just as by recounting successful deeds they raise posterity to a certain courage, so by the example of misfortunes set before them they make those same persons more cautious in similar circumstances.

For writers of annals are accustomed, by duty, to commit to writing not what they themselves desire, but what the times supply. The outcome of affairs—and especially of wars—is ordinarily variable and uneven: neither unbroken prosperity nor the opposite misfortune is without bright intervals. We are defeated, therefore; yet whatever subsequent times shall provide, as we began—would that they may be fortunate and happy!—with the Lord as author and life as companion, we shall diligently take care to commit to writing, having been recalled from our second intention.

## CHAPTER I. The long-nourished hostility between the king and the count of Jaffa breaks out into execrable disputes; no hope of reconciliation appears. The count of Tripoli obtains administration of the kingdom and royal guardianship.

Meanwhile, the tinder of hatred between the king and the count of Jaffa was, from hidden causes, increasing more and more each day; and resentment had grown to such a pitch that the king now seemed openly to be seeking grounds on which to separate his sister from him by dissolving the marriage. Accordingly, in pursuance of this intention, he publicly approached the patriarch, asking that a day be fixed for him—as though he meant to accuse the marriage—on which, in the patriarch’s presence, a divorce might be solemnly pronounced.

But the count, fully informed of all this, on his return from the expedition separated himself from the rest of the army and set out by a short route for Ascalon. He warned his wife, who was then staying at Jerusalem, to leave that city promptly before the king entered it and proceed to Ascalon; for he feared that, if the king could get possession of her, he would not allow her ever again to return to her husband.

The king therefore sent a messenger to summon the count and explain the reason for the summons. The count, resisting, pleaded reasons for his absence and alleged illness. When, though summoned repeatedly, he delayed coming, the king determined to go there in person and formally cite the count before the court by word of mouth. On arriving with an escort of some of his princes, he found the city gates barred. Touching them with his hand and three times ordering that they be opened to him, he found no one who obeyed his command; and he returned with due indignation, while all the people of the city watched. Having heard of the king’s arrival, they had stationed themselves on the towers and walls, awaiting the outcome.

The king then proceeded directly to Jaffa. Before he reached the city, he met many of its citizens coming out to meet him, leading men from both classes. When they opened the city to him, the king entered without difficulty; and, after appointing a governor to take charge of the place, he came to Acre.

A general court was therefore summoned at that city. When the princes of the kingdom had assembled on the appointed day, the patriarch, having with him as associates in this business both masters—the Master of the Temple and the Master of the Hospital—approached the lord king. Kneeling, he interceded for the count, asking that the king put aside his resentment and restore him to favor. Since they were not immediately heard, they departed together in indignation, not only from the court but also from the city.

Before the assembled princes, a proposal had been made to send envoys to the kings and other princes beyond the mountains, inviting them to aid Christendom and the kingdom. When this matter should have received prior discussion, the patriarch, as we have said, intervened, preferring the principal issue and turning to the earlier subject. Thus, as stated above, they departed Acre in intemperate anger.

But when the count of Jaffa learned that the king would not incline his mind toward peace with him, he added worse deeds to those already done. Taking with him the soldiery at his disposal, he made for the castle called Darum. He suddenly fell upon the encampments of certain Arabs who, for the sake of pasture, had pitched their tents in those regions. They had received safe-conduct from the king and were living securely under his protection. Finding them unprepared, he carried off plunder and booty and returned to Ascalon.

When the king heard of this, he again summoned the princes and entrusted to the count of Tripoli the care and general administration of the kingdom, placing his hope alike in that count’s prudence and greatness of spirit. In doing so he appeared to have satisfied the desires of most of the people and princes; for everyone regarded it as the one and only path to safety if the care of royal affairs were entrusted to the said count.

[Col. 0891] The remainder is wanting.

## [Continuation of William of Tyre’s History of the Holy War.]

[Col. 0891]

## Notice concerning the Continuation of William of Tyre’s History of the Holy War

(D. Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. V, col. 581.)

[Col. 0891] Among the historians of the Holy War published by Jacques Bongars, the history of William, archbishop of Tyre, has always been held in the highest esteem, both because of the multitude and variety of the matters it treats and because of the author’s own dignity. That dignity was surely so great that he was called the prince of all historians: a man of learning not ordinary, and graceful beyond that age; of varied experience, keen judgment, and, so far as one may judge from his life and intellect, upright; elegant and weighty also in expression. (Bongars, in the preface cited above.)

He divided his work into twenty-two books, and, having begun the twenty-third, departed this life before completing it. In an old manuscript belonging to the most illustrious Lord Gaston de Noailles, formerly bishop of Châlons, we found these books translated into French five hundred years ago by an anonymous author, with certain interpolations. That author also continued the history of the archbishop of Tyre down to the year 1275: a work assuredly not unworthy, in the judgment of all who have read it, of public publication. For it carefully describes events in the East over approximately one hundred years and reports many things which one would not easily find elsewhere. It also touches here and there upon affairs at Constantinople, in France and England, and matters concerning the Empire.

Some urged us to publish here the translator’s work entire, especially since he incorporated into his version many things absent from the Tyrian. But several considerations dissuaded us from this purpose: (1) the immense bulk of the work; (2) the very ancient French idiom, which can be understood only with great labor; and (3) the possibility that the materials added by the author to the Tyrian may perhaps become known from elsewhere. Let it therefore suffice here to publish the continuation of the History of William, archbishop of Tyre; for its easier understanding we shall append a glossary of unfamiliar words.

Concerning the translator’s date, however, two things can be determined with certainty. First, he lived at least to the year 1275, in which he completed his work. Second, he put the finishing touch to his work before 1295. For in that year the manuscript we used was written, at the end of which we read:

> This book was written and completed at Rome in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1295, in the month of May, in the time of Pope Boniface the Eighth, born in a city in the Campagna named Anagni, who was elected pope after Pope Celestine the Fifth, named Brother Peter of Morone, who resigned in the city of Naples.

## Continuation of William of Tyre’s History of the Holy War, written in the French language by an ancient author five hundred years ago

(D. Martène, cited above, from the manuscript of the most illustrious Lord Gaston de Noailles, formerly bishop of Châlons.)

[Col. 0893A] So great was the hatred between the king and the count of Jaffa that it grew ever greater day by day, until matters reached the point that the king was seeking grounds on which he might openly dissolve the marriage between the count and his sister. He asked the patriarch to summon them, saying that he wished to accuse this marriage and prove by reason that it was neither good nor lawful.

When the count heard this, he secretly withdrew from the other barons and came to Jerusalem, where his wife was then staying. He strongly urged her to leave the city before the king arrived, as he was returning from his army. For he feared that, if the king found her there, he would not let her return to him; therefore he urgently asked her to follow him to Ascalon, whither he went directly.

The king heard that the count had left the army and sent messengers after him, summoning him to come to his court. The count replied that he could not go because he was ill. The king sent several messengers, one after another, but they could never bring him; for he continually excused himself on grounds of illness. The king said that, since the count would not come to him, he himself would go and speak to him and summon him. The barons followed him.

He went directly to Ascalon, but found the gates very securely closed. He called and commanded that they be opened to him; three times he touched the gate with his hand, but no one came to obey his command. The townsmen of the city had climbed onto the walls and towers, and did not dare move, but awaited the outcome of the affair. The king left there greatly angered and set off for Jaffa. Many knights and townsmen of that city met him and led him in without any resistance. He took the city into his control and placed his bailiff there. Then he departed and came to Acre, where he ordered a great council of his prelates and barons to be summoned.

When they had assembled, the patriarch took with him the Master of the Temple and the Master of the Hospital. They went directly before the king, prayed him very humbly, and pleaded with him on their knees to forgive his anger against the count of Jaffa and consent that he come before him. But the king would not listen to them; rather, he replied quite plainly that he would do no such thing. They were greatly offended that a man whose body was in so poor a condition still bore such great resentment in his body. In anger they left the court and departed from the city.

The council had been called because envoys were to be sent to the princes of France and of other lands, to ask them to aid the land of Jesus Christ and His people. When the patriarch ought first to have spoken of that business, he began instead the other matter I have told you of; and because the king would do nothing for him, he and his companions left. These were the two masters of the Temple and the Hospital. Thus nothing was done about the affair for which they had assembled.

The count of Jaffa heard that the king would show him no mercy and that he could obtain peace neither through affection nor through entreaty. Thereupon he considered how he might provoke the king. He took as many knights with him as he could obtain and went directly toward the castle of Darum. There were encamped Arabs called Bedouins, who kept a great abundance of livestock in the pastures. They had given so much gold to the king that he allowed them to remain there, and they were under his protection. Consequently all were secure and expected no attack from anyone. The count and the knights came suddenly upon them, surprised them, killed some of them, and carried all the booty they found—garments and possessions—to Ascalon.

News came to the king, who was greatly disturbed. He summoned the count of Tripoli, and because he trusted his good sense and loyalty, immediately entrusted to him all power and the entire administration of the kingdom. The barons and common people rejoiced greatly, because it had long been said that the land could not otherwise be brought into good order unless the whole burden and direction of affairs were entrusted to the count of Tripoli.

[Col. 0893] Here the published William of Tyre ends.

[Col. 0895A] The count of Tripoli answered that he would gladly accept the administration, provided that he should not be guardian of the child, lest, if the child died by chance within ten years, it should be said that he had died through him. He also wished the castles and fortresses to be placed in the hands of the Hospital and the Temple, for he did not wish to be mistrusted or to have a thousand wicked charges spoken against him.

He also wished to be assigned an income from which he could support himself if the kingdom incurred any expense; for he then had no truce with the Saracens, and the land yielded insufficient revenue for him to maintain an army against them without great cost. Therefore he wished to be assured of holding the administration for ten years, on the condition that, if the child died within those ten years, the administration should revert as before until such time as, by the counsel of the pope of Rome, the emperor of Germany, the king of France, and the king of England, the kingdom should be adjudged to one of the two sisters—the elder or the younger.

For King Aimery had divided land to the younger sister before he became king, and the younger was of royal and Roman [imperial?] descent. Therefore the barons did not agree that the elder sister should succeed if the child died, without the counsel of the four whom I have named. Thus the count of Tripoli arranged matters, because he did not wish discord to arise in the land if the child died, and he wished to hold the administration until the four had given their counsel.

This arrangement pleased the king and the barons exactly as the count had set it out. They agreed that Count Jocelyn, the child’s maternal great-uncle, should guard him; and that the count of Tripoli should have Beirut and its dependencies, because he was incurring expense for the kingdom, assigned to him by the barons of the land until he had recovered his costs.

When they had thus arranged their affairs, the king ordered that the child be crowned. They took him to the Holy Sepulchre and crowned him. Because he was small, he caused him to be carried in a knight’s arms as far as the Temple of the Lord, so that he should not be lower than God. The knight was tall and of high stature; his name was Balian of Ibelin, one of the barons of the land.

It is the custom in Jerusalem, when the king bears the crown at the Sepulchre, that he wears it upon his head from there to the Temple where Jesus Christ was presented. There he offers his crown, but offers it as a redemption. Thus it was formerly done: as soon as a woman had borne a male child, she first offered him at the Temple, then redeemed him with a lamb, or two doves, or two turtledoves.

When the king had offered his crown in the Temple, he descended steps outside the Temple and entered his palace in the Temple of Solomon, where the Templars lived. There tables had been set for eating. The king sat there, together with his barons and all those who wished to eat, except only the burgesses of Jerusalem, who served them. For they owed the king this service: whenever the king had worn the crown, they served him and his barons at their meal.

Not long after the young king had worn the crown, the leprous king died. Before he died, he summoned all his barons to come to him in Jerusalem, and they came. At the moment they arrived, the leprous king passed from this world; all the barons of the land were present at his death. The next day they buried him in the church of the Sepulchre, where the other kings had been buried since the time of King Godfrey of Bouillon. They were buried between Mount Calvary, where Jesus Christ was put upon the cross, and the sepulchre where He was laid; Mount Calvary and Golgotha are both within the church of the Sepulchre.

## HERE BEGINS BOOK XXII

[Col. 0895]

### I. The child king, having received the homage of the barons, is entrusted to Count Jocelyn for guardianship. Scarcity of water in the city. A well near the Fountain of Siloam is discovered.

[Col. 0895C] When the king was dead and the child had borne the crown, he caused all the barons of the land to render him fealty and homage as their lord and king; afterward he had them render it to the count of Tripoli as bailiff. He also made all the barons and knights of the land swear that they would abide by what had been said concerning the two sisters, and would hold and assist the count of Tripoli in maintaining and guarding the land if the child died within ten years.

When the leprous king was dead and the child had borne the crown, the child was entrusted to Count Jocelyn to guard, and he took him to Acre. He guarded him as well as he could, while the count of Tripoli was bailiff of the land.

It happened in that first year that no rain fell in the land of Jerusalem, nor did any water enter the cisterns, so that there was exceedingly little to drink. There was then in Jerusalem a burgess who very willingly did good for God’s sake. His name was Germain. In Jerusalem he had three marble vaults enclosed within walls; in each of the three vaults he had two basins with chains, and he always had them kept full of water. All men and women who wished to drink went there.

When Germain saw that there was little water in his cisterns and that it was not raining, he was deeply grieved and distressed, because he greatly feared that he would lose the almsgiving which he had begun for poor people out of love for God. Then he remembered what he had heard the old men of the land say: that beside the Fountain of Siloam there was an ancient well which Jacob had made, but it was covered and filled in, grass grew over it, and it would scarcely be found.

Then the worthy man prayed to Our Lord that He would enable him to find this well, enable him to continue the good work he had begun, and permit him, according to His pleasure, to provide His poor people with aid of water. The next morning he rose, went to church, and prayed God to counsel him. Then he went to the marketplace, hired workmen, and went to the place where he had been told the well was. He had them dig until the well was found.

When they found it, he had it emptied and rebuilt anew, all at his own cost. Then he had a wheel constructed above it, with buckets turned by a horse: when the full bucket rose, the empty one went down. He also had stone troughs placed where the water drawn from the well ran. All the people of the land who wanted water came there and carried it into the city.

The burgess had water drawn day and night by his horses and gave it to all who wished to take it, freely and at his own cost, until God sent rain to their cisterns. Nor did the worthy man cease even then: he had two pack animals and three servants whose only task was to carry water to the basins he had in the city, to provide drink for poor people. The well from which he had this water drawn was fully fifty fathoms deep and more. Later the citizens demolished and filled it in when they heard that the Saracens of Egypt were coming to besiege the city.

### II. Concerning the Fountain of Siloam. The count of Tripoli makes a truce with Saladin.

[Col. 0897C] Hereafter we shall tell you of the Fountain of Siloam, which is near the well. It is not good for drinking, but salty. With that water they tanned the city’s hides, washed clothes, watered horses, and irrigated the gardens in the valley below. This fountain does not flow on Saturday, but is completely still.

I shall tell you what happened in connection with this fountain. One day, when Jesus Christ walked upon the earth, He was in Jerusalem among His apostles. They passed through a street and saw a man who had no eyes. The apostles asked Jesus Christ whether he was without eyes because of some sin of his father, mother, or relatives. Jesus Christ answered that it was not because of the sin of his father, mother, or relatives, but so that He might work in him.

Then Jesus Christ spat upon the ground, took a little mud, put it where the eyes should have been, and told him to go to the Fountain of Siloam and wash himself. He went and washed, received eyes, and saw. Then he returned to the city of Jerusalem to his relatives, who greatly marvelled that he had eyes. They asked how this had happened, and he told them; but they would not believe him, and sent to discover whether it was certainly he. They said that it was.

Now we shall speak of the count of Tripoli, bailiff of the kingdom of Jerusalem. When the count saw that it did not rain and that the sown grain did not grow, he feared a dearth. He summoned the barons of the land and the masters of the Temple and the Hospital, and said to them: “Lords, what counsel will you give concerning the fact that it does not rain and the grain does not grow? I fear that the Saracens may perceive that we have scarcity and attack us. What counsel will you give? Shall I make a truce with the Saracens because I fear dearth?”

The barons advised him to make a truce with Saladin. He requested it, and Saladin willingly granted him one for four years. When there was a truce between Saracens and Christians, the Saracens brought so much food to the Christians that they enjoyed very good times indeed. Had the truce not been made, all would have died of hunger. For this truce which he made with the Saracens, the count of Tripoli was greatly loved by the people of the land, who gave him many blessings.

I forgot to tell you, when I spoke of the Fountain of Siloam, of an almsgiving which the burgesses of Jerusalem performed; but now I shall tell it to you. They performed it on the forty-day observance, on the day when the Gospel is read about the poor man to whom Jesus Christ restored sight with a little mud and commanded to go and wash at the Fountain of Siloam. He did so, received eyes, and saw. In memory of this, the burgesses of Jerusalem performed the almsgiving I shall describe.

They had tubs brought to the fountain and filled them all with wine. They had pack animals loaded with bread and wine and brought to a place where all poor people who came received bread and wine in great abundance, together with money. Men and women also went in procession on that day for the purpose of performing this almsgiving.

### III. Boniface, marquis of Montferrat, takes the cross, as does his son Conrad, who arrives at Constantinople.

I have told you of the almsgiving performed at the Fountain of Siloam. Now I shall tell you of a great lord of Lombardy named Boniface, marquis of Montferrat. This marquis was the grandfather of King Baldwin. When he heard that his nephew was king of Jerusalem, he was very glad and joyful. He took the cross, left his land to his eldest son, and crossed the sea.

When he arrived, the king, the count of Tripoli, and all the barons of the land received him with great honor and rejoiced greatly at his arrival. The king gave him a castle in the desert beyond the river, near the place where God fasted for forty days. This castle is seven miles from Jerusalem and three miles from the river. It stands upon a high mountain and is called Saint Elijah. It is called thus because the people say that it is the place where Elijah fasted forty days and then fell asleep, and that God sent him there a piece of bread and water in a vessel. An angel awakened him so that he might drink and eat; he drank and ate. Therefore the people of that country call the place where the castle stands Saint Elijah.

This Boniface the marquis had a son named Conrad. He took the cross in order to go overseas after his father and see his nephew, king of Jerusalem. He set out and was at sea, but at that time Our Lord did not will that he should cross. Instead, He sent him weather that carried him to Constantinople, because He had provided for the destruction of the land, and through this Conrad a part of it would be aided, as you shall hear later.

Our Lord did not will to destroy everything, but left a small remnant, as He did to Solomon’s son. For God was angered with Solomon because of the sin of lust which he committed with a pagan woman whom he kept and ought not to have kept. He loved her so much that he had three idol temples made for her on three mountains, each three miles from Jerusalem. Our Lord was more angered by the idolatry which he had established upon the Mount of Olives than by all the other sin he had committed before. For it was from the Mount of Olives that He ascended into heaven before His apostles when He had risen from death to life, and there He will descend at the Judgment.

Then Our Lord told Solomon that he had angered Him; and, were it not for the great love He had had for his father David, He would utterly destroy him. Yet He would not punish him so severely during his lifetime. But Solomon should know that after him his son would not retain the kingdom, except only a little part; and He would leave him that small part for the love He had borne toward his father David.

Likewise, Our Lord did not wish entirely to disinherit Christendom for the sake of a certain worthy man who was in the land. As He left something to Solomon’s son for David’s sake, so He left a city named Tyre for Conrad, who was at Constantinople, as you shall hear afterward.

At the time Conrad arrived at Constantinople, Quirsac was emperor and his eyes had not yet been put out. There was at Constantinople a great lord named Livernas, who had been cousin to Emperor Manuel. This Livernas had concealed himself and withdrawn during the time when Andronicus was emperor, because he feared that Andronicus would mutilate him as he had mutilated his relatives.

When Livernas heard that Andronicus was dead and that Quirsac was emperor, and that he had delivered the world from Andronicus, as I shall tell you: one night, after Andronicus had had Alexius—who had charge of the empire of Constantinople and of the child, son of Emperor Manuel—beheaded, Andronicus conceived a great treason. By the counsel of one of his clerks named Langosse, he had the young child—who was married to the daughter of King Louis of France and whom he ought faithfully to have guarded—seized one night, put in a sack, carried out to sea in a boat, and thrown into it; thus he was drowned.

Before this deed became known, Andronicus summoned the emperor’s relatives and, as they arrived, had them thrown into prison. Then he had their eyes put out; and there were some whose noses and lips he had cut off. He thus dealt with many of the emperor’s relatives. Then he became emperor, wore the crown in the church of Saint Sophia, and committed much wickedness, as you shall hear.

### IV. The unchastity of Andronicus, emperor of Constantinople. He summons Quirsac, or Isaac, to have him killed; but Quirsac himself kills Langosse and seizes the imperial crown.

When Andronicus was emperor in Constantinople, there remained no beautiful nun in an abbey, nor daughter of knight or burgess, whom—if she pleased him—he did not take by force and sleep with. He was greatly hated by all because of the wickedness he did.

One day Langosse came to him and said: “Lord, there is in this city a knight who was related to Emperor Manuel. If you believe me, summon him and put him in prison, or have him killed. For I know truly that, if you leave him as he is, he will make war upon you, because he is [uncertain: *rous de putaire*].”

The emperor summoned him to come and speak with him. The knight was named Quirsac and had a brother named Alexius. When Quirsac heard the summons, he told the messenger to go on and said that he would follow. Then he summoned his brother and companions and told them how the emperor had summoned him. “I know well,” he said, “that I have been accused to the emperor so that I may be killed. What counsel do you give me?”

His brother and companions said: “We advise you to go there, and we will go with you and hear what he says.” “Since you advise it,” Quirsac said, “I shall go.” Then he armed himself beneath his clothes, girded on his sword, and he and his companions mounted and went to Blachernae, where the emperor was. Blachernae is an imperial residence situated at the landward end of Constantinople.

As Quirsac went toward the emperor and came into a narrow street, he met Langosse, who was going to dine at his lodging. Quirsac saw that Langosse could not turn back without passing him. He rushed upon him and cut off his head. Then, spurring back, he rode down through the city with his drawn sword, crying: “Lords, come after me, for I have killed the devil!”

When the cry arose in the city that Quirsac had killed Langosse, all went after him to the Lion’s Mouth. Quirsac took the Lion’s Mouth, fortified it, and put his men within it. This was an imperial residence on the sea, where most of the emperor’s treasure was kept. Quirsac then took the crown and the emperor’s garments, went to Saint Sophia, and crowned himself emperor. When he had worn the crown, he summoned all the people of the city and had them arm to go and assault Blachernae.

### V. He permits Andronicus, shamefully treated, to be killed by the fury of women.

When Andronicus heard that Quirsac had killed Langosse, seized the Lion’s Mouth and its treasure, and assumed the crown, he did not know what to do. He had as many men as he possessed armed for his defence, but it was of no avail. When Quirsac came before Blachernae, those within, seeing that their defence would accomplish nothing, surrendered. Quirsac then had Andronicus taken [Col. 0901A] and brought to the Lion’s Mouth. Afterwards he decided to put him to a shameful death, because of his rightful lord, whom he had caused to be drowned in the sea—Manuel’s son, who had been emperor—and because of the other wicked acts he had committed.

Quirsac had him stripped entirely naked, and had a string of garlic brought, though the bulbs were not very large. He had a crown made from it and crowned him as king; then had him beaten and his hair shorn in the form of a cross. He made him mount a she-ass backwards, holding its tail in his hand as a bridle. Thus he had him led through all the streets of Constantinople. I shall tell you what the women did: they had prepared pisas and longuamis [uncertain terms, perhaps types of refuse or missiles], and threw them upon his head through all the streets. Thus Andronicus wore a crown in Constantinople until he was outside [Col. 0901B] the city. Then Quirsac delivered him to the women, and they rushed upon him as dogs upon carrion. They tore him wholly limb from limb; and whichever woman could get a piece as large as a bean ate it, while they gnawed his bones with knives. Not a morsel or joint remained which they did not eat. They said that all those who had eaten of him were saved, because they had helped avenge the wickedness he had committed.

## VI. Alexius seizes the empire after his brother has been captured and blinded.

This emperor Quirsac was greatly loved by the people of the land because he had so well avenged the wickedness of Andronicus and Langosse. He was especially loved by the abbeys: there was no abbey in Constantinople on whose gate [Col. 0901C] his image was not painted. He had no wife when he assumed the crown. He asked the king of Hungary to send him a sister whom he had, to take as his wife. The king sent her very willingly and gladly. When she was in Constantinople, the emperor married her and had her crowned. They afterwards had a son named Alexius.

One day Emperor Quirsac was riding through his land and came to an abbey near Philippi. King Alexander had been born in that city of Philippi. It lies five days’ journey from Constantinople. In that city St Paul composed part of his epistles, whence they are called “To the Philippians.” Emperor Quirsac stayed at that abbey. When his brother Alexius heard that he was lodging there with few men, [Col. 0901D] he had him seized and his eyes put out. He left him in the abbey, returned to Constantinople, became emperor, and wore the crown. Afterwards he summoned his brother Quirsac and had him brought to Constantinople; there he had him guarded and attended, and supplied with what he needed.

## VII. The empress prudently sends her son Alexius to the king of Hungary for protection. The young king of Jerusalem dies.

When the empress learned that Alexius had thus put out the eyes of his lord, the emperor, she was deeply distressed and feared that he would have her son Alexius, who was a child, killed. She quietly entrusted him to knights and sergeants and sent him to the king of Hungary, her brother, whose nephew he was, to be kept. The king guarded and reared him until a time when a movement arose from France and other lands for an expedition overseas.

Alexius, who, as I have told you, had had his brother the emperor’s eyes put out, held and governed the empire. But Livernas, of whom I have spoken above, because he was more closely related by blood to Emperor Manuel than Alexius was, assembled a great force, promised them money, and paid it out. He came before Constantinople with an army. When the emperor learned that he was coming against him with an army, he begged Marquis Conrad, who had then come to Constantinople, to remain with him and with his men until he had ended his war. The marquis remained.

When Livernas arrived before Constantinople, he drew up all his armed divisions and stood in front. The emperor would not go out against Livernas, because Livernas had great kindred within the city. But the marquis armed himself and rode out against Livernas. Livernas was pointed out to him, and he charged him. Livernas and all his troop thought that he had left the city to come to their aid; but when he came near Livernas, he spurred the horse of Ravine and struck him through the body, [Col. 0902B] knocking him down dead. Then he returned to Constantinople. When those outside saw that their lord was dead, they fled. Conrad returned to the city to the emperor, who kept him with him, because he did not wish the citizens whose kinsman he had killed to harm or molest him. He remained with the emperor until it was time to go to the land overseas to guard the city which God had provided for him, and which he would leave to Christendom.

Here we shall cease speaking of Conrad and speak of King Baldwin. The child who was at Acre in the custody of Count Jocelin, his mother’s uncle, fell ill and died. Count Jocelin conceived a great treachery. He came to the count of Tripoli and told him not to go to Jerusalem with the king to bury the body, nor to allow any of the barons of the land to go there; instead, the body should be entrusted to the Templars, who would carry it to Jerusalem. Count Tripoli foolishly accepted Jocelin’s counsel. The Templars bore the king’s body to Jerusalem, while the count of Tripoli went to Tiberias.

Then Count Jocelin seized the city of Acre and afterwards went to Beirut, which the count of Tripoli held in pledge. He entered it by treachery and garrisoned it with [Col. 0902D] knights and sergeants. Afterwards he sent word to the countess of Jaffa, the king’s mother, that she and all her knights should go to Jerusalem, and, once her son the king had been buried, should seize and garrison the city and assume the crown. When the count of Tripoli heard that Count Jocelin had thus betrayed him, he summoned all the barons of the land to come to him at Nablus. All went there except Count Jocelin and Prince Reynald. Count Jocelin would not leave Acre; and the countess of Jaffa was in Jerusalem with her husband and her knights. She had her son the king buried; there came out the Marquis Boniface, his grandfather, as well as the patriarch, the master of the Temple, and those of the Hospital.

## VIII. The countess of Jaffa is adorned with the crown of the kingdom.

[Col. 0903A]

When the king had been buried, the countess of Jaffa came to the patriarch, the master of the Temple, and the master of the Hospital, and asked them to advise her. The patriarch and the master of the Temple told her not to be troubled: they would crown her despite all the people of the land—the patriarch for love of her mother, and the master of the Temple because of the hatred he bore Count Tripoli.

They summoned Count Reynald, who was at Krak, to come to Jerusalem. He came; then they decided that the countess should summon the count of Tripoli and the barons to come to her coronation, since the kingdom had fallen to her. She sent them messengers. The barons replied that they would not go; instead, they sent [Col. 0903B] two Cistercian abbots to the patriarch and the masters of the Temple and Hospital. In the name of God and of the pope, they forbade them to crown the countess of Jaffa until they had consulted those to whom they had sworn an oath in the time of the leprous king.

The abbots went to Jerusalem to deliver the message. The patriarch and the master of the Temple said that they would observe neither faith nor oath, but would crown the Lady. The master of the Hospital would not be present at all; rather, he said that it would be contrary to God and to their oath. Then the gates of the city were closed, so that no one could enter or leave. They feared that the barons at Nablus, twelve miles away, might enter the city while they were crowning [Col. 0903C] the Lady and cause a disturbance.

When the barons at Nablus heard that Jerusalem was thus shut, so that no one could enter or leave, they dressed a sergeant who had been born in Jerusalem as a monk and sent him to Jerusalem to spy out how the Lady would receive the crown. He went there but could not enter by the gate. He came to the leper-hospital [Col. 0904A] of Jerusalem, adjoining the walls. There was a small postern through which one entered the city. He prevailed upon the master of the hospital to admit him through that postern. He went to the Holy Sepulchre and remained there until he had seen and learned what he had been sent to discover.

The master of the Temple and Prince Reynald took the Lady and led her to the Sepulchre to crown her. When she came to the Sepulchre, the patriarch asked the master of the Temple for the keys to the treasury where the crowns were. He gave them to him. They then summoned the master of the Hospital to give up his own key. He replied that he would give none, unless it were by counsel of the barons of the land. The patriarch, the master of the Temple, and Prince Reynald went to him for the keys, but he withdrew; and it was close to None (mid-afternoon) before they found him. They asked him to give them the key. He answered that he would not. They begged and importuned him so much that, fearing that someone of the house might take the keys he held in his hand and give them to the patriarch, he threw them into the middle of the house. The patriarch took them, and they went to the treasury. They brought out two crowns and carried them to the Sepulchre. The patriarch placed one upon the altar and crowned the countess of Jaffa with the other.

## IX. Guy of Lusignan becomes king of Jerusalem.

When the countess had been crowned, the patriarch said to her: “Lady, you are a woman; it is necessary that you have with you someone, a man, who may govern your kingdom. Take this crown and give it [Col. 0904C] to such a man as can govern your kingdom.” She took the crown and called her lord, who stood before her. She said: “Lord, come forward and receive this crown, for I do not know where I could better bestow it.” He knelt before her, and she put the crown upon his head. Thus he was king and she was queen.

## BOOK XXIII BEGINS.

[Col. 0903]

## I. The barons, after Guy’s elevation to the kingdom, decide to make Humphrey king; but he refuses the royal crown.

[Col. 0903D]

When the sergeant dressed in a monk’s robe saw this, he returned through the postern by which he had entered. The sick people let him out, and he came back to Nablus, where the barons were, and told them all that he had seen. When Baldwin of Ramla heard that Guy of Lusignan was king of Jerusalem, he said: “By an agreement, he shall not be king for a year.” And he was not: for he was crowned in mid-September, and he lost the land at the feast of St Martin the Burning, before August.

Then Baldwin said to the count of Tripoli and the other barons: “Lords, do as best you can, for the land is lost; but I shall leave it, because I do not wish to bear blame or reproach for having been present at the land’s destruction. For I know the king well enough: he is now foolish and vacillating, so that neither by my counsel [Col. 0904C] nor by yours will he accomplish anything; rather, he will act by the counsel of people who know nothing. Therefore I shall leave the country.”

Then the count of Tripoli said: “Sir Baldwin, have mercy on Christendom, and let us take counsel as to how we may save the land. We have here the daughter of King Amalric and her lord Humphrey. We shall go to Jerusalem and crown him, for we have the support of all the barons and the master of the Hospital, except Prince Reynald, who is with the king in Jerusalem. I have a truce with the Saracens and shall have it as long as I wish; they will not harm us, but will help us if we need it.” Thus they all agreed and pledged that they would crown Humphrey the next day.

When Humphrey learned that they wished to crown him, he thought that he could not endure the burden of guarding the kingdom. During the night he mounted with his knights and entered Jerusalem. But the next day, when the barons were ready [Col. 0905A] and wished to crown Humphrey, they heard that he had gone to Jerusalem. When Humphrey came before the queen in Jerusalem—she was his sister—he greeted her; but she did not greet him, because he had opposed her and had not attended her coronation. He began scratching his head like an embarrassed child and said: “Lady, I could not help it: they wished to make me king against my will, and so I fled here.”

“Since you have done this,” said the queen, “I forgive you my displeasure; but do homage to the king.” He then did homage to the king and remained with the queen in Jerusalem. When the count of Tripoli and the barons at Nablus learned that Humphrey had fled to Jerusalem, they were greatly distressed and did not know what to do. Then they said to the count of Tripoli: “Lord, advise us concerning the oath which the leprous king made us swear; for we do not wish to do anything for which we may incur blame or reproach.” The count advised that they keep the oath they had made.

The barons took counsel and said to the count: “Lord, since there is a king in Jerusalem, we cannot reign against him without disgrace. We ask you not to take it ill. But go to Tiberias and remain there; we shall go to the king, do our homages, and give all the assistance we can. Saving our honours, we shall procure that you recover all the expenses you have incurred in the land for which the leprous king gave you Beirut in pledge.” Baldwin of Ramla would not join in this counsel.

## II. The barons render homage to King Guy.

[Col. 0905C]

When the count of Tripoli saw that all the barons had failed him, he went to Tiberias; and the barons went to Jerusalem to do homage to the king. Only Baldwin of Ramla did not go, but he sent one of his young sons. He told the barons to ask the king to put his son in possession of his land and receive his homage.

After the barons had done homage to the king, they asked him, on behalf of Baldwin of Ramla’s son, to put him in possession of his father’s land and receive his homage. The king replied that he would neither put him in possession of the land nor receive his homage until his father himself had done homage; then it would be good counsel to put the son in possession [Col. 0905D] of the land. Baldwin understood well that, unless he did homage, the king would seize his land.

When Baldwin heard that he must do homage to King Guy, he was greatly distressed. He came before the king but did not greet him; instead he said: “King Guy, I do homage to you, as one who will not hold land from you.” Thus Baldwin of Ramla did homage to the king, but did not kiss him. He had his son invested with the land and made him do homage. Then he departed, entrusted his son and all his land to the care of his brother Balian of Ibelin, took leave, and went away. This was a great loss to the land; but the Saracens rejoiced greatly, for they feared him and his brother Balian more than any baron of the land. His knights escorted him until he was beyond [Col. 0906A] the king’s power. He took leave of his brother Balian and the other knights and went to the prince of Antioch, who received him well, rejoiced greatly at his arrival, and gave him as much land as he had left behind. Let us now leave Baldwin of Ramla and speak of King Guy, who remained in Jerusalem.

## III. King Guy prepares an army against the count of Tripoli, who summons Saladin to his aid. The king sends messengers to offer peace to the count.

King Guy took counsel with the master of the Temple as to what he could do concerning the count of Tripoli, who would not do him homage. The master advised him to summon his host and besiege Tiberias. When the count of Tripoli learned that the king had summoned his army to come against him, he was not pleased. He sent to Saladin, [Col. 0906B] lord of Damascus, saying that King Guy had assembled his host to come against him, and asking that, should he need help, Saladin would aid him.

Saladin sent him a considerable force of armed knights and sergeants and told him that, if the king besieged him in the morning, he would relieve him in the evening. Saladin then summoned and assembled his host at Baisan, a city five leagues from Tiberias. King Guy, who had assembled his army at Nazareth, was deeply troubled. Balian of Ibelin came to him and said: “Lord, why have you assembled this host? Where do you intend to go? This is not the season to keep an army in the field against winter.”

The king told him that he intended to besiege Tiberias. “By what counsel, lord,” said Balian, “do you intend to do this? That counsel is bad; no wise man ever gave you such counsel. Know, lord, that neither by my counsel nor by that of your barons will you set foot there. There is a great chivalry of Christians and Saracens within Tiberias, while you have too few people to besiege them. Know that if you go there, not one foot will escape; and as soon as you have besieged it, Saladin will relieve it with a very great force. Instead, disband this host; I and some of your barons will go to the count of Tripoli and make peace between you, if we can, for this enmity is not good.”

The king accepted his counsel, disbanded his host, and sent messengers to Tiberias. When they came to the count, they spoke of peace. The count replied that he would make no peace until he was restored to that of which he had been dispossessed; but if he were restored, he would do such things that the king and barons would be grateful to him. The messengers returned to the king and reported what they had found. Thus the matter remained throughout the winter until Easter.

Then King Guy heard that Saladin was assembling his armies to enter his land. He summoned the archbishops and bishops to come to him in Jerusalem. When they had come, he asked their counsel concerning Saladin, who was assembling his host to attack him. The barons advised him to come to terms with the count of Tripoli, since otherwise he could not withstand the Saracens. The count of Tripoli had a great truce with Saladin; he was a wise man and a good knight. If matters with him were settled and the king would heed [Col. 0907A] his counsel, he would have little to fear from the Saracens. Moreover, he had lost the best knights of the land, namely Baldwin of Ramla; and if he lost the aid of the count of Tripoli, everything would plainly be lost.

The king replied that he would willingly make peace with him and would agree in good faith to whatever they advised. He then told the master of the Temple, the archbishop of Tyre, Balian of Ibelin, and Reynald of Sidon to go to the count of Tripoli to make peace; whatever peace they made, he would keep. The three came and went to spend the night at Nablus. Reynald of Sidon went by another road. That night Balian told his companions that the next day was the day to lodge at La Fève; but he would remain at Nablus, where he had a little business, and would hurry so as to overtake them [Col. 0907B] the next day.

## IV. Meanwhile the count allows Saladin’s son free passage into Christian lands. The Knights Templar confront the Saracens and are destroyed by them.

Here we shall leave the messengers for a while and speak of one of Saladin’s sons, who had newly arrived at Dūbīs. He sent to the count of Tripoli, requesting that the next day he be allowed to enter the Christians’ land through the count’s territory in order to make a raid. When the count heard this, he was greatly distressed. He thought that, if he refused, he feared losing the aid and counsel of Saladin, the young man’s father; but if he granted it, he would incur great shame and blame from Christendom.

Afterwards he thought he would warn the Christians so thoroughly that they would lose nothing, while Saladin’s son could not justly be angry with him. He sent word to Saladin’s son that he gave him permission to pass through his land and enter Christian territory on the condition that he cross the river at sunrise and cross back again before sunset; that he should take nothing from within a town or house, nor inflict damage. Saladin’s son agreed. The next morning he crossed the river, came before Tiberias, and entered Christian territory.

The count of Tripoli had the gates of Tiberias closed, so that those within would not come out and harm the raiders. Since the count already knew that the king’s messengers were coming to him, he caused letters to be made and sent them to a knight of the land who was stationed at Nazareth [Col. 0907D] and to others with him; indeed, everywhere that he knew the Turks would go. He ordered that, whatever they saw that day, they should not leave their towns or houses. The Turks were to enter the land, and if they remained quiet, they would be safe; but if they came out into the open, they would all be captured and killed. He also sent word to the castle of La Fève, where the king’s messengers were, that they should not move the next day.

When the master of the Temple heard that the Saracens were to enter the land, the next day he dispatched a courier to a convent of the Temple four miles away, at a town named Caco, and ordered them to mount and come to him as soon as they saw his letters, because the Saracens were to enter the land the next morning. [Col. 0908A] As soon as the convent received the master’s order, they mounted and came to him before nightfall, lodging before the castle. The next morning they set out and went to Nazareth.

The knights of the garrison of La Fève numbered ninety, from both the Temple and the Hospital; at Nazareth they took forty knights stationed there on the king’s behalf. They left Nazareth and went seven miles toward Tiberias. They found the Saracens at a spring called the Spring of Cresson. The Saracens had already returned to the ford to cross the river and re-enter their own land, without having done any harm to the Christians, because the Christians had kept themselves safe as the count of Tripoli had ordered.

Then the master of the Temple and those with him charged the Saracens. The Turks received them boldly and enclosed them so that the Christians could not be seen among them. For the Turks numbered some seven thousand, while the Christians were only one hundred and forty. There the master of the Hospital was killed, and likewise all the knights of the Temple and Hospital, except only the master of the Temple, who escaped with two other knights. The forty knights stationed at Nazareth on the king’s behalf were all killed. When the squires of the Temple and Hospital saw that their masters had charged among the Saracens and were getting the worse, they fled with all their equipment, so that none of the Christians’ equipment was lost. [Col. 0908C]

## V. The Turks carry away the heads of the slain Christians. Balian, receiving news of the Christians’ rout, reports it to the queen. The messengers come to the count and reconcile him with the king.

I shall now tell you what the master of the Temple did when he passed through Nazareth utterly defeated. He sent a sergeant into Nazareth and had it cried throughout the city that all who could bear arms should follow him to the Gaaing, for he had defeated the Turks. They followed him; all of Nazareth who could go came out, and they ran until they reached the place where the battle had been. There they found the Christians dead and defeated. The Turks rushed upon them and captured them all.

When Coredier, Saladin’s son, had defeated and killed our Christians with the help of his Turks, [Col. 0908D] he had the heads of the knights of the Temple and Hospital fastened upon the points of Turkish lances. They led the prisoners away bound and passed in this fashion before Tiberias. When those of Tiberias saw that the Christians had been defeated, that the Turks were carrying their heads upon their lances and leading the others away as prisoners, bound in shame, they grieved exceedingly.

Thus Saladin’s son crossed the river at sunrise and recrossed it before sunset. He kept his agreement with the count of Tripoli well: never in castle, house, or town did he inflict evil or damage, except upon those whom he found in the fields. This battle took place on a Friday, in the year of the Incarnation of Our Lord 1187, on the feast-day of St James and St Philip, the first day of May.

We shall now speak of Balian, who had remained at Nablus. When night came, Balian, as he had agreed with the master of the Temple and Hospital, left Nablus to follow them. After he had ridden two miles, he came to a city called Sebaste. He thought that it was a fine day and that he would go no farther until he had heard Mass. He went to the bishop’s house and had him rise. They talked together until the watch sounded daybreak. Then the bishop had one of his chaplains vest, and he sang Mass for him.

When Balian had heard Mass, he went away at great speed, until he came to the castle of La Fève. There, outside the castle, he found the tents of the convent of Caco pitched, [Col. 0909B] but there was no one to tell him what this might mean. He had one of his young men enter the castle to inquire what it could be. The young man entered the castle and found no one who could tell him anything concerning what he sought, except two sick men lying in a chamber; they could tell him nothing. He returned to his lord and said that he had found no one who knew anything of it.

They then went toward Nazareth. When they had gone a little way from the castle of La Fève, a brother of the Temple rode out and came swiftly to them. Balian asked him what news there was. He answered: bad news. He told him that the master of the Hospital had been beheaded; that of all the brothers of the Temple only three had escaped—the master of the Temple and two others—and that the knights whom the king had left in garrison at Nazareth had all been captured and killed.

When Balian heard this news, he was deeply grieved. He sent a sergeant back to Nablus to tell the queen, his wife, this news and to command that all the knights of Nablus should come to him at Nazareth. Near there he encountered the squires and the equipment of the knights of the Temple who had escaped from the rout. Know that, if Balian had not turned back to Sebaste to hear Mass, he would have arrived in time for the battle.

When he came to Nazareth, he heard such grief throughout the city for those who had been killed or captured in the battle that there were few houses in which there were not dead or captives. There he found the master of the Temple, who had escaped. Balian waited there [Col. 0909D] for his knights until they arrived. When they had come, he informed the count of Tripoli, who was at Tiberias, that he was staying at Nazareth. When the count of Tripoli heard that Balian had not been in the battle, he was very glad. The next day he sent fifty knights to escort him.

Balian asked the master of the Temple how the battle had occurred. He said that the Christians had fought well and had killed many Saracens; they would have defeated them, had not an ambush which the Saracens had placed on a hill enclosed them, whereby they were defeated. Then they sent to the place where the battle had occurred for the bodies of the knights, and buried them. The next day the archbishop of Tyre, Balian of Ibelin, and the master of the Temple set out to go to Tiberias. When they had left the city, the master of the Temple turned back because he could not ride. Balian and the archbishop went to Tiberias.

When the count learned that they were coming, he went out to meet them, greatly distressed by the misfortune that had occurred there the day before, entirely through the pride of the master of the Temple. He received them honourably and brought them to his lodging. They then delivered their message. The count told them that he was very grieved and ashamed at what had happened, and that whatever settlement they arranged between them, he would make, for he knew well that they would not give him bad counsel. They told him to put the Saracens out of the city and come to the king; just as he had committed himself to them, so had the king committed himself to making peace. [Col. 0910B] The count willingly agreed. They then sent a swift messenger to the king, informing him that they were bringing the count with them.

## VI. The king goes to meet the count. The True Cross is brought to the army.
