When the king heard this news, he was greatly pleased. He set out from Jerusalem, where he was, to meet the count of Tripoli. They met before a castle called St Job. As soon as the king saw the count from afar, he dismounted and went to him. When the count saw that the king had dismounted, he likewise dismounted and came to him. When one was near the other, the count knelt before the king. The king raised him and kissed him; then they returned to Nablus.

There the king took counsel with the count of Tripoli and the other barons concerning what he should do. The count advised him to summon his host and assemble it at the Spring of Saffuriya, for he knew that Saladin was assembling his host to enter his land. He advised him to send to the prince of Antioch for aid. The king did as the count advised, went to Saffuriya, and assembled his host. The prince of Antioch sent him one of his sons with fifty knights.

The patriarch had the True Cross carried to the army and informed the king that he had an excuse and could not go there. Here was fulfilled the prophecy which the archbishop of Tyre spoke when he was elected patriarch: that Heraclius had won the True Cross in Persia and brought it back to Jerusalem, and that Heraclius would take it out and it would be lost in his time. From that hour Heraclius took the True Cross out of Jerusalem; it never entered there again, but was lost in battle, as you will hear below. [Col. 0910D]

When the Holy Cross had been brought to the army, the master of the Temple advised the king to proclaim throughout his land that all who wished to receive wages should come to him, and he would give them good pay. He would then distribute the treasure which King Henry of England had in the house of the Temple.

## VII. The treasure of the king of England is handed over to the king. Saladin besieges Tiberias.

I shall now speak of the treasure which King Henry had at the Temple and the Hospital. When the king of England had caused St Thomas of Canterbury to be martyred, he reflected that he had done wrong and that he would go overseas [Col. 0911A] and be reconciled with Our Lord for that offence and others. Thus it came about that, every year after St Thomas was martyred, he sent great wealth to be put in reserve in the houses of the Temple and Hospital at Jerusalem. He intended, when he came there, to find the wealth ready to aid the land.

The treasure held by the master of the Temple he gave to King Guy, saying that he wished him to gather so many men that he could meet the Saracens in battle and avenge the shame and injury they had done. The king took the Temple’s treasure and distributed it among the knights and sergeants. He ordered the constables of the sergeants that each should make a banner from the arms of the king of England, because it was from his wealth that they were paid and retained. [Col. 0911B]

When the king had remained there another five weeks with all his men, Saladin crossed the river and besieged Tiberias. The wife of the count of Tripoli was within when Saladin besieged it. There were no knights within; all were in the army with the king, together with the four knightly sons she had, sons of the castellan of Saint-Omer. The eldest was named Hugh of Tiberias, the second William, the third Ralph, and the fourth Odo.

## VIII. The count of Tripoli judges that no aid should be brought to Tiberias; the master of the Temple takes the opposite view, and the king follows his counsel.

When the countess saw that the Turks had besieged them, and that she could not hold out against so many Saracens, she sent a messenger to King Guy and to her lord [Col. 0911C], the count, telling them that unless they relieved her promptly, she would lose the city; for she had not enough people to defend herself against so great an army as the Saracens had. The messenger came to the king on the countess’s behalf. When the king heard the message, he summoned the Master of the Temple and the barons. When they had assembled, he told them that Saladin had besieged Tiberias, and that the countess had sent him word to relieve her swiftly, lest otherwise she lose the city; and therefore counsel had to be taken.

“Lord,” said the Count of Tripoli, “I shall give you good counsel, if I am believed; but I know well that no one will believe me.”

“Nevertheless,” said the king, “say what you wish.”

“Lord,” he replied, “I advise that Tiberias be allowed [Col. 0911D] to fall. I shall tell you why. Tiberias is mine, and my wife is there; no one will lose as much as I shall if it is lost. Yet I know well that if the Saracens take it, they will not retain it, but will destroy it; nor will they come seeking us in this place. And if they take my wife and my men and demolish my city, I shall recover them when I can. For I should sooner endure that my city were taken and destroyed than that the whole land were lost. For I know well that, if you go to relieve it, it is lost; and I shall tell you how. Between here and Tiberias there is no water except a small spring, namely the Spring of Cresson. That is little enough for an army; and as soon as you set out to relieve it, the Saracens will be before you, and will continually harass you as far as Tiberias, and will force you [Col. 0912A] to encamp, so that you cannot fight them because of the heat, while the foot-sergeants will have nothing to drink. And if you charge, the Saracens will scatter and flee toward the mountains; nor can you proceed without your sergeants. Thus they will make you encamp where your men and horses will have nothing to drink. They will die of thirst. On the next day they will take you all; for they will have water and provisions and will be entirely fresh, while we shall all be hungry and dying of thirst and heat. Thus all will be dead or captured. Therefore I advise you to let Tiberias fall rather than the land be lost.”

Then the Master of the Temple said that he still had the wolf’s fur. The count paid no heed to these words, but said to the king: “Lord, if what I have told you does not happen, I grant you my head to be cut off, if you go there.”

The king asked the barons what they thought of the counsel which the count gave. They said that the count spoke truly, and they all agreed with him. The king himself and the Hospitallers agreed, and all were in agreement except the Master of the Temple. Nevertheless, the king and all the barons pledged that they would do this. Then everyone went to his tent; it was nearly midnight. The king went to supper.

When he had supped, the Master of the Temple came to him and said: “Lord, do you believe the counsel which that traitor has given? It is intended to dishonour you. You are newly made king, and never before did a king of this land have so great a host in so short a time. It will therefore be a great disgrace if, with five thousand of your [Col. 0912C] men, you allow a city to be lost; and this is the first undertaking entrusted to you. Know that the Templars would sooner lay down their white mantles and sell all that they possess than leave unavenged the dishonour which the Saracens have done me. Lord, have it proclaimed through the army that they arm themselves, and let every man go to his division, and let the Holy Cross be brought there.”

The king did not dare refuse him, because he had made him king and had entrusted the great treasure to the King of England. He therefore had his proclamation made, that all should arm themselves and each should go to his division. When the barons heard the king’s proclamation, they were all astonished and asked one another by whose counsel the king was doing this. They all went to the king’s tent to dissuade him from setting out. But the king would not listen to them; rather, he told them [Col. 0912D] to go and arm themselves and follow him. They returned to their equipment and carried out the king’s command. They armed themselves with great sorrow, as men who well knew that no good could come of it.

That day Balian of Ibelin commanded the rearguard, and he lost many of his knights there. Before the king had departed from the encampment, the Turks were present, as the Count of Tripoli had said, and began to shoot very thickly.

## IX. Saladin attempts, through a sorceress, to bewitch the Christian army.

Before I say more about the army, I shall tell you of a marvel which may perhaps seem a fable. The sergeants of the rearguard of the army found [Col. 0913A] an old Saracen woman on an ass. She was the slave of a Syrian of Nazareth. They seized her and put her under such duress that she said who she was and what she sought in that army.

She said that she was going around the army in order to bind it by her enchantment and her words; she had already gone around it for two nights. If she could go around it once more that night, they would be so bound that not one foot would escape from the battle to which they were going. They ought to know that, if they advanced, scarcely anyone would escape; and those few would escape only because she could not complete her circuit. Saladin had given her great wealth to perform this binding.

They asked her whether she could undo it. She answered that she certainly could, provided that every man returned to his tent just as they had been [Col. 0913B] when she bound them; if they did not go there, she could not undo it. Then the sergeants made a great fire from their huts in order to burn her, and threw her into it; but she came out and could not be burned. They thrust her back into the fire, and she came out as before; however much they knew how to throw her in, she always emerged again. Then one of the sergeants struck her with an axe and killed her.

Now do not regard this old woman as a fable, for one finds in writing that long ago there was a man in Jerusalem who so bound an army, provided that he went around it, that there was no man in the army able to use any limb he had. This man was named Balaam the prophet, and it was he who prophesied that a star would come forth from Jacob. That star was our Lady Saint Mary, [Col. 0913C] who is called Star of the Sea. For just as sailors are guided by the star, so sinners are guided back by our Lady Saint Mary, who sprang from the lineage of Jacob.

It happened once to Balaam, who was in Jerusalem, that a great host came before Jerusalem. When the people of Jerusalem saw them, they were greatly afraid. They prayed earnestly to Balaam and gave him gifts, so that he went out to bind the army. When he came to a hill outside Jerusalem, his ass stopped. Balaam struck it, and the ass drew back; and the more he struck it, the further it drew back.

Then the ass spoke to Balaam and said: “Why do you strike me? I feel no evil from anything that you do to me. The angel of the Lord God strikes me in the middle of the muzzle with a sword, so that I cannot go forward.”

Then Balaam knew certainly that God did not [Col. 0913D] wish him to proceed. He returned and told those of Jerusalem that they should do the best they could, because he could do nothing by his art: God did not wish him to go further, for his ass had thus spoken to him.

The next day those of the army assaulted the city. When the citizens saw that they were being so fiercely attacked, they begged Balaam, for God’s sake, to do or say something through which they might defend themselves against them. Balaam said that he could do nothing against the will of the Lord God. Nevertheless they begged him to advise what they might do.

He advised them to dress and adorn all the young women of the city handsomely and send them into the army. If the enemy sent them back, they should surrender the city. He knew no other counsel to give them. But if they kept them two or three days, then on the fourth day they should open the gates of the city, go out, and fight them; they would defeat them.

They did as Balaam advised. They sent their women into the army. The enemy did not refuse them; rather, each took his own and did with her as he pleased. Those inside saw that the men of the army did not send them back and were doing with them as they pleased. They opened the gates and attacked them. They killed and defeated them all. Thus the siege was lifted from the city.

In the place where the ass spoke to Balaam stood the women’s leper-house of Jerusalem. For the women’s leper-house is not together with the men’s leper-house. The women’s leper-house stood by the walls of Jerusalem, while the men’s leper-house was [Col. 0914B] a considerable distance higher up.

Now I shall tell you of Heraclius, Patriarch of Jerusalem.

## X. On the election of Heraclius as patriarch. The Archbishop of Tyre opposes his election.

As I told you before, in the time of Baldwin the Leper there were two clerics in Jerusalem: one was Archbishop of Tyre and the other Archbishop of Caesarea. This is not the Caesarea called Caesarea Philippi, but another one. The Archbishop of Tyre was called William and was born in Jerusalem. No better cleric in the land was known. The Archbishop of Caesarea was born in Auvergne and was called Heraclius. He was a handsome cleric, and because of his beauty the king’s mother loved him and [Col. 0914C] made him Archbishop of Caesarea.

In the time of these two clerics the Patriarch of Jerusalem died. The king summoned the archbishops and bishops of the land to come to Jerusalem in order to elect a patriarch. They came; and when they had assembled, Archbishop William of Tyre said to the canons of the Holy Sepulchre, to whom belonged the election of the patriarch:

“Lords, I have found it written that Heraclius won the Holy Cross in Persia and brought it to Jerusalem, and that Heraclius would cast it out, and that in his time it would be lost. Therefore, for God’s sake, I beg you not to elect him patriarch. For if you name him in your election, I know well that the king will choose him; and know that the land will be lost during his lifetime if he is patriarch. For God’s sake name [Col. 0914D] one of the others; and if you do not find one in this country, we shall advise you well to seek in France a worthy man to be patriarch.”

The canons did nothing of the kind, because the king’s mother had already asked them, concerning Heraclius, Archbishop of Caesarea, to name him in their election. Thus they named him first, and the Archbishop of Tyre afterwards. For this is the election of the patriarchs and archbishops in the overseas lands: they name two and present them to the king. The king chooses one. If he is presented in the morning, he must choose him before vespers ring; if he is presented in the evening, he must choose him before high Mass in the morning.

The apostles made this election. When Judas was dead, they chose two—Joseph and Matthias—and cast lots; and the lot fell upon Matthias [Col. 0915A]. Thus they still do in the land of Syria. The king takes whichever he wishes.

The two archbishops were presented to the king, and the king chose Heraclius, because his mother had asked him to do so. In this manner Heraclius became Patriarch of Jerusalem. When he was patriarch, he commanded the archbishops and bishops of the land to render him obedience. They all did so except the Archbishop of Tyre. The latter appealed to Rome and said that he would show reasons why Heraclius ought not to be patriarch. Having made his appeal, the archbishop prepared for his journey and went to Rome. The pope and the cardinals were greatly pleased by his arrival. He then so prevailed with the pope and the cardinals that, had he lived until the patriarch came to Rome, the latter would have been deposed. I shall tell you how he died [Col. 0915B] before the patriarch came there.

## XI. Heraclius, given to impurity, kills the archbishop by poison.

When Patriarch Heraclius learned that the Archbishop of Tyre had gone to Rome to injure him, he knew well that, if the archbishop lived long, he would be deposed. Therefore he told one of his physicians to go after him and poison him. This the physician did, and the archbishop died.

Afterwards the patriarch went to Rome and did what he wished, then returned to Jerusalem. When he had returned from Rome, he became acquainted with the wife of a merchant who was at Nablus, twelve miles from Jerusalem. He frequently sought her. She went there, and he gave her enough of his wealth so that she might be well disposed toward her husband. Not long afterwards her husband died. Then the patriarch brought her to [Col. 0915C] Jerusalem and bought her a good stone house. He kept her openly before the world as a man keeps his wife, except that she did not live with him.

When she went to church, she was dressed in rich garments like an empress, with her servants before her. When people who did not know her saw her, they asked who that lady was. Those who knew her said that she was the patriarch’s wife. Her name was Pasque de Riveri. She had children by the patriarch. While the barons were in council, a fool came to the patriarch and said: “Lord Patriarch, give me a good gift, for I bring you good news. Pasque de Riveri, your wife, has a beautiful daughter.”

I have said this because the patriarch lived such a life, and the clerics and priests of the city took their example from him. When Jesus Christ saw the sin and filth committed there where He was crucified, He could bear it no longer. Rather, He cleansed the place of the inhabitants who were in the city in Heraclius’s time, so that there remained only two men: one named Robert of Corbie and the other Fouque Fiole. These were the first two men born in the city. Saladin then caused all that they needed to be given them. They had sufficient for as long as they lived in the city.

## XII. The Saracens meet King Guy and utterly rout the Christians after capturing the king.

Now I shall tell you of King Guy and his army, which came from the Springs of La Forbie to relieve the city of Tiberias. But as soon as they moved, the Saracens [Col. 0916A] came before them to harass them, just as the Count of Tripoli had told them. It was already well past noon when they were midway between Tiberias and the Springs.

Then the king asked the Count of Tripoli what counsel he gave and what they should do. The count then gave bad counsel, for he advised that they pitch the tents and encamp. But some in that army said truly that, had they then charged against the Saracens, the Saracens would have been defeated. King Guy now believed the bad counsel, though before he had refused to believe the good counsel.

When the Saracens saw our Christians encamp, they were very glad. They encamped so close to them that one side could speak to the other; not even a cat could leave the Christian army without the Saracens seeing it. That night there was great distress in the army, for no man or beast drank during the night. The day of Rames appeared as Friday; the next day, Saturday, was the feast of Saint Martin boiling before the army. That night the Christians watched under arms, and their suffering from thirst increased greatly.

On the next day all moved armed and ready to fight, and the Saracens likewise on the other side. Yet they drew back, for they did not wish to fight until the heat had risen. There was a great thicket of grass where our Christians were. The Saracens set fire to it so that our men might suffer greater distress from both fire and sun, and thus held them until the hour of terce.

Then five knights of the company of the Count of Tripoli left and came to Saladin, saying to him: [Col. 0916C] “Lord, what are you waiting for? Charge upon them; they can no longer help themselves: they are all dead.”

The foot-sergeants, without doubt, threw down their arms and surrendered to the Saracens without striking a blow, under the distress caused by thirst. When the king saw the anguish and distress of the sergeants surrendering to the Saracens, he sent for the Count of Tripoli and told him to charge first; because the battle was in his land, he ought to make the first attack.

The count charged against the Saracens down a slope. As soon as the Saracens saw him coming and charging upon them, they parted and made way for him, and the count passed through. Once he had passed through, the Saracens closed up again and charged the king. They captured him and all [Col. 0916D] the barons in his company, except only those in the rearguard who escaped.

When the Count of Tripoli, who had passed straight through the Saracens, heard that the king had been captured, he departed and went to Tyre. Tiberias was only two miles from there. He did not dare turn toward it for fear of being captured. The son of the Prince of Antioch and the knights whom he had brought fled with him, as did his four stepsons. Balian of Ibelin, who was in the rearguard, escaped and fled to Tyre, as did Reynald, lord of Sidon.

## XIII. The loss of the True Cross.

In that battle the Holy Cross was lost. No one knew what became of it for a long time, until the time when Count Henry of Champagne was lord of the kingdom of Jerusalem. Then a brother of the Temple who had [Col. 0917A] been in the battle said to him: “Lord, if a thousand men could be found in this land who knew how to lead me to the place where the battle took place, I could certainly find the Holy Cross. For I buried it with my own hands while the battle was taking place.”

Count Henry summoned one of his sergeants who was born in the land, and asked him whether he knew how to point out the place where the battle had taken place. He said that he did, and identified the place where the king had been captured. The count then commanded him to lead there the brother of the Temple who had buried the Holy Cross. He said that he could go only by night, for if they went there by day he would be seized and detained. They went there by night and dug for three nights, but found nothing.

## XIV. Saladin orders the captive king and other noblemen to be brought before him. He has Prince Reynald beheaded. He sends the king in chains to Damascus and takes Tiberias.

[Col. 0917B]

When Saladin had defeated and captured our Christians, he encamped and gave thanks to Our Lord for the honour He had done him. Then he commanded that all the knights whom he had captured be brought into his tent. This was done. He ordered the barons and great men to be brought separately, for he wished to see them before him; the others were left outside.

The king was brought in, Prince Reynald of Kerak, Humphrey of Toron, the Master of the Temple, Marquis Boniface of Montferrat, Count Jocelin, Constable Aimery, and [Col. 0917C] the king’s marshal. All these great men were captured with the king in the battle.

That day was Saturday, the feast of Saint Martin the Boiling. This defeat took place in the year of the Incarnation of Our Lord 1187, on the fifth day of June.

When Saladin saw the king and barons before him, at his mercy, he was very glad. He saw that the king was hot and knew well that he would gladly drink. He had a full cup of syrup brought to drink for refreshment. When the king had drunk, he held out the cup to Prince Reynald to drink. When Saladin saw that the king had given drink to Prince Reynald, the man in the world whom he hated most, he was greatly angered. He told the king that he was displeased that he had given Reynald drink, and that, since it was so, he might indeed drink—but on one condition: that he would never drink from another.

Then Saladin asked for a sword and himself cut off Reynald’s head with his own hand, because Reynald had never kept faith or oath in the truces that Saladin had granted him. Saladin then had Prince Reynald’s head taken and ordered it dragged through all the cities and castles of the land; and this was done.

Afterwards Saladin had the king and all the prisoners taken to Damascus in captivity. Then he left there and encamped before Tiberias. When the countess learned that the king had been captured and the Christians defeated, she surrendered Tiberias to Saladin. That same day Saladin sent part of his knights to Nazareth, and it was surrendered to him. On Wednesday he went to Acre, and it was surrendered to him. Afterwards he went to Tyre, but he would not besiege it, because [Col. 0918A] the knighthood which had escaped from the battle was still inside.

Then Balian of Ibelin sent word to Saladin asking for safe-conduct to go to Jerusalem to bring out his wife and children to the queen. Saladin willingly granted it, provided that he remain in Jerusalem only one night and bear no arms against him.

## XV. Balian comes to Jerusalem and is retained there by the patriarch, as it were against his will.

When Balian came to Jerusalem, the people there were very glad and rejoiced greatly at his arrival. They begged him, for God’s sake, to guard the city and become its lord. He said that he could not do this, because he had pledged his faith to Saladin that he would remain only one night.

The patriarch said to him: “Lord, I absolve you from the sin and [Col. 0918B] oath which you have made to Saladin. Know that you will commit a greater sin by keeping the oath than by abandoning it. For it will be a great shame to you and your heirs if at this point you leave the city of Jerusalem; nor ought you ever again to have honour in the land.”

Then Balian of Ibelin promised that he would remain. Those of the city did him homage and received him as lord.

The queen, King Guy’s wife, was still then in Jerusalem. At that time there were only two knights in the city who had escaped from the battle. Balian of Ibelin then made fifty sons of burgesses knights. Know that the city was so full of women and children who had fled inside when they heard that the king was captured and the Christians defeated that they could not fit inside the houses, but had to remain in the streets.

Then the patriarch and Balian caused the covering over the Sepulchre, which was covered with silver, to be stripped off. They had coin made from it to give to the knights and sergeants. Every day the knights and sergeants went through the country around the city and brought in whatever provisions they could, for they knew well that it would be besieged.

Now we shall cease to speak of Jerusalem and shall tell of Saladin, who came before Tyre.

## XVI. Saladin takes several cities. God preserves Tyre for the Christians.

Saladin thought that he would accomplish nothing before Tyre because of the knighthood that was there. He passed on and [Col. 0918D] went to besiege a city six miles from Tyre, called Sidon. He took it, and also a city called Gibelet. Afterwards he took a castle called Boterim. The lady of that castle was the woman whom the Count of Tripoli would not give to Gerard of Ridefort, who entered the Temple in resentment; and from this arose the hatred through which the land was lost.

When the Count of Tripoli learned that Saladin had entered his land, he embarked, together with the son of the Prince of Antioch and all the knights he could have, and went to Tripoli. But once he had arrived there, he did not live long; rather, as people say, he died of grief. He left his land to the son of the Prince of Antioch, who afterwards became count.

When Reynald of Sidon and the castellan of Tyre saw that all the knights had gone away and that there were few people and little food, they sent word to Saladin to return from where he was, and they would surrender Tyre to him. When Saladin heard this news, he was very glad. He took a knight and gave him Saladin’s banner to place above the castle. But the castellan answered him that he did not dare raise it because of the people of the city; as soon as Saladin came, however, he would raise it, and the banner would remain displayed.

The knight returned and told Saladin. Saladin then hastened greatly to come to Tyre. But before he arrived, God sent it help, because He did not wish it to be lost. Rather, He wished to leave this city to the Christians, as you have heard above, so that He might leave the Christians at least a little land. I shall tell you what counsel and help God sent it.

## XVII. Conrad, son of the Marquis of Montferrat, leaves Constantinople and comes to Acre.

[Col. 0919B]

Conrad the marquis, who was living in Constantinople, came to the emperor and said: “Lord, my knights wish to go to the Sepulchre, and I cannot keep them back; but they have promised me that as soon as they have made their pilgrimage, they will return to me.”

He made the emperor understand this because he did not wish the emperor or the people of the city to know that he himself wished to depart. He feared that the relatives of Livernas, whom he had killed, would watch for him and kill him.

The emperor had ships prepared and sufficient provisions and arms put aboard. The marquis’s household entered them; and when the time came, they departed. The emperor and the marquis were then at the Mouth of the Lion.

“Lord,” he said to the emperor, “I have forgotten a matter which I ought to tell my men.”

Then he entered a ship, went after them, and joined his men. They had a good wind and sailed without stopping until they came before Acre. When they ought to have cast anchor, they saw no vessels coming out against them; so they would not cast anchor but drew back. When the Saracens of Acre saw that they would not enter the port, a Saracen knight came to the ship to discover who they were. When the marquis saw him approaching, he forbade his men to speak, saying that he would speak himself.

The Saracen came before the ship and asked what people they were. The marquis answered that they were merchants.

“Why then do you not land?” asked the Saracen.

The marquis answered that they would not come ashore because they did not know [Col. 0919D] what people were in Acre.

The Saracen said that they could safely land under Saladin’s protection, for Acre was his and he had conquered it. He had captured the King of Jerusalem and imprisoned all his barons, and he had conquered all the land except Tyre and Jerusalem, which he was besieging. If they wished to land under Saladin’s protection, they should land.

When the marquis heard this news, he was very grieved. He drew back and commanded the sailors to make haste.

## XVIII. He then hastens to Tyre, whose defense is entrusted to him. Saladin besieges Tyre, lifts the siege, and takes Caesarea and Jaffa. He takes Ascalon and grants liberty to the captive king.

When the Saracen saw that they would not enter the port, [Col. 0920A] he returned to have the vessels of Acre armed, so that they might capture the ship if they could. But God, who had sent Conrad to help Tyre, would not permit it; rather, He sent him a favourable wind.

When they came before Tyre, those of the city came out before them to discover who they were. When the marquis saw them coming, he was very glad, because they were Christians. They earnestly begged him to land at Tyre, which was a marvel, and to have pity upon Christendom. He willingly landed there.

When those of Tyre learned that he was the son of the Marquis of Montferrat, they were very glad. They came out to meet him in procession and brought him and his knights into the castle. When Reynald of Sidon and the castellan of Laïens saw that the city of Tyre had been entrusted to the marquis, they were greatly afraid because they had promised to surrender it to Saladin. At night they entered a little boat and fled to Tripoli.

When the marquis was within the castle, he searched it to discover how it was supplied with arms and other things. He found there the two banners of Saladin which he had sent to be placed above the castle. He asked whose banners these were. A man told him that they were Saladin’s banners, which were to be placed above the castle on the next day, since the city was to be surrendered to him.

The marquis had the two banners taken and thrown into the city ditches. On the day after the marquis had arrived, Saladin came before Tyre, fully believing that the city would immediately be surrendered to him. But God sent it help.

When Saladin saw that he would not have Tyre, he was greatly astonished at what had been reported to him. He asked why this was. They told him that the son of the Marquis of Montferrat—whose father Saladin held in prison—had arrived there; the city had been entrusted to him, and he would defend it well against Saladin and his army, with God’s help.

When Saladin heard this, he besieged Tyre and sent to Damascus for the marquis, the father of the man within Tyre, to be brought to him. When the marquis was brought into the army before Tyre, Saladin sent word to Conrad, his son, that if he surrendered Tyre, he would give him great wealth and restore his father to him.

The marquis answered that he would not give the smallest stone of Tyre for his father; rather, Saladin should bind him to a stake in the army and shoot at him, for he was too old.

When Saladin saw [Col. 0920D] that he could accomplish nothing there, he departed and went to besiege Caesarea, which he took. Then he went to Jaffa and took it. Afterwards he went to Ascalon and besieged it; but it was strong, and he did not take it as readily as he had thought. Instead he sent to Damascus and had the King of Jerusalem brought into the army.

When he had come, Saladin told those of Ascalon that, if they would surrender the city, he would let them and their king go entirely free. The king spoke to his men who were in the city and said that he did not wish them to surrender Ascalon for his sake, because it would be a great loss to surrender a city for one man. But he begged them, for God’s sake, that if it happened that they could not hold Ascalon, they should surrender it, doing what they could to secure his release.

Then the burgesses assembled and took counsel. They said that they could see no source from which help might come to them. It was better to surrender the city, saving their lives, persons, and possessions, than to be starved or taken by force. Thus they surrendered the city to Saladin, as I shall tell you.

Their persons and possessions were released, and Saladin had them safely conducted into Christian territory. The king was released as the tenth man, choosing nine prisoners from Saladin’s prison; but it was stipulated that the king should remain in prison until the end of March. Ascalon had been surrendered at the end of the preceding August. When Saladin had Ascalon, he sent the king to stay at Nablus, and told the queen, the king’s wife, to go to him at Nablus, because he did not wish the king to remain in Jerusalem when he went to besiege it. When the queen heard the [Col. 0921B] message, she went to the king at Nablus, and they remained there until Saladin had taken Jerusalem.

## XIX. Saladin announces to the citizens of Jerusalem that they must surrender the city to him.

On the day when Ascalon was surrendered to Saladin, the people of Jerusalem whom he had summoned came to him, because he wished to make peace with them if he could obtain the surrender of the city. That day was Friday, and at precisely the hour of none the sun changed, so that it seemed to be night.

Then Saladin told the burgesses of Jerusalem that he saw clearly that he had conquered the whole kingdom of Syria except Tyre and Jerusalem. If they would surrender the holy city to him before he took it by force, they would act wisely.

I had forgotten to tell you that, on the day Ascalon was lost, all the surrounding castles were surrendered to him.

The burgesses of Jerusalem answered Saladin that, if God pleased, they would not surrender the city to him.

“I shall tell you,” Saladin said, “what you shall do. I believe that Jerusalem is the house of God, and that is our belief; and I would not willingly lay siege to the house of God, nor have it assaulted, if I could have it by peace and friendship. I shall give you thirty thousand besants to fortify the city of Jerusalem, and a space of five miles in which to go wherever you wish and cultivate land for five miles around the city. I shall have provisions brought to you in such abundance that nowhere in all the land are provisions so cheap; and you shall have a truce until Pentecost. When that time comes, if you see that you can obtain help, hold out well; but if you cannot obtain it, surrender the city, and I shall have you, your persons and your possessions, safely conducted into Christian territory.”

They answered that, if God pleased, they would never surrender the city where God suffered death and shed His blood for us.

When Saladin saw that they would not surrender Jerusalem to him by goodwill or entreaty, he swore that he would never take it except by force.

## XX. Saladin takes the entire kingdom except Tyre and Jerusalem.

Meanwhile, while Saladin was before Ascalon, Balian of Ibelin asked him, for God’s sake, to grant safe-conduct to his wife and children so that she might go to Tripoli. For he could not keep the agreement which he had granted him when he went into Jerusalem, because he was so closely guarded that he could not get out. Saladin sent a knight there and had her conducted as far as Tripoli.

Saladin had taken the whole kingdom except Jerusalem, Tyre, and the Crac. He never laid siege to the Crac; rather, after he had conquered the land, he waited two years, until sheer famine compelled them to surrender it. Before they surrendered, they sold their wives and children to the Saracens in order to obtain food; and there remained neither beast nor any thing in the castle which they could eat. When they had nothing more to sell or to eat, they surrendered the castle to Saladin, because they clearly saw that they would receive no relief. Saladin was very glad [Col. 0922B] when they surrendered it to him. He caused the wives and children whom they had sold to be bought back and restored to them; moreover, he gave them great wealth and had them conducted into Christian territory. He did this because they had guarded the castle so well and loyally, as long as they could, and without a lord.

Saladin came from Ascalon to besiege Jerusalem on a Thursday evening. On the following day he encamped from the leper-hospital for women to the leper-hospital for men, and as far as St Stephen’s Gate.

## XXI. Saladin besieges Jerusalem; the Christians resist manfully. Saladin changes the position of the siege.

Before Saladin assaulted the city of Jerusalem, he sent word to those within that they should surrender it to him and that he would keep for them the terms which he had granted them before Ascalon—provided only that they surrendered the city. But they should know well that he had sworn that, if he made an assault upon them, he would never take them except by force. The people of Jerusalem sent him word that he should do the best he could, for they would never surrender the city to him.

Then Saladin had his men arm for the assault. Those in the city came out fully armed and fought against the Saracens; but the battle did not last long, since they all had the morning sun directly in their eyes. They withdrew until evening, when the Saracens began the assault again and continued until night. Saladin did this on that side for eight days; yet the Saracens could not force the Christians in, because the Christians were always outside the gates while daylight lasted, and twice or three times each day drove the Saracens back to their tents. On that side the Saracens could never erect a stone-thrower, mangonel, or any other engine.

Hear then how the Saracens assaulted the Christians. They did not attack until after noon. Then the Saracens had the sun behind them, while the Christians had it, and the dust, in their eyes. The Turks attacked with shovels, with which they threw sand and dust upward; it flew into the Christians’ eyes and faces. When the Saracens saw that they could accomplish nothing on that side, they moved the siege and went to encamp on the other side, from St Stephen’s Gate to the Gate of Jehoshaphat and to the Abbey of the Mount of Olives [Col. 0923A]; and they could see everything that those of Jerusalem did, except in the covered streets.

This relocation of the siege took place on Friday. Once they had thus besieged the city, the Christians were enclosed so that they could not leave it. For from St Stephen’s Gate to the Gate of Jehoshaphat there was no gate or postern through which they could go out into the fields, except the postern of St Mary Magdalene, by which one went out between two walls. On the day when Saladin moved his siege, he had a stone-thrower erected which struck the city walls seven times that same day; and during the night he had so many stone-throwers and mangonels erected that on the following day twelve of them, all set in place, were counted.

In the morning Saladin had his knights arm and formed three battle-divisions to assault the city. The shields were before them; behind were the archers, shooting as thickly as hail. No man in the city was so bold as to dare show himself upon the walls. The Turks came up to the ditches, sent in miners, and set ladders against the walls of the barbicans. In two days they undermined fifteen toises of wall. When they had mined beneath it and propped it up with timber, they set fire within; and the wall collapsed into the ditch over as much as they had undermined. The Christians could not counter-mine, because they feared the stone-throwers, mangonels, bolts, and arrows, and therefore could not remain there.

## XXII. The Christians deliberate on surrendering the city. Meanwhile the attacking Turks are repulsed.

[Col. 0923C]

Then the Christians assembled to take counsel about what they should do. They came to the patriarch and Balian of Ibelin and told them that they wished to go out by night and strike the camp. For they would rather die honourably in battle than be captured in the city and shamefully slain; they clearly saw that they could no longer hold it, nor could any defence avail them. And they preferred death in the place where Jesus Christ suffered death for them to surrendering the city.

The burgesses, knights, and serjeants agreed to this counsel; but the patriarch replied: “Lords, I should judge this good, but there is more to consider. If we abandon ourselves and allow the souls whom we can save to perish, that is not good. For every man in this city has perhaps fifty women and children dependent upon him; and if we die, the Saracens will take the women and children, not kill them, but make them convert to the law of Muhammad, and thus they will be lost to God. But if, with God’s aid, we could do so much with the Saracens as to go out and make our way to Christendom, that would seem better to me than going to fight at hazard.”

All agreed to this counsel. They then chose Balian of Ibelin and asked him to go to Saladin to learn what peace they might make. He went and spoke with him. While he was speaking with Saladin about surrendering the city, the Turks made an assault upon it and brought ladders [Col. 0924A], which they raised against the walls. As many as ten or twelve banners had climbed upon the walls, and they had already entered through the place where the wall had been mined and had fallen.

When Saladin saw his men and banners on the walls, he said to Balian: “Why do you ask me for the surrender of the city and for peace, when you see my people prepared to enter it? It is too late, for you see clearly that the city is mine.”

At the very moment when they were speaking thus, Our Lord gave such courage to the Christians upon the walls that they made the Saracens who were on the walls retreat and fall to the ground, and drove them entirely beyond the ditches. When Saladin saw this, he was greatly ashamed and grieved. He told Balian to return, saying that he would do no more at present, but that he should come again on the following day to speak with him; he would gladly hear what he wished to say.

Now I shall tell how that night the stone from a stone-thrower struck the timberwork of a tower so violently that the timberwork fell, causing a very great crash. The rabble of the camp and of the city were so frightened that everyone began crying, “Treason! Treason!” Those in the city thought that the Saracens had entered, while those outside thought that the Christians had come into the camp.

## XXIII. Because of their sins God does not hear the Christians’ prayers. Negotiations with Saladin concerning the surrender of the city.

The ladies of Jerusalem had tubs brought and set in the square before Mount Calvary, filled with cold water. They made girls enter them up to the neck, cut off their braids, and throw them away. Monks, priests, and nuns went barefoot in procession upon the city walls, carrying the Holy Cross before them, which the Syrians bore. The priests carried the Body of the Lord upon their heads. But Our Lord Jesus Christ would not hear the prayers which they made, because the foul stench of lust and adultery that was in the city did not allow prayer or supplication to rise before God. Our Lord would suffer it no longer, but so cleansed the city of its inhabitants that neither man, woman, nor child remained there, except two aged men, who did not live long afterward.

We shall now leave this subject and speak of Balian of Ibelin, who went to Saladin [Col. 0924D] to surrender the city. When Balian came before Saladin, he told him that the Christians would surrender the city, their lives being spared. Saladin answered that he had spoken too late: when he had made them the fair offer of surrendering the city, they had not wished to surrender it, and he had sworn that he would not take them otherwise than by force. But if they wished to surrender to his mercy and do as he pleased, he would take them; otherwise not. “For,” he said, “you see well that they have no relief and have no choice but to be taken in the city.”

Balian begged him, for God’s sake, to have mercy on them. Saladin answered: “Sir Balian, for love of God and of you, I shall have mercy upon them in one manner. In order to preserve my oath, they shall surrender to me as persons taken by force. I shall leave them their movables and possessions, to dispose of as their own; but their persons shall be in my prison. Whoever can and wishes to ransom himself, I shall let go for a stated ransom; whoever cannot ransom himself shall remain in my prison, as one taken by force.”

Balian answered: “Sir, what shall be the amount of the ransom?” Saladin answered that the rate should be the same for poor and rich: a man should pay twenty pounds, a woman ten, and a child ten; whoever could not pay this ransom should be a slave.

Then Balian said: “Sir, in this city there are few who can help themselves except the burgesses; and for every man here who can pay the ransom, there are a hundred who do not possess even two pounds. For the city is full of people from the surrounding country and of common folk who have crowded inside it. For God’s sake, sir [Col. 0925B], devise such counsel and measure as may ransom them.”

Saladin said that he would take counsel and that Balian should return to him the next day. Balian returned to the city, came to the patriarch, and summoned all the barons to report what he had found out from Saladin. When he had told them, they were greatly grieved for the common people of the city. They took counsel and said that there was a great sum belonging to King Henry of England in the Hospital; if they could persuade the Hospitallers to release that money to ransom a portion of the common people, it would be well done.

Likewise, King Guy had prevailed upon the master of the Temple to hand over the treasure of the king of England which was in the house of the Temple. From it he hired knights and serjeants, whom he led into the battle in which he was captured and in which the True Cross was lost.

Then the patriarch and Balian summoned the men of the Hospital and told them of the plan they had discussed: they wished to have the treasure of the king of England which the Hospitallers held in custody, to ransom the common people of the city, if they could negotiate a ransom with Saladin. The commander said that he would take counsel with his brothers. They told him to consider carefully what counsel they adopted, for they knew well that if they did not hand over King Henry of England’s money to ransom the poor, they would make Saladin take it, and would have no thanks for it.

The commander consulted his brothers. They said that this would be well done; and, if the treasure were theirs, they would willingly have the poor ransomed from it. Then the master of the Hospital came to the patriarch and Balian and told them that he and his brothers willingly consented that the treasure of the king of England should be assigned to ransom the poor people. Then all begged Balian of Ibelin to go to Saladin and make the best peace he could; and he went.

Saladin asked what he had come to seek. “Sir,” said Balian, “I have come to you concerning that for which I had asked you.” Saladin answered that he would keep what he had agreed with him; but if he granted anything further, it would be nothing, for the city and what was within it were his.

## XXIV. Terms of the agreement.

“Sir,” said Balian, “for God’s sake set a reasonable ransom for the poor people, and I shall do what I can to see that it is paid to you; for out of a hundred there are not two who can pay that ransom.” Saladin said that, for God’s sake first and for Balian’s sake afterward, he would set such a reasonable ransom as they could meet. He then fixed it so that a man should pay ten pounds, a woman five, and a child one. Thus the ransom was fixed for those able to redeem themselves; and whatever movable goods or other things they had left, they could carry away safely, and would find no one to wrong them in this.

Afterward Balian said to Saladin: “Sir, you have fixed the ransom for the rich; now you must settle the ransom for the poor. For there are some twenty thousand who could not pay the ransom for one man. For God’s sake make some equitable provision, and I shall obtain the assistance of the Temple, the Hospital, and the burgesses, so that they may be freed.”

Saladin said that he would willingly make such provision and would let all the poor go for one hundred thousand bezants. “Sir,” said Balian, “when all those who can ransom themselves have been ransomed, not half the ransom which you demand for the poor will remain to them.” Saladin said that he would do no otherwise.

Then Balian considered that he would not bargain for redeeming all together. For if he had redeemed one part, perhaps, with God’s help, he might obtain terms for the rest. He therefore asked Saladin for what price he would release and free seven thousand persons. Saladin said: for one hundred thousand bezants. “Sir,” said Balian, “that cannot be; but for God’s sake set a moderate sum.” They spoke together so long that they made an agreement for thirty thousand bezants for seven thousand persons [Col. 0926C], counting two women as one man and ten children below age as one man.

When this had been settled, Saladin fixed a time within which they might sell and pawn their goods and pay their ransoms: fifty days. Whoever should be found in the city after the fifty days would have person and property belong to Saladin. Once they were outside the city, he would have them conducted safely into Christendom. He also told Balian that all those in the city who had arms should arm themselves; and that, should thieves or rebels mingle among them, they should defend the people and guard the narrow passages until the unarmed had passed.

## XXV. The city is surrendered to Saladin.

[Col. 0926D] When the matter had been thus arranged, Balian took leave of Saladin and returned to the city. The patriarch summoned the Templars, Hospitallers, and burgesses of the city to hear the agreement which Balian had made with Saladin. They came, and Balian told them all that he had done. They said that it pleased them well, for he could not have done better.

Then the keys of the gates were sent to Saladin. When he received them, he was very glad and gave thanks to God. He sent guards into the Tower of David and had his banner raised over it. He had every city gate closed except one, namely the Gate of David. There he stationed knights and serjeants, so that no Christian could go out; through it the Saracens entered and departed to buy what the Christians had for sale.

The day on which the city of Jerusalem was surrendered was Friday, the feast of St Leodegar, the second day of October, in the year of the Incarnation of Our Lord 1188. When Saladin had thoroughly provisioned the Tower of David and the city gates, he proclaimed that they should bring their ransoms to the Tower of David and deliver them to the officials whom he had appointed to receive them, without waiting until the fifty days had elapsed. For whoever should be found after the fifty days, body and goods would remain his.

The patriarch and Balian went to the Hospital, had thirty thousand bezants taken, and carried them to the Tower of David for the ransom of seven thousand poor persons. When the thirty thousand bezants had been paid, they summoned the burgesses of the city. When these had come [Col. 0927B], they chose from each street two of the worthiest men they knew and made them swear upon holy things that they would spare neither man nor woman for hatred or affection; rather, they were to make each swear how much he possessed and retain for him only as much as he needed to travel to Christendom, using the rest to ransom poor people.

The number of poor people in each street was written down, and it was determined how one might take more and another less in proportion to what they possessed. In this way they made up the number of seven thousand persons. Then all the seven thousand persons were put out of the city of Jerusalem. When they were outside the city, little was visible of the remainder.

Afterward the patriarch and Balian summoned the Templars, Hospitallers, and burgesses, and begged them, for God’s sake, to devise means to ransom the poor people remaining in Jerusalem. They gave aid, but not as much as they ought, for they no longer feared that their possessions would be taken from them by force, since Saladin had guaranteed their safety. Otherwise they would have been far more generous toward the poor. From what they took from the poor who had gone out, beyond the surplus needed for their expenses, they ransomed some poor people; but I shall not tell you their number.

Now I shall tell how Saladin caused the city of Jerusalem to be guarded, lest the Saracens commit wrong or outrage against the Christians who were in the city. In each street he placed two knights and ten serjeants to guard the city. They guarded it so well that no one ever heard of any offence committed against the Christians. As the Christians left Jerusalem, they encamped before the Saracen host, so close that there was not an arrow’s flight between them. Saladin had the Christians’ camp guarded day and night, so that they should suffer no harm and thieves should not fall upon them.

When all those who had been ransomed had left the city of Jerusalem, very many poor people still remained. Then Saphadin, Saladin’s brother, came to him and said: “Sir, I helped to conquer the land and the city; therefore I ask you to give me a thousand slaves from among those in the city.” Saladin asked what he wished to do with them. He said that he would do with them as he pleased. Saladin granted them to him and ordered his officers to deliver him two slaves; and they did so.

## XXVI. Saphadin grants freedom to a thousand captives. Many others are freed.

[Col. 0928A]

When Saphadin had the thousand poor people, he freed them for God’s sake. Then the patriarch asked Saladin, for God’s sake, to give him some of the poor who could not ransom themselves. Saladin gave him seven hundred; the patriarch freed them. Then Balian asked Saladin for poor people, and Saladin gave him five hundred; Balian freed them.

Then Saladin said to his people: “My brother Saphadin has performed his almsgiving, as have the patriarch and Balian. Now I wish to perform mine.” He then ordered his officers to open the postern on the side toward St Lazarus, and had it proclaimed throughout the city that all poor people should leave. He ordered that, if there were among those poor any who could redeem themselves [Col. 0928B], they should be taken away and carried into prison; young men and young women were to be placed between the two walls, while old people were put outside the city.

This inquiry and expulsion lasted from sunrise to sunset, and they were put out through the postern. Saladin thus gave alms to countless poor people. Afterward those who remained were counted, and eleven thousand were still found. The patriarch and Balian came to Saladin and begged him, for God’s sake, to hold them as hostages and free the poor people until they had procured their ransoms in Christendom, whereupon they would be redeemed. Saladin said that he would not accept two men for eleven thousand, and that they should speak of it no more; and they did not.

## XXVII. How well Saladin treated the Christians. The count of Tripoli refuses to receive Christians.

[Col. 0928C]

Saladin performed a great act of courtesy. The noblewomen, the burgesses’ wives, and the daughters of knights who had fled to Jerusalem—whose lords had been captured or killed in battle—when they had left Jerusalem and been ransomed, went before Saladin, crying for mercy. When Saladin saw them, he asked who they were. He was told that they were the wives and daughters of knights who had been killed or captured in battle. He asked what they wanted. They told him that, for God’s sake, he should have mercy upon those whose husbands he held in prison and whose lands had been lost, and that God might provide them counsel and help.

When Saladin saw them weeping, he took great pity on them. He told the ladies to inquire whether their lords were alive; and all whom he had in prison, as many as could be found, he had released. Afterward he ordered that the ladies and young women whose fathers or lords were dead should be generously given from his own goods—more to some, less to others, according to their condition. So much was given them that they praised God and the world for the goodness and honour Saladin had shown them.

When all the Christians who were required to leave Jerusalem had gone out, the Saracens were greatly astonished at the vast people who had come forth. They said to Saladin that so great a multitude had left the city that they could not travel together. Saladin ordered them divided into four groups [Col. 0929A], with the Temple to lead one group, the Hospital another, and the patriarch and Balian the third. When he had thus arranged their departure, he assigned fifty knights to each group to conduct them safely into Christendom.

I shall tell how they conducted and guarded them. Twenty-five knights formed the vanguard. When those in the vanguard had eaten, they lay down to sleep and had their horses given their daytime fodder. When they had supped, they mounted their horses and rode throughout the night among the Christians, lest robber Saracens should fall upon them. Those forming the rearguard, when they saw a weary man, woman, or child, made their squires dismount and carry the exhausted people as far as the lodging-place; they themselves carried children before and behind them on their horses.

When they came to their lodging-place and had supped, they lay down to sleep. Those who had been the vanguard during the day served as the rearguard on the following day. When they came to narrow places where danger was feared, they had those Christians who possessed arms arm themselves and guard the passes until all had gone through. Wherever they lodged, the country people brought food in great abundance, so that the Christians obtained it cheaply.

Of the three groups thus arranged, the Templars led one, the Hospitallers another, and the patriarch and Balian the third. The patriarch and Balian remained to the last because they thought to overcome Saladin entirely by the prayers of the Christians who remained behind. Saladin had them conducted safely throughout his territory as far as the land of Tripoli. But when they came before Tripoli, the count of Tripoli had the gates shut and allowed none to enter. He had his knights go out into the fields and seize all the wealthy burgesses, taking from them the goods that Saladin had allowed them to retain.

Most of the poor went into the land of Antioch and Armenia; the other part remained before Tripoli and afterward entered it. But those from Ascalon and the neighbouring castles were not received in this manner when they went to winter at Alexandria. For when the Christians came before Alexandria, the governor had them lodged and good enclosures made around them [Col. 0929D]; he had them guarded day and night so that they should suffer neither harm nor loss. There they wintered very comfortably until March, when they embarked to cross to Christian territory.

## XXVIII. The Saracens’ charity toward the Christians.

Now I shall tell what those of Alexandria did. The worthy Saracens of the city of Alexandria went out every day and made great gifts of bread and money to the poor Christians. Wealthier persons who had money used it in merchandise, which they loaded aboard ships when they crossed the sea, thereby gaining great wealth.

Now I shall tell what befell them. Thirty-eight ships of Pisans, Genoese, Venetians, and other people wintered in the harbour of Alexandria; in March they obtained cheap passage. When March came and those who had hired the ships had been received aboard them, fully a thousand poor Christians remained who had nothing with which to hire ships or buy provisions to put aboard them.

The masters of the ships came to the governor of Alexandria, duly paid what they owed, and said that he should release their cables and rudders, for when they had weather and wind they wished to depart. The governor told them that he would not restore their cables and rudders until they had put all the poor Christians aboard their ships. They said they would not put them aboard, because they had hired no ships or bought no provisions for them.

“What then do you intend to do with them?” said the governor. They replied that they would leave them and would never undertake to carry them. [Col. 0930B] The governor asked whether they were Christians. They said yes. “How then,” said the governor, “do you wish to leave them here to become Saladin’s slaves? That cannot be: you must take them. I shall tell you what I shall do for God’s sake and for their sake: I shall give them enough bread and water, and you shall put them aboard the ships; otherwise you cannot have your rudders and cables.”

When the sailors saw that they could manage no differently, they said that they would carry them across. “You shall swear to me upon holy things that you will carry them well and loyally into Christendom; that, because I have compelled you to take them, you will not put them ashore anywhere except where you put ashore the rich people; and that you will do them no harm. If I can learn that you have done them shame or villainy, I shall exact vengeance from the merchants of your land who come into this country.”

Thus the Christians who had gone to winter at Alexandria through Saracen territory departed safely. Now I shall tell what Saladin did.

## XXIX. Saladin has the Temple washed with rosewater. He besieges Tyre.

When Saladin had taken Jerusalem and sent away the first group of Christians with the Templars, he would not leave Jerusalem until he had been in the Temple and worshipped, and until all the Christians had gone out. He had sent to Damascus for enough rosewater to wash the Temple before he entered. As people say, there were four or five camels [Col. 0930D] fully laden with it.

But before he had the Temple washed with that rosewater, or entered it, he caused a great gilded cross that stood upon the Temple to be thrown down. The Saracens bound it with ropes and dragged it to the gate of the Tower of David. There they broke it into pieces, and made a great outcry after the Cross as they dragged it. I do not say that this was done by Saladin’s command.

When the Temple had been washed, Saladin entered and gave thanks to God for granting him lordship over His house. Afterward he sent one part of his army to besiege Tyre and the other before Jerusalem, until all Christians who were to depart had left; then he went after the army which he had sent to Tyre.

When Saladin came before Tyre, he summoned the marquis of Montferrat. He was brought before him. Then he sent word to Conrad, the marquis’s son, concerning the marquis, whom he had captured at Jerusalem: if he would surrender Tyre, he would restore his father and give him great wealth. The marquis sent back word that Saladin should do his utmost, for he would never surrender Tyre; rather, with God’s help, he would defend it well against him.

Then Saladin sent to Acre and had fourteen galleys armed and brought before Tyre to guard the sea, so that no provisions could enter. On land he had fourteen stone-throwers and mangonels erected, which hurled missiles day and night. Yet they did little good, and there was no day on which our Christians did not make sorties against the Saracens two or three times. All this was led by a Spanish knight who was in Tyre and bore green arms. Whenever he came out before them, the Saracens in the camp were more astonished by the sight of his fine bearing than by anything else. The Turks called him the Green Knight. He wore an iron chain over his helmet.

The marquis had leather-covered vessels made, fashioned so that they could go very close to land. Crossbowmen were inside, with openings through which they shot. These vessels did great harm to the Saracens, for neither galleys nor other vessels dared approach them; they were called *barbotes*.

When the marquis saw that he was besieged by sea and land, he had a boat armed, sent it out by night, and dispatched it to the count at Tripoli, asking him to assist with men and provisions.

## XXX. Assistance sent from Tyre is driven back by force of the winds. Through Conrad’s ingenuity the Saracens before Tyre suffer loss.

[Col. 0931C]

When the Count of Tripoli heard what the marquis requested of him, he had twenty galleys armed and put knights and provisions aboard them, and sent them to Tyre; but God did not will that they should enter there. For when they came within two miles of Tyre, a storm arose which shattered fully half of them and drove them back to Tripoli, though no one perished. When the marquis saw that he had no help at all, he prayed God to counsel him; and he did as you shall hear.

It happened that he had in Saladin’s army a young man, the son of an emir, who had quarrelled with his father and entered Tyre, becoming a Christian.

[Col. 0931D]

Now I shall tell you what the marquis did after the young man had been in Tyre for some time. The marquis caused a letter to be written in the name of that young man who had become a Christian. It was addressed to Saladin as to his lord, and said that he knew all the secret plan of Tyre, that the Christians intended to flee by night, and that, if Saladin would not believe him, he should have listeners posted who would hear the commotion at the harbour. When the letters had been written, the marquis had them fastened to the shaft of an arrow and made one of his sergeants shoot it into the army. When the Saracens saw the arrow and the letters, they took them and brought them to Saladin. He had the letters read and learned what they said. He made the matter known to the emirs and put his best men into galleys to lie in wait for the Christians.

The marquis had the tower above the principal gate of Tyre provisioned, and set guards upon the walls, so that if the Saracens wished to climb the walls by ladders, they might defend them. He commanded the guards to remain entirely silent, so that they should neither be heard nor seen, in any way whatsoever, until there was need. Then he had the gates of the barbicans shut; he left no man in them, and all day they remained entirely quiet inside the city. When he had thus provided for the walls and tower, he went to the harbour and had his galleys thoroughly armed. He commanded all who could bear arms to be at the harbour that night, and so they were. They made a great uproar throughout the night.

Then the Saracens perceived that what had been reported to them was true. They too armed themselves and entered the galleys to await the Christians.

[Col. 0932A]

[Col. 0932B]

At daybreak the Saracens came to the harbour. The chains were lowered, because the Christians wished the galleys to enter. The three towers at the chain were well manned, and their men acquitted themselves very well that day. When the marquis saw that so many galleys had entered the harbour, he had the chain raised, captured five galleys that had come in, and killed all those aboard them. He then manned these five galleys with knights and sergeants, together with the two galleys that he had inside Tyre.

When the Saracens saw them coming, they drew back, for they clearly saw that they could not withstand them. But the men of Tyre charged them. Without doubt, the shore was entirely covered with mounted Saracens, who entered the sea as far as they could in order to aid their galleys; thus many of them were drowned.

When those in the galleys saw that they could endure and resist no longer, they ran ashore toward the camp, and two of the galleys went off to Beirut.

[Col. 0932C]

These two galleys which fled to Beirut later did great harm to our Christians, as you shall hear below.

### XXXI. The Saracens, defeated in naval and land battle, raise the siege of Tyre.

While the battle was taking place at sea, part of the Saracen army brought ladders to the walls of the barbicans, entered them, and went as far as the principal wall. But it was too high, and they could not set the ladders against it; moreover, although the ladders were long enough, they could not climb them because of the guards upon the walls.

[Col. 0932D]

When they saw that they could not climb the walls, they undermined the outer facing and the core of the wall; and they had only to push it down when God sent help. When the Christians had defeated the Saracens at sea, they were told that the Turks were undermining the city walls and already had great numbers within the barbicans. When the marquis heard this, he returned, had a gate opened, and they went out and charged the Turks. When these saw men coming upon them, they fled. Some threw themselves down from the barbicans; those whom they could catch were killed, and the number slain there was reckoned at as many as a thousand.

This defeat inflicted by our Christians upon the Saracens occurred on New Year’s Day; the siege before Tyre had begun on the preceding All Saints’ Day. When Saladin saw that he had been defeated by sea and land, he was greatly enraged and forbade any further assault upon the city. Reluctantly, he ordered fire set to his galleys and his engines and had everything burned. That night he broke camp and went to lodge a mile from Tyre.

[Col. 0933A]

The following day he divided his army and went to remain at Damascus.

### XXXII. The Archbishop of Tyre comes to Rome. King William of Sicily blames himself for the loss of the Holy Land.

Here we shall leave Saladin for a little and tell of the Archbishop of Tyre, who came as an envoy to the pope. He brought news of the great calamity that had befallen the Land of Promise. He arrived in the realm of the king of Sicily, Calabria, and Apulia.

[Col. 0933B]

King William had as his wife a daughter of the king of England, named Joan. The Archbishop of Tyre learned that the king was nearby. He came to him and told him of the great damage which had occurred in the kingdom of Jerusalem. The king was greatly grieved and thought himself somewhat guilty of the loss of the land; and I shall tell you why.

When Alexius had caused the eyes of his brother, who was emperor, to be put out, and had made himself emperor, he took counsel with his people of Constantinople about guarding the land at his own expense. They strongly advised him to do so. Therefore he caused a great expedition of ships and galleys to be prepared. He sent throughout the overseas land and other countries for knights and sergeants, promising them pay according to each man’s rank. He detained pilgrims intending to cross to the Holy Land, and for two years kept the ports so that no one could pass. Because he held back the crossing, and because of those who came from overseas, the land was greatly weakened; and the king of Jerusalem, having few men against the Turks, was defeated.

[Col. 0933C]

For when Saladin came against the cities and castles, he found no one to oppose him; rather, the whole kingdom was surrendered to him, except Tyre alone. For this reason King William said that he was greatly culpable for the loss of the land and kingdom.

I shall tell you what became of that expedition. Afterwards you shall hear of the help that he sent to the overseas land. King William did not go with that expedition, but remained in order to send men and provisions. If need arose, he sent some of the greatest men of the land to guide and keep watch over those troops.

### XXXIII. The King of Sicily sends aid to the Holy Land.

When the ships and galleys had been prepared, they departed and arrived at Dyrrachium in Greece. They captured and garrisoned it. Then they went to Thessalonica, conquering and garrisoning all the land between Dyrrachium and Thessalonica. Afterwards they advanced toward Constantinople.

When the Greeks of the country saw that these men had conquered so much from them, they were greatly troubled. They came to the commanders of the expedition and said that they were welcome, for they were very glad at their arrival; and they would have great joy if they could avenge the worthy man whose eyes had been put out, who had avenged the wicked deed done by Andronicus.

[Col. 0934A]

They then told them that the sea route to Constantinople was much too long, but that they should go by land; the Greeks would go with them, guide them, and provide abundant provisions from the country, for they did not love the emperor at all.

The Greeks so urged the leaders of the expedition that they went with them and abandoned their fleet. The Greeks led them on until they came seven days’ journey from Constantinople, near a city called Philippi. There they lodged in a valley. While the Greeks were leading them, they secretly notified the people of the country to be armed against them at Philippi; and so they were. When the cry of the country went up there and they had all assembled, they armed at daybreak on the following day, charged the men of the expedition, killed and captured them.

[Col. 0934B]

Few escaped; thus that expedition was lost.

Now I shall tell you what help King William sent to the overseas land. He sent one hundred galleys and three hundred knights, to help preserve the little land that remained to the Christians. Then he caused a great expedition of ships and galleys to be prepared to send afterwards, and to follow the king of England, whose daughter he had married. I have not said that he had taken the cross; but not long after that expedition he died without an heir, before the king of England went there. When King William was dead, the people of the country chose his first cousin, who was Count of Apulia. His name was Tancred, and they made him king.

Here we shall leave Tancred for the moment and speak of the Archbishop of Tyre, who had arrived in King William’s realm. The king gave him mounts and expenses for his journey as far as Rome.

[Col. 0934C]

### XXXIV. The pope summons Christian princes to bring aid to the Holy Land. The Emperor of Germany is the first to take the cross; he is drowned in the waters of Armenia. The kings of France and England take the cross. Saladin besieges Tripoli and raises the siege.

When the Archbishop of Tyre came to Rome, he found the pope and told him of the great harm overseas, and how the Saracens had conquered the land. When the pope heard it, he was greatly grieved. He sent his messengers throughout Christendom to proclaim the news which had been brought to him from the Land of Promise. He summoned all the great men of Christendom—kings, dukes, counts, barons, knights, and sergeants—and declared that, for all who took the cross in order to go to the overseas land, he took upon himself all the sins they had committed, provided that they had confessed and repented of them, and held them absolved between themselves and God.

[Col. 0934D]

He also declared that to all who wished to levy a tithe upon their men, he granted permission to take it from all their property of value, and freely allowed it for the service of the Lord God.

When the great men of Christendom, knights, townsmen, and sergeants heard the news, they took the cross and prepared to go. The first great man to depart was the Emperor of Germany. He went by land and led fully fifty thousand mounted men, besides those on foot. They travelled until they reached Constantinople, crossed the Strait of Saint George, and entered Turkey.

[Col. 0935A]

The emperor of Constantinople ordered that provisions be brought to them in abundance, and instructed the admiral Docoine, his liege man, to have provisions brought from his land along their route at a reasonable price and to have them safely conducted through his territory.

When the Germans entered the land of Turkey and of Docoine, they began to take away the food from the peasants who brought it to them. The peasants drew back when they saw themselves being robbed and brought no more provisions. Thus the Germans marched for three weeks without food except their horses, until they came to Armenia. Nearly half had died before reaching it.

One day the emperor was lodged beside a river in Armenia. He wished to bathe and was drowned.

[Col. 0935B]

When the emperor of Germany departed, he had three sons. He took one with him; after his father’s death, this son went to Antioch with those who had escaped the famine. The eldest of the three sons, who had remained to guard the empire, was named Henry. He had as wife the aunt of King William of Sicily, his father’s sister. The other brother was named Otto and was Duke of Burgundy; he had as wife the daughter of Count Theobald of Blois and died without an heir. The third was named Philip and was Duke of Swabia. I have begun to speak of the emperor’s children because hereafter you shall hear what became of them and what they did.

The king of France, though he had taken the cross, did not depart so soon because he was at war with the king of England. I shall say no more now about their war until the proper point, but you shall hear of Saladin, who was staying at Damascus.

[Col. 0935C]

News came to Saladin that the king of France and the king of England, together with all the other barons of Christendom, had taken the cross in order to march against him. He was neither pleased nor secure. He had Acre very strongly fortified and supplied with knights, sergeants, and provisions, placing there those in whom he had greatest trust.
