For he knew well that the Christians would arrive there, and that so great a host could land nowhere else. He commanded them not to leave Acre for the sake of a small force or for anything at all, but to remain quiet and closely shut within the city; and if Christians besieged them, as they were to inform him, he would immediately come to their aid.

When he had thus provisioned Acre, he had his cities and castles which he had conquered along the coast provisioned as well. Then he moved his army and went to besiege Tripoli.

[Col. 0935D]

At the moment when Saladin had laid siege to Tripoli, the ships and galleys of King William and the three hundred knights arrived at Tyre. Then the marquis had part of these galleys armed to relieve Tripoli, and commanded King William’s knights to go there. They went with the knights whom the marquis sent. The Green Knight of Spain was among them.

When the relieving force had arrived at Tripoli and rested a little, they made a sortie into the Turks’ camp; the Green Knight was at the very front. When the Saracens saw the Green Knight, they were greatly astonished that they had such abundance of men. They told Saladin that he had come in relief.

[Col. 0936A]

Saladin sent to ask him, under safe-conduct both coming and going, to come and speak with him. He went. Saladin made him great welcome and offered him many horses and much wealth, but he cared nothing for it. Saladin told him that, if he would remain with him, he would give him great lands. The knight answered that he would not remain, and that he had not come into the land to aid the Saracens, but to overthrow and injure them to the utmost of his power. Then he took leave and returned to the city.

When Saladin saw that Tripoli had so many armed Christians for its relief and that he could do nothing there, he departed and went ten miles away to a city called Tortosa. But before leaving, the queen, wife of King Guy, who was there within the city, sent him word to keep the agreement which he had made with her lord when he departed from Ascalon, and that it was high time for her lord to be released. Saladin said that he would gladly do so. He sent to Damascus, ordering that the king and ten of his knights, such as he would choose from the prison, be sent to him; and he commanded that the marquis be brought to Tyre and be presented there to his son on his behalf. Thus it was done as he commanded.

[Col. 0936B]

### XXXV. Saladin captures Valence and Byblus.

When the king and those whom he had chosen from prison came before him, he made them swear upon the saints that they would never again bear arms against him. Then he sent them to Tripoli. One of those released with the king was the Master of the Temple; another was the constable Bauneris; and the third was the marshal. I do not know how to name the others.

The king and his barons were released. Saladin sent Count Reynald’s son, Humphrey, free. Then Saladin went to a city five miles from Tortosa called Valence, captured and ravaged it. He did not wish to garrison it because of a castle nearby in the mountains called Margat. From there he went to a city called Gibel, captured it, and garrisoned it.

[Col. 0936C]

From there he went to Antioch, but did not besiege it. There, I heard, was a knight whom he mortally hated, in a castle in the territory of Antioch. This castle was named Guillaume’s Rock; and he went to besiege it more for the sake of this knight than for any other reason, because, if he could take him, he would cut off his head, just as he did to Count Reynald—and he would have been justified. For this knight had done him evil in return for the good he had received from him; and you shall hear how.

This knight killed his liege lord together with his lord’s wife, and went to Saladin, to whom he was related as a cousin. Saladin received them kindly and gave them great lands. After the knight had been with Saladin for some time, he became very friendly with one of Saladin’s nephews. One day he asked him to go with him; the nephew went. The knight led him into the Christians’ land and put him in a Templar castle called Safed, in prison.

[Col. 0936D]

He gave the Templars half the ransom that would be obtained for the young man, in order to protect himself against the relatives of the liege lord whom he had killed. This knight was named John Gale.

Here we shall leave Saladin, who went to besiege this knight, and shall speak of King Guy, who was at Tripoli.

## BOOK XXIV BEGINS

[Col. 0937]

### I. King Guy proceeds to Tyre, where he is denied entry. He besieges Acre.

[Col. 0937A]

The king who had been released and absolved was told to go with the queen to remain at Tyre until he had help to besiege Acre; and so he did. When the marquis learned that King Guy and the queen were coming to Tyre, he had his men armed and the gates shut.

When King Guy came near Tyre, he was told that the marquis had ordered the gates closed against him. He went as far as the gate and ordered it opened. The marquis asked who he was who so boldly demanded that the gate be opened. He said that he was King Guy, with the queen his wife, and that he wished to enter his city. The marquis said that it was not theirs, but his, for God had given it to him; he would guard it well, and the king would not set foot within it. They should go elsewhere to lodge.

[Col. 0937B]

When King Guy heard this news, he was greatly grieved. He took a knight and sent him to Tripoli to the knights, commanding them to lead King William’s fleet before Acre, for he wished to besiege it. Then he departed from Tyre with all his people. It was a great marvel that he should besiege Acre with so few men, for there were four men within Acre for every one of his.

When the king came there, he lodged on a hill outside Acre, in the land of Saint Nicholas. There they made good defensive lines, and had water from the river, from which they drank and watered their horses. As they saw ships and galleys arriving, they armed themselves, went out against them, broke up the vessels, carried them into the camp to make barricades, and continually advanced their position.

When the men of Acre saw that the army was growing, they sent a messenger to Saladin, who was besieging Guillaume’s Rock, telling him that King Guy and the Christians had besieged Acre.

[Col. 0937C]

When Saladin heard it, he raised the siege and came to Acre, where he besieged the Christians before Acre. Know that if the Saracens had then attacked the Christians, they could have inflicted great harm upon them; for there were ten Saracens for every Christian. Thus the siege before Acre continued for a year: the men of Acre never ceased going to the Saracen camp, nor did those in the camp cease going into the city.

### II. War between the kings of France and England. Peace between them. King Richard is crowned.

[Col. 0937D]

When the emperor of Germany’s son, who was staying at Antioch, and the Germans learned that the Saracens had besieged Acre, they went toward the siege as far as they could by land; and when land failed them, they went by sea.

The king of France and the king of England were the last to go there because of a war between them. I shall tell you how it began. The king of England had two sons: one was called Richard and was Count of Poitou; the other was called John. Before the king of England went overseas, he wished to have his son John crowned king of England and to give Richard all the land on this side of the sea. When Richard learned this, he was not pleased. He came to the king of France and begged his mercy: “Lord, for God’s sake, do not suffer me to be disinherited, as my father intends to do. I have your own sister, pledged to me, and I ought to have her as my wife. Help me maintain my right and that of your sister.”

[Col. 0938A]

The king summoned his army and marched against the king of England at Le Mans. He captured Le Mans. The king of England fled to Tours; the king of France followed, crossed the Loire, and captured Tours. The king of England fled to Chinon.

When the king of France had taken Tours and Le Mans, they made peace on these terms: Auvergne was surrendered to the king of France.

[Col. 0938B]

Not long afterwards, the king of England died, as people said, of grief. When he was dead, Richard came to the king of France and did homage to him for the land of Calame; and the king restored to him what he had conquered from his father, Tours and Le Mans. Then King Richard crossed into England and was crowned. When he had been crowned and his land was secured, he crossed back and came to Normandy. He and the king of France intended fully to arrange their expedition and the day of departure.

### III. The two kings, having taken the cross, set out for the Holy Land with many other princes and nobles.

When the two kings had met, King Richard said to the king of France: “Lord, I am a young man and have undertaken such a journey as going overseas; therefore I should not need to take a wife. I pray you now to grant me a delay until I return; and I promise you that within forty days after God has brought me back, I shall marry your sister.”

[Col. 0938C]

The king of France granted this. They arranged their expedition so that the king of France would take scrip and staff at Saint-Denis on the feast of Saint John and would go directly by sea to Genoa, from which, with God’s help, he would cross to the Holy Land. King Richard pledged that on that same day he would take scrip and staff at Saint-Martin in Tours and would go, with God’s help, to Marseilles.

At that same time took the cross the Duke of Burgundy, Count Henry of Champagne, Count Theobald of Blois, Count Stephen of Sancerre, the Count of Clermont, the Count of Ponthieu, the Count of Flanders, the Count of Saint-Pol, many other counts whom I do not know how to name, and a great chivalry of France.

[Col. 0938D]

Count Reynald of Dammartin remained, because the king left him with the Archbishop of Reims, his uncle, to guard France. I do not say that all these knights embarked at the port from which the king departed; rather, they sailed from several ports.

The king of France had his provisions and engines loaded at Genoa, and when God gave them fair weather, they departed. King Richard and his barons likewise departed from Marseilles. Some sailed directly to Acre, while others could not pass there and arrived in Sicily. King Philip’s fleet had not gone far by sea when a storm seized it and did the king great damage, for his provisions and engines were thrown into the sea.

[Col. 0939A]

Count Henry of Champagne, who arrived at Acre before any of the others, took the provisions and engines from the king’s ships when they arrived and had them set up against Acre’s walls for the assault. Thus, when the king arrived at Acre, had it not been for the provisions which he had loaded at Messina, he would have lacked those which he had sent ahead. The king did not cross during the winter; after the storm he arrived at Messina.

### IV. The king of France winters at Messina. Dearth at Acre.

When Tancred, king of the land, heard that the king of France had arrived in his realm, he went to meet him, received him gladly, and begged him not to put to sea again, but to remain in his city until March. He placed his land at the king’s disposal. The king agreed to remain. Tancred gave him his own residence at Messina; the king of France lodged there and wintered until March.

[Col. 0939B]

[Col. 0939C]

During this passage, so many people arrived at Acre that they surrounded it completely, from one sea to the other. They made a ditch through the sandy ground outside Acre, by which they diverted the river that ran through Acre itself, taking the fresh water from the Saracens. Within Acre there was no water except salt water and a few cisterns of rainwater. But there was little of it, and it was nothing for so many people as were in the city. The Saracens within Acre were in great distress, for they had lost the fresh water and the route by which food had come to them from the Saracen army, except that they were sometimes aided from a town near Acre called Caiphas.

Saladin had won that town and had vessels loaded with food, which he ventured across the sea; they entered Acre whenever they could.

[Col. 0939D]

At times the dearth in the camp was so great that a muid of wheat sold for fifty bezants, and a muid of flour for sixty. The muid of that country was as much as a porter could carry once upon his back. An egg sold for twenty deniers, a hen for ten sols, and an apple for six deniers. Wine and flesh were so costly that they could not be had at all, except horseflesh when a horse died. Many people died in that camp of hunger and misery.

### V. Christians seeking food in the Saracen army are killed. On the queen’s death, the kingdom passes to Isabella, wife of Humphrey, who is separated from him.

One day as many as two thousand sergeants chose themselves out and told the barons: “For God’s sake, give us food to eat; otherwise we will go and win it from the Saracens.”

[Col. 0940A]

They could endure no more. One morning they left the camp and charged into the Saracen camp. When the Turks saw them coming, they emptied their lodges and let them enter. The Christians loaded themselves with provisions and then began to return, all burdened with them. When the Saracens saw them returning thus laden, they spurred upon them, cut them all to pieces, stripped them afterwards, threw them into the river, and sent them down into the Christians’ camp. Thus this company of sergeants was lost; they never received help from their own camp.

Know that just as the Christians had besieged Acre from one shore to the other, the Saracens besieged the Christians from behind, from one sea to the other. When the Christians assaulted Acre, the Saracens assaulted the Christians from the rear.

[Col. 0940B]

At that time the queen, King Guy’s wife, died in the camp, together with the four children she had; and the land fell to Isabella, wife of Humphrey, who fled when the barons of the land were to crown him.

When Marquis Conrad of Montferrat learned that the kingdom had passed to Isabella and Humphrey, he went to the Bishop of Beauvais, who was in the camp, and begged him for God’s sake to devise a way by which Humphrey might be separated from Isabella his wife and she might be married to him. For Humphrey was so cowardly that he could never hold land.

The bishop said that he would gladly undertake it. He discussed it with the barons of the army and the clergy, setting before them Humphrey’s cowardice. Some agreed to the separation; others said that it could not be done.

[Col. 0940C]

The bishop went to Humphrey and so prevailed upon him that, for money given, he renounced his wife to the marquis. When Humphrey had been separated from Isabella, the marquis married her and took her to Tyre.

### VI. The king of England lands at Palermo. The king of France arrives at Acre. Richard rejects the French king’s sister and marries the daughter of the king of Navarre.

Here we shall stop speaking of the siege of Acre and tell of the king of England, who had departed from Marseilles and put to sea. When he came opposite the island of Sicily, he decided to land there in order to hear news of the king of France and to see his sister, who had been queen of that land. He had his course turned toward shore and arrived at a city called Palermo, at Sicily’s seaward end; Messina lies at the other end toward the mainland, seven days’ journey from it.

[Col. 0940D]

When the king of England had arrived, he asked news of the king of France and was told that he had arrived at Messina and was wintering there. When he heard this, he went to Messina and wintered with the king of France until March.

When the king of France learned that the king of England was coming, he went to meet him, and they rejoiced greatly that they were safe and well. The king of France was lodged in King Tancred’s palace; the king of England lodged on the other side of the city, outside the town, because he did not wish to lodge near the king, lest their men become entangled with one another.

There he fortified a castle upon a hill and named it Mategrifon. He did so in case conflict should arise between his own men and those of King Tancred, so that they might withdraw there. From this later arose great contention, but the king of France made peace between them.

[Col. 0941A]

After this, King Richard asked his sister to sell her dower, take the money, and go with him overseas; when God should bring him back, he would restore her money and marry her richly. She answered that she would gladly do what he wished. Afterwards he married her to the Count of Saint-Gilles, by whom she had a son who became Count of Saint-Gilles.

When peace was made in the land of Aubuiois, King Richard spoke with King Tancred about buying his sister’s dower. Tancred willingly bought it and paid the money.

When March came, the king of France and the king of England had provisions bought; when all was ready, they departed. The king of France went by ships and arrived at Acre before the king of England. King Richard went in galleys, and an adventure happened to him, as you shall hear, which prevented him from coming so quickly to Acre.

[Col. 0941B]

The old queen, his mother, was in Poitou. She heard that her son the king was wintering at Messina; and because she did not wish her son to marry King Philip’s sister, she asked the king of Navarre to send one of his sisters to her son King Richard. She would send the lady to Messina where he was wintering and have him marry her. The king of Navarre was very pleased and sent her. Then the queen prepared for her journey and went by land as far as Messina.

### VII. The king and queen of England come to Cyprus.

[Col. 0941C]

When the queen came to Messina, her son the king had already departed. But Queen Joan, his sister, had not departed and was to leave on the following day. The queen of England said to her: “Fair daughter, take this young lady to your brother the king, and tell him that I command him to marry her.” Joan gladly received her, and the queen returned to Poitou.

Now I shall tell what happened to Queen Joan. When she came near the island of Cyprus, she told the sailors to make land in order to discover whether they might hear news of her brother, the king of England. They turned toward shore and dropped anchor before a city called Limassol.

At that time the emperor of Cyprus was at Limassol with his whole army, so that if those who travelled to and from overseas wished to use force on the island or to plunder, he might be ready to defend it.

[Col. 0941D]

When the emperor saw the ship arrive, he sent a boat to learn what people they were. Those on the ship said that it was the queen of Sicily and wife of the king of England. The boat returned and told the emperor who the people were.

Then the emperor sent two knights to Queen Joan and instructed her to come ashore to refresh herself, promising to give her whatever he could. The queen replied that she would not come ashore. Then she asked them whether they knew if the king of England had passed by. They said that they knew nothing. They returned to the emperor and told him that she would not come ashore.

When he heard this, he had four galleys armed in order, if possible, to capture the ship.

[Col. 0942A]

But the queen’s knights saw the galleys being armed and thought it could mean no good. They weighed anchor and withdrew into the open sea. Yet they had not gone far when the king of England came with his galleys. He turned toward the ship to discover what people they were. When he learned that it was his sister’s ship, he entered it.

### VIII. The king of England captures the island of Cyprus. Acre is surrendered to the king of France; peace is made with Saladin.

While they were speaking thus, he saw the maiden and asked who she was. She replied that she was the sister of the king of Navarre, whom her mother was sending to him, with word that on no account should he fail to marry her. Then she told him how the lord of Cyprus had made them weigh anchor. When the king heard this [Col. 0942B], he entered a galley and had all his men land at Limassol. The emperor saw the galleys and learned that the king of England was there. Barefoot, he leapt upon a horse and fled.

When the men of the host saw that their lord was fleeing, each thought how to escape. The king landed and took the city, together with everything that had remained in the emperor’s camp. There he gained many horses and beasts, and great wealth. When the king had taken the city, he had his sister disembark, and then had the maiden brought to a church, where the king married her. He stayed there for some time.

King Guy, who was at Acre, when he learned that the king of England was coming, entered a galley, went to meet him, and found him at Limassol. They rejoiced greatly together. [Col. 0942C] Afterwards they arranged that King Guy should conduct the king of England’s fleet to a harbour near a city called Nicosia, which lies in the middle of Cyprus, so that, should the king need his fleet, it might be near him; for he intended to pursue the emperor by land. Thus King Guy went by sea, and the king of England by land. The latter pursued the emperor until he besieged him in a castle and took him, his wife, and a daughter whom he had; he also captured barons of the land and great wealth that was in the castle, for all the island’s treasure had been brought there because the castle was strong.

When King Richard had taken the island and the emperor, he entrusted it to the Templars to guard and wished to give it to them. They said that they would not take it, but would guard it. Then the king went [Col. 0942D] overseas, taking the emperor, his wife, and his daughter with him. He arrived at Acre.

The king of France learned that the king of England was coming and had married a wife, and was greatly displeased. Yet he nevertheless went to meet him, and showed such great courtesy that he dismounted from his horse, took King Richard’s wife in his arms, and led her from the boat to land, as the story relates.

After King Richard had arrived, he and the king of France attacked Acre every day. In one assault the French forced their way between two walls. There the marshal of France was killed. The siege had already lasted more than a year, and the Turks were greatly distressed and weakened in men and provisions. They sent word to Saladin that he should devise some means by which they might be delivered, for they could no longer hold out. Saladin knew well that they were in great distress, and it grieved him deeply. He asked the two kings for a truce while he spoke with those inside, and for a day of peace. During this truce peace was made, as I shall tell you.

Saladin surrendered Acre to the king of France, and was to restore to him the Holy Cross; for every Saracen within the city, one Christian was to be returned, while a specified ransom was to be paid for the emirs and high-ranking men within. He set a date for bringing the Cross and producing the ransom. When the peace had been arranged, the Christians entered Acre and put the Saracens in prison. The king of France received the castle of Acre and had it provisioned, while the king of England lodged in the house of the Temple. Thus Acre was taken and surrendered in the year of the Incarnation [Col. 0943B] of Our Lord 1191.

## IX. After Acre Has Been Taken, Each Person Is Restored to His Former Inheritance

The burgesses of Acre and those who had held inheritances there before the Saracens took it went to claim their inheritances and wished to possess them. But the mercenary knights who had taken them said that they would return nothing, because they did not know these claimants and had conquered the properties from the Saracens.

The burgesses of Acre came to the king of France and begged him for mercy, that they should not be disinherited. They said that they had neither mortgaged nor sold their inheritances, but that the Saracens had taken them away; and since God had restored the city to the Christians, it did not seem right to them [Col. 0943C] that they should lose them. They begged him, for God’s sake, to provide a remedy.

The king said that he would gladly do so. He summoned the king of England and the barons of the host. When they had come, the king told them that the burgesses of Acre had asked them to devise a means of recovering their inheritances. Then he said that he had not come into the land to acquire houses or inheritances, but to aid the land and place it in Christian hands; and it seemed right to him that, since they had conquered the land, those who had held inheritances there ought not rightly to lose them. Such was his counsel.

They all agreed and said that it was right to do so. There the two kings and all the others granted that whoever could prove by good witnesses [Col. 0943D] that an inheritance had been his should have it restored to him. They further arranged that the knights who had taken houses within Acre should live together in the house with those to whom the inheritances belonged, for as long as the knights wished to remain there.

## X. Saladin Refuses to Restore the Holy Cross and Pay the Ransom for the Emirs. The King of France Falls Ill and Returns to France. King Richard Marches toward Jerusalem

When the day came on which Saladin was to deliver the Holy Cross to the king and pay the ransom for his emirs who were inside Acre, he sent word to the king of France that he should grant him another day, for he had not yet prepared what he was bound to deliver. The king [Col. 0944A] granted it to him.

When the second day came, Saladin did not deliver it, but asked him to grant another day. The king was angered that Saladin was deceiving him in this manner. He set him a day on the condition that, if he did not deliver what he owed, he would have the heads cut off all the Saracens who were in Acre. When the day came, Saladin did not deliver it. Then the king had the Saracens taken, except for the emirs, led out of Acre, and beheaded.

He kept the emirs because the war was not yet ended, and because, if a high-ranking man were captured, one could be exchanged for another. Of these emirs who were detained, the king of France had one half and the king of England the other.

When Saladin had surrendered Acre, he withdrew into his own land. He sent to the city of Ascalon, which he had conquered from the Christians, and had it demolished because he feared that the Christians might come to besiege it. Not long after this Count Philip of Flanders died, and King Philip of France fell seriously ill. But as soon as he began to recover, he had a galley prepared, entered it, and returned safely to France.

He left the duke of Burgundy in his place, together with his resources and men. Some people said that, when Count Philip died, he summoned the king and told him to go away because his death had been sworn. Others said that he had returned because the county of Flanders had fallen to him, which he had given to his niece in marriage, and because he [Col. 0944C] feared that the count of Hainaut would seize it.

Here we shall leave the king, who arrived safely and came by Rome to see the pope. We shall speak of the king of England and the barons who remained at Acre. King Richard was informed that the Saracens had evacuated Jerusalem and that he could readily have the city if he went there without bowshot or lances. He informed the duke of Burgundy and the barons of the host. They resolved to go and to provision Acre well.

They loaded ships with provisions and sent them to Jaffa. From there they came and encamped five miles from Jerusalem, at a town called Batenuble. There they arranged their battle formations and determined who should command the vanguard and the rearguard. King Richard formed the vanguard and the duke of Burgundy the rearguard.

## XI. The Duke of Burgundy, with the French Barons, Returns to Acre. Saladin Besieges Jaffa. King Richard Recovers the Castle of Jaffa and Avoids Saladin’s Ambushes

[Col. 0944D]

When the battle formations had been arranged, each man went to his lodging. Then the duke of Burgundy thought deeply; and, after reflection, he summoned the barons of France and said to them:

> “Lords, you know that our lord the king of France has returned, that the whole flower of his kingdom has remained here, and that the king of England has but few men compared with us. If we go to Jerusalem and take the city, men will not say that we have taken it; rather, they will say that the king of England has taken it. This will be a great shame and reproach to France. Men will say [Col. 0945A] that King Philip fled and King Richard took Jerusalem; and France will never cease to be reproached for it.”

Many agreed to do as he wished, though some did not. The duke of Burgundy had the French armed and returned toward Acre. Some of the barons, who loved the king of England, informed him that the French were returning to Acre. When the king heard this, he returned to Jaffa, provisioned it well with men and food, and then came to Acre after the duke of Burgundy.

Not long afterward the duke died. Saladin then gathered his host and went to besiege Jaffa. When those in Jaffa were besieged, they sent to King Richard, asking him to relieve them, for they could not hold out against so great a host. When King Richard [Col. 0945B] heard this, he informed the French barons that Jaffa was besieged and asked whether they would go with him. They replied that, wherever holy Christendom needed their aid, they agreed to go.

They arranged their battle formations and set out to relieve Jaffa. King Richard told the French barons to proceed safely by land, while he would go by sea, so as to reach the castle more quickly until they arrived. The king had his galleys armed; he and his men entered them and travelled day and night until they reached Jaffa.

When they came before Jaffa, the castle had already been taken and the Saracens were binding the Christians to lead them into the camp. When King Richard learned that the castle had been [Col. 0945C] taken, he landed, hung his shield about his neck, and took a Danish axe in his hand. He recovered the castle and killed the Saracens within; then he pursued those outside as far as the camp. He and his men halted on a hill before the camp.

Saladin asked his men why they were fleeing. They replied that the king of England had arrived at Jaffa, had killed and captured many of their men, and had rescued the castle. Saladin asked where he was. They answered:

> “Lord, see him there upon that hill, entirely on foot with his men.”

“How,” said Saladin, “is a king on foot among his men? He has no fear.”

Then Saladin sent him a horse and instructed the messenger to tell him that such a man as he ought not to be on foot among his men in so great a danger. The sergeant carried out [Col. 0945D] his lord’s command. He came to the king and presented him with the horse on Saladin’s behalf. The king thanked him for it. Then he had one of his own sergeants mount the horse and spur it in front of him. When that man had spurred the horse and thought to turn back, he never could do so: the horse carried him off against his will into the Saracens’ camp.

## XII. Saladin Raises the Siege of Jaffa and Fights the Christians. The King of England Takes Ascalon

Saladin was greatly ashamed by this. He had another horse made ready. King Richard returned to Jaffa. Saladin did not break camp that day, but remained until the next.

Because of the prowess which King Richard displayed there and elsewhere, especially at the castle of Darum, which he took from the Saracens, he was greatly feared throughout all pagan lands. It sometimes happened, as the story says, that when Saracen children cried, people said to them, “Be quiet, for the king of England!” And when a Saracen rode a restive horse, and the horse saw its own shadow and drew back, the Saracen spurred it and said: “Do you think King Richard is hidden in this bush, or in whatever it is that the horse fears?”

When Saladin learned that the Christians were coming to Jaffa by land, he raised the siege and went to meet them. He encountered them before the castle of Arsuf. There they joined battle and fought. The Christians suffered greater losses than the Saracens, but nevertheless departed without defeat and went to Jaffa, where King [Col. 0946B] Richard was. In that encounter the good knight James of Avesnes was killed.

Then it happened that a Saracen caravan came from Egypt and was travelling to Damascus. It had heard that Saladin was at Jaffa and therefore travelled more confidently; it encamped five miles from Jaffa. King Richard was informed that there was a rich caravan and that he could gain great wealth if he captured it. The king had his men armed, captured it, and brought it to Jaffa.

Afterwards he assembled the barons of the host and said that he wished to go and fortify Ascalon, for if it were fortified, the land would be greatly strengthened. They went there, took Ascalon, and provisioned it well. They also took two castles nearby, Gadres and Darum. [Col. 0946C] The king of England and the barons remained there, because that region was healthier than elsewhere.

Here we shall cease speaking of the land overseas and speak of the island of Cyprus.

## XIII. The Greeks Are Slain by the Latins. Richard Sells the Island of Cyprus to King Guy

It happened that the Greeks assembled and resolved to attack and kill the Latins who were with the Templars, to whom King Richard had entrusted the island. The Latins were informed that the Greeks were gathering to kill them; they were advised to send for aid and to place themselves in a fortress until relief arrived.

All assembled and came to Nicosia, where they entered the castle. There were no more than one hundred Latins inside. [Col. 0946D] Yet so many Greeks gathered round about that no one could count them.

The Latins were inside the castle. On the eve of Easter they assembled and saw plainly that they had no power to hold the castle and were not strong enough against so many men. They said among themselves that it would be better to die by arms than by hunger. They resolved to go out and hazard body and soul. On the following day they confessed and received communion; then they armed themselves and went out. Ten of the weaker men remained inside to open the gate if necessary.

Then the Latins emerged and struck among the Greeks as among sheep, for the Greeks defended themselves no more than sheep would have done. The Latins killed so many that it was marvellous, for they did not cease killing and pursuing throughout the whole day, until they had emptied the city, leaving neither man nor woman. On the following day they found the whole city full of provisions and wealth, and carried everything into the castle. [Col. 0947A]

Afterwards they informed the king of England and the master of the Temple what they had done. The Templars then told the king that he should do with the island as he pleased, because they could no longer guard it. When King Guy, who possessed no land, learned that the Templars had surrendered the island of Cyprus, he came to the king of England and, on the master of the Temple’s advice, bought it. The king of England sold it to him.

Now I shall tell what King Guy did when he had bought the island. He sent messengers into Armenia and Antioch and to other places, and summoned men of those regions who wished to come to the island, promising them lands and fiefs in great abundance. [Col. 0947B]

## XIV. Guy, King of Cyprus, Is Succeeded by His Brother Aimery

The knights who had been disinherited and whose lands the Saracens had taken, as well as maidens and widowed ladies, went there. King Guy gave them land in great abundance, married off the orphan girls, and gave them great wealth, until he enfeoffed three hundred knights in the land and two hundred mounted sergeants, besides the burgesses, to whom he gave much land and great endowments.

After giving so much, he had not enough left to maintain twenty household knights. Thus King Guy populated the island of Cyprus; and, when he had populated it in this way, he did not live long thereafter. The land fell to his brother, Constable Aimery.

Aimery saw that he had little land, and that the lands which his brother King Guy had given for a thousand bezants were worth twice that amount, because each recipient had taken as much as he wished. He summoned all the knights of the land and said to them:

> “Lords, my brother King Guy gave you so much that nothing remained to him. The land has fallen to me, and I am its lord, so long as God pleases. You are my men, but I have no land. There are some among you who possess more than I do. How shall I be poor while you are powerful and rich, and have nothing to spend? That is not fitting. Take counsel among yourselves and let each return to me enough that I may be among you as lord, and may aid you as my [Col. 0947D] men.”

They took counsel, and each gave him from his land whatever came to his heart. Constable Aimery did so much, by force as well as by affection, that when he died the lands of Cyprus were worth to him two hundred thousand bezants.

When the island fell to Count Aimery, he would not wear a crown until he received it from the high prince from whom he held the island. Here we shall leave the island of Cyprus and speak of the land overseas.

## XV. The Marquis, Having Plundered Ships of the Assassins, Is Murdered—Believed to Be at the King of England’s Instigation. Henry, Count of Champagne, Marries His Wife

One day a merchant ship from the land of the Assassins arrived at Tyre. The marquis needed money, so he sent to the ship and had as much of its goods taken as pleased him. The merchants landed [Col. 0948A] and complained to the marquis that they had been robbed, begging him, for God’s sake, to restore their goods. The marquis replied that they would not recover the goods, but should guard well what remained.

They said that, since he would not restore them, they would complain to their lord. He replied, “By God, do so.” They returned, told their lord, and complained of their loss.

When the lord of the Assassins heard this, he ordered the marquis to return his men’s goods. The marquis sent word that he would not return them. A second time the lord of the Assassins sent word that he should restore the goods of his people and should know well that, if he did not restore them, he would harm him for it. The marquis said that he would not return them.

Then the lord of the Assassins ordered two of his men to go to [Col. 0948B] Tyre and kill the marquis. They went there. When they came to Tyre, they became Christians. One remained near the marquis, and the other near Balian of Ibelin, who had Queen Maria as his wife and was then living at Tyre.

One day the marchioness had gone to the baths. The marquis would not eat until she returned. Thinking that she stayed too long, he grew hungry. He mounted with two knights and went to the lodging of the bishop of Beauvais to eat with him. When he arrived, the bishop had already eaten, so he returned.

As he entered a narrow street near the exchange, one man rose from one side of the street and another from the other side. When he came opposite [Col. 0948C] these two men, they stood against him. One held out a letter to him; the marquis took it. The other drew a knife and struck him through the body, and he fell dead. Thus those of the land testify that he was killed.

People said that the king of England had caused this to be done by Assassins, and that he had also sent someone into France to have King Philip killed—though perhaps this was not truly so. King Philip was informed that the king of England had done this. He was greatly afraid and guarded himself closely; for a long time he allowed no one to come before him unless he knew him well.

At the time when the marquis was killed, the king of England was at Acre. When he learned that the marquis had been killed, he mounted at once and came to Tyre, bringing with him Count Henry of Champagne, [Col. 0948D] his nephew. Thus many people suspected him of complicity in the marquis’s death, because the marquis was killed on Tuesday and he had the marquis’s wife married to Count Henry of Champagne on the Thursday following.

## XVI. Richard, Having Demolished Ascalon and Two Castles, Makes a Truce with Saladin and Returns Home

When Count Henry departed from Champagne, he was lord and ruler of the county of Champagne. He left it in his mother’s care. As long as she lived, she sent him the revenues of the land and paid the debts there which he incurred at Acre with merchants coming from Champagne. Thus Count Henry held the land as long as [Col. 0949A] he lived, at which many people greatly marvelled, since his heirs were disinherited of the land and county.

There remained to the countess a son and a daughter. The daughter was married to Count Baldwin of Flanders, who later became emperor of Constantinople. After the death of Count Henry and then of his mother the countess, King Philip made the young man a knight and gave him the county. His name was Theobald, and he married a sister of the queen of Navarre and sister of the queen of England, King Richard’s wife.

King Richard had given a wife to his nephew, the count of Champagne. He saw that the knights and pilgrims were returning to their own countries and that few people remained in the land. He told Count Henry that he would make a truce with the Saracens and return to his own country, where he would raise [Col. 0949B] great forces and great wealth to assist and relieve him when the truce should end.

The count said that, since he wished to do this, it would please him; but, for God’s sake, he should not forget him, since he saw plainly in what condition he was leaving him in the country. Since Count Henry was remaining in the land, it would fall to him to request the truce. He requested it from Saladin.

Saladin knew well that the king of England and the pilgrims who were there were returning to their own countries, and that this was why the count sought a truce. He sent him word that he would grant no truce unless the king had Ascalon, Gades, and Darum, which he had fortified, demolished.

When the king heard that his nephew’s land would be diminished by so much valuable territory as that of Ascalon, he said to Count Henry:

> “Fair nephew, I can remain no longer in this country. Yet I shall not refrain from departing because Ascalon must be demolished. I shall have it demolished in order to obtain a truce; and, with God’s help, if I have life and health, I shall return with so many men that I shall recover Ascalon and all the land, and you shall wear a crown in Jerusalem.”

Thus the truce was made, and Gadres, Darum, and Ascalon were demolished.

When the truce had been made, Saladin took pity on the high-ranking men of the land who had been disinherited and still lived. He gave the lord of Sidon a good town four miles from Tyre, called Sarepta; and he gave Balian of Ibelin, the baron of Queen Maria, a castle five miles from Acre with the land belonging to it. The castle was called Laqueimont. To the lord of Haifa [Col. 0949D] he restored Haifa; to the lord of Caesarea he restored Caesarea; to the lord of Arsuf he restored Arsuf and its dependencies; and to Count Henry he gave Jaffa.

Count Henry afterwards had three daughters by his wife. He arranged marriages for all three with the three sons of Constable Aimery, lord of Cyprus: the eldest to the eldest when they should be of age. Therefore the eldest said to the eldest that, if one of them died, he should not lose his right, so that the eldest should have the eldest. He gave Jaffa to the king of Cyprus together with his daughters.

He could give them no more land, because his wife had a daughter by the marquis, who later became queen, as you shall hear. The lord of Cyprus received Jaffa, provisioned it with knights, sergeants, and food, and held it.

## XVII. Richard Travels in Disguise and Is Taken by the Duke of Austria

[Col. 0950A]

When the king of England had made a truce with the Saracens, he had his ships prepared and his galleys loaded with provisions and men. He placed aboard his wife, the wife of the emperor of Cyprus, who had died in his prison, their daughter, and his own men.

Then he said to the master of the Temple:

> “Master, I know well that I am not loved by everyone. If I cross the sea and people know why, I shall arrive nowhere without being either killed or captured. Therefore I ask you to lend me some of your knight-brothers and sergeants, who will come with me in a galley. When we are there, they shall conduct me as though I were a Templar brother, as far as my own country.”

Indeed, the king had committed an outrage against certain Templars before Acre when he arrived, especially against the duke of Austria; it is not necessary for the book to relate this. The master [Col. 0950B] told him that he would gladly do so. He had knights and sergeants quietly prepared, and they entered a galley.

The king took leave of Count Henry, the Templars, and those of the land, and entered a ship. In the evening he entered the Templars’ galley and took leave of his wife and household. Thus they went, one party one way and the other another.

The king could not conceal his business so secretly that the man who entered the galley in order to have him captured was not prepared; he travelled with him until they had arrived and beyond. They reached a harbour at the entrance to Germany, on the side of the Greek sea.

When [Col. 0950C] the king and the Templars had arrived, they sought mounts, mounted them, and travelled through Germany until they lodged in one of the duke of Austria’s castles in Germany. It happened that the duke was then staying in that castle. When the man who was with the king of England in order to have him captured learned that the duke was in the castle, he came to him and said:

> “Lord, now do well: the king of England is lodged in that town; see that he does not escape you.”

The duke was very glad of this news, because some people said that the king had affronted him before Acre. He commanded that all the gates of the castle be shut, that his men arm themselves, and he himself went to the lodging where the king was staying. [Col. 0950D] He brought with him the man who had brought this news so that he might identify him.

The king was informed that men were coming into the house to capture him. He was taken by surprise and did not know what to do. He therefore took a poor coat, entered the kitchen, and sat by the fire to turn the capons. I do not say that this is true, but some people say so.

The duke’s men entered the house and searched here and there, finding only Templars and those preparing food in the kitchen. The man whom the king had accused entered the kitchen and saw, as the story relates, who was turning the capons. He said to the knights, “See, here he is; seize him.” They took him, and he remained in the duke’s prison until he was ransomed.

## XVIII. King Philip Invades England’s Lands; Richard, Having Promised a Ransom, Is Set Free

[Col. 0951A]

When King Philip heard that the king of England had crossed the sea and had been detained in Germany, because of the disgrace Richard had done him concerning his sister—whom he had betrothed to marry when he returned, but had taken another woman instead—he summoned his host and entered Richard’s land. He took Gisors and other castles, burned part of his land, and captured the count of Chester, who was guardian of Normandy.

At the time when King Richard was captured, Henry, son of Emperor Frederick, was in Germany; Frederick had left him to guard his land. After the king of England had been in prison a long time, [Col. 0951B] he begged the emperor, for God’s sake, to set him to ransom. He would give him whatever he dared demand; and he was more distressed that the king of France was burning and ravaging his land than by his own imprisonment.

The emperor summoned the duke of Austria in order to set a ransom for the king. They set his ransom, by the counsel of King Philip, as the story says, at a great sum: one hundred and sixty thousand marks. The emperor received the larger part of this ransom, the duke the other part, and the king of France received his share in return for allowing the ransom to pass through his land.

The king of England swore to pay the ransom and furnished good hostages. When he was released, the emperor had him conducted through his land. He then entered the sea and went to England. When he was in his own land, he raised his ransom lawfully and sent it [Col. 0951C] to the emperor, who released his sureties.

When his ransom had been paid, he entered the sea, crossed to Normandy, and summoned his host to march against the king of France, if he could, to recover his losses. Thus began the war between the two kings; but I shall say no more of it now.

## XIX. Emperor Henry Becomes King of Sicily

The kingdom of Sicily, Apulia, and Calabria had fallen to Emperor Henry’s wife after her nephew King William died, and Tancred had been made king in that land. When the kingdom fell to him, he had no opportunity to go there, because the greatest lords and barons had gone with his father, along with most of the knighthood.

After his father died and he became emperor, he had enough to do travelling through his land and receiving [Col. 0951D] his homages. When he had received the ransom of the king of England, he assembled men and went to Apulia, leaving his brother, duke of Swabia, as guardian of the land.

Before the emperor died, King Tancred died, and one of his sons had been made king. The king of Sicily heard that the emperor was coming into his land, gathered his host, and went to meet him. They encountered one another before a city called Naples in the Terra di Lavoro; there they fought, and the emperor was defeated.

He remained in the land and summoned men. While he was gathering them in order to enter Apulia and Calabria, the king of Sicily died. When the men of the land had lost their lord, they surrendered Apulia and Calabria to the emperor.

There was a high-ranking man in Sicily who wished to hold the island against the emperor and make one of his nephews king; but he lacked the power, for some people opposed him. When the emperor had secured Apulia and Calabria, he crossed into Sicily and took it. He pursued that high-ranking man who opposed him until he captured him, put him to a cruel death, and had his nephew’s eyes put out. He and his wife wore the crown at Palermo.

When the emperor came into Sicily, he had never had a child. There, as the story says, the empress bore him a son. Yet many people could not believe that she had carried him, because she was of such great age that, in their view, she could not have borne a child. The child was called Frederick.

## XX. Emperor Henry Prepares a Fleet for a Holy Expedition

[Col. 0952B]

When Emperor Henry had conquered his land, he had ships and galleys equipped to send a great force to the land overseas. Throughout Germany he sent out a proclamation that all who wished to go to the land overseas, poor and rich alike, would be provided with passage and provisions if they wished to take them.

Then many people took the cross and went where the emperor was in order to depart. When the Germans and those whom the emperor sent at his own expense had assembled, they were reckoned to include four hundred knights and a great number of foot soldiers. The emperor also sent the chancellor of Germany to be commander of the host and caused all those going to promise that they would obey [Col. 0952C] his will.

The emperor promised them that he would not leave the land in which he was while they were overseas, and that he would send them men and a great abundance of provisions. When the passage and the ships had been prepared, they departed.

At this time the king of Hungary died, and the queen remained a widow without an heir. The land fell to her lord’s brother. She sold her dower for a great sum and went to the land overseas, taking knights and sergeants with her. She travelled in the passage by which the Germans crossed and arrived at Tyre.

Count Henry received her with great honour, as indeed he ought, for she was his mother’s sister; she had been wife to the old king of England, his uncle, and sister to King Philip of France. After she arrived, that lady lived only eight days. Thus this wealth remained to Count Henry, but little of it was left. [Col. 0952D]

### XXI. Emperor Henry. The King of Cyprus is crowned. Death of Saladin. Saladin, son of Saladin, besieges and takes Jaffa by force. The grievous death of Count Henry.

Of the Germans who crossed over, one part arrived at Acre and the other in Cyprus. The chancellor was with those who arrived in Cyprus. When the King of Cyprus learned that the chancellor had arrived on the island, he went to meet him, did him great honour, and told him that, since he stood in the emperor’s place, he wished him to crown him; for he wished to hold his land from the emperor. The chancellor said that he would gladly do so, since the king requested it, and he was very pleased. He took some of his Cypriot knights and went with the lord of Cyprus to Nicosia, where he crowned him. Once he had crowned him, he went to the ships, and afterwards arrived with the others at Acre.

Before the Germans arrived, Saladin had died. He had apportioned what he had conquered and given it where he wished. But to the brother who had helped him conquer it he gave nothing; rather, this brother went with his nephew into Egypt, to whom Saladin had given that land. To his eldest son Saladin gave the kingdom of Damascus and Jerusalem; to another, the kingdom of Aleppo; and to the others he gave enough that he apportioned his possessions among the twelve sons he had.

At the time when Saladin died, there was a high-born lady at Tripoli who had formerly been lady of Gibelet. She negotiated so effectively with the Saracens to whom Saladin had entrusted Gibelet’s defence that they withdrew; and the lady entered it with her knights and provisioned the city and castle.

When the Germans arrived at Acre, the truce made in King Richard’s time was broken because of Saladin’s death. Saladin’s son, lord of Damascus and Jerusalem, assembled his army in order to attack the Christians. He went to besiege Jaffa. This was the son of Saladin to whom the Count of Tripoli had granted leave to pass through his territory into the Christians’ land. When the people of Jaffa were besieged, they sent to Count Henry for help, for he knew well that the castle was not strong.

When the count heard the news, he summoned his army and the Germans and made them set out for Cayhas, four miles from Acre. He told them that he would depart the next day, since he had accounts to settle with his men and affairs to arrange. The army left, and the count remained behind. He settled accounts with his men, and it was evening when he had finished. He ordered the tablecloths laid for supper. He asked to wash, and water was brought to him beside a window high in the tower where he lived. As he washed his hands, he leaned forward and fell out of the window to the ground, and so died.

The servant holding the towel threw himself down after him, because he did not wish people to say that he had pushed him. He was not killed, but his thigh was broken. Some say that, had he not thrown himself down, the count would not have died. The servant, who had fallen between two walls, dragged himself until he came near a postern gate; he heard people passing outside and began to cry out. When they heard the cries, they came there and asked what had happened. He told them, for God’s sake, to bring knights and carry away the count, who lay there dead. The count’s servants and sergeants went there and found him dead. They carried him to the church and buried him.

He had often commanded that the window be barred because of the children, for his heart told him that it would cause harm. Great was the mourning made for the count. Word was sent after the army to return, because the count was dead. The army returned, and the count was buried in the church of the Holy Cross. The Saracens before Jaffa took it by force, demolished the castle, and carried away all the Christians who were within.

### XXII. Death of the Sultan of Egypt. The King of Cyprus is granted the crown of Jerusalem.

[Col. 0954A]

At this time the Sultan of Egypt, Saladin’s son, went hunting one day, fell from his horse, and broke his neck. When his uncle, who possessed no land, saw his nephew dead, he seized the land and fortified it. He sent throughout all pagan lands to seek knights and sergeants, promising them good pay.

When the Sultan of Damascus, who had taken Jaffa, learned that his brother was dead and that his uncle had occupied and fortified the land, he withdrew to Damascus and assembled men, for he knew well that his uncle would disinherit him if he could; and this he did.

When Count Henry had been buried, counsel was taken about making a lord in the land and marrying his wife. There was a high-ranking man in the country, named Hugh of Tiberias, who had been stepson to the Count of Tripoli and had married the sister of that lady. He had a brother called Ralph, and advised that the lady should be married to him, saying that she would be well bestowed upon him. Some agreed; but the Temple and the Hospital opposed it, saying that on their advice she should certainly not be given to him.

“For with all the aid that came to the count from his land of Champagne, he could not maintain the land, and was often in very great poverty and need. How, then, shall we give the land to a man who has nothing, when he who had all the aid from Champagne could not govern it? We shall take counsel and, God willing, give her to such a man as will govern the land.”

They took counsel and agreed that the King of Cyprus wished to marry her; they did not know where she could be better bestowed, nor by what means the land might be more swiftly relieved. They agreed to this, and, on the advice of the Chancellor of Germany, sent for Aimery, King of Cyprus, gave him the lady, and he married her and wore the crown. Then for the first time she became queen.

### XXIII. King Aimery besieges Beirut.

After King Aimery had married the lady, it happened one day, as he was riding outside Tyre with his knights, that two men on horseback came against him to kill him. They did not kill him, but he was severely wounded. They were captured and exiled, and never confessed who had caused them to do this; therefore Hugh of Tiberias was suspected, on account of his brother, who had not obtained Queen Isabella.

He summoned all the knights who possessed revenues within Acre and told them to choose two knights with his bailiffs to guard and collect the revenues of Acre, in order to divide them among themselves and render to each what he ought to have, if possible. For he did not wish to lose or spend his own resources in paying their revenues; rather, he and his knights would live on the revenues of his own land, while they should live on the revenues assigned to them.

Afterwards he took counsel with the Temple, the Hospital, the Chancellor of Germany, and the barons of the land about attacking the Saracens. They advised besieging Beirut. Then they loaded ships with provisions and armed galleys to travel by sea, while the army went by land.

When the Saracens at Beirut learned that the Christians were coming against them, they emptied the castle of women, children, weak persons, and all the slaves who were within, except for a carpenter dwelling there. But they sent his wife and children as hostages into pagan territory, lest he commit some treachery.

When the Saracens learned that the Christians were coming by sea and land, they armed themselves and went to meet them. When the carpenter saw that all the Saracens had left the castle, he came to two Christian slaves who remained and said to them: “Now act bravely: if you will believe me, the castle is taken.” They told him they would help him.

They went to the castle gate. The carpenter made one of the slaves climb onto the gate, so that, if the Saracens returned, he might throw stones and defend himself stoutly. He himself would go up onto the great tower near the gate and help defend it. To the other slave he said that he should go to the other tower over the sea, climb it, make the sign of the cross when he saw the ships nearby, and cry, “God help us and the Holy Sepulchre!” Then he should come down and open the gate for those entering.

### XXIV. He takes the city.

After arranging this, each went to his assigned place. The Saracens had left the castle and saw that the Christians were rapidly approaching by sea and land. They turned back, intending to enter the castle, but found the gate shut. Those upon the gate and the great tower began to throw stones and cry, “God help us and the Holy Sepulchre!”

The Saracens saw that they had lost the castle, and that, if they remained there, they would be captured and killed, since Christian relief was near. They fled, and the castle remained to the Christians. Thus Beirut was taken.

When the Christians saw the man on the tower crying, “God help us and the Holy Sepulchre,” they wondered what it could mean and thought it might be done by treachery. The man on the tower came down, opened the gate facing the sea, and cried to them to come in safely, for there was no one in the castle, since all the Saracens had fled.

Then as many as ten sergeants armed themselves and went there, entering with great fear. When they came near the land and saw that no one was in the castle, they sent to meet the king, who was coming by land, and told him to come, for the castle had been taken.

### XXV. Aimery enters Beirut. On the emperor’s death, he makes a truce with the sultan.

When those who came by sea had entered the castle, they seized the two slaves and tortured them, so that they would show them where the wealth and treasure had been hidden. The slaves said that they knew nothing of it, and that the Christians acted wrongly and sinfully in torturing them. They tortured them until they died.

Afterwards they came to the main door of the tower and thought to break it down; but it was iron and securely barred inside. The man in the tower told them to move back and strike the door no more, or otherwise, however many of them came, he would kill them, and no one would enter the tower until he saw the king or his messenger.

After the ships had arrived, the king came before Beirut with the whole army. They rejoiced greatly and gave thanks to Jesus Christ for restoring the castle to them in such a manner. When the king was encamped before Beirut and learned that the carpenter was in the great tower and would not come down until he saw the king or his messenger, he sent him a knight and instructed him to come and speak with him safely.

When the carpenter saw the king’s messenger, he came down and went to the king. The king showed him great joy and asked how the Saracens had evacuated the castle. He related how it had happened. Since the castle had been taken through him, the king granted him a large revenue within the castle for himself and his heirs, and secured the release of his wife and children, who were in pagan territory.

Thus God restored these two castles to the Christians, Gibelet and Beirut, which are only five miles apart. The king furnished Beirut with knights and sergeants, for no other garrison was needed: it was well supplied with arms and provisions for five years, except only wine.

It was found written in the castle that the two galleys—of which I told you above—that escaped from Tyre and came to Beirut had caused the loss of more than fourteen thousand men, whom they had captured and sent into pagan territory, besides those whom they had killed. I shall tell you how. Before Beirut is a mountain promontory that projects into the sea. At the foot of that mountain the galleys always lay armed. On the mountain were watchers who constantly watched the sea for vessels coming from Armenia, Antioch, and Tripoli and sailing toward Tyre and Acre. All had to pass that way. When the watchers saw them, they made this known to the galleys, which put out, captured them, and killed all whom they could. Thus these two galleys harmed the Christians as long as Beirut belonged to the Saracens.

After King Aimery had provisioned this castle, he went to the castle of Toron, five miles from Tyre, besieged it, and pressed the siege so hard that those in the castle wished to surrender it, provided their lives were spared. He would not accept it. He had not been there long after they had offered to surrender the castle when a messenger came and said that the Emperor of Germany was dead.

When the chancellor and the Germans heard this, they raised the siege and departed like defeated men, without waiting for one another. They prepared their fleet to cross back over the sea; they loaded their provisions and knights into the ships and departed.

When King Aimery saw that the Germans were leaving, he made a truce with the sultan, who had been Saladin’s brother and had disinherited his nephew. He made it on the same terms as Saladin had made it with Count Henry, respecting the territory he had restored to him between Beirut and Gibelet.

### XXVI. The King of Armenia captures the Prince of Antioch and devastates his land. Count Henry of Champagne makes peace between them. On the death of the Prince of Antioch, the Count of Tripoli succeeds him. He allies himself against the Armenian with the Sultan of Aleppo. The Armenian overcomes Antioch and is crowned king.

[Col. 0957A]

I told you above that I would tell how Armenia first came to have a king, though it had never had one before. Now I shall tell you.

In the time of the Count of Champagne, who was lord of the Christians’ land overseas, the Prince of Antioch summoned the King of Armenia, who was his man, to speak with him at a place he named. The lord of Armenia said that he would not go, because he dared not: on a previous occasion the prince had summoned his brother Rupen, who was lord, and when he went there, the prince had imprisoned him. Since he had done this to his brother, he did not dare go.

The prince sent word that he might come safely, and that he would be no more than one tenth of the prince’s force. The lord of Armenia said that he would go. They fixed a day, and he went, as I shall tell you. He armed two hundred men, knights and sergeants, and placed them in ambush near the place where the conference was to occur. He commanded them that, as soon as they heard a horn, they should come to his aid, for he feared the prince might have him seized.

The lord of Armenia went as one of three to meet the prince, taking with him a servant carrying a horn. He stationed him apart and told him that, if he saw the prince attempt to have him seized, he should immediately sound the horn.

When the lord of Armenia and the prince were together, they spoke together. After they had talked for a while, the prince saw that the lord of Armenia had only two companions, and ordered him seized. His knights took him. When the servant saw his lord being seized, he blew the horn. Those lying in ambush immediately sprang out and rescued their lord. They captured the prince and his knights, carried them away, and imprisoned them.

The lord of Armenia summoned his army to enter the land of Antioch. He entered it, devastated it severely, and captured cities and castles. When the prince saw that the lord of Armenia was thus taking his land and showed him no mercy, he sent a messenger to Count Henry at Acre, begging him to come into the country and help him out of prison; for unless he did so, he would never leave it.

Count Henry prepared for his journey and went to Armenia. When the lord of Armenia learned that the count was coming, he went to meet him, received him with great honour, and was very glad at his arrival. He placed all his land, so far as he could, at the count’s command, except for the Prince of Antioch, whom he held in prison.

After the count had remained some time in the country, he obtained permission to speak with the prince, in order, if possible, to make peace between them. The lord gave him leave to speak with him. The count arranged peace between them both, as you shall hear, and caused the prince to be released from prison.

The peace was this: the prince renounced the homage owed to the King of Armenia and became his man; the land which the lord of Armenia had conquered from him would remain with the latter; and a marriage was arranged between a niece of the King of Armenia—the daughter of his brother Rupen—and the eldest son of the Prince of Antioch. The prince was to give his son as a pledge in exchange for the land, but did not give him.

Afterwards, when this son had married the niece of the King of Armenia, he died before his father, leaving a son. The prince sent the mother and the child to Armenia. The lord of Armenia kept them until the prince was dead, for he wished to keep them because he thought thereby to obtain Antioch and the land outright. For the prince had made all the people of the land swear upon relics that, after his death, they would render Antioch and the land to his grandson; but he had not otherwise invested him with them.

When the prince died, the people of Antioch sent for the Count of Tripoli, who was the prince’s son, asking him to come to Antioch, and they would render it to him. They did render it to him. When the lord of Armenia heard that the prince was dead, he took the child and his mother and came before Antioch, for he thought to enter it. The Count of Tripoli, who was inside, opposed him.

The lord of Armenia sent into his land to summon his army to come before Antioch. The count in Antioch sent to the Sultan of Aleppo, begging him for God’s sake to help him, since the lord of Armenia intended in this way to disinherit him. The sultan replied that whenever he made it known to him, he would assist him, for he did not love the King of Armenia. The sultan faithfully kept this promise; otherwise the count could not have held Antioch against the lord of Armenia.

This war lasted fully seven years. Then Antioch was surrendered to the King of Armenia by treachery.

After the count had made peace between the prince and the King of Armenia, he took leave of them and returned to his own land. But first the lord of Armenia said to Count Henry: “Lord, I have enough land, cities, castles, and great revenues to be a king. The Prince of Antioch is my man. I ask you to crown me.” The count willingly crowned him. Thus Armenia had a king.

### XXVII. Count Henry is honourably received by the Prince of the Assassins.

When the count set out, the King of Armenia gave him great wealth and escorted him until he was beyond his land. The lord of the Assassins heard that Count Henry was in Armenia and sent him a request that, on returning from Armenia, he should come by way of his territory; he would be grateful to him, for he greatly desired to see him.

The count replied that he would gladly go, and did so. When the lord of the Assassins learned that the count was coming, he went to meet him, received him very joyfully and with great honour, and led him through his land and castles until one day they came before a castle. In that castle was a high tower; upon each battlement stood two men dressed entirely in white.

The lord of the Assassins said to him: “Lord, your men would not do for you what mine would do for me.”

“Lord,” he said, “that may well be.”

The lord of the Assassins cried out, and two of his men who stood on the battlements threw themselves down and broke their necks. The count marvelled greatly and said truly that he had no man who would do such a thing for him.

The other said to the count: “Lord, if you wish, I shall make all those whom you see above leap down.”

The count replied, “Certainly not.”

When the count had stayed as long as he pleased in that land of the Old Man, he took leave to depart. The lord of the Assassins gave him an abundance of jewels and escorted him out of his land. At parting he told him that, in return for the honour Count Henry had done him by coming through his land, he assured him of his protection forevermore. If any great man did anything displeasing to him, he need only make it known, and the lord would have him killed.

### XXVIII. Emperor Henry provides for his son before his death.

It happened that Henry I, Emperor of Germany, who was in Sicily and had sent the Germans to the land overseas, died. The empress, his wife, had borne him a son in the year before the emperor died, and had named him Frederick, after his grandfather.

When he was about to die, he summoned two high men of Germany and had them brought before him. He entrusted Apulia and Calabria to one, named Theobald, to guard for his son until he came of age. To the other he entrusted the island of Sicily, his wife, and his son. He commanded his brother Philip, Duke of Swabia, to guard the empire well until his son came of age. Philip did so as long as he lived; but afterwards he was killed, as you shall hear.

### XXIX. The empress dies after having her son crowned.

[Col. 0959C]

When the emperor had thus arranged his realm, he died. Less than a year later the empress died. But before she died, she summoned the archbishops, bishops, and barons of her land to come to her at Messina. When all had assembled, she told them that she wished to crown her son and secure to him the land as its rightful heir. She did not wish to wait until she herself was dead; rather, she wished him to be secured in it and recognized as lord during her lifetime.

The barons said they would take counsel. When they returned from counsel, they said: “Lady, we do not wish him to be crowned, nor will we do homage to him or recognize him as lord; for you are of such an age that we do not believe you could have borne such a child in your womb.”

The lady replied: “Why should I burden my soul and disinherit another person by crowning this child? I would not do so. Since all of you are my men, consider what I ought to do; for I bore this child, he is the emperor’s son, and I shall do it.”

They decided among themselves that she should swear upon relics that he was her son, and she did so. Afterwards they received him as lord and crowned him. Once the lady had secured the child in possession of the land, she had letters drawn up and sent them to the pope, informing him that she left her son and her property in his guardianship. When the lady had thus arranged her affairs, she died.

After she was dead, the pope sent a cardinal to guard the child, and he was taken to Palermo, where they guarded him for a long time. When the empress was dead, the high men of the land could not endure the Germans whom the emperor had left to guard the country. They attacked them to drive them out; but the Germans held out as long as their lord Markward lived. When he died, the Germans evacuated the land.

After they had departed, war began among the high men of Sicily, each wishing to be lord. They made war on one another for a long time, and there was great dearth in the land, so that the fields could not be cultivated. For each said that he wished to possess the land together with the child; and they took so much from one another that the king had nothing. Only two cities in Sicily remained to him, Messina and Palermo.

They took the castle of Palermo from the king. They also conquered from the king a city in Sicily named Saragossa. After the Pisans had taken it, the Genoese besieged it and captured it by force. When the Saracens of Sicily saw the war among the Christians, they gathered together and went into a mountain. There they fortified themselves so strongly that no one could approach them. They raided through the Christians’ land, gaining plunder from them and killing many.

### XXX. Count Walter of Brienne is killed.

There was in Apulia a maiden who had been the daughter of King Tancred. On the counsel of the pope and certain worthy men, she went into Champagne to Count Walter of Brienne and brought it about that he married her. When he had married her, she led him into Apulia, and they went by way of Rome.

Because he had married that lady on his counsel and recommendation, the pope gave him of his own resources, supplied him with men, and commanded him to enter the land of Apulia. The people of the country were very glad, and a great part of them rendered the land to him; indeed, they would all have rendered it, had not Theobald—whom the emperor had entrusted with its guardianship—opposed him.

Theobald had a great force with him, including Count Gauthier, so that Count Walter was encamped before a city. At night, when the count was asleep, Count Gauthier entered the camp secretly with his knights. They went straight to the count’s tent, cut its ropes, brought the tent down upon him, and killed him. When the count was dead, all his men were defeated. Theobald recovered the land from the count’s wife. Walter left a son named Walter, who later became Count of Brienne.

### XXXI. Alliance between the King of England and Baldwin, Count of Flanders, against the King of France.

When the King of England was released from prison, he was deeply grieved over the land he had lost. He summoned his army throughout his land and sent for raiders throughout Provence. He and Count Baldwin of Flanders agreed that neither would cease from war nor make peace without the other until they had restored all their losses: Count Baldwin was to recover all the land which King Philip held, having taken it with his sister in marriage; and the King of England was to recover what King Philip had conquered from him.

The King of England had dealt so effectively with the barons of France that he possessed their hearts, although their persons remained in the service of the king. When the King of England and Count Baldwin had sworn together, Count Baldwin summoned his army and began war from Flanders, while the King of England did so from Normandy.

One day their raiders rode before Beauvais. The bishop and his men came out and pursued them. Some others lying in ambush then emerged and captured them. On another occasion the king was near Gisors with no more than eighty knights. He rode through the land until he came upon an ambush of the King of England’s numerous men, the king himself being with them.

When the French saw that they had rashly fallen into danger and could not leave without shame and loss, they begged their king to return toward Gisors, saying that if he remained there he would be captured, while they would stay and resist as long as they could. By his barons’ counsel the king left them and reached Gisors safely. When the King of England saw the French, he charged them, surrounded them, and captured them all. He believed that he had captured the King of France himself, because a knight wearing the king’s arms was there, as people said.
