The king at Gisors was greatly angered by the knights he had lost and the disgrace that had happened to him. He sent throughout his land, summoned his army, and assembled a great force. Count Baldwin entered the king’s land from Flanders. Aire and Saint-Omer were surrendered to him, and then he went to besiege Arras; but he accomplished nothing there, because a strong chivalric force was inside, sent by the king. Except that, in one assault, a contest was made against one of France’s best knights, named Sir John of Haugert.

Count Baldwin saw that he would accomplish nothing at Arras, raised the siege, rode through the king’s land, and inflicted great damage. One day the Count of Namur, Baldwin’s brother, raided before Arras. The people of Arras came out, captured him, and sent him into France.

When King Philip had assembled his army, he went to meet the King of England, who came against him. When the armies were about to engage, the barons went between them and made a truce.

I had forgotten to say that, after the King of England had returned from overseas and been released from prison, he besieged King Philip at Aumale and took it. There the alliance of the Count of Flanders and the King of England to wage war against the King of France was made.

### XXXII. The King of England is killed by an arrow in the district of Limoges. Otto becomes emperor.

After the King of England had made a truce with the King of France, he was informed, as people said, that one of his men, lord of a castle, had found a great treasure of gold in the ground. The King of England ordered him to send the treasure that he had found in the king’s land; if he did not, the king would besiege him in his castle.

The knight replied that he had none of the king’s property and would send him nothing. The King of England went there and besieged the castle. This castle lies in the land of Limoges. When the king was before it, he told the knight to surrender it, and that, if he did not surrender it, he should know that the king would take it.

While he was threatening him, a crossbowman in the castle cocked a crossbow, shot at him, and struck him through the body. The king put his hand to the bolt and pulled it out; not long afterwards he died. Thus the King of England died, as people say.

Before the King of England died, he had with him a nephew, the son of his sister and of the Duke of Soissons. He had brought him with him from Germany when he had left prison and had made him Count of Poitiers. His name was Otto. During his lifetime the king heard that Emperor Henry had died, and told Otto, his nephew, to go to Germany. He said that he would exert such influence with the pope that Otto would become emperor.

Otto went to Germany. King Richard sent to the pope and the barons of Germany, promised and gave so much that he obtained their consent to make his nephew Otto emperor, except for the Duke of Swabia, who opposed him. This duke had been brother to the deceased Emperor Henry, and declared that there would be no emperor while he lived except his nephew Frederick, who was in Sicily and ought to become emperor, and for whom he guarded the land.

For a long time he maintained the empire in this way against the pope and against those Germans. At last, one day, a knight cut off his head in his own chamber. When the Duke of Swabia was dead, Otto was made emperor.

### XXXIII. Many barons of France take the cross.

[Col. 0962C]

Before I tell you more about Otto—how he became emperor and what end he met—I shall tell you what the Count of Flanders and the French barons who had opposed the king did. They proclaimed a tournament on and beside the Somme, and all went there. When they were all armed on one side and the other for the tournament and were about to engage, they took off their helmets, ran to the crosses, and took the cross to go overseas.

Some said that they took the cross through fear that the King of France might oppress them because they had opposed him. At this gathering Count Baldwin of Flanders took the cross; so did Henry of Anjou, his brother; Count Theobald of Champagne; Count Louis of Blois; the Count of Perche; the Count of Saint-Pol; Count Simon of Montfort; John of Nesle; Enguerrand of Boves and his three brothers; Count Renaut of Dampierre; and many other barons and great knights. Those who took the cross beyond the mountains were estimated at a thousand knights or more.

### XXXIV. Concerning Fulk of Neuilly.

Before the barons took the cross, there was in France a priest named Fulk of Neuilly, who preached the cross and induced many knights and other people to take the cross. Great wealth was collected and given to him to spend in the land overseas. But he did not carry it there, for he died.

Before the expedition moved, some said that he died of grief because of the wealth entrusted to him which had been concealed from him. Nevertheless, the greater part of his money was at Cîteaux; but it may well be that he had entrusted some of it elsewhere and that this had been kept concealed from him.

The wealth entrusted at Cîteaux was carried to the land overseas, and never did such a great sum do so much good in that land as this did. For the Crolles [reading uncertain] had been there, and all the walls of Tyre, Acre, and Beirut had been broken down; all were rebuilt with this money.

### XXXV. Those who took the cross depart from France by different routes, and all are captured by the sultan.

The French barons who had taken the cross conferred together and resolved to procure a fleet for themselves. Their counsel advised them to send to Venice [Col. 0963B] and have Venetians come to make an agreement with them for that fleet. When the Venetians heard this, they were greatly pleased, and sent some of their wisest men into France to make an agreement with the barons.

When the Venetians were in France, the barons assembled at Corbie. There the agreement was made: ships and galleys were to be in the crusaders’ service for two years, wherever they wished to be conveyed by sea. A great sum of money was involved, together with half the conquests beyond the Land of Promise. There the counts and great men present at that conference swore to uphold the agreements and pay the money. And the Venetians swore upon relics that they would have ready, at the appointed time, ships, galleys, and transports.

[Col. 0963C] When the great men had approved the fleet, they spoke among themselves and said that they would make one of themselves their lord, whom they would obey and who would administer justice over them. They considered Count Theobald of Champagne and made him their lord; then they departed. Not long afterwards Count Theobald died.

The barons assembled again to determine whom they should make their lord. Their counsel advised them to make the Marquis of Montferrat their lord, since he was a crusader and a worthy man. They sent for him, made him their lord, and prepared for their departure.

There were many knights in France who had not been at the court of this expedition and did not go there. Some crossed by way of Marseilles, and others by other routes. John of Nesle [Col. 0963D] then embarked, with a great part of the Flemings, and they went by the Straits of Morocco. All the crusaders on this side of the mountains crossed at one port, passed overseas, and arrived at Acre—except those who reached Venice. There were certainly three hundred knights or more, from every land, and very many common people crossed as well.

On this crossing went the Count of Forez, but he did not live long: he died shortly after arriving at Acre. Count Renaut of Dampierre was there. He came to the king and told him that he wished to break the truce, since there were so many men who could wage war effectively against the Saracens. The king replied that he was not so good a man as to break the truce, but would wait for the great men of France, who had gone to Venice.

The count was greatly ashamed that [Col. 0964A] the king had thus spoken to him and would not allow him to break the truce. He spoke abusively to the king. The king was wise: he listened and let him say what he pleased, since he did not wish to cause strife or conflict among the pilgrims.

When the count saw that he could accomplish nothing in the land, he spoke with several knights who had crossed at that time. They took counsel together and said that they would not remain in that land, but would go to Antioch. They travelled until they had left the land of the Christians and came to a Saracen city called Gibel. This city lies between Margat and Laodicea.

When the lord of Laodicea heard that so great a company was going there, he went to meet them, because he had a truce with the Christians, and greeted them. He did them great honour and had them lodged outside the city. [Col. 0964B] Afterwards he had food brought in great abundance for them to buy. He asked where they wished to go. They said that they would go to Antioch.

The lord of the city told them that they could not go to Antioch unless they had safe-conduct from the sultan of Aleppo, through whose land they had to pass. If they wished, he would send to the prince and inform him that a great force of knights and important men was there to aid him, so that he might obtain from the sultan security for their passage through his land.

They said that they would not delay until the messenger returned, but would pass through safely enough, since they were a great company. The Saracen said that they would not act wisely if they went before he had informed the prince; for if they went, not one of them would escape. Nevertheless, they said that they would go.

The Saracen [Col. 0964C] said: “Why do you not believe me? You are not wise. You have an excellent market for provisions here; nowhere will you find such a market.” Yet the Christians made ready and said that they would remain no longer.

When he saw that he could not keep them by entreaty, he said: “Lords, I have a truce with the Christians, and I would not for anything incur blame for what might happen to you. I shall conduct you safely through my land. But know truly that as soon as you leave my land, you will be taken, for men are lying in wait for you.”

They would not believe him and went away; and he conducted them as far as his territory extended. When they had left his land, they came near Laodicea. A great company of Saracens lying [Col. 0964D] in ambush there captured them all, except for one knight who had been taken but escaped during the night. His name was Sohier of Entreseignes. Thus, as you have heard, they were captured through their folly, because they would not heed counsel.

### XXXVI. The Sultan of Egypt prepares to resist the Christians. The Sultan of Aleppo besieges Damascus.

The Sultan of Egypt, who was Saladin’s brother, had seized the land after his nephew’s death and had disinherited another nephew of the land of Damascus and Jerusalem. When he heard that the Christians had prepared their fleet to come into Egypt, he placed a strong garrison in Damascus for the nephew whom he had disinherited, and came into [Col. 0965A] Egypt to take counsel on how he might defend his land against the Christians who were to come there.

When he had arrived, he summoned the bishops and priests of his law and said to them:

“Lords, the Christians have prepared a great fleet to come into this land and, if they can, to take it. You must have horses and arms and be well equipped to defend the land; for I am at war with the Sultan of Aleppo and with my nephews. I cannot have all my men here, but must maintain forces here and there; therefore you must help me.”

They said that they would not bear arms or fight, for their law forbade them to fight, and they would never act against their law. Rather, they would go to their mosques and pray to God that He defend the land. [Col. 0965B] For they ought to do nothing else.

The sultan said to them: “If the Christians came here and took the land from you, what would you do?”

“We shall do what God pleases.”

“Since you cannot fight,” said the sultan, “I shall seek men who will fight for you.”

Then he had a clerk brought before him, summoned the highest-ranking bishop, and asked him how much land he possessed, where it lay, and warned him not to lie. The man told the truth, and the sultan had it written down. Afterwards he called the others one by one and had their holdings recorded. When all had been written down, he had their revenues totalled. He found that they had twice as much revenue in the land as he himself had.

“Lords, you have more land than I, and you will suffer great loss if [Col. 0965C] you lose it. I shall seize your lands and give you your maintenance; from the remainder I shall hire knights and sergeants to defend the land.”

They said: “Lord, God willing, you will not do this—take away the alms which your ancestors have given.”

He said that he did not wish to take them away, for it would be contrary to reason to take or diminish them. Rather, he wished to preserve and protect them to the best of his power. He seized all their revenues and lands and joined them to his own; from his own resources he granted each man maintenance according to what he had possessed.

Afterwards he sent messengers and agents to Venice, giving them great wealth and rich gifts to convey to the doge and Venetians. With these he sent greetings and friendship, saying that, if they could in any way divert the Christians [Col. 0965D] from going into Egypt, he would give them great wealth and extensive privileges at the port of Alexandria.

The messengers came to Venice, accomplished well what they sought there, and returned as quickly as they could.

Meanwhile, while the sultan was in Egypt, the Sultan of Aleppo and Saladin’s disinherited son besieged Damascus with a great army and great force. When the men of Damascus saw themselves besieged, they sent word to the sultan, their lord, asking him to relieve them. When the sultan heard this news, he was greatly angered and went to relieve Damascus with as many men as he could gather.

He came as quickly as he could to Jerusalem. There he assembled his army and all his people at Naples, which is one day’s journey from Acre and five days’ journey from Damascus. There, by his wisdom and ingenuity, [Col. 0966A] he caused the siege of Damascus to be raised; and he never relieved them more closely than this.

### XXXVII. The Venetians refuse to convey the crusaders to the Holy Land unless the latter first help them capture a certain city of Slavonia. On this account the King of Hungary complains to the pope.

The pilgrims who were to embark on the ships at Venice were brought, as they arrived, to an island near Venice called Saint Nicholas, and lodged there. Each great man was assigned his ship and told what he was to pay. Payment was received from each person according to his assessment.

When this had been done, the fleet was not even half paid for according to the agreement. Many of the common people [Col. 0966B] returned to their own country, and many dispersed through the land to seek their subsistence.

When the Venetians had received from the pilgrims the payments assessed upon them, they told their sailors to take them across. But the Venetians said that they would not put to sea until they had received all that had been agreed to them, for they had fully kept their own part of the agreement. The great men wished to give good pledges and promise repayment. The Venetians said that they would do nothing and would not sail until they were paid.

They endured such hardship on the island that summer passed and winter approached. They could not sail because of the cold. The great men were greatly grieved and angered by the wealth they had wasted and lost, and because they could accomplish nothing of what they had intended.

When the Venetians saw them in such distress and sorrow, they were greatly pleased. The doge came to the great men of the host and said that there was nearby a city that had done him great injury and harm. If they would agree to go with the Venetians and help take the city, he would remit the money due to him for the fleet and take them where they were meant to go.

[Col. 0966C] The great men said that they would take counsel with the pilgrims of the host. They discussed it and said that they must either do a thing they ought not to do, or return shamefully homeward. They agreed to do the Venetians’ will and go where the latter wished. When the Venetians heard this, they were greatly pleased.

They had provisions loaded, gathered the pilgrims onto the ships and vessels, went toward the city, landed, and besieged it. This city was called Ladres (elsewhere, Gadres) in Slavonia, and belonged to the King of Hungary.

When the King of Hungary learned that the pilgrims bound overseas had besieged his city and ravaged his land, he was greatly distressed. He sent to the barons and pilgrims of the host, saying that they were doing wrong to ravage his land, since he was a crusader as they were. For God’s sake, he asked them to raise the siege; and, if they wished, he would give them abundantly from his own resources and go overseas with them.

[Col. 0966D] They sent back word that they could not withdraw, since they had sworn aid to the Venetians and would aid them.

Then the King of Hungary sent to the pope, praying, for God’s sake, that he provide a remedy concerning the pilgrims going overseas who were ravaging his land.

### XXXVIII. The pope excommunicates them. Crusaders depart by various routes. They proceed toward Antioch.

When the pope heard this news, he was not pleased. He sent a cardinal there to admonish them to leave the king’s land; if they did not leave, he would excommunicate them. The cardinal went and admonished them, but they would do nothing of the kind; instead, they took the city. The cardinal excommunicated them on the pope’s behalf.

When they had been excommunicated, they assembled and conferred. They sent to the pope, begged his mercy, informed him why they had gone there, and begged him, for God’s sake, to have mercy upon them. This embassy was undertaken by Robert of Boue.

[Col. 0967B] When the cardinal had excommunicated them, he returned. Robert of Boue, after delivering his message on behalf of the pilgrims, did not return to them, but went into Apulia to cross into the land overseas. He crossed and arrived at Acre.

Enguerrand would not remain under excommunication, but went to the King of Hungary and remained with him for a long time. Count Simon of Montfort and his brother Guy likewise went to a port and crossed when the weather was favourable, together with two abbots of Cîteaux: the Abbot of Vaux and the Abbot of Cercanceaux. Stephen of Perche, Renaut of Montmirail, and many other knights crossed overseas.

The others wintered at Gadres after they had taken it and remained there throughout the winter. John of Nesle and the [Col. 0967C] Flemings then embarked. They went through the Straits of Morocco and took a Saracen city, where they made great gains. Having taken the city, they did not wish to remain there, but gave it to the Brothers of the Sword, who fortified it and still hold it. They then went to winter at Marseilles.

Among these Flemings was a knight related to Count Baldwin. He became acquainted with a woman who was in Marseilles, a daughter of the King of Cyprus, and sought her hand in his own country. As she was travelling there, the Count of Saint-Gilles took and married her. When he had kept her as long as he wished, he expelled her from his land. She came to Marseilles, and the count married the sister of the King of Aragon.

The knight of whom I have spoken found her there, won her favour, and married her. He believed [Col. 0967D] that, with the aid of the Count of Flanders, his kinsman, and the Flemings, he would recover the island of Cyprus, which had belonged to her father.

When it was time to cross, John of Nesle and the other pilgrims who had wintered at Marseilles and elsewhere crossed and arrived in the land overseas. When they had arrived, the knight who had married the King of Cyprus’s daughter took some of his friends and Flemings and went before King Aimery. The knight asked him to restore Cyprus to him, since he had married the emperor’s daughter—for that was what she was—and it ought to be hers.

When King Aimery heard this, he regarded him as a fool and commanded him to leave his land, on pain of bodily banishment; if he did not, he would banish him. The knight had no counsel but to leave the land of the King of Cyprus.

[Col. 0968A] In the crossing by which the Flemings travelled, a great many people crossed and arrived in the land overseas; but no military action was undertaken there because there was a truce. One party went to Tripoli, another to Antioch, to the prince who was at war with the King of Armenia. John of Nesle went to remain in Armenia and was with the king at a siege before Antioch; his banners were seen there, as is said.

Those who went into Armenia and Antioch did not go as foolishly as those who had earlier gone there and were captured; rather, they had safe-conduct for their journey.

### XXXIX. The men of Acre intercept a Saracen convoy.

There was an admiral in Egypt who possessed castles in the land of Sajette. He had galleys armed [Col. 0968B] and put to sea, sending them out to make captures during the truce. The galleys came before the island of Cyprus and captured two boats, containing only five men. They did no more harm to the Christians.

King Aimery was informed that Saracen galleys had captured his men off Cyprus. When he heard this, he sent to the sultan, demanding the restoration of his men, who had been captured during the truce. The sultan ordered the admiral to restore them. The admiral said that he would restore none of them. The king said that he would make him pay when he could.

That admiral who had captured the king’s men one day had twenty vessels loaded with wheat, barley, and merchandise, to supply the castle which he possessed in the land of Sajette and to pay its garrisons. For he feared that, when the pilgrims arrived at Acre, they would not remain at Gadres but would besiege it.

[Col. 0968C] When the vessels had been loaded and the weather was favourable, they set out. When they came near Acre, the men of Acre saw that they were passing by and not turning into the harbour. They therefore knew well that they were Saracen ships. They hurried to the ships and galleys, sailed out against them, captured them, and brought them into Acre.

There were more than two hundred Saracen knights in those ships. All this gain of grain and vessels went to the king; it was reckoned that there were fifteen thousand muids of wheat and barley, according to the measure of that land. The gain made in that enterprise was worth sixty thousand bezants.

### XL. King Aimery violates the truce agreed with the Saracens.

[Col. 0968D]

When the king had had the goods unloaded and placed in safety and the Saracens imprisoned, he had Acre’s gates firmly closed and guarded, so that no one could enter or leave. He did not wish the Saracens to be told what he intended to do.

Then he ordered the knights of Acre and those who had arms and horses to provide themselves with supplies, and, as soon as they heard the kettledrums sound, to arm, mount, and follow him. Those in Acre did so willingly, for they greatly desired to go against the Saracens.

That night, when the king had the kettledrums sounded and the knights had eaten, he had them arm; they set out, [Col. 0969A] with many foot-soldiers, and travelled throughout the night. The Templars and Hospitallers—one formed the vanguard and the other the rearguard. At daybreak they entered Saracen territory and spread through the country, collecting booty. They captured many women and children and made great gains.

They returned to Acre. The sultan, who was at Damascus, was told that King Aimery had entered his land, captured his people, and inflicted great damage. When the sultan heard this, he was greatly pleased and said that the king was welcome to take and ravage enough: neither he nor his counsel would hinder him; let each man guard what he had to guard. King Aimery was now indeed repaid for the five men whom the admiral had captured.

When John of Nesle, who was in Armenia, and the other knights heard that the truce had been broken, they went to Acre, where war was being waged against the Saracens. The king often entered their land, bringing back booty and making great gains from them.

[Col. 0969B] On one occasion he went beyond the river, found nothing on this side, and crossed far over it. They gathered booty and made great gains. Then they crossed back over the river and returned, lodging there. On that day there was great fear for them in Acre. For when they had collected the booty and were returning, before they had crossed the river, they caught a pigeon, tied a red thread around its neck, and sent it to Acre.

When the pigeon arrived and was captured, no letter was found on it, only the red thread; and this caused great fear. [Col. 0969C] For they supposed it to be a sign of battle and shed blood.

When the king had crossed to this side of the river, he wrote letters, tied them about another pigeon’s neck, and sent it to Acre, informing them that he was safe and well, that he had crossed the river, and all that he had done. On the following day the king returned safely with all his gains.

### XLI. The king ravages Saracen lands and, finally, when the crusaders depart, makes a truce with them.

One of the sultan’s sons, named Coredin, greatly hated the Christians. He learned that King Aimery was ravaging his father’s land and capturing booty and people, while his father took no measures against it; and he was [Col. 0969D] greatly angered. He gathered a large force and went to lodge eight miles from Acre at the spring of Safforie. Once or twice every day he made raids toward Acre.

When the king saw that the Saracens were lodged so near Acre, he had his tents pitched outside Acre, prepared to move, and kept his knights with him. It often happened, while they were eating in the camp, that Saracen raiders came so near the lodgings that arrows could readily be shot at them.

One day Coredin came with all his people to a place one league from Acre, at a Templar village called Doc. When the king learned that Coredin had come with all his men so near him, he armed himself and all his people who could bear arms, on foot and horseback. They advanced against the Saracens and arranged their battle-lines.

[Col. 0970A] They were so near the Saracens that each side shot at the other. There the king received many requests to charge. He asked them to wait until there was a suitable opportunity, for he sent out scouts to reconnoitre the country, fearing that the Saracens had laid an ambush in order to retreat toward the city.

They remained thus from noon until evening, without either side attacking the other, except for two knights who left their battle-line, charged two Saracens, and unhorsed them; but the foot-soldiers killed the knights. One was from Orléans and was named William Prunel; the other was also named William and was a native of Calabria.

When the scouts returned, they told the king that they had seen nothing and that there was no ambush. He called upon the knights who had asked him to charge, telling them to charge. Yet there was no battle-line bold enough to charge, however much the king urged them; instead, they all remained quiet until night, when the Saracens withdrew. The Christians returned to Acre without doing more.

[Col. 0970B] Those who had been there were held in little esteem by the knights. On the following day illnesses began among them, and on the third day still more; there were so many sick and dead that afterwards, despite all his power, the king could never assemble five hundred knights.

The king had galleys and vessels armed and sent them, with a great company, into the land of Damietta. There they made great gains and returned safely. King Aimery made great gains by sea and land against the Saracens because of the five men whom the Saracens had captured during the truce.

When the crossing-season of September came, most of the knights hired ships and returned home. John of Nesle, Robert of Boue, Count Simon of Montfort, and his brother Guy remained in the land. Guy married the Lady of Sajette. When the king saw that the knights were returning and the land was left empty, [Col. 0970C] he made a truce with the Saracens.

### XLII. A plan for restoring Isaac to the empire of Constantinople.

Now we shall cease speaking of the land overseas until the occasion arises, and shall speak of the counts and pilgrims who were at Gadres, and of the son of the Emperor Isaac. The emperor had sent him into Hungary as a pledge to his brother the king, so that the man who had had his father’s eyes put out might not kill him.

The youth had become a grown young man, and he was advised to go to Gadres and so deal with the pilgrims and Venetians there—by promises and gifts—that they would go with him to Constantinople and help him recover the land of which he had been disinherited. He would give them whatever they might specify.

The Venetians said that they would take counsel. They conferred and their counsel advised them to help him, if he would meet their terms. They came to him and said that they had taken counsel and would aid him if he would grant their request. He told them to state what they would demand.

They stipulated that the Count of Flanders should have one hundred thousand marks, and the marquis one hundred thousand marks. This money was promised to them—for themselves, for him, and for the knights of his land—and [Col. 0971A] the Doge of Venice was to have one hundred thousand marks and the Count of Saint-Pol fifty thousand marks. He also swore that he would repay every pilgrim, rich or poor, what he had paid for the fleet for two years, together with the cost of maintaining it for those two years; that he would ask them for five hundred knights for two years; and that he would provide provisions for the whole host for two years.

The youth swore to observe these terms if they could bring him to Constantinople and enable him to recover the land; and they pledged that they would not fail him, but, with God’s help, would all aid him until he became emperor and recovered the land of Constantinople.

When this had been promised on both sides, the young man went into Hungary to take counsel with his uncle and to win him over to go with the pilgrims. The Venetians had the ships and galleys made ready, provisions loaded, and pilgrims gathered aboard. [Col. 0971B] When the time came, they set out from Gadres and went to the island of Corfu. This island lies between Dyrrachium and Apulia. They waited there for the youth until he arrived; when he had come, they departed and went to Constantinople.

Thus the Venetians had well heeded the sultan’s request, of which I told you before, that they divert the pilgrims so that they did not go to Alexandria.

### XLIII. Emperor Alexius prepares to resist Isaac’s nephew.

When Emperor Alexius of Constantinople heard that his nephew was bringing so great a fleet against him, he was not pleased. He summoned all the great men of his land and told them that his nephew was bringing such a great force against him, and that they must prepare their arms to defend themselves. They promised to aid him as their lord.

When they learned that the Venetians were approaching Constantinople, they raised a chain at the entrance to the harbour, so that ships and vessels could not enter. This chain was more than four bowshots long and as thick as a man’s arm.

One end was at one of the towers of Constantinople; the other was at a place called Parte. At the end of that place stood a tower where one end of the chain coming from Constantinople was fastened. The tower was well garrisoned because the emperor knew that our men would land on that side, and it was fortified in this manner to guard the tower.

[Col. 0971C] This tower was called the Tower of Galata. Saint Paul wrote part of his epistles there.

The French pilgrims travelled until, on a Saturday, they came before Constantinople. They could not enter the harbour, but went to a place beyond the Golden Horn, near the Red Abbey. There the French landed without any opposition from the men of Constantinople.

When the men of the city saw the French, they came to the emperor and said: “Lord, let us go out and prevent them from landing.”

The emperor said that he would not do so. He would let them land and occupy the ground; once they were lodged, he would send out all the prostitutes of Constantinople, have them climb a hill facing the place where the French were lodged, and make them urinate so much that [Col. 0972A] the French would be drowned and die a death so vile.

I do not say this as true, but some people say that the emperor said this in pride.

### XLIV. The French, having landed at Constantinople, attack and take the tower called Golgotha. Alexius sallies from Constantinople against the Latins.

On the next day, after our people had landed on the other side of Constantinople, they attacked the Tower of Galata. The assault was not great, but they took it. They set fire to the wooden structure and defeated the Greeks who had come from Constantinople to relieve the tower. Many were drowned when the chain was broken apart, for they had climbed upon it to flee safely into Constantinople. For when the French had taken the tower, they broke the chain.

[Col. 0972B] When the French had opened the harbour for entry, they brought the ships onward as far as the end of the Castle of Blachernae, which lies at the landward end of Constantinople. One of the emperor’s residences was there, and it was where he most often stayed.

The ships entered near the castle. The knights and pilgrims took up quarters and besieged Constantinople on that side. They made barriers before themselves so that the men of the city could not come out to harm them. They were lodged in a valley near their ships, with behind them, on the mountain, an abbey called Beaumont, which they had fortified.

After they had been there for some time, they arranged their battle-lines so that, if those inside came out to fight them, each man would go to his own division.

Not long afterwards the men of Constantinople came to the emperor and said: “Lord, unless you deliver us from these dogs who have besieged us here, we shall surrender the city to them.”

He said that he would indeed deliver them. He then summoned his knights, ordered them to arm, and had it proclaimed throughout the land that he would fight the Latins. When they were armed, they left Constantinople by a gate called the Roman Gate, a mile from where the Latins were lodged.

[Col. 0972C] When the emperor and all his armed people had left Constantinople, he sent as many as five battle-lines toward the Latin quarters. When the Latins heard that the men of the city were coming out to fight them, they armed and came outside their barriers. They all remained still, and the Greeks remained still on the other side.

### XLV. The Venetians take the city. The French restore the rightful emperor to his throne.

The Venetians who were aboard the ships, without informing the Latins, learned that the emperor and his men had left Constantinople and that the Latins were all armed outside the barriers awaiting battle. They armed themselves, entered boats, took ladders with them, and came to the city walls on the Blachernae side. They raised ladders, entered the city, opened the gates facing the sea, and set fire to the city.

They then sent word to the French that, if they needed knights, the Venetians would send them, for [Col. 0973A] they were in the city and had taken it.

When the emperor saw that the city was burning and the Venetians had taken it, he departed with his knights. The French lodged in the city and restored to possession the man whose eyes had been put out; but he did not live long afterwards. The French crowned the youth who had brought them to Constantinople.

Then they selected a great man of the land, who seemed to them a worthy man, and made him guardian of the land and of the young man, because the latter was young and so that the guardian might obtain the agreements which the youth had promised them.

After this arrangement, the man came and said to them:

“Good lords, you are here in this city with us, and you have chosen me to be guardian of the empire. It seems to me, if you approve among yourselves, that you should leave the city and go to lodge over there at Parte, near the Tower of Galata, where the Greeks were before they were burned out. I shall send you abundant provisions and shall seek and endeavour to ensure that you have the agreements that are owed you.”

[Col. 0973B] The French took counsel and spoke with the Venetians. They agreed, and went to lodge near the Tower of Galata.

This guardian of whom I speak was named Marcofles. When the Latins had taken up quarters and their fleet was near them, Marcofles summoned the Venetians and required them to have in writing the sums that the pilgrims had paid for ships. He was informed of the total amount. He had the money taken and restored to each person what was found recorded in writing. Afterwards he sent each of them wheat, wine, and meat according to his need.

Not long after he had done this, a great conflict arose in Constantinople between Greeks and Latins who had lived there before the fleet came. The Greeks greatly feared that those outside would become involved, and so they set fire to the houses of the Latins. The fire did not cease burning for nine days and nine nights, across the city from one sea to the other.

### XLVI. Marcofles, having killed the emperor, seizes the empire. The French and Venetians capture Constantinople.

Marcofles gained entry into the emperor’s chamber at Blachernae and had him strangled one night; thus the dream which the emperor had dreamed was fulfilled. [Col. 0973D] He had a wild boar fashioned of copper at the Lion’s Mouth, which stood by the sea. The emperor lived there, and dreamed that this boar strangled him. On the following day, out of the fear he felt, he had it broken to pieces; but this availed him nothing: nevertheless he was strangled. When the emperor was dead, Marcofles was informed of it. Marcofles went to Blachernae and had him buried; and when he had buried him, he summoned his knights, went to Saint Sophia, assumed the crown, and became emperor. But before assuming the crown, he had the gates carefully guarded, so that no one could go out or enter, lest the army learn of the emperor’s death or of the conspiracy in the city.

There was a great lord in the city who had been related to the emperor. It seemed to him that he ought rather to be emperor [Col. 0974A] than Marcofles. One day, while Marcofles was at Blachernae, he gathered such men as he could find and went to Saint Sophia. There he seated himself in the chair and assumed the crown. When Marcofles heard of it, he went there with his men and killed him.

When the French and Venetians saw that the city gates were shut, so that no one could come or go, they greatly wondered where the emperor had gone. But they were not allowed inside; rather, they were told that the emperor was ill. This could not remain hidden for long, and all learned how the emperor had died and in what manner Marcofles had become emperor. Not long afterwards Marcofles began to wage war upon the Latins and to restrict their provisions.

[Col. 0974B] I shall tell you what he did one day. He had as many as fourteen ships filled with thorns; and when they had a wind blowing from their direction toward the Latin army, he had fire set within them. The wind carried them straight toward the Latin fleet. But the Venetians, who were well equipped, defended themselves very well against them and against this fire, so that they suffered no damage either in their persons or in their goods.

Our French wintered there until Lent came. Then the men of Venice made bridges from their masts and their ships. They arranged them by such a device that armed men could climb above them; and when they descended, they were above the highest towers facing the sea, at the point where they were to make the assault. Thus they prepared their enterprise and fixed the attack for Palm Sunday. When morning came on the following day, they armed themselves and entered the ships; and God gave them such a favourable wind that it bore them to Constantinople.

The first ship to reach the walls was that of the bishop of Soissons. It immediately drew up beneath a tower below the bridge; Frenchmen and Venetians climbed onto the bridge and took that tower. The first man to enter was a Venetian, and he was killed there. The next was a French knight, named Audin Durebouche. The former gained one hundred marks, and the latter fifty. As soon as this tower was taken, they opened the gates and entered. When the emperor saw that the Latins had entered the city, he fled. Thus Constantinople was taken.

Before [Col. 0974D] the French and Venetians besieged the city, they had agreed that they would take nothing from within a church, and that the goods captured in the city would be gathered together and divided fairly; for the Venetians were to have half of everything. Such had been their covenant when they undertook the expedition: from all conquests, apart from the land of Jerusalem, they were to receive one half wherever it might be.

After they had established this, the three bishops present—the bishop of Soissons, the bishop of Troyes, and a German bishop—excommunicated all who diverted anything, or who did not bring what they found to the place established for division. Afterwards they excommunicated all who took anything within a church, robbed priest or monk, or laid hands upon a woman. Thus the excommunication was ordained.

Before the Latins entered Constantinople and possessed it, they were full of God’s grace and had great charity among themselves: if they saw one hundred Greeks, they would be two Latins.

### XLVII. The Latins plunder Constantinople

When the Latins had taken Constantinople, they had embraced before themselves the shield of God; but as soon as they were inside, they cast it down and embraced the devil’s shield. First they ran to Holy Church and robbed the abbeys. Such greed arose among them that those who ought to have borne love bore it down. Such hatred and [Col. 0975B] rancour arose among them that the knights said the poor people had everything; the poor said that the knights had carried off everything; and the clerks and priests had hidden everything—of which there was clear evidence in one party.

Those who acquired most were the Venetians, who carried goods by night to their ships. After Constantinople had been taken, the doge of Venice wished to make an arrangement with the Latins concerning the wealth in Constantinople: he would have his men gather the goods and set the movable property apart, and would give each knight four hundred marks, each priest and mounted sergeant two hundred marks, and each foot-soldier one hundred marks. He would indeed have done and granted this, but the French would not agree; rather, so much was stolen and diverted before the division [Col. 0975C] with the Venetians that, from the French share, a knight received only twenty marks, a priest or mounted sergeant ten marks, and a foot-soldier five marks.

### XLVIII. Baldwin, Count of Flanders, becomes Emperor of Constantinople

When they had thus divided the wealth, they divided the city, so that the Venetians received one half and the French the other. The Venetian share lay toward the land, and the French share toward the sea. When they had divided both the wealth and the city, they deliberated as to whom they should make emperor and patriarch. They agreed that, if the emperor were chosen from this side of the mountains, those from beyond the mountains would make the patriarch; and that the Venetians would give the emperor the fourth part of the city on the landward side, while the French would give the fourth part near the Lion’s Mouth.

[Col. 0975D] Having thus arranged matters, they chose as emperor Count Baldwin, Count of Flanders, and he assumed the crown. Once crowned, the emperor distributed the lands and islands of the region, giving the Venetians the share which they were to possess. Afterwards, leaving the Venetians and his bailiffs in Constantinople, he went to Salonica in order to take it and give it to the marquis to whom he had granted the kingdom of Salonica.

The marquis went with him and brought the empress, his wife, whom he had married. She had been the wife of Emperor Quirsac [Isaac], the mother of the emperor whom Marcofles had strangled, and sister of the king of Hungary. This lady had a son who afterwards became king of Salonica. Salonica is fully twenty-five days’ journey from Constantinople.

The emperor went from [Col. 0976A] Constantinople to Salonica, and everywhere he came the whole land acknowledged him as lord. When he reached Salonica, it was surrendered to him, and he gave it to the marquis. Afterwards a great territory on the coast toward Apulia was surrendered to him; he gave it to Cape Peneis, which was later held by Geoffrey of Villehardouin. When all this land had been delivered up and he had bestowed it upon those of whom I have told you, he returned to Constantinople.

There came Henry of Anjou, his brother. He gathered men and crossed the arm of Saint George. He went into Turkey and conquered much land. Payen of Orléans, Baldwin of Beauvais, and Peter of Brachuel gathered men with them, crossed the strait, went into Turkey, and conquered much land.

On the other hand, Emperor Baldwin and Count Louis remained in Constantinople. Before Count Baldwin became emperor and had taken Constantinople, because the expedition had lasted longer than they had agreed, he summoned his wife to come to him wherever he might be. When the lady heard the news sent by her lord, she prepared herself, crossed the sea, and arrived at Acre. At this point her lord became emperor. News came to the emperor that his wife was at Acre. He sent knights to bring her to Constantinople. He also sent word into the land overseas and had it proclaimed everywhere that whoever wished to have land or a garrison should come to him.

Fully one hundred knights from the overseas land went there by that route, and as many as ten thousand other people also went. But when they arrived, [Col. 0976C] he would give them nothing. They departed and went to Salonica and wherever else they could do best in the country. The countess of Flanders, who was at Acre, did not live long after she had come to Constantinople.

### XLIX. Conspiracy against the Latins at Adrianople. The Latins besiege Adrianople

Now I shall tell you what the Greeks of Adrianople did. The city of Adrianople belonged to the Venetians, for it had fallen to their share. They treated the inhabitants of the city very badly and did them many outrages. Therefore the citizens sent to the castles and cities near them, begging them for God’s sake to unite and to summon the lord of Blachernae to aid them; they would restore all the land to him, since the Latins treated them too badly.

The cities and castles of that region agreed, and they all gathered at the tower of Adrianople. They sent to the lord of Blachernae to ask for aid. He replied that he would gladly assist them at Easter with a great force. The message had gone fifteen days before the beginning of Lent; and Constantinople is four very long days’ journey from Adrianople.

When the inhabitants of the castles and of Adrianople had the assurance that the Blachernes would aid them, they came to the Venetian garrisons stationed there and ordered them to evacuate the city. If they did not leave, they would kill them; but they might depart [Col. 0977A] in peace before being killed. The garrisons saw that they could not hold out; they went away and proceeded to Constantinople. The same was done to all the garrisons of the castles in that region.

The garrisons sent a messenger to the emperor, informing him that they were coming and that the Greeks had expelled them. The messenger reached Constantinople on Ash Wednesday, just as the emperor was leaving his chapel, where he had heard the service. He delivered his message. When the emperor heard it, he was greatly distressed. He summoned the doge of Venice, Count Louis, and the knights who were in Constantinople. They all came to him and were greatly angered when the emperor told them the news he had heard.

They deliberated and agreed to go and besiege Adrianople, putting everything to the sword, since through Adrianople the whole country had revolted. The emperor commanded that all should be ready to march by Mid-Lent, and that all able to bear arms should go, except those assigned to remain and guard the city. It was done as he commanded. When Mid-Lent came, they marched and laid siege to Adrianople.

They had not been long before Adrianople when the Blachernes and Cumans came near. Every day they rode close to the army and so watched the provisions that they could scarcely be obtained. The Latins also made defensive barriers around the rear, so that the Blachs and Cumans might not break into the camp.

### L. The citizens of Adrianople wish to surrender to Emperor Baldwin, provided the Venetians do not rule them. The Venetians prevent the emperor from making an agreement with them. Blachs and Cumans come to Adrianople’s aid, and kill Count Louis

[Col. 0977C]

When the emperor learned that the lord of Blachernae had brought such a great force against him, he was greatly afraid. He took messengers and sent them to Turkey, to Henry of Anjou his brother, ordering him to come with all the men he had, because the Blachs and Cumans had besieged him before Adrianople. He sent the same message to Payen of Orléans, Baldwin of Beauvais, and Peter of Brachuel, who had another army in Turkey.

When the emperor came before Adrianople, all the townsmen came out to meet [Col. 0977D] him and greeted him well as their lord. They asked why he had come against them and why he had come to besiege the city. They acknowledged him fully as lord and would gladly surrender the city to him if he would govern them justly as his men. But they would not surrender it if he wished to put them under another’s authority; rather, they would let themselves all be cut to pieces, limb by limb. What they had done to the garrisons, they had done in defence of their own persons, because the garrisons had abused their wives and children so greatly that they could endure them no longer. Never, as long as they lived, would Venetians exercise jurisdiction over them.

When the emperor heard this offer from the people of Adrianople, he took counsel. He was advised that, if the doge would take land elsewhere, he should give it to him, provided he left Adrianople in peace. The emperor asked the doge; but the doge answered that he would make no such exchange, for he would avenge the outrage done to himself and his men. He told the emperor to assist him, as he ought, in assaulting the city. The emperor replied that he would not fail him.

The emperor then drew up his men and attacked the city. He sent part of his miners, who undermined one section of the wall, shored it up, and placed the supports so that nothing remained except to set fire to them. When all was prepared, so that nothing remained but to set the fire and enter the city, the emperor summoned the knights of the army for the assault. He ordered some to guard the barriers and others to enter the city, for he did not wish [Col. 0978B] the common people to enter and divert the goods inside. He then commanded and had it proclaimed that, whatever they might see or hear, no one was to leave the barriers.

It was already well toward noon when they had completed these preparations. They dispersed, each going to his lodging. This was done on the Thursday before Easter. Count Louis was seated at dinner. While he ate, the Blachs and Cumans came as far as the barriers, shouting and howling. When Count Louis heard them, he was greatly angered and said: “See, these scoundrels will not let us eat in peace. Go,” he said to one of his squires, “bring me my horse.” To another he said: “Go, tell Stephen of Perche, Robert of Montmirail, and my knights to follow me.”

He asked for a light hauberk, put it on his back, mounted his horse, and rode out beyond the barriers, with his knights and household after him. When the Blachs and Cumans who were at the barriers saw them coming, they began to flee, and he pursued them. When those in the army saw Count Louis ride out, they cried “To arms!” and followed him. When the emperor heard the noise and cry, he asked what it was. He was told that Count Louis had gone out and was pursuing the Cumans. The emperor ordered a horse brought to him, saying that he would go after him and make them turn back. He commanded the marshal of Champagne that no one but knights should follow him, and that he should guard the barriers and the engines against the townsmen, while he himself went after Count Louis to bring him back.

[Col. 0978D] Count Louis pursued the Blachs and Cumans until he fell into their ambush, having already chased them three miles or more. When he saw the ambush, he turned back; but part of those lying in ambush sprang after him, mortally wounded him, and killed those who were with him. More than two hundred of the best knights of the army rode out after the emperor, among whom were Venetians, to rescue Count Louis. When the ambush saw the emperor’s men coming, it withdrew. The emperor went forward and found the count dying. He was greatly grieved and made great lament.

Count Louis said to him: “Lord, do not grieve for me; but, for God’s sake, have mercy upon yourself and upon Christendom. For I am dead. But remain quiet, all of you, and draw your men together; night will soon fall, and then you can go to your lodgings. For I have been at their ambush and have seen them; and know that, if you go farther forward, not one foot will escape.”

The emperor replied: “May God never permit that I should incur reproach, or that it should be said that I left Count Louis dead in the field. Either I shall carry him away, or I shall die there.”

### LI. The emperor attacks the Blachs and Cumans and is killed by them. The siege of Adrianople is raised

The emperor now rode forward, with the knights after him. The Blachs and Cumans sprang from their ambush and surrounded them. There they fought and killed all those of the emperor’s company, the emperor included, except I do not know how many knights and sergeants who escaped and returned to their lodgings.

When the Venetians and those with them saw [Col. 0979B] the battle, they turned back, knowing well that if they advanced they would not survive. It was already early evening when they reached their lodgings. They informed the doge of Venice and the marshal of Champagne of the disaster that had occurred. When they heard it, they quietly raised the siege, left their equipment, and travelled throughout the night toward a city on the coast belonging to the Venetians, named Rodosto.

Some went to Constantinople, but these were few. After travelling all night, when daylight came, they looked out and saw a great body of horsemen in the distance. Thinking they were Blachs, they began to flee toward Rodosto. But the horsemen were the army of Baldwin of Beauvais, Payen of Orléans, and Peter of Brachuel, who were coming to assist the emperor.

Peter of Brachuel first recognized them. He greatly wondered who the fleeing people were and why they fled. Looking closely, he recognized some of the banners and thought they were his own people. He said to his companions: “Come very gently, and I will spur toward them and learn what this is.” He spurred forward and overtook them. Seeing him come alone, they halted. When he reached them, he recognized them, and they recognized him. He asked for their news, and they told him.

When Peter of Brachuel heard the news, he made great lament and summoned his companions. They came to him, and once assembled they went directly [Col. 0979D] to Rodosto. There they remained, waiting to see whether God would send them help from any quarter.

### LII. Henry, hearing of the death of the emperor whose aid he was coming to give, withdraws to Rodosto

After the Blachs had killed the emperor and his knights, and learned that Henry his brother had crossed the arm of Saint George and was coming to Adrianople, they went to meet him, intending to kill him if they could find or reach him. But God would not permit it. Rather, He sent him a countryman of the region to tell him of the deaths of the emperor, Count Louis, and the knights; of the raising of the siege of Adrianople; and that the survivors had gone to Rodosto. He told him that the Blachs were coming against him and, if they found him, would kill him. “Therefore, for God’s sake,” he said, “think how to save yourself and your companions, and do not cease travelling day and night.”

[Col. 0980A] When Henry heard the news of the death of the emperor his brother and of his companions, he was deeply angered and grieved. He was greatly afraid for his own death and for those with him, and did not know what to do. He had brought with him fully thirty thousand Armenian householders, with their wives, children, and equipment, intending to settle them in Constantinople. He had sworn that, whatever happened, he would not abandon them until he had brought them to Constantinople.

Now he did not know what to do. He saw clearly that, if he went away and left them, he would commit a great sin and act contrary to his oath. Therefore he took counsel from the knights of the army concerning what he should do. The knights advised him that it was better to leave this common people to fortune and go to Rodosto, to their own men, so that they might rally there, rather than remain and have themselves killed. For they knew well from what the countryman had said that not one foot would escape. It was better that the Armenians should die than they. For they knew well that, if he were killed, neither Constantinople, Rodosto, nor any part of the land would retain a single foot that was not delivered to the sword.

Henry considered that the knights had given him good advice. He called the countryman and asked whether he could lead them to Rodosto. He replied, “Yes, certainly; but, for God’s sake, hasten your departure.” Henry set out with his knights and the countryman. They travelled for two nights without ever eating, and lost many horses which gave out, so that many had to go [Col. 0980C] on foot. They travelled until they came to Rodosto, where they found their companions who had escaped. When they found themselves assembled there, they were very glad, considering the disaster that had occurred. They made great lament for those who had died.

The Blachs surrounded the Armenians whom Henry had left behind, attacked them, and killed them, with their wives and children, and the Armenians themselves, except for some who escaped and went to Constantinople.

### LIII. Henry, the emperor’s brother, is appointed administrator of the empire, and afterwards emperor after one year

When the news concerning Count Louis and the knights reached Constantinople, and no news was known of the army which had departed from the siege of Adrianople, [Col. 0980D] the people were greatly alarmed and grieved. This was no wonder. Count of Béthune, who had remained in Constantinople, and a cardinal also heard the news. They summoned all the Latins of Constantinople and had them gather in one place to deliberate what should be done. They ordered everyone to be ready to defend himself, should need arise; for at that time there were a hundred Greeks for every Latin in Constantinople, and the whole country was in uproar.

They decided to equip a vessel and send it to Rodosto, searching the coast to learn whether they could hear any news of Henry of Anjou or of the others who had departed from Adrianople. Thus they arranged and sent by sea what they could not send by land. They equipped a vessel and sent it by sea. It was more than eight days after the vessel had found them at Rodosto before the people at Rodosto informed those in Constantinople; indeed, they did not tell them until the vessel returned.

They remained there fully fifteen days and more after arriving at Rodosto, not daring to depart because of the Blachs. When they learned that the Blachs had withdrawn, they left Rodosto and went toward Constantinople. They sent ahead the vessel that had come seeking news of them and informed the city that they were coming.

When they were in Constantinople, they all assembled and deliberated about making a lord in the land. They decided to make Henry, the emperor’s brother, bailiff [Col. 0981B] of the land until they learned whether the emperor was dead or alive. There they did him homage as bailiff. He remained bailiff for more than a year. He had people seek and search, and gave great wealth to monks and other persons to find the emperor; but no news of him could ever be learned, except that one day a man came to him and said that he, together with two other men, had carried off the emperor and taken him into a forest. They had left him there with the two men guarding him. If Henry sent knights and sergeants with him by sea, they would bring him back.

Henry had two galleys equipped and placed knights and sergeants aboard, together with the count of Béthune. He sent them to the forest to which the man led them. This forest was on the Greater Sea. When they reached it, they landed and went to the tree beneath which the man said they had left the emperor. They did not find him there; rather, they found remnants of bread and salt, but did not know who had eaten there. The man swore to them that they had left the emperor beneath the tree with two men. They searched the forest but found nothing. Seeing that they found nothing, they returned to Constantinople.

This is all the news that could ever be learned concerning Emperor Baldwin after he disappeared. I had forgotten to tell you of the count of Saint-Pol, who was at Constantinople: he died a natural death fully fifteen days before the emperor marched to Adrianople.

When Henry had been bailiff of the land for more than a year and no news of Emperor Baldwin could be discovered, [Col. 0981D] the people of the city made him emperor. A part of the land lost around Constantinople was restored to him. Adrianople was likewise restored on the condition that it would have a Greek lord and would not be subject to the lordship of the Venetians or of the Latins. Nevertheless the emperor accepted what was restored to him and gave it to a great lord of the land named Livernas, who afterwards served him well.

This Livernas had as his wife the sister of King Philip of France, who had been the wife of the son of Emperor Manuel, whom Andronikos had caused to be drowned. Emperor Henry made peace with the Blachs and with the lord of Blachernae in order to have the aid of him and his land. He then brought it about that his territory was restored to him as far as Salonica, and he went there. When he arrived, he found that the marquis was dead. There he found one of the marquis’s sons, whom he crowned and made king of Salonica.

Not long after he had stayed there for some time, he died. His knights and men who were with him returned in order to guard Constantinople. They then took messengers and sent them to Count Peter of Auvergne, who was first cousin to King Philip of France and had as his wife the countess of Namur, sister of Emperor Baldwin and Emperor Henry. They ordered him to go with his wife to Constantinople, for the empire had fallen to his wife; they would make him emperor, and the empress would be so entitled.

### LIV. Peter goes to Rome, where the pope crowns him emperor; he proceeds toward Constantinople

[Col. 0982B] When he heard the news, he and his wife set out and went directly to Rome. He brought knights and sergeants with him, but left behind two knightly sons, the elder of whom was count of Namur. When Count Peter was at Rome, he prevailed upon the pope to crown both him and his wife. Once they were crowned, they went to Brindisi in Apulia, and the pope sent a cardinal with them.

When the emperor came to Brindisi, he had ships and vessels prepared. They embarked and crossed to Durrës. When they had arrived before Durrës and its lord learned that it was the emperor, he came out to meet him, showed him great joy, received him as lord, did him homage, and surrendered his land to him. Durrës is the first city at the entrance to Greece from the side of Apulia.

When [Col. 0982C] the emperor had remained there for a time, the lord of Durrës came to him and said: “Lord, you will go to Constantinople by land, and I shall go with you as long as my land extends. Once it is known through Greece that I have surrendered my land to you and am going with you, no one will oppose you. Instead, they will come to you for mercy and surrender all the land to you.”

The emperor believed him. They set out and travelled overland. The empress was pregnant and did not go by land, but by sea to Constantinople. Before reaching Constantinople, she arrived in the land of Geoffrey of Villehardouin, who showed her great honour. The empress had a daughter, and Geoffrey of Villehardouin had a son named Geoffrey. Seeing that he possessed great land and that her daughter would be well married there, the empress gave him her daughter; he took her as his wife and married her.

[Col. 0982D] Afterwards the empress went to Constantinople. Not long afterward, she gave birth to the son with whom she was pregnant.

### LV. The emperor is killed. The brother of the count of Namur becomes emperor

Now I shall tell you what the lord of Durrës did, he who was conducting the emperor by land. They had not travelled more than three days from Durrës when they lodged in a very strong castle. When they had lodged there and were sleeping at night, the lord of Durrës had his men well armed. He had the emperor and his men seized; many were killed, and the rest were imprisoned. He held them prisoner so long that the emperor died, as did the count of Sançerre.

When the Greeks heard that the emperor was in prison, they rose up and reconquered all the land which Emperor Henry had conquered. Not long after the emperor’s death, the empress died in Constantinople. When the empress was dead, the knights of the land summoned the count of Namur, who was her son, to go to Constantinople, because the land had fallen to him.

When the messenger came and delivered his message, he said that he would take counsel. He did so, but his counsel did not advise him to go. Instead, he sent his younger brother and instructed them to crown him, since he himself could not go. This Henry went by Hungary, because the empress was [Col. 0983B] his sister and he had safe-conduct from the king of Hungary through his land and through Blachia. He reached Constantinople safely and assumed the crown.

Once he had assumed the crown, he accomplished little in the land, for he had not brought men with whom he could accomplish much. He would have lost all the land had he not had the aid of the Blachs; but the Blachs helped him maintain and retain what he found there.

### LVI. The emperor’s mother is drowned. His wife’s nose and lips are cut off. He himself dies

There was a worthless lady in Constantinople, who had been the daughter of a knight of Arras named Baldwin of Neuville. This lady had a mother. The emperor loved her so much that he could not be without her; he married her secretly and installed her with him in his residence, together with her mother.

When the knights of Constantinople learned that he had married her, they were greatly distressed, because he was so absorbed in her that he could not be made to leave his chamber. They deliberated what they should do. Following their decision, they went into the chamber where the emperor was, seized him and held him. They took the mother of his wife, placed her in a boat, and sent her out to be drowned at sea. Then they came to his wife and cut off her nose and lips. With this they left the emperor in peace.

When the emperor saw the shame inflicted upon his wife and her mother, he was greatly grieved. He had galleys armed, embarked, left Constantinople, and went to Rome. When he arrived there, he complained to the pope of the outrage his men had done him. The pope strongly comforted him, gave him of his own resources, and urged him so earnestly and worked so effectively upon him that he returned to Constantinople. As he was returning, he arrived in the land of Geoffrey of Villehardouin; there he contracted an illness from which he died.

### LVII. Emperor Otto, having been crowned, invades the lands of the Church. He is excommunicated
Frederick, who was king of Sicily and whom his own men had disinherited of his land, while his uncle the duke of Swabia was safeguarding for him the land of Germany, was to be emperor. It happened one day that a knight entered the duke’s chamber and killed him. When the great men of Germany learned that the duke was dead—he who, through the promises and gifts he had received from the king of England, had opposed their crowning Otto—they summoned Otto and crowned him at Aachen. When Otto had worn the crown, he had the knight who had murdered and killed the duke sought out, and searched for so thoroughly that he was taken, in order to remove from himself the blame that was laid upon him for the duke’s death. He had the knight dragged and hanged.

Afterwards he went to the pope at Rome to be crowned. The pope crowned him very willingly, because the king of England had given him a great present for it. On the day after Otto was crowned emperor of Rome, he entered the pope’s territory and began to wage war upon him, taking the castles and fortified places from the pope. When the pope learned that he had taken his castles and entered his land—this man whom he had made emperor, though he ought not to have done so, and whom he had aided through covetousness in disinheriting the one who ought to have been emperor—he was greatly distressed. He could do nothing else, nor take any other vengeance, except to excommunicate Otto throughout Christendom. He excommunicated him and caused him to be excommunicated throughout Christendom.

When Theobald, who was bailiff of Apulia, to whom the emperor had entrusted the land of Apulia and Calabria and the guardianship of his son Frederick, learned that Otto had worn the crown, he went to him and told him to go into Apulia, and that he would surrender the whole land to him. Afterwards, he would go into Sicily, seize Frederick, and kill him. And if he did not do so, he knew well that, if Frederick came of age, he would take it from him.

### LVIII. Otto vainly attempts to invade Sicily. Frederick, king of Sicily, seeks the sister of the king of Aragon as his wife.

The emperor well provisioned the castles he had taken from the pope, then went into Apulia with Theobald; but he accomplished little there, for the people of the country opposed him and never wished to surrender to him. When he saw that he would accomplish nothing there, he left Theobald in his place and went into Lombardy and Tuscany to secure guarantees. In Germany all remained excommunicated.

The pope waited more than a year, believing that Otto would make amends for the offence he had committed against him; but he did not come and would not make amends. The pope then took the counsel that you will hear of. But first I shall tell you of Frederick, who was at Palermo. The archbishops who guarded him advised him to marry in such a place that he might have help and support in recovering his land, which his own men had taken from him. He said that he would gladly do whatever they wished on their advice.

They then said that the king of Aragon, who bordered upon him by sea, had a sister who had been queen of Hungary; and if he could arrange to have her as his wife, they knew of no place from which he could better obtain help by sea and land. Then Frederick came and said that they should send there: if she were willing to be sent to him, he would gladly marry her. The archbishops had galleys armed and sent to the king of Aragon to request his sister for the king of Sicily.

### LIX. It is granted to him.

[Col. 0985A]

When the messengers came to the king of Aragon and had delivered their message, the king was very joyful. He had galleys and ships armed and loaded with weapons and provisions; he put his sister aboard and sent her to the king of Sicily. He also sent with her his brother, who was count of Provence, and five hundred knights to help him recover the land which his own men held against him.

After they departed from Aragon, they arrived at a city called Palermo, where the king of Sicily was. When they had arrived, they came ashore. The king went to meet them and married the lady. After he had married her, they departed from Palermo and went into Sicily, where at first they conquered little of the country. But the king, queen, and knights did so much that he went on conquering all. From Palermo to Messina is five days’ journey.

After the count of Provence came to Messina, it was not long before the count died, together with a great part of his knights; the rest returned to their own country. The king remained at Messina with his townsmen, for he had few knights with him.

### LI. The pope urges Frederick to cross into Germany and be crowned at Aachen.

Now I shall tell you the counsel which the pope adopted against Otto. He heard that the king of Sicily was at Messina and had married a wife. He sent him word that, if he could manage to be in Germany, he would order the archbishops and bishops to crown him at Aachen; after he had worn the crown at Aachen, he himself would crown him at Rome.

When the king of Sicily heard this news, he was greatly pleased. He had a galley made ready, embarked, and went to a city of his own, three days’ journey from Rome, at the edge of his territory, called Gaeta. But before going there, because he did not know what might happen, he crowned one of the sons he had by his wife. He remained a long while at Gaeta, because he did not dare go farther on account of the Pisans, who were watching for him in order to kill him.

After he had stayed there a long time, he sent to the Genoese, asking them for God’s sake to aid him, since he did not dare leave Gaeta. The people of Genoa armed galleys, sent for him, and brought him to Genoa. There he remained for a full eight months and never left the city. For when Otto heard that the pope had summoned Frederick in order to crown him against Otto and send him into Germany, he sent messengers into Lombardy and Tuscany, to the cities and passes, offering great presents and promising great gifts to those who could seize and hold Frederick; and he earnestly entreated them to do so.

### LXI. Once crowned, he takes the cross. Otto vainly attempts his death.

When King Philip of France heard that the king of Sicily was at Genoa and that the pope was sending him into Germany to be crowned, he was very glad. Knowing that Otto had the passes and roads watched in order to seize him, he sent word to Genoa that they should spare no expense or effort to get Frederick quickly into Germany, and he would reward them well.

The Genoese accomplished so much with the people of Lombardy that the king crossed into Germany and wore the crown at Aachen. As soon as he was crowned, he took the cross for overseas and vowed to God that he would go to the Promised Land and help, to the best of his power, to deliver the land from the hands of the Saracens. When the king of Sicily had worn the crown at Aachen, the archbishops and bishops adhered to him by the pope’s command, as did all the knights of a part of Lorraine.

It happened one day that he was in a castle in Lorraine, and his death had been arranged by means of a promise Otto had made. A knight who knew of this treachery came to him and told him that his death had been planned, that he was to be killed that night, and that, if he would follow his counsel, he would contrive that he should not die. The king said that he would gladly do so.

“Lord,” he said, “if you leave now, you are watched on every side. You cannot go that way without being killed. I shall tell you what you must do. When night comes, you shall have a servant sleep in your bed, while you remain behind the door of the chamber. When those who must kill you know that you are asleep, and see the man lying in your bed, they will think that it is you. They will pass on and set about killing him; then you shall immediately leave the chamber. I shall have everything prepared with mounted men and shall take you away. The cry will arise that you have been killed, and, with God’s help, I shall lead you to safety during the night.”

The next day the cry spread through the whole city and country that the king of Sicily had been killed in his bed. When the count of Bar and the duke who bordered on Lorraine learned this, they had it made known to the king of France. When he heard it, he was greatly distressed, because he feared Otto: if Otto came into possession, he would harm him. That same day the count of Bar and the duke again let the king of France know that Frederick had escaped, and how; the king was greatly pleased when he learned it.

After this it happened that the king of Sicily sent word to the king of France that he wished to speak with him at Vaucouleurs. King Philip could not go there, but sent his son Louis, and they met there and spoke together. Of their counsel I can tell you nothing, except that some people said that King Philip lent him great wealth in order to maintain his war against Otto.

### LXII. King Philip opposes Otto, who forms an alliance against him with the English and Flemings. The king of England is defeated by Louis, son of the king of France. The battle of Bouvines, in which the king of France is victorious.

Otto knew well that the king of France loved the king of Sicily and aided him from his own resources against Otto. He knew that his uncle, the king of England, and the count of Flanders, named Ferrand, were united and gathering men to wage war upon the king of France. He assembled a great force of dukes and counts and went into Flanders to help the count injure the king of France.

The king of England sent a great body of knights to the count of Flanders to oppose the king of France. He also sent his brother, named William Longsword, Count Renaud of Boulogne, who was serving with him in the war, and Hugh of Boves. Afterwards the king of England crossed into Poitou with a great army and many knights.

When the king of France learned that the king of England had arrived in Poitou to enter his land, he sent there his son Louis, the count of Nevers, and many knights. They did so much that they would have captured the king of England in a castle, had it not been for a cardinal of Rome who was English and was in that country to preach the cross for the overseas expedition.
