When he saw that the king of England was getting the worse of it, he pleaded so earnestly with Louis, the king of France’s son, that a truce was granted and the king departed. Thus the cardinal caused the king of England to escape, so that he was not taken.

When the king of France heard that the count of Flanders was gathering men, and that Otto, the brother of the king of England, and Renaud, count of Boulogne, had come to the count’s aid, he summoned his host and went into Flanders to meet him. He lodged four leagues away, near a city called Tournai. The day on which the king came to Tournai was Saturday, and the next day was Sunday. The king said that he would not move because of the holiness of the day.

When the Flemings learned that the king was so near them, they armed and came against him, believing that they would find him at Tournai. The king was told that the Flemings were coming upon him. He had his men arm, rose from there, and returned to a lodging from which he had departed the day before. He placed his rearguard and charged the men of Champagne with it. He halted at a bridge called the bridge of Bouvines. There he waited for his rearguard to come up, for he did not wish to go against the Flemings in battle because it was Sunday.

The count of Flanders was told that the king of France was fleeing and did not dare wait for him. Then the count came and charged until he struck the rearguard. They received him with the help of the squadrons of knights close to them. They captured the count of Flanders, William Longsword, a count of Germany called Count Pelvi [reading uncertain], Renaud of Boulogne, a great part of the Flemings, and many other knights.

### LXIII. Frederick pursues Otto, who surrenders to him the imperial insignia.

[Col. 0987D]

Otto fled, together with the duke of Brabant who was with him and Hugh of Boves. They escaped, and Otto went into Germany. When Frederick heard that Otto had been defeated in Flanders and had fled, he assembled a great force and marched against him. When Otto heard that King Frederick was advancing upon him with a great force, he evacuated Germany and went to Soissons, in his brother’s land. King Frederick followed him, pursued him until he caught up with him, and besieged him in a castle.

There Otto fell ill and died. But before he died, he renounced the empire and surrendered to King Frederick the crown of Rome and the insignia which he wore when he was emperor. As you have heard, God helped Frederick from the very poor condition in which he was at the beginning.

We shall now leave off speaking of King Frederick, who was in Germany and remained there a long time before he went to Rome, until the proper time comes to speak of it. King Frederick sent for his son and his wife, whom he had left in Sicily.

### LXIV. John of Brienne is made king of Jerusalem.

Now we shall tell of the land of Jerusalem. It happened that Count Henry died, and the land fell to the daughter of the marquis whom the Assassins had killed. She had no lord; rather, one of her uncles was made bailiff of the land until such time as a man could be found to whom they would give her and whom they would make lord.

The knight who was made bailiff and was her uncle was named John of Ibelin. He was the son of Balian and Queen Maria, wife of King Amalric. He was bailiff of the land before anyone had been found to whom the young lady could be given, and he kept the land well at peace with the Saracens.

It happened that the patriarch, bishops, knights of the land, Templars, and Hospitallers gathered together and took counsel as to whom they could give the young lady and make king of the land. A knight was present when they were assembled. He rose to his feet and told them that he knew a knight in France who had no wife, was a noble and worthy man, and, if they wished to agree to it, he thought that the kingdom would suit him well and that she would be well bestowed upon him.

They asked who he was and what his name was. He told them that he was called Count John of Brienne. They discussed the matter together and took counsel. Many among them knew him well or had heard of him. They all agreed to seek him out, give him the young lady, and make him king. They took messengers and sent them to summon him.

The messengers came to him where he was in France and told him that those of the overseas land were summoning him in order to make him king. When he heard this, he said that he would take counsel. He went to the king of France and told him that he had been summoned to become king in the overseas land. The king advised and urged him strongly to go.

He went and arrived at Acre, where he was received with great honour and great lordship. Then he went to Tyre, married his wife, and they wore the crown. When the Saracens learned that Acre had a king, they broke the truce which they had made with the bailiff and war began.

After King John had worn the crown, he sent word to the king of Cyprus to take as his wife the daughter of Count Henry. Count Henry, the young lady’s father, had arranged this marriage before his death. The king of Cyprus sent for her, married her, and made her queen.

King John had a first cousin named Erard of Brienne. One day he learned that the king had gone to Tyre. He persuaded the queen to give him the other daughter of Count Henry, who was her sister. He married her secretly as soon as the queen had given her to him, because he did not wish the king to be blamed, nor for it to be said that the king had given her to him. He immediately crossed the sea and came to France.

### LXV. The pope orders the cross to be preached. James of Vitry is elected bishop of Acre.

I shall now tell you no more of Erard or his wife, though perhaps you will hear of them again later. King John, who was at Acre, sent word to the pope, asking him for God’s sake to aid him, because he had great need of men. When the pope heard the news from the overseas land, which needed help, he ordered throughout Christendom that the best clerics he knew should preach the overseas cross. Afterwards he sent cardinals to encourage them and confirm what they said, and many people took the cross throughout all lands.

There was in France a cleric who preached the cross, called Master James of Vitry; he enrolled many people under the cross. While he was preaching, the canons of Acre elected him and sent word to the pope to send him to them as bishop of Acre. Know that, had he not received the pope’s command, he would not have accepted. Nevertheless he crossed overseas, was bishop for a long time, and did much good in the land. But afterwards he resigned, returned to France, and later became a cardinal of Rome.

The first great lord of that crusade to cross over was the king of Hungary, who brought many men. Many people from all lands crossed on that expedition and arrived at Acre. At the time when the king of Hungary crossed over, Queen Maria, King John’s wife, died, leaving him a daughter. The king did not wish to remain without a wife. Instead he sent to the king of Armenia, asking him to send one of his daughters, whom he would take as wife. The king sent her and he married her. Afterwards the king of Armenia came to Acre. When King John had married his wife, the king of Cyprus came to Acre with a great force.

### LXVI. The Christians besiege Mount Tabor. They raise the siege.

There were now four kings at Acre, and a very great multitude had arrived there. They took counsel that they would go to besiege a castle four miles from Acre, called Mount Tabor. They went there and besieged it, but did not take it, for the sultan had assembled a great force and came to relieve his castle.

When the Christians learned that the sultan was near them and was coming to harm them, they raised the siege and went out to meet him in battle. The Saracens were high in the mountains and the Christians on the plain. Coredain, the sultan’s son, came to his father and said: “Lord, come down into the valley, and let us fight the Christians.”

The sultan said that he would not do so. “See, fair son,” he said, “how eagerly and fiercely they come to fight. If we descend into the valley, perhaps we shall get the worse of it. For they value death as dearly as life. It seems to me that they have all abandoned themselves to death, and I do not wish to have my men killed. See,” he said, “how great a multitude they are; they have no lord to govern them, and each lives from his own resources. When they have spent what they possess, they will depart.”

The sultan remained quite still in the mountains. When the Christians saw that they would not come down, they did not dare remain at the siege, lest the Saracens place themselves between them and Acre and cut off their provisions. They had not been back at Acre long when the king of Hungary embarked and returned to his country; the king of Armenia returned to Armenia; and the king of Cyprus returned, arrived at Tripoli, fell ill, and died.

King John was at Acre and had many men, while many more came every day. He considered that he could accomplish nothing in that land and that, if he had the advice of the Temple, the Hospital, and the knights of the land, he would willingly go to besiege Alexandria or Damietta, if they advised it. It seemed to him that if he had one of these cities, he could through that city obtain the kingdom of Jerusalem. Having conceived this plan, he summoned the Templars, Hospitallers, and knights of the land to take counsel concerning it.

### LXVII. King John resolves to besiege Damietta.

When all were assembled, the king came and told them: “Lords, for God’s sake counsel me concerning what I shall tell you. We have a very great force; many crusaders from all lands will come, and many more will yet take the cross. It seems to me that we cannot accomplish much here against the Saracens. If you see that it would be good to do and give your consent, I would willingly go into the land of Egypt to besiege Damietta or Alexandria. For if we can have one of these cities, it seems to me that we could obtain this whole land through either of the two, if God granted us to take it.”

The Templars, Hospitallers, and knights discussed it together, and their counsel was that it would be good to do. They agreed and promised that they would go. When the king saw that they had agreed together, he commanded each man to prepare his ships and load the galleys with arms and provisions, each according to his means. They fixed a day for departure.

When the fleet was ready, the king well supplied Tyre and Acre with knights and sergeants. When he went into Egypt, he left at Acre fully five hundred knights, both natives of the land and pilgrims. After he had thus supplied Tyre and Acre, he had it proclaimed throughout Acre that all able-bodied men, except those remaining in the garrisons, should board the ships and go with him, under pain of excommunication.

When the ships and galleys were ready, they embarked. When God gave them a favourable wind, they departed and travelled until they came in a short time to Damietta. They landed and disembarked upon an island before Damietta, where they encamped on the river. They remained there for a full year and could accomplish nothing against Damietta, except that they took a tower near the riverbank where they were encamped, which was well garrisoned.

One end of a chain was in that tower and the other at Damietta; they raised it whenever they wished to prevent vessels from going up or down the river. When the Christians had taken the tower, they garrisoned it and broke the chain, so that vessels arriving to join their army could come up the river directly to the bank on their side.

### LXVIII. The pope sends crusaders and legates to Damietta.

When the pope learned that the Christians had besieged Damietta, he ordered throughout Christendom that the crusaders should set out. Afterwards he commanded the archbishops and bishops of the ports to serve as legates in releasing the common people from their vows to take the cross, sending home those who were not fit for defence so that they should not waste their money. According to what some people said, those released from their vows at Rome were not left with money except enough to return to their own country.

Afterwards the pope sent legates through all lands to release men from the cross and to cause those who were not released to set out. He ordered everywhere that no one should be regarded as bound by the cross who did not set out or give of his own goods as much as would reasonably be required for the overseas land.

Then he sent two cardinals eastward to Damietta: Cardinal Robert, who was English, and Cardinal Pelagius, who was Portuguese. Cardinal Robert died there; Pelagius lived, which was a great misfortune, for he did much harm there, as you will hear in due course.

### LXIX. The sultan destroys the walls of Jerusalem and neighbouring castles.

When the sultan learned that the Christians had set out for Egypt, he was not pleased. Instead he had the walls and castles around Jerusalem demolished, except only the Crac. For he thought that, once Jerusalem’s walls and the castles had been destroyed, the Christians would turn back, go to Jerusalem to make their pilgrimage, and then return to their own countries.

But they did not do so; rather, as you have heard, they landed and encamped before Damietta. When the sultan saw that the Christians did not turn back and was told that they had landed and besieged Damietta, he was greatly distressed. He assembled men and went there, taking with him one of his sons, named Loquemel, to whom he gave the land of Egypt when he died. He left his other son in the country to guard it, entrusting to him the land of Damascus and Jerusalem.

The sultan went into Egypt. When he arrived and saw that the Christians were near Damietta on the other side of the river, he was greatly distressed. He lodged before Damietta and did not live long afterwards, but died. His son became lord of the land and maintained the army. He had the river blocked with great stakes from one bank to the other, so that the Christians could not go up the river and land on his side. Afterwards he had the bank well fortified from the palisade to Damietta on the side where he was, so that the Christians could not land there.

### LXX. The Christians attempt to cross the river.

After the Christians had been on the island a long time, they took counsel as to what they should do. They could achieve nothing there, and it was necessary for them to cross toward Damietta. They said that they could by no means land between Damietta and the palisade; but if they could break the palisade and pass beyond it, they would, with God’s help, make a landing. They took counsel there and agreed to go.

After they had agreed, they very well prepared their army and their defensive lines. Then they armed and boarded the ships and galleys. When they were aboard, God gave them a favourable wind and they set out. In the ship that led the way was Walter, chamberlain of the king of France, through whom the king had sent great wealth for the needs of the land. That ship was strong and had a good wind; it struck the palisade, broke it, and passed beyond, opening the way for the other ships, which afterwards passed safely, except for one of the Temple which ran aground and which the Saracens burned, though its men escaped.

When the Saracens saw that the Christians were preparing to go up the river, they armed and went to the bank to prevent them from landing; they shot at them and threw Greek fire. When the Christians had gone some distance from Damietta, they found a bank where they thought they could land well. They saw that all the land and the entire shore were covered with Saracens. They said that they could not land there, for the land was too thickly covered with Saracens.

They took counsel that they would land on the bank of the island from which they had set out, and that the next day at dawn they would land on the other side. They landed and cast anchor along the riverbank. On the other side, the Saracens strongly fortified their bank and went to their lodgings.

### LXXI. The Christians cross the river and besiege Damietta. The Saracens fortify castles near Acre.

Now I shall tell you how it happened and how God aided the Christians. There was discord between a great man of the Saracen army and the sultan. The sultan wished to put him inside Damietta as part of the garrison, but he said that he would never enter it. For Saladin, his uncle, had put his father in the garrison of Acre and had allowed him to be captured when the Christians took Acre.

This great man withdrew from the army, he and his men and a great multitude with him; but he left his equipment and tents behind, because he did not wish anyone to notice his departure or to think that he had been captured. When those stationed on the bank to guard against the Christians heard the uproar and noise of those who were departing, they thought that they had been betrayed. They abandoned the shore and departed.

When day began to dawn, those unloading the ships and guarding the army looked across to the far bank. They saw no one; instead, they saw the bank entirely empty. They made this known to the Christians, who armed, raised their anchors, crossed over, and landed on the other side. The knights and sergeants disembarked, except for the mariners, who took the fleet downriver.

They drew themselves up in order and marched towards Damietta. When the Saracens learned that they had crossed the river, they armed and left their lodgings to come against them. The sultan was informed that the great man whom he had asked to enter Damietta had departed with all his men and with a great part of the army. When the sultan heard this, he did not wish to go against the Christians, but abandoned his lodgings and departed.

The Christians plainly saw him go, but did not wish to pursue him. Instead they went to the Saracens’ lodgings, which they had left behind. They made their camp there and besieged Damietta. They found the lodgings well furnished, which was of great use to them, and won much wealth there. Afterwards they divided the provisions, distributing the spoil to each according to his station.

Then they made two bridges across the river, from one camp to the other. They made good ditches and strong defensive barriers behind them, so that the Saracens could not attack them. Then they set up stone-throwers, mangonels, and trebuchets to cast missiles against the walls of Damietta, but could do nothing. They made assaults every day, and remained thus for a full year without accomplishing anything.

[Col. 0993C]

When the Saracens had abandoned their lodgings and all withdrawn, and learned that the Christians were encamped and had set up engines before the city and were making assaults, they camped two miles away and arranged to send some of their men every day to attack the defensive lines.

Afterwards the sultan summoned his brother Coredin, who was in the land of Jerusalem, to aid him with as many men as he could obtain, because the Christians had crossed the river and besieged Damietta all around. He also sent to the caliph of Baghdad, who is the pope of the Saracens, asking him by Muhammad to aid him; if he did not aid him, he would lose the land. For the pope of Rome was sending so many men there that they were beyond counting or measure. He asked that the caliph have preaching carried out among paganism just as the pope did throughout Christendom, and the caliph sent the sultan great assistance in men through his preaching.

Before the Christians left Acre for Egypt, they fortified a castle at the end of a city on the sea called Caesarea. They began to build another seven miles from Acre and five from Caesarea, in a place called “the Narrows.” The castle which they left under construction when they embarked was named Pilgrims’ Castle, because the pilgrims began to build it. The Templars hold that castle because it was built on their lands.

### LXXII. Battle between Christians and Saracens near Acre. The Christians are defeated by the Saracens.

[Col. 0994A]

Coredin, who was the son of the sultan of Damascus, had assembled a very great force. On the feast-day of the Beheading of St John, which falls at the end of August, he laid an ambush near Acre, and then sent men riding before it. When the garrisons of Acre saw the raiders coming, they sallied out after them and pursued them so far that they came upon the ambush. They halted, refusing to go farther, and considered themselves fools for having pursued those men so far. When the Saracens saw the Christians, they sprang out and fought them. There were many dead on both sides, until the Christians could endure no longer. Then whoever could escape fled towards Acre [Col. 0994B], and the Saracens pursued them to Acre’s gates, capturing and killing many. When the Christians in Acre saw their men returning utterly defeated, they ran to arms, shut the gates, and secured them so that the Saracens could not enter.

When Coredin had defeated Acre’s garrisons, he besieged the castle. When those in the castle were besieged, they sent to Acre for help. The people of Acre sent them galleys and instructed them to abandon the castle and come to Acre, since they could not rescue them. When those in the castle heard the news, they boarded the galleys by night, went to Acre, and abandoned the castle. On the following day, the Saracens armed themselves to assault it; and when they came near the walls [Col. 0994C], they found no one opposing them. They had ladders brought, climbed the walls, and entered the castle. When they had taken it, they did not wish to garrison it, but demolished it. Having demolished it, they went to besiege Castle Pilgrim.

When Coredin received word that his brother the sultan was ordering him to go to his aid with as many men as he could obtain, he raised the siege, secured his territory, and went to Egypt to his brother.

When the Christians had remained before Damietta for a while, they took counsel and agreed that they would go out to attack the Saracens and fight them. Having adopted this plan, they appointed those who were to remain and guard the barriers, and those who were to go against the Saracens. [Col. 0994D] King John went out ahead of the army, together with the elect of Beauvais, who afterwards became bishop, Walter the chamberlain, and a great body of cavalry from every land; and a wonderful multitude of foot soldiers went out as well. They marched until they came near the Saracen army. When the Saracens saw them coming, they withdrew and mounted their horses. Our foot soldiers entered the tents, loaded themselves with provisions and whatever else they could find, and turned back. When the Saracens saw that the Christians were laden, they charged them. The king and the cavalry who were protecting them went to meet the Saracens; they joined battle and fought, so that the Christians had the worse of it and were defeated. The elect of Beauvais and Walter the chamberlain were captured, together with a great [Col. 0995A] part of the men from France and elsewhere. Not one of the foot soldiers escaped: all were killed or died of thirst. For it was exceedingly hot that day, and they had no water where they had gone. The day was the feast of St John at the end of August, and on that day it was one year since the Christians had been defeated before Acre. The Saracens greatly rejoiced over the Christians whom they had captured, who were high-ranking men, and because they had defeated the king. The Christians made great lamentation; yet I tell you that every day they killed or captured Saracens.

## LXXIII. Damietta captured by the Christians. Division between the king and the cardinal.

Those within Damietta were struck by a severe sickness, so that many died there, and they died [Col. 0995B] every day. They made this known to the sultan and sent him word that he should either surrender the city or send them men able to defend it, since they could not defend themselves. The sultan had five hundred well-mounted knights prepared and told them that, if they could manage to get inside Damietta, he would give them whatever they asked. They said that they would go and enter it.

They prepared themselves and made ready to enter by night. When they were ready, they let those in Damietta know that, when they heard noise and disturbance in the Christian camp by night, they should open a gate through which they could enter. When the time came in the first sleep of the night and the Christian army was asleep, the Saracens, well armed and well mounted, [Col. 0995C] struck into the camp through the guards who watched the barriers. The Saracens within Damietta opened the gate, and the others entered. On the side where they entered was encamped the count of Nevers, for which he was greatly blamed and banished from the army.

Not long after the Saracens had entered Damietta, the cardinal’s men kept the night watch one night on the side facing the city. It was arranged that every high-ranking man should perform the night watch in turn, and that night it fell to the cardinal. That night they raised the customary cry, and wondered what it could mean. They spoke together, prepared ladders, set them against the walls, and when daylight came [Col. 0995D], they climbed up and found no one. They made this known in the camp, went down to the gates, opened them, and entered without resistance. Dead men and sick persons lay throughout the streets, so that the entire city stank. The Saracens able to take refuge gathered in a tower, where they were captured. All the dead were thrown into the river and went out to sea.

When the Christians had captured Damietta, they gave each person his share of the city and its property according to his rank. Not long afterwards, serious hostility arose between the king and the cardinal. The cardinal consequently excommunicated every day all men and women who dwelt in, or rented, a house in the portion of Damietta held by King John. The king was greatly grieved by what the cardinal did [Col. 0996A], for he had expended cost and labour in capturing Damietta.

## LXXIV. Damietta having been abandoned, the king goes to Armenia, then to Acre. The cardinal harasses the army and the pilgrims.

News was brought to King John that the king of Armenia, whose daughter he had married, was dead. He was very glad, and had a highly respectable reason for leaving the army, since he was greatly distressed because the cardinal exercised authority over him and had forbidden anyone in the army to do anything on his behalf. He summoned the knights of the army, took leave of them, and said that he must go to Armenia, because the land had fallen to him through his wife. Those in the army were greatly grieved when they learned that the king was departing.

King John went to Armenia, and when he arrived he claimed the land. [Col. 0996B] The Armenians said that they did not acknowledge him as lord; but if they saw the king’s daughter, they would render the land to her as their lady. King John went to Acre to bring his wife to Armenia. When he was at Acre, some people caused him to believe that his wife intended to poison his daughter, through whom he held the kingdom. The king was greatly grieved and beat his wife with his spurs, so that, it was said, she died from that beating.

The king did not remain at Damietta but stayed at Acre. He remained there for a full year after returning from Damietta before he went back there, by which he was in danger of losing his life. When the king left Damietta, the cardinal remained lord of the army. Before Damietta was captured, and thereafter as well, he had ordained that no man—even if he had left behind a poor wife, [Col. 0996C] children, or debts—could send anything back; rather, he had to leave everything in the army. Every day the cardinal had excommunicated all men and women who carried away anything belonging to a man who had died in the army. Afterwards he made those who hired out ships swear that they would let no pilgrim enter them, and that none should cross unless they saw his seal. Moreover, he had them excommunicate such persons. He made the same order in Acre and throughout the land.

When pilgrims who had hired ships and loaded their provisions thought to embark, and heard the sailors tell them that they could not enter unless they saw the cardinal’s seal, they were greatly distressed. They went to the cardinal and asked him [Col. 0996D] why he had forbidden the sailors to carry them across. He said that he had forbidden it so that they should leave what was theirs in the army. Some said: “Lord, we have already stayed here one or two years; have we not spent enough?” Nevertheless, he took from everyone according to his means when he wished to depart or obtain his seal. He did exactly the same at Acre.

## LXXV. The cardinal rejects salutary advice. Pilgrims captured by the Saracens.

The Saracens learned that the Christians had no galleys at sea and that the sea was unguarded. They had galleys prepared, armed, and put to sea to capture the Christians coming to Damietta. Spies came to the cardinal and said that [Col. 0997A] the Saracens had galleys ready, and that he should prepare against them; if he did not, he would suffer loss. The cardinal would not believe them, but gave them food and dismissed them.

When the galleys were at sea, the spies returned to the cardinal and said to him: “Now beware: the galleys are at sea.” The cardinal said: “Whenever these peasants want food, they come telling some news. Go, give them wine to drink and food to eat.”

The Saracen galleys at sea did not neglect their business. They went to the island of Cyprus and found many ships laden with pilgrims in a harbour before Limassol. They went forward and burned both the ships and the pilgrims. They remained there for a long time, burning and capturing every ship going to Acre or Damietta. News came to the cardinal [Col. 0997B] that the Saracen galleys had inflicted great harm upon the Christians and were in Cyprus, and that they had already captured, killed, or burned more than thirteen thousand Christians. When the cardinal heard the news, he was deeply grieved, and rightly so: the loss had occurred through his fault, because he had not believed those who had warned him. He had galleys armed, but too late, for the others had returned richly laden with goods and people they had won.

## LXXVII. Two Christians go to the sultan to preach Christ. The sultan offers the Christians the kingdom of Jerusalem in exchange for Damietta.

Now I shall tell you that there were two clerics in the army [Col. 0997C] at Damietta. They came to the cardinal and told him that they would go to preach to the sultan, and wished to go with his permission. The cardinal said that they would not go with his permission, for he knew well that, if they went, they would never escape. Nevertheless, they said that he should allow them to go, and begged him earnestly. When the cardinal heard that they were so eager to go, he said to them: “I do not know your intentions; but see to it, if you go, that your hearts are always with God.” They said that they would not go there unless for a very great good, if they could accomplish it. Then the cardinal said that they might indeed go, if they wished.

So they departed from the Christian army and went to the Saracen camp. When the Saracens on night watch [Col. 0997D] saw them coming, they thought that they came as envoys or to renounce their faith. They went to meet them, captured them, and brought them before the sultan. When they came before the sultan, they greeted him, and he greeted them likewise. Then he asked them whether they wished to be Saracens or had come as envoys. They answered that they would never be Saracens, but had come as messengers from God, to save his soul if he would believe them.

“For we say truly that, if you die in this law, you are lost. Therefore we have come to you; and if you will hear and understand us, we shall show you by right reason, before the wisest men of your land, that you are all lost and are all nothing.”

[Col. 0998A] The sultan said that he had archbishops and bishops of his law who were very learned clerics, and that he could not hear what they said without them. The clerics replied: “We are very glad of this; send for them.” The sultan summoned them, and they came to him in his tent. There were also some of the highest and wisest men of the land, as well as the two clerics. When they had arrived, the sultan told them why he had sent for them and recounted what the clerics had said to him. They answered:

“Lord, you are the sword of the law, and you ought to uphold and defend it. We command you, in the name of Muhammad, who gave it to us, to have their heads cut off. For we shall not hear anything that they may say. The law forbids belief in any preaching; and therefore we command you to have their heads cut off.”

[Col. 0998B] With this they took leave and departed. The sultan remained with the two clerics. Then the sultan came to them and said: “Lords, they have commanded me, in the name of Muhammad and of the law, to have your heads cut off, for the law commands this. But I shall act against the command, for what an evil reward would I give you for having put yourselves in danger of death to save my soul?”

Afterwards he asked whether they wished to remain with him; he would give them great lands and great possessions. They said that they would not remain, but would gladly go back if it was his command. The sultan said that he would gladly have them safely conducted back. Afterwards he had gold, silver, and abundant silk cloths brought to them [Col. 0998C], and ordered them to take whatever they wished. They said that they would take nothing, since they could not bring his soul to God; they would value his soul brought to God more highly than all that he possessed would be worth in their eyes. Yet, they said, he would do well to give them food, and they would depart since they could not do otherwise. The sultan had them given abundant food and drink; and when they had eaten, they took leave of the sultan, who had them conducted as far as the Christian army.

When the Saracens had lost Damietta, they were greatly distressed. They sent word to the Christians that, if they wished to surrender Damietta, they would restore to them the whole land of Jerusalem as the Christians had held it, except the Crac, and all Christians imprisoned among the pagans. [Col. 0998D] The Christians discussed it and took counsel. Their counsel advised that they should not surrender it, because through Damietta they could conquer the whole land of Egypt and afterwards the land of Jerusalem. For the man who was emperor of Germany was everywhere taking the cross, and many others would take it. If the emperor were there with all his power, and the crusaders still to come to their aid, together with what they had already begun and with God’s help, they could well have the whole land of Egypt and Jerusalem. When King Philip heard that they could have a kingdom for one city, he considered them fools and simpletons for not doing so.

## LXXVII. The pope summons Frederick to Rome, crowns him, and orders him to cross the sea to recover the Holy Land; he temporarily refuses.

[Col. 0999A]

The cardinal informed the pope that God had granted them the capture of Damietta, that it was the key to Egypt, and that the Saracens were willing to restore to them the whole land of Jerusalem except the Crac. But the people of the land would not agree, because of the help they expected from the emperor and other Christians. When the pope heard this, he was greatly pleased. He made it known throughout Christendom and ordered all pilgrims who had taken the cross to set out.

Afterwards he summoned Frederick, who was in Germany, ordering him to come to Rome, receive the crown, and then go to the land overseas. The emperor immediately [Col. 0999B] sent to Messina and ordered many galleys and horse-transports to be made ready for his crossing. When Frederick heard the message, he took leave in Germany, left his son there, and went with his wife to Rome, where they received the crown. But before he received the crown, he restored to the pope the cities and castles which Otto had taken from the pope.

When Frederick had been crowned, the pope ordered him to go to the land overseas. The emperor said that he could not go so soon, because he had many Saracens in his land and in Sicily, whom he wished first to remove. For if he went before they were expelled, he might well lose it. Moreover, he did not have Apulia, Calabria, or Sicily at his command, for his own men held them against him. But if he had put his land in order, [Col. 0999C] he would cross with God’s help and do much good in the land.

Afterwards the emperor went to Apulia, to a city called Capua. When the knights and high-ranking men heard that Frederick had received the crown and was at Capua, many came to his mercy and restored their lands to him. Some did not dare await him or come to his mercy, but fled to the land overseas. Some surrendered to the Temple; and there were some to whom he would show no mercy, but had hanged. Thus all the land of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily was restored to him, except the Saracens who were there. But afterwards he captured them and sent them into Apulia. A great city was established for them there, where they still are; but not all of them remain there, for some went to dwell in the towns of Apulia.

## LXXVIII. The Christians resolve to besiege Babylon.

[Col. 0999D]

Now we shall leave speaking of the emperor of Germany until the proper time and tell you of the Christians who were at Damietta. They heard that the emperor had received the crown and was making great preparations to cross the sea and aid them. They spoke together and said that they could well go and besiege Cairo. He who gave them this counsel gave them counsel to drown themselves; for I shall tell you the nature of the land.

There are sluices on a river throughout the land of Egypt, for retaining the river water. When this river reaches Egypt, it divides into seven branches, and all seven flow into the Greek Sea. The largest of these seven reaches [Col. 1000A] Babylon and Cairo. Babylon is a city, and Cairo is a castle below Babylon. This arm of water branches into two: one branch goes toward Damietta, while the other runs to a city called Fae and also falls into the sea. Each of these rivers carries shipping. Between these two rivers the Christians took land when they came before Damietta.

Every year, in the middle of August, the sluices are broken, so that the water spreads throughout the land, and the grain is then sown. Otherwise, unless this water spread in that manner, no grain would grow in the land, however much rain there might be. It has sometimes happened in our time that the river did not run or spread, nor could it spread because of lack of water; and then all the people of the land died of [Col. 1000B] hunger.

## LXXIX. The sultan offers the Christians a thirty-year truce together with the kingdom of Jerusalem.

At the moment when the river was to overflow, they set out for Cairo. When the Saracens had lost Damietta, they knew well that the Christians would not stop there, but would go on to Babylon and Cairo. They made a bridge across the river where the water was strongest, covered it entirely with iron, and built it in the strongest current because they did not want the Christians to go to the other arm of the river on their way to Babylon.

When the Christians had taken counsel and agreed to go to Cairo, they strongly garrisoned Damietta and made ready to depart. Before setting out, the cardinal summoned King John, who was at [Col. 1000C] Acre, asking him to come to Damietta, because they were prepared to go and besiege Cairo. The king said that he would not go, but would guard his land; he had good cause to attend to the land of which he was lord, which had come to him and which he had helped conquer.

When the Saracens heard that the Christians were preparing to go to Babylon and Cairo, they went to encamp and lodge at the iron bridge, in order to guard the passage there. Afterwards the sultan sent word to the cardinal that, if he would surrender Damietta, he would restore to them the whole land of Jerusalem as the Christians had held it, except the Crac; he would rebuild Jerusalem at his own expense, and all the castles destroyed after the Christians had begun their expedition towards Damietta; and he would grant a truce for thirty years, so that they could properly fill the land with Christians. [Col. 1000D]

## LXXX. The cardinal refuses peace.

The Templars, Hospitallers, and people of the land agreed to this peace, but the cardinal would not agree. Instead, he caused the army, except the garrisons, to set out. They went upstream along the river; the fleet went by water and they went by land, so that every day they encamped opposite each other.

When the cardinal had set out, he sent to King John, begging him for God’s sake to have pity upon Christendom, since they were setting out to go to Cairo; for God’s sake, he should follow them. The cardinal would pay what the king owed—fully one hundred thousand bezants, which he owed for the army at Damietta. When the king heard that the army had set out for Cairo, he was greatly grieved that it had moved at such a time [Col. 1001A], for it was in great danger of losing everything, as it did in the end. The king saw clearly that he had to go after them: if he did not, and misfortune befell them, he would bear great blame. So he left Acre and followed them, travelling until he reached them at the iron bridge, where they were encamped near the Saracen army. The vessels of the army went each day to Damietta and brought provisions to the camp, so that the army was well supplied.

## LXXXI. The Saracens block the Christians’ routes and open the water-barriers.

Now I shall tell you what the Saracens did. They had their galleys, which were on the river of Foe, sail upstream as far as the bridge, and then quietly sail downstream on the river of Damietta, [Col. 1001B] so that the Christian fleet on the other side neither knew of nor perceived it. The Saracen galleys placed themselves between the army and Damietta. There they remained, capturing the vessels that went from the army to Damietta and from Damietta to the army. Thus they blocked the waterway, so that provisions could not reach the army. For eight days or more no provisions went from Damietta to the army, and those in the army greatly wondered what this could mean, since they could receive no news from Damietta, nor could those at Damietta receive news from the army.

It happened that, just as the Saracen galleys were sailing down from the river of Foe into the river of Damietta, one hundred armed galleys, sent there by the emperor of Germany, had arrived on the river of Damietta and remained there. Had they known that galleys stood between them and the army, [Col. 1001C] they would have captured them and relieved the army, and Damietta would not have been lost.

When the sultan learned that the Christian galleys had arrived at Damietta, he said that he might delay no longer in harming the Christians. He had the sluices cut, and the water spread into the Christian camp. Some were in it up to the neck, and many drowned. All their provisions were lost. They could go neither forward nor back, in their vessels or on land. They were so surrounded by water that, unless the sultan granted them leave to return safely to Damietta, not one of them could escape drowning.

## LXXXII. Meeting between the king and the sultan, and peace between them.

[Col. 1001D]

When the king saw the army’s disaster, he sent word to the sultan that he would gladly fight him. The sultan sent him word that he would not fight: they were all dead if he wished it, and not one would escape drowning. He sent to the king asking whether it pleased him to come speak with him. The king went with the cardinal’s permission, taking with him Master James, bishop of Acre.

When the sultan saw the king, he made great celebration, had him sit beside him, and then said: “Lord king, I have great pity for you and your people, who are dying there in great misery from hunger and will also be drowned. Yet, if you wish, you can save them well from death.”

The king said: “Lord, how?”

[Col. 1002A] “I shall tell you how,” said the sultan. “If you will surrender Damietta, I shall bring them all to safety.”

The king said that Damietta was not his alone, but that it had many co-sharers; if the sultan wished, he would inform them and would gladly abide by what they decided. The sultan said that this would please him greatly and that he should send. The king sent the bishop of Acre to the cardinal and to those in the water, informing them of the sultan’s request. The cardinal and those in the army agreed together, were greatly pleased at the request, and sent word to the king that he should make the best agreement he could, provided that they might get out of where they were; whatever he did, they would uphold. The bishop returned to the king and told him what he had found.

Then the king and the sultan made peace between themselves [Col. 1002B], as I shall tell you. They surrendered Damietta to the sultan, together with all Saracens whom they held captive on this side of the sea. The sultan restored to them the Christians imprisoned in his land and in the land of Coredin, his brother. He said that he would restore the Holy Cross lost in the battle before Acre. They made an eight-year truce, upon the terms existing when King John received the crown.

## LXXXIII. Damietta restored to the Saracens. The king crosses the sea and comes to Rome.

When the peace had thus been concluded on both sides, the sultan sent peasants of his land to make bridges and sluices by which the Christians could get out of the water and reach dry land. Afterwards the sultan told the king that he wished to have hostages for the peace until his own people were inside Damietta and the Christians outside it. [Col. 1002C] The king and the bishop of Acre remained as hostages.

Afterwards men were sent to Damietta; the Christians were made to leave it, and it was handed over to the sultan, together with all prisoners within it. When this had been done, the king sat before the sultan and began to weep, while Christians were still in the water, dying of hunger. [Col. 1002D] The sultan looked at the weeping king and said: “Lord, why do you weep? It does not befit a king to weep.”

“Lord, I have good cause,” said the king, “for I see the people entrusted to me by God dying in such great wretchedness as hunger.”

The sultan pitied what he saw when the king wept, and wept also. Then he told him not to weep any longer, for they would have food. He sent them thirty thousand loaves to distribute among poor and rich alike. For four days he sent them thus, until they were out of the water. Once they were out, he sent a market of bread and meat for those able to buy, and to poor people he sent fifteen days’ bread for each person. They remained there until the messenger whom the sultan had sent to Damietta returned. When the messenger had returned, the sultan gave them leave, and each went his own way.

The king went to Acre and left knights in the land to inspect the cities, castles, and towns and release the prisoners. When the king had done this, he made a kinsman of his, named Eudes of Montbéliard, bailiff of the land [Col. 1003A]. Then he crossed the sea to go to Rome and France, to speak with the pope, the emperor, the king of France, and the king of England, in order to obtain help and support for the land overseas; to complain to the pope of the disgrace which the cardinal had inflicted upon him before Damietta; and to seek a husband for his daughter who could maintain the land.

## LXXXIV. The king visits France, England, and Spain. The emperor marries his daughter. Conflict between the emperor and the king.

When the emperor learned that he had arrived, he went to meet him, received him with great honour, rejoiced greatly at his arrival, and accompanied him until he came to the pope. The pope received him with great honour and went out to meet him. [Col. 1003B] The king complained of the disgrace which the cardinal had inflicted upon him. There the pope, emperor, and king agreed that never again should there be a division of anything conquered once they had gone to the land overseas, but all should belong to the king of Jerusalem.

At the time the king arrived in Apulia, the lady who was the emperor’s wife had died. When they had agreed that conquests should remain with the king, the pope spoke to the emperor about taking King John’s daughter as his wife. The emperor said that he would gladly take her because of the affection he had for her father. There the pope joined their hands. When this had been done, they separated. The emperor went to Apulia, and the king went to Rome, where he was received in procession. From there he went to France, to King Philip, who showed him great honour. Afterwards he went to the king in England and returned to France.

And I tell you truly that, in every land through which he passed, and in the good towns, people went out to meet him and received him in procession. Not long after King John was in France, King Philip died and left great wealth to King John for carrying to the land overseas. King John was at Saint-Denis for King Philip’s burial. Afterwards he attended the coronation at Reims of King Louis, Philip’s son. Then he went to Santiago. On his return, the king of Spain met him at Burgos and showed him great honour. There the king of Spain gave him in marriage one of his own sisters, whom he had.

When King John had married a wife, he went to [Col. 1003D] France. After he had been there a while, he took leave of the king and barons, saying that he had to go, because the emperor awaited him in Apulia to cross the sea and marry his daughter. He went and travelled until he reached the emperor in Apulia. When he was there, the emperor had his daughter summoned, married her, and had her crowned. He loved King John greatly and made him lord of his land.

The devil, seeing the great love between the emperor and King John, was greatly grieved. He entered the emperor’s body and made him desire a niece of King John who had come with his daughter. He deflowered her and hated his wife. One day King John went to see his daughter and found her in her chamber greatly distressed. He asked what was the matter, and she told him that the emperor had done the same to his niece: [Col. 1004A] he had deflowered her, kept her, and hated his wife. When the king heard this, he was greatly grieved. He comforted his daughter, then took leave and went to the emperor.

When he arrived, the emperor rose to meet him and greeted him courteously. But the king told him that he did not return his greeting, and that all those through whom he was emperor—except the king of France—were dishonoured; and, if it were not for sin, he would kill him. When the emperor heard this, he was greatly afraid and ordered him to leave his land. King John said willingly that he would never remain in the land of so disloyal a man. He left the land and went to Rome. The Romans went out to meet him, received him with great honour, and promised that they would help him with sixty thousand écus if he needed it. He thanked them, left Rome, and went to [Col. 1004B] Lombardy, to Bologna the Fat, where he and his wife remained.

## LXXXV. The king and emperor are reconciled. The emperor pretends to cross to the Holy Land.

When the people of Lombardy heard that King John was at Bologna la Grassa, the podestàs of the cities assembled and went to him. They greeted him courteously and told him that, if he wished, they would restore the land to him and crown him. The king thanked them and said that he did not refuse, but that the land belonged to his daughter, who was its lady. Nevertheless, if they offered it, he would remain in the land as long as he wished.

When the emperor had banished the king from his land, he was greatly distressed at the reproach which the king had spoken to him. He went to his wife and beat her harshly, so that she nearly lost the child which she had [Col. 1004C] in her womb; afterwards he had her shut up in a castle, where she remained for a long time. The emperor greatly feared that the king would take his land from him; therefore he sent him word that he would come to him for mercy and would make amends for the affront he had done him. The king did not wish to wage war against the emperor, but sent back word that he would gladly forgive him if he made amends.

The emperor went into Lombardy with a great host and begged the king for mercy, and the king forgave him. Afterwards the king made peace between the emperor and the Lombards in the manner I shall tell you. All the communes and cities of Lombardy were to make amends for their offence by bringing five hundred knights, at their own expense, for two years into the land overseas. Afterwards the emperor went into Apulia, [Col. 1004D] while the king remained at Bologna, because he did not wish to go with the emperor.

When the pope heard that there was hostility between the king and the emperor, he summoned the king to come to him, and he went. The pope entrusted his land to his keeping, and granted him the revenues for his maintenance. It happened that the emperor’s wife gave birth to a son; not long afterwards she died, at which he was greatly grieved, yet he was nevertheless glad that he had an heir remaining. The pope ordered the emperor to cross overseas and perform his pilgrimage; if he did not cross, he would exact justice from him. The emperor sent word that he would gladly cross, and set a day for it.

When the pope learned the day, he sent throughout all Christendom to those who had taken the cross, ordering them to set out and go to Brindisi, for the emperor would cross. The emperor made [Col. 1005A] great preparations of ships and galleys, and had provisions and men loaded aboard. When the pilgrims had arrived, the ships were ready, and they had been taken on board, the emperor entered a galley; the fleet and the vessels set sail after it. But when evening came, the emperor had his galley quietly turn back, without anyone knowing it except those in the galley; thus he returned to Brindisi, while the pilgrims crossed overseas and came to Acre.

### LXXXVI. The emperor is excommunicated by the pope. After Coradin’s death, the pilgrims fortify certain castles.

When the pope heard that the emperor had thus returned, he was greatly distressed, excommunicated him, and caused him to be excommunicated throughout all Christendom as a traitor and disloyal man. The emperor sent to the sultan [Col. 1005B] in order to make a forced peace, as you shall hear.

At the time when the pilgrims arrived, Coradin was dead, and his land remained to his children. He left the land and the children in the guardianship of a knight who was from Spain and had formerly been a brother of the Temple; he entrusted them to him because he had served him loyally and had faithfully kept his religion, except only that he went against the Christians. Therefore he entrusted them to him, knowing well that he would guard them loyally. He did not wish to leave them to the Saracens, because he knew well that they would hand them over to his brother, the sultan of Babylon.

When the sultan died, his truces in the land overseas died with him. The pilgrims there took counsel that they should go and fortify a castle seven miles from Tyre, in a place called Sajette. They went there; but when they [Col. 1005C] arrived, their deliberation brought them to the conclusion that they would not fortify it, since too much work would be required and it would not be very defensible. Rather, they would fortify a castle on an island lying before the city and build a causeway of earth to it; if the castle were made, it would fear no assault either by sea or by land.

All those in the host agreed, remained there, fortified the castle throughout the winter, and made the causeway; at its end they made a strongly defensible gate. There were many Englishmen in that host, and two bishops, who did much good in the host and elsewhere, as you shall hear. The Germans fortified another castle, called the Franks’ Castle. When they had fortified these two castles during the winter, they went [Col. 1005D] to Caesarea in the summer, where they fortified another castle. The Spaniard who held the land in guardianship did not dare abandon what he guarded, lest the sultan, who was seeking to disinherit his nephew, should enter it.

### LXXXVII. The emperor crosses overseas without informing the pope and negotiates peace with the sultan. He asks the pope for absolution.

When the messengers whom the emperor had sent to the sultan returned, he immediately went to sea and sailed to the land overseas, without making this known to the pope; thus he went, wholly excommunicated. When he came opposite the island of Cyprus, he landed and stayed there. He sent his marshal to Acre, with a large company, to speak with the sultan.

At the time when the marshal had been sent to Acre, [Col. 1006A] the pilgrims were still at Caesarea. One day they had sent foragers into pagan territory to seek provisions. They brought back great quantities of livestock and booty. The marshal heard of it, mounted with his knights fully armed, and went out against them. When they saw the marshal, they recognized the banners and were very glad, for they thought that he had come to aid them. But he had no such intention: rather, he fell upon them, killed and wounded them, and took away what they had won.

After doing this, the marshal returned to Acre. From there he went to a place in the country as envoy to the sultan, to discuss peace, because he did not wish them to come to Acre or the people of the land to know their counsel. The people of the land sent a messenger to the pope and informed him how [Col. 1006B] the emperor’s men had maltreated them and how they often went to speak with the Saracens.

When the emperor had remained for some time in the island of Cyprus, his marshal informed him of what he had found out from the sultan. The emperor immediately went to sea and arrived at Acre. At that time the Christians were before Caesarea, where they had fortified a castle; from there they went to Jaffa, where they fortified another very strong castle.

When the emperor was at Acre, he immediately had a galley armed, put messengers aboard, and sent them to the pope, making known that he was in the Holy Land and would sustain it. He promised that he would never return until he had conquered all the land of the Saracens and put it into the hands of the Christians. The pope said that he would not absolve [Col. 1006C] him, for he did not regard him as a Christian; rather, he had crossed as a false man and a traitor. Afterwards he instructed the patriarch, the Temple, and the Hospital neither to take his counsel nor to agree with him, and to take good care, for he would never do good, as the pope believed.

### LXXXVIII. The emperor is badly received by the Templars and makes peace with the sultan.

One day the emperor conceived a great treachery. He went to a castle of the Temple called Château Pèlerin and entered it. Finding it strong and well supplied, he said that he wished to possess it and that they must evacuate it. The Templars ran to the gates, shut them, and said that unless he departed, they would put him in [Col. 1006D] such a place that he would never leave it. Seeing that he did not have the power, the emperor went out and returned to Acre.

He armed his men and went to the house of the Temple, intending to demolish it. The Templars defended it well, until the emperor withdrew and went to Jaffa, where a castle was being fortified. He sent to the sultan, ordering him to keep his agreements. The sultan knew of the discord between him and the pope and the people of the land, and sent word that he could not keep them; for his brother Coradin was dead, and he could not dispose of his land as he pleased, since it remained under guardianship.

The emperor swore an oath and sent word that, unless the sultan kept his agreements, he should know well that he would never have rest until he had disinherited him. When the sultan [Col. 1007A] heard this, he summoned those who had his nephew in guardianship, since he could not make peace without them on the terms agreed between them. The guardians came to the sultan, and the sultan said:

“Lords, behold the emperor, who has come for a peace which we had negotiated between myself and my brother, and which we had promised him. You too must promise it; and if you will not promise it, he will move against you.”

When they heard this, they said that he should do so and they would grant it, because it seemed to them that they could lose more in war than in peace.

### LXXXIX. Terms of the peace.

Now I shall tell you what the peace was. The sultan restored all the land of Jerusalem as the Christians had held it on the day when the Saracens [Col. 1007B] conquered it from them, except only the Crac of Montreal and three castles in the territory of Tyre and Sajette, which powerful men had garrisoned and would not surrender. Yet this could not matter greatly, because they were not so strong that they would need to be besieged. But the Crac was a loss: all Christendom might sit before it, provided it had food, before it was taken.

The city of Jerusalem was restored on these terms: three Saracens would be there to guard the Temple where God was offered; the Christians would have no lordship there; and Saracen pilgrims would come and go safely and without tribute to the Temple and to Solomon’s palace, where the Templars had been when the land was lost. The emperor placed Saracens in the city, to the shame [Col. 1007C] of the pilgrim Templars, because he did not wish them to be in the city. The emperor might fortify castles and cities already fortified, but he could make no new fortification, nor could the Saracens fortify themselves.

This peace was agreed by both sides, and a truce was made for ten years. When this was done and the truce made, the sultan had the Saracens evacuate the city, except only the Temple. The emperor entered it with his men and wore the crown for half a Lent. When he had worn the crown, he gave the royal palace, which stands before David’s Tower, to the German Hospital.

Neither the Temple nor the Hospital nor the patriarch was party to this peace or truce, because the pope had instructed them [Col. 1007D] not to take the emperor’s counsel or aid him. Moreover, even had the pope not so instructed them, they would not have helped to make this peace, for it was held to be false and bad.

### XC. The pope supplies King John with forces, and he invades the emperor’s lands. The emperor recovers his lands, makes peace with the pope, and is absolved by him.

When the emperor had worn the crown in Jerusalem, he sent one of his clerks to the pope, to his son in Germany, and to the king of France, informing them that the land had been restored to him. When the pope heard this news, he was not glad, because the emperor was excommunicated and because it seemed to him that he had made an evil peace, since the Saracens held the [Col. 1008A] Temple. Therefore he would not permit it to be known as having been done through him, nor permit Holy Church to celebrate it; rather, he ordered throughout all Christendom that the emperor be excommunicated as an apostate and unbeliever.

Afterwards he gathered a great force, entrusted it to King John, and had it enter the emperor’s land in order to lay waste the emperor’s own domain, not his imperial territory. King John entered it, took castles and towns, and made great conquests from the emperor. Word was brought to the emperor, who was overseas, that the pope had assigned troops to King John and that he was taking his castles, cities, and men.

When the emperor heard this, he assembled galleys, embarked in them, left a guardian in the land of Jerusalem, crossed the sea, and arrived in Apulia. When he had arrived, he sent [Col. 1008B] throughout all his cities to seize all houses of the Temple and drove every Templar out of his land. Then he assembled a great host and marched against King John, sending word to his son in Germany to aid him as best he could.

When King John saw that the emperor was coming against him with all his strength, he withdrew and informed the pope. The pope sent to France for assistance. The bishop of Beauvais went there with a great body of knights. The emperor recovered all the land which King John had taken from him.

The duke of Austria, who had gone to aid the emperor with his son, came to the pope and told him that the war did not befit either him or the emperor, but that he should make peace. The pope said: “What peace should I make? He has lied to me so much that I could scarcely [Col. 1008C] believe anything he told me, or any oath he swore to me.”

“Lord,” said the duke, “you shall be secured concerning the peace.”

There they negotiated a peace between the pope, the cardinals, and the duke. The pope sent two cardinals and the duke to the emperor with the terms of the peace. He said that he would not make that peace, but proposed another which he would make. The cardinals did not agree; they contended on both sides. The duke urged the emperor so earnestly that he submitted himself to the duke and the two cardinals, and swore upon saints that whatever they decided, he would uphold. He gave good assurance of this, and the cardinals pledged it on the pope’s behalf. The peace was agreed on both sides, and the emperor was absolved.

### XCI. The Saracens are defeated by the Christians.

[Col. 1008D]

A little after the emperor had departed from the land of Jerusalem, peasants of the country joined the Saracens and went one morning to Jerusalem to kill the Christians within. The Christians defended themselves well, it is said, killed fully five hundred Saracens, and lost only one Christian, an Englishman.

### XCII. The empire of Constantinople is offered to King John, who refuses it. But he gives his daughter in marriage to the heir of the empire and administers the empire.

Now we shall cease speaking of the land of Jerusalem until the proper time and occasion, and shall speak to you of Constantinople. The Christians within had lost all the land except [Col. 1009A] the city and a little territory outside it. They took counsel together. Several said that they should abandon and sell the city; others said that they would never do this, since they would have great shame and reproach wherever they went if they abandoned so rich a city for nothing. Rather, they sent to the pope for aid, informing him of the condition of the land and begging him, for God’s sake, to give them King John as lord; for if they could have him, with God’s help he would hold the land well, and as soon as he came into the land they would deliver it to him and make him lord. All agreed to this counsel.

They sent to the pope and King John. When the pope heard the news, he ordered King John to come and speak with him, and he came. When he had come, the pope [Col. 1009B] told him what had been sent to him from Constantinople and earnestly urged him to do it and take counsel upon it.

The king told him that he had already fully taken counsel and would not go. A child remained from Emperor Pirron, the heir of the land; thus he would not put himself at risk in order to defend another man’s land. The pope strongly urged him to go and promised him great aid in men and resources. The king said that he would not go for that promise, nor would he accept or refuse the promise.

Because the king saw the land’s need, and because the pope urged him, he said that he would go on this condition, if the knights of the land granted it and the pope approved: the heir of the land would marry a daughter [Col. 1010A] whom he had and would wear the crown. After marrying his daughter, he would swear upon saints that, as long as the king lived, he would remain under guardianship and have no lordship over him. Afterwards the knights would do homage to the king for his lifetime; all the land he conquered which his ancestors had held would belong to the emperor, while any land he conquered which his ancestors had not held would belong to the king’s heirs and would be held by them from the emperor. If they wished to do this, he would go.

The pope greatly approved what the king had said and agreed to it fully. The messengers said that they would return and inform the knights. They returned to Constantinople and informed them. The knights discussed it and all agreed readily to what the pope and king had sent them. [Col. 1010B] They sent back and summoned the king to come to Constantinople, promising to do everything he had set forth.

When the king heard these messengers, he went to the pope and took leave of him. The pope gave him from his resources and promised to help him with men and money if necessary. Then the king made preparations, went to Venice, embarked, and sailed to Constantinople. He summoned all the knights of the land and had his daughter married to the youth who was to be emperor. When the youth had married her, the king required him, together with the knights of the land, to fulfil his agreements. The emperor and the knights did what he had stipulated, according to their agreement, and the king was satisfied with this.

## BOOK XXV BEGINS

[Col. 1009]

### I. Alice, queen of Cyprus, claims the kingdom of Jerusalem as due to her.

[Col. 1009C]

At the time when the emperor departed from the land of Syria and Cyprus, Alice, queen of Cyprus and mother of King Henry, came to Acre and claimed the kingdom of Jerusalem as the nearest apparent heir of King Aimery, her grandfather. The people of the land took counsel and answered that they were men of Emperor Frederick, who held the land through the guardianship of his son Conrad; therefore they could not do what she requested. Yet, because they had never seen that son Conrad and he had never been present in the kingdom, they would send word to the emperor that he must send them his son Conrad within a year. If he sent him, they would keep him as their lord; [Col. 1009D] otherwise they would do toward him what they ought.

To carry out this matter they sent two knights as messengers to the emperor: one was Geoffrey Litors, a native of the country; the other was John of Bailou, born in Flanders. These two crossed to Apulia in a galley and arrived at Brindisi. From there they travelled until they found the emperor at Saint-Laurent, as he was going to Capua. As you have heard, [Col. 1010C] they delivered their message, to which he replied that within a short time he would do what he ought.

### II. How King John conducted himself at Constantinople.

Here we shall tell you what befell King John when he went to France. It happened at Constantinople after Emperor Robert had died. Philip, his brother, count of Namur, had given up and surrendered the empire to him. There remained to him a son, very young and a very small child, named Baldwin. By agreement, the barons of the land made as guardian and keeper of the empire and of the child a worthy man called Anseau, who maintained the land well, considering its poor condition.

To maintain it better, he made peace and alliance with the Cumans and married the daughter of a Cuman in order to draw them more closely to himself. As a result [Col. 1010D] the land became more secure and more abundant.

Since the land of Constantinople was in so weak a state, the barons took counsel and, by agreement, sent worthy messengers to King John asking him to come and receive the empire of Constantinople on the conditions they offered him. King John consented in the way that had been set forth, brought fine men with him, and supplied great wealth.

Among the conditions [Col. 1011A] was that the child who was the rightful heir should marry one of the king’s daughters, whom he had had by the sister of the king of Castile; and that all he conquered beyond the Strait of Saint George, in Bithynia, should belong to him and his heirs, but should be held by them from the empire; and that he should hold the empire as long as he lived.

When he came to Constantinople, he was crowned emperor and received the homages and fealties. Just as he thought he ought to ride out and begin the war, he became involved in litigation with the Venetians. Afterwards he found himself much reduced in men and resources. Nevertheless, as best he could, he crossed the Strait of Saint George and besieged a strong castle called Lespigas. He remained there until he took it, not by force but through treachery. He then garrisoned it, went forward, and rode through [Col. 1011B] the land of Vatatzes.

This Vatatzes was a Greek, who held the land beyond the Strait of Saint George and called himself emperor, considering himself emperor. He held the land through his wife, who had been the daughter of Lascaris, who called himself emperor because he belonged to the imperial line and to the lineage of the good Emperor Manuel, of whom this book spoke earlier.

When Emperor John had ridden through that land and lived at the expense of his enemies for a while, the Greeks never daring to come to battle but always avoiding him, he afterwards returned to Constantinople. Never again did he go out to harm his enemies, but returned to litigation. With so little profit he spent all the wealth which he had brought into the country. Therefore his men abandoned him, and thereafter he remained alone in [Col. 1011C] poverty as long as he lived.

### III. The sultan of Babylon besieges and captures Damietta.

It happened after Emperor Frederick departed from the land of Syria that the sultan of Babylon, al-Malik al-Kāmil, together with his brother al-Malik al-Farrāj, and with a great host of foot and horse, went to besiege the city of Damascus. They made a show of cutting down the gardens, of which the people of Damascus were greatly afraid, since these were among their great riches and all their great delight.

They found themselves disordered, like men who had no lord but a child and were under the power of a guardian. They feared destruction because they had no lord to sustain them; therefore they came to terms with [Col. 1011D] al-Kāmil and surrendered the city to him. He immediately gave it to his brother al-Ṣarāf, and that man gave him four eastern cities in exchange.

When Sayf al-Dīn Bār learned that the people of Damascus intended to surrender the city and disinherit their lord al-Malik al-Nāṣir, son of Coradin, and that he could devise no remedy, he took his lord and secretly led him out of the castle of Damascus through a postern. He brought him to the Crac, where his mother was, left his treasure there, and went to his own castle of Salqet. He rescued the child because he feared that his uncle al-Kāmil and al-Ṣarāf would kill him.

### IV. Frederick, after making peace with Pope Gregory, pretends that he wishes to cross to the Holy Land.

After the peace had been made between Pope Gregory [Col. 1012A] and Emperor Frederick, the emperor made a great show of wishing to take action in the land overseas. It had been reported to him that the Saracens were observing the truces with him very badly, along with the other outrages and wrongs which they committed against Christians: they were killing pilgrims on the road to Jerusalem. Indeed, more than ten thousand had been killed in that time.

The Saracens committed an even greater offence: they assembled more than fifteen thousand footmen in the land of Saint Abraham, in the mountains of Jerusalem, in Nablus, and in the surrounding country. They said that they would not allow the city of Jerusalem to remain in Christian hands, nor permit Christians to have the power to enter the *templum Domini*—the Temple of the Lord—which was God’s house. They made it appear that they did this without the sultan’s will and that their *faquis*, that is, their priests, had set them on to it. [Col. 1012B] All armed, they entered the city, ran wildly through the streets, broke into houses, robbed, and killed many Christians, though not very many.

### V. The Christians of the Holy Land take refuge in the safest places.

The Christians in Jerusalem—Latins, Syrians, and all other nations—when they learned of the coming of these men, shut themselves in, with their wives, children, and best possessions, in David’s Tower, in a fortification made there, and in the strongest houses nearby.

The bailiff of the city, named Renaud of Haifa, [Col. 1012C] chamberlain of the kingdom, sent to Acre to the lord of Sajette and to Garnier the German, who remained there as the emperor’s bailiff of the kingdom, and informed them of this assembly. He took knights and sergeants; they set out from Acre and went as far as Jaffa. They sent ahead a knight named Baldwin of Pignegi, accompanied by Tricople, to inspect the Saracens’ plot, while the host followed after.

They set out at early evening and took the road to Emmaus—the castle where Our Lord appeared to two pilgrims after the Resurrection. They rode all night and at daybreak were at Bethlehem.

### VI. The Christians kill the Saracens at Jerusalem.

[Col. 1012D]

When the Christians who had taken refuge in David’s Tower saw those coming from Bethlehem appear, they recognized the banners and knew that help was coming. They were greatly glad, for they were in very great fear, like men whom the Saracens had enclosed and were attacking on every side. This had already lasted two days, and they were then in the third.

Then they took heart, rushed upon the Saracens, defeated and scattered them, so that they did not dare rally or recover themselves. Rather, the Christians pursued them through the streets, striking and killing them. One part fled out through Saint Stephen’s Gate, another through the Gate of Jehoshaphat, another toward the Temple and Mount Sion, descending down from the walls. When those coming from [Col. 1013A] Bethlehem approached the city, they saw the rout and recognized the pursuit; they spurred after those fleeing, overtook and killed several. It was found that, inside and outside, fully two thousand or more were dead.

They then sent to the host to announce the news. The messenger found the host at the Knights’ Tower; when he had told them the news, they were greatly glad and did not advance farther, but returned to Acre.

Above all, the emperor, under cover of these events and with the pope’s knowledge, had three hundred knights and two hundred crossbowmen and mounted sergeants equipped. At Brindisi he had horses, arms, and provisions loaded into twenty-eight transport ships. They set sail and travelled until they arrived at Gavata, the point before Limassol. When they arrived, they dropped anchor and stayed there awaiting their commander, [Col. 1013B] Richard, son of Augier, the emperor’s marshal, who was to set out after them with fifteen galleys.

### VII. The emperor orders John of Ibelin expelled from the kingdom of Cyprus. The king refuses to do so.
