When the transport ships were to depart from Brindisi, a ship of the German Hospital sailed ahead of them and came to Acre. A spy of John of Ibelin, lord of Beirut, came aboard it and informed him of the arrival of the emperor’s men and all their purpose. Therefore John came immediately to Acre, gathered as many men as he could have, some for pay and some among his friends, went to Beirut, and from there to Cyprus.

When he arrived, he took the king and a small company and went to lodge at Quit. He had all the rest of his men, knights and sergeants, quartered at Limassol, and made Balian, his eldest son, their commander.

At that time two galleys arrived at Limassol. In them were the bishop of Melfi and two knights who held their fiefs at Acre. One was called the German; the other, John of Balle; they were Flemings. They asked for the king in order to speak with him, and were told that he was at Quit. They departed from Limassol with their galleys and went to Quit, where the king was lodged.

When they arrived, they said to the king in the lord of Beirut’s presence: “My lord, the emperor commands you, as one who is his man, to dismiss and expel from your land John of Ibelin, his children, nephews, and kinsmen. They have wronged him; therefore he commands and forbids you to receive or protect them in your land.”

The king, who was a child and young in age, took counsel and had one of his knights, his man, named William the viscount, answer for him. He said: “Lords, the king has commanded and charged me to tell you that he is amazed that the emperor, your lord, has given him such a command; for the lord of Beirut is the uncle of his mother, and it is well known that he, his nephews, and a great part of his kin are his men. Therefore he cannot fail them. Saving the emperor’s grace, the king cannot [Col. 1014A] and ought not do what you have asked him; if he did, he would wrong them.”

After this John of Ibelin rose and said to the king: “Lord, I am your man, and I ask you to maintain me in my right, for I am ready to do right before you and in your court, if anyone has any claim against me.”

Thereupon the messengers rose and said to the king: “Lord, you have well understood what we have told you on the emperor’s behalf, and we have understood your reply.” Then they departed, withdrew to their galleys, and went to Gavata, where their transport ships were.

### VIII. The castle of Beirut is besieged.

When those in the transport ships had waited there several days for the marshal, who was their commander, and saw that he did not come, they took counsel and departed from Gavata. They sailed until they came to an island before Beirut. There they disembarked, unloaded their horses, armed themselves, formed into squadrons, and rode in ordered squadrons toward the city of Beirut.

When the people of Beirut saw them coming, some entered the castle; others opened the city gates and received them. Thus the newcomers spread through the city and lodged in the houses, where they found great abundance of provisions and other things. They began to besiege the castle and make engines. They made a great trebuchet which threw a weight of one quintal. Between lesser trebuchets and mangonels there were one hundred and twenty. They pressed the men in [Col. 1014C] the castle so hard that no one could enter or leave.

### IX. Emperor Frederick appoints Richard, son of Augier, administrator of the kingdom.

After this, it was not long before Marshal Richard, son of Augier, arrived at Limassol with all fifteen galleys. When he came there and learned that the transports had gone to Beirut, he set out from there, went by sea, and came to Beirut. He found the siege there, maintained it as it had been begun, and pressed it as vigorously as he could. Thereupon he sent his brother Henry to Tyre and instructed him to tell Aimery of Layron to surrender to him Tyre, which he held in custody. The latter received the order and delivered up the city and the castle. When the marshal had been for some time at Beirut, he went with all speed to Acre.

[Col. 1014D] When he had arrived there, he assembled the knights and burgesses. When they had all gathered at the castle before the great palace, he had a letter read in their presence, sealed with a golden seal and sent on behalf of Emperor Frederick to all the people of the kingdom. It contained many fine and friendly words, and among other things said: “I have sent you the emperor’s marshal, Richard, son of Augier, legate of Macoste, to be bailiff of the kingdom, to uphold justice and right, and to preserve great and small, rich and poor alike in their rights.”

When these letters had been read, Richard rose and said: “Lords, you have heard the letters of my lord the emperor; and just as they declare, so he has commanded me, and I am ready [Col. 1015A] to act by the counsel of the worthy men of the land.” If his conduct and deeds had corresponded to his words and the letters, the people of the country would indeed have remained at peace and accepted him as bailiff. But not long afterward in the land his behaviour proved altogether different: he revealed his heart and intention, as one who was proud and arrogant and not very well endowed with sense. Thus the people of the land perceived that his purpose was to destroy everything and reduce it to nothing.

### X. Balian’s address to Richard, administrator of the kingdom, which he holds in little regard

When they had perceived this and were certain of his wickedness and ill will, they assembled, [Col. 1015B] took counsel, and by common agreement came before Marshal Richard. Balian of Sidon said to him:

“They have charged me to say a word to you on my own behalf and theirs. They make known to you that, when this land was conquered, it was not conquered through any lord’s misfortune, but by crusading, pilgrims, and people gathered together. When they had conquered it, they made a lord by common agreement and election, and gave him lordship over the kingdom. Afterwards, by common agreement and with the knowledge of the worthy men, they established ordinances and assizes, which they wished to be observed and used in the kingdom, for the preservation of the lord and the other people and for the maintenance of right. Then they swore them and caused [Col. 1015C] the lord to swear them; and from that time until now every lord who has been in the kingdom has sworn them, and the emperor likewise ought to swear them.

“Among the other ordinances and assizes is this assize: no lord can or ought to dispossess anyone of his property without judgment. Yet John of Ibelin, lord of Beirut, who is the emperor’s man—and you, who stand in his place to guard the land and uphold right—have laid hands upon these possessions and tenures, dispossessed him of the city of Beirut and the surrounding lands, and besieged his castle without the decision of a court and without judgment. Therefore we require of you, by right and reason, and to preserve the oath and faith of your lord the emperor, that you and your men withdraw from Beirut. Thus [Col. 1015D] the lord of Beirut may be restored to his possession. If you wish to bring any charge or claim against him, summon him according to the usage of the kingdom and proceed against him by the judgment of the land. If he is cast by judgment of court, we are ready to assist you to the full extent of our power and to do what is necessary for amends to be made.”

### XI.

When Marshal Richard heard this speech, he was greatly astonished that they had ever dared to say it. For he thought that no one would dare oppose anything he wished to do. But he now saw clearly that the matter would not proceed as he had intended. Nevertheless, he disclosed what he could not remedy and told them that he could not answer concerning this until he had taken counsel with the great men of the empire who had come with him and were at Beirut. But he would go [Col. 1016A] there and take counsel with them, and they should send him their reply there.

Thereupon he departed early the next morning and went to Beirut. When he arrived, he constrained and harassed the castle more severely than before. John of Sidon, John of Caesarea, Hugh of Montbéliard, Garnier the German, and the other knights of the kingdom sent two knights to Beirut to request the marshal’s reply, as he had promised them. One of these knights was named Reynald of Haifa, chamberlain of the kingdom, and the other was Daniel of Malembec. When these men arrived at Beirut, they notified the marshal that they had come to hear his answer to what the emperor’s men had said and required of him.

His answer was this: “Lords,” [Col. 1016B] he said, “I make known to you that I am the emperor’s man and am bound to carry out his command. Therefore I wish everyone to know that I do not wish to transgress in anything that is reasonable. For it is well known how John of Ibelin has shown and conducted himself toward the emperor—not because I am only a serjeant and the emperor is lord. If you consider that the emperor does anything to you which he ought not to do, send word to him; he is so good and loyal a lord that he will set it right as he ought.”

The messengers returned to Acre and reported the marshal’s answer to those who had sent them.

### XII. The inhabitants of the kingdom seek to defend their immunities and privileges

[Col. 1016C]

When the people of the kingdom heard the reply, they understood clearly that the marshal’s intention was as they had been led to believe. They reflected that, unless they took counsel for themselves and their cause, they were in a bad position. Therefore the wisest and most prudent among them took counsel together. They saw that they had no other recourse except to be bound together by oath to preserve and protect their rights, claims, and the franchises of the kingdom.

They then remembered that in the land there was a confraternity of Saint Adrian, granted by King Baldwin and confirmed by his privilege. This confraternity had established ordinances, regulations, and privileges. Among [Col. 1016D] its other ordinances was this: all those who wished to enter this confraternity could be received by the brothers and members of the confraternity. Then all the knights, burgesses, and great men assembled. When they had gathered, they summoned the counsellors of the confraternity and the privileges. When these had come, they brought forward the two charters of privilege and had them read. Then they considered the confraternity, and most of the people swore it, willingly doing so from fear of Marshal Richard’s household. Thus they were bound to one another. Afterwards this was reported to Cyprus, to make it known to John of Ibelin, lord of Beirut.

### XIII. John of Ibelin asks the king of Cyprus to assist him in recovering his land, and the king grants this

[Col. 1017A]

When he learned what had been done at Acre and among the people of the kingdom in the manner you have heard, he was greatly pleased. It seemed to him that this was substantial aid in maintaining his cause. He came to King Henry, who was still under age, and said before the barons whom he had assembled:

“Lord, you know that I am your man; therefore I make known to you what foreign people have done to me and are still doing: great violence and great wrong. They have taken and seized my city of Beirut and the surrounding land, and have seized my castle of Beirut. Therefore I pray you, as my lord and as one bound to help me, to deliver and rescue [Col. 1017B] my land and castle of Beirut. Come yourself and bring the men who are here; and I pray all of them, as my friends and brothers, to provide counsel and aid.”

The king answered that he would willingly go and bring as many of his men as he could. The king’s men who were there replied that they were ready to help him. Some would very unwillingly have granted it, had they dared refuse it; and afterwards, when they saw the time had come, they showed this clearly.

They arranged for ships to be procured, had galleys armed, and gathered at Famagusta. There they awaited favourable weather, until they set out on the first day of Lent. They crossed in very calm weather and landed at the Hill of the Constable, between Nefin and Bouceron; there they all disembarked. Then it happened that Amaury, Balian, and Aimery of Besançon, Eudes of Gibelet, and their companions fled by night, leaving their armour and lodgings, and went to Tripoli. Marshal Richard sent them a galley there, in which they went to Beirut. The reason why they withdrew from the king was that they said the king was under age and under another’s control, while they were men of the emperor directly and owed him a stronger allegiance than they did the king.

### XIV. He likewise asks the barons then at Acre

Afterwards John of Ibelin departed from the Hill and took [Col. 1017D] the king with his army. He crossed the Hill and went before Gibelet, continuing until they came before Beirut at a place called Senefil. There they lodged beside the river.

When they had arrived, John of Ibelin sent a messenger to Acre, one of his squires named Droon. He sent several letters to Balian of Sidon and John of Caesarea, who were his sister’s sons, and to many other friends; he also sent a letter to the community of the land. These letters contained the following after the greeting:

“Lords, I make known to you that foreign people from other lands have fallen upon me, seized and taken my city and land, and besieged my castle. Since I have no power to come to you [Col. 1018A] or to send you my men, for they are shut up in my castle, I make known my need to you by these letters. In them I pray, require, and summon you, as my brothers and friends, to support me according to the usages and customs of the kingdom of Jerusalem, and to help me recover and deliver my city, castle, and land.”

These letters were read in Balian of Sidon’s house, where most of the emperor’s men had gathered. John of Caesarea requested an answer for his uncle John of Ibelin. It came about that a great part agreed that they ought to help and rescue him, and offered themselves for that purpose. The others said that they had not considered the matter.

Those who agreed to go [Col. 1018B] were John of Caesarea, Bohart of Haifa and his father Reynald, Geoffrey the Strong, Geoffrey of Estreni, Baldwin of Bonvoisin, and other knights, sixty-three in all. They equipped themselves, set out, and came to where the king of Cyprus was with John of Ibelin. Then the Cypriot host moved from Senefil and lodged near the city at a place called Loros.

They remained there until Gerard, patriarch of Jerusalem; Peter, archbishop of Caesarea; John of Sidon; Hugh of Montbéliard; Brother Garin, master of the Hospital of Saint John; Brother Hermann of Pierregort, master of the Temple; the bailiff of Venice; and the councils of Pisa and Genoa departed from Acre and went to [Col. 1018C] Beirut. They lodged below the city and spoke to both parties to discover whether they could bring about counsel and peace. After speaking sufficiently with the two sides, they saw that they could accomplish nothing in any way, and so withdrew and returned to Acre.

John of Ibelin saw and knew that he was accomplishing nothing where he was. Nor had he used force to harass those before Beirut who had besieged his castle. For, had they been in the open field, they would have had to give battle against the Cypriots; for he had more mounted and foot soldiers than John of Ibelin possessed.

### XV. John of Ibelin goes to Acre and urges the people to seize the marshal’s transports. He besieges Tyre

[Col. 1018D]

When he understood this, he departed from the place where he was, took King Henry and the Cypriot army with him, and went to Sidon. There he left Anseau of Brie to guard it for him, with the greater part of the army; he took the others with him and went to Acre. When he arrived, he assembled the people of the city—knights, burgesses, and the rest of the populace—and before them all swore the confraternity of Saint Adrian at the church lectern.

After he had sworn, he addressed all the people, made his complaint, and told them that the transports belonging to their adversaries had arrived and were still in the harbour, and that they could still inflict great damage upon them. Therefore he advised that they should be detained. As soon as [Col. 1019A] he had said this, a cry rose in the church: everyone called out against the transports. They immediately moved and ran to the sea, entered boats, went to the transports, and seized seventeen of them; one escaped, being at the quay.

The reason they found the transports at Acre was this: when the Lombards had disembarked at Beirut, the marshal had sent them to Acre to winter, because he thought he would have the whole land at his command. But in this he found himself deceived. When the transports had been taken, as you have heard, the marshal, who was at Tyre, learned it and was greatly distressed.

After the transports had been seized, the king departed from Sidon and came to Acre. Once he had arrived, John of Ibelin took counsel and resolved, with the court, the people [Col. 1019B] of the city, and their assistance, to besiege Tyre; the Genoese aided him in men and provisions. Thus he set out and encamped at Casal Imbert.

When Marshal Richard heard of this undertaking, he sent to Beirut to his third brother, who was acting in his place, ordering him to raise the siege and bring the army to Tyre. He did this because he feared the arrival of the force that was to go before Tyre. The third brother did what his brother had commanded: he set fire to the engines, departed from Beirut, took the men with him, as well as the galleys and other vessels, and came to Tyre.

### XVI. Marshal Richard captures the unsuspecting Cypriots

When John of Ibelin learned the news that those of the army before Beirut had departed, abandoned the siege, and come to Tyre, he was greatly pleased. He returned to Acre and left the king with the Cypriots near Casal Imbert, at the Sablon towards Acre.

While John of Ibelin was at Acre taking counsel as to what he should do, the marshal at Tyre learned of the Cypriots’ plan. He prepared his men and galleys, departed Tyre at the first hour, and travelled throughout the night. At dawn, they fell upon the Cypriots’ camp by land and sea and captured them. They found most of them in their beds, and very few were able properly to arm themselves.

Spies had given them warning at nightfall. But Anseau of Brie, whom John of Ibelin had left as commander of the army in his place, would not believe the spies. Rather, he mocked them and said that it was very difficult to believe that the enemy would come six leagues by such bad roads to attack them, when they had not done so while they were two bowshots from them before Beirut. Therefore he would take no precautions and would not guard himself against his enemies. He had nevertheless appointed knights for the watch, as he did every evening; but those on watch were not on the side from which the enemy would come. Instead, they were stationed outside the camp, towards Acre, sitting in a tent wholly unarmed in their beds beneath their hawks. The captain of these watchmen was John of Ibelin, nephew of the lord of Beirut.

### XVII. The king of Cyprus is taken to Acre

[Col. 1020A]

When the men of Apulia had fallen upon the camp, the outcry was very great. A knight who was the king’s tutor and guardian put him on a horse and entrusted him to men who took him to Acre. He himself remained in the fighting, where he was captured and very badly wounded in the face. This knight was named John Babin.

Such Cypriots as could mount their horses, armed or unarmed, gathered together in one part and defended themselves. There were good blows until daylight came; then they found themselves few in number and unable to bear the burden, so they withdrew into a settlement. For one part of their people had taken counsel about nothing except going towards Acre. Then the men of [Col. 1020B] Apulia struck the camp, and those from the galleys disembarked and did likewise. They thought only of plunder, and so took everything the Cypriots had in their camp and carried the booty to Tyre.

As soon as the cry and news came to Acre, John of Ibelin, lord of Beirut, Balian of Sidon, Hugh of Montbéliard, John of Caesarea, Rohard of Haifa, and the other knights of Acre sprang to arms and went without delay as far as Casal Imbert. There they found those who had withdrawn into the settlement. Then they all passed the Casal and hurried to the foot of the mountain called Passe-Poulain. When they came there, they found that the others had already crossed the pass; seeing that they could not catch them, they returned [Col. 1020C] to Acre.

The day on which this affair happened was Tuesday, the third day of May, in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1232. On that day King Henry of Cyprus completed his fifteenth year of age.

### XVIII. John of Ibelin withdraws with the king to Cyprus

When the Cypriots returned to Acre, they found themselves in great hardship and poverty, having all returned naked, as it were. They had lost arms, garments, clothing, money, and jewels, and had brought back nothing except what they wore and the horse upon which they sat. They were so dismayed and alarmed by this that it was scarcely otherwise than that a great part of them would have turned to the other side and carried off the king with them, for he was a child and easily deceived.

When John of Ibelin perceived this, he showed no sign of it, but concealed his thoughts and considered what he could do. He arranged for John of Caesarea, his nephew, to sell to another of his nephews a casal called Caferlet for sixteen thousand bezants; and his other nephew, John of Ibelin, sold to the Temple another casal called Arames for fifteen thousand bezants. When they had assembled this money, he gathered all the Cypriots, encouraged them, and lent them part of these funds. With the other part he took men, armed galleys and ships, and prepared to cross into Cyprus. He took the king with him and arranged that the king granted fiefs to several knights, in order to take them with him to Cyprus. Then they loaded the transports that had belonged to the men of [Col. 1021A] Apulia, and loaded the horses and other equipment into the other vessels, and made ready to depart.

### XIX. Richard conquers a great part of the kingdom of Cyprus

Now let us return to Marshal Richard. After he had inflicted the defeat at Casal Imbert, he sent the Cypriots who were with him, together with some of his own men, to Cyprus. When they had arrived in Cyprus, they obtained the castle and city of Keryneia, the Caudare, and the tower of Famagusta, and besieged Dieudamors.

Within the castle of Dieudamors were two sisters of the king, Lady Mary and Lady Isabel. There was also a castellan named Philip of Cafran, and Ernoul of Gibelet, whom the lord of Beirut had left as commander [Col. 1021B] in the land. He made very little provision, so that he did not even supply the castle in which the king’s two sisters were, nor did he himself do so. It would have had to be surrendered because of the shortage of food and the great distress, and they endured great hardship until they were rescued.

As soon as the marshal learned that the Cypriots at Acre were preparing to go to Cyprus, he departed from Tyre. He took his men with him, except for a few whom he left to guard Tyre, and crossed to Cyprus. When he arrived there, he sent his men throughout the land, so that he had the whole country in his hand and under his command except the castle of Dieudamors and the castle of Bufavent.

### XX. King Henry returns to Cyprus and pursues Richard

[Col. 1021C] King Henry and the Cypriots who were with him embarked and departed from the harbour of Acre on the day of Pentecost. They went as far as Sidon; from there they set out for Cyprus, arrived on the island before Famagusta, and disembarked without resistance or opposition. Marshal Richard was in the city of Famagusta with all his army, yet they offered no opposition to the landing. Rather, at midnight that evening, he had the galleys in the harbour set on fire and did not stop until he came to Nicosia with all his men.

The king, John of Ibelin, and those with him crossed the island on the next day, went on, and lodged within the city. After they had been there two days, they departed on the third and travelled by short stages until they [Col. 1021D] came to Nicosia. As soon as the marshal learned that they were approaching, he and all his men departed and went to lodge between the mountain and the valley of the hill, on the road which leads from Nicosia to Keryneia, where they remained.

The king, John of Ibelin, and those with him left Nicosia on the very day they entered it and lodged outside the city in a place called Tracona. From there they departed early the next morning, on Tuesday, the eleventh day of June, and rode towards where their enemies were. They continued until they came near a casal called La Gride. There they wished to lodge, and some of their equipment and serjeants had already entered the casal, while the others followed. When they looked about them, they saw the men of Apulia descending the pass towards them, their squadrons divided and assigned each to its own commander, all prepared for battle.

### XXI. Battle between the Cypriots and the Apulians, who are defeated

When the Cypriots recognized that they were coming to fight, they prepared and advanced towards them. They approached until they collided, and the battle lasted a long time between them. Many were unhorsed. But one thing greatly aided the Cypriots: they had foot-serjeants. Thus, when one of their knights was unhorsed, the serjeants raised him and put him back on horseback; but when one of the others was unhorsed, the serjeants immediately killed or captured him. Therefore [Col. 1022B] many of the men of Apulia were killed and captured in that battle. More than sixty knights were killed and fully forty of the Apulians captured. Of the Cypriots only one knight died, named Sierge, a native of Tuscany.

When the battle had lasted so long, the men of Apulia could endure no longer or bear the burden, for they were receiving too much damage. They left the field and retreated in defeat up the pass towards Keryneia. The Cypriots attacked and pursued them; they went on together in a confused mêlée and drove them as far as the gates of Keryneia, where they took refuge with great difficulty.

### XXII. Richard withdraws into Armenia. King Henry besieges Keryneia

[Col. 1022C] When the Cypriots had won the battle and gained the field, as you have heard, they returned to a place on a hillside at the foot of the mountain and lodged there. The marshal saw that he was enclosed and that he had enough men and provisions; accordingly, he sent to Jaffa for the galleys that were there. When they had come to him, he appointed such men as he wished to remain at Keryneia, while he and the others withdrew into Armenia and entered [“en la fois,” reading uncertain]. There the king and his father Constantine received and honoured them greatly. They remained there for a long time, until illness took hold among them. Consequently many died, and most were ill. When they saw [Col. 1022D] that they could not remain in the country, they departed and went to Tyre.

As soon as those of whom you have heard left Keryneia for Armenia, King Henry and his men lodged beside the walls of Keryneia and besieged it so closely that no one could leave or enter. Through the battle which had taken place, the king and the men with him remained securely and peacefully in his lordship.

The siege before Keryneia lasted until after Easter. Then an agreement was made: King Henry released and restored all the prisoners whom he held, and they restored Keryneia to him, together with all the prisoners whom they had captured at Casal Imbert and all the ladies whom they had taken in Nicosia, in churches, and in religious houses when they entered the land.

### XXIII. Death of Queen Alice and of Bohemond; war between the sultan of Hama and the Hospital

[Col. 1023A]

While the siege was before Keryneia, Queen Alice, King Henry’s wife and daughter of the marquis of Montferrat, who had shut herself up within Keryneia with the men of Apulia, was delivered of a child while ill in bed from an illness of which she died. When she had died, those within Keryneia prepared her as a queen should be prepared. Then they requested a safe-conduct from the king to send a man to speak to him. The safe-conduct was granted, and the man came to the king and told him that the queen, his wife, had departed this world; those within Keryneia sent word that, if it pleased him, he should have her taken and buried as befitted a queen and should do with her as with his wife.

The king agreed. A truce was given, so that no one shot from outside or within until the queen was brought out and carried to the king’s camp. Then those in Keryneia’s castle put her outside; those outside received her and bore her to Nicosia with a very great company of people. She was honourably buried in the mother church of Saint Sophia by Archbishop Estorquet.

Not long afterward Bohemond IV, prince of Antioch and count of Tripoli, departed this world. Thus Bohemond V, his son, succeeded him and held the two lordships.

At that time the sultan of Hama refused to pay the Hospital of Saint John a payment which he had customarily rendered for the Crac. Therefore the truce between the Hospital and the sultan was broken, and the Hospital assembled men to wage war upon the sultan of Hama. Present in this force were Brother Hermann of Pierregort, master of the Temple, with his whole convent; one hundred knights from Cyprus, commanded by John of Ibelin, lord of Beirut; Walter, count of Brienne, who in that same year had married Mary, sister of King Henry, then living in Cyprus, where the king had given him land; and eighty knights of the kingdom, commanded by Peter of Avalon, nephew of Hugh of Montbéliard. Henry, brother of the prince, was also there with thirty knights whom his brother had assigned to him, because the prince himself could not go owing to the truce he had with the sultan of Hama.

Brother Garnier, master of the Hospital of Saint John, assembled all this force. He had with him his whole convent and all his power; and in that army there were fully one hundred knights, eighty mounted serjeants, and more than fifteen hundred foot-serjeants.

### XXIV. They make peace. The Knights of the Temple also make peace with the Armenians

When all this force had assembled and they were at the entrance above the Crac, after they had remained there two days, they departed at nightfall and rode throughout the night, so that at dawn they were at Montferrand. They advanced towards the town, and the town was taken and pillaged. But few people were found there, because those who had been in it fled into the castle as soon as they saw the Christians moving and coming against them. They had enough time to gather themselves [Col. 1024A] inside the castle, since the streets and entrances of the town were barred by good towers and strong walls, which the Christians had to destroy before they could enter.

When they had taken what they found and had demolished and devastated a great part of the town, they went on and lodged two leagues from there at a casal with a spring called Mergemit. They remained there two days and sent out their foragers and raiders through the land; these plundered the casals and carried off the booty. On the third day they left and returned before Montferrand. If anything remained in the town to take or destroy, they did not spare it.

From there they went to lodge at a casal called Lafonsaquiée. The next day they returned [Col. 1024B] to the entrance from which they had departed. After they had been there about eight days and intended to make another new raid, news came to them that the sultan of Babylon and his brother the Seraph, with fifteen thousand mounted men and a great number of foot-serjeants, had departed Damascus and come to Hama in order to go towards the frontier between themselves and the sultan of Iconium, with whom they were at war.

When they arrived there and learned of the Hospital’s affair, they halted in order to settle the business of the sultan of Hama, who was their sister’s son. Thus peace was made between him and the Hospital, and from that time forward the payment which had been withheld from them was restored. Then the men dispersed, each going to his own region.

When the master of the Temple and his brothers [Col. 1024C] had departed from that affair, they joined the prince of Antioch. Each brought his full force, and they went into Armenia to avenge an outrage which the king of Armenia had committed against the Temple: he had had an unspecified number of their brothers—some hanged, others flayed, because, he said, they wished to bring people into the land in order to harm him. The prince willingly joined in this undertaking because of the hatred he bore the king of Armenia and his father over what they had done to his brother Philip.

When Constantine, the king’s father, saw the force coming against him, he was afraid and sent word to the master of the Temple that he wished to make an agreement with him. This he did; he and the king made amends to the Templars for what they had done wrong. Thus the Templars [Col. 1024D] remained fully at peace and returned home, which greatly displeased the prince, for he would gladly have avenged himself in some measure upon his enemies.

### XXV. Envoys sent to Rome make peace with the emperor, which is disapproved by the inhabitants of the kingdom
At that point the people of the kingdom of Jerusalem sent envoys to Rome concerning the arrangement made by Haymar, master of the Hospital of the Germans, in order to negotiate between them and the emperor. The envoys were two knights of Acre, Philip of Tyre and Henry of Nazareth. When they had come to Rome, they did everything that the master of the Germans wished, wholly in accordance with the emperor’s pleasure, and received his letters, sealed with his seal, setting forth the terms of the peace. When they had returned to Acre [Col. 1025A] and delivered the letters, they were read aloud. When the people of the kingdom learned the terms of the peace from the tenor of the letters, they were greatly angered—and with good reason: for that peace was to their harm and disgrace, and contrary to the command and authority which the envoys had received. Thus they reviled them, held them to be traitors and false men, and scarcely refrained from doing violence to their persons.

The people of the kingdom took counsel and, by common agreement, sent to the king of Cyprus. Thus it came about that the king of Cyprus and those of the kingdom of Jerusalem jointly sent an envoy to the pope at Rome, to excuse themselves and show why they ought not to receive that peace; for they maintained to the pope [Col. 1025B] that the peace had been made before him and with his knowledge. The envoy whom they sent was a knight of Cyprus who was from Syria, but had gone to live in Cyprus on account of a great fief which King Henry had granted him. The king later made him chamberlain of Cyprus. This knight was called Geoffrey Le Tort; and for this reason the king joined in the common cause of the people of the kingdom of Jerusalem.

### XXVI. Geoffrey Le Tort comes to the pope, who also condemns the peace. Death of the sultan of Babylon.

The peace of which we have spoken was greatly to his harm. He departed from Cyprus and came to Acre, where he received letters from the barons of the land, together with their instructions and those he had received from the king of Cyprus. Then [Col. 1025C] he embarked on a Genoese ship and crossed to Genoa; from there he went to Viterbo, where the pope and the entire court were. He brought fine and rich gifts to the pope and cardinals, delivered his message, and showed the pope the points and reasons why that peace should not be accepted.

The pope received him graciously and listened very willingly. He replied that it was no wonder that they rejected it. For from the very time when it had been made, he had regarded it as false and evil; and he could do no otherwise. For the envoys said that they had authority to do what they had done, and that, if they said they would not observe it, that was within their own power and no force would be used against them. Rather, he promised them the aid and support of the Church, and sent them letters [Col. 1025D] in which he commanded that the two kingdoms should be one thing. He ordered the four regions of Acre and all the communes subject to the king of Cyprus and his land, and those of the kingdom of Jerusalem, to assist in guarding and defending them and their possessions. He gave this command very particularly; and he sent the same command to the podestà and commune of Genoa.

Geoffrey Le Tort obtained all these letters, and many others, from Pope Gregory. He carried them away, returned to Genoa, embarked there upon a ship, crossed to Acre, and then went from there to Cyprus.

At this time the sultan of Babylon died; he was called al-Kāmil. His second son, called al-Malik al-ʿĀdil, remained in his place and became sultan, because his elder son, called al-Malik al-Ṣāliḥ, was in the land of the East which his father had given him, and had made him sultan there during his own lifetime. At this time Bohemond, prince of Antioch and count of Tripoli, had separated from Queen Alice, because it had been found that he was related to her within the third and fourth degrees through King Hugh of Cyprus, whose wife she had been. After his separation, he did not wish to remain without a wife; accordingly he sent to Rome, and Luciana, daughter of Count Paul, son of Count Richard, who had been brother to the good Pope Innocent, was brought to him. King Henry of Cyprus then married Stephanie, daughter of King Hethum of Armenia, and had her crowned also, as he had crowned Alice, daughter of the marquis of Montferrat.

### XXVII. Emperor Frederick enters Lombardy and attacks the Milanese.

[Col. 1026B]

At this time Emperor Frederick assembled a great host and entered Lombardy. All who adhered to him received him with great joy: the city of Cremona and all the cities which supported him. Opposed to him were the city of Milan and all the cities of its party. Then a great and fierce war began between them and lasted a long time. At last the men of Milan could no longer bear the burden and withdrew from the field like defeated men. But many people were killed and captured on both sides. The podestà of Milan, son of the doge of Venice, was captured; the emperor had him hanged in the land of Trani from a high tower standing on the shore of the sea.

Thereupon the Milanese captured [Col. 1026C] a son of the emperor, called Enzo. He was taken at the siege of the castle called Gorgonzola. The carroccio of Milan was also captured and carried to Cremona, where it was placed in the principal church of the city. The carroccio is the great banner set upon a four-wheeled cart. This Enzo, the emperor’s son who was captured, was the son of a high-born German lady, and his father had made him king of Sardinia. Yet he was not long in prison, for the Germans took him back from the castle in which he had been imprisoned.

After this battle the emperor went to besiege with great force a strong city belonging to the district of Milan, called Vicenza. He pressed it hard by siege and assault, and caused a town to be built which he called Victory. [Col. 1026D] The people of Vicenza were greatly distressed, for they could neither leave nor enter, and expected aid from no side. When they saw themselves in such misery, which had endured a long time, they began to lack provisions; and the thirst was so severe that a great number of them lost their teeth. Therefore they resolved to risk all, judging it better than waiting longer in the condition in which they were. They watched their opportunity, came out suddenly and vigorously, attacked the emperor’s camp, routed it, and won the victory. They set fire to Victory and burned it entirely. Thus they were freed from the siege and hardship in which they had been.

### XXVIII. Pope Gregory summons a general council, whose routes Frederick blocks. He captures the envoys and casts them into chains.

[Col. 1027A]

At that time Pope Gregory, who was born at Anagni, a city one day’s journey from Rome, wished to assemble a general council in order to proceed against the emperor. He therefore sent beyond the mountains to summon the prelates to come to him at Rome. When the emperor learned this, he caused their road to be obstructed, so that they could not pass through his land. The pope then sent to the Genoese, asking and summoning them to send galleys to Provence to bring the prelates from beyond the mountains to Rome.

For love of the pope and in hostility to the emperor, the Genoese sent no fewer than sixty armed vessels. Their admiral—that is, their commander—was a Genoese of the lineage of the Embriaci, called William the Black. This William was proud and overbearing, and showed it well in this affair, for through his arrogance the whole undertaking was lost.

The Genoese fleet went to a city in Provence which stands on the sea and is called Nice. There the prelates assembled in a great multitude, with a cardinal among them who had gone as legate beyond the mountains and was bishop of Palestrina. Once assembled, they set out to come to the mouth of the Tiber, which runs through Rome. When the emperor learned of this, he sent into the kingdom and had galleys and other vessels armed. He also asked the Pisans to assist him with armed ships, [Col. 1027C] which they willingly did. So many vessels were equipped that their ships and those of the kingdom amounted to forty armed vessels. Their admiral was a valiant man of Pisa called Ugolino Bonaccorsi.

When these vessels had assembled, they positioned themselves at a port called Ferrara, in a region named Lecce. The Genoese fleet was approaching; and when it reached the end of the island of Corsica, it learned the news of the emperor’s fleet, which lay in wait on its route. They took counsel and agreed to avoid battle and sail outside the islands; and they could easily have done so, had they wished. But William the Black, being such as you have heard before, spoke first and said that the Genoese would never avoid battle with the Pisans or Lombards, and that he would pass through them to their shame and that of their lord.

He therefore headed toward them. Had he gone as one ought to go into battle against one’s enemies, and arranged his vessels as the business required, it might have profited him; for he had greater strength in ships and men than they possessed. But he made no arrangement and devised no plan. As soon as he saw them near, he shouted to attack them. Ugolino had arranged his ships and set a vanguard and rearguard. They came together and clashed at Permerains, so that in the first encounter they captured three Genoese galleys. Thereby the others were thrown into defeat [Col. 1028A] and fled. The Pisans and men of the kingdom did not pursue them, but held fast to the galleys that fell into their hands, captured them, and made very great profit. They took a great multitude of prelates, including Cardinal Blanc, bishop of Palestrina, and a chaplain of the pope, legate at Genoa, called Gregory of Romagna. All these were brought to the emperor, who had them imprisoned throughout his lands.

### XXIX. Many who had taken the cross in France cross the sea.

At this time a very great crusading movement arose in the kingdom of France to cross into the land of Syria. Thus they left their country and went to Marseilles and Aigues-Mortes, where they embarked in ships to cross to Acre. In this expedition [Col. 1028B] were Theobald, king of Navarre and count of Champagne; Henry, count of Bar; Peter of Dreux, count of Brittany; the count of Forez, who was count of Nevers through his wife; Amaury, count of Montfort; John of Dreux, count of Mâcon; and many other rich men.

When these pilgrims came to Acre, they lodged throughout the city and outside it at the Sablon. There they took counsel and by common agreement set out to fortify Ascalon. They rode until they came to Jaffa. When they had arrived, a spy came to the Templars and informed them that at Gadres [perhaps Gaza] one thousand and fifty Turks were encamped, commanded by an emir called Croc Elgevi. When the Christians heard this news, they agreed that four hundred knights should undertake the expedition. The count of Bar went, and the count of Montfort, Balian of Sidon, Odo of Montbéliard, John of Arsuf, the Temple, and the Hospital. They left Jaffa at evening and rode until, at daybreak, they were near Gaza. Then they armed themselves and advanced in ordered squadrons toward the place where the Turks were encamped.

### XXX. The Christians are destroyed by the Turks.

When the Turks saw them coming toward them, they mounted and drew back toward a hill. Al-Kurj took counsel with his men, who advised him to leave, since he had not enough men to fight them. Croc Elgevi replied that they would have ample time to depart, but that he would send out his main force and test the Christians’ formation. He did as he had planned, sending two hundred Turks to skirmish.

As soon as the skirmishers approached, they began to retreat. The Christians began to lose formation and to press one another. When the skirmishers saw this, they hurried them more closely and kept near them. Al-Kurj perceived the Christians’ poor formation, came down from the hill where he had been, and advanced rapidly against our men. As soon as he and his people were near, they struck with their spurs and charged so closely among the Franks, because of the bad formation they had seen them make, that they dealt them very badly. The Christians, without taking any counsel [Col. 1029A] among themselves, fled in defeat; and whoever could escape did so.

Amaury, count of Montfort, was captured there, and the count of Bar was killed. A great multitude of knights, both secular and religious, were either killed or taken. All the foot-sergeants were lost, along with most of the equipment. Those who escaped from the battle came to Ascalon, where they found the king of Navarre, the count of Brittany, and the entire host. As soon as they arrived, so great a panic seized them all that it seemed to them the Saracens were about to come and capture them all. Consequently, as soon as night fell, every man set out for Jaffa without order and without waiting for another; they went like defeated men and left [Col. 1029B] a great abundance of provisions and equipment behind. When they reached Jaffa, they remained there very little time, then departed and did not stop until they came to Acre.

### XXXI. The sultan of Hama deceitfully offers his lands to the Christians.

When they had arrived there, they remained and stayed a long time without doing anything. Meanwhile a cleric of Tripoli, called William, came into the host and told the barons that the sultan of Hama sent them word that, if they would come through his land so that he might have the strength and aid of the Christians, he would put his fortresses into their hands and become a Christian. He sent this message with earnest prayers and requests that they would not delay.

The barons took counsel and agreed to pursue the matter. Then the host departed from Acre and rode all along the coast until they reached Tripoli. There they halted and lodged within the city of Mont-Pèlerin. From there they sent envoys to the sultan in the company of William the cleric, to learn whether he could carry out and complete what he had promised them. He pretended to seek terms, led them on with words for some time, and in the end failed them altogether, as one who was merely making mockery of them. The appearance which he had made was only because he feared the lady of Aleppo, the sultan’s mother, who was at war with him. That lady held the lordship of Aleppo because her son, the sultan, was a child and under age.

When the Christians perceived the sultan of Hama’s lie and deceit, after they had stayed some time before Tripoli and Bohemond, prince of Antioch, had honored them greatly, they departed and returned to Acre. But John, count of Mâcon, died at Tripoli and was buried in the church of the Hospital of Saint John.

### XXXII. The sultan of Damascus offers a truce to the Christians.

After they had come to Acre, not long afterward they went to lodge at the Palm Grove of Haifa, to pasture their horses. When that lodging ended, they went to lodge at the fountain of Sepphoris. While they were there [Col. 1030A], an envoy came to them from the sultan of Damascus to negotiate a truce.

This sultan was called al-Malik al-Ṣāliḥ. He had been, and still was, lord of Baalbek; he was son of al-ʿĀdil Sayf al-Dīn. The manner in which he became sultan of Damascus was as follows. When al-Ashraf died, al-Kāmil took Damascus, as you have heard above. After his death the city remained without a lord, because al-Kāmil’s elder son was in the land of the East in his own lordship and was called al-Malik al-Ṣāliḥ, just like his uncle of whom you have heard speak; and the other son, called al-ʿĀdil, was in Egypt, of which he was lord. Therefore, because of these circumstances, they chose a nephew of Saladin called al-Malik al-Jawād. He went to Damascus, was received as lord, was made sultan, and held the [Col. 1030B] land for a considerable time.

At length Ṣāliḥ, who was in the East, moved with a great host and came to Damascus. Al-Jawād went out against him, surrendered Damascus to him, and remained with him. He surrendered it because he saw that the people of Damascus would not support him against Ṣāliḥ. Ṣāliḥ prepared his army to go into Egypt and take the land from his brother, but did not go, because he saw clearly that he lacked the power to do it. With a great part of his people he returned to Damascus, and there stayed carelessly at Nablus.

The son of the sultan, called al-Nāṣir, who was at the Crac, learned that Ṣāliḥ was staying carelessly at Nablus. He therefore came suddenly from the Crac to Nablus, captured Ṣāliḥ, carried him to the Crac, and put him in prison in heavy irons. Ṣāliḥ [Col. 1030C] of Baalbek learned this, moved upon Damascus, and was received and made sultan.

### XXXIII. The truce is sworn.

It happened at that time, while the Christians were at Sepphoris, that this Ṣāliḥ of whom you have heard sent his envoy to the Franks. The matter proceeded so far that a truce was made between him and the Christians. For the truce he restored to them the castle of Beaufort and promised to restore all the land which the Franks had held from the coast to the Jordan River. They promised him that they would make neither truce nor peace with the sultan of Babylon without him and without his agreement; that they would assist him; and that they would lodge at Ascalon or Jaffa with all their forces [Col. 1030D] in order to prevent the sultan of Babylon from crossing the frontier and entering the land of Syria, where he was to encamp beside them at the place where the river of Jaffa issues forth.

All these agreements which you have heard were sworn by all the barons of the host, by the sultan, and by the emirs. In accordance with the agreement, he restored Beaufort, the land of Sidon, and that of Tiberias. The sultan of Babylon, against whom the sultan of Damascus had made these agreements with the Christians, was his nephew: namely, the Ṣāliḥ of whom you have heard that al-Nāṣir captured and put in prison at the Crac.

After capturing him, al-Nāṣir thought to recover the land of Damascus. But when he learned that their uncle Ṣāliḥ held Damascus, and saw that matters were not as he had believed, he conceived another plan. He told his cousin Ṣāliḥ, who was in his prison, [Col. 1031A] that if he would marry his sister and swear that he would aid him to the utmost of his power in obtaining Damascus, which had belonged to his father, then, when he had it, he would offer it to him to hold in good peace. Al-Nāṣir was ready, if Ṣāliḥ would do this, to bring his brother al-ʿĀdil into his hands and make him sultan of Babylon. He had secured the assent to this from part of the emirs of Babylon. Moreover, being one who had a great treasure left him by his father, he had given and promised great wealth.

### XXXIV. The king of Navarre, the count of Brittany, and the Hospitallers also swear a truce.

When Ṣāliḥ had given al-Nāṣir the security which he demanded, married his sister, and placed himself wholly in his power, al-Nāṣir secretly sent into [Col. 1031B] Babylon and arranged to be assured of the agreements which the emirs had promised and sworn to him. Then he gathered all his force quickly; he had seven hundred mounted Turks. Five hundred Turks came to Ṣāliḥ as soon as they learned that he had been released. They crossed the desert and traveled so secretly and as swiftly as they could that they reached Cairo.

Upon their arrival, they found that the emirs had captured their lord al-ʿĀdil and delivered him to his brother Ṣāliḥ, who put him in prison elsewhere; but he was never afterward seen. Thus Ṣāliḥ became sultan of the land of Egypt. This was the man whom the other Ṣāliḥ, sultan of Damascus, feared, and for this reason he allied himself with the Christians.

When the truce had been sworn as you have heard above, the Christians went to lodge at Jaffa. Ṣāliḥ of Damascus and the lord of Hama lodged with all their host at the head of the river. This truce, of which you have heard, had been procured and made through the influence of the Temple and without the agreement of the Hospital. Therefore the Hospital in turn procured a truce separately, apart from the Christians. The king of Navarre, the count of Brittany, and many other pilgrims swore it; nor did they refrain because of the oath they had made to the sultan of Damascus.

When this truce had been made in the manner you have heard, the king of Navarre, the count of Brittany, and the other pilgrims who had sworn it departed from Jaffa, went to Acre, hired ships, and crossed to their own lands. The master of the Hospital, Brother Peter of Vielle-Bride, [Col. 1031D] who had sworn the truce with the sultan of Damascus, departed from Jaffa with his convent and went to Acre, where he remained with the people of the land. The Temple, the count of Nevers, and part of the pilgrims remained at Jaffa. They would neither depart from nor withdraw from the agreements made with the sultan of Damascus. Thus the Christians ended in contention and discord, some adhering to one truce and others to the other.

### XXXV. Raoul of Soissons marries Alice, mother of the king of Cyprus, and obtains the administration of the kingdom of Jerusalem.

At the time when the pilgrims were at Acre, Alice, mother of the king of Cyprus, married a high nobleman of [Col. 1032A] France called Raoul of Soissons, brother of the count of Soissons. After marrying her, he came forward with the assent of part of the people of the country and claimed, for his wife the queen, the guardianship and lordship of the kingdom of Jerusalem. He claimed it because he was the nearest apparent heir in the land among the heirs of King Amalric, her grandfather, and because no one had been there since the death of his niece, Empress Isabella.

The people of the kingdom took counsel among themselves and replied that Queen Isabella, wife of the emperor, had had a son in Apulia, who was the rightful heir of the kingdom. But because he was neither present nor had ever been present, they would receive Alice as lady and deliver the kingdom to her keeping, while preserving the claims and rights [Col. 1032B] of King Conrad, son of Empress Isabella, her niece. And this was done.

When Raoul of Soissons acquired the lordship in the manner you have heard, he exercised it rather weakly. For those through whom he had been installed were kinsmen of his wife, the lady, and had more power and authority than he did. Thus he seemed no stronger than a shadow. In resentment, he abandoned everything, left his wife, and went away to his own country.

### XXXVI. Richard, brother of the king of England, crosses to the Holy Land and soon returns home.

In that passage to the Holy Cross in which the king of Navarre and the count of Brittany went, Richard, count of Cornwall and brother of [Col. 1032C] King Henry of England, came to Acre. He brought with him a fine company of knights and much wealth. When he arrived at Acre, he lodged in the house of the Hospital of Saint John. After he had stayed some time there, he and his men equipped themselves and went to Jaffa, where he lodged with the other Christians who were there.

While he was there, the Templars strongly urged him to adhere to and uphold the truce and agreements of the sultan of Damascus. The Hospitallers sent him messages and earnestly entreated him concerning this; indeed, they had discussed it with him at Acre itself, asking him to adhere to the truce of the sultan of Babylon. But he would do neither the one nor the other. Rather, he said that, if the Christians were at Jaffa and wished to go to lodge at Ascalon, he was ready to fortify the castle.

The barons of the host, the Templars, and the Hospital of the Germans took counsel and swore to what he requested, judging it to be a continuation by the Christians of the truce they had made with the sultan of Damascus and beneficial to Christendom. They agreed and departed from Jaffa. When they had procured workmen and everything necessary for the labor, they went to Ascalon. Upon arriving, they made their arrangements and began their work. The castle was fortified in the same fashion in which King Richard—the uncle of this Richard now fortifying it—had fortified it. When he had fortified it, he supplied it as well as he could.

Then he summoned from Jerusalem a knight called Walter of Penampié, who was bailiff there on the emperor’s behalf [Col. 1033A] and held the land of Jerusalem under the protection and truce of the sultan of Babylon. As soon as Walter came to Ascalon, Count Richard surrendered and delivered the castle to him, for him to guard on the emperor’s behalf. After doing this, he returned to Acre, hired his ship, and went to his own country. The host returned to Jaffa; and wherever the Christian host went, the sultan of Damascus, with all his host, was always encamped near them.

After they had remained a long while at Jaffa, the pilgrims who had remained after the others wished to return to their own country. They went to Acre, hired ships there, and crossed to their lands; and all the other Christians returned to Acre.

### XXXVII. Balian captures the city of Tyre.

[Col. 1033B] At that time Richard, marshal of the emperor, who was at Tyre, embarked in a ship to cross to Apulia to the emperor who had summoned him. When he departed, he left his brother Lothair in his place and entrusted to him the city and castle of Tyre.

After Richard had left, Balian of Ibelin, lord of Beirut, and Philip of Montfort, lord of Toron, worked so effectively that they obtained supporters in Tyre. They departed from Acre by night and rode until they came before Tyre. As soon as they were near the walls, those who supported them were all armed at the postern by the butchery and signaled to those outside. They struck spurs, entered the sea, and went along the city wall by the Hospital [Col. 1033C] of the Germans. They entered the city with those who awaited them and then went with great haste toward the castle.

Lothair, son of Augier, perceived what was happening, armed himself, left the lodging in which he was, and went to the castle. All the men of Apulia who were in the city made for the castle, if they could reach it. Thus the city of Tyre was taken from the emperor’s men.

### XXXVIII. Raoul of Soissons demands it and is refused. Innocent IV summons the Council of Lyons and cites the emperor before it. He excuses himself to the pope through envoys.

When Raoul of Soissons, who knew nothing of this undertaking, learned that Balian of Ibelin and Philip of Montfort had Tyre and held it, he and his wife Queen Alice departed [Col. 1033D] from Acre and came to Tyre. Once there, Raoul demanded from Balian and Philip, for himself and for the queen, the city of Tyre, which he wished to possess in the same manner as he possessed the other things of the kingdom. They replied that they would neither deliver nor hand it over to them, but would keep it until they knew to whom they ought to restore it. This was one of the reasons why Raoul of Soissons departed.

As you have heard, Pope Innocent IV saw that he could not assemble a council at Rome or in that region. He therefore sent to Genoa to ask that galleys be sent secretly to the mouth of the Tiber. When they had arrived, he left Rome, came there, embarked in the galleys, and went to Genoa. The reason he did these things at that time was [Col. 1034A] so that Emperor Frederick might not intercept him.

When he was at Genoa, he stayed there for some time; then he departed, crossed the mountains, and went to Lyons upon the Rhône. There he remained, summoned the prelates, and assembled all whom he could obtain. Then he sent envoys to the emperor and had him admonished concerning thirteen articles of accusation, commanding him to submit himself to the mercy of the Church. For previously he had informed him that he was accused of these matters; and because he had not come to answer the charges, he had made an inquiry against him and had found the accusations brought against him to be true. Thus he was convicted and proved guilty, and the pope wished him therefore to submit himself to the mercy of holy Church.

When the emperor heard the pope’s command, he sent his envoys to Lyons. One was the marquis of Froborc, and the other was his jurist and able advocate, called Master Peter of the Vines. They came before the pope, and when they stood before him Master Peter began to speak, saying:

“Lord, the emperor commends himself to your feet as to his lord and father. He makes known to you that he would have come to your feet to hear your command and obey in everything that should please you; but he has a bodily impediment, being sick in bed and unable to move. Therefore, lord, he asks you to grant him a delay until he can come to you to perform your commands. And if it pleased you to release him from all the matters which you demand of him and lay to his charge, and leave him in peace as a Catholic Christian in the faith of Jesus Christ, he is ready, within one year, to put Jerusalem and all the land which belonged to the Latins into the hand and power of the Christians.”

The pope asked him whether he had an instrument by which one might believe that he was the emperor’s messenger and that he spoke on his behalf what he had said. He replied that he did. Then he produced letters sealed with gold, and another letter of a notary-public, containing the manner in which he was to be believed and accepted as messenger. The pope then asked whether his lord the emperor had the power to do concerning the land of Syria what he had said; and he replied yes, affirming it strongly.

Then the pope turned toward the cardinals and prelates and spoke so loudly that all who were there [Col. 1034D] could hear him: “Lords, you may now see what sort of Christian the emperor is. When he can recover the Holy Land and the holy places of Jerusalem, restore them to the Christians, and remove them from the hands and power of unbelievers, he neither does it nor wishes to do it unless it is upon terms.”

He then told the emperor’s envoys that the excuse they had offered was insufficient and that he did not accept it, for they had neither proved it nor offered to prove it. He said that he would proceed further with the case and commanded them not to appear before him again.

### XXXIX. The emperor is deposed. Count William of Holland is elected emperor.

The pope then assembled a general council and brought forward the emperor’s case. The matter proceeded so far that the emperor and [Col. 1035A] his heirs were condemned and deposed. The pope sent word everywhere to make this known, and excommunicated all who would recognize him as emperor or call him emperor.

Afterward the pope sent a legate into Germany and had preaching carried out against the emperor. Thus many people rebelled against him and adhered to the pope, especially all the clergy, which had great power in that land. When the pope learned that matters stood thus and that the greater power of Germany was on his side, he acted so that a king was elected in Germany and crowned at Aachen. The man whom they made king was William, count of Holland. The pope promised him that, as soon as he had come to Rome and had opportunity, he would crown him emperor.

Then a great and fierce war began between those who adhered to the new King William and those who adhered to Emperor Frederick. The pope took great pains to sustain this war, sending it all the men and money he could, and granting as great an indulgence as that for the land overseas. Thus the war and contention endured for a long time, until the emperor’s death. When the emperor died, the pope returned to Rome. The men of the kingdom sent for King Conrad, son of the emperor, who was in Germany and whom his father had made king; he continued the war against the Church and against King William.

### XL. Richard, Frederick’s marshal, tossed by many contrary winds, returns to Tyre, where it is delivered to Balian.

And now let us return to speak of the land of Syria. It happened, as you have heard, that Richard, son of Augier, the emperor’s marshal, had departed from Tyre; Henry, his brother, and their wives were with him. They carried away great wealth and set out to cross to Apulia. When they had been nine days at sea, a storm caught them and kept them long upon the sea, where they suffered hardship. At last the weather carried them to the land of Tripoli in Barbary; and when they were there, they found that their ship was coming entirely apart and that water was entering it in many places. They looked about and saw a Saracen vessel, which had come from Tunis and was bound for Alexandria. They drew alongside it, went aboard, and transferred their possessions; they handed their own ship over to the Saracens. But just as they thought to depart, a very violent storm overtook them and drove them back. Thus, after the weather had held them several days at sea, they returned to Tyre, whence they had departed. When they were in the harbour, they cast anchor and thought to disembark in the city as in one which was theirs—or so it seemed to them—for they did not know what had happened there since their departure. When they arrived, the people of the city became aware of them; they went and seized the marshal, his brother, their wives, and all that they possessed, and brought them to Balian, lord of Beirut. Balian had them brought before the castle, caused gallows to be erected, and sent word to their brother Lothair that he must surrender the castle and he would release his brothers; otherwise, he would have them hanged before his eyes. Lothair took counsel [Col. 1036A] and, seeing that he could not hold the castle, surrendered it; and the other restored and released his brothers.

### XLI. The Sultan of Babylon destroys the Christians.

At this time it happened that Ṣalāḥ, who was Sultan of Babylon, sent great wealth to the East, over which he was lord, in order to bring men to his aid. He sent word that he would give them the whole land of Egypt if they would remain there. Consequently, a great host from a city called Khwarazm came—fully twenty thousand mounted men—and set out to join him. The reason they did this was fear of the Tartars, who had entered their country.

These Khwarazmians rode until they came to Gaza. There they found the army of the Sultan of Egypt. On their way they did great damage in the land of Tripoli and elsewhere; and they came upon Jerusalem so suddenly that few people could flee. Rather, they were so taken by surprise that more than thirty thousand men, women, and children were killed there; for he took no one alive, but killed all. The Sultan of Damascus, who was called Salāṭh, sent his army toward Acre. Its commander was the Sultan of al-Karak, and there were four thousand mounted men. When they were before Acre, the Christians who were there—the Hospital of St John, the Temple, the Hospital of the Germans, the knights of the country, and others who had come from Cyprus and Tripoli—departed from Acre; the Turks were with them, as were Robert, patriarch of Jerusalem, and many others. They rode until they came to Ascalon. Count [Col. 1036C] Walter of Brienne, who was at Jaffa, joined their march; and the Christians numbered fully six hundred knights, apart from other mounted and foot soldiers.

When they reached Ascalon, they took counsel among themselves as to what they should do. Then the Sultan of al-Karak said to them:

> Lords, you have to deal with a great foreign host which has no refuge; thus they are like desperate men. Therefore I do not recommend battle; rather, I advise that we remain here, for we have provisions enough, and more will come to us from Acre. They have little food and are a great host, so they cannot endure long; they will have to depart. It will be enough if they leave us the place. Because they are foreigners without refuge, they cannot last but will disperse; and unless they have support in the land of Babylon—which I do not believe the Sultan will give them—we shall be rid of them.

Many Christians agreed with the Sultan’s counsel, while the others insisted that they should go out to fight them where they were. Then, through the hatred and envy among the Christians, and because of their sin and misfortune, the worse counsel prevailed. They departed from Ascalon at dawn on a Tuesday and rode until they reached Gaza. There they found the army of Babylon, three thousand Turks, and the Khwarazmians, numbering fully twenty thousand. Then the battle-lines joined, and there was a great melee, but it lasted only a short time. For the Sultan of al-Karak and the Turks who were with him at once [Col. 1037A] left the field and went away; they lost all their equipment as well.

The Christians then began to weaken, so that squires and foot soldiers crowded among the squadrons, preventing the horses from charging or reaching the Turks. Then part of them began to flee, and the affair ended in defeat. This misfortune befell the Christians through their folly, pride, and envy. In this manner were captured William of Châteauneuf, master of the Hospital of St John, and Hermann of Perigord, master of the Temple, who died in prison; John and William, sons of Raymond, lord of Botron; and many other secular and religious knights. A very great number of other men were also killed or taken; scarcely a quarter of the entire army escaped. Peter of Sergines, archbishop of Tyre, and the bishop of St George of Ramla were killed there.

When those who had escaped that defeat came to Ascalon, they did not remain there long but went on to Acre. The Turks of Babylon departed from Gaza with all their booty and returned to their own land. They left the Khwarazmians in expectation that the Sultan would send for them; but he feared the power they possessed and that they might offend against him, and therefore would not draw them to himself. Instead, he placed troops against them at Belbeis to prevent them from passing into Barbary. When the Khwarazmians learned this, they considered themselves greatly betrayed and abandoned. Then they scattered through the country in many places and had several encounters with many people. They were always in the open country, as men who had neither refuge, city, nor castle. Therefore the people of the land, who were all against them, often caught them unawares and inflicted great losses upon their men; and their situation deteriorated so greatly that within three years they had been so dispersed that none remained in the country.

This defeat took place on a Tuesday, in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1254, in the month of October; and it was the day of St Luke the Evangelist.

### XLII. St Louis, King of France, takes the Cross.

At this point Pope Innocent IV was at Lyons on the Rhône, as you have heard above. It happened in France that the king fell ill with a severe sickness, by which he was so afflicted that he lost speech and was in such a condition that people thought he was dead. His mother, Queen Blanche, his wife, and his brothers made as great lamentation as those who regarded him as dead; they had assembled the clergy to perform the office for his burial.

At that moment he drew breath again, opened his eyes, looked around him, and said: “Bring me the Bishop of Paris.” Those about him were as glad and joyful as persons whose mourning had been turned to joy. They brought the Bishop of Paris before him. When the king saw him, he said: “Lord Bishop, I ask you to give me the cross for overseas.”

When his mother the queen and his brothers heard this, they knelt before him and said: “Lord, for God’s mercy, wait [Col. 1038A] until you are recovered, and then do what you please.”

Then he became angry and said to them: “Know well that I shall neither eat nor drink until I have the cross upon my shoulder to go overseas.”

He then called for the Bishop of Paris and again requested the cross. The bishop did not dare refuse him. He took a piece of silk ribbon, made it into a cross, knelt before the king weeping, and gave it to him. The king took it, kissed it, raised it to his eyes, and then had it fastened to his shoulder. Then he said: “Know truly that I am healed.”

There was such great weeping, both in the chamber and outside it, and such lamentation, that they did not make more when they had thought him dead. When he had risen and was healed, he had letters drawn up and sent word to the land of Syria that he was crusaded; they were to take heart and provision their cities and castles, for, with God’s help, he would soon be in the Holy Land.

### XLIII. The Sultan of Damascus is defeated by the Sultan of Aleppo. The Sultan of Babylon besieges and takes Damascus and several other cities and castles.

At this time Salāṭh, Sultan of Damascus, went to Baalbek, which was his original inheritance. He had a dispute with the Sultan of Aleppo, and they came to battle. The lord of Damascus was defeated, captured, and imprisoned in Aleppo.

When the Sultan of Babylon learned that the Sultan of Damascus was imprisoned at Aleppo, he set out with a great army, went to Damascus, and besieged it, making a show of cutting down its gardens. [Col. 1038C] The people of the land became afraid and saw that they had no lord to defend them. They were always weak people and a base populace, being all merchants and craftsmen, with very few men-at-arms among them; for this reason they receive anyone who brings even a few men. So they surrendered to him.

After he had Damascus, he went to al-Karak and Baalbek and took them. Not long afterwards, he sent his army to besiege a castle which Eudes of Montbéliard had fortified at Tiberias. They pressed it so severely that they took it by force; all who were inside were captured or killed. From there they went to besiege Ascalon. They established a very strong siege and assaulted it harshly with engines and mines, and with very fierce assaults upon the walls. They pressed the castle so severely that it could not be supplied by sea with men and provisions. The Sultan therefore had twenty-two galleys and one small vessel come from Alexandria, carrying food and the necessities for the galleys. They remained before Ascalon, so that no vessel could go there.

### XLIV. The Christians bring supplies and aid to Ascalon.

When the Hospitallers, who held Ascalon in custody for the emperor, who had entrusted it to their keeping, heard this, they requested aid from all those of Acre—prelates, religious orders, communes, and all other people—that they might assist them in the cost of armed vessels [Col. 1039A] by which the galleys before Ascalon could be driven away and those inside be resupplied with a garrison.

For this purpose they sent to the king in Cyprus, asking him to aid them. The king sent eight galleys, well armed and well supplied with knights and sergeants. Their commander was Baldwin of Ibelin, seneschal of Cyprus. They set out from Famagusta and went to Acre. There they joined the vessels which the people of Acre had also prepared; from there they all departed together. There were fifteen galleys and at least fifty other small vessels, saities and gameles. They sailed and rowed until they reached Ascalon.

When the Saracens saw them, they drew their galleys and their small vessel as close to the city as they could, so that they might be defended from land if the Christian ships should attack them. The Christian ships lay some distance from them at sea, at anchor, and remained for five days. Then, one evening, a strong west wind arose at sea. All the Christian vessels were in great danger, but nevertheless remained at their anchors without damage; it helped them that they were some way out at sea. For that coast swells more with the wind, and the sea is rougher near land than farther out. Thus the Turkish galleys could not endure there: they struck the shore, and all twenty-two galleys and the small vessel were wrecked. In the morning the Christians saw all the Saracen galleys broken up along the shore. They put many things into the castle to refresh our people. The weather at sea and the wind were so violent that they could endure no longer; therefore they raised their anchors and sails and returned to Acre.

### XLV. The Saracens take Ascalon by storm.

When the Turks saw what had happened to them, they exerted themselves still more to besiege and harass the castle. What had been intended to help the castle turned to its damage. For after the galleys had been broken up, the Saracens used the timber and planks to make mantlets, screens, and covered approaches; from the trees they made engines to cast missiles into the castle. Thus they pressed the castle so hard that those within could not endure it. Yet they made so great a defence that for a long time no men had been seen who endured so much, defended themselves so well, or behaved so vigorously [Col. 1040A] as they did.

But none of this availed or helped them: the castle was taken by force. They were so harassed by frequent assaults that they could have neither rest nor respite. Moreover, the attackers drove towers over the whole mound on which the castle stood, and mined deeply into the middle of the castle, until the Turks were mixed pell-mell with those within. But some of those inside perceived this, went to the shore, and embarked in vessels; in this way many escaped. The others who remained were killed or captured, and the castle was thus taken and destroyed.
