Thus it happened that, of the castles which had been fortified at the coming of the King of Navarre, the Count of Brittany, and the Count of Cornwall, none remained that was not lost, except the castle of Safed, which the Temple had fortified.

### XLVI. The Turcomans rise against the people of Antioch.

At this time it happened at Antioch that a people called Turcomans rose up because of the contention, oppression, and injury inflicted upon them. They began to ravage the land of Antioch, raid and harass the villages, and kill the peasants. These Turcomans are a wild people, having neither city nor castle; rather, they lodge each day in tents of felt. They possess great quantities of animals—sheep, rams, some goats, and also oxen and cows—and live as shepherds. They engage in no gainful occupation; and among all the Saracens there is no sort of people held in less esteem for deeds of arms. Therefore the people of Antioch despised them. For this reason they ventured to pursue them in disorder, without equipment or escort, holding them so cheap.

It happened that the Turcomans considered their situation and saw that those pursuing them were scattered and dispersed. They rallied, turned back, attacked them, defeated them, captured many, and killed them. This happened so often that the people of Antioch fell into great fear, while the Turcomans gained excessive confidence. We shall now cease to speak of the affairs of Antioch and the Turcomans, because we must pursue the subject of this book and set out in order how matters occurred in the kingdom of Jerusalem [Col. 1040D] and the land of Syria.

## HERE BEGINS BOOK XXVI.

[Col. 1039]

### I. St Louis crosses the sea and takes Damietta.

[Col. 1039D]

Louis, King of France, who had taken the cross, as you have heard above, made his preparations and arrangements to cross into the land of Syria. A year before his departure he sent some of his men, who arrived on the island of Cyprus. He sent them there to procure provisions and other things that he might need; they brought fifty valuable horses, and their commander was a worthy sergeant named Nicholas of Sours.

In the year after these men had come to Cyprus, the king departed from France to go to Aigues-Mortes. This was in the year of the Incarnation of Jesus Christ 1248. On the twenty-eighth day of September he arrived in Cyprus, and Count Patris died at Marseille. The lord of Arsuf relinquished the bailiwick, and John Fuinon became bailiff; Eudes of Tusculum was legate.

In 1249, on the twentieth day of May, the king left Limassol for Damietta and arrived there on the fourth day of June. On the fifth day he landed by force, and on the sixth day the city of Damietta was taken without a blow being struck.

At Acre there was war between the Pisans and the Genoese. It lasted twenty-eight days, and they hurled against one another twenty-two kinds of engines: stone-throwers, trebuchets, and mangonels. John Fuinon was removed from the bailiwick, and the lord of Arsuf was again made bailiff; he made a truce between the communes for three years. After the war, a storm wrecked seventy-two vessels, small and large, in the harbour of Acre; at the harbour of Damietta, thirty-two ships and ten other vessels, besides many others on the river. On the twenty-seventh day of November the king departed with his whole army for Mansurah. [Col. 1041B] He arrived there on the twenty-second day of December, and on the way the Templars and the Count of Artois, who had the vanguard, defeated the Saracen vanguard at Seresaph. They killed about one hundred and fifty-five men; and on the next day fully a thousand Saracens were captured, killed, or drowned after crossing the stream on foot to challenge the Christians.

On the eighth day of January, the lord of Arsuf and the forces of the kingdom went to destroy Bechsen, a Turcoman encampment, where they gained sixteen thousand head of livestock, large and small, and captured the admiral who was their commander.

### II. At Mansurah the Counts of Artois, Salisbury, and Coucy are killed.

[Col. 1041C]

In 1250, on the eighth day of February, the king crossed the river of Tinnis with his whole army, but many knights and other people were drowned there. Afterwards the king surprised the Saracens’ camp, and many were killed. The vanguard of the army broke into Mansurah because the common soldiery desired to plunder the city. The Saracens became aware of this and returned; then they killed the Count of Artois, the Count of Salisbury, Count Raoul of Coucy, and many others.

On the fifth day of April the king and his army, lacking provisions, departed for Damietta; all were captured on the road at Setansaf. On the second day of May the Saracens killed their Sultan. Then the king and the barons swore a truce to the Saracen amirs and ransomed themselves for one hundred thousand marks of silver. The king and his brothers, the legate, the patriarch, many other barons and knights, and other people were released, and came to Acre on the eighth day of May.

Then the king fortified the suburb of Acre. On the day of St Lawrence, Count Alphonse of Poitiers, Charles Count of Anjou, and William Count of Flanders departed to cross the sea. King Henry of Cyprus married Plaisance, daughter of the Prince of Antioch, in September. Brother William, master of the Hospital, and one hundred and twenty knights, with about eight hundred other persons, were released by the Saracens. Emperor Frederick died on the day of St Lucy.

### III. The evil conduct of Conrad, Frederick’s son. St Louis strengthens Caesarea and Jaffa with fortifications.

[Col. 1042A]

Conrad, King of Jerusalem and son of Frederick, lived two years, five months, and fifteen days. He closely followed his father’s wickedness, detested and greatly despised the female sex. He was a drunkard, a squanderer, unstable, a ravisher, and a persecutor of the Church. As was said, he had Henry the Younger, nephew of the King of England, and Frederick, his own nephew, son of King Henry his brother, poisoned. He killed certain Friars Minor and other religious persons by various tortures. He had the walls of Naples and Capua pulled down. In the time of Count William of Holland, who had been elected king and held the right of the Empire, Conrad caused himself to be called emperor by the people, contrary to permission and justice. This Conrad was excommunicated until his death by the authority of Pope Innocent IV.

The Sultan of Aleppo was defeated in Egypt with thirty thousand mounted men; more than two thousand Egyptians were killed in that battle. King Henry of England took the cross and forbade the passage of the great men of his land.

In 1251, the King of France fortified Caesarea; Peter Larcat was made Archbishop of Tyre; and Beaumont died, after whom his son, Beaumont, became prince and count. Then Alexander, son of the King of Scotland, married the daughter of the King of England.

In 1252, King Louis fortified Jaffa, and his mother Lady Blanche died. Beaumont, Prince of Antioch, was made a knight at Jaffa by the hand of King Louis; and Julian, lord of Sidon, married the daughter of Hethum, King of Armenia.

In 1253, the Saracens of Damascus came before Acre, destroyed Doc and Ricordane, took Sidon, killed eight hundred men or more, and carried off into prison fully four hundred masons and other people. The king again fortified Sidon. King Henry of Cyprus died; so did Guy of Nîmes, bishop of Jaffa; Walter, bishop of Acre; and Nicholas Larcat, Archbishop of Tyre. [Note: [Col. 1041D] Above, Peter Larcat is mentioned.] After him Giles, who had been at Damietta, was postulated as archbishop. Hethum, King of Armenia, went to the Tartars.

In 1254, work was carried out on the walls of Sidon, and the king came to Acre. Balian of Ibelin, son of the lord, who afterwards married [Col. 1042D] Plaisance, Queen of Cyprus, was made a knight. After the feast of St Mark, the king and queen departed from Acre with their people to cross the sea. He left to my lord Geoffrey of Sergines, seneschal of the kingdom, one hundred knights to guard the kingdom of Syria. Margaret, lady of Sidon, died on the fifth day of June. On the following day Peter of Biaune, marshal of the Hospital, died. King Conrad died on the twenty-first day of May, and Robert, Patriarch of Jerusalem, died on the eighth day of June. Eudes, patriarch, arrived in Acre; John of Ibelin, Count of Jaffa, was bailiff of the kingdom. In mid-September, Eudes, Bishop of Tusculum, the legate, departed from Acre to cross the sea. Afterwards Beaumont, Prince of Antioch, married Sibyl, daughter of Othon, King of Armenia. Five months into the winter Pope Innocent died, and Alexander succeeded him.

### IV. Concerning Pope Alexander IV. Various events from 1255 to 1260.

Alexander IV was made pope. He had been Bishop of Ostia and granted St Lazarus of Bethany and its dependencies to the Hospital of St John and Mount Tabor.

In 1255, a truce was made with the lord of Damascus, and the boundary ran from the river of Arsuf to the boundary of Beirut. Otho the cardinal came into the kingdom of Apulia with Pope Alexander’s army; Foggia, St Lawrence of Siponto, Monte Sant’Angelo, and the entire coast as far as Otranto were surrendered to him.

In 1256, John of Ibelin gave up the bailiwick, and John of Ibelin, lord of Arsuf, became bailiff. On the third day of June, the vigil of Pentecost, Master James, Patriarch of Jerusalem and formerly bishop of Verdun, arrived at Acre. After the feast of St John, Master Florent, bishop of Acre, consecrated at Rome, came to Acre. Huguelin Bozacharie, Pisan consul at Acre, died; he had seized the prelates who were travelling to the council at Rome. The war between Genoese and Venetians began over possession of the house of St Sabas. The Genoese, aided by the Pisans, defeated the Venetians, captured them, and pursued them through their street as far as St Mark’s. Brother Renaud of Vichiers, master of the Temple, died; after him Brother Thomas Bérard was made master.

[Col. 1043C]

In 1257 the Genoese came to an agreement and swore to guard and preserve the lordship for themselves, because the Venetians and Pisans had reconciled and sworn together against the Genoese. Afterwards Beaumont, Prince of Antioch, came and brought to Acre, on the first day of February, his sister Plaisance, Queen of Cyprus, and his nephew Hugh, son of that queen and heir of the kingdoms of Cyprus and Jerusalem, through the instigation of the Temple and of Count John of Ibelin of Jaffa.

In 1258, peace was made between Prince Beaumont and the lord of Arsuf, who had been at odds. Balian, son of the lord of Arsuf, released Queen Plaisance, and she him, from the marriage that had existed between them. The queen, her son, and the prince returned to Tripoli, while the bailiwick of the kingdom of Jerusalem remained with John of Ibelin, lord of Arsuf.

The Rous of Turkey, commander of the Genoese, came before Acre with fifty Genoese galleys and four ships. He was defeated by forty Venetian galleys, and twenty-four galleys were captured between Acre and Haifa; fully one thousand seven hundred Genoese men were killed or taken. Afterwards an agreement was made: the Genoese abandoned their tower and street and went to Tyre. They were not to carry a banner on their ships in Acre harbour, nor hold court or staff within Acre. Afterwards their tower and all the houses in their street were demolished and carried to Venice. From the foundation-stones of the tower, its pillars, and other stones, the Pisans and Venetians fortified their streets. The Tartars took the land of the Assassins in Persia. John of Ibelin, lord of Arsuf and bailiff of the kingdom of Jerusalem, died. King Conrad, who had been reconciled after the death of his father Frederick, died; he had taken Naples by force when it rebelled against him.

In 1259, Brother Thomas of the Order of Preachers came to Acre as legate from the pope. Geoffrey of Sergines became bailiff of the kingdom; he maintained very strict justice and had many thieves and murderers arrested and hanged.

### V. The Tartars take Jerusalem, then are defeated by the Sultan of Babylon.

In 1260 the Tartars took by force Aleppo, Aarene [identification uncertain], Hama, al-Karak, and Damascus. They came into the kingdom of Jerusalem and took the deserted city. Afterwards they were defeated by the Sultan of Babylon on the third day of September, on the plains of Tiberias. Afterwards Bandocdar killed the Sultan as he was returning to Babylon, and was made Sultan in his place.

At this time Julian sold Sidon and Beaufort to the Temple, from which great hatred afterwards arose between the King of Armenia and the Temple. Afterwards John of Ibelin, lord of Beirut, John of Giblet, marshal of the kingdom, and Brother Stephen of Sisse, master of the Temple, were defeated by the Turcomans with the entire convents of Acre, Château Pèlerin, Safed, and Beaufort. The lord of Beirut, Brother Matthew the Savage, commander of the Temple, John of Giblet, Count Judans, and several other knights were taken, while many others mounted and on foot were killed or captured. The Templars lost all their equipment. Afterwards the lord of Beirut was ransomed for twenty thousand bezants; the commander of the Temple, James Judans, marshal of the kingdom, and several others were also ransomed.

In 1261 Pope Alexander died, and Urban succeeded him.

### VI. Concerning Pope Urban IV. The Saracens besiege Antioch and raise the siege. The siege of Tyre and its lifting.

After Alexander came Urban IV, born at Troyes in Champagne and descended from poor people. He was Bishop of Verdun, legate in Germany, and afterwards Patriarch of Jerusalem. In his time the great war between Venetians and Genoese took place at Acre, by which the city was almost destroyed; he supported the Venetians.

After that war, Brother Thomas of Lantil, Bishop of Bethlehem, came to Acre as legate. Resenting that one who ought to have been subject to him had come as legate above him, he departed from Syria and went to the Roman court, though he found another pretext. He led people to believe that he was going to have revoked the grant which Pope Alexander had made of St Lazarus of Bethany to the Hospital of St John. After he had come to the Roman court and remained there a short time, Pope Alexander died, and he was elected pope and called Urban. He was of very great courage, made many cardinals at the beginning of his pontificate, and gave the kingdom [Col. 1045A] of Sicily and the land of Apulia to Charles, Count of Anjou. He made him vicar of the Church, drew up the privileges, and confirmed the whole matter. But he died before Charles came into the land, and therefore the affair could not be completed in his time.

He revoked the grant which Pope Alexander had made to the Hospital of St John of St Lazarus of Bethany. He caused the church of St James at Troyes, which was later burned, to be built. Balian of Arsuf sold Arsuf Castle with all its dependencies to the Hospital of St John. Plaisance, Queen of Cyprus, died on the twenty-second day of September, and Hugh of Lusignan was made bailiff of Cyprus.

On the twenty-first day of June the Greeks took Constantinople from the Latins. Palaiologos made himself emperor and caused himself to be called Constantine.

[Col. 1045B]

In 1262 Antioch was besieged by the Saracens of Babylon; but through the intervention of the King of Armenia, the Tartars set out to come against them, and they abandoned the siege and departed. Charles, Count of Anjou and Provence, besieged Marseille. Those within submitted to him by force; he became its lord and established his own justice in the city.

In 1263 Bandocdar, who had killed the Sultan of Babylon and made himself Sultan of Egypt, came before Acre on the fourteenth day of April. On the fifteenth day of April his men rode as far as Acre’s gates, so that the city was in great danger. The bailiff, my lord Geoffrey of Sergines, and many other knights and sergeants were wounded; several died of their wounds. The reason he came was that the Temple and the Hospital would not return his slaves, as they had agreed to do under the truce, while he wished to return theirs. The Count of Jaffa returned his slaves to him, and he kept the truce with him well for a long time; but at last he took Jaffa and destroyed it.

That year Henry, son of Prince Beaumont of Antioch, came with his wife Isabella, daughter of King Hugh of Cyprus and Queen Alice, through whom the lordship of the kingdom fell to him. They requested from the lords of Acre the bailiwick of the kingdom of Jerusalem. They were received without rendering homage or oath, because they had not brought with them the rightful heir. The said Isabella returned to Cyprus and left her husband as bailiff in Acre. On the twenty-fifth day of September, William—formerly Bishop of Argens—came to Acre as legate, Patriarch of Jerusalem, and administrator of the bishopric of Acre; and Thomas, the legate who was Bishop of Bethlehem, returned to Rome.

In 1264 fifty galleys and transports came and suddenly besieged Tyre, belonging to my lord Philip of Montfort; but it defended itself with the aid of the people of Acre. When the Venetians saw that they could not harm the city, they returned shamefully. The Genoese captured at sea a great part of the Venetian caravan which was following the course of those galleys to come to Acre. Pope Urban IV died on the first day of October, as did John of Ibelin, lord of Beirut; Hugh, heir of Caesarea; and Isabella, wife of Henry, son [Col. 1046A] of the prince. Master Guy of Saint-Gilles in Provence was made pope.

### VII. Concerning Pope Clement IV. Charles of Anjou becomes King of Sicily. Death of Pope Clement; election of Gregory XI.

Pope Clement, born at Saint-Gilles in Provence, was descended from knights and worthy people. He was a great jurist and a good advocate, the best in the land, and had the reputation of being a loyal man—a quality not often found among people of his profession. He had married a wife, by whom he had two daughters. After his wife’s death he adopted the clerical life and was attached to King Louis of France; thereafter he became bishop of Le Puy, then archbishop of Narbonne, and thence was called to be a cardinal of Rome. Afterwards he was sent as legate to [Col. 1046B] England, to make peace in the war between the king and his barons. While he was there Pope Urban died; he was elected pope and called Clement.

He completed what Pope Urban had begun. For in his time King Charles came to Rome, since the people of the city had made him senator of Rome. He caused him and his wife to be crowned at Rome by a cardinal who was bishop of Albano, as king and queen of the kingdom of Sicily; and the banner of the Church was delivered to him against all men. At this time King Charles went into Apulia and fought King Manfred; he defeated and killed him in the field, gained the lands of Apulia and Sicily, and held them.

Shortly afterwards, in that same time, Conradin of Germany, son of the other Conrad, came into Apulia with a very great host, at the instigation of the Pisans and [Col. 1046C] Romans, who had rebelled against King Charles, and at the urging of Lord Henry of Castile, who had been made senator of Rome against King Charles. By the inducement of these and many others, the said Conradin fought King Charles; in the end he was defeated, and nearly all his men were either killed or captured. At last he himself was taken and beheaded, as were many other high-born men within a short time.

Afterwards Pope Clement was seized by an illness of which he died. This was a great loss, for he was a very worthy man and of good life. After him the see remained vacant for more than three years because of discord among the cardinals, who could not agree to make a pope. But at last they elected a wise cleric, a worthy man and of good life, born at Piacenza in Lombardy, called Sir Theobald. He was archdeacon of Liège and had gone on pilgrimage overseas with Lord Edward. On the ninth day after the end of October, messengers were sent to fetch him: Brother Stephen of Sissi, a Templar brother and commander of Apulia; Sir Fulk of Lérre, a knight and great baron of Provence who was with King Charles in Apulia and came on his behalf; and two notaries of the Roman court. They departed from Acre in three galleys on Saint Martin’s Day in winter and travelled from land to land because of the winter.

The king of Castile defeated the king of Granada between Córdoba and Seville, killing [Col. 1047A] three thousand Saracen horsemen and many others on foot. Olivier de Termes arrived at Acre.

## VIII. The Sultan of Babylon captures the castle of Arsuf

In the year 1265, Bandocdart, sultan of Babylon, besieged the castle of Arsuf, held by the Hospitallers, on 15 March. By force of engines and mining he took it on the last day of April. More than a thousand persons within were captured: religious knights, secular men, and sergeants-at-arms.

At Acre there was seen a bright sign like a sword, the length of a lance and the breadth of a moon, which came from the east and seemed to strike the bell-tower of Holy Cross.

Hugh of Lusignan, son of Henry the prince, who was bailiff of Cyprus, came to Acre with a fine fleet of galleys and vessels as relief; he had with him 130 knights [Col. 1047B] and mounted sergeants.

Sir Simon de Montfort, who was count of Leicester and had the king of England’s sister as his wife, so prevailed with the barons of England that he captured the king, his brother Count Richard—who was called king of Germany—and Edward his son. But Edward escaped from prison; his men rallied to him, fought Simon de Montfort, and defeated him. Then the said Simon and his eldest son were killed, along with many others of their party. Afterwards they killed the count of Ferrières, the lord of Attinges, and fully four thousand knights.

## IX. On Charles of Anjou, king of Sicily

Charles was the son of King Louis of France and the youngest of his sons. He married the daughter of the count of Provence, through whom he acquired that county. Before he possessed that county, he was count of Anjou. He was a very wise and knightly man, always seeking tournaments. He undertook to support the countess of Flanders against John, her son, Lord John of Avesnes; from this arose a very great war, in which many people died and were ruined. He worked hard to become king of Vienna, but could not achieve it.

At last the Church granted him the kingdom of Apulia and Sicily, if he could conquer it, under agreements made between them. Therefore he had galleys armed at Marseilles, embarked, and went by sea to Pisa, where he was received with great honour. From there he went to Rome, of which he was senator, and waited until [Col. 1047D] his wife, who was coming with a very great force of men-at-arms, had arrived there. When he was at Rome, by the pope’s command he and his wife were crowned king and queen of Sicily by the hand of the cardinal named Sir Raoul Grosparmi.

After he had worn the crown, he assembled all the men-at-arms he could obtain, entered Apulia, and on his arrival took San Germano, L’Aquila, and many other places. He then learned that King Manfred was at Benevento with all his men-at-arms. The king went to meet him, fought him, and defeated him in the field; King Manfred was killed on the spot. Thus King Charles possessed the whole country and captured King Manfred’s wife, children, and all his treasure.

Yet indeed, part of the counts and [Col. 1048A] barons of the land rebelled against Manfred and aligned themselves with King Charles. After the victory, however, they treacherously rebelled against King Charles; therefore they were later destroyed by King Charles himself. Henry of Castile, who had been at the victory of Tunis, came to King Charles after that victory and remained with him a long time. Afterwards, in anger, he departed and went to Rome. There he was made senator and caused the land to rebel against the king; the Pisans also stirred up war against him.

At this time Charles’s wife, the daughter of the count of Provence, died. The Pisans and Romans, by the instigation of Count Gawain and certain others, brought Conradin of Germany, who was defeated, as you have heard above. The Saracens too had rebelled, along with a great part of Apulia and Sicily.

Taken with Conradin were the son of the duke of Austria, Lord Henry of Castile, Count Gerard of Pisa, Count Gawain, and his sons. King Charles caused all these to be beheaded, by judgment and by the judgment of the land of Naples, on the shore and in his own presence—except Lord Henry of Castile. He pardoned that man’s death because he was his kinsman; but he had him kept in such a place that he preferred death to the life he endured there.

At this time King Charles married the daughter of the count of Nevers, niece of the duke of Burgundy. Afterwards the Saracens of Lucera saw that they could not hold out and expected help from no quarter; [Col. 1048C] therefore they surrendered their land and submitted to King Charles’s mercy. Thereupon the whole country remained at peace.

## X. On Manfred, son of Frederick

You should know that Manfred was the son of Emperor Frederick, who begot him by a noble lady of Lombardy. He was prince of Taranto and married the daughter of a great lord of Greece named Nicalixe. He was a very handsome person, wise and courteous, and laboured much in astronomy, making all his deeds according to it. He was very crafty.

As people say, he had King Conrad and his brother King Henry poisoned; the latter was the lawful and legitimate heir. After their deaths he spread reports that Conradin, Conrad’s son, had died, and brought forward practised messengers who solemnly declared that they had been present at [Col. 1048D] Conradin’s death. By spoken assertions and forged letters they maintained that Conradin had left Manfred, in his testament, the kingdom of Sicily and the land of Apulia, and had made him his heir.

After these reports Manfred had himself crowned king and seized the whole country. He laboured greatly to make peace with the Church, but could never reach an agreement with it. At last he set himself wholly against the Church, doing it all the harm and injury he could. He received, honoured, and kept near him all who were hostile to the Church. He greatly loved the Saracens and often gave them rich presents.

But at last the Church, unable longer to suffer his disloyalty, granted his land to King Charles, who defeated him, as you have heard above. Thus [Col. 1049A] Manfred ended his life badly, because he had begun badly. It is said that the greater part of his barons failed him and abandoned him in the field, and that a great part turned against him—especially those whom he had raised up, enriched, and made from nothing. But that is the custom and nature of the land: all those of the country fail at need, and every day each would like to have a new lord.

## XI. The Sultan of Babylon captures the castle of Safed

In 1265 the count of Nevers, Erard de Valéry, Erard de Nanteuil, and fully fifty knights came to Acre.

In 1266 Baudocdar, sultan of Babylon, came before Acre on 2 June and remained before the city for eight days. He then went to besiege Safed and took it on [Col. 1049B] 22 June, saving the lives of those inside. Under the agreement negotiated by Brother Leo, the chancellor, he was to conduct them to Acre; but the sultan broke the agreement and had them all killed outside the castle, and the said Brother Leo became an apostate.

Afterwards the sultan entered Armenia by force with all his host, killed Thoros, son of the king of Armenia, and captured Luion, his other son. He captured and killed a very great number of Armenians, because their king had gone to the Tartars. The count of Nevers died at Acre in August.

That month Hugh of Lusignan, bailiff of Cyprus, came to Acre with a fine company of men-at-arms. He made a raid with the Templars, Hospitallers, German brethren, and French knights, together with many other people on foot and horseback, toward Tiberias. An alarm was raised in the land, and the Turks of Safed lay in ambush at Caroublier, near the plain of Acre. Through greed for gain, the first guard of our men was fully three leagues away from the others; consequently they all fell upon them and defeated them shamefully. The Hospitallers, the Germans, the company of knights of Lord Geoffrey of Sergines, and many others—more than five hundred on foot and horseback—would largely have escaped alive; but the peasants of the Casaux killed them by night when they came seeking their armour and clothing.

At this time John of Ibelin, count of Jaffa, died in October, and Lucian, archbishop of Caesarea, in January; [Col. 1049D] and the archbishop of Tyre was summoned overseas.

## XII. The Sultan of Babylon besieges Acre. Saint Louis again takes the cross

In 1267 Baudocdar, sultan of Babylon, came before Acre with all his army on 2 May. They bore the banners of the Temple and the Hospital, by which they surprised the common people who were outside seeking gain. They rode as far as before the city and killed, behind Toron, more than five hundred common people whom they had captured. There was not one whose gall had not been drawn from his body, and the skins of their heads, including the ears, were flayed.

The next day he withdrew to Safed. On 16 May he returned before Acre, had the mills and garden-towers demolished, and caused the trees, gardens, and [Col. 1050A] vineyards outside Acre’s walls to be cut down.

On 16 August Liques de Grimaut, with twenty-eight Genoese galleys, took the port of Acre. In the harbour they burned two Pisan ships and did much as they pleased for twelve days. But twenty-eight Venetian galleys surprised some of the Genoese galleys which thought to return, and held five galleys with their crews. Many were either killed or captured.

Hugh, heir to the kingdom of Cyprus, died in November. Hugh of Lusignan was crowned king on Christmas Day by the hand of William, patriarch of Jerusalem, who had gone there to visit the churches and kingdom of Cyprus. At this time Louis, king of France, the king of Navarre, the royal children, and many other counts and barons of France, England, and Germany took the cross for the aid of the Holy Land.

## XIII. The Sultan of Babylon captures Jaffa and Antioch

On 25 March Pope Clement IV died, and Charles, king of Sicily, defeated Conradin with all his army. Baudocdar, sultan of Babylon, took Jaffa treacherously and during a truce on 7 March. He killed many common people, but allowed the others to go to Acre with all their possessions and gave them safe-conduct. He took the head of Saint George and had the body of Saint Christina burned, which Bishop John of Troyes had left at Jaffa.

From there he went to Beaufort and took it from the Templars by force on 25 April. Afterwards he went to Antioch [Col. 1050C] and took it without any defence on 27 May. After the city was captured, seventeen thousand persons or more were killed within it; more than one hundred thousand men, women, and children, both laypersons and religious, were taken. The Templars abandoned their two castles, Gaston and Roche de Roussel, and the territory of Port-Bonnel at the entrance to Armenia.

Luion, son of the king of Armenia, was released from the sultan’s prison in exchange for Saugor, a kinsman of the sultan whom the Tartars had captured. Henry, archbishop of Nazareth, died. Brother Geoffrey of the Order of Preachers was made bishop of Saint Abraham. Balian of Ibelin, lord of Arsuf, was made constable and bailiff of the kingdom of Jerusalem.

## XIV. Various matters for the year 1269. Battle between Saracens and Christians

[Col. 1050D]

In 1269 there was a great earthquake in Armenia, which brought down one castle, three Armenian abbeys, and fully twelve villages. Geoffrey of Sergines died on 11 April.

At this time, on 26 August, King Charles took Lucera from the Saracens; and on 24 September Hugh of Lusignan, king of Cyprus, was crowned king of Jerusalem in the city of Tyre. In that time there was dearth in Syria of every commodity, and wheat rose to eight and a half bezants.

That year the king of Aragon was to cross to Syria. He and his host embarked, but on the fourth day a great storm overtook him and wrecked his ship. When he saw this, he returned to port with two other ships, while all the rest of the fleet came to Acre, together with his two [Col. 1051A] illegitimate sons, for they thought the king was coming; but he had returned. Never afterwards would he embark because of his fear of the storm and the death of his beloved lady Berengaria, which brought him great shame and reproach.

On the Wednesday before Christmas, Robert de Crésèques, Olivier de Termes, the lord of Pacy, and fully two hundred knights had gone to an ambush a league outside Acre. The host of Jaffa came and surprised them, falling upon our men. Ours received them very well; but so many Saracens arrived that our men could not withstand them. It is said that the sultan himself was present with a thousand horsemen. Robert de Crésèques and Brother Olivier de Termes were killed there, as were some two hundred others, knights and sergeants; and at least as many, or more, Saracens died.

Then the chivalry of Acre, the Temple, the Hospital, the Germans, and the sons of the king of Aragon saw the battle before them and wished to go to rescue those fighting. But Peter of Aragon, the king’s son, dissuaded them, saying that, even if his father and brothers were in the battle, he would not advise that all Christendom be placed in such danger for two persons, since the Saracens were too numerous.

## XV. Louis crosses the sea

In the following year, 1270, thirty-two ships arrived at Acre with five hundred Frisians who had come from Tunis, from the great host of the king of France. In their time there was great abundance of goods at Acre, and the great dearth which had prevailed ceased. Know that they were very good and Catholic people.

That year William, patriarch of Jerusalem, died at Acre on 21 April. Then the king of France came to Aigues-Mortes with his three sons, his brother the count of Poitiers, and a great part of his equipment. He remained in Provence awaiting his host and baronage; on 2 June he departed with all his host, made port at Cagliari in Sardinia, and soon thereafter left for Tunis. He took Carthage. His son John Tristan died before Tunis; after him the legate died; then the good king of France died; then the king of Navarre; and so many other counts, barons, knights, and people died [Col. 1051D] that it was a wonder.

After the death of the king of France, King Charles came to the host and negotiated peace, which was made. He and the other barons received great wealth from the king of Tunis and returned to Trapani. On their return, in the harbour itself, more than forty ships were wrecked, and the wealth, people, and horses aboard were lost. The wife of Sir Philip, who was travelling to France, died; and the queen of Navarre died at Aix in Provence on the return from Tunis.

## XVI. Various matters for the year 1271

In 1271 Sir Henry of Germany, son of Richard, king of Germany, was murdered at Viterbo inside the church while Mass was being sung, by the sons of Simon de Montfort, Sir Guy and Sir Simon.

After this deed Lord Edward, son of the king of England, crossed to Syria with a great force. The sultan of Babylon took the Crac of the Hospital, the tower of Chastel-Blanc, and Gibelacar, which belonged to the prince. He made a truce with the count of Tripoli; he took Montfort from the Germans and demolished it. From there he came before Acre. The sultan took a castle of the Old Man of the Mountain. Fourteen Saracen galleys were wrecked at Limassol in Cyprus, and fully three thousand Saracens were either captured or killed. The king of Cyprus came to Acre as relief.

The count of Poitiers, who had long lain ill at Palermo after the return from Tunis, died. As he was travelling to his country, he fell ill at Albenga, a city near Genoa, and died there. This was a great loss to the lands on this side [Col. 1052B] of the sea. Shortly afterwards his wife, the countess, died while travelling to France. Great treasure therefore remained to King Philip of France, together with the counties of Toulouse and Poitiers and many other possessions which he held.

Lord Edmund, brother of Lord Edward, came to Acre with a small company. Lord Philip was crowned king of France. At this time Palaeologus, emperor of the Greeks, defeated the men of Negroponte at sea with galleys he had equipped; he captured most of the people of the island and its knights, and took a castle on the island of Negroponte.

Lord Theobald, a valiant cleric born at Piacenza, was elected pope of Rome. The messengers whom Lord Edward and Christendom had sent to the Tartars to seek aid returned to Acre. They had conducted the business so well that they brought the Tartars, who raided throughout the lands of Antioch and Aleppo, of Hama and La Chamelle, as far as Caesarea the Great, killing every Saracen they found. Thence they returned to the marshes at the entrance to Turkey, with great booty of slaves and much livestock. They encamped there to rest after the great hardships of the long journey they had made, and for the pasture and plentiful waters they found in that country for the great livestock they were driving.

In that same season, on 12 June, Sir Edward and his men, together with those of Acre, went to destroy Saint George. The English died from heat and thirst on the road, though they carried so much fruit, grapes, and honey that they fell dead at once.

On 23 November Sir Edward and his brothers, the king of Cyprus, the Templars, Hospitallers, Germans, all the Cypriots, all the pilgrims, and all the foot sergeants rode into the land of Caesarea to destroy the tower of Qaqun. When they arrived, they found several encampments of Turcomans, who were encamped there and knew nothing of their coming. Thus they took their camps, killed fully a thousand people, captured fully five thousand beasts, and returned safe and sound to Acre with little loss. Nevertheless, because of the great booty they found, the tower of Qaqun remained standing: they did not attack it. For this they were much mocked by the Saracens; [Col. 1053A] the sultan himself told the messengers of King Charles, who had come to him to negotiate truces between him and Christendom, that since so many men had failed to take one house, there was no appearance that they could conquer such a land as the kingdom of Jerusalem.

## XVII. Truce between the king of Cyprus and Jerusalem and the Sultan of Babylon

In 1272, on 22 April, a truce was made between Hugh of Lusignan, king of Jerusalem and Cyprus, and Baudocdar the sultan. The truce included only the plain of Acre and the road to Nazareth. In May Sir Edmund, brother of Sir Edward, departed; and on 18 June an Assassin wounded Sir Edward in his chamber. On 23 August Lord William of Valence, uncle of Sir Edward, crossed overseas; on 14 September Lord Edward again crossed overseas; and on 8 October Brother Thomas of the Order of Preachers, patriarch of Jerusalem, legate for all Syria, and bishop of Acre, arrived at Acre.

That same year Brother Bonacourt of the Order of Preachers, son of Henry of Gloire, was made archbishop of Tyre; and the lady of Beirut was married to Sir Edmund the Stranger. At this time discord arose between the king of Cyprus and his men concerning the service which the king demanded from them outside Cyprus, and which they did not think they owed him. On his arrival the patriarch brought, at the Church’s expense, five hundred men, on foot and horseback. Brother John of Saint-Messan of the Order of Preachers, archbishop of Tyre, died; and Brother Bonacourt of Gloire was made archbishop in his place, as I said above.

## XVIII. Deaths of the king of Armenia and the duke of Burgundy

Hethum, king of Armenia, died, and his son Luion became king and was crowned according to their custom. The duke of Burgundy died; his son Robert, who had no land, succeeded him as duke and married the sister of King Philip of France. Then the customs of Burgundy were changed for him. For according to the ancient customs, the heir of the count of Nevers, who was the duke’s eldest son, ought to have had the duchy of Burgundy.

The master of the Temple, the marshal of the Hospital, the commander of the Germans, Sir John de Gresly, and [Col. 1053D] many others went to Cyprus to reconcile the king and his barons, but returned without accomplishing anything. Sir John de Gresly was made seneschal of the kingdom of Jerusalem; William de Canet, nephew of Olivier de Termes, marshal; and John of Ibelin, lord of Arsuf, constable.

## XIX. Death of the master of the Temple

In 1273, on 8 April, Olivier de Termes returned to Acre with twenty-five mounted men and one hundred crossbowmen on foot, paid by the king of France. Brother Thomas Bérard, master of the Temple, died on the feast of Our Lady in March; and on 13 May Brother William of Beaujeu, who was overseas as commander of the Temple in Apulia, was made master. Brother William de Pousson, who had held the master’s office, and Brother Bertrand de Fox went to fetch him. Brother Goufier was made great commander, acting in the master’s place.

An agreement was made between the king of Cyprus and his barons: they were to serve him outside the kingdom of Cyprus, wherever it pleased him, in the kingdom of Jerusalem or elsewhere on this side of the sea, for four months of the year, precisely wherever his person or his son might be.

For Sir Hugh of Lusignan, king of Cyprus, and on behalf of the Christians across the sea, the archbishop of Tyre, the bishop of Jaffa, John de Gresly, seneschal of the kingdom, Brother William of Corcelles of the Hospital, Jacques Visal, and Enguerrand de Jorni went as messengers to the council at Lyons. Some of them went as procurators for the king of Cyprus against Lady Mary, who claimed and demanded before the court the kingdom of Jerusalem as her inheritance.

Estorgue, bishop of Tiberias, died; William of Salonica, archdeacon of Saint George of Lydda, was made bishop in his place.

King Philip of France married the sister of the duke of Brabant. P. Geu, the Venetian bailiff, came to Acre and would not permit John of Montfort, who called himself lord of Tyre, to remain in Acre, where he had arrived, because he wronged them regarding the right they claimed in Tyre. But the religious orders, to avoid conflict, had him go to Nazareth; from there he went to Tyre without entering Acre on that occasion.

Sir Giles de Sauci came to Acre with four hundred crossbowmen paid by the king of France and the Church; afterwards Sir Peter Daminnes came with three hundred crossbowmen [Col. 1054C] under the same arrangement.

## XX. The Council of Lyons

In 1274 the council was held at Lyons on the Rhône by Pope Gregory X. At the council the bishop of Liège and the bishop of Rodez were deposed. The Greeks were reconciled and swore obedience to the Church of Rome; they proved the articles of faith concerning which they had been doubtful, confessed them, and acknowledged them to be true.

Count Rudolf of Habsburg was elected king of Germany and emperor and was confirmed by the Church. He received the crown of the kingdom of Germany, but was not crowned emperor, because the pope died before he could come to Rome. At this council many good ordinances were made for aid to the Holy Land, as you shall hear later.

The king of Castile came to Beaucaire with a small company to speak with the pope concerning a claim he believed he had to the empire of Germany, since he had been elected to it by the princes of Germany and had expended much wealth thereupon. But he achieved nothing in the matter, for the pope supported Count Rudolf’s party, and he returned to Castile without accomplishing anything.

At the council Brother Peter of Tarentaise, archbishop of Lyons on the Rhône; the archbishop of Aix in Provence; Brother Bonaventure, the great master of the Friars Minor; and Master Peter the Spaniard were made cardinals. Aymar de Roussillon was made archbishop of Lyons. Peace was made between the canons and burgesses of Lyons, who had long warred together. Brother William de Roussillon, abbot of Savigny, was made bishop of Valence and Die, while retaining the abbey of Savigny.

Bohemond, prince of Antioch and count of Tripoli, died on 20 March. His son Bohemond was made prince and went to Armenia to be made a knight by the hand of the king of Armenia, his uncle, on the advice of his mother the princess and Bartholomew, bishop of Tortosa, who managed all his affairs because he was under age. Olivier de Termes died on 12 August.

Then King Henry of England died, and his son Lord Edward was crowned king. Adam de Romery, bailiff of the patriarch and dean of that same church of Safed, was made bishop of Safed. William of Salonica, bishop of Tiberias, died, and William the Hairy, cantor of Saint George of Lydda and chancellor of Armenia, was made in his place.

## XXI. Death of the Sultan of Babylon

In 1275, on 25 May, Baudocdar, sultan of Babylon, called Melet-Medavar, died. He ravaged the plain of Armenia and put to the sword everything he found. The number of dead, it is said, was more than two hundred thousand persons. He carried off as captives ten thousand or more girls and boys, and seized more than four hundred thousand mounts, other large beasts, and smaller livestock.

The king withdrew into the mountains with the armed men he had and the people who were besieged in Armenia. Those who had opportunity took refuge at sea. A great many merchants and other people who had escaped the Saracens and were travelling by sea fell into the hands of corsair robbers.

Sir William de Roussillon came to Acre on behalf of the king of France, bringing one hundred mounted men: namely, forty knights, sixty mounted sergeants, and four hundred foot crossbowmen, paid by the Church.

Brother Julian of the Order of the Trinity, formerly lord of Safed and a brother of the Temple, died at Tripoli. King James of Aragon died; his eldest son, Lord Peter, was made king of Aragon and count of Barcelona, while Lord James, the other son, was made king of Majorca and lord of Montpellier.

After the death of the prince, his first cousin the king of Cyprus came to Tripoli with a great and fine company of men-at-arms to advise and assist the prince’s son, who was under age. But the bishop of Tortosa, who had arrived earlier and had already assumed the child’s guardianship through the instigation of the princess his mother, prevented the king from accomplishing the purpose for which he had come. Therefore he departed from Tripoli and came to Acre.

## XXII. War between Saracens and Spaniards
Brother William of Beaujeu, Master of the Temple, who had been at the Council of Lyons, came to Acre on the day of Saint Michael. A great multitude of Saracens from Barbary crossed into Spain and, upon their arrival, defeated a great number of knights and [Col. 1056A] other men-at-arms. There were slain the archbishop of Toledo, brother of the king of Aragon and of the queen of Castile, several other valiant knights, and many other people. Afterwards the Saracens were defeated by the people of Spain and driven out of the country; they went into Aragon, defeated the king of Aragon, took many prisoners, killed many people, and captured castles and towns. There the commander of the Temple was taken, together with several others, both religious and secular, and a great number of other people. Afterwards the king of Aragon assembled a great force of men-at-arms, defeated the Saracens, recovered a large part of the castles and territory which he had lost, and the commander of the Temple in Aragon, together with several other [Col. 1056B] prisoners who had previously been captured, was released.

At that time a dispute arose at Tripoli between the knights and the people of the city, because the Romans, who had possessed all the power of the court in the time of the former prince, had inflicted many injuries and troubles upon the knights of the land. John Peter and two other Romans with him were killed. Because the bishop of Tripoli supported the Romans—as one himself born at Rome [the phrase *des perfes* is uncertain] and the prince’s uncle—while the bishop of Tortosa, who had the prince and the entire administration of Tripoli in his hand, supported the knights of the land, great hatred and conflict arose between these two bishops. This was the root and beginning of the great war that afterwards occurred between the [Col. 1056C] prince and the Temple, from which many evils ensued, as you will hear below.

And the lord of Gibelet, because he made peace with the bishop of Tripoli through the mediation of the Temple, in whose custody the bishop of Tripoli was, fell, together with him and these affairs, into the prince’s hatred through the contrivance of the bishop of Tortosa. Thus the war intensified, and many persons were harmed and ruined by it.

At that time Sir Amaury de Montfort, son of Count Simon de Montfort, through whom the war in England began, was escorting one of his sisters into Wales to marry her to the prince of Wales. A storm drove him into the territory of Lord Edward, king of England; he was captured and delivered to the king of England, who was their first cousin. On this account, and for several other reasons, war arose [Col. 1056D] between the prince of Wales and the king of England.

## XXIII. The Kingdom of Navarre Passes to the French

King Henry of Navarre and count of Champagne died. He had become king after the death of King Theobald, his brother, who died upon returning from Tunis without an heir, as you have heard above. Henry, whose wife was the sister of the count of Artois, left a young daughter. By dispensation of the court of Rome, she was promised in marriage to the son of King Philip of France, who was her cousin once removed. For this reason the kingdom of Navarre and the county of Champagne came into the hand of the king of France. This displeased the king of Castile greatly, for he did not wish to be so close to the lordship of the crown of France; and this was a very [Col. 1057A] great cause of the war which arose between the two kings.

Afterwards the widow of the said King Henry of Navarre was married to Sir Edmund, brother of Lord Edward, king of England; and the county of Champagne was sworn to him as the lady’s dower, to hold until her daughter, who was heir, should be married and of age.

In the same year Don Ferdinand, the eldest son of the king of Castile, who had married Lady Blanche, daughter of King Louis of France, was married upon this condition: if they had children together, those children were to have the kingdom of Castile without dispute, in whatever way it might happen—whether the king died before Don Ferdinand or Don Ferdinand before the king. The king and queen and the greater part of the barons of Castile swore this. [Col. 1057B] By this marriage peace was made between the king of France and the king of Castile, ending the quarrel which had existed between them. For the king of France claimed and demanded as his own the kingdom of Castile, which had devolved upon him through Lady Blanche his mother, who was the rightful heir of the kingdom of Castile and the king’s daughter.

## XXIV. Queen Blanche of Castile Returns to France

Lady Blanche had two sons by her husband. After his death she was greatly distressed, being in a foreign land, and the king of Castile was not such good company to her as he ought to have been. Therefore she so prevailed upon her brother Philip, king of France, that he sent for her and had her brought to France. But the king of Castile did not permit [Col. 1057C] her to take the children with her.

Some time afterwards the queen of Castile, who did not consider herself well treated by her husband, feared that the children might be badly brought up, and wished to preserve her oath. Through the agency of her brother, the king of Aragon, she went into Catalonia and took with her the two children of Lady Blanche; from there they were summoned to France. Thus the two children were saved and restored to their mother.

## XXV. War between the Kings of France and Castile

After the death of Don Ferdinand, Lady Blanche’s husband, Don Sancho, the other son of the king of Castile, with his father’s consent took possession of a great part of the land and caused a great part of the barons to swear that he should have the kingdom after his father’s death, contrary to the oath which the king and his barons had made. Therefore [Col. 1057D] war arose between the king of France and the king of Castile. For the king of France wished to uphold the rights of his nephews, and wished them to have the kingdom of Castile after the death of their grandfather as their rightful inheritance, under the agreements stated above. But the king of Castile opposed this and caused a great part of the kingdom of Navarre, which was in the king of France’s hand, to revolt, because it was the approach to his own territory.

But the king of France summoned a great number of knights and other men-at-arms, recovered the whole kingdom of Navarre, and they turned toward the king of France in order to uphold the children’s rights and preserve their oath. Afterwards the king of France set out to attack the king of Castile and advanced as far as the entrance into Gascony. [Col. 1058A] He had in his company, it was said, sixty thousand mounted men and innumerable armed foot soldiers. But worthy men intervened between the two and made a truce between them; therefore the king of France dismissed his men and returned to France.

## XXVI. Concerning Pope Gregory X

Pope Gregory the Tenth was born at Piacenza in Lombardy. He was of noble stock, descended from counts, and was named Master Theald. He was a canon of Lyons on the Rhône and archdeacon of Liège, a good man of good life. He had a great dispute with his bishop of Liège, chiefly because the latter did not lead a good life or conduct himself as a prelate ought. He had departed, as it were, in anger with the bishop and gone on pilgrimage to the Holy Land; and he was [Col. 1058B] at Acre when he was elected.

Thus it appeared clearly that the election had been without deceit. He was elected by the common will of the cardinals on the feast-day of Saint Giles, the first day of September. Brother Stephen of Sissy, a brother of the Temple, and Sir Fulk of Puyricard, knights, came to fetch him at Acre on behalf of the cardinals and King Charles of Sicily. Great rejoicing was held at Acre over this election, for the people of the land had great hope that he, having seen the distress in which it stood, would devote great counsel to its deliverance.

He took leave of all the worthy people of the land and embarked upon the sea in galleys on the octave of Saint Martin; he arrived at Brindisi on New Year’s Day. There [Col. 1058C] he was received with great celebration by King Charles and by a part of the cardinals who awaited his arrival there; from there he went to Rome, where he was ordained and consecrated. He knew well the poor condition in which he had left the Holy Land. Since he knew that he could not carry out his purpose at Rome as well as beyond the mountains, nor obtain as readily the counsel of the kings and princes of those lands or so great an abundance of prelates, he arranged his affairs and went to Lyons. There he assembled a general council.

At that time important messages came to him from Germany, informing him that the affairs of Germany were proceeding badly, and particularly the affairs of the Church, for want of a king. He gave them permission to elect. They went into Germany, and Count Rudolph of Habsburg was elected, by common will, [Col. 1058D] king of Germany and emperor; he was confirmed by the pope and crowned at Aachen.

## XXVII. A Tenth of Church Goods for Aid to the Holy Land

After the death of Count Richard of Cornwall, brother of the king of England, who had been king of Germany, King Philip of France came to Lyons before the council in order to confer with the pope. He restored to him the county of the Venaissin, which his ancestors had held from the Church for a long time. There the pope held the general council, at which there were one thousand four hundred persons bearing crosses. King James of Aragon was there, having come in hope of being crowned by the pope as his predecessors had been; but he failed in this, and made a very great offer, according to his means, for [Col. 1059A] aid to the Holy Land.

At this council was Brother William of Beaujeu, Master of the Temple, who was in the land overseas, as you have heard above, when he was made master. There were messengers of kings, dukes, princes, great barons, and prelates who could not attend in person. There were the envoys of Palaeologus, emperor of the Greeks, and of their patriarch. They swore upon the soul of their lord to be obedient henceforward to the Church and to believe all the articles of faith as Rome commands. They acknowledged the articles of faith concerning whose truth they had been in doubt; therefore they were reconciled to the Church and absolved from the sentence under which they had long remained.

There were also envoys from the Holy Land, who very well laid before the council the poor state in which the Holy Land stood; indeed, the council had been assembled especially [Col. 1060A] for this purpose, and they would have accomplished their business very well if the pope had lived. It was decreed there that the tenth of the churches of Christendom should, for six years, be devoted to aid for the Holy Land; that every Christian should give, for the aid of the Holy Land, one denier of the currency current in the land where he was; and that in every church there should be a chest with three keys, guarded by three worthy men, in which the money should be placed.

There usurers were condemned, and under pain of excommunication it was forbidden that anyone should go to trade, or carry merchandise, into the land of the Saracens. At this council all the poor religious orders which had been devised and established since the Lateran Council were condemned and abolished, on condition that they might remain in their religion.

[Col. 1059]

# Glossary of Unusual French Words

## A

**Abandonnement:** boldly.  
**Achaison:** cause, reason, occasion.  
**Acocher:** to lodge.  
**Acouser:** to join.  
**Acre:** Acco, Ptolemais.  
**Acreanter:** to promise.  
**Ajume:** helmet, casque.  
**Amenuiser:** to diminish.  
**Amouiller:** to soften, mollify.  
**Ançois:** before, formerly; to be distinguished from *ainseois*, “thus”; *ains* also sometimes means “formerly.”  
**Annuitier:** to become night.  
**Antain:** uncle.  
**Antaine:** aunt.  
**Aourner:** to worship.  
**Apostole:** the pope.  
**Appareiller:** to prepare oneself.  
**Ardre:** to burn.  
**Ars:** burned.  
**Assener:** to consign, secure.  
**Assené:** agreed upon.  
**Asseoir:** to besiege.  
**Atainement:** quarrel.  
**Atirer:** to negotiate, compose, settle.  
**Atirement:** settlement.  
**Atorner:** to prepare, surround.  
**Auner ses ost:** to assemble, arrange one’s army.  
**Auques:** more; also.  
**Autiers:** altar.  
**Avaler:** to descend.  
**Avoyer:** to lead astray.  
**Avoir:** wealth, goods, resources.  
**Avoutir:** adultery.

## B

**Bandor:** publicly.  
**Barat:** deceit.  
**Barbacane:** a defence or wooden covering made against enemies.  
**Baron:** husband.  
**Batan:** great courier.  
**Beer:** to stretch out.  
**Bertauder:** to shear irregularly.  
**Besilier:** to drive away.  
**Bobaucher; Bouter:** to put, place.  
**Bouir:** to drink.  
**Brucroy; Bruir:** to burn.  
**Bruissier:** [uncertain; no definition supplied].

## C

**Caintre:** to hide.  
**Carros:** the great standard.  
**Cecile:** Sicily.  
**Celéement:** secretly.  
**Chaane:** chain.  
**Chalanger:** to reclaim an inheritance.  
**Chaloir:** to sup.  
**Chatiax:** castles.  
**Chatre:** prison.  
**Chevax:** horses.  
**Chevetaine:** captain.  
**Chevir:** to negotiate, accomplish, avoid.  
**Cil:** those.  
**Clamer:** to call.  
**Coiment:** very softly, without noise.  
**Congier:** to dismiss.  
**Conroy:** design, intention.  
**Consuir:** to strike.  
**Contens:** dispute, contention.  
**Convine:** the state of affairs.  
**Convintaille:** agreement; that which is agreed.  
**Convoyer:** to accompany.  
**Corredier:** steward.  
**Coulon:** pigeon.  
**Coust:** expense.  
**Covine:** a retinue of persons; train.  
**Covins:** armed fighting wagons.  
**Creanter:** to promise, assure.  
**Crole:** credible.  
**Cuens:** count.  
**Cuider:** to think.

## D

**Damage:** damage.  
**Dame Dieu:** Lord God.  
**Deen:** dean.  
**Desconfir:** to defeat.  
**Desconfiture:** rout.  
**Deshaitié:** sick, languishing, troubled.  
**Departir:** to separate.  
**Descroisier:** to dispense from the crusade.  
**Desevrer:** to separate, break off, annul.  
**Desogler:** to disconcert.  
**Desroi:** rout.  
**Destorber:** to trouble.  
**Dex:** God.  
**Distrent:** they said.  
**Drecier:** to raise, set up.  
**Duel:** mourning.  
**Dui:** two.

## E

**Embler:** to carry away.  
**Embatir:** p. 618, “lest thieves enter.”  
**Empereor; emperere:** emperor.  
**Emperris:** empress.  
**Encelées:** inserted, enclosed.  
**Enchauchier:** to chase, give chase.  
**Enchir:** to pray, beseech.  
**Enclotier:** to enclose, shut in, surround.  
**Encombrer:** to shut up, overwhelm.  
**Endemantier:** meanwhile; previously.  
**Enfes:** child.  
**Enfouir; enfoir:** to bury.

**Engroisser:** to grow large.  
**Ennuiter:** to become night.  
**Erre:** way, circuit, course.  
**Errer:** to run.  
**Eschargaillier:** to take booty; plunder; carry off spoils.  
**Eschargalter:** to keep guard.  
**Escharrement:** [no definition supplied].

**Haities:** according to one’s wish.

[Col. 1065]

According to the traditions of the ancients, and also certain writings which possess no small authority among the Palestinians, and especially among the Greeks, the Church of Jerusalem, down to the time of Justinian Augustus of holy memory, had a bishop enjoying no, or only slight, prerogative of dignity. In the time of the aforesaid God-beloved prince, a general synod was gathered at Constantinople, in the time of Pope Vigilius, Eutychius of Constantinople, Apollinaris of Alexandria, the lord of Antioch, and Eustochius of Jerusalem, patriarchs, concerning the Three Chapters: namely, the writings of Theodoret of Cyrrhus; likewise the writings of Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia; and the letter of Ibas to Maris the Persian.

In this synod, after other institutions necessary for the Church of God which it decreed should be promulgated according to the times, the authority of the holy Fathers who had assembled there decreed by common consent that the aforesaid God-beloved Church should be honoured and that its bishop should be given a place among the patriarchs, in reverence for the Holy Resurrection. Since the aforesaid city devoted to the worship of God lay, as it were, on the boundary of the patriarchates of Alexandria and Antioch, and since those patriarchates would have no cities from which to appoint suffragans unless something were taken from each, it was judged expedient to cut something away from both, so that subject sees might be appointed for it according to the model of the other patriarchates.

Accordingly, from Antioch they removed the metropolitan sees of Caesarea and Scythopolis; from Alexandria, likewise the metropolitan sees of Rabba and Beteris. Since the same patriarch also had to have, besides the above-mentioned metropolitan sees, immediate suffragans, whom the Greeks call *cyncelli*, they removed certain bishops from the aforesaid metropolitan sees and created others anew, up to twenty-five. We have appended the number and names of these cities, first reckoning the metropolitans and their suffragans. The arrangement is as follows:

First see: Caesarea Maritima. Under this see are nineteen bishoprics.

Dora. Antipatris. Jamnia. Nicopolis. Onus. Soscuris. Raphia. The district of Apatos. The district of Jericho. The district of Livas. The district of Gadaron. Ashdod-by-the-Sea. Ashdod-hippum. Estomason. Estilion. Tricomias. Toxtus. Saltum. Constantiniaquis.

Second see: Scythopolis. Under it are nine bishoprics.

Capitoliados. [Col. 1066] Miru. Gadaru. Pelos. Vilisippus. Tetracomias. Oluna. Galanis. Komanas.

Third see: Rabba of Moab. Under this see are twelve bishoprics.

Augustopolis. Arindila. Kara. [Col. 1067] Serapolis. Mempsidos. Eulitis. Zora. Virosum. Pentacomia. Mamapson. Mitroconeras. Saltum Hieraticum.

Fourth see: Beteris of Arabia. Under it are thirty-five bishoprics.

Adrasson. Dias. Medadon. Gerasa. Nein. Philadelphia. Hierapolis. Essmos. Neapolis. Themistus. Philippopolis. Dionysia. Constantinu. Pentacomias. Tricomias. Canastados. The district of Votanios. Exacomias. Enacomias. Comogonias. Comogeros. Comosthonis. Comis. Mahadaron. Comocoreatas. Comis Capron. Comis Insuavos. Comis Pirroareton. Comis Pecius. Comis Ariathon. Comis Neotis. Lydda. [Col. 1068] Joppa. Ascalon. Gaza. Meimas. Diocletianopolis. Beitt Gerbein. Neapolis. Sebastia. Jericyntus. Tiberias. Diocaesarea. Legionum. Capitolina Mauronensis. Gedera. Nazareth. Tabor. Caracha, or Petra. Adroga. Afra. Aelis. Faram. Elinopolis. Mount Sinai.

# In the Year of the Lord 1185: Lucius III, Roman Pontiff

[Col. 1067]

## Notice

*(Mansi, Councils, XXII, 473.)*

“Pope Lucius the Third,” says William of Tyre, *History of the Sacred War*, book XXII, chapter 7—he was also Humbert, bishop of Ostia, a Tuscan by nation and from Lucca by birthplace, a man very advanced in years and only moderately learned—“was the first pontiff created, on 29 August in the year of the Lord 1181, according to the form prescribed by the Third Lateran Council.”

At the beginning of his pontificate, this pope devoted himself entirely to fostering Christian peace. When the emperor had set out for Italy, Pope Lucius left the city of Rome, as Krantz says in the *Saxon History*, book VI, chapter 47, to meet him and discuss with him the affairs of the Christian commonwealth, which had begun to decline severely in Asia. The two highest powers of Christendom met at Verona. An immense multitude of churchmen had gathered, requesting reconciliation with the Apostolic See, because in the schism they had followed the emperor and had been ordained and installed by antipopes. Emperor Frederick intervened for them, asking that they should be received into favour. The pope graciously consented.

But when hands were to be laid on each of them the following day, his policy changed, because he said that decrees made at the Venetian council could not be annulled except by another council. He promised that he would soon summon another assembly, in which a decision on these matters would be made. The Germans’ threats were heard, as was their custom, but the cardinals were not moved by them. This alteration of policy was thought to have originated with Conrad, archbishop of Mainz and bishop of Worms.

Thereupon the emperor began negotiations with the pontiff about the inheritance of the powerful Lady Matilda in Italy. Under the emperors Henry father and son, she had done much for the Church; at her death she left much property to that Church, to possess as its own, while the emperor claimed it for the imperial right. As stated, she was the daughter of the margrave of Saxony. Yet chronology proves that she died long before this age, unless someone maintains that there were two Matildas and that one flourished in Italy after the other. The dispute between priesthood and monarchy was long debated, but no conclusion could be reached; they separated without end. —Krantz.

Baronius adds from Arnold of Lübeck’s *Chronicle*, book III, chapter 10, that at the same place a schism arose between emperor and pope concerning the election of the bishop of Trier; its details are set forth fully by the same author.

He urged Christian princes to prepare themselves collectively to bring aid to the faithful who were fighting barbarians in Asia. But while he was arranging for the expedition to be hastened with oars and sails, he was seized by illness and died at Verona on 25 November. He was buried in the cathedral church, in the year of the Lord 1185, after governing the Church for four years, two months, and twenty-seven days. He adorned the city of Lucca, from which he came, with many gifts. From Emperor Frederick, with whom he had the most intimate and friendly relations, he obtained that throughout all Etruria no coinage should have currency or use except that of Lucca, just as the Lombards accepted no other than the coinage of Pavia. At this time Abbot Joachim flourished; more concerning him will be said below in the notes to the Fourth Lateran Council. The Maronites, rejecting the error of Maron the Monothelite, returned to the bosom of the Church, retaining the name derived, as they say, from Saint Maron the abbot.

[Col. 1069]
