# Letters and Privileges of Pope Lucius III

For the books used, see the index prefixed to volume CLXXIX.

## Year 1181

[Col. 1071A]

I. He receives the monastery of Saint Peter ad Vincula at Ravenna under protection and confirms its goods and rights, imposing upon the monks an annual rent of twelve denarii of Pavia coinage.  
*(Velletri, 28 September.)*

[See Rubeus, *History of Ravenna*, p. 353, where mention of this privilege occurs.]

II. He receives the monastery of Saint Mary of Gallomonte under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges.  
*(Velletri, 14 October.)*

[*Neustria Pia*, p. 873.]

Lucius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Geoffrey, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Gallomonte, and the brethren of the same place, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity, etc.

Whenever a request is made of us which is recognized as consonant with religion and propriety, it befits us willingly to grant it and to afford appropriate support to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and take the aforesaid monastery of St Mary of Gallomont, in which you are devoted to the divine service, under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves, strengthening it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree, first of all, that the monastic order which is known to have been instituted in that monastery according to God, the Rule of Blessed Benedict, and the observance of the brothers of Hambye, shall be inviolably observed there for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings and princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, through the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit to specify in their own terms: the place itself on which the aforesaid monastery stands, with all its appurtenances, etc., as in the confirmation of King Henry of England.

> [Note: Col. 1071B]
>
> **Charter of foundation**
>
> Since, amid the changefulness of things and succession of times, human memory swiftly slips away—as the Psalmist says, “like grass” (Psalm 102)—and since the efforts of that pestilential sower of tares, envious of the love of the faithful and rejoicing in his own malice, may be wholly weakened by the passage of time and by the concealment of his envy, I, Nicholas of Stoteville, have thought it fitting to record and confirm in this present charter of mine the gifts and alms which, with God as author and with the consent of Robert, my son and heir, I give to God, to the abbey of St Mary of Gallomont, and to the monks serving God there, for the salvation of the soul of King Henry, son of the Empress Matilda; and for the salvation of my own soul, of Juliana my wife, of Robert my son, of my other sons, and of all my predecessors.
>
> First, the site and situation of the abbey itself; and all the land I possess as far as the riverbank; and the wood before the abbey itself; and all the land around the wood, as far as the enclosure extends; and the meadow between the wood and my fishpond; and the hides of the animals of my park for making books; and at Tirondivilla, thirty-three acres of land which I held there in demesne; and at Rivilla, my wood and my entire demesne; and two tenants with their holdings, namely Robert Costart and Walter the smith; and the church of Logiis, the church of Tegervilla, the church of Pervilla in England, and the church of Estrefled, with the hermitage of St Leonard; at Tristevilla, one tenant with his holding, namely William son of Roses; at Gallomont, two burgage holdings, namely those of Gilbert Merant and Guarin of Grinville; and the holding of Troistete of Alneto; near Logiis, fifty acres of land; at Vallibus, twenty acres of land; near Logiis, one tenant with his holding, namely Guy of Mara; and a certain part of my wood at Logiis, as far as the enclosure extends, between my wood and the wood of Geoffrey Affagard; and a mill near Gaufevilla called Flascart; near Gallomont, the mill of Alneto and half the mill of Vado; my meadow at Grandcamp; ten acres of land near Tigervilla; and wherever my animals have grazing and my swine pannage, there likewise shall the animals and swine of the monks have them. All these gifts, etc.
>
> **Charter of confirmation by the King of England**
>
> HENRY, by the grace of God King of England, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and Count of Anjou, to archbishops, bishops, abbots, counts, justiciars, sheriffs, and all his ministers and faithful subjects throughout all his land, greeting.
>
> Know that I have granted and by this my present charter confirmed to God, to the abbey of St Mary of Gallomont, and to the monks serving God there, all gifts of churches, lands, persons, and alms which have reasonably been made to them, both in ecclesiastical things and in temporal possessions—namely, from the gift of Stoteville, etc., as above. It then adds:
>
> From the gift of Juliana, wife of the aforesaid Nicholas: in England, near Norwich, one hundred shillings’ worth of land from her first marriage portion; and from the gift of Robert of Stoteville, son of the same Nicholas, the church of Gomerville, the church of Magnaville, and the church of Wimonville, with the altar of St Stephen; and a certain mill near Beverdam, of the honor of Ramorum, with everything belonging to the mill, in its mill-toll and in every respect; his water-rights at Stoteville; and eighteen acres of land in the same vill, which he had purchased from Robert his son-in-law; and above Gallomont, fifty acres of land from the land of Tronquay; and from the gift of Nicholas of Stoteville, son of the aforesaid Nicholas, fifty shillings’ worth of land at Arville; and from the gift of William of Stoteville, son of the aforesaid elder Nicholas, a certain mark’s worth of land at Estrefled; and from the gift of Richard of Stoteville, son of the aforesaid elder Nicholas, forty shillings annually from his mill at Herecourt, called Turmolin; from the gift of Peter of Hotot and Juliana his wife, their mill at Caney in its entirety; and by the grant of Richard of Alfay and John his son, the whole mill with its appurtenances which Nicholas of Stoteville and Juliana his wife gave to the aforesaid abbey near Gauseville; and one measure of grain which William Burdet held in that same mill, which the abbot and convent of that abbey held from William himself, with the consent of Ainfrid, his son and heir; and from the gift of the same Richard of Alfay, thirty-five acres of land near Stigal, in discharge of the remainder which his mother had given to the aforesaid abbey; and from the gift of Reginald of Gerponville, one measure of grain annually from his mill at Hamel, and one load of wheat annually to be received near Clivilla, as his charter contains; and from the gift of Robert Affargart and Geoffrey his son, one measure of grain annually from the mill at Noet, ten acres of land at Logiis, and at Hacquaville the holding of Gosca the carpenter in full; and from the gift of Matthew of Gerarville and William his son, half a measure of salt to be taken annually from his own salt-store.
>
> And from the gift of Walter of Castrillon, four and a half acres of land by the causeway of Goufrediville, seventeen cartloads of oats, and four capons from two tenants of his forest land; and the tithe of all land and revenue which he shall acquire. And from the gift of William of Canoville, half a measure of grain annually to be had from his mill on his bank at Witeflend. And from the gift of Walter of Arfay, Patricia his wife, and William their son, the church of Devilla. And from the gift of Richard Tallebot, Amicia his wife, and their sons Hugh and William, one measure of oats at Belvay, from the holding of Hugh son of Jefrey Larduin, which he holds in Canuta Wood. Therefore I will and firmly command, etc.]

It further adds:

No one shall presume to exact tithes from you of your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen fleeing the world, free and unencumbered, and retain them without any contradiction. Moreover, we forbid any of your brothers, after making profession in that place, to depart from it without his abbot’s permission, unless for the sake of a stricter religious observance; and no one shall dare to retain one who has departed without letters of authorization from the community. When a general interdict has been laid upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a low voice.

In the parish churches which you possess, you may choose priests and present them to the diocesan bishop. If they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust them with the care of souls, so that they shall answer to him concerning spiritual matters and to you concerning temporal matters. Furthermore, we decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while preserving the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no person shall be placed over it by any trick of intrigue or by force, except one whom the brothers, by common consent, or the sounder part of their counsel, shall, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict, provide to be elected.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but, preserving all things whole, they shall in every way benefit the uses for which they were granted—for its governance and support—saving the authority of the Apostolic See, the canonical right of the diocesan bishop, and the due reverence owed to the monastery of Hambye, etc.

Given at Velletri, on the second Ides of October, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1181 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Lucius III.

### III. He takes the Church of Lucca under his protection and confirms its possessions and privileges.  
*(Lateran, 12 November.)*

[*Memoirs for the History of Lucca*, II, II, 194.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WILLIAM, bishop of Lucca, and to his successors canonically appointed for ever.

The order of justice requires that it should not be thought alien to our office that we love the Church entrusted to you more ardently and devote ourselves more diligently to its advancement and increase, inasmuch as, by reason both of our native land and of the benefit which we received from that Church, we acknowledge ourselves to be under greater obligation to it. For it is fitting that, since we received the grace of baptism in that Church, we should preserve it and its rights with a particular concern and extend apostolic protection to it, so that it may remain peaceful in future times against the assaults of the wicked.

Therefore, venerable brother bishop in Christ, moved by the matters we have stated and by consideration of your devotion, we take under our protection the Church over which, by God’s providence, you are known to preside, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, Alexander II, Paschal II, and [lacuna] Urban II, Roman pontiffs; under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, [lacuna] by the privilege of this writing [lacuna], decreeing that whatever possessions [lacuna] goods that Church at present [lacuna] possesses [lacuna] are seen to belong to it.

To these we add the parish church and estate of Marlia, with the church of St Terentius and with all its holdings, lands, and every appurtenance. Also the two castles of Moriano, with all their appurtenances and adjacent lands, as [lacuna] we know [lacuna]. And the land called Cerbajola; also the castle called Fundanium, with all its appurtenances; likewise the castle of Decimo and the parish church [lacuna], with everything belonging to it. Also the parish church [lacuna], the land of Cerignana, and the castle and estate of Verrucla, which is in the Alps. The tithes [lacuna] also of Verrucla, which is near Bojanum [lacuna]. We include the parish church, castle, and estate of St Mary called “at the Mountain,” with every appurtenance; and the land of the place called [lacuna]; the castle and estate of St Gervasius, with all that belongs to it. The parish church of Ficeclo with its chapels; the chapel of St Vitus of the Valley [lacuna] (of the Arno) [lacuna]; the parish church of Appiano with all its chapels; the estate of Camuliano with its appurtenances [lacuna], and the parish church there with all its chapels; the parish church of Gello with all its chapels; that of Triano with all its chapels; that of Aquis with all its chapels; the castle of Monte di Castello with all its appurtenances; and the parish church of St Stephen with all its chapels.

Moreover, following in the footsteps of our predecessor of pious memory Pope Calixtus, we grant, by the kindness of the Apostolic See, to you and your successors the use of the pallium during the solemnities of Mass in your church, provided only that you use it on those days on which it has been granted to you by our predecessors.

Furthermore, by [lacuna] authority, we decree that no monastery or church shall be established in your bishopric without the assent of you or your successors, without prejudice to [lacuna] privileges. We forbid the anointing of catechumens and the sick among the people by monks, or the imposition of public penances, without the permission of you or your successors.

But if the people of the monastery [lacuna] assemble for the reception of the divine office, those same sacraments shall be administered through a priest-chaplain to whom the bishop has entrusted the government of the people and the care of souls, while preserving the reasonable customs [lacuna] of the churches. Concerning parish churches held by monks in your bishopric, following the synodal ruling of Pope Urban of blessed memory, we decree that they shall in no way install a priest in them without the authority of you or your successors; rather, when they fall vacant, they shall be presented to you and to the abbots and priors to whom those churches belong, and you shall entrust the care of souls to them if they are suitable, so that [lacuna] they shall answer concerning the care of the people and their own order.

Moreover, if the parishes, monasteries, or churches of Lucca have disputes among themselves and [lacuna] a complaint comes before the bishop, the controversy shall be decided by his judgment, saving the authority of the Roman Church. We also decree [lacuna] that no one shall have power to receive persons excommunicated or interdicted by the bishop of Lucca into a prohibited [lacuna].

By this present writing we further enact that the bishop of Lucca shall be elected not through the violence of any lay persons whatsoever, but by the canons of the Church according to the enactments of the canons. We likewise confirm to you and your successors those things which have been granted or confirmed by our predecessors Alexander II and Paschal II, Roman pontiffs [lacuna].

We decree that the decision reasonably given between your predecessor and the abbot of Ficeclo concerning tithes, churches, and other matters by Ildebrand, formerly bishop of Pistoia, Argentim the archpriest, and R. the primicerius, shall be observed in future times as it is contained in the public instrument and has hitherto been observed. We likewise decree that the renunciation made by Bulgarus, count of Ficeclo, to John your predecessor concerning certain possessions and churches, shall remain valid henceforth, as the public instrument of Gerard the notary contains. We hold valid, and confirm by apostolic authority, the canonical customs which you are known still to possess from ancient times in the parish churches of monks and in the other parts of the bishopric, both in receiving synodal dues and in other matters [lacuna].

Furthermore, out of reverence for the Church entrusted to you, and yielding to the prayers of you and your canons, as well as of the clergy, consuls, and people of your city, we grant to you and your successors, with the counsel of our brothers, the use of the cross throughout your bishopric, and confirm it by apostolic authority.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, remove or retain its possessions, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations [lacuna], but that they may be preserved whole for the uses for which they were granted, to their full benefit, saving the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Theodorus, bishop of the see of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina.  
I, James, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin.  
I, Rainerius, cardinal deacon of St Gregory at the Golden Veil.  
I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St [lacuna].  
I, Gratianus, cardinal deacon of SS Cosmas and Damian.  
I, Vivianus, cardinal priest of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill.  
I, Rainerius, cardinal deacon of St Adrian.  
I, Cynthius, cardinal priest of the title of St Cecilia.  
I, Matthew, cardinal deacon of St Mary the New.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the second Ides of November, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1181 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Lucius.

### IV. To P[hilip], archbishop [of Cologne]: he reports that he has ordered the provost of Bonn to excommunicate the count of Sayn if he has not compensated the monastery of Siegburg for the damages inflicted upon it.  
*(Lateran, 1 November.)*

[LACOMBLET, *Urkund.*, I, 341.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother P., archbishop, and to his beloved sons, the chapter of Cologne, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because of certain injuries which the nobleman, the count of Sayn, inflicted upon the monastery of Siegburg, and because of a castle which he built upon its freehold estate, we instructed our beloved son the provost of Bonn that, if the aforesaid count does not make amends for the aforesaid acts, he is not to delay in binding him and the inhabitants of the castle, excepting little children and women, with the bond of excommunication. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, when the provost has pronounced sentence on the count and the other persons aforesaid on this account, you shall cause it to be inviolably observed throughout your whole diocese until they have amended their conduct.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of November.

### V. Privilege for the abbey of St Mary of Soissons.  
*(Lateran, 16 November.)*

[D. GERMAIN, *History of Our Lady of Soissons*, 443.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter in Christ, the abbess of St Mary of Soissons, greeting and apostolic blessing.

You have informed us that Matilda, formerly abbess, while she lived at the church of Blessed Peter, promised four prebends, before they fell vacant, to certain clerics at her pleasure, but assigned none of them before she died. For this reason, those to whom such a promise was made do not cease unreasonably to harass your monastery. Since the sacred Lateran Council condemns such promises, lest anyone be seen to desire his neighbor’s death, we absolve you and that monastery, through the kindness of the Apostolic See, from promises of this kind, strictly forbidding anyone to trouble you or your monastery on this ground for any reason.

Moreover, wishing profitably to provide for you and your sisters, we forbid by the authority of this writing that anyone holding a prebend in the greater church shall henceforth be admitted in yours in any manner, and that prebends shall not be promised to anyone before they fall vacant.

Given at the Lateran, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December.

### VI. He takes the monastery of Siegburg under his protection and confirms its goods and rights.  
*(Rome, St Peter’s, 18 November.)*

[LACOMBLET, *Urkund.*, I, 337.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GERARD, abbot of the monastery situated on Mount Siegburg, and his brothers, both present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

Whenever a request is made of us which is recognized as consonant with religion and propriety, it befits us willingly to grant it and to afford fitting support to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to our just petitions; and, following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Innocent of happy memory, we take under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of St Michael the Archangel, situated on Mount Siegburg, in which you are devoted to the divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing.

We decree that whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, through the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their own terms.

The place itself on which the aforesaid monastery stands, with all its appurtenances. The whole church at Achara and the whole church at Hanefe; the church in Lower Pleysa and that in Upper Pleysa; the church at Bercheim. Likewise, what you hold in the church of Geisteinghen, the church of Mendene, the church of Hare, the church of Olma, and the church of Strala; and the church at Wizenchirken. By apostolic authority we confirm to you these aforesaid churches, free from every payment and exaction, with their tithes, as they are known to have been canonically granted to your monastery by Anno, archbishop of Cologne of good memory, and by his successors, and confirmed by their writings.

Moreover, we likewise confirm to you the dependent houses and estates belonging by right to this monastery: namely, the cell at Pleysa, the cell of Hirzenove, the cell at Rimago, the cell at Thidrode, the cell at Zulpich, the cell at Millen, the cell at Furstenberg near the church of Xanten, and the cell at Stokheim, with all their appurtenances.

Likewise the estate at Hanefa, with tithes and the other appurtenances, which your church received in exchange from the canons of Bonn, given in exchange for the custody of Bonn for the use of themselves and their church. The vill of Mandene, which it received from the provost and canons of the mother church in exchange for the tithe at Badelecca. Your places, namely Achera; likewise Achera, Strala, Gestingen, Lara, Mandene, Aschemere, Gulsa, with the tithes of Salic land, whether cultivated by your own labor or by your tenants. Leia, Bettendorp, Ulma, Moffendorp, Flattena, Pirna, Venheim, Kerchich, Sulze, Meimedorp, Dorendorp, Mulindorp, Irmindiroth, Hofstede, Anrufle, Lwesberg, Quintinachin, Edelenkirchen, Hunefe, and the vill of Hirzenowin, which King Henry IV bestowed upon that monastery. The tithes of that vill; likewise estates at Hanepha, Wedowo, Tevirnich, Henaena, Nistre, Rupretherode, Brath, Ocherode, Winkinberg, and Alpach; the tithe at Heisterscorzzim; the tithe at Wizinkirchen; the tithe at Hanepha; and the tithe at Brathcozzim.

At Kercich, a benefice acquired by purchase. At Flattina, the benefice of Herrad, acquired by purchase. Likewise Dudlingin, Unkilbach, Brubach, Crichesdorp, Walerdop, and Geislere. A holding at Wosnich; a holding at Kessenich. Two parts of the vineyards at Brubach, which Louis, count of Thuringia, gave you for the soul of his mother Gunegunda. An estate at Vennehusen, Spele, Wolpinrode, Godingouin, Auvich, Dalehusin, and Reginsagen. An estate at Hanepha, received in exchange from the brothers of Werden. An estate at Ulpich, which Walter of Roulant and his wife Voda bestowed upon you. Likewise tithes at Ghimminich; tithes at Geseche, which were canonically conferred by the diocesan bishops. Also the unrestricted grant of the deanery in which the mountain itself is situated, as it was reasonably conferred upon your monastery by the archbishops of Cologne.

We forbid the advocates to whom the advocacy of the monastery is entrusted from time to time to appoint an advocate from elsewhere, or to demand from the goods supplied for their stipends, or from payments made in judicial matters, more than is shown to have been prescribed by the ordinance of Archbishop Anno. We therefore decree, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Theodinus, bishop of the see of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina.  
I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St Susanna.  
I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin.  
I, Gratianus, cardinal deacon of SS Cosmas and Damian.  
I, Matthew, cardinal deacon of St Mary the New.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1181 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Lucius.

### VII. He takes the monastery of St Peter of Cerreto, in the diocese of Volterra, under his protection and confirms its goods and privileges.  
*(Rome, St Peter’s, 26 November.)*

[MITTARELLI, *Camaldolese Annals*, IV, Appendix, p. 108.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons MAURO, abbot of the monastery of St Peter of Cerreto, and his brothers, both present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

Whenever a request is made of us which is recognized as consonant with religion and propriety, it befits us willingly to grant it and to afford fitting support to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and take the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to the divine service, under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, strengthening it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree, first of all, that the monastic order which is known to have been instituted in that place according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict shall be inviolably observed there for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, through the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their own terms: the place itself on which the aforesaid monastery stands, with all its appurtenances; the church of St Saviour of Fungeto, with all its appurtenances. We also confirm to you by apostolic authority the tithe of your agricultural produce, as you have held it without challenge for forty years and still possess it, provided that you are obliged to give it to no one except your hospice.

You may also receive into conversion clerics and laymen fleeing the world, free and unencumbered, without anyone’s opposition, and retain them in your monastery. When a general interdict has been laid upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, without ringing bells, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, and in a low voice. Furthermore, we decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while preserving the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove or retain its possessions, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but all things shall remain unimpaired and whole, and shall in every way benefit the uses for which they were granted—for its governance and support. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

HELP US, O GOD OF OUR SALVATION; ST PETER; ST PAUL; POPE LUCIUS III.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Theodorus, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St Susanna.  
I, Vivianus, cardinal priest of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill.  
I, Hugh, cardinal priest of the title of St Clement.  
I, Arduinus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem.  
I, Matthew, cardinal priest of the title of St Marcellus.  
I, Laborans, cardinal priest of the title of St Calixtus at St Mary across the Tiber.  
I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin.  
I, Rainerius, cardinal deacon of the title of St George at the Golden Veil.  
I, Rainerius, cardinal deacon of St Adrian.

*(Place of the + sign.)*

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of December, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1181 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

### VIII. Bull for the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem.  
*(Rome, St Peter’s, 29 November.)*

[*Privileges of Saint John of Jerusalem*, p. 87.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brothers archbishops and bishops, and to the beloved sons abbots, priors, archdeacons, deans, priests, and other prelates of churches to whom these letters shall come, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have heard—and, hearing, have wondered—that although it has been granted to our beloved sons, the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem, by our fathers and predecessors, and afterward allowed and confirmed by ourselves, that they are bound to pay tithes to no one from the lands which they cultivate by their own hands and at their own expense, certain persons presume, contrary to the indulgence of the Apostolic See, to demand and extort tithes from them. By a wrongful and perverse interpretation of apostolic privileges, they distort the clause and assert that where it is written “from their labors,” it ought to be understood as referring to newly cleared lands.

Since it is manifest to all right-thinking persons that such an interpretation is perverse and contrary to sound understanding, because under that clause they are wholly free and exempt from payment of tithes both on lands which they have brought or may bring under cultivation and on cultivated lands which they till by their own hands or at their own expense, we command and command by these apostolic letters that you ensure that all your parishioners are forbidden by our authority ever to presume to demand or extort in any way from the aforesaid brethren tithes or even first-fruits from newly cleared land, from other land which they cultivate by their own hands and at their own expense, or from the increase of their animals. For, if we had intended “from newly cleared lands” alone where we write “from their labors,” we should have written “from newly cleared lands,” as we do in the privileges of certain others.

And because it is neither fitting nor proper that persons should act against the enactments of the Apostolic See, which ought to retain inviolable force, we command and firmly enjoin you that, if any canons, clerics, monks, or laymen burden the aforesaid brethren by demanding tithes contrary to the privileges of the Apostolic See, you shall suspend canons, clerics, and monks from office, without contradiction, appeal, or delay; and strike laymen with sentence of excommunication. You shall cause both the sentence of excommunication and that of suspension to be inviolably observed until due satisfaction is made.

By the authority of this writing we further command you that, if anyone lays violent hands upon the aforesaid brethren, you shall publicly denounce him as excommunicated with lighted candles, and cause all persons carefully to avoid him as excommunicated until he has made suitable satisfaction to the brethren aforesaid and has presented himself before the apostolic presence with letters from the diocesan bishop containing the truth of the matter.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the third day before the Kalends of December.

### IX. To the archpriest and canons of the Church of Lucca: he reports that the prior of St Fridianus came before him to have privileges confirmed. He affirms that he will protect their rights.  
*(Rome, St Peter’s, November–December.)*

[BALUZE, *Miscellanies*, ed. MANSI, IV, 596.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the archpriest and canons of the Church of Lucca, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We received your letter with the kindness we owed you, [Col. 1082C] and from its tenor we learned that our beloved sons, the prior and canons of St. Fridian, did not duly answer the letters which we sent on your behalf; but that, within the appointed term, the prior set out upon a journey and came to the Apostolic See. You therefore requested more urgently that our will be communicated to you as quickly as possible. Let it accordingly be made known to you by these present letters that we desire the matter between you and them to be brought to an end, in your vicinity, either by agreement or by judgment; but if this perhaps cannot be done, it shall necessarily be referred to the Apostolic See. Know, moreover, that the prior has presented himself before us in order to renew his privileges and to transact matters concerning St. Salvator of Ficarolo and certain other affairs which do not concern you; but, with the Lord as author, he has not done and will not do anything from which prejudice to your right may arise. [Col. 1082D] For our part, so far as we can consistently with propriety, we shall take care, by virtue of our office, to preserve your right. Nor should you wonder at the brethren who refused to subscribe to your privilege, since nothing is ordinarily confirmed for anyone which he does not possess at all. Hence you know that our beloved son D., contrary to our will and advice, laboured to renew that very privilege. But lest we should appear to wish to deny you what we could in any manner grant, we acquiesced in his wish so far as lay within our power.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s.

## X. Privilege for the convent of St. Hilary. (Lateran, 29 December.)

[LAMI, *Ecclesiastical Monuments of Florence*, I, 202.]

[Col. 1083A]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, CAPITINIGRO, abbess of the monastery of St. Hilary situated in the diocese of Fiesole, and her sisters, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

The Apostolic See ought to afford protection to prudent virgins who, beneath the habit of religion, with lamps kindled by works of holiness, continually prepare themselves to go forth to meet the Bridegroom (Matt. 25), lest perhaps an assault of any rashness either turn them back from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of sacred religion. [Col. 1083B] Therefore, beloved daughters in Christ, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of blessed memory, Alexander, Celestine, Eugenius, and Adrian, Roman pontiffs, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery of St. Hilary, situated in the diocese of Fiesole, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and those who succeed you.

[Col. 1083C] Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: the monastery of St. Gorgonius with its appurtenances; the monastery of St. Gregory with its appurtenances, situated near the city of Bologna; the church of St. Mary of Agnano with its appurtenances; the church of St. Martin of Musignano with its appurtenances; the church of St. Stephen of Pitiana with its appurtenances; the church in the castle of St. Hilary with its appurtenances; the church of St. Mary, which is within the castle and monastery, with its appurtenances; the castle of St. Hilary with all its appurtenances; and the castle of Remulo with its appurtenances. We likewise confirm to you the revenues, rights of patronage, and reasonable ancient customs which you have in the monastery at Vallombrosa. [Col. 1083D]

No one shall presume to exact tithes from you on your newly cleared lands (*novalia*) which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. You may receive women fleeing the secular world, free and unencumbered, into conversion, and retain them without any opposition. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. In the parish churches which you possess, you may choose priests and present them to the diocesan bishop; and, if they are suitable, the bishop shall commit the care of souls to them, so that they shall answer to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters. [Col. 1084A]

Following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Adrian, we decree that the monastery itself shall remain forever in the same condition and religious character—namely, that of religious women—daily advancing in religion, as was established from its beginning. By apostolic authority we prohibit new customs or exactions from being imposed upon you, your churches, or your people. Baptism also, as has been ancient custom, shall always be celebrated in your church at the proper time, with all opposition by any person set aside. Moreover, we prohibit anyone from daring to usurp for himself the viscountship of that same convent; rather, the abbess who at the time presides over the monastery may, after taking counsel with her entire chapter, confer that office and, where fault or another manifest reasonable cause requires it, remove it. [Col. 1084B] You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordination of clerics to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to furnish these things freely and without any improper demand.

Furthermore, we decree that the burial-place of your monastery shall be free; and no one shall obstruct the devotion and last will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted, while preserving nevertheless the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. [Col. 1084C]

Upon the death of yourself, the present abbess of this place, or of any woman who succeeds you, no one shall be placed over it through any trick of intrusion or violence, except the woman whom the sisters by common consent, or the sounder part of the sisters’ counsel, shall determine ought to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, or diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be kept whole for the full benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. [Col. 1084D] If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St. Susanna.  
I, Vivianus, cardinal priest of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill.  
I, Cynthius, cardinal priest of the title of St. Cecilia.  
I, Ugo, cardinal priest of the title of St. Clement.  
[Col. 1085A] I, Ardricus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem.  
I, Matthew, cardinal priest of the title of St. Marcellus.  
I, Hyacinthus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin.  
I, Rainerius, cardinal deacon of St. Adrian.  
I, Matthew, cardinal deacon of St. Mary Nova.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January [29 December], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1181 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

## XI. To the German clergy. (Lateran, 29 December.)

[LE PAIGE, *Library of the Premonstratensian Order*, p. 634.]

[Col. 1085B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the archbishops and bishops established throughout the German kingdom, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We desire that those things which ecclesiastical men reasonably establish for the preservation of religion and order in the Church of God should remain firm and unimpaired, lest, if they are rendered void by anyone’s rashness, the vigour of discipline perish and grave danger arise to souls. Now it was established long ago in the Premonstratensian Order that abbots and provosts must assemble every year for the general chapter. Yet some, summoned on account of the past schism, refuse to come there, despising the command of the abbot of Prémontré and of the Apostolic See. [Col. 1085C] Therefore, by apostolic writings, we command your whole body that if any persons subject to your jurisdiction, summoned to the chapter by the said abbot, refuse to attend—unless this has been remitted to them by the decision of the superior abbot, or some other reasonable and necessary cause has excused them—you shall observe, and cause to be inviolably observed until due satisfaction is made, the sentence which he has pronounced against them on that account.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January [29 December], in the year of the Lord 1181.

## XII. To Canute, king of Sweden: he commends to him Ægidius, bishop of Århus. (Lateran, 30 December.)

[HILJEGREN, *Swedish Diplomatic Records*, I, p. 117.]

[Col. 1085D]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to CANUTE, illustrious king of Sweden, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Behold: in accordance with the urgency of your prayers and our promise, we send to you our beloved son Ægidius, whom we have made bishop of Århus in place of the deceased Ilianus. He is indeed a pious and prudent man, conspicuous for honourableness, and especially dear to us among our other brethren because of his merits. [Col. 1086A] We have fully granted him the office of bishop throughout the diocese of Århus, which now lies within your jurisdiction, that he may root out paganism, extirpate harmful things, plant Christianity, and accomplish similar salutary works, according as, with the prudence given him by God, he sees each thing ought to be done or left undone.

We therefore ask your royal highness to receive him—or rather, to receive us in him—to treat him readily and honourably, and to cause all your subjects, especially those dwelling in the above-named diocese, to show him due honour, so that the devotion which we trust you bear toward the Apostolic See may be made manifest in effect. Thus we and our brethren may deservedly increase in your affection, and Bishop Ægidius himself—upon whose most sacred office our supreme bishop, God, may bestow his blessing—may, through himself and his people, be bound for all time to your love by a grateful return in whatever way he can promise it. [Col. 1086B]

Given at L[ateran], on the third day before the Kalends of January [30 December], in the second year of our pontificate.

[Note: The words “in the second year of our pontificate” are thought to have been added by another hand. JAFFÉ.]

## XIII. Privilege for the church of SS. Crispin and Crispinian of Cavea Suessionensis.

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, X, Documents, 126.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons THEOBALD, abbot of the church of Saints Crispin and Crispinian of Cavea Suessionensis, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

The vigour of equity and the order of reason require that just petitioners be granted their request, especially when piety supports the will of those asking and truth does not abandon it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church of the holy martyrs Crispin and Crispinian of Cavea Suessionensis, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. [Col. 1086C] First, we decree that the canonical order known to have been established in that church according to the rule of the Lord and of Blessed Augustine shall there be observed inviolate for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, through grants of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names. [Col. 1086D]

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; whatever Paganus, knight of Cella, gave you in alms at Bellomonte, with the consent of his wife Ermentrude, his sons, and Renaud, knight of Guni, from whose fief it was held, both in land-rent (*terragium*), wine-rent (*vinagium*), quit-rent (*census*), and other rights; your vineyard adjoining the aforesaid place; whatever Odo, knight of Chrosni, possessed at Mont-Nantoil and gave you in alms for Mary, his daughter, a convert of that church, with his sons’ consent, both in wine-rent and in quit-rent; and one muid of wine which Tesso gave in alms to the aforesaid church in the same village; [Col. 1087A] the cultivated land of Sancei in the village of St. Audoen, saving the land-rent and tithe belonging to that church; whatever Dudo Lombard possessed in Neuville, which he gave your church in alms in return for four muids of grain payable annually, both in judicial rights, land-rent, and other matters; the land which Fredessendis, daughter of Odo, knight of Pont-Saint-Médard, gave you in alms at Valrain, with the consent of her husband Warner and her sons; the tithe of the cultivated land of Lisiard, knight of Virzi, near Old Town; the tithe of your land at Lorval, in the parish of Nancel, together with the tithe of the church; the vineyard of Bordain given you by Berenger the Butler and his sister Ascelina; the land of Beneroles given you in alms, without any redemption, by Radulf, son of Engelbert Faucillons, and his sister, with the consent of Gerard of Cherisi, from whose fief it was held; the tithe of Loiri; three solidi of quit-rent, nine denarii, one obol, and the land which Bartholomew, knight of Fessoma, gave in alms to your church at Valresis; [Col. 1087B] all the right which you have in the altar of Chaveigni; one and a half muids of wine given you in alms by Radulf Renel out of his wine-rents at Billi; and one muid of wine given in alms to your church by the son of Renaud of Vassen out of his wine-rents at Chuisi.

No one shall presume to exact tithes from you on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. You may receive clerics or laypersons fleeing the secular world, free and unencumbered, into conversion and retain them without any opposition. [Col. 1087C]

Moreover, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving it without his abbot’s permission, except for the sake of a stricter religious life; nor may anyone dare retain one who has departed without the common security of letters. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. We also decree that the burial-place of that place shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted, while preserving nevertheless the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. [Col. 1087D] Upon the death of yourself, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any trick of intrusion or by violence, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall determine ought to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine. [Col. 1088A]

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be kept whole for the full benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See, the canonical right of the diocesan bishop, and the due reverence owed to the church of Arras. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

In the year 1181 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

## XIV. Privilege for the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Paris.

[Bouillart, *History of the Abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés*, Proofs, p. 48.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Paris, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Though unworthy, we have been placed by the Lord’s disposition in the exalted chair of Blessed Peter so that we ought gladly to admit just petitions and endeavour to grant them effective favour. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory—Paschal, Innocent, Lucius, Eugenius, Anastasius, Adrian, and Alexander, Roman pontiffs—we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing, the monastery of Blessed Germanus of the Meadows, in which you are devoted to divine service and which belongs properly to the jurisdiction of Blessed Peter. [Col. 1088C] We decree that whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire through grants of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

By the page of this present privilege we therefore confirm to you and your successors forever that whatever liberty and whatever dignity was conferred on your monastery by the privilege of Blessed Germanus and by the written grants of Childebert, Chlothar, and other kings of the Franks shall remain unimpaired. [Col. 1088D] We command that chrism, holy oil, consecrations, ordinations, and whatever things you need from pontifical ministry shall not be denied to you or your successors by any Catholic bishop. We prohibit any bishop or clergy of the Church of Paris from celebrating masses, ordinations, or stations in the monastery without the will of the abbot or community. Nor do we grant them power to command anything there, to forbid them divine offices, to excommunicate them, or to summon to synod the abbot or monks, priests or clerics of the churches of that place. [Col. 1089A]

We further add that, in the parish churches which you hold outside the borough of St. Germanus, priests shall be chosen by you and presented to the bishop. If they are suitable, the bishop shall commit the care of souls to them, so that they shall answer to him concerning the care of the people, and to you concerning temporal matters belonging to the monastery. But if they should refuse to do this, you shall have by apostolic authority free power to withdraw from them the temporalities which they hold from you. Every abbot, beloved son Hugh, who after you is elected by the community of the monastery entrusted to you, in accordance with the Rule of Blessed Benedict, shall receive blessing from the Roman pontiff or from whichever Catholic bishop he prefers, provided that bishop enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See. [Col. 1089B]

We also decree by apostolic authority, and grant you by the customary clemency and kindness of the Apostolic See, that henceforth you shall not be subject or subordinate to any legation unless a legate has been specifically deputed from the side of the Roman pontiff. No one may, under pretext of a legation granted to him by the Apostolic See, burden you, your successors, your monastery, or the churches within the borough of St. Germanus with any sentence of interdict or excommunication, or exercise any jurisdiction over you or those churches, unless the Roman pontiff has specifically commanded this to him. [Col. 1089C]

Moreover, since the archbishop of Sens was accustomed, in the time of our aforesaid predecessor Alexander, to visit certain churches which you have in his diocese with such a number of persons and horses that his visitation was very burdensome to those churches, and since before the council that predecessor mercifully provided for your monastery in this respect, we likewise, following in his footsteps, grant you by apostolic authority that, if the aforesaid archbishop or his successors exact procuration from your churches from which they ought to receive it for more than forty horses at most and forty-four persons, neither those churches nor you may be compelled on any ground to pay it to them or furnish anything under the pretext of procuration, unless you do so as a favour. [Col. 1089D] If the archbishop now presiding, or his successors, should wish to exceed the number of horses or persons defined above in the procurations owed to the archbishop of Sens by some of your churches, you shall be free to deny what is requested. If, because of this, they pronounce any sentence against those churches, monks, or clerics, we decree by apostolic authority that it shall have no force.

Furthermore, we prohibit anyone, except the Roman pontiff, a legate sent from his side with a special mandate of the Apostolic See, or the abbot to whom their care and custody belongs, from excommunicating or placing under interdict the monks of your monastery, wherever they live. [Col. 1090A] No one shall presume to exact or extort from you tithes on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. By apostolic authority we grant you that, within the parishes of churches belonging to the aforesaid monastery, no one may dare build an oratory, chapel, or church, or establish a cemetery, without the consent of the diocesan bishop and of yourselves—unless they are perhaps Templars or Hospitallers, to whom this is known to have been granted by privileges of the Apostolic See.

Therefore, desiring by pontifical provision to safeguard your peace and advantage, we decree by this present privilege that if anyone transfers lands lawfully belonging to you, or fields in which you hold a share, to another church or religious house by gift, sale, or any other form of alienation, those churches or religious houses may not retain them without your consent beyond a year and a day. [Col. 1090B] Rather, according to the custom of the Gallican Churches, they shall grant them by price or gift to persons who will pay in full to you and your monastery your rights.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person to rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall remain unimpaired and whole for the full benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice, of course, to the authority of the Apostolic See. [Col. 1090C] If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church, sign. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, sign., etc.

Given . . . in the year 1181 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

(Chronicle of W. Thorn, in TWISDEN, *Histories of English Writers*, II, 1834.)

(Ibid.)

# YEAR 1182

[Col. 1091B]

## XXII. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the church of St. Saviour, Venice. (Lateran, 8 January.)

[CORNELIUS, *Church of Venice*, XIV, p. 104.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons MARTIN, prior of the church of St. Saviour of Rialto, and his brethren, present and future, professing the canonical life, in perpetuity.

Apostolic protection ought to be present for those choosing the religious life, lest perhaps an assault of any rashness either turn them back from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of sacred religion. [Col. 1091C] Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, Innocent, Eugenius, Anastasius, and Alexander, Roman pontiffs, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First we decree that the canonical order known to have been instituted in that place according to God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine shall there be observed inviolate for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire through grants of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. [Col. 1091D]

By apostolic authority we confirm to you one half of the tithes paid by the parishioners of your church, as our predecessor Pope Eugenius of blessed memory commanded and John Polanus, formerly diocesan bishop of good memory, granted us by his privilege, both for the clerics and for repairing the roofs (*sartatecta*). We grant full authority to the prior of your church to pronounce sentence of excommunication against parishioners who presume to defraud us concerning one half of these tithes, just as our predecessors of happy memory, Adrian and Alexander, Roman pontiffs, are known to have granted in their writings. [Col. 1092A]

We further grant, as is known to have been granted by our aforesaid predecessors, that the prior of your place at the time may freely provide security of the land in respect of those same tithes. You may also receive clerics and laypeople fleeing the secular world, free and unencumbered, into conversion without anyone’s opposition, and retain them in your church. We further prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving the cloister without his prior’s permission; nor may anyone dare retain a person who has departed without the security of common letters. Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority the judgment reasonably pronounced after long litigation by our venerable brother Henry, patriarch of Grado, and Ildebrand of good memory, cardinal priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles and then legate of the Apostolic See, concerning the dispute between you and Dominic, plebanus of St. Bartholomew, about certain parish households—namely, the households of the Giusti, Morosini, Gradonici, Greeks, Leonardo Fradelli, and Domenico Aureo—which each party claimed as belonging to his own jurisdiction, as is known to be contained in their authentic written instrument made on the matter. [Col. 1092B]

We also decree that the burial-place of that place shall be free, so that no one shall obstruct the devotion and last will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted, while preserving nevertheless the right of the churches from which bodies of the dead are taken. We decree that no one without your consent may dare give penance to your parishioners when they are ill, anoint them, or receive them for burial, except with the right of your church as established by the sacred canons. [Col. 1092C] Upon the death of yourself, the present prior of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any trick of intrusion or violence, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall canonically determine ought to be elected according to God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatever rashly to disturb your church, or take away its possessions, or retain what has been taken away, or harass it by any vexations; [Col. 1092D] but that all things shall be preserved whole for the full benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempts rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by due satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself answerable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; and let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ, [Col. 1093A] and at the last judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance. But for all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina.  
I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St. Susanna.  
I, Vivianus, cardinal priest of the title of St. Stephen.  
I, Cynthius, cardinal priest of the title of St. Cecilia.  
I, Hugh, cardinal priest of the title of St. Clement.  
I, Arduinus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem.  
I, Matthew, cardinal priest of the title of St. Marcellus.  
I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of St. Callixtus.  
I, Hyacinthus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin.  
I, Rainerius, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil.  
I, Gratianus, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.  
I, Rainerius, cardinal deacon of St. Adrian.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the sixth day before the Ides of January [8 January], in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1181 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

## XXIII. He grants G., abbot of Vézelay, and his successors the use of the mitre. (Lateran, 13 January.)

[LAUNOII, *Complete Works*, II, part I, p. 288.]

LUCIUS III, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons G., abbot, and the brethren of Vézelay, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our brother bishops and cardinals humbly and devoutly requested us, out of reverence for Blessed Mary Magdalene, whose body rests there, to take care to adorn your monastery with the gift of our generosity, so that it might thereby become more celebrated among people and be held in greater veneration in the future. Therefore, that it may glory more fully in the bounty of the grace of the Apostolic See and be held in greater veneration among people, we grant to you, son abbot, and to your successors, by the customary kindness of the Apostolic See, the use of the mitre; and we graciously permit you to use it freely on the principal solemnities and processions of the monastery, at councils of Roman pontiffs, in assemblies of bishops, and at the funerals of the dead.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of January [13 January].

## XXIV. He confirms the peace between the monks and burgesses of Tournus. (Lateran, 15 January.)

[JUENIN, *New History of Tournus*, Proofs, p. 179.]

[Col. 1094A]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and monks of Tournus, greeting and apostolic blessing.

To grant the requests of religious men and readily to accord assent to their just petitions is required both by the order of law and by rightly ordered charity. We have indeed heard that, when a dispute arose between you and the burgesses of Tournus concerning certain customs, it was at length settled by an amicable [Col. 1094B] composition through Louis, of venerable memory, then king of the Franks. Since grounds for a renewed dispute have arisen, we confirm by apostolic authority the composition as it was made and accepted by both parties, and as it is more fully contained in the king’s authentic charter; and we strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February.

In lead: Pope Lucius III.

XXV. He takes the monastery of Bonfaget under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Lateran, January 15.)

[HUGO, *Annals of the Sacred and Canonical Order of Prémontré*, vol. I, Documents, p. CCCXI.]

[Col. 1094C]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WIARD, abbot of the Church of Bonfaget, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

It befits apostolic protection to be present for those choosing the religious life, lest perhaps an assault of any rashness call them back from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church [Col. 1094D] of Blessed Mary of Bonfaget, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order which is recognized to have been established in that church according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the institution of the brethren of Prémontré, shall be observed there inviolate in perpetuity. Therefore, whatever possessions and whatever goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, acquire through the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and undiminished to you and your successors.

[Col. 1095A] Among these we have thought fit to state expressly the following: namely, the place in which the abbey was founded, called Bonlays, with all its appurtenances—lands, meadows, woods, waters, and pastures necessary for every kind of animal—which William of Bernole gave you with the counsel and assent of all his heirs and of Matthew, duke of Lorraine; the grange of Grusillis with its appurtenances, lands, meadows, woods, and pastures; the freehold of Feischal with its mills and other appurtenances, lands, meadows, woods, and pastures; whatever you possess at Brantigny; the grange of Moironcourt with all its appurtenances, meadows, woods, lands, and pastures; the freehold of Janneio, which you received from the hand of Wideric, abbot of Clairlieu, with the counsel and consent of all [Col. 1095B] his brethren, monks as well as laymen, after you had paid thirty pounds in Toul currency; which freehold the noblemen Holderic of Geanceyr and his son Holderic, Gerard of Forcherul and his sons Peter, Gauselius, and Gerard, gave to them and to their church, also with the counsel and consent of Duke Matthew, under the testimony of Theodoric of Romunt, Gerard, advocate of Bruyères, and William of Arches; likewise the entire holding of Theobald of Jorseo, in fields, woods, meadows, and pastures adjoining the aforesaid freehold, commonly called Benevilis, which Theobald of Jorleio himself and Willer of Floremont had formerly given to the aforesaid church of Clairlieu, with the assent of his son Gerard, at the request and by the counsel of Duke Matthew, Duchess Beathar, and [Col. 1095C] their sons Simon and Frederick; likewise the tithes of the aforesaid freehold at Benevilis, from meadows, fields, and all other things from which tithes are paid, which Henry, formerly bishop of Toul, had previously granted to the said church of Clairlieu to possess in perpetuity, by the counsel of Odo the archdeacon, at the request and with the assent of the abbess of Remiremont and her entire chapter; also with the assent of the clerics to whom the aforesaid tithes belonged, namely Gerard of Jorseio, his nephew Wideric, and Hefrid, priest of Janneio. To them and their successors you shall pay five shillings in Toul currency each year at the feast of blessed Martin, or within its octave, placing them upon the altar of the aforesaid church of Janneio. [Col. 1095D] You received these tithes, together with the holding of Theobald of Jorseio and the freehold of Janneio, from the hand of the aforesaid Wideric, abbot of Clairlieu, with the consent of his entire chapter, and in the same freedom and integrity in which the said church of Clairlieu had previously possessed them.

Indeed, no one shall presume to demand tithes from you on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. You may also receive clerics or laymen who flee the world, free and unencumbered, for conversion, and retain them without any opposition.

Moreover, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, to leave it without his abbot’s permission; and no one shall dare retain one who leaves without letters of authorization from the community. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, without ringing bells and in a low voice. In the parish churches which you possess, you may appoint at least three or four of your canons, one of whom shall be presented to the diocesan bishop so that he may entrust him with the care of souls; provided that he shall answer to the bishop in spiritual matters, but to you in temporal matters and in observance of the order. For chrism, holy oil, consecrations of churches, ordinations of clerics to be promoted to sacred orders, conducting an abbot to his seat, or any [Col. 1096B] other ecclesiastical sacraments, no one shall dare demand anything from you, whether under pretext of custom or in any other manner. But should anyone presume to act contrary to this, let him know that he shall have a portion with Gehazi, whose deed he imitates by exacting a shameful gift (4 Kings 5).

Furthermore, we decree that the burial place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; saving, nevertheless, the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Desiring also, with fatherly care, to provide for your peace and tranquillity, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone within [Col. 1096C] the enclosures of your houses or granges from daring to commit violence, robbery, theft, or arson, or to seize or kill a person.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things granted for the governance and support of those concerned shall be preserved whole and serve every purpose beneficial to their uses, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. [Col. 1096D] I, Theodorinus, bishop of Porto. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St. Susanna. I, Vivian, cardinal priest of the title of St. Stephen on the Mount. I, Cynthius, cardinal priest of the title of St. Cecilia. I, Arduin, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross. I, Matthew, cardinal priest of the title of St. Marcellus. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of St. Mary Messoris. I, Rainerius, cardinal deacon of St. Gregory at the Golden Veil. [Col. 1097A] I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Rainerius, cardinal deacon of St. Adrian.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1181 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Lucius III.

XXVI. He commands the apostolic delegates to investigate the disobedience of the parish priest of the church of St. Bartholomew and, if they find it, to punish it. (Lateran, January 16.)

[CORNELIUS, *Venetian Church*, XIV, 106.]

[Col. 1097B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother . . . bishop of Torcello [Note: [Col. 1097D] Leonard Donato, bishop of Torcello.], and to the beloved son . . . prior of the church of St. Mary of Charity [Note: [Col. 1097D] Ildebrand, prior of St. Mary of Charity.], greetings and apostolic blessing.

When a serious dispute concerning certain parishioners was being conducted between the church of St. Saviour of Rialto and that of St. Bartholomew, it was entrusted by delegation of the Roman pontiff to our venerable brother, the patriarch of Grado, and to I., of good memory, formerly cardinal priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles, for due settlement. Having heard and examined the arguments of both parties, they adjudged the said parish churches to St. Saviour’s [Col. 1097C]. That sentence our predecessor Pope Alexander of blessed memory, as is clearly shown by his letters, confirmed by apostolic authority; and he caused certain priests of that church, because they had acted against the sentence, to be suspended from office.

Since, therefore, J. Praemarenus [Note: [Col. 1098D] John Praemarenus, parish priest of St. Bartholomew.] is said, after an appeal, to have received the administration of the aforesaid church in a manner less than canonical, and after the appeal to have caused divine services to be celebrated for the aforesaid parishioners by hired priests: lest he should glory in the impunity of such presumption, and others take from his example the audacity to offend, we strictly command your discretion by apostolic writings to investigate the truth of the matter more diligently; and, if this is established to you, [Col. 1097D] suspend from office, notwithstanding the obstacle of appeal, the aforesaid J. and the hired priests whom he caused to celebrate divine services for the aforesaid parishioners, and cause them to remain suspended until they make satisfaction to the aforesaid prior and brethren according to canonical requirements, or come to the Apostolic See having made satisfaction. You shall admonish the witnesses whom they consider fit to name to give testimony to the truth; and if they omit this through favor or fear, you shall compel them more strictly by our authority to tell the truth.

Given at the Lateran, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February.

XXVII. He confirms the settlement made between the count of Joigny and the abbess of St. Julian of Auxerre. (Lateran, January 27.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, XII, Documents, 138.]

[Col. 1098A]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, HEL., abbess, and the sisters of St. Julian of Auxerre, greetings and apostolic blessing.

From the tenor of an authentic document it has become known to us that, when a dispute arose between Agnes, abbess of that same monastery of yours, and R., count of Joigny, concerning four men—namely Gosbert, Anulph, Rainard, and Huric—whom the abbess had established as her servants under the authority of Migania, and the matter had, through appeal, come [Col. 1098B] before the hearing of our predecessor Pope A. of holy memory, who was then at Sens, he entrusted it to us and to Odo of good memory, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, for settlement.

After long and extended litigation of the case, with the consent of the parties and through our mediation, it reached its conclusion by the following settlement: the count released to the abbess herself and to your monastery, forever and free, the said four men, their wives, and their children, so that he shall have no right over them, namely no claimed exaction, so long as they remain servants and officials of the aforesaid monastery; but when they cease to be servants or officials, they shall have in them the same [rights] as in the monastery’s own men. The count also confessed and declared that he had nothing in the wood of St. Julian, which is in Otha, except the office of forester. Yet he wholly withdrew from the dispute concerning the men and the wood out of reverence for our prayers, in consideration of his sister, who was in your monastery, and on account of the abbess. You request that this aforementioned settlement, for greater firmness, be confirmed by our writing. Assenting to your requests, we confirm it by apostolic authority as it was freely accepted and observed by the parties, and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly [Col. 1098D] oppose it.
