If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person [violates this provision, etc.]

Fare well.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Holy Roman Church, have subscribed. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina, have subscribed. I, Peter, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St. Susanna, have subscribed. [Col. 1126A] I, Vivian, cardinal priest of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill, have subscribed. I, Cynthius, cardinal priest of the title of St. Cecilia, have subscribed. I, Hugh, cardinal priest of the title of St. Clement, have subscribed. I, Ard[uinius], cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Callixtus, have subscribed. I, Hyacinthus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, Rainerius, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Gratian, [Col. 1126B] cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Ides of March, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1181, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

### XLIV. Privilege granted to the canons of the Church of Piacenza.  
*(Lateran, March 10.)*

[CAMPI, *History of Piacenza*, II, 366.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, [lacuna] provost and canons of the Church of Piacenza, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting and consonant with reason that we preserve with diligent care the dignities and rights of each [Col. 1126C] church and take suitable measures to prevent their disturbance through anyone’s malice. Moved by this consideration, and persuaded by your prayers, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone to build a church or oratory within the parishes of your churches without the assent of the diocesan bishop and yourselves, saving, of course, the authentic documents of the Roman Church.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of March.

### XLV. Ratifies the statute of the canons of Piacenza.  
*(Lateran, March 10.)*

[IBID.]

[Col. 1126D] LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the provost, etc. (in the manner stated above).

It has been reported to us on your behalf that, having carefully considered the resources of your church and wishing to avoid grave scandal, you have jointly decreed that there shall be only eighteen canons and five custodians in your church. You seek confirmation of this constitution by apostolic authority, so that it may have greater force.

Accordingly, moved by your prayers, and following the example of our predecessor Pope Alexander of happy memory, we confirm by apostolic authority the number stated above for the canons and custodians, and fortify it by the protection of this present writing. We establish that you shall by no means exceed that number unless your resources have increased to such an extent that they may properly be judged sufficient [Col. 1127A] for a larger number, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of March.

### XLVI. To the bishops and clergy of Scotland—concerning the absolution of William, king of Scotland.  
*(Velletri, March 17.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXII, 474.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren, the bishops and abbots, and to the clergy and people established throughout Scotland, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the Apostle has ordained that honor be shown to kings as those who excel, it is fitting and consonant with reason that we honor them more earnestly as most beloved sons and, by granting their just requests, give heed to their devotion toward blessed Peter and the most holy [Col. 1127B] Roman Church. We have learned that, when our most beloved son in Christ William, illustrious king of the Scots, resolutely opposed the election and consecration of our venerable brother John, bishop, Roger, archbishop of York of good memory, and the bishop already mentioned, relying upon letters of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of holy memory, pronounced a sentence of excommunication against him and the kingdom, and against certain persons of the kingdom.

Moreover, our venerable brother Jocelin, bishop of Glasgow, and our beloved sons Arnald, abbot of Melrose, Osbert, abbot of Kalkoensis [Kalrensis], and Walter, prior of St. Columba on the Island, came to the Apostolic See on this account. By their representation they showed us [Col. 1127C] that the archbishop pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the king and an interdict against the kingdom, and that the bishop already mentioned pronounced a sentence of excommunication against certain persons of the kingdom. They reasonably demonstrated before us and our brethren, on multiple grounds, that this sentence ought to be revoked. Therefore, showing deference to the aforesaid king as our most beloved son in Christ, by apostolic authority and with the common counsel of our brethren we remitted every sentence pronounced by the said bishop for the aforesaid cause against him, his people, or his kingdom; and we established that neither he nor his people are bound by excommunication, nor the kingdom by interdict, under the foregoing sentence. Wherefore, by these apostolic writings, we command your whole body that you are not to hesitate [Col. 1127D] to communicate with him as a Catholic king who enjoys communion with the Apostolic See, but shall render him due honor in all things. For the more certain we are of the sincerity of his devotion toward the churches and ecclesiastical persons of his kingdom, the more fully we wish him to be honored in all matters in which we can do so according to God.

Given at Velletri, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April.

### XLVII. Takes the monastery of Bellelay under protection and confirms its possessions and rights.  
*(Velletri, March 19.)*

[HUGO, *Annals of the Sacred and Canonical Premonstratensian Order*, vol. I, Documents, p. 217.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1128A] sons, the abbot of the monastery of Bellelay and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life in perpetuity.

Those who choose the religious life ought to receive apostolic protection, lest an assault of any rash person perhaps turn them from their purpose or—God forbid—impair the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and, following the example of our predecessors, Innocent and Eugenius, Roman pontiffs of happy memory, take the aforesaid church of Bellelay, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and our own, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we establish that the canonical order known to have been instituted in that church according to [Col. 1128B] God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the form of the Premonstratensian institution shall there be observed inviolably in perpetuity. Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by grant of popes, benefaction of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, acquire through the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the church of Thuvenna with the chapel of Reconvilber, with their appurtenances, [Col. 1128C] both endowment and tithes; the church of Boecurt with the court of that place and its other appurtenances; the church of St. Ursicinus of Nugerol, with the court which you possess there and its other appurtenances; the court of Salmuris with vineyards; Corceles and Marves; Cascale with its fields; Loueresce and Taragna; an allod in fields and meadows; the allod of the knight Manegold near Belvilar and near the monastery; the allod of Vernath, in woodland as well as fields and meadows; the allod of Fornas; the court of Racina with its appurtenances; the court of Corcelum, with its appurtenances near Divilier; an allod near Laimunt; an allod near Corfawre; an allod near Sonillier; an allod near Wingelies; the allod of Cunegund near Zazingeim; [Col. 1128D] the allod of Fridelvo near Bethelaica; the allod of Cono near Corginnart; an allod near Villar; an allod near Buires; an allod; the court of Montagis with its appurtenances near Chouna; an allod; the monastery of Grangurt with its appurtenances, namely the allod of Cordemasche; the court of Langier with its appurtenances; the court of Girevilar with its appurtenances; and an allod near Althorielie, with all their appurtenances.

No one shall presume to demand tithes from you on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. You may also receive for conversion clerics or laymen fleeing the world, free and unencumbered, and retain them without any opposition whatever. Moreover, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, to leave it without the permission of his abbot; nor may anyone dare retain one who has departed without letters of authorization from the community. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. You are to receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of clerics to be advanced to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to supply these things freely and without any burden upon you. Otherwise, [Col. 1129B] you may approach whichever bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. We also forbid anyone other than the bishop of Basel to presume to assume the advocacy of that place. Furthermore, we decree that the burial-ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted; the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken being nevertheless preserved.

Upon the death of yourself, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any trickery of surreption or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall have judged to be elected in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Augustine. Moreover, wishing with paternal solicitude to provide for your peace and tranquillity, by apostolic authority we forbid anyone within the enclosures of your houses or granges to commit violence, robbery, or theft, to set fire, or to seize or kill a person. Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, to take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things granted for the governance and support of those for whose use they were bestowed shall be preserved entire and be of advantage to them in every respect, saving [Col. 1129D] the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been admonished a second or third time, unless he correct his offence by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve their rights for that same place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 1130A] I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Peter, bishop of Tusculum.

Given at Velletri through the hand of Albert, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1181 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

XLVIII. Privilege for the monastery of Saint-Quentin of Mont. (Velletri, April 8.)

[GUIBERT, Abbot of Nogent, *Works*, p. 620.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot of Mont-Saint-Quentin and his brethren, present and future, etc.

To grant the effect sought by just petitioners is required both by the force [Col. 1130B] of equity and by the order of reason, especially when piety supports the petitioners’ wish and truth does not abandon it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just requests; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have judged the following to be expressly named:

[Col. 1130C] Two parts of the tithe which you acquired in the lands of John Bortel: twenty shillings, etc.

You may also receive for conversion clerics and laymen fleeing the world, free and unencumbered, without anyone’s opposition, and retain them in your monastery. Moreover, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in the same place, to leave it without his abbot’s permission, except for the sake of a stricter religious life; nor may anyone dare retain one who has departed without letters of authorization from the community.

When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, without ringing bells, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, and in a subdued voice.

No one shall presume to demand or extort from you tithes on your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. In the parish churches which you possess, you may choose priests and present them to the diocesan bishop, so that, if they are suitable, he may commit the care of souls to them; they shall be accountable to him in spiritual matters, but to you in temporal matters.

We also decree that the burial-ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose [Col. 1131A] the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted; the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken being nevertheless preserved. For chrism, holy oil, consecrations of churches, ordinations of clerics to be advanced to sacred orders, the conducting of an abbot to his see, or any other ecclesiastical sacraments, no one may dare demand anything from you, whether under pretext of custom or in any other way.

We also prohibit any church, land, or other benefice conferred upon your church from being granted personally to anyone or alienated in any other manner without the consent of the entire chapter, or of its greater and sounder part. If any gifts or alienations have been made otherwise than as stated, we judge them void.

Moreover, none of the brethren or converts bound by profession to your house may stand surety for anyone, or borrow money from anyone, without the consent and permission of the abbot and the greater part of your chapter, beyond the amount provided by the prudent determination of the chapter, unless this is for an evident benefit to your house. If they presume to do so, the convent, without whose permission and consent they acted, shall not be bound to answer in any way for them.

Furthermore, in your causes you may bring forward suitable brethren as witnesses and, where right permits, by their testimony both repel violence and vindicate justice.

[Col. 1131C] Upon the death of yourself, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any surreption, trickery, or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall have judged to be elected according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

Therefore we decree, etc., as above in the letters of Pope Eugenius.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodinus, bishop of the see of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Peter, bishop of Tusculum. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna. [Col. 1131D] I, Vivian, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Cynthius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Arduinus, cardinal-priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Laborans, cardinal-priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Saint Callixtus. I, Reinerius, cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

Given at Velletri through the hand of Albert, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of April, in the year 1181, in the first year of Pope Lucius III.

XLIX. To Theobald, abbot of Cluny.—He decrees that no other order or religious observance may be established in parishes under Cluniac jurisdiction. (Velletri, April 11.)

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, p. 76.]

[Col. 1132A]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son THEOBALD, abbot of Cluny, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

The apostolic office entrusted to us by God, and consideration for the welfare of the Church, exhort and admonish us to cherish with fuller charity those churches which we see to be more fervent in the observance of holy religion and which we know to flourish in honorableness and religion, and continually to show them greater [Col. 1132B] honor and favor. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord Theobald, adhering to the footsteps of our predecessors, we sincerely and tenderly love your church as a special daughter of the Apostolic See, wholly devoted to it; and we have judged it fitting to assent to your petitions. We therefore grant to you and your successors in perpetuity that in parishes belonging to your right no order or religious observance other than the Cluniac shall be established in future times, so that goods or rights conferred upon your church by the generosity of Roman pontiffs may not be diminished or taken away under pretext of any new or subsequently introduced religious observance. We nevertheless decree that no one may presume to establish a cemetery within the boundaries of your parishes without your consent, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. It shall therefore be lawful for no person whatsoever to infringe the tenor of this our decree or rashly disturb it. If in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been admonished a second or third time, unless he corrects his presumption by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve their rights for that same place may there be the peace [Col. 1132D] of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen!

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Peter, bishop of Tusculum. I, Rainerius, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Vivian, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Cynthius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Laborans, cardinal-priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber.

Given at Velletri through the hand of Albert, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Ides of April, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1182 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

L. He confirms the goods and rights of the priory of Saint Peter of Rumilly, diocese of Boulogne. (Velletri, April 11.)

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, p. 77.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the prior of the monastery of Blessed Peter of Rumilly and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life in perpetuity.

Whenever a request is made of us which is recognized as consonant with religion and honorableness, we ought gladly to grant it and afford suitable support to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, [Col. 1133B] we mercifully assent to your just requests; and, following the example of Pope Eugenius of blessed memory, our predecessor, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have judged the following to be expressly named:

In the diocese of London: the church of Stanford; [Col. 1133C] the church of Lagefara; the church of Little Lagefara; the church of Cogeshala; the church of Teja; the church of Lanversoch, by the gift of Eustace, count of Boulogne; the estate called Rumilly, and Burdes, Fosseneis, and Pochim, with lands from the sea as far as Fon. [uncertain OCR], mills, waters and watercourses, rights of access to water, meadows, pastures, woods, male and female serfs, and all their other appurtenances. In England, by the gift of Count Eustace: land yielding twenty pounds sterling annually in the estate called Fobinges. Moreover, the place itself—namely, the aforesaid monastery of Rumilly with all its appurtenances—shall remain forever in the obedience and subjection of the monastery of Cluny, as it is known to have done hitherto.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, to take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things granted for the governance and support of those for whose use they were bestowed shall be preserved entire and be of advantage to them in every respect, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. If in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Peter, bishop of Tusculum. I, Vivian, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. [Col. 1134A] I, Cynthius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Laborans, cardinal-priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Saint Callixtus. I, Rainerius, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

Given at Velletri through the hand of Albert, priest of the Holy Roman Church, cardinal and chancellor, on the third day before the Ides of April, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1182 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

LI. He receives the monastery of Reichenbach under protection, confirms its possessions, and enlarges its privileges. (Velletri, April 14.)

[RIED, *Codex diplomaticus Ratisbonensis*, I, 254.]

[Col. 1134B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons REIMBOTO, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary at Reichenbach, situated in the diocese of Regensburg, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life in perpetuity.

Whenever a request is made of us which is recognized as consonant with religion and honorableness, we ought gladly to grant it and afford suitable support to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just requests. The aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary of Reichenbach, situated in the diocese of Regensburg, founded by Diepald, margrave of blessed memory, and his wife Adelaide, and offered to blessed Peter, in which you are devoted to divine service, we receive, following the example of Pope Calixtus of blessed memory, our predecessor, under the guardianship of blessed Peter and our protection, and strengthen by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been instituted in the same monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions or goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, [Col. 1134D] the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. No one shall presume to demand tithes from you on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. You may also receive for conversion clerics or laymen fleeing the world, free and unencumbered, and retain them without any opposition. Moreover, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, to leave it without his abbot’s permission, except for the sake of a stricter religious life; nor may anyone dare retain one who has departed without letters of authorization from the community. When a general [Col. 1135A] interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. For chrism, holy oil, consecrations of churches, ordinations of clerics to be advanced to sacred orders, the conducting of an abbot to his see, or any other ecclesiastical sacraments, no one may dare demand anything from you, whether under pretext of custom or in any other way.

If anyone presumes to act against this, let him know that he will have a portion with Gehazi, whose conduct he imitates in exacting a shameful payment (4 Kings 5). Furthermore, we decree that the burial-ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will [Col. 1135B] of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted; the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken being nevertheless preserved. Upon the death of yourself, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any trickery of surreption or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall have judged to be elected in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Benedict. We make the same provision concerning the appointment of an advocate; but if that advocate proves burdensome to the brethren and useless to the monastery, we grant you the unrestricted authority, once he has been removed, to substitute another in his place.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever [Col. 1135C] rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, to take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things granted for the governance and support of those for whose use they were bestowed shall be preserved entire and be of advantage to them in every respect, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the customary right of the diocesan bishop. As a token of the freedom received from the Roman Church, you shall pay one gold coin each year to us and to our successors, as is known to have been instituted by the aforesaid Margrave Diepald. If in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

[Col. 1135D] Ten cardinals subscribed with the pope, giving their assent to the aforesaid charter of protection.

Given at Velletri through the hand of Albert, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1182 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Lucius III.

Lead seal: LUCIUS PP. III.

LII. At the request of Patriarch Henry, he confirms the privileges of the Church of Grado. (Fragment.) (Velletri, April 18.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, V, 1131. Here only the subscriptions and date of the diploma are printed, the reader being referred to the bull granted by Adrian IV to the Church [Col. 1136A] of Grado. See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXIII.]

[Col. 1136A]

Given at Velletri through the hand of Albert, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1182 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Peter, bishop of Tusculum. I, Vivian, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Cynthius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Arduinus, cardinal-priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Laborans, cardinal-priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Saint Callixtus. [Col. 1136B] I, Rainerius, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Ardicius, cardinal-deacon of Saint Theodore.

LIII. He confirms the possessions of the monastery of Saint Mary of the Upper Cell, in the diocese of Würzburg. (Velletri, May 1.)

[HUGO, *Annals of the Sacred and Canonical Order of Prémontré*, vol. I, documentary proofs, p. 387.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons RABENOLD, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary Ever-Virgin at Cella, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life.

[Col. 1136C] … Among these we have judged the following to be expressly named: the place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is built, with the adjoining cell of nuns and the estates contiguous to the monastery—namely Herstart and the one situated beyond the river Wrogi—with their lands, tithes, and all appurtenances, cultivated and uncultivated; also the hill called Rotemberc, with all its revenues. Further, that exchange which was made between you and the bishop of Neuenburg and his church, through the hands of the advocate of that church, namely Count Theotinis, son of Margrave Conrad, and through the hand of a certain noble Manegold of Wilpere and his sons, as Pope Alexander of blessed memory, our predecessor, Emperor Frederick, Herold bishop of Würzburg, Tuto bishop of Neuenburg, [Col. 1136D] and the Church of Neuenburg itself confirmed by their privileges. The following are all the properties of the Church of Neuenburg given in exchange: properties in Hinsmisart and Hosteim, in Carbach and Birckinvald, for each of which twenty-eight marks are paid annually to the Church of Neuenburg. The following properties were received in exchange: the estate of Haselbrunen; the estate called Walprunnen; two-thirds of the estate called Albestatt—the remaining third of the same estate you hold from the canons of the greater church at Würzburg for an annual rent—together with the estate called Lusenbach and certain properties in Hisingen, for which you pay annually six pounds in Würzburg currency. Also sixteen holdings which Herold, bishop of Würzburg of blessed memory, granted to your monastery for the use of the infirm, together with three pounds and tithes in Turrebach, for which you pay him annually one pound. Further, the estate at Mose and the estate at Richesbrunnen, with their tithes and all appurtenances; the estate at Würzburg; your properties at Gernestatd and Karbach; and the estate at Hetingesfeld with the vines belonging to it. No one shall presume to demand or extort from you tithes on your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. Wishing also with paternal solicitude to provide for your peace and tranquillity, by apostolic authority we forbid anyone within [Col. 1137B] the enclosures of your houses or granges to commit violence, robbery, or theft, to set fire, or to seize or kill a person. You may also receive for conversion, without anyone’s opposition, clerics or laymen fleeing the world, free and unencumbered, and retain them in your church.

Moreover, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in the same place, to leave it without the abbot’s permission; nor may anyone dare retain one who has departed without letters of authorization from the community. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, without ringing bells, excluding the excommunicated [Col. 1137C] and interdicted, and in a subdued voice. Upon the death of yourself, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any trickery of surreption or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall have judged to be elected in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Augustine. We also decree that the burial-ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there; the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken being nevertheless preserved. Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, etc.

I, Conrad, minister of Sal. [uncertain], bishop of Galina. [Col. 1137D] I, Theodinus, bishop of the see of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Peter, bishop of Tusculum. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Vivian, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Cynthius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Arduinus, cardinal-priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Matthew, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Laborans, cardinal-priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Saint Callixtus. I, James, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Arditio, cardinal-deacon of Saint Theodore. [Col. 1138A] I, Rainerus, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Rainerus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian.

Given at Velletri through the hand of Albert, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of May, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1181 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

LIV. He receives the church of Saint Mary of Reno under protection and confirms its goods and rights. (Velletri, May 3.)

[TROMBELLI, *Memoirs of Reno*, p. 376.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1138B] sons GERARD, prior of the church of Saint Mary of Reno, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life in perpetuity.

Although unworthy, we have been entrusted with the care and concern of all churches; therefore we are bound to exercise pastoral concern for the condition of your church and, insofar as the Lord gives us power, diligently to attend to your peace. Accordingly, that you may be fortified by apostolic defense against the assaults of evildoers, moved by your pious prayers and just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, [Col. 1138C] the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have judged the following to be expressly named:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is built, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Andrew at Turricella; the church of Saint Domini near Bognum; the church of Saint Saviour; the possessions formerly belonging to Gerard de Sala; the church of Saint Praxedes, as it was granted to you by our predecessors Anastasius and Alexander, Roman pontiffs of pious memory, saving the right and reverence due to the cardinal who for the time being holds that church; the church of Saint James called Casa Dei, with its appurtenances; and the bridge situated over the Reno next to your church, with its possessions. We ratify and confirm the liberties and immunities reasonably granted by Henry and Gerard, bishops of Bologna of blessed memory, to your church and to the other churches mentioned above: namely, that with all their goods, movable and immovable, they shall be altogether free and exempt from every condition, service, tribute, lordship, or control—whether of monks and clerics, laymen, or any person great or small—arising from holdings under the bishop, except for episcopal right; and we decree that they shall remain unimpaired for all time. [Col. 1139A] You may also receive for conversion clerics and laymen fleeing the world, free and unencumbered, and retain them in your church without any opposition. Moreover, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in your place, to leave it without his prior’s permission, except for the sake of a stricter religious life; nor may anyone dare retain one who has departed without letters of authorization from your community. If any of these brethren dares to remain outside the cloister without the aforesaid permission and, after being admonished a second or third time, should refuse to return to his senses, the prior of the same place may pronounce against him a sentence of excommunication as against one professed to him.

Furthermore, by apostolic authority we confirm to you and your church the tithes which you have held undisturbed for forty years and are known now to retain peacefully. We also forbid anyone to impose new and undue exactions upon you or your church. We decree that the burial-ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted; the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken being nevertheless preserved. [Col. 1139C] Moreover, we grant you free authority to receive the ordinations of your clerics from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, as the bishops mentioned above are known to have granted you this authority by authentic writings. We confirm to you the tithes on the produce of your property coming from anywhere within the diocese of Bologna, as those same tithes were granted to your church by the provident care of those bishops. Upon the death of yourself, the present prior of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any trickery of surreption or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall have judged to be elected in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Augustine. Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; [Col. 1139D] but that all things granted for the governance and support of those for whose use they were bestowed shall be preserved entire and be of advantage to them in every respect, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the bishop of Bologna. If in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Conrad, minister of Sal… and bishop of Sabina, subscribed. I, Theodinus, bishop of the see of Porto and Santa Rufina, subscribed. I, Peter, bishop of Tusculum, subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna, subscribed. [Col. 1140A] I, Vivian, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, subscribed. I, Cynthius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, subscribed. I, Arduinus, cardinal-priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, subscribed. I, Matthew, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, subscribed. I, Laborans, cardinal-priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Saint Callixtus, subscribed. I, Hyacinthus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, subscribed. I, Ardicio, cardinal-deacon of Saint Theodore, subscribed. I, Rainerius, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, subscribed. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, [Col. 1140B] subscribed.

Given at Velletri through the hand of Albert, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Nones of May, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1182 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

LV. He confirms the enactments of Burgundius, bishop of Strasbourg, concerning the rights of the provost of Haslach and the canons there. (Velletri, May 9.)

[WURDWEIN, *Nova subsidia diplomatica*, vol. X, p. 121.]

Lucius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1140C] sons, the canons of Saint Florentius of Haslach, present and future, lawfully appointed, in perpetual remembrance.

Those things which are reasonably established by the authority of prelates for the worship of God ought to remain in their stability, and, lest they can be torn from their position through anyone’s malice, ought to be secured by apostolic protection. Accordingly, since frequent discord had arisen among you concerning the distribution of the prebends of your church, Bishop B. of Strasbourg, of blessed memory, as appears from his document, being anxious to allay the discord and having taken the counsel of his brethren, with the aid of heavenly grace at last brought it about that, all division being set aside, he set forth what was due to you, as it had been assigned.

[Col. 1140D] Indeed, your former provost B. granted to you, at the urging of the aforesaid bishop, the tithes pertaining to your church: namely, from Hosthoven and from Hernoldeshseim, tithes of wine only; and, after his death, tithes of grain and other produce, and moreover tithes from Hurmaten in Brussetal. The same bishop, while he held the provostship of your church in his own hand, granted the tithes of Sulcen, six fields of vineyard at Buytenheim, and three at Westhoven, on the condition that no provost whatsoever who might at any time preside over your church should have the power to take these away from you. Furthermore, the aforesaid provost B., by pious devotion, granted to the same church a certain mill which he held by proprietary right, together with the adjoining estate in the village of Tunguenesin,

[Col. 1141A] provided nevertheless that, while he lived, he should enjoy them freely; but upon his death they should revert to your church without any objection, and that on his anniversary you should distribute from the aforesaid mill four quarter-measures of grain to the poor. Moreover, B. of Cunze bequeathed to you for the salvation of his soul a certain estate in the aforesaid village, on the condition that his son C., your fellow canon, should possess that estate during his life; and, on his father’s anniversary, should distribute to the poor twelve cloister loaves, a pail of wine, and twelve denarii; and that, upon his death, the aforesaid church should succeed to that estate without anyone’s opposition. All these things, therefore, as you reasonably possess them, we confirm to you and to your church by apostolic authority.

[Col. 1141B] Moreover, when a question arose concerning the reroofing of your church and other matters, it was acknowledged before the aforesaid bishop, as his document contains, that the provost ought to repair one half and the bishop the other half of the church whenever it requires repair in any respect. Moreover, the provost shall diligently take care that no neglect causes any deficiency in the brothers’ buildings—namely, throughout the cloister, dormitory, refectory, bakehouse, cellar, and mill; and if any of these should fall from their condition, he shall restore them at his own expense and shall provide with all diligence for the needs of the household and of divine worship. If through his negligence or carelessness your church suffers any loss in these matters,

[Col. 1141C] the same provost shall be bound to make good the damages incurred. He shall also manage the brothers’ cellar with all diligence, so that their prebends—namely, the grain and wine assigned to his custody—may be faithfully rendered for the brothers’ use, lest they be lost through any mishap. If they are lost, he shall restore everything. Nor shall he have authority to admit anyone to a canonry except by the common election of the brothers. Likewise, he shall appoint neither dean, schoolmaster, keeper, porter, nor cellarer except by the election of the brothers; nor shall he take action to appoint a baker unless the brothers’ election concurs. He shall also supply at his own expense as many wine vessels as are necessary for the brothers’ use; and when these have been worn out by decay or age,

[Col. 1141D] he shall be bound to provide other new ones. He shall lease none of the courts whose grant pertains to him by right of the provostship without the brothers’ election. Whenever a cloister benefice becomes vacant, it shall not be conferred upon anyone by hereditary right. The provost, however, shall not refuse it to that canon who holds the place immediately after him, provided that he requests it out of devotional zeal. But if he does not wish to request that benefice, the provost shall have authority to confer it upon whichever canon of your church he prefers, regard nevertheless being had for the means of each, and not so as to seem, by intending to enrich one, to provide the others with occasion for scandal.

Moreover, the provost must receive the brothers’ prebends from the court of Kircheim, from which he owes you every year

[Col. 1142A] one hundred and thirty quarter-measures of grain according to the measure of the churches of the city of Strasbourg, and five cartloads of wine, besides the ten quarter-measures of grain which he owes the dean, and besides the five quarter-measures which he is bound to give to the alms prebend. The provost shall also supply the money assigned for the brothers’ clothing, so that the brothers may not grow lax in the celebration of the divine offices. He shall also have the warming-house heated each day for the brothers’ use by his servant from the feast of St. Martin until Maundy Thursday, and shall have the hay of the meadow of Urmatten cut at his own expense for the brothers’ benefit.

Therefore, lest the provost be able to withhold anything from you contrary to what has been established, or lest you

[Col. 1142B] ought to demand from him something which he is not bound to pay or give you, we command that these matters which we have set forth, as established by the authority of your bishop and to be observed in your church, remain entire for future times.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, or take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things granted for the governance and support of those concerned shall be preserved entire and shall benefit them in every way, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical justice of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

[Col. 1142C] I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Susanna. I, Vivian, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Cynthius, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Cecilia. I, Arduin, cardinal-priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Matthew, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Marcellus. I, Laborans, cardinal-priest of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of St. Callixtus. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Ardicio, cardinal-deacon of St. Theodore. I, Rayner, cardinal-deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil.

[Col. 1142D] I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Conrad, bishop and minister of the Church of Salzburg. I, Theodinus, bishop of the see of Porto and St. Rufina. I, Peter, bishop of Tusculum. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina.

Given at Velletri, through the hand of Albert, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Ides of May [9 May], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1182 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

## LVI. He confirms to the monastery of Repsholt the income granted by Liemar, formerly archbishop of Hamburg. (Velletri, 15 May.)

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburg Documents*, I, 230.]

[Col. 1143A]

Lucius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the provost of the church of St. Maurice of Ripesholt and his brethren, present and future, canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

The care of the governance entrusted to us urges and exhorts us more earnestly to watch diligently over the adornment of the Lord’s house, so that its ministers may observe canonical ordinances in their conduct and obtain the necessary support for this present life, according to the Apostle’s rule: “Let him who serves at the altar live from the altar.”

Beloved sons in the Lord, you have represented to us that Liemar, bishop of Bremen of good memory, solicitous in the administration of the episcopal office for the service of our Creator and the maintenance of His ministers in your church, took care, as is set down below, to provide the clerics serving the Lord in your church with necessary allowances, and ordained that they be supplied in perpetuity: every day, namely, one loaf of such size that seven could be made from the measure of one local bushel; four beakers of beer; one denarius in the currency of Gavar; and ten shillings annually

[Col. 1143B] for buying clothing. He also ordained and added, every Sunday, a fine rye loaf and a denarius with a beaker of mead or two of beer. On the greater feast days—namely, at the Nativity of the Lord, on its four days; the Circumcision of the Lord; the Epiphany; the Purification of St. Mary; the feast of St. Matthias; the laying aside of the flesh [Shrove Tuesday]; holy Easter Day and the following three days; the feast of the Apostles Philip and James; the Ascension of the Lord; holy Pentecost Day, Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday; the feast of St. John the Baptist; the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, and of James and Lawrence; the Assumption of St. Mary; the feast of St. Bartholomew; the Nativity of St. Mary; the feast

[Col. 1143C] of St. Matthew the Apostle; St. Maurice; and the dedication of the same church; the feast of St. Michael; the holy Apostles Simon and Jude; All Saints; St. Willehad; and the Apostles Andrew and Thomas—each person shall receive a fine loaf, and for every four persons together, a suckling pig and a chicken, or separately a denarius. Each priest shall receive three beakers of mead, each deacon two, and each subdeacon likewise two; or twice that quantity of selected beer. Furthermore, he added, as a supplement to the prebend for the discharge of the debt of charity, whatever might be piously offered for the burials of the dead, whether in money or estates. Whatever income or rent remains beyond the expenses of the brothers’ prebend is ordained to be collected and applied, with the counsel and assent of the brothers and parishioners, to the building and fabric of the church,

[Col. 1144A] or to increasing its ornaments and books. Upon the death of the provost then in office, no one shall be put in charge there by any trickery of surreption or by force, except one whom the brothers by common consent, or the sounder part of the brothers’ counsel, in the fear of God shall judge fit to elect.

Now therefore, because you have requested that this be strengthened by the protection of apostolic authority against the assaults of malicious persons, we, following the example of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of holy memory, gladly assent to your petition; we confirm the aforesaid ordinance by apostolic authority, judge that it shall remain valid in future times, receive your church

[Col. 1144B] under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and secure it by the privilege of this present writing.

We decree, therefore, that it shall be lawful for no person whatever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things granted for the governance and support of those concerned shall be preserved entire and shall benefit them in every respect, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical justice of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

Given at Velletri, through the hand of Albert, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of June [15 May], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1181 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius

[Col. 1144C] III.

## LVII. He orders Gerard, archbishop of Ravenna, “to require the inhabitants of the parish of St. Mary in Porto, of the parish of St. Martin in Maiera, and others in the territory of Ferrara, whom Pericinus, their envoy, had exempted by order of the consuls of Ferrara after they had sworn obedience to the archbishop, to take the oath before him.” (Velletri, 21 May.)

[See RUBEUS, *History of Ravenna*, p. 353.]

## LVIII. He takes the monastery of Dudley under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Velletri? 16 June.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, I, 614.]

[Col. 1144D] Lucius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Everard, prior of the church of Dudley, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Those who, setting aside worldly desires, have vowed their service to the Lord under regular discipline ought to be secured by apostolic protection, lest they grow lax in carrying out their purpose if they are harassed by the injuries of wicked persons. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just petitions; we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church in which you are devoted to divine service, and we secure it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we establish that the monastic order known to have been instituted in that church according to God and the Rule of St. Benedict

[Col. 1145A] and the institution of the Cluniac brethren shall be observed there inviolate in perpetuity. Furthermore, whatever possessions or goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God granting, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit to specify by their own names: the church of St. James of Dudley and the chapels of the same village, of St. Edmund and St. . . .; the church of Deggestei, with its appurtenances; the church of Porlfeld with the chapel of Cotton; the church of Angle . . . with its appurtenances; the church of Bratetelde with the chapel of Englefeld, given by Gervase Paganell; the church of Wombourne with the chapel of Tresel and its other appurtenances, given by Guy of Offeni; the church of Settle with its appurtenances, given by Ralph of Settle; from the gift of Agnes of Somery, the village of Chyrchille with its appurtenances; from the gift of Osbert of Kenefara, the village of Saredune with its appurtenances; from the gift of Robert of Chandeu, one virgate of land in the village of Wolztone; and the lands of Angepenne, given by John Mansell.

[Col. 1145B] We further decree that the burial-place of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last wishes of those who have determined to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken remaining intact. Whenever there is a general interdict upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices with closed doors, without ringing bells, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, and in a low voice. No one shall presume to demand or extort from you tithes on your newly cultivated lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the offspring of your animals. In the parochial churches which you possess, you may choose clerics or priests and present them to the diocesan bishop; if they are suitable, the bishop shall commit to them the cure of souls, so that they are answerable to him in spiritual matters,

[Col. 1145C] but to us in temporal matters. You may also receive into your religious life and retain without any opposition clerics or laymen fleeing from the world, free and absolved. We further prohibit anyone, after making profession in your church, from presuming to leave that place except to embrace a stricter religious life; and no one shall dare retain one who has departed without the assurance of common letters. We also decree that the ancient and reasonable customs hitherto observed in your church shall remain valid in future times.

We therefore decree that no person whatever may disturb the aforesaid monastery in any respect, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them,

[Col. 1146A] or harass it with any vexations; but that all things granted for the governance and support of those concerned shall be preserved entire and shall benefit them in every respect, saving the authority of the Apostolic See, the canonical justice of the diocesan bishop, and due reverence to the Church of Cluny. If in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our ordinance, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offense by appropriate satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment.

[Col. 1146B] But upon all who preserve their rights to that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given, etc., on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July [16 June], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1190 [read 1182] of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

## LIX. Privilege for the church of St. Mary of Alteriacum. (Velletri, 18 June.)

[HUGO, *Monuments of Sacred Antiquity*, I, 210.]

Lucius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Milo, abbot of the church of St. Mary of Alteriacum,

[Col. 1146C] and the other brethren, present and future, and all others, apostolic blessing in perpetuity.

It is fitting that those choosing the religious life should have apostolic protection, lest perhaps an assault of someone’s rashness should either turn them aside from their purpose or, which God forbid, break the strength of holy religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of St. Mary of Alteriacum, in which you are devoted to divine service, and secure it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we establish that the canonical order known to have been instituted in that church according to God and the Rule of St. Augustine shall be observed there inviolate in perpetuity. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God granting, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings

[Col. 1146D] or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by their own names:

Namely, the place called Alteriacum, in which the aforesaid church is founded, with its tithes and all its appurtenances—cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, waters, and woods—within the boundaries marked out: through the two Chillimonts (Chillemont), through the hill of Alteriacum, through the stream or spring of Chelmini (*la goutte ou source de Chillemont*), as far as Mortania; and on the other side through the ford of Sapinci (*le void du sapiné*) as far as Mossur (Mossoux), and all the lands of Nunfai, owing no rent, together with pasture rights throughout the whole ban of Rambertivilla; the place of Guandeborzoch (la Souche), with tithes and pastures throughout the whole ban of Nozuncurt (Nossoncourt), to be held in perpetuity, on condition that the aforesaid church shall pay twelve denarii of Metz currency each year to the chapter of St. Stephen at the synod after the feast of All Saints; provided, however, that if there are within the boundaries of Alteriacum things useful for the construction of God’s church, they shall be taken without prohibition or objection, with the consent and approval of Theodoric of Danubrium,

[Col. 1147A] advocate of the same place, and of the other ministerials. One half of the mill of Anglemont, granted to you by Stephen, formerly bishop of Metz, subject to a rent of one denarius. The allod which Theodoric, advocate of Rambertivilla, held at Vicus; the land at Nozuncurt which Wideric, knight of Spinis, with the consent of his son Wideric, gave you, together with ten *journals* of land, for which and for the remaining land you pay six denarii every year to his steward on the feast of St. Remigius. The tithes of your own labours which your brethren gather in the barn situated on the aforesaid land. The fishery in the water called Mortania, between Mossur (Moussoux) and Baldincha (Baldonchamp),

[Col. 1147B] which Theodoric, formerly elected bishop of Metz, gave you to possess peacefully and without disturbance from any of the surrounding inhabitants. By way of liberty, no one may presume to fish within the boundaries against your will; provided that the aforesaid elect retains in his hand the beavers and the ban of that place. The site of a mill in the ban of Nuzuncurt, granted to you by the aforesaid elect, together with the channeling of water through his meadow, so far as shall be necessary for the mill.

Three lands which you possess at Vicus free from every rent and exaction. Pasture rights in the ban of Volmecurt, which Theodoric, advocate of the same village, granted you subject to a rent of one denarius of Toul currency, which you pay annually to the steward of Volmecurt on the feast of St. Martin

[Col. 1147C] or within its octave. The tithes of your labours which Guarinus, priest of Rambertivilla, and his nephew Albric granted you, subject to a rent of seven denarii payable every year on the Kalends of October [1 October]. The tithes of your labours which Cono, priest of Dillonis-villa, with the assent of Peter, bishop of Toul, granted you in perpetuity, both from crops and from meadows and animal offspring, subject to a rent of twelve denarii of Toul currency payable on the Kalends of October; and whatever William, knight of Rambertivilla, acknowledged that he held in the tithes of your church and your granges. Also, whatever your brethren had cultivated from Atrium of Joanmesni (Joanmenil) and from Thiarmenni upward, which he granted you in perpetuity, with the approval of his wife and children, his brother Raynald the cleric, and the assent of Peter, bishop of Toul, subject to a rent of six denarii payable on the feast of St. Remigius. The lands and tithes belonging to the church of Dillonisvilla (Glonville), which Hermann, formerly abbot of the monastery of Moyen, with the assent of his chapter, granted you on condition that on the feast of the deposition of St. Idulphus you pay his church every year two shillings of Toul currency for the tithes of each ploughland.

[Col. 1147D] The tithe which you have from Gerard, abbot of the monastery of Senones, with the assent of his chapter, from the village of Berrue and upward, and from the village of Thiarmesnil and upward, both in animal offspring and in agriculture, subject to a rent of two shillings payable at the Nativity of St. John upon the altar of St. Stephen in the cell of Danubrium (Deneuvre); the holding which lies within the common boundaries of the two parishes of Distorchium (Destord), namely, and St. Helena, which Walter, formerly dean of St. Deodatus, with the assent of his chapter, granted you subject to a rent of eighteen denarii of Toul currency payable annually on the feast of St. Deodatus. Also, whatever Albert, knight of Froville, possessed in the forest pastures of St. Stephen and throughout the whole ban of Rambertivilla, and the part of the forests of the ban of Danubrium within its fixed boundaries, from the water called Mortania as far as the other called Murz.

[Col. 1148A] Furthermore, we likewise confirm to you the liberties which Stephen, formerly bishop of Metz of good memory, and Theodoric, formerly elect of the same church, granted your house as alms in meadows, fields, woods, and pastures. No one shall presume to demand tithes from you on your newly cultivated lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the offspring of your animals.

You may also receive into your church and retain without any objection clerics or laymen fleeing from the world, free and absolved. We further prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from being permitted to depart without his abbot’s leave, except to embrace a stricter religious life; and no one shall dare retain one who departs without the assurance of common letters.

[Col. 1148B] Whenever there is a general interdict upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices with closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells, and in a low voice. We further prohibit churches, lands, or any benefice granted to your church from being given to anyone personally or alienated under any other title without the consent of the whole chapter, or its greater and sounder part. If any gifts or alienations are made otherwise than stated, we decree them void. Moreover, we add that no canons or lay brothers bound by profession to your house may stand surety for anyone or borrow money from anyone beyond the sum established by the prudent judgment of your chapter, without the consent and permission of the abbot and the greater and sounder part of your chapter, unless this is for the manifest benefit of your house.

[Col. 1148C] If they presume to do so, the convent, without whose permission and consent they acted, shall not be bound in any way to answer for these matters.

Furthermore, in your cases you may produce your brethren who are competent to testify, and, if right requires it, by their testimony repel violence and vindicate justice. For chrism, holy oil, consecrations of churches, ordinations of clerics who are to be promoted to holy orders, the bringing of an abbot to the episcopal see, his installation, or any other ecclesiastical sacraments, no one shall dare demand anything from you, whether under the pretext of custom

[Col. 1148D] or in any other way. If anyone presumes to act against this, let him know that he will have a share with Gehazi, whose conduct he imitates by exacting a shameful payment. We further decree that the burial-place of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last wishes of those who have determined to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken remaining intact. Wishing also, with paternal care, to provide for your peace and tranquillity, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone, within the enclosures of your places or granges, from presuming to commit violence, robbery, or theft, set fire, or take, cut down, or kill any animal.

[Col. 1149A] We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things granted for the governance and support of those concerned shall be preserved entire and shall benefit them in every way, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical justice of the diocesan bishop. If in future, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Susanna.

[Col. 1149D] I, Vivian, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Cynthius, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Cecilia. I, Arduin, cardinal-priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Matthew, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Marcellus. I, Laborans, cardinal-priest of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of St. Callixtus. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Damaso. I, Theodinus, bishop of the see of Porto and St. Rufina. I, Peter, bishop of Tusculum.

[Col. 1150A] I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina. I, James, cardinal-deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Ardicio, cardinal-deacon of St. Theodore. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

Given at Velletri . . . through the hand of Albert, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July [18 June], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1182 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

## LX. He confirms the possessions of the Church of St. Mary Magdalene of Besançon. (Fragment.) (Velletri, 26 June.)

[*Unpublished Memoirs and Documents of Franche-Comté*, vol. II, p. 318.]

[Col. 1150B]

Lucius, bishop, to his beloved sons Manogold, cantor, and the canons of St. Mary Magdalene established at Besançon, present and future, canonically appointed, in perpetuity, etc.

We confirm at Besançon the chapel of St. James within the sands, with all its appurtenances; the land which you possess from that chapel to the city walls, to be allocated and assigned without opposition for whatever uses you know will best benefit your church; the holding of Peter of Osma; the holding of John the knight, beside the well of Lord Dudin

[Col. 1150C] in the Field of Mars; the holding of Constantine beside the mill in the quarter of Baptenti; the holding of Hugh the monk; what you possess in the mill of Baptenti; a share in the oven situated at the junction of Calvimont; two holdings; and whatever you possess at Valentinum.

Given at Velletri, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July [26 June], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1182 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the year [not supplied in the surviving text] of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

## LXI. He takes the Church of St. Mary of Lausanne under protection and confirms the canons’ possessions. (Velletri, 26 June.)

[*Memoirs and Documents of the Society of French-speaking Switzerland*, vol. VII, p. 27.]

[Col. 1150D]

Lucius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Arducius, provost, and the canons of the Church of Lausanne, and their successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

Both the force of equity and the order of reason compel us to grant the effect sought by those who make just requests, especially when piety assists the petitioners’ wish and truth does not abandon it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the Church of Blessed Mary, in which you are devoted to divine service, and secure it by the privilege of this present writing. We establish that whatever possessions . . . among which . . . we have thought fit to specify by their own names: the benefice

[Col. 1151A] which you possess at the high altar and at the altar of the Holy Cross; the church of St. Protasius; the church of Domno Martino; the church of Essertines; the church of Bota; the church of Alba Aqua with all its rights, appurtenances, and ancient liberty; the church of St. Mary; the church of St. Peter; the church of St. Lawrence with its appurtenances; the church of St. Stephen; the church of Tolochina; the church of Juleus with its appurtenances; the church of Sugnens; the church of Baises; the church of Orba with its appurtenances; the church of Evonant; the church of Dalens; the church of Muratel; the church of Pentola; the church of Chavornay with its appurtenances; the church of Corrovald; the church of Crisie; the church of Dessilus; the church of Villaricomite; the church of Viveyo;

[Col. 1151B] the church of Bollo; the church of Granges with its appurtenances; the church of Danesse; the church of Utfinis; the church of Crans; the church of Nivillins; the village of Crans; the village of St. Protasius; the village of Tolochina; the village of Dellens; the village of Spanengis; the village of Domno Martino; the village of Bomanel; the village of Bota in Ogo; the village of Alba Aqua; the village of Essertines; the village of Warrens; and what you possess at Crissie; what you possess at Viviacum; the tithes which you receive on the bishop’s lands; what you possess at Pulliacum; what you possess in Burgo; what you possess in the town of Lausanne; the alms which Peter of Scandens made to you; the donation which Cono of Grandson and his wife Algui are said to have made to you from their right;

[Col. 1151C] and the donation which our venerable brother Roger, your bishop, made to your church on behalf of Peter of Escandens, as compensation for the *majoria* [the mayoralty/right of a mayor] which the same bishop had at Bellomontem; likewise, the amicable settlement concerning the church of St. Marius, concerning the tithe on expenses and candles . . . and concerning the procuration due to you and your successors on the Monday of Easter, made without impropriety by Peter, formerly bishop of Pavia and legate of the Apostolic See, of good memory.

Furthermore, we likewise confirm to you by apostolic authority the ancient and reasonable customs hitherto preserved for you and your church. We also decree that the liberty which your church has reasonably possessed in villages and over persons up to this time shall remain unimpaired,

[Col. 1151D] expressly prohibiting anyone from presuming to impose new and unlawful exactions upon them, or upon your chaplains or clerics.

We decree, therefore, etc.

Given at Velletri.

## LXII. Confirmation of the goods of the Church of Senlis. (Velletri, 30 June.)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, X, 220.]

Lucius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Stephen, dean of the Church of St. Mary of Senlis, and his brethren, present and future, canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

[Col. 1152A] By virtue of the office of the apostolate entrusted to us, we are obliged to give more diligent assistance to the devoted children of the Church and effectively to grant their just petitions, so that, through the fulfillment of their requests, they may be more earnestly moved to devotion toward the Roman Church and, protected by apostolic guardianship, may render more fervently to the Lord the service due to Him. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves your Church of St. Mary of Senlis, in which you are dedicated to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions, goods, or revenues that same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by grant of pontiffs, bounty of kings [Col. 1152B] or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with the two streets adjoining it and its other appurtenances; the church of St. Peter, situated in the suburb of your city; the church of St. Hilary before the Rheims Gate; the church of St. Geneviève with its appurtenances; the church of St. Anianus; the church of St. Martin, situated in the Paris quarter; the church of St. Martin of Ermenold’s estate, with certain tenants, lands, a certain portion of the tithes, and the other things which your church is known to possess in that estate and its territory; [Col. 1152C] the church of Ver with its appurtenances; the church of St. Mary of Eva, with certain tenants, a portion of the tithes, judicial rights, and the other things which you reasonably possess there; the church of Moleignon, with that estate, lands, vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, and its other appurtenances.
