Further, from the alms of Asthon, of good memory, formerly cantor of your church: four tenants paying you a fixed annual rent, whom he had acquired from the knight Odo of Gonesse by valid title of purchase; the church of Monte Spiculatorio; the church of Ogerio of St. Medard; the church of Duviacum with its appurtenances; the church of Ruilliacum with half the greater tithe of the lands of that estate; [Col. 1152D] moreover, half of a certain new tithe, called the tithe of newly cultivated land; the church of Borreto with a portion of the tithes; the church of Tremiliacum with the chapel of Veterinis, and that estate with its judicial rights and appurtenances; the church of Rareio; the church of St. Mary of Chamant with the tithe of that estate, saving nevertheless a certain portion of that tithe assigned to the priest of the same place; the church of St. Leonard of Deep Valley, with that estate, lands, pastures, judicial rights, and appurtenances; the church of the Fountain of St. Firmin; the tithe of Chantilly; the church of Gouvieux, with that portion of the tithes which your church is known to possess in the lands and vineyards of that estate; and also the mayoralty in that estate, with all belonging to it, [Col. 1153A] which our venerable brother Henry, now bishop, acquired from his own property and gave you with pious liberality; the church of New Town, called Lamorlaye, with the tithes of that place.

Within the enclosed borough of your city: tenants, lands, and their judicial rights and customs, according to the observance hitherto maintained. Outside the enclosed borough, as distinguished by the ancient ditch: tenants, vineyards, lands, revenues, and the whole jurisdiction of all your land without diminution. In the Paris quarter: half of the mill called St. Mary’s Mill; the greater part of the small tithes from the gardens, yards, and the raising of animals and geese of that city, as your church is known to have held hitherto; seven muids [modii] [Col. 1153B] of grain, ten muids of wine, and fifty sols in Parisian money, which, from the alms bestowed upon your church by Guy of the Tower, of good memory, the butler of Senlis or his heirs succeeding one after another are bound to pay you yearly for the brethren’s Lenten meal, as is more fully set forth in the charter made concerning this; four mines of salt, which your bishop for the time being is bound to render you yearly for the same brethren’s meal; in the quarter of St. Geneviève, two sols of quit-rent, which the knight Odo of the Ditch assigned to you upon his land for the soul of his father Adam; the lands of Long Water, with a certain share of the harvest and their tithes; at the same place, the wood called St. Mary’s Brushwood; the meadows which you possess between the two fords; in the meadow of Percebot, one cartload or two wagonloads of hay, to be had there yearly when the hay is gathered; [Col. 1153C] in the bishop’s meadow near the Fountain of the Sands, the same quantity of hay, to be received at the same season; furthermore, whatever you reasonably possess in the territory of the said city in tithes or any possessions, customs, and judicial rights; tithes from certain lands of the estate called Montis; at the place called Viaria, lands, a share of the harvest, and tithes paid to you; in the diocese of Beauvais, at St. Lupus beside the river called the Oise, a meadow paying you two sols of quit-rent; ten sols of quit-rent, which [Col. 1153D] Theobald of Crépy left you as an alms through the hand of your aforesaid bishop; the estate called Olriacum, with its lands, woods, and other appurtenances; also the fishpond and mill adjoining that estate; the lands which you have at the estate called La Chapelle; the tenants, lands, customs, and rights which you have at Bazoches; at St. Christopher of Halatte, two-thirds of the tithes from certain lands of that estate; the lands and revenues which you have at Saintines; what you have at Pomponne; in the estate of Bernosa, one tenant with a vineyard and certain possessions; the vineyards which you have at Hautmont from the alms of William, formerly cantor of your church; half a tenant at Chamissiacum, [Col. 1154A] paying you yearly nine mines of grain, four denarii, and one capon; in the territory of that same estate, lands paying you an annual rent; at Baleigniacum, one tenant with the small tithe of that house and the annual rent which he is bound to pay you; furthermore, a tithe from certain dwelling-plots and lands situated in the territory of that same estate.

Moreover, just as the aforesaid bishop granted and confirmed to you by his pontifical authority and by the protection of his written instrument that, when your churches situated in his diocese are vacant, you may have them served by chaplains until rectors are appointed to them, so we too confirm this to your devotion by the authority of this privilege. Furthermore, just as the people of your church [Col. 1154B] have hitherto enjoyed without dispute the liberty that they are bound to pay toll to no one for goods which they sell in the city or acquire for their own use, and that your houses and households are not subject to lay authority, so we decree that these persons, houses, and households shall enjoy the same liberty in times to come.

We also hold valid, and decree to remain perpetually unimpaired, the ancient and reasonable customs of your church hitherto observed: namely, that if one of you dies, or enters religious life, having received from his prebend one mina or more of the new harvest of that year, the portion of the harvest due to him may usefully be applied to payment of debts incurred, or to other uses according to the direction of himself [Col. 1154C] or another person to whom he entrusted the disposition of his property. But if, which God forbid, one of you should die intestate, then, after debts usefully incurred have been paid and expenses deducted, whatever remains from the property acquired by that deceased person through the church shall devolve upon the church, in accordance with the decrees of the Lateran Council. When your churches become vacant, you may present persons to the diocesan bishop; if they are suitable, they shall receive from him the care of souls, so that they owe accountability to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters.

We further decree that, on the death of your bishop, or of you, son dean, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over that church by any trickery or violence, [Col. 1154D] except one whom you, by common consent, or the sounder part of you, shall deem to be elected in the fear of God and according to the ancient canonical custom of your church. In elections or any other business of your church, we forbid the decisions of the greater and sounder part of you to be impeded by the opposition of others, provided that what is decided does not conflict with ecclesiastical ordinances. We also prohibit anyone from promulgating against you or your church a sentence of suspension, excommunication, or interdict without manifest and reasonable cause.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, [Col. 1155A] or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be kept whole for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, to be of service in every respect, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the due reverence owed to your bishop. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly presume to act against it, etc.

Given at Velletri, through the hand of Alberic, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of July [30 June], in the fifteenth indiction; in the year 1182 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the first year of the pontificate of Pope Lucius III.

A collation was made with the original on 24 April 1336, after Easter.

LXIII. To Peter, abbot of Monte Cassino: he declares that the church of St. Nicholas of Gurgo was bestowed by Barason, judge of Arborea. (Velletri, 30 June.)

[MONTFAUCON, *Diarium Italicum*, p. 327.]

[Col. 1155B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, abbot of Monte Cassino, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We desire that gifts bestowed upon religious places out of regard for piety should remain secure and unimpaired, and that they be fortified by apostolic protection lest they be disturbed by the wickedness of evil men. Induced, therefore, by this reasonable consideration, and likewise granting your prayers, we confirm to you and, through you, to your monastery, by apostolic authority, and fortify with the protection of this present writing, the church of St. Nicholas of Gurgo with all its appurtenances, [Col. 1155C] which your monastery has canonically acquired, committed to your care, from our beloved son, the noble man Barason, judge of Arborea, with the consent of the diocesan bishops, as is contained in his authentic instrument, and which you possess justly and without dispute. For fuller notice of this act, we have thought fit to set down that instrument below:

“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. For those weighed down by the burden of sins, a principal remedy is found in hastening to distribute temporal substance to Christ’s poor, the Lord Himself saying: ‘Give alms, [Col. 1155D] and behold, all things are clean for you’; and again: ‘Make for yourselves friends from unrighteous mammon, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings.’ Therefore, hearing this saying, I, Barason, king and judge, following to the best of my ability the pious footsteps of my grandfather and father, with the consent of my wife Queen Algaburga, and also of our bishops, Marianus Zorachi of Terralba and Comitanus Pais of Ala, for the redemption of our souls and of those of our parents, deliver, donate, and grant to the church of St. Benedict of Monte Cassino the church of St. Nicholas of Gurgo, with all its appurtenances: serfs and maidservants, lands, vineyards, cultivated and uncultivated ground, woodland pastures and meadows, woods, fisheries, animals, and all things written in the charter of that [Col. 1156A] same church. This is done upon the following pact and agreement: that it shall send there twelve monks to serve God, provided that the aforesaid church can support them without injury to itself; and three or four of them shall be sufficiently learned that, if necessary, they may be chosen as archbishops and bishops, and may also be competent to conduct the affairs of our realm at the Roman curia, at the emperor’s court, and everywhere. But if the aforesaid church cannot support so many, it shall send seven, or as many as shall seem appropriate according to our counsel. From this church, the church of St. Benedict of Monte Cassino shall receive twenty bezants yearly, and no more, unless some impediment should arise for that church on account of the Roman curia, war, some business of its realm, or the purchase of some land. Neither I nor any other person shall in any manner be permitted to reclaim or disturb the aforesaid church of St. Nicholas, if they are willing to observe the aforesaid agreement.

“Witnesses: Marianus Zorraki, bishop of Terralba; Comitanus Pais, bishop of Ala; Ponthus, curator of Bonorzuli; Comitanus Fronsacute, curator of Campitanno; Comitanus de Lacon Pedes, curator of Valensa; Constantinus Spanus, curator of Frodoriane and judge; Parason de Gallun, curator of Miili; Orzocho de Lacon, my son, curator of Giltiber; Orzocor de Lacon Arborikesus, curator of Barbaria of Meana; Constantinus Manca, curator of Mantra Olisai; John of Vinea, major of the Bujakesi, with all his associates; and Peter Paganus, though unworthy, the priest who wrote all these things.

[Col. 1156C] “But should anyone wish to contrive anything against this charter of our donation, may he incur the curse of almighty God—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—likewise of blessed Mary, ever Virgin and Mother of God, and of all the heavenly powers, the holy patriarchs and prophets, apostles, evangelists, disciples, Innocents, martyrs, confessors, virgins, and all the elect. Amen. But those who consent to this charter, confirm it, and believe it to be true, may they have the blessing of almighty God—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—likewise of blessed Mary, ever Virgin and Mother of God, [Col. 1156D] and of all the heavenly powers, the holy patriarchs and prophets, apostles, evangelists, disciples, Innocents, martyrs, confessors, virgins, and all the elect. Amen. All these things were ordained and confirmed in the year 1182.”

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the wrath of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Velletri on the second day before the Kalends of July [30 June].

(There is appended a hanging lead seal, inscribed on one side [Col. 1157A]: “SAINT PAUL, SAINT PETER”; and on the other: “POPE LUCIUS THE THIRD.” [Note: [Col. 1157] In the archive of Monte Cassino there also appear many other diplomas of the kings of Sardinia, written in the vernacular language of the island.])

LXIV. He commands all prelates of churches to excommunicate those who lay ambushes for monks travelling to the general chapter of Cluny. (Velletri, 14 July.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 414.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, all prelates of churches in whose dioceses there are evildoers who lay ambushes for monks coming to the general chapter of Cluny or take away their possessions, greeting and apostolic blessing.

As we have learned, the malice of evil men [Col. 1157B] has now reached such madness, and their greed has so burned beyond measure, that it spares neither decency nor religion, but everywhere seeks from every quarter fuel for its avarice. As has been reported to us, certain evildoers lay ambushes for monks coming to the general chapter of Cluny; having forcibly taken the goods which they carry from those whom they can catch, they presume to inflict many injuries upon them. Therefore, wishing to restrain such men from so great wickedness, we command your discretion by apostolic letters to ensure that those whom you know to be entangled in such crimes are, without opposition from anyone, strictly avoided by all as excommunicated persons until they restore the damages inflicted and make suitable satisfaction [Col. 1157C] for the injuries.

Given at Velletri, on the second day before the Ides of July [14 July].

LXV. To [Guy], archbishop of Sens. (Velletri, 5 August.)

[*Antiquités de Saint-Aignan d’Orléans*, p. 85.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the archbishop of Sens, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son, the abbot of St. Maximin, having submitted a question to us, showed that, although his monastery had received for a very long time, by ancient custom, a certain prebend in the church of St. Anianus of Orléans, [Col. 1157D] the dean and canons had rashly withdrawn it by their own act, without judgment and without justice. Therefore, wishing to provide that his monastery not be defrauded in this matter, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, after summoning the parties, if the abbot’s assertion is established by lawful witnesses, you shall cause the prebend, with the revenues received, to be restored to the monastery without delay and without appeal. Once restoration has been made, if any disputed matter appears, hear it more carefully and decide it by means of justice.

Given at Velletri, on the Nones of August [5 August].

LXVI. He receives the monastery of St. Mary of Murelo under protection and confirms its possessions. (Velletri, 23 November.)

[MANRIQUE, *Annal. Cisterc.*, III, 25.]

[Col. 1158A]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, abbot of St. Mary of Murelo, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life.

Those who profess the religious life ought to have apostolic protection. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your supplications and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are dedicated to divine service, etc. Furthermore, whatever possessions [Col. 1158B] or goods that same monastery now possesses or may in future acquire shall remain secure and unimpaired to you. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: the place of Murelo itself, in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with its appurtenances; the grange of Ovila with its appurtenances; the grange of Alcaramaz with its appurtenances; the grange of Azagron with its appurtenances, etc.

Given at Verona, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December [23 November], in the first indiction, in the year 1182 of the Lord’s Incarnation and the second year of the pontificate of the same Lord Pope Lucius III.

LXVII. He receives the church of Segni under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Velletri, 2 December.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 1237.]

[Col. 1158C]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother PETER of Segni and to his successors who shall canonically enter office, in perpetuity.

Both the order of reason requires, and consideration for ecclesiastical advantage invites us, to love our brothers and fellow bishops with a fuller charity and to fortify more earnestly by the protection of the Apostolic See the churches committed to their governance, so that in carrying out the office they have undertaken they may always be the more watchful, the more secure they see themselves to be from the assaults of wicked men. Therefore, venerable brother bishop in Christ, we graciously [Col. 1158D] assent to your just petitions; following the example of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the Church of Segni, over which by God’s authority you are known to preside, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses—whether houses, small holdings, or property outside the city; vineyards; fruit-bearing or fruitless trees; cultivated and uncultivated lands; woods, meadows, waters, mills, pastures; or other things on mountains or on the plain—or may in future acquire by grant of pontiffs, bounty of kings or princes, [Col. 1159A] offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s provision, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

In the city of Segni: the church of St. Peter with all its appurtenances; the church of St. Lucy with all its appurtenances; the church of St. Stephen with all its appurtenances; the church of St. Mark with all its appurtenances. In the castle of Collemezzo: the church of St. Mary with all its appurtenances. In the castle of Metellanico: the church of St. Angel, the church of St. Peter with all its appurtenances, the church of St. Giles, the church of St. Mary of Vacariis with all its appurtenances, the church of St. Nicholas of Montenero with all its appurtenances, [Col. 1159B] the monastery of St. Mary of Roscillis with the chapel of St. Margaret and the chapel of St. Archangel of Gabiniano, together with all its appurtenances and liberties. In the castle of Gabiniano: the church of St. Thomas with all its appurtenances, the church of St. John of Montefocale, the church of St. Mary of the Archpriest, and the church of St. Valentine with all its appurtenances. In the castle of Plumbinaria: the church of St. Mary, the church of St. Anastasius, the church of St. Nicholas with all its appurtenances, the monastery of St. Cecilia with all its appurtenances, the church of St. Barbara with all its possessions, the church of the Savior of Viculo, the church of St. Mary with all its appurtenances, the church of St. Anastasia, and the church of St. George with all its appurtenances. In the castle [Col. 1159C] of Vallismontone: the church of St. Mary, the church of St. Andrew, the church of St. Lawrence with all its appurtenances, the church of St. John of the Wood, the church of St. Nicholas with all their appurtenances, the church of St. Zoticus with all its appurtenances, and the monastery of St. Mary in Silice with all its appurtenances and liberties. In the castle of Sacco: the church of St. Angel; the church of St. Hilary with all its appurtenances; the church of St. Leonard of the Rock; and that of St. Sylvester with all its appurtenances. In the castle of Montfortino: the church of St. Mary, the church of the Holy Cross, the church of St. Stephen with all its appurtenances, the church of St. Peter at Versa Acqua with the chapel of St. Sylvester and all its appurtenances, [Col. 1159D] the church of St. Archangel, and the church of St. Nicholas of the Turf Wood with all its appurtenances.

The garden before the gate of the aforesaid city of Segni, with its *plaigis* and *longara* [local land terms; precise sense uncertain], and all its appurtenant benefits. The greater hemp-field beside the road leading to Anagni, at the foot of the *placae* beneath the ford, together with the other land above that hemp-field and part of the wood of the hill of Fenaltulo. We also decree that the castles of Collemezzo, Metellanico, Gabiniano, Plumbinaria, Vallismontone, Sacco, and Montfortino are subject to you and your successors by episcopal right, as they are known to have been subject to your predecessors. We likewise confirm by this present writing the boundaries of your bishopric, as they are known to be contained in the privileges of our predecessors and as your predecessors and you yourself at present [Col. 1160A] possess them. We decree that the reasonable liberties which you have in your fief-holders and people of Segni shall remain valid and secure, and forbid them henceforth to be violated by any rashness. We also prohibit anyone within the boundaries of that bishopric, without the assent of you or your successors, saving the privileges of the Apostolic See, from presuming to build a new church or chapel.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all shall be kept whole for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, to be of service in every respect, [Col. 1160B] saving the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Vivianus, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Arduinus, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St. Mary in Trastevere, title of Callixtus. [Col. 1160C] I, Rainerius, deacon-cardinal of St. George at the Golden Veil. I, Gratianus, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

Given at Velletri through the hand of Albert, priest and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Nones of December [2 December], in the first indiction, in the year 1182 of the Lord’s Incarnation and the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

LXVIII. At the request of Bishop John, he receives the church of Ravello under protection and confirms its possessions. (Velletri, 4 December.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 1185.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother [Col. 1160D] John, bishop of Ravello, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

Since, by the office of the apostolate entrusted to us by God, through which by the Lord’s ordinance we have preeminence among all Christ’s faithful, we ought to concern ourselves with the peace and tranquillity of every individual, we especially ought to be solicitous for the peace of those who are endowed with pastoral dignity, promoted to episcopal office, and known by special prerogative to belong to the jurisdiction of the Roman Church. For unless we attend to their welfare, preserve their dignities and rights unimpaired insofar as we can with God’s permission, and defend them by apostolic authority from the assaults of wicked men, they cannot truly be solicitous for the salvation of those who, by the Lord’s dispensation, [Col. 1161A] have been entrusted to them for governance. Therefore, venerable brother John, bishop in Christ, we graciously assent to your just petitions. Following the example of our predecessors of blessed memory, Popes Adrian and Alexander, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the church of Ravello, over which by God’s authority you are known to preside, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire by grant of pontiffs, bounty of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

[Col. 1161B] The monastery of St. Tryphon, the monastery of the Holy Trinity, and the monastery of St. Mary of Castiglione. We further confirm to you and your successors in perpetuity the whole extent of the parish of Ravello, as it has hitherto been reasonably possessed by your predecessors and by yourself.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all shall be kept whole for the benefit of those for whose support they were granted, to be of service in every respect, saving the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

[Col. 1161C] I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodinus, bishop of the see of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Vivianus, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Albinus, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St. Mary in Trastevere, title of Callixtus. I, Rodulphus, deacon-cardinal of St. George at the Golden Veil. I, Gratianus, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

[Col. 1161D] Given at Velletri, through the hands of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Nones of December [4 December], in the first indiction, in the year 1182 of the Lord’s Incarnation and the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

LXIX. He commands [Stephen], bishop of Autun, and [Manasses], bishop of Langres, to ensure that nothing is done contrary to the privilege granted to Cistercian monks. (Velletri, 21 December.)

[LILJEGREN, *Diplomat. Suec.*, I, 116.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the bishops of Autun and Langres, and to his beloved sons, abbots, priors, and other prelates of churches established in their bishoprics, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1162A] We have heard—and, hearing it, have been astonished—that, although it has been granted to all brethren of the Cistercian Order by the Fathers and our predecessors, and subsequently confirmed by ourselves, that they are bound to pay tithes to no one from the *laboribus* (“labours” or produce) which they cultivate by their own hands or at their own expense, certain persons nevertheless presume, contrary to the grants of the Apostolic See, to demand and extort tithes from them. By a perverse interpretation of the clauses of apostolic privileges, they assert that *laboribus* (“labours” or produce) must be understood as referring to newly cultivated lands. But it is evident to all persons of sound judgment that such an interpretation is perverse and contrary to sound understanding, since, according to that clause, they are entirely exempt from payment of tithes, both from lands which they have brought or bring [Col. 1162B] into cultivation and from cultivated lands which they till by their own hands or at their own expense. For if the Roman Church had intended only newly cultivated lands where we have written “from *laboribus* [labours],” we would have written “from newly cultivated lands,” as is inserted in the privileges of certain others.

Therefore, since there is no doubt that it would result in common injury to the Church if anyone should believe that he could go unpunished in acting contrary to ordinances of the Apostolic See which ought to remain perpetually binding, we command and enjoin you by apostolic letters, lest anyone take from this a pretext for maliciously assailing the aforesaid brethren and in any way harassing them contrary to justice, carefully to prohibit more strictly by our authority all persons subject to your jurisdiction [Col. 1162C] from presuming in any way to extort tithes from the brethren of Fontaines, or any others of the same order living in your bishoprics, whether from newly cultivated lands, other lands which they till by their own hands or at their own expense, or the raising of animals.

If any canons, clerics, monks, or laymen burden the aforesaid brethren by demanding tithes contrary to the privileges of the Apostolic See, then, without appeal, strike laymen with both excommunication and interdict; suspend clerics from office; and cause both the sentence of excommunication and that of interdict to be observed inviolably until fitting satisfaction has been made. Moreover, by the authority of these present letters we command you to announce publicly, with lighted candles, that those who have laid violent hands upon brethren of the aforesaid monasteries are excommunicated, [Col. 1162D] and cause them to be strictly avoided by all as excommunicated persons until they have made fitting satisfaction to the aforesaid brethren and presented themselves before the Apostolic See with letters from the diocesan bishop containing the truth of the matter. Know further that they have been granted the right, in their cases—whether cases which they themselves have against others, or which others have against them—to bring suitable brethren as witnesses and, by their testimony, both to repel violence and obtain justice.

Given at Velletri, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January [21 December] 1182.

LXX. He receives the monastery of St. Mary of Baumgarten under protection and confirms its possessions and rights. (Velletri, 21 December.)

[SCHOEPFLIN, *Alsat. diplom.*, I, 276.]

[Col. 1163A]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons CONSTANTINE, abbot of the monastery of St. Mary of Borgar, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Those choosing the religious life ought to have apostolic protection, lest the assault of any rashness either recall them from their purpose or, God forbid, weaken the strength of holy religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions [Col. 1163B] and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of blessed Mary, Mother of God and ever Virgin, in which you are dedicated to divine service; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order established in that monastery according to God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institution of the Cistercian brethren shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions or goods that same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire by grant of pontiffs, bounty of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure [Col. 1163C] and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The very place in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances, and with the adjoining grange of Bongart; and whatever you possess in landed estates or in pasturage for animals, as is contained in the legal instruments made concerning this by the bishops of Toul and Strasbourg, and by Matthew, duke of Lorraine. Whatever likewise you possess in vineyards, lands, and other property near the village of Aphec and its surroundings; also your grange of Anisseheim with all its appurtenances; the alms-gift of Walfred of Bixosseheim, as he conveyed it to your church through the hand of the bishop of Strasbourg, in vineyards, lands, meadows, courts, houses, holdings, and a mill at Bixosseheim, Engresseheim, and other places [Col. 1163D]. The grange of Baudeneheim with all its appurtenances. Likewise, rights of use in woods and pastures, namely for the necessary use of yourselves and all your animals. The grange of Fossa, as it was granted to you by Matthew, duke of Lorraine, and Simon of Parreia, and bounded by its other limits; likewise pastures for every kind of your animals. Also rights of use in woods for all your uses throughout the land of the castle called Spiceberg. The grange of Fresonevillari with all its appurtenances and dependencies. Likewise pastures and all rights of use necessary to you and your animals throughout the entire ban of Lord Juvinus, Magnumuiler, and Wios [Col. 1164A].

Indeed, of the lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, and of the increase of your animals, let absolutely no one presume to demand tithes from you. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen fleeing the world, free and unencumbered, and retain them without any objection. Moreover, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, to leave it without the permission of his abbot; and no one may dare retain one who has departed without letters of authorization from the community. Further, wishing with paternal concern to provide for your peace and tranquillity, by apostolic authority [Col. 1164B] we forbid anyone within the enclosures of your establishments or granges to presume rashly to commit violence, robbery, or theft; to set fire; or to seize or kill a person.

If the bishop in whose parish your house is founded, though requested three times at intervals with the humility and devotion fitting in the matter, should perhaps refuse to bless a substitute abbot, it shall be lawful for that abbot to bless his own novices and to perform the other acts belonging to his office, until that bishop reconsiders his harshness and does not refuse to bless the abbot who is to be blessed. Furthermore, in your causes you may produce brethren suitable to give testimony [Col. 1164C], and by their testimony, if it is right, both repel violence and vindicate justice.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, or to take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass them by any vexations; but let all things be preserved whole for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, to be useful to them in every way, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodinus, bishop of the church of Porto and of the see of Santa Rufina [Col. 1164D]. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St. Susanna. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Vivian, cardinal priest of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Arditio, cardinal deacon of St. Theodore. I, Arduin, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross of Viterbo. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of SS. Cosmas and Damian. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Callixtus. [Col. 1165A] I, Ranerius, cardinal priest of SS. John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Albinus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary the New.

Given at Velletri, through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, in the first indiction, in the year 1182 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

LXXI. He confirms the settlement made by Guichard, archbishop of Lyons of blessed memory, with Guigo, count of Forez. (Velletri.)

[MENESTRIER, *History of Lyons*, Proofs, p. XII.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons [Col. 1165B], the dean and chapter of Lyons, greeting and apostolic blessing.

By the administration of the office entrusted to us, we are compelled to grant the just petitions of individuals and to fortify with apostolic protection those arrangements made by agreement of the parties without wrongdoing, lest what has been established by amicable settlement with care and labor be later annulled through anyone’s malice. Accordingly, your devotion has requested that we should strengthen by the protection of our written instrument that settlement which Guichard, your late archbishop of good memory, made with the nobleman Guigo, count of Forez, with our assent and in our presence. Granting your petitions, we hold that settlement [Col. 1165C] valid; and, since it was made and accepted by the spontaneous will of the parties, we have directed that it be recorded word for word in writing for the memory of future generations, as it is contained in the authentic instrument, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, for the establishment of perpetual peace between Lord Guichard, etc.

Given at Velletri, through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of [lacuna], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1182 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius.

YEAR 1182–1183.

LXXII. He confirms for the canons of Asti the church of St. Michael of Intercisio. (Velletri, March 20.)

[*Monuments of National History*, Charters I, 935.]

[Col. 1165D]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the archpriest and canons of Asti, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant the just wishes of petitioners, and bring to fulfillment, with the result following, vows that do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, concurring gratefully in your just petitions, we confirm for you and your successors by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this writing, the church of St. Michael of Interisio, granted to you by An[selm], your late bishop of good memory, as you possess it canonically and without dispute [Col. 1166A]. We decree that no person whatsoever may violate this page of our confirmation or presumptuously oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Velletri, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April.

LXXIII. Privilege for the chapter of Reims. (Velletri, March 26.)

[VARIN, *Administrative Archives of the City of Reims*, vol. I, part 1, p. 403.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons R., dean, and the chapter of Reims, etc.

[Col. 1166B] Granting your just petitions, by these present letters we permit that no one may release R. of Roscio, his heirs, or any other wrongdoers against your church, from the sentence by which they have canonically been bound on account of their offences, unless they first render suitable satisfaction to your church according to their means.

Given at Velletri, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April.

LXXIV. At the request of the canons of Piacenza, he confirms the judgment rendered between the church of Piacenza and Alfonso, former bishop of Pavia. (Velletri, March 28.)

[CAMPI, *History of Piacenza*, II, 367.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons [Col. 1166C] A., provost, and the canons of Piacenza, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Matters which come into controversy and are ended by friendly agreement or judgment ought, lest they relapse into the difficulty of renewed contention, to be committed to the trust of writing and strengthened by apostolic protection. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, gratefully concurring in your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen by the protection of this writing the judgment formerly pronounced by us, when we exercised the office of legate in those regions, between the church of Piacenza and Alf[onso], bishop of Pavia of good memory, concerning two parts of the tithe of the whole estate of Porto Albara; as it was canonically rendered and accepted by the parties [Col. 1166D]. We decree that no person whatsoever may violate this page of our confirmation, etc.

Given at Velletri, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, 1182.

LXXV. He confirms for the monastery of St. Denis churches granted by the archbishops of Sens. (Velletri, April 2.)

[DOUBLET, *History of Saint-Denis*, vol. I, p. 516.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and monks of Saint-Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Those things which are conferred upon religious places by our brethren and fellow bishops out of pious regard ought to be strengthened by apostolic protection, lest they can be disturbed by anyone’s malice [Col. 1167A]. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, gratefully concurring in your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen by this present document the grant made to you, and through you to your monastery, by our venerable brother G., archbishop of Sens, and by his predecessors of good memory, Daibert and William, concerning the churches of Belna, Saint-Loup, Josenuilla, Ver, Fericiac, Grand Puits, and Saint-Ouen, and concerning the presentation of priests in those churches; as it was canonically made and observed, and is contained in authentic writings. We decree that no person whatsoever may, etc.

Given at Velletri, on the fourth day before the Nones of April, 1182.

LXXVI. He confirms for the monastery of St. Denis the church of Forest and certain altars granted by the bishops of Cambrai. (Velletri, April 4.)

[Ibid., p. 517.]

[Col. 1167B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and monks of Saint-Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen by the protection of this writing the grant made to you, and through you to your monastery, by our venerable brother the bishop of Cambrai and by his predecessors of good memory, Walter, Odo, Nicholas, and Roger: namely, the church of Forest, the altar of Solempna, the altar of Vertiniolo, and a portion of a certain tithe of Kevi; as it was canonically made [Col. 1167C], hitherto observed, and is contained in authentic writings. We decree that no person whatsoever may violate this page of our confirmation or presumptuously oppose it. Should anyone, etc.

Given at Velletri, on the second day before the Nones of April, 1182.

LXXVII. To Henry, bishop, and William, dean, and the canons of Bayeux, he grants “that both they and their successors may be buried at the cathedral church.” (Velletri, April 11.)

[*Works of Peter of Blois*, p. 771.]

[Col. 1167D] LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, bishop, and his beloved sons WILLIAM, dean, and the canons of Bayeux, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the report of our beloved son Master Radulf, your canon, it has become known to us that, although the monks of Saint-Vigor had obtained apostolic confirmation from our predecessor Pope Honorius of blessed memory for an ordinance of one of your bishops, which, under pain of excommunication, decreed that none of the bishops or canons of your church should have burial anywhere except at the monastery, your predecessors were nevertheless buried at your church. But you, humbly fearing the said ordinance, requested to be protected in this matter by apostolic authority [Col. 1168A]. Therefore, favorably inclined to your prayers, and decreeing with the counsel of our brethren that the aforesaid excommunication is not binding, by apostolic authority we grant that both you and your successors may be buried at the cathedral church, notwithstanding objection or appeal. Let no person whatsoever therefore violate this page of our decree and grant, or presumptuously oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Velletri, on the third day before the Ides of April.

LXXVIII. He rebukes Abbess A[delheid] and the sisters of Quedlinburg “because they reduce the payment due to the Roman Church as a token of the liberty received, and although those same privileges expressly state that they ought annually to pay a pound of silver to the Roman pontiff, they are willing to pay only a mark, maintaining that ‘pound’ there ought to be understood as ‘mark.’” Nevertheless, at the request of the provost of Mainz, S., he grants “that henceforth they shall pay annually no more than a mark of refined silver, by the Cologne weight.” (Velletri, April 14.)

[See ERATH, *Codex Diplomaticus of Quedlinburg*, 103.]

[Col. 1168B]

LXXIX. To Peter, abbot, and the chapter of Monte Cassino. (Velletri, March 20.)

[TOSTI, *History of Monte Cassino*, II, 210.]

[Col. 1168C] LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons P., abbot, and the chapter of Monte Cassino, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since your monastery is burdened and oppressed in many ways, and is compelled to incur very great expenses in providing hospitality to those from our curia who frequently pass through your territory, we wish to provide with paternal care for your burdens and to lighten those burdens in which we can do so according to God. Therefore, since at times persons from our curia and from among our brethren stay at the monastery’s expense at Saint-Germain, not from necessity but by choice, by these present letters we grant that you are not required to furnish hospitality at Saint-Germain to anyone from our curia or among our brethren for more than one or two [Col. 1168D] days, unless illness or some other manifest necessity should detain him.

Given at Velletri, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May.

LXXX. He grants various privileges to the monastery of St. Remigius at Reims. (Velletri, May 10.)

[VARIN, *Administrative Archives of the City of Reims*, I, II, p. 395.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons P., abbot, and the brethren of St. Remigius of Reims, etc.

By apostolic authority we grant you that you may receive, free and unencumbered, and retain without any objection both clerics and laymen who flee to your religious house [Col. 1169A]. In the parish churches which you possess, you may freely choose suitable persons and present them to the diocesan bishop, who shall entrust the care of souls to them, so that they must answer to him in spiritual matters, but to you in temporal matters. Moreover, with episcopal authority, you may, according to your discretion and judgment, provide two priests serving the church from the revenues of one parish, so that one is subject to the other, provided that the revenues are sufficient to support both suitably. Furthermore, providing with paternal concern for your peace and security, by apostolic authority we forbid anyone within the enclosures and precincts of your establishments [Col. 1169B] and granges rashly to commit any violence or to seize or kill a person. Moreover, we forbid anyone rashly to seize any of your people, remove them from your lordship, or dare burden them with undue demands for lodging and service, or with any unjust exactions. Indeed, of your newly cultivated lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, and of the increase of your animals, let no one presume to demand tithes from you.

Further, by these present letters we forbid anyone, on your land or in possessions belonging to you which you retain under your lordship for your own use, to construct any building without your permission and authority. Wishing also to remove an undue burden [Col. 1169C] from you, we forbid a sentence of interdict or excommunication to be pronounced against you or your churches without manifest and reasonable cause. We further decree that the burial places of your establishments in which there are at least six monks shall be free, so that no one may hinder the devotion and final wish of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while preserving the canonical right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

When a general interdict of the land is in force, you may commit to Christian burial in your cemeteries the brethren and servants dwelling in those houses, and those who have given themselves to your religious community, unless they have been specifically placed under interdict or excommunicated [Col. 1169D], or some other consideration of right stands in the way. Let no one therefore. . . .

Given at Velletri, on the sixth day before the Ides of May.

LXXXI. He confirms “the renunciation of the wrongful custom which Bulcard of Montmorency had in the vineyards of the monastery of Saint-Denis situated in the village of Dioilo, and the toll (*rotaticum*) which the same Bulcard had on his land, as he remitted them to the monastery.” (Velletri, May 14.)

[DOUBLET, *History of Saint-Denis*, vol. I, p. 516.]

Whenever anything is remitted to pious places and religious persons, or bestowed upon them out of pious regard, it ought, lest it later be disturbed by anyone’s malice or called into doubt [Col. 1170A], to be committed to the trust of writing and strengthened by the protection of apostolic guardianship. Therefore, beloved sons, gratefully concurring in your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen by the protection of this writing the renunciation of the wrongful custom which Bulcard of Montmorency had in your monastery’s vineyards situated in the village of Dioilo, and the road toll (*rotagicum*) which that same Bulcard had in his land, as he reasonably remitted and granted them to your monastery, with the consent and approval of his brothers Hervé and Theobald of Marly. We decree that no person whatsoever may violate this page of our confirmation or presumptuously oppose it. Should anyone, etc.

[Col. 1170B] Given at Velletri, on the second day before the Ides of March, 1182.

LXXXII. To the chapter of Narbonne. (Velletri, May 16.)

[*New Gallia Christiana*, VI, Documents, 46.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons of the chapter of Narbonne, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brethren, the bishops of Maguelonne and Béziers, appearing before us, informed our court that, when your Church was deprived not only of an archbishop but also of other officeholders, you promised under oath [Col. 1170C] that you would obey without any objection the command of our venerable brother the bishop of Albano, who was then exercising the office of legate in those regions, concerning the ordering of that Church. But because that bishop returned to the Apostolic See before he had ordered your church, and because we wished to provide lest any harm come to that Church through lack of persons, we commanded the said bishop to order the aforesaid Church, as you had bound yourselves to him by the solemnity of an oath. He, with the counsel of the aforesaid bishops, filled three vacant archdeaconries and the sacristy in that church with suitable persons, and appointed a certain canon [Col. 1170D], commanding you by force of the oath you had made not to delay in admitting those persons to their offices and prebend, and to allow them freely to possess their revenues and places.

Accordingly, holding valid what was done by the bishop of Albano, we command and order you, in obedience to his command—as you are bound by oath—to hold his appointment valid and firm, with objection and appeal set aside; nor may any of you hinder the persons appointed by him, as we have said, from peacefully possessing through the investiture of the aforesaid bishop of Béziers the aforesaid offices and prebend.

Given at Velletri, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June.

LXXXIII. He orders the abbot and monks of Urano to obey the archbishop of Ravenna. (Velletri, May 18.)

[MITTARELLI, *Camaldolese Annals*, IV, Appendix, p. 111.]

[Col. 1171A]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and monks of Urano, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brother, the archbishop of Ravenna, has informed us that, although you monks had been suspended from office because you did not elect an abbot, you neither observed the suspension nor took care to make satisfaction to the said archbishop for contempt of the sentence, as we enjoined; yet you elected an abbot upon a renewed apostolic command. Since, therefore, from a time beyond human memory, all the abbots of your monastery, down to our beloved son P., now prior of Camaldoli, are asserted to have promised an oath of obedience to his predecessors, to you, son abbot, we command and strictly order by apostolic letters that within forty days after receipt of these letters [Col. 1171B] you promise and render to that archbishop every obedience and reverence which your predecessors promised to his predecessors, the archbishops. . . . notwithstanding that our predecessor Pope A. of holy memory is known personally to have granted something for the time being to the aforesaid prior. Further, by the authority of these letters we enjoin [lacuna] the grants of the Church of Ravenna which you hold, to the archbishop without difficulty [lacuna] or, if you cannot reach an amicable agreement with him, [lacuna] to our venerable brethren, the bishops of Fetrano and Faenza, and our beloved son, the provost of Fetrano, [lacuna] to render the fullness of equitable justice [Col. 1171C].

Given at Velletri, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June.

I, Peter of Torre, notary of Cesena, have written and copied this exactly as I saw and read it in Catholic letters sealed with the apostolic seal.

LXXXIV. He commands the abbots of Vézelay and Flavigny to compel the canons of Chalon and Mâcon to restore churches taken from the monastery of Tournus. (Velletri, May 23.)

[JUENIN, *New History of Tournus*, Proofs, p. 179.]

[Col. 1171D] LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbots of Vézelay and Flavigny, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received a complaint brought before us by our beloved sons, the abbot and monks of the monastery of Tournus: namely, that the beloved sons, the canons of Chalon, have unjustly taken from them the church of Giniac and the church of Molesia. Furthermore, the prior and regular canons of the church of St. Peter of Mâcon have, as is alleged, presumed to take from the said monks the church of Saint-Taur near the castle of Rainald. Therefore, unwilling to permit the aforesaid monastery to suffer loss of its rights, we command your discretion by apostolic letters diligently to admonish and, by ecclesiastical compulsion, require the possessors of the aforesaid churches to restore them to the aforesaid monks, or to render them full justice in your presence [Col. 1172A].

Given at Velletri, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June.

On the lead seal: LUCIUS POPE III.

LXXXV. He confirms the sentence pronounced against the count of Geneva by the archbishop of Vienne and the bishop of Geneva. (Velletri, June 1.)

[SPON, *History of Geneva*, 1730 edition, duodecimo, vol. III, p. 64.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren, the archbishop of Vienne and the bishop of Geneva, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1172B] Whenever a sentence of ecclesiastical coercion is canonically pronounced against wrongdoers against Churches on account of their offences, it must remain firmly in force until those wrongdoers themselves are compelled, by suitable satisfaction, to amend the things they have done wrongly. Therefore, we confirm by apostolic authority the sentence which you have canonically pronounced against the count of Geneva and his land on account of damages and injuries done to the Church of Geneva, and command that it be observed inviolate until due satisfaction has been made.

Given at Velletri, on the Kalends of July.

LXXXVI. He confirms the immunity of the church of Basenvilla. (Velletri, June 2.)

[MARTENE, *Anecdota*, I, 589.]

[Col. 1172C]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the prior and brethren of Basenvilla, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant the just wishes of petitioners, and bring to fulfillment, with the result following, vows which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, gratefully concurring in your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority for your devotion, and strengthen by the protection of this writing, the immunity and exemption from rents, procurations, customary dues, exactions, and other burdens—except knights’ fiefs—granted to you and your successors in pious devotion by the nobleman Simon of Nealfa, for the soul of the nobleman Simon of Maurepast, in the presence of L., the late illustrious king of the Franks of good memory [Col. 1172D], and of our venerable brother W., then archbishop of Sens and now archbishop of Reims, as is found in the authentic instruments of the aforesaid persons.

> [Note: [Col. 1171] See the letters of King Louis concerning the satisfaction made by Simon of Nealfa for the killing of Simon de Malrepast, knight, in Martene, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 589.]

We decree that no person whatsoever may violate this page of our confirmation or presumptuously oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Velletri, on the fourth day before the Nones of June.

LXXXVII. To [William], archbishop of Reims—He complains that he releases persons bound by the bishop of Beauvais. (Velletri, June 9.)

[Ibid., 622.]

[Col. 1173A]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the archbishop of Reims, cardinal of Santa Sabina and legate of the Apostolic See, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the prudence of your brotherhood cannot be unaware how greatly, for many reasons, you ought to love and honor more earnestly our venerable brother Ph., bishop of Beauvais, we are exceedingly grieved and troubled that, as we have heard from his complaint, you release, without consulting him, his parishioners whom he binds for their offences [Col. 1173B]; in this matter his authority and honor are gravely diminished. Indeed, as we have learned from his own report, after he had, on your command and advice, subjected the nobleman and count of Clermont to excommunication, and his land to interdict, you at your own discretion granted him the benefit of absolution without any satisfaction, receiving an oath but ordering nothing relevant to satisfaction.

Therefore, the more sincerely we love that bishop in consideration of himself and his people, and freely preserve his honor unimpaired, the less are we willing to endure what redounds to his injury. By apostolic authority we forbid your brotherhood to derogate from his dignity in any respect, or to mitigate the sentences which he has pronounced to his own loss or prejudice [Col. 1173C]. Otherwise, however much we may wish to spare you, as a venerable brother and a great member of the Church, we shall not be able to leave his injury uncorrected.

Given at Velletri, on the fourth day before the Nones of June.

LXXXVIII. He grants the monks of St. Pancras that the sons of those who held the monastery’s churches shall not have those churches by right of inheritance.

(This bull belongs to Lucius III; following Mansi’s *Councils*, we wrongly attributed it to Lucius II. See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXX, under Lucius II, no. 94.)

YEAR 1183.

LXXXIX. He takes under protection the monastery of St. Mary of Miravallis and confirms its property and privileges. (Velletri, January 12.)

[HUGO, *Premonstratensian Annals*, vol. II, Proofs, p. 171.]

[Col. 1173D]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GUILLELMUS, abbot, and the church of St. Mary of Miravallis, and its brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

Those who choose the religious life ought to have apostolic protection at hand, lest an assault of any rash person either turn them back from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of holy religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully grant your just petitions, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid church of St. Mary of Miravallis [Col. 1174A], in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it with the privilege of this writing. First, we decree that the canonical order which is recognized as instituted in that church according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the institution of the Premonstratensian brethren, shall there be observed inviolate for all time.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire, with the Lord’s help, by grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and undiminished to you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following in their own terms [Col. 1174B]:

The very place in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the place of Morinivallis with all its appurtenances, which Peter, bishop of Toul, granted to your church and fortified by the protection of his writing, for you to establish an oratory there; the chapel of the castle of Brisseio, with its offerings and other appurtenances; the parish church of Brisseio, with the village, tithes, offerings, and other appurtenances. The private lands called *Croadas*, adjacent to that place, which the same bishop granted you, extending as far as Morinummons; and from that mountain, over the higher plain and lower slope, as divided by the path descending from the castle and proceeding over the mountain plain as far as the spring that flows down the side of that mountain [Col. 1174C]. Also, the free use of the common pastures, beneficial for animals of every kind, throughout the entire ban of the aforesaid castle, with the approval and assent of Gerard the advocate, on this condition: that if any of your brethren at any time cause loss to someone, they shall restore the loss to the injured party without litigation and without any exaction.

Indeed, of your newly cultivated lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, and of the increase of your animals, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you.

You may also receive into your community clerics or laymen fleeing the world, free and unencumbered, and retain them without any objection. Moreover, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place [Col. 1174D], to leave it without the permission of his abbot; and no one may dare retain one who has departed without letters of authorization from the community. For chrism, holy oil, consecrations of churches, ordinations of clerics who are to be promoted to holy orders, the bringing of an abbot to the episcopal see, or any other ecclesiastical sacraments, no one may dare demand anything from you, whether under pretext of custom or in any other manner. Should anyone presume to act contrary to this, let him know that he will have a share with Gehazi, whose deed he imitates by exacting a shameful payment (4 Kings 5).

In your causes you may also produce brethren suitable to give testimony, and by their testimony, if it is right [Col. 1175A], both repel violence and vindicate justice. Moreover, we decree that the burial place of this establishment shall be free, so that no one may hinder the devotion and final wish of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while preserving the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Further, wishing with paternal concern to provide for your peace and tranquillity, by apostolic authority we forbid anyone within the enclosures of your establishments or granges rashly to commit violence, robbery, or theft; to set fire; or to seize or kill a person.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, or to take away its possessions, or retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved intact, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they have been granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; and let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and at the last judgment be subject to divine vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights to that same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good works and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodinus, bishop of the See of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Vivian, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. [Col. 1175D] I, Laborans, cardinal priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Calixtus. I, Ranerius, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Hubert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, Hyacinthus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Gratian, deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo. I, Gerard, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Albinus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New.

[Col. 1176A] Given at Velletri, through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the second Ides of January, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1182 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

XC. He receives the Church of Saint Denis of Pas into protection and confirms its possessions. (Velletri, January 12.)

*[Collection des Cartulaires*, vol. V, p. 501.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of the Church of Saint Denis of Pas, both present and those canonically to be appointed in future, in perpetuity. . . .

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just [Col. 1176B] petitions; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid Church of Saint Denis of Pas, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods . . . we have judged proper to specify in the following terms: the revenues which you hold from the Chapter of Paris, namely two *modii* and eight *sextarii* of the purer grain from its granary, measured by the royal mina, excepting the seven *modii* called “of the altars”; and, for each canon of your church, as much bread and wine called “of Lent” as is allotted to one of the resident canons of Blessed Mary; the house within the cloister beside your church; and the houses [Col. 1176C] outside the cloister gate, by the postern, which have been assigned to two canons from the gift of Simon of Saint Denis; the mill of Genestai; houses, vineyards, meadows, the rent from Botunvileir, pasture, land, and jurisdiction, with all appurtenances, in the diocese of Meaux; the tithe of Little Nanteuil, the tithe of Vinants, the tithe of Tuiz, and the fief of the tithe of Saint Maximus, which Bulchard of Sanci holds in fief from your church, in the diocese of Paris; the tithe of Alnet and the tithe of Dimiach, which, by the grant of Maurice, bishop of Paris, you possess through the gift of Peter, canon of your church; five solidi from the rent at Argenteuil, and the wine tithe belonging to [Col. 1176D] that same rent; three solidi and four denarii near the borough of Saint Denis; the arable land of Miliac, vineyards, meadows, a house, and the mill situated at Mibreyo, called the Fourth Mill, one half of which was bought for twenty pounds in Parisian money, and the remaining part for sixteen pounds; from the house of Barbedaur, dean of Blessed Mary of Paris, vineyards at Mont Camac, for the lighting of your church; and, from the gift of Richeldis, sister of Simon of Saint Denis, four solidi of annual rent at Saint-Merry. We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever, etc. . . .

Given at Velletri, through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the second Ides of January, in the first indiction, in the year [Col. 1177A] 1182 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

XCI. He receives the Church of Saint Eusebius of Vercelli into protection and confirms the canons’ possessions. (Fragment.) (Velletri, January 16.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IV, 783.]

Given at Velletri, through the hand of Albert, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1182 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate.

XCII. He grants Peter, bishop, and the chapter of Chartres that “the benefices of the Church of Chartres shall henceforth not be granted to others, except to those who promise that they will reside.” (Velletri, January 17.)

[D’ACHERY, *Spicilegium*, folio edition, III, 547.]

[Col. 1177B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother PETER, bishop, and to his beloved sons G., dean, and the chapter of Chartres: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since more is required of him to whom more is entrusted, it is fitting and consonant with reason that those who are honoured above others in your Church should serve it more zealously and devote themselves to its welfare. Moved by this consideration, we have judged it proper to decree by apostolic authority that the benefices of the Church of Chartres shall henceforth not be granted to anyone except those who, according to the [Col. 1177C] ancient and reasonable custom, have promised that they will reside. If, after making this promise, they do not fulfil it, let them be deprived of those benefices. Moreover, by apostolic authority we forbid anyone holding a benefice in another church to be admitted either as a canon of your church or as a parish priest, unless he has relinquished the former benefice and has been released by his own bishop.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no one whatsoever to infringe this page of our constitution or rashly to act against it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

[Col. 1177D] Given at Velletri, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February.

XCIII. He confirms certain churches to John, bishop of Maguelone. (Velletri, January 24.)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, VI, Instruments, 362.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother JOHN, bishop of Maguelone: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has come to us that your bishopric has in large part been laid waste by the incursion of raiders. Since the priests of certain churches belonging to episcopal right have died, you have specially reserved them for yourself, requesting confirmation of them from the Apostolic See. Therefore, favourably assenting to your petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority to your person, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the church of Saint Genesius of Gigean, Saint Andrew of Cucullo, Saint Michael of Mujulan, Saint Michael of Aguzanics, the church of Cazillac, and Saint Peter of Agantic, as you possess them reasonably and without dispute.

Given at Velletri, on the ninth day before the Kalends of February, in the third year of the pontificate.  
[Note: At [Col. 1177], another hand added the words “third year of the pontificate.” Read: “second.”]

XCIV. He deprives the bishop of Catania, having become a suffragan of the archbishop of Monreale, of the power to wear the pallium. (Velletri, February 4.)

[PIRRI, *Sicilia sacra*, I, 532.]

[Col. 1178B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WILLIAM, archbishop of Monreale, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

Lest a dispute arise between the Church of Monreale and the bishop of Catania on account of the pallium, the use of which the bishop of Catania has customarily enjoyed through the indulgence of the Apostolic See, we decree by apostolic sanction and confirm to you and your successors by this present document that, after the death of our venerable brother who is now bishop of Catania, his successor shall not use the pallium.

Given at Velletri, on the second Nones of February, 1184.

XCV. He establishes the monastery of Monreale as an archiepiscopal see. He consecrates Abbot William as archbishop, invests him with the pallium, and declares him metropolitan of the bishopric of Catania. (Velletri, February 5.)

[Ibid., 458.]

[Col. 1178C]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WILLIAM, archbishop of Monreale, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

Although the Lord Jesus Christ, in establishing His Church, gave His disciples authority to bind and loose believers therein, He nevertheless willed that one among them—namely the blessed Apostle Peter—should take precedence, saying: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16). By this He gave all believers to understand that, just as there was one mediator between God and humankind, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2), reconciling things in heaven and things upon earth (Colossians 1), breaking down the dividing wall and making both one (Ephesians 2), so there is in the Church one head of all things from Him and through Him, lest there be any division among the members; through the authority and providence of the one head they are brought back to the one truth of faith and the same [Col. 1179A] religion and worship. This is also shown in the passage where the command given him by our Lord is read, concerning both strengthening his brethren (Luke 22) and feeding the Lord’s sheep (John 21).

From this power which came to blessed Peter through the Lord’s institution, the most holy Roman Church—founded and established through the Lord Jesus Christ by that same blessed Peter—received authority over all Churches, so that whatever its prudence ordained should everywhere be valid and firm. This has likewise been received and observed by all Churches spread throughout the whole world, so that through it dignities have been distributed, and what appeared to pertain to worship has been appointed and ordered for Christ’s faithful and devoted people. From this power given by the Lord to blessed Peter, he and his successors established bishops in diverse regions of the world and divided dignities among the provinces. We also, who have succeeded them at the Lord’s call, though unequal to them in merits, have judged that a metropolitan see should be established at the place called Monreale, for the great benefit of the Christian people.

For when our dearest son in Christ, William, illustrious king of Sicily, burning with the fire of divine charity, had founded a monastery there for the glory of God and the salvation of himself and his parents, and had first offered the site for that purpose to blessed Peter and the Roman Church, by the authority of our predecessor of happy memory, Pope Alexander, and with the assent of our venerable brother Walter, archbishop of Palermo, he rendered it free and exempt from episcopal subjection. Thereupon, devoting royal care to erecting buildings, in a short time he built for the Lord a church through a most worthy administration; he enriched it with very strongly fortified castles and revenues, adorned it with books, sacred vestments, silver, and gold; and at length introduced a multitude of monks of the Cava order. He raised this place so greatly in buildings and other resources that no comparable work by any king has existed from ancient days, so as to bring into amazement persons to whom report alone could bring knowledge of what had been done.

Then, thirsting for this good work as a stag for fountains of water, and reckoning little whatever he had done in longing for eternal things [Col. 1179D]—as Wisdom says: “Those who eat me shall still hunger, and those who drink me shall still thirst” (Ecclesiasticus 24)—he earnestly petitioned our aforesaid predecessor, ourselves, and our brethren to endow that same place with metropolitan dignity. This was especially appropriate because he had begun, and planned further, to gather people there who might, from that side, furnish an impregnable defence to the whole land against the assaults of all enemies.

Now, after substantial deliberation with our brethren, and considering the common benefit hoped for from the growth of that place, we have judged that we should not refuse his desire and petition.
