Otherwise, where he had proved most generous from his own treasury and estates, we might seem reluctant in those matters which concern the office of the apostolate laid upon us by God; and his great devotion and ours might be diminished by our delay, whereas by our zeal for what is good it was fitting that it should be stirred toward something better. In view of his desire, it seemed no small consideration that, although it was unusual for two metropolitan sees to exist so near one another, this new establishment would in no way further diminish anyone’s right, since the monastery itself had already been exempted by archbishops and bishops, both in itself and in all its places, from every episcopal jurisdiction, and endowed with complete liberty in all things, so that it was subject to no archbishop or bishop, but only to the Roman pontiff.

Therefore we consecrate you, our venerable brother in Christ William, as archbishop of that same [Col. 1180B] place by our hands, as it were by the hands of blessed Peter, and decree that you be adorned with the dignity of the pallium. Receiving, moreover, under the safeguard of apostolic protection and confirming by our privilege—which has been made—the church founded by royal generosity in honour of the Lord our God and in memory of the blessed Virgin Mary, we decree first of all that the monastic order known to have been established in that place according to the fear of God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the observances of the monastery of Cava, shall be inviolably observed there for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that same church now reasonably possesses through the gift of the aforesaid king and of any others, or may in future acquire through grants of pontiffs, gifts of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to that church forever. Among these we have judged it proper expressly to designate the bishopric of Catania, which, by the common counsel of our brethren and at the repeated request of the aforesaid king, we establish to be subject in perpetuity, by metropolitan right, to you and your successors as its proper archbishops. We also confirm by apostolic authority to you and your successors the episcopal jurisdiction and all that you hold in the places written below through the grants of our brethren and fellow bishops, and decree that they shall remain firm and unimpaired forever:

Through the grant of our venerable brother Walter, archbishop of Palermo, with the will, counsel, and assent of all his canons, and also with royal approval: the whole parish and diocese of the castle of Corleone, together with the monastery of Saint Mary Magdalene and other churches, with tithes and other rights which the Church of Palermo had customarily received from the barons and other inhabitants of that castle and its dependencies, and with all episcopal jurisdiction which it appeared to possess in that parish and diocese; furthermore, the church of Saint Sylvester, formerly under the dominion and proper jurisdiction of the Church of Palermo, which, because it was very near your church and much more useful to it than to the Church of Palermo, the aforesaid archbishop, [Col. 1181A] as his authentic instrument states, freely and voluntarily transferred to that same church with the counsel and consent of all his brethren, together with all its estates, villeins, possessions, and all his rights.

Through the grant of Nicholas of good memory, formerly archbishop of Messina, with the consent of his whole chapter: all episcopal right which the Church of Messina ought to have in the monastery and all its dependencies, which Margaret, mother of the king of illustrious memory, once glorious queen, had built through her devotion at the place called Monachium, in the diocese of Messina, in honour of God and in memory of the blessed ever-Virgin Mary; and which she obtained through the said archbishop as free and exempt from every claim and jurisdiction of the Church of Messina.

Through the grant of Thomas, archbishop of Reggio, with the common consent of his chapter: the whole episcopal right, and whatever else belonged to the Church of Reggio, in the monastery of Saint Saviour of Martello, built by John Calomenus, formerly the royal chamberlain; and in the nunnery of Saint John Exocalnia, outside the walls of the city of Reggio, with the cells, obediences, possessions, estates, and dependencies of those monasteries, as is contained in the privilege of the aforesaid archbishop.

Through the grant of Bartholomew, bishop of Agrigento, with the assent of his chapter: both the parish and diocese, and the entire episcopal jurisdiction, with all tithes and other rights and revenues which the Church of Agrigento received from the barons and other inhabitants of the castle of Battalazio and its dependencies, and of the hamlet of Busachini; likewise all tithes and other revenues which the Church of Agrigento held from the castle of Corleone and its dependencies, as is shown in the bishop’s document.

Through the grant of Matthew, bishop of Mazara: the parish, diocese, episcopal jurisdiction, all tithes, and other revenues which the Church of Mazara had in the township of Iato and the township of Calatrasi, with all their dependencies, as is more clearly contained in the document of the aforesaid bishop.

Through the grant of R., bishop of Anglona, with the common assent of his chapter: in the monastery of Carboni, with its cells, obediences, and possessions, the whole episcopal [Col. 1181D] jurisdiction and whatever else the Church of Anglona possessed therein, as is expressly recorded in that bishop’s document.

Through the grant of the bishop of Bisignano, with the assent of his chapter: the church of Saint Mary of Maccla, with episcopal jurisdiction and all its obediences and dependencies, as is shown in the privilege of that bishop; likewise the church of Saint Martin, built on land belonging to the church by Peter Indulfus, which Peter himself offered to that same church together with its estates, possessions, and dependencies.

Furthermore, from the generosity of the Apostolic See we grant your brotherhood the pallium, namely the fullness of the pontifical office. You are to use it within your church in the celebration of the solemnities of Mass on the following days: the Nativity of the Lord; the feast of Saint Stephen; the Octave of the Lord’s Nativity; the Epiphany; the Hypopante; Palm Sunday; the Lord’s Supper; Holy Saturday; Easter and the two following days; the Assumption; Pentecost; the three feasts of Mary, Mother of God and Virgin; the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; the commemoration of All Saints; the solemnities of all the apostles; the principal feasts of your church; dedications of churches; consecrations of bishops; ordinations of clerics; and the anniversary of your consecration.

Take care, therefore, that the honour of this garment is preserved by the modest vigour of your conduct, so that the adornments of your morals may correspond to it; and that, with God as author, you may be more conspicuous through good deeds than through such an ornament. You whom the office of pastoral care binds should show love to the brethren, so that, grounded in the virtue of humility, you may neither be elated by prosperity nor wearied by adversity. Let even adversaries be united to you in affection according to the Lord’s command; so far as it depends upon you, have peace with all, and strive to bring the discordant back to peace. Let the breastplate of judgment shine upon your breast, joined with the shoulder-piece of reason; and proceed before God and men in such a way that you provide an example of virtue to the Lord’s flock entrusted to you, and conduct yourself in deed and word so that, seeing your good works, they may glorify our Father who is in heaven (Matthew 5), and rejoice that they have such [Col. 1182C] a ruler, through whom they may be instructed in faith and stirred up to good works.

Upon the death of you or any of your successors, let no one be set over that place by any artifice of fraud or violence, except one whom the monks of that place, or the greater part of the sounder counsel from among that same community, if a suitable person is found there, believe should be elected according to God and the canonical sanctions. But if a suitable man cannot be found there, a monk from elsewhere shall be chosen by the brethren of that place, and he shall indeed use the regular food and clothing.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved intact, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they have been granted. Indeed, as a token of his devotion and to show that the same church was subject only to the Roman pontiff, the above-named son of ours, the king, when he began to found it under the name of a monastery, established an annual payment of one hundred *tarenos* to the Roman pontiff. If in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, LUCIUS, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and the See of Santa Rufina. [Col. 1183A] I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Vivian, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Saint Calixtus. I, Raynerius, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Ubertus, cardinal priest of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, Pandulfus, cardinal priest of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Hyacinthus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary [Col. 1183B] in Cosmedin. I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo. I, Gerard, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Goffredus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Albinus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New.

Given at Velletri, through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest [Col. 1183C] and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of February, in the first indiction, in the year 1182 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

XCVI. He orders the bishops of Cefalù and Patti to obey Richard, archbishop of Messina. (Velletri, February 9.)

[PIRRI, *Sicilia sacra*, I, 398.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, the bishops of Cefalù and Patti, and to his beloved sons, the abbots and prelates of other Churches subject by metropolitan right to the Church of Messina: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We believe that it has not escaped any of you that the providence of the heavenly dispensation has willed that there be ranks in the Church and has established distinct orders, so that, while inferiors show reverence to superiors and superiors bestow love upon inferiors, true concord may arise and the administration of each office may be rightly carried out. Hence the Apostle says: “Whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Romans 13). Therefore, by apostolic letters we command and enjoin you to show due obedience and reverence to our venerable brother Richard, your archbishop; whatever he shall enjoin upon you according to God, receive humbly without opposition and observe steadfastly. Thus you may be commended for virtue and teach those subject to you by example how superiors ought to be honoured; [Col. 1184A] for it is just and consonant with canonical sanction that one who is himself [lacuna] set over others should himself render the reverence which he demands.

Given at Velletri, on the fifth Ides of February.

XCVII. He receives the Church of Saint Stephen of Prato into protection and confirms its goods and rights. (Velletri, February 12.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 334.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, PLEBANUS, provost of the Church of Saint Stephen of Prato, and his brethren, both present and those canonically to be appointed in future, in perpetuity.

Equity and the order of reason require that just petitions be granted their effect, especially when piety supports the petitioners’ will and truth does not abandon it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your petitions; and, following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Innocent of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid Church of Saint Stephen, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, with the Lord’s favour, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these [Col. 1184C] we have judged it proper to specify the following by their proper names:

The church of Saint Mary in the Castle with its dependencies; the church of the Holy Trinity with its dependencies; the church of Saint Peter at the Fuya Gate with its dependencies; the church of Saint Vincent; the church of Saint James; the church of Saint Thomas with its dependencies; the church of Saint Mark with its dependencies; the church of Saint Saviour with its dependencies; the church of Saint Mary of Ribaldo with its dependencies; the church of Saint Martin with its dependencies; the monastery of Saint Martin of Cojano with its dependencies; the right which you have in the monastery of Saint Fabian; the church of Saint Bartholomew of Cojano with its dependencies; the church of Saint Lucy with its dependencies; the church of Saint Peter [Col. 1184D] of Figline with its dependencies; the right which you have in the church of Saint Michael of Cerreto; the right which you have in the church of Saint Peter of the Island; the right which you have in the church of Saint Martin of Sorriana; the right which you have in the church of Fabio; and the right which you have in the church of Saint John of Pistoia.

By this present privilege we also decree that no one may receive your parishioners for divine offices as long as they have been condemned by you by sentence of excommunication or interdict. We further decree that, within the parish of that same church, no person whatsoever may, against your will and objection, build a church or inflict any injury upon you in this matter, saving, however, the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. We grant you the tithes, without anyone’s opposition, of those who belong to your church by parochial right. We also prohibit anyone from daring to pronounce a sentence of interdict or excommunication against you or your church without just and reasonable cause. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordinations of clerics to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide these to you freely and without any improper exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic prelate you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what you request. Furthermore, we confirm to you and your church the burial-right of that place [Col. 1185B] for the use of those reckoned as your parishioners, provided that, if they choose burial in a religious church, your canonical share of the testament shall be reserved. We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and the See of Santa Rufina. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Vivian, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. [Col. 1185C] I, Ranerius, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Calixtus. I, Pandulfus, cardinal priest of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Jacob, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo. I, Gerard, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Goffredus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Albinus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New.

[Col. 1185D] Given at Velletri, through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eleventh Ides of February, in the first indiction, in the year 1183 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

XCVIII. He confirms the settlement between the monasteries of Kaltenborn and Rode. (Velletri, February 25.)

[SCHOETTGEN and KREYSIG, *Diplomatarium*, II, 702.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the provost of Kaltenborn: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Matters known to have come into dispute and to have been settled by an amicable agreement ought to be recorded in writing and strengthened by apostolic protection, lest they relapse into the difficulty of renewed contention. It has indeed come to us that between the Church of Kaltenborn, in which you administer the office of provost, and the Church of Rode, a certain controversy had formerly been long debated. Our venerable brother Wichmann, archbishop of Magdeburg, and the beloved son, bishop-elect of Halberstadt, settled it with the consent of the parties, on these terms: the provost of Rode, with the assent of his canons, assigned to your church six and a half *mansi* situated at Elvenstedt, one situated at Amalungesdorf, and two plots at Blackeneim yielding two solidi, on the condition that the complaint concerning the aforesaid estates should be settled forever. We therefore confirm this settlement by apostolic authority, as it was canonically made and accepted by both parties, and strengthen it by the page and protection of this present writing.

Moreover, certain estates—namely, at Gerendorf, two *mansi* yielding thirty solidi; at Gerbenstedt, three *mansi* yielding two talents and six solidi; and at Gorditz, one *mansus* yielding fourteen solidi—which they bought from canons of the Church of Merseburg; and certain estates which they received in exchange from our dearest son in Christ Frederick, illustrious emperor of the Romans, namely at Vinkele, yielding ten talents and ten solidi; at Wulfferstede, five talents and ten solidi; and at [Col. 1186C] Warrenstede, four talents. We have judged that all these should be confirmed by apostolic authority to the aforesaid Church of Kaltenborn, which it possesses peacefully and without dispute, and fortified by the text of this present writing. We decree that no one may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly act against it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His holy apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Velletri, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March.

XCIX. Privilege for the monastery of Wilbacensis. (Velletri, February 27.)

[SCHATEN, *Annales Paderbornenses*, I, 858.]

[Col. 1186D]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HENRY, abbot, and to the nuns of the monastery of Wilboldessen, both present and those who shall profess the monastic life in future, in perpetuity.

To grant effect to just requests is required alike by the force of equity and the order of reason, especially when piety supports the petitioners’ will and truth does not abandon it. Therefore, beloved daughter in the Lord, we graciously assent to your petitions; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your monastery, in which you are dedicated to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order, which is acknowledged to have been established in that monastery according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, shall be inviolably observed there for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods the monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names:

Wilbodesson, Watervelde, Trevere, Atride, Ossenthorp, Hemelhusen, Rocethehusen, Northen, Wellethe, Ilrenhusen; likewise Northen, Histniche, Wetere, Hathesbatthessen, Volmarsen, Guntersen, [Col. 1187B] Adenem, Othehem, Honrothem, Overethe; the manor at Suthem and the tithe over that same village; Esnethe Gheveburche, Limgo, Winnethe; the tithe at Eddessen, the tithe at Hatheburgusen, the tithe at Richersen, the tithe at Harderenssen; Sundram at Hornen; a house within the walls of the city of Patherburn and five building-plots; and, near the city, three holdings; the tithe of all our newly cleared lands and all tithes within the bounds of your tithe-districts.

When a general interdict has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding those excommunicated and under interdict, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. We likewise grant that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict—without prejudice, nevertheless, to the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. On the death of you, the present abbess of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any deceitful contrivance or violence, except one whom the sisters, by common consent, or the sounder part of the council, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of St. Benedict.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever to disturb the aforesaid church, to take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole, to be of every benefit for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter knowingly attempts rashly to violate this page of our decree, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not correct that presumption by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor; let such a one know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let such a one be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and let such a one be subject, at the last judgment, to stern vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that [Col. 1188A] they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Theodinus, bishop of the see of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, Henry, bishop of Albano.  
I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.  
I, Vivian, cardinal priest of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill.  
I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St. Mary across the Tiber.  
I, Ranerius, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius.

[Col. 1188B] Given at Velletri, by the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of March [27 February], in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1183, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Lucius III.

## C. He receives the monastery of St. Lawrence of Aversa under protection and confirms its goods and rights. (Velletri, 18 March.)

[MARGARINI, *Bullar. Casin.*, II, 200.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BONOHOMINI, abbot of the monastery of St. Lawrence of Aversa, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: forever.

[Col. 1188C] To grant effect to just requests is required alike by the force of equity and the order of reason, especially when piety supports the petitioners’ wishes and truth does not abandon them.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, Urban and Alexander, Roman pontiffs, the aforesaid monastery—which belongs especially to the right of blessed Peter and in which you are dedicated to divine service—and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order which is acknowledged to have been established in that monastery according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict shall be inviolably observed there for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, through the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. We likewise confirm by apostolic authority to you and to that monastery all churches, lands, and towns which the monastery reasonably possesses. We utterly forbid public masses to be celebrated in that monastery by any bishop, stations to be held, or processions conducted, without the consent of the abbot or brethren, lest [Col. 1189A] any occasion for secular gatherings be afforded in the retreats of God’s servants. Certainly, no one shall presume to exact or extort tithes from you on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or upon the increase of your animals. Nor may any bishop place the monastery itself or its cells under interdict, or excommunicate the monks. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordination of clerics and monks belonging to the monastery who are to be promoted to holy orders, from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. We forbid any bishop to excommunicate or suspend from office, or summon to synod, the chaplains or clerics serving the monastery itself or its cells.

Furthermore, by reason of the special freedom of that monastery, which is known to adhere directly, without intermediary, to the Roman Church; and in honor and reverence of the most glorious martyr Lawrence, whose relics are deposited there, we grant to you and your successors, without anyone’s opposition, the use of the mitre anywhere in the celebration of divine offices, and the daily use of the ring. We likewise grant that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict—without prejudice, nevertheless, to the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. On the death [Col. 1189C] of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any deceitful contrivance or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. The elected person shall come to the Roman pontiff to receive blessing.

Therefore, most beloved sons in Christ, you ought diligently to devote yourselves to the ordinances of regular discipline, so that, the freer you are from secular tumults, the more earnestly you may strive to please God with all the powers of mind and soul. We therefore decree, etc. If anyone therefore, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Theodinus, bishop of the see of Porto and St. Rufina.  
I, Henry, bishop of Albano.  
I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina.  
I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St. Susanna.  
I, Vivian, cardinal priest of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill.  
I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Calixtus.  
I, Rainerius, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius.  
I, Ubertus . . . [lacuna]

Given at Velletri, by the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April [18 March], in the first indiction, in the year [Col. 1190A] of the Lord’s Incarnation 1182, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

## CI. At the request of Bishop Rainald, he receives the Church of Isernia under protection and confirms its goods. (Velletri, 20 March.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VI, 296.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother RAINALD, bishop of Isernia, and to his successors to be appointed in perpetuity.

Set, by the Lord’s ordering, in the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, we ought to love with brotherly charity our brothers and fellow bishops, whether near or far, and preserve to the churches in which they are known to serve the Lord their rights. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, we graciously assent to your just petitions, and, following the example of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the Church of Isernia, over which by God’s authority you are known to preside, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and whatever goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. [Col. 1190C] Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names:

The bounds and limits of your bishopric, which you are now known to possess peaceably: beginning at the river Volturno near its confluence with the river Sesti; extending through the castle of Mastralis, the castle of Zurlani, the castle of Capriata, and the castle of Fossaecaeca; through the uplands, the castle of Gualdo, Felesti, the castle of Pizuti, the castle of Pestorano, and the castle of Carpinone with St. Mark; the castle of Sexano with St. Benedict; and, ascending by Mount Rosini, the castle of Periculo, the castle of Monte Negro, the castle of Rocca Siconis, and the castle of Forunli; then extending through the land of St. Vincent and by Mount Alze to Portella, where the Melerinum rises; [Col. 1190D] thence stretching to the boundary of the lands, woods, and mountains of the monastery of St. Benedict; again extending along the borders of the territory, woods, and mountains of the aforesaid monastery, by the summit of Mount Aquilo and Sambuculi as far as the market of St. Martin; by the summit of Mount Cesino; stretching to the ford of Francis on the river Sesti itself; and descending along the river Volturno, which is the first boundary.

At Sesto, the parish church of St. Eustace; at Mastralis, the parish church of St. John; at Torcino, the parish church of St. Mary; at Capriata, the parish church of St. Mary; at Capperellis, the parish church of St. John; at Camposacco, the parish church of St. John; at Monte Odonis, the parish church of St. Michael; at Gualdo, the parish church of St. Michael; at Falesto, the parish church [Col. 1191A] of St. Mary; at Longono, the parish church of St. Bartholomew; at St. Agapito, the parish church of St. Nicholas; at Riperta, the parish church of the Savior; at Pizzuto, the parish church of St. Agatha; at Pestorano, the parish church of St. Mary; at Carpinone, the parish church of St. Mary; at Sexana, the parish church of St. Mary; at Fara, the parish church of St. Nicholas; at Monte Negro, the parish church of St. Mary; at Rocca Siconis, the parish church of St. Leonard; at Forulo, the parish church of St. Blaise; at Conestellis, the parish church of St. Lawrence; at Rocca Beraldi, the parish church of St. Nicander; at Armana, the parish church of the Holy Cross; at Conveula, the parish church of St. Michael; at Meronda, the parish church of St. Nicholas; at Periculo, the parish church of St. Mary; at Ovano, the parish church of St. Mary; at Saxo, the parish church of St. Lawrence; at Valle Jampelli, the parish church of St. Mary; at Macchia, the parish church of St. Nicholas; at Ravindola, the parish church of St. Michael; at Venafro, [Col. 1191B] the parish church of St. Mary with its appurtenances; at Rocca Venefri, the church of the Holy Cross; at Rocca Peperoli, the church of St. Mary; at Monte Aquilo, the parish church of St. Mary; at Valle St. Locheri, the parish church of St. Mary; at Cerasolo, the parish church of St. Christopher; at Casali, the parish church of St. John; in the territory of Venafro, the churches of St. Barbara, St. Nicander, and the Holy Cross; at Peperolo, the churches of St. George and St. Nazarius; at Camposacco, the church of St. Andrew; at Monte Rodono, the church of St. Nazarius; at Macchia, the church of St. Mary; at Isernia, the churches of St. Vitus and St. Agapitus, and the church of the Savior in the territory of Exano; and the monastery of St. Mary situated within the walls of the city of Isernia itself; in the territory of Longana, the churches of the Holy Sepulchre and St. [Col. 1191C] Erasmus; at St. Agapito, the church of St. Helena; at Gualdo, the church of St. Nicholas; at Pizzuti, the churches of St. Lawrence and St. Peter; at Carpinone, the churches of St. Maurus and St. Romanus; at Sexanti, the churches of St. Michael and St. Benedict; at Miranda, the church of St. Michael; at Forulo, the churches of St. Peter, St. Onuphrius, and St. Pancras; at Monte Aquilo, the church of St. Paul with its three chapels and their appurtenances.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid Church of Isernia, to take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole, to be of every benefit for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the due reverence owed to the bishop of Capua. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, etc.

## CII. Privilege for the abbey of St. Ghislain. (Velletri, 4 April.)

[REIFFENBERG, *Monuments*, VIII, 393.]

[Col. 1192B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot of the monastery of St. Ghislain and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: forever.

To grant effect to just requests is required alike by the force of equity and the order of reason, especially when piety supports the petitioners’ wishes and truth is not abandoned. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are dedicated to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic [Col. 1192C] order which is acknowledged to have been established in that place according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict shall be inviolably observed there for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, God being favorable, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; in the village of Logia (Slogia), the manor, demesne, and a ploughland [*carrucata*] of arable land with its curtilages, together with every tithe, both of that land itself and of all the fiefs of the same village; the tithes which you have in the lands of St. Peter; the tithe of the tithe [from the vineyard] of Hugh; the hamlet called Ultramontes with its appurtenances, and the church of that place with its dependencies, Harminiac and Beuweniis; the tithe from the manor and lands of St. Landolin; at Novella, one ploughland of arable land; a fourth part of the village of Blelgiis, with its appurtenances and jurisdiction; in the village called Wamia, the allod of Gonter and his son Aegidius of Cing; the land of Hugh of Aengien, with other lands, curtilages, rents, meadows, and woods; part of the village of Durni, with its village and jurisdiction; the village of Waherias and its demesne manor, free from every advocacy and tithe; [Col. 1193A] the church which you possess from the church of St. Gaugeric for an annual rent of one hundred solidi in the currency of Cambrai; in the village of Chavren, the demesne manor, with lands, meadows, woods, waters, curtilages, and a portion of the tithe free from every lordship and divided from the other portions; in the village called Harcheis, three fertons by the weight of Flanders, which the church of Aulne owes for the land of Heluidis; at Resbaco, the demesne manor and three parts of the whole allod, in lands, woods, waters, meadows, rents, and jurisdiction; at Roncherias, six marks of silver by the weight of Cologne, which the church of Cambron owes as an annual rent for the lands of that place; and the altar with the chapel of Herieriponte; the altar of Cella, with its dependencies Hornuth and Quaternione; the church of Durno, with its dependencies Blelgiis, Hercana, Astices, and Slogio; the church of Villari, with its dependencies Harminiaco and Bewengiis; the church of Wama, with its dependencies Wamiolo and Reseniis; Bassecles with its appurtenances; Altregia, with the chapel of the village, with all its appurtenances, free from every exaction except the bishop’s procuration; at Imbrechies, the manor and demesne lands with meadows and waters, two parts of the common allod free from every exaction; the altar of Bosut, free from the *personatus* [parochial benefice] and every exaction, save an annual payment of six denarii for the bishop’s procuration; [Col. 1193C] the altar of Baldurno with its dependency Willeroth, free from every exaction save an annual payment of three solidi for the bishop’s procuration; the altars of Lingniis and Tumaide; the chapel of Rameniis, free from the *personatus* and every exaction except the bishop’s procurations; Abechias with its dependencies Belchi, Molembois, Popiola, Petrewez, and its other dependencies; likewise the altars granted to you by Nicholas, bishop of Cambrai of good memory, and confirmed by his privileges; Harchies with its dependencies Grandiecclesia and Stambrusia, and the chapel of Equi Campo; the altar of Blathum, free and without a *personatus*; the chapel of Wieres, free except for a payment of twelve denarii termed *sonegium*; the altar of Tulin with its dependencies Hainin; the altar of Huncheniis; the altar of Hersella; the altar [Col. 1193D] of Rascengien; the altar of Humberges; the altar of Goi with land and its appurtenances; the altar of Longiis with its dependencies Dolciis (Doulzies) and the chapel of Squeri; the chapel of Delfait (Defait, Defayt) and the chapel of Herieriponte, free from every exaction and *personatus*; in the village of Alemannis, the demesne manor and the tithe of that manor and of the land belonging to that same village, in lands, vineyards, meadows, woods; everything which St. Ghislain justly and peacefully possesses in the district of Soissons; the manor and demesne lands at Altregium, and portions of the common allod in lands, waters, meadows, woods, and rents, free from every exaction or advocacy; the village of Bassecles with all its appurtenances, and the administration of that village granted in alms to your monastery.

[Col. 1194A] Certainly, no one shall presume to exact or extort tithes from you on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or upon the increase of your animals. You may also receive into your conversion, and retain without opposition, clerics or laypersons who have fled the world and are free and absolved. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding those excommunicated and under interdict, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. We likewise decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless perhaps they are excommunicated or under interdict—without prejudice, nevertheless, to the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. On the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any deceitful contrivance or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. We ratify the ancient customs, liberties, and immunities granted to that monastery and observed until now, and decree that they shall remain unimpaired in future times. Moreover, we prohibit anyone from daring to pronounce against you or your churches a sentence of excommunication or interdict without manifest and reasonable cause.

[Col. 1194C] We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, to take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole, to be of every benefit for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter knowingly attempts rashly to violate this page of our decree, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not correct that offense by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor; let such a one know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let such a one be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and let such a one be subject, at the last judgment, to stern vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

## CIII. He confirms the privileges of the brethren of the military Order of the Temple of Jerusalem. (Velletri, 28 April.)

[RYMER, *Foedera*, etc., I, p. 37.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ARNALD, master of the religious military Order of the Temple situated at Jerusalem, and his brethren, present and future: forever.

[Col. 1195C] “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change nor shadow of turning” (James 1:17). Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we praise almighty God concerning you and for you, because throughout the whole world your religious order and venerable institution are proclaimed (Romans 1:8). For whereas by nature you were children of wrath (Ephesians 2:8) and devoted to the pleasures of the world, now, through the grace breathed forth by the Gospel, having become hearers who are not deaf, you have left behind worldly pomp and private possessions; you have also abandoned the broad road which leads to death, and humbly chosen the arduous way which leads to life (Matthew 7:13–14). To demonstrate that you are specially numbered among those in God’s service, you continually bear upon your breast the sign of the life-giving cross (2 Corinthians 4:10).

To this is added that, like true Israelites and most well-trained warriors in the divine contest, kindled by the flame of true charity, you fulfill in deeds the Gospel saying: “No one has greater love than this: that he lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). Hence, since you do not fear to obey the voice of the supreme Shepherd by laying down your lives for your brethren (1 John 3:16), defending them from the assaults of pagans, and since you are called soldiers, you have been appointed by the Lord defenders of the Catholic Church and assailants of Christ’s enemies.

Although your zeal and praiseworthy devotion [Col. 1196A] labor with all heart and mind in so sacred a work, nevertheless we exhort your entire community in the Lord; and, by the authority of God and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we enjoin upon you and your servants, for the remission of sins, that you labor fearlessly, invoking Christ’s name, to defend the Catholic Church and to rescue from pagan pollution that Church which is under pagan tyranny, by fighting the enemies of the cross.

Moreover, whatever you take from their spoils, you may confidently apply to your own uses; and we forbid anyone to compel you, against your will, to give any person a portion of it. We decree that the House or Temple in which you are gathered for the praise and glory of God, for the defense of his faithful people, and for the liberation of God’s Church, together with all possessions and goods which it is known lawfully to possess now or may acquire hereafter by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favor, shall remain for all future time under the guardianship and protection of the Apostolic See. By this present decree we also establish that the religious life instituted in your house there through divine inspiration shall be inviolably observed, and that the brethren serving almighty God there shall live chastely and without private property; proving their profession in word and conduct, they shall in all things and through all things be subject and obedient to their master or to those whom he has commanded.

[Col. 1196C] Moreover, just as that house itself deserved to be the source and origin of your sacred institution and order, so it shall likewise be held for ever as the head and mother-house of all places belonging to it. Further, we order that, upon your death, beloved son Arnalde in the Lord, or the death of any of your successors, no one shall be set over the brethren of that house except a person both military and religious who has professed the habit of your way of life; nor shall the person to be set over them be elected by anyone other than all the brethren gathered together, or the sounder and purer part of them.

Furthermore, it shall not be lawful for any ecclesiastical or secular person to violate or diminish the customs jointly established by the master and brethren for the observance of your religious order and office. Nor may those same customs, at any time observed and confirmed by you in writing, be altered except by the master, with the consent, however, of the sounder part of the chapter. We forbid and utterly prohibit any ecclesiastical or secular person from daring to demand from the master and brethren of that house the fealties, homages, oaths, or other securities customary among secular persons. But know this: just as your sacred institution and religious military order have been established by divine providence, so it is likewise not fitting for you to hasten away to another place under the pretext of a more religious life. For God, who is unchangeable and eternal, does not approve fickle hearts; rather, he wishes a sacred purpose once undertaken to be carried through to the end of its proper work.

[Col. 1197A] How many and how great were those who, beneath a military belt and cloak, pleased the Lord of earthly empire and left behind an everlasting memorial of themselves? How many and how great, standing in arms of war, fought bravely in their own times for God’s covenant and the defense of their fathers’ laws, and, consecrating their hands to the Lord in the blood of unbelievers, attained after the toils of war the prize of eternal life? See, therefore, to your calling, brethren both knights and servants; and, in the Apostle’s words, let each of you remain in the calling in which he was called. We therefore command that your brethren, once devoted and received into your sacred fellowship, after making their profession in your military order and assuming the habit of religion, shall have no permission to return to the world. Nor may any of them, after making profession, once taking up the Lord’s cross and assuming the habit of your profession, cast it off or transfer to another place—or even to a monastery—under the pretext of a stricter or looser religious life, against the will or without the knowledge of the brethren or of whoever is master. Nor shall any ecclesiastical or secular person have permission to receive or retain them.

Certainly, no one shall presume to exact or extort tithes from you on the produce of your lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. [Col. 1197C] Furthermore, we confirm for you by apostolic authority the tithes which you are able to hold, by the advice and consent of bishops, from the hand of clerics or laypersons, and those which you acquire with the consent of bishops and their clerics.

That nothing may be lacking to you for fullness of salvation and the care of your souls, and that ecclesiastical sacraments and divine offices may be supplied more conveniently to your sacred fellowship, we likewise establish that you may receive honorable clerics and priests, ordained according to God, so far as you know, who come to you from wherever they may be, and retain them with you both in your principal house and in obediences and places subject to it; provided that, if they are from nearby, you seek them from their own bishops, and that they are not bound to any other profession or order. But if the bishops should perhaps refuse to grant them to you, you shall nevertheless have authority from the Holy Roman Church to receive and retain them. If any of these, after making profession, prove to be disturbers of your religious order or house, or otherwise useless, you may remove them with the sounder part of the chapter, grant them permission to transfer to another order in which they wish to live according to God, and appoint other suitable persons in their place. These too shall be tested in your fellowship for the space of one year. If, in that manner, their conduct [Col. 1198A] requires it and they are found suitable for your service, then at last they shall make profession to live regularly and obey their master; provided, nevertheless, that they share the same food, clothing, and bedding with you, except that they shall wear closed garments. Nor may they rashly involve themselves in the chapter or in the administration of your house, except insofar as you assign them. They shall have the care of souls only so far as you require of them. Moreover, they shall be subject to no person outside your chapter, and shall render obedience, according to the statutes of your order, to you, beloved son Arnalde in the Lord, and to your successors, as to their master and superior.

[Col. 1198B] You shall receive the consecrations of altars or churches, the ordinations of clerics to be promoted to holy orders, and the other ecclesiastical sacraments from the diocesan bishops, provided that they are Catholic, enjoy the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, and are willing to confer these upon you freely and without any improper exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whatever Catholic bishops you prefer, who, supported of course by our authority, shall grant what is requested. We prohibit clerics from preaching for money or gain, and you from sending them to preach for such a reason, unless perhaps the Master of the Temple for the time being determines, for definite reasons, that this ought to be done.

If at any time deserted places are bestowed upon the same venerable house by someone in pious devotion, you may [Col. 1198C] build villages there and construct churches and cemeteries for the use of the people dwelling there, provided that there is no abbey or community of religious persons in that neighborhood which could thereby be disturbed. But when cultivated lands are conferred upon you under any just title, you shall have the power and permission to build oratories there and establish cemeteries for the use of travellers and only of those who belong to your table. For it is unseemly, and close to perilous for souls, for religious brethren, on the pretext of going to church, to mingle with crowds of men and gatherings of women.

Moreover, all who are received into your community shall promise stability of place, conversion of morals, and that they will serve as soldiers of the Lord [Col. 1198D] for the days of their life under obedience to the Master of the Temple, by placing upon the altar a written document containing these matters. We therefore decree that the collectors of your fraternities or alms-collections shall stand under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, without prejudice to the right of their lords, and shall have peace throughout the lands in which they are found. Likewise, we enact that whoever has been received into your fraternity, if the church to which he belongs should be prohibited from divine offices and it happens that he dies, shall not be denied ecclesiastical burial, unless he is excommunicated or individually placed under interdict.

Furthermore, if any of your brethren sent by you to receive these fraternities or collections come to any city, castle, or village, [Col. 1199A] and that place happens to be under interdict from divine offices, then, out of reverence for almighty God and for the joyfulness of their arrival, the churches shall be opened once a year and, with excommunicated persons excluded, divine offices shall be celebrated there. We also establish that no bishop may promulgate a sentence of interdict or excommunication in churches subject to you by either law. Nevertheless, if a general interdict has been pronounced in those places, you may celebrate the divine offices with excommunicated persons and those individually interdicted excluded, behind closed doors and without ringing bells.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we decree that, wherever you happen to come, you may receive penance, anointing, or any other ecclesiastical sacraments [Col. 1199B] from honorable and Catholic priests, lest anything perhaps be lacking to you in receiving spiritual benefits. And because we are all one in Christ and there is no distinction of persons before God, we also wish your household and servants to share both in the remission of sins and in every other beneficence and apostolic blessing granted to you.

Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted rashly to disturb the aforesaid place, or take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them with any vexations; rather, let all be preserved intact for your uses and those of the other faithful of God, to be wholly beneficial, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See. [Col. 1199C] If anyone, knowing this text of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends for his offense by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But those who observe these provisions shall obtain the blessing and grace of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodinus, bishop of the See of Porto and Santa Rufina. [Col. 1199D] I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St Susanna. I, Rainerius, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints John and Paul, the title of Pammachius. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St Mary across the Tiber, the title of Callistus. I, Ubertus, priest-cardinal of the title of St Lawrence in Damaso. I, Pandulphus, priest-cardinal of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, James, deacon-cardinal of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Ardicio, deacon-cardinal of St Theodore. [Col. 1200A] I, Bobo, deacon-cardinal of St Angelo. I, Gerard, deacon-cardinal, etc. I, Octavian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Soffredus, deacon-cardinal of St Mary in Via Lata. I, Albinus, cardinal of St Mary Nova.

Given at Velletri, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 28 April, in the first indiction, in the year 1183 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

(With a lead seal suspended from red silk threads.)

### CIV. He receives the Church of St Peter of Regensburg into protection and confirms its privileges and possessions. (Velletri, 30 April.)

[RIED, *Codex diplomaticus Ratisponensis*, I, 260.]

[Col. 1200B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons RAPOTO, dean of the Church of Regensburg, and his brethren, present and future, canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

Whenever something is requested of us which is recognized as suitable to religion and integrity, it is fitting for us willingly to grant it and to accord an appropriate effect to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Eugenius of happy memory, [Col. 1200C] we receive your church, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings, the gifts of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or by other just means, with the Lord’s assistance, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify in their proper terms:

The Church of Blessed Peter of Regensburg itself, with all its possessions and appurtenances; the parish of the greater church; the estate of Gislingen, with all its possessions and appurtenances; [Col. 1200D] your cloister buildings and the plots of your houses situated in the city of Regensburg; the church of Persen, with the liberty granted to you by Hartwic, bishop of Regensburg, of good memory, and which you peacefully and reasonably possess; the church of Wibelsdorf; the church of Illinchoven; the church of Hovechirchen; the church of Waltkeringen; the church of Pfaffenberge; the church of Hitinchoven; the church of Pfolenchoven; the church of Lirendorf; the church of Leuchingen; the church of Punnechoven; the church of Otelhaim; the church of Chirphinholze; the church of Hazenchoven; the tithe of Wimtingen; the tithe of Samtingen; tithes in Toenkove; tithes in Norkowe; the estate which you possess in the village called Holzen; the estate which you possess in the village called Heitemchoven; the estate [Col. 1201A] which you possess in the village called Strazze; and the holding which you possess in the village called Talmazzingen.

In addition, we decree that administration of the archdeaconries of the same church shall be entrusted to none except canons of your church. And so that, secure from secular disturbance, you may more freely devote yourselves to the celebration of divine offices, we forbid under threat of anathema that any prince—except our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, the illustrious ever-August Roman emperor—shall have the right, against your will, to quarter his men or horses in your lodgings. When, however, a solemn court has been assembled by the imperial majesty, only ecclesiastical persons may lodge with you, and then without bringing in horses. [Col. 1201B]

Furthermore, because, as the Apostle says, no one ought to judge another’s servant, since he stands or falls to his own master, we prohibit by apostolic authority any secular judge, contrary to the ancient custom observed down to modern times, from having authority to judge any of your servants without your consent, unless an offense has been committed which entails blood-vengeance and which is not fitting to be exercised through an ecclesiastical man. Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid place, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them with any vexations; rather, let all be preserved intact, wholly beneficial for the uses of those for whose governance [Col. 1201C] and maintenance they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See, the canonical right, and the due reverence of the diocesan bishop. If any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this text of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offense by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him recognize himself as guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that [Col. 1201D] they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and the See of Santa Rufina, have subscribed. I, Henry, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Vivianus, priest-cardinal of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill, have subscribed. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St Mary across the Tiber, title of Callistus, have subscribed. I, Rainerius, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, title of Pammachius, have subscribed. I, Hubertus, priest-cardinal of the title of St Lawrence in Damaso, have subscribed. [Col. 1202A] I, Eander, priest-cardinal of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed. I, Arditio, deacon-cardinal of St Theodore, have subscribed. I, Gerard, deacon-cardinal of St Adrian, have subscribed. I, Soffredus, deacon-cardinal of St Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed. I, Albinus, deacon-cardinal of St Mary Nova, have subscribed.

Given at Velletri, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 30 April, in the first indiction, in the year 1183 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

The lead seal is appended: LUCIUS PP. III.

### CV. He receives the monastery of St Martin on Île Barbe into protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Velletri, 11 May.)

[LE LABOUREUR, *Les Mazures de l’abbaye royale de l’Isle Barbe*, vol. I, p. 115.]

[Col. 1202B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GUICHARD, abbot of the monastery of St Martin situated on Île Barbe, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Equity’s strength and reason’s order require that just petitioners be granted what they seek, especially when piety supports the petitioners’ will and truth does not abandon it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your many petitions and receive the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine office, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, following the example of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Innocent and Alexander of happy memory, [Col. 1202C] and fortify it by the privilege of this present document.

First, we decree that the order and monastery known to have been established in that place according to God and the Rule of St Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, God being favorable, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify in their proper terms:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, [Col. 1202D] with all its appurtenances and the churches built on that island. In the borough outside, on the bank of the Saône, the church of St Nicholas and of Saints Minervius and Eleazar. At Mont d’Or, the church of St Nicetius; in the village of Pomerii, the church of St Julian and St Cyprian of Cassania; the chapel of St Bartholomew. At Arderia, the church of St John and of St Germanus at Taponac. The church of St Mary and St Justus of Ranciac; the church of Beo; the church of St Andrew of Cimaloc; the church of St Christopher; the chapel of St Bartholomew; the church of St Martin of Franchelams; the church of St Euphemia of Inviniac; the church of St Florentius and the church of St Mary of Visiniac; the church of St Peter of la Montaneyo; the church of St Bartholomew; the church of St Martin of Floriac; the church [Col. 1203A] of St Paul of Pierre-Encise. The church of St Peter of Firminiac; the church of St Peter of Biriac; the church of Bressola. At Jalliac, the church of St Vincent; the church of Pisiac; the church of Holy Cross; the church of Corziac; the church of Romaneche; the chapel of Miribello; the church of Maximiac Mortuo; the church of St Peter at Rilliac; the church of Buxiac; the church of Fironda; the church of Crispiac; the church of Beyno; the church of Villorges; the churches of Noyosc, Gordanis, and St Maurice; the church of St Peter of Mura; the church of St Julitta; the church of St Peter of Balma; the chapel of St Mary; the church of St Romanus of Solemiac; the church of St Gregory; the church of Asnières; the chapels on the hills, of Villeta, Jons, and Moiffone; [Col. 1203B] the church of Pusiniac and Joennages; the chapel of Antone; at Fluriac, the church of St Bartholomew; the church of Tartarac; the church of Taurinis; the church of Castellucio; the church of Constantiis; the church of Cruento; the church of Claipiac; the church of Marsiliac; the church of Cella; the church of Magniac; the church of Mareloco; the church of Versiac; the church of Benerone; the church of Boteone; the church of St Lawrence; the church of St Romanus; the church of St Peter of A [lacuna]; the church of St Benebert of Novellis; the church of St Romanus Vetulus; the church of St Faith; the church of St Mary Magdalene; the right which you possess in the church of the Castle of St Germanus; the church of St Agatha; the church of St Andrew of Suriac; the church of St Martin of Folliosa; the church [Col. 1203C] of St Julian of the Tower; the church of St Justus on the Loire and the chapel of Grangent; the church of Chambla; the monastery of St Ragnebert; the church of Saints Cosmas and Damian; the church of St Peter; the church of St Mary; the church of St Martin; the church of St Justus of Velay; and the church of St Clement.

In the diocese of Chalon, the church of St Lawrence and the church of St Martin of la Carre. In the diocese of Clermont, the church of St Mary. In the diocese of Le Puy, the church of St Ferreolus; the church of St Romanus of Junsiac; the church of St Martin of Tirangiis; and the church of St Hilary. In the diocese of Vienne, the church of Cabanosc; the church of St Ragnebert of Fulcimagnia; the church of St Saturninus; the chapel of Sarreria; the church of Sablone; [Col. 1203D] of Baudinis; of Jossanis; and of Appesiac. In the diocese of Valence, the church of St Desiderius of Revoria; the churches of Montélimar—St Peter, Holy Cross, St Martin of the Hospital, and another church of St Martin; the church of St Praejectus; of St Michael and St Marcellus; and the church of Piosac. At Aiguno, the churches of St Mary, St Desiderius, and St Saturninus. In the diocese of Tricastin or Orange, the church of St Andrew of Barres; the church of St Mary of Alono and the chapel of that castle; the church of St Peter of Sallas; the monastery of Abolena; the church of St Genesius; the church of Mota of Mont Dragon; the church of St John of Lagoneria; the church of Torcularibus with its tithes; the church of St Arigius; the church of Belgione of Sprarancian; the church of St Mary of Albuna; the church [Col. 1204A] of St Nazarius with the chapel of Balma of St Dalmatius of Causanti; the church of Mulieratis; and the church of St Thyrsus.

In the diocese of Carpentras, the church of St Mary of the Innocents. In the diocese of Vaison, the church of Malatera; the monastery of St Benedict of Capella; the church of St Romanus; the church of Podium Almeradum; the church of St George; the church of St Marcellus; the church of Tilletoupis; and the church of St Blaise with the chapel of Placian. In the diocese of Sisteron, the monastery of St Marius; the church of St John with the chapel of the Castle of Assarna; St Peter; St Julian; the church of Lingosterio; of Cibarrano; and the churches of Torrendos and St Mary Sisa. In the diocese of Die, the church of St Mary; St James of Arrolas; the church of Cassabone; the church of Brusac; and the church of [Col. 1204B] Castilione. In the diocese of Gap, the monastery of St Peter of Lent; the church of Pellona; of Tornareto; the church of St Plandicius and St Mary; the chapel of Phara; the church of St Michael of Durfort; the churches of Cornilio, St Michael, the chapel of St John, the church of St Mary of Burienis, the church of Assenac, the church of St Leontius, St Alban, and St Veranus in the Valley of Brosius, the church of St Peter, St John, and St Mary, the chapel of the Castle, the church of Torretis, the church of St Mary of Carcere and the chapel of Carcer, the church of St Romanus and the chapel of Pomariolo, the church of St George, the chapel of the Castle of Lazarus, the monastery of Alomonis with the churches situated within and around the town, the church of St Clement, the chapel of St Victoria; in the territory of the Castle [Col. 1204C] of Larderii, the two churches which you possess and the castle chapel, the church of Clemensana and the chapel of that castle. In the diocese of Embrun, the church of St Mametus; the churches of Bayonne; the church of Augustodunum; of St Martin; of St Mary and another church of St Mary; the churches of St Peter and St Domitian; and the churches of Sallone.

Further, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and your monastery the castle of Ligniac with its lands, woods, and other appurtenances, as you reasonably and peacefully possess it by the gift of Stephen of Villars.

Certainly, concerning your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, and the produce of your animals, let no one presume to extort tithes from you. [Col. 1204D] You may also receive into your profession clerics or laymen fleeing the secular world, who are free and absolved, and retain them without contradiction. Moreover, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving it without the permission of his abbot, save for the purpose of embracing a stricter religious life; and let no one dare retain those who depart without the common security of your letters. In the parish churches which you hold, you may elect priests and present them to the diocesan bishops; if suitable, the bishops shall entrust them with the care of souls, so that they must answer to the bishops in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters.

We also grant you that within the boundaries of your parishes no one shall have authority, without the consent of the diocesan bishops and ourselves, to build a new church or oratory, saving the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. [Col. 1205A] We have likewise decreed that the burial-ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, saving nevertheless the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a low voice. Furthermore, by apostolic authority we forbid [Col. 1205B] any person to promulgate against you or your monastery a sentence of excommunication or interdict without manifest and reasonable cause.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, we decree that no one shall be set over it by any craft of deception or by force, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the decision of the sounder part of the brethren, shall, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of St Benedict, provide to be elected. Therefore no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them by any vexations. Rather, let all be preserved intact for the uses [Col. 1205C] of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, to be wholly beneficial, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. In acknowledgment of this protection received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay to us and our successors two gold bezants annually. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, etc.

Given at Velletri, through the hand of Albert, cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 11 May, in the first indiction, in the year 1183 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

### CVI. He receives the monastery of St Denis into protection and confirms its possessions and rights. (Velletri, 3 June.)

[FÉLIBIEN, *History of the Royal Abbey of Saint-Denis*, Proofs, p. 112.]

[Col. 1205D]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WILLIAM, abbot of St Denis, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Equity’s strength and reason’s order require that just petitioners be granted what they seek, especially when piety supports the petitioners’ wishes and truth does not abandon them. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive the aforesaid monastery—which belongs especially to the jurisdiction of blessed Peter—[Col. 1206A] in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document.

First, we decree that the monastic order known to have been instituted in this place according to the fear of God and the Rule of St Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, through the grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s aid, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify in their proper terms:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the right of disposal over prebends in the church of St Paul; in the diocese of Paris, [Col. 1206B] the church of St Leodegarius, the church of St Martin in Strata, and the church of Trembleac; in the archdiocese of Rouen, the church of Charz, the church of Cergi, and the church of Bussiac; in the diocese of Chartres, the church of Trapis; in the diocese of Orléans, the church of Tauriaco; further, the settlement which our venerable brother Henry, bishop of Senlis, ordered to be observed concerning the various disputes between you and the nobleman William of Melloto, both concerning tallages and forced labor-services and concerning rent-paying lands [Col. 1206C] and certain other matters.

The grant made to you and, through you, to your monastery by our venerable brother Guy, archbishop of Sens, and his predecessors, concerning the churches of Belna, Saint-Loup, Josenvilla, Ver, Fericiac, Grand Puteo, and Saint-Ouen; likewise the presentation of priests in those churches; the grant similarly made to you by our venerable brother Roger, bishop of Cambrai, and his predecessors of good memory, Walcher, Odo, and Nicholas, concerning the church of Forest, the altar of Solemma, and the altar of Vertinolis; a share of a certain tithe of Kivi; likewise, the settlement which the aforesaid bishop of Senlis ordered to be observed concerning the dispute between you and Albert of Mont Homéry about a certain road and certain wrongful customs; the grant also made to your monastery by our venerable brother Philip, bishop of Beauvais, concerning both the parsonage and the presentation of priests in the churches—namely, the church [Col. 1206D] of St Martin of Colle, the church of Ulliac, the church of Ciris, the church of Croy, the church of Asnières, the church of Moranciac, the church of Masters, the church of Noisiac, the church of Murno, and the church of Buxorta; further, the renunciation of the wrongful custom which Buccard of Montmorency held over the vineyards of your monastery situated in the village of Dioillo and over the land of Rotagici; likewise, the agreement made between your monastery and the church of St Exuperius of Corbeil, in the presence of John, formerly bishop of Chartres, of good memory, concerning the entirety of the prebend of that church.

[Col. 1207A] We fortify by apostolic protection all these settlements and renunciations, insofar as they were made and received without impropriety, are contained in authentic documents, and have also been observed down to the present. Let no one presume to extort tithes from you on your newly cleared lands cultivated by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the produce of your animals.
