You may receive clerics and laymen, free and absolved, fleeing the secular world, into conversion, and retain them without any [Col. 1207B] contradiction. Moreover, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving it without the permission of his abbot, except for the purpose of embracing a stricter religious life; and let no one dare retain one who departs without the security of your common letters.

In the parish churches which you possess, you may elect priests and present them to the diocesan bishop; if suitable, the bishop shall entrust them with the care of souls, so that they shall answer to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters. By apostolic authority we further prohibit the judicial rights or lay offices which you, son Abbot, have lawfully reclaimed into your own hands from persons dwelling in the borough of St Denis from henceforth being assigned to others; likewise, we prohibit the regular customs hitherto observed by your predecessors and by you from being changed on any frivolous pretext, unless this occurs through the provision of you or your successors, with the consent of the chapter or its greater and sounder part. [Col. 1207C] We entirely forbid new and undue exactions to be imposed upon you by archbishops, bishops, archdeacons, deans, or other prelates of churches. You may receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordinations of clerics or monks to be promoted to holy orders from whatever bishop you prefer, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favor of the Apostolic See, and is willing to confer these upon you freely and without any improper exaction.

[Col. 1207D] Moreover, we forbid anyone to presume to build a chapel or oratory within the boundaries of the parishes of your churches without the consent of the diocesan bishop and yourselves, saving the privileges of the Roman Church. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, without ringing bells, with excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, and in a subdued voice. Further, we decree that the burial-ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, saving nevertheless the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that [Col. 1208A] place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any deceitful contrivance or force, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the counsel of the sounder part of the brethren, shall, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of St Benedict, provide to be elected. Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them with any vexations; rather, let all be preserved intact, wholly beneficial for the uses of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and, in the aforesaid churches, the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. If any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, etc.

[Col. 1208B] I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St Susanna, have subscribed. I, Vivianus, priest-cardinal of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill, have subscribed. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St Mary across the Tiber, title of Callistus, have subscribed. I, Pandulphus, priest-cardinal of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and the See of Santa Rufina, have subscribed. I, Henry, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Arditio, cardinal-deacon of the title of St Theodore, [Col. 1208C] have subscribed. I, Gratianus, deacon-cardinal of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Bobo, deacon-cardinal of the title of St Angelo, have subscribed. I, Gerard, deacon-cardinal of St Adrian, have subscribed. I, Soffredus, deacon-cardinal of the title of St Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed. I, Albinus, deacon-cardinal of St Mary Nova, have subscribed.

Given at Velletri, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 3 June, in the first indiction, in the year 1183 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope [Col. 1208D] Lucius III.

### CVII. He receives the monastery of Saints Flora and Lucilla of Arezzo under the protection of the Holy Roman Church, and enumerates and confirms its possessions. (Velletri, 6 June.)

[MARGARINI, *Bullarium Casinense*, II, 202.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons CHARITY, abbot of the monastery of St Flora, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

[The supplied source ends here, mid-document.]

The granting of what is justly requested is required both by the force of equity and by the order of reason, especially when piety supports the petitioners’ wish and truth does not abandon justice [Col. 1209A]. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; and, following the example of our predecessors Innocent and Alexander, Roman pontiffs, we receive the aforesaid monastery of Saint Flora, in which you are devoted to the service of God, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, with the Lord’s aid, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and undiminished for you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify these in the following terms [Col. 1209B]:

The castle of Saint Flora, with the chapels situated in that castle—namely, the chapel of Saint Anastasius, the chapel of Saint Angelus, the chapel of Saint Apollinaris, the chapel of Saint Zeno—and whatever right you have in the chapel of Saint Mary; the monastery of Saint Peter Major in the city of Arezzo, with its lodging-house and all its appurtenances, adding that, according to your ancient and reasonable custom, you may freely regulate it; the chapel of Saint Gregory and whatever right you have in the church of Saint Laurentian; the monastery of Saint Michael of Mount Pinculi, with its chapels and other appurtenances; the church of Saint Peter and Saint Tiburtius at Gargonsa, with its appurtenances [Col. 1209C]; the parish church of Saint Martin of Galognano, with all its appurtenances; whatever right you have in the parish church of Saint Mustiola; whatever right you have in the church of Saint Vincent at Cortona; the castle of Quarata, with the church of Saint Andrew and its estate; whatever you have at Saint Mamma; the castle of Muglano, with the church of Saint Angelus and its estate; whatever right you have in the estate of Saint Prosper; whatever right you have in the church of Saint Mary at Villa Alba; the castle of Fontiano, with the church of Saint Peter and its appurtenances; the castle of Rughitino, with its churches and estate; the church of Saint Leo, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Flora Minor, with half of its estate and of the estate of Bulgari, together with the right which you have in the church of Saint Lawrence and [Col. 1209D] Saint Sebastian; the church of Saint Peter at Maiano, with the right which you have in it; and whatever you have at Polliciano, Pilli, and in the village.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any device of deception or violence, except the person whom the brethren, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall determine ought to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. We likewise decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever, etc. If anyone therefore in the future, etc.

[Col. 1210A] I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and Saint Rufina. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna, have subscribed. I, Vivianus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, have subscribed. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Calixtus, have subscribed. I, Landus, priest-cardinal of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed. I, Hyacinthus, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, Ardicio, deacon-cardinal of the title of Saint Thomas, have subscribed. I, Gratianus, deacon-cardinal of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian [Col. 1210B], have subscribed. I, Bobo, deacon-cardinal of the title of Saint Angelus, have subscribed. I, Gerardus, deacon-cardinal of the title of Saint Adrian, have subscribed. I, Octavianus, deacon-cardinal of the title of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Soffredus, deacon-cardinal of the title of Saint Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed. I, Albinus, deacon-cardinal of the title of Saint Mary Nova, have subscribed.

Given at Velletri, through the hand of Hugh, notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Ides of June [6 June], in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1182 [Col. 1210C], in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

The sign of Pope Lucius III.

Help us, O God of our salvation.

CVIII. He receives the monastery of Saint Himerius under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (18 June.)

[MABILLON, *Annals of the Benedictines*, VI, 696.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the prior of the church of Saint Ymerius and its brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It befits apostolic protection to be present for those who choose the religious life [Col. 1210D], lest perhaps the assault of any rash person either recall them from their purpose or, which God forbid, in any degree weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we decree that the monastic order which is known to have been established in your church according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, with the Lord’s aid, by grants of pontiffs [Col. 1211A], gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify these in the following terms:

The site itself on which your monastery is situated, granted by Hugh of Montfort, with all its appurtenances: namely, with the chapel of Saint Mary in the village of Saint Ymerius; the chapel of Saint Michael at Pont-l’Évêque; tithes of the mills of Corneville, and of other woods, forests, fisheries, fishponds, dairies, thickets, and of everything liable to tithe from the honour of Montfort in Normandy and England. In England, the churches of Bradbourne [Bradeburna], Tilton [Tiltentona], and Esbrugge, with all their appurtenances; and specifically the tithes of fish at Heca and one house at Irea, as the charters of the donors [or: grants; *donationum*] attest. By the gift of Hugh, son of Gilbert of Ghent: that portion of woodland called Herold’s Wood and Valliscorvi, and the thicket formerly belonging to Richard Poree at Perrefita, and tithes from the saltworks and fairs of Pont-l’Évêque and the valley of the Ancre, as his charter attests. By the gift of the illustrious Henry, king of the English: the chapel of Bello-loco, with its tithes and all appurtenances. By the gift of William of Perrefita, with the consent of his wife and sons and of his lord Hugh of Montfort: the tithe from dead water and from all his mills, as is contained in his charter. [Col. 1211C] By the gift of Robert Mauviel, with the consent of his wife and sons: the thicket, land, and wood which the clerk Hebert held from him; the wood of Quarreria; and a garden beside the spring of Saint Ymerius. At Ferraville, one garden and one acre of land. By the gift of Hugh, provost of Torta Quercus: three acres of land in the same village. By the gift of William Furtel, at Magnaville: one vavassor paying ten shillings, with his appurtenances. By the gift of Robert of Montfort: pasture and land on the hill above the house of Hugh Peissun; the water and fishery of Ivea; the garden formerly belonging to William the priest; and the tithe of the new mill and of Fulleret’s mill. By the gift of Elias of [Col. 1211D] Baillolio: land at Torta Quercus in forest clearings, and one saltwork at Tolca, with the consent of his lord Robert of Montfort. By the gift of Walter Pipard: the land of Guvifosse, which Hugh of Montfort had given him for his service. By the gift of Oliver of Aubigné: one vavassor rendering five shillings, with the *reguards* [rights of oversight] and all appurtenances. By the gift of Albreda of Tilly and her son Robert: a third part of the tithe of the mill of Perrefita, with all appurtenances. By the gift of William of Beteville: the tithe of his mill in the same village and the land which he gave them near Saint Ymerius beside the forest, as is contained in the authenticated writings of each donor.

Certainly, from your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate with your own hands [Col. 1212A] or at your own expense, and from the sustenance of your animals, no one may presume to demand or extort tithes from you. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen, free and absolved, who flee the world, and retain them without any objection. Moreover, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving it without his prior’s permission, except for the sake of a stricter religious life; and no one shall dare retain a departing brother without the common security of letters. When a general interdict has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. In the parish churches which you possess, you may choose clerics or priests and present them to the diocesan bishop. If they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust the care of souls to them, so that they owe him an account in spiritual matters, but [Col. 1212B] owe you an account in temporal matters.

Moreover, ancient and [lacuna] which we have hitherto [lacuna] in your church, and we [lacuna] them unimpaired to future [lacuna]. Furthermore, we decree that [lacuna] bishop, dean, archdeacon, or their official [lacuna] your churches or the clerics of your household [lacuna] upon a manifest and reasonable cause, it may be lawful to publish a sentence of interdict, excommunication, or suspension. We likewise decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wishes of those desiring burial there, unless perhaps they are excommunicated or interdicted [Col. 1212C], saving nevertheless the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact and in every respect serve the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and of the see of Saint Rufina [Col. 1212D]. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Vivianus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Calixtus. I, Pandulf, cardinal of the title of the Twelve Apostles. [lacuna] deacon-cardinal [lacuna] of Saint Theodore. I, Gra[lacuna], deacon-cardinal of the title of Saint Angelus. I, [lacuna] of Oriani, deacon-cardinal [lacuna]. [Col. 1213A] I, Galfredus, deacon-cardinal of the title of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Albinus, deacon-cardinal of the title of Saint Mary Nova.

[lacuna] Through the hand of Hugh, notary of the Holy Roman [lacuna], on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July [18 June], in the indiction [lacuna], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1182, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Lucius III.

CIX. He writes to the abbot of Siegburg that he should either bring or send the evidence necessary for what he had often requested: that Anno, patron of the monastery, should be declared a saint. He urges him to grant some suitable ecclesiastical benefice to the messenger carrying this letter. (Segni, 24 June.)

[LACOMBLET, *Charters*, I, 343.]

[Col. 1213B]

CX. He receives the church of Saint Anianus at Orléans under protection and confirms its goods. (Segni, 24 June.)

[*Antiquities of Saint-Aignan of Orléans*, Preface, p. 118.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, CADURCUS, dean of the church of Saint Anianus at Orléans, and his brethren, present and future, to be canonically appointed: in perpetuity.

Although, by the office of the apostolate entrusted to us by God, we ought to exercise vigilant care and solicitude for all churches, we must nevertheless be especially concerned for those which are known to pertain more particularly to the right and property [Col. 1213C] of the most holy Roman Church and which rely with fuller devotion upon the protection of the Apostolic See. And, lest they should be harassed by the rash attacks of any persons upon their goods or even their dignities, it is fitting that they should also be protected by the aid of our authority. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests, and, following the example of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, receive the aforesaid church of Saint Anianus, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future [Col. 1213D] acquire, God being propitious, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and undiminished for you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify these in the following terms:

Namely, the village of Sentilly [Sentiliacum] with its church; the village of Rum with its church; the village of Tilly with its church; the church of Chalo and the village of Artenay, granted to you by our most beloved daughter in Christ, Alizia, illustrious queen of the Franks, to be held and defended, with respect to the village of Chalo, with the freedom and immunity in which Louis, of good memory, once illustrious king of the Franks, is known to have held it, as is contained in his authenticated writing; likewise half the revenues, both from small tithes [Col. 1214A] and from offerings and all benefices of the living and dead, in the aforesaid church of Chalo, in accordance with the grant formerly made to you by our venerable brother W., formerly archbishop of Sens and now archbishop of Reims, cardinal of Saint Sabina and legate of the Apostolic See, as recorded in his authenticated writing. This is on the condition, however, that if several parish churches should be built in the same village, you shall have in all those erected there the same right which you are known to have had, and to have, in the aforesaid church. The village of Herbilly with its church and all its tithes and appurtenances; the church of Old Saint Anianus, called the Chapel, and the church of Saint German within the city walls; whatever you have in the village of Fontenet, and the church of that village with [Col. 1214B] its tithes and other revenues belonging to your right; the water of the Loire from the wall of the old city as far as Saint Lupus, and all the mills which you have in that water with their fisheries; whatever you have beyond the Loire and in Sologne; whatever you have in Gâtinais; the village of Bardezac with all its appurtenances; whatever you have in the forest called Boloma; the village of Cazelles; whatever pertains to the mayoralty of Jarria; and the village of Seteis.

In the above-mentioned parish churches—namely, those of Sentilly, Ruem, Tilly, Fontenay, Centolio, Herbilly, and Chalo—which you hold, you shall choose priests and present them to the bishops. If they are suitable, the bishops shall entrust to them, without payment, the care of souls, so that they are accountable to the bishops for the care of the people, but shall render you due obedience and customary subjection in temporal matters [Col. 1214C]. In the other two churches, namely Saint Anianus and Saint German, and for the service of the altar of the Crucified in the church of Saint Anianus, you may freely appoint priests, without anyone’s objection or presentation, as hitherto and henceforth. You may also, when your parish churches are vacant, as is customary and has been observed from ancient times until now, appoint supply priests, who shall serve almighty God until you agree upon suitable persons to be instituted in them. Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority the fairs on the two feasts of blessed Anianus, intended to provide lights for the same church, granted to you and your church by Louis, the illustrious king of France of good memory, and by John, formerly bishop of Orléans, and strengthened by the authority of their writings, as is contained in their authenticated documents. Furthermore [Col. 1214D], by this decree which is to endure forever, we establish that two prebends and the annual payments of canons, however the prebends may change, shall remain assigned to the office of the confraternity. We also confirm and strengthen by the protection of the Apostolic See the vineyards and all things bestowed upon the aforesaid confraternity, for you and through you for the confraternity itself, as has been established by the common consent of the chapter and confirmed in writing; and we decree that this constitution shall remain valid and unshaken for future times.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of your canons or clerics who are to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour of the Apostolic See, and is willing to confer these things freely upon you, without money or any exaction. Otherwise, have recourse to whichever bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is sought. Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority all liberties, immunities, and royal customs granted to you and your church by the kings of France and strengthened by their writings, and decree that they shall remain perpetually unimpaired [Col. 1215B].

We likewise enact and establish by this present decree that no archbishop, bishop, or any person may excommunicate the church entrusted to you, or you or the clerics of your choir, nor place you under an interdict or suspend you from divine offices, except the Roman pontiff, his legate, or one acting under a special command of the Apostolic See. Furthermore, we prohibit any ecclesiastical person or person of whatever order from imposing undue exactions upon your churches or chapels, or upon their priests. We decree, therefore, that no one whatsoever, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and Saint Rufina. [Col. 1215C] I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Peter, cardinal of Saint Susanna. I, Vivianus, priest-cardinal of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Calixtus. I, Pandus, priest-cardinal of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Ardicio, deacon-cardinal of Saint Theodore. I, Gratianus, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gerardus, deacon-cardinal of Saint Adrian. I, Soffredus, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Albinus, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary Nova.

[Col. 1215D] Given at Segni, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July [24 June], first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1183, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

CXI. He confirms the privileges granted by Alexander III to the nunnery of Saint Zacharias at Venice. (Segni, 6 July.)

[CORNELIUS, *The Church of Venice*, XI, 376.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, CASOTA, abbess of the monastery of Saint Zacharias of Venice, and her sisters, present and future, to be regularly appointed: in perpetuity.

[Col. 1216A] The Apostolic See ought to grant protection to prudent virgins who, beneath the habit of religion, with lamps lit through deeds of holiness, continually prepare themselves to go out to meet the Bridegroom, lest perhaps the assault of anyone’s rashness either turn them aside from their purpose or, God forbid, weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and, following the example of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, receive the aforesaid monastery of Saint Zacharias at Venice, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we decree that the monastic order known to have been instituted there according to God and the observance [Col. 1216B] of the brethren of Cluny shall be observed inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, God being propitious, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and undiminished for you and those who succeed you. We have thought fit to specify these in the following terms:

The estate situated in the place called Petrolio, with the church of Saint Thomas and all its appurtenances; the estate located in the place called Clugia, with all its appurtenances; the holdings situated [Col. 1216C] in the place called Runcaberto, with all their appurtenances; the holdings situated in the county of Treviso, with their appurtenances; the possessions at Treviso; and the possessions which you have in the bishopric of Cittanova, with all their appurtenances; and whatever you have in Sacco and Lupa, in the district of Padua, in Livenza, and Laurentiaca, together with their dependencies. We likewise confirm to you the tithes of all the tenants and lands which you rightfully possess in the aforesaid places and estates according to ancient tenure. We prohibit, however, the admission henceforth into the same monastery of any sister who may presume in any way to retain private property. We likewise decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who choose to be buried there [Col. 1216D], unless perhaps they are excommunicated or interdicted, while preserving the rights of the churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. We decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations. Rather, all things shall be preserved intact and in every respect serve the benefit of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If indeed any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. (L. S.) [Col. 1217A] I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and Saint Rufina. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Vivianus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Calixtus. And six others.

Given at Segni, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Nones of July [6 July], in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1183, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

CXII. He receives the monastery of Ebersheim into his protection and confirms its possessions and rights. (Segni, 19 July.)

[SCHOEPFLIN, *Alsatian Diplomatic Documents*, I, p. 278.]

[Col. 1217B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, EGELOLF, abbot of the monastery of Saints Peter, Paul, and Maurice at Ebersheim, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: for perpetual remembrance.

Whenever something is requested of us which is recognized as consonant with religion and uprightness, it befits us willingly to grant it and to give suitable assistance to the petitioners’ wishes. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests, and receive the aforesaid monastery of Saints Peter and Paul [Col. 1217C], and Maurice and his companions, at Ebersheim, situated in the district of Alsace beside the river called Ill, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in the same monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s aid [Col. 1217D], shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify these in the following terms:

The place itself where the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances. At Sulza, the estate of Porte with its tithes and the tithes of the demesne estate in fields, meadows, and vineyards. At Regenesheim, the tithes of two holdings. At Gundolvesheim, the tithes of five holdings. At Bercholtz, the tithes of one vineyard. At Balteresheim, Battenheim, Bolichesheim, and Bollenwilre, the tithes which you possess in them. The chapel of Zelle with the tithes of its allodial estate. The chapel of Sarmonzhe with the tithes of its allodial estate. At Egenesheim, the tithes of one demesne estate. At Sigoltesheim, the demesne estate with [Col. 1218A] all its dependencies—vineyards, fields, meadows, and ban-right—and the chapel of that estate with all the tithes of its property, together with the tithes of twelve holdings and of another two holdings of the church of Strasbourg. At Orheswilae, the demesne estate with the tithes of that property and its ban-right. At Bunegesheim, an estate with the allodial land of vineyards and fields, together with all its tithe, which Queen Ringardis gave you. Also, an allodial estate in that village which Odalric gave you. At Scerwilre, the demesne estate with vineyards, fields, meadows, tithes, and the ban-right of that property. At Tamwilre, an allodial estate with fields, meadows, watercourses, and a chapel with tithes. At Ebersheim, the demesne estate with forests and a fourth part of the ban-right of that village. At Kagenheim [Col. 1218B], the demesne estate with all its dependencies and ban-right. At Sermesheim, the demesne estate with the tithe of salic land, and the church with the tithes of that village. At Hittenheim, the tithes of one demesne estate. At Mazenheim, the tithes of sixty-eight *jugera*. At Outenheim, the demesne estate and the church with the tithes of that village. At Northus, the tithes of one demesne estate; and likewise at Hundenesheim and Lumersheim. At Valna, the demesne estate with a fourth part of the ban-right of that village. At Birenheim, the demesne estate with half the ban-right. At Hiltesheim, the demesne estate with tithes of salic land, the church with the tithe of that village, its ban-right, and all its *mundiburd* [protective jurisdiction] and liberty. Likewise in that village, the demesne estate belonging to the sacristy, with its tithes and dependencies, namely Cellesheim, Conenheim, and Hagenheim. At Azolveswilre [Col. 1218C], the demesne estate with church, ban-right, and all lordship. At Mutersholz, the demesne estate with church, the tithes of that village, and half the ban-right. At Baldenheim, a chapel with half the tithes of that village. At Wittensheim, the demesne estate with three parts of the ban-right, and the church of that place with tithes. At Niveratesheim, an allodial estate and church with the tithes of that village. At Swavesheim, the demesne estate with half the ban-right. At Artusvesheim, the demesne estate with church, the tithes of that village, and ban-right. The chapel at Bireheim with its tithes. At Cruzenheim, the demesne estate with three parts [Col. 1218D] of the ban-right, all lordship of that village, and the church with its tithes. At Arzenheim, the demesne estate with all its rights. At Burheim, the tithes of the demesne estate. At Castineto, one landed property. At Tambaco, one landed property. At Llichirchen, three holdings. At Offenheim, two holdings. In the district of Breisgau, the demesne estate in the village of Wizwilre, with all its dependencies, and the church with the tithes of that village, ban-right, and all lordship. At Baldovesheim, nine holdings. At Ibenheim, one holding. At Widensoln, one and a half holdings. At Uresheim, one holding. At Otrateswilre, three holdings. At Ostheim, one holding; at Onheim, two holdings; at Veltchirichen, one vineyard and half a holding. At Roleswilre, two [Col. 1219A] holdings; moreover, a vineyard of three *jugera* with its estates, and likewise another vineyard. At Bateresheim, two holdings. At Burcheim, half a holding. At Berolvesheim, nine holdings. At Bliemaresheim, a fourth part of a holding. At Stocesheim, two and a half holdings. At Hessenheim, half a holding. At Amricheswilre, one vineyard. At Pfassenheim, one vineyard. At Dubelsheim, two holdings. At Hedolvesheim, one and a half holdings. And at Mochenheim, half a holding; and the chapel situated at Ebersheim, with all its appurtenances.

Certainly, from your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, and from the sustenance of your animals, no one may presume to demand or extort tithes from you. You may also receive clerics [Col. 1219B] or laymen, free and absolved, who flee the world, into conversion and retain them without any objection. Moreover, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving it without his abbot’s permission, except for the sake of a stricter religious life; and no one shall dare retain a departing brother without the security of common letters. When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. Furthermore, we decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who choose to be buried there, unless perhaps they are excommunicated or interdicted [Col. 1219C], while preserving the rights of the churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any device of deception or violence, except the person whom the brethren, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall determine ought to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but all things shall be preserved intact and in every respect serve the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted [Col. 1219D], saving the authority of the Apostolic See and its canonical right. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and of the see of Saint Rufina. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Vivianus, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. [Col. 1220A] I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Calixtus. I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, James, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary [lacuna]. I, Arditio, deacon-cardinal of Saint Theodore. I, Gratianus, cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Bobo, deacon-cardinal of Saint Angelus. I, Octavianus, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Goffredus, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Albinus, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary Nova.

Given at Segni, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August [19 July], in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1183 [Col. 1220B], in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

CXIII. He receives the monastery of Saint Nicholas of Hermeries under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Segni, 28 July.)

[HUGO, *Premonstratensian Annals*, I, Proofs, p. 648.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, ROBERT, abbot of the church of Saint Nicholas of Hermeries, and its brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Whenever that is requested of us which is recognized to accord with virtue and propriety, it is fitting that we grant it willingly and afford suitable support to the desires of the petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and take under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We first decree that the canonical order which is known to have been established in that church according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be observed inviolably there for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that church now possesses justly and canonically, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s favor, by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself upon which the aforesaid church is situated, with its lands, meadows, and the King’s Wood [Note: [Col. 1219D] *Bois du roi*], and all appurtenances of the abbey; all the houses and vineyards which you possess at Lagny [Note: [Col. 1219D] *Latiniacum*], and whatever you possess at Conche [Note: [Col. 1219D] Conche near Lagny], whether in houses, vineyards, or other holdings; the estate which you have at Sery [Note: [Col. 1220D] *Sarias*], with lands, meadows, woodland, and all that belongs to you by right; and whatever you have acquired at Medium Meldum [Note: [Col. 1220D] Melun or Meaux], both woodland and meadows, [Col. 1221A] from the alms of Count Henry; two mills at Butrerches and Espault [Note: [Col. 1221D] Buire and Espaux, near Château-Thierry]; and one hundred sols to be paid annually at Barcho de Ari [Note: [Col. 1221D] Berchère]; the church of Saint Medard [Note: [Col. 1221D] Damard near Lagny], with the houses, lands, vineyards, and meadows belonging to the priest of that church, free and exempt from every customary due, rent, and tithe belonging to Lord Simon of Glisy [Note: [Col. 1221D] *Gliseria*], his brother, and his heirs; one half of the small tithes of Tournant [Note: [Col. 1221D] *Turnonium*], Chatres [Note: [Col. 1221D] *Castris*], Champrose near Tournant [Note: [Col. 1222D] *Campus Roboris*], Houssaye [Note: [Col. 1222D] *Urscia*], Bernay near Rosay [Note: [Col. 1222D] *Bernaïum*], the chapel of Hewidis [Note: [Col. 1222D] Les Chapelles near la Houssaye], and the chapel of Morcengin [Note: [Col. 1222D] Marchange near Neuf-Moutier, as I suppose]; two measures of grain, to be paid yearly in the grange of Champrose, from the alms of Guy of Garlande [Note: [Col. 1222D] Gui de Garlande, lord of Tournant] and his son Ancel; likewise two measures [Col. 1221B] of grain from the alms of Lord Ralph of Bucy.

Moreover, no one shall presume to exact or extort from you tithes on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, nor on the produce of your animals, gardens, or trees. You may also receive for conversion clerics or laymen fleeing the world, provided they are free and released from obligation, and retain them in your community without anyone’s opposition. Furthermore, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, to leave your cloister on any frivolous pretext without his abbot’s permission; and no one shall dare retain one who leaves without letters of authorization from the community. [Col. 1221C] In addition, by apostolic authority we forbid anyone to pronounce against your churches a sentence of interdict, or against you or your clerics a sentence of excommunication or suspension, without manifest and reasonable cause. We strictly forbid anything whatsoever to be demanded from you for the blessing of an abbot, for conducting him to or installing him in his seat, for any other sacraments, whether under the pretext of custom or in any other manner.

Desiring also, with paternal solicitude, to provide for your peace and tranquility, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone within the enclosures of your houses or granges to commit violence, robbery, or theft; to set fire; to seize or kill a person; or to lay violent hands upon anyone. [Col. 1221D] In the parish churches which you possess, you may appoint at least three or four of your number, one of whom shall be presented to the diocesan bishop to receive from him the care of souls; provided, however, that he shall answer to the bishop in spiritual matters, but to you in temporal matters and in observance of the order. When a general interdict has been laid upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, with excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, bells unrung, and voice subdued. We further decree that the burial-place [Col. 1222A] of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last wishes of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted—while preserving, nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain or diminish what has been taken away, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole, entirely benefiting the uses of those for whose governance and support they have been granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, [Col. 1222B] etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and of the see of Saint Rufina. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of Saint Mary across the Tiber and of Calixtus. I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, James, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Ardicio, deacon-cardinal of the title of Saint Theodore. [Col. 1222C] I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

Given at Segni, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, in the first indiction, in the year 1183 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Lucius III.

### CXIV. Privilege for the canons of Reggio. (Segni, August 13.)

[TIRABOSCHI, *Memorie Modenesi*, III, p. 89.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the canons of Reggio serving Saint Prosper, both present and future, canonically appointed in succession, forever.

[Col. 1222D] Both the force of equity and the order of reason require that we grant effect to just petitions, especially when piety supports the petitioners’ wish and truth does not leave it unsupported. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and take under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the church of blessed Prosper, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that same church now [Col. 1223A] possesses justly and canonically, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s favor, through grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself on which the said church is situated, with all appurtenances belonging to it; in the city of Reggio, the chapel of Saint Stephen, the chapel of Saint Faustinus, the chapel of Saint Apollinaris near the Bernone gate, the chapel of Saint Martin of the *Vinea passiva*, the chapel of Saint Maurice in the Street, and the chapel of Saint Adalbert in the Disbracato quarter beside the city; in the county, moreover, the parish church of Bagnolo [Col. 1223B] with its chapels and appurtenances; one third of the parish church of Nebularia with its appurtenances; one third of the parish church of Saint Stephen with its appurtenances and one third of the estate of that place; the church of Saint Martin of Pinizo; the church of Saint Dalmatius of Sisso; the church of Saint John of Corigia; and the *braida* of Fontaneto, with its cultivated land and all its appurtenances.

Moreover, by this present decree we ordain that the liberties and immunities reasonably granted to you and your predecessors by the predecessors of our venerable brother, the bishop of Reggio, and observed hitherto, together with the reasonable and ancient customs of that church, shall remain whole and unimpaired. When [Col. 1223C] a general interdict has been laid upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, bells unrung, excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, and voice subdued. Furthermore, we forbid anyone to pronounce against you or your dependents a sentence of interdict or excommunication without manifest and reasonable cause.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain or diminish what has been taken away, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole and unimpaired, entirely benefiting the uses of those for whose governance and support they have been granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical [Col. 1223D] right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Theod… bishop of Porto and Saint Rufina, have subscribed. I, Henry, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Euphemia, have subscribed. I, Vivian, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, have subscribed. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Calixtus, have subscribed. I, Pand… priest-cardinal of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed. [Col. 1224A] I, Andrew, deacon-cardinal of Saint Theodore, have subscribed. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Girard, deacon-cardinal of Saint Adrian, have subscribed. I, Octavian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Albinus, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary the New, have subscribed.

Given at Segni, through the hand of Hugh, notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of August, in the first indiction, in the year 1183 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

### CXV. To all prelates of Germany.—He commends to their prayers Christian I, archbishop of Mainz, who had died piously. (Segni, September 2.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXII, 480.]

[Col. 1224B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the archbishops and bishops, and to his beloved sons the abbots, communities, and other prelates of the German Church: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We wish it to come to your knowledge that Christian, archbishop of Mainz, of good memory—a very prudent and distinguished man—had long served magnificently our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, illustrious emperor of the Romans and ever Augustus, [Col. 1224C] and had in many respects transgressed against the obligation of his office. Since we could not otherwise restrain the treachery of the Romans, who were devastating the patrimony of the Church in hostile fashion and wickedly besieging Tusculum, we summoned that archbishop to the service of the Church. He, however, becoming obedient unto death, hastened, disregarding the unhealthiness of the air, to bring aid to the Church tossed by the storm with a vast multitude of troops, so that, as he had previously offered his members to iniquity for iniquity, he might now offer himself and his men to serve righteousness unto holiness of life. And it came to pass, by the Lord’s will, that the Romans twice fled at the terror of his name alone. When he had entered Tusculum, [Col. 1224D] we caused the city walls, which had long since fallen down for the greater part, to be repaired through his assistance before his death.

At last the Lord, having mercy on him, caused a feverish illness to scourge him, so as beneficially to fulfill in him what is written: “Where I find you, there I shall judge you”; and likewise: “Whom the Lord loves he corrects; and he scourges every son whom he receives.” Accordingly, that archbishop, in true confession and great contrition of heart, wholly intent upon the service of blessed Peter and the Roman Church, took up the cross, resigned every dignity, and closed his final day on the eighth day before the Kalends of September. Since we are greatly bound to be concerned for the salvation of one who did not refuse to die in the service of the universal Church, and since from his end we may [Col. 1225A] derive great confidence of his remedy, we admonish the whole of you, exhort you in the Lord, and command that, keeping his memory in your prayers, you assist that archbishop by your intercessions before the Lord, and that in all conventual churches you perform for him a thirty-day observance and an annual commemoration, so that divine mercy may pardon and wipe away the stains that clung to him from earthly contagions, and that you may deserve to receive from the Lord an unfailing reward for this work of mercy.

### CXVI. To Peter, abbot, and the brethren of Monte Cassino. (Segni, September 5.)

[TOSTI, *Storia di Monte-Casino*, II, 209.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1225B] sons PETER, abbot, and the brethren of Monte Cassino: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Those arrangements which are made in religious houses out of fraternal charity, devoutly and reasonably, ought to remain secure and obtain perpetual force through the authority of the Apostolic See. Therefore, by the authority of this present document we decree that the provisions which Richerius, abbot of good memory, and others who governed your monastery are known to have granted by regular provision to the infirmarer of your house for the use of sick brethren shall remain firm and unimpaired for them, wholly benefiting the needs of the sick brethren, as reason requires. If any of these have been alienated or, through any reckless presumption, diverted to other uses, [Col. 1225C] we command that they be restored to their former condition and assigned to the needs of those sick persons. Therefore no person whatsoever may infringe this document of our constitution or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Segni, on the Nones of September.

### CXVII. He takes the chapter of Terracina under protection and confirms its goods. (Anagni, September 22.)

[CONTATORE, *Historia Terracinae*, p. 365.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1225D] sons LEO, archpriest, and the chapter of Terracina: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The most holy Roman Church is accustomed, by the duty of its habitual piety, to love devoted and humble sons with especial affection and, like a loving mother, to cherish them with the defense of its protection, lest they be harassed by the troubles caused by wicked men. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, concurring favorably with your just petitions and considering the devotion which you are known to have toward blessed Peter and ourselves, we take under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your persons, together with all the ecclesiastical and temporal goods which you now possess justly and canonically or may hereafter acquire by lawful means, God granting it; and we fortify them with the safeguard of this present writing, [Col. 1226A] strictly forbidding anyone to dare molest you or presumptuously lay hands upon your property. Whoever should presume to do so shall know that he has incurred the sentence of excommunication.

Therefore no person whatsoever may dare infringe this document of our protection and prohibition or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, he shall incur the indignation of almighty God, etc., etc.

Given at Anagni, on the tenth day before the Kalends of October.

### CXVIII. He takes the monastery of Saint Peter at Thierhaupten under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Anagni, November 1.)

[*Monumenta Boica*, XV, 101.]

[Col. 1226B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, the abbot and community of the monastery of Saint Peter at Thierhaupten, both present and future, professing the regular life: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Apostolic protection ought to be granted to religious men who continually prepare themselves for immortal life through works of holiness, lest an assault of rashness draw them back from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of their religious life. Therefore, beloved sons in Christ, we graciously assent to your just petitions and, following the example of our predecessor Pope Eugenius of blessed memory, [Col. 1226C] take your aforesaid monastery under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We establish and grant you free election of an abbot, and decree that the monastic order known to have been established in your church according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be inviolably observed there for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions or goods that monastery possesses justly and canonically, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s favor, through grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and those who succeed you. You may also [Col. 1226D] receive free and released persons for conversion and retain them without any opposition. No one shall presume to demand or extort from you tithes from the newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands and at your own expense, or from the produce of your animals. When a general interdict has been laid upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, bells unrung, and voice subdued.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain or diminish what has been taken away, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole, entirely benefiting the uses of those for whose governance and support they have been granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If in future any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly [Col. 1227A] attempts rashly to contravene this document of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offense by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be estranged from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards [Col. 1227B] of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church, etc. …

Given at Anagni through the hand of Hugh, notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of November, in the second indiction, in the year 1183 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius.

### CXIX. Sentence against sacrilegious invaders of ecclesiastical rights, from whom every remedy of appeal is removed. (Anagni, November 8.)

[PETIT, *Theodori Poenitentiale*, p. 561.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons G., dean, and the chapter of Chartres: greeting and [Col. 1227C] apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us that certain of your parishioners violently invade the goods of your church and do not fear to inflict injuries at their own pleasure both upon you and upon your people; and, though warned, they cannot be recalled from their wickedness. Since it is therefore incumbent upon us to provide churches and ecclesiastical persons with their due peace and tranquility and to afford apostolic protection against the insolence of laymen, we grant you by apostolic authority that, whoever among your parishioners—whether he be B., count of Perche, B. of Dreux, of Vendôme, of Évreux, or of Montfort, or any baron or other person whatsoever—has inflicted or inflicts losses or injuries upon your church or people, and, when warned, scorns to make satisfaction, you shall compel them, without impediment of appeal, by ecclesiastical censure, to render due justice until worthy satisfaction has been made; and in their lands, apart from baptism and penances, you shall prohibit the celebration of divine [Col. 1227D] offices. No letters obtained from us or from Adrian, apostolic lord of blessed memory, may stand in the way.

Given at Anagni, on the sixth day before the Ides of November, 1183.

### CXX. Privilege for the abbey of Longpont. (Anagni, November 9.)

[MULDRAC, *Historia abbatiae Longipontis*, p. 72.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1228A] sons …, abbot, and the brethren of Longpont: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily give our consent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to effect what does not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, favorably concurring with your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority for you and your monastery, and fortify with the protection of this present writing, those things which the noblewoman Agatha, lady of Pierrefonds, has bestowed upon your monastery as a devout and reasonable alms, as you justly and peacefully possess them. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: the wood of Caisueto, with every right which she possessed therein—hunting rights, *grieria* [an uncertain forest-right term], or any other thing—for clearing or for whatever you may wish to do; likewise full right of use of dead wood in the forest of Retz and pasturage there for your animals; and, moreover, all her arable land which she cultivated at Fontemmort, with two small meadows, one at Matherival and the other at Bulbul, as our venerable brother Nivelon, bishop of Soissons, from whose fief they were held, likewise granted and approved. [Col. 1228B]

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this document of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul. [Col. 1228C]

Given at Anagni, on the fifth day before the Ides of November.

### CXXI. He confirms the agreement made by the canons of Saint Ursus of Aosta with the bishop of Aosta, through Haimo, archbishop of Tarentaise, concerning certain churches. (Anagni, November 11.)

[*Monumenta Historiae Patriae*, *Chartae*, I, 936, from the archive of Saint Ursus of Aosta.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the prior and brethren of the church of Saint Ursus: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily give our consent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to effect the wishes which do not depart from the path [Col. 1228D] of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, favorably concurring with your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority for you and your church, and fortify with the protection of this present writing, the settlement which was canonically made, upon the counsel of religious and wise men, between you and our venerable brother, the bishop of Aosta, concerning the church of Saint Mary and Saint Peter at Château-Argent, the church of Saint Stephen of Gressan, the church of Saint Saviour of Valais, and a certain *casaria*; and which was peacefully and quietly received by each party, as is contained in the authentic instruments drawn up concerning it. [Col. 1229A] Therefore no person whatsoever may infringe this document of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Anagni, on the third day before the Ides of November.

### CXXII. To Peter, abbot of Cîteaux, and Peter, abbot of Clairvaux: he writes that the time has not yet come to enroll Peter, former archbishop of Tarentaise, among the saints. He commands them to have committed to writing what is certain concerning his deeds and manner of life. (Anagni, December 9.)

[See *Acta Sanctorum Bollandiana*, May, vol. II, p. 322.]

### CXXIII. Judgment against robbers who abused the remedy of appeal against ecclesiastical ordinances. (Anagni, December 12.)

[*Theodori Poenitentiale*, p. 562.]

[Col. 1229B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons G., dean, and the chapter of Chartres: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the remedy of appeal was devised to assist the oppressed, but is used for the defense of evildoers, we wish and ought to provide that wrongdoers may not, under the pretext of appeal, lay violent hands upon ecclesiastical goods with impunity. Induced by this consideration, we establish by apostolic authority that, [Col. 1229C] if anyone has plundered property of your church and his offense is manifest, or if you have canonically proved your claim before the bishop or archdeacon in whose archdeaconry the wrongdoer resides, the robber shall not be permitted, by evasion through appeal, to escape ecclesiastical discipline. Therefore no person whatsoever may infringe this document of our constitution or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Anagni, on the second day before the Ides of December, 1183.

### CXXIV. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Matthew of Castello. (Anagni, December 15.)

[GATTULA, *Historia Casinensis*, II, 402.]

[Col. 1229D]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JOHN, abbot of the monastery of Saint Matthew of the servants of God at Castello, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

Placed, though unworthy, by the Lord’s gift upon the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, we ought to extend the gaze of our care over the whole body of the Church and provide with more attentive concern for the peace of the servants of God. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and, following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Alexander of happy memory, take the aforesaid [Col. 1230A] monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We first decree that the monastic order known to have been established in your monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be inviolably observed there for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now possesses justly and canonically, or may hereafter acquire, with the Lord’s favor, through grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

[Col. 1230B] The place itself upon which the aforesaid monastery is built, with all its appurtenances; the lands and vineyards which you possess in the land of Saint Benedict; the *terragium*; the allowance of bread and wine which you receive daily from the monastery of Monte Cassino under an old grant observed hitherto, and that which you receive from the church of Saint Mary of Albaneta and Saint Nicholas of Siconia, as the aforesaid monastery of Monte Cassino granted them to you in perpetuity out of piety; likewise the freedom granted to your monastery by Rainald Theodinus of good memory and by Peter, beloved son and abbot of Monte Cassino, with the chapter’s assent, as contained in their authentic writings; the good customs observed hitherto; [Col. 1230C] and also the church of Saint Martin on Mount Montano and the church of Saint Leonard near Mount Sambuco, with their appurtenances, reasonably granted to you by the abbots of that same monastery; together with the men whom you hold from the aforesaid monastery of Monte Cassino. All these things we likewise confirm by apostolic authority for you and your monastery.

You may also receive for conversion clerics or laymen fleeing the world, provided they are free and released from obligation, and retain them in your monastery without any opposition. Furthermore, no brother of yours, after making profession in your house, may leave it without his abbot’s permission; and no one shall dare retain one who leaves without letters of authorization from your community. We also forbid anyone to introduce a monk into the same house against your will or, against your will and without reasonable cause, remove any brother from it. [Col. 1230D] No one whatsoever shall presume to exact tithes from you on your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the produce of your animals. We further decree that no one at all may impose upon your monastery unlawful exactions or new rents, or increase old ones contrary to the enactments of the sacred canons. We also decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last wishes of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted—while preserving, nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which [Col. 1231A] the bodies of the dead are taken. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it through any cunning of deceit or violence, except the person whom the brethren, by common consent or by the counsel of the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain or diminish what has been taken away, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole, entirely benefiting the uses of those for whose governance and support they have been granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and to the due right and reverence owed to the monastery of Monte Cassino. [Col. 1231B] If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Theodore, bishop of Porto and Saint Rufina, have subscribed. I, Henry, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Mark, have subscribed. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Calixtus, have subscribed. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna, have subscribed. I, James, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, [Col. 1231C] have subscribed. I, Ardicio, deacon-cardinal of Saint Theodore, have subscribed. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Octavian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the second indiction, in the year 1184 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

## YEAR 1184

### CXXV. To Maurice, bishop of Paris.—Against priests accused of fornication. (Anagni, January 4.)

[*Collection des Cartulaires*, vol. IV, p. 35.]

[Col. 1231D]

LUCIUS TO MAURICE, bishop.

It has been reported to us on your behalf that certain priests established in your diocese are under public disgrace because they are not ashamed publicly to keep concubines. When you seek to correct them, they raise the obstacle of an appeal in order to evade canonical correction; yet they do not depart from their vice and evil custom. Since the remedy of appeal was not devised to furnish anyone with an incentive to sin, we grant your brotherhood by apostolic authority that, if priests publicly accused of this offense cannot or will not, when warned, perform canonical purgation within forty days, you shall suspend them without contradiction or appeal; and if they do not then repent, remove them from office and deprive them of ecclesiastical benefice. [Col. 1232A]

Given at Anagni, on the second day before the Nones of January.

### CXXVI. He confirms the judgment rendered by Theodinus, bishop of Porto, and Octavian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, between Oderisius, bishop of Penne, and Senebald, abbot of Saint Quiricus of Intethroco. (Anagni, January 19.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 1120.]

[Col. 1232B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ODERISIUS, bishop of Penne: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the controversy which had long been conducted between you and our beloved son Senebald, abbot of St. Quiricus of Intrethoco, concerning churches and certain other matters, had by our command been entrusted to our venerable brother Theodinus, bishop of Porto, and our beloved son Octavius, cardinal deacon of SS. Sergius and Bacchus, they, by the counsel of prudent men, established between you the agreement written below. For its greater clarity, we have thought fit to set down below, word for word, the instrument which they drew up concerning the same affair [Col. 1232C]:

> “Theodinus, by the grace of God bishop of Porto and of the see of St. Rufina, and Octavius, cardinal deacon of SS. Sergius and Bacchus, to all to whom these letters shall come, eternal salvation in Christ.
>
> Let all of you know that, since a dispute concerning the churches and other matters written below had arisen before us between our venerable brother Oderisius, bishop of Penne, and Senebald, abbot of St. Quiricus of Intrethoco, we, acting by the command of Lord Pope Lucius and hearing the case, received a free and unconditional submission to our arbitration from the aforesaid abbot and Master Bert., procurator of the aforesaid bishop. The latter had been appointed by that bishop, in this case and in the presence of Lord Pope Lucius and certain cardinals, as procurator both to litigate and to settle [Col. 1232D]. They bound themselves mutually, by a stipulated penalty of one hundred pounds, the abbot himself or the convent on the one hand, and the procurator or bishop on the other, promising that they would always hold valid whatever we should determine between them.  
>
> [Note: [Col. 1231D] The passage is corrupt.]
>
> Having taken the counsel of prudent men, and for the good of peace with the consent of both parties, we determine that the bishop, or his messenger, shall once a year be honourably received and provided for in these two churches—namely St. John on the Island and St. Mary of Ronzano—with as many horses and companions as he has when visiting the other churches of the bishopric; and that, upon his departure, he shall be honoured from the resources of the church in the customary manner [Col. 1233A].
>
> In the church of St. John of Casanello, he himself or his messenger shall once a year be honourably received and provided for. The chaplains of the aforesaid churches—namely St. John on the Island and St. Mary of Ronzano—and the other clerics serving in those chapels, shall pay the bishop cathedraticum; and those of their parishioners or of the clerics residing in the chapels whom the bishop excommunicates they shall not admit to communion. Clerics having the care of souls shall attend when summoned to the synod; and those whom the bishop promotes to the care of souls shall swear fealty to him and to the Church of Penne.
>
> With respect to the chapel of St. John at Casanello, which is at Old Atri, the bishop shall have a fourth part of the tithes and mortuary dues; and the person who there has the care of souls [Col. 1233B] shall swear fealty to the bishop and Church of Penne. The abbot, however, shall have by full right the power of appointment and removal in these five churches: St. John on the Island, St. Mary at Ronzano, St. John at Casanello, St. Nicholas at Galbano, and St. Saviour at the Fano. Any interdict which he imposes upon the aforesaid churches, and any monks or clerics residing in the said churches whom he excommunicates, the bishop shall not absolve.
>
> If the bishop promotes to sacred orders any monks or clerics in the said churches, he shall not require an oath from them, unless he promotes them to exercise the care of souls. The bishop shall preserve inviolate the privileges granted by the Holy Roman Church to the monastery of St. Quiricus, provided nevertheless [Col. 1233C] that those privileges remain intact, that the aforesaid monasteries and all things situated under those monasteries remain at the abbot’s disposition, and that the provisions contained in this agreement be preserved.
>
> The bishop shall absolve the monks and clerics of St. John at Casanello whom he has caused to swear to him, except the man who holds and shall hold the chapel of Old Atri, who shall remain bound by an oath of fealty. Clerics having the care of souls in the chapel of the church of St. John at Casanello shall receive that care from the bishop’s hand and shall be bound by oath to the bishop and Church of Penne. In the other aforesaid churches, he shall absolve those whom he has caused to swear to him, except those who exercise the care of souls in those churches.
>
> Moreover, on the visitation of the parish, the bishop or his messenger shall be received and honourably entertained [Col. 1233D]. In the church of St. Saviour at the Fano and St. Nicholas at Galbano, the customary rent shall be paid to him. In the church of St. Saviour, from which he had been removed, and all clerics who are in churches in which baptism is celebrated and the care of souls exercised—both in all the chapels of St. John at Casanello and in all other churches, whether chapels or not, in which the care of souls is exercised—shall receive that care from the bishop’s hand, shall pay him cathedraticum, and shall be bound to him by an oath of fealty.
>
> Of the fourth part of the tithes and mortuary dues of all the aforesaid churches, excepting the chapel at Atri, the bishop shall have one half and the abbot the other half [Col. 1234A]. Spiritual correction shall pertain to the bishop, temporal correction to the abbot. Manifest crimes of all lay parishioners of the aforesaid churches shall be referred to the bishop.
>
> That all these provisions may obtain perpetual force and firmness, we have marked this page of writing with the impressions of our seals. These things were done in the city of Anagni, in the year of the Lord 1183, in the third year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Lucius, the second indiction, on the twenty-second day of December.”

Therefore, as this settlement was made and accepted between you, and as we have set it down above word for word, we confirm it by apostolic authority and fortify it with the protection of this present writing, decreeing that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly contravene it [Col. 1234B].
