Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Anagni, 14 Kalends of February.

## CXXVII. Confirms the privileges of the monastery of Léhon.  
*(Anagni, 16 February.)*

[MORICE, *Mémoires pour servir à l’histoire de Bretagne*, I, 689.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the prior and monks of the monastery of Léhon: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We cannot be unaware how great a loss to its property your monastery has incurred on account of the case which it is known to have had against the monastery of St. Magloire at Paris [Col. 1234C], since we have so often heard the complaint itself and have understood, for the most part, the expenses and labour which your monastery has borne. But because Durandus, who at that time acted as abbot in your monastery, made promises concerning churches and benefices that were not vacant, and drew up charters of his own concerning such promises so that he might thereby acquire the favour of more persons—under the pretext of which promise your house is grievously harassed—we have thought fit by this present document to grant you that you shall be obliged to answer no one on the pretext of a promise made by him concerning benefices or churches which were not vacant. We strictly forbid you henceforth to presume to make such promises; and, if any are made, we decree that they shall lack force [Col. 1234D].

Given at Anagni, 14 Kalends of March.

## CXXVIII. Takes the Florentine monastery of the Holy Trinity under protection and confirms its possessions and rights.  
*(Anagni, 17 February.)*

[LAMI, *Ecclesiae Florentinae Monumenta*, vol. I, p. 200.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Jerome, abbot of the Florentine monastery of the Holy Trinity, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Whenever a request is made to us which is known to accord with religion and honour, it is fitting that we grant it with willing mind and bestow suitable support upon the desires of the petitioners [Col. 1235A]. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, receive under the protection of St. Peter and ourselves the aforesaid Florentine monastery of the Holy Trinity, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it with the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order which is known to have been established in that monastery according to God, the Rule of St. Benedict, and the institution of the brethren of Vallombrosa, shall there be inviolably observed for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and inviolate to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with its parish defined by fixed boundaries; the estates of Ripule and Varliano; the estate of Lignaria; the estate of Monte, with all their appurtenances; and the fields of Mugnone and Turri with their appurtenances [Col. 1235B]. No one shall presume to exact tithes from you on your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the sustenance of your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen fleeing the world, provided that they are free and absolved, and retain them without any contradiction.

Moreover, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in the same place, to leave it without permission of his abbot, except for the sake of a stricter religious life; and no one shall dare retain one who leaves without authorization from the community. When a general interdict of the land is in force, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice.

[Col. 1235C] Furthermore, we forbid anyone within the boundaries of your parish to dare construct a new church or oratory without the consent of the diocesan bishop and yourselves, saving nevertheless the privileges of the Roman [Col. 1235D] Church. We also decree that the burial place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wishes of those who resolve to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted, while preserving the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any trickery or violence, except a person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of St. Benedict.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them [Col. 1236A], or harass it with any vexations; but that all things granted for the support and governance of those for whose use they were granted shall be preserved intact and shall profit them in every way, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical rights of the diocesan bishop. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should in future rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third admonition, unless he corrects his offence by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find with the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Theoduinus, bishop of Porto and St. Rufina, have subscribed.  
I, Henry, bishop of Albano, have subscribed.  
I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.  
I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Mark, have subscribed.  
I, Laborans, cardinal priest of the title of St. Callistus at St. Mary across the Tiber, have subscribed.  
I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St. Susanna, have subscribed.  
I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the title of the basilica of the Twelve [Col. 1236C] Apostles, have subscribed.  
I, James, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed.  
I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of SS. Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed.  
I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of St. Angelo, have subscribed.  
I, Sofridus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Albert, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, 13 Kalends of March, in the second indiction, in the year 1183 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Lucius III.

## CXXIX. Forbids the appointment of canons in the Church of Modena unless they are elected by all the canons or by their sounder part.  
*(Anagni, 27 February.)*

[TIRABOSCHI, *Memorie Modenesi*, III, 91.]

[Col. 1236D]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the provost and canons of Modena: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whenever the Apostolic See is asked for something which accords with law and reason, we ought readily to grant the petitioners’ desires, lest we appear—God forbid—difficult in a matter which should be granted promptly. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we forbid canons to be appointed in your church contrary to the ancient custom hitherto observed, except those whom the canons shall elect by common consent [Col. 1237A], or whom their sounder part shall provide to be elected, saving, of course, the constitution of the Lateran Council, should you fail within the prescribed time to make provision for the church from among the canons. Let no person whatsoever, therefore, infringe this page of our prohibition or rashly contravene it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Anagni, 3 Kalends of March.

[Note: [Col. 1237D] Lucius III, elected pope in 1181, was compelled by Roman disturbances to remain for a long time outside Rome, and for the most part at Anagni, until in 1184 he came into Lombardy; having settled at Verona, he died there on 25 November 1185. Hence these three briefs, dated on the same day, appear to belong to the year 1163, or at any rate to a year not far from it.]

## CXXX. Confirms to the canons of Modena the chapel of St. Dalmatius.  
*(Anagni, 27 February.)*

[Col. 1237B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Boniface, provost, and the canons of Modena: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily assent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to effect the requests which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, concurring favourably with your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and your successors, and fortify by the privilege of this present writing [Col. 1237C], the chapel of St. Dalmatius, which Ildebrand, of good memory, formerly cardinal priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles, while he held the administration of the bishopric of Modena, reasonably granted to your community, just as you possess it without dispute. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly contravene it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Anagni, 3 Kalends of March.

## CXXXI. Confirms the cell of St. Mark to the monastery of St. George in the Black Forest.  
*(Anagni, 10 March.)*

[NEUGART, *Codex diplomaticus Alemannicus*, II, 110.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Manegold and the chapter of St. George: greeting and [Col. 1237D] apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily give assent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to effect the requests which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously consenting to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and your monastery, and fortify with the protection of this present writing, the cell of St. Mark, founded by the priest Semannus [Note: [Col. 1237D] Semannus was pastor of the church at Gebweiler, a town of Upper Alsace, and restored at his own expense in 1105 the convent of St. Mark, which had been consumed by fire in 1105. Father Bernard Lenz, in the manuscript *History of St. George*.] and entrusted to your care for the observance of regular discipline, just as you justly and peacefully possess it [Col. 1238A]. We decree that the nuns who are known to be devoted there to divine offices under your governance shall peacefully possess the land of the place with its appurtenances, as belongs to them by right, and shall render you regular obedience and reverence for your spiritual pastoral care. Let no person whatsoever infringe this page of our confirmation and constitution or rashly contravene it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur [Col. 1238B] the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Anagni, 6 Ides of March.

[Note: [Col. 1238D] Lucius III may have stayed for some time at Anagni in 1183 before returning to Rome in that same year, since he had previously resided at Velletri and, from 1184, at Verona, to free himself from the harassment of the Romans.]

## CXXXII. Takes the Premonstratensian Order under protection and confirms its laws and privileges.  
*(Anagni, 10 March.)*

[LE PAIGE, *Bibliothèque Prémonstratée*, book III, p. 635.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Hugh, abbot of Prémontré, and the other abbots and canons of the Premonstratensian Order, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Although unworthy, we have been placed by the Lord’s disposition upon the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See; and we are compelled to be solicitous for the condition of each person [Col. 1238C], and are bound sincerely to embrace what pertains to the increase of religion and the adornment of virtues, so that the repose of religious persons may be secure from every disturbance and, strengthened by apostolic protection, remain unharmed by the yoke of worldly oppression. Considering, therefore, how your religion and order, shining with much glory of merits and fragrant with the grace of holiness, has extended its branches from sea to sea, we have thought fit to cherish under the safeguard of apostolic protection and fortify by this present privilege the order itself and all the houses of the same order.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, after the example [Col. 1238D] of our predecessor Alexander of blessed memory, we ratify by apostolic authority and fortify by the privilege of this present writing all the regular institutions and ordinances which you have made by common consent or by that of the greater and sounder part, as they are set out below. Namely: that the canonical order, as it is known to have been established in the church of Prémontré [Col. 1239A] in the white habit according to the Rule of blessed Augustine and the ordinance of Norbert, of reverent memory, former founder of the Premonstratensian Order, and of his successors, shall be inviolably observed in every church of the same order for all time; and that the same observances and the same books pertaining to the divine office shall be uniformly maintained by all churches of the same order. Nor may any church or person of your order seek, or in any way retain if obtained, any privilege contrary to the common institutions of that order.

Nor shall any church impose upon a church which it has begotten any exaction of temporal advantage whatsoever; but the father abbot alone shall have care for the advancement both of the son abbot and of the brethren of that house, and shall have authority according to the order to correct what he knows ought to be corrected therein; and they shall humbly render him filial reverence as to a father. But the abbot of the church of Prémontré, which is known to be the mother of the others, shall hold the rank and office of father not only in those churches which it established, but also in all other churches of the same order; and due obedience to a father shall be rendered to him by all, both abbots and brethren [Col. 1239B].

Moreover, every year, setting aside every excuse, all the abbots of your order shall assemble at the general chapter at Prémontré, except only those whom bodily illness has hindered from the hardship of travel. They shall nevertheless be obliged to appoint a suitable messenger for themselves, through whom their necessity and the reason for their delay may be reported to the chapter [Col. 1239C]. Those dwelling in more distant regions who cannot present themselves at the chapter every year without grave difficulty shall meet at the term assigned them in that chapter itself.

If, through obstinacy, any abbots or provosts cease to attend your chapter, the abbot of Prémontré, with the counsel of his chapter, may strike them with regular sentence until they have made fitting satisfaction. No archbishop or bishop, except perhaps by command of the Roman pontiff, may relax a sentence which the aforesaid abbot of Prémontré, whether in general chapter or outside the chapter, has canonically pronounced upon prelates or subjects of your whole order with the counsel of his fellow abbots [Col. 1239D].

Therefore, in your general chapter, with the abbot of Prémontré presiding and the others trusting and cooperating in the Spirit of God, diligent discussion shall be held concerning matters pertaining to the edification of souls, instruction in morals, formation in virtues, and the advancement of regular discipline. In every question and complaint, spiritual as well as temporal, put forward in that chapter, that shall be held inviolably and observed which the abbot of Prémontré, together with those who appear to be of sounder counsel and more suitable, shall justly and prudently decide.

If any abbot of your order is found to be of ill repute, unfit, or a violator of his order, and, after first being admonished by his father abbot or by his messengers, neglects to correct and amend his fault, or refuses voluntarily to resign if he ought to be removed, he shall be deposed by authority of the general chapter. Once deposed, he shall return without delay, without any condition of temporal advantage, to the house from which he came or to another house of the same order which he chooses, and shall remain firmly in obedience to its abbot, as do the other brethren of that house [Col. 1240A]. The same may be done at another time, if necessary and if the chapter cannot be awaited without scandal or danger, by the abbot of Prémontré, the father abbot, and such other abbots as he shall summon. If the deposed man should obstinately attempt to oppose the sentence pronounced against him, both he and the principal supporters of his obstinacy who belong to your order shall be restrained by ecclesiastical censure of the abbot of Prémontré and the other abbots, until they make satisfaction [Col. 1240B].

But whenever one of your churches is deprived of its own abbot, or an election of abbot has not been regularly held there, it shall remain under the authority and administration of the father abbot, and, with his counsel, the person to be elected shall be chosen by the canons. Upon his election, the brethren of the church shall at once promise obedience to him; and he, not as one freed from the authority of the father abbot or of his order, shall be presented to the archbishop or bishop in whose diocese he is, to receive from him the fullness of the office [Col. 1240C]. Yet, after making profession to his archbishop or bishop, he shall not on that account transgress the constitutions of his order or become in any respect their violator.

If any of you canonically elected abbot, having once and twice been presented to the diocesan bishop by the abbots of your order, cannot obtain his blessing from him, then, lest the church to which he has been called be endangered through lack of counsel, he shall fully exercise in it, according to the order, the office and position of abbot, both in providing outward matters and correcting inward ones, until he obtains the blessing either through the intervention of your general chapter, by command of the Roman pontiff, or from the metropolitan.

No ecclesiastical person shall exact from you a price for chrism, consecrations, ordinations, burial, the blessing of an abbot, or leading him to his seat on a palfrey; nor shall any of you presume to give anything even if it is demanded, because the mark and peril of simoniacal depravity involve both the person who demands and the person who gives [Col. 1240D].

Further, if any of your churches is deprived of a pastor’s support, and discord or division should arise among the brethren concerning the appointment of an abbot, and they cannot readily be restored to concord or unity, the father abbot, with the counsel of his fellow abbots, shall prudently provide them with a suitable person; and they shall receive him as abbot without contradiction. If they disdain to receive him, they shall be subject to the sentence which the father [Col. 1241A] abbot, with the counsel of his fellow abbots, shall think fit to promulgate against them by authority of the order.

Moreover, since the church of Prémontré is the first mother of all the churches of the whole order and has no other father over it, an annual visitation shall be held there, as was established for the protection and preservation of the order by the first three abbots—of Laon, Floreffe, and Cuissy. If anything in that house requires correction, it shall be corrected by them without a further hearing. But if the abbot is negligent in correcting and the brethren, though frequently warned, remain incorrigible, the matter shall be referred to the general chapter; it shall be amended with the counsel of the general chapter as seems best; and the chapter’s sentence in this matter shall be observed without any reconsideration.

Whenever the church of Prémontré is without an abbot, its care shall belong to the aforesaid three abbots. With their counsel, the canons of that church shall elect a suitable person as abbot, having also summoned to their counsel four other abbots belonging to the same church, whom the canons themselves shall decide to summon [Col. 1241B]. Each mother church of your order may also, with the counsel of the abbot of Prémontré, choose as its own abbot whomever it wishes from the abbots of churches known to have proceeded from it, or from another inferior church of the same order, provided he is suitable.

No one of your churches shall elect as its abbot a person from another order, nor shall anyone of your order be appointed abbot of a monastery of another order, except by authority of the Roman Church. Nor may anyone receive or retain after receiving your canons or lay brothers without the permission of their abbots. No church of your order may rashly transfer itself to another profession. But if churches of canons from another order enter your order, they shall without objection owe allegiance to the church of your order in which they are known to have assumed your order [Col. 1241C].

Moreover, if a dispute concerning temporal matters should arise between any churches of your order, no ecclesiastical or secular hearing shall be sought outside the order. Rather, through the mediation of the abbot of Prémontré and those others whom he summons [Col. 1241D], the matter shall either be settled charitably between them or, after hearing both sides, the controversy shall be concluded by a just judgment. For the better preservation of peace in your order, we strictly forbid any of your prelates or subjects, in matters pertaining to the discipline and institutions of the order, to dare appeal, as established by the Lateran Council. If anyone attempts an appeal, those concerned shall nonetheless be obliged to exercise regular discipline.

Furthermore, because you are removed from worldly noise and tumult and love peace and quiet, we decree that your granges, courts, and likewise the precincts of your churches shall be free from the incursions and violence of evil persons. We forbid anyone there to dare seize, despoil [Col. 1242A], beat, or kill a person, or commit theft or robbery. To avoid the frequent presence of secular persons, you may, saving the rights of the diocesan bishops, build oratories in your granges and courts; and, when necessary, celebrate divine offices therein for yourselves and your household. You may receive that household, unless some persons have their own residences nearby, to confession, communion, and burial with the propriety appropriate to your order.

You may also receive into conversion free and absolved persons fleeing the world, and retain them with their goods without any contradiction. No one shall presume to hinder free persons who are ill and have resolved in their final wishes to be brought to you or buried among you, or to retain their lawful goods [Col. 1242B], saving nevertheless the lawful share of the heirs and the canonical rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

For the greater reverence of your order and observance of regular discipline, we grant you, sons who are abbots, full power to bind and loose your subjects. Since all the matters which you have ordained for the advancement of religion and the salvation of souls could not be attached to this present abridgment, together with what is written we ratify by apostolic authority your customs which, with regard to religion, you have regularly established among yourselves and shall hereafter establish by God’s authoring; and we decree that they shall be inviolably observed for all time by you, your successors, and all who profess your order [Col. 1242C]. Nor shall any letters have force which have been obtained, without naming the Premonstratensian Order, against the liberty granted you by the Apostolic See.

No one shall presume to demand or extort tithes from you on the fruits of your labour from possessions held before the general council; on newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense and from which no one has hitherto received anything; or on gardens and shrublands, meadows, pastures, your fisheries, or the sustenance of your animals. We forbid bishops and other prelates of churches to lodge in your monasteries unless they observe the number of their retinues established by the Lateran Council [Col. 1242D]. They shall turn aside to your granges and courts for lodging only in great necessity; and then they shall be content with the customary food of those dwellings, provided with propriety and charity. No secular or ecclesiastical person may eat meat in any of your houses, except manifestly on account of illness and only in your conventual monasteries.

Furthermore, we forbid any person, brethren, to dare summon members of your order before secular courts. If anyone believes that he has a legal claim against you, he may pursue it under examination by an ecclesiastical court. You may also bring forward suitable brethren to testify in your cases [Col. 1243A], and by their testimony, as is right, repel violence and vindicate justice. We likewise forbid any ecclesiastical or secular person, contrary to the statutes of the Lateran Council, to impose tallages in your churches or any other burdensome and unjust exactions upon you. We also forbid you to presume to accept from anyone, to be fed or kept to the detriment of your order, wild beasts, birds, dogs, or other animals of this sort kept for curiosity.

Finally, so that you may serve God more quietly and be spared the necessity of travelling about, we have thought fit by this present writing to grant that, if your bishops maliciously delay or, owing to a just impediment, are unable to confer upon you ordinations and the other ecclesiastical mysteries [Col. 1243B], should you have as a guest a bishop whose ordination and office are fully known to you, you may freely receive from him ordinations and the other sacraments, provided this does not create prejudice to the diocesan bishop.

Moreover, graciously inclining to your petition, we have thought fit by this present document to prohibit any archbishop or bishop, or their officials, from presuming to interdict or suspend your churches or their religious persons without manifest and reasonable cause. If anything in them requires correction, it shall be referred to the hearing of the general chapter at Prémontré, and there amended as justice and propriety require [Col. 1243C]. Further, if any bishops or their officials pronounce any sentence against your persons or churches contrary to the liberty granted them by your predecessors or by us, we decree that the same sentence shall be annulled, as having been issued against grants of the Apostolic See.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb your churches, remove their possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass them with any vexations whatever; but that all things be preserved whole for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, to their benefit in every way, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. [Col. 1243D] If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, having been warned a second and third time, unless he correct his offence by appropriate satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. [Col. 1244A] I, Theodinus, bishop of the see of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Laborans, cardinal-priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Saint Callixtus. I, Pandarus, cardinal-priest of the title of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, James, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Arditio, cardinal-deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Octavian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. [Col. 1244B] I, Albinus, cardinal of Saint Mary the New.

Given at Anagni, through the hand of Albert, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 10 March, in the second indiction, in the year 1183 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Lucius III.

### CXXXIII. He commands the abbot and monks of Classe to obey the archbishop of Ravenna. (Anagni, 20 March.)

[MITTARELLI, *Annals of Camaldoli*, IV, 111.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons [Col. 1244C] . . . , abbot and monks of Classe: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since it ought not to have escaped your memory how many and how great are the benefits you receive from the Church of Ravenna, and how great an increase your monastery may receive, both spiritually and temporally, through the grace and favour of our venerable brother its archbishop, you yourselves ought sufficiently to be zealous in devotion toward him and, by your example, to invite others to his obedience and service. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command and enjoin upon your whole community that—excepting only the matter of rendering fealty, from which Walter, of blessed memory, formerly archbishop of Ravenna, released you—in all other matters, especially the promise of obedience and the enthronement of the see, [Col. 1244D] whenever successors have been elected for you, son abbot, you shall render to the aforesaid archbishop and his Church due obedience and customary reverence, all contradiction and excuse ceasing; so that you cannot be reproved for the fault of disobedience or incur any censure for disregarding an apostolic command. Otherwise, since we neither wish, nor can with a clear conscience, fail the aforesaid archbishop in the matter of his right, we shall, by the Lord’s authority, hold valid and command to be inviolably observed whatever sentence he may canonically pronounce on this account.

Given at Anagni, 20 March.

### CXXXIV. He informs the brethren of Casa Dei that, “at the Lord’s Supper” (29 March), he granted Abbot Lantelmus and his successors the use of the mitre. (Veroli, 8 April.)

[MAB., *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, century VI, pt. II, p. 187.]

[Col. 1245A]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the community of Casa Dei: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The authority of the Roman See, from which ecclesiastical honours have flowed, customarily honours by the bestowal of its office those who, being endowed with integrity, are known to be bound to blessed Peter and his successors by sincere devotion. Giving this our more careful consideration, when on Maundy Thursday we were to celebrate the solemnities of Mass [Col. 1245B] and many persons stood before us wearing mitres upon their heads, we observed that our beloved son Lantelmus, your abbot, did not have a mitre on his head. No petition concerning this having been presented to us, and no suggestion having induced us, both on account of the abbot’s own integrity and the constancy of his devotion, and because your monastery is subject directly, without intermediary, to the jurisdiction and governance of blessed Peter and ourselves, we granted him a mitre, to be worn upon his head according to custom.

Although afterward he urgently pressed us to release and exempt him from wearing the mitre, nevertheless, by virtue of obedience we enjoined him to use the mitre on the principal feasts, [Col. 1245C] as is customary for other persons. By this document we also command you to urge him to carry out what we have enjoined. And, in the customary benevolence of the Apostolic See, we grant both to him, as we have said, and to his successors the use of the mitre. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our constitution or rashly oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he shall incur the indignation of almighty God and of his apostles, the blessed Peter and Paul.

Given at Veroli, 8 April.

### CXXXV. He confirms the goods and rights of the priory of Saint Arnulf at Crépy, of the Cluniac order, in the diocese of Senlis. (Veroli, 20 April.)

[*Cluniac Bullary*, p. 78.]

[Col. 1245D]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUMBERT, prior of the monastery of Saint Arnulf the martyr at Crépy, and the other brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetual remembrance.

The granting of due effect to just petitioners is required both by the strength of equity and by the order of reason, especially when piety assists the petitioners’ desire and truth does not abandon it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your petitions. Following in the footsteps of our predecessors of holy memory, John, Paschal, Innocent, Eugenius, and Alexander, Roman pontiffs, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of this document, the aforesaid [Col. 1246A] monastery of Saint Arnulf the martyr at Crépy, in which you are devoted to divine service. It is recognized as subject to no lordship or power except that of the Roman pontiff and the abbot of Cluny.

First, we decree that all things known to have been granted and conveyed to your monastery by the founders of your house—namely Walter, formerly count of Amiens, and his wife Adela—shall be preserved for you and your successors, after the example of those same predecessors of ours, in the liberty in which they were conveyed. Moreover, whatever possessions or goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grant of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors, to be possessed, administered, and governed in perpetuity both by you and by others appointed as priors through the abbots of Cluny. [Col. 1246B] Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with its lands, vineyards, tithes, and all other appurtenances; namely the market and suburb of the castle of Crépy, with the cultivated land adjoining that castle, on part of which the castle is built; the altar and village of Oger, with tithes and all appurtenances belonging to that place; [Col. 1246C] one mill situated below the slope of the hill of the castle of Crépy; one [mill] in the village of Dilveiro; one meadow and vineyards upon the river Alturna; the village of Chasia, situated in the district of Othis, with all its appurtenances—lands, woods, meadows, mills, and two churches: namely, the mother church of that village, founded in honour of Saint Denis the martyr, and the dependent chapel of Saint Gangulf with its tithes; the church of Saint Martin situated near the castle of the bridge of Arens, with its lands, vineyards, and other appurtenances. In accordance with the tenor of your privileges, this church shall be subject both to you and to your successors and shall be ordered with your approval and counsel.

In the wood of Biera, the village called Fagil, with all [Col. 1246D] its appurtenances; in the district of Meaux, one church in the village called Mallos, with lands, people, and tithes. In the bishopric of Senlis, the church of Saint Agatha, with the entire parochial right of the whole castle of Crépy and all its appurtenances; the altar of Frenco. In the bishopric of Beauvais, the altar and village of Locelles with all their appurtenances; the cell of Frenceriis with all its appurtenances; the holding of Noirello, namely houses, vineyards, and tithes at Harcheri. In the bishopric of Amiens, the cell called Morandi; the monastery with the grange of oats and all its appurtenances, which we decree shall always remain in the liberty in which it is recognized to have remained hitherto. [Col. 1247A] Possessions in the village of Vilet near Mont-Didier; the altar of Villaris; the altars of Germiniac, which you possess by the charter of Falcon, formerly bishop of Amiens, with all parochial right of that village and its tithes. In the bishopric of Soissons, the church of Bunoculo with grange, lands, vineyards, meadows, tithes, and other revenues. The allod of the knight Guido at Meromont; the allod of Leotold at Dilucium, with other things you hold there; the village of Vallis, the New Village, the village of the knight Galcherius, and the allod of Frovesta.

Furthermore, by the authority of the Apostolic See we decree that, as our predecessor of holy memory Pope John established and confirmed when that place was offered to him at the beginning of its foundation by the aforesaid Walter, count of Amiens of good memory, and when that house was adopted by him as a new planting into the special and proper daughterhood of the holy Apostolic See: [Col. 1247B] no archbishop or bishop whatsoever may pronounce a sentence of excommunication or interdict against that monastery without the assent and command of the Roman pontiff, or of his legate specially sent from his side; nor may anyone exact customs there, celebrate public Masses against your will, or lay a hand upon it for the purpose of imposing any burden.

For it is not fitting that those known to belong to the right of the sacred Roman Church, which is the head and mother of all churches, should be burdened by anyone’s oppressions or harassed by incursions. You may also choose priests for your churches and present them to the diocesan bishop; if they are found suitable, the bishop shall commit the care of souls to them, provided that they answer to him concerning spiritual matters and to you concerning temporal matters, without any contradiction.

If you judge that some priest is to be retained for celebrating the divine offices in the place where you are devoted to divine service, he shall not meanwhile be required to answer to anyone concerning the altar of the Cross, which belongs to you. Nor may anyone presume to demand from you tithes of your newly cultivated lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or of the increase of your animals; rather, you shall henceforth possess them peacefully, without any contradiction from bishops [Col. 1247D] and episcopal officials—you who distribute your goods to pilgrims and the poor. Nor may anyone have authority to trouble you concerning alms canonically given to you for the salvation of the souls of the living or the dead. Rather, you may retain and possess, saving the right of the mother church, gifts and offerings brought to you both by the living and by the dead, for the benefit of the servants of God and the poor. Moreover, the same monastery with all its appurtenances shall remain, as it is known hitherto to have remained by grant of the holy Apostolic See, under the free ordering and governance of the monastery of Cluny.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, [Col. 1248A] remove its possessions, retain or diminish what has been removed, or harass it with any exactions whatever; but that all things be preserved whole for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, to their benefit in every way, saving in all matters the dignity of the Apostolic See and, in the above-mentioned churches, the canonical right of the diocesan bishops. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mark. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna. [Col. 1248B] I, Laborans, cardinal-priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Saint Callixtus. I, Paul, cardinal-priest of the title of the basilica of the Holy Apostles. I, James, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Laborans, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo. I, Geoffrey, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata.

Given at Veroli, through the hand of Albert, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 20 April, in the second indiction, in the year 1184 of the Lord’s Incarnation, [Col. 1248C] in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

### CXXXVI. He orders R., dean and chapter of Rouen, since the archbishop has died, to ensure that W[illiam], bishop-elect of Coutances, is consecrated by the suffragan bishops of the Church of Rouen. (Veroli, 24 April.)

[MARTÈNE, *Treasury*, III, 987.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons R., dean and chapter of Rouen: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have learned from the report of our beloved sons, the chapter of the Church of Coutances, that when they had canonically and unanimously elected our beloved son W., formerly dean of Bayeux, as bishop, [Col. 1248D] the election was solemnly confirmed by your archbishop R., of blessed memory, and a date was appointed for consecration. But meanwhile the archbishop, as it pleased the Lord, closed his final day; and thus, through this misfortune, the consecration has until now been delayed, not without serious loss, since that Church has now remained deprived of pastoral governance for six years and more.

Therefore, because delay brings danger with it, by apostolic letters we command and enjoin upon your discretion that, if the matter stands thus, after summoning to your church the suffragan bishops, you shall cause the office of consecration to be conferred upon the aforesaid elect without difficulty, delay, or appeal. Thus, having attained the fullness of episcopal office, he may administer health-giving sacraments to the flock entrusted to him [Col. 1249A] and provide, as necessary, both for the ordination of clerics and for the dedication of churches, and for the other matters that pertain to a bishop alone.

Given at Veroli, 24 April.

### CXXXVII. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Severus at Ravenna. (Veroli, 27 April.)

[MITTARELLI, *Annals of Camaldoli*, IV, 113.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HENRY, abbot of Saint Severus at Ravenna, and his brethren, present and future, to be regularly appointed: in perpetuity.

Whenever a request is made to us which is recognized as consonant with religion and integrity, it is fitting that we willingly grant it [Col. 1249B] and give appropriate effect to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this document. We decree that whatever possessions or goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grant of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

[Col. 1249C] The place itself where the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Pulio; the church of Saint Mary at the Hospice; the church of Saint Thomas; half of Saint Lawrence’s gate, with the riverbank as far as the tower of Saint Cyprian, including that tower; and from that gate as far as the palace of King Theodoric of former times, with the houses and holdings; whatever you possess within the city of Ravenna or throughout the territory of that city; the island from Badanero to the port of Candiano and from your monastery to the sea, with rights of fishing and grazing; whatever you possess in the county of Imola; the church of Butrio with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Cassian within the city of Faenza, with all its appurtenances, and [Col. 1249D] whatever you possess in that city or its bishopric; whatever you possess in the bishopric of Bologna and in the bishopric of Forlì; the church of Saint Sophia in the bishopric of Ferrara, and whatever you possess in that bishopric; the church of Saint Giles at Carpenella and one third of the church of Saint Mary of that village, together with the village itself; the chapel of Saint Severus, the chapel of Saint Martin, the chapel of Saint Christopher, the chapel of Saint Andrew at Catignano, and the chapel of Saint Paternian, with all their appurtenances; the entire estate of Sclao and whatever you possess in the bishopric of Populonia; the church of Saint Paul of Casameruli with its appurtenances, and whatever you possess in the city or bishopric of Ficocle; the church of Saint Angelo in the city [Col. 1250A] of Rimini; the church of Saint Mary of Marignano; the church of Saint Stephen at Pereto; the church of Saint Martin at Luciano, with all their appurtenances; and whatever you possess in the bishopric of Rimini; the church of Saint James in the city of Pesaro, with its appurtenances, and whatever you possess in that city or bishopric; whatever you possess in the bishopric of Fano, Cagli, or Gubbio; whatever you possess in the county of Castello; the castle of Coria with its churches and appurtenances; one third of the castle of Afra with one third of the church of that castle; the monastery of Saint Benedict of Castagnola with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint John of Cassiano; the church of Saint Andrew; the church of Saint Peter at Caniano with all its appurtenances; and [Col. 1250B] whatever you possess in the county of Senigallia; the monastery of Castagnola; the church of Saint Mary of Remorta with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Stephen at Lemiciano; the church of Saint Sergius; the church of Saint Cassian; and whatever you possess in the bishopric of Jesi, with churches and appurtenances; the church of Saint Angelo at Casabie with its entire estate; the church of Saint Ariacus at Gaona with its entire estate; the church of Saint John at Palumbice with its entire estate; the church of Saint John of Agello with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Camorata; and whatever you possess in the counties of Ancona and Osimo.

Certainly, no one may presume to exact from you tithes of your newly cultivated lands, which you cultivate by your own hands [Col. 1250C] or at your own expense, or of the increase of your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laypersons fleeing from the world, free and absolved, and retain them without any objection. Moreover, we forbid that any of your brethren, after making profession in the same place, may leave it without the permission of his abbot; and no one may dare retain one who departs without letters of authorization from the community.

When a general interdict of the land is in force, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, without ringing bells, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, and in a low voice. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it by any craft of deceit or violence, [Col. 1250D] except one whom the brethren, by common consent or the sounder part of the brethren, shall determine to elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

Furthermore, we decree that the burial-place of your monastery shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted; saving, however, the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Moreover, we hold valid by apostolic authority, decree that it shall remain in force in future times, and confirm by this present privilege, the constitution made and authenticated in a formal document by our dearest son in Christ Frederick, the illustrious ever-august emperor of the Romans, concerning the non-alienation of the monastery’s possessions or revenues by those who hold them in your name. [Col. 1251A]

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain or diminish what has been removed, or harass it with any vexations whatever; but that all things be preserved secure and whole for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, to their benefit in every way, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

**Help us, O God, our Saviour.**

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. [Col. 1251B] I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Vivian, cardinal-priest of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Laborans, cardinal-priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Callixtus. I, Pandulf, cardinal-priest of the title of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, James, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Bobo, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo. I, Octavian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Soffredus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. [Col. 1251C] I, Albinus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary the New.

Given at Veroli, through the hand of Albert, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 27 April, in the second indiction, in the year 1184 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

### CXXXVIII–CXXXIX. He receives the church of Caput Ursuli under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Veroli, 4 May.)

[MURATORI, *Italian Antiquities*, III, 1179.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, priest and rector of the church of Caput Ursuli: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We are moved by the benevolence of the Apostolic See and prompted by the duty of the office entrusted to us to cherish venerable places with paternal affection and to grant them the safeguard of apostolic protection against assaults by evil men. Therefore, after the example of Pope Paschal, our predecessor of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify by the patronage of this document, the house over which, by God’s agency, you are known to preside, together with everything which you now reasonably possess. We decree that whatever goods have been offered to that house by the sons of Gualandus, Theodoric and Groffolellus; by Ranerius and Gottolus, sons of Gotto; by Heigo and Theodoric, sons of Bennus; by Bernard and Henry, sons of Bennus; by Rudolf and Ildebrandinus, sons of Ildebrand; [Col. 1252A] or by any faithful persons, and whatever may hereafter be offered, shall remain peacefully, whole, and unimpaired in the possession of that house, for the benefit of pilgrims and the poor.

We also forbid anyone to assault that house, rashly disturb it, plunder its goods, or presume to alienate them in any manner. Therefore no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our protection or rashly oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he shall incur the indignation of almighty God and of his apostles, the blessed Peter and Paul.

Given at Veroli, 4 May.

### CXL. He lists the possessions of the collegiate church of Blessed Mary at Bruges and confirms them by apostolic privilege. (Veroli, 4 May.)

[MIRAEUS, *Diplomatic Works*, II, 977.]

[Col. 1252B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GILBERT, provost of Saint Mary of Bruges, and his brethren, present and future, canonically appointed: in perpetuity.

The granting of due effect to just petitioners is required both by the strength of equity and by the order of reason, especially when piety assists the petitioners’ desire and truth does not abandon it.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, [Col. 1252C] after the example of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory; and we fortify it by the privilege of this document. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grant of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: the church of Sijsele with its tithes and other appurtenances; the rents that your people pay to you annually; and the grant made by Balderic, bishop of Noyon of good memory, to your parish church of Saint Mary, situated near the town of Bruges. Following in the footsteps of our predecessors of happy memory, Popes Paschal and Alexander, we confirm this grant by apostolic authority: namely, that the altar of Blessed Mary, as our predecessor decreed, shall be free from every exaction.

The canons established there shall have canonical and free authority, as expressed in the canons, to elect their own provost—such authority as canons are known to have when they elect a provost either from their own church or from another. The bishop shall assign to him the spiritual care of the canons and oversight of their temporal substance. He, however, shall receive both offices from the bishop and render him canonical reverence [Col. 1253A] and subjection in respect of both.

When a general interdict of the land is in force, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, without ringing bells, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, and in a low voice.

Furthermore, we decree that the burial-place of your church shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted; saving, however, the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Moreover, we hold valid the liberties, immunities, and reasonable customs hitherto observed in your church, and decree that they shall remain in force in future times.

[Col. 1253B] We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain or diminish what has been removed, or harass it with any vexations whatever; but that all things be preserved whole for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, to their benefit in every way, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. [Col. 1253C] I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Vinciamus, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Hill. I, Laborans, cardinal-priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Callixtus. I, Isandus, cardinal-priest of the title of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, James, deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Bobo, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Soffredus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. [Col. 1253D] I, Albinus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary the New.

Given at Veroli, through the hand of Albert, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 4 May, in the second indiction, in the year 1184 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

### CXLI. Statute concerning the oath of officeholders regarding residence. (Veroli, 4 May.)

[PETIT, *The Penitential of Theodore*, p. 453.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons G., dean, and the canons of the Church of Chartres: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1254A] When measures have been established for the benefit of churches which are not contrary to reason, they ought to be fortified by apostolic sanction, lest anyone’s rashness presume to violate them. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority the statute established in your chapter, with the common counsel of the brethren, by J., your bishop of good memory: namely, that whoever thereafter received a benefice or office in your church must swear in chapter to reside within your city. Those to whom the benefices and offices of your church have subsequently been conferred are said to be bound by this oath. Since this statute was reasonably enacted and has hitherto been observed without objection for the benefit of that church, we confirm it by apostolic authority. [Col. 1254B] We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he shall incur the indignation of almighty God and of his apostles, the blessed Peter and Paul.

Given at Veroli, 4 May.

### CXLII. He confirms the agreement of Guichard, archbishop of Lyon. (Veroli, 6 May.)

[JUENIN, *New History of Tournus*, Documents, p. 179.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the prior and brethren of the house of Balgiac: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1254C] [lacuna] Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, concurring with your just petitions in favourable assent, we confirm by apostolic authority, and fortify with the patronage of this document, the agreement and settlement made by Guichard, formerly archbishop of Lyon of good memory, concerning the dispute long conducted between your house and Peter, precentor and custodian of Saint Stephen, over the parochial right of the castle of Balgiac; insofar as that settlement and agreement was reasonably made, accepted by both parties, and contained in an authentic document. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly [Col. 1254D] oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he shall incur the indignation of almighty God and of his apostles, the blessed Peter and Paul.

Given at Veroli, 6 May.

### CXLIII. He confirms the possessions of the monastery of Laët. (Veroli, 6 May.)

[REIFFENBERG, *Monuments*, VII, 643.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HELGOT, abbot of the monastery of Laët, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Whenever a request is made to us, etc. Therefore, etc., decreeing that whatever possessions or goods [Col. 1255A] the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire by grant of pontiffs, gifts of kings and princes, etc.

Given at Veroli, through the hand of Albert, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 6 May, in the second indiction, in the year 1184, in the third year of the pontificate of the aforesaid Pope Lucius III.

### CXLIV. He receives the monastery of Capey under protection and confirms its possessions. (Veroli, 6 May.)

[D. MARRIER, *History of Saint Martin of the Fields*, 341.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ROBERT, prior of the monastery of Capey, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular [Col. 1255B] life: in perpetuity.

To grant effect to just requests is demanded both by the force of equity and by the order of reason, especially when piety supports the will of the petitioners and truth does not abandon it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of this present writing, the aforesaid monastery in which you are devoted to the divine service. We decree that whatever possessions, whatever goods, the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, with the Lord’s help, acquire by grant of pontiffs, gift of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The church of St. Medard at Capy, and a third part of the tithe of that castle, and whatever you possess there. The altar-right of Longueval, a third part of the tithe of that place, and whatever you possess there. The right and possession which Geoffrey the cleric, son of Matthew of Péronne, a distinguished man, held in the altar-right of Clary, together with the part of the tithe which you possess there and whatever you possess in that same place. One prebend in the church of St. Fursey in the castle of Péronne, by donation of Count Ralph of Vermandois. The altar-right of Framerville, with a third part of the tithe and whatever you possess there. The altar-right of Vauvillers, with the third part and the tithe and the land and court that you possess there. The altar-right of Old Amiens, free and exempt from every customary due, and whatever you possess there in tithe or land. The land of Rémécourt and whatever you possess there. The land of Foucaucourt and whatever you possess there. The allod of Choinnoles, its tenants, and whatever you possess there. The altar-right of Mames and whatever you possess in the tithe of that place. Whatever you possess in the tithe of Carnay. The altar-right of Fontaines, with the court and whatever you possess there. Twenty solidi annually for the lighting of the church, to be collected at Péronne from the merchants’ toll, commonly called *Guionagium*, and paid on the feast of St. Remigius, by gift of Ralph, count of Vermandois, and his wife Adelaide. The land called St. Cornelius’s, subject to payment of a rent of five solidi. Sixty solidi of Arras currency. At Warneston, three *bonucria* of land, by gift of Peter, knight of Capy, with the assent and consent of his wife Eva and their daughter Gila. [Col. 1255C–1256A]

Moreover, no one shall presume to exact tithes from you on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the produce of your animals. In the parish churches which you hold, you may choose priests and present them to the diocesan bishop; if they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust the care of souls to them, so that they shall answer to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters. You may also receive clerics or laymen who flee from the world, free and unencumbered, into conversion, and retain them without any opposition.

When a general interdict has been laid upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices with closed doors, without ringing bells, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, and in a low voice. Furthermore, no one shall presume, on his own authority and without authorization from the Roman pontiff, to subject the prior or monks to excommunication or interdict, as was established by Pope Lucius of blessed memory and other Roman pontiffs. But if, God forbid, violence should happen to be committed in your precinct—by bloodshed, assault, or anything of that kind—your church shall by no means on that account be prohibited from divine offices. [Col. 1256B]

Moreover, we decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who have chosen to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted; nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken are reserved.

Furthermore, we prohibit anyone from presuming, without your consent, to build a chapel or oratory within the bounds of your parishes, saving the privileges of the Roman Church. We also establish that, if the prior appointed from time to time in your church should judge it appropriate to entrust for a time the prebend which you are to have in the church of St. Fursey at Péronne to a suitable person who will serve there continually, that person shall receive the whole fruits, as do others who serve continually. [Col. 1256C–D]

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars, ordinations of clerics, and the other ecclesiastical sacraments from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, is in the grace and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide them to you freely and without any improper demand. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, and he, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. We hold valid the liberties, immunities, and reasonable customs hitherto observed in your church, and decree that they shall remain unimpaired in future times.

Moreover, wishing in paternal solicitude to provide henceforth for your peace and tranquillity, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone from daring, within the enclosures of your houses or your granges, to commit theft, set fire, seize, or kill a person. By the same apostolic authority we further prohibit any bishop from holding stations in your church or celebrating public masses without your consent, lest the simplicity of monastic discipline—which ought to be fostered by church prelates—be disturbed by popular tumults. [Col. 1257A]

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole and intact, for the complete benefit of the uses for which they were granted, namely the governance and support of those concerned, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the due reverence owed to the monastery of Cluny and the church of St. Martin-des-Champs. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person shall knowingly attempt in future rashly to act against this page of our constitution, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make amends for the offence by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and office, acknowledge himself or herself answerable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and be subject to divine vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. [Col. 1257B–C]

Given at Veroli, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the second day before the Nones of May, in the second indiction, in the year 1184 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

### CXLV. He confirms the privileges, immunities, and possessions of the canons of St. Ursus of Aosta. (Veroli, 7 May.)

*[Historiae Patriae Monumenta, Chartae, I, 930.]*

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ULRICH, prior of St. Peter and St. Ursus of Aosta, and the canons of the same church, present and future, professing the canonical life: in perpetuity.

The office of the government entrusted to us invites us to assent to religious vows and to fulfill them by effective action; the order of reason seems to demand it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of this present writing, the aforesaid church in which you are devoted to divine service. First, we decree that the canonical order, known to have been established in that church according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine, shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, with God’s help, acquire by grant of pontiffs, gift of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the churches of St. Mary and St. Peter of Château-Argent, with their appurtenances; the church of St. Alban of Mosterio, with all its appurtenances; the church of St. Lawrence of Mount Girolt, with its tithes and appurtenances; the church of St. Ursus of Conia, with its tithes and appurtenances; the church of St. Stephen of Grazano, with its tithes and appurtenances; the church of St. Martin of Varaia, with its tithes and appurtenances; the church of the Holy Saviour of Valesia, with its appurtenances; the church of St. James of Ussonia and the place of Stillano, with their appurtenances; the church of St. John of Quarto; the church of St. Andrew of Pavone, with its tithes and appurtenances; the church of Salugia, with its tithes and appurtenances; and the church of St. Paul of Verzel, near the Sesia, with its appurtenances. [Col. 1258A–B]

Moreover, no one shall presume to exact tithes from you on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the produce of your animals. You may receive clerics or laymen who flee from the world, free and unencumbered, into conversion, and retain them without any opposition.

Furthermore, we prohibit any of the brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving it without permission of his prior, except in pursuit of a stricter religious life; and no one shall dare retain one who leaves without letters of authorization from the community. When a general interdict has been laid upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices with closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a low voice. In the parish churches which you hold, you may choose priests and present them to the diocesan bishop; if they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust the care of souls to them, so that they may answer to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters. [Col. 1258C–D]

We also decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who have chosen to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted; nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken are reserved. On the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be put in charge there by any deceitful contrivance or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall determine ought to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine.

We also forbid anyone to give personally, or otherwise alienate, churches, lands, or any benefice conferred upon your church without the consent of the whole chapter or of its greater and sounder part. If any gifts or alienations are made otherwise than has been stated, we judge them void. [Col. 1259A]

Furthermore, no canons or lay brothers bound by profession in your house may, without the consent and permission of the prior and the greater and sounder part of your chapter, stand surety for anyone or borrow money from anyone beyond the amount provided by the foresight of their chapter, except for a manifest benefit to your house. If they presume to do so, the community, without whose permission and consent they acted, shall not be bound in any way to answer for it. [Col. 1259B]

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid churches, take away their possessions, retain what has been taken, or harass them by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved for the complete benefit of the uses for which they were granted, namely the governance and support of those concerned, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person shall in future, etc.

Farewell.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Susanna, have subscribed. I, Vuccanus, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill, have subscribed. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Callixtus, have subscribed. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina, have subscribed. I, Henry, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Paul, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, James, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, Ardicio, deacon-cardinal of St. Theodore, have subscribed. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Ottonianus, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. [Col. 1259C–D]

Given at Veroli, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the Nones of May, in the second indiction, in the year 1184 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

### CXLVI. Bull for the chapter of St. Martin of Tours. (Veroli, 28 May.)

*[Défense des priviléges de Saint-Martin de Tours, p. 24.]*

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the dean, treasurer, and chapter of Blessed Martin of Tours: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since your church belongs directly to the Apostolic See, you fear that, if we delegate to our venerable brother the archbishop of Tours cases brought against it, he may seek, by occasion of the delegation, to claim permanent jurisdiction over you. Therefore, desiring in accordance with our office to provide for your liberty, we grant you by apostolic authority that, if any letters against your church have been obtained addressed to the aforesaid archbishop, or shall hereafter be sought, you may, by apostolic permission, refuse him. Let no person whatsoever therefore infringe this page of our concession or rashly act against it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul. [Col. 1260A–B]

Given at Veroli, five days before the Kalends of June.

### CXLVII. Bull for the church of St. Martin of Tours. (Veroli, 28 May.)

*[Ibid.]*

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PHILIP, dean, Ro., treasurer, and the chapter of St. Martin of Tours: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to effect the prayers which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, joining your just petitions with favourable assent, we grant you full authority and confer upon you the power, without impediment from appeal, to withdraw the benefices which persons are known to hold in the name of that church from those who have promised fidelity and also confirmed by oath that they will abide by the judgment of your chapter according to the customs of your church, if they refuse to fulfill what they have sworn to you, until they make suitable satisfaction. Confirming also by apostolic authority the liberties, dignities, and approved customs of your church, we decree that they shall remain unimpaired and whole. Let no person whatsoever therefore infringe this page of our concession and confirmation or rashly act against it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul. [Col. 1260C–D]

Given at Veroli, five days before the Kalends of June.

### CXLVIII. Bull for the chapter of St. Martin of Tours. (Veroli, 28 May.)

*[Ibid.]*

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PHILIP, dean, Ro., treasurer, and the chapter of St. Martin of Tours: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more particularly your church is known to belong to the right and property of the Apostolic See, the more incumbent it is upon us to provide that the integrity of its peace and liberty may continually remain in its full strength, and that its status may not more dishonourably suffer any loss of its rights through the wickedness of unlawful innovation. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting to your just petitions, we decree that the ancient dignity of that church shall remain in its established condition according to what is contained in the privileges of Roman pontiffs and kings, and we confirm it by apostolic authority.

By the common counsel of our brethren, we establish that all common oaths or conspiracy which your burgesses of Châteauneuf have made under the designation of a commune or a common oath, by whatever name it may be called, are void and null; and that their principal authors, together with their supporters, shall be bound by the bond of anathema if they refuse to abjure them. We also decree void the oath by which the people had rashly bound themselves to those persons, and order that it shall not be observed; nevertheless, they shall make satisfaction by worthy penance for the rashness of that oath, because they made it against the Church of God with condemnable presumption. This is especially so because through it the liberty of the Church would be lost, and in matters known to belong to its jurisdiction many things would frequently occur contrary to the order of law and the justice hitherto observed.
