## CLXVI. Privilege for the Church of Magdeburg.  
*(Verona, 25 October.)*

[**Origin. Guelf.**, Preface, p. XXV.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WICHMANN, archbishop of Magdeburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Attentive to the duty of our office, by which we are bound to all in granting what they worthily request, we give special thought to ensuring that those who are called with us to share the burden of solicitude may always and everywhere receive welcome assistance from the fullness of our authority. Therefore, beloved brother in the Lord, commending with fitting praise in the Lord the zeal of your charity, by which you are known to have provided so beneficially for the church entrusted to you that you are deservedly to be held worthy of commendation in the Lord, we willingly assent to your just petitions. We confirm by apostolic authority to that church, and fortify by the privilege of this present writing, the castle of Seburg which you have conferred upon it together with the rest of the inheritance; decreeing that Sumersemburg also with its appurtenances, and Juterburg with its dependencies, and the other possessions and estates which the zeal and industry of your solicitude have acquired for the aforesaid Church of Magdeburg, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you, and shall not be separated from its lordship and ownership by any rash alteration.

[Note: [Col. 1287D] The pope uses so mild an expression that he attributes even the enrichment of churches with the spoils of others to the zeal and [Col. 1288D] industry of episcopal solicitude. Yet, to say this in passing, the sons of Henry the Lion did not acquiesce in this decree, nor did they believe it sufficient to confirm the archbishop’s unjust possession. Rather, since they knew it to be a principle of natural law that things unjustly taken may at any time be reclaimed from an unjust possessor, the fact that they expressly counted the castle of Summerseburg among their own possessions is proved, among other documents, by the charter of partition presented elsewhere; for we are taught that it belonged to Otto IV’s hereditary share.

Nor should you suppose that they were herein disobedient or violators of papal commands. For the clause, “if the petitions rest upon truth”—which, by the nature of the case, inheres in all papal rescripts—had rendered these very artifices of Wichmann null from their first beginnings, immediately and by operation of law. Henry the Lion, whose hide was being played with in the tale, had neither been heard, nor had any just title by which that occupation might be consolidated been alleged in judgment; rather, all had been done tumultuously by Wichmann, and thus the papal confirmation itself had, in the language of jurists, been obtained by suppression and surreption.

The image is indeed a jeu d’esprit, arising more from ingenuity than from the truth of the matter, when the provinces plundered and despoiled from Henry the Lion are represented by a picture of a horse torn to pieces and stripped of flesh. Yet it presents a most truthful spectacle: on one side ecclesiastics, on the other certain secular magnates, wonderfully enriched by these spoils. Since the picture is not recent, one need not fear that he who recounted Henninges’s explanation in order more rightly to divine its meaning would appear to have written a satire. But because those epigrams are utterly without wit, we shall explain the depicted panel in our own fewest words.

On the right side are seen the possessions claimed by: 1. the Archbishop of Mainz (although Henninges’s opinion is false that Eichsfeld had already been acquired by the archbishop out of the Lion’s spoils); 2. the Archbishop of Cologne; 3. the Bishop of Paderborn; 4. the Bishops of Bremen and Verden; 5. the Bishops of Halberstadt and Magdeburg (who are nevertheless incorrectly joined in a single person, since each separately increased his resources greatly from this calamity); 6. the Bishop of Hildesheim; 7. the Bishop of Minden; 8. the Bishop of Lübeck (although, since those advantages resulting from Henry the Lion’s proscription accrued not so much to the bishop as to the city—which, having now acquired self-rule, began to be subject to the Emperor, or to the duke through an intermediary—it is less correctly included among the spoils of sacred-order bishops [Col. 1290D]).

On the left side are represented the possessions that devolved upon secular magnates. Thus appear here the arms of: 1. the princes of Anhalt or Ascania, from whom came Bernard, the first Duke of Saxony after Henry the Lion; 2. Brunswick (which, however, is quite ridiculous, since the Brunswick line descended from Henry the Lion and did not grow through his misfortune); 3. Bavaria, or more properly Schyren; 4. the Palatinate (again, however, by a manifest error, since the Palatinate was taken not from Henry the Lion but from his son); 5. Holstein; 6. Meissen; 7. Hesse (although that house had not yet then arisen, while the Landgraves of Thuringia still survived); 8. Goslar. But let what has been said concerning Henninges’s riddle suffice. Since it explains the matter less accurately and altogether omits much that ought also to be said, I would not have repeated it had I not thought the figure reproduced in a copperplate engraving should be illustrated by a brief word.] 

That these may be observed more cautiously in all future times, we decree by the present constitution that whoever succeeds you in the archiepiscopal dignity shall, upon receiving the pallium, give a special undertaking that he may not, without the licence of the Apostolic See and the counsel of the greater and sounder part of the chapter, alienate under any title those things left by you or found among the ancient possessions of the church; but that he shall always keep and defend them in good faith for the benefit of the Church of Magdeburg.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatever to infringe this page of our confirmation and constitution, or in any way to oppose it. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowingly, rashly attempts to act against this page of our constitution, then, having been warned a second and a third time, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance.

But let all who observe it have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action, and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. [Col. 1289C] I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence, have subscribed. [Col. 1290A] I, Laborans, cardinal priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber and of Saint Callixtus. I, Hubert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, Paul, cardinal priest of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Conrad, Bishop of Sabina and Archbishop of the See of Mainz. I, Theodinus, Bishop of Porto and of the See of Saint Rufina. I, Henry, Bishop of Albano. I, Theobald, Bishop of Ostia and of the Church of Saint Velletri. I, Ardicio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. [Col. 1290B] I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Soffredus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Albinus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary Nova.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Hugh, notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November [25 October], in the third indiction, in the year 1184 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

## CLXVII. Privilege for the monastery of Saints Peter and Paul at Münster.  
*(Verona, 28 October.)*

[HUNDIUS, *Metropolis of Salzburg*, II, 521.]

[Col. 1290C]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HARTWIC, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter situated in the [Col. 1291A] place called Münster, and his brethren, both present and future, to be regularly appointed, for ever.

It befits us to grant assent to just wishes and to lend our ears to just petitions, since, though unworthy, we are seen, by the Lord’s disposition, to have been placed as guardians and heralds of justice upon the lofty watchtower of the chief apostles Peter and Paul. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Hartwic, we grant assent to your petitions with the affection due to charity; and, receiving under the guardianship and protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of Blessed Peter over which, by God’s authority, you preside, we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing.

First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order established there according to the Rule of Saint Benedict shall be observed inviolate for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions or goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire, by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: namely, two parts of the tithes and offerings from the two parishes of Altenhoven and Menching, which are known to belong to the aforesaid monastery.

Moreover, concerning your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, and concerning the produce of your animals, no one shall presume to exact tithes from you. [Col. 1291C] We further forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in your house, to depart from your cloister without his abbot’s licence; and no one shall dare to retain one who has departed without documentary assurance from the community.

We also prohibit anyone, under pretext of advocacy, wickedly to harass your monastery or persons belonging to it, or to vex them with unjust exactions. In the parish churches which you possess, you may choose three or four priests; nevertheless, they shall be presented to the diocesan bishop, in order that they may receive from him the care of souls, and shall be accountable to him in spiritual matters, but to you in temporal matters and in observance of the order. [Col. 1291D] Upon the death of you, the present abbot of this place, or of any of your successors, no person shall be placed there by any artifice of deception or violence, save one whom the brethren by unanimous consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, shall provide to be elected.

We also decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, without prejudice to the rights of the mother church.

We therefore decree that no person whatever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things [Col. 1292A] shall be kept whole and intact, to be of every benefit for the uses for which they were granted—for the governance and support of those concerned—without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, etc.

SAINT PETER, SAINT PAUL.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Callixtus. I, Hubert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, Theodinus, Bishop of Porto and of the See of Saint Rufina. [Col. 1292B] I, Henry, Bishop of Albano.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Hugh, notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November [28 October], third indiction, in the year of the Lord 1184, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

## CLXVIII. He receives the Church of Feltre under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges, at the request of Bishop Drudo.  
*(Verona, 29 October.)*

[VERCI, *History of the Trevisan and Veronese March*, vol. I, p. 33.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother DRUDO, Bishop of Feltre, and his successors [Col. 1292C] canonically appointed, for ever.

Placed by the Lord’s disposal upon the watchtower of the Apostolic See, we ought to love our brethren, whether near or far, with brotherly charity, and to provide with paternal solicitude for the churches committed to them by God. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, bishop, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following the example of Anastasius, our predecessor of happy memory, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of the present writing, the Church of Feltre, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same Church now justly and canonically possesses, [Col. 1292D] or that you may in future acquire, by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The possessions which you have at Pergino, Levigo, Calcedraniga, Lavaron, and Ravesia; Suvia, Alsugo, Tongeno, and throughout the whole valley of Sugana, both in castles and in villages belonging to the church; at Grino, in the meadow of Imolano, at Crivulis—which you possess in the Brenta canal; the possessions which you have at Lamone; at Primerio, with every right which you have there; the possessions which you have in the parish of Arsedi, in the parish of Fungasi, and in the parish of Sini; and in all villages [Col. 1293A] situated on the plain of the city of Feltre; the possessions which you have beyond the river Cantani, with the castle of Tocho in the parish of Ceto, in the parish of Formicano, and whatever you possess in the valley of Belluno with the right which you have in the Plavis canal, in the mountains as well as in the plains; the possessions and rights which you have at Masserio, with the castle of the same place, the possessions of Malzagi, and all other things which you have in the county of Tar. [uncertain abbreviation]; and whatever right you have in the city of Feltre, Soro, and other places, with lands, buildings, vineyards, meadows, pastures, fields, woods, courts, waters and watercourses, mills, fisheries, mountains, valleys, cultivated and uncultivated grazing lands; with the toll of Saint Victor and of All Saints, with the toll of Cuvoli on the Brenta, and of the city of Soro.

We also decree that whatever King Conrad of good memory justly granted to your church and confirmed by the text of his authentic charter shall remain ratified and unshaken for ever. We further prohibit anyone from presuming to retain or harbour this church’s own servants against the will of the bishop of that place. Furthermore, we ratify the liberties and immunities reasonably granted to your church by our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, Emperor of the Romans, as is more fully contained in his authentic charter; and we decree that they shall remain unimpaired in future times.

We therefore decree that no person whatever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its [Col. 1293C] possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all shall be kept intact, to be of every benefit for the uses for which they were granted—for the governance and support of those concerned—without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the due reverence owed to the Patriarch of Aquileia. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber. I, Ubertus, cardinal priest of the title of Jerusalem in Damaso. I, Pandulfus, cardinal priest of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve [Col. 1293D] Apostles. I, Theodinus, Bishop of Porto and of the See of Saint Rufina. I, Henry, Bishop of Albano. I, Theobald, Bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Arditio, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Sofredus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Albinus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary Nova.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Hugh, notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November [29 October], in the third indiction, in the year 1184 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

## CLXIX. He confirms the privileges and possessions of Corvey Abbey.  
*(Verona, 29 October.)*

[FALKE, *Codex Traditionum Corbeiensium*, p. 741.]

[Col. 1294A]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons CONRAD, Abbot of Corvey, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

The requirement of justice and the kindness of the Apostolic See demand that we extend more abundantly the hand of our protection to persons and places especially attached to Blessed Peter and more devoutly remaining in fidelity and obedience to the Holy Roman Church, and that with due kindness we preserve for them their rights and the dignities conferred upon them. Therefore, beloved son in Christ, Conrad, Abbot of Corvey, attentively considering the devotion which you bear toward the Apostolic See, we too wish, by the Lord’s favour, that the dignity handed down to your predecessors through the privileges of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, shall remain unimpaired.

Accordingly, by the authority of this decree, we grant you the right, on principal solemnities, to use sandals and a dalmatic, to sit beside the altar, and to instruct the people within the monastery committed to you or in the conventual priories in matters pertaining to the salvation of souls. Furthermore, by the grace of God and the Apostolic See, we grant in perpetuity to you and your successors the use of the mitre and ring on those same solemnities, as it was granted to your predecessors by the Roman pontiffs.

Moreover, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of this present writing, the monastery of Corvey itself, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, [Col. 1294C] or may in the future acquire by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

Namely, the tithe from the estate of Luithardessen; the tithe from the estate of Beneringen; the tithe from the estate of Dasborg; the tithe from the estate of Mulenhusen; the tithe from the estate of Heldorp; the tithe from the estate of Munden; the tithe from the estate of Boderike; the tithe from the estate of Munichusen; the tithe from the estate of Bederinkhusen; the tithe from the estate of Wlnelage; the tithe from the estate of Homburstelde; the tithe from the estate of Nienstede; the tithe from the estate of Wolkmarese; the tithe from the estate of Luithmaresun; the tithe from the estate of Luitheressen; the tithe from the estate of Erclen; the tithe from the estate of Brumelinktorp; the tithe from the estate of Leziaci; the tithe from the estate of Castinaci; the tithe from the estate of Hostepe; the tithe from the estate of Nuthlon; the tithe from the estate of Keflikc; the tithe from the estate of Nen; the tithe from the estate of Croppenstide; the tithe from the estate of Hemmenthorp; the tithe from the estate of [Col. 1295A] Holthusen; and the tithe from the estate of Gruminge.

In Frisia, a possession called Nerthen; and at the same place the church of Linguord; the island of Rumena; and the fishery of Hocwar. We also grant that no one may alter or take away, without the common consent of the brethren, any arrangement which you have already made or shall hereafter make in your memory, or which others have established before you or shall establish after you. We further decree that any abbot who grants in benefice to anyone the castle of Wilborg, which you are known to have fortified for the defence of the Church of Corvey, shall be bound by the bond of anathema until he comes to his senses.

We also enact that the monastery itself shall never, on any pretext, be granted in benefice to any person whatsoever, but shall always remain under the protection of the Roman pontiffs and the defence of emperors or kings. We add that the monastery of Heresburg, with the tithes around the mountain extending for two Saxon *rastae*, as they are known to have been first conferred by Pope Leo of blessed memory at the request of Charlemagne, who had captured that mountain; likewise the monastery at Groningen and the monastery at Keminata, shall never be alienated from the same monastery of Corvey. Rather, they shall always be governed by the abbot of that place and be rightly ordered under the Rule of monastic discipline. Nor shall anyone be permitted to alter, grant in benefice, or alienate anything from the goods of those three monasteries belonging to the use and provision of those serving the Lord there, [Col. 1295C] without the assent of the brethren living in those monasteries and with the approval of the chapter of Corvey.

We also will that the provostship of the clerics of the Church of Saint Paul, which is called the New Church, shall always remain, as hitherto, under the administration of the same Abbot of Corvey. Nor may the abbot or provost confer, exchange, or dispose of the prebends of the canons in benefice without the consent of the clerics. Furthermore, we decree that, within the circuit of the wall of the frequently mentioned monastery of Corvey, no cleric or layman shall at any time possess any dwelling by right of property or benefice; rather, the whole precinct of that place shall be available for the uses and dwellings of the abbot, monks, and other religious persons.

[Col. 1295D] We forbid any bishop, other than the Roman pontiff, to exercise any jurisdiction in that monastery, so that, unless invited by the abbot of that monastery, he may not presume even to celebrate the solemnities of Mass there. Therefore, in order that all these matters which we have stated above may have full force in the future, as they are contained in the authentic privileges of our predecessors, we confirm them by the authority of our favour both to you and to your successors.

We therefore decree that no person whatever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole and unimpaired, to be of every benefit for the uses for which they were granted—for the governance and support of those concerned—without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mary across the Tiber. I, Hubert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, Pandulfus, cardinal priest of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Conrad, Archbishop of the Sees of Sabina and Mainz. [Col. 1296B] I, Theodinus, Bishop of Porto and of the See of Saint Rufina. I, Henry, Bishop of Albano. I, Theobald, Bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Arditio, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Theodore. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Soffredus, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Albinus, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Mary Nova.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Hugh, notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November [29 October], in the third indiction, in the year 1184 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

## CLXX. Privilege for the Church of Saint Martin of Tours.  
*(Verona, 30 October.)*

[*Defence of the Church of Saint-Martin of Tours*, 25.]

[Col. 1296C]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother W[ILLIAM], Archbishop of Reims, cardinal of Saint Sabina, legate of the Apostolic See, and to his beloved son . . . abbot of Marmoutier, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When, some time ago, a complaint from the Church of Blessed Martin of Tours reached our hearing concerning a conspiracy which that Church alleged had been formed by the burgesses of Châteauneuf under the designation of a commune or common oath, we gave our beloved sons, the canons of that Church, free authority by apostolic power that, if any of the participants in that conspiracy, after being warned, refused to abjure it, they might, without appeal, bind them and their supporters with the bond of anathema.

But the canons, as the burgesses assert, are said to have exceeded the bounds of this concession and to have pronounced a sentence of anathema against persons insufficiently warned in accordance with canon law, although the burgesses were prepared—as they are said still to be—to observe the apostolic mandate. The canons, on the contrary, maintain that they proceeded to that sentence while observing the terms of the concession. Therefore, lest the absolution of those said to be bound should result in danger [lacuna], we will and firmly command that, after receiving from those held excommunicated sworn security that they will obey our mandate, you shall, strengthened by our authority and without appeal, release them from the bond of this sentence; and you shall cause their release to be publicly announced throughout the dioceses in which they were denounced as excommunicated.

Thereafter you shall diligently endeavour to restore peace between the aforesaid canons and burgesses. If peace cannot be achieved, you shall reasonably compel the aforesaid burgesses, notwithstanding any appeal, to obey our command in accordance with the form of the concession under whose authority the canons pronounced their sentence. If any among them deny that they took the oath concerning the aforesaid commune or conspiracy, whatever name it bears, they shall swear that they did not take that oath and that henceforth they will not be oath-takers. If they refuse to obey our mandate in these matters, then, without impediment of appeal, you shall more strictly compel them as contumacious persons by sentence of excommunication.

If they should decide to litigate between themselves concerning damages and injuries inflicted on either side, summon the parties, hear the case, and bring it to a canonical conclusion without appeal. If both of you cannot be present for the absolution and the announcement of absolution which we have directed, one of you and a messenger of the absent one bearing his letters shall nevertheless carry these measures out without appeal. But in the other articles, your colleague the archbishop shall not proceed without your presence, notwithstanding any letters that may have been obtained from the Apostolic See contrary to the tenor of these letters without the consent of the parties.

Given at Verona, on the third day before the Kalends of November [30 October].

## CLXXI. Decree against heretics.  
*(Verona? November?)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXII, 476.]

To abolish the perversity of the various heresies which in modern times have begun to spring up in many parts of the world, ecclesiastical vigour must be roused. For, with the power of imperial strength lending its support, both the obstinacy of heretics is crushed in the very attempts of its falsehood [variant: “in wicked falsehoods or attempts”], and the truth of Catholic simplicity, shining forth in the holy Church, shows that Church to have been cleansed from every abomination of false doctrines. Therefore, supported alike by the presence and power of our dearest son Frederick, illustrious Emperor of the Romans, ever Augustus, and with the common counsel of our brethren, as well as of other patriarchs, archbishops, and many princes assembled from various parts of the world, we rise by the general sanction of this present decree against those heretics, upon whom their profession of various falsehoods has bestowed various names [variant: “heads/chapters”]; and, by the authority of the Apostolic See, through the tenor of this constitution, we condemn every heresy, by whatever name it is called.

First, therefore, we decree that the Cathars, Patarines, and those who falsely call themselves the Humiliati or the Poor of Lyons, the Passagians, Josephites, and Arnoldists, shall be subject to perpetual anathema. And since some persons, under the appearance of piety, deny its power, as the Apostle says, and claim for themselves the authority to preach, although the same Apostle says, “How shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Romans 10), we bind with the same bond of perpetual anathema all who, having been forbidden or not sent, presume to preach publicly or privately without authority received from the Apostolic See or the bishop of the place; and all who are not afraid to think or teach concerning the sacrament of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, baptism, remission of sins, marriage, or the other ecclesiastical sacraments, otherwise than the most holy Roman Church preaches [Col. 1298B] and observes.

Likewise, we bind with the same bond all whom the Roman Church itself, or individual bishops in their dioceses with the counsel of their clergy, or the clergy themselves during a vacancy of the see, with the counsel—if need be—of neighbouring bishops, shall judge to be heretics. We decree that their receivers and defenders, and likewise all who furnish the aforesaid heretics with any protection or favour in order to foster in them the perversity of heresy—whether they are called *Consolati*, *Credentes*, *Perfecti*, or by any other superstitious names—shall be subject to the like sentence.

Since, however, as sins demand, it sometimes happens that the severity of ecclesiastical discipline is condemned by those who do not understand its power, we nevertheless enact by the present ordinance that whoever is manifestly found in the above-mentioned errors, if he is a cleric or is disguised under the guise of any religious order, shall be stripped of every prerogative of ecclesiastical rank. Thus deprived alike of every ecclesiastical office and benefice, he shall be left to the judgment of secular authority for punishment by due penalty, unless, immediately after the discovery of his error, he voluntarily returns to the unity of the Catholic faith, consents publicly to abjure his error at the discretion of the bishop of the region, and makes suitable satisfaction.

But a layman tainted by notorious or private guilt of any of the aforesaid pestilences, unless, as has been said, after abjuring heresy and making satisfaction, he promptly flees to the orthodox faith, shall be left to the judgment of the secular judge, to receive the due punishment according to the character of his crime.

Those found suspect on the Church’s suspicion alone, unless at the discretion of the bishop, according to the degree of suspicion and the standing of the person, they demonstrate their innocence by adequate purgation, shall be subject to the same sentence. But those who, after abjuring error or after clearing themselves, as we have said, by examination of their own bishop, are found to have relapsed into the heresy they abjured, we decree shall be handed over to secular judgment without any hearing whatever; the goods of the condemned shall be assigned, according to lawful enactments, to the churches which they served.

Moreover, we decree that the aforesaid excommunication, to which we desire all heretics to be subject, shall be renewed by all patriarchs, archbishops, and bishops on the principal feasts, whenever they hold solemnities, or on any occasion, for the glory of God and the condemnation of heretical perversity. By apostolic authority we establish that if any member of the episcopal order is found negligent or remiss in these matters, he shall be held suspended from episcopal dignity and administration for three years.

Furthermore, at the episcopal counsel and suggestion of the imperial majesty and its princes, we have added that every archbishop or bishop, personally or through his archdeacon or other honourable and suitable persons, shall once or twice yearly make a circuit of any parish in which there is a report that heretics live. There he shall compel three or more men of good repute—or, if it seems expedient, the entire neighbourhood—to swear that, if anyone knows heretics to be there, or knows any persons holding secret conventicles or differing from the common way of life and conduct of the faithful, he shall endeavour to report them to the bishop or archdeacon.

The bishop or archdeacon shall summon the accused before him. Unless they clear themselves of the charge at his discretion according to the custom of the country, or if, after having made such purgation, they relapse into their former perfidy, they shall be punished by the judgment of the bishops. If any of them, rejecting an oath out of damnable superstition, happen to refuse to swear, they shall thereby be judged heretics and struck with the penalties named above.

We further establish that counts, barons, governors, and consuls of cities and other places, upon the admonition of archbishops and bishops, shall promise under bodily oath that, whenever called upon in this regard, they will strongly and effectively assist the Church against heretics and their accomplices in all the matters aforesaid. They shall also endeavour in good faith, according to their office and ability, to put into execution both ecclesiastical and imperial enactments concerning the matters we have described. If they refuse to observe this, they shall be stripped of the office which they hold and shall by no means be admitted to others; moreover, they shall be bound by excommunication and their lands subjected to an interdict of the Church.

Any city that decides to resist these decretal ordinances, or that neglects, contrary to the bishop’s admonition, to punish those who resist, shall be deprived of commerce with other cities and shall know that it is deprived of episcopal dignity.

We decree also that all supporters of heretics, as persons condemned to perpetual infamy, shall be excluded from advocacy, testimony, and all other public offices. If there are any who, exempt from the law of diocesan jurisdiction, are subject only to the power of the Apostolic See, they shall nevertheless submit to the judgment of archbishops or bishops in those measures established above against heretics, and in this matter shall obey them as delegates of the Apostolic See, notwithstanding the privileges of their liberty.

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, V, 76.]

[Col. 1300B]

I, Ubertus, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Lawrence in Damaso. I, Pandulphus, priest-cardinal of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Ardicio, deacon-cardinal of St. Theodore. Given at Verona, through the hand of Ugo, notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Ides of November, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1184, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Lucius III, pope.

CLXXIII. To the chapter of Rouen.—He receives favorably the election of the bishop of Lincoln as archbishop of Rouen. (Verona, Nov. 17.)

[MARTEN, *Anecdota*, I, 622.]

[Col. 1300D]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the dean and chapter of Rouen: greeting and apostolic blessing.

You sent to us our beloved sons Master Hubert, archdeacon of Évreux, and Elias, canons of your church. We received them with that honor which it was fitting to show, both in view of your devotion and of their own worthiness. We received their petitions with due kindness and, insofar as we were able according to God and justice, brought what they desired to its effect. Indeed, we have gladly accepted the election of our venerable brother, the bishop of Lincoln, duly celebrated by the unanimous consent of your whole body, [Col. 1301A] granting our assent the more readily because we love the person of the said bishop with a warmer affection and, by the Lord’s authority, are especially concerned to provide for his advancement and honor.

At your urgent request, we have arranged for the pallium, the fullness of the pontifical office, to be sent through our beloved son Hubald, our subdeacon. Receive, therefore, the aforesaid Hubald, whom we hold exceedingly dear and welcome, with kindly affection; for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves, render him the honor due to him; and hold him especially commended to you.

[Col. 1301B] Given at Verona, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December.

CLXXIV. To the abbots of the Cistercian Order he grants “that absolutely no one may pronounce against them, their monasteries, or the brethren established there, a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict; nor may abbots be compelled to make any profession.” (Verona, Nov. 21.)

[MANRIQUE, *Annales Cistercienses*, III, 131.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot of Cîteaux and all his fellow abbots serving the Lord under the same order: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The integrity of monastic discipline, which the providence of the eternal Creator has restored in the purity [Col. 1301C] of the order which you maintain, has always found in the Apostolic See that mercy by which your purpose of virtue might grow in the Lord and the devotion of others might be stirred by your examples, so that through the path of heavenly commandments it might hasten successfully toward the proposed prize. Yet, among other things, although your order has maintained itself subject to bishops with such humility that, while preserving its original institutions, it has always wished to submit to their direction, it has nevertheless hitherto obtained from the favor and protection of the Apostolic See that no one should pronounce any ecclesiastical sentence against the monasteries or abbots of the said order, or burden persons established in that order by a promulgation of excommunication, [Col. 1301D] suspension, or interdict.

But since, as the charity of many grows cold, wickedness is known to have so abounded that some of those who in these times are set over the Churches of God transgress the boundaries established by their predecessors, and do not hesitate especially to inflict undue punishment upon your order, by this present letter we decree and confirm by apostolic authority that absolutely no one may pronounce against you, your monasteries, or the brethren established there, contrary to what is known to have been observed from the beginning of the order, a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict. If such a sentence has been pronounced, we decree by apostolic authority that it shall have no force.

Moreover, we decree [Col. 1302A] that, in receiving the professions offered by abbots already blessed or to be blessed, archbishops and bishops shall be content with the form and wording known to have been established from the beginning of the order: namely, that the abbots themselves must make profession, with their order preserved, and must not be compelled to make any profession contrary to the institutions of the order. Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our constitution and confirmation, or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Verona, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December, in the third year of the pontificate of the same Lord Pope Lucius.

CLXXV. Privilege for the congregation of Verona. (Verona, Nov. 22.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, V, 801.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons SICHERIUS, archpriest of the congregation of Verona, and his brethren, present and future, forever.

“Whenever,” etc., “may remain inviolate.” Among these, we have thought fit to specify for you in express terms the following: land at the castle of Victor; land of Roverina; land of Piscantina; land of Bondi; land of Valdesassa; land of Casana; land of Avera; land of Saxi; land [Col. 1302C] of Subcleva; land of St. Mary in the Stars; land of Polana; land of Montisauri; land of Novalis; land of Illasi; land of Calegnola; land of Porcilli; the land of Pupeclara with its tithes; land of Leniaci; Maralisca with all its jurisdiction; Cavaredum with its tithe; the church of St. George with its appurtenances; the church of All Saints with its appurtenances; the church of St. Mark with its appurtenances; the church of Saints James and Philip with its appurtenances; land of Tumula; and the land which is at the Cross of Maratica.

Since rights of justice are known to have been granted to churches both in the old and in the new law, we forbid, under threat of anathema, that any layman should presume to exact tithes from you. We further forbid anyone to dare to promulgate against you [Col. 1302D] or your churches a sentence of excommunication or interdict without manifest and reasonable cause. We also hold valid the ancient liberties and immunities reasonably granted to you in your churches and hitherto observed, and decree that they shall remain inviolate in times to come. Moreover, we prohibit anyone from imposing new and undue exactions upon you or your churches. Therefore we decree, etc., with the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop preserved. If, therefore, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Mark, have subscribed. I, Theodinus, cardinal-bishop of the Apostolic See of St. Rufina. I, Henry, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, Octavian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Ugo, notary of the Holy Roman Church, [Col. 1303B] on the tenth day before the Kalends of December, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1184, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Lucius III, pope.

CLXXVI. Privilege for the church of St. Ursus of Aosta. (Verona, Nov. 29.)

[*Monumenta Historiae Patriae*, Charters, I, 933.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GONTERUS, prior, and the canons of the Church of St. Ursus of Aosta, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

The force of equity and the order of reason require that just requests be granted; especially when piety supports the will of those who ask and truth does not leave it unsupported. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, [Col. 1303C] we graciously assent to your just petitions, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of St. Ursus of Aosta, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order known to have been established in the same church according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be observed there inviolate in perpetuity.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods it now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter obtain, by the grant of popes, the gifts of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and inviolate to you and your successors. [Col. 1303D] Among them we have thought fit to specify in express terms:

The place itself on which the aforesaid church stands, with all its appurtenances; the land given to you by William de Palatio; the land given to you by Vuilencus Moranti; the land given to you by Albor and his mother Mary; the alpine pasture of Gerzola and Terre; the tithes of Thaone, Ouri, and Varaia; the tithe of the vineyard lying between the hospice and Clement’s village, and of that which lies between the Orchard and the Arch; the tithe of Morgi, Liverogni, and Aruer; and others which you hold elsewhere.

Furthermore, under threat of anathema, we forbid any layman to presume to seize or invade your property, to capture men belonging to your church, or improperly to burden those men [Col. 1304A] with tallages or exactions. You may receive into conversion clerics or laymen fleeing the world, provided they are free and released from obligation, and retain them without any contradiction. We further forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, to depart from it without the permission of his prior, except for the purpose of embracing a stricter religious life; and no one may dare retain a departing brother without letters of the community attesting the matter.

In the churches which you possess, you may place three or four of your brethren, one of whom you shall present to the diocesan bishop; he must answer to the bishop regarding spiritual matters, but to you regarding temporal matters and observance of the order. [Col. 1304B] We further decree that the burial ground of your church shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while preserving the rights of the churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it through any cunning of fraud or violence, except the person whom the brethren, by common consent—or the sounder part of the brethren—shall determine ought to be elected in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Augustine. Furthermore, by apostolic authority we forbid any bishop, contrary to the decrees of the Lateran Council, henceforth to burden you or your churches with tallages or exactions, [Col. 1304C] or to subject you to interdict or excommunication without manifest and reasonable cause. Therefore we decree that no one whatsoever, etc. If anyone therefore in the future, etc. But to all who preserve the rights of that place, etc.

Farewell.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, John, of the title of St. Mark, have subscribed. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Callistus, have subscribed. I, Humbertus, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Lawrence in Damaso, have subscribed. I, Pandulphus, priest-cardinal of the title of the Basilica [Col. 1304D] of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and St. Rufina, have subscribed. I, Henry, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri, have subscribed. I, Ardicio, deacon-cardinal of St. Theodore, have subscribed. I, Gratianus, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Albinus, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary the New, have subscribed.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Hugh, notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of December, in the third indiction, in the year [Col. 1305A] of the Lord’s Incarnation 1184, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

CLXXVI bis. Bull for Hermann, abbot of Reinhardsborn. (Verona, Dec. 5.)

[*Thuringia sacra*, p. 177.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HERMANN, abbot at Reinhardsborn: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the holy Roman Church, by the Lord’s ordinance, is mistress of all churches, it orders their rights with such moderation that it establishes some as preeminent over others and grants distinctive dignities a special privilege. Thus, just as in the structure of the human body certain members are honored above others, so also, in the unity itself of ecclesiastical order, some churches are adorned before others with privileges granted to them. Therefore, beloved in the Lord, induced by the prayers and supplications of the noble man Louis III, landgrave of Thuringia, we have thought fit by this present page to grant to you and your successors in perpetuity that, for the honor of God and the future enlargement of your house, you may use a mitre. [Col. 1305B]

Moreover, as an increase of the grace and liberty bestowed, we have handed to the aforesaid Landgrave Louis the mitre which we took from our own head, for him to present to you as a token of our favor. We therefore will that, in memory of so great an honor granted through his favor, special prayers shall henceforth be offered to the Lord in that church for his salvation and that of his parents. [Col. 1305C]

Therefore, that this our concession may possess unfailing force in future times, we confirm it by apostolic authority and fortify it with the protection of this present writing, decreeing that absolutely no one may infringe this page of our confirmation and concession, or rashly oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Verona, on the Nones of December.

CLXXVII. To Robert, archbishop of Vienne, and his suffragans, he commends the Carthusian Order. (Verona, Dec. 10.)

[*Privileges of the Carthusian Order*, ed. 1510, fol. 26.]

[Col. 1305D]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the archbishop of Vienne and his suffragans: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although we ought to extend apostolic protection to all, we are bound especially to provide for those who abound in works of charity and, having despised the vanities of the world, are found devoted to divine exercises of penitence. Therefore we earnestly ask and exhort your brotherhood in the Lord to take care to cherish and support our beloved sons, the Carthusian brethren, and their order; to preserve their houses and rights from every kind of malice, that they may remain inviolate and secure; to punish their wrongdoers and favor their benefactors; and to grant them favor and support, so that the aforesaid house under our protection may experience no deficiency, but, by the Lord’s aid, may receive increase day by day. [Col. 1306A]

And since we receive their defenders and benefactors under the defense of apostolic protection, you too, by apostolic authority, shall defend them from every injury and disturbance with greater confidence and favor, notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See through suppression of the truth.

Given at Verona, on the fourth day before the Ides of December.

CLXXVIII. He receives the Carthusian house under protection and confirms its possessions. (Verona, Dec. 21.)

[*Privileges of the Carthusian Order*, fol. 2.]

[Col. 1306B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the prior and brethren of the Carthusian house, present and future, professing the eremitical life, forever.

It is fitting that apostolic protection be present for those choosing the religious life, lest perhaps an assault of any rashness either recall them from their purpose or, which God forbid, weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; following in the footsteps of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the Carthusian house in the wilderness, wherein you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege [Col. 1306C] of this present writing.

First, indeed, we decree that the order of eremitical life known to have been established in that place according to God shall be observed there inviolate in perpetuity. Furthermore, we confirm to you and your successors all possessions granted to your house by Christ’s faithful out of piety, contained within your boundaries—namely: within the place called Cluss; the rock enclosing the valley and extending as far as the millstone-marker which encloses and divides Comba Chalda and extends as far as the rock below Bochgelos; then another millstone-marker which, ascending, reaches to the rock of Bonviant; thence another millstone-marker which, ascending, runs along the edge of the plane-tree grove from Bonviant [Col. 1306D] to the rock above the furnace of la Follia.

Likewise, from that mountain which stretches from the same rock to Mount Aillinart; and from Mount Aillinart, descending, it extends along Morta westward to the rock above Carreria, and from that rock it continues to the rock of Pertuso. Finally, it stretches downward to the river called Dead Guerus (*Guerus Mortuus*). From Dead Guerus it proceeds upward along the rock enclosing Lesser Carreia as far as the terrace; and from the terrace, along the edge of the plane-tree grove and by *lo Foleys*, turning toward Januarius. From Januarius, as the Alps slope toward Proveysien, it extends to Calmeta Goncelim; from Calmeta Goncelim it runs along the edge to the rock of Chalvienton, and thence [Col. 1307A] descends along Herard’s rock to the closure.

Since the donors of these possessions have forbidden fishing, hunting, bird-catching, the pasture and passage of sheep, goats, and all domestic animals within the prescribed boundaries, we likewise strengthen this prohibition by apostolic authority.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb your house or take away, retain once taken, diminish, or harass by any vexations its aforementioned possessions; but that all shall be kept intact and shall in every way benefit the uses for which they were granted, namely, the governance and support of those concerned. The authority of the Apostolic See is preserved in all things. [Col. 1307B] If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1184, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

CLXXIX. Privilege for the monastery of St. Bertin of Saint-Omer. (Verona, Dec. 22.)

[*Collection des Cartulaires*, III, 363.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons SIMON, abbot of the monastery of St. Bertin, and his brethren, present and future, professing the monastic life, forever.

[Col. 1307C] Set, by the Lord’s disposition, in the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, we ought, as we must imitate our predecessors in good works, likewise to exercise the greatest care lest what they established by pious provision should, through our negligence—which may the Lord avert—be disturbed by anyone’s assault. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, following the footsteps of our predecessors of pious memory, the Roman pontiffs Eugenius and Alexander, we confirm by apostolic authority and decree to remain valid the settlement of the controversy between your monastery and Peter, of blessed memory, formerly abbot of Cluny, concerning the subjection which that abbot claimed over your monastery, as it was made by our predecessor Pope Innocent of happy memory, with his brethren presiding and approving, and strengthened by the authority [Col. 1307D] of his written instrument.

Accordingly, since Innocent, as justice required, annulled the privileges which the Cluniacs said they possessed from the Apostolic See on this matter, we, after the example of the aforesaid predecessors, Roman pontiffs, release both you and your successors, as well as the monastery itself of St. Bertin, from such litigation and from subjection to the Cluniacs. We decree that the same monastery, restored to its own freedom, shall remain forever under the rule and protection of the Roman [Col. 1308A] Church alone, without prejudice to the right of the church or bishop of Thérouanne. As a token, etc., as in the above-mentioned privilege of Pope Innocent. [Note: [Col. 1307D] *Patrologiae*, vol. CLXXIX, no. 398.]

The place itself, beside the castle of Saint-Omer, in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances. In the parish of Morinie, etc., as in the same privilege of Innocent. In the parish of Canterbury, the church of Trulega and the church of Cilliam, with their chapels and other appurtenances.

Furthermore, we hold valid and confirm by apostolic authority the agreement made between you and the abbess of Broburg concerning the boundaries of your parish, with the consent of the parties, as it has been accepted on both sides and is contained in the authentic written instrument of our venerable brother, the bishop of the Morini. What was ordained and confirmed in his written instrument [Col. 1308B] concerning the chapel and cemetery of the lepers of Broburg by Milo, bishop of the Morini of blessed memory, we decree shall remain valid: namely, that in that chapel the divine office shall be celebrated only for lepers and those serving them, and that in their cemetery no one except lepers and their households shall be buried.

Also, in the monastery of St. Silvin at Alchiacum, your abbot for the time being shall, as hitherto, have full authority, as in a special daughter-house, to correct what needs correction according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, with the counsel of religious men.

We also decree that within the bounds of [Col. 1308C] your parishes no one may presume to build a church or oratory without your consent, while preserving the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. We absolutely forbid public stations by the bishop in your monastery, or the bishop’s coming there, unless he has been summoned by the abbot and brethren. Furthermore, by apostolic authority we confirm to the monastery itself, in all respects and through you, the possessions and tithes which your monastery has held without disturbance for forty years and which you now hold without controversy.

Indeed, no one may presume to exact or extort tithes from your newly cleared lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. You may receive into conversion clerics or laymen fleeing the world, provided they are free and released from obligation, and retain them without any contradiction. [Col. 1308D] When a general interdict of the land is in force, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, with excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice.

In the parish churches which you possess, you may elect priests and present them to the diocesan church; if they are suitable, the bishop shall commit the care of souls to them. They must answer to him regarding spiritual matters, but to you regarding temporal matters. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordinations of monks to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to supply these to you freely and without any improper demand. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. [Col. 1309A]

We likewise decree that the burial ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who determine to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while preserving the rights of the churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any craft of fraud or violence, except the man whom the brethren, by common consent—or the sounder part of the brethren—shall determine ought to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever, etc., to the end, as in the above-mentioned privileges of Pope Innocent and Celestine. [Note: [Col. 1309D] *Patrologiae*, vol. CLXXIX, no. 30.]

I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Mark. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Callistus. I, Humbertus, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Lawrence in Damaso. I, Pandulphus, priest-cardinal of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. [Col. 1309C] I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

SAINT PETER. SAINT PAUL.

Given at Verona, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1184, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Lucius III, pope.

CLXXX. He renews privileges for the Regular Canons of the monastery of St. Mary at Carceri in the territory of Este. (Verona, Dec. 22.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, V, 265.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1309D] sons LIVALDUS, prior of the church of St. Mary of Carceri, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life.

Whenever that which appears fitting to religion and uprightness is requested of us, it is proper for us to grant it willingly and to extend apostolic assistance to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; following the example of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the church of St. Mary of Carceri, wherein you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it with the privilege of this present writing.

[Col. 1310A] First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order known to have been established in the same place according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the institution of the brethren of Porto, shall be observed there inviolate in perpetuity. Furthermore, whatever possessions, etc., among which we have thought fit to specify in express terms the following:

The place itself on which the aforesaid church stands, with all its adjoining lands and appurtenances; and the tithes of newly cleared lands throughout the place called Carrateculum, as the privilege of our predecessor Alexander states more fully; and, in Augutiano and throughout Scudechia, in Fracta, Montagnana, and Vigosolo; whatever you possess in Cavalligo; whatever you possess in Craterolo, Carpo, Porto, Minevio, [Col. 1310B] Bonadico, Urbano, Casale, Milliarino, Pause, Vigezolo, Este, the parish of Villa, Monteselice, and Baone; and whatever blessed Paduanus, bishop, reasonably granted you there. We likewise confirm whatever was canonically given to you by Bellinus and Sinibald, bishops of Padua of blessed memory: the church of St. Saviour with all its possessions, etc., as you justly and peaceably possess it; the land which you possess at Vicotineoso and Gazolo; the church of St. John of Vighizolo, with all its possessions and other things known to belong to that church, namely lands, marshes, fisheries, and tithes; likewise the tithing-rights of the whole marsh of Baone, as they were reasonably granted to you by the bishop of Padua and as his instrument states more fully; and the tithe from the territory of the village called Cavallile.

We hold valid and confirm by apostolic authority the sentence which the aforesaid B. lawfully pronounced concerning the dispute between you and the clerics of St. Thecla of Este over the person of Hugo Balisterius, his son, and his property. Furthermore, we likewise confirm to you and your church the sale reasonably made to you by the archpriest of Runco and his brethren of certain land at Minerva. We decree that no layman may presume to exact tithes from possessions which your church now holds or may hereafter acquire. [Col. 1310D]

Indeed, no one may presume to exact or extort tithes from your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. You may receive clerics and laymen fleeing the world, provided they are free and released from obligation, into conversion, and retain them without any contradiction. In the parish churches which you possess, you may elect priests and present them to the diocesan bishop. If found suitable, the bishop shall entrust them with the care of souls, so that they must answer to him regarding spiritual matters and to you regarding temporal matters.

We strengthen by apostolic authority the ancient and reasonable customs of the church, preserved down to the present time, and the tithes which you have possessed from forty years ago until now. [Col. 1311A] When a general interdict of the land is in force, you may celebrate the divine offices without ringing bells, behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, and in a subdued voice. We further grant that the burial ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who determine to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated, while preserving the rights of the churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever, etc., with the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop preserved. If, therefore, etc.

[Col. 1311B] Given at Verona, through the hand of Albert, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1184, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Lucius III, pope.

CLXXXI. To Henry, king of the English.

[TWISDEN, *Historiae Anglicanae Scriptores*, I, 624.]

LUCIUS III, pope, to the illustrious king of the English.

Those things which we believe pertain to your salvation and to the exaltation of royal majesty we lay before your Highness all the more willingly because with ever more sincere affection we desire the glory of your name, together with an increase of salvation and peace. Therefore, by these letters we have thought fit to admonish the piety of your Highness [Col. 1311C]: setting before the eyes of your heart, in wholesome reflection, the love of God; recalling and bringing again to mind the love of Louis, king of the French, of pious memory; and considering the good of the tranquillity and peace commonly desired between you and our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the French—take pious care and prudent concern for the condition in Christ of our most dear M. [Margaret], queen and widow, namely the relict of your son H. [Henry] of good memory. Thus make an arrangement with her concerning her dower and her marriage-gift which leaves her, and those acting for her, no ground for murmuring or complaint; nor should you yourself, on this account, fear a stricter sentence of judgment from the Father of orphans and Judge of widows [Col. 1311D]. Since, therefore, at the urging of certain of her friends, you have decreed that she be satisfied concerning a specified sum of money, we ask your Excellence, exhort you in the Lord, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of your sins: at our intervention, for the preservation of peace and charity, suitably increase for her the sum, as Peter Bermund has informed us on your behalf; and do not fail to assign it to her in specified revenues. Thus, having received the consolation of this relief, she may remain in peace, and you may expect from almighty God an unfailing reward for the deed of kindness you have bestowed.

## CLXXXII. To the Same. — For aid to be given to the land of Jerusalem.

[MANSI, XXII, 475.]

[Col. 1312A]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HENRY, illustrious king of the English: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since all your predecessors, beyond the other princes of the earth, shone conspicuously in the glory of arms and nobility of spirit, and the people of the faithful learned in their adversity to have them as patrons, men rightly have recourse, with a certain confident assurance, to you, heir not only of the kingdom but also of your fathers’ virtues, wherever peril—indeed, extermination—is feared to threaten the Christian people. Let aid be furnished through the arm of royal greatness to the members of Him who, by His mercy, granted you to attain so lofty a summit of glory and preeminence, and made you an impregnable wall against the wicked assailants of your name [Col. 1312B].

First, let your Serenity know—already assailed in these days by frequent and distressing complaints—how the land of Jerusalem, the special inheritance of the Crucified One, in which the mysteries of our salvation were foretold and fulfilled in the event itself, and which He who created all things assigned to Himself as a peculiar possession by special privilege, is worn down and hemmed in by the oppressions of a faithless and utterly foul nation. Unless swift aid is brought to it, it is on the point of ruin; and from this, God forbid, the Christian religion would suffer irreparable loss. For that Saladin, the most savage persecutor of the holy and terrible Name [Col. 1312C], has so burned with the spirit of fury and exerts all the powers of his wickedness for the destruction of the faithful people that, unless the violent onset of his savagery is restrained as though by barriers set against it, he will conceive certain hope and confidence that the Jordan may flow into his mouth; that the land consecrated by the sprinkling of life-giving blood may be defiled by the contagion of his utterly foul superstition; and that the land which your glorious and noble predecessors delivered from the dominion of the unbelieving nation through many labours and perils may once more be subjected to the impious rule of that most wicked tyrant.

Accordingly, because of the urgency of this necessity and imminent sorrow, we have thought fit to entreat your Magnificence by apostolic letters—indeed, with hearts opened wide, to appeal to you with the utmost earnestness [Col. 1312D]. Look to the honour of Him who established you on high and bestowed upon you a glorious name alongside the names of the great ones of the earth. Turn yourself, with zeal for piety, toward the desolation of the aforesaid land; and exert effective effort so that the disgrace of Him who, for your sake, chose to be mocked in that very land may in this respect be removed. Following in the footsteps of your predecessors, preserve by your diligence, with the Lord’s help, in the worship of the great God that land which they snatched from the jaws of the prince of darkness.

Your Highness ought to labour all the more diligently amid so great a crisis of oppression because you understand that the land itself is deprived of the protection of its king, and its leading men have placed all hope of its defence in the patronage of your greatness [Col. 1313A]. Your Serenity may recognize this still more clearly from the fact that they have sent to your Excellence the greatest and most distinguished defenders of that land, our venerable brother Heraclius, patriarch, and our beloved son, the Master of the Hospital. By considering their dignity from their very presence, you may judge how pressing was the necessity for which they endure to be so long without their aid, so that through them they may more readily incline your devotion to meet their wishes.

Receive these men, therefore, as sent to you by the Lord Himself, kindly and treat them with due charity. More readily accede to their requests in proportion as, in view of their gravity and integrity, favour and kindness ought to be shown them. Moreover, let your prudence recall and carefully ponder within itself [Col. 1313B] that promise by which your Highness bound itself to furnish aid to the often-mentioned land. In this matter show yourself so watchful and zealous that, at the dreadful judgment, your conscience may not accuse you and the examination of the strict Judge, who is not deceived, may not condemn you.

ANNO 1181–1185.

## CLXXXII bis. Privilege for the church of St. German at Mons.

[MIRAEUS, *Opera diplomatica*, II, 1187.]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons NICHOLAS, provost of the church of St. German, and his brethren, both present and future, canonically established, in perpetuity.

A devout request ought to be fulfilled by an effective result, so that sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the benefit requested may undoubtedly acquire force. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests, and receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of St. German of Mons, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and whatever goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the gifts of kings or princes [Col. 1313D], the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure to you, your successors, and that church.

Among these we have thought fit to specify by their proper names: the place itself in which the aforesaid church of St. German is situated, with its appurtenances; all the altars of the churches of the castle called *Castri locus*; the site and also the church of St. Waudru; the church of St. Peter; the right of the other church at the gates of St. Peter; the chapel of St. Andrew; the count’s chapel above the gate; the chapel of St. Nicholas at Bertoimont; and the chapel of the infirm.

We also confirm free and canonical appointment of priests, together with the offerings and revenues of the altars assigned to your use [Col. 1314A]; the meadows, mills, yards, hollows, houses, and whatever you possess in places adjoining the said castle; likewise whatever you are known to have at Quem, Jemappes, Genly, and Elonges; also the wheat and oats owed by the church of St. Waudru specifically to the priest-canons of your church; further, the rent which, on Maundy Thursday, your parish priest, who has the care of souls, is bound to pay you each year—namely fifteen *fertons* of silver; the male and female serfs belonging to your church; and the ancient and reasonable customs of your church observed hitherto. We hold these valid and decree that they be inviolably observed. By apostolic authority we also decree that no one pronounce against you or your churches a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict without manifest and reasonable cause [Col. 1314B].

Moreover, no one shall presume to demand or exact tithes from you of your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or from the fodder of your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics and laypersons fleeing the world, if free and absolved, and retain them without opposition. Furthermore, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving it except under the pretext of embracing a stricter religious life; and no one shall dare retain a person who leaves without letters of guarantee from the community. When a general interdict is imposed upon the land [Col. 1314C], you may, with the doors closed, bells not rung, excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, and the voice subdued, celebrate the divine offices.

We also forbid anyone to presume to build anew a chapel or oratory within the enclosures of your sites or granges without the consent of the diocesan bishop and yourselves, saving the privileges of the Apostolic See.

In the parish churches which you possess, you may choose priests and present them to the diocesan bishop. If they are suitable, the bishop shall commit the care of souls to them; they shall answer to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters.

Furthermore, we decree that the burial-ground of that place shall be free [Col. 1314D], and that no one shall obstruct the devotion and last will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict—without prejudice, however, to the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away or retain its possessions once taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact and shall in every way benefit the uses of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the canonical rights of the Apostolic See and of the diocesan bishop. If in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it [Col. 1315A], then, after a second or third warning, unless that person corrects the presumption by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and office; let that person know that he or she stands guilty before divine judgment for the wrong committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ; and let that person be subject, at the last judgment, to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that same place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

ANNO 1184–1185.

## CLXXXIII. He orders the bishops of Patti and Cefalù to obey R[ichard], archbishop of Messina. (Verona, 25 July.)

[PIRRI, *Sicilia sacra*, I, 399.]

[Col. 1315B]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren, the bishops of Cefalù and Patti: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since our Lord and Saviour, in handing down to His faithful the pattern of humility to be observed, took care to show reverence to those set above Him, a person who does not render due reverence to his superiors is rightly considered not a disciple but an opponent. Therefore, by apostolic writings we command your brotherhood [Col. 1315C] to render due reverence and obedience to our venerable brother R[ichard], archbishop of Messina; to visit his church at the appointed times in accordance with his admonitions; and humbly to assist him in his needs and expenses.

Given at Verona, 25 July.
