The parish church of St. Florian of [Col. 1369D] Zaudo with its chapels, and the county, with jurisdiction and district over the appurtenances of Zaudo itself. The district and right of appointment of the castle of Lavatio. Mount Farra with its tithes. The wood of the Canal of the Holy Cross, extending from Levina Leverada toward the church of the Holy Cross, with its tithes and appurtenances. The court of Fregona, with the castles of Carone, the chapel of St. Justus, and the chapel of St. Martin, with its lordship and appurtenances. The village of Pinedo. The castle of Oderzo, with its court, villages, and fields. The chapels of St. Blaise, St. Peter, St. Martin, and St. Mary, together with another chapel and fields, all of which are said to lie among the appurtenances of the castle of Oderzo. The right of appointment to these in the parish church of St. John of Oderzo; the chapel of the court of Francone; and the *livellaticum* [leasehold right] of the other churches and their appointments among the appurtenances of Oderzo; the court and castles of Soligo with their villages and appurtenances; the court of Cendon with its chapels.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we have thought fit to forbid that any advocate or his official should presume to burden your church or its appurtenances, or harass them with any undue exactions. We further forbid anyone within the bounds of your parish, without your consent, to dare to construct a new chapel or oratory, saving the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. Furthermore, by apostolic authority we forbid new and undue exactions to be imposed by patriarchs, bishops, or any other ecclesiastical or secular persons upon you, your ecclesiastical or secular officials, your people, or your property [Col. 1370B]. We also decree by this present ordinance that the liberties and immunities reasonably granted to that church by kings, princes, and other ecclesiastical or worldly persons, and its ancient and reasonable customs, shall remain whole and unimpaired. We likewise prohibit anyone from presuming to admit those whom you have interdicted or excommunicated to office or ecclesiastical communion without fitting satisfaction. When you, now elect of the same church, or any one of your successors dies, no one shall be set over it by any cunning of fraud or by violence, save one whom the canons of that church by common consent, or the sounder part of the chapter according to the fear of God [Col. 1370C] and the ordinance of the holy Fathers, shall provide to be elected.

We also decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the governance and support of those for whom they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and due reverence toward the Church of Aquileia. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodinus, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. [Col. 1370D] I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Mary in Trastevere. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of the title of St. Mark. I, Ubertus, cardinal priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Damaso. I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul. I, Adelard, cardinal priest of the title of St. Marcellus. I, Melior, cardinal priest of the title of the Twelve Holy Apostles. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross. I, Ardicus, cardinal deacon. [Col. 1371A] I, Roland, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Rodulf, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Verona by the hand of Albert, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1185, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

## CCXLIV. He receives the Church of St. Mary of Garz into protection and confirms its property and rights.  
*(Verona, November.)*

*[Monumenta Boica, vol. I, p. 61.]*

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons [Col. 1371B] BERTHOLD, provost of the church of St. Mary at Garz, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

Whenever a request is made to us which is recognized as consonant with religion and uprightness, it becomes us willingly to grant it and to afford fitting support to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church of St. Mary at Garz, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, [Col. 1371C] or may hereafter, by the Lord’s favor, acquire through grants of pontiffs, benefactions of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among them we have thought fit to specify the following in their proper names:

All tithes of your parish, in which your monastery stands, and the other tithes which your church justly and lawfully possesses either in the bishopric of Salzburg or in that of Freising. Likewise, all tithes from the newly cultivated lands of the forest of Garz, between Bramberg and Hollenstein, and also from the wood of Aichenawe, which Archbishop Conrad the Elder granted to your church. We also confirm for the common use of the regular brethren there serving God the chapel of Burthen, with its endowments and tithes, which the provosts of that place [Col. 1371D] have held. Likewise all estates which Aura of Isen gave to your church, together with the chapel situated on the same estate of Isen, which Conrad, archbishop of the Church of Salzburg, at Aura’s request, delivered and confirmed to your church with all its appurtenances; also the estate of Bettenhaim, with the chapel situated upon it, and the other chapels belonging by right to your church. In the bishopric of Freising we likewise confirm the chapels situated on the land of your church at Sewen and Pennanigen, with the tithes which the provosts of that church proved before Otto, bishop of Freising, that your church possessed justly and lawfully.

[Col. 1372A] Certainly, no one shall presume to demand or extort tithes from you on your newly cultivated lands which you cultivate either by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals. You may also receive into conversion, without anyone’s opposition, clerics and laymen fleeing from the world who are free and released, and retain them in your church.

We further prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving the cloister without permission of his provost, except for the sake of a stricter religious life; and no one may dare to retain one who leaves without letters of authorization from the community.

When a general interdict is imposed upon the land, [Col. 1372B] you may celebrate divine offices in a low voice, behind closed doors, without ringing bells, excluding those excommunicated and under interdict. In the parish churches which you hold, you may choose priests and present them to the diocesan bishop; if they are suitable, the bishop shall commit the care of souls to them, so that they are answerable to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters. Furthermore, if the advocate of your church behaves badly, you may, without any opposition, remove him from that monastery and, if necessary, appoint another suitable person in his place. When you, now provost of that place, or any one of your successors dies, no one shall be placed over it by any fraudulent contrivance or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren according to God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine, shall provide to be elected. Furthermore, we decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken are preserved.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb your church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the benefit in every respect of the uses for which they were granted, saving [Col. 1372D] the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Lucius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theodinus, bishop of the see of Porto and San Rufino. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Mark. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St. Mary in Trastevere, of the title of Calixtus. I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the title of the Twelve Apostles. I, Hubertus, cardinal of the Roman Church, of the title of St. Lawrence in Damaso. I, Albinus, of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. [Col. 1373A] I, Melior, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Adelard, cardinal priest of the title of St. Marcellus. I, Arditio, cardinal deacon of St. Theodore. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Goffredus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata. I, Rollo, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Adulfus, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Verona by the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, … November, in the fourth indiction, in the year [Col. 1373B] 1185 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

## CCXLV. He receives the Church of Uppsala into protection and confirms its possessions and rights, at the request of Archbishop John.  
*(Verona, November 5.)*

*[LILJEGREN, Diplomatarium Suecanum, vol. I, p. 119.]*

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother John, archbishop of Uppsala, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

By the office of apostleship entrusted to us, we ought to love our brethren and fellow bishops, whether near at hand or far away, with sincere affection of charity, and [Col. 1373C] to preserve for the churches in which they are known to serve the Lord their dignity and rights. Therefore, venerable brother in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the Church of Uppsala, over which by God’s authority you are known to preside, strengthening it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the Lord’s favor, acquire through grants of pontiffs, benefactions of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among them we have thought fit to specify the following in their proper names:

The residence at Uppsala with its appurtenances; Ramby with its appurtenances; Collem with its dependencies; Liusabec with its appurtenances. Fishing rights at Elwa Karlaby with their appurtenances, and the residence at Munseo with its appurtenances. We ratify the liberties and immunities reasonably granted to your church by kings and other persons, both with respect to tenants and in other matters, and decree that they shall remain unimpaired for all time. We further ordain, and prohibit under threat of anathema, that when your church is vacant no person may with condemnable rashness presume to plunder its property, disturb it in any manner, or impede the canonical election of an archbishop. We further prohibit [Col. 1374A] anyone from admitting those whom you have interdicted or excommunicated to office or ecclesiastical communion without your knowledge or consent, or from presuming to act contrary to your canonically promulgated sentence—unless perhaps danger of death is imminent, so that, when they cannot have your presence, the bound person must, after satisfaction has first been made, be absolved by another according to the form of the Church.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the governance and support of those for whom they were granted, to their advantage in every respect, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Theodinus, bishop of the see of Porto and Santa Rufina, subscribe. I, Henry, bishop of Albano, subscribe. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri, subscribe. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Mark, subscribe. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St. Mary in Trastevere, of the title of Calixtus, subscribe. I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the title of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles, subscribe. I, Albert, by divine permission cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross [Col. 1374C] in Jerusalem, subscribe. I, Melior, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius, subscribe. I, Adelard, cardinal priest of the title of St. Marcellus, subscribe. I, Arditio, cardinal deacon of St. Theodore, subscribe. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, subscribe. I, Soffredus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata, subscribe. I, Rollandus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico, subscribe. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in [Col. 1374D] the Tullian Prison, subscribe. I, Radulfus, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil, subscribe.

Given at Verona by the hand of Albert, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of November, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1185, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Lucius III.

## IN THE YEARS 1181–1185

## CCXLVI. To the Archbishop of Split

*(From MANSI, Councils, XXII, 482, as are also the other fragments which follow.)*

But concerning the fact that certain persons in your province are said to be joined in the fourth and fifth degrees of consanguinity, on account of the harshness of the people, you may pass over in silence and dissimulation marriages already contracted, although they are contrary to the institution of the sacred canons.

## CCXLVII. To the Dean and Canons of Vocestem

Because you have asked us whether you ought to proceed to hold an election, declaring that you do not dare to do so without royal consent: if it cannot be done otherwise, approach H., our beloved son in Christ, king of England. Diligently represent to him that B., formerly your bishop, has been deposed permanently; and, having obtained the assent of the same king, unanimously agree upon an honourable, learned, and suitable person [Col. 1375B], and elect him concordantly as pastor and bishop, so that through his foresight and governance welcome increase may accrue to the church in spiritual as well as temporal matters.

## CCXLVIII. To …

Robert of Colombelles procured against his adversary duplicate letters concerning the church of a certain village of Colombelles, addressed to the archdeacon of Rouen and the judges of Tours, so that, if he could not obtain the archdeaconry before the archdeacon of Rouen [the text reads “archdeaconry”; perhaps read *archidiacono*, “before the archdeacon”], he might not cease to harm his adversary before the judge of Tours. Since, therefore, such malice ought not to be indulged, we command that both sets of letters shall have no force, and that whatever has been done through them shall be held void and invalid.

## CCXLIX. To the Archbishop of Canterbury

Since, in seeking advice, you ask to be instructed whether it belongs to you to confirm a judgment rendered by judges delegated by us in your province, although nothing concerning the cases has been dealt with in your presence: we answer your inquiry as follows. You are not bound to confirm the judgment itself unless you wish to do so; but you should know that it is incumbent on you by duty of office that, if at the command of the same judges the judgment cannot be put into execution, you shall afford them assistance [Col. 1375D] and support. You may also confirm it if you know that it has been reasonably rendered.

## CCL. To …

W., a clerk of Cothosinori [Cotosmor], informed us that, although he has canonically obtained that church and possessed it peacefully for more than thirty years, S., a clerk said to possess several ecclesiastical benefices, presumes repeatedly to harass him by drawing him into litigation on the strength of certain letters which he is said to have procured from Pope Alexander, our predecessor of holy memory, alleging that he is the son of the man who most recently ministered in that church. Since it is unjust and contrary to reason that W. should be deprived of the same church on such a ground after having, as is said, been in it for so long: say … through A. … If you know that the foregoing rests upon truth, do not permit him to be harassed in any degree by the aforesaid clerk over that church on the pretext of such a claim; rather, cause him, as you see to be just, peacefully to possess it [“the same church”].

## CCLI. To the Bishop of Barch., the Abbot of Abanden, and the Prior of St. Fridae

[Col. 1376B] From the complaint of B., clerk, … and below: Since, therefore, reason demands that things contrary to the discipline of the Church be corrected: say V. through A. … If you know that what is alleged rests upon reason, cause the aforesaid R. to be removed from the aforesaid church, notwithstanding an appeal …; and cause the same church to be assigned to the aforesaid B., if he is suitable, notwithstanding letters procured from the Apostolic See while an appeal is pending. But if R. does not show a reasonable impediment, because he has not prosecuted the appeal which he lodged, condemn him to the necessary expenses of the other party on appeal.

## CCLII. To …

[Col. 1376C] The wicked plague of forgery, which certain forgers living in the land of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious H., king of the English, are known to have devised for fabricating [variant readings: “for authenticating,” “for breaking,” “fabricating”] public letters, has grown into a common ruin; so that the authority of our letters was already wavering in some places in a state of doubt, unless the censure of the Church should both investigate and correct the excess of so great a presumption. Therefore, being especially confident in your diligence, we have thought fit to commit to you the execution of this matter, commanding through A. … that whatever forgers you may, God willing, be able to discover by any means—if they are clerics—shall be deprived without any delay or appeal of their order and of any benefice [Col. 1376D] they possess, and be held under strict guard until fuller directions as to what ought to be done with them are conveyed to you in our reply. But if you apprehend any laymen among them, hand them over to our dearest son in Christ, R., king of the English, to be judged according to their deserts, so that in judicial proceedings, both ecclesiastical and secular, that plague, known to be harmful to all alike, may be condemned together with its authors.

[Col. 1377]

# DECREES OF LUCIUS III

## I. To the Master and Brethren of the Military Order of St. James—On the Cohabitation of Clerics and Women

[Col. 1377A]

Your devotion has thought fit to inquire whether we should give counsel to your brethren who attend parish churches whose clerics keep concubines; for different rulings of the sacred canons appear to have been issued on this matter. For in one place it is said: “Let no one hear the Mass of a priest who unquestionably has a concubine”; elsewhere, “No one, however defiled, can defile God’s sacrament, which purges all thoughts,” etc., because all things are purified in faith in Christ. Yet it is one thing when the priest does not deny that the crime is notorious, or has been canonically condemned for it; another when it is wholly concealed [Col. 1377B], or is still tolerated by the Church. Likewise, it is one thing to abstain from the offices of such persons so that the license to sin may be taken away from others and they may be drawn to the fruit of worthy repentance; another if their ministries are regarded [Col. 1378A] as those of innocent men. Therefore hold without doubt that divine offices may lawfully be heard and the other ecclesiastical sacraments received from clerics and priests, even though fornicators, so long as they remain concealed and the deed has not become manifest.

## II. To the Bishop of Norwich

It has been asked of us on your behalf whether an ordinary judge, or another person whom a delegated judge has ordered to summon the parties or to execute a judgment, is bound to obey the delegated judge. Since they act not in their own capacity but in that of the delegator, and since, when jurisdiction is delegated, everything pertaining to jurisdiction is seen to be delegated, the delegated judge may rightly compel both the ordinary judge [Col. 1378B] and any other person whom he has instructed to carry out what is ordered, and impose an appropriate penalty upon one who refuses obedience.

[Col. 1377]

# VARIOUS LETTERS TO POPE LUCIUS III

## I. From Bertrand, Bishop of Agen, to Lucius—That King Henry the Younger of England Chose Burial in the Church of Rouen  
*(About the year 1182.)*

*[MARTEN., Ampl. Collect., I, 951.]*

[Col. 1377C]

To his most blessed lord and father LUCIUS, by the grace of God supreme pontiff of the universal Church, B., by God’s grace and his own mercy the humble minister of the Church of Agen, sends greeting and a ready will, with due submission, for whatever service he may be able to render.

From the testimony of the Scriptures we have learned that both the person through whom truth is concealed and the person through whom falsehood is uttered are liable to the same punishment. Therefore, at the request of the clerics of the Church of Rouen [Col. 1377D] concerning the burial of King Henry the Younger, lest justice suffer injury through our silence, we report to Your Blessedness the truth of what occurred. Let Your Fatherhood therefore know that, when we had come to him by command of his lord father, King H., for the sake of restoring peace, we found him lying upon a bed of sickness. After he had received from us, with the greatest humility and devotion, extreme unction and the other ministrations customarily administered to those at the point of death, he finally chose burial in the named church of Blessed Mary at Rouen. But although we and very many other religious men, taking account of the difficulty of the journey and the remoteness of the place, earnestly advised him to choose burial at the monastery of Grandmont, we were in no way able to turn him from his purpose. May the glorious prudence of Your Holiness determine what ought to be done concerning this. May the Lord preserve Your Holiness unharmed for many years.

## II. From Odo, Duke of Burgundy, to the Same—On the Same Matter

*[Ibid.]*

[Col. 1378D] To the most holy father and lord LUCIUS, supreme pontiff by God’s grace, and to all the faithful to whom this present writing shall come, ODO, duke of Burgundy, greeting.

Holy Father, I wish it to come to your knowledge and that of all the faithful that I was present and heard when King Henry, son of King Henry of England, while at the point of death, chose for himself burial at Rouen, earnestly asking to be buried in the cathedral church in the city of Rouen, etc.

## III. From the Castellan of Saint-Omer to the Same—On the Same Matter

*[Ibid.]*

[Col. 1379A]

To the venerable father and lord L., supreme pontiff by God’s grace, the castellan of Saint-Omer sends greeting and due and devoted reverence.

Let Your Holiness know that I was present and heard when King Henry, son of Henry, king of the English, while at the point of death, chose burial for himself in the cathedral church in the city of Rouen, and humbly entreated that his body be carried there. May Your Holiness prosper now and always.

## IV. From R., Duke of Narbonne, to the Same—On the Same Matter

*[Ibid.]*

[Col. 1379B]

To his most reverend father and lord in Christ, L., pontiff of the Romans by God’s grace, R., by the same grace duke of Narbonne, count of Toulouse, marquis of Provence, sends greeting and himself.

By this present letter we inform Your Fatherhood that we were present at the death of the younger king of England, who, in our hearing, chose burial for himself in the church of Rouen. Although many begged or advised him to choose burial in the church of Grandmont, he could never be recalled from his resolve that he should ask for a tomb to be placed for him in the church of Rouen beside the burial-place of his uncle William, etc.

## V. From Roland, Subdeacon of the Roman Church, and Silvanus, Abbot of Rievaulx, Legates of the Apostolic See, to Lucius—On the Affair of the Bishopric of St Andrews in Scotland  
*(1182.)*

*[MANRIQUE, Annal. Cisterc., III, 119.]*

To the reverend father and lord LUCIUS, supreme and universal pontiff by God’s grace, ROLAND, by the same grace elect of Dol, servant of his holiness and foster-child of the Apostolic See, least of the subdeacons, and Silvanus, called abbot of Rievaulx, send the reverence of due submission.

When we had given to Bishop Hugh the letters which he had denounced as forgeries, and the letters in which the course of the affair is set out, and when, having received leave from the lord king of the Scots, we wished to depart in haste, the lord king earnestly and affectionately asked me, the elect of Dol, to make an approach through Lord Bishop John and offer him, on the king’s behalf, the bishopric of Dunkeld with the revenues which he had previously possessed in the bishopric of St Andrews, together with an increase of forty marks to be received annually; and also the royal chancellorship as a token of affection. He added that he would restore to him and his people everything taken away, except only that which he knew had come into his own hands, and would receive him into the fullness of his favour, as had previously been offered to him. Yet he required that the same Bishop John should burn all his documents which had been obtained from Alexander, your predecessor of pious memory, concerning the affair of St Andrews. He also allowed that Bishop Hugh might be transferred to the bishopric of Glasgow, if Bishop John would not otherwise consent. And if that could not be done, he would nevertheless grant what he had offered; but he would not love Bishop John so greatly or restore to him his full favour. When, in the presence of Lord Hugh, bishop of Durham [Col. 1380B], I had offered all this to Lord John, he graciously accepted it, yet said that he would never permit Bishop Hugh to remain in the Church of St Andrews. He also wished the aforesaid documents to be deposited somewhere, so that he could never use them contrary to the king’s will.

Thus, as we returned to the king’s presence, Bishop John looking on near Roxburgh, the lord king told us that it would please him greatly if Bishop Hugh could remain in the Church of St Andrews, and asked me to endeavour to induce the bishop to this. When I told him that I would never again ask him about this, because I could make no progress in the matter, he said: “I firmly believe that, since Lord John has returned to peace and friendship with me, he will endure this out of consideration for my affection and at the urgency of my prayers; and I would gladly speak with him about it.” The king asked me to advise him to come and speak with him. Clerics of the king having therefore been sent to Bishop John, he replied that he would not come because he had heard from certain counsellors of the lord king that the king was always striving by every means to have Hugh remain in the bishopric of St Andrews; and that, if he wished to come, they could not furnish him with a safe-conduct. When they returned with this response, the lord king sent a certain bishop, abbots, counts, and barons to the same bishop [Col. 1380D], asking him to come to speak with him; and he commanded them to offer that bishop every assurance of safety. On their return they said that Lord John, perceiving that the lord king wished Bishop Hugh to remain in the Church of St Andrews, had replied that he would never come to the king unless they first swore that the king would observe everything which he had offered him through me; but they were unwilling to swear. Thus Lord John returned home. We, however, fixed for the aforesaid Bishops John and Hugh the Kalends of October as the date for coming before you and obeying your judgment. Farewell.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1186: ALAN, BISHOP OF AUXERRE

[Col. 1381]

## NOTICE

*(Gallia Christiana nova, vol. XII, col. 293)*

[Col. 1381A] After Bishop Hugh’s death, his nephew appealed to the supreme pontiff that no other should be elected in his uncle’s place before he himself had gone to Rome and returned, having obtained confirmation of his provostship. But, disregarding him, eleven priests and nine deacons, besides others of lower rank, assembled together. In order to commend their choice to the supreme pontiff, they dispatched the dean of St. Peter and the prior of St. Eusebius, acting both for themselves and for the abbot of St. Lawrence; the opposing party, however, intimidated them through the count of Nevers so that they did not depart. For on the third day after the first election, Hugh’s same nephew, abandoning his own appeal, arranged a second election. Its instigators were the cantor, archdeacon, and treasurer of the church; among the priests, one Hugh, brother of Brother Geoffrey, [Col. 1381B] whom they suppose to have been elected, since he held the seal of the church; and among the deacons, Stephen alone—so that, when one man was named, two might be excluded, and thus a third, whom they wanted, might be appointed.

Eugenius III committed the whole affair to three persons, one of whom was St. Bernard; and he charged them to promote the abbot—apparently the abbot of Rigny—who had been nominated by St. Bernard. Bernard’s vote and that of one other agreed in favour of the person Eugenius had indicated, while the third protested and disclosed the supreme pontiff’s confidential instruction. Accordingly St. Bernard asked Pope Eugenius (Letter 280) to supply what was lacking. The electoral assembly having therefore been reconstituted, and St. Bernard having attended it (from Letter 282), the clerics who had formerly divided into factions united in agreement upon Alan, abbot of Ripatore, [Col. 1381C] on the day before the Kalends of December, 1152. Although King Louis VII at once opposed him because his consent had not been obtained, he seems soon to have been placated by St. Bernard; for in the same year Alan was a witness to churches granted to the monastery of Arremar by Geoffrey, bishop of Langres. In the following year he witnessed the judgment rendered by Louis VII in favour of the same Geoffrey against Odo, duke of Burgundy. In 1154 Anastasius IV, in a bull issued to Alan, confirmed his right concerning the abbacy of St. Germanus. Delegated by that same pontiff, in the same year he reconciled at Sens the monks of La Charité and the canons of Château-Renard, who were in dispute over a prebend to be received by the monks in the canons’ church.

At about this time he was appointed by the pope, together with Theobald, bishop of Paris, as judge in the accusations brought against the abbot of Latiniacum. In 1156 he attended the discovery and exposition of the tunic of Jesus Christ at Argenteuil. Invited by the abbot, he celebrated solemn ordinations at Vézelay on 10 March 1156. In 1157 Count William of Auxerre made his declaration of fealty before him according to the customary formula, and came to an agreement [Col. 1382B] concerning the jurisdiction of Conada and other matters. In the same year Alan exempted the monks of Pontigny from the rent which they were bound to pay to the monks of La Celle. In 1159, by decision of the chapter, he confirmed for the regular canons of Saint Eusebius the right to the vacant canonical grain allowance, granted by his predecessor Humbald; Alexander III and Adrian IV confirmed it by apostolic authority. He attended the exposition of the relics of Saint Geneviève at Paris on 10 January 1161. The following year he met Alexander III at Montpellier and, together with him, pronounced a sentence of excommunication against Octavian the schismatic. He obtained from him the bull which, following the Sainte-Marthe brothers, we reprint in the appendix [Note: [Col. 1381C] See *Patrologia*, vol. CC, under Alexander III.], authorizing him to employ witnesses, documents, and other proofs in place of judicial combat. But the bull is mistaken either as to the place where it is said to have been issued [Col. 1382C] or as to the year of the pontificate. For Alexander was still in Gaul in his fourth year.

In 1163 he confirmed, by completed charters, the gifts made by his predecessor Hugh to the Premonstratensian canons of Saint Marianus, together with the addition of the church of Tangiacum. In the same year he united the priory of Saint Amator to the monastery of Saint Satyrius of Bourges; and, as arbitrator together with Hugh, bishop of Sens, he restored to concord William, abbot of Molesme, and Heribert of Merry, who were in dispute. In 1164 he appeased Count William, then most hostile and odious to the king because of the attacks he was making upon the people of Vézelay. In the same year, when the controversy formerly existing between Hugh and William, count of Nevers, broke out anew, Geoffrey, formerly bishop of Langres, then living a private life at Clairvaux, settled it at the command of the supreme pontiff. He decreed that the terms formerly arranged between Bishop Hugh and the count by Bernard, of holy memory, formerly abbot of Clairvaux, should be inviolably observed. Still in the same year he confirmed to the monks of Donzy the churches of Pigny and Bouhy. [Col. 1383B] In 1165 he exempted Ascelin, abbot of Rigny, from paying the tithes of his monastery in the diocese of Auxerre. By a new diploma he buried once more the extinct, yet already so often revived, provostship of the cathedral church [Col. 1384A] and granted its rights and revenues to the canons in 1166.

The following year, having resigned his dignity into the hands of the archbishop of Sens without the permission of the supreme pontiff, who complained of this, he withdrew, eager for solitude, to Ripatorium, in the fourteenth year after attaining the episcopate. There he made his will in 1182; it may be found in Camusat and in our appendix. Still alive in 1183, he reconciled the monks of Ripatorium and Arremar, who were in dispute; indeed, in 1185 he subscribed Count Peter’s charter for the monks of Bon Repos. At last he returned to Clairvaux, where he died most holy on the day before the Ides of October, in Saint Bernard’s own cell, which he had undertaken to inhabit after the death of Geoffrey, bishop of Langres. He lies at the right hand of that same Geoffrey, toward the monks’ choir [Col. 1384B]. Besides several letters of Alan, there survives in print an epitome of the *Life of Saint Bernard* composed by him.

[Col. 1383]

## FIVE LETTERS OF ALAN, BISHOP OF AUXERRE, TO LOUIS THE YOUNGER, KING OF THE FRANKS, that he may protect the Church of Auxerre against the vexations of the count of Nevers. About the year 1164.

(Duchesne, *Rerum Francicarum Scriptores*, IV, 642.)

## LETTER I

[Col. 1383C]

To his dearest lord LOUIS, magnificent king of the Franks, A., styled bishop of Auxerre, greeting and devoted service in all things.

Let not Your Royal Majesty wonder that, when necessity presses, we so often trouble the ears of your magnificence; harassed as we are by repeated attacks, we are compelled to flee beneath the shadow of your wings. For the hand of the count is still stretched out, and he has not turned away his indignation from the Church. He still bends his bow, breathing threats, seeking to order all things according to his will and to place all beneath his feet. Indeed, the neighboring lords on every side, following his example—not, I would say, induced to this by him, but having found a pretext in his favor and friendship—raise claims [Col. 1383D]. They maintain that many things belong to their *casamentum* [estate or territorial holding]; and because we do not satisfy them according to their wishes, they seek to plunder everything and, having already seized much, threaten daily to inflict still greater injuries.

Since there is no one who dares to set himself as a wall for the house of God, and none to help except my lord [Col. 1384C] the king, we beg your magnificence, from whom we hope for no small aid, and for whom it is easy to command silence from all, to send us one of your men to guard and defend Varzy, Pigny, and our other lands. For the count has not yet done homage to me, nor does he promise that he will do so. Unless the Lord who commands the winds and the sea stretches out to us the hand of His help, we expect that still more troubles will be inflicted upon us hereafter.

## LETTER II

To his dearest lord LOUIS, magnificent king of the Franks, A., styled bishop of Auxerre, greeting and devoted service.

Your Highness has often been informed [Col. 1384D] of the oppression by which the count of Nevers afflicts and grievously crushes the church of Saint Stephen of Auxerre and the other churches belonging to it; and I believe that you sympathize. How he and I met before the lord pope, what was done there, how the count conducted himself there, [Col. 1385A] how he made threatening gestures and movements, and how he departed in anger, the lord of Nevers will explain to you more fully in person.

Moreover, our land is yours; it stands under your protection and power, and your officers have been appointed to guard the land. We therefore beg your magnificence to summon the count of Nevers, as you know how and as is expedient, lest he dare violently to stretch out his hand against our possessions—or rather, yours—and inflict any damage. Furthermore, concerning the lord of Bourges, who is most faithful and a principal pillar of the Church in your kingdom, we earnestly entreat you to bear with so great a man, as befits your royal dignity, with your customary kindness; lest the bishops of your kingdom be scandalized by his grievance [Col. 1385B], and rather that, because of the manifestation of your kindness toward him, we all may render fitting thanks. If anyone whispers anything adverse concerning him, do not, out of reverence for his religious character, believe every word.

## LETTER III

To his dearest lord LOUIS, most excellent king of the Franks, A., styled bishop of Auxerre, wishing him so to reign as to be able to please the supreme King.

We give thanks to Your Sublimity because you graciously received our messenger, who had gone to Sens to report to you the evils which the lord of La Ferté does not cease to inflict upon our land, and because you commanded that peace should henceforth be preserved for us, as befitted [Col. 1385C] royal majesty. Yet because of the frequent incursions of wars which have long been accustomed to harass our land, it is clear that it has hitherto been so crushed by countless persecutions that scarcely anything remains in it and that it has been reduced to poverty and want.

Now the lord of La Ferté and his men so harass and oppress Pigny and the adjoining territory that our people dare not go out to cultivate the land. For after your command to him that he preserve peace with us, he presumed to carry off our plunder. Apply your counsel to these matters, therefore. For if their malice remains unpunished, perhaps nothing will remain to us except the cultivated lands and vineyards.

## LETTER IV

[Col. 1385D]

To his reverend lord LOUIS, magnificent king of the Franks, A., by the grace of God bishop of Auxerre, greeting and service.

The third day before the Purification was appointed [Col. 1386A] as the day between myself and the count of Nevers in the presence of the lord of Sens. On that day the lord of Troyes, the abbot of Saint Columba of Sens, and many other prudent men assembled, acting as mediators in the matters to be negotiated. I demanded of the count that he do homage to me as his father had done; he plainly denied that he owed it, although many stood by ready to prove that his father had done homage to me. Rejecting their proof, he would not submit to judgment as to whether their proof ought to be admitted; nor would he restore the damages done to our Church and to the other churches. When he said that he possessed nothing belonging to the churches, though many were ready to prove that he had possessed many things, he rejected their proof and appealed to a date fifteen days [Col. 1386B] after Easter.

## LETTER V

To his illustrious and dearest lord LOUIS, magnificent king of the Franks, A., styled bishop of Auxerre, wishing him so to reign as to be able to please the King of kings.

To Your Serenity and royal magnificence we render whatever thanks we can for the watchful care and concern you have shown toward our Church—or rather, yours—in preserving and maintaining its possessions. All who heard of it rejoiced and glorified God in you and because of you. Your messenger came and appointed me a day [Col. 1386C] fixed between myself and the count; receiving it gladly, I was ready, all pretexts set aside, to go there. But before he arrived, the count of Nevers had sent his letters to the Cistercian chapter. After these had been examined, the lord and venerable Geoffrey, formerly bishop of Langres, the abbot of Pontigny, and the abbot of Clairvaux appointed a day for myself and the count, wishing to restore peace between us and the count.

Accordingly, when I and a company of reputable and religious men had appeared on the appointed day, the count declared himself quite graciously willing to do what pertained to peace, and promised to abide by the judgment of Lord G., formerly bishop of Langres, and of the abbots of Pontigny and Clairvaux. But while all urged and approved that we should submit the entire case to their judgment [Col. 1386D], we deferred doing so until we had first learned your counsel and will on this matter. Inform us, therefore, what pleases you; for we are prepared to act in this affair according to your counsel and will.

[Col. 1387]

## CHARTER by which Geoffrey, formerly bishop of Langres, Wichard, abbot of Pontigny, and Geoffrey, abbot of Clairvaux, settle the controversy which had arisen between Alan of Auxerre and the count of Nevers. (Year 1164.)

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. XII, *Instrum.*, col. 127.)

[Col. 1387A] I, GODEFREY, formerly bishop of Langres, wish it to be known to present and future persons that, concerning certain complaints litigated between the lord Alan, venerable bishop of Auxerre, and William, illustrious count of Nevers, by God’s help, through our agency and that of Wichard, abbot of Pontigny, and Geoffrey, abbot of Clairvaux, after the truth concerning the rights and customs of the aforesaid bishop and count had been more carefully investigated, an amicable settlement was made in the following manner.

First, with the charter preserved and approved which Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, of holy memory, made between the predecessor of this bishop, Lord Hugh, and the grandfather of this count—the count, namely, who became a Carthusian—it was decreed by us that [Col. 1387B] whatever is determined in it and ratified by their seals shall stand, and shall be observed inviolably for all days by both bishop and count.

Concerning the market-land, which belongs jointly to the bishop and the count, it has been established that neither may grant it to anyone or do anything there without the other’s consent. The sole exception is that the count may grant stalls there to money-changers alone, only for money-changing; these stalls may not be transferred by them to other uses. If the count receives a payment from this, the bishop is to have half. The count’s officials shall have no involvement whatever in the toll collected by the bishop and the viscount. It is clear that the land called Kalends of May belongs to the bishop; consequently the count has no right to do anything [Col. 1387C] there, and the building which he erected there is to be demolished. Likewise, the house by the bridge is to be demolished, since it has been established and is manifest that it was built over the water below the bridge, which is under the bishop’s jurisdiction.

The count’s officers may not take the riding services of the bishop’s men or of the churches’ men for any work or dispatch [Col. 1388A]; nor may anything be exacted from the bishop’s men or the churches’ men for building or repairing fortifications. Sometimes the bishop’s men complain before the count’s officers, and those officers refuse to do them justice unless they render justice to those officers in return; yet they themselves owe this only if they live by the market. It is therefore clear that justice ought not for this reason to be withheld or denied them.

Moreover, it used to happen that the count’s men extended credit to the bishop’s men and, when they could not recover what had been lent, seized the goods of other men of the bishop. It was decreed that this must not happen at all, for debts are to be demanded from no one except the person to whom the credit was extended. It was further acknowledged that the count has no jurisdiction or authority whatsoever, either in the market or elsewhere, over the bishop’s enfeoffed servants at Auxerre or elsewhere, even if they live by the market, for any offense, except through the bishop [Col. 1388B].

Therefore, that the aforesaid settlement may remain valid and unshaken forever, we have confirmed it with the seals of the bishop, the count, and ourselves, the witnesses being recorded who were present with us: Henry, venerable bishop of Troyes, and Gerard, archdeacon of the same place; Guy, provost of Auxerre; William, dean; Stephen, cantor; Stephen, cellarer; Garnier, seneschal; Stephen of Pierre-Perthuis, knight; Stephen, the bishop’s [Col. 1388C] provost; Raaudus; and the burgesses of Auxerre.

Done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1164, in the reign of Louis, most Christian king of the Franks.

[Col. 1387]

## DIPLOMAS OF ALAN

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, XII, *Instrum.*, col. 126 and following.)

### I. Charter of Bishop Alan for the Monastery of Saint Marianus

[Col. 1387D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, [Col. 1388D] ALAN, bishop of Auxerre. Since it is certain that a bishop is Christ’s vicar, he ought to assist the needs of the poor of that same Christ. [Col. 1389A] Therefore our predecessor Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, bestowed many gifts upon the regular canons of the Premonstratensian Order, whom, aflame with zeal for religion, he established at Auxerre to serve God there in the church of Saint Marianus.

Indeed, he gave them the aforesaid church of Saint Marianus, with certain vineyards attached to that church; the church of Saint Martin; the church of Saint Salvius; and the site of a mill upon the river Belcha, with the land and rent belonging to the mill. He also gave them the church of Blessed Mary situated in the suburb, with its rents and vineyards, lands, tithes, meadows, male and female serfs, and all appurtenances located near Longene, and a full prebend in the Church of Saint Stephen. Having received all these from the bishop’s hand, the canons did not confirm them by the episcopal seal, whether through simplicity or excessive trust in the donor. They now ask us to confirm them.

Therefore, lest they suffer any claim concerning these things in the future, we grant the very same things that he gave, with the assent and concession of the entire chapter of Saint Stephen and at the request of William, count of Nevers, who later became a Carthusian, although that chapter itself did not give its approval. To these gifts, by episcopal generosity, we add the church of Tangiacum. And that these may remain valid and unshaken for them, we have caused this to be written and authenticated with the devices of our seals, namely our own and that of the common chapter of Saint Stephen.

Done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1163.

### II. The priory of Saint Amator is united to the monastery of Saint Satyrius of Bourges

[Col. 1389C]

It belongs to the discernment of the episcopal office not merely to protect and preserve religious places, but also to advance religion itself to a better condition. Accordingly, I, ALAN, by God’s grace styled bishop of Auxerre, by the office laid upon me and by command of apostolic authority, grant in perpetuity to the church of Saint Satyrius the church of Blessed Amator, together with those possessions which the regular canons then held, preserving the arrangements existing between the church of Saint Amator and Blessed Stephen, and on the condition that a prior from that house be appointed there by the bishop; that he live there in accordance with the custom and discipline [Col. 1389D] of the aforesaid church; that he and his [Col. 1390A] brethren, with the Lord’s grace assisting, observe the Rule of Blessed Augustine; and that, once appointed, he be removed only by the bishop.

To prevent any occasion of dispute hereafter between the bishop and the canons, it has been settled with my assent and theirs that the bishop shall pay every year twelve measures of wine from the bishop’s vineyards, in which the canons claimed the tithe: ten of red and two of white. In the land called Cunemine, whenever it is cultivated, the canons shall receive the tithe. This settlement was made on the octave of Blessed Stephen in the chapter at Auxerre, Guy the provost, Rainaud the archdeacon, Rudolph the treasurer, and Stephen the cantor being present and assisting, with the assent also of the whole chapter, in the year from the Incarnation [Col. 1390B] of the Lord 1163, in the pontificate of Pope Alexander III, in the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, and under William the Younger, count of Nevers.

### III. Alan confirms certain churches to the monks of Donzy

I, ALAN, by God’s grace bishop of Auxerre, wish it to be known to present and future persons that Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, of good memory, who had been raised to the episcopate from the church of Saint Germanus of Auxerre, over which he had long presided, gave to Saint Mary of Donzy and to the monks serving the Lord there the church of Saint Vincent at Pigny and the church of Saint Peregrinus at Bouhy. Subsequently, in my time, when a dispute arose concerning the presentation of the priest of Bouhy, [Col. 1390C] after the testimony of trustworthy men on this matter had been received, I, following in the footsteps of that holy man, confirmed the gift made of the church of Pigny and the church of Bouhy, together with presentation of the priest, saving the episcopal right; retaining that portion of the tithes which belonged to the Church of Auxerre in the time of Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, who had been raised to the episcopate from the church of Pontigny, and that portion of rent which the priest Benedict possessed.

Witnesses to this matter are Rainard, abbot of Bon Repos; Maurice, prior of Donzy, in whose time this was done; Stephen the cellarer; Rainaud, canons of Auxerre; Arnaud and Geoffrey, monks of Donzy; Arnaud the provost; and William *canis putidus* (“stinking dog”).

[Col. 1390D] Done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1164.

[Col. 1389]

## TESTAMENT OF ALAN

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. XII, col. 136.)

[Col. 1389D] What has been done and confirmed by the counsel and will of our chapter, lest it be weakened in any way, we commit to the trust of letters, so that posterity may hold as certain and ratified what is written in this document. Therefore [Col. 1390D] I, the styled abbot of Ripatorium, leave in writing for the knowledge of present and future persons that the venerable lord Alan, formerly bishop of Auxerre, so disposed his testament through our hand, lest anything of the goods which he possessed [Col. 1391A] should remain intestate:

First, concerning the grange called Via-Domange (today Vaudemanche), it was ordered and decreed that the boundaries of his possessions are not to be transferred from it in any way; rather, as it presently possesses them, so it shall possess them forever, if it remains a grange forever. But should it ever happen that the boundaries within the walls of Doschia (today Dosches) are enlarged so that it has four ploughlands of land adjoining it, then the boundaries of the lands lying beyond the stream of Germont may be transferred at the discretion of the abbot and the brethren of sounder counsel.

Also, every year, on each solemnity on which the brethren assemble to hear the word of God, and on the feasts of Saint Bernard and on the anniversary [Col. 1391B] of this same Alan, one pound of white bread from the grain of that grange shall be given to each person. If, because of the pressure of circumstances, one of these solemnities is transferred or the sermon omitted, the provision of this ordinance is nevertheless not to be omitted in any way. Concerning the vineyard at Valière, it was said and agreed that all of it should be assigned to the use of the convent; and lest the cellarers be burdened by its cultivation, he assigned to them five arpents of vineyards lying on the hill of Teneleriis (today Tennelières), which he had purchased for himself, so that they might devote the fruit received from them to the cultivation of that vineyard.

Furthermore, he gave us seven chalices and all his books, both cloister books and church books, decreeing, commanding, and ordering that no book or chalice be taken out of Ripatorium or carried away by any means. All this was done for this reason and by this counsel: if he should be buried at Clairvaux in the tomb of his fathers, all that has been said concerning the books shall remain ratified and established; but if not, all shall be void, and shall neither remain ratified nor established. Although we took this clause ill, since we did not love the absence of so great a father, yet because it concerned his soul, and because from long ago it had been in his heart to be buried with Saint Bernard so that he might rise again with him, we granted the burial as he requested, though unwillingly. And, lest all these matters as stated and written should perish with the passage of time, we inserted them [Col. 1392B] under the threat of anathema and ordered them to be validated by the impression of our seal and the affixing of his ring.

Nevertheless, since nothing greater is owed to a person than that the affection of love shown while he lives should not be denied when he dies, we decree, adding to this present writing, that when he has passed from this world, the priests shall perform five Masses, the clerics two psalters, and the lay brothers three hundred *Our Fathers*. On the anniversary the observance shall be as follows: a Mass shall be said for him in the convent every year; the priests shall celebrate the Divine Office for that day; the clerics shall perform fifty psalms; and the lay brothers shall perform one hundred *Our Fathers*. Done in the year of the Incarnation of the Word, 1182. [Note: [Col. 1391] The authentic parchment instruments of this testament, furnished with their seals intact, are still preserved in the Public Archives at Troyes.]

[Col. 1391]

## LIFE OF SAINT BERNARD, BY ALAN

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXV, *Works of Saint Bernard*, vol. IV.)

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1186. BLESSED PETER, EIGHTH ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX

[Col. 1391]

## HISTORICAL-LITERARY NOTICE

(Oudin, *Script. eccles.*, II, 1561)

PETER, surnamed Monoculus (“the One-Eyed”), eighth abbot of Clairvaux, a Frenchman by nationality and of noble stock, first became a monk at Clairvaux. Then, after Geoffrey was transferred by election from the church of Igny to the governance of Clairvaux, Peter was elected abbot at Igny in Geoffrey’s place in 1162. He presided over [Col. 1393] that church until 1179, when, though unwilling, he was moved from being abbot of Igny to administer the renowned mother church of Clairvaux.

He wrote elegant letters on diverse subjects. I saw them collected from manuscripts in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés at Paris by the monk Transmundus; Bertrand Tissier printed them in volume III, p. 264, of the *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum Ordinis Cisterciensis*. As an apostolic judge, together with the abbot of Cîteaux, he was sent to the dissident Grandmontines; he kindly received at Clairvaux their clerics or priests, who had been driven from their own houses by the insolent lay brethren. He also discharged an embassy to Emperor Henry.

Finally, while visiting the churches of his order in the course of his office, he breathed his last at Fusniacum on the fourth day before the Kalends of December, in 1186. The Chronicle of Auxerre reports that he died celebrated for a reputation of holiness. Brought to Clairvaux, he was placed in Saint Bernard’s first stone tomb or coffin, beside Gerard, under the following common epitaph:

> Beneath this stone cell lie Lord Gerard, distinguished martyr, sixth abbot of Clairvaux, and Lord Peter, the eighth, renowned for miracles, whose Life is found in the volume of Blessed Bernard.

Caesarius treats of Peter, abbot of Clairvaux, in his work *On the Miracles of His Time*, and Abbot Conrad in the *Great Cistercian Exordium*; consult them if you wish for more. Thus the Sainte-Marthe brothers in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, p. 256, under the Abbots of Clairvaux.

[Col. 1393]

## LETTERS OF BLESSED PETER

(Dom Tissier, *Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensis*, vol. III, p. 264.)

### I. To Pope Alexander III

He complains that the Cistercian Order is harassed by secular persons through lawsuits, plundering of property, and so forth, and implores the pope’s help against these evils.

[Col. 1393A]

“The evil of the day increases,” etc. See among the various letters to Alexander III, after his *Registers*, *Patrologia*, vol. CC.

### II. To the Same

He thanks the pontiff for favors conferred, especially upon the monastery of Balerne (which belongs to the line of Clairvaux), and desires that its pending legal case against wicked persons may quickly be concluded.

“What are we to do, holy Father,” etc. See above.

### III. To the Chancellor

He commends to him the bishop of Autun, whom some of his own people had summoned before the Apostolic See.

[Col. 1393B]

Contempt is not to be feared as importunate where the gaze of compassion is extended, because charity is never importunately requested: it is always ready to grant more abundantly than is asked. This is what, in the Apostle and apostolic men—such as I may without impropriety say that you are—not only bestows itself, but is bestowed beyond measure. This is what burns with those who are scandalized and is weak with those who are weak (2 Cor. 11). Finally, this is what, from contemplation of the holy men who have preceded us, promises us good hope in you for the future.

Accordingly, relying upon this charity, we seek your aid not merely for our necessities [Col. 1393C] but also for our obligations, and commend to you the case of our bishop of Autun. His religious devotion builds his good reputation, and the goodness of his religion builds his conscience; virtue has produced rivals for him where malice could not produce enemies. For certain members of his own household, foolishly kicking against the goad to their own hurt, recently raised their heel against him and summoned a man of conspicuous innocence before the Apostolic See. These wicked men, accustomed to the scandals of disputes, do not know how to refrain from rising up to disturb this man too, in obedience to their old habit, after the disturbances and lawsuits brought against his predecessors. We therefore commend to you his simplicity and justice, and ask and beseech that his position, shaken by the winds of hostile malice, may be supported by the strength of your kindness.

### IV. To the Archbishop of Mainz

He extols his virtues, then commends to him the monastery of Eberbach and its abbot.

After the victory over the old hostility, through which holy mother Church triumphed in your hands when the schism had been overcome; after the laborious contests of proven fidelity [Col. 1394B], through which the strength of the Empire and the glory of imperial majesty shone forth through you, there was not lacking for you an angel of Satan to strike you with the blows of his malice even in triumph, lest either the greatness of so great an achievement should exalt you or the uninterrupted prosperity of successful outcomes should fail to show the merit of your patience.

Zion heard and rejoiced at the things you accomplished by the integrity of your faith. We heard and sympathized with the things you endured through another’s faithlessness, giving thanks to Him who exposed you to the assaults of temptation for the increase of your glory, yet did not permit you to be tried beyond endurance. Therefore, hearing with most joyful ears through glad reports that you have been delivered from the hands of the impious, we do not cease to pray and give thanks for you, that the Lord our God [Col. 1394C] may repay you with everlasting glory for your stewardship of public peace and wipe away the sweat of your endurance with the hand of gentle consolation.

And because divine grace has restored you to the expectation of our sons at Eberbach, we ask that your presence now much more cherish them and that house itself, which until now has been preserved and prospered in all things beneath the shadow of your name, and that you not permit it to be harmed or troubled in anything. May the favor toward it increase which it received from you when you departed; its condition is especially set aright by the opportunity of your return, if your old mercy is heaped up with new acts of compassion. In particular, we commend to your goodwill our dearest brother, your most devoted son, A., abbot of that place, who succeeded Lord G. when he returned from there. Through the gentleness of Jesus Christ we ask that you cherish him in the Lord as our own inward parts, knowing without doubt that whatever peace and consolation are granted to him by the gift of your charity will be reckoned as shown to us and to the whole Order. If anyone suggests anything adverse to you in disparagement of him, let iniquity rather lie to itself, and let the mouth that speaks wicked things be silenced by your rebukes.

### V. To the Abbot of Cîteaux

He reports the death of the abbot of Trois-Fontaines, murdered by a most wicked man. [Note: [Col. 1395D] Blessed Gerard of Igny, killed shortly before.]

[Col. 1395B]

Drenched in bitterness of spirit and inwardly pierced by pain of heart, I do not know, Father, what to say to you or what to do, overwhelmed by grievous affliction and misery. But attend to what will be written, and see whether there is sorrow like my sorrow (Lam. 1:12). For a harsher blow has lately torn open the scar covering the former wound: so that I, who long ago mourned the parricidal funeral occasioned by the killing of a Father, am compelled now to lament the same thing in the firstborn of Clairvaux.

To increase still further the sum of my miseries [Col. 1395C], each of them in some manner died in my hands; each was killed in my presence. Thus the sword of this grief might pierce the soul of an old man bereaved all the more cruelly because it struck me, wretched as I am, from close at hand and wounded me more deeply from nearby. For it happened a few days ago that we were carrying out the duty of visitation in the house of Trois-Fontaines, which is the first among our daughters. Behold, the abbot of that place entered the sanctuary of the church, where he had lately erected an altar of Blessed Bernard, intending, as usual, to offer a private prayer, so that afterward, when the solemnities of the Masses had been celebrated, he might be more devoutly prepared for us and for the pressing business at hand.

While he remained there and stood with the angels of God before the Lord, Satan too appeared among them, permitted to stretch out [Col. 1395D] his hand against him, so that that most innocent Father might receive death where he sought the Author of life. For after him entered a man of Belial named Simon. Having shut the door in order to kill in secret, he attacked the said abbot, his Father, striking the blade of an axe against his head. Nor did he cease from cutting his face and crown until that Father—no longer unhappy, but still pitiable—crowned with his own blood, breathed out his spirit in the hands of Him to whom he was praying.

After one hour had passed, that most cruel parricide went away and did not fear to celebrate Mass, seeking to assume the devotion of the priesthood as a veil for his crime. For a long time the murderer lay hidden, unrecognized amid the tumult of mourners and monks gathering together [Col. 1396A], although the voice of blood flowing without cease pointed out the man of blood, whenever he approached the bier, by a kind of dripping testimony. Thereupon, later confronted with these and certain other circumstantial signs, he confessed himself guilty of the deed he had committed—indeed deserving to obtain no pardon, since he found in the victim no cause of death.

And now, best Father, he has been captured, chained, and kept in bonds. We most urgently beg you that, after counsel has been fixed for the appointed day and deliberation held with the brethren, such punishment may be determined for him that it ought to put an end to the inducement for a similar presumption.

### VI. To the community of Trois-Fontaines

He admonishes that community carefully to guard the murderer and not to kill him by hunger.

[Col. 1396B]

Those who have one heart and one soul in the Lord necessarily hold other things also in common, whether an unchangeable law of fixed equity has granted them the free kindness of a better lot, or the sad collision of a harsher chance has inflicted it upon them. This is proved, in the pain of your wound, by the unrestrained fellow-feeling of the Fathers of the Order: whatever it is by which your brotherhood is distressed because of the enormity of a recent crime is poured into their breasts through participation in your grief. They feel—indeed they feel—that what you lament concerns them according to the measure of their ability; for what burns you by the singularity of the calamity kindles them through the kinship of charity. They advise you, moreover, and desire of you, that, now at last having received consolation in this grief, you should fortify your actions with prudent circumspection, and show yourselves henceforth such that the bitterness of the present misfortune may be judged not so much a punishment for past neglects as a safeguard for merits to follow.

Concerning that wretched parricide, after deliberation they have decreed that, although not merely his presence but even his memory alike renews horror and grief, nevertheless, in order to avoid a greater scandal, you are to keep him under strict guard until the chapter; sustaining the miserable man’s life with bread and water alone, except that your humanity may provide him with some pottage on three days of the week. For both we and you must take care that, while we wish him not to escape from our bonds, violence of hunger does not destroy him in our hands. See, therefore, that you do not disregard either of these two points; for what the authority of the Order has decreed, your religious devotion must wholly emulate. As for what further must be done in your affairs, behold, we are at home, ready for every aid of consolation and peace whenever the time for counsel shall come before you.

### VII. To the abbot of Carilocus.—He orders that what is just be restored to a merchant who says he was cheated in a livestock transaction.

[Col. 1397A]

No small advance in charity is shown when the gain of brotherly peace is preferred to private profits. For, as the Apostle says, godliness with sufficiency is great gain (1 Tim. 6); and we especially ought to attend to this, since we are believed to have forsaken earthly things for heavenly ones. Therefore, since that man maintains that in the livestock transaction involving animals which he bought from your brethren he was defrauded of almost three hundred shillings, we wish your discretion diligently to investigate the matter and, if what is asserted is found true, to moderate the said N.’s loss by reasonable compensation. Thus God too will be glorified here: for an acceptable sacrifice is kindled upon the altar of the heart [Col. 1397B] when the fat of earthly greed is burned in the fires of charity.

### VIII. To Simon of Montacute.—He exhorts him to persevere in works of mercy toward his neighbours.

We gladly behold, and reverently esteem, the grace of our God at work in you—a grace which the Almighty planted like a fruitful olive tree in your breast. We know that it would never spread itself so widely into the branches of good works unless the dew of heaven made it fruitful in that turf of charity from which it springs. Rejoicing, therefore, with all our affections in Christ over this grace, we pray for its continual progress and abundant fruits: that through saving actions it may thus continually break forth publicly [Col. 1397C], while receiving unfailing growth inwardly.

And it will receive such growth if it does not cease to give; for the oil of godliness and the ointment of compassion, the more abundantly it is poured out upon the necessities of brethren, is increased by gifts of greater worth. Divine grace does not know how to be subject to failure; rather, becoming richer through its own diminution, it is restored to gain from the very source from which it seemed to have suffered loss. Persist, therefore, as you do, in works of mercy, so that you may acquire for yourselves the crown in recompense for your merits, and may cause enduring joy concerning your salvation to flow to us.

### IX. To the bishop of Winchester.—He says that in a certain matter he did not dishonour the king, but provided for the purity of the Order against a false brother; and he commends the house of Mortuimaris.

[Col. 1397D]

Having received with thanksgiving the letter which you sent, we dispatch messengers and writings to appease the king’s mind.

> [Note: [Col. 1397D] Understand here the king of England.]

We hope that, if he learns the integrity of what was done, the clemency of his countenance will grow calm and he will turn to mercy that which he had purposed in anger. You also, lest you should accept doubtful things as certain when the truth is unknown, should rather believe us—if you please, entrusting our word to most faithful testimony—that whatever was done and decreed concerning that man was compelled by the necessity of law and the sincerity of equity. [Col. 1398A] There was no perverse consideration there that diminished the king’s honour; rather, there was a straightforward and timely provision, lest the purity of the Order and the name of the person should be cheapened as disgrace increased.

As to his assertion that he has been seized and placed, as it were, in prison, he himself should consider what he is saying. Perhaps he counts it more a prison because he is not allowed to go about the earth and walk through it, so as to go forth speaking against his brethren and setting scandal against the sons of his mother. Therefore close your ears henceforth to empty insinuations; and, we ask, act on our behalf and stand before the lord king, that he may not restrain his mercies in anger nor, judging them himself, hold guilty those whom the sincerity of blameless action proves innocent. Let him also regard the house of Mortuimaris with his accustomed mercy, [Col. 1398B] lest it too suffer punishment in its place because, after the likeness and habit of the living sea, it does not retain dead flesh.

### X. To the abbot of Vallibus.—He complains that a book he had lent was ruined by dripping water and returned by night so that the damage might not be discovered.

A loss is serious, and burdened by several injuries, when the damage done to a material object goes so far that the simplicity of charity is also deceived. We say this because the book which you sent back to us, ruined through excessive neglect and drenched by an inundation of dripping water, though you had kept it carelessly, you returned very cautiously. The bearer, namely, arranged to restore it at night, and himself to pass on before dawn on the following day, while the cause was not yet [Col. 1398C] known. As though it were not enough that the late-arriving guest concealed the injury of the damage done, unless he should again make our confidence the sport of his sudden flight and haste.

Why, then, should those who left the former book in such disgraceful condition through such mockery still receive another book from us? Although, therefore, for the charity which bears all things, we for the present overlook the past offence, yet fearing like conduct from the like persons, we require that another book of ours which you have be immediately returned to us. For he knowingly turns danger back upon himself who, taught by experience of a previous injury, does not avoid the misfortunes of future loss.

### XI. To Queen Tarasia.—He praises the queen, especially for her generosity toward the poor and toward the Order.

[Col. 1398D]

The page of the letter which you sent has reached us, full alike of the sweet grace of exceptional devotion and shining with the brightness of royal faith. For from its tenor we have plainly learned that, although the exalted rank of sovereign honour is at your disposal, the humility of your mind honours you far more: it restrains the pride of worldly power in your most serene heart while raising that heart toward the pursuit of heavenly blessedness.

Hence it is that, unlike the other women of our time, you are not ashamed of Christian poverty in Christ’s poor, while you most devoutly seek the prayers [Col. 1399A] of those whom you yourself more truly sustain by your aid. And whence comes so great a current of humility in a virgin, unless from love and imitation of him who emptied himself and deigned to be born of a virgin?

Now therefore, Lord Jesus Christ, sower of mercy and of humble counsel, receive the fruits of the seeds which you have sown in Tarasia. But you, most excellent lady, whom the heavenly Lord has anticipated with so great a blessing that you learned to love heaven before earth, do what you do; love what you love; so that, after the flourishing sovereignty of present glory, you may exchange the corruptible crown of this kingdom for an incorruptible diadem. We commend to your magnificence our poor brethren—indeed, now rich through your household—though there is no need for us to do so, [Col. 1399B] in order that we may show our fatherly solicitude toward them and that the reward of your work may be doubled, if what you do out of spontaneous generosity you also do in obedience to our admonition.

### XII. To the king of Portugal.—He commends the humility of the king, who had anticipated him with a letter, and his charity toward the Order; and he accepts the monastery of Castineria offered by the king.

We embrace with outstretched arms [Col. 1399C] of lowly humility the favour of your graciousness, by which you anticipated us with the address of a royal greeting. We give thanks to God, who has made you lofty in the glory of earthly dignity in such a way that he has made you more glorious still by the summit of humility and love for heavenly things. For with such humility and kindness does your glory make itself known to us in the letter which you sent that it seems to speak rather of a knight than a prince—except that this is indeed the most exalted sovereignty which is seen to be supported by faith in Christ and humility.

What letter, indeed, can we send back to you, who do not allow the poverty of our brethren to remain poor, but increase it with the gifts of your continual beneficence and the extension of landed endowments? Look upon these holy works also, we pray, Christ Jesus, as acceptable works of this royal piety, so that he who gives your poor freedom from the anxieties of this world may, through your gift, [Col. 1399D] have with them an everlasting dwelling in the house of your Father.

For our part, most pious prince, revering according to our measure the riches of your benevolence, we gladly accept the offering of the monastery of Castineria, which out of love for holy religion you have resolved to transfer under the title of our Order. We have a ready will in the Lord that, when the abbot of that place comes, he may receive from us fitting assistance and support. As for the aid of prayers which you requested: can you fail to share in our good things, to whom we are so greatly indebted for such great benevolence?

### XIII. The community of Clairvaux, to Pope Alexander.—The community asks the pontiff not to deprive it of its abbot Henry, who was being sought for the bishopric of Toulouse.

[Col. 1400A]

“We are guided by the example of Christ’s disciples,” etc. See under Alexander III, above.

### XIV. The community of Clairvaux, to the king of the French.—It asks the king not to allow its abbot to be taken away and made bishop of Toulouse.

You have been accustomed to add the most ample affections of royal love, which you extend to all the Churches of your realm out of reverence for the supreme King, to the fullness of the charity already begun toward us, so that you might make singular for us, without prejudice to others, a favour common to all through your piety. Thus [Col. 1400B] the riches of heavenly grace enlarge your most pious heart, so that it abounds with that from which all may draw, and yet does not lack that which familiar affection may claim as its own by right of possession.

Therefore, rejoicing in the prerogative of special favour, we approach the throne of your majesty in our necessities with greater confidence, inasmuch as we already possess more evident proofs of certainty from the very privilege of your affection. Now, therefore, it is greatly necessary that you be present to your Clairvaux. If, while you reign, it should lose its shepherd through human interference, it has no one left in whom it can thereafter either wish or be able wholly to trust as a man.
