We have sent you our messengers, who must surely be found trustworthy if what you answered us through them concerning the magnificence of your protection is fulfilled. [Col. 1400C] For the lord cardinal has shown, by an unexpected change both of journey and of intention, how he fulfilled what he promised.

It remains, therefore, for the sincerity of your faith to restore to us the consolation of which we have been deprived, by writing to the lord pope that he should neither now consent to this destruction of our peace nor hereafter admit the appeals of any desolated Church as a customary cause of our disturbance. For it is unjust, and forbidden by sacred laws, that one person should be enriched at another’s loss. And indeed we seem vainly to persist in the devoted labour of prayer for the advantageous election of a shepherd if it happens that we have shed our tears for the consolation of others rather than for our own.

### XV. The community of Clairvaux, to the lord Cador, archdeacon.—It says that it is distressed not to have been honoured by his visit, and announces the death of its prior.

[Col. 1400D]

Your prudence rightly, yet no less graciously, excuses the fact that, occupied with the duties of royal service, you could not provide the joy of your promised visit at the appointed time. Yet you must recognize this: the excuse does not satisfy our desires, even if it seems to have satisfied judgments, because whatever unforeseen occurrence has brought in, however justly, the necessity of an obligation does not prescribe terms to the affections of charity.

For what if you cannot fulfil [Col. 1401A] what I desire? Yet I cannot cease to love what I love; nor does the stubborn flame of ardent love cease in turn to rise to the height of its desires, even when restrained by the obstacle of an imposed difficulty. For even here the not blameworthy excess of love has its own excess: often, when we cannot obtain what we desire, we desire still more ardently what impossibility denies. Henceforth it is yours by every means to ensure that what had been arranged in pious friendship concerning your visit is not taken away from us but merely postponed.

Furthermore, your request that knowledge of our condition be given you by letter proceeded from that charity through which you rightly make your own whatever prosperity may bring us that is joyful or adversity that is sorrowful. By God’s grace, both we and your Clairvaux fare quite prosperously, except that most recently, in these days, the hand of the Lord has touched us not lightly. In the absence of the abbot, the death of the prior struck us most grievously on one and the same day, depriving us of the consolation of both parents. We, mourning the death of one and awaiting the return of the other,

> [Note: [Col. 1401D] Abbot Henry was then made a cardinal.]

sigh between sorrows and joys—indeed, more sorrowful because, through weariness at the delay, we cease to hope for the coming of the aforesaid Father, which we have long awaited in vain.

### XVI. To religious persons established in Germany.—The community of Clairvaux shares with the abbots of Germany participation in its prayers, etc.

[Col. 1401C]

We know, brethren, that the gifts of heavenly graces grow through the common fellowship of brethren, and that they overflow more abundantly within the minds of their possessors the more liberally they flow out, through a channel as it were of transmitting charity, to the aid of neighbours. Therefore, requested for the suffrages of our brotherhood, we gladly assent to your wishes, granting you perpetual fellowship with God through participation in our prayers, so that we too may obtain, as we earnestly ask, a share pleasing to God through fellowship in yours.

For when we divide our good things between one another, we unite our inmost minds in the love of God under the bond of peace; and what was possessed by each person through divine gift is increased for all through this unity. Therefore we warn and exhort you [Col. 1401D] in the Lord that henceforth, with a view to this fellowship and to earning God’s grace alike for us and for yourselves, you may be more zealous in the ministry of the divine work, sowing blessings with a full hand, so that at last you may harvest with a full sickle in the eternal fields.

May his righteousness be enlarged in your hearts; may the gate be closed to follies; and may love of the world, or of secular powers, be subordinated to the guardianship of divine love. Let natural ties also not prejudice truth in your affections; for flesh and blood do not inherit the kingdom of God, nor is it in any way expedient for you, if you have left the world for Christ, to abandon Christ for the world in a damnable exchange. [Col. 1402A]

### XVII. To the community of Mortuimaris.—He exhorts those in distress to exercise courage and display patience.

Having heard the roaring of the rising storm, which the blast of diabolical malice is stirring up against you and your house, we persist with anxious prayer, insofar as we can, in awakening Jesus again as he sleeps, that he may now rise and help you and not abandon you in so great a necessity. Yet we hope and trust in him that, rising, he will rise to command the winds and waves, so that calm may come from the disturbance and the fixed tempest of this trouble may become [Col. 1402B] a breeze; that its waves may grow mild and be still.

But to you, dearest brethren, an opportunity has been granted to exercise virtue, so that you may show in persecution what progress you have made in peace, and now unfold from your treasures for merit whatever you suppose has come to you as gain while you were trading. For behold, a pitch-black night of gloomy tribulation is spread over you; but act so that night may be illuminated like day, and that this night may become your illumination amid your delights, when, in the darkness of the storm, that shines forth which you once kindled in the light of brightness.

For thus it is written: “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night his song” (Ps. 41). What is this song except thanksgiving and the voice of praise—the song into which we are especially commanded to break forth when the evils of the present life break forth more grievously against us? He invited his disciples to this song when he said: “Count it all joy, my brethren, when you fall into various trials” (Jas. 1). And lest any doubt concerning the severity of the trial creep in, observe that another preached with no different spirit: “God,” he says, “is faithful, and will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear; but with the temptation he will also make the outcome, that you may be able to endure it” (1 Cor. 10).

You therefore, brethren, set it in your hearts to preserve unceasing patience, and make from the malice of the deceiver a gain for charity. Make your paths straight and let your endeavors be directed toward the Lord, so that what you read may be fulfilled in you: “When a man’s ways please the Lord, he will turn even [Col. 1402D] his enemies to peace.” For who will harm you, if you are imitators of what is good? Let the discipline of the Order, love of the brotherhood, and sincerity of charity persist among you; and let no adversity now be feared where no iniquity rules. Let the fear of God and contempt of the world live in you, and all things are conquered.

We also, as you yourselves requested, have sent messengers and letters to the lord king

> [Note: [Col. 1402D] Understand the king of England.]

and to other persons. We hope that peace and tranquillity will soon smile upon you in due season, provided only that the rod of discipline which you bear neither falls before these blasts nor withers.

### XVIII. To the bishop of Bath and the abbot of Forde.—He commends the case of the monks of Fountains.

[Col. 1403A]

We write to you more than is necessary concerning the case of our brethren of Fountains, which the lord pope has committed to your piety, since we believe that it is more than sufficiently implanted in your hearts to judge the poor in righteousness and to render judgment in equity for the meek of the earth. The case itself too, as we confidently hope, is so supported by the benefit of law that it should require little from the office of a judge. Yet, because it seemed right to them, it has seemed right also to us humbly to implore your excellence, that the groaning of the afflicted may enter into your sight and that you may not permit the poor of him who will weigh the judgments of human decisions in the balance of equity to be burdened with unjust laws. [Col. 1403B]

That day will come—indeed, it will come—whatever Christ’s poor may suffer meanwhile, when they will stand in great steadfastness against those who afflicted them and took away their labours. We too bear witness to the truth: the venerable lord Philip, upon whose statement the lord of York seems to rely, as though he had renounced, on behalf of the community, both the case and the complaint, wholly maintains and testifies the contrary. He recalls that he said only this: that it was more expedient for them to await the mercy of himself, their patron, and their bishop than to contend with him in the contest of an uncertain lawsuit.

Therefore we ask and beseech you in Christ Jesus that, just as you have received from the lord pope the manner in which you ought to proceed and to conduct the examination of the case, so, Fathers, strive to act and determine the matter entrusted [Col. 1404A] to you according to the bare merits of the case. For you know how dangerous it is to show deference to a person if justice thereby suffers any loss.

### XIX. To the bishops of Albano and Palestrina.—He asks that their wrongdoers be restrained.

Why should even one stroke of the pen separate in a letter those who are joined by one summit of dignity? Or why should distinction be sought on pages where the simple unity of charity flourishes? We therefore write to you two as to one; for while we receive the one in either of you, we cultivate a singular affection in the plurality of two. The condition of our Church is domestic to you; its affection is not alien from you.

It has been placed, as you know, [Col. 1404B] among untamed nations, stubborn in French ferocity; and, while they squander their own goods through excess, they seize and plunder the goods of others through violence. Therefore, through your intervention, we request that an apostolic rescript be granted to us, establishing by a general mandate the authority of the archbishops and bishops of our land to render us full justice against our malefactors. No absolution thereafter is to issue for them unless worthy satisfaction first precedes.

Let villages, towns, and cities cease from participation in the sacred mystery as long as the plunder of Blessed Remigius remains there, so that restitution without loss may come to us for the goods taken away while the celebration of divine offices is forbidden them. For the present we request these things from you, and great things indeed; if your love answers us in these matters, it will come about that, when necessary, we shall ask greater things.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1187: LETTERS OF AIMERIC, PATRIARCH OF ANTIOCH, AND TERRIC, GRAND PRECEPTOR OF THE TEMPLARS

[Col. 1403]

# LETTERS

### I. Aimeric, patriarch of Antioch, to Louis, king of the French.—Having related the victory of the Turks over the Christians, he implores the king’s help.

(Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 870.)

[Col. 1403D]

In the year 1164 from the Incarnation of the Lord, this letter was sent by the patriarch of Antioch to Louis, king of the French, as follows.

AIMERIC, by God’s grace patriarch of Antioch of the holy apostolic see, to LOUIS, illustrious king of the French: greeting and patriarchal blessing.

It was fitting that we should always write joyful things to your royal majesty [Col. 1405A], and cherish the splendour of its heart by the splendour and affection of our words. Yet the opposite has always happened with us. For our occasions are continual occasions of weeping, continual pain and groaning; nor can we speak except of the things amid which we live. Thus the common saying runs: where pain is, there are tongue and hand.

The frequent deaths and captivities of Christians which we behold daily, and likewise the destruction of the Eastern Church, afflict us with inexpressible grief. Utterly tormented almost to annihilation, we die while living amid bitterness of soul; and, living a life more bitter than death, to complete our miseries we cannot die altogether. Nor is there anyone who reflects in his heart and, moved by compassion, extends a hand to lift us up.

But, not to linger longer over words, [Col. 1405B] the very scanty Christian people who remain among us cry with us to you, choosing your clemency as that which, after God, is sufficient to free us and the Church of God in the East. And that the whole sequence of events done around us may be known to you: in the Lent just past, a certain man among the Saracens who are around us—one held greater than all the rest, and who oppressed our Christianity more than any who had existed long before—entered Egypt with a great force of Turks. He was commander of their army and governor of Damascus.

[Col. 1405C]

The king of Egypt, who is also called the sultan of Babylon, distrusting his own strength and that of his followers, devised a plan, by whatever means he could, to seek the king of Jerusalem as helper against the coming most warlike nation of Turks. He acted wisely, preferring to reign under tribute rather than to be deprived at once of life and kingdom. That man, then, as we have said, entered Egypt and, with certain inhabitants of that land favouring him, seized and fortified a certain city.

Meanwhile the sultan, negotiating agreements with the lord king concerning an annual tribute to be paid and the release from Egypt of all Christian captives, accepted the lord king as his helper. When the moment of his departure was imminent, the king entrusted to us and to our new prince, his kinsman Bohemond, son of that Prince Raymond, the care of both his kingdom and land until his return.

[Col. 1405D]

That great destroyer of the Christian people, situated near us, gathered from every side the kings and peoples of the unbelievers. Wishing to pass more freely to ravage the kingdom of Jerusalem and bring whatever aid he could to his dependent who was struggling in Egypt, he offered and repeatedly sought peace and truces from our prince. But the prince had no intention of agreeing to peace with him until the lord king’s return. Therefore, seeing that he could not fulfil his purpose, he turned his furious arms against us and besieged one of our castles, named Harenc, twelve miles from our city.

The besieged continually cried out to us—there were about seven thousand of them, fighting men, women, and children—and did not cease day and night to beg us to pity them. A day was even fixed beyond [Col. 1406A] which they could not hold out. Having gathered forces from every side, our prince set out on the feast day of Saint Lawrence and proceeded safely, with all who were with him, from Antioch to the castle. But the Turks, being cunning as they are, abandoned the siege and halted not far from the castle amid the narrow passes in their own territory.

On the next day our men pursued the Turks to that place. Acting less wisely than they ought, they gave way when battle was joined; and the fighting went so disastrously that almost none of us of any rank escaped, save one whom the strength of his horse or some chance delivered from that tumult. The prince was captured; the count of Tripoli was captured; likewise a certain Greek, Calamannus, a duke of Mamistia of great name; Hugh of Lusignan; [Col. 1406B] and certain brothers of the Temple and Hospital who had come from the land of Tripoli with the count. Some were cut down, others captured; none or very few of the people were saved. Men, horses, and arms were utterly destroyed almost to the last.

After the slaughter of the Christians, the Turks returned to the aforesaid castle and took it, leading its helpless population—women, children, and wounded alike—to Antioch under terms of agreement. They afterwards approached the city and ranged over the whole land as far as the sea, exercising their tyranny at will with the sword and fire upon everything that came before their eyes.

God is witness that the remnant left to us is entirely insufficient for the day-and-night watches upon the walls. [Col. 1406C] Because of the scarcity of men, we entrust their guarding and defence even to those whom we suspect. Clerics and priests guard the gates, with the use of the churches abandoned. We ourselves rise for watches upon the walls and, with great labour and without interruption, repair as best we can the many breaches caused by the earthquake. Yet all this is in vain unless God looks upon us with a more favourable countenance. For we do not hope to endure long, seeing that the strength of men in this age has failed and is altogether absent. Still, we do this so that nothing which could have been done may remain unattempted by us.

[Col. 1406D]

Above all, the sole anchor which remains to our hope encourages us in this: from all men we have heard of your greatness, that among all the kings of the West you have the East continually upon your lips and breathe forth concern for us. Hence we understand that your joy will not be complete until you fulfil what, on account of our sins, has not hitherto been granted to us. It is our hope that through your hand the Lord will visit his people and have mercy upon us.

May the sighs and groans of Christians enter the ears of the highest and incomparable prince; may the torments and sufferings of captives pierce his heart. And, lest we exceed the measure of a letter by writing further, or fail under this vain expectation and be consumed longer beneath the shadow of death, may royal majesty deign to write back and communicate its pleasure to us. Whatever we must endure at his word will not be burdensome to us. May the Lord Jesus Christ increase in the king’s heart the desire that we desire [Col. 1407A], so that he may kindle it—the one in whose hand are the hearts of kings. Amen.

### II. Aimeric to Henry, king of the English.—On the same subject.

(Baronius, *Annals*, under the year 1187, no. 5.)

AIMERIC, by God’s grace patriarch of Antioch of the holy and apostolic see, to HENRY, by the same grace most illustrious king of the English, beloved lord and friend: may you reign in him through whom kings reign.

With tears and sobs we announce to your excellence by this present letter our fittingly immeasurable grief at the unexpected and terrible calamity which has recently befallen us—or rather all Christendom. Let the whole age hear with you [Col. 1407B] our grief, that it may know whence our mourning and lamentation come and whither they tend.

On the fourth day of July in the year 1187 from the Incarnation of the Word, Saladin, having gathered a foreign multitude of enemies, gave battle to the Christians who were in the land of Jerusalem. Having routed their forces, he triumphed over them as he pleased. The life-giving Cross was exposed to the mockery of the Turks; the king and the Master of the Temple were taken; likewise Raymond the prince was killed by the wicked Saladin’s own hands. Bishops, Templars, Hospitallers, and nearly the whole multitude—twelve hundred [the designation is omitted in the supplied text] and thirty thousand foot soldiers—were slaughtered by the sword in defence of the Holy Cross, apart from the large number later killed or captured in the cities which he took.

Having been sated with Christian blood, he captured and fortified Tiberias; then the noble city of Acre, Caiphas, Caesarea, Joppa, Nazareth, Sebaste, Neapolis, Lydda, Ramla, Arsuf, Hebron, Bethlehem, and finally the holy city of Jerusalem. He besieged the Lord’s Sepulchre, swearing that he would break it into fragments and cast its pieces into the depths of the sea. [Col. 1407C]

Concerning the survivors, dreadful uncertainty holds us: we do not know the day or hour when they will be subjected to his dominion and their inhabitants either carried captive or slain—especially since they are known to be stripped of provisions, horses, arms of war, and defenders.

[Col. 1407D]

Because of this great wrath and indignation of God poured out from above upon us, we eat our bread with tears and are shaken by terrible fear: lest the Lord’s Sepulchre be handed over to foreign nations; lest the few who remain in the Christian land, if help is delayed and our enemies press upon us, place our necks beneath the swords of those who strike. You surpass the other kings of the West in prudence, reputation, and wealth, and we have always awaited your help. We pray that you may swiftly bring powerful aid to the Holy Land.

If you delay, the Lord’s Sepulchre, together with the noble city of Antioch and the land adjoining it, will lie under foreign nations in everlasting reproach. Remember your praise and renown, so that God, who raised [or: exalted] you to a kingdom, may be exalted through you. And if you will undertake this most worthy work on a great scale—[Col. 1408A] by coming yourself or sending us the aid we desire—the liberation of the whole Holy Land will, after God, be credited to you.

And we ourselves, mourning as we can and striking our guilty breasts, cry to God that he may grant you both the will and the power to accomplish this for the praise and glory of his name, so that in this extremity of the Holy Land’s death you may mercifully aid both it and us. Otherwise, we, exposed to various dangers and succumbing to prolonged weakness, must now expire; and, with Christian blood shed, the Lord’s Sepulchre and the noble city of Antioch with its adjoining territory must lie subject to foreign nations in everlasting reproach. We further ask that you keep commended to you the beloved brethren, the bishops of Chalon [Cabilonensis] [Col. 1408B] and Valence [Valeniensis], whom we have sent to you for this very purpose. Farewell.

### III. Aimeric to Hugh Eterianus.—He praises Hugh’s book against the doctrine of the Greek Church.

(See under Hugh Eterianus, *Patrologia*, vol. CCII [202].)

### IV. Terric, Grand Preceptor of the Templars, to all the brethren of the Temple.—Concerning the disaster of the Christians.

(Baronius, *Annals*, under the year 1187, no. 4.)

Brother TERRIC, called Grand Master of the most poor House of the Temple, and the poorest of all the brethren, [Col. 1408C] together with a convent almost wholly reduced to nothing, to all the preceptors and brethren of the Temple to whom these letters shall come: greeting, and that they may sigh for Him at whom sun and moon marvel.

By how many and how great calamities the wrath of God, our sins demanding it, has permitted us to be scourged at present, we are unable to set forth either in letters or in a lamenting voice—alas for sorrow! For the Turks, having gathered an immeasurable multitude of their peoples, began fiercely to invade the borders of our Christians. Gathering the battle-lines of our own peoples against them, within the octave of the blessed Peter and Paul we ventured to engage them and to set out toward Tiberias, which they had violently taken, leaving only the castle. When they had driven us upon most unfavorable rocky ground, [Col. 1408D] they attacked us so fiercely that, the Holy Cross and our king being captured, and all our multitude slain, and two hundred and thirty of our brethren, as we truly believe, beheaded on the same day (besides those sixty who were killed on the first day of May), scarcely the lord Count of Tripoli, the lord Reginald of Sidon, the lord Ballovius, and we ourselves were able to escape from that miserable field.

Then the pagans, having raged upon the blood of our Christians, did not delay to come with all their multitude against the city of Acre. Having violently taken it, they invaded almost the whole land, leaving to us and to Christendom only Jerusalem, Ascalon, Tyre, and Beirut. Even these cities, almost all their inhabitants having been slain, we shall in no way be able to retain unless divine [Col. 1409A] and your ready aid is at hand. They are also at present fiercely besieging the city of Tyre; day and night they do not cease from assaulting it. Their numbers are so great that, like ants, they have covered the whole face of the land from Tyre to Jerusalem and as far as Gaza. Therefore deign to bring aid as speedily as possible to us and to Eastern Christendom, now wholly ruined, so that through God and the eminence of your brotherhood we may, supported by your assistance, save the remaining cities. Farewell.

V. Of the same to Henry, king of England.—Concerning the capture of Jerusalem.

(Ibid.)

[Col. 1409B]

To the most dear lord HENRY, by the grace of God illustrious king of the English, duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and count of Anjou, brother TERRIC, formerly Grand Master of the House of the Temple at Jerusalem: greeting in Him who grants salvation to kings.

Know that Jerusalem, with the Tower of David, has been surrendered to Saladin. The Syrians, however, have custody of the Sepulchre until the fourth day after the feast of Saint Michael; and Saladin himself has permitted ten brethren of the Hospital to remain in the house of the Hospital, to care for the sick, for one year. The brethren of the Hospital at Belvoir still resist the Saracens most effectively, and have already captured two Saracen caravans. In capturing one of these, they valiantly gained all the arms, equipment, [Col. 1410A] and provisions that had been in the castle of Faba, which the Saracens had destroyed.

Still resisting Saladin are Gragchus [Gregeus] of Mont Royal, Mont Royal, Safed of the Temple, Gragchus of the Hospital, Margat, the White Castle, the land of Tripoli, and the land of Antioch. After Jerusalem had been taken, Saladin ordered the cross to be removed from the Temple of the Lord, and had it carried through the city for two days as a spectacle, being beaten with sticks. Then he caused the Temple of the Lord to be washed inside and out, above and below, with rose-water, and ordered his law to be proclaimed over it from its four sides amid a remarkable tumult.

From the feast of Saint Martin until the Circumcision of the Lord, he besieged Tyre with thirteen *pierrariae* [stone-throwing engines], which day and night hurled stones into it without cease. On the vigil of Saint Sylvester, the lord Marquis Conrad stationed knights and foot-soldiers along the city wall; and, having armed seventeen galleys and ten other small vessels, he fought against Saladin’s galleys with the aid of the house of the Hospital and the brethren of the Temple. Having defeated them, he retained eleven of their galleys and captured the great admiral of Alexandria together with eight other admirals, while a multitude of Saracens was slain. The remaining galleys of Saladin, escaping Christian hands, fled to Saladin’s army. By his order they were hauled ashore, and Saladin himself, applying fire, caused them to be reduced to ashes and cinders. Overcome with extreme grief, he cut off his horse’s ears and tail, and rode that horse through the whole army before the eyes of all. Farewell.

LXIV.—To Pope Alexander. 92.

LXVII.—To Henry, king of the English. 95.  
LXVIII.—To Pope Alexander. 97.  
LXIX.—To the same. 97.

LXXII.—To the abbot of Cîteaux and his brethren. 102.

LXXVI.—To Bartholomew, bishop of Exeter. 105.  
LXXVII.—To the abbot of Saint-Évroult. 105.  
LXXVIII.—To the abbot of the Court of God. 106.  
LXXIX.—To the abbot of Cîteaux. 106.  
LXXX.—To Henry, abbot of Fécamp. 107.  
LXXXI.—To Pope Alexander. 107.  
LXXXII.—To Henry, abbot of Fécamp. 108.  
LXXXIII.—To the lord William of Pavia, cardinal. 109.  
LXXXIV.—To the legates Albert and Theodwin. 110.  
LXXXV.—To Albert and Theodwin, cardinals. 111.  
LXXXVI.—To Pope Alexander. 112.  
LXXXVII.—To Henry, bishop of Bayeux. 112.  
LXXXVIII.—To the archbishops of Canterbury and Tarentaise. 113.  
LXXXIX.—To Rotrou, archbishop of Rouen. 114.  
XC.—Form of an agreement concerning a certain commission. 114.  
XCI.—To Henry, the elder king of England. 115.  
XCII.—To the same. 117.  
XCIII.—To the same. 117.  
XCIV.—To William, dean of Bayeux. 118.  
XCV.—To . . . 119.  
XCVI.—To Pope Alexander. 120.  
XCVII.—To the same. 120.  
XCVIII.—To Hugh, archdeacon of Lisieux, his nephew. 121.  
XCIX.—To Henry, the elder king of England. 122.  
C.—To Walter of Coutances. 123.  
CI.—To Henry, the elder king of England. 123.  
CII.—To Pope Alexander. 124.  
CIII.—To the same. 125.  
[Col. 1412] CIV.—To Lord Peter, cardinal. 125.  
CV.—To Pope Alexander. 126.  
CVI.—To the same. 127.

CIX.—To Pope Alexander. 131.  
CX.—To the same. 131.  
CXI.—To the same. 133.

CXIX.—To Pope Alexander. 141.  
CXX.—To Bartholomew, bishop of Exeter. 142.

CXXII.—To Richard, bishop of Winchester. 143.

CXXIV.—To the abbot of Clairvaux. 144.  
CXXV.—To William, archbishop of Reims. 145.

CXXVII.—To Henry, king of the English. 146.

ARNULF’S SERMONS. 151.

I.—Sermon delivered at the Council of Tours. 151.  
II.—Sermon on the same subject. 157.  
III.—Sermon at a synod. 161.  
IV.—Sermon on the Annunciation of the glorious Virgin Mary. 167.

TREATISE ON THE SCHISM which arose after the death of Pope Honorius II. 173.

I.—On the Nativity of the Lord. 195.
