WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF TYRE.

Historical-literary notice. 201. Second notice. 201. HISTORY OF DEEDS DONE IN THE PARTS BEYOND THE SEA, from the time of the successors of Muhammad to the year of the Lord 1184. 209. Prologue. 209.

BOOK ONE.

CHAPTER I.—How, in the time of the Emperor Heraclius, Omar, son of Khattab, the third leader of the Arabs after Muhammad, occupied all Syria. 213.

CHAPTER II.—What was the reason that he occupied the East so suddenly; and how, upon coming to Jerusalem, he ordered the Temple of the Lord to be rebuilt. 214.

CHAPTER III.—For how long Syria endured the yoke of slavery under successive rulers; and how the friendship contracted with Aaron, king of the Persians, by the magnificent Emperor Charles was useful to the faithful living under the dominion of unbelievers. 215.

CHAPTER IV.—How it came under the power of the Egyptian caliph; how, during the reign of the most wicked Heque, the yoke of servitude became more intolerable for the faithful; and concerning the destruction of the church at Jerusalem. 217.

CHAPTER V.—What was the condition of the faithful among unbelievers at that time. 218.

CHAPTER VI.—How the excellent Daber succeeded his wicked father as governor of the kingdom; and how, through the prayers of the lord Romanus, emperor of Constantinople, the church was rebuilt, with John Cariamte cooperating and the monk Constantine supplying what was necessary. [Col. 1413] 219.

CHAPTER VII.—On the rise and earliest origin of the Turkish people. 220.

CHAPTER VIII.—How many and how great vices held the world subject at that time. 223.

CHAPTER IX.—How, sins demanding it, the Persians occupied all regions as far as the Hellespont. 224.

CHAPTER X.—How, at the same time, crowds of the faithful came to the Holy City, and under what conditions they were treated both within and without; and how the city was again delivered into Turkish hands. 226.

CHAPTER XI.—On the arrival of Peter the Hermit, a man of God; and his conference with the venerable Simeon, patriarch of Jerusalem. 227.

CHAPTER XII.—The revelation made to the same Peter in the church of the Holy Resurrection. 228.

CHAPTER XIII.—On the dispute between Emperor Henry and Pope Gregory VII; and how Urban, his successor, kindly received Peter upon his return from Jerusalem. 229.

CHAPTER XIV.—On the journey of Pope Urban into the lands beyond the mountains, and the synod held at Clermont. 231.

CHAPTER XV.—The pope’s exhortation to the people concerning the journey to Jerusalem. 231.

CHAPTER XVI.—Which princes offered themselves for the journey; and concerning the sign of the cross, which those who intended to go impressed upon their garments as a sign of their vow and future pilgrimage. 234.

CHAPTER XVII.—Names of the princes from the kingdoms of the Franks and Germans who undertook the journey. 236.

CHAPTER XVIII.—Walter Sans-Avoir, the first to set out, arrives at Constantinople. 237.

CHAPTER XIX.—Peter the Hermit follows; passing through Hungary, he experiences the treachery of the Hungarians. 239.

CHAPTER XX.—At Niš, a city of Bulgaria, a dangerous disturbance arises between pilgrims and Bulgarians. 240.

CHAPTER XXI.—Peter recalls his fleeing army and again seeks to reach a peaceful agreement with the Bulgarians; but the latter error is worse than the former, and his legions are scattered. 241.

CHAPTER XXII.—Peter, having gathered the remnant of his routed legions, arrives at Constantinople; after crossing the Bosporus, he encamps in Bithynia. 242.

CHAPTER XXIII.—His army, while he is absent, drives off plunder from the region of Nicaea and captures a town near Nicaea. 243.

CHAPTER XXIV.—Soliman, leader of the Turks, recovers the aforesaid town and puts to the sword all whom he finds there. 244.

CHAPTER XXV.—The whole army is stirred up against the same Soliman because of the slaughter of their brethren, and, fighting against him, is destroyed. 245.

CHAPTER XXVI.—Soliman, victorious, plunders our camp, carries away the remnant of the people either captive or kills them; he besieges the castle of Civetot, but withdraws upon hearing the emperor’s embassy. 246.

CHAPTER XXVII.—A certain German priest, Godescalc, again leading an army, arrives in Hungary. 246.

CHAPTER XXVIII.—Letter of the king of the Hungarians to the aforesaid Godescalc and his army; and their wretched destruction. 247.

CHAPTER XXIX.—How the preceding armies were followed by an innumerable multitude of irrational men, who killed the Jewish people and proceeded without discipline. 248.

CHAPTER XXX.—How they besieged the castle of Meeszburg and killed seventy Hungarians; and how at last, divinely turned to flight, nearly all were killed by the Hungarians. 249.

BOOK TWO.

CHAPTER I.—At what time Duke Godfrey set out, which nobles were with him, and how he reached Hungary. 249.

CHAPTER II.—The embassy of the same duke to King Coloman of Hungary through Godfrey of Ascha, and that king’s reply to the same duke. 251.

CHAPTER III.—The king and our princes meet one another; Baldwin, the duke’s brother, is given to the king as a hostage; after Hungary has been crossed and his brother recovered, the duke is honored by the king with many gifts. 253.

CHAPTER IV.—Our legions enter the emperor’s land: the entrance is described, and the misery of the Greeks is made known. 254.

CHAPTER V.—The duke sends envoys to the emperor, demanding that he release Hugh the Great [Col. 1414] and other nobles whom he held in chains; the whole region is exposed to plunder, and at last our men arrive at Constantinople. 255.

CHAPTER VI.—The emperor invites the duke to him; he refuses to enter. Serious hostilities arise between them. By the emperor’s deceit, the duke’s army is moved to a narrower place. 256.

CHAPTER VII.—Description of the city of Constantinople. The duke sends envoys to the emperor; our army unexpectedly suffers an ambush by the Greeks. 257.

CHAPTER VIII.—The army returns to the city and a great battle is fought; a very great slaughter of Greeks takes place. 258.

CHAPTER IX.—The people rush to arms and lay waste the whole region; in the camp there is a great abundance of provisions. 259.

CHAPTER X.—A messenger of Bohemond comes to the duke, asking him not to confer with the emperor; the duke’s reply. 260.

CHAPTER XI.—The emperor, having sent his son John Porphyrogenitus and given a hostage, invites the duke to him. The duke enters to him; the emperor adopts him; peace is restored between them. 260.

CHAPTER XII.—The duke, heaped with gifts and taking leave for the time being, departs. A market for merchandise is provided; the duke’s legions cross the Bosporus and encamp in the district of Chalcedon. 261.

CHAPTER XIII.—Bohemond hastens on; the nobles following him are described; the emperor secretly prepares an ambush for him. 262.

CHAPTER XIV.—Letter of Emperor Alexius to Bohemond. The emperor’s army secretly rushes into Bohemond’s camp. Some are captured who disclose the emperor’s malice. 263.

CHAPTER XV.—The duke meets Lord Bohemond and brings him, almost against his will, before the emperor, where he is most greatly honored. Meanwhile Tancred moves his legions into Bithynia, where they join the duke’s cohorts. 264.

CHAPTER XVI.—Robert, count of Flanders, arrives with his men, is brought in when summoned by the emperor, and, after receiving immense gifts, crosses the sea and joins the aforesaid princes. 265.

CHAPTER XVII.—The count of Toulouse and the bishop of Le Puy hasten through Dalmatia with their forces, having endured much difficulty of travel in that region. 266.

CHAPTER XVIII.—At Dyrrachium an imperial envoy meets the same count; the bishop of Le Puy is captured by Bulgarians but, through the Lord’s mercy, is freed. Again at Rhaidestos an embassy of both the emperor and our princes meets him. 268.

CHAPTER XIX.—The count, leaving the army, hastens to the emperor but does not meet with him. The emperor deceitfully orders an attack upon his army. 269.

CHAPTER XX.—The count’s army, in his absence, is secretly attacked by the Greeks. The count is angry; the emperor, repenting of the deed and fearing for himself, requests the intervention of the princes, asserting his innocence. 269.

CHAPTER XXI.—Through the intervention of the princes, the count is reconciled with the emperor. He invites the emperor to proceed with the remaining princes. Those who had crossed the sea hasten toward Nicaea; the count immediately follows them. 271.

CHAPTER XXII.—Robert, count of the Normans, and Lord Eustace, the duke’s brother, arrive at Constantinople with their legions, receiving great gifts and much honorable attention from the emperor. Then, crossing the Hellespont, they join the remaining princes. 272.

CHAPTER XXIII.—A certain Tatinus, a familiar of the emperor, joins our princes: a man exceedingly deceitful and notorious for wickedness. 274.

BOOK THREE.

CHAPTER I.—Description of the city of Nicaea and its prerogatives; how Soliman, who ruled there, had assembled against us immense Turkish forces from the whole East, lying in ambush in order to attack our men. 274.

CHAPTER II.—Our men attack the city fiercely, but its citizens still have free movement across the lake. Soliman sends the citizens a letter of encouragement. 276.

CHAPTER III.—The carrier of the letter is captured and reveals all the enemy’s secrets to the princes. The count of Toulouse, who alone was absent, arrives swiftly when summoned by the other princes. 276.

CHAPTER IV.—Soliman descends from the mountains and violently rushes into the camp; his army is overthrown; tokens of victory are sent to the emperor, who rewards the princes. 277.

CHAPTER V.—The princes take up positions allotted to them; the city, besieged on every side, is attacked. Certain nobles fall in battle. 278.

CHAPTER VI.—A certain machine placed against the wall is crushed by the citizens, and many of our men perish beneath it. The lake hinders our [Col. 1415] efforts. 279.

CHAPTER VII.—Our men bring ships from the sea on wagons, occupy the lake; the citizens marvel at our device and despair. 280.

CHAPTER VIII.—The city is again attacked from every side. The count of Toulouse strives with engines and every skill to weaken the tower opposite him; but, the citizens resisting, the work is wasted. 281.

CHAPTER IX.—A memorable deed of Godfrey. The citizens set fire to our engines; the lamentable death of a certain nobleman. 281.

CHAPTER X.—A certain craftsman offers his services to the princes, constructs an engine, undermines a tower, and brings down the undermined tower. 282.

CHAPTER XI.—Soliman’s wife, fleeing with two sons, is captured. The citizens despair; they negotiate surrender with the Greek Tatinus. Envoys concerning this matter are sent to the emperor by the princes. 284.

CHAPTER XII.—The emperor, having sent envoys, receives the city. Thanking the princes, he sends gifts. The people are indignant and complain that the agreements have been broken. The emperor sends back to their own homes, honored with gifts, the captives taken to Constantinople. 285.

CHAPTER XIII.—The siege lifted, the army sets out. The princes separate from one another. Soliman again meets them with innumerable forces. 286.

CHAPTER XIV.—Battle is joined. William, Tancred’s brother, falls, and Bohemond’s whole army is placed in the direst straits. Tancred is almost captured. 287.

CHAPTER XV.—The remaining princes arrive and aid their oppressed brethren. Soliman is put to flight; his army perishes; our men carry off exceedingly rich spoils. The army is again fortified. 288.

CHAPTER XVI.—Entering Pisidia, the legions suffer beyond measure from lack of water. The army is wretchedly endangered. 289.

CHAPTER XVII.—Certain princes separate from one another and roam the neighboring regions. The duke, fighting a bear, is nearly killed. 290.

CHAPTER XVIII.—The count of Toulouse falls gravely ill unto death. The army, passing through Lycaonia, arrives at Maresia. Baldwin’s wife dies. 291.

CHAPTER XIX.—Tancred descends into Cilicia and besieges Tarsus. He receives as an enemy Baldwin, the duke’s brother, coming into the same region. 292.

CHAPTER XX.—Baldwin orders Tancred’s banner to be thrown down from the citadel of the city and sets up his own there. Tancred, angered, withdraws. Guelf occupies Adana. 294.

CHAPTER XXI.—Tancred violently takes Mamistra in the same region. 295.

CHAPTER XXII.—Baldwin occupies Tarsus. Three hundred of our men perish in a miserable accident before the city gate. 295.

CHAPTER XXIII.—The people take up arms against Baldwin, but are at last pacified. A fleet of Western men puts in at Tarsus. 296.

CHAPTER XXIV.—Baldwin, after taking Tarsus, comes to Mamistra. He and Tancred fight one another, but are soon reconciled. 297.

CHAPTER XXV.—Baldwin returns to the main army. Tancred attacks and takes all Cilicia. Neighboring rulers hasten to win his favor by presenting gifts. 298.

BOOK FOUR.

CHAPTER I.—Baldwin, the duke’s brother, having returned to the main army and, at the urging of Pancratius, again taken up military service, descends northward and occupies the whole region as far as the Euphrates. 299.

CHAPTER II.—His fame spreads far and wide; he is summoned by the citizens of Edessa. After crossing the Euphrates, he hastens there, having suffered ambushes on the road. The people of Edessa meet him and bring him into the city with great joy. 300.

CHAPTER III.—The ruler of the city, repenting of his action, envies Baldwin’s successes and attempts to annul the agreements; but at last, overcome by the people, he deceitfully adopts him as his son. 301.

CHAPTER IV.—At the request of the citizens he besieges Samosata. The citizens conspire against their ruler, a useless man, recalling how many injuries he had inflicted upon them. 302.

CHAPTER V.—The people of Edessa kill the aforesaid ruler and appoint Baldwin as their lord. Baldwin then purchases Samosata, at great price, from Balduc, who held it. 303.

CHAPTER VI.—He besieges the city of Sororgia. He violently takes it while under siege, winning boundless favor among his people. 304.

CHAPTER VII.—Certain men sent from the main army violently take the city of Artah. Stirred by this report, the people of Antioch hasten there with a great force, [Col. 1416] lay ambushes for our men, and attack the city. Accomplishing nothing, they return, having first nevertheless fortified the bridge. 304.

CHAPTER VIII.—The main army arrives at Artah. From there, having sent ahead certain men to reconnoitre the routes, they come to the bridge and cross the river despite the enemy’s opposition. 306.

CHAPTER IX.—Description of the city of Antioch and its distinction. 307.

CHAPTER X.—In which province it is situated; likewise, a description of its location. 308.

CHAPTER XI.—Who was its ruler, and how, upon hearing of our arrival, he had previously fortified the city by gathering forces into it from neighboring cities. 311.

CHAPTER XII.—The deliberation of our princes, and the arrival of the expeditionary forces at the city. 312.

CHAPTER XIII.—The princes are stationed around the city in suitable positions and confine the city in a strong siege; the citizens are overwhelmed by fear. 313.

CHAPTER XIV.—Our men build a wooden bridge over the river so that they may go out more freely to forage. The citizens make sudden sorties against the camp of the count of Toulouse. 314.

CHAPTER XV.—The count employs various devices against them; at length the gate is blocked by masses placed before it. 315.

CHAPTER XVI.—When our men went out to forage, the enemy met them; a most fierce conflict occurs. Many on both sides fall, some pierced by weapons, others drowned in the river. 317.

CHAPTER XVII.—Necessary supplies being exhausted, famine begins to prevail; the people suffer want; tents rot from the excessive rains; the army wastes away. 318.

CHAPTER XVIII.—Bohemond and the count of Flanders go out to forage with a great force of troops. Meanwhile the citizens secretly rush into the camp, inflicting loss and injury upon our men. 319.

CHAPTER XIX.—Those who had gone out to forage find and defeat the enemy; they return with plunder and abundant spoils. 320.

CHAPTER XX.—Sven, son of the king of the Danes, following the army with his forces, is slain by Turks near the city of Finiminis. 321.

CHAPTER XXI.—Tatinus, a deceitful man, leaves the army, allegedly to arrange provision-trading and to ask the emperor for aid, never to return. 321.

CHAPTER XXII.—As famine grows worse and a deadly plague seizes the people, a three-day fast is proclaimed by the bishops. Duke Godfrey recovers full health, and the army is comforted by his recovery. 322.

CHAPTER XXIII.—The vexatious activity of spies sent by the enemy is checked through a memorable deed of Lord Bohemond. 323.

CHAPTER XXIV.—The Egyptian caliph sends envoys to the princes, requesting an alliance and seeking to win their favor. 324.

BOOK FIVE.

CHAPTER I.—The citizens of Antioch summon and obtain help from their neighbors; their auxiliaries pitch tents around the castle of Harenc. 324.

CHAPTER II.—Our princes, leaving the infantry to guard the camp, advance with the cavalry to meet the enemy, returning victorious to camp. 326.

CHAPTER III.—The citizens of Antioch are grievously dismayed when they learn of the fate of their auxiliaries. 327.

CHAPTER IV.—Our men build a castle. Genoese ships put in at the harbor. The people go down to the sea and, suffering an ambush, are partly cut down. 328.

CHAPTER V.—The duke’s plan and admirable achievement in response to the adverse event that had occurred. 329.

CHAPTER VI.—The enemy, returning in triumph, are cut down by our men’s swords before the city gate; two thousand of them fall. The duke cuts a man in armor in two through the middle. 330.

CHAPTER VII.—Our men construct a fortified post at the bridgehead and send a token of victory to the ships. 332.

CHAPTER VIII.—The city is suddenly more tightly pressed, a new fortification having been established on the western side. 333.

CHAPTER IX.—Those who had scattered return to the army. Baldwin sends gifts from Edessa to each prince. 334.

CHAPTER X.—The arrival of hostile forces is reported in the camp. Stephen, count of Blois, feigning illness, goes down to the sea, never to return. 336.

CHAPTER XI.—The condition of the city is described. Bohemond’s friendship with a certain faithful man in the city is described. 337.

CHAPTER XII.—A plan arranged through intermediaries between Bohemond and the aforesaid faithful man. 338.

CHAPTER XIII.—Bohemond works to have the city granted to him; only the count of Toulouse objects. 339.

CHAPTER XIV.—Those hurrying to aid the Antiochenes besiege Edessa; but Baldwin’s valiant resistance causes them to withdraw empty-handed and cross the Euphrates. 339.

[Col. 1417]

CHAPTER XV.—Our men send out scouts, concerned about the enemy’s arrival. 340.

CHAPTER XVI.—Meeting together, they deliberate. Bohemond reports the secret entrusted to him by his friend. 341.

CHAPTER XVII.—The rejoicing princes grant the city to Bohemond; he negotiates more secretly with his friend for the surrender of the city. 342.

CHAPTER XVIII.—The citizens suspect the aforesaid man; before the ruler, he declares his innocence. 343.

CHAPTER XIX.—The great straits under which the people of the faithful within the city were oppressed; and how the slaughter intended for them was averted. 345.

CHAPTER XX.—Following the plan of the aforesaid man, the army leaves camp, intending to return around nightfall. 346.

CHAPTER XXI.—Bohemond urges his friend to complete the undertaking; the latter kills his brother, who does not consent. He admits Christians into the city by a lowered ladder. 347.

CHAPTER XXII.—Those admitted open the gate; the army, now aware of the deed, rushes into the city. The city is captured by assault. 348.

CHAPTER XXIII.—The citizens withdraw into the fortress; Acxianus, fleeing outside the city, is killed; many are hurled headlong from the mountain. 349.

BOOK SIX.

**Chapter I.**—The mountain is described, and part of it is occupied by the enemy, guards having been stationed there. Men are sent to the sea to summon the people; provisions are brought in, and the city is secured. 351

**Chapter II.**—Three hundred men, sent ahead by the main enemy army, range before the city. Roger of Barneville, meeting them too incautiously, is killed. 352

**Chapter III.**—The chief prince approaches, pitches camp on the mountains above the fortress. The duke is struck down at the Eastern Gate; two hundred of our men perish. 353

**Chapter IV.**—Within the city our men draw a rampart along the foot of the mountain; battle is fought there, and the enemy are defeated. The enemy commander descends from the mountain and besieges the city on its lower side. 354

**Chapter V.**—The people within the city suffer severely from famine. Certain nobles secretly flee from it; Bohemond is placed in command of all. 355

**Chapter VI.**—The Count of Flanders voluntarily abandons and burns the fortress before the Gate of the Bridge, since he could not hold it. The enemy prince sends some of our captives into Persia. 356

**Chapter VII.**—As famine grows stronger, the people are reluctantly reduced to unclean foods. 358

**Chapter VIII.**—The enemy secretly occupy almost one of the towers. Henry of Ascha resists bravely; having killed many, he forcibly holds the citadel. 359

**Chapter IX.**—The enemy descend to the sea, burn the ships, and kill many of our men on the road. 360

**Chapter X.**—Stephen, Count of Chartres, sets out for Constantinople to the emperor. 361

**Chapter XI.**—His address to that same emperor, full of falsehood and ruinous to the faithful. 362

**Chapter XII.**—The emperor returns to his own lands and disbands the forces which he had assembled to aid our people, believing the word of the aforesaid count. 363

**Chapter XIII.**—The enemy, learning of the emperor’s departure, press their attack more vigorously. Our people despair and refuse their services. Bohemond sets the city on fire to draw them out of hiding; the princes contemplate flight, but the duke resists. 364

**Chapter XIV.**—A revelation is made to a certain Peter; the Lord’s lance is found. The people are encouraged anew. 365

**Chapter XV.**—By the common counsel of the princes Peter the Hermit is sent as envoy to the enemy; undaunted, he carries out the embassy. 366

**Chapter XVI.**—Peter returns to the magnates and reports to our people the enemy’s arrogance; war is declared. 367

**Chapter XVII.**—Their battle-lines having been arranged, they leave the city, leaving the Count of Toulouse behind to guard it. 369

**Chapter XVIII.**—The enemy commander prepares to prevent their sortie, but our men break out bravely. 370

**Chapter XIX.**—As our men come out, dew is poured down from above, in which all receive consolation. 371

**Chapter XX.**—Kerbogha arrays his battle-lines; close combat is joined. Süleyman, attacking from the rear, severely overwhelms Bohemond’s division; the princes come to its aid. As the Turks weaken, they set fire so as to raise smoke. 372

**Chapter XXI.**—The enemy commander flees; their legions are destroyed; those who escape are put to flight. 374

**Chapter XXII.**—Returning from the slaughter of the enemy, our men bring back from their camp limitless spoils. 375

**Chapter XXIII.**—When the city has been set in order, they cleanse and restore the churches, and diligently install clergy in them. [Col. 1418] 376

### Book Seven

**Chapter I.**—Hugh the Great and the Count of Heumaucorum are sent as envoys to the emperor; Count Baldwin dies on the way; Hugh the Great does not return. The Bishop of Le Puy dies; a plague arises. 377

**Chapter II.**—The people clamour to proceed to Jerusalem; the journey is postponed until the Kalends of October. Bohemond descends into Cilicia and recovers the whole region. 378

**Chapter III.**—Lord Hasarth asks the duke for help against his lord Rodohan. The duke summons his brother Baldwin and hastens there. 379

**Chapter IV.**—Baldwin meets his brother with immense forces. The remaining princes provide assistance. Rodohan flees. Some of our men perish on the road; about ten thousand of the enemy are killed. 380

**Chapter V.**—Avoiding disaster, the duke withdraws into his brother’s territory; there he destroys the towns of certain traitors. Some other princes also hasten there, to obtain Baldwin’s generosity. 381

**Chapter VI.**—The citizens of Edessa, angered because their count employed Latins alone, conspire against him. Warned of this, Baldwin kills the conspirators. 382

**Chapter VII.**—Balas plots treachery against the count; the count takes precautions. Some of Balas’s associates are captured. Fulcher of Chartres makes the incident less serious. The traitor Balduc is killed. 383

**Chapter VIII.**—The Count of Toulouse occupies Albara and establishes a bishop there. A German fleet arrives in the harbour. The pestilence does not cease. 385

**Chapter IX.**—They besiege the city of Ma‘arrat and capture it after besieging it. Lord William, Bishop of Orange, dies. Gulfer of the Towers is held in distinction. 385

**Chapter X.**—The duke returns to his brother and obtains leave. On his way back to the army he suffers an ambush, but escapes unharmed. 387

**Chapter XI.**—At Ma‘arrat a dispute arises between the Count of Toulouse and Bohemond. Bohemond occupies the count’s territories near Antioch. The princes meet at Rugia but decide nothing useful. The people suffer from famine. 387

**Chapter XII.**—The count enters enemy territory and leads away spoil from it. Unable to endure the people’s clamour, he sets out. The Count of the Normans and Tancred join him. 389

**Chapter XIII.**—The count’s army withstands an attack by raiders on the march; the count wisely charges them. A resisting castle is broken through. Camp is pitched before Arqa, and envoys from neighbouring peoples come to the princes. 390

**Chapter XIV.**—Arqa is described. Captives of our people held in the city of Tripoli indicate that the city ought to be besieged. 391

**Chapter XV.**—Some men who have gone out from camp bravely occupy the city of Antaradus; whence they return to camp with abundant spoils and continue the siege. 392

**Chapter XVI.**—Duke Godfrey, with the Count of Flanders and the remainder of the expedition, arrives at Laodicea, frees Guynemer from chains, and restores his fleet to him. Bohemond pursues them as they depart as far as the aforesaid city. 392

**Chapter XVII.**—The duke and the army with him besiege Gabelum. The deceit of the Toulousans intervenes. Hastening to Arqa, they join the remaining princes; the siege makes no progress. 393

**Chapter XVIII.**—The controversy over the Lord’s lance is renewed. Its discoverer enters a lighted pyre and dies a few days later. 395

**Chapter XIX.**—The envoys whom our princes had sent to Egypt return. 396

**Chapter XX.**—The emperor’s envoys are present. Complaining of Bohemond, they announce that the emperor will come. The princes disagree; battle is fought with the Tripolitans, the enemy are defeated, and our men return victorious to camp. 397

**Chapter XXI.**—The governor of Tripoli obtains peace from our men by a great sum of money and gifts. On the counsel of the faithful who live in those regions, the princes choose the coastal road. 398

**Chapter XXII.**—Proceeding on their way, they pass the cities situated along the seacoast and arrive at Lydda and Ramla. 399

**Chapter XXIII.**—The Jerusalemites diligently fortify their city with brave men, arms, and provisions. For the most part they drive the faithful citizens out of the city. 401

**Chapter XXIV.**—The people of Bethlehem send envoys to the princes; Tancred is sent there, and he occupies the church and the place. 402

**Chapter XXV.**—The army advances and arrives at Jerusalem; meanwhile a disturbance arises in which some of the enemy fall. 404

[Col. 1419]

### Book Eight

**Chapter I.**—A description of the site of the Holy City, showing what regions and places it has around it. 405

**Chapter II.**—By what names, and how many, the city is called; and that David made it the throne of his kingdom. How Aelius Hadrian transferred it from the slope to the mountain summit. And further matters concerning its site. 406

**Chapter III.**—That it contains within the circuit of its walls part of two mountains; that the church of the Lord’s Resurrection lies below, while the Temple of the Lord is above; and the form of each church. 408

**Chapter IV.**—That the city is situated in a dry and waterless place. Concerning the spring of Siloam. And how the citizens, having heard of our approach, destroyed the pools and blocked up the springs. 410

**Chapter V.**—At what time our army arrived before the city; what was the number of our people and of the enemy; and in what order the camps were laid out. 412

**Chapter VI.**—On the fifth day after the siege began they assault the city. Under the guidance of a certain faithful man, they descend into the forests, carry timber away, and erect engines. 413

**Chapter VII.**—The people are worn out by thirst; while seeking water at distant places and the other necessities of life, they are frequently killed by the enemy. 414

**Chapter VIII.**—The citizens construct engines and prepare to resist; they subject the faithful who are among them to forced labour. 415

**Chapter IX.**—A Genoese fleet arrives at Jaffa. Men are sent from the army to bring them to the siege; those sent suffer enemy ambushes on the way. 417

**Chapter X.**—Those who arrived in the fleet join the army and render very great assistance in constructing the engines. The Count of Toulouse and Tancred are reconciled. 418

**Chapter XI.**—Litanies are proclaimed to the people. The whole people ascend the Mount of Olives. 419

**Chapter XII.**—The duke and the two greater counts transfer their camps by night; the engines are raised in a circuit before the city. 420

**Chapter XIII.**—The city is attacked, and a most violent conflict takes place on both sides; but night intervenes and ends the contest. 421

**Chapter XIV.**—That night both the besiegers and the besieged remain in great anxiety. 423

**Chapter XV.**—The following day they return to the same task, and the city is attacked more violently than usual. The sorceresses who had come to bewitch our engine perish. 423

**Chapter XVI.**—A sign is given divinely from the Mount of Olives; the people, who had been exhausted, return more fiercely to battle. 424

**Chapter XVII.**—On the southern side the Count of Toulouse, with his men, attacks the city no less vigorously. 425

**Chapter XVIII.**—The duke and those with him lower a bridge from the wooden tower over the wall and send in their men. The city is taken, the gate is opened, and our army is admitted. 426

**Chapter XIX.**—The duke, ranging through the city with his men, carries out an innumerable slaughter. The Count of Toulouse forcibly enters on the southern side and brings in his troops. Part of the citizens withdraw to the city’s stronghold. 427

**Chapter XX.**—The citizens gather in the court of the Temple. Tancred pursues them there. An innumerable slaughter takes place, and immeasurable blood is shed there. 428

**Chapter XXI.**—Once the city has been set in order, the tumult is calmed; laying down their arms, they visit the venerable places in prayer and keep the day as a festival. 429

**Chapter XXII.**—The Bishop of Le Puy and certain others who had died on the journey are seen in the city and appear to many. 430

**Chapter XXIII.**—The faithful men who lived in the city render immense thanks to Peter the Hermit, to whom they had entrusted their embassy, and honour him as was due. 431

**Chapter XXIV.**—The city is cleansed of the bodies of the slain. Those who had withdrawn into the citadel surrender to the Count of Toulouse. That day is established as forever celebrated. 432

### Book Nine

**Chapter I.**—On the eighth day after the city’s capture, the princes meet to choose one of themselves to rule the city and territory; the clergy indiscriminately strive to oppose this. 433

**Chapter II.**—The princes disregard the clergy’s opposition, elect the lord duke, and bring the elected man with hymns and songs to the Lord’s Sepulchre. 434

**Chapter III.**—Having been promoted, the duke demands back from the Count of Toulouse the Tower of David, which the count had received from the enemy. The princes disagree, but he nevertheless obtains the tower he requested. [Col. 1420] 435

**Chapter IV.**—The Bishop of Marturano, a crafty and wicked man, endeavours to promote as patriarch a certain Arnulf, like himself; but he does not succeed. The Lord’s Cross is found. 436

**Chapter V.**—It is explained who Duke Godfrey was, whence he came, and from what ancestors he was descended. 437

**Chapter VI.**—His mother’s prophecy concerning the future condition of her sons. 438

**Chapter VII.**—His memorable deed in a certain single combat is recounted. 438

**Chapter VIII.**—A notable deed of the same man in Emperor Henry’s victory over Rudolph, the false king of the Saxons. 439

**Chapter IX.**—How abundantly he showed pious generosity toward the churches at Jerusalem; and how, from humility, he refused to be invested with the royal diadem. 441

**Chapter X.**—The Egyptian prince rouses all his forces and military strength against our people and directs them into Syria. 441

**Chapter XI.**—Conversely, after litanies and prayers have been completed at Jerusalem, the duke assembles the princes around Ramla and gathers forces. 442

**Chapter XII.**—Battle is joined, and victory is divinely granted to our men, who acquire innumerable riches. 443

**Chapter XIII.**—The princes separate. The Norman and the Fleming return home; the Toulousan returns to Constantinople; Tancred is placed in command of the city of Tiberias. 445

**Chapter XIV.**—Bohemond, prince of the Antiochenes, and Baldwin, count of the Edessenes, come to Jerusalem and celebrate there the Lord’s Nativity. 446

**Chapter XV.**—Daimbert, archbishop of the Church of Pisa, is placed over the Church of Jerusalem as patriarch. 447

**Chapter XVI.**—Through the efforts of malicious men, serious disputes, accompanied by hostility, arise between the duke and the patriarch over the Tower of David and the fourth part of the city. 448

**Chapter XVII.**—How the fourth part of the city came into the right and power of the lord patriarch. 448

**Chapter XVIII.**—Again concerning the same matter: and what venerable places that often-mentioned quarter contains within itself. 449

**Chapter XIX.**—What was the state of the kingdom at that time; how the duke besieged the coastal city of Assur; and why he lifted the siege. 451

**Chapter XX.**—A deed worthy of remembrance which happened to him during that siege. 452

**Chapter XXI.**—Bohemond, prince of the Antiochenes, is captured near the city of Melitene. 453

**Chapter XXII.**—A memorable deed of the duke in the land of the Arabs. 453

**Chapter XXIII.**—The duke’s death and burial. 454

### Book Ten

**Chapter I.**—Lord Baldwin, Count of Edessa, succeeds his deceased brother in the kingdom. 455

**Chapter II.**—Concerning the bodily appearance and character of that same Lord Baldwin. 455

**Chapter III.**—Count Warner, after the duke’s death, occupies the tower and secretly summons the aforesaid Baldwin by messengers. 456

**Chapter IV.**—Letter of Lord Daimbert to the prince of Antioch. 457

**Chapter V.**—Baldwin approaches Jerusalem and finds enemy ambushes near the River Dog. 459

**Chapter VI.**—The enemy are defeated; the road having been cleared, Baldwin reaches Jerusalem. 460

**Chapter VII.**—Patriarch Daimbert, fearing Baldwin’s arrival, leaves the patriarchal residence and withdraws into the church on Mount Zion. 461

**Chapter VIII.**—The count sends troops toward Ascalon, crosses the Jordan, enters enemy territory, and finally returns to Jerusalem. 462

**Chapter IX.**—The patriarch and count having been reconciled, the count is anointed king. 463

**Chapter X.**—Tancred, remembering an earlier injury, leaves him when summoned by the Antiochenes. 463

**Chapter XI.**—The king crosses the Jordan, takes innumerable booty from the enemy’s territory, and a commendable deed of his is described. 463

**Chapter XII.**—Western princes again prepare for the expedition and arrive at Constantinople with immense forces. 464

**Chapter XIII.**—The emperor, named Alexius, according to his customary practice plots against them through the Turks. Most of the pilgrims are cut down; those remaining reach Jerusalem following the Count of Toulouse. 465

**Chapter XIV.**—The king besieges Antiopatrida and forcibly captures it after besieging it. 466

**Chapter XV.**—The same king besieges the coastal city of Caesarea and attacks it while under siege. 468

**Chapter XVI.**—An innumerable multitude of citizens is killed in the city’s chapel, and an archbishop is appointed to the captured city. [Col. 1421] 469

**Chapter XVII.**—The king, arriving at Ramla, awaits the enemy army said to be coming; fighting them, he gains victory. 469

**Chapter XVIII.**—From there he goes to Jaffa and encourages its terrified citizens. 471

**Chapter XIX.**—The newly arrived princes capture Tortosa and hand it over to the Count of Toulouse; then they hasten to Jerusalem. The king goes out to meet them as far as Beirut. 472

**Chapter XX.**—The Egyptians enter our territories with immeasurable forces. The king meets them, fights them too incautiously, and is defeated. 473

**Chapter XXI.**—Fleeing from battle, the king takes refuge in the castle of Ramla. Through the aid of a certain Arab he is rescued, while others are killed there. 474

**Chapter XXII.**—The king, fleeing by byways, reaches Arsuf and thence Jaffa. All assemble from the kingdom to assist the king; battle is fought with the enemy, and our men emerge victorious. 475

**Chapter XXIII.**—Meanwhile Tancred brings the most distinguished cities of Apamea and Laodicea under his authority. 477

**Chapter XXIV.**—Baldwin of Le Bourg, Count of Edessa, marries the daughter of Duke Gabriel. 477

**Chapter XXV.**—Bohemond, released from the enemy’s chains, returns to Antioch and kindly receives Patriarch Daimbert, who has fled to him. 478

**Chapter XXVI.**—After Daimbert’s expulsion, a certain Ebremar is irregularly placed over Jerusalem. The king besieges Ptolemais but makes no progress; on his return he is wounded. 479

**Chapter XXVII.**—Count Raymond of Toulouse builds a castle before the city of Tripoli, called Mount Pilgrim. 480

**Chapter XXVIII.**—The king again besieges Ptolemais and, relying on Genoese assistance, forcibly captures the besieged city. 480

**Chapter XXIX.**—Carrhae in Mesopotamia is besieged by Tancred, Baldwin, and others. Driven by famine, the citizens deliberate about surrendering the city. 481

**Chapter XXX.**—Our men, disputing over authority in the city, lose it; the citizens receive reinforcements; close battle is fought there; our men are defeated, and a most dangerous disaster befalls them. 482

### Book Eleven

**Chapter I.**—Bohemond, prince of the Antiochenes, entrusts the principality to Tancred, crosses the sea, hastens to France, and marries the daughter of the king of the Franks. The patriarch of Jerusalem goes to Rome. The king abandons his lawful wife without examination of the case. 483

**Chapter II.**—Lord Raymond, Count of Toulouse, dies. His nephew William Jordan succeeds him. Rodohan, the great prince of the Turks, enters our territories; Tancred meets him and puts him, discomfited, to flight. 485

**Chapter III.**—The Egyptians pour into the kingdom with immense forces. The king meets them, captures some, kills many more, and drives the rest into flight. 486

**Chapter IV.**—Patriarch Daimbert, returning with enforcement of apostolic letters, dies at Messina, a city of Sicily. Ebremar, intruder upon that see, hastens to Rome. Ghibelin, Archbishop of Arles, is sent as legate and is later installed as patriarch. 488

**Chapter V.**—The nobleman Hugh of Saint-Aldemar, lord of Tiberias, builds a castle in the mountains overlooking the city of Tyre, called Toron. Not long afterward, fighting the Damascenes, he is mortally wounded but nevertheless victorious, and dies. The Ascalonites also, intending to lay an ambush for our men, fall into the trap they had prepared. 489

**Chapter VI.**—Bohemond returns from France to Apulia and enters Greek territory with immense forces to ravage it. At last, wishing to return to Syria, he dies, leaving behind his son Bohemond. 490

**Chapter VII.**—Likewise, immense Turkish forces from the eastern regions attempt to occupy the lands of Edessa; but Tancred and the king resist them bravely. 491

**Chapter VIII.**—Baldwin, Count of Edessa, returns from enemy captivity, with Joscelin; they raise war against Tancred. 493

**Chapter IX.**—Bertrand, son of the Count of Toulouse, comes down into Syria with a Genoese fleet, seeking to succeed his father; William Jordan opposes him. Byblos is captured. 493

**Chapter X.**—King Baldwin hastens to Tripoli; the siege is intense, and the city is taken. 495

**Chapter XI.**—Baldwin, Count of Edessa, goes down to Melitene to his father-in-law Gabriel, where a deed of his sufficiently worthy of memory is recorded. [Col. 1422] 496

**Chapter XII.**—Through the king’s efforts, the church of Bethlehem is raised to cathedral rank. 497

**Chapter XIII.**—The city of Beirut is besieged by land and sea and taken in the second month. 499

**Chapter XIV.**—A fleet of Danes and Norwegians comes down into Syria. With its help the king besieges and takes Sidon; a remarkable event concerning the king is related. 501

**Chapter XV.**—Ghibelin, patriarch of Jerusalem, dies; the impious and wicked Arnulf succeeds him. 502

**Chapter XVI.**—An immense host and innumerable forces of Turks pour from the east into the territory of Antioch; but Tancred, together with Count Bertrand of Tripoli, resists bravely. 503

**Chapter XVII.**—Tyre is besieged; but the citizens resist powerfully, and the besiegers’ purpose is frustrated. 504

**Chapter XVIII.**—Lord Tancred dies, leaving the principality to Roger, son of Richard. 505

**Chapter XIX.**—Mawdud, the most powerful prince of the Turks, again enters the kingdom with immense forces. The king meets him and is defeated; the entire region is strained beyond its strength. 505

**Chapter XX.**—The Ascalonites attack Jerusalem; but at last the enemy battle-lines are broken up, and they return home. 507

**Chapter XXI.**—The Countess of Sicily, the future wife of the king, arrives in the harbour of Acre. 507

**Chapter XXII.**—A severe famine arises in the region of Edessa. Baldwin captures his kinsman Joscelin and forcibly compels him to leave the whole region. 508

**Chapter XXIII.**—A great earthquake shakes the territory of Antioch. Bursuq, the most powerful Turkish satrap, also ravages that same region. 510

**Chapter XXIV.**—The Ascalonites besiege the city of Jaffa; but fearing the king’s approach, they withdraw home without accomplishing their undertaking. 511

**Chapter XXV.**—Bursuq again harasses the territory of Antioch; but Prince Roger meets him with his forces, routs him, and puts him to flight, his legions scattered. 513

**Chapter XXVI.**—Arnulf, patriarch of Jerusalem, accused on many counts, goes to Rome. In Syria, beyond the Jordan, the king builds the castle of Sobal, called Mount Royal. 514

**Chapter XXVII.**—Seeing the Holy City empty of inhabitants, the king brings faithful Syrians from Arabia; giving them dwellings, he establishes them as inhabitants of the city. 515

**Chapter XXVIII.**—At the clergy’s urging, the king asks the lord pope that whatever cities he conquers may be subject to the Church of Jerusalem. The replies of various letters are appended. 516

**Chapter XXIX.**—The king descends to the Red Sea and surveys the region. Worn out by illness, he sends the Countess of Sicily, whom he had taken as wife, back to her own country. 519

**Chapter XXX.**—Before the city of Tyre, the castle of Alexandria, commonly called Scandalion, is built. 520

**Chapter XXXI.**—The king descends into Egypt, captures Pharamea, falls ill, and dies from that illness during the same journey; he is buried at Jerusalem beside his brother. 520

### Book Twelve

**Chapter I.**—Baldwin, Count of Edessa, is elevated to the kingdom; it is described who he was and whence he came. 521

**Chapter II.**—Why he set out for Jerusalem when he was elected king. 522

**Chapter III.**—The manner of the election is explained, and a memorable deed of Eustace, Count of Boulogne, is described. 523

**Chapter IV.**—Concerning the bodily appearance, morals, and manner of life of that same king. 524

**Chapter V.**—Alexius, emperor of Constantinople; Pope Paschal; and the Countess of Sicily, who had been queen of Jerusalem, die. 525

**Chapter VI.**—The Egyptian army, by sea and land alike, enters the kingdom. The king meets them with his men, but they do not join battle. Arnulf, patriarch of Jerusalem, dies; Gormond succeeds him. 525

**Chapter VII.**—The Order of the Knighthood of the Temple is established at Jerusalem. 526

**Chapter VIII.**—Pope Gelasius dies; Calixtus succeeds him. 527

**Chapter IX.**—Gazzi, a most powerful Turkish satrap, pours with immense forces into the territory of Antioch, ravaging everything. 528

**Chapter X.**—Prince Roger falls in battle, and our army is defeated. [Col. 1423] 529

**Chapter XI.**—The king and the Count of Tripoli hasten to Antioch in order to resist the aforesaid Gazzi. 530

**Chapter XII.**—The king and the same count engage the aforesaid Gazzi; putting him to flight, they overthrow his battle-lines, many being killed, and the care of the principality is entrusted to the king. 531

**Chapter XIII.**—A council is held at Nablus, a city of Samaria. 533

**Chapter XIV.**—The aforesaid Gazzi again enters Antiochene territory with renewed forces; the king meets him. But Gazzi, struck by apoplexy, dies. 534

**Chapter XV.**—The king grants the citizens of Jerusalem complete freedom and confirms it by his privilege. 535

**Chapter XVI.**—Doldequin, king of the Damascenes, ravages the territory of Tiberias. The king meets him and destroys the city of Gerazum. 535

**Chapter XVII.**—Balak, a most powerful Turkish prince, forcibly enters Antiochene territory. Count Joscelin is captured by him; the king also falls into his chains, captured by the same man. 535

**Chapter XVIII.**—Certain Armenians expose themselves to grave danger to free the king. They capture the castle in which the prisoners were held, and Count Joscelin is released. 537

**Chapter XIX.**—Balak again forcibly recaptures the same castle, having put the aforesaid Armenians to the sword. 538

**Chapter XX.**—Count Joscelin assembles a great force to free his lord the king and arrives at Antioch; but shaken by the unexpected news of what had happened, he sends his dispersed battle-lines back home. 539

**Chapter XXI.**—Again the Egyptians enter the kingdom with immense forces; but our men meet them with strong force and miserably crush them. 540

**Chapter XXII.**—The Doge of Venice comes down into Syria with a numerous fleet. 541

**Chapter XXIII.**—The same doge violently breaks and puts to flight an enemy fleet found near Jaffa, retaining many galleys. 542

**Chapter XXIV.**—The princes of the kingdom meet with the same doge, and Tyre is besieged. 543

**Chapter XXV.**—Text of the charter of privilege containing the agreed terms between the Venetians and the princes of the kingdom of Jerusalem concerning the siege of Tyre. 544

### Book Thirteen

**Chapter I.**—The antiquity and distinction of Tyre are described together. 547

**Chapter II.**—How far Syria extends, and what regions it contains. 549

**Chapter III.**—A description of the region adjoining that city and of the advantages it provides. 550

**Chapter IV.**—That it was frequently besieged in ancient times. 552

**Chapter V.**—The city is described, and the condition and circumstances of its citizens are explained. 553

**Chapter VI.**—The siege is established, stations are assigned to the princes in that sector, and the city is attacked as an enemy. 554

**Chapter VII.**—The Damascenes who are in the city resist more vigorously, while the citizens are somewhat less resolute. 555

**Chapter VIII.**—The Ascalonites come to Jerusalem to attack the city, but on their return are badly treated by its inhabitants. 555

**Chapter IX.**—Doldequin, king of the Damascenes, approaches to lift the siege; our men meet him, and he withdraws from his purpose in fear. 556

**Chapter X.**—The citizens apply fire to our engines; our men resist bravely. A man skilled in shooting missiles is summoned by our people from Antioch. 557

**Chapter XI.**—Balak is killed near Hierapolis. On hearing the report, our army becomes more cheerful and presses the attack upon the city more vigorously. 558

**Chapter XII.**—The Ascalonites again ravage the territory of Jerusalem while our army is still detained at the siege. 559

**Chapter XIII.**—The citizens suffer under the severity of famine and prepare to surrender. Doldequin hastens to assist them, but in vain; the city is yielded to our men. 559

**Chapter XIV.**—When the city has been taken, the citizens go out into the camp, and our men occupy the city. 561

**Chapter XV.**—The king is released from chains. He besieges Aleppo, but the arrival of allies causes the siege to be lifted. The king returns to Jerusalem. Pope Calixtus dies, and Honorius succeeds him. 562

**Chapter XVI.**—Bursuq, prince of the Turks, ravages Antiochene territory. The king meets and engages him; the enemy army is overthrown. 563

**Chapter XVII.**—The king defeats the Ascalonites and also the Egyptians who had come to aid them. 564

[Col. 1424]

**Chapter XVIII.**—The king enters Damascene territory; Doldequin meets him; battle is joined, and our army returns victorious. 565

**Chapter XIX.**—The Count of Tripoli captures the city of Rafaniya. Henry, emperor of the Romans, dies; Lothair succeeds him. 567

**Chapter XX.**—Bursuq again enters Antiochene territory and is eventually killed by his own men. An Egyptian fleet comes up into Syria but, having achieved nothing and suffered loss, returns. 568

**Chapter XXI.**—Young Bohemond arrives at Antioch. The king restores his land to him and gives him his daughter Alice in marriage. 569

**Chapter XXII.**—Serious hostilities arise between the same king, Bohemond, and Joscelin, Count of Edessa; but the king swiftly comes and settles them. Africans forcibly break into Syracuse, a city of Sicily. 570

**Chapter XXIII.**—At Tyre, the first Latin archbishop is established. 571

**Chapter XXIV.**—Fulk, Count of Anjou, comes when summoned, and Melisende, the king’s firstborn daughter, is given to him in marriage. 573

**Chapter XXV.**—Gormond, patriarch of Jerusalem, dies; Stephen succeeds him. Difficult disputes arise between the king and the patriarch. 573

**Chapter XXVI.**—The king, the prince of Antioch, the Count of Tripoli, and the Count of Edessa enter Damascene territory; but, defeated and having lost part of their army, they return. Patriarch Stephen dies; William succeeds him. 574

**Chapter XXVII.**—Bohemond, prince of the Antiochenes, is killed in Cilicia near Mamistra. The king hastens to Antioch. Bohemond’s wife attempts to repel her approaching father; but through the citizens’ agency the city is handed over to the king, the princess having been excluded. 576

**Chapter XXVIII.**—The king returns to Jerusalem; seized by a severe illness, he dies and is buried with the other kings in the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre. 578

### Book Fourteen
**Chapter I.**—What were the character and ancestry of Lord Fulk, the third king of Jerusalem. 577  
**Chapter II.**—How, before being summoned by King Baldwin, he had come to Jerusalem on pilgrimage; and concerning his elevation to kingship. 580  
**Chapter III.**—Joscelin the elder, count of Edessa, though ill, meets the enemy in a litter; after victory has been won, he expires; and concerning his son Joscelin. 581  
**Chapter IV.**—The king is summoned by the people of Antioch, and the wickedness of the princess is revealed. 582  
**Chapter V.**—As he hastens to Antioch, the count of Tripoli opposes him, but is defeated by the king. Antiochene affairs are placed in safety. 583  
**Chapter VI.**—He is again recalled by the Antiochenes. Zengi besieges a certain castle in Tripolitan territory; through the intervention of the king’s sister, Zengi raises the siege. 584  
**Chapter VII.**—The king hastens to Antioch; he puts to flight the assembled enemies, and the Antiochenes are enriched with the enemy’s spoils. 584  
**Chapter VIII.**—The patriarch of Jerusalem and the princes of the kingdom found a highly necessary fortress, called Arnald’s Castle. 585  
**Chapter IX.**—At the king’s counsel, a mission is sent to Raymond, son of the count of Poitou, that he may marry Constance, daughter of Bohemond. 586  
**Chapter X.**—Bernard, patriarch of Antioch, dies; Ralph, archbishop of Mamistra, succeeds him amid disorder. 587  
**Chapter XI.**—Pope Honorius dies; Innocent succeeds him; a dangerous schism arises. William, archbishop of Tyre, departs this life; Fulk succeeds him, goes to Rome, requests and receives the pallium. 588  
**Chapter XII.**—The Roman Church orders that he obey the bishop of Jerusalem and hold under him the position which he had formerly held under the Antiochenes. 589  
**Chapter XIII.**—His suffragans are ordered to obey him, and letters to this effect are sent to them. 590  
**Chapter XIV.**—It is explained whence and for what reason this controversy arose between the two patriarchs, and upon what grounds each defends his own position. 592  
**Chapter XV.**—The count of Jaffa is accused before the king, and great unrest is stirred up in the kingdom. 594  
**Chapter XVI.**—Walter of Caesarea challenges the count to single combat; the latter goes over to the enemy and is abandoned by his own men. 595  
**Chapter XVII.**—The city of Jaffa is besieged; the princes of the kingdom negotiate peace; meanwhile Balian is captured by the enemy. 596  

[Col. 1425]

**Chapter XVIII.**—The count of Jaffa is maliciously wounded at Jerusalem; unrest again arises; but after recovering his health, he crosses the sea by agreement. 596  
**Chapter XIX.**—A truce is made with the Damascenes; captives taken at Belinas are restored. 598  
**Chapter XX.**—Raymond, son of the count of Poitou, arrives secretly; reaching Antioch, he marries Constance, daughter of Bohemond, against the will and resistance of the princess, the girl’s mother, and obtains the principality. 599  
**Chapter XXI.**—The identity, character, and ancestral lineage of Raymond are described. 600  
**Chapter XXII.**—To restrain the insolence of the people of Ascalon, the king builds a castle called Gybelin, also known as Beersheba. 601  
**Chapter XXIII.**—The count of Tripoli is killed near Mount Pilgrim through the treachery of certain of his own men; his son Raymond succeeds him and avenges his father’s death. 602  
**Chapter XXIV.**—The emperor John of Constantinople, hastening toward Antioch, occupies all Cilicia. 602  
**Chapter XXV.**—Zengi besieges the castle called Montferrand; the king and the count of Tripoli attempt to raise the siege but fail; defeated, the count is captured, while the king withdraws into the castle. 604  
**Chapter XXVI.**—Zengi again besieges the castle; the besieged summon help from all the neighboring regions. 605  
**Chapter XXVII.**—Bezeuge, governor of Damascus, burns and devastates Nablus. 606  
**Chapter XXVIII.**—Help for the king is hastened forward; but meanwhile the besieged suffer still greater hardships. 607  
**Chapter XXIX.**—Relief arrives; meanwhile the king inclines toward surrender, and, after terms of peace have been made, returns safely to his own lands. 608  
**Chapter XXX.**—The prince, returning to Antioch, finds the city besieged; he opposes the emperor with all his strength, but at last, through the intervention of certain persons, is reconciled with him. 609  

### Book Fifteen

**Chapter I.**—The emperor besieges Caesarea, while the prince and the count of Edessa are in his service. 609  
**Chapter II.**—Angered, he raises the siege before completing the undertaking and returns to Antioch. 612  
**Chapter III.**—The emperor demands from the prince a garrison for the city, as though he intended to remain in the region. 612  
**Chapter IV.**—An uproar is raised in the city; the emperor becomes afraid and withdraws his demand; the disturbance is calmed when he leaves the city. 614  
**Chapter V.**—Envoys are sent to mitigate the emperor’s anger and succeed; the emperor returns home. 615  
**Chapter VI.**—The king of Jerusalem besieges and forcibly takes a fortress beyond the Jordan. Near Tekoa our men are miserably overthrown. 616  
**Chapter VII.**—Zengi harasses the kingdom of Damascus; the Damascenes seek aid from our people and obtain it upon stipulated terms; Zengi returns to his own country. 618  
**Chapter VIII.**—The city of Banias is besieged, with the Damascenes providing assistance. 629  
**Chapter IX.**—The prince of Antioch and the count of Tripoli join the same siege, and the city is attacked with the utmost vigor. 620  
**Chapter X.**—In the presence of the prince and count, an engine is erected for attacking the city, while the citizens stoutly defend themselves in hope of relief. 621  
**Chapter XI.**—The legate of the Roman Church arrives and joins the siege; the city is taken, a bishop is appointed there, and all the princes proceed to Jerusalem. 622  
**Chapter XII.**—The prince of Antioch conspires with the opponents of the Antiochene patriarch; the patriarch sets out for Rome. He is captured by Roger, duke of Apulia, but at last makes peace with him and reaches Rome. 624  
**Chapter XIII.**—He is accused by his opponents; at last he returns home with the fullness of favor. 625  
**Chapter XIV.**—On his return, his clergy, at the prince’s instigation, refuse to receive him; he withdraws into the territory of the count of Edessa; eventually reconciled with the prince, he enters Antioch. 626  
**Chapter XV.**—The archbishop of Lyons, legate of the Apostolic See, dies at Acre; Alberic, bishop of Ostia, is sent in his place. A synod is summoned at Antioch. 627  
**Chapter XVI.**—At the assembly of bishops an accusation is brought against the patriarch; he is summoned but delays coming. Serlo, archbishop of Apamea and his supporter, is deposed. 627  
**Chapter XVII.**—The patriarch, as though contumacious, is deposed in his absence;  

[Col. 1426]

he is shamefully treated and committed to chains. Setting out again for Rome, he obtains partial favor; but on his return he dies of poison. 629  
**Chapter XVIII.**—The legate returns to Jerusalem, holds a synod, and dedicates the church of the Lord. 630  
**Chapter XIX.**—The emperor again comes down into Syria and invites the prince to honor the agreements formerly made. 631  
**Chapter XX.**—The citizens, having sent an embassy to the emperor, oppose the agreements and forbid his entry. 632  
**Chapter XXI.**—The emperor sends messengers to the king of Jerusalem, pretending that he intends to visit the holy places; he receives the king’s response on the matter. 633  
**Chapter XXII.**—While delaying in Cilicia, the emperor is mortally wounded while hunting. 633  
**Chapter XXIII.**—Having elevated his younger son to the empire, the emperor dies. The army returns home after Manuel has been installed as emperor. 634  
**Chapter XXIV.**—The king and princes of the kingdom establish before Ascalon a castle called Ibelin. 635  
**Chapter XXV.**—Again before Ascalon, by the common counsel of the princes, a fortress called Blanchegarde is built. 636  
**Chapter XXVI.**—The queen builds a monastery at the place called Bethany, endows it with an extensive estate, and sets her sister over it. 637  
**Chapter XXVII.**—While hunting a hare on the plains of Acre, the king is thrown headlong from his horse and dies; he is buried at Jerusalem among his predecessors. 638  

### Book Sixteen

**Chapter I.**—A brief preface is supplied. Upon Fulk’s death, his son Baldwin III succeeds him; his bodily appearance is described. 639  
**Chapter II.**—Concerning his character and manner of life. 640  
**Chapter III.**—Concerning his elevation to the kingship and how long he reigned under his mother’s guardianship. 642  
**Chapter IV.**—Zengi besieges Edessa, and the situation of that city is described. 642  
**Chapter V.**—The city is taken and its people are killed. 644  
**Chapter VI.**—A fortress beyond the Jordan called Moses’ Valley is acquired by the king. 645  
**Chapter VII.**—Zengi dies while besieging Calagembar; his son Nur ad-Din succeeds him. 646  
**Chapter VIII.**—A nobleman of Damascus, governor of the city of Bosra, makes an agreement with the king; the army of the kingdom hastens toward Bosra; Ainard, governor of Damascus, endeavors to obstruct the undertaking. 647  
**Chapter IX.**—The advancing army suffers countless dangers. 648  
**Chapter X.**—Having reached the appointed place, they find the city occupied by the enemy; the undertaking fails and a return is ordered. 650  
**Chapter XI.**—On its return the army suffers intolerable dangers; the enemy marvel at our men’s endurance. 652  
**Chapter XII.**—An envoy is sent to the enemy for peace; a certain nobleman among the enemy falls; the enemy army breaks up, and ours proceeds more freely. 653  
**Chapter XIII.**—Our legions reach Gadara; the place is described; the army returns home. 654  
**Chapter XIV.**—The citizens of Edessa summon the count; he hastens there and retakes the city without the enemy’s knowledge. 655  
**Chapter XV.**—Nur ad-Din comes against him; besieging the city, he cruelly afflicts our people. 656  
**Chapter XVI.**—The count, leaving with his men, endeavors to return home; Nur ad-Din pursues, massacres the army, and the count escapes by flight. 656  
**Chapter XVII.**—William, patriarch of Jerusalem, dies; Fulk, archbishop of Tyre, succeeds him; Ralph, the king’s chancellor, is forcibly intruded upon the church of Tyre by royal power. 658  
**Chapter XVIII.**—The western peoples are stirred up; the emperor of the Romans, Conrad, and Louis, king of the Franks, with many other princes, set out to aid the eastern Christians. 659  
**Chapter XIX.**—The emperor, going ahead with his forces, reaches Constantinople. The sultan of Iconium lays ambushes against him. 660  
**Chapter XX.**—After crossing the Hellespont, Emperor Conrad is misled by Greek treachery, and his army is led into extremely dangerous places. 661  
**Chapter XXI.**—The guides supplied to his army by the Greek emperor maliciously absent themselves, and the emperor’s army is endangered. 662  
**Chapter XXII.**—The Turks suddenly rush upon the German legions and slaughter them; yet the emperor escapes. 664  

[Col. 1427]

**Chapter XXIII.**—After crossing the Hellespont, the king of France arrives at Nicaea in Bithynia with his legions; the two rulers confer, and the emperor returns to Constantinople. 665  
**Chapter XXIV.**—The king of France proceeds by another route and reaches Ephesus; Guy, count of Ponthieu, dies there. The Franks cross the river Maeander despite the enemy. 666  
**Chapter XXV.**—By a remarkable mischance, the army of the Franks is overthrown; the contingent which had gone ahead escapes. 667  
**Chapter XXVI.**—The king, escaping the disaster, joins those who had preceded him; the remainder of the army reaches Attalia and from there crosses into Syria. 668  
**Chapter XXVII.**—Raymond, prince of Antioch, honorably receives the king of France at the port of Saint Symeon and leads him to Antioch; but in the end they part in hostility. 670  
**Chapter XXVIII.**—After the winter has passed, Emperor Conrad reaches Syria by ship; Count Anfossus also arrives at Acre and dies at Caesarea. 671  
**Chapter XXIX.**—The king of France, departing from Antioch, hastens to Jerusalem; the patriarch of Jerusalem is sent to meet him. 671  

### Book Seventeen

**Chapter I.**—A general council is held at the maritime city of Ptolemais, and the princes who had assembled there are named. 673  
**Chapter II.**—They propose to besiege Damascus and, as agreed, proceed to it. 674  
**Chapter III.**—The site of the city of Damascus is described. 675  
**Chapter IV.**—Our men forcibly break into the city’s orchards and seize the river by force of arms despite the enemy. A remarkable and admirable deed of the emperor is described. 676  
**Chapter V.**—The citizens despair and consider flight; they corrupt certain of our princes with money, and through their persuasion the army is transferred to the opposite side of the city. 677  
**Chapter VI.**—Provisions fail in our camp; the treachery of the traitors is exposed; our men raise the siege and return. 678  
**Chapter VII.**—Various opinions are set forth as to who was responsible for so great a betrayal. They again propose to besiege Ascalon, but achieve nothing. 679  
**Chapter VIII.**—Emperor Conrad returns home, while the king of France remains in Syria. 680  
**Chapter IX.**—Nur ad-Din enters Antiochene territory; Prince Raymond confronts him; battle is fought between them. Prince Raymond is killed. 681  
**Chapter X.**—Nur ad-Din treats the entire region according to his own will. The king hastens there to offer assistance. The sultan of Iconium enters the territory of the count of Edessa. 682  
**Chapter XI.**—After the king has departed from Antioch, the count of Edessa is captured by the enemy, among whom he dies dishonorably. 684  
**Chapter XII.**—The king, with the princes of the kingdom, rebuilds Gaza near Ascalon. 685  
**Chapter XIII.**—Serious hostilities arise between the king and his mother; without his mother’s knowledge, the king is crowned. 686  
**Chapter XIV.**—Son and mother divide the kingdom between themselves. The king forcibly enters Jerusalem and besieges his mother in the Tower of David; finally peace is restored in tranquility. 687  
**Chapter XV.**—The sultan of Iconium again enters the county of Edessa; the king hastens there with all speed. 688  
**Chapter XVI.**—The emperor of Constantinople sends an army into Antiochene territory; he demands that the county of Edessa be surrendered to him, obtains what he requests, and its castles are yielded to the Greeks; the king then leads out the Latins. 689  
**Chapter XVII.**—Nur ad-Din confronts the king and seeks to prevent his departure. The king returns to Antioch, though with difficulty. Nur ad-Din expels the Greeks and occupies the whole region. 690  
**Chapter XVIII.**—The king urges the princess to take one of the princes as husband, so that he may govern the region; but he does not succeed. The king then goes to Tripoli, intending to return home. 692  
**Chapter XIX.**—The king and his mother meet at Tripoli in order to reconcile the count with his wife, but fail. The count is killed at the city gate by the Assassins. 693  
**Chapter XX.**—An enormous multitude of Turks comes to Jerusalem to seize it, but our men go out and overthrow them with great strength. 694  
**Chapter XXI.**—The king and princes of the kingdom hasten to Ascalon to ravage the orchards around the city; but, pursuing a greater purpose, they besiege the city. 695  
**Chapter XXII.**—The site and advantages of the city are described.  

[Col. 1428]

696  
**Chapter XXIII.**—The siege is organized; commanders are appointed for the fleet and for the legions on land. 698  
**Chapter XXIV.**—In the second month of the siege, pilgrims arrive, bringing many resources useful for the siege. 699  
**Chapter XXV.**—In the fifth month, the Egyptian fleet reaches the city, giving great comfort to the besieged citizens. 700  
**Chapter XXVI.**—Constance, princess of Antioch, marries Reynald of Châtillon. Nur ad-Din also forcibly occupies the kingdom of Damascus. Amalric is appointed to the church of Sidon. 700  
**Chapter XXVII.**—Those at the siege press their attack upon the city. The citizens try to burn an external engine. Part of the city wall collapses; our men, seeking to enter, perish in part; our army despairs. 701  
**Chapter XXVIII.**—Our men are encouraged again and urged to continue the siege, pressing the attack more boldly. 703  
**Chapter XXIX.**—The people of Ascalon despair and by common counsel incline toward surrender. 705  
**Chapter XXX.**—The leading citizens, sent to the king, obtain free departure with their wives, children, and all their possessions, and surrender the city. 706  

### Book Eighteen

**Chapter I.**—Reynald of Châtillon, prince of Antioch, shamefully mistreats the patriarch of Antioch; the latter flees to the kingdom. A severe famine arises throughout the land. 707  
**Chapter II.**—Upon Anastasius’s death, Adrian succeeds him. Emperor Frederick is crowned at Rome. Serious hostilities arise between the pope and William, king of Sicily. 709

**Chapter IV.**—The origin and beginning of the house of the Hospital are described. 711  
**Chapter V.**—How the Egyptian caliph, at the request of the Amalfitans, ordered a site assigned to them where they might build a church. 712  
**Chapter VI.**—The patriarch, with the greater part of the eastern bishops, sets out for Rome to Pope Adrian. 714  
**Chapter VII.**—The emperor of Constantinople, with the pope’s consent, invades Apulia. The lord patriarch and his companions arrive at the papal court. 715  
**Chapter VIII.**—Pope Adrian hastens to Benevento; the patriarch hurries there and presents his case, but the court, corrupted by gifts, suppresses justice. The patriarch returns without accomplishing his purpose. 716

**Chapter XI.**—Contrary to the terms and peace treaty which he had made with them, the king captures Turks and Arabs in the forest of Banias. 720

**Chapter XV.**—Nur ad-Din again besieges Banias, but fails when the king again confronts him. 725

**Chapter XVII.**—The king, with all the forces of the kingdom and the count of Flanders, hastens to Antioch. Nur ad-Din falls into a desperate illness. 727  
**Chapter XVIII.**—Caesarea is besieged and shortly thereafter forcibly taken. 728  
**Chapter XIX.**—Nur ad-Din’s brother comes over to us. Fulk, patriarch of Jerusalem, dies. A cave beyond the Jordan is restored to our people. The king besieges and takes the castle of Harenc in Antiochene territory. 730  
**Chapter XX.**—At Jerusalem Amalric, prior of the church of the Lord’s Sepulchre, is elected patriarch; controversy about his election arises among the bishops. 732  

[Col. 1429]

**Chapter XXI.**—Nur ad-Din besieges our cave in the region of Sueta; the king arrives and raises the siege; Nur ad-Din fights with our men and is defeated. 732  
**Chapter XXII.**—The envoys sent to Constantinople for the royal marriage return and bring the king a wife, the emperor’s niece. 733  
**Chapter XXIII.**—The emperor of Constantinople comes to Antioch; Prince Reynald, making satisfaction for what he had committed against the Cypriots, is reconciled with him. 734  
**Chapter XXIV.**—The king hastens to those regions, is honorably received by the same emperor, and brings back countless gifts. 736  
**Chapter XXV.**—The emperor enters Antioch and displays great generosity toward its citizens; afterward he returns home. 737  
**Chapter XXVI.**—After Adrian’s death, a dangerous schism arises in the Roman Church. 738  
**Chapter XXVII.**—Nur ad-Din, entering the territory of the sultan of Iconium, forcibly occupies part of it. The king ravages the territory of Damascus. 739  
**Chapter XXVIII.**—Reynald, prince of Antioch, is captured by the enemy and put in chains at Aleppo. 740  
**Chapter XXIX.**—A certain John, cardinal-priest of the Roman Church, comes down to Syria as legate; disagreement arises among the bishops concerning his reception. A son, Baldwin, is born to Amalric, count of Jaffa and brother of the king. 741  
**Chapter XXX.**—Summoned by the Antiochenes, the king hastens there; imperial envoys are present, seeking for their lord a wife from among the kinswomen of the lord king. 742  
**Chapter XXXI.**—He assigns to him the sister of the count of Tripoli, an illustrious maiden named Melisende; but after a year the emperor repudiates her and marries Maria, daughter of Prince Raymond. 743  
**Chapter XXXII.**—Near Antioch the king rebuilds the castle called Iron Bridge. Queen Melisende, his mother, dies. 745  
**Chapter XXXIII.**—Angered by his sister’s repudiation, the count of Tripoli inflicts upon the emperor every injury he can. 745  
**Chapter XXXIV.**—At Antioch the king drinks poison; brought thereby into a final illness, he seeks to return home, but as the illness worsens he dies on the journey at Beirut. 746  

### Book Nineteen

**Chapter I.**—Amalric succeeds his brother, Lord Baldwin, in the kingdom. 747  
**Chapter II.**—His character, life, and conduct are described. 748  
**Chapter III.**—His physical constitution is described, together with a certain question which he gave to one of his familiars to solve. 750  
**Chapter IV.**—Before he was crowned, he was compelled to separate from his wife, whom he had married contrary to the sacred canons. 751  
**Chapter V.**—The king goes down into Egypt and engages Sultan Dargan in battle. Shawar brings Shirkuh into Egypt; Dargan sends envoys to the king to seek peace. 752  
**Chapter VI.**—Peter, archbishop of Tyre, dies; Lord Frederick, bishop of Acre, succeeds him. 754  
**Chapter VII.**—Dargan, sultan in Egypt, is killed by the treachery of his own men. Shawar becomes sultan, invites the king, and the king descends into Egypt; Shirkuh is forcibly expelled. 754  
**Chapter VIII.**—Nur ad-Din is defeated in Tripolitan territory and scarcely escapes our hands by flight. 755  
**Chapter IX.**—Nur ad-Din besieges the castle of Harenc in Antiochene territory; the prince of Antioch, the count of Tripoli, and Calamannus, governor of Cilicia, are captured. 755
