**Chapter XII.**—The return of the author of this history to his homeland is described, and some particulars of his advancement are set forth. Shirkuh goes down into Egypt, taking a large force with him. 759  
**Chapter XIII.**—The king, pursuing Shirkuh, likewise goes down into Egypt to aid the Egyptians. 760  
**Chapter XIV.**—Cairo is described, and its first founder is identified. 761  

[Col. 1430]

**Chapter XV.**—The king meets Shirkuh as he approaches; Shirkuh forestalls the king and crosses the river. 762  
**Chapter XVI.**—Sultan Shawar works to detain the king by renewing the agreements. 762  
**Chapter XVII.**—Persons are sent to the caliph to renew the treaty; the magnificence of the royal palace is described. 763  
**Chapter XVIII.**—The agreements are fulfilled, and in their confirmation the caliph gives his right hand to Hugh of Caesarea. 764  
**Chapter XIX.**—The reason why the ruler of Egypt is called *Mulene* is explained. 765  
**Chapter XX.**—It is further explained why he is called caliph and how he is the opponent of the caliph of Baghdad. 766  
**Chapter XXI.**—The king builds a bridge over the Nile. Shirkuh enters the island; the king pursues him. 767  
**Chapter XXII.**—The island is described, along with how many mouths of the Nile enter the sea and which they are. Our men drive out the enemy and occupy the island; Shirkuh flees into the desert. 768  
**Chapter XXIII.**—The land of Egypt is described and its nature explained. 770  
**Chapter XXIV.**—Battle is joined between the king and Shirkuh in the desert, with great danger to both sides. 771  
**Chapter XXV.**—Shirkuh withdraws within Alexandria. The king hastens there and besieges the city. 773  
**Chapter XXVI.**—The site of Alexandria is described. 774  
**Chapter XXVII.**—The king continues the siege and most severely harasses the citizens of Alexandria. 775  
**Chapter XXVIII.**—Hearing this, Shirkuh discusses peace with Hugh of Caesarea. 777  
**Chapter XXIX.**—Hugh, together with the king and princes, fulfills the terms of the treaty. 778  
**Chapter XXX.**—The city is surrendered to the king, and peace is proclaimed for the Alexandrians. 778  
**Chapter XXXI.**—Having gained the victory and recovered all his men, the king returns home. 779  

### Book Twenty

**Chapter I.**—Lord Ernisius, archbishop of Caesarea, and Odo of Saint Amand, the king’s butler, return from Constantinople, bringing with them the king’s future wife. The king is crowned in the church of Tyre and marries her. 779  
**Chapter II.**—Andronicus, a kinsman of the emperor, takes Theodora, widow of King Baldwin, with him through enemy lands. 780  
**Chapter III.**—The churches of Petra and Hebron are organized with bishops appointed. Stephen, chancellor of the king of Sicily and bishop-elect of the church of Palermo, comes to Syria. William, count of Nevers, dies among us. 781  
**Chapter IV.**—The emperor’s envoys come to the king seeking certain agreements from the lord king. The archdeacon of Tyre is sent and concludes the proposed agreements with the emperor. 782  
**Chapter V.**—The king goes down into Egypt with his forces and, contrary to the terms of the treaty he had made with the Egyptians, wages war against them. 783  
**Chapter VI.**—The city of Bilbeis is besieged and taken by assault. The sultan deceives the king with promises of limitless money. 784  
**Chapter VII.**—The king pitches camp before Cairo, awaiting the money promised by the sultan. 785  
**Chapter VIII.**—Our fleet, sent up the Nile, attempts to join our army but, accomplishing nothing, returns home. 785  
**Chapter IX.**—While Cairo is besieged, the king awaits the money promised by the sultan. But the sultan tries to withdraw from the agreements and calls for Turkish assistance. 786  
**Chapter X.**—Milo of Plancy corrupts the king’s judgment with harmful counsel. Shirkuh, summoned by the Egyptians, arrives; the king meets him in the desert, but, not finding him, returns home without success. 786  
**Chapter XI.**—Shirkuh occupies Egypt, kills the sultan, and himself dies shortly afterward. 788  
**Chapter XII.**—Saladin, his nephew through his brother, succeeds him after his death and gains the kingdom of Egypt. 789  
**Chapter XIII.**—Bernard, abbot of the monastery of Mount Tabor, is appointed over the church of Lydda. Frederick, archbishop of Tyre, is sent to the western lands to seek aid from the western princes. 789  
**Chapter XIV.**—The emperor, wishing to fulfill the agreements, sends a fleet and certain of his princes into Syria. 790  
**Chapter XV.**—The king goes down into Egypt with his forces, while the Greeks follow him both by sea and by land. 791  

[Col. 1431]

**Chapter XVI.**—The king besieges Damietta, and in attempting to take it both the Latin and Greek armies toil fruitlessly. 792  
**Chapter XVII.**—Famine arises in the camp, and nearly the entire fleet is burned; finally, after labor has been wasted fruitlessly, the siege is raised. 794  
**Chapter XVIII.**—The expeditions are recalled and the king returns home. On the return journey almost the entire Greek fleet perishes, driven by adverse winds. 795  
**Chapter XIX.**—A very great earthquake shakes nearly the whole East and brings down cities of greatest antiquity. 796  
**Chapter XX.**—Saladin enters our territories and besieges the castle called Darum. 797  
**Chapter XXI.**—The king confronts him with a small force of knights; many of our people, both in the city of Gaza and on the road, are slaughtered by the enemy. 799  
**Chapter XXII.**—Saladin returns home. The king too, having repaired the castle, which had been partly destroyed, returns to Ascalon. 800  
**Chapter XXIII.**—In the same year Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury and glorious martyr of Christ, is killed in his own church. 801  
**Chapter XXIV.**—The king, taking several of his princes with him, goes to Constantinople; the emperor strives to anticipate him with manifold honor. 801  
**Chapter XXV.**—Brought before the emperor, he is honorably received and holds frequent conversations with him regarding necessary affairs. 803  
**Chapter XXVI.**—Once affairs have been completed and gifts bestowed in abundance, both the king and his princes return home. 804  
**Chapter XXVII.**—The king summons an army at Sepphoris. Frederick, archbishop of Tyre, returns from the lands beyond the mountains. Lord William, bishop of Acre, is killed in Romania. 805  
**Chapter XXVIII.**—Milo the Armenian, brother of Lord Toros, allied with Nur ad-Din, harasses Antiochene territory; the king hastens there to restrain his malice. 807  
**Chapter XXIX.**—Saladin besieges the castle beyond the Jordan called Montreal, but gains nothing and returns home. 809  
**Chapter XXX.**—Saladin devastates all the land beyond the Jordan. The king keeps his army at a place called Carmel. Raymond, count of Tripoli, returns from captivity. 809  
**Chapter XXXI.**—The sect of the Assassins is described, together with the dispatch of their envoy to the lord king. 810  
**Chapter XXXII.**—The envoy of the Assassins is killed by the brethren of the Knights Templar, and great unrest arises in the kingdom. Ralph, bishop of Bethlehem, dies. 811  
**Chapter XXXIII.**—Nur ad-Din dies. The king besieges Banias and, after making a truce, departs; falling ill, he goes to Jerusalem, where within a few days he dies. 813  

### Book Twenty-One

**Chapter I.**—The first auspices of Baldwin IV, sixth king of Jerusalem: his character, age, and bodily appearance. 813  
**Chapter II.**—At what time he was anointed and crowned. 815  
**Chapter III.**—In the first year of his reign, a fleet of the king of Sicily comes to Alexandria and suffers enormous losses. The count of Tripoli, as nearest agnate, claims the administration of the kingdom and guardianship of the king. 816

**Chapter XI.**—The king again enters hostile Damascene territory and plunders the valley surnamed Bachar. Reynald of Châtillon and Joscelin, the king’s uncle, are freed from enemy chains.  

[Col. 1432]

824  
**Chapter XII.**—The lord emperor of Constantinople is shamefully defeated near Iconium. 826  
**Chapter XIII.**—William the Younger, marquis of Montferrat, comes to Syria and marries the king’s sister. 826  
**Chapter XIV.**—The long-awaited count of Flanders enters the kingdom. 828  
**Chapter XV.**—Those who had come with the count mislead him, warning him not to comply with the princes of the kingdom. 829  
**Chapter XVI.**—Envoys of the emperor of Constantinople arrive, urgently demanding fulfillment of the agreements made by the king with their lord and the preparation of expeditions against Egypt. 830  
**Chapter XVII.**—The count obstructs this action, being alien to an honorable purpose. 831  
**Chapter XVIII.**—The emperor’s envoys return home. The count proceeds toward Antiochene territory. Balian marries the widow of Lord King Amalric. 832

**Chapter XXI.**—The enemy ravage the region far and wide, burning towns and suburbs. 835  
**Chapter XXII.**—The king leaves Ascalon and confronts the enemy; battle-lines are arranged on both sides, and preparations for combat are made. 836  
**Chapter XXIII.**—Battle is joined; Saladin is defeated and put to flight with utmost peril and disgrace. 837  
**Chapter XXIV.**—Unseasonable rain and unusual cold exhaust beyond endurance those who fled from the battle; countless numbers are killed and very many captured. The king returns victoriously to Jerusalem. 838

**Chapter XXVI.**—A general synod is summoned at Rome. The king builds a castle on the waters of the Jordan under ill-omened birds; once built, he gives it to the Templars. 841

## BOOK TWENTY-TWO

**Chapter I.**—The king gives his sister, who had been the wife of the marquis, in marriage to a certain young man, namely Guy of Lusignan. A truce is confirmed with Saladin on equal terms, contrary to custom. 847  
**Chapter II.**—Saladin invades the territory of Tripoli as an enemy, and devastates both the crops and the resources of the land. 848  
**Chapter III.**—The Egyptian fleet comes to the island of Aradus; the count of Tripoli makes an alliance with Saladin. 849  
**Chapter IV.**—The archbishop of Tyre returns from Constantinople; Lord Louis, king of the Franks, dies. 849  
**Chapter V.**—The king gives his younger sister in marriage to Humphrey the Third. The emperor of Constantinople dies. 851  
**Chapter VI.**—The prince of Antioch is subjected to anathema because of a concubine whom he had taken in addition to his living wife. A conspiracy is formed against Emperor Alexius. 852  
**Chapter VII.**—The patriarch of Jerusalem is sent to Antioch to attempt a remedy for its endangered condition. Pope Alexander dies. 852  
**Chapter VIII.**—The son of Nūr al-Dīn dies, leaving his inheritance to the lord of Mosul, his kinsman. 855  
**Chapter IX.**—A dangerous quarrel arises between the king and the count of Tripoli, and proceeds as far as open hatred. 856  
**Chapter X.**—A disturbance arises at Constantinople; and when the wicked man Andronicus prevails, the Latin population is expelled. 857  

[Col. 1433]

**Chapter XI.**—The causes of the disturbance and dissension are set forth. 858  
**Chapter XII.**—Having killed the nobles, Andronicus occupies the city and the palaces, and oppresses the people by a violent rule. 859  
**Chapter XIII.**—The Latin population, which had taken refuge in galleys, ravages the islands and coastal places as an enemy. 860  
**Chapter XIV.**—Saladin breaks the treaty which he had concluded with the lord king; the king confronts him beyond the Jordan. The Turks break into the village of Bury, carrying its inhabitants away into captivity. 862  
**Chapter XV.**—The same man violently occupies our fortress in our territory of Suicide: namely, a most strongly fortified cave. 863  
**Chapter XVI.**—The same man violently enters our borders; battle is joined near the castle of Torbelet, with victory uncertain. 865  
**Chapter XVII.**—The same man, having summoned a fleet from Egypt, besieges the city of Beirut. 867  
**Chapter XVIII.**—The king, hastening to relieve it, reaches Tyre. Saladin raises the siege. 868  
**Chapter XIX.**—Saladin crosses the Euphrates and enters Mesopotamia. 870  
**Chapter XX.**—The king ravages the territory of Damascus as an enemy. 871  
**Chapter XXI.**—The same king besieges the stronghold which Saladin had recently occupied; he takes it when besieged and restores it to Christendom. 872  
**Chapter XXII.**—The king again enters the territory of Damascus with his expeditions. 874  
**Chapter XXIII.**—A tax is collected in the kingdom, by which it may defend itself against future contingencies. 875  
**Chapter XXIV.**—Saladin besieges Aleppo and obtains it, subject to certain stipulated conditions. The prince of Antioch exchanges Tarsus with Rupen, leader of the Armenians. 878  
**Chapter XXV.**—The king, seized by a severe illness at Nazareth, appoints Guy of Lusignan, count of Jaffa, governor of the kingdom. 879  
**Chapter XXVI.**—Saladin, having entered our territory with immense forces, encamps around the region of Scythopolis. Our men meet him. 881  
**Chapter XXVII.**—Severe famine arises in the army; at last, without a battle being joined, both our men and the enemy withdraw from one another. 882  
**Chapter XXVIII.**—Saladin besieges the city of Petra beyond the Jordan and attacks it fiercely while it is under siege. 884  
**Chapter XXIX.**—The king removes the administration of the kingdom from the count of Jaffa; he crowns his nephew Baldwin with the royal diadem. 886  
**Chapter XXX.**—The king, having assembled his forces, hastens beyond the Jordan to assist those under siege. Saladin raises the siege. 887  

## BOOK TWENTY-THREE

**Preface.** 889  
**Chapter I.**—The long-nurtured hostility between the king and the count of Jaffa breaks out into execrable disputes; no hope of reconciliation appears. The count of Tripoli obtains the administration of the kingdom and the royal guardianship. 890  

**Continuation of William of Tyre’s History of the Sacred War.** 891  

## BOOK TWENTY-TWO IN THE CONTINUATION

**I.**—The child king, having received homage from the barons, is entrusted to Count Jocelin for guardianship. Scarcity of water in the city. A well is discovered near the spring of Siloam. 895  
**II.**—On the spring of Siloam. The count of Tripoli negotiates a truce with Saladin. 897  
**III.**—Boniface, marquis of Montferrat, takes the cross, as does his son Conrad, who arrives at Constantinople. 898  
**IV.**—The lewdness of Andronicus, emperor of Constantinople. He approaches to kill Quirsac, or Isaac; the latter in turn, after killing Langosto, seizes the imperial crown. 900  
**V.**—He allows Andronicus, shamefully dressed in women’s clothing, to be killed by an enraged mob. 900  
**VI.**—Alexius seizes the empire, having captured and blinded his brother. 901  
**VII.**—The empress cautiously sends Alexius, her son, to the king of Hungary for safekeeping. The younger king of Jerusalem dies. 901  
**VIII.**—The countess of Jaffa is adorned with the crown of the kingdom. 903  
**IX.**—Guy of Lusignan becomes king of Jerusalem. 904  

## BOOK TWENTY-THREE

**I.**—The barons, upon learning of Guy’s elevation to the kingdom, resolve to establish Humphrey as king. But he refuses the royal crown. 903  

[Col. 1434]

**II.**—The barons render homage to King Guy. 905  
**III.**—King Guy prepares an army against the count of Tripoli, who summons Saladin to his assistance. The king sends envoys to offer peace to the count. 906  
**IV.**—Meanwhile the count permits the son of Saladin free entry into Christian lands. The Knights Templar confront Saladin and are annihilated by him. 907  
**V.**—The Turks carry off the heads of the slain Christians. Balian, having received news of the Christians’ defeat, reports it to the queen. Envoys come to the count and reconcile him with the king. 908  
**VI.**—The king comes to meet the count. The True Cross is brought to the army. 910  
**VII.**—The treasure of the king of England is delivered to the king. Saladin surrounds Tiberias with a siege. 910  
**VIII.**—The count of Tripoli judges that no assistance should be brought to Tiberias. The master of the Temple takes the opposite view, and the king follows his counsel. 911  
**IX.**—Saladin endeavors to bewitch the Christian army through a sorceress. 912  
**X.**—On the election of Patriarch Heraclius. The archbishop of Tyre opposes his election. 914  
**XI.**—Heraclius, given over to sexual immorality, kills the archbishop with poison. 915  
**XII.**—Saracens confront King Guy and utterly defeat the Christians after the king has been captured. 915  
**XIII.**—Loss of the True Cross. 916  
**XIV.**—Saladin orders the captive king and other noblemen to be brought before him. He cuts off the head of Prince Raynald. He sends the king in chains to Damascus and takes Tiberias. 917  
**XV.**—Balian comes to Jerusalem and is kept there by the patriarch, seemingly against his will. 918  
**XVI.**—Saladin takes several cities. God preserves Tyre for the Christians. 918  
**XVII.**—Conrad, son of the marquis of Montferrat, leaves Constantinople and comes to Acre. 919  
**XVIII.**—He then hastens to Tyre, whose custody is entrusted to him. Saladin besieges Tyre, raises the siege, and takes Caesarea and Jaffa. He takes Ascalon and grants freedom to the captive king. 919  
**XIX.**—Saladin orders the citizens of Jerusalem to surrender the city to him. 921  
**XX.**—Saladin takes the whole kingdom except Tyre and Jerusalem. 921  
**XXI.**—Saladin besieges Jerusalem, where the Christians resist bravely. Saladin changes the location of the siege. 922  
**XXII.**—The Christians deliberate upon surrendering the city. Meanwhile the Turks, attacking it, are driven back. 923  
**XXIII.**—God does not hear the Christians’ prayers because of their sins. Negotiations are held with Saladin concerning the surrender of the city. 924  
**XXIV.**—Terms of the treaty. 924  
**XXV.**—The city is surrendered to Saladin. 926  
**XXVI.**—Saladin grants liberty to a thousand captives. Many others are freed. 928  
**XXVII.**—How well Saladin treated the Christians. The count of Tripoli refuses to receive the Christians. 928  
**XXVIII.**—The Saracens’ charity toward Christians. 929  
**XXIX.**—Saladin has the Temple washed with rosewater. He besieges Tyre. 930  
**XXX.**—Aid sent from Tyre is driven back by force of the winds. Through Conrad’s resourcefulness, the Saracens suffer losses before Tyre. 931  
**XXXI.**—The Saracens, defeated in sea and land battle, raise the siege of Tyre. 932  
**XXXII.**—The archbishop of Tyre comes to Rome. William, king of Sicily, ascribes to himself the loss of the Holy Land. 933  
**XXXIII.**—The king of Sicily sends aid to the Holy Land. 933  
**XXXIV.**—The pope calls upon Christian princes to bring aid to the Holy Land. The emperor of Germany is the first to take the cross; he is drowned in Armenian waters. The kings of France and England take the cross. Saladin besieges Tripoli, then raises the siege. 934  
**XXXV.**—Saladin takes Valania and Byblos. 936  

## BOOK TWENTY-FOUR

**I.**—King Guy proceeds to Tyre, but is refused entry. He besieges Acre. 937  
**II.**—War between the kings of France and England; peace between them. King Richard is crowned. 937  
**III.**—The two crusading kings depart for the Holy Land with many other princes and nobles. 938  
**IV.**—The king of France winters at Messina. Charity at Acre. 939  

[Col. 1435]

**V.**—Christians searching for provisions in the Saracen army are killed. At the queen’s death, the kingdom devolves upon Isabella, wife of Humphrey, who is separated from him. 939  
**VI.**—The king of England arrives at Palermo. The king of France arrives at Acre. After the latter’s sister is rejected, Richard marries the daughter of the king of Navarre. 940  
**VII.**—The king and queen of England come to Cyprus. 941  
**VIII.**—The king of England takes the island of Cyprus. Acre having been surrendered to the king of France, peace is made with Saladin. 942  
**IX.**—Once Acre has been taken, each person’s former inheritance is restored to him. 943  
**X.**—Saladin refuses to restore the Holy Cross and to pay the ransom of the admirals. The king of France falls ill and returns to France. King Richard proceeds toward Jerusalem. 943  
**XI.**—The duke of Burgundy withdraws to Acre with the French barons. Saladin besieges Jaffa. King Richard recovers the castle of Jaffa and escapes Saladin’s ambushes. 944  
**XII.**—Saladin raises the siege of Jaffa and fights with the Christians. The king of England captures Ascalon. 945  
**XIII.**—The Griphii are slain by the Latins. Richard sells the island of Cyprus to King Guy. 946  
**XIV.**—Aimery, Guy’s brother, succeeds King Guy as king of Cyprus. 947  
**XV.**—The marquis, after plundering ships of the Assassins, is murdered treacherously, as is believed, at the instigation of the king of England. Henry, count of Champagne, marries his wife. 947  
**XVI.**—Richard, having destroyed Ascalon and two castles, concludes a truce with Saladin and returns to his homeland. 948  
**XVII.**—Richard travels in disguise and is captured by the duke of Austria. 950  
**XVIII.**—The king Philip invades English lands. Richard is released upon payment of the promised ransom. 951  
**XIX.**—Emperor Henry becomes king of Sicily. 951  
**XX.**—Emperor Henry prepares a fleet for a holy expedition. 952  
**XXI.**—Emperor Henry is crowned king of Cyprus. Death of Saladin. Saladin, Saladin’s son, besieges Jaffa and takes it by force. The grievous death of Count Henry. 952  
**XXII.**—Death of the sultan of Egypt. The king of Cyprus is adorned with the crown of Jerusalem. 954  
**XXIII.**—King Aimery besieges Beirut. 954  
**XXIV.**—He takes the city. 955  
**XXV.**—Aimery enters Beirut. After the emperor’s death, he concludes a truce with the sultan. 955  
**XXVI.**—The king of Armenia captures the prince of Antioch and devastates his land. Count Henry of Champagne makes peace between them. Upon the death of the prince of Antioch, the count of Tripoli succeeds him. He allies himself against the Armenian with the sultan of Aleppo. The Armenian defeats Antioch and is crowned king. 957  
**XXVII.**—Count Henry is honorably received by the prince of the Assassins. 958  
**XXVIII.**—Emperor Henry provides for his son before his death. 959  
**XXIX.**—The empress dies after crowning her son. 959  
**XXX.**—Count Walter of Brienne is killed. 960  
**XXXI.**—Alliance between the king of England and Baldwin, count of Flanders, against the king of France. 960  
**XXXII.**—The king of England is killed by an arrow in Limousin. Otto becomes emperor. 961  
**XXXIII.**—Many barons of France take the cross. 962  
**XXXIV.**—On Fulco of Milli. 962  
**XXXV.**—The crusaders depart from France by various routes and are all captured by the sultan. 963  
**XXXVI.**—The sultan of Egypt prepares to resist the Christians. The sultan of Aleppo besieges Damascus. 964  
**XXXVII.**—The Venetians refuse to transport the crusaders to the Holy Land unless they first assist them in capturing a certain city of Slavonia. The king of Hungary complains to the pope about this. 966  
**XXXVIII.**—The pope excommunicates them. The crusaders depart by different routes and proceed toward Antioch. 967  
**XXXIX.**—The people of Acre intercept the Saracens’ supplies. 968  
**XL.**—King Aimery violates the truce made with the Saracens. 968  
**XLI.**—The king plunders Saracen territory and, when the crusaders finally depart, makes a truce with the Saracens. 969  
**XLII.**—A plan to restore Isaac to the empire of Constantinople. 970  
**XLIII.**—Emperor Alexius prepares to resist Isaac, his nephew. 971  
**XLIV.**—The French, having reached Constantinople, attack and capture the tower called Golgotha. Alexius sallies from Constantinople against the Latins. 972  

[Col. 1436]

**XLV.**—The Venetians take the city. The French restore the lawful emperor to his throne. 972  
**XLVI.**—Marcofles, after killing the emperor, seizes the empire. The French and Venetians capture Constantinople. 972  
**XLVII.**—The Latins plunder Constantinople. 973  
**XLVIII.**—Baldwin, count of Flanders, becomes emperor of Constantinople. 975  
**XLIX.**—A conspiracy against the Latins at Adrianople. The Latins besiege Adrianople. 976  
**L.**—The citizens of Adrianople wish to surrender to Emperor Baldwin, provided that the Venetians do not rule them. The Venetians prevent the emperor from making peace with them. Vlachs and Cumans come to Adrianople’s aid; Count Louis is killed by them. 977  
**LI.**—The emperor attacks the Vlachs and Cumans and is killed by them. The siege of Adrianople is raised. 979  
**LII.**—Henry, hearing of the emperor’s death, whose aid he was coming to provide, withdraws to Rodosto. 979  
**LIII.**—Henry, the emperor’s brother, is appointed administrator of the empire and, after a year, emperor. 980  
**LIV.**—Peter, having gone to Rome, is crowned emperor by the pope. He proceeds toward Constantinople. 982  
**LV.**—The emperor is killed. The brother of the count of Namur becomes emperor. 982  
**LVI.**—The emperor’s mother is drowned. His wife has her nose and lips cut off. He himself dies. 983  
**LVII.**—Emperor Otto, once crowned, invades the lands of the Church and is excommunicated. 983  
**LVIII.**—Otto attempts in vain to invade Sicily. Frederick, king of Sicily, seeks in marriage the sister of the king of Aragon. 984  
**LIX.**—She is granted to him. 985  
**LX.**—The pope urges Frederick to proceed into Germany to be crowned at Aachen. 985  
**LXI.**—Having been crowned, he takes the cross. Otto attempts his death in vain. 985  
**LXII.**—King Philip opposes Otto, who makes an alliance against him with the English and Flemings. The king of England is defeated by Louis, son of the king of France. The battle of Bouvines, in which the king of France is victorious. 986  
**LXIII.**—Frederick pursues Otto, who surrenders the imperial insignia to him. 987  
**LXIV.**—John of Brienne becomes king of Jerusalem. 988  
**LXV.**—The pope orders the Cross to be preached. James of Vitry is elected bishop of Acre. 989  
**LXVI.**—The Christians besiege Mount Tabor, then raise the siege. 989  
**LXVII.**—King John resolves to besiege Damietta. 990  
**LXVIII.**—The pope sends crusaders and legates to Damietta. 991  
**LXIX.**—The sultan destroys the walls of Jerusalem and of neighboring castles. 991  
**LXX.**—The Christians attempt to cross the river. 992  
**LXXI.**—The Christians cross the river and besiege Damietta. The Saracens fortify castles near Acre. 992  
**LXXII.**—Battle between Christians and Saracens near Acre. The Christians are defeated by the Saracens. 994  
**LXXIII.**—Damietta is captured by the Christians. Division between the king and the cardinal. 995  
**LXXIV.**—Having abandoned Damietta, the king proceeds to Armenia and then to Acre. The cardinal harasses the army and the pilgrims. 996  
**LXXV.**—The cardinal rejects salutary counsel. The pilgrims are captured by the Saracens. 996  
**LXXVI.**—Two Christians go to the sultan to preach Christ. In exchange for Damietta, the sultan offers the Christians the kingdom of Jerusalem. 997  
**LXXVII.**—The pope crowns Frederick, summoned to Rome, and orders him to cross the sea for the recovery of the Holy Land; he declines for the present. 999  
**LXXVIII.**—The Christians resolve to besiege Babylon [Cairo]. 999  
**LXXIX.**—The sultan offers the Christians a truce of thirty years together with the kingdom of Jerusalem. 1000  
**LXXX.**—The cardinal refuses peace. 1000  
**LXXXI.**—The Saracens block the Christians’ routes and open the barriers of the waters. 1001  
**LXXXII.**—A conference between the king and the sultan, and peace between them. 1001  
**LXXXIII.**—Damietta is restored to the Saracens. The king crosses the sea and comes to Rome. 1002  
**LXXXIV.**—The king visits France, England, and Spain. The emperor marries his daughter. Discord between the emperor and the king. 1003  

[Col. 1437]

**LXXXV.**—The king and emperor are reconciled. The emperor feigns that he will cross the sea to the Holy Land. 1004  
**LXXXVI.**—The emperor is excommunicated by the pope. After Conradin’s death, the pilgrims fortify certain castles. 1005  
**LXXXVII.**—The emperor crosses the sea without informing the pope and negotiates peace with the sultan. He asks the pope for absolution. 1005  
**LXXXVIII.**—The emperor is badly received by the Templars and makes peace with the sultan. 1006  
**LXXXIX.**—Terms of the peace. 1007  
**XC.**—The pope supplies forces to King John, who invades the emperor’s lands. The emperor recovers his lands, makes peace with the pontiff, and is absolved by him. 1007  
**XCI.**—The Saracens are defeated by the Christians. 1008  
**XCII.**—The empire of Constantinople is offered to King John, who refuses it. But he gives his daughter in marriage to the heir of the empire and administers the empire. 1008  

## BOOK TWENTY-FIVE

**II.**—How King John conducted himself at Constantinople. 1010  
**III.**—The sultan of Babylon [Cairo] besieges and captures Damietta. 1011  
**IV.**—Frederick, having made peace with Pope Gregory, feigns that he wishes to cross the sea to the Holy Land. 1011

**VI.**—Christians kill Saracens in Jerusalem. 1012

**VIII.**—The castle of Beirut is besieged. 1014

**X.**—Balian’s address to Richard, administrator of the kingdom, which he regards as of little account. 1015  
**XI.**—[Without heading.] 1015  
**XII.**—The inhabitants of the kingdom endeavor to preserve their immunities and privileges. 1016  
**XIII.**—John of Ibelin asks the king of Cyprus to help him recover his land, and the king grants this. 1017  
**XIV.**—He makes the same request of the barons at Acre. 1017

**XVII.**—The king of Cyprus is brought to Acre. 1020

**XIX.**—Richard conquers a large part of the kingdom of Cyprus. 1021

**XXI.**—Battle between Cypriots and Apulians, who are defeated. 1022

**XXIX.**—Many crusaders cross the sea from France. 1028

[Col. 1438]

**XXXVII.**—Balian takes the city of Tyre. 1033

**XLV.**—The Saracens capture Ascalon. 1039

**I.**—Saint Louis crosses the sea and takes Damietta. 1039

## LUCIUS III, ROMAN PONTIFF

**Notice.** 1067  
**Diplomatic notice.** 1069  

## LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF POPE LUCIUS III

### THE YEAR 1181

**I.**—He takes the monastery of St. Peter in Chains at Ravenna under protection and confirms its goods and rights, imposing upon the monks an annual payment of twelve Pavia-mint denarii. 1071  
**II.**—He takes the monastery of St. Mary of Gallomont under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. 1071  
**III.**—He takes the church of Lucca under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. 1071  
**IV.**—He informs Philip, archbishop of Cologne, that he has instructed the provost of Bonn to excommunicate the count of Sayn if he has not compensated the monastery of Siegburg for the losses inflicted upon it. 1077  
**V.**—Privilege for the abbey of St. Mary at Soissons. 1077  
**VI.**—He takes the monastery of Siegburg under protection and confirms its goods and rights. 1077  
**VII.**—He takes the monastery of St. Peter at Cerreto, in the diocese of Volterra, under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. 1079  

[Col. 1439]

**VIII.**—Bull for the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem. 1081  
**IX.**—He informs the archpriest and canons of the church of Lucca that the prior of St. Fridianus has come to him to obtain confirmation of privileges. He affirms that he will protect their rights. 1082  
**X.**—Privilege for the nunnery of St. Hilary. 1083  
**XI.**—To the German clergy. 1085  
**XII.**—He commends Ægidius, bishop of Aarhus, to Canute, king of Sweden. 1085  
**XIII.**—Privilege for the church of Saints Crispin and Crispinian at La Cave, Soissons. 1086  
**XIV.**—Privilege for the abbey of St. Germain at Paris. 1088  
**XV.**—He confirms the privilege, established by Alexander III, concerning the blessing of the abbot of the monastery of St. Augustine at Canterbury. 1090  
**XVI.**—He forbids Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, and the archdeacon of Canterbury in any way to interfere in the possession of the monastery of St. Augustine—its tenants, clerics, or churches—while litigation concerning its privileges is pending. 1090  
**XVII.**—He forbids those subject to the jurisdiction of the monastery of St. Augustine at Canterbury, both clerics and laypeople, to answer the archbishop or his officials in any matter until the question of the false privileges has been settled. 1090  
**XVIII.**—He forbids Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, to demand in any way a profession from the abbot of St. Augustine. 1090  
**XIX.**—He forbids Roger, abbot of St. Augustine at Canterbury, to make or promise a profession to the archbishop. 1091  
**XX.**—He commends the monastery of St. Augustine at Canterbury to Henry, king of the English. 1091  
**XXI.**—He forbids the monastery of St. Augustine at Canterbury to be subjected to an interdict by command of the Apostolic See. 1091  

### THE YEAR 1182

**XXII.**—He confirms the possessions and privileges of the Venetian church of St. Saviour. 1091  
**XXIII.**—He grants Abbot G. of Vézelay and his successors the use of the mitre. 1093

### THE YEARS 1182–1183

**LXXII.**—He confirms that the church of St. Michael of Intercisio belongs to the canons of Asti. 1165  
**LXXIII.**—Privilege for the chapter of Reims. 1166

**LXXVII.**—He grants Henry, bishop, William, dean, and the canons of Bayeux that both they and their successors may be buried at the cathedral church. 1167  
**LXXVIII.**—He reproves Abbess A[delheid] and the sisters of Quedlinburg “because they diminish the payment due to the Roman Church as a sign of the liberty they have received; and because, although the same privileges expressly state that they ought to pay the Roman pontiff a pound of silver annually, they are willing to pay only a mark, maintaining that in this passage a pound must be understood as a mark.” Nevertheless, at the request of the provost of Mainz, he grants “that thereafter they shall pay yearly only a mark of refined silver, according to the Cologne weight.” 1168  

[Col. 1441]

**LXXIX.**—To Peter, abbot, and the chapter of Monte Cassino. 1168  
**LXXX.**—He grants various privileges to the monastery of St. Remigius at Reims. 1168  
**LXXXI.**—He confirms “the renunciation of the wrongful custom which Bulcard of Montmorency exercised in the vineyards of the monastery of St. Denis, situated in the village of Deuil, and the *rotaticum* [wheel-toll] which the same Bulcard possessed in his own land, insofar as he remitted them to the monastery.” 1169  
**LXXXII.**—To the chapter of Narbonne. 1170  
**LXXXIII.**—He orders the abbot and monks of Urano to obey the archbishop of Ravenna. 1171

**LXXXVI.**—He confirms the immunity of the church of Basenville. 1172  
**LXXXVII.**—To William, archbishop of Reims.—He complains that he releases persons bound by the bishop of Beauvais. 1173  
**LXXXVIII.**—He grants the monks of St. Pancras that the sons of those who held churches belonging to the monastery shall not possess those churches by hereditary right. 1173

# Blessed Peter, Eighth Abbot of Clairvaux

Historical and literary notice. 1391  

## Letters of Blessed Peter

I.—To Pope Alexander III. He complains that the Cistercian Order is harassed by secular persons through lawsuits, plundering of property, and the like, and implores the pope’s aid against these evils. 1293  
II.—To the same.—He thanks the pope for the benefits bestowed, especially upon the monastery of Balerne (which is of the line of Clairvaux), whose begun lawsuit against the wicked he hopes may be brought swiftly to an end. 1393  
III.—To the chancellor.—He commends to him the bishop of Autun, who has been appealed against by his own people to the Apostolic See. 1393  
IV.—To the archbishop of Mainz.—He extols his virtues, then commends to him the monastery of Eberbach and its abbot. 1394  
V.—To the abbot of Cîteaux.—He reports the death of the abbot of Trois-Fontaines, murdered by a most wicked man. 1395  
VI.—To the community of Trois-Fontaines.—He urges that community to keep the murderer carefully and not to kill him by starvation. 1396  
VII.—To the abbot of Kerlouan.—He orders that what is just be restored to a merchant who said that he had been defrauded in trading livestock. 1396  
VIII.—To Simon of Montaigu.—He exhorts him to persist in works of mercy toward his neighbours. 1397  
IX.—To the bishop of Winchester.—He says that in a certain matter he did not dishonour the king, but safeguarded the purity of the Order against a false brother; and he commends the house of Mortemer. 1397  
X.—To the abbot of Vaux.—He complains that a book which he had lent was ruined by dripping water and returned at night so that the damage might not be discovered. 1398  
XI.—To Queen Tarasia.—He praises the queen, especially for her generosity to the poor and to the Order. 1398  
XII.—To the king of Portugal.—He commends the king’s humility, of which he had been apprised by letter, and his charity toward the Order; and accepts the monastery of Castineria offered to him by the king. 1399  
XIII.—The community of Clairvaux to Pope Alexander.—The community asks the pope not to deprive it of its abbot Henry, who was being sought for the bishopric of Toulouse. 1400  
XIV.—The community of Clairvaux to the king of the Franks.—It asks the king not to allow its abbot to be taken from it and made bishop of Toulouse. 1400  
XV.—The community of Clairvaux to Lord Cadou, archdeacon.—It says that it is distressed that it could not be honoured by his visit, and reports the death of its prior. 1400  
XVI.—To religious persons established in Germany.—The community of Clairvaux communicates to the abbots of Germany a share in its prayers, and so forth. 1401  
XVII.—To the community of Mortemer.—He exhorts the afflicted to exercise virtue and show patience. 1402  
XVIII.—To the bishop of Bath and the abbot of Forde.—He commends the cause of the monks of Fountains. 1403  
XIX.—To the bishops of Albano and Palestrina.—He asks that their wrongdoers be restrained. 1404  

[Col. 1447]

# Aimeric, Patriarch of Antioch, and Terricus the Templar

## Letters of Aimeric and Terricus, Grand Master of the Templars

I.—Aimeric, patriarch of Antioch, to Louis, king of the Franks.—Having reported the Turkish victory over the Christians, he implores his assistance. 1405  

[Col. 1448]

II.—Aimeric to Henry, king of England.—On the same subject. 1407  
III.—Aimeric to Hugh Etherianus.—He praises his book against the teaching of the Greek Church. 1408  
IV.—Terricus, Grand Master of the Templars, to all the brethren of the Temple.—Concerning the defeat of the Christians. 1408  
V.—The same to Henry, king of England.—Concerning the capture of Jerusalem. 1409  

[Col. 1447] **End of the Two Hundred and First Volume.**
